p.seg: 1 Original Preface to the Commentary on the Waterways Classic
The Preface states:
The Book of Changes states that Heaven generates water from the One,
thus its vital energy is subtle in the northern region,
and it is the foremost among all things.
The Records of the Mysterious Center states:
What is most abundant under heaven
is water.
It floats the heavens and bears the earth,
reaching all places, high and low;
it moistens all things without exception.
When its energy flows and meets rocks,
its essence, even as thin as a layer of skin,
can, before a single morning passes, gather moisture to nourish the spiritual realm—
no divine power can compare to it.
Therefore, even the enlightened cannot fathom its profound depths
nor exhaust its vast immensity.
In the past, the Records of the Great Yu described the mountains and seas,
but it was comprehensive yet incomplete;
the Treatise on Geography recorded its contents,
but it was brief and not exhaustive;
the Book of Documents, the Basic Annals, and the Offices of Zhou were all too sketchy;
the descriptions in the rhapsodies on capitals
were too limited to convey the full meaning;
although the Waterways Classic roughly connected the threads of waterways,
it lacked extensive cross-references.
As the saying goes, each speaks his own mind,
but few can provide comprehensive guidance.
Now, those who seek maps and explore mysteries
exhaustively listen to accounts of regional domains,
yet those who travel across lands and journey afar
rarely can grasp their illuminating connections.
Even if they vaguely recall previous accounts,
they cannot help but remain deeply perplexed.
In my youth, I had no interest in seeking out mountains;
as I grew older, I lacked the disposition to inquire about fords.
My knowledge fell short of profound classics;
my understanding of the Way was obscured by the need for breadth.
In advancement, I lacked the opportunity to inquire about one and know two;
in retreat, I lacked the wisdom to observe one corner and infer three.
Studying alone without hearing others,
the ancients lamented such isolation and narrowness;
abandoning and losing books,
the enlightened sighed at such wall-facing ignorance.
Seeking depth in a silent room,
asking about distant places from a closed boat—
this too is difficult indeed.
Yet, peeking at the sky through a hair-thin tube,
or glimpsing time through a calendar tube;
drinking from rivers and sipping from the sea—
each follows its own nature to completion.
Taking advantage of my ample leisure,
and idly passing the years,
I have ventured to expound upon the Waterways Classic,
expanding upon the earlier text.
The Great Tradition states:
Great rivers are separated by intervals,
small rivers are connected in sequence,
all flowing eastward to return to the sea.
Tracing the inflow and outflow of their tributaries,
examining the paths they follow along their courses,
searching out waterways and channels,
I have compiled and connected them.
Where the Classic contains errors,
I have examined and appended what the main text does not record.
What are not the constant sources of the main waterways
are not within the scope of this commentary.
However, antiquity is vast and obscure;
Chinese and foreign dynasties succeeded one another;
cities and towns were left empty and in ruins;
rivers and streams were altered or destroyed;
different names and varied designations
arose across generations;
waterways sometimes hidden, sometimes visible,
books and maps often contradict themselves;
some, with chaotic flows, assume misleading names;
others, cutting straight across, acquire common appellations;
winding islets interweave in strange patterns;
whirling rapids and reversing currents;
the network of paths and branches is intricate;
the system of connections is vast and complex.
Even with the Twelve Classics as reference,
it is still difficult to speak definitively;
minor streams and subtle ripples
are inherently hard to investigate thoroughly.
I can only offer my own straightforward views,
and fully present the theories of cartographers and travelers.
What I do not know,
I shall leave unaddressed.
Therefore, in compiling evidence for this Classic,
and appending its essential branches,
I hope to provide a private guard against forgetfulness and error,
and to make it easier for seekers to consult and understand.
1 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Volume One
1.1 The River
1.1 The River
The Kūnlún Ruins lie in the northwest.
Three tiers form the Kūnlún Hill.
The Discourse on Kūnlún states:
The mountain of Kūnlún has three levels.
The lower one is called Fántóng,
also known as Bǎntóng;
the second is called Xuánpǔ,
also known as Lángfēng;
the upper one is called Céngchéng,
also known as Tiāntíng,
and this is the dwelling of the Great Emperor.
It is fifty thousand lǐ from Sōnggāo,
and is the center of the earth.
The Basic Annals of Yǔ agrees with this.
Gāo Yòu states that the river emerges from the Kūn Mountains,
flows hidden underground for thirteen thousand lǐ,
and was channeled and opened by Yǔ,
emerging at Mount Jīshí.
According to the Classic of Mountains and Seas,
from Kūnlún to Jīshí is one thousand seven hundred and forty lǐ.
From Jīshí, exiting Lǒngxī Commandery to Luò,
based on the Treatise on Geography, it is approximately over five thousand lǐ.
Also according to the Biography of King Mù,
the Son of Heaven traveled from the Kūn Mountains to the ancestral Zhōu,
and calculated the distance of the western lands.
From the ancestral Zhōu, west of the Chán River,
to the state of Hé Zōng and Mount Yángyū,
was three thousand and four hundred lǐ;
from Yángyū west to the head of the river was four thousand lǐ,
totaling seven thousand four hundred lǐ.
The Maps of Foreign Lands further states:
From the great state of Jìn heading due west for seventy thousand lǐ,
one reaches the ruins of Kūnlún,
where various immortals dwell.
These accounts differ in their figures;
the roads are obstructed and long;
records in the classics are scattered and lost;
water and land routes are distinct;
paths and returns are not the same.
With my shallow insight and limited knowledge,
I cannot investigate these matters in detail.
I cannot but briefly relate what I have heard and seen,
to record the discrepancies.
Its height is eleven thousand lǐ.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states it is eight hundred lǐ square
and ten thousand rèn high.
Guō Jǐngchún estimated it to be over two thousand five hundred lǐ from top to bottom.
The Huáinánzǐ states its height is eleven thousand lǐ, one hundred fourteen steps, three feet, and six inches.
The River,
The *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* states:
The word “hé” (river) means “to bear.”
It bears and distributes essence,
embracing yin and guiding measurement.
The *Shìmíng* states:
Hé (river),
means “below,”
flowing through according to the low places of the earth.
The *Kǎoyìyóu* states:
The river is
the pneuma of water,
the essence of the Four Watercourses,
that which flows and transforms.
The *Yuánmìngbāo* states:
The Five Phases begin here,
it is whence the myriad things are born,
the interstitial fluid of the primal pneuma.
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
Water is
the blood and pneuma of the earth,
like sinews and vessels through which it flows,
therefore it is said water possesses wealth.
Among the five calamities,
water is the greatest.
Water has its large and small,
its far and near.
Water that emerges from mountains and flows into the sea
is called a main river;
that which draws other waters into a large watercourse or the sea
is called a branch river;
that which emerges from ground ditches,
flows into a large watercourse,
and reaches the sea,
is again called a stream river.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
When the autumn floods arrive in their season,
the hundred streams pour into the river,
such is the greatness of its main flow.
The *Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì* states:
The river is
the elder among waters,
corresponding above to the Celestial Han.
The *Xīnlùn* states:
Among the sources of the Four Watercourses,
the Yellow River is the highest and longest.
Pouring down from high places,
the water flow is swift and steep,
therefore its current is rapid.
Xú Gàn’s “Qìdū Fù” states:
Among rivers and watercourses, the vast Yellow River is majestic,
issuing from Kūnlún,
its nine streams parting and flowing away,
paying court northward to the Cāngyuān,
its startling waves surging fiercely,
floating foam tossed and racing.
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
The Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jì are the Four Watercourses.
“Dú” (watercourse)
means “to penetrate,”
that which penetrates and carries away the filth of the Central Lands.
The *Báihǔtōng* states:
Its virtue is prominent and great,
therefore it is called “dú.”
The *Shìmíng* states:
“Dú” (watercourse)
means “solitary.”
Each independently emerges from its source and enters the sea.
It emerges from its northeastern corner.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
The Kūnlún Ruins lie in the northwest,
the river water emerges from its northeastern corner.
The *Ěryǎ* states:
The river emerges from the Kūnlún Ruins,
its color white.
The channels it joins number one thousand seven hundred and one streams,
its color yellow.
The *Wùlǐlùn* states:
The reason the river’s color is yellow
is the flow of the multitude of streams,
which muddies it.
A hundred lǐ brings a small bend,
a thousand lǐ brings one bend and one straight stretch.
The Han Grand Minister of War Zhāng Zhòng deliberated, saying:
The river water is muddy.
To clarify one shí of water,
yields six dǒu of silt.
Yet the people compete to draw from the river to irrigate fields,
causing the river not to flow freely.
By the third month,
when the peach blossom flood arrives, the river then breaches its banks,
because it is choked and cannot drain.
He prohibited the people from again drawing from the river.
Thus, the Yellow River also bears the name “Muddy River.”
The *Shùzhēngjì* states:
The Méngjīn and Héjīn fords are perpetually muddy.
Compared to the Jiāng, they are narrow;
compared to the Huái and Jì, they are broad.
In cold weather, the ice is several zhàng thick.
When the ice first solidifies,
carts and horses dare not cross.
One must wait for a fox to walk
— it is said this creature hears well —
and only when there is no water beneath the ice does it cross.
People see the fox walk,
then they cross.
I note that the *Fēngsútōng* states:
A village saying claims, “The fox wishes to cross the river,
but what can it do about its tail?”
Moreover, the fox’s nature is suspicious,
hence the common saying about “fox-doubt.”
So it is not necessarily entirely as Yuánshēng’s words describe.
It bends and follows its southeastern flow,
entering the Bó Sea.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
To the south is the Abyss of the Utmost Reach,
also called the Abyss of the Central Pole,
three hundred fathoms deep,
where only Féng Yí has his capital.
The Map of the Encompassing Lands states:
Féng Yí constantly rides a cloud chariot drawn by two dragons.
The River water again emerges from the Yángyūlíngmén Mountain,
and flows into the Féngyì Mountain.
The Biography of King Mù states that the Son of Heaven campaigned westward,
reaching Mount Yángyū,
the place where the River Earl Féng Yí had his capital,
this being the clan of the River Ancestor.
The Son of Heaven then sank jade tablets and discs as a ritual offering.
The River Earl then, together with the Son of Heaven, unrolled maps and examined texts,
to view the Son of Heaven's precious vessels:
jade fruits, xuán pearls, luminous silver, golden ointment, and other objects,
all recorded in the River Chart.
The River Earl, with ritual propriety,
and King Mù, viewing the chart,
only then guided him to proceed westward.
In the time of Fú Xī,
he received the Dragon-Horse Chart from the River,
which is the Eight Trigrams.
Therefore, the Preface to the Mandate and Calendar states:
The River Chart,
is the stepping stone for emperors and kings.
The chart depicts the divisions of the rivers, mountains, and the boundaries of the provinces.
Later, Yáo built an altar at the River,
received the Dragon Chart,
and composed the Record of Grasping the River.
Reaching the times of Shùn of Yú, the Xià, and the Shāng,
they all also received it.
Lǐ Yóu's Inscription on the Měng Ford:
Vast and mighty is the River water,
paying homage to the sea.
Flowing directly from the Central Province,
is where the Dragon Chart resides.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
In the past, when Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he performed prayers at Yángyū,
which was probably here.
Gāo Yòu considered Yángyū to be a marsh in Qín,
but this is incorrect.
The Buddhist Records of the Western Regions states:
On Mount Ānòudá,
there is a great abyssal water on its summit,
with palaces, towers, and pavilions of great size.
This mountain,
is the Kūnlún Mountain.
The Biography of King Mù states:
The Son of Heaven ascended Kūnlún,
viewed the palace of the Yellow Emperor,
and sealed the tomb of Fēng Lóng.
Fēng Lóng,
is the Duke of Thunder.
The Yellow Emperor's palace,
is the Ānòudá Palace.
This mountain gives rise to six great waters.
West of the mountain is a great water,
named the Xīntóu River.
Guō Yìgōng's Extensive Records states:
It is the Gān Water,
located east of the Western Regions,
named the Xīntáo Water.
The mountain is west of the Tiānzhú country,
the water is sweet,
therefore called Gān Water (Sweet Water).
There is rock salt,
white like crystal,
large pieces are broken for use.
Kāng Tài said:
Ānxī, Yuèzhī, Tiānzhú, down to Jiānàdiàoyù,
all rely on this salt.
The monk Fǎxiǎn said:
Crossing the Cōng Mountains,
one already enters the territory of Northern Tiānzhú.
From here, following the mountains southwest for fifteen days,
the path is arduous and obstructed,
the cliffs and banks perilous and precipitous.
The mountains consist only of rock,
sheer cliffs stand a thousand fathoms high.
Looking down from them causes dizziness.
Wishing to advance, one finds no place to set foot.
Below there is water,
named the Xīntóu River.
In the past, people chiseled a path through the rock and erected ladders.
In total, one crosses seven hundred ladders.
After crossing,
one treads on suspended ropes to cross the river.
The two banks of the river
are about eighty paces apart.
It is cut off even after nine translations,
Hàn's Zhāng Qiān and Gān Yīng never reached it.
I have examined various historical records,
this is the so-called territory of Jìbīn.
There is a stone-paved ascent,
the path is narrow, barely over a foot wide.
Travelers, riders and pedestrians supporting each other,
pulling each other along rope bridges,
for about twenty lǐ,
finally reach the Hanging Crossing.
The obstructing dangers and perils
are beyond description.
Guō Yìgōng said:
West of Wūchá,
there is the country of Xuándù (Hanging Crossing).
Mountains and streams are impassable,
they cross by pulling on ropes,
hence the country gets its name.
Its people dwell in the mountains,
cultivating among the stone cliffs.
They pile stones to make dwellings.
The people drink by joining hands,
the so-called "ape drinking."
There is white grass, small-paced horses,
there are donkeys but no oxen.
Is this the Xuándù?
The monk Fǎxiǎn also said,
crossing the river brings one to the country of Wūcháng.
The country of Wūcháng is Northern Tiānzhú,
a country the Buddha reached.
The Buddha left his footprint here.
The length of the footprint depends on one's mind and thoughts,
and remains so to this day.
The stone for drying robes is also still there.
The Xīntóu River flows further southwest,
bends and flows southeast,
passing through Central Tiānzhú country.
The land on both banks is flat.
There is a country named Pítú,
where the Buddha's teachings flourish.
It also passes the Pú Nà Bān River.
On the left and right banks of the river,
there are twenty saṅghārāmas (monasteries).
This water passes through the country of Mótóuluó,
and then downstream joins the Xīntóu River.
West of this river,
the various countries of Tiānzhú,
and south from here,
are all called "Zhōngguó" (the Middle Kingdom).
The people are prosperous and wealthy.
"Zhōngguó" means
their clothing and food are the same as in (our) Zhōngguó,
hence it is named "Zhōngguó."
Since Nirvāṇa,
the practices of the holy assembly,
their dignified demeanor and rules,
have been transmitted without interruption.
From the Xīntóu River to Southern Tiānzhú country,
reaching the Southern Sea,
is forty thousand lǐ.
The Buddhist Records of the Western Regions states:
The Xīntóu River passes through the countries of Jìbīn, Jiānyuè, Móhēlà, and others,
and enters the Southern Sea.
Southwest of Mount Ānòudá there is water,
named Yáonú;
southwest and slightly east of the mountain there is water,
named Sàhǎn;
slightly further east there is water,
named Héngjiā.
These three waters issue from the same mountain,
and all enter the Héng Water (Ganges).
Kāng Tài's Account of Fúnán states:
The source of the Héng Water
lies at the extreme northwest,
emerging from within the Kūnlún Mountains.
There are five great sources.
The various waters that divide and flow
all come from these five great sources.
The great river Zhīhùlí emerges from the mountain and flows northwest,
turning southeast to empty into the great sea.
Zhīhùlí,
is the Héng Water.
Therefore, the Buddhist Records of the Western Regions has the designation Héng Qū (Ganges Bend).
North of the Héng are four countries,
the westernmost one within the Héng Qū is it.
There is the country of Jūyínàhè.
The Biography of Fǎxiǎn states:
The Héng Water flows southeast,
passing south of the country of Jūyínàhè.
Between twin trees north of the city,
there is the Xīliánchán River.
By the river,
the World-Honored One, with his head to the north, entered Parinirvāṇa here,
the place where the relics were divided.
Zhī Sēngzǎi's Account of Foreign Lands states:
After the Buddha's Nirvāṇa,
the devas and humans wrapped the Buddha in new white cotton cloth,
making offerings with incense and flowers.
After seven full days,
they placed him in a golden coffin,
and carried him out of the royal palace.
They crossed a small stream of water,
named Xīlánnà,
about three lǐ or so from the royal palace,
north of the palace.
Using sandalwood as firewood,
the devas and humans each used fire to ignite the wood,
but the wood would not catch fire at all.
Mahākāśyapa returned from the desert sands,
overcome with grief and wailing,
which moved heaven and earth.
From that time onward,
other firewood would ignite and burn of its own accord.
The king collected the relics,
using a golden vessel to measure them,
obtaining eight hu and four dou.
The various kings, heavenly dragon kings, and spirit kings each received a small portion,
which they took back to their own countries,
to build Buddhist temples.
King Aśoka erected a stūpa at the place where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa,
but the twin trees and the stūpa
are no longer there today.
These trees are called sāla trees,
and their flowers are called sāraka.
The color of these flowers is white like frost and snow,
and their fragrance is incomparable.
Zhú Zhī's Fúnán Jì says:
Línyángguó is two thousand li by footpath from Jīnchénguó,
accessible by carriage and horse,
with no waterways.
The entire country serves the Buddha.
There was a monk who passed away and was cremated for burial.
After burning thousands of bundles of firewood,
he remained seated in the fire,
and was then placed in a stone chamber.
Over sixty years have passed since then,
yet his body remains as before, uncorrupted.
Zhú Zhī witnessed this with his own eyes.
The vajra is eternal and abiding,
its radiance everlasting.
The relics appear in the stūpas,
enduring through the ages without decay.
This is what is meant by the wisdom of emptiness being boundless,
and the great enlightenment being unfathomable.
The waters flow chaotically into the Ganges.
The Ganges River then flows east past the north of the city of Pìshělì.
The Buddhist Xīyù Jì says:
Pìshělì
is the country of Wéiyélí.
Zhī Sēngzǎi's Wàiguó Shì says:
The country of Wéiyélí is fifty yojanas from the city of Rājagṛha.
The city's circumference is three yojanas.
Vimalakīrti's home is south of the palace within the great city,
about seven li from the palace.
The buildings have completely collapsed,
and only the site remains.
The monk Fǎxiǎn says:
North of the city is a great forest with multi-storied pavilions,
where the Buddha resided.
Originally, it was the home of the courtesan Āmrapālī, who donated it to the Buddha to build a stūpa.
Three li northwest of the city,
there is a stūpa named "Laying Down the Bow and Weapons."
Upstream on the Ganges, there was a country
where the king's minor consort gave birth to a fleshly lump.
The chief consort, out of jealousy,
said, "Your birth
is an inauspicious omen."
She then placed it in a wooden box,
and cast it into the Ganges River.
Downstream, a king was touring and sightseeing
when he saw the wooden box floating on the water.
He opened it to look,
and saw a thousand small children, all exceptionally handsome and well-formed.
The king took them in and raised them.
They grew up
to be extremely brave and strong.
Wherever they went to wage war,
they crushed and subdued all opposition.
Next, they intended to attack their father's original country.
The king was greatly distressed and worried.
The minor consort asked:
"Why are you so distressed and worried?"
The king said:
"The king of that country has a thousand sons,
incomparably brave and strong,
who intend to come and attack our country.
That is why I am distressed."
The minor consort said:
"Do not worry.
Just build a tall tower west of the city.
When the enemy comes,
place me atop the tower,
and I will be able to repel them."
The king did as she said.
When the enemy arrived,
the minor consort spoke to them from the tower:
"You are my sons.
Why are you committing such rebellious acts?"
The enemy said:
"Who are you,
claiming to be our mother?"
The minor consort said:
"If you do not believe me,
all of you open your mouths and look upward."
The minor consort then pressed her breasts with both hands,
and milk flowed in five hundred streams,
all falling into the mouths of the thousand sons.
The enemy realized she was their mother,
and immediately laid down their bows and weapons.
The parents, reflecting on this,
both attained the state of pratyekabuddha.
The stūpa still exists today.
Later, when the World-Honored One attained enlightenment,
he told his disciples,
"This is the place where I once laid down my bow and weapons."
Later generations learned of this,
and erected a stūpa at this place,
hence the name.
The thousand small children
are the thousand buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
The Buddhist Xīyù Jì says:
East of the bend in the Ganges,
there is the country of Sēngjiāshàn Nàijiēchéng, where the Buddha descended the three precious steps.
The Fǎxiǎn Zhuàn says:
The Ganges flows southeast,
passing south of the country of Sēngjiāshī.
It was here that the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven on three precious steps
to preach the Dharma for his mother.
After the precious steps vanished,
King Aśoka built a stūpa at the site of the precious steps.
Later, a stone pillar was erected,
with a lion image on top.
Non-Buddhists had little faith,
but when the lion roared,
it frightened them into sincere belief.
The Ganges then flows east past the city of Jìbīn Ráoyí.
The southern part of the city connects to the Ganges.
Six or seven li northwest of the city,
on the northern bank of the Ganges,
is where the Buddha preached the Dharma to his disciples.
The Ganges then flows southeast past the north of the country of Shāqí.
Outside the city of Shāqí,
east of the southern gate road,
the Buddha chewed a willow twig and stuck it in the ground.
It grew to a height of seven feet,
neither increasing nor decreasing,
and still exists today.
The Ganges then flows southeast,
passing north of the city of Jiāwéiluówèi,
which was the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Fifty li east of the city is the royal garden,
where there is a pond.
The queen entered the pond to bathe,
and after emerging, walked twenty steps north of the bank.
Facing east, she raised her hand
and grasped a tree, giving birth to the prince.
When the prince fell to the ground,
he took seven steps.
Two dragons spat water to bathe the prince,
forming a well-pond,
from which the monks draw water for their needs.
The prince wrestled with Nanda and others, matching strength with an elephant,
and shot an arrow into the ground.
Today, there is a spring there,
which travelers rely on for drinking water.
The Buddhist Xīyù Jì says:
Three li north of the city on the Ganges,
at the place where the king welcomed the Buddha,
a stūpa was built,
with an image of the king embracing the Buddha.
The Wàiguó Shì says:
The country of Jiāwéiluóyuè no longer has a king today.
The city walls and moats are desolate and overgrown,
with only empty spaces remaining.
There are upāsakas surnamed Śākya,
about twenty or more households,
who are descendants of the former King Śuddhodana.
Thus, they belong to the four castes,
living in the old city,
as upāsakas.
They still diligently practice,
preserving ancient customs.
At that time, the stūpa was completely ruined.
King Tiáo Mí repaired and restored one stūpa,
and King Sīhētiáo sent materials to assist in its completion.
Today, twelve monks reside there.
When the prince was first born,
the tree that Queen Māyā grasped
was named "Xūhē."
King Aśoka made a green stone image of the queen grasping the tree and giving birth to the prince.
The original tree no longer exists,
but later monks took saplings from the original tree and planted them.
Passed down through successive generations to the present day,
the tree's branches remain as before,
still shading the stone image.
Furthermore, the footprints from the prince's seven steps
are still visible today, with their patterns preserved.
King Aśoka placed green stones on both sides of the footprints,
and covered them with a long green stone on top.
The people of the country today constantly make offerings of incense and flowers there.
The shape of the seven footprints is still visible,
with clear and distinct patterns.
Although covered with stones today, it is no different.
Some people also place several layers of cotton cloth
over the stones,
making the patterns even clearer.
When the prince was born,
dragon kings flanked the prince on both sides.
Dragons spewed water to bathe the Crown Prince.
One dragon spewed warm water,
another spewed cold water,
thus forming two pools,
which to this day remain one cold and one warm.
Ten days before the Crown Prince left home,
he went out and sat under the Nyagrodha tree in the royal field.
The tree deity offered the Crown Prince the seven treasures,
but the Crown Prince did not accept them.
Thereupon, he contemplated leaving home.
The royal field was one *jù* from the palace.
*Jù*
means ten *lǐ* in Jin language.
The Crown Prince left home on the night of the fifteenth day of the third month.
The Four Heavenly Kings came to welcome him,
each supporting a horse's hoof.
At that time, various deities and heavenly beings filled the surroundings,
scattering celestial fragrant flowers in the sky.
At this time, he reached the Hénán Móqiáng River,
and right by this river, he became a śramaṇa.
The Hénán Móqiáng River is north of Jiāwéiluóyuè,
ten yojanas away.
This river is in the country of Luóyuèzhī Píngshā,
thirty yojanas away.
The Bodhisattva then passed by temporarily.
King Píngshā came out to see the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva stayed for one day in King Píngshā's Suílóunà orchard,
and at dusk, he left to stay overnight at Bàndá Bōchóu.
Bàndá
means white in Jin language;
Bōchóu
means mountain in Jin language.
White Mountain is ten *lǐ* north of the country of Píngshā.
The next morning, he left,
and at dusk, he stayed at Tánlán Mountain,
six yojanas from White Mountain.
Then he went directly to the Bodhi tree.
The Bodhi tree is north of Yuèzhī,
twenty *lǐ* from Tánlán Mountain.
The Crown Prince left home at the age of twenty-nine,
and attained the Way at thirty-five.
This account differs from the sutras,
hence it is recorded as a variant.
Zhú Fǎwéi said:
Jiāwéiwèi country
is the Tianzhu country where the Buddha was born.
It is the center of three thousand suns and moons, and twelve thousand heavens and earths.
Kāng Tài's *Fúnán Biography* says:
In the time of Fàn Zhān,
there was a man from the Mìyáng country named Jiā Xiánglí,
who once traveled from his own country to Tianzhu,
and after trading and traveling, reached Fúnán.
He told Zhān about the customs of Tianzhu,
saying the Dharma was widely propagated,
gold and treasures were amassed,
the mountains and rivers were fertile,
and one could indulge in whatever they desired.
It was respected by neighboring great countries
generation after generation.
Zhān asked:
"How long would it take to go there now,
and how many years to return?"
Lí said:
"Tianzhu is about
over thirty thousand *lǐ* from here,
and the round trip would take over three years."
When he set out,
it took four years to return,
and he considered it the center of heaven and earth.
The Ganges River then flows east past the Lánmò Pagoda.
Beside the pagoda is a pool,
guarded by a dragon in the pool.
King Aśoka wanted to destroy the pagoda
to build eighty-four thousand pagodas,
but upon realizing it was offered by the dragon king,
he understood it was not of this world,
and stopped.
This place is desolate and uninhabited,
and elephants use their trunks to fetch water and sprinkle the ground,
like in Cāngwú and Kuàijī,
where elephants plow and birds weed.
The Ganges River then flows east to the estuary of five rivers,
likely where five waters converge,
though the details are unclear.
Ānanda went from the country of Magadha toward Vaiśālī,
intending to enter nirvana by boat.
The heavenly beings informed King Ajātaśatru,
who pursued him to the river.
The Licchavis, hearing Ānanda was coming,
also came to welcome him.
They all arrived at the river.
Ānanda thought to himself:
If he went forward, King Ajātaśatru would bear resentment;
if he turned back, the Licchavis would also bear a grudge.
So, in the middle of the river,
he entered the *samādhi* of fire-light,
burned his body, and entered nirvana.
His body split into two parts,
each landing on one bank.
The two kings each took half of the relics,
and built two pagodas.
Crossing the river and going south one yojana,
one reaches the city of Pāṭaliputra in the country of Magadha.
This city
is the one ruled by King Aśoka.
The palaces in the city all have walls and towers,
carved and engraved with patterns,
and large stones are piled to form a mountain.
Below the mountain is a stone chamber,
three *zhàng* long,
two *zhàng* wide,
and over one *zhàng* high.
There was a great Mahāyāna brahmin's son,
named Luótài Sīpó,
also called Mañjuśrī,
who lived in this city.
He was intelligent and wise,
understanding all matters,
and lived a pure life.
The king revered and served him as a teacher.
Relying on this one person,
the Buddha-Dharma was widely propagated,
and outsiders could not encroach.
Among all the countries,
only this city was the largest,
with prosperous people
who competed in practicing benevolence and righteousness.
King Aśoka destroyed seven pagodas
to build eighty-four thousand pagodas.
The first great pagoda he built
is over two *lǐ* south of the city.
In front of this pagoda are the Buddha's footprints,
and a vihāra was built
with its north door facing the pagoda.
South of the pagoda is a stone pillar,
four or five arm-spans thick,
over three *zhàng* high,
with an inscription
that reads:
"King Aśoka gave Jambudvīpa as alms to the four directions.
The monks then used money to redeem the pagoda."
Three hundred paces north of the pagoda,
King Aśoka built the Niraya city here.
In the city is a stone pillar,
also over three *zhàng* high,
with a lion capital.
There is an inscription
recording the cause and conditions for building Niraya city,
as well as the year, month, and day.
The Ganges River then flows southeast past the Small Solitary Stone Mountain.
On the mountain top is a stone chamber,
facing south.
The Buddha once sat inside it,
and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked the Buddha forty-two questions.
The Buddha used his finger to draw on the stone for each one,
and the marks of the drawings remain.
The Ganges River then flows west past the new city of Rājagṛha,
which was built by King Ajātaśatru.
Going four *lǐ* south from the city,
one enters a valley and reaches the area of five mountains.
The five mountains surround it,
shaped like a city wall.
This is the old city of King Bimbisāra.
It is five or six *lǐ* from east to west,
and seven or eight *lǐ* from north to south.
This is where King Ajātaśatru first intended to harm the Buddha.
The city is desolate,
and there are no paths.
Entering the valley and following the mountain,
going southeast for fifteen *lǐ*,
one reaches Vulture Peak Mountain.
Before reaching the summit, three *lǐ* away,
there is a stone cave facing south,
where the Buddha sat in meditation.
Forty paces to the northwest,
there is another stone cave,
where Ānanda sat in meditation.
Māra Pāpīyān transformed into a vulture to frighten Ānanda,
but the Buddha used his divine power
to reach through the stone and pat Ānanda's shoulder,
and the fear immediately ceased.
The bird's footprints and the handprint are all preserved,
hence it is called the Vulture Cave.
The mountain peak is elegant and dignified,
the highest among the five mountains.
The Buddhist *Records of the Western Regions* says:
Vulture Peak Mountain is northeast of Rājagṛha in Anavatapta.
Looking west at the mountain,
two peaks stand side by side,
two or three *lǐ* apart.
In between, vultures
often dwell on the ridge,
and the locals call it Vulture Peak Mountain.
In the Hu language, *qíshé*
means vulture.
Also, Zhú Fǎwéi said:
The country of Rājagṛha has the Divine Vulture Mountain,
called Vulture Peak Mountain in the Hu language.
The mountain is made of blue stone,
and the stone resembles a vulture.
King Āshùwáng had people carve the stone,
artificially attaching two wings and two feet,
carving and shaping its body.
It can still be seen today,
and from a distance, it resembles the shape of a vulture,
hence it is called Língjiùshān (Vulture Peak).
There are various accounts,
differing in detail and distance.
Now, because Fǎxiǎn personally stayed on this mountain,
recited the *Shǒuléngyán* Sutra,
and made offerings of incense and flowers,
his account is considered authoritative.
Further west, passing thirty lǐ south of the city of Jiānàchéng,
one reaches the place where the Buddha practiced austerities for six years under a tree.
There are woods there.
Traveling west for three lǐ,
one reaches the place where the Buddha entered the water to bathe and where the Heavenly King held a tree branch for him to grasp to climb out of the pool.
Traveling north for another two lǐ,
one reaches the place where the girl Sujātā offered the Buddha milk porridge.
From here, traveling north for two lǐ,
one reaches the place where the Buddha sat facing east on a stone under a large tree and ate the porridge.
Both the tree and the stone are still there.
The stone is six chǐ in length and width,
and its height is slightly less than two chǐ.
The climate in this country is temperate,
and some trees are several thousand years old,
even up to ten thousand years.
From here, traveling northeast for twenty lǐ,
one reaches a stone cave.
The Bodhisattva entered it,
sat facing west in the lotus position,
and thought to himself:
"If I attain enlightenment,
there should be a divine sign."
Immediately, the shadow of the Buddha appeared on the stone wall,
about three chǐ long,
and it remains bright to this day.
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently,
and the devas in the sky said:
"This is not the place where past or future Buddhas attain enlightenment.
Travel southwest from here,
less than half a yojana,
under a Bodhi tree,
is where past and future Buddhas attain enlightenment."
The devas guided the Bodhisattva to rise and walk.
After walking thirty paces from the tree,
a deva offered him auspicious kusha grass.
The Bodhisattva accepted it,
walked another fifteen paces,
and five hundred green sparrows flew over,
circled the Bodhisattva three times, and then flew away to the west.
The Bodhisattva proceeded to the Bodhi tree,
spread the auspicious grass,
and sat facing east.
At that time, the demon king Mára sent three beautiful women from the north to tempt the Bodhisattva,
while Mára himself came from the south.
The Bodhisattva pressed the ground with his toe,
and Mára's army scattered.
The three women turned into old hags,
and could not restore themselves.
The Buddha sat facing east on a square stone under a Nyagrodha tree,
and the place where Brahmā came to visit the Buddha,
as well as the place where the Four Heavenly Kings presented the alms bowl, all have stūpas erected.
The *Foreign Accounts* states:
The Buddha Vipassī practiced austerities under this tree for six years.
A wealthy man's daughter offered the Buddha milk porridge in a golden bowl.
After receiving the milk porridge,
the Buddha went to bathe in the Nairañjanā River.
After bathing,
he finished eating the porridge by the river,
threw the bowl into the water,
and it floated upstream for a hundred paces
before sinking into the river.
The Nāga king Kālika retrieved it and enshrined it in his palace for worship.
The bowls of the three previous Buddhas are also said to be there.
The Buddha sat by the river under the great Bodhi tree.
The great Bodhi tree is two lǐ from the Bodhi tree.
Under this tree, after seven days,
he attained enlightenment through contemplation.
Mára's army tested the Buddha.
Shi's *Records of the Western Regions* states:
The Nairañjanā River flows south into the Ganges.
West of the river is the Buddha's tree,
where the Buddha practiced austerities,
eating only one grain of rice per day for six years.
About five lǐ west of the city,
east of the tree by the river,
is where the Buddha entered the water to bathe.
On the eastern bank, under a Nyagrodha tree, he sat and practiced,
and it was here that the girl offered him porridge.
Then he crossed the river to the west,
and sat under the Bodhi tree south of the six-year tree,
where he subdued Mára and attained Buddhahood.
Fótúdiào said:
The Buddha's tree withered,
but when the Buddha came, it sprouted new branches and leaves.
Zhú Fǎwéi said:
The six-year tree is five lǐ from the Buddha's tree,
recording the differences.
Fǎxiǎn traveled southeast from here,
returning to the city of Bāliánfúyì.
Sailing west down the Ganges,
he reached a monastery,
named Kuàngyě (Wilderness),
where the Buddha once stayed.
Continuing west down the Ganges,
he reached the city of Bōluónài in the country of Jiāshī.
Zhú Fǎwéi said:
The country of Bōluónài is 1,200 lǐ south of the country of Jiāwéiluówèi,
with the Ganges in between,
flowing southeast.
The place where the Buddha turned the Dharma wheel
is twenty lǐ north of the country,
under a tree named "Chūnfú,"
where Vimalakīrti stayed.
Fǎxiǎn said:
About ten lǐ northeast of the city,
is the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva),
originally inhabited by Pratyekabuddhas.
Wild deer often rested there,
hence the name.
Fǎxiǎn returned from here
to reside in Bāliánfúyì.
Sailing east along the Ganges,
on its southern bank is the great country of Zhānpó.
Shi's *Records of the Western Regions* states:
East of the bend of the Ganges is the city of Zhānpó country.
To the south is Lake Bǔkuōlán,
with the Ganges to the north.
This is where the Buddha descended to preach the precepts.
The Ganges then passes by the country of Bōlì,
which is the Buddha's maternal grandfather's country.
Fǎxiǎn said:
The Ganges flows east to the country of Duōmólíjiān,
which is the river's mouth to the sea.
Shi's *Records of the Western Regions* states:
Dàqín (the Roman Empire) is also called Líjiān.
Kāng Tài's *Account of Fúnán* states:
From the southwest of Jiānàdiàozhōu, entering a large bay,
about seven or eight hundred lǐ,
one reaches the mouth of the great Zhīhùlí River.
Crossing the river and traveling west,
one eventually reaches Dàqín.
It also says:
Departing from the mouth of Jūlì,
entering a large bay,
heading directly northwest,
after about a year or more,
one reaches the river mouth of Tiānzhú (India),
named the Ganges.
At the river mouth is a country,
called Dānzhì,
belonging to Tiānzhú.
A eunuch named Xìng was sent to be the king of Dānzhì.
Shi's *Records of the Western Regions* states:
The Ganges flows east into the Eastern Sea.
It seems the two rivers flow into
and are received by two seas,
naturally forming east and west.
Shi's discussion of Fótúdiào cites the *Shānhǎijīng* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), saying:
South of the Western Sea,
by the shores of the Flowing Sands,
beyond the Red River,
before the Black River,
there is a great mountain,
named Kūnlún.
It also says:
Six hundred lǐ west of Zhōngshān is Mount Kūnlún,
from which five rivers originate.
This is based on Fótúdiào's account.
Further, recent research on Kāng Tài's *Account of Fúnán*
shows that its description of Mount Kūnlún matches Diào's account.
According to the account,
the shortest route from Jiāozhōu to Tiānzhú
is known from Tài's account, which also identifies Mount Anavatapta as Mount Kūnlún.
Shi said that thanks to Diào's account,
it became clear,
and he thus composed the *Map of the Western Regions*,
which he discussed with Fǎtài.
Fǎtài, finding it strange based on common knowledge,
said that since the Han dynasty, various renowned scholars
should not have been unaware of the location of Mount Kūnlún, even though the Yellow River is several thousand lǐ south of Dūnhuáng.
Shi replied,
and further wrote, citing the *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn* (Story of King Mu):
King Mu feasted with the Queen Mother of the West by the side of Mount Kūnlún and on the Jasper Lake,
saying it was 11,100 lǐ from Zōngzhōu's Chánjiàn.
How could this not align with Diào's words?
Now that you have seen Tài's account,
it is not that earlier people were unaware.
From now on,
it is known that Mount Kūnlún is Mount Anavatapta.
How can it be said to be outside the foreign lands?
I have examined Shi's words,
but they are not strong evidence.
The *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn*, *Zhúshū* (Bamboo Annals), and *Shānhǎijīng*
have all been buried and obscured for ages,
their bindings worn and scattered,
and the texts disordered.
It is difficult to piece together;
later generations have arbitrarily combined them,
often deviating far from the original meaning.
As for attempting to trace the veins of the earth and rivers,
they do not align with the classics,
and when verifying distances and routes,
they naturally do not correspond.
The Buddhists do not further investigate the grand purpose of the masses' return,
nor do they elaborate on the subtle details
to refute what is incorrect,
which is not appropriate.
Now, according to the *Shānhǎi Jīng*, it says:
The ruins of Kūnlún are in the northwest,
the lower capital of the Emperor.
The ruins of Kūnlún
are eight hundred *lǐ* square,
ten thousand *rèn* high.
On top, there is the Tree of Grain,
and on its face are nine wells,
with jade as their railings.
On its face are nine gates,
each guarded by the Kāimíng beast.
This is where the hundred gods reside.
Guō Pú said:
This refers to a separate Lesser Kūnlún.
Also, according to the *Huáinánzǐ*, on Kūnlún,
there are the Tree of Grain, Pearl Trees, Jade Trees, and Xuán Trees.
The Immortal Tree is to its west,
Shātáng and Lánggān are to its east,
the Crimson Tree is to its south,
and the Green Trees and Yáo Trees are to its north.
Beside it are four hundred and forty gates,
each gate spaced four *lǐ* apart,
and between each *lǐ* are nine *chún*,
each *chún* measuring fifteen feet.
Beside it are nine wells,
and a jade beam supports its northwestern corner.
The northern gate is open
to admit the winds of Bùzhōu.
The Leaning Palace, Spinning Chamber, Xuánpǔ, Liángfēng, and Fántóng
are within the Chānghé of Kūnlún.
This is its Sparse Garden,
and the pond of the Sparse Garden
is filled with Yellow Water.
The Yellow Water circulates three times and returns to its source.
This is called the Cinnabar Water,
and drinking it grants immortality.
The Hé River emerges from its northeastern corner,
the Chì River emerges from its southeastern corner,
and the Yáng River emerges from its northwestern corner.
All these four rivers
are the divine springs of the Emperor,
used to harmonize all medicines
and moisten the myriad things.
The hill of Kūnlún, if one ascends twice its height,
is called the Mountain of Liángfēng.
Climbing it grants immortality.
If one ascends twice its height again,
it is called the Mountain of Xuánpǔ.
Climbing it grants spiritual power,
enabling control over wind and rain.
If one ascends twice its height again,
it reaches the heavens.
Climbing it grants divinity,
and this is called the dwelling of the Great Emperor.
Yǔ then used Xìtǔ to fill the Great Flood,
creating famous mountains,
and excavated the ruins of Kūnlún to form the lower earth.
Gāo Yòu said:
"Earth" might also be read as "pool."
This somewhat resembles the theory of Fótú Diào.
The six waters of Ānòudá,
the boundaries of the Cōnglǐng and Yútián rivers,
compared with the classics, histories, and various texts,
are entirely contradictory and divergent.
Also, according to the *Shízhōu Jì*,
Mount Kūnlún is located in the Xū direction of the Western Sea,
and the Hài direction of the Northern Sea.
It is 130,000 *lǐ* from the shore,
and there is the Ruò River,
which encircles the mountain.
To the southeast, it connects to the Jīshí Garden,
to the northwest, it connects to the Room of the Northern Door,
to the northeast, it faces the Well of the Great Gate,
and to the southwest, it is near the Valley of Chéngyuān.
These four great mountains at the corners
are indeed the supporting branches of Kūnlún.
At the southern end of the Jīshí Garden,
it is said that Xīwángmǔ once told King Mù of the Zhōu dynasty:
"It is 460,000 *lǐ* from Xiányáng.
The mountain rises 36,000 *lǐ* above the flat land,
and on top, there are three peaks.
The face is square,
ten thousand *lǐ* wide,
shaped like an overturned basin,
narrow at the bottom and broad at the top.
Therefore, it is said that Mount Kūnlún has three peaks.
One peak faces due north,
shining with the brilliance of the morning star,
and is named the Lángfēng Summit.
One peak faces due west,
named the Xuánpǔ Terrace.
One peak faces due east,
named the Kūnlún Palace.
In that place, there is accumulated gold,
forming the Heavenly Wall City,
with a face a thousand *lǐ* square.
On the city, five golden platforms are installed,
and twelve jade towers.
At the Běihù Mountain and Chéngyuān Mountain, there are also walled cities,
with golden platforms and jade towers,
similar and uniform.
The Gate of Yuānjīng,
the Hall of Guāngbì,
the Chamber of Qiónghuá,
the Purple and Emerald Cinnabar Rooms,
illuminated by the sun's radiance,
with crimson clouds and nine lights—
this is where Xīwángmǔ governs,
revered by true officials and immortal spirits.
Above, it connects to the rotating mechanism,
where primordial *qì* flows and spreads.
The Jade Balance is constantly regulated,
aligning with the Nine Heavens and harmonizing *yīn* and *yáng*.
All categories of things and living beings,
rare and extraordinary, emerge here.
All are found in this place.
Celestial beings and humans gather in great numbers,
too numerous to record in full.
Beyond the Northern Sea,
there is also Zhōng Mountain,
on which there are golden platforms and jade gates.
This too contains primordial *qì*,
and is the place where the Celestial Emperor resides and governs.
Examining the words of Dōngfāng Shuò
and the text of "50,000 *lǐ*" in the *Classic*,
it is difficult to say that the accounts of Fótú Diào and Kāng Tài are correct.
Within the six directions,
the stores of water and marshes,
the large are not necessarily immense,
the small are not necessarily minute,
the visible are not necessarily existent,
the hidden are not necessarily nonexistent—
what they encompass is vast.
Among them, places with the same name but different locations,
and designations that are confused,
are also not few.
For example, Fāngzhàng in the Eastern Sea
also bears the name Kūnlún.
The Bronze Pillar in the Western Continent
also has the governance of the Nine Bureaus.
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shízhōu Jì* says:
Fāngzhàng is in the center of the Eastern Sea.
The distances from its east, west, south, and north shores
are exactly equal.
Each face of Fāngzhàng is five thousand *lǐ*,
and above, it is exclusively where dragons gather.
There are palaces of gold, jade, and lapis lazuli,
where the Three Heavens' Director of Destinies governs.
Immortals who do not wish to ascend to heaven
all come and go here.
Zhāng Huá, narrating Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shényì Jīng*, said:
On Kūnlún, there is a bronze pillar,
so high it reaches the heavens,
called the Pillar of Heaven.
It is three thousand *lǐ* in circumference,
round and smooth as if polished.
Below, there is a winding chamber,
where the Nine Bureaus of Immortals govern.
Above, there is a great bird,
named "Xīyǒu,"
facing south.
It spreads its left wing to cover Dōngwánggōng,
and its right wing to cover Xīwángmǔ.
On its back, there is a small area without feathers,
spanning 19,000 *lǐ*.
Each year, Xīwángmǔ climbs onto its wing
to visit Dōngwánggōng.
Therefore, the inscription on the pillar says:
"The Bronze Pillar of Kūnlún,
so high it reaches the heavens,
round and smooth as if polished,
its form is beautiful."
The inscription on the bird says:
"There is a bird named Xīyǒu,
green and crimson, resplendent and bright.
It does not sing nor eat.
To the east, it covers Dōngwánggōng;
to the west, it covers Xīwángmǔ.
When Wángmǔ wishes to go east,
she climbs it to pass through.
*Yīn* and *yáng* depend on each other,
only meeting enhances their work."
The *Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú* says:
The Five Dragons appeared to teach,
and the Heavenly Emperor left his traces.
Gazing beyond the boundless,
on Zhōuzhōu, Mount Kūnlún.
Róng's commentary says:
The Five Dragons govern in the five directions.
They are the gods of the Five Elements.
The Five Dragons descended, and the twelve brothers of Tiānhuáng,
divided the five directions into twelve regions,
following the traces of the Five Dragons,
practicing the transformation of non-action,
and the immortals and sages governed the world.
They dwelled on the Kūnlún Mountains in Zhùzhōu.
The Wúwài Mountain is located twelve thousand lǐ southeast of Kūnlún.
The Five Dragons
and Tiānhuáng all emerged from here,
serving as the gods of the twelve hours.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"The hill of Kūnlún
is indeed the lower capital of the Emperor.
Its deity is Lùwú,
who oversees the nine divisions of heaven
and the Emperor's garden and seasons."
Yet within the six directions,
its encompassment is vast.
Its profound and subtle essence,
difficult to grasp through emotion,
and the myriad images and deep mysteries,
defy exhaustive inquiry.
Without ascending two dragons on cloud tracks,
or driving eight steeds on tortoise paths,
how can one compare to Xuānyuán's visits to the hundred spirits,
or Dà Yǔ's gatherings for accounting?
The theories of Confucians and Mohists—
who can distinguish them clearly?
It also flows beyond the sea,
south to the foot of the Jīshí Mountain,
where there is a stone gate.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"The Yellow River flows into the Bó Sea,
then emerges beyond the sea,
and enters northwest into the Jīshí Mountain, which Yǔ channeled."
The mountain is located in the southwest of Héguān County, Lǒngxī Commandery, within Qiāng territory.
I have examined various texts,
all stating that the Yellow River originates from Kūnlún,
its source hidden and emerging again,
submerging at Púchāng,
and emerging from the sea.
Thus, the Luòshū says:
"The River from Kūnlún,
emerges from the double wilderness."
This refers to it.
It passes through Jīshí and becomes the River of the Central Kingdom.
Therefore, Chéng Gōngzǐ'ān's "Ode to the Great River" states:
"Observing the grandeur of the hundred rivers,
none surpass the beauty of the Yellow River;
hidden in the lofty peaks of Kūnlún,
emerging from the towering heights of Jīshí."
The Buddhist Records of the Western Regions states:
"The River from Púchāng
flows hidden underground,
emerging south at Jīshí."
However, the text here
seems not to compare to Jīshí,
and should be placed below Púchāng Sea.
2 Commentary on the Water Classic, Volume 2
2.1 The Yellow River
2.1 The Yellow River
It flows south into the Cōnglíng Mountains,
then emerges from Cōnglíng and flows northeast.
The Yellow River has three sources,
not merely two.
One source emerges in the west from the country of Juāndú on the Cōng Mountains,
over two hundred li west of Xiūxún,
both being of the former Sài race.
To the south they belong to the Cōng Mountains,
which are a thousand li high.
The *Xīhé Jiùshì* states:
"The Cōng Mountains are eight thousand li west of Dūnhuáng.
These mountains are lofty and great,
and onions grow on them,
hence they are called the Cōng (Onion) Mountains."
The source of the River secretly emerges from these mountains,
dividing into two streams.
One stream flows west past the south of the country of Xiūxún,
which lies west of the Cōng Mountains.
Guō Yìgōng's *Guǎngzhì* states:
"The country of Xiūxún is situated on the Cōng Mountains,
where the mountains have many large onions."
It then flows past the north of the country of Nándōu,
which borders Xiūxún to the north,
and is three hundred and forty li southwest of the country of Jìbīn.
The River then flows west past the north of the country of Jìbīn.
After the Yuèzhī were defeated,
the Sài king moved south and ruled Jìbīn,
governing from the city of Xúnxiān.
The land is peaceful and harmonious,
lacking nothing.
Gold, silver, precious treasures,
rare animals, and exotic goods
surpass those of the Central Plains.
It is a great country.
The mountains are perilous,
with the Great Headache and Small Headache Mountains,
red earth,
and the Fever Slope,
which affects humans and animals alike.
The River then flows west past the south of the country of Yuèzhī,
which is governed from the city of Jiānshì.
Their customs are the same as those of Ānxī.
The Xiōngnú Chányú Mòdú defeated the Yuèzhī,
killed their king,
and used his skull as a drinking vessel.
The country then split,
with the main body traveling far beyond Dàyuān,
settling west in Dàxià,
becoming the Dà Yuèzhī;
the remaining smaller groups who could not leave
jointly defended the Southern Mountains and Qiāng territory,
and were called the Xiǎo Yuèzhī.
Hence there are the names Dà Yuèzhī and Xiǎo Yuèzhī.
It then flows west past the south of the country of Ānxī,
whose city borders the Guī River.
Its territory extends several thousand li,
making it the largest country.
There are merchants, carts, and boats traveling to neighboring countries,
and they write on leather, writing sideways.
The River, together with the Níluóqídì River, flows into the Léizhù Sea.
The Buddhist *Xīyù Jì* states:
"The Níluóqídì River emerges north of Mount Ānòudá,
and flows west past the country of Yútián."
The *Hànshū Xīyù Zhuàn* states:
"West of Yútián,
all rivers flow west,
emptying into the Western Sea."
It then flows west past the north of the Four Great Stupas,
which is the country of Jiūshīluó mentioned by the monk Fǎxiǎn.
In Chinese, it means "Severed Head."
When the Buddha was a Bodhisattva,
he gave his head to someone,
hence the country was named accordingly.
East of the country is the place where he threw himself to feed a starving tiger,
and stupas were erected at both sites.
It then flows west past the north of the country of Jiāntuówèi,
which is the city ruled by King Āyù's son, Fǎyì.
When the Buddha was a Bodhisattva,
he also gave his eyes to someone in this country,
and a great stupa was erected at that place as well.
There is also the country of Fúlóushā,
where the god Śakra transformed into a cowherd boy,
piled up earth to make a Buddha stupa,
and the Dharma King subsequently built it into a great stupa.
These are the so-called Four Great Stupas.
The *Fǎxiǎn Zhuàn* states:
"The country possesses the Buddha's alms bowl.
The king of the Yuèzhī raised a great army
to attack this country,
intending to take the bowl away.
He placed the bowl on an elephant,
but the elephant could not move forward.
He then made a four-wheeled cart to carry the bowl,
pulled by eight elephants together,
but again it would not advance.
The king realized the bowl's karmic connection had not yet arrived,
so he erected a stupa and left the bowl there for veneration.
The bowl holds two dǒu,
is variegated in color with black predominating,
has four clearly defined rims,
is about two fēn thick,
and is very glossy.
If a poor person offers a few flowers, it becomes full;
if a rich person offers many flowers in veneration,
even a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand hú,
it still will not fill up."
Fótú Diào said:
"The Buddha's bowl
is made of green jade,
holds about three dǒu,
and is treasured by that country.
When making offerings,
if one wishes for incense and flowers to not fill it all day,
it is as said;
if one wishes for a handful to fill it,
it also becomes as said."
Also, according to what the monk Zhú Fǎwéi said,
the Buddha's bowl is in the country of Dà Yuèzhī.
A pagoda was built,
thirty zhàng high,
with seven stories.
The bowl is on the second story,
suspended by golden chains and locks.
The bowl is made of green stone.
Some say the bowl hangs in midair.
Subhūti placed the bowl on a golden stand.
A footprint of the Buddha and the bowl are together in one place.
The king, ministers, and people
all offer sandalwood incense, the seven treasures, and jade discs in veneration.
The stupa footprint, Buddha's tooth, monastic robe, and uṣṇīṣa relic
are all in the country of Fúlóushā.
The Buddhist *Xīyù Jì* states:
"Northwest of the royal city of Jiāntuóyuè is the city of Bōtǔluóyuè,
the city of the Buddha's robe.
To the east there is a monastery."
Returning to follow the river course:
ten li to the northwest is the Hé Bùluó Dragon Abyss,
where the Buddha came to the bank to wash his robes.
The washing stone still exists.
This water reaches Ānxī
and empties into the Léizhù Sea.
It also says:
"West of Jiāntuóyuè,
in the Western Sea, is the country of Ānxī."
Zhú Zhī's *Fúnán Jì* states:
"The country of Ānxī is twenty thousand li from the country of Sīhētiáo.
Its territory borders the sea.
This is the Tiānzhú Ānxī country mentioned in the *Hànshū*."
It has nearly a million households,
making it the largest country.
The *Hànshū Xīyù Zhuàn* also says:
"Líjiān and Tiáozhī border the Western Sea.
According to elders' accounts,
Tiáozhī has the Weak Water,
which even the Queen Mother of the West has never seen.
Traveling by water west from Tiáozhī,
for about a hundred days,
one approaches where the sun sets."
Perhaps this is where the River connects to the Western Sea.
Therefore, the *Liángtǔ Yìwùzhì* states:
"The waters of the Cōng Mountains
divide and flow east and west.
Those flowing west enter the great sea;
those flowing east become the source of the River,
which is what the *Yǔ Jì* calls the Kūnlún."
Zhāng Qiān was sent to Dàyuān and traced the River's source to its limit,
saying it ended here,
and did not reach Kūnlún.
The River, dividing from its source at the Cōng Mountains,
flows east past the country of Jiāshèluó.
The Buddhist *Xīyù Jì* states:
"There is a country named Jiāshèluóshì.
This country is narrow and small,
yet all the vital routes of the myriad countries pass through it."
South of the city there is water,
flowing northeast,
emerging from the Luóshì Western Mountains,
which are the Cōng Mountains.
It passes through the Qíshā Valley,
and upon exiting the valley, divides into two streams.
One stream flows east,
passing north of the country of Wúléi,
which is governed from Lú City.
Its customs are the same as those of Xīyè and Zǐhé.
It then flows east past the north of the country of Yīnài,
which is five hundred and forty li from Wúléi,
and its customs are the same as Zǐhé.
The River then flows east past the north of the country of Púlí,
which is governed from the Púlí Valley,
five hundred and fifty li north of Shūlè.
Its customs are the same as Zǐhé.
The River then flows east past the north of the country of Píshān,
which is governed from Píshān City,
three hundred and eighty li northwest of Suōjū.
Another source emerges from the Southern Mountains of the country of Yútián,
flows north and joins the river emerging from the Cōng Mountains,
then flows east and empties into the Púchāng Sea.
The river water flows east again and converges with the Yútián River.
Its southern source originates from the southern mountains of Yútián,
commonly called Qiúmózhì.
From Zhì, it flows north,
passes west of the state of Yútián,
whose capital is Xīchéng.
The land abounds in jade and stones.
West to Píshān is 380 lǐ,
east to Yángguān is over 5,000 lǐ.
The monk Fǎxiǎn traveled southwest from Wūdì,
encountering no people along the way,
traversing the sands with great difficulty.
The hardships endured on the journey
were beyond human comparison.
After one month and five days on the road,
he reached Yútián.
The state was prosperous and populous,
its people devoutly faithful,
mostly adherents of Mahāyāna Buddhism,
dignified and orderly in conduct.
Their bowls and utensils made no sound.
Fifteen lǐ south of the city is the Lìchà Temple,
within which is a stone boot,
and on the stone is a footprint.
Local tradition says it is the trace of a Pratyekabuddha.
Since Fǎxiǎn did not record this,
it is suspected not to be a Buddha's footprint.
[The river] flows northwest again,
and empties into the [Yellow] River.
This is what the "Classic" refers to as "flowing north and emptying into the Cōnglǐng River."
The Southern River flows east again, passing north of the state of Yútián.
The Buddhist "Records of the Western Regions" states:
"The river water flows east for 3,000 lǐ,
reaching Yútián,
then bends and flows northeast."
The "Book of Han: Treatise on the Western Regions" states:
East of Yútián,
all waters flow east.
The Southern River flows northeast again, passing north of the state of Wūmí,
whose capital is Wūmí City,
located 390 lǐ west of Yútián.
The Southern River flows east again, passing north of the state of Jīngjué,
located 460 lǐ west of Wūmí.
The Southern River flows east again, passing north of the state of Qiěmò,
then continues east,
and on the right converges with the great waters of Ānòudá.
The Buddhist "Records of the Western Regions" states:
"Northwest of Mount Ānòudá is a great body of water,
which flows north and empties into the Láolán Sea."
This water flows north, passing the southern mountains of Qiěmò,
then flows north again, passing west of Qiěmò City.
The state's capital is Qiěmò City,
connected to Jīngjué 2,000 lǐ to the west,
and 720 lǐ east to Shànshàn.
They cultivate the five grains,
and their customs are roughly similar to those of the Han.
It also states:
"The Qiěmò River flows northeast, passing north of Qiěmò,
then flows and on the left converges with the Southern River.
The converging streams flow eastward,
becoming the Zhùbīn River."
The Zhùbīn River flows east again, passing north of the state of Shànshàn,
whose capital is Yīxún City,
formerly the land of Lóulán.
The king of Lóulán was disrespectful to the Han,
so in the fourth year of Yuánfèng,
Huò Guāng dispatched the Pinglè Supervisor Fù Jièzǐ to assassinate him,
and established a new king.
The Han also installed the former king's hostage, Yùtúqí, as king,
and renamed the state Shànshàn.
Officials bade him farewell at the Héng Gate,
and the king personally requested of the Son of Heaven:
"Having lived in Han for a long time,
I fear being harmed by the former king's sons.
The state has Yīxún City,
with fertile and beautiful land.
I wish to send generals to garrison and farm, accumulating grain,
so that I may rely on their authority."
Thus, garrison farms were established to pacify and control the region.
Suǒ Mài of Dūnhuáng,
styled Yànyì,
was talented and strategic.
The Inspector Máo Yì recommended him to act as General of the Èrshī Army,
leading troops from Jiǔquán
and Dūnhuáng, a thousand men in total,
to Lóulán for garrison farming.
They built simple houses,
summoned a thousand soldiers each from Shànshàn, Yānqí, and Qiūcí,
and dammed the Zhùbīn River.
On the day the river was blocked,
the water surged with fierce force,
waves crashing over the embankment.
Mài sternly declared:
"Wáng Zūn established his authority,
and the river embankment did not overflow;
Wáng Bà acted with utmost sincerity,
and the Hūtuó River ceased to flow.
The divine power of water virtue
is the same in ancient and modern times."
Mài personally prayed and made offerings,
but the water still did not recede.
So he arrayed his troops, armed them,
beat drums, shouted, and roared,
stabbing and shooting [at the water].
After a great battle lasting three days,
the water finally receded and turned back.
The irrigation enriched and expanded the fields,
and the Hu people proclaimed it divine.
After three years of extensive farming,
a million measures of grain were accumulated,
awing foreign states into submission.
The water flows east and empties into a marsh.
The marsh is north of Wūní City in the state of Lóulán,
locally called the Eastern Old City.
It is 1,600 lǐ from Yángguān,
1,785 lǐ northwest to Wūlěi,
1,865 lǐ to the state of Mòshān,
and 1,890 lǐ northwest to Chēshī.
The land is sandy and saline, with little farmland,
relying on grain from neighboring states.
The state produces jade,
and has abundant reeds, tamarisk, diversiform-leaved poplar, and white grass.
The state is located on the eastern frontier,
facing the Báilóngduī,
lacking water and grass.
They often provided guides,
carrying water and shouldering grain,
to welcome and send off Han envoys.
Therefore, local custom calls this marsh the Láolán Sea.
The Buddhist "Records of the Western Regions" states:
"The Southern River, from east of Yútián northward for 3,000 lǐ,
reaches Shànshàn and enters the Láolán Sea."
The Northern River branches off from the Southern River east of Qíshā,
which is what the Buddhist "Records of the Western Regions" calls "the two branches flow north,
pass Qūcí, Wūyí, and Chánshàn,
and enter the Láolán Sea."
The Northern River flows northeast again,
dividing into two streams,
from which a tributary flows out.
The Northern River flows from Shūlè, passing north of the Southern River.
The "Book of Han: Treatise on the Western Regions" states:
"East of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
there are mountains to the north and south,
separated by over a thousand lǐ,
and six thousand lǐ from east to west,
with the river emerging between them.
South of Wēnsù,
on the left it converges with a tributary,
which receives water from the Northern River east of Shūlè;
it flows northwest, passing south of the state of Shūlè,
then flows northeast and converges with the waters from the northern mountains of Shūlè;
these waters emerge from a northern stream,
flow southeast past the city of Shūlè,
560 lǐ south to Suōjū,
with markets and rows of shops,
facing west on the route to the Great Yuèzhī, Dàyuān, and Kāngjū.
The Buddhist "Records of the Western Regions" states:
"The state has a Buddha's bathing bed,
made of red sandalwood,
four feet square,
which the king venerates in his palace."
In the 18th year of the Hànpíng era of the Han dynasty,
Gěng Gōng, as the Colonel of Wù-Jǐ,
was besieged by the Zuǒ Lùlí King of the Xiōngnú.
Gěng, considering this city flanked by streams and beside water,
moved from Jīnpú to reside in this city.
The Xiōngnú attacked again,
damming and cutting off the stream water.
Gěng dug a well within the city,
fifteen zhàng deep,
but found no water.
The officers and soldiers were parched and exhausted,
squeezing and drinking juice from horse dung.
Gěng then looked up to heaven and sighed:
"In the past, General Èrshī drew his sword and stabbed the mountain,
and a spring gushed forth.
Now, with the Han's virtuous and divine power,
how could it be exhausted?"
He straightened his clothes,
bowed twice toward the well,
and prayed for his officers and soldiers.
After a short while,
water rushed forth from the spring,
and all exclaimed 'Long live!'
He then splashed the water to show it,
and the enemy, thinking it divine,
immediately withdrew.
Later, Chēshī rebelled,
joining the Xiōngnú to attack Gěng.
With provisions exhausted and in dire straits,
they boiled their armor and crossbows,
eating the sinews and leather.
Gěng shared life and death with his soldiers,
all without disloyalty.
Unable to capture Gěng after besieging him,
Guān Chǒng sent a memorial requesting rescue.
In the first year of the Jiànchū era, Emperor Zhāng accepted the advice of Minister over the Masses Bào Yù,
and dispatched troops to rescue them.
Reaching Liǔzhōng,
they divided the troops under Colonel Guān Chǒng to enter the fortifications of Gāochāng.
Attacking the city of Jiāohé,
Chēshī surrendered,
and they dispatched Fàn Qiāng, an officer under Gōng’s command,
leading two thousand soldiers to meet Gōng.
They encountered over ten feet of heavy snow,
barely able to reach the destination.
Hearing the sound of troops and horses at night in the city,
the people were greatly terrified.
Qiāng shouted from afar:
“I am Fàn Qiāng.”
Everyone in the city cheered “Long live!”,
opened the gates, and embraced one another, shedding tears.
Only twenty-six men remained,
their clothes and shoes torn and worn,
their appearances haggard and emaciated,
supporting one another as they returned.
The Zhī River flows east again, passing south of the Shāchē Kingdom,
whose capital is Shāchē City,
located seven hundred and forty lǐ southwest of Púlí.
Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty opened up the Western Regions,
establishing military agricultural colonies here.
There is an iron mountain,
which yields green jade.
The Zhī River flows east again, passing south of the Wēnsù Kingdom,
whose capital is Wēnsù City,
its land and produce
are similar to those of Shànshàn.
It is six hundred and ten lǐ north to Chìgǔ of Wūsūn,
and two hundred and seventy lǐ east to Gūmò.
Here,
the Zhī River enters the Northern River from the right.
The Northern River flows east again, passing south of the Gūmò Kingdom.
The Gūmò River flows into it,
its source originating northwest of Gūmò,
passing by Chìshā Mountain,
flowing southeast along the west of the Gūmò Kingdom,
whose capital is Nánchéng.
It is fifteen days’ journey on horseback south to Yútián.
The land yields copper, iron, and orpiment.
The water flows southeast again,
entering the Northern River from the right.
The Northern River flows east again, passing south of the Qiūcí Kingdom,
then east again,
joining the Qiūcí River from the left,
which has two sources.
The western source emerges from the south of the Northern Great Mountain.
The Buddhist “Records of the Western Regions” states:
Two hundred lǐ north of Qūcí, there is a mountain
that glows with fire at night
and emits smoke during the day.
People take coal from this mountain
to smelt iron from this mountain,
which constantly supplies the needs of the thirty-six kingdoms.
Thus, Guō Yìgōng’s “Guǎngzhì” says:
Qiūcí is skilled in casting and smelting.
The water flows south, passing by Chìshā Mountain.
The Buddhist “Records of the Western Regions” states:
Forty lǐ north of the kingdom,
there is a temple on the mountain,
named Quèlí Dà Qīngjìng.
It emerges from the mountain and flows southeast again,
with a branch diverging to the left.
Flowing southeast again,
the water divides into three streams.
The two right streams both flow southeast,
entering the Northern River.
The Eastern River emerges northeast of Qiūcí,
passing south by Chìshā and Jīlí,
with a branch diverging to the right,
flowing southwest into Qiūcí City.
Pronounced Qūcí,
it was formerly Yánchéng.
It is six hundred and seventy lǐ west to Gūmò.
The river flows southeast again, passing east of Lúntái.
In the past, when Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn first opened the Western Regions,
he established a military commandery
and stationed agricultural colonies here.
Sōusù Dūwèi Sāng Hóngyáng memorialized:
East of the former Lúntái,
the land is vast,
rich in water and grass,
capable of irrigating over five thousand qǐng of fields.
The climate there is mild,
the land fertile,
suitable for expanding canals and ditches,
planting the five grains,
with harvests comparable to those of the Central Plains.
At that time, the Xiōngnú were weak,
not daring to approach the Western Regions.
Thus, they relocated Shāchē,
over a thousand lǐ away,
which is this station.
The water flows southeast again,
joining the western branch from the right.
The water has two sources,
both receiving water from the Western River,
flowing east past the south of Qiūcí City,
merging into one stream.
Within the water lies an old city,
likely guarded by the military agricultural colonies.
The water flows southeast into the Eastern River.
The Eastern River flows southeast again, passing south of the Wūlěi Kingdom,
whose capital is Wūlěi City,
three hundred and fifty lǐ west of Qiūcí,
and two thousand seven hundred and thirty-eight lǐ east of Yùmén and Yángguān.
It is close to the agricultural officials of Qúlí,
with fertile and abundant land,
making it the central capital of the Western Regions, where the Protector General governed.
The Hàn envoy holding the imperial tally, Zhèng Jí,
also oversaw the Northern Route,
hence the title Protector General.
The establishment of the Protector General
began with Jí’s appointment.
The water flows southeast again into the Great River.
The Great River flows east again,
joining the Dūnhōng River from the right.
The water emerges north of Yānqí,
from Dūnhōng Mountain,
located west of the Xiōngnú
and east of Wūsūn.
The “Classic of Mountains and Seas” states:
Dūnhōng Mountain,
from which the Dūnhōng River emerges,
flows west into Yōuzé.
It emerges from the northeastern corner of Kūnlún,
truly the source of the River.
The two sources flow together,
the western source flowing east,
dividing into two streams.
The left stream flows southwest,
emerging west of Yānqí,
passing through the wilderness of Yānqí,
turning southeast,
entering the marshes of Dūnhōng.
The right stream flows southeast,
dividing again into two,
flanking the kingdom of Yānqí.
The city lies amidst four waters,
on an islet in the river,
with its capital at Yuánqú City,
four hundred lǐ west of Wūlěi.
It meets two streams to the south,
which together enter the marshes of Dūnhōng.
The eastern source flows southeast,
dividing into two streams,
with twin torrents surging,
great rapids gushing forth,
both flowing southeast,
passing east of Yānqí,
leading west of Wēixū Kingdom.
The kingdom’s capital is Wēixū City,
one hundred lǐ west of Yānqí.
Flowing southeast again,
it enters the marshes of Dūnhōng.
Where the river accumulates,
the pond waters swell,
overflowing to form a sea.
The “Records of the Grand Historian” states:
Yānqí, near the sea, abounds in fish and birds.
To the northeast, it is separated by a great mountain from Chēshī.
The Dūnhōng River flows from the Western Sea past the Yùlí Kingdom,
whose capital is Yùlí City,
three hundred lǐ west of the Protector General’s seat,
and one hundred lǐ north of Yānqí.
The water emerges west again from Tiěguān Valley in Shāshān,
flowing southwest again,
passing by Liánchéng and branching off,
diverted for agriculture.
Sāng Hóngyáng said:
In my humble opinion, west of Liánchéng,
agricultural colonies could be established
to assert authority over the western kingdoms.
This is the place.
The water turns south again,
passing west of the Qúlí Kingdom.
Thus, the “Records of the Grand Historian” states:
To the west is a great river,
which is this water.
Flowing southeast again,
it passes through the Qúlí Kingdom,
whose capital is Qúlí City,
three hundred and thirty lǐ northwest of Wūlěi.
When Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn opened the Western Regions,
he established agricultural colonies at Qúlí,
which is this place.
It borders Jīngjué to the south
and Yùlí to the northeast.
Flowing south again, it enters the River.
The “Classic of Mountains and Seas” states:
The Dūnhōng River
flows west into Yōuzé.
It seems the disordered river flows from the southwest into it.
The River flows east again, passing south of the Mòshān Kingdom,
whose capital is Mòshān City,
two hundred and forty lǐ west to Yùlí.
The River flows east again, passing south of Zhùbīn City.
Flowing east again, it passes south of Lóulán City and then flows east.
Likely, it was where agricultural colonies were stationed,
hence the city bears the kingdom’s name.
The river water flows eastward and pours into the Yōu Marsh,
which is what the *Classic* refers to as the Púchāng Sea.
The water accumulates northeast of Shànshàn
and southwest of Lóngchéng.
Lóngchéng
was originally the ruins of Jiānglài,
a great kingdom of the Hú people.
When the Púchāng Sea overflowed,
it swept away and destroyed the kingdom.
The foundation of the city still remains and is extremely large;
setting out from the west gate at dawn,
one reaches the east gate by dusk.
The water eroded its banks,
and the remaining currents, blown by the wind,
gradually took the shape of a dragon,
facing west toward the sea.
Hence, it was named Lóngchéng.
The land stretches for a thousand *lǐ*,
all covered in hard, solid salt.
Travelers passing through
spread felt mats for their livestock to lie on.
Digging beneath the surface,
one finds large salt blocks,
square like giant pillows,
piled one upon another.
It resembles mist rising and clouds floating,
with few stars or sun visible,
scarce in birds and animals,
and abundant in ghosts and strange phenomena.
To the west, it borders Shànshàn;
to the east, it connects to Sānshā,
forming the northern barrier of the sea.
Therefore, Púchāng is also called the Salt Marsh.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
From the Bùzhōu Mountains,
looking north toward the Zhūpí Mountains,
overlooking the lofty Yuèchóng Mountains,
and gazing east toward the Yōu Marsh,
where the river water submerges.
Its source is turbulent and bubbling.
It lies thirteen hundred *lǐ* east of Yùmén and Yángguān,
spanning four hundred *lǐ* in breadth.
Its waters are clear and still,
neither decreasing in winter nor summer.
Within it, whirlpools spin like lightning,
forming hidden, submerged currents.
Above its swirling streams,
birds soaring in the sky
all fall into the deep waves.
This is where the river water submerges
and emerges again at Jīshí.
Further east, it enters the frontier,
passing south of Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Zhāngyè commanderies.
The Yellow River originates from Púchāng,
where there is evidence of hidden currents,
and it begins its winding journey into the frontier passes.
From this point onward,
the Classic should be examined for factual accuracy.
The Yellow River has a dual source,
emerging again beyond the western frontier,
flowing out from the Jīshí Mountains.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
At the Jīshí Mountains,
there is a stone gate below,
and the Yellow River surges westward through it.
This mountain
contains all things in existence.
This is what the Tribute of Yu refers to as "channeling the Yellow River from Jīshí."
The mountains lie within the territory of the Western Qiāng,
where the Shāodāng tribe resides.
In the second year of the Yánxī era,
the Western Qiāng Shāodāng tribe invaded the frontier,
and the Protector of the Qiāng, Colonel Duàn Jiǒng, led a campaign against them,
pursuing them beyond the frontier
to the Jīshí Mountains,
where he beheaded them and returned.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
The Western Qiāng
extend west from Xīzhī,
dwelling along the upper reaches of the Yellow River.
The Yellow River bends and flows northeast,
