passing through the land of Xīzhī,
which is known as the River Bend.
Yìng Shào said:
According to the Tribute of Yu,
Xīzhī belongs to Yōngzhōu,
lying west of Héquān,
over a thousand li east of Héquān,
inhabited by the Qiāng people,
and is called the River Bend Qiāng.
To the northeast, it passes through Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and south of Zhāngyè.
Yìng Shào's Records of Geography and Customs states:
Dūnhuáng
and Jiǔquán
are named for their water, which is as sweet as the taste of wine;
Zhāngyè
means "extending the nation's arm and armpit"
to intimidate the Qiāng and Dí tribes.
The Shuōwén explains:
The system of commanderies,
under which the Son of Heaven's domain spans a thousand li,
is divided into one hundred counties,
with four commanderies per county.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals states:
High ministers governed counties,
while lower ministers governed commanderies.
By the Qín dynasty,
thirty-six commanderies were first established
to oversee the counties.
The character for commandery (郡)
combines the radical for "settlement" (邑) with the phonetic component for "ruler" (君).
The Shìmíng explains:
A commandery (郡)
means "a group" (群),
a place where people gather.
Huáng Yìzhòng's Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
The term "commande ry" (郡) relates to "ruler" (君),
changing from the enfeoffment of dukes and marquises;
the ruler
is the most revered.
The commandery governor holds exclusive authority,
and the rituals between ruler and subject are highly esteemed.
In the character for commandery (郡),
"ruler" (君) is on the left,
and "settlement" (邑) is on the right.
The ruler is the head,
and the settlement supports the people.
Thus, it takes its name from "ruler,"
and is called a commandery.
The Hàn Official Records state:
Qín adopted Lǐ Sī's proposal,
dividing the realm into thirty-six commanderies.
Commanderies were named variously:
some after ancient states,
such as Chén, Lǔ, Qí, and Wú;
some after old settlements,
such as Chángshā and Dānyáng;
some after mountains,
such as Tàishān and Shānyáng;
some after rivers or plains,
such as Xīhé and Hédōng;
some after local features,
such as Jīnchéng, where gold was found beneath the city,
Jiǔquán, where spring water tasted like wine,
Yùzhāng, where camphor trees grew in courtyards,
and Yànmén, where wild geese nested;
some after historical events,
such as Kuàijī, named after Yǔ summoning the lords
for a grand assembly at the Dōngyě Mountains.
The Yellow River passes south of it and winds far into the distance.
The Yellow River flows from the River Bend
eastward past the south of the Xīhǎi Commandery.
During the reign of Emperor Píng of Hàn,
Wáng Mǎng held power
and sought to display his might and virtue
to subdue distant regions.
He persuaded the Qiāng to cede the Xīhǎi territory,
established the Xīhǎi Commandery,
and built five counties there.
Beacon towers stood in view along the coast.
After Wáng Mǎng's usurpation brought chaos,
the commandery was abandoned.
The Yellow River then flows east through Yǔnchuān
and passes north of the Dàyú and Xiǎoyú Valleys.
This was the dwelling place of the Qiāng tribes Mítáng and Zhōngcún.
In the fifth year of the Yǒngyuán era,
Guàn Yǒu replaced Niè Shàng as Protector of the Qiāng Colonel,
attacked Mítáng,
beheaded over eight hundred,
and seized tens of thousands of hu of ripe wheat,
building a city on the Féngliú River to store the wheat;
he also constructed large ships
and built a bridge across the river gorge to ferry troops.
Mítáng then retreated far to the River Bend.
In the ninth year of Yǒngyuán,
Mítáng again joined Zhōngcún to raid eastward before returning.
In the tenth year,
the court attendants Wáng Xìn and Gěng Tán
marched west to attack Mítáng
and subdued him.
An edict permitted his return to the Dàyú and Xiǎoyú Valleys.
Mítáng believed the Hàn construction of the river bridge
meant troops could arrive at any time,
so the land was uninhabitable.
He rebelled again,
settled at the River Bend,
and became enemies with other Qiāng tribes.
His people joined official troops to attack him.
Yǔnchuān was several tens of li from Mítáng;
after encamping,
they sent light troops to provoke battle,
then withdrew to lure him.
Mítáng pursued them
to the camp, where battle ensued,
and Mítáng fled in defeat.
Thereafter, Xīhǎi and the Dàyú and Xiǎoyú Valleys
were left without settlements.
The Chancellor of Yúmí, Cáo Fèng, memorialized:
Since the Jiànwǔ era,
the Western Róng have repeatedly violated the law,
often starting with the Shāodāng tribe.
The reason for this
is their residence in the Dàyú and Xiǎoyú Valleys,
where the land is fertile and rich,
close to the frontier,
and adjacent to other tribes.
To the south, they gained Zhōngcún,
expanding their numbers;
to the north, the great river provided a natural barrier,
making their position secure.
They also benefited from the fish and salt of Xīhǎi,
cultivating fields along the mountains and rivers
to expand agriculture and livestock,
thus growing powerful
and often dominating the other tribes.
Now their alliances are broken,
and their kin have turned against them.
Their remaining able fighters
number no more than a few hundred.
We should seize this moment
to reestablish the Xīhǎi Commandery and counties,
secure the two Yú Valleys,
expand garrison farms,
block the routes of interaction between the Qiāng and Hú,
grow grain to enrich the frontier,
and reduce the burden of transport.
The emperor appointed Fèng as Chief Commandant of the Western Region of Jīnchéng,
who then opened twenty-seven garrison farm divisions,
lining them along both sides of the river,
connecting with Jiànwēi in a continuous line.
Later, when the Qiāng rebelled again,
these were abandoned.
According to Duàn Guó's Records of Shāzhōu,
the Tǔyùhún built a bridge over the river,
called the "Hé Lì,"
measuring one hundred fifty paces long.
Stone foundations were piled on both banks,
laid in successive sections,
with large timbers crisscrossed and weighted down,
level on both sides,
three zhang apart.
Large beams were placed horizontally with planks in between,
and railings were installed with elaborate decoration.
The bridge lies east of Qīngshuǐchuān.
Further east, it passes north of Héquān County in Lǒngxī,
where the Táo River flows from the southeast and joins it.
The Yellow River flows right past the north of Shāzhōu (Sand Prefecture).
Duàn Guó said:
One hundred and seventy lǐ southwest of Jiāohé, there is yellow sand,
the sand stretches one hundred and twenty lǐ from north to south,
and seventy lǐ from east to west,
reaching Dàyángchuān to the west.
Looking at the yellow sand,
it is as if someone scattered dried provisions on the ground;
no grass or trees grow there at all,
just barren yellow sand
extending for several hundred lǐ in circumference.
Shāzhōu (Sand Prefecture) thus derived its name from this.
The "Geographical Records" states:
In the second year of the Shénjué era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Héguān County was established,
likely named after the strategic pass on the river.
The "Fēngsú Tōng" says:
An area of one hundred lǐ is called a tóng,
and its collective name is a xiàn (county).
Xiàn (county),
means xuán (mysterious, profound),
means shǒu (head, leader).
It is composed of the radical "silk" (糸) with an inverted "head" (首).
Raising the head easily leads to bias.
This means one should be profound and tranquil,
and equalize corvée duties.
The "Shìmíng" further states:
Xiàn (county),
means xuán (suspended),
as it is suspended under the commandery.
Huáng Yìzhòng's "Record of the Thirteen Provinces" says:
Xiàn (county),
means xián (string of a bow),
a string is used for correctness and straightness.
It refers to the position of the lower body,
the place adjacent to the people,
not taking its oath lightly,
applying laws with a measuring cord,
not bending like a string.
The sound of xián (string) is close to xiàn (county),
hence it was used to derive the name.
Nowadays, the character xiàn (county) has the radical "silk" (糸) on the left side.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
he ordered all counties and towns in the realm to build walls.
Zhāng Yàn said:
This meant each was to build its own city walls.
The Yellow River then flows northeast,
entering the boundaries of Xīpíng Commandery.
To the left, it joins two rivers,
which flow south into the Yellow River.
Further northeast,
the Jìchuān River flows into it.
This river originates southwest from Làndú,
flows northeast into a great valley,
called the Dàgǔ River (Great Valley River).
It passes north by the southwest of Jiāohé City,
flows north and empties into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past the north of the old Jiāohé City.
There are two cities leaning against each other at the eastern and western corners,
located two hundred and twenty lǐ northeast of Xīpíng.
During the Jǐngpíng era of Emperor Shào of Sòng,
Tǔyùhún Āchái was appointed General Ānxī and Duke of Jiāohé,
based in this city.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past Huángchuān City.
The Yellow River then flows east past the south of Shíchéng (Stone City).
To the left, it joins the Běigǔ River.
In the past, Duàn Jiǒng attacked the Qiāng at Shíchéng;
over eight hundred people fell into the river or pits and died,
which happened here.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past Huánghéchéng (Yellow River City).
It is two hundred and seventeen lǐ northwest of Xīpíng.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past the north of Guǎngwéi City.
To the right, it joins the Wūtóuchuān River.
This river originates from Yuǎnchuān,
drawing from the Wéizhī tributary,
flows north past the east of the city and then north,
emptying into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past the south of Hánchuān City.
To the left and right of the city,
through a valley, there are two rivers
originating from the northern mountains,
flowing south past Hán Pavilion,
and emptying into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east,
and the Línjīn Creek flows into it.
This water comes from the southern mountains,
flows north past the west of Línjīn City and then north,
emptying into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past the north of Línjīn City and the south of Báitǔ City.
The "Record of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
Sixty lǐ west of Zuǒnán Crossing is Báitǔ City,
located north of the great river,
serving as a crossing point along the river.
Guō Huái, the Sīzhōu Cìshǐ of Wèi, defeated the Qiāng
and blocked them at Báitǔ,
which is this place.
The Yellow River then flows east,
and to the left meets the Báitǔchuān River.
This river emerges from below the northwest of Báitǔ City,
flows southeast past the north of Báitǔ City,
and then southeast into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows northeast and meets two rivers,
joining two waters on the right.
They flank the banks unevenly, with connected lands,
facing each other across perilous terrain.
North of the river are layered mountains,
very numinous and beautiful.
On the mountain peaks,
stand stones hundreds of zhàng high,
tall and upright,
vying in height and imposing presence,
looking jagged and precipitous from afar,
as if a piled-up painting were propped against the sky.
Below, the layered cliffs rise steeply,
with sheer banks offering no steps.
Within the overhanging cliffs,
there are many stone chambers.
Inside the chambers, it seems as if there are accumulated scrolls,
but few worldly scholars have ever reached them.
Therefore, it is called the Jīshūyán (Accumulated Books Cliff).
Within the cliff halls,
divine beings are often seen coming and going.
They are likely individuals dressed in feathers and garments of great geese,
masters who refine their essence and consume special diets.
Common people, not realizing they are immortals,
call them spirits and ghosts.
The Qiāng people call ghosts "tángshù",
hence they also named it Tángshù Mountain.
Pointing to the dense dwellings in the halls,
they call them the Tángshù Caves.
Those who cherish the Way and revere the mysterious,
and those with shaven heads and pure hair,
also go there to lodge and entrust themselves.
Therefore, the "Record of Qínchuān" states:
By the cliffs of the river gorge, there are two caves.
One is called the Tángshù Cave,
forty zhàng high.
Two lǐ to the west is the Shí Liàng Cave,
one hundred zhàng high,
twenty zhàng wide,
and thirty zhàng deep,
storing five bamboo chests of ancient books.
Liàng
was a man from Nán'ān.
Below the seal, there is water
originating from this mountain stream,
flowing south into the Yellow River,
called the Tángshù River.
The Yellow River then flows east to Yětíng (Wild Pavilion) south,
then flows northeast,
passing through Yánchuān,
called the Yánchuān River.
It then flows northeast into the Yellow River,
called the Yětíngkǒu (Wild Pavilion Mouth).
The Yellow River then flows east past the north of Fènglín (Phoenix Forest).
Fènglín
is the name of a mountain.
Five peaks stand together.
Elderly worthies say:
In the past, there was a phoenix
that flew and roamed among the five peaks,
hence the mountain has this name.
The "Record of Qínzhōu" states:
North of Fūhǎn Plain is called Fènglínchuān (Phoenix Forest Plain),
through which the Yellow River flows east.
The Yellow River then flows east and joins the Lí River.
This river originates from beyond the frontier among the Qiāng,
hence the "Geographical Records" states:
This river emerges from beyond the western frontier,
flows northeast,
passes through the wild barbarian territories,
passes west of Xiāotóng City,
then flows northeast past east of Lièchéng.
Examining the "Dì Shuō", it has no entry,
likely because it originates from the Róng region.
To the left, it joins the Liè River.
This river originates from a northwestern stream,
flows northeast past the north of Lièchéng,
and enters the Lí River on the right.
The city lies at the confluence of the two rivers.
The Lí River then flows north past the west of Kěshígū City,
a name from the Western Róng.
Further northeast,
to the right, it joins the Hēichéng Creek.
This water originates from below the northwestern mountains,
flows southeast past the south of Hēichéng,
then southeast,
where a branch stream diverges to the left.
Then it flows southeast into the Lí River.
The Lí River then flows northeast past the east of Yúchéng,
and the Yúchéng Creek flows into it.
This water originates from below the northwestern mountains of Sùhé Xìyuè,
flows southeast through Xìyuèchuān,
a local name from the barbarian customs.
Then it flows southeast out of Dízhōu Gorge,
and southeast joins the branch of the Hēichéng Creek.
This tributary water receives the creek water from above,
flows northeast past the east of Hēichéng,
and flows northeast into the Yú Creek.
Then it flows southeast past the south of Yúchéng.
It flows northeast and empties into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows northeast past the Shímén Kǒu,
where the mountains are high, perilous, and extremely steep.
The opposite banks resemble a gate,
hence the gorge acquired this name.
It is suspected that this is the Gāolán Shānmén.
In the third year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the Swift Cavalry General Huò Qùbìng set out from Lǒngxī,
reached Gāolán,
which refers to the mountain pass and fortress of this mountain.
Yìng Shào's "Hànshū Yīnyì" states:
Gāolán is located outside the frontier fortress of Báishí County in Lǒngxī,
and is the name of a river.
Mèng Kāng said:
It is the name of a mountain pass.
Now, this mountain is not far from the river,
therefore commentators suspect it lies between the river and the mountains.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows northeast,
and the Gāolánshān Shuǐ from the left and right flanks empties into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows east,
and the Báishíchuān Shuǐ empties into it.
The water originates from the mountains northwest of the county,
flows southeast,
and a branch flows east and empties there.
The Báishíchuān Shuǐ again flows south past the west of Báishí Chéng and empties into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows east past the old city of Báishí County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed to Shùnlì.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Báishí County is 285 lǐ northwest of Dídào,
and the Lí Shuǐ passes north of it.
Now the Lí Shuǐ passes south of it,
and does not pass north of it.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows east past the north of Báishí Shān.
Yìng Shào said:
Báishí Shān lies to the east,
and the Luóxī Shuǐ empties into it.
The water originates from the mountains southwest,
and flows east into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows east,
and on the left joins the Hànjiān Nánxī Shuǐ.
The water originates west of Hànjiān,
flows southeast past the south of Hànjiān and empties into it.
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" states:
Guǎngdà Bǎn is northwest of Fúhǎn,
and Hànjiān is located there.
In the past, Mùróng Tǔyùhún journeyed from Yān past the Yīn Shān westward,
and established his residence here.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows east past the old city of Fúhǎn County.
Yìng Shào said:
This was the former fief of the Marquis of Fúhǎn.
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" states:
Fúhǎn County is 210 lǐ west of the commandery,
and the Lí Shuǐ passes east in front of the city's south gate.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows northeast,
and the Gùchéngchuān Shuǐ empties into it.
The water has two sources:
the southern source originates from the mountains southwest,
flows northeast past the north of Jīnniǔ Dàlǐng,
again flows northeast past an old city,
and again flows northeast to meet the northern water.
The northern source flows from the southwest past the north of the old city,
and on the right enters the southern water.
The combined flow goes northeast and empties into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows northeast,
and on the left joins a branch of the Báishíchuān Shuǐ.
The water above receives the Báishíchuān Shuǐ,
flows east past the north of Báishí Chéng,
again flows east crossing the Hànjiān Xī,
again flows east past the south of Fúhǎn Chéng,
and again flows east into the Lí Shuǐ.
The Lí Shuǐ again flows northeast out of the gorge,
flows north and empties into the Hé.
The "Dìlǐ Zhì" states:
The Lí Shuǐ originates outside the western frontier of Báishí County,
and flows east to Fúhǎn where it enters the Hé.
The Hé Shuǐ again flows past the south of Zuǒnán Chéng.
The "Shísánzhōu Zhì" states:
140 lǐ west of Shíchéng is Zuǒnán Chéng,
and the ferry also takes its name from this.
The Dà Hé again flows east past the north of Chì'àn,
which is the river's bank.
The "Qínzhōu Jì" states:
Fúhǎn has a river bank,
the bank is 40 zhàng wide.
During the Yìxī era,
Qǐfó built a flying bridge over this river here,
the bridge was 50 zhàng high,
and it took three years to complete.
The Hé Shuǐ again flows east,
and the Táo Shuǐ empties into it.
The "Dìlǐ Zhì" states:
The water originates from among the Qiāng outside the frontier.
The "Shāzhōu Jì" states:
The Táo Shuǐ and the Diànjiāng Shuǐ both originate from Jiāngtái Shān;
south of the mountain is the source of the Diànjiāng;
east of the mountain is the source of the Táo.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
The Bái Shuǐ originates from Shǔ.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Commentary" states:
From Líntáo's Xīqīng Shān it flows southeast into the Hàn,
and reaches Diànjiāng,
therefore Duàn Guó considered it the Diànjiāng Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ originates from the same mountain,
therefore it is known that Jiāngtái
is another name for Xīqīng.
The Táo Shuǐ flows northeast,
passing through Tǔyùhún territory.
Tǔyùhún
originally were a collateral branch of the Eastern Yān Mùróng clan,
who took their clan name,
and used it as the tribal name for their leader's kind.
Therefore they are called wild captives.
From the Táo and Jiāng area, for 300 lǐ north and south,
the ground is covered with dragon's beard grass,
and there is no firewood.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows northeast past the north of Táoyáng Zēngchéng.
The "Shāzhōu Jì" states:
300 lǐ northeast of Jiāngchéng is Zēngchéng,
a city facing the Táo Shuǐ.
In the second year of the Jiànchū era,
the Qiāng attacked the Southern Commandant at Líntáo.
The emperor sent the Acting Chariot and Cavalry General Mǎ Fáng and the Chángshuǐ Colonel Gěng Gōng to rescue him.
The various Qiāng retreated and gathered at Táoyáng,
which is this city.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows east past the south of Hónghé Shān,
the city is amidst four mountains.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows east past the north of Míhé Chéng,
a Qiāng name.
It again flows east past Gānzhī Tíng,
passes Wàngqū,
which is southwest of Líntáo,
200 lǐ from Lóngsāng Chéng.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows east past the north of the old city of Líntáo County.
When Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he went west to the banks of the Táo Shuǐ,
saw a tall man,
and received the "Black Jade Book" on this water.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows northeast,
bends and flows past the west of Suǒxī Chéng.
In the second year of the Jiànchū era,
Mǎ Fáng and Gěng Gōng came out from the Wǔxī Xiángtǎn Valley to Suǒxī,
fought the Qiāng,
defeated them,
built Suǒxī Chéng,
and moved the Southern Commandant of Lǒngxī to reside there.
It is commonly called Chìshuǐ Chéng,
also known as the Eastern City of Líntáo.
The "Shāzhōu Jì" states:
From the Eastern Táo to the Western Táo is 120 lǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ again bends and flows north,
passes the west of Lóngsāng Chéng and flows northwest.
In the second year of the Jiànchū era, Mǎ Fáng
came from Āngù Wǔxī to Lóngsāng,
opening the old road,
commonly called Lóngchéng.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows northwest past the east of Bùhé Tíng,
and the Bùhéchuān Shuǐ empties into it.
The water originates from the western mountains,
flows northeast out of the mountains,
passes north of Bùhé Tíng,
and flows northeast into the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows north out of Ménxiá,
passes Qiújué Chuān,
and the Xùnchuān Shuǐ empties into it.
The water originates from the western stream of Sānglán,
flows east through Sānglán Chuān,
again flows east past the north of Xùn Chuān,
and flows east into the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows north through a gorge,
passes Piānqiáo,
emerges from Yíshǐ Liáng,
and on the right joins the Xùnkǎichuān Shuǐ.
The water originates southeast from beneath Héngdǐ Shí,
flows north through Xùnkǎi Chuān,
and flows northwest into the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows northeast past the east of Sāng Chéng,
and again flows north to meet the Lánchuān Shuǐ.
The water source originates from the northwestern stream of Qiújué Chuān,
flows northeast through Lán Chuān,
passes north of Sāng Chéng,
and flows east into the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows north past the west of Wàiqiāng Chéng,
and again flows north past the east of Hébó Chéng,
the city is within the mountains,
and on the left joins the Hébóchuān Shuǐ.
The water originates from the mountains southwest of the city,
flows northeast past the south of Hébó Chéng,
and flows northeast into the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ flows north past the west of the old city of Āngù County.
The "Dìlǐ Zhì" states it is a subordinate county of Lǒngxī.
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" states:
The county is 47 lǐ south of the commandery.
Gài Yán turned to attack the rebellious Qiāng of Dídào, Āngù, and Wǔxī,
and heavily defeated them,
which was here.
The Táo Shuǐ again flows north past the west of the old city of Dídào.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Now it is called Wǔshǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ flows northwest of the city,
and again flows north,
The Longshui River flows into it,
which is the Lan River mentioned in the *Classical of Mountains and Seas*.
The river originates from the Gāochéng Ridge northwest of the Niǎoshǔ Mountains,
flows west past Lǒngzhǐ,
where landslides from the mountain cliffs
can be heard for hundreds of *lǐ*,
hence Yáng Xióng’s description “the sound is like the collapse of Zhǐ” refers to this.
It then flows northwest past the foot of the Báishí Mountain,
and the *Treatise on Geography* states:
To the east of Dídào is the Báishí Mountain.
The Lan River then flows northwest past the south of Wǔjiē City,
and further northwest past the east of the old Dídào City.
The *Table of Officials* states:
A county inhabited by barbarians is called a *dào*,
while a fiefdom granted to a princess is called a *yì*.
Yìng Shào explains:
They speak a different language and wear their garments left-over-right,
unlike the Huáxià people.
An interpreter is required
for communication.
The Hàn dynasty’s Lǒngxī Commandery was established here,
founded in the 28th year of King Zhāo of Qín.
Yìng Shào explains:
Since Lǒngzhǐ lies to its east,
it is called Lǒngxī (West of Lǒng).
The *Biographies of Immortals* records:
Fēng Jūndá,
a native of Lǒngxī,
ingested refined mercury,
lived to be over a hundred years old,
yet looked only about thirty,
and rode a black ox,
hence he was called the Black Ox Taoist.
Wáng Mǎng changed the names of commanderies and counties,
renaming the commandery Yànróng,
and the county Cāolǔ.
In the past, when Mǎ Yuán served as the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī,
in the sixth year,
he opened a canal for Dídào,
diverting water to grow *jīng* rice,
bringing prosperity to the commandery,
using this very river.
The Lan River then flows northwest
and empties into the Táo River.
The Táo River converges with two tributaries on the right
and meets the Dàxiàchuān River on the left.
The Dàxiàchuān River originates from the western mountains,
where two sources merge and flow turbulently,
passing south of Jīnniǔ City.
The *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
To the west of Dàxià County lies the old Jīnniǔ City,
forty *lǐ* from the county,
originally the seat of a Commandant.
It then flows northeast past the old city of Dàxià County.
The *Treatise on Geography* notes it was renamed Shùnxià by Wáng Mǎng.
The *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* records:
The county has a temple of Yǔ,
as Yǔ was born here.
It then flows northeast out of the mountains
and empties into the Táo River.
The Táo River continues north,
joined by three tributaries on both sides,
and flows turbulently north into the [Yellow] River.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
The Táo River flows north to Fúhǎn
and enters the [Yellow] River to the east, which is accurate.
It then flows east past the north of Yūnyá County in Jīnchéng.
It is the seat of Jīnchéng Commandery.
Established in the sixth year of the Shǐyuán era of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn,
it was called Xīhǎi by Wáng Mǎng.
Wáng Mǎng also changed Yǔnyá to Xiūyuǎn County.
The Yellow River flows past its south,
not to its north.
To the south, the Huángshuǐ emerges beyond the frontier.
Flowing east, it passes north of the stone chamber of the Queen Mother of the West, the stone cauldron, and the Xīhǎi Salt Lake.
Thus, Kǎn Yīn said:
To its west lies the source of the Huángshuǐ.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
It is where the Huángshuǐ emerges.
The Huángshuǐ then flows southeast past Lóngyí City,
which was formerly the land of Xīlíng.
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
The city is located three hundred and ten lǐ west of Línqiāng New County.
Wáng Mǎng accepted the tribute of Xīlíng,
and established Xīhǎi Commandery,
with its seat in this city.
The Huángshuǐ then flows southeast past the north of Bēihé Qiāng Lake,
where there is a salt lake.
Kǎn Yīn said:
West of the county lies Bēihé Qiāng Lake.
It is commonly called Qīnghǎi,
and is two hundred and fifty lǐ east of Xīpíng.
The Huángshuǐ flows east past the north of Huángzhōng City,
which was formerly the land of the Lesser Yuèzhī.
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
Between Xīpíng and Zhāngyè,
a branch of the Greater Yuèzhī,
was the state of the Lesser Yuèzhī.
Fàn Yè's "Book of the Later Hàn" states:
The Huángzhōng Yuèzhī Hú
had their king killed by the Xiōngnú,
and the remaining tribes dispersed.
Some crossed the Cōnglǐng mountains to the west,
while the weaker ones entered the mountains to the south,
settling among the Qiāng,
hence receiving the name Lesser Yuèzhī.
The "Biography of the Western Qiāng" in the "Book of the Later Hàn" states:
Among the Qiāng was Wúyì Yuánjiàn.
During the time of Duke Lì of Qín,
he fled as a slave into Sānhé.
The Qiāng, amazed, regarded him as a deity,
and elected him as their leader.
Between the Yellow River and the Huángshuǐ, there were many birds and beasts,
so they engaged in hunting.
Thus, he was revered and trusted,
and many followed him.
His great-grandson, Rěn,
remained in Huángzhōng,
becoming the Huángzhōng Qiāng.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
controlled on the right by four streams,
which originate from four valleys,
flow northeast, and empty into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the north of Chìchéng,
and enters eastward through the Róngxiá Gorge mouth,
where it joins on the right with the Qiāngshuǐ.
This water emerges from the mountains to the southwest,
flows past the east of Hùqiāng City,
which was formerly the seat of the Protector of the Qiāng Commandant,
then flows northeast past the west of Línqiāng City,
continuing northeast,
and empties into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the old city of Línqiāng County,
which in the first year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
was enfeoffed to Sūndū as a marquisate.
It was called Jiānqiāng by Wáng Mǎng.
It is called Suīróng City,
but this is incorrect.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Lúxīshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges from Lúchuān to the southwest,
flows northeast,
and empties into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the old city of Línqiāng New County.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Línqiāng New County is one hundred and eighty lǐ west of the commandery seat,
and the Huángshuǐ flows past the south of the city.
The city has east and west gates,
and in the northwest corner, there is a citadel.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and on the right joins with the four streams of Liūxī, Fúliū, Shídù, and Lí,
which flow northeast and empty into it.
On the left, it meets the Línqiāng Xīshuǐ.
This water originates northwest of the new county,
flows southeast,
passes north of the county,
and enters the Huángshuǐ to the southeast.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Lóngjūchuānshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges on the right from the mountains to the southwest,
flows northeast past Lóngjū City,
then north, emptying into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Chángníngchuānshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges from Sōngshān,
flows southeast past Jìnchāng City,
where the Jìnchāngchuānshuǐ empties into it.
The Chángníngshuǐ then flows southeast,
and the Yǎngnǚchuānshuǐ empties into it.
This water originates from Běishān north of Yǎngnǚ,
with two sources,
both flowing swiftly from afar,
converging south into a single stream,
passing Yǎngnǚshān,
and is called Yǎngnǚchuān.
Kǎn Yīn said:
North of Chángníng Pavilion lies Yǎngnǚ Ridge,
which is Hàoménshān,
the northern mountain of Xīpíng.
The waters flow turbulently through the mountain gorge,
south past the east city of Chángníng Pavilion.
It has east and west gates,
and in the northeast corner, there is Jīnchéng,
located forty lǐ northwest of Xīpíng.
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states sixty lǐ,
which is too far.
The Chángníngshuǐ then flows southeast and joins with another stream,
which emerges from the western mountains,
flowing southeast.
On the mountain south of the water,
there is a shrine to the Wind God,
where sacrifices are made in spring and autumn.
This water flows southeast past the south of Chángníng Pavilion,
and enters the Chángníngshuǐ from the east.
The Chángníngshuǐ then flows southeast,
and empties into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Niúxīnchuānshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges from distant mountains to the southwest,
flows northeast,
passes east of Niúxīnduī,
then north past the west of Xīpíng Pavilion,
and enters the Huángshuǐ from the northeast.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the north and east city of Xīpíng City,
which was the old pavilion.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Gōngsūn Húnxié, the Administrator of Lǒngxī from Běidì, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
During the Huángchū era of Wèi,
Xīpíng Commandery was established,
relying on the old pavilion,
with additional construction of southern, western, and northern walls to serve as the commandery seat.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the south of Tǔlóu,
with the tower leaning against the mountain plain to the north,
its peak three hundred chǐ high,
as if carved out.
Below the tower is a shrine,
with carved walls and old remnants still existing.
Kǎn Yīn said:
North of Xīpíng Pavilion lies the Tǔlóu Shrine.
Now it is located five lǐ northeast of the pavilion.
On the right, five springs empty into it,
which emerge north of Xīpíng Pavilion,
lined up like geese in a row,
flowing northeast to the south of Tǔlóu,
and entering the Huángshuǐ from the north.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and on the right joins with the Cōnggǔshuǐ.
This water has four sources,
each emerging from a valley,
flowing turbulently and emptying into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the north of Dōng Pavilion,
exiting east through Qīxiá,
a mountain gorge.
Flowing east,
on the right, the Chángxī of Qīgǔ empties into it,
while on the left, the Gānyíchuānshuǐ enters.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Ānyíchuānshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges from distant mountains,
flows northwest,
controlling and drawing from numerous streams,
bends north past the northwest of Ānyí City,
and enters the Huángshuǐ from the east.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the old city of Ānyí County,
which has east and west gates,
located seventy lǐ east of Xīpíng Pavilion.
Kǎn Yīn said forty lǐ.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and on the left joins with the Yíchūnshuǐ.
This water emerges from the Yíchūnxī northeast,
flows southwest to the south of Ānyí City, and enters the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and the Lèqiěxīshuǐ empties into it.
This water emerges from the Lèqiěxī southeast of the county,
flows north past the east of Ānyí City,
and enters the Huángshuǐ from the north.
The Huángshuǐ has the name Lèqiě,
which likely originates from this.
Kǎn Yīn said:
The Jīnchéng River first joins with the Hàomén River,
and then with the Lèqiě River.
The Huángshuǐ flows further east,
and on the left, the Chéngliúgǔshuǐ enters from the south,
while on the right, it meets the eastern and western streams of Dáfú,
which flow unevenly northward,
turbulently exiting east,
and the Qīdùn and Jīgǔ streams flow north and empty into it.
Further east,
the Tǔnàgū and Chángmén rivers
flow south into the Huángshuǐ.
Liùshān,
is a name,
the Huángshuǐ then flows east past the south of Lèdū city,
flowing eastward,
it joins on the right with the Láigǔ and Qǐjīn rivers,
and on the left meets the Yángfēi,
Liúxī, and Xìgǔ rivers,
flowing east past the old city of Pòqiāng County.
Yìng Shào said:
It was established in the second year of the Shénjué era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
the city lacks a south gate.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* says:
The Héhuángshuǐ passes east in front of the south gate,
the Liùgǔshuǐ comes from the south,
the Pòqiāngchuān comes from the north,
flanking and flowing into it.
The Huángshuǐ then flows southeast past the north of Xiǎojìnxīng city,
which was formerly the seat of a Commandant.
Kǎn Yǐn said:
Forty *lǐ* west of Yǔnyá County is Xiǎojìnxīng city.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east and joins the Gémén River,
which is the Hàomén River.
It emerges from beyond the western frontier,
enters the frontier eastward,
passes south of Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Zhāngyè,
flows southeast past the old city of the Xiāngǔ Frontier Post Commandant of Xīpíng,
and further southeast joins the Zhànshuǐ.
This river has two sources,
the western source emerges below Báilǐng,
the eastern source arises from Bái'àngǔ,
they converge into one river.
Flowing southeast to Wùshān,
it flows into the Gémén River.
The Gémén River then flows east past the southeast of Yǎngnǚběishān,
joining on the left with the Nánliúchuānshuǐ,
which emerges from Běishān,
flowing south into the Gémén River.
The Gémén River then flows east past the old city of Hàomén County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Xīngwǔ.
Kǎn Yǐn said:
Hào,
is pronounced gé.
Therefore it is also called Géménshuǐ,
bearing both names.
It then flows east and empties into the Huángshuǐ.
Therefore the *Dìlǐ Zhì* says:
The Hàoménshuǐ flows east to Yǔnyá and enters the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the north of Yǔnyá County, where it is called Zhèngbó Ford,
and joins the Jiànshuǐ,
which emerges from beyond the northwestern frontier of Língjū County,
flowing south past the west of its old county seat.
It was established in the second year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
called Hǎnlǔ by Wáng Mǎng.
It then flows south past the west of Yǒngdēng Pavilion,
traverses Hēishígǔ flowing south,
and empties into Zhèngbó Ford.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past the old city of Yǔnjiē County,
established in the second year of the Shénjué era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
called Xiūyuǎn Pavilion by Wáng Mǎng.
The county has a Lóngquán,
emerging from Yǔnjiēgǔ,
within the spring's eye,
the water patterns form intertwined dragons,
if one tries to disturb and break them,
they soon reform into dragons.
Livestock about to drink,
all fear and avoid it, running away,
it is called Lóngquán,
and flows down into the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east past Zhīyáng County,
where the Nìshuǐ flows into it.
The water emerges from Cānjiēgǔ in Yǔnyá County,
flows southeast past Jiētíng city,
further southeast past the north of Yángfēi Pavilion,
further southeast past the west of Guǎngwǔ city,
formerly the seat of the Guǎngwǔ Commandant.
Guō Huái defeated the rebel Qiāng leader,
Zhì Wúdài,
at this place.
About twenty *lǐ* southwest of the city,
west of the water is Mǎtígǔ.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn heard that Dàyuān had heavenly horses,
and sent Lǐ Guǎnglì to attack it,
first obtaining these horses,
having horns was their peculiarity,
therefore Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Song of the Heavenly Horse" says:
The heavenly horse comes, traversing barren lands,
passing a thousand *lǐ*, following the eastern road.
The Hú horses, moved by thoughts of the north wind,
then broke their halters and tethers,
raised their heads and galloped,
departing the capital at dawn,
reaching beyond the northern frontier of Dūnhuáng by dusk,
gave a long neigh and departed,
therefore the place was named Hòumǎ Pavilion.
Now, south of Jìnchāng Commandery and on the boulders of Mǎtígǔ in Guǎngwǔ,
horse hoofprints are as if trodden in mud,
having a natural form,
therefore the common name is Tiānmǎ Path,
the frontier tribesmen imitated and carved them,
hence there are traces of varying sizes,
their forms differ,
and looking at them one can distinguish them.
The Nìshuǐ then flows east past the old city of Zhīyáng County,
and flows southeast into the Huángshuǐ.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* says:
The Nìshuǐ emerges east of Yǔnyá,
and reaches Zhīyáng to enter the Huáng.
The Huángshuǐ then flows east,
and empties into the Jīnchéng River,
which is the Huáng Hé at Jīshí.
Kǎn Yǐn said:
The river reaching Jīnchéng County,
is called the Jīnchéng River,
its name changes with the locality.
The Buddhist *Xīyù Jì* says:
East of Láolán Sea, the subterranean flow at Lóngshāduī,
is at Ābùgān Xiānbēishān, four hundred *lǐ* southeast of Túnhuáng.
Flowing east to Jīnchéng it becomes the Great River.
The river emerges from Kūnlún,
Kūnlún is Ānòudáshān.
The Héshuǐ then flows east past the south of Shíchéng,
called Shíchéng Ford.
Kǎn Yǐn said:
It is northwest of Jīnchéng.
The Héshuǐ then flows southeast past the north of the old city of Jīnchéng County.
Yìng Shào said:
When first building the city, gold was obtained,
therefore it is called Jīnchéng.
Xuē Zàn in the *Hànshū Jízhù* says:
Jīn (gold/metal),
signifies taking its firmness,
therefore Mòzǐ has the saying of a 'metal wall and boiling moat'.
Wáng Mǎng called it Jīnpíng.
The *Shìběn* says:
Gǔn built the first city wall.
The *Fēngsútōng* says:
Chéng (city),
means shèng (full/containing),
composed of tǔ (earth) with chéng as phonetic.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
Inside is the chéng (inner wall),
outside the chéng is the guō (outer wall),
outside the guō is the tǔláng (earthen rampart).
Where the land is high, dig moats,
where low, build dikes,
call it a 'metal city'.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* says:
The Great River is north of Jīnchéng's north gate.
Flowing east,
the Liángquán flows into it,
emerging from the southern mountains of the county.
According to elders' accounts:
Liáng Huī,
courtesy name Shǐ'é,
was a descendant of the Hàn Grand General Liáng Jì,
after Jì was executed,
he entered Qiāng territory.
Later, his grandfather was supported by the Qiāng,
becoming a chieftain and residing in this city.
The land was desolate and the people in turmoil,
Huī intended to move to Fúhǎn,
and encamped at this mountain,
was surrounded and pressed by a group of Qiāng,
with no water,
Huī planted the elm whip he held into the ground,
prayed to the mountain with a black sheep,
a divine spring gushed forth,
elm trees formed a grove,
its water flows north from the county and empties into the Hé.
Further east, it passes north of Yúzhōng County,
formerly Méng Tián, for Qín, drove the Róng people northward,
opening up the land of Yúzhōng.
According to the *Dìlǐ Zhì*,
it is a subordinate county of Jīnchéng Commandery,
therefore Xú Guǎng's *Shǐjì Yīnyì* says:
Yúzhōng is in Jīnchéng,
which is what Ruǎn Sìzōng in his "Quànjìn Wén" calls 'south of Yúzhōng'.
Further east, it passes the northern border of Tiānshuǐ,
The Yuànchuān River originates from the Zǐchéng Southern Mountains in Yǒngshì County,
flowing northeast,
passing through this formed plain,
which is commonly known as Zǐchéng Plain.
It then flows north past the Pastoral Enclosure,
the former site of the Han dynasty's pastoral grounds.
The Qiang chieftain Míwú and over ten thousand followers
reached Xiāngwǔ, Shǒuyáng, Píngxiāng, and Yǒngshì,
plundered the horses from this enclosure,
and burned down the postal stations,
all of which occurred at this very location.
It is also said:
the land along the Yuànchuān River
is fertile soil for dragon horses,
hence Mǎ Yuán requested to share the land with farmers to sustain himself.
There are two enclosure cities, east and west,
seventy li apart.
The western city
was the capital of Qǐfó.
It then flows north into the Yellow River.
Further northeast, passing south of Wēnwéi County in Wǔwēi,
the Yellow River flows northeast along its eastern border,
with a spring source in the southwest of the county,
flowing east past the south of the county,
then northeast into the Yellow River.
Further northeast, passing north of Tiānzǐ Yǒngshì County,
the *Geographical Records* state:
Mǎnfú,
governed by a Commandant of Dependent States,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Jìdé.
A river originates west of the county,
commonly known as the Twenty-Eight Crossings River.
Flowing northeast,
through winding ravines and streams,
with paths running through them,
passing twenty-eight crossings,
travelers toil in fording and wading,
hence the name.
It flows north past the county and then empties into the Yellow River.
There is also the Chìyèchuān River,
originating south from Chìhāo Valley,
flowing north through Chìyè Plain,
then north through Niúguān Plain.
Further north past the northwest of Yìchéng,
flowing north through Sānchéng Plain,
and then north into the Yellow River.
Further northeast, passing north of the Màitián Mountains on the northern border of Āndìng.
The Yellow River flows northeast, passing northwest of the old city of Zǔlì County in Āndìng.
In the third year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty,
he visited Yōng,
then crossed over Lǒng and ascended Kōngtóng,
and returned after reaching the Zǔlì River to the west,
which was precisely this place.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiānglǐ.
Lǐ Fěi said:
its pronunciation is "lài".
Further to the northeast,
the Zǔlì Chuān River flows into it.
The water originates from the southern mountains of Zǔlì,
flows north past Zǔlì County, then turns northwest,
and empties into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past the west of Màitián City,
and further north, it merges with the Màitián Spring water.
The water emerges northwest of the city,
flows southwest, and empties into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows northeast through the western valley of Màitián Mountain,
which lies six hundred and forty lǐ northwest of Āndìng.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past the north of Hēichéng,
and further northeast,
the Gāopíng Chuān River flows into it,
which is the Kǔshuǐ.
The water originates from the Kǔshuǐ Valley in the Dàlǒng Mountains of Gāopíng.
In the eighth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ campaigned against Wěi Xiāo,
and Wú Hàn entered from the Kǔshuǐ Valley at the First City of Gāopíng,
which is this valley.
It flows northeast past the east of the old city of Gāopíng County,
established in the third year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty,
and served as the seat of Āndìng Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed the county Pùmù.
Ten lǐ to the west is a solitary mound,
on which stands an old terrace,
and beside the terrace is an altar to the Wind God,
hence commoners call this mound "Fēngduī".
The water then flows north,
and the Lóngquán water flows into it.
The water emerges from Lóngquán, seven lǐ northeast of the county.
It flows northeast
and empties into the Gāopíng Chuān.
The Chuān water then flows north out of the Qín Great Wall,
which lies fifteen lǐ north of the county.
It then flows northwest past the north gate of the old eastern and western Tǔlóu cities,
merging with another stream.
This water has five sources,
all emerging west of the Lǒng Mountains.
The eastern water originates from Qiūyuān, twenty-six lǐ southwest of the county.
The deep pool lies within four mountains.
The Qiū water flows north,
then northwest out of the north of the Great Wall,
where it meets the second water.
This water originates from the mountains west of the Great Wall, forty lǐ southwest of the county.
It flows north past the east of the old palace of the Wèi imperial lodge,
and further north,
the third water flows into it.
It emerges from the mountains forty lǐ southwest of the county,
flows north past the west of the old palace of the imperial lodge,
and further north merges with the fourth water.
This water originates forty-eight lǐ southwest of the county,
flows northeast,
and again merges with the fifth water.
This water originates from Suānyáng Mountain, sixty lǐ southwest of the county,
flows northeast,
and on the left meets the right-hand water,
converging into a single stream.
It flows east past the north of Xīlóu,
and empties eastward into the Kǔshuǐ.
Duàn Jiǒng served as Protector Colonel of the Qiāng,
and at Kǔshuǐ in Gāopíng, Āndìng, he campaigned against the Xiānlíng,
beheading eight thousand men above this water.
The Kǔshuǐ then flows north and merges with the Shímén water.
This water has five sources.
The eastern water originates eighty lǐ west of Gāopíng County,
flows northwest,
and the second water flows into it.
This water emerges from Rúzhōu Spring, one hundred and twenty lǐ west of the county,
flows northeast,
and enters the eastern water from the right.
The mingled flow then meets three streams on the left,
converging irregularly,
and together they flow northeast as a single stream.
The turbulent waters pass through a gorge,
the gorge
being the northern edge of the Lǒng Mountains' exit,
called Shíménkǒu,
and the water is called Shímén water.
It lies over eighty lǐ northwest of the county.
The Shímén water then flows northeast and empties into the Gāopíng Chuān.
The Chuān water then flows north,
and the Zìyán water flows into it.
The water emerges from Zìyán Creek to the west,
flows east through a gorge,
called Zìyánkǒu,
which lies one hundred lǐ northwest of the county.
It then flows northeast past the south of Yánchéng,
and enters the Gāopíng Chuān from the east.
The Chuān water then flows north past the east of Liánchéng.
According to the "Treatise on Geography",
Běidì had a Lián County,
and Kǎn Yīn stated
it was north of Fùpíng.
Since ancient times, when the Xiōngnú invaded the Hàn,
the lands of Xīnqín
largely became Dī territory.
Old cities and former walls
all took on Hú names.
Geography has shifted and been lost,
making it impossible to recognize again,
so it must be that people have mistakenly identified it.
The Chuān water then flows north,
and the Kǔshuǐ flows into it.
The water emerges from a mountain one hundred lǐ northeast of the county,
flows and empties into the Gāopíng Chuān.
The Chuān water then flows north,
passes west of Sānshuǐ County,
and the Féishuǐ flows into it.
The water originates west of Qiāntiáo Mountain, two hundred lǐ northwest of Gāopíng County,
flows northeast,
and merges with Ruòbó Creek.
This water has two sources,
which converge into a single channel,
flowing northeast into the Féishuǐ.
The Féishuǐ then flows northeast,
and the Wéiquán water flows into it.
The spring's flow emerges
east of Ruòbó Creek,
and flows northeast into the Féishuǐ.
The Féishuǐ then flows northeast out of a gorge,
and empties into the Gāopíng Chuān.
East of the water is a mountain,
and east of the mountain lies the old city of Sānshuǐ County,
originally the seat of a Dependent State Commandant,
and Wáng Mǎng's Guǎngyán Pavilion.
It lies three hundred and forty lǐ southwest of Āndìng Commandery.
Court Gentleman for Discussion Zhāng Huàn served as Dependent State Commandant of Āndìng,
and governed here.
When the Qiāng offered a golden horse,
Huàn summoned his Registrar Zhāng Qí before the Qiāng,
poured wine on the ground, and said:
"Even if horses were as common as sheep,
I would not take them into my stable;
even if gold were as plentiful as grain,
I would not take it into my bosom."
He returned everything and accepted nothing,
and his authority and influence spread widely.
East of the county are hot springs,
and east of the hot springs is a salt pond.
Thus, the "Treatise on Geography" says the county had a Salt Official.
Now, northeast of the city is an old walled town,
north of which are three springs,
which may be the Salt Official of the county.
The Gāopíng Chuān water then flows north into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows northeast past the west of the old city of Xùnjuǎn County.
The "Treatise on Geography" says the Yellow River branches off here as the Hégōu,
flows east to Fùpíng,
and enters the Yellow River from the north.
Here, the Yellow River has the name Shànghé.
3 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Three
3.1 The Yellow River
3.1 The Yellow River
Further north, it passes west of Fùpíng County in Běidì.
By the river there are two mountains facing each other,
water emerges between them,
which is the Upper River Gorge,
commonly known as the Qīngshān Gorge.
The river water passes through the gorge and flows northward,
branching off eastward.
The river then flows north past the west of the old city of Fùpíng County,
where the Qin established the Northern Commandant,
governing the county seat.
Wáng Mǎng renamed the commandery Wēiróng,
and the county Chíwǔ.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Cáo Fèng, styled Zhònglǐ,
served as the Grand Administrator of Běidì,
and his governance and transformative influence were particularly outstanding.
A yellow dragon appeared in response at the Gāogāng Pavilion in Jiǔlǐ Valley,
with horns three feet long,
and a girth of ten arm-spans,
its tail reaching over ten zhang.
The Son of Heaven praised him,
bestowing one hundred bolts of silk,
and increasing his rank to that of a two-thousand-dan official.
The river flows further north,
where the town of Bógǔlǜ Garrison is situated on a river islet,
a city built by Hèlián.
Mulberry and fruit trees remain,
still arrayed on the islet.
However, the name comes from a northern dialect,
and the origin of the city's name is unclear.
Inquiring among the elders,
they all say that the old and learned men recounted:
During Hèlián's time,
a fine horse died here,
and they took the horse's color as the name of the settlement,
hence the city was called Báikǒuliú, but due to a phonetic error,
it has been called as it is today,
though the details are unknown.
The river then passes east of the Diǎnnóng City,
commonly known as Hú City.
Further north, it passes east of the Shànghé City,
commonly known as Hàn City.
Xuē Zàn said:
"Shànghé is in Xīhé Commandery, Fùpíng County,"
which is this place.
Féng Cān served as the Diǎnnóng Commandant of Shànghé, governing here.
The river flows north again, passing east of the Diǎnnóng City,
commonly called Lǚ City,
all places where Féng Cān stationed troops
to engage in agriculture.
The river then flows northeast past the east of the old city of Lián County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Xīhé Pavilion.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
"Bēiyí Mountain lies to the northwest."
The river then flows north and merges with a distributary.
The water originates from the Great River,
flowing northeast past Fùpíng City,
where it splits into channels
to irrigate fields and gardens,
then flows north into the river,
but now it is dry.
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Yōng flows back in."
This refers to the river breaking its banks and flowing back in.
The river having a yōng
is like the Hàn River having a qián.
The river then flows northeast past the west of Húnhuái Barrier,
as recorded in the "Treatise on Geography,"
where the Húnhuái Commandant governed outside the frontier.
In the early Tàihé era,
when the Three Qí were pacified,
residents from Lìxià were relocated here,
hence the name Lìchéng,
located three hundred lǐ south of Běidì.
The river then flows northeast past the west of Shíyá Mountain,
five hundred lǐ from Běidì.
On the mountain rocks,
there are naturally formed patterns,
all resembling tigers and horses,
vivid and distinct,
similar to paintings,
so it is also called Huàshí Mountain.
Further north, it passes west of Línróng County in Shuòfāng.
The river flows northeast past the east of the old city of Sānfēng County,
established in the third year of Yuánshòu under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The "Record of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
"It is located one hundred forty lǐ west of Línróng County."
The river then flows north past the west of the old city of Línróng County,
established in the fifth year of Yuánshuò,
formerly the seat of Shuòfāng Commandery,
which Wáng Mǎng called Tuīwǔ.
The river flows further north,
where a distributary branches eastward,
called Tóngkǒu,
flowing east past the south of the old city of Wòyě County,
established in the third year of Yuánshòu under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
which Wáng Mǎng called Suíwǔ.
The distributary flows east to irrigate fields,
truly a case of "wisdom lies with us."
The river then bends north and becomes the Southern River.
The river flows north, then turns west and overflows east of the old city of Yǔhún County,
established in the second year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
when Shuòfāng Commandery and its counties were opened,
and it served as the seat of the Western Commandant.
There is a road
leading northwest from the county to Jīlù Barrier.
Wáng Mǎng renamed the commandery Gōusōu,
and the county Jíwǔ.
The water accumulates to form Túshēn Marsh,
which spans one hundred twenty lǐ from east to west.
Thus, the "Treatise on Geography" states:
"Túshēn Marsh lies east of the county."
This is that marsh.
Kǎn Yīn called it Yǔhún Marsh.
Bending, it flows east from the north of the county.
The river then bends and flows east,
becoming the Northern River.
In the second year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
General-in-Chief Wèi Qīng crossed Zǐ Ridge
and bridged the Northern River here.
It flows east past the south of Gāoquē.
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
After King Wǔlíng of Zhào adopted Hú attire,
he advanced from Dài along the Yīn Mountains
and established Gāoquē as a barrier.
Below the mountain lies the Great Wall,
and where the Great Wall ends,
mountains rise piercing the sky.
The mountain is split in the middle,
with two cliffs like gate towers,
soaring into the clouds,
appearing like a gate tower from afar.
Thus, based on its appearance,
it was named Gāoquē.
North of the gate tower lies the wilderness,
and at the mouth of the gate tower, there is a fortress,
spanning the mountain and forming a stronghold,
called Gāoquē Garrison.
From ancient times to the present,
it has always been heavily garrisoned
to guard the frontier route.
In the fourth year of Yuánshuò under the Hàn,
Wèi Qīng led a hundred thousand troops
and defeated the Right Wise King at Gāoquē.
This is that place.
The river then flows east past the north of the old city of Línhé County,
established in the third year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
where Liú Xián, son of Prince Gōng of Dài, was enfeoffed as a marquis,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jiānhé.
It reaches west of Hémù County.
The Yellow River flows east from Línhé County past the southern side of Yángshān,
as noted in the Hànshū Commentary:
"Yángshān lies north of the river,"
referring to this mountain.
It then flows east past the western side of Shíjìfù,
a hill where the cracked stones
all bear marks resembling deer and horses,
hence it bears this name.
Turning south, it passes by Hémù County,
located in Běijiǎ,
a place name.
From Gāoquè eastward,
between the mountains and along the river,
and beyond Yángshān,
all is Běijiǎ.
The Shǐjì states:
"Qín sent Méng Tián with a force of one hundred thousand men
to attack the Hú in the north,
crossing the river to capture Gāoquè and occupy the area of Yángshān and Běijiǎ."
The Northern River then joins the Southern River further south.
The Southern River originates from the Western River,
flowing east past the old city of Línróng County to the north,
then east past Línhé County to the south,
and further east past the old city of Guǎngmù County to the north,
where the Eastern Commandant had his seat.
It was the Salt Office under Wáng Mǎng.
Flowing for about two hundred lǐ,
it converges with the river to the east.
The Yellow River then flows south past the western side of Mǎyīnshān.
The Hànshū Pronunciation and Meaning states:
"Yángshān lies north of the river,
and Yīnshān lies south of the river,"
referring to this mountain.
But in reality, it is not south of the river.
The Shǐjì Pronunciation and Meaning states:
"North of Ānyáng County in Wǔyuán lies Mǎyīnshān."
Now, the mountain lies north of the county,
so to say Yīnshān is south of the river
is again a matter of doubtful transmission,
which is incorrect.
I note that south of the Southern River, the Northern River, and Ānyáng County,
there are only sandy hills,
with no other unusual mountains.
Thus, the Guǎngzhì states:
"North of Shuòfāng Commandery, there are seven shifting sands,
but no mountains to compare with them."
This shows the inaccuracy of the Pronunciation and Meaning and the Guǎngzhì.
It would be correct to say Yīnshān lies southeast of the river.
The Yellow River then flows southeast past the old city of Shuòfāng County to the northeast,
as mentioned in the Shī: "Build that city in Shuòfāng."
In the second year of Yuánshuò of the Hàn,
General-in-Chief Wèi Qīng captured the lands south of the river and established Shuòfāng Commandery,
commissioning Colonel Sū Jiàn to build Shuòfāng City,
which is this city.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wǔfú.
According to the Treatise on Geography:
Jīnlián Salt Marsh and Qīng Salt Marsh are both south of the county.
Further, according to the Wèi Land Records:
The county has a large salt pond,
whose salt is large, bluish-white,
and named qīngyán.
Also called róngyán,
it is used in medicine.
The Hàn established an office for salt administration.
The pond is 1,200 lǐ from Píngchéng Palace,
located within Xīnqín.
Fú Qián said:
"Xīnqín
is a place name,
a thousand lǐ to the north."
Rú Chún said:
"North of Cháng'ān,
south of Shuòfāng."
Xuē Zàn said:
"Qín expelled the Xiōngnú,
reclaimed the lands south of the river,
and relocated people to populate it,
calling it Xīnqín."
Turning south, it passes by the southern side of Xī'ānyáng County in Wǔyuán.
The Yellow River turns east from Shuòfāng,
passing by the old city of Qúsōu County to the north.
The Treatise on Geography
states that Shuòfāng had Qúsōu County,
where the Central Commandant had his seat.
It was Gōusōu Pavilion under Wáng Mǎng.
The Lǐ Sāncháo Jì states:
"To the north, reach Qúsōu;
to the south, pacify Jiāozhǐ."
This pairs north with south.
It is the Qúsōu mentioned in the Yǔgòng alongside Xīzhī.
The Yellow River then flows east,
passing by the old city of Xī'ānyáng County to the south,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Zhāng'ān.
The Yellow River then flows east,
passing by Tiánpì City to the south.
The Treatise on Geography states:
It was the former seat of the Western Commandant.
Turning east, it passes by the southern side of Jiǔyuán County.
The Yellow River then flows east past the old city of Chéngyí County to the south,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Àilǔ.
The Yellow River then flows east past Yuántíng City to the south.
Kǎn Yīn's Shísānzhōu Zhì states:
It was the seat of the Central Commandant.
The Yellow River then flows east past the old city of Yíliáng County to the south.
Kǎn Yīn said:
"Sixty lǐ southwest of Wǔyuán,
now called Shíyá City."
The Yellow River then flows east past Gùyáng City to the south,
where the Eastern Commandant had his seat.
It then passes by the old city of Héyīn County to the north,
and further east past the old city of Jiǔyuán County to the south.
Qín Shǐhuáng established Jiǔyuán Commandery,
administered here.
In the second year of Yuánshuò of Hàn Wǔdì,
it was renamed Wǔyuán.
It was Huòjiàng Commandery and Chéngpíng County under Wáng Mǎng.
To the northwest, facing another city,
likely the old city of Wǔyuán County,
which was Tiánhé Pavilion under Wáng Mǎng.
The Zhúshū Jìnián
records: In the seventeenth year of King Xiāng of Wèi,
Hándān ordered officials, nobles, and slaves to relocate to Jiǔyuán,
and also ordered generals, nobles, and their sons serving as garrison officers
all to wear Hè clothing.
The city faces the long river to the south,
and backs against连绵的山脉 to the north.
Qín Shǐhuáng expelled the Xiōngnú,
and from the river eastward,
up to Yīnshān,
built outposts and barriers as fortifications along the river.
Xú Guǎng's Shǐjì Pronunciation and Meaning states:
"Yīnshān lies north of Wǔyuán,"
referring to this mountain.
In the thirty-third year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
starting from Líntáo,
east to Liáohǎi,
west along Yīnshān,
he built the Great Wall and opened up lands in Nányuè.
Working day and night,
the people were exhausted and resentful.
Thus, Yáng Quán's Wùlǐ Lùn states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng sent Méng Tián to build the Great Wall,
and the dead lay one upon another.
A folk song said:
'If you bear a son, do not raise him;
if you bear a daughter, feed her with gruel.
Do you not see beneath the Great Wall,
skeletons propping each other up?'"
Such was the anguish and suffering.
Méng Tián said before his death:
"Starting from Líntáo,
reaching Liáodōng,
building walls and moats over ten thousand lǐ,
I could not avoid severing the earth's veins.
This is surely why I deserve to die."
Further east, it passes by the southern side of Línwò County,
which was Zhènwǔ under Wáng Mǎng.
The Yellow River then flows east,
where a distributary branches off.
The Yellow River then flows east,
and Shíménshuǐ flows into it from the south,
originating from Shíménshān.
The Treatise on Geography states:
"It emerges north from Shímén Barrier,"
referring to this mountain.
It flows northwest toward Guānglù City.
In the third year of Gānlù,
when Hūhányé Chányú returned,
an edict dispatched Chánglè Guard Commandant, Marquis of Gāochāng, Dǒng Zhōng,
Chariot and Cavalry Commandant Hán Chāng, and others,
leading sixteen thousand cavalry,
to escort the Chányú to reside south of the desert,
protecting the city built by Guānglù Xú Zìwèi.
Hence, the city derived its name.
Northeast of the city
is Huáishuò Garrison City.
The water flows southeast from the barrier,
passing by Línwò City to the east,
and then flows southeast into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past the old city of Gùyáng County to the south,
which was Gùyīn under Wáng Mǎng.
The Treatise on Geography states:
"North from the county emerges Shímén Barrier."
The Yellow River breaches its southwestern corner,
then flows southeast,
where a distributary flows into it.
The water originates from the Great River at Línwò County,
flows east for seventy lǐ,
irrigates fields to the north,
covering twenty lǐ north to south,
and then flows into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past Sèquán City to the south and then flows east.
Further east, it passes by the southern side of Zhēnlíng County in Yúnzhōng,
and further east past the northern side of Shānán County.
From the east of the county, it turns south,
passing by the western side of Shālíng County.
The great river flows east past the old city of Xiányáng County to the south.
It is the Bìng Wǔ of Wáng Mǎng.
The river bends and flows,
with Bái Qú River pouring into it.
The river emerges from outside the pass.
It flows west past the old city of Dìngxiāng Wǔjìn County to the north,
governed by the western section commander.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it "Fámán."
In the middle of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Zhào Lǜ was enfeoffed as a marquis state.
Bái Qú River flows northwest past the north of Chénglè City.
The "Records of Commanderies and States" states:
Chénglè,
formerly belonged to Dìngxiāng.
According to the "Records of the Land of Wèi":
There is Chénglè City eighty lǐ east of Yúnzhōng City.
It is now governed by Yúnzhōng Commandery,
also known as Shílú City.
Bái Qú River continues west past the south of the Wèi's Yúnzhōng Palace.
The "Records of the Land of Wèi" records:
The Yúnzhōng Palace is forty li east of the old city of Yúnzhōng County.
Bái Qú River further flows southwest past the south of the old city of Yúnzhōng,
formerly the land of Zhào.
"Records of Yú Shì" states:
Marquess Wǔ of Zhào built a long wall from Wǔyuán and Héqū,
extending east to Yīn Mountain.
Additionally, he constructed a large city west of the river,
which collapsed before completion,
thus he chose another location at Héqū of Yīn Mountain to pray.
During the day, he saw a flock of swans playing over Yúnzhōng,
wandering back and forth for days,
and saw a great light beneath them.
Marquess Wǔ said:
"Is this for me?"
Thus he built a city at that spot,
which is now the city of Yúnzhōng.
In the thirteenth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Yúnzhōng Commandery was established.
Wáng Mǎng renamed the commandery to Shòuxiáng
and the county to Yuǎnfù.
Bái Qú River further flows northwest past the south of the old city of Shālíng County,
known as Xī'ēn County in the time of Wáng Mǎng.
Its waters flow west into Shālíng Lake.
Additionally, there is Mánggān River emerging from outside the pass,
flowing south past Zhōng Mountain,
which is Yīn Mountain.
The former courtier Hóu Yìng stated to the Hàn that Yīn Mountain stretches over a thousand lǐ east to west,
and it was the garden park of the Chányú.
Since Xiàowǔ sent troops out,
it was annexed north of the desert,
leaving the Xiōngnú devoid of Yīn Mountain,
when passing by,
they have never not wept.
This refers to the mountain.
Its waters flow southwest past Wǔgāo County,
known as Yǒngwǔ during Wáng Mǎng's rule.
Further south, it flows past the west of the old city of Yuányáng County,
then southwest converging with Wǔquán River.
Its waters originate east from the old city of Wǔquán County, to the southwest of it,
the county,
referred to by Wáng Mǎng as Shùnquán.
The water flows south, then bends west,
passing the south of the old city of Běiyú County.
According to the "Geography Treatise,"
there is Nányú County in Wǔyuán,
known as Nánlì in Wáng Mǎng's time,
hence the prefix Běi here,
formerly governed by the middle section commander.
"Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
Guǎnglíng has Yú,
hence the prefix Běi is added here.
Suspecting too far and loose.
Its waters further flow southwest into Mánggān River.
Mánggān River flows southwest past the southern valley mouth of Báidào,
there is a city to the right,
surrounded by a long wall,
backed by mountains and facing marshes,
called Báidào City.
Exiting north from the city, there is a high ridge,
known as Báidào Ridge.
Along the way, there are only earth caves,
where springs emerge,
drawing water endlessly.
When I read "Qíncāo," seeing Qín Shèn harmonize,
"The Records of Elegant Songs" states:
"Watering horses in the holes of the long wall."
As I traversed this path,
I deeply pondered ancient events,
and began to understand and believe it.
It is not mere empty words.
Looking around left and right,
atop the hill,
there are ruins as if from a crumbling foundation.
Following the stream across the ridge,
with no end from east to west,
believed to be built by Marquess Wǔ Lìng of Zhào.
Mánggān River further flows southwest,
passing north of Yúnzhōng City,
with water from Báidào central creek flowing into it.

hence it is called Kǒngshān (Hollow Mountain).
The mountain lies over thirty li southwest of Púchéng.
The Yellow River then joins the Qūshuǐ on the right.
The first mountain in the "Western Fourth Range" of the Classic of Mountains and Seas is Yīnshān,
and 170 li to the northwest is Shēnshān,
where the upper slopes abound with paper mulberry and oak,
the lower slopes with wild jujube and oak,
and the southern side with gold and jade.
The Qūshuǐ emerges from there,
flowing eastward into the Yellow River.
It is commonly called Qīngshuǐ (Clear Water),
flowing east into the Great Wall of Shàngjùn.
It passes by the foot of Lǎorénshān,
then flows northeast,
reaching Lǎoréngǔ,
where the water emerges northward alongside the valley,
and following the stream leads to the water's source.
The Qīngshuǐ then receives the mouth of Lóngwěishuǐ to the east,
which emerges from Lóngwěixī on the northern side of Shénquánzhàng in Běidì,
flowing northeast into the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then joins the Sānhúshuǐ to the east,
which emerges from Sānhúgǔ in the southern mountains,
flowing northeast into the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then passes east through Gāonú County,
where it merges with the Fēnglínshuǐ.
The Treatise on Geography calls it Wěishuǐ.
Thus, it is said that Gāonú County has the Wěishuǐ,
which contains fat that can be burned.
There is fat on the water,
which can be scooped and used.
The Records of the Investigation of Things states that in Yánshòu County of Jiǔquán, a spring emerges from the southern mountains,
as large as a basket,
pouring onto the ground to form a ditch.
The water contains fat like meat broth,
which, when collected in a vessel,
is yellow at first and then turns black,
like solidified grease,
yet extremely bright,
indistinguishable from grease.
It is excellent for greasing carts and water-powered trip-hammers,
and the locals call it shíqī (stone lacquer).
Such fatty water is found in many places,
not only in the Wěishuǐ of Gāonú County.
Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed Dǒng Yì as the King of Dí,
residing in one of the Three Qín,
and this is one of them.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn conquered it and made it a county,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lìpíng.
Due to folk dialect corruption,
it is called Gāolóuchéng.
The Fēnglínchuān, a long river, pours down,
flowing north to join the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then flows south,
joined by the Xīgǔshuǐ,
which emerges from Xīchuān to the west,
flowing southeast into the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then flows east into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows south,
and the Púchuānshuǐ emerges from Shílóushān,
passing south through the east of Púchéng.
This is where Chóng'ěr fled.
It then passes south through the west of the old city of Púzǐ County,
which is now the seat of Fēnzhōu of the Great Wèi.
Xú Guǎng's Annals of Jìn states
that Liú Yuān moved south from Líshí to Púzǐ.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Púchéng is to the northwest,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The water emerges southward,
receiving the mouth of Huánglúshuǐ,
which emerges east from the south of Púzǐchéng,
entering a valley to the northeast,
and following the stream leads to the water's source.
The Púshuǐ then merges south with the Zǐchuānshuǐ,
which emerges northeast from Zǐchuāngǔ,
joining the Jiāngshuǐ to the southwest.
The Jiāngshuǐ emerges from Jiānggǔ,
flowing northwest into the Zǐchuānshuǐ.
The Zǐchuānshuǐ then flows northwest into the Púshuǐ,
and the Púshuǐ flows southwest into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then merges south with the Hēishuǐ,
which emerges from the western mountains of Dìngyáng County,
with two extraordinary sources,
pouring together into a single ravine.
It flows southeast past the north of the county,
then flows southeast,
joining the Dìngshuǐ on the right,
commonly called Báishuǐ.
The water emerges west from Dìngshuǐgǔ in the southern mountains of the county,
flowing east past the old city of Dìngyáng County.
Yìng Shào said:
The county lies on the southern bank of the Dìngshuǐ.
The Dìngshuǐ then flows east into the Hēishuǐ,
and the mingled streams flow southeast into the Yellow River.
4 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll 4
4.1 Yellow River
4.1 Yellow River
It then flows south past the west of Hé Dōng Běiqū County,
The Yellow River flows south past the west of the old city of Běiqū County.
Forty lǐ to the west is Fēng Mountain.
On it is a cave like a wheel,
from which a desolate wind constantly blows,
never ceasing.
Where it strikes directly,
scarcely any living grass grows.
This is likely because it is perpetually unstable,
being the gateway for many winds.
Forty lǐ west of Fēng Mountain,
south of the river, is Ménɡmén Mountain.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"Ménɡmén Mountain
has much gold and jade on its summit,
and much yellow earth and alum stone at its base."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Before Lóngmén was opened,
before Lǚliáng was chiseled,
the Yellow River emerged from above Ménɡmén,
greatly overflowing and flowing backward.
There were no hills or mounds;
even high ridges were submerged.
This was called the Great Flood.
When the Great Yǔ dredged and cleared it,
it was named Ménɡmén."
Therefore, the *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* states:
"He ascended Ménɡmén in the north,
the ascent of the Nine Rivers."
Ménɡmén
is precisely the upper entrance of Lóngmén.
It truly is a great constriction of the river,
and also bears the name Ménɡmén Ford.
This rock formation was first chiseled by Yǔ.
The river channel, scoured wide,
has high, deep banks on either side.
Precipitous cliffs lean and resist,
with massive rocks perched perilously,
seeming about to fall yet still leaning.
As the ancients had a saying:
"Water is not a chisel of stone,
yet it can penetrate rock."
How true!
Where the water currents clash within,
white vapor floats like clouds.
Those viewing from afar
often feel as if mist and dew dampen them,
and peering into the depths startles the soul.
The water still sends up crashing waves ten thousand xún high,
with hanging currents a thousand zhàng long.
The turbid flood roars in fury,
surges like mountains leaping,
with deep waves piling and collapsing,
all the way to the lower outlet.
Only then does one understand why, in the story of Shènzǐ, bamboo cast into the river at Lóngmén
could not be overtaken by a team of four horses.
Furthermore, Yànwán Shuǐ flows into it.
From different sources they converge,
flowing west to join the Yellow River.
The Yellow River, flowing south, then receives Lǐyú [River].
It passes east through a ravine,
reaching the head of the stream where its source lies.
The *Ěryǎ* states:
"Zhān
is wěi."
They emerge from Gǒng Cave.
In the third month, they ascend and cross Lóngmén.
Those that succeed in crossing become dragons.
Those that fail
return with bruised foreheads.
If not for this coming and going to gather,
how could such a name have arisen?
The Yellow River flows further south,
where Yángqiú Shuǐ enters it.
The water issues east from Yángqiú Chuān,
flows west past the old city of Běiqū County,
a city
that is precisely the town to which Yíwú fled.
It was called Zhènběi under Wáng Mǎng.
The *Jíjūn Gǔwén* states:
"Dí Zhāng came to rescue Zhèng,
and encamped at Nánqū."
Yìng Shào said:
"Because there was a Nán[qu],
Běi[qu] was added."
The *Guóyǔ* states:
"Èr Wǔ said to Duke Xiàn:
'Pú and the two Qū
are your lordship's borders.'"
Its waters flow west
and empty into the Yellow River.
The river, further south, becomes the Cǎisāng Ford.
In the eighth year of Duke Xī of the *Chūnqiū*,
this is where Jìn's Lǐ Kè defeated the Dí at Cǎisāng.
Chìshuǐ issues from the east of Bà Gǔ Chuān in the northwest,
and is called Chìshí Chuān.
It flows east into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River, flowing south, then joins with Pú Shuǐ.
To the west, two sources arise together,
both issuing from the same mountain.
They emerge from Yīnshān County of Xīhé,
called Shānníng under Wáng Mǎng.
From the eastern foothills of Yīn Mountain,
the southern water flows northeast and joins with Chángsōng Shuǐ.
Chángsōng Shuǐ issues east from Dānyáng Mountain,
flows northeast,
and enters Pú Shuǐ from the left.
Pú Shuǐ then flows northeast and meets with Běixī,
combining into a single stream,
which flows northeast into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River flows further south.
Dān Shuǐ issues southwest from Dānyáng Mountain,
flows northeast past the east of the Yěguān [Smelting Office],
commonly called Dānyáng City.
To the left and right of the city,
traces of copper still remain.
Its waters join the mouth of Báishuǐ to the northeast.
Báishuǐ issues east from Dān Mountain
and flows northwest into it.
Dān Shuǐ then flows northeast into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River flows further south.
Hēishuǐ issues west from Dān Mountain
and flows northeast into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River flows south to È Valley.
Following the valley northeast to the end of the ravine
is where the water source arises.
It flows southwest into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River flows further south.
Luò Shuǐ branches off east from Liè Mountain,
flowing southeast into the Yellow River.
In the past, Marquis Wén of Wèi built a lodge north of the Luò,
referring to this water.
Further south, it passes west of Píshì County.
Píshì County
was called Yánpíng under Wáng Mǎng.
Its old city lies southeast of Lóngmén.
One cannot extend the course past Píshì
and then reach Lóngmén.
Further south, it exits the mouth of Lóngmén,
where Fén Shuǐ comes from the east to join it.
In ancient times,
the Great Yǔ channeled the Yellow River through Jīshí,
dredged and breached Liáng Mountain,
referring to this very place.
This is what the "Classic" calls Lóngmén.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" states:
North of Liáng Mountain is Lóngmén Mountain,
excavated by the Great Yǔ,
connecting to the mouth of the Mèngjīn River,
with a width of eighty paces.
Traces of chiseling remain on the cliff faces,
and the vestiges of his labor still endure.
On the banks, there are also temples and shrines,
in front of which stand three stone steles.
The inscriptions on two of the steles are worn and illegible,
no longer decipherable,
while one stele was erected during the Tàihé era.
The "Zhúshū Jìnián" records:
In the first year of Jìn Zhāogōng,
the Yellow River ran red for three lǐ at Lóngmén.
In the fourth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
the river water turned red at Lóngmén for three days.
Jīng Fáng's "Yì Yāo Zhàn" says:
When the river water turns red,
it signifies the resentment of the common people.
The river then flows south,
where it converges on the right with Chànggǔ Stream.
This stream flows southeast from the valley,
passing northwest of Xiàyáng County,
and empties into the Yellow River to the southeast.
The river then flows south past the eastern side of Liáng Mountain Plateau.
The plateau extends from the mountain southeastward to the river,
a place of significance for the state of Jìn,
located northwest of Xiàyáng County in Féngyì,
overlooking the river.
When the mountain collapsed,
it blocked the river for three days, halting its flow.
The Marquis of Jìn consulted Bó Zōng about this,
and it was precisely at this location.
