The "Chūnqiū Gǔliáng Zhuàn" states:
In the fifth year of Duke Chéng,
Liáng Mountain collapsed,
damming the river,
so that it did not flow for three days.
Bó Zūn encountered a cart-puller who did not yield,
and ordered his carriage attendant to whip him.
The cart-puller said:
"The reason you whip me
is because you seek a distant path."
Bó Zūn then questioned him,
and the cart-puller replied:
"If the ruler dons plain mourning garments
and leads his ministers in weeping,
the river will flow again."
They followed his words,
and the river resumed its flow.
The river then flows south,
where Jūgǔ Stream joins it.
This stream originates from Liáng Mountain northwest of the county,
flowing southeast,
and is joined by Héngxī Stream.
Héngxī Stream emerges from Sānlěi Mountain,
a mountain with three layered peaks,
hence the common name Sānlěi Mountain.
According to the "Ěryǎ",
a mountain with three tiers is called a Kūnlún mound.
Could this mountain also be a Kūnlún mound?
At the foot of the mountain by the water's edge,
there are two stone chambers,
likely the former dwellings of recluses.
A small stream flows east,
emptying into Jūgǔ.
South of the side valley mountain, there is a stone chamber,
with two stone chambers facing west,
and two stone chambers facing north,
all built into the cliffs with windows,
connected by doors and gates,
forming what is called a cluster of stone chambers.
On the eastern side of the stone chamber,
traces of a mortar and pestle are still said to remain;
in the courtyard, there are also remnants of old structures,
vaguely resembling their former foundations;
on the northern earthen chamber,
there is a trickle of water seeping over the rocks,
sufficient for a gourd dipper to drink from,
seeming like a place for seclusion, study, or dwelling.
In the past, Zǐxià taught west of the river,
and it is suspected that this was the place,
though there is no way to verify it.
The stream then flows southeast past the old city of Xiàyáng County to the north,
which was formerly known as Shǎoliáng.
In the eleventh year of King Huìwén of Qín,
it was renamed to its current name.
It was called Jìtíng during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The water flows southeast and empties into the Yellow River.
In the past, when Hán Xìn attacked King Bào of Wèi,
he crossed here using wooden jars.
The river then flows south,
where it converges on the right with Táoqú Stream, which originates from Liáng Mountain in the northwest,
flowing southeast past the south of the retreat of Yīn Jì, the governor of Hànyáng,
commonly known as the Temple of Zǐxià.
Táoshuǐ then flows south past Gāomén to the south,
likely due to the layered hills being broken and incomplete,
hence the name Gāomén (High Gate) for the stream.
It then flows southeast past Huáchí to the south.
The pool is three hundred and sixty paces square,
located about four lǐ northwest of Xiàyáng City.
Thus, Sīmǎ Qiān's "Stele Inscription" states:
"Gāomén and Huáchí
are here in Xiàyáng."
Today, Gāomén lies three lǐ east of Huáchí.
The stream then flows southeast past the old city of Xiàyáng County.
Fú Qián said:
"Xiàyáng
is a city of Guó.
It is thirty lǐ east of Tàiyáng."
It then passes north of Gāoyáng Palace,
and flows southeast past the north of Sīmǎ Zǐcháng's tomb.
In front of the tomb, there is a temple,
and in front of the temple, a stele.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiā,
Yīn Jì, the governor of Hànyáng, admired the surviving writings,
magnified his merits and virtues,
and thus built a stone chamber,
erecting a stele and planting pillars.
"The Autobiography of the Grand Historian" states:
"Qiān was born at Lóngmén."
This is the location of his tomb mound.
The stream flows southeast into the Yellow River.
In the past, Marquis Wén of Wèi and Wú Qǐ floated down the river,
admiring the strength of the river and mountains,
precisely at this place.
The river then flows south,
where Xúshuǐ joins it.
This water originates from Liáng Mountain in the northwest,
flowing southeast past the east of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Ascension Palace,
then southeast,
cutting through the Qiángliáng Plateau.
On the right, it passes north of Liú Zhòng City,
which was the fief of Liú Zhòng, elder brother of the Han founder.
Thus, Xú Guǎng's "Shǐjì Yīnyì" states:
"Héyáng
is the name of a state.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Marquis Liú Zhòng was enfeoffed here."
The water flows southeast past the north of Zǐxià's tomb mound,
and enters the Yellow River to the east.
The river then flows south past the east of Zǐxià's stone chamber.
There are two stone chambers, one north and one south,
perched beside the river cliff,
which are the temple chambers of Zǐxià.
It then flows south past the west of Fényīn County.
The Yellow River flows eastward to the border of the Fényīn Shuí.
The old county town lies beside the Shuí.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn,
Zhōu Chāng was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Eighty lǐ north of Hédōng Commandery is Fényīn City.
It is three lǐ north of the Fén River.
The northwestern corner of the city is called Shuí Hill,
upon which stands the Temple of Hòutǔ.
The *Fēngshàn Shū* states:
In the fourth year of the Yuándǐng era, the Temple of Hòutǔ was first established at Fényīn Shuí Hill, which is this very place.
There is also the Wànsuì Palace.
In the first year of the Shénjué era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn, he visited the Wànsuì Palace,
crossed the great river eastward,
and divine fish danced in the water.
Long ago, Zhào Jiǎnzǐ sank Luán Yǐng here,
saying:
"I am fond of music and beauty,
and this man provided them;
I value worthy men,
yet for six years he did not recommend a single one.
This is to encourage my faults and suppress my virtues."
Gentlemen considered him capable of self-censure.
The Yellow River then passes east of Héyáng City.
In the seventeenth year of King Wēiliè of Zhōu,
Marquis Wén of Wèi attacked Qín, reaching Zhèng.
Upon returning, he built Fényīn and Héyáng,
which is this city.
It was formerly the city of Yǒushēn,
the state of Tàisì.
The *Shī* says:
"In Hé's southern side,
By the Wèi's riverside."
It also says:
"The maiden from Shēn,
Eldest son, she went."
This refers to this place.
North of the city is the Fèn River.
It is several lǐ south of two other waterways.
Its waters flow east through the city,
then east into the Yellow River.
Also, from within the city's interior,
a Fèn stream flows southeast out of the city,
emptying into the Yellow River.
South of the city is yet another Fèn stream,
which flows east and empties into the Yellow River.
South of the water still stands the Temple of Wénmǔ.
Before the temple is a stele,
fifteen lǐ from the city.
The water,
namely the Hé River,
gives the county its name.
Thus Yìng Shào said:
"It lies on the southern side of the Hé River."
The Yellow River flows further south,
where the Fèn River joins it.
The Fèn River emerges forty lǐ south of Fényīn County,
three lǐ west of the Yellow River.
Its source opens on level ground,
with gushing springs welling up,
almost as large as a wheel,
its depth unfathomable.
Common folk call it Fènkuí.
In ancient times, people dammed its flow to create a pond,
planting rice there.
It measured two hundred paces east-west,
and over a hundred paces north-south.
It and the Héyáng Fèn River flank the Yellow River.
On an islet in the river,
there is another Fèn spring,
all secretly interconnected.
Thus Lǚ Chén said:
According to the *Ěryǎ*,
waters that emerge separately but flow together are called Fèn.
Its waters flow southwest,
pass west of Púbǎn,
then flow west into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows south past west of Táo City.
Shùn made pottery by the riverbank.
Huángfǔ Shì'ān believed this was Dìngtáo,
but it is not here.
However, Táo City lies north of Púbǎn City.
This city,
is where Shùn made his capital.
It is not far south of Lìshān.
Whether farming or potting,
he could do it wherever he was.
Why must it be Dìngtáo
to be considered potting?
Shùn's potting
might have been one such instance.
Méngjīn has the name Táohé,
which likely originated from here.
To the south, it faces the Pújīn Pass.
The bamboo annals from the Jízhǒng tomb record:
In the seventh year of King Xiāng of Wèi,
the King of Qín came to meet at the Púbǎn Pass.
In the fourth month,
the King of Yuè sent Gōngshī Yú to present boats,
beginning with nets and three hundred vessels,
five million arrows,
and rhinoceros horns and elephant tusks.
It then flows further south past west of Púbǎn County.
The Geographical Treatise states:
The county
was formerly called Pǔ.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Pǔchéng.
Yìng Shào said:
When Qín Shǐhuáng toured eastward,
he saw there was a long slope,
hence the addition of 'bǎn' (slope).
Mèng Kāng said:
Duke Wén of Jìn gave [this place] to Qín as a bribe,
and the people of Qín returned Pǔ to Wèi.
The people of Wèi rejoiced,
saying:
"Pǔ has returned!"
Hence it was called Pǔfǎn.
Xuē Zàn, annotating the *Book of Han*, said:
"The Basic Annals of Qín in the *Records of the Grand Historian* takes Yuán to be Pǔfǎn."
This means it was originally not Pǔ.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
It was the capital of Shùn.
Some say it was Púbǎn,
others say it was Píngyáng and Pān.
Today, within the city walls there is a temple to Shùn.
It was the seat of the Qín Province Governor of Wèi.
After the capital was moved to Tàihé, the province was abolished,
and the Hédōng Commandery was established.
The commandery had many drifting and mixed [peoples],
who were called relocated people.
Among the people was one surnamed Liú, named Duò,
who long excelled at the craft of brewing.
Drawing water from the river's flow,
he fermented a fragrant, rich wine.
It was hung up to mature until the year of the withered branches,
and tapped during the time of the fallen mulberry leaves,
hence the wine got its name.
Moreover, the color of this fragrant, clear wine
was pure white like starch-water,
with a distinct, ethereal aroma,
unlike any other.
Its orchid-like fragrance surpassed even musk,
naturally achieving an exquisite aroma.
As a local tribute,
it was selected as the finest vintage.
From princes and dukes to common friends,
those who urged and invited each other
would often say:
"Suǒláng has regard for us,"
thinking it was fellow-traveler's talk.
"Suǒláng" is a *fǎnyǔ* (inversion) for "Sāngluò,"
and it further became an elegant phrase for the registers,
a witty saying among the secretariat officials.
South of the commandery is Lìshān.
It is called Lìguān,
the place where Shùn ploughed.
There is Shùn's Well,
from which flow the two rivers, Guī and Ruì.
The southern one is called the Guī River,
the northern one the Ruì River.
They flow west past the foot of Lìshān,
on top of which is a temple to Shùn.
Zhōu Chù's *Record of Local Conditions* says:
According to an old account,
Shùn was buried in Shàngyú.
Also, the *Record* states:
He ploughed at Lìshān.
And on the border between Shǐníng and Shàn counties,
in the fields ploughed by Shùn,
there were many oak trees below the mountain.
In the region between Wú and Yuè,
oak is called "lì,"
hence the name Lìshān.
I find Zhōu Chù's record in this matter to be unreasonable.
Transmitting doubts is permissible,
but proving it as fact is incorrect.
How can one borrow a different name for a tree,
attach a special designation to a mountain,
forcibly associate it with the great Shùn,
and claim this is indeed the place,
thereby further losing the fundamental nature of records and annals,
and deviating from the constant principles of factual recording?
Lìshān and Guīruì—
if one speaks of these, then it is settled.
Regarding that other place, it is erroneous.
This is what the *Book of Documents* means by "He sent down his two daughters to the Guīruì."
Kǒng Ānguó said:
They dwelt within the Guī River.
Wáng Sù said:
Guīruì
is a place name in Yú.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
He married the two daughters at the bend of the Guī River.
Mǎ Jìcháng said:
The place where a water emerges is called "ruì."
If so,
then "ruì" does not seem to be a water name.
But now we see there are two rivers with different sources that join together,
their mingled flow running west to empty into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River flows south past the west of Léishǒu Mountain.
The mountain faces the great river,
thirty *lǐ* north of Púbǎn.
This is what the *Book of Documents* calls Húkǒu and Léishǒu.
It is commonly also called Yáoshān.
On the mountain is an old city,
which the world also calls Yáochéng.
Yān Yīn said Púbǎn
was the capital of Yáo.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*:
The county has temples for Yáoshān and Shǒushān,
and Léishǒu Mountain is to the south.
There are matters that seem so but are not,
and are not but seem so.
A thousand years is vast and remote;
these are not details we can ascertain.
Further south,
the Sù River flows into it.
The river rises from Léishǒu Mountain in Héběi County.
The county's north is divided from Púbǎn.
The mountain has a temple to Bóyí and Shūqí.
Yān Yīn's *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* says:
The mountain
is also called Dútóu Mountain,
where Bóyí and Shūqí lived in seclusion.
South of the mountain is an ancient tomb mound,
where cypress trees grow lushly,
clustering thickly on the hill,
commonly called the tomb of Bóyí and Shūqí.
This water flows southwest,
and is also called Léi Water.
The *Biography of King Mu* says:
On the rénxū day,
the Son of Heaven reached Léishǒu.
The Quǎnrōng barbarians toasted the Son of Heaven at the slope of Léishǒu,
and then presented twenty-four fine horses.
The Son of Heaven had Kǒng Yá receive them on the bank of the Léi Water—this was the place.
In the past, when Zhào Dùn hunted on Shǒushān,
he fed Qí Mímíng beneath the shaded mulberry tree—
this was also here.
The Sù River again flows southwest,
and empties into the Yellow River.
This is what the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒ Tradition* call the Sù River.
It is commonly called Yáng'ān Jiàn Water.
Further south [the Yellow River] reaches Tóngguān at Huàyīn,
where the Wèi River comes from the west and flows into it.
The *Bamboo Annals* from Jíjùn states:
In the fifteenth year of Duke Huì of Jìn,
Duke Mù of Qín led troops to escort Prince Chóng'ěr,
crossing from Héqū.
The *Zuǒ Commentary* to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, under the twenty-fourth year of Duke Xī,
records that the Earl of Qín installed him,
and when they reached the river,
Zǐfàn handed a jade disc to the prince, saying:
"I, your servant, have borne the halter and reins,
following you, my lord, in roaming the world.
My offenses are many;
even I know them,
how much more must you, my lord?
I beg to depart from here."
The prince said:
"If I do not share the same heart with my maternal uncle,
may the White River be my witness."
He then cast the jade disc into the river here.
Zǐtuī laughed and said:
"Heaven opened the way for the prince,
yet Zǐfàn claims it as his own merit.
I cannot bear to share rank with him,"
and so he fled.
The Hé River passes by Chuánsīkōng,
where it converges with the Wèi River.
The *Treatise on Geography* in the *Book of Hàn* states:
This was formerly a county under the jurisdiction of Jīngzhàoyǐn.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng's *Discourses of the States* says:
Mount Huàyuè was originally a single mountain blocking the river,
and the Hé River, upon encountering it, curved its course.
The river god, the Giant Spirit,
pushed with his hands and kicked with his feet,
splitting it into two.
The imprints of his palm and foot
still remain on Huà Rock.
The *Chart of Opening Mountains* states:
There was a Giant Spirit named Hú,
who fully mastered the Way of the Primordial Earth,
capable of creating mountains and rivers,
and bringing forth rivers.
This is the so-called Giant Spirit Bìxì,
whose head crowns the Divine Mountain.
There have often been curious gentlemen
who ascended Mount Huà to observe these traces.
From the lower temple, passing by rows of cypress trees and heading south for eleven lǐ,
then turning east for three lǐ,
one reaches the central shrine.
Proceeding southwest another five lǐ,
one arrives at the southern shrine,
called the Běijūn Shrine.
All those wishing to ascend the mountain
come here to pray and make offerings.
From here, entering a valley southward for seven lǐ,
one reaches another shrine,
called Shíyǎngfùmǔ,
where a stone niche and wooden tablets are preserved.
Going south another lǐ,
one reaches Tiānjǐng,
a well just large enough to accommodate a person.
The cavity is hollow,
winding and twisting upward,
reaching a height of over six zhàng.
On the mountain above, there is also a trickle of fine water
that flows into the well,
but it does not drench people much.
Those ascending all use this route,
as there is no other path.
Wishing to exit the well and gaze at the sky,
one sees brightness as if looking through a window from inside a room.
Exiting the well and heading southeast for two lǐ,
one encounters a steep slope, precipitously ascending and descending.
Descending this slope for about two lǐ,
one then ascends eastward to the Bǎizhàng Cliff,
where both ascent and descent require grasping ropes and clinging to vines to proceed.
Ascending southward for four lǐ,
the path reaches a stone wall.
Following alongside it and advancing slightly,
after a distance of over a hundred paces,
from here heading southwest for six lǐ,
one reaches another shrine,
named the Húyuè Temple,
whose deity statue has the appearance of a youth.
From the shrine, heading south past a narrow ridge,
which is only about three chǐ wide,
with cliffs tens of thousands of rèn high on both sides,
and peering down to an unfathomable depth,
if prayers at the shrine are answered,
clouds will level with it,
and only then dare one cross.
Even then, one must straddle the ridge and pull oneself along,
gradually making progress.
Thus, the world calls this ridge the "Gripping Ridge."
Crossing this for two lǐ,
one reaches the mountain peak.
On the summit, spanning seven lǐ,
there are two divine springs:
one called Púchí,
which flows west into the ravine;
the other called Tàishàng Spring,
which flows east into the ravine below.
The Upper Palace shrine is near the northeastern corner,
its interior cluttered with various objects,
details too numerous to record fully.
From the Upper Palace, heading northeast for four hundred and fifty paces,
there is Qū Ridge.
Looking southeast from here toward the Giant Spirit's handprint,
one sees only vast cliffs and red walls,
with no distinction between the view from above or below the mountain.
The river flows south within the pass,
surging against the pass mountains,
hence it is called Tóngguān.
The Huò River flows into it,
originating from Mount Sōngguǒ.
It flows north through Tōnggǔ,
also known in the world as Tōnggǔ Water,
and empties northeast into the Hé River.
This is what the *Record of Campaigns* calls Tónggǔ Water.
Some say the place was named after the water.
The Hé River flows northeast from Tóngguān,
beside which there is a long slope,
called Huángxiàng Slope.
The slope is bordered by a deep ravine,
and ascending this slope leads to Tóngguān,
which is what is meant by "following Huángxiàng to cross Tóng."
Passing north and exiting Dōngxiáo,
it is generally called Hángǔ Pass.
The banks are profound, the sky high,
the empty valleys deep and secluded.
The ravine paths are so narrow
that two carts cannot pass abreast,
earning it the name "Heaven's Barrier."
Therefore, the *Rhapsody on the Western Capital* says:
"With perilous cliffs encircling firmly,
like a girdle and collar easily defended,
it is said that Qín, with such a two percent advantage,
could annex the various lords."
Thus, Wáng Yuán advised Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"I ask to use a single pellet of clay
to seal Hángǔ Pass to the east.
If aiming for kingship fails,
the worst outcome would still suffice for hegemony."
Guō Yuánshēng's *Record* states:
During the turmoil at the end of the Hàn,
when Cáo Cāo campaigned against Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo,
they fought successive battles in this area.
West of the river, by its banks,
there is Lord Cáo's Fort.
On the plain east of the road,
it is said to be Lǐ Diǎn's camp.
In the thirteenth year of the Yìxī era,
the imperial army once occupied this fort.
The *Record of a Western Campaign* says:
Following the winding road,
entering the Hán road for six lǐ,
there is an old city,
with a circumference of over a hundred paces,
facing the great river to the north,
and high mountains to the south.
The Yáo clan established a pass here to guard the gorge.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liú Sòng entered Cháng'ān,
Tán Dàojì and Wáng Zhèn'è
either camped on the mountains
or built forts on level ground,
establishing seven forts, large and small,
bordering the perilous river.
The Yáo clan also held positions on the mountains, plains, and hills,
and traces of these still remain.
Directly north of the pass,
across the river, there is a layered hill,
towering and uniquely elegant,
standing alone on the northern bank of the river,
known in the world as Fēnglíng.
This is what Dài Yánzhī called Fēngduī.
To the south are the riverside camps of the Yáo clan,
facing Jìn across the river.
The Hé River flows further northeast,
where the Yùjiàn Water flows into it.
This water originates from Yùxī in the south,
flowing north past the west of Huángtiānyuán.
The *Records of the Surrounding Regions* states:
At the eastern end of the opened mountain, the top is flat and broad,
about a lǐ square,
with sheer cliffs on three sides,
rising about a thousand rèn high.
During the Hàn dynasty, sacrifices to Heaven were held here,
hence it was named Huángtiānyuán.
On it stands Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Sīzǐ Terrace.
It then flows north past the west of Wénxiāng City.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
Hú County in Hóngnóng has Wénxiāng,
and the world calls it Wénxiāng Water.
This is the former town of Wèi Shàngshū Púyè, Marquis of Wénxiāng, Hé dōng Wèi Bórú.
The water flows north and empties into the Hé River.
The Hé River then flows east past the north of Wénxiāng City,
where it converges with the Quánjiūjiàn Water to the east.
This water originates from the southern mountains,
flowing north past the east of Huángtiānyuán.
The *Record of Campaigns* says:
Quánjié
is a place name.
To its west is named Táoyuán,
the ancient Táolín,
where King Wǔ of Zhōu rested his oxen after conquering Yīn.
The "Rhapsody on the Western Expedition" says:
all sought fame in Táoyuán.
The "Geographical Records of Tàikāng" of the Jìn dynasty states:
Táolín lies in the southern valley of Wénxiāng.
The river then flows northward and empties into the Hé.
Further east, it passes south of Héběi County.
The county is separated from Hú County by the river.
The Liǎo River originates from Liǎo Valley on Xiāng Mountain,
flowing southwest to join the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east,
where the Yǒnglè Stream flows into it.
This stream originates from Bó Mountain in the north,
flows south past the west of the old city of Héběi County,
which was the former state of Wèi.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed Wèi
and enfeoffed it to Bì Wàn.
The diviner Yǎn said:
"Wèi is a great name;
Wàn's descendants will surely flourish."
Later, it was made a county,
located north of the Yellow River,
hence the name Héběi County.
Today, the city's southern and western sides are about twenty-some lǐ from the great river,
about ten lǐ north of Shǒu Mountain,
situated between the river and the mountains,
where the land is narrow and confined,
which is why the "Wèi Fēng" section includes the poem "Ten Acres."
Within the city, there is a Dragon Spring,
which flows south out of the city,
continues south,
then breaks off and ceases to flow.
The Yǒnglè Stream then flows south into the Yellow River.
I note that according to the "Classic of Mountains: Central,"
this is the Qúzhū River.
In the "Fēngshàn Treatise" by Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
it is said that among the seven famous mountains west of Huà Mountain,
Bó Mountain is one.
Bó Mountain
is Xiāng Mountain.
Xú Guǎng said:
Púbǎn County has Xiāng Mountain.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
At the head of Pú Mountain,
there is Gānzǎo Mountain,
from which the Gòng River originates,
flowing west to join the Yellow River.
To the east is Qúzhū Mountain,
from which the Qúzhū River originates,
flowing south to join the Yellow River.
If we follow the "Fēngshàn Treatise,"
these two rivers could not logically flow southwest into the Yellow River.
Now, examining the Liǎo River,
the direction of its flow
aligns with that of the Gòng River.
The Yǒnglè Stream originates and flows into the Yellow River,
matching the course of the Qúzhū River.
The general designation of Pú Mountain
is also no different from Xiāng Mountain.
Therefore, Yáng Xióng's "Hédōng Rhapsody" says:
"The river spirit leaps in alarm,
trampling Huà and treading Xiāng."
The commentary states:
"Xiāng Mountain is over ten lǐ north of Tóngguān."
From this, it can be inferred
that Xiāng Mountain is at Púbǎn, and the stream
is the Qúzhū River.
The Yellow River flows south of Héběi County's city,
then east past Ruìchéng.
Between these two cities,
lies the tomb of Duàngān Mù.
Duàngān Mù
was a worthy man of Jìn.
When Marquis Wén of Wèi passed by his gate,
he bowed in respect toward his cottage,
showing a virtue revered through the ages,
whose fragrance reaches to the present.
The "Bamboo Annals" from the Jí tomb states:
"In the first year of Duke Wǔ of Jìn,
Shàng Yījūn of Ruì occupied Jīng,
and the Xún and Dǒng clans both rebelled."
Not only Dàlì,
but also ancient Ruì,
is mentioned here.
The "Annals" also say:
"In the seventh year of Duke Wǔ of Jìn,
Ruì Jiāng, mother of Ruì Bó Wàn, expelled Wàn,
who fled into exile."
"In the eighth year of Wèi,
the armies of Zhōu and Guó besieged Wèi,
captured Ruì Bó Wàn, and took him east."
"In the ninth year,
the Róng people welcomed Ruì Bó Wàn in the suburbs."
This city may also have been part of Ruì Bó's former territory.
The Yellow River then joins with the Pán Stream on the right,
which originates from Kuāfù Mountain in Hú County,
flows north past the east of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Sīzǐ Palace and Guīlái Wàngsī Terrace,
then north into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east past the north of the old city of Hú County,
where long ago, Fàn Shū entered the pass
and encountered Ráng Hóu here.
The Hú Lake originates from Kuāfù Mountain in the Táolín Pass,
spanning three hundred rèn in circumference.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and the world was settled,
the king toured the mountains and rivers,
released his horses at Huàyáng,
and scattered his oxen at Táolín,
which is this very place.
There were many wild horses here,
and Zàofǔ obtained steeds like Huáliú, Lǜ'ěr, and Dàolí here,
which he presented to King Mù of Zhōu,
who drove them to visit the Queen Mother of the West.
The lake water then flows north past the east of Hú County,
and north into the Yellow River.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
"In Hóngnóng's Hú County, there is the place where Xuānyuán the Yellow Emperor ascended to immortality."
The Yellow Emperor mined copper from Shǒu Mountain,
cast a tripod at the foot of Jīng Mountain,
where a dragon lowered its beard to the tripod.
The Yellow Emperor mounted the dragon,
followed by seventy others,
and ascended to heaven.
Hence, the place was named Dǐnghú.
Jīng Mountain is in Féngyì,
and Shǒu Mountain is in Púbǎn,
connected to Hú County.
Both the "Jìnshū Dìdào Jì" and the "Tàikāng Jì" refer to it as Hú County.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn changed it to Hú.
Folklore says the Yellow Emperor mounted a dragon here to ascend to heaven.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
"In Jīngzhào's Hú County, there are two temples to the Son of Heaven of Zhōu,
hence the name Hú."
It does not mention the Yellow Emperor ascending on a dragon.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"Ninety lǐ to the west is Kuāfù Mountain,
where the trees are mostly palm and nanmu,
with many bamboo groves.
Its southern side is rich in jade,
its northern side in iron.
To the north, there is a forest
named Táolín,
where many horses roam.
The lake water originates here,
flowing north into the Yellow River."
Therefore, the "Sānqín Jì" says:
"Táolín Pass is four hundred lǐ east of Cháng'ān.
If armies and horses pass through,
if they behave well, they may pasture at Huà Mountain,
resting beneath the forest;
if they behave poorly, the river will burst its banks and flood,
preventing men and horses from crossing."
The Yellow River then flows east and joins with the Bǎigǔ Stream,
which originates from Shídī Mountain south of Hóngnóng County.
Below the mountain is the Shídī Shrine,
with an inscription that reads:
"In the fourth year of Gānlù of Wèi,
this was built by the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Conquers the South, Inspector of Yù Province, Administrator of Hóngnóng, and Duke of Nánpíng."
The water flows north,
passing below the pavilion.
When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn fled into exile,
he reached Bǎigǔ,
where he divined about going to Qí.
Hú Yǎn of Chǔ said:
"Better to go to Dí."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn once traveled incognito to this pavilion,
where he was fed by the pavilion chief's wife.
Thus, Pān Yuè's "Western Expedition Rhapsody" says:
"Long was the journey of the guest at Bǎigǔ,
where the wife, seeing his appearance, offered a meal."
This refers to that pavilion.
The valley water then flows north into the Yellow River.
The Yellow River then flows east,
joining with the Mén River on the right.
The Mén River
is a branch of the Luò River.
The Luò River, from northeast of Shàngluò County to northwest of Jùyáng City,
divides into two streams.
The branch channel flows northeast,
becoming the Mén River.
The Mén River then flows northeast past Yánghuá Mountain,
which is the Yánghuá Mountain mentioned in the "Classic of Mountains and Seas,"
from which the Mén River originates.
It then flows northeast through a gorge,
called the Hóngguān River.
East of the water is a city,
which is the Guān Pavilion.
West of the water is a fortress,
called the Hóngguān Fortress.
It is also popularly called the "Place Where Liú and Xiàng Divided the Land,"
but this is incorrect.
I note that in Shàngluò, there is the Hónglú Enclosure Pond,
where waterways and channels flow along,
hence this stream is called the Hónglú Stream.
The name Hóngguān
originates from this.
The Mén River then flows northeast past Yìchuān,
where two streams join it.
The left stream originates from the northern side of Yánghuá Mountain,
flows northeast,
passes west of Shèngqiáng Pavilion,
then northeast,
joining the right stream.
The right stream originates from the southern side of Yánghuá Mountain,
flows northeast,
passes east of Shèngqiáng Pavilion,
then northeast, joining the left stream.
This refers to the Shuǐ of Lŭgū mentioned in the "Shānhǎi Jīng," which originates from Yánghuá's northern side,
flowing northeast into Mén Shuǐ.
Again northeastwards,
Zhú Shuǐ flows into it.
The river has two sources,
with the left source emerging south from Yá Lǐng,
known as Shíchéng Mountain by the people.
This water flows northeast,
passing west of Shíchéng,
and merges northeast with the right water.
The right water originates from Shíchéng Mountain,
flows northeast past the east of Shíchéng,
and northeast into the left water.
The "Dì Lǐ Zhì" records:
Zhú Shuǐ originates from the valley below Yá Lǐng.
The "Kāi Shāntú" states:
Yá Mountain is southwest of Hángǔ Mountain.
This water flows turbulently,
eastward into the Shuǐ of Lŭgū.
The two waters, thus, were comprehensively named.
The Lì Jiàn flows northeastward.
Called Kāifāngkǒu,
there is a mound beside the water,
called Fāngbódūi.
Sòng Fènwǔ General Lǔ Fāngpíng,
Jiànwǔ General Xuē Āndū, and others,
marched into the north with Jiànwēi General Liǔ Yuánjǐng,
and the army camped at Fāngbódūi.
There is a city atop the mound,
built by Fāngpíng.
Further northeast, it passes south of the Yìchuān City,
the old territory of Dòumén in the Hàn,
named after the river,
also called Dòumén,
the city lies seven lǐ south of Hángǔ Pass.
Again northeast,
Tiánqú Shuǐ flows into it,
sourced from the Bái Shí Valley of Yá Mountain,
flowing northeast past the east of Gùqiūtíng,
which is where Xuē Āndū's troops traversed.
Its water further flows past the west of Lùtí Mountain,
on the mountain rocks, there are deer hoof prints,
naturally formed,
not carved by human effort.
It traverses Tiánqú Valley,
called Tiánqú Shuǐ,
flowing northwest into Zhú Shuǐ.
Zhú Shuǐ further enters Mén Shuǐ from the north.
The waters to its sides,
is Hángǔ Mountain.
Mén Shuǐ further flows past the east of the old city of Hóngnóng County,
the city was the former administrative site of Hángǔ Pass’s inspector.
Zhōng Jūn discarded the straw mat here.
Yān Dān, Mèngcháng,
also performed righteous deeds like the crowing of a rooster at its rise,
which could be said to move the heart deeply,
and the integrity of their ambition is hard to alter.
In the past, Lǎozǐ entered the pass from the west,
and Yǐn Xǐ observed the atmosphere here.
Therefore, Zhào Zhì in "Yǔ Jī Màoqí Shū" said:
"Lǐ Lǎo entered Qín,"
and at the pass, he sighed.
It also mentions in "Yǔ Jī Shūyè Shū" about the place of observing Qi by Yǐn at the pass,
with conflicting accounts,
and hasn't been conclusively determined.
In the 4th year of Yuán Dǐng under Hàn Wǔdì,
the pass was relocated to Xīn'ān County,
and the old pass became the administrative site for Hóngnóng County and Prefecture.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yòuduì.
Liú Huángōng became the prefect,
and tigers followed him across the river,
leading Guāngwǔ to praise him upon inquiry.
The city's waters flow north beside the river,
discharging into the river.
The river there
has the name Dòu Jīn.
Commentators all claim
that Hàn Wǔ traveled incognito to Bǎigǔ,
encountering disrespect at Dòumén,
and was deeply moved by his wife's profound recognition of gifts,
he returned the jade stairs,
generously rewarding,
granting a ferry,
allowing them to sell ferry passages,
this is now Dòu Jīn.
Therefore, Pān Yuè noted in the "Xīzhēng Fù":
"The wife's recompense was too excessive,
thus her husband's improper official position,
followers like Yuán Bào,
all regarded it likewise.
I note on the southern shore of the river,
there are ferry crossings by the water banks,
called Dòu Jīn.
In the county of Héběi, there is Dòu Shuǐ,
flowing south into the river,
hence the river has the name Dòu Jīn,
not started from Mén,
with similar names due to the nature of the matter,
hence authors were confused by it.
"Zhú Shū Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" records:
"The Emperor from Tiánlíng,
then camped at the sunny side of Dòu Shuǐ,
on the day Dīnghài,
entered Nánzhèng.
Examining the paths it passed through,
the route directly crossed this ferry,
thus developing this infers,
that it wasn't because of Mén,
it is commonly known as Yǎnxiāng Jiàn Shuǐ.
The river flows east again,
joining with a left-side water,
this water has two sources diverged and drawn,
both directing towards Bó Mountain.
Flowing south, they join into one river.
Within these two waters,
it's known as Xián Yuán,
referring to the land disputed between Yú and Ruì,
its details remain unexplored.
Then flowing south into the river.
On the river's right,
Cáo Shuǐ flows into it,
the water springs from Nán Shān,
flows north past Zāo Yángtíng west,
where Chén Shè sent Zhōu Zhāng into Qín,
and Shaofu Zhāng Hán was beheaded here.
Wèi believes this was Hàoyáng.
"Jìnshū Dì Dào Jì" says:
The pavilion is thirteen lǐ east of Hóngnóng County.
Its water flows northwest,
entering the river.
Further east, the river joins Zāi Shuǐ,
the water springs from Chángzhēng Mountain,
flowing northwest past south of Qūwò City,
then winding past the city westwards,
flowing northwest into the river.
Those who described it,
all remarked Qūwò is in the north,
which isn't the case.
Wèi's Sītú Cuī Hào,
believed it was the name of a place in Qūwò.
I verify in the "Chūnqiū" fourteen years of Wén Gōng,
Jìn Hóu appointed Zhān Jiā to guard the Taolin barrier,
stationed there to defend against Qin,
thus it was guarded with offices from Qūwò,
therefore, the name Qūwò
has been handed down through ancient history.
Continuing east, the river reaches Qīlǐ Jiàn,
which is seven lǐ west of Shǎn City.
Hence it was named accordingly.
Its water flows from Nán Shān into the river,
also called Cáoyáng Kuò.
Thus Pān Yuè's "Xīzhēng Fù" states:
"Traveling at the Màn Dú's mouth,
resting at Cáoyáng's market."
Yuán Bào and Cuī Hào also don't refute this location.
I note in the "Hànshū,"
during the time of Xiàn Dì’s eastern move,
compelled by bandit disruptions,
Lǐ Jué and Guō Sī pursued and battled in Hóngnóng Valley,
the emperor then camped in Cáoyáng,
with Yáng Fèng and Dǒng Chéng,
pretending to negotiate outside with Jué,
while inside they allied with Bái Bō and Lǐ Lè to defeat Jué,
the imperial carriage could advance,
fought again,
Fèng and others suffered a great defeat,
with troops arrayed
spanning over forty lǐ before reaching Shǎn.
From this, it seems not to be Cáoyáng.
Yet, if sought in the "Shānhǎi Jīng,"
Zāi and Cáo characters are similar,
this might indicate a place named Cáoyáng.
Continuing east, the river joins with Xiāo Shuǐ,
sourcing from Chángzhēng Mountain,
commonly called Gān Mountain,
possibly a previous or alternate name.
The mountain is eighty lǐ south of Shǎn City,
with two streams as twin leads,
flowing together into a ravine,
and northward and westward into the river.
Further east, passing north of Shǎn County.
The Tuó River originates from Tuó Mountain,
flowing northwest.
Additionally, there is the Yá River that originates from the northern valley of the southern mountain,
passing through the Yá Gorge,
flowing north to converge with the waters of Gān Mountain.
This water originates from the eastern valley of Gān Mountain,
and the two streams merge and flow into the Yá River.
It then flows northeast to join the Tuó River,
and the Tuó River flows north out of the valley,
referred to as Mànjiàn.
It merges with the Ānyáng Creek,
which originates from south of Shíxiáo,
flowing west past the south of Ānyáng city,
where Emperor Hàn Zhāo, bestowed the title of marquis on Shàngguān Jié.
Pān Yuè referred to it as "I followed to Ānyáng."
It merges east with the Mànjiàn water,
where north of the water lies a traveler's pavilion,
known as the Mànkǒu Guesthouse.
It flows west past the old city of Shǎn County to the south,
then merges with another river,
known as the Dúgǔ River,
originating south from the nearby stream,
flowing north to join the Tuó.
The Tuó River then flows northwest past the west of Shǎn City,
entering the Yellow River to the northwest.
North of the river faces Máo City,
which used to be Máo Pavilion,
the settlement of the Máo Rong people.
The "Gōngyáng" states:
"Jìn defeated it at Dàyáng."
The name of the ford is also derived from this.
In the third year of Duke Wén of Spring and Autumn Annals,
Duke of Qín attacked Jìn,
crossing from Máo Ford,
and returned after burying the bodies at Xiáo.
To the east, the Xiányáng Jiàn River flows into it,
originating from the south of Běiyú Mountain,
flowing to Shǎn Ford into the Yellow River,
south of the river is Shǎn City.
In the past, Zhōu and Zhào divided vassal states,
using this city to separate east and west,
the eastern city is Upper Yáng of Guóyì,
where Guó Zhòng established his capital,
becoming Southern Guó,
the three Guó,
this being one.
Inside its large city is a smaller city,
once the state of Jiāo.
King Wǔ bestowed it upon the descendants of Shénnóng here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huángméi.
Dài Yánzhī said:
"The southern city leans against the mountain plain,
facing the Yellow River to the north,
with cliffs over a hundred rèn high,
those standing on the edge are filled with awe.
Northwest it borders the river,
where water surges for several tens of zhàng,
something resides in the water,
the elders say,
it is where the copper Wēng Zhòng sank.
It is also said,
the stone tiger carried a classic here and sank,
the two objects existed together,
causing the water to surge,
but the details are unknown.
Some say:
"Wēng Zhòng's headbun often appears,
rising and falling with the water level,
always even with the water;
when the Jìn army was about to arrive,
the bun did not reappear,
only the strange water is seen now,
its sound resonating,
heard for several miles.
In the twenty-sixth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
twelve colossal Dí people appeared at Líntáo,
each over five zhàng tall,
considered a good omen,
twelve golden men were cast to resemble them,
each weighing two hundred forty thousand jīn,
placed before the palace gate,
known as "Golden Dí".
They were inscribed on their chests, stating:
"In the twenty-sixth year of the Emperor,
unifying the world for the first time,
creating counties,
establishing laws,
standardizing measures,
great people came to see at Líntáo,
each five zhàng in height,
feet six chǐ,
written by Lǐ Sī.
Therefore, Wèi Héng's "Xù Zhuàn" states:
"Qín's Lǐ Sī,
was renowned for his zhuàn script,
and writings on mountain stelae and bronze inscriptions,
all by him.
The Hàn moved them from Āpáng to the wilderness in front of the palace,
commonly called "Wēng Zhòng".
In the second year of Dìhuáng,
Wáng Mǎng dreamt of a crying copper man,
detested it,
remembering that the copper man had inscriptions mentioning the emperor's initial unification of the world,
ordered artisans from Shàngfāng to erase the dream-related inscription on the copper man's chest.
Later, Dǒng Zhuó destroyed nine of them to make money.
Of those remaining, three,
Wèi Míngdì wanted to move them to Luòyáng,
but they were too heavy to carry,
stopping west of Bàshuǐ.
"Han Jin Chunqiu" says:
some say the "Gold Dí" wept,
so it was abandoned there,
Shí Hǔ took and placed it in Yè Palace,
then Fú Jiān moved it to Cháng'ān,
destroyed two to make money,
one never arrived as Fú Jiān was overthrown,
the people pushed it to shun the north of Huáng Hé,
whereupon the "Gold Dí" vanished.
I believe that such a grand river as Hóng Hé,
should not be obstructed by slight interruptions in its rapids;
and in the vast Lang of Zhǎngjīn,
minor objects should not impede its flow.
The roaring of these waters,
as recounted in "Historical Records," stated that in the twenty-sixth year of Wèi Wénhóu,
Guó Mountain collapsed,
blocking the river, causing it.
When Xiàn Dì moved east,
crossing by night and day,
falling into pits, competing for boats,
boats were within reach,
it was in this place as well.
Further east, it passes south of Dàyáng County.
The Jiaojian River originates from Wú Shān,
flowing southeast into the Hé River,
and the Hé River continues east.
The Lujian River also originates from Wú Shān,
flowing east past the west of Dàyáng City,
then southwest into the Hé River.
The Hé River continues east past the old city of Dàyáng County.
The *Bamboo Annals* records:
In the nineteenth year of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Duke Xiàn allied with the army of Yú to attack Guó,
destroying Xiàyáng;
Duke Chǒu of Guó fled to Wèi,
and Duke Xiàn ordered Xiàfù and Lǚshēng to settle in the capital of Guó.
The *Geographical Records* states:
This was Northern Guó,
where there was a temple to the Son of Heaven,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Qíntián.
Yìng Shào’s *Records of Geography and Customs* says:
The city lies to the north of the Great River.
The Hé River continues east,
and the Shājiàn River flows into it,
which originates from Yú Shān to the north,
flowing southeast past Fùyán,
passing in front of the hermitage of Fù Yuè,
commonly known as the Sage’s Cave.
Kǒng Ānguó’s *Commentary* states:
Fù Yuè lived in seclusion between Yú and Guó.
This is the very place.
About ten *lǐ* northeast of Fùyán,
is Diānlíng Slope.
This is the Diānlíng mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn* as the entry point.
There are eastern and western steep ravines,
with deep, hollow cliffs on both sides,
and a road built through the valley,
guiding the north-south route,
called the Líng Bridge.
Fù Yuè, while laboring in seclusion,
rested here,
and it was here that Emperor Gāozōng sought him in a dream and found him.
Northeast of the bridge is Yúyuán,
and east of the road on the plateau is Yú City,
where Yáo married Shùn to his daughter, who came to Yú.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Yú Zhòng, a descendant of Tàibó, here,
making him Duke of Yú.
This is the Northern Yú mentioned in the *Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Records*.
East of the city is a mountain,
commonly called the Wǔjiā Tomb,
atop which is the Temple of Duke Yú.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Gǔliángzhuàn* record:
When Duke Xiàn of Jìn was about to attack Guó,
Xún Xī said:
“Why does my lord not use the steeds of Qūchǎn
and the jade of Chuíjí
to borrow a path through Yú?”
The duke said:
“These are treasures of the state of Jìn.”
Xún Xī replied:
“This is merely moving them from the inner treasury to the outer treasury.”
The duke agreed,
and after conquering Guó and destroying Yú,
he led back the horses and retrieved the jade.
The jade remained as before,
but the horses’ teeth had grown longer.
This is what Gōng Zhīqí meant when he said that Yú and Guó were like the cheekbone and the jawbone depending on each other,
and that if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.
Once Guó perished,
Yú would perish as well.
The city faces a long slope about twenty *lǐ* to the north,
called Yú Slope.
Dài Yánzhī said:
“From top to bottom,
seven mountains lie stacked.”
The *Strategies of the Warring States* records:
“Once, a fine steed pulled a salt cart up Yú Slope,
struggling and straining under the yoke, unable to advance.
This was likely the place of its hardship.”
Northeast of the bridge, in the mountain stream,
a small stream flows southwest into the Shājiàn River,
meandering past the east of Dàyáng City,
which is the seat of Héběi Commandery.
The Shājiàn River flows south into the Hé River.
The Hé River continues east,
joining on the left with the Jīshí and Tǔzhù streams.
Both originate from Dàyáng Mountain to the north,
flowing south into the Hé River.
This mountain
is also commonly called Bó Shān.
Thus, the *Travels of King Mù* states:
“The Son of Heaven departed from Gǔ,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
ascended south to Bó Shān at the Diānlíng Pass,
and then lodged in Yú.”
Further east, it passes between the Dǐzhù rocks.
Dǐzhù is the name of a mountain.
In ancient times, when Yǔ was controlling the great flood,
he cut through mountains that blocked the water's path,
thus breaking open the mountains to allow the river to flow through.
The river water divided and flowed around the mountain,
and the mountain appeared in the water like a pillar,
hence it was called Dǐzhù (Pillar).
After three channels were cut through,
the water flowed in separate streams,
and based on its appearance, it was also called Sānmén (Three Gates).
The mountain is located northeast of Guóchéng and east of Dàyángchéng.
The Sōushénjì records that Duke Jǐng of Qí was crossing the Jiāng and Shěnzhī River,
when a giant turtle seized the left trace-horse,
dragging it under,
and everyone was terrified.
Gǔ Yězǐ then drew his sword and pursued it,
moving diagonally for five lǐ,
then upstream for three lǐ,
until he reached the base of Dǐzhù.
It was the giant turtle;
he held the turtle's head in his left hand,
and with his right hand, he grasped the left trace-horse,
leaping out like a soaring swallow or a soaring swan,
shouting up to the sky,
causing the water to flow backward for three hundred paces.
The onlookers all thought he was the River Earl.
Some versions also use the characters "Jiāng" or "Yuán."
If the name were based on the location,
then it should be in Shǔ or Chángshā.
According to the Chūnqiū,
these two regions were places Duke Jǐng never reached,
and Gǔ Yězǐ would have had no opportunity to display his bravery there.
Liú Xiàng, in his preface to the Yànzǐ Chūnqiū,
quotes Gǔ Yězǐ as saying:
"I once crossed the Hé River,
and a giant turtle seized the left trace-horse, dragging it into the flow at Dǐzhù.
At that time,
I pursued and killed it,
and upon looking, it was indeed a giant turtle."
He does not mention the Jiāng or Yuán rivers.
Furthermore, examining the Shǐqiān Jì, it states:
"In the twelfth year of Duke Jǐng's reign,
he visited Duke Píng of Jìn;
in the eighteenth year,
he visited Duke Zhāo of Jìn."
The route taken by his carriage would have passed directly by this ford.
The incident with the giant turtle at Dǐzhù likely occurred here.
It also says:
"The onlookers thought he was the River Earl,"
which is stronger evidence than the Jiāng or Yuán versions.
The River Earl is not a river god of the Jiāng,
so it is clear it refers to the Hé River.
To the right of the Hé River,
the Xiáo River flows into it.
The river originates from Pánxiáo Mountain in Hénán,
flowing northwest.
There is a bridge over the river,
commonly known as the Yā Bridge.
It passes through a ravine and flows northeast,
merging with the Shíxiáo River.
The Shíxiáo River originates from Shíxiáo Mountain,
which has two ridges:
the southern ridge is the tomb of Xiàhòu Gāo;
the northern ridge is where King Wén took shelter from wind and rain.
It is said that the mountain paths are winding and deep,
with peaks and hills providing overlapping shade,
making it suitable for sheltering from wind and rain.
When the Qín general was about to attack Zhèng,
Jiǎn Shū offered advice, but the duke dismissed it.
Jiǎn Shū wept and said to his son:
"I will see them depart,
but I will not see them return.
The Jìn people will surely ambush the army at Xiáo,
and I will collect your bones there."
Mèng Míng indeed met defeat here with the Qín army.
The Xiáo River continues north,
merging with the Xī River on the left,
and their combined flow empties into the Hé River.
The Hé River then flows east,
and the Qiānxiáo River flows into it.
The river originates from Qiānxiáo Mountain in the south,
flowing north,
winding through two paths.
During the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
Cáo Gōng campaigned westward against Bā and Hàn,
and disliking the danger of the southern route,
he opened a northern route instead.
Since then, most travelers have taken this route.
Now, beside the mountain along the road, there is a stone inscription that reads:
"In the third year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty,
Liáng Liǔ, the Tàishǒu of Hóngnóng, repaired the old road."
East of Tàixiáo and west of Xīxiáo,
it is clear that there is not just one Xiáo.
To the west, there are two stones,
and fifty paces further south,
beside the stream, there is the Yìshén Bēi of Tiánmò Xiānshēng,
who likely lived in seclusion in this mountain.
The river flows north and empties into the Hé River.
The Hé River flows between banks flanked by mountains,
with towering peaks rising high,
layers of mountains displaying their beauty,
and ridges piled upon ridges reaching the sky.
Zhèng Xuán, according to the Dì Shuō,
stated that the Hé River flows east,
passes through Dǐzhù,
and meets the Èliú.
What is now called Dǐzhù
is likely the Èliú.
Dǐzhù should be in Xīhé,
but this is not certain.
In my opinion,
Zhèng Xuán's explanation is incorrect;
there is no mountain in Xīhé that resembles it.
From Dǐzhù downstream,
above Wǔhù,
over a distance of one hundred twenty lǐ,
towering rocks rise prominently in the river,
their formations connecting to the high land.
This was likely also cut by Yǔ to allow the river to flow through,
and I suspect this is the Èliú.
Although the mountain was cut open,
it still obstructs the rushing flow,
stirring up clouds of swirling water against the rocks,
with turbulent waves angrily overflowing.
There are nineteen rapids in total,
where the water flows swiftly and fiercely,
comparable to the Three Gorges,
damaging boats and ships,
a peril since ancient times.
In the fourth year of Hóngjiā of the Hàn dynasty,
Yáng Yān proposed that from upstream on the Hé River,
the narrowness of Dǐzhù was problematic
and could be widened by carving.
The emperor then ordered Yáng Yān to carve it,
but the rocks merely sank into the water,
unable to be removed,
and instead made the water even more turbulent and fierce,
causing more harm than before.
In the second year of Jǐngchū of the Wèi dynasty, in the second month,
the emperor dispatched the Dūdū of Shāqiūbù and the Jiānyùn Jiànyì Dàfū Kǒu Cí,
leading five thousand workers,
to carry out annual repairs
to calm the river's obstacles.
In the third year of Tàishǐ of the Jìn dynasty, in the first month,
Emperor Wǔ dispatched the Jiānyùn Dàzhōng Dàfū of Zhàoguó, Dūjiàng Zhōngláng Nàihé Dōnglè Shì,
leading over five thousand men,
to repair the river rapids,
as recorded in the Wǔhù Cí Míng.
Although efforts were made across generations,
the water remained torrential and turbulent,
with waves still piling up.
When merchant boats anchored here,
few could avoid hesitation and difficulty in crossing,
hence the saying about the many gorges and rapids.
Wǔhù is the name of a rapid,
with a spirit shrine,
commonly called General Wǔhù,
though the reason for this name is unknown.
Further east, it passes north of Píngyīn County,
and the Qīngshuǐ River flows from the northwest to join it.
The Qīngshuǐ River originates from the western ridge of the Qīnglián Mountain,
also known as Qīngyíng Mountain.
Its waters flow southeast,
exiting the gorge,
where there is a city on the left of the gorge,
which served as an ancient checkpoint.
The Qīngshuǐ River passes by to its south,
flowing east past the north of Gāoluò City.
Fú Qián said:
"It was the capital of the Chì Dí."
People call it Yǐbó City,
due to a similar sound in pronunciation,
thus losing its true form.
This is what the "Spring and Autumn Annals" refers to when it mentions the Jìn Marquis sending Crown Prince Shēnshēng to attack the Eastern Mountain Gāoluò Clan.
It converges with the Yǐbóchuan River,
whose waters originate in Kuàng Valley of the northern mountains,
and flows southeast to merge with the Qīng.
The Qīngshuǐ continues east past south of Qīnglián City,
then flows southeast,
joining with the Nánxī River on the right,
whose waters originate from the southern mountains and flow east into the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then continues east to merge with the Qiánzǎojiàn River,
whose waters issue from beneath the Shírén Ridge,
flow south,
commonly known as Fúsū River,
then travel south past Jiànmiáo north of Mǎtóushān,
also called Bái Shuǐyuán,
southwest past north of the old city of Yuánxiàn.
"Records of the Grand Historian" states,
"In the second year of Marquis Wǔ of Wèi, Yì City was built extending to Yuán."
This refers to the county.
Its waters flow southwest,
merging with the Qīngshuǐ.
The water appears white and turbid,
upon meeting the clear current,
showing a contrast of dark and bright colors.
Qīngshuǐ then flows southeast past east of Yánghu City,
which is the Wūbīng Pavilion in Yuán County.
It was the residence of five great ministers of Jìn migrating to Sòng.
The Qīngshuǐ continues southeast, merging into the river.
The river then flows east to merge with Jiào River,
whose waters originate from Jiào Mountain north of Yuán County,
flowing south past Fǔ Mountain.
The mountain is about thirty lǐ high,
with a spring source on top,
of unfathomable depth,
and a circumference of five to six lǐ at the summit,
with little vegetation.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"Southeast of Mèngmén lies Píng Mountain,
from where the water emerges,
disappearing underground.
It is next to Wángwū,
presumed to be Píng Mountain."
Its waters flow south,
traversing Gǔzhōng Upper Gorge,
with a five-zhàng cascade,
pouring into the valley below,
with steep cliffs rising vertically against the banks,
with graceful edges towering beautifully,
over one hundred zhàng tall,
followed by green pines on the peaks,
red stones hanging from cliffs,
with verdant cypresses growing within them,
separated into red, green, and brocade sections,
appearing like a painting from afar.
The water broadens over ten steps,
flowing south through Gǔzhōng Valley,
splitting into two ravines:
one ravine exits to the northwest,
about one hundred and sixty lǐ,
meandering through mountain passes,
barely traversable by horses,
with remnants of dry riverbeds still at the northeastern valley entrance of Wénxǐ County,
yet containing no water today.
Another water course flows past Yěguān westward,
known as Gǔzhōng City,
where relics of copper and coins remain scattered here.
A great spring beneath a mound west of the city,
flows west into the ravine,
converging with Jiào water,
submerging beneath stones,
traveling south to the lower gorge.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"Gǔzhōng's mountain was used by the Celestial Emperor's platform to host all spirits."
That is this mountain.
Its waters restart from another source,
heading south until it reaches lower Ma Tóu Mountain east of Jié Pō,
submerging and flowing south over ten lǐ,
resurfacing,
known as the submerging flow,
then entering the river south.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"Jiào Mountain,
from which Jiào River emerges,
flows south into the river."
In winter, these waters dry up; in summer, they flow,
indeed known as Dry River by locals,
now commonly referred to as Dry Ravine.
The river then merges with Zhěn Water.
This water emerges from Qīngyào Mountain in Xīn'ān County,
known as Jiāng Mountain today,
flowing north into the river.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" records:
"Qīngyào's Mountain,
from where Zhěn Water emerges,"
that is this water.
The river continues east,
receiving Zhènghuí River,
whose waters come from Guī Mountain,
east of Jiāng Mountain.
Flowing east,
it is commonly known as Jiāngchuān River,
merging with Shíguāchóu River,
whose waters emerge from the northwest among stone streams,
flowing southeast to merge into Jiāngchuān River.
Jiāngchuān River continues east past Jiāng Yěguān eastward,
flowing northeast into the river.
The river further incorporates Yōngyōng Water,
originating from Yísū Mountain in Hé Dōng Yuánxiàn,
commonly called the Long Spring Water.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"Water abounds with yellow shells;
this is the source of Yīluò."
Its waters flow north,
dividing into two,
one entering the river northward,
another flowing northeast into the river.
The river continues east past north of Píngyīn County.
"Geographical Custom Records" claims:
"The county of Hénán Píngyīn,
former land of Jǐnyīn,
was an area inhabited by Yīn Róng."
It adds:
"Located south of Píngchéng,
hence called Píngyīn,
the abode where Elder Dǒng instructed Gāozǔ,
also where Lù Jī refers to as old man Dǒng,
whom I plan my Píngyīn with."
Emperor Wén of Wèi renamed it Héyīn.
The river meets Qíshuǐ.
This water originates from Wángwū Mountain in Yuán County Qísī Valley,
flowing southeast between mountains,
passing the old city eastward,
identified as Qíguān.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ of Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Sīkōng Wáng Liáng was sent north to defend Qíguān, Tiānjǐngguān,
striking the Chìméi separate division,
making all concede.
Emperor Xiàn crossed north from Shǎn to Ànyì,
exiting east at Qíguān,
indicating this pass.
Qíshuǐ turns westward,
passing south of the checkpoint city,
through Zhǐguān south,
past Miáopavilion westward.
The pavilion,
a former Miáoyì of Zhōu,
flows east into the river.
The "Records" document Qīngshuǐ incorrectly.
It is actually Qíshuǐ.
Continuing east arrives at Dèng.
Forty-two lǐ northwest of Luòyáng,
formerly Dèng Town.
5 Annotated Water Classic, Volume Five
5.1 The River Water
5.1 The River Water
flows east again past north of Píng County,
where Zhànshuǐ water comes from Wèi to merge with it.
The river flows east past the old city of Héyáng County.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records: "The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng."
On the rénshēn day,
the Duke had an audience with the king at his temporary residence.
The Marquis of Jìn captured the Marquis of Wèi and took him back to the capital.
In the 28th year of Duke Xī of the Zuǒzhuàn,
in winter,
a meeting was held at Wēn,
and the Marquis of Wèi was captured.
At this meeting,
the Marquis of Jìn summoned King Xiāng to meet with the feudal lords,
and had the king go hunting.
Zhòngní said:
"For a minister to summon his sovereign
cannot serve as a model."
Therefore, the Classic records: "The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng,"
indicating it was not his proper hunting ground.
Fú Qián and Jiǎ Kuí said:
"Héyáng
is Wēn."
Bān Gù's "Treatise on Geography" from the Book of Hàn,
Sīmǎ Biāo and Yuán Shānsōng's "Treatise on Commanderies and States,"
the "Records of the Regions" from the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
and the "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" all state:
"Héyáng is a separate county,
not the town of Wēn."
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Chén Juān was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and it was called Hétíng under Wáng Mǎng.
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" says:
"Its administration is on the river,
the river
being the Mèngjīn River."
Guō Yuánshēng's "Record of Campaigns" says:
"Jiàntǔ
is now Yěbǎn City."
This name differs from that in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
but it is incorrect.
What is seen north of the river today
is the old county seat of Héyáng City,
located northwest of Yěbǎn.
It was likely part of the territory of Wēn in Jìn times,
hence many scholars have debated its connection to Wēn.
The "Records of Wèi Lands" says:
"Yěbǎn City was formerly called Hànzǔ Crossing.
The city is strategically fortified,
facing the Mèngjīn River to the south."
The river flows right past north of Línpíng Pavilion.
The "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ was buried south of Línpíng Pavilion,
overlooking Píngyīn to the west."
The river then flows east past north of Luòyáng County.
On the southern bank of the river stands a stele,
inscribed on the north face:
"Northern boundary of Luòyáng.
The river's two islets
are divided and belong here."
Above, there was formerly a shrine to the Marquis of Hépíng,
with a stele in front of the shrine,
but its current location is unknown.
Guō Bān's "Tales of the Ages" says:
"During the time of King Wén of Jìn,
a giant fish appeared at Mèngjīn,
hundreds of paces long,
five zhàng tall,
its head at the southern bank,
its tail at the central islet.
The shrine to the Marquis of Hépíng is this very shrine."
The river then flows east past north of the old city of Píng County.
In the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Suì, son of the Prince of Jìběi, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It was called Zhìpíng under Wáng Mǎng,
commonly known as Xiǎopíng.
There is Gāozǔ's military training ground.
On the northern bank, two cities face each other,
housing the Northern Central Guard Command,
where convict laborers and garrison households were relocated,
and guarded by Yǔlín and Hǔbēn troops under command.
South of the river faces Shǒuyáng Mountain,
referred to as Shǒudài in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
This is why the "Song of Bóyí and Shūqí" says: "I climb that western mountain."
On the mountain stands a temple to Bóyí and Shūqí,
with two steles in front.
Both were erected by Chén Dǎo, Governor of Hénán in the Later Hàn, Xú Xún, Magistrate of Luòyáng, along with the recluses Sū Téng of Píngyuán and Hé Jìn of Nányáng,
as recorded on the steles.
There is also a temple to the Duke of Zhōu.
The Wèi dynasty built the Xuánwǔ Observatory at Mángchuí.
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Rhapsody on the Xuánwǔ Observatory" describes it as a towering structure,
soaring high and steep,
standing alone and upright,
catching the clear breeze from a thousand lǐ away.
The court also established an icehouse on this mound,
with an ice well inside.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"When the sun is in the northern constellation, ice is stored."
Often in the twelfth month,
ice was collected from narrow passes along the river,
from the bends of gorges and rocks,
in the northern shadows,
as described in the Bīn Odes: "In the second month,
they chisel ice with a chōng-chōng sound."
It was then placed in the well chamber,
which is "stored in the icehouse."
South of the river is Gōuchén Fort,
traditionally said to be where King Wǔ, attacking King Zhòu,
met with eight hundred feudal lords.
This is what the Book of Documents means by "unplanned yet simultaneous."
The Purple Forbidden constellation has the Gōuchén star as its host,
governing disputes and military formations.
Thus, in Dùnjiǎ tactics for attack,
the method involves aligning the attacking deity
with the energy of Gōuchén descending to control
the celestial hour it oversees,
ensuring victory over the enemy.
Hence, the fort derives its name from this.
At this point on the river,
it is called Méngjīn.
The Lùnhéng says:
"When King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
boarding a boat,
Yánghóu stirred the waves,
with fierce winds against the current.
King Wǔ brandished a yellow battle-axe and commanded them,
and the wind and waves ceased.
Midstream,
a white fish entered the boat,
which was roasted as an offering to Heaven,
and he made a covenant with the eight hundred feudal lords."
This is what the Book of Documents means by "unplanned yet speaking in unison."
Thus, it is called Mèngjīn,
also Méngjīn.
This is what the Book of Documents means by "eastward to Mèngjīn."
It is also called Fùpíngjīn.
The Jìnyángqiū says:
"Dù Yù built a bridge over the river at Fùpíngjīn."
This is "constructing boats to form a bridge."
It is also called Táohé.
Dù Jī, Imperial Secretary of Wèi,
when the emperor was about to visit Xǔ,
tested a tower ship,
which capsized at Táohé,
referring to this place.
In ancient times, when Yǔ controlled the floods,
he observed the river and saw a tall figure with a white face and fish body emerge, saying:
"I am the essence of the river."
He gave Yǔ the "River Chart" and returned to the depths.
Later, when Zǐ Cháo usurped the throne
and fought against King Jìng,
he took Zhōu's precious jades
and sank them in the river to pray for blessings.
Two days later,
a ferryman found them on the riverbank.
When about to sell them,
they turned to stone.
After King Jìng's position was secured,
the finder presented them,
and they became jade again.
The river flows further east,
where the Jú River joins it.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"Hé Mountain,
with no grass or trees on top,
but abundant yáo and bì jade,
is truly the ninefold confluence of the river.
This mountain
has five bends,
and nine waters flow from it,
converging and flowing north,
entering the river.
Its southern side has much dark jade,
guarded by the auspicious spirit Tàiféng,
who resides south of Fù Mountain,
emitting light when coming and going."
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi says:
"Kǒng Jiǎ of the Xià dynasty
hunted at Fù Mountain in Dōngyáng,
encountered a great storm,
became lost,
and entered a commoner's house."
Huángfǔ Mì's "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" identifies this as the eastern Shǒuyáng Mountain,
likely a different name for the same mountain.
Now, east of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
there is no water corresponding to this,
likely due to the vast gap between ancient and modern times,
and changes in river courses and terrain.
In ancient times, Emperor Yáo built an altar by the river and Luò,
selected auspicious moments for sacrifices,
and led Shùn and others up Shǒu Mountain,
following the river islets,
where five elders roamed.
They said to each other:
"The River Chart will come to inform the emperor.
He who knows us
is the double-pupiled one."
The five elders then transformed into shooting stars and ascended to the Pleiades,
which happened here.
Further east,
the Jì River flows into it.
Further east, it passes north of Gǒng County.
Here, the Yellow River has the Wǔshè Crossing,
which is the Wǔshè Ford.
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Zhū Wěi dispatched the imperial envoy Jiǎ Qiáng and the General for Suppressing Difficulties Sū Mào,
leading thirty thousand men,
to cross from the Wǔshè Ford,
and attack Wēn.
Féng Yì dispatched a colonel to join forces with Kòu Xún in attacking them,
inflicting a major defeat,
pursuing them to the riverbank,
capturing over ten thousand alive,
with several thousand drowning in the river.
North of the county, there is a mountain overlooking the river,
called Yínyuán Hill.
Below it is a cave,
called the Gǒng Cave,
said to connect underground to Huáipǔ,
reaching north to the Yellow River.
Directly by the cave is an islet,
called Wěi Islet.
Chéng Gōngzǐ'ān's "Rhapsody on the Great River" says:
"The sturgeons and king sturgeons,
come to roam in late spring."
The "Rites of Zhōu" states,
"In spring, offer sturgeon."
However, they are not present out of season or in other places.
Thus, the river above the Sturgeon Cave
also bears the name "Sturgeon."
The "Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ" states that King Wǔ, on his campaign against Zhòu, reached the Sturgeon River,
where Zhòu sent Jiāo Gé to await the Zhōu army—
this is the very place.
The Luò River flows from the northwest of the county and joins it.
The Luò River, at Gǒng County,
flows east past Luòruì,
facing north toward Lángyá Islet,
and enters the Yellow River,
which is called the Luò Estuary.
Coming from west of the county,
it flows north and joins the Yellow River,
clear and turbid waters flowing separately,
distinct and sharply divided.
Yìng Chàng's "Rhapsody on the Divine River" says:
"Drawing from the distant source of the divine river,
emerging from the divine hills of Kūnlún,
traversing the slopes and springs of Jīn and Luò,
spreading nine courses across the Central Plain."
Further east, it passes north of Chénggāo County,
where the Jì River flows from the north and joins it.
The Yellow River flows east from the Luòkǒu,
passes left by the south of Pínggāo County,
then east by the south of Huái County,
where the old course of the Jì River entered,
dividing the river with Chénggāo.
The river flows right by the north of Huángmǎ Bǎn,
which is called Huángmǎ Pass.
This is where Sūn Dēng departed,
and Yáng Jùn wrote a letter to an old friend in Luòyáng.
The river flows east again by the north of Xuánmén Bǎn,
which is the great slope west of present-day Chénggāo.
Ascending this slope,
one heads east toward Chénggāo.
Cáo Dàjiā’s "Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition" says:
"Gazing upon the confluence of the Hé and Luò,
viewing the Xuánmén of Chénggāo."
The river flows east again by the Dàpī Mountain of Chénggāo.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"A mountain of one layer is called pī."
Xǔ Shèn, Lǚ Chén, and others
all considered it a mound of one layer.
Kǒng Ānguó considered a two-layered mound as pī,
and some also took it as a place name,
but this is incorrect.
The "Yǔgòng" chapter of the *Shàngshū* says:
"Passing the confluence of the Luò,
reaching Dàpī."
Zhèng Kāngchéng said:
"It is the throat of the land,
from which the Yǎn emerges at the pī’s edge."
It lies on the border between Xiūwǔ and Wǔdé in Hénèi,
where the waters of the Jì and Yǎn enter and exit the Yíngbō Marsh.
Thus, Dàpī is indeed this mountain.
North of Pī,
is what the *Classic* refers to as the Jì River coming from the north to join it.
Now the Jì River enters the Yellow River from Wēn County,
not here.
What enters here
is merely the Fènggōu River,
which is the old course of the Jì and Yǎn.
The old city of Chénggāo County is atop Pī,
winding around the Pī mound,
with steep cliffs,
about forty zhàng high.
The city expands and contracts with the perilous terrain,
rugged and uneven.
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Zhì
is a fortified city,
where Guó Shū died,"
which is Eastern Guó.
In the seventh month of the second year of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ,
Duke Chéng of Jìn met with the feudal lords at Qī,
then fortified Hǔláo to pressure Zhèng into seeking peace.
This was likely repairing the old fortifications.
The *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn* says:
"The Son of Heaven hunted birds and beasts in Zhèng’s park,
ordering the foresters to clear the woods.
A tiger was among the reeds;
as the Son of Heaven approached,
the warrior Gāo Bēnróng of the Seven Elite Guards captured it alive and presented it to the Son of Heaven.
He ordered it caged and kept in Eastern Guó,
hence the name Hǔláo (Tiger Cage)."
Thus, the name Hǔláo
originated from this.
The Qín made it a pass,
and the Hàn established it as a county.
In the northwest corner of the city is a small fortress,
three lǐ in circumference,
with watchtowers on the north side,
towering alone overlooking the river.
During the Jǐngmíng era,
on my way to Shòuchūn,
passing by this town,
I ascended to gaze afar,
the landscape stretching over rivers and plains.
A traveler arriving on a journey,
I felt deeply moved.
South of the river faces Yùmén,
where in the past Hàn Gāozǔ and Téng Gōng secretly crossed,
fording the river at this spot.
East of the gate faces the riverbank,
where on the side there is an earthen cave.
When Wèi attacked the Northern Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Máo Dézǔ at Hǔláo,
the battle lasted two hundred days,
without success.
The city had only one well,
forty zhàng deep.
The mountain terrain was steep,
making defense difficult,
so they secretly dug a tunnel to reach the well.
I recently went there on official business,
and sought it out;
the cave site still remains.
The river flows east again to join the Sì River,
which originates south from Fúxì Mountain,
commonly called Fāng Mountain.
It flows north to join the Dōngguān River.
The Dōngguān River originates from Sōngzhǔ Mountain,
with a spring emerging from a layered mound,
splitting into two branches from one source,
flowing and pouring separately,
commonly called Shíquán Spring.
The eastern branch is the Suǒ River,
the western is the Dōngguān River.
Flowing northwest,
the Yánglán River joins it,
originating from Fēi Mountain,
flowing northwest into the Dōngguān River.
The Dōngguān River flows northwest further,
where the Qīng River enters.
The Qīng River flows west from the eastern shore,
joining the Dōngguān River,
then merging chaotically into the Sì.
The Sì River flows north again,
joining right with the Shíchéng River,
which originates from Shíchéng Mountain.
This mountain has layered ravines and ridges,
stacked steeply like a city wall.
From the mountaintop, springs flow,
waterfalls cascade down,
with overflowing springs below,
flowing east and pouring out.
Alongside are several dozen stone plots,
each with wild vegetables.
On the cliff side are several cave openings,
traces of seclusion remain,
but it is unknown who first established them.
It flows northeast further into the Sì River.
The Sì River flows north again to join the Màn River,
which originates west from Lóu Mountain.
In winter it becomes warm,
hence commonly called Wēnquán (Hot Spring).
Flowing northeast past Tiánmàn Valley,
it is called Tiánmàn Creek,
flowing east into the Sì River.
The Sì River flows north past the east of Hǔláo City,
where Hàn defeated Sīmǎ Xīn and Cáo Jiù on this river.
The Sì River flows north further into the Yellow River.
As the "Zhēngjiān Rhapsody" says: "Treading on fragrant grass at the Sì estuary,
mourning at the humble lodge of King Xiāng of Zhōu."
I note that according to earlier scholars,
King Xiāng of Zhōu resided in Xiāngchéng County of Yǐngchuān,
which is a city name,
not a water name.
The origin of the error
lies in both being named after Sì and Zhèng,
which is mistaken.
Also, according to Guō Yuánshēng’s *Shùzhēng Jì*
and Liú Chéngzhī’s *Yǒngchū Jì*,
both say Gāozǔ ascended the throne on the north bank of this river.
Now the old altar site is no longer known.
Lú Chén and Cuī Yún
also said this.
I note that Emperor Gāo received the Mandate of Heaven at the Sì River in Dìngtáo,
not here.
Thus, seeking the altar
yields no trace.
The river flows east again past the north of Bǎnchéng,
where there is a ford,
called Bǎnchéng Zhǔkǒu.
The river flows east again past the north of Wǔlóng Wù,
a fortress facing the long river,
with a Wǔlóng Shrine.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Kūnlún Mountain Temple is in Yíngyáng County, Hénán."
Perhaps this is that shrine,
though it is unclear.
Flowing east further past the north of Yíngyáng County,
the Làngdàng Canal emerges from here.
The Great Yǔ blocked the Róngzé Marsh,
opening it to connect the Huái and Sì Rivers.
This is the Làngdàng Canal mentioned in the Classic.
During the reign of Emperor Píng of the Hàn,
the Yellow River and the Biàn Canal breached and were damaged,
and before they could be repaired,
the Biàn Canal encroached eastward,
spreading wider day by day,
so that the former sites of gates and alleys
were all submerged in water.
In the twelfth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of the Hàn,
discussions were held on managing the Biàn Canal,
and the emperor summoned Wáng Jǐng, a man from Lèlàng, to inquire about the advantageous water conditions.
Jǐng presented the benefits and harms,
responding with agility,
and the emperor greatly approved of him,
bestowing upon him the Classic of Mountains and Seas, the Records of Rivers and Canals, the Tribute of Yǔ Map, along with money and silk.
Later, when constructing the embankments,
hundreds of thousands of conscripts were mobilized,
and an edict appointed Jǐng and the Palace Attendant Wáng Wú to manage the canal.
They built embankments and repaired weirs,
starting from Xíngyáng,
east to the estuary at Qiānchéng,
spanning over a thousand lǐ.
Jǐng then assessed the terrain,
cut through mountains and opened valleys,
fortified strategic points against surges,
dredged and cleared blockages,
establishing a sluice gate every ten lǐ,
allowing water to circulate and flow back,
eliminating the risk of seepage and leakage.
The following year, the canal was completed,
and the emperor personally inspected it,
issuing an edict for the commanderies and states along the river to appoint officials for river embankments,
following the old system of the Western Capital.
Jǐng thus gained fame,
and Wáng Wú along with all those involved in the work
were promoted one rank.
During the Yángjiā era of Emperor Shùn,
from east of the Biàn estuary,
stones were piled along the river,
forming a weir to connect the canal.
All called it the Golden Embankment.
During the Jiànníng era of Emperor Líng,
the stone gate was further repaired and expanded,
to block the canal entrance.
When water was abundant, it flowed through;
when the flow diminished, it ceased.
The river then flows northeast past the north of the Hù Pavilion in Juǎn,
as stated in the Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒ's Commentary:
In the seventh year of Duke Wén,
Zhào Dùn of Jìn formed an alliance with the feudal lords at Hù.
According to the Bamboo Annals,
in the twelfth year of Duke Chū of Jìn,
the Yellow River cut off at Hù,
which is precisely this place.
The river then flows east past the north of the Bājī Embankment.
In the seventh year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān of the Hàn,
the Attendant Yú Cén from Tàishān
piled stones in eight places east of the stone gate,
each like a small hill,
to withstand the surging waves,
called the Bājī Embankment.
The river then flows east past the north of Juǎn County,
where during the battle between Jìn and Chǔ,
the Jìn army fought to cross,
and fingers in the boats could be scooped up by handfuls.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ sacrificed to the river, declared victory, and returned,
which was at this very place.
The river then flows northeast past the north of Chì'àn Fort,
and turns northeastward.
Further northeast, it passes east of Wǔdé County,
where the Qìn River flows from the northwest to join it.
The river flows from Wǔdé County,
in the first year of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn's Yánkāng era,
Cáo Rùi was enfeoffed as a marquis state,
who later became the Emperor Míng of Wèi.
To the east, it reaches the west of Suānzǎo County,
where the Pū River flows east.
In the thirty-ninth year of the Hàn dynasty's rise,
during the time of Emperor Xiàowén,
the river breached at Suānzǎo,
and broke through Jīn Dī to the east,
and a large number of troops were dispatched to block it.
Therefore, Bān Gù stated:
Wén built a dam at Zǎoyě,
Wǔ composed the "Ballad of the Gourd,"
referring to blocking this mouth.
Now there is no water.
The river then flowed northeast,
and people call it Yánjīn.
When Shí Lè attacked Liú Yào,
he passed through here,
using the melting river ice as if aided by divine spirits,
and named this place Língchāngjīn.
