In the past, Dàntái Zǐyǔ carried a jade disc worth a thousand gold coins to cross the river,
the waves of Yánghóu arose,
and two dragons flanked his boat.
Zǐyǔ said:
"I can seek righteousness,
but cannot be threatened.
He wielded a sword and killed the dragons,
and when the dragons died, the waves subsided,
then he threw the jade into the river,
three times it floated back up,
so he broke the jade and left,
showing no reluctance."
During Zhào Jiàn Wǔ's time,
a pontoon bridge was built over the ford,
using stones to make a mid-river crossing.
Regardless of the size of the stones,
they drifted away immediately,
with millions of laborers involved,
but after a year, it was not completed.
Shí Hǔ personally inspected the construction work,
sank a jade into the river,
and the next day,
the jade floated back on a sandbar,
washed onto the shore by the waves,
so he executed the craftsmen and returned.
The river then flowed east past the north of the old city of Yān County,
where it was known as Jíjīn,
also called Shíjìjīn,
which was the Southern Ford.
In the twenty-eighth year of Duke Xī of the "Chūnqiū",
Jìn planned to attack Cáo,
Cáo being east of Wèi,
they requested passage through Wèi,
but the people of Wèi did not allow it,
so they crossed from the southern river,
which is this place.
Jìn attacked Lùhún,
also crossing here.
During the Sòng Yuán Jiā era,
General Xiāo Bīn was sent to assist the state,
leading General Wáng Xuánmó northwards,
while General Yuán Hùzhī guarded Shíjì with naval forces,
which was this location.
The river then flowed east,
where the Qí River enters it,
and east again past Zhēhāi Pavilion southward.
The "Hànshū: Gōuxùzhì" states:
Eighteen lǐ east of the Qí River's mouth,
there is a golden embankment,
with a height of one zhàng,
from Qí's mouth eastward,
the land gradually descends,
while the embankment gradually rises,
reaching Zhēhāi Pavilion,
rising four to five zhàng high.
Also, there is Sùxū Mouth,
where the old river water flowed northward.
The river then flows east by the right past Huátái City's northern wall,
with three layers of walls enclosing the city.
The small inner city is called Huátái City,
it is said that Huátái people themselves built this city,
naming it accordingly.
The city was formerly Zhèng Lǐnyán's city,
with an older Yánjīn below.
The "Chūnqiū Zhuàn" states:
Kǒng Kuī was exiled by Kuǎi Kuì,
he transported Bó Jī to Píngyáng,
traveling through Yánjīn, that is this place.
The old city south of Lǐnyán,
was then Wèi's Píngyáng Pavilion,
nowadays people call this ford Yánshòujīn.
During the Sòng Yuán Jiā period,
General Dào Yànzhī,
left General Zhū Xiūzhī to guard this city,
when the Wèi army invaded south,
Xiūzhī upheld his post without yielding,
his mother sorrowed and worried,
one day her milk suddenly flowed,
she cried out,
telling her family,
"I am an old cow,
it is not the time for milk,
something must have happened to my son."
Xiūzhī, cut off from supplies,
indeed, fell on that day.
The city,
used to be the administrative seat of the Eastern Prefecture.
The "Xùhànshū" states:
In the ninth year of Yánxǐ,
the waters of the Ji River in Jìyīn, Dōng Prefecture, Jìběi, and Píngyuán were clear.
Xiāngkǎi presented a memorial saying:
"The 'Chūnqiū' notes have not recorded the river water being clear,
and now it is so."
The "Yì Qián Záo Dù" states:
"When Heaven is about to descend a good omen,
the river water first becomes clear."
Jīngfáng’s "Yìzhuàn" says when the river is clear,
heaven is bright,
heaven gives omens,
earth emits monstrosities,
people suffer epidemics,
when the three occur together and the river water clears,
the unicorn in the 'Chūnqiū' was not supposed to appear but did,
and Confucius wrote it as an anomaly.
The river symbolizes the feudal lords,
the clear water is a sign of brightness and clarity,
how could it only signify the feudal lords' peeping into the capital?
The following year,
the emperor departed,
summoning Jiédúhóu as the Hàn successor,
who became Emperor Líng.
In the fourth year of Jiànníng in February,
the river's water cleared again.
The river also flows northeast past Líyáng County to the south.
Lí was a marquisate.
The poem "Shì Wēi"
in the Shījīng refers to the Marquis of Lí taking refuge in Wèi.
Jìn Zhuó said:
"Mount Lí lies to its south,
and the Yellow River flows past its east."
A stele on the mountain states:
"The county takes its name from the mountain,
and from the north side of the river,
hence its name."
It was called Lízhēng under Wáng Mǎng.
The old city northeast of present-day Mount Lí
is likely the old city of Líyáng County.
The mountain lies west of the city,
the city's foundation rests upon the mountain,
and it is bounded by the river to the east.
Therefore, Liú Zhēn's "Rhapsody on Mount Líyáng" says:
"Shaded by the Yellow River to the south,
covering Jīnchéng to the left,
green altars receive sacrifices,
tall steles praise the spirits."
In the past, Mùróng Xuānmíng led his troops from Yè south to Huátái.
Lacking boats,
he intended to secure Líyáng.
At dusk, drifting ice
froze solid overnight.
After they finished crossing,
by morning the ice had melted.
The Yàn people called this place Tiānqiáo Ford.
On the eastern bank is an old city,
strategically positioned along the long river.
Dài Yánzhī called it Lùmíng Fort,
with a circumference of twenty lǐ.
He said Lùmíng
was one of Shí Lè's eighteen cavalrymen,
and the city was named after him.
Guō Yuánshēng said:
"The city
was built during Yuán Shào's time."
Both are incorrect.
I, based on the Zhúshū Jìnián,
note: In the eleventh year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Marquis Lí of Zhèng sent Xǔ Xī to cede territory—
the towns of Píngqiū, Hùyǒu, Shǒuyuán,
and the Zhèng post road.
"We took Zhǐdào and Zhènglù."
This refers to this city.
Inside the present city is an old terrace,
still called the Lùmíng Terrace,
also known as Lùmíng City.
It was where Wáng Xuánmó fled from Huátái to Lùmíng.
The ford took its name from this,
hence also called Lùmíng Ford,
and also Báimǎ Ford.
Southeast of the ford is Báimǎ City.
When Duke Wén of Wèi moved east,
he crossed the river and made it his capital.
Therefore, the ford took its name from it.
Yuán Shào sent Yán Liáng to attack Liú Yán, Governor of Dōngjùn, at Báimǎ.
Guān Yǔ, for Lord Cáo, beheaded Liáng to repay his favor—
this was the place.
Báimǎ had the Wéi district and Wéi city,
so the ford was also called Wéi Ford.
The Shǐjì mentions "descending to Xiūwǔ,
crossing Wéi Ford."
The Yellow River formerly overflowed south of Báimǎ County, connecting to the Pú, Jì, and Huánggōu rivers.
Therefore, Sū Dài advised Yān:
"Breach the mouth of Báimǎ,
and Wèi will lose Huáng and Jìyáng."
The Zhúshū Jìnián records:
In the twelfth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
the Chǔ army diverted the Yellow River
to flood beyond Chángyuán.
After the Jīndī was built,
the old channel was cut off,
but it is still called the Báimǎ Channel.
The old channel flows east past the south of Lùmíng City,
then northeast past the north of Liángchéng in Báimǎ County.
The Qíjiù Zhuàn says:
"The Divine Horse Pavilion in Báimǎ County, Dōngjùn,
is solidly built with layered foundations,
two hundred paces north-south,
about fifty paces east-west,
resembling a hill carved into a city wall.
Outside, plowing, cultivation, and cutting
have leveled it completely.
Directly south are stepped paths leading up,
wide enough for two carriages abreast.
Southwest of the city wall is the Divine Horse Temple,
with well-tended trees.
It is about twenty lǐ west of Báimǎ Ford,
and about fifty lǐ southeast of the old city of Báimǎ County.
It is likely the Báimǎ Mountain mentioned in the Kāishān Tú.
Herds of white horses often roamed below the mountain.
When they neighed mournfully, the river would breach;
when they galloped, the mountain would collapse."
The commentary states:
"The mountain is north of Zhèng,
the old Zhèng."
The details are unclear.
Liú Chéngzhī said:
"There is a Báimǎ Pass,
which Mèng Dá ascended and sighed deeply."
This can be said to be a careless error regarding the geography.
A Liángchéng was formerly established at the pavilion,
and the county seat was located here.
The Báimǎ Channel also flows southeast past Púyáng County,
dispersing into the Pú River.
Wherever it breaches and converges,
it interconnects and flows,
forming a reciprocal cycle.
The Yellow River flows northeast from the ford past Liángchéng County.
North of the river is the Bān Shrine.
The Mèngshì Jì says:
"The shrine is in the middle of the river,
built on a piled-stone foundation.
When the river rises high,
it is always level with the water."
Dài's Xīzhēng Jì says:
"Now the shrine is seen on the eastern bank,
with stones piled against the river to form walls.
Its buildings are just large enough for a person.
It seems utterly devoid of spiritual presence,
unlike what the Mèngshì Jì records.
I fear this statement is excessive."
The river flows further northeast,
passing south of the Wǔ Zǐxū Temple.
The shrine is within the boundaries of Dùnqiū Commandery on the north bank,
adjacent to the long river.
In front of the temple is a stele,
erected in the third year of Qīnglóng of Wèi.
The river flows further northeast to become Chángshòu Ford.
The Shùzhēng Jì says:
"From Liángchéng to Chángshòu Ford is sixty lǐ,
where the old course of the river emerges."
The Hànshū Gōuxù Zhì says:
"The harm caused by the Yellow River in the Central Plains was especially severe,
so the river was channeled from Jīshí,
passing through the Lóngdòu and two other channels to divert the river.
One was the Tà River,
which is the present course;
the other was the northern channel,
which was empty during Wáng Mǎng's time,
hence commonly called Wáng Mǎng River."
The old channel flows northeast past the west of Qīchéng.
In the second year of Duke Āi of the Chūnqiū,
Zhào Yāng of Jìn led troops
to install the Wèi crown prince Kuǎikuì in Qī.
Lost at night,
Yáng Hǔ said:
'Keep the river on the right and head south, and you will surely arrive.'
This is present-day Qī Pavilion west of Wèiguó County in Dùnqiū.
It was a Wèi town on the river.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
General Lǐ Bì was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The old channel also flows past the east of the old city of Fányáng County.
The Shǐjì records:
"Zhào general Lián Pō attacked Wèi and took Fányáng."
It flows north past the west of the old city of Yīn'ān County.
In the fifth year of Yuánshuò of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Wèi Bùyí was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The old channel flows further northeast past the east of the old city of Lèchāng County.
The Dìlǐ Zhì records:
"It was a subordinate county of Dōngjùn."
Emperor Xuān of Hàn enfeoffed Wáng Zhìjūn as a marquis here.
The old channel flows further northeast past the west of Píngyì's outer walls.
The Zhúshū Jìnián records:
In the second year of Duke Liè of Jìn,
Zhào built the city of Píngyì.
In the fifth year,
Tián Gōngzǐ Jūsī attacked Hándān
and besieged Píngyì.
In the ninth year,
Tián Xī of Qí and Hán Jǔ of Hándān
fought at Píngyì.
The Hándān commander was defeated,
and Hán Jǔ was captured fleeing,
taking Píngyì's new city.
It flows further northeast past the northwest of the old city of Yuánchéng County,
reaching the Shāqiū Weir.
The Shǐjì says:
"Yuán, son of Marquis Wǔ of Wèi, had his fief here,
hence the county's name."
East of the outer walls is Wǔlù Ruins.
To the left and right of the ruins are many sunken cities.
The Gōngyáng says:
"Xí
means a town."
The explanation says:
"Xí
means sunken."
The Jùnguó Zhì says:
"Wǔlù
was formerly Shālù,
with a Shā Pavilion.
When King Mù of Zhōu lost Shèng Jī,
he campaigned east and lodged at Wǔlù.
His daughter Shū Suǒ arrived here, weeping in grief.
This is called the Hill of Shū Suǒ."
It is another name for Shālù.
In the fourteenth year of Lord Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Shālù collapsed,
and a diviner of Jìn said:
"Yīn overwhelms Yáng,
earth and fire overpower each other,
thus Shālù collapsed."
Six hundred and forty-five years later,
a sage woman was expected to rise,
would it be Qí Tián?
Later, Wáng Wēngrú moved from Jǐnán to Yuánchéng,
and the place became upright,
with the sun and moon above it.
The Wáng family was a descendant of Shùn.
The earth is because of this,
and Hàn is the fire.
Wáng Jìn gave birth to Zhèng Jūn,
whose mother dreamt of the moon entering her bosom.
At the age of eighteen,
she was summoned to the Crown Prince's palace,
to give birth to Emperor Chéng,
becoming Empress Yuán.
The Hàn dynasty was in decline,
with four generations holding power.
Thus it is said, earth and fire overpower each other to become powerful.
With her collapse,
Lord Yángxióng wrote an epitaph stating "The essence of Tàiyīn,
the spirit of Shālù,
conjoined with Hàn,
matching the creation of Yuan and Chéng."
During the Jiàn'ān period of Emperor Xiàn,
Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo resisted each other at Guāndù.
Xiào was forced by Yuán Shào to follow the army despite being ill,
and died on arrival.
Over a thousand disciples and mourners from the district's officials and others below,
wearing mourning garments, attended.
Xiào's annotations on the "Five Classics," prognostications, celestial observations,
were renowned in the world.
Therefore, Fàn Yè stated in the "Appraisal":
"Kǒng's teachings were thus illuminated,
and were interrupted in the middle of the Hàn era."
To the north of the county is the Shāqiū Dam,
the dam blocks the water.
The "Shàngshū: Yǔ Fù" states:
"It heads north past Xiáng water.
Not following its path is called Xiáng,"
it is also called Kuì,
reaching the mainland,
and spreading northward to form the Nine Rivers.
"Fēngsú Tōng" says the river spreads out.
The division into Nine Rivers begins here.
In the "Yǔgòng" chapter, Yǎn Province,
the Nine Rivers had their paths,
referring to Túdǎi, Tàishǐ, Mǎjiá, Fùfǔ, Húsū, Jiǎn, Jié, Jūpán, and Géjīn,
collectively forming opposing rivers.
Zhèng Xuán said:
"The combination of lower branches forms opposing rivers."
This refers to receiving each other,
facilitating the flow to the river and sea.
During Qí Huán's powerful era,
a wide field was closed,
merging into a single river.
Therefore, north from the dam,
Guǎntáo, Yíngtáo, Bèiqiū, Gébān, Guǎngchuān, Xìndū, Dōngguāng, Héjiàn, and Lèchéng to the east,
the city sites remained,
but many river deltas were lost.
During the Hàn dynasty, the river broke,
the Golden Dam separated north and south from its harm,
yet debate always sought the traces of the Nine Rivers to dig them,
without knowing their location.
Hence Bān Gù said:
"From here to the north of the Hàn,
eight branches were lost."
The old river course,
divided from the Shāqiū Dam to the south,
produced the old river at Túnshì.
The old river of the waters runs northeast through the ruins of Fǎgān County to the west,
then reaches its north,
what Wáng Mǎng called Jíshùn.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, for the merit of the Great General Wèi Qīng defeating the Right Sages,
enfeoffed his son Dēng as a marquis state.
The old river also flows east through the ruined city of Bèiqiū County to the south.
Yīng Shào stated:
"In the 'Zǔo's Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals',
Lord Xiāng of Qí hunted at Bèiqiū."
I examined Jīng Xiāngfán and Dù Yù's statements that it was in Bóchāng,
as described in Sīmǎ Biāo's "Records of Commanderies and Kingdoms" as Bei Zhongju.
Yīng's annotation on this matter is slightly incorrect.
The old river again flows east through the ruins of Gānlíng County to the south,
known as Cù in the "Geographical Records,"
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Cùzhì.
Emperor Xiào Dé of Hàn, father of Emperor Ān,
was forced to be demoted to a prince,
and died here,
thus was buried in this land,
naming the mausoleum Gānlíng,
and the county also took the name.
In the second year of Huán Emperor Jiànhé,
the Qīnghé was renamed Gānlíng.
It was the market area of Gānquán in the Zhou period.
The mausoleum lies north of the old river,
its mound grand and high,
even though it was damaged midway,
it still resembled a mausoleum with layers,
known as the tomb of Tánghóu.
The city is called Yìchéng,
but this is incorrect.
In the past, Wénshǔ Láng of Nānyáng,
served as the official of Gānlíng during Jiàn'ān,
and one night stayed by the water.
Zhào's Lánxiāng dreamt of requesting reburial.
Wénshǔ investigated the water and found a coffin,
indeed by the water's edge,
half submerged.
Wénshǔ told his friends,
"If someone heard this,
I would certainly not believe it."
Thus he moved the burial,
offered sacrifices, and left.
The old river continues east past the ruins of Àitíng to the south,
then east past the ruins of Píngjìn to the south.
In the current city, there is a pagoda with five layers,
with a golden dew bowl on top,
inscribed:
"In the eighth year of Zhào Jiànwǔ,
Bǐ Shì Dàolóng and Héseì Zhú constructed the pagoda Chéng,
promoting virtuous deeds and encouraging transformation,
establishing the temple to the divine.
The pagoda has decayed,
yet the dew bowl remains,
bright and radiant.
The old river again turns northeast past the ruins of Líng County to the south,
called Bōtíng by Wáng Mǎng.
A separate river, Míngdú, emerges from the water at the county.
The old river again flows east past the ruins of Shù County to the east,
in the fourth year of Lü Hòu,
due to the accomplishments of her father Yīng,
conferred the son Tuó inheriting as a marquis state,
renamed Shànlù by Wáng Mǎng.
The old river again flows east past the ruins of Píngyuán County to the west,
and north it cuts across Túnshì's three channels,
flowing north past the ruins of Yìmù County to the northeast,
flowing west past the ruins of Píngyuán Gē County to the west.
"Geographical Records" states:
"Gē,"
is a ferry,
named Hépíng Pavilion by Wáng Mǎng,
it was the former domain of the obscure Hòuyī.
Yīng Shào stated,
"Gē,"
is the surname Yǎn,
descendants of Jiù Yáo,
the 13th year of Jiànwǔ during the reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
General Zhū Hù, influential in righteousness,
was enfeoffed as a marquis state.
The old river continues north past the ruins of Xiū County to the east,
then north past Ānlíng County to the west,
originally Xiū County's Ānlíng Township.
"Records of Geographical Customs" says:
"Forty li east of Xiū County lies Ānlíng Township,
an old county."
Northwards to the northeast past the ruins of Dōngguāng County to the west,
merging north with Zhāng River.
A watercourse diverges from the old river,
northwards emerges as Túnshì River,
passing east of Guǎntáo County,
and emerges northeast.
"The Hàn Shū's Waterways and Canals Records" states:
"From closing Xuanfang,
the river again broke north at Guǎntáo County,
dividing as Túnshì River,
as wide and deep as the Great River;
during Emperor Chéng's time,
the river broke at Guǎntáo and Jīndǐ of the Eastern Commandery,
the court appointed Envoy of the Damming, Wáng Yánshì, to block it,
completing the dike in thirty-six days.
An edict named the fifth year of Jiànshǐ as the first year of Héping,
Wáng Yánshì was promoted to Grand Minister,
this water was thus halted.
The course of Túnshì's old river further east-northeast,
with a separate river emerging from it.
The separate river continues east-northeast past Xìnchéng County,
where Zhāng Jiǎ River emerges from it.
"Geographical Records" says the Zhāng Jiǎ River originates from Túnshì's separate river at Xìnchéng County.
The old course of Zhāng Jiǎ River cuts north across Qīnghé at Guǎngzōng County.
It splits into two channels,
the left channel passing west of Guǎngzōng County's old city,
and further north past the ruins of Jiànshǐ County.
Tián Róng said:
"In the twelfth year of Zhào Wǔdì,
established Jiànxīng Prefecture,
governing Guǎngzōng,
with Jiànshǐ,
and Xìngdé, governing five counties under its jurisdiction.
The left channel continues north past Jīngchéng to the east and Liáochéng to the west,
further past the west of Nángōng County,
and flows north into Jiàng channel.
The right channel flows northeast past the south of Guǎngzōng County's old city,
further northeast past Jièchéng Pavilion to the north,
and further northeast past the old city of Zǎoqiáng County in Chánglè Commandery to the east.
This was formerly Xìndū,
and in the fifth year of the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
it was changed to its present name.
It then flows northeast past Guǎngchuān County,
where it joins the old course of the Jiàngdú River.
It then flows northeast past the west of the old Guǎngchuān County city,
and east past the south of the Jíjīn Tíng.
Xú Guǎng said:
"Jíjīn is in Guǎngchuān."
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
"North of the county is the city of Jíjīn,
where Lǚ Shàng suffered hardship selling food;
it is suspected to be here."
Liú Chéngzhī said:
"Northeast of Cuó County in Qiáo Commandery is the Jíjīn Tíng,
which is an old settlement,
the place where Lǚ Shàng suffered hardship."
I have examined the *Zuǒzhuàn* to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
which records "attacking Cháo, conquering Jí, and entering Zhōulái,"
but there is no mention of a "jīn."
Dù Yù's *Explanations of Places in the Spring and Autumn Annals* also states
that the Jí Tíng is northeast of Cuó County,
but similarly does not mention a "jīn."
So, I do not know where Chéngzhī obtained this claim.
However, there are many places in the world named Jí,
and not all of them can be called Jíjīn.
Also, in the seventeenth year of Duke Zhāo of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Wú to lead troops across from Jíjīn,
sacrificed animals at Luò,
and then destroyed Lùhún.
Dù Yù's *Explanations of Places* omits this and does not record it.
Fú Qián said:
"Jíjīn
is like Mèngjīn."
Xú Guǎng's *Jìn Jì* also states
that Shí Lè, invading Héběi from Gébēi,
attacked Xiàng Bīng of Jí at Fāngtóu,
and crossed from Jí.
Jíjīn lies between Dōng Commandery and Hénèi,
and Tián Róng believed it to be the southern ferry of Shíjì.
Although ancient times are obscure and distant,
and the principles of governance are profound,
scattered texts and lost phrases
may still be found,
and the hidden and visible traces along the route can be verified by local conditions.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Lǚ Wàng
was a man from the eastern sea,
who grew old without meeting opportunity,
and used fishing to seek out King Wén of Zhōu."
He also said:
"At the age of fifty, Lǚ Wàng
sold food at Jíjīn;
at seventy,
he slaughtered oxen in Zhāogē;
and at ninety,
he became the teacher of an emperor."
Huángfǔ Shì'ān said:
"He wished to retire by the shores of the eastern sea,
but hearing that King Wén cherished the elderly,
he went to Zhōu to fish."
Today, the city of Jíshuǐ also claims to have the retreat of Lǚ Wàng.
Starting from the eastern sea
and reaching Fēngyōng,
following his route and direction,
Zhào and Wèi are closer,
while placing it in Qiáo and Sòng
seems more distant.
The old course of the Zhāngjiǎ River flows further northeast to the east of Xiū County, where it joins the Qīnghé River.
*The Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
"The Zhāngjiǎ River flows northeast to Xiū County and enters the Qīngzhāng River."
The Bié River of Túnshì flows east,
where a branch emerges,
flowing east past the south of the old Xìnchéng County city,
and further east past the south of the old Qīngyáng County city,
north of Qīnghé Commandery,
which was moved here from Qīngyáng during the Wèi dynasty.
It then flows northeast past the south of Língxiāng,
further northeast past the south of the old Dōngwǔchéng County city,
and further northeast past the south of the old Dōngyáng County city.
*The Treatise on Geography* states:
"Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Xūlíng,"
but common people call it Gāolíguō,
which is incorrect.
Yìng Shào said:
"Thirty lǐ northeast of Dōngwǔchéng is Yángxiāng,
which was formerly a county."
Further east, it disperses and ends,
with no further ferry or route.
The Bié River of Túnshì flows further northeast past the south of Qīnghé Commandery,
and further northeast past the west of the old Qīnghé city.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Wáng Xī.
*The Records of Geography and Customs* states:
"Seventeen lǐ southeast of Gānlíng Commandery is the old Qīnghé city,
which people call Quèchéng."
It then flows further northeast past the south of Yìmù County,
where it divides into two courses:
the northern course of the Bié River of Túnshì flows east past the south of the old Yìmù County city,
crosses east over the old course of the Great River,
and further northeast past Píngyuán County,
where a branch emerges northward,
ending at Ānlíng County.
The northern course of the Bié River of Túnshì flows further northeast past the south of the old Chóngpíng County city.
Yìng Shào said:
"Eighty lǐ southwest of Zhònghé County is Chóngpíngxiāng,
which was formerly a county."
It then flows further northeast past the south of the old Zhònghé County city,
and further northeast past the south of the old Dìng County city.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Yuè, son of Prince Xiào of Qí.
*The Records of Geography and Customs* states:
"Thirty lǐ southeast of Ráo'ān County is Dìngxiāngchéng,
which was formerly a county."
The northern course of the Bié River of Túnshì flows further east into Yángxìn County,
but now has no water.
Further east, it becomes the Xián River,
flowing northeast past the north of the old Yángxìn County city.
*The Treatise on Geography* states:
"It is a subordinate county of Bóhǎi,
and flows east into the sea."
The southern course of the Bié River of Túnshì crosses east over the old course of the Great River from Píngyuán,
and flows past the north of the old Píngyuán County city,
where a branch emerges to the right,
flowing northeast to the boundary of Āndé County,
and east to join the Shāng River.
The southern course of the Bié River of Túnshì flows further northeast within the boundary of Píngyuán,
where another branch channel emerges to the right,
ending at Āndé County.
The southern course of the Bié River of Túnshì begins at the old course of the Great River north of Píngyuán city,
flowing eastward,
and is also commonly called the Dǔmǎ River,
which is what *The Treatise on Geography* refers to as the Dǔmǎ River in Píngyuán County,
flowing northeast into the sea,
covering a distance of five hundred and sixty lǐ.
It flows northeast past the west of the old Āndé County city,
and further northeast past the south of Línqí city.
Initially, when eastern Qí had not submitted,
the great Wèi built a city to face it,
hence the city got its name.
It then bends and flows past the east of the city,
with the old course forty paces wide,
and further northeast past the west of the old Chóngqiū County city.
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xiāng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
in autumn,
an alliance was formed at Chóngqiū,
due to the campaign against Qí.
Yìng Shào said:
"Fifty lǐ north of Āndé County is Chóngqiūxiāng,
which was formerly a county."
It then flows further northeast past the north of the old Xīpíngchāng County city.
Since there is a Píngchāng County in Běihǎi,
"west" was added to distinguish it.
In the first year of the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Wáng Chángjūn.
The old channel and streams
flow east into Bān County, becoming the Bān River.
This is likely one of the courses of the Nine Rivers.
*The Book of the Later Hàn* records that Gōngsūn Zàn defeated the Yellow Turbans at the Bān River,
which is this course.
Further east, it becomes the Báilùyuān waters,
three hundred paces from north to south,
over a thousand paces from east to west,
and over three zhàng deep.
The water is clear in winter and turbid in summer,
stagnant and not flowing,
but if summer floods occur,
the water depth reaches five zhàng,
and only then does it flow and connect.
The Bān course flows further past the north of the old Bān County city,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Fēnmíng.
It flows east past the north of the old Lèlíng County city.
*The Treatise on Geography* states:
"It was formerly the seat of a commandant,"
and Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó said it was a town of Píngyuán,
but now it is divided into a commandery.
It then flows further northeast past the south of the old Yángxìn County city,
and northeast into the sea.
The old course of the Túnshì River flows east from the Bié River past the south of the old Xìnxiāng County in Gānlíng.
*The Treatise on Geography* states:
"Emperor Ān changed its name to Ānpíng."
Yìng Shào said:
"Seventeen lǐ northwest of Gānlíng is Xìnxiāng,
which was formerly a county."
The old course of Túnshì flows further east past the north of the old Gānlíng County city,
further east past the north of Líng County,
and further northeast past Shū County,
where it joins the old course of the Míngdú River,
which begins at the old course of the Great River south of Líng County.
*The Treatise on Geography* states:
"The river water separates from Líng County to become the Míngdú River."
It flows northeast past the east of Líng County,
east into Shū County,
and north to join the Túnshì course.
The Túnshì course also bears the name Míngdú.
It flows further east past the north of the old Shū County city,
northeast to join the old course of the Great River,
which is called the Míngdú Mouth.
*The Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
"The Míngdú River flows northeast to Xiū and enters the Túnshì."
Examining the course of the river, it does not reach that far.
Further northeast, it passes south of Wèi County,
and further northeast, it passes north of Púyáng County,
where the Hùzǐ River emerges.
The river flows east past the south of Tiěqiū,
as recorded in the *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn*,
in the second year of Duke Āi,
when Zhèng Hǎndá led his troops,
Yóu Wúxù drove the chariot for Jiǎnzǐ,
with the crown prince of Wèi as the right-hand guard,
they ascended Tiě,
and saw the Zhèng army.
The crown prince of Wèi threw himself from the chariot,
which happened at this very place.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Tiě
is the name of a hill.
Dù Yù said:
South of Qī and on the northern bank of the river,
there is an ancient city,
which is the town of Qī.
In the eastern part of the city is the tomb of Zǐlù.
On the western bank of the river is Gānchéng.
The *Jùnguó Zhì* states:
Wèi County has Gānchéng.
South of the river is Lóngyuān Palace.
During the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
the river breached at Púyáng and flooded sixteen commanderies,
so a force of one hundred thousand men was dispatched to block the breach,
and Lóngyuān Palace was constructed.
It was likely that Emperor Wǔ built the palace beside the breached river,
next to Lóngyuān,
hence it was called Lóngyuān Palace.
The river flows northeast past north of Púyáng County,
forming the Púyáng Ford.
The old city lies to the south, separated from Wèi County by the water,
and ten lǐ north of the city is the mouth of the Hùzǐ River,
where the Jīndī and Xuānfáng Weir are located.
During the Hàn dynasty,
the river breached at Jīndī.
Wáng Zūn of Zhuō Commandery,
who had been transferred from the post of Inspector of Xúzhōu to Governor of Dōng Commandery,
faced a great overflow of the river,
which inundated Hùzǐ,
and the Jīndī was breached and damaged.
Wáng Zūn personally led the officials and people,
sacrificed a white horse by sinking it,
prayed to the river god Hé Bó,
personally held the guī and bì jades,
and offered his own body to fill the breach in the dike.
He built a hut and lived atop it,
while the officials and people all fled.
Wáng Zūn stood firm and unmoving, and the floodwaters rose only to his feet and then stopped.
Both the court and the common people admired his courage and integrity.
The river flows further northeast past south of Wèiguó County,
and to the east is the Guōkǒu Ford.
The river flows further east past north of Juànchéng County,
with the old city located eighteen lǐ south of the river.
It was called Juànliáng during Wáng Mǎng's time,
and was the former seat of Yǎnzhōu.
Cáo Cāo began his enterprise here.
Among the cities along the river, this one was the most formidable and secure.
The *Jìn Bā Wáng Gùshì* records:
Dōnghǎi King Yuè governed from Juànchéng,
but the city wall inexplicably collapsed for over seventy zhàng.
Yuè considered this ominous,
and moved his seat to Púyáng.
South of the city is the temple of Dèng Ài, the Wei envoy with imperial credentials, General Who Conquers the West, Grand Commandant, and Marquis of Fāngchéng.
South of the temple is a stele for Dèng Ài,
erected in the twelfth year of the Jiànyuán era of the Qín dynasty,
by Péng Chāo of Āndìng, General of Guǎngwǔ, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, and Marquis Within the Passes.
On the southern bank of the river is Xīnchéng,
built by Wáng Xuánmó, General of Níngshuò of the Sòng, as a forward position when he entered the river.
On the northern bank are the grand foundations of Xīntái,
with multiple layers spanning several zhàng in height and width,
built by Duke Xuān of Wèi as the New Terrace,
which is the subject of the poem by Qí Jiāng in the *Shī*.
This is the Lúguān Ford.
East of the terrace is a small city,
rugged and dilapidated,
with the terrace's base resting against the river.
Commonly called Dǐgéchéng,
it is suspected to have been the seat of the commandant of the pass and ford,
though this is not certain.
The river flows further northeast past west of Qíntíng in Fàn County,
as recorded in the *Chūnqiū Jīng* regarding the building of a terrace at Qín.
The river flows further northeast past Wěisù Ford,
north of the Great River,
which is Dōngwǔyáng County.
To the left, it meets the old course of the Fúshuǐ.
This old course originates from the Great River at Dùnqiū County and flows northward,
then east past the old city south of Fányáng County.
Yìng Shào said:
The county is located north of the Fán River.
Zhāng Yàn said:
The county has the Fányuān.
In the twentieth year of Duke Xiāng of the *Chūnqiū*,
the *Jīng* records the duke forming an alliance with the Marquis of Jìn and the Marquis of Qí at Chányuān.
Dù Yù said:
It is south of Dùnqiū County,
now called Fányuān.
Chányuān
is Fányuān,
also called Fúshuǐ.
In the past, when Wèi moved to Dàliáng,
Zhào exchanged Zhōngmóu with Wèi.
Thus, the *Zhì* states:
Zhào's southern boundary reaches Fúshuǐ and Fányáng.
This refers to this watercourse.
The old course crosses the Great River to the east,
and then passes east through the wilderness of Wǔlù,
where Duke Wén of Jìn received a clod of earth from a rustic,
which happened at this very place.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Thirty lǐ northwest of present-day Wèi County,
there is the city of Wǔlù,
now under the jurisdiction of Dùnqiū County.
The old course of Fúshuǐ flows further southeast past north of the city of Wèiguó Yì,
which was the old state of Duke Wèi.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn enfeoffed it to a descendant of the Zhōu.
It then flows east past the old city south of Wèiguó County,
the ancient Zhēnguān.
Yìng Shào said:
In the Xià dynasty, there were Guān and Hù,
which is this city.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* records:
In the second year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Tián Shòu of Qí led troops to attack us,
besieged Guān,
and Guān surrendered.
The old course of Fúshuǐ flows further east past Hémùchéng and then northeastward.
The *Jùnguó Zhì* states:
Wèi was originally the old state of Guān,
of the Yáo surname.
It has Hémùchéng.
Further northeast, it enters Dōngwǔyáng County,
and then east into the river.
There is also the Tàshuǐ that emerges here,
which Dài Yánzhī called Wǔshuǐ.
The river flows further east past east of Wǔyáng County and west of Fàn County, then northeastward.
Further northeast, it passes north of Dōng'ē County.
The river flows northeast from Fàn County to form the Cāngtíng Ford.
The *Shùzhēng Jì* states:
Cāngtíng Ford is within the boundaries of Fàn County,
sixty lǐ from Dōng'ē.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
The ford is seventy lǐ northeast of Wǔyáng County.
The ford
is named for the Hé and Jǐ rivers.
The river passes to the right through Kēzé,
as recorded in the *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*,
in the fourteenth year of Duke Xiāng,
where Sūn Wénzǐ of Wèi defeated the duke's followers at Āzé.
Further northeast, it passes west of the old city of Dōng'ē County,
and then flows northeastward to discharge.
A branch of the river flows eastward,
called the Dènglǐ Canal.
Further northeast, it passes west of Chípíng County.
The river flows northeast from the Dènglǐ Canal past the north of Chāngxiāng Pavilion,
then continues northeast past the west of the Qiáo'áo city.
The Shùzhēng Jì states:
"Qiáo'áo
is the name of a ford.
Those who cross by boat from the Yellow River
all use this ford.
The city faces the water,
and its southwestern side has collapsed into the river."
In the twenty-seventh year of the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty,
Wáng Xuánmó was appointed as General Níngshuò,
leading the vanguard into the river,
pacifying Qiáo'áo
and defending it.
The Commander Liú Yìgōng deemed the sand city indefensible,
so he summoned Xuánmó and ordered him to destroy the city and withdraw.
Later, the city was rebuilt.
When the Wei established Jìzhōu,
its administration was located here.
The river water struck its southwestern corner,
and it collapsed into the river again,
which was the former Chípíng County.
Yìng Shào said:
"Chí
is the name of a mountain.
The county lies on level ground by the mountain,
hence it is called Chípíng."
Wáng Mǎng's achievements were lofty indeed.
The Jīng states: "The Great River lies to its west,
and the Dènglǐ Canal passes to its east."
This refers to this town.
In the past, when Shí Lè was subordinate to Shī Huān,
he camped and farmed in Chípíng.
He heard the sounds of drums, horns, small drums, and bells
in this county.
To the west, it is divided from Liáochéng by the river.
The river then flows northeast and joins the Dènglǐ Canal.
The canal receives water from the Great River west of Dōng'ē County,
flows east past the north of the old Dōng'ē County city,
which was formerly a town of Wèi.
Yìng Zhòngyuàn said:
"Because there is a west,
it is called east."
The Wei enfeoffed Cáo Zhí as king of this domain.
Inside the north gate of the great city, on the western side,
there is a large well on the mound,
as large as a wheel,
six or seven zhàng deep.
In years past, glue was boiled here
to be presented to the imperial court.
This is the so-called Ējiāo mentioned in the Běncǎo.
Hence, it is commonly known as the Ē Well.
The county produces fine silk fabrics,
which is why the Shǐjì states:
"King Zhāo of Qín wielded the Tài'ē sword
and wore Ēgǎo garments."
Further east, it passes Línyì County,
where it joins the Jiàng Canal.
Then it flows north past the east of Chípíng County
and the west of the old Línyì County city,
finally entering the river to the north.
The river then flows northeast past the Sìdú Ford.
On the western bank of the ford,
facing the river, stands the Temple of the Four Waterways,
which looks east toward the mouth of the Four Waterways.
The river divides eastward into the Jì,
also said to be where the Jì River receives water from the Yellow River.
However, the stone gate at the Yíngkǒu was blocked and not yet cleared,
so from here it flows northeast,
passing for nine lǐ before merging with the Qīngshuǐ.
Thus, the Jì Waterway flows from the Yellow River into the Jì,
from the Jì into the Huái,
and from the Huái reaches the Jiāng.
The waterways connect and circulate,
hence the name "Four Waterways."
In the past, when Zhào killed Míngdú,
Zhòngní stood by the river and sighed.
Turning back from there, he said:
"Qiū's failure to cross
is fate."
The Qíncāo records that Confucius sang by the Dí River,
saying:
"The Dí waters surge, oh, the wind raises waves;
oars and boats are overturned, adding to the chaos."
I note that Línjì
was formerly Dí.
This is the route the Jì passes through,
hence it shares the general name.
The river then passes east of the old city of Yángxū County,
which is still commonly called Yángchéng.
The river also passes east of Chípíng City,
likely due to the county's relocation.
Within the city, there is an old terrace,
commonly called Shípíng City,
but this is incorrect.
It is probably because "Chí" and "Shí" sound similar.
Further northeast, it passes east of Gāotáng County.
The Yellow River passes by the county,
and the Tà River flows into it.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Tà River originates from Dōngwǔyáng.
Today, the Tà River receives water from the Yellow River southeast of Wǔyáng County,
flows northwest past the east of Wǔyáng New City,
which was the seat of the Dōng Commandery under Cáo Cāo.
Water was channeled from the stone sluice at the east gate and flowed north into the Hall Pond,
and the old foundation south of the pond still remains.
Inside the city, there is a very large stone.
The west gate of the city is named the Ice Well Gate,
and inside the gate, in a winding area,
the ice well still exists.
Outside the gate, there is an old terrace,
called the Wǔyáng Terrace,
and around the terrace, there are also remnants of corner battlements.
The water flows northeast from the city past the old city of Dōngwǔyáng County.
Yìng Shào said:
The county is located north of the Wǔ River,
and it was called Wǔchāng under Wáng Mǎng.
Thus, the Tà River may also be called the Wǔ River.
Zāng Hóng served as the Grand Administrator of Dōng Commandery,
governing here.
When Cáo Cāo besieged Zhāng Chāo in Yōngqiū,
Zāng Hóng, out of loyalty and righteousness,
requested Yuán Shào to rescue him,
but Yuán Shào refused.
Zāng Hóng then severed ties with Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào besieged Zāng Hóng,
and the city ran out of food.
Zāng Hóng called out to his officers and soldiers, saying:
For the sake of great righteousness,
I cannot avoid death.
You all have no reason
to suffer this calamity in vain.
The crowd wept and said:
How could we bear to abandon you, our wise governor?
More than eight thousand men and women
lay down together and died.
Zāng Hóng did not yield,
and Yuán Shào killed him.
A townsman named Chén Róng, who served as an assistant,
said:
I would rather die on the same day as Zāng Hóng
than live on the same day as you, General.
Yuán Shào also killed him,
and the scholars lamented and sighed.
Today, around the city,
the outer walls of Yuán Shào's siege still remain.
The water encircles the moat,
and northeast of the city, it converges into a single channel,
flowing northeast out of the outer walls,
passing west of the Gǎngchéng City in Yángpíng County.
The "Records of Commanderies and States" states:
Yángpíng County has the Gǎngchéng Pavilion.
Further north, it passes east of the old city of Yángpíng County.
In the first year of the Yuánpíng era of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn,
the Chancellor Cài Yì was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Tà River further flows north, cutting across the northwest of Shēndào City,
where there is the Shēn Pavilion.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Huán of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Duke Xuān of Wèi sent Jí to Qí,
ordering bandits to wait at Shēn.
Jí and Shòu both perished at this pavilion.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Today, ten lǐ north of Yángpíng County in Píngyuán,
there is the old Shēn Pavilion,
a narrow and strategic pass,
on the road from Wèi to Qí.
Gazing at the New Terrace above the river,
moved by the two sons from their youth,
the poet's "Riding the Boat"
is truly lamentable.
Today, east of the county, there is a temple for the two sons,
still called the Filial Piety Shrine.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the east of the old city of Lèpíng County.
The county
was formerly called Qīng.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Zhì Zhōngtóng was enfeoffed at Qīng.
Emperor Xuān enfeoffed Xǔ Guǎnghàn's younger brother, Wēngsūn, at Lèpíng,
both as marquisates.
Under Wáng Mǎng, it was called Qīngzhì.
During the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
it was changed to its current name.
The Tà River further flows north past the west of the old city of Liáochéng County.
Inside the city, there is a Jīn City,
surrounded by water,
with a galloping road at the south gate,
cutting across the water and extending southward,
allowing boats to travel from the outside.
Beside the east gate, there is a multi-tiered terrace,
towering into the clouds,
where Lǔ Zhònglián once said, "Withdraw the troops from Gāotáng
and repel the masses from Liáochéng."
The Tà River further flows northeast past the north of the old city of Qīnghé County.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
Gānlíng
was formerly Qīnghé.
Qīnghé is seventeen lǐ to the south,
but today, southeast of the old city of Gānlíng County,
there is no city to match it.
Directly east, twenty lǐ away, is the Àitíng City,
and forty lǐ southeast is this city,
which is likely the Qīnghé City.
Later, the Mán people settled there,
so it is commonly called Mán City.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the southeast of Wénxiāng City,
and further northeast past the south of the old city of Bópíng County.
Inside the city, there is a multi-tiered terrace rising elegantly,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Jiāmù.
To the right, it joins the Huáng Ditch and flows into the river marsh.
The Huáng Ditch receives water from the outer walls of Liáochéng,
flowing abundantly when the water is high
and ceasing when the water is low.
It emerges northeast of the city,
passes south of Qīnghé City,
and further northeast passes north of Shè City.
This is what the "Spring and Autumn Annals" refers to as east of Liáo and Shè.
It is commonly called Guō City,
but this is incorrect.
The city is three lǐ from east to west
and two lǐ from north to south.
At the eastern and western corners, there is a Jīn City,
which is low-lying,
with ruins of the outer walls still remaining,
and many tombs on both sides.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Thirty lǐ northeast of Liáochéng County is the old Shè City.
Today, this city is about twenty-five or six lǐ west of Liáochéng,
which is Shè City.
Further east, it passes north of Wénxiāng City,
and further southeast passes north of Wáng City.
In the seventh year of the Tàicháng era of Wèi,
the Prince of Ānpíng, Zhèn, built it while stationed in Píngyuán,
and it is commonly called Wáng City.
In the twenty-third year of the Tàihé era,
the garrison was abolished, and Píngyuán Commandery was established,
with its seat in this city.
The Huáng Ditch further flows northeast,
merging with the Tà River in a concealed manner,
its force stabilizing the riverbanks,
emerging east at Gāotáng County,
where the great river bends to the right,
flowing east into the Tà River.
Sāng Qīn's "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Tà River originates from Gāotáng.
I, based on the "Bamboo Annals" and "The Travels of King Mù," note that
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the Son of Heaven marched east from Wǔlù,
fished in the Tà River,
and offered sacrifices to the virtuous,
calling it the Sacrificial Mound;
on the day Jǐsì,
the Son of Heaven marched east,
and fed his horses on the banks of the Tà River.
Tracing its course and direction,
it could not have originated near Gāotáng.
What Sāng said
likely refers to the point where the river emerges,
which is somewhere in between.
It is commonly believed that this water receives its source from the Yellow River,
and is also called the Source River.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the west of the old city of Yuán County,
which was called Dōngshùn Pavilion under Wáng Mǎng.
Dù Yù's "Explanation of Geography" states:
Northwest of Zhù'ā County in Jǐnán is Yuán City.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the east of the old city of Gāotáng County.
In the past, King Wēi of Qí sent Xìzǐ to guard Gāotáng,
and the people of Zhào did not dare to fish in the river.
This is what Lǔ Zhònglián said to Tián Bā:
"Now the Chǔ army is at Nányáng,
and Zhào is attacking Gāotáng."
In the tenth year of Duke Āi in the "Zuǒzhuàn" of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Zhào Yǎng led troops to attack Qí,
capturing Lí and Yuán,
and destroying the outer walls of Gāotáng.
Dù Yù said:
Yuán is the same as Yuán.
Northwest of Zhù'ā County is Gāotáng City.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the north of the old city of Tàyīn County.
The county
was formerly the settlement of Lí.
In the third year of the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, a surrendered king of the Xiōngnú was enfeoffed here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yìchéng.
It passes by the south of Běitàyīn City.
Fú Chēn called it Tàyáng,
and south of the city, there is a stele for Liú Dài, the Governor of Yǎn Province of Wèi.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
Tàyīn County in Píngyuán
is today's Jùtà Pavilion.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the south of the old city of Zhù County,
and further northeast passes north of Cuīshì City.
In the twenty-seventh year of Duke Xiāng in the "Zuǒzhuàn" of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Cuī Chéng requested to retire in Cuī.
Dù Yù's "Explanation of Geography" states:
Northwest of Dōngcháoyáng County in Jǐnán is Cuīshì City.
The Tà River further flows northeast past the south of the old city of Dōngcháoyáng County.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
the Commandant Zǎi Jì was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The *Record of Geography and Customs* states:
Nányáng had a Cháoyáng County,
hence the addition of "Eastern" [to distinguish it].
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
this was Xiūzhì under Wáng Mǎng.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of the tomb of Fú Shēng, a recluse-scholar of the Hàn,
whose stele still exists.
He was made a court erudite of the Qín for his mastery of the *Classics*.
When the Qín buried the Confucian scholars alive,
Fú Shēng went into hiding.
When the Hàn arose,
he taught in the regions between Qí and Lǔ,
compiling the *Five Classics* and the *Great Commentary on the Book of Documents*.
Emperor Wén sent a comfortable carriage to summon him.
He was too old to travel,
so he had the archivists, including Ōuyáng Shēng, receive instruction on the *Book of Documents* from the recluse-scholar,
who was known as Fú Shēng.
The Luò River then flows east past the north of the old city of Zōupíng County,
the ancient state of Marquis Zōu,
whose descendants of Shùn bore the surname Yáo.
It then flows northeast past the north of Eastern Zōu City.
The *Treatise on Geography*
states that the Qiānchéng Commandery had an Eastern Zōu County.
The Luò River then flows northeast past the north of the old city of Jiànxìn County.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Lóu Jìng was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
Yìng Shào states:
fifty *lǐ* northwest of Línjì County is Jiànxìn City,
the old city where the commandant had his seat.
The Luò River then flows northeast between the two cities of Qiānchéng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
this was made Qiānchéng Commandery,
which was called Jiànxìn under Wáng Mǎng.
In the fourth year of the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng, it became a kingdom.
In the seventh year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé,
it was changed to Lè'ān Commandery,
which was formerly Qí territory.
Fú Chēn states:
Qiānchéng City is one hundred and fifty *lǐ* northwest of Qí City,
separated by the Huì River,
which is another name for the Luò River.
It then flows northeast to become the Mǎcháng Depression,
which is eighty *lǐ* from east to west
and thirty *lǐ* from north to south.
The disorderly branches of the river flow into the sea here.
The abundance of the river and the sea
is greatest here.
The *Record of Geography and Customs* states:
the Luò River flows northeast to Qiānchéng and enters the sea.
When the river is full, it forms a thoroughfare reaching the sea;
when the water diminishes, it becomes a tiny trickle, its flow cut off.
The *Book* [of Documents] states:
"floated upon the Jǐ and the Luò."
This refers to this waterway.
It then flows northeast past the east of Yángxū County,
where the Shāng River emerges.
"Geographic Treatise":
Yángxū is a subordinate county of Píngyuán.
In the fourth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Jiānglǘ, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí.
The city lies southwest of Gāotáng City.
The "Classic" places it here,
which is incorrect.
The Shāng River first receives water from the Hé River,
and is also a deep pool formed by the Luò River and the Zé River.
Deep and stagnant,
it is commonly called Qīngshuǐ (Clear Water).
Since then, although sand has silted and filled it,
traces still remain.
Passing north through the marsh,
it is commonly called Luòlǐkēng.
It passes west of Zhānggōng City,
then north,
where its source resurges underground,
also called Xiǎo Zhāng River.
"Shāng" and "Zhāng" sound similar,
hence the character and pronunciation shifted.
The Shāng River then flows north past the east of Píngyuán County,
then past the old city of Āndé County south,
then northeast past the old city of Píngchāng County south,
then east past the old city of Bān County south,
then east past the old city of Lèlíng County south.
In the fourth year of Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Shǐ Zǐcháng, a Palace Attendant.
The Shāng River then flows east past the old city of Lè County south.
In the eighth year of Empress Dowager Gāo,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Pìguāng, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhāngxiāng.
Yìng Shào said:
Sixty lǐ southeast of Bān County is Lèxiāng City,
the old county seat.
The Shāgōu River flows into it.
The water emerges south from the sunny side of the Great River,
the spring source being two hundred paces from the river.
Its water flows north into the Shāng River.
The Shāng River then flows northeast past the northwest of Mǎlǐng City,
bends east, turns south,
and passes east of the city.
The city lies within a river bend.
Prince Yuè of Dōnghǎi beheaded Jí Sāng at this city.
The Shāng River then flows northeast past the old city of Fùpíng County north.
"Geographic Treatise" says:
It was a marquisate.
Wáng Mǎng called it Lè'āntíng.
Yìng Shào said:
Emperor Míng renamed it Yàncì.
Kàn Yīn said:
Yàncì County was originally the fief of Fùpíng Marquis, General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Ānshì.
This is incorrect.
According to "Hànshū",
in the sixth year of Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
Right General Zhāng Ānshì was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fùpíng.
Upon his death,
his son Yánshòu inherited the state,
located in a separate estate in Chénliú,
within Wèi Commandery.
"Chénliú Customs Biography" says:
Ānlíng Township in Wèishì County, Chénliú,
was the old Fùpíng County.
This was indeed Ānshì's fief.
Annual income from rents exceeded ten million.
Yánshòu felt he had no merit or virtue,
and could not long occupy his ancestor's great state,
so he petitioned to reduce his households.
The Son of Heaven considered him modest,
transferred his fief to Píngyuán,
combined it into one city,
with household registration unchanged,
but taxes reduced by half.
"Thirteen Provinces Treatise" says:
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng,
it was renamed Yàncì.
According to "Shǐjì: Yearly Table of Marquises, Meritorious Officials of Emperor Gāo",
in the sixth year of Emperor Gāo,
Yuán Qǐng was enfeoffed as a marquisate.
Xú Guǎng's "Pronunciation and Meaning" says:
"Hànshū" writes it as Yuán Lèi.
Thus, Yàncì is an old name,
not originating from Emperor Míng,
but rather restored.
West of the county is the tomb of Dōngfāng Shuò,
with a shrine beside it,
which has divine efficacy.
Beside the water is Yún City.
In the fourth year of Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Xìn, son of Prince Xiào of Qí.
The Shāng River then divides into two streams:
the southern stream is called Chángcóng Ditch,
flowing east into the sea.
South of the ditch by the sea,
there is a Pú Platform,
eight zhàng high,
two hundred paces square.
"Sān Qí Brief Records" says:
Southeast of Gé City is Pú Platform.
When Qín Shǐhuáng traveled east to the sea,
he coiled rushes on the platform and tethered his horse.
To this day, rushes grow each year,
twining as if tied,
resembling water willows,
usable for arrows.
Now it is thirty lǐ east of the sea.
The northern stream is also commonly called Bǎipú Ditch,
flowing northeast into the sea.
The Great River then flows northeast past the old city of Gāotáng County west.
"Zuǒzhuàn", nineteenth year of Duke Xiāng:
Duke Líng of Qí deposed Crown Prince Guāng and established Prince Yá,
appointing Sùshā Wèi as Junior Tutor.
When the Marquis of Qí died,
Cuī Zhù welcomed Guāng.
Guāng was established,
and killed Prince Yá at Qiū of Gōudòu.
Wèi fled to Gāotáng and rebelled.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Originally part of Píngyuán County,
the western border of Qí.
The Great River passes its west, not its east.
The "Classic" says it passes east,
which is an error.
The Great River then flows north past Zhānggōng City,
adjacent to the riverbank.
Wèi's Governor of Qīngzhōu, Zhāng, governed here,
hence commonly called Zhānggōng City.
There is a ferry on the water,
named Zhānggōng Crossing.
The river water then flows north past the old city of Píngyuán County east.
"Geographic Customs Record" says:
"Yuán" means broad and level,
hence Píngyuán (Level Plain).
The county was the old seat of Píngyuán Commandery.
Established in the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Hépíng.
Jīn Zhuó said:
West of Qí is Píngyuán.
The river water passes northeast through Gāotáng.
Gāotáng is Píngyuán.
Therefore, the "Classic" says
the river passes east of Gāotáng County.
This is incorrect.
According to "Geographic Treatise":
Gāotáng is where the Luò River emerges,
while Píngyuán is where the Dǔmǎ River originates.
Clearly, Píngyuán is not Gāotáng,
and the Great River cannot pass its east—this is certain.
The Great River overflows on the right,
commonly called Gānzǎo Ditch.
The banks have many jujube trees,
hence the common name.
When the river is full, it floods;
when water diminishes, it stops flowing.
The ditch then flows northeast past the long dike,
passes north of Luòyīn County,
east past north of Zhù City,
east forming interconnected ponds and deep pools,
commonly called Huìyě Marsh.
The river water then flows northeast past the old city of Āyáng County west.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Wàn Xīn, a Gentleman of the Palace.
Yìng Shào said:
Fifty lǐ southeast of Luòyīn County is Āyáng Township,
the old county seat.
Further northeast, it passes north of Luòyáng County.
The river water from Píngyuán passes left past east of Āndé City,
then north as Lùjiǎo Ford.
Northeast, it passes Bān County, Lèlíng, Lèxiāng to the old city of Yàncì County south,
becoming the Yàncì River.
In the second year of Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
the fierce bandit Bì Háo and several hundred others sailed to raid Píngyuán.
County Magistrate Liú Xióng,
with his subordinate clerk Suǒ Fǔ,
pursued by boat to Yàncì Ford,
engaged the bandits,
and both were captured.
[Suǒ Fǔ] begged to substitute for Xióng.
Háo released Xióng at this ford.
Suǒ Fǔ can be said to have fulfilled filial devotion and reverence,
and exemplified the utmost loyalty between ruler and minister.
The river water passes right past the old city of Luòyīn County north,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jùwǔ County.
The river water then flows northeast as Luòwò Ford,
located south of the old city of Luòwò County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Yántíng.
"Geographic Customs Record" says:
Fifty lǐ northwest of Qiānshèng County is the Great River,
north of which is Luòwò City,
the old county seat.
Wèi renamed it Hòubù Pavilion,
now commonly called Yòufǔ City.
The river water then flows east past north of Qiānshèng City,
which is what Fú Chēn called Qiānshèng North City.
Further northeast, it passes north of Lì County,
then further northeast, it passes Jiǎxià Town.
The Jì River comes from the west and flows into it,
then further northeast, it enters the sea.
The Hé River then flows east and divides into two streams.
The branch stream flows east past the south of Jiǎxià City,
then southeast through Mǎcháng Kēng and flows into the Jì River.
The "Classic" says the Jì River flows into the Hé River,
but this is incorrect.
The Hé River flows northeast from the branch stream,
passing north of Jiǎxià Town,
which is commonly called Cāngzǐ City.
It then flows further northeast
and enters the sea.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
With nine bends it flows into the sea,
yet its flow never ceases—
this is the conveyance from Kūnlún.
The "Shàngshū Yǔgòng" says:
Passing right by Jiéshí, it enters the Hé River.
The "Shānhǎijīng" says:
The mountain of Jiéshí,
from it emerges the Shéng River.
Flowing east, it enters the Hé River.
The point where the Hé River enters the sea
was originally at Jiéshí.
But the course of the river today
is not the channel dredged by Yǔ.
In the fifth year of King Dìng of Zhōu,
the Hé River shifted from its old channel.
Therefore, Bān Gù said:
It dried up in the Shāng,
and shifted in the Zhōu.
Also, in the second year of the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the Hé River shifted again to Dōngjùn,
and changed its course to flow into the Bó Sea.
Therefore, the Hàn Dynasty Sīkōng Yuàn Wáng Huáng stated:
In the past,
heaven once brought continuous rain,
with a northeast wind,
the seawater overflowed,
advancing southwestward and flooding several hundred lǐ.
Thus, Zhāng Zhé said:
Jiéshí is in the sea.
It must have sunk into the seawater.
In ancient times, Yān and Qí were vast and distant,
and Yíngzhōu was established there.
Now the city reaches the seashore,
and the seawater encroaches from the north,
so half the city is on the verge of sinking.
The words of Wáng Huáng
are credible and well-founded;
the submergence of Jiéshí into the sea
is not without evidence.
6 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll Six
6.1 Fén River
6.1 Fén River
The Fén River originates from Guǎncén Mountain north of Fényáng County in Tàiyuán.
The "Shānhǎijīng" says:
The beginning of the "Second Northern Classic,"
east of the Hé River,
its head rests on the Fén,
called Guǎncén Mountain.
On its summit there are no trees,
but below there is much jade.
The Fén River emerges from it,
flowing west into the Hé River.
The "Thirteen Provinces Gazetteer" says:
It emerges from Yānjīng Mountain in Wǔzhōu.
This is another name for Guǎncén.
This mountain has layered mounds and long cliffs,
with grass but no trees.
A spring source emerges below the southern foothills,
merely a small, meandering stream.
Further southwest,
the banks are flanked by continuous mountains,
with peaks connecting in succession.
Liú Yuān's nephew Liú Yào once hid in Guǎncén Mountain.
One night, two youths suddenly entered,
knelt and said:
"The King of Guǎncén sends his humble servants to pay respects to the Zhào Emperor."
They presented a sword,
placed it before him,
bowed twice, and left.
By candlelight, he examined it:
the sword was two chǐ long,
with an extraordinary luster.
On the back was an inscription:
"The divine sword commands,
eliminates all poisons."
Yào then wore it.
The sword would change into five colors according to the time,
and later Yào became king of the Hú.
The Fén River flows further south
and joins the East and West Wēn Streams.
The water emerges from nearby streams on the left and right,
their sounds flowing and converging like wings.
On the water, various trees cast intertwined shadows,
clouds hang low, and mist connects.
From here, the water flows into deep pools and swells,
waves surge and swirl.
Further south, it passes east of a city,
which relies on ramparts and piled stones,
and rests beside the Fén River.
Commonly called Dài City.
Further south, it emerges between two cities.
These cities are angled,
resting like wings on the Fén flow,
commonly called Hóumògān City.
This likely comes from a Róng dialect,
and has been mispronounced in transmission.
The Fén River flows further south past the east of the old city of Fényáng County.
The land is broad and flat,
with low hills and gentle waters.
The "Geographical Treatise" says:
The Fén River emerges from the northern mountains of Fényáng County,
flowing southwest.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Jìn Qiáng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Later, agricultural garrisons were established,
and grain was stored here,
called Yángcháng Granary.
The mountain has Yángcháng Slope,
northwest of Jìnyáng.
The stone steps wind around,
like sheep intestines,
hence the granary and slope get their name.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Hàn,
the Hūtuó and Shíjiù Rivers were managed.
According to Sīmǎ Biāo's "Treatise on the Commanderies and States of the Later Hàn,"
Nánxíngtáng County in Chángshān has Shíjiù Valley.
It likely utilized the waters of the Hūtuó River
to transport supplies east of the mountains.
From Dūlǜ to Yángcháng Granary,
they intended to use the Fén River to transport goods to Tàiyuán,
to supply Qín and Jìn.
The labor was arduous for years,
and along the transport route,
there were 389 narrow passes in total,
and countless people died.
Dèng Xùn was appointed as an Attendant,
to oversee the water project.
Xùn assessed and understood the difficulties,
immediately reported in detail to Emperor Sùzōng,
and Emperor Sùzōng followed his advice,
saving the lives of several thousand people.
When Empress Héxī Dèng was established,
her uncle Dèng Gāi believed it was due to Xùn's accumulated good deeds.
Yángcháng refers to this granary.
Further south, it passes east of Xiùróng City.
The "Wèi Land Records" say:
Xiùróng—
the Hú people moved to live here,
and the Xiùróng Protectorate was established.
It is sixty lǐ east of the Fén River.
To the south, it joins the Suān River.
The water source emerges west from Shàoyáng Mountain,
flowing southeast into the Fén River.
The Fén River emerges further south from the mountains,
flowing southeast.
Luòyīn River flows into it.
The water emerges from Xīnxīng Commandery,
flowing west past north of Luòyīn City,
then further west past the old city of Yú County.
In the twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhāo in the "Spring and Autumn Zuǒzhuàn,"
the seven counties of the Qí clan were divided among the senior officials as fiefs,
and Yú Bǐng was made the senior official of Yú.
Luòyīn River flows further west,
past the old city of Lángmèng County.
This is Lángdiào under Wáng Mǎng.
Left and right, deep ravines flank it,
with a great gorge to the south,
commonly called Lángmǎ Ravine.
In the past, the ravine was cut off to form a city,
with southern and northern gates.
The old walls of the gate barriers still remain.
Luòyīn River flows further southwest past north of Yángqū City.
The "Wèi Land Records" say:
Yángqū—
the Hú people settled within Tàiyuán's borders,
and the Yángqū Protectorate was established.
The water flows southwest
and enters the Fén River.
The Fén River flows further south past the southwest of Yángqū City and enters it.
Southeast, it passes east of Jìnyáng County,
and the Jìn River flows from the south of the county eastward into it.
The commandery seat of Tàiyuán Commandery was at Jìnyáng City,
established in the third year of King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín.
This is what the *Shàngshū* refers to as "having already cultivated Tàiyuán."
The *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* says:
A high and level place is called Tàiyuán.
Yuán (原) means
duān (端),
level and having measure.
The *Guǎngyǎ* says:
Dàlǔ (大鹵)
is Tàiyuán.
The *Shìmíng* says:
Land that does not produce living things is called lǔ (鹵).
Lǔ (鹵) means
lú (罏).
The *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* says:
In the Central States it is called Tàiyuán,
among the Yí and Dí tribes it is called Tàilǔ.
The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* says:
The eastern plain was made level,
that which is vast, high, and level is called Tàiyuán,
and the commandery takes its name from this.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* says:
East of the city, the Fén River flows southward.
East of the river is a stele for Jìn's Commissioner with Credentials, Commander of Military Affairs in Bīngzhōu, General Who Guards the North, and Prince Chéng of Tàiyuán.
On the river there was formerly a bridge.
Qīng Pīng perished beneath the bridge,
and Yù Ràng died by the ford's side.
This is also the place where Xiāngzǐ took off his garment.
The Fén River flows west past the south of Jìnyáng City.
There was formerly a shrine for Jiè Zǐtuī.
In front of the shrine was a stele.
The temple buildings have collapsed,
and only a solitary stele remains.
Now the writing is worn away,
and nothing can be discerned.
Further south,
the Dòngguò River comes from the east and flows into it.
The Fén River then flows south past the east of the old city of Gěngyáng County,
which was formerly the Gěngyáng Township of Yúcì.
This was the fief given by Wèi Xiànzǐ to the district magistrate Wèi Wù.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Gěngyáng
was a town of Jìn.
Now, sixty lǐ south of Jìnyáng County in Tàiyuán, within the boundaries of Yúcì, there is Gěngyáng City.
The Fén River flows further south,
and this is where it meets the Dòngguò River.
It then flows south past the east of Dàlíng County.
In the past, King Wǔlíng of Zhào traveled to Dàlíng,
dreamed of a maiden
playing the qín and singing,
and longed to see this person.
Wú Guǎng presented Mèng Yáo,
and this occurred within this county.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Dàníng.
The Fén River, at the left side of the county, meanders to form the Wū Marsh.
The *Guǎngyǎ* says:
Water flowing out from the Fén forms the Fén Embankment.
This embankment is four lǐ from east to west,
and over ten lǐ from north to south.
South of the embankment it connects to Wū.
The *Dìlǐzhì* says:
The Nine Marshes are to the north,
and are the marshlands of Bīngzhōu.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* calls it Dàlù.
It is also called the Ōuyí Marsh,
and commonly known as Wūchéng Marsh.
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuōwén* says:
The Yān River emerges from the northern sands of Zhōngyáng County in Xīhé,
and flows south into the [Yellow] River.
This is that river.
The Yān River also meets the waters of Yīnghóu.
The *Shānhǎijīng* mentions Mount Yèlì,
from whose northern side the waters of Yīnghóu emerge,
flowing north into the Sì River.
The Sì River emerges from Mount Sì.
These waters, though from different sources, share a common course,
and flow into the waters of Yīnghóu.
They then flow turbulently past the south of Zhōngdū County,
and are also commonly called the Zhōngdū River.
The Hóujiǎ River flows into it.
This river originates from Mount Hújiǎ in Qí County.
There is a long slope,
called Hújiǎ Ridge,
which is what Liú Xīn referred to in his *Suìchū Fù* as "crossing Hóujiǎ and driving far."
Cài Yōng said:
Hóujiǎ
is also the name of a town,
located in Qí County.
The Hóujiǎ River then flows northwest past Yísuìjiāo,
passes through Tàigǔ,
and is called the Tàigǔ River.
Emerging from the valley, it flows northwest,
passes by the old city south of Qí County,
and from the county stretches continuously,
connecting west to the Wū Marsh.
This is the Qí Marshland.
It is what the *Ěryǎ* calls Zhāoyúqí.
This was the fief of Jiǎ Xīn.
Xīn was ugly in appearance,
and his wife would not speak to him.
He went with her to Gāo to shoot pheasants,
and when he hit one with a single shot, she laughed.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shì County.
It then flows west past the old city north of Jīnglíng County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Zhìchéng.
In the *Chūnqiū*, this was the region of Jiǔyuán.
Therefore, the *Guóyǔ* says:
Zhào Wénzǐ was traveling with Shūxiàng at Jiǔyuán,
and said:
"If the dead could be revived,
with whom would I associate?"
Shūxiàng said:
"Perhaps with Yángzǐ?"
Wénzǐ said:
"Yángzǐ conducted himself uprightly in Jìn,
yet could not save himself.
His wisdom is not worthy of praise."
Shūxiàng said:
"Perhaps with Jiùfàn?"
Wénzǐ said:
"Jiùfàn, upon seeing advantage, did not consider his lord.
His benevolence is not worthy of praise."
"Shall I then follow Zēng?"
"He accepted remonstrance without forgetting his teacher,
in speech and action he did not fail his friends,
in serving his lord he did not cling to gain advancement,
nor did he flatter to avoid dismissal."
Its old capital still exists.
When Hàn arose,
a mound was added below it,
hence it was called Jīnglíng.
The Hóujiǎ River then flows northwest past the old city south of Zhōngdū County,
the city bordering the water's edge.
In the second year of Duke Zhāo of the *Chūnqiū*,
the Marquis of Jìn detained Chén Wúyǔ at Zhōngdū.
Emperor Wén of Hàn, when he was King of Dài,
made this his capital.
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ,
the emperor visited the Zhōngdū Palace.
Light was seen in the hall,
and he pardoned all in Zhōngdū from capital offenses downward.
The Hóujiǎ River then flows west,
joins with the waters of Yīnghóu,
passes by the old city south of Wū County,
which was the fief of Jìn's senior minister Sīmǎ Mímóu.
It is called the Wū River,
and commonly also called the Lǜ River.
The sounds of lǜ and wū are similar,
hence the change occurred.
It then flows northwest into the Wū Embankment,
and returns to the flow of the Fén.
It then flows south past the east of Píngtáo County,
and the Wén River comes from the west and flows into it.
The Fén River further flows south and joins with the Shítóong River,
which is the Mián River.
The river originates from Mián Mountain in Jièxiū County,
flowing north past the west of Shítóong Temple,
which is the shrine of Jiè Zǐtuī.
In the past, Zǐtuī fled from the reward of Duke Wén of Jìn,
and hid in the mountains of Miánshàng.
Duke Wén of Jìn sought him but could not find him,
so he enfeoffed Mián as Jiè Zǐtuī's fields.
He said:
"To mark my fault,
and to honor a good man."
Thus, this mountain was named Jiè Mountain.
Therefore, Yuán Shānsōng's *Jùn Guó Zhì* states:
Jièxiū County has Jiè Mountain, Miánshàng Settlement, and Zǐtuī Temple.
Wáng Sù's *Sāngfú Yāojì* states:
In the past, Duke Āi of Lǔ held a funeral for his father,
and Confucius asked:
"Should we set up a cassia tree?"
Duke Āi replied:
"No.
The cassia tree
originated from Jiè Zǐtuī.
Zǐtuī
was a man of Jìn.
Duke Wén faced internal troubles,
and left the state for the Dí region.
Zǐtuī followed him on his journey,
cutting his own flesh to sustain the army's provisions.
Later, when Duke Wén restored the state,
he suddenly forgot about Zǐtuī.
Zǐtuī sang while holding a chant,
and Duke Wén then realized
that he should have received titles and emoluments.
Zǐtuī fled to Jiè Mountain,
embraced a tree and burned to death.
The people of the state buried him,
fearing that his spirit might fall to the ground,
so they made a cassia tree.
My father was born in a palace,
and died on a pillow and mat.
What need is there for a cassia tree?"
I note that Confucius even disapproved of using jade for burials,
so how could he ask about the cassia tree as a ritual?
Wáng Sù's evidence here
is close to being false.
The Shítóong River further flows west and empties into the Fén River.
The Fén River further flows southwest past the west of the old city of Jièxiū County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Jièměi.
East of the city are two steles for the recluses Guō Línzōng and Sòng Zǐjùn.
Sòng Chōng was summoned as a virtuous man to the office of Minister of Education,
and Línzōng was a native of the county.
He was appointed to the Ministry of Education,
recommended for the position of Grand Commandant,
but declined due to illness.
His stele inscription states:
"He was about to tread the distant traces of Hóngyá,
to follow the untrammeled paths of Cháo Fú and Xǔ Yóu,
to soar beyond the mundane world with outstretched wings,
to transcend the heavenly path and stand aloft.
His allotted life was not long,
and he lived only forty-two years,
passing away on the dinghài day of the first month in the second year of Jiànníng."
All of us, his friends from all directions,
forever cherish sorrow and pain,
and thus erected a stele to mark his tomb,
to clearly inscribe his shining virtue."
Cài Bójiē from Chénliú, Lú Zǐgàn from Fànyáng, Mǎ Rìdī from Fúfēng, and others
came from afar to mourn,
wearing the attire of friends.
Those who observed a year of heartfelt mourning, such as Hán Zǐzhù, Sòng Zǐjùn, and twenty-four others,
and the remaining disciples who wore coarse mourning garments numbered in the thousands.
Cài Bójiē said to Lú Zǐgàn and Mǎ Rìdī:
"I have written many stele inscriptions for the world,
and all have caused me shame,
but only for Guō Yǒudào,
I feel no shame."
To the right of the Fén River is Zuǒbù City,
situated beside the Fén River,
likely built by Liú Yuān when he was a commandant of Jìn.
Further south, it passes Guānjué Ford,
a ford on the Fén River,
located southwest of Jièxiū County,
commonly known as Quèshǔ Valley.
For tens of lǐ, the road is narrow and perilous,
with cantilevered plank roads built on both sides of the river,
stones piled to form the road,
winding along the cliff sides.
Sometimes it is one zhàng above the water,
sometimes five or six chǐ high,
with mountains above,
and deep ravines below.
It is commonly called the Lǔ Bān Bridge,
likely an ancient strategic ford,
and still a treacherous place today.
Further south, it enters the territory of Hédōng,
then passes west of Yǒng'ān County,
which was formerly Zhì County.
King Lì of Zhōu was exiled to Zhì,
which is this city.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huángchéng,
and in the third year of Yángjiā under Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
it was changed to Yǒng'ān.
The county
was the capital of the Earl of Huò.
Passing east of Tángchéng,
Xuě Zàn's annotation to the *Hànshū* states:
"It was the capital of Yáo."
It is ten lǐ east of Zhì.
The Fén River further flows south and joins with the Zhì River,
which originates from Tàiyuè Mountain in the northeast,
referred to in the *Yǔ Gòng* as Yuèyáng.
This is Huòtài Mountain.
On it is the tomb of Fēilián,
who served King Zhòu for his swift running,
while Èlái was known for his great strength.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked King Zhòu,
he also killed Èlái.
Fēilián had previously been sent north by King Zhòu as an envoy,
and upon returning with no report to make,
he built an altar on Huòtài Mountain and delivered his mandate there.
He obtained a stone coffin,
with an inscription stating:
"The Emperor orders Chǔfù
not to participate in the chaos of Yīn,
and bestows upon you a stone coffin for burial."
He died,
and was thus buried there.
Huòtài Mountain has a temple to the mountain deity,
which is very numinous.
Birds do not roost in its forests,
and fierce tigers often guard its courtyard.
There is also a numinous spring used for sacrifices;
when drums are beaten, the spring flows,
and when the sound ceases, the water dries up.
In Yīnshān County of Xiāngdōng, there is Hóután Mountain,
on which is a numinous altar.
In front of the altar is a stone well several chǐ deep,
usually without water,
but when prayers are offered,
sweet spring water gushes forth,
ceasing once the use is complete.
This is similar to the aforementioned case.
The Zhì River further flows west past the north of Guānfù,
which was formerly Bǎiyì.
Yuán Guò, who followed Xiāngzǐ,
received bamboo texts at Wángzé,
and reported them to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ fasted for three days,
then personally split the bamboo,
finding red writing that said:
"I am the heavenly envoy of the Marquis of Shānyáng of Huòtài Mountain.
On the bǐngxū day of the third month,
I will enable you to counter and destroy the Zhì clan.
You shall also establish me at Bǎiyì."
Xiāngzǐ bowed and accepted the command of the three deities,
then destroyed the Zhì clan,
and made sacrifices to the three deities at Bǎiyì,
putting Yuán Guò in charge.
Later generations called this place Guānfù.
The Zhì River further flows west past the south of the old city of Yǒng'ān County,
then flows southwest,
and empties into the Fén River.
The Fén River further flows south past the east of Huòchéng,
which was the former state of Huò.
In the past, Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed Huò,
with Zhào Sù as his charioteer,
and Duke Huò Qiú fled to Qí.
A great drought struck the state of Jìn,
and divination indicated
that Huòtài Mountain was causing the calamity.
They sent Zhào Sù to summon the lord of Huò to resume sacrifices.
Jìn then regained prosperity.
This was likely the former residence of Duke Huò Qiú.
The Fén River further flows southwest of Zhàochéng,
where King Mù enfeoffed Zàofù,
and the Zhào clan began from here.
The Fén River further flows south,
where the Huò River joins it.
