The river originates from Huòtài Mountain,
forming a deep pool at its source,
spanning seventy steps with unfathomable depth.
It flows southwest past the south of Zhàochéng,
then west into the Fén River.
Further south, it passes east of Yáng County.
The Jiàn River emerges from the Western Mountains of Gǔyuǎn County to the east,
flows southwest past the southern side of Huò Mountain,
and then west past the northern side of the old city of Yáng County.
This was the fief of Liáo Ān, a senior official of Jìn.
Yìng Shào said:
It was the former state of Marquis Yáng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yǒunián Tíng.
This river flows west into the Fén River.
The Fén River passes west of Yáng City,
not to the east.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Píngyáng Commandery had its seat at Yáng County,
and the river flowing south west of the commandery is the Fén River.
(The Fén River) passes southwest west of Gāoliáng Town.
The Hēi River emerges from Hēi Mountain,
flows west past the southern side of Yáng City,
and then west joins the waters of Cháo Mountain.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
From Niúshǒu Mountain,
the Láo River emerges,
flows west and empties into the Jué River.
It is suspected this is that river.
The Jué River,
is the water of Cháo Mountain.
The river's source emerges from the eastern valley of Cháo Mountain to the southeast,
flows north past the east of Fú Mountain,
then northwest and joins the Láo River.
The combined flow runs northwest past the north of Gāoliáng City,
and enters the Fén River to the west.
The Fén River then flows south past the west of the old Gāoliáng City,
the ruins of ancient Gāoliáng.
In the 24th year of Duke Xī of the *Chūnqiū* (636 BCE),
Duke Mù of Qín escorted Prince Chóng'ěr into Jìn,
and killed Duke Huái here.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* records:
In the 13th year of Duke Chū of Jìn (462 BCE),
Zhì Bó Yáo fortified Gāoliáng.
In the 12th year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn (195 BCE), it was made a marquisate,
enfeoffing Marquis Gōng Lì Jiè to this town.
(The Fén River) then passes south east of Píngyáng County.
The Fén River flows south past the west of Báimǎ City.
Wèi sacrificed a white horse when building it,

It is now the seat of Píngyáng Commandery.
The Fén River then flows south past the east of the old city of Píngyáng County.
This was the former fief of Zhào Cháo, a senior official of Jìn.
Yìng Shào said:
The county lies north of the Píng River,

Wèi established Píngyáng Commandery,

By the water is a temple of Yáo,

The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Ten *lǐ* east of Píngyáng City,

South of here, the Fén River joins the Píng River.

The water flows east past the north of Húgǔ Tíng.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
the Dí invaded Jìn

It then flows east past the south of Píngyáng City,

Commoners call it the Jìn River,
but that is incorrect.
The Fén River then flows south past the west of the old city of Xiānglíng County.
This was the fief of Xì Chōu, a senior official of Jìn,

To the northwest is the tomb of Duke Xiāng of Jìn.
The county
was likely named after the tomb.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Gànchāng.
(The Fén River) then passes south east of Línfén County.
The Tiānjǐng River emerges southwest of the Eastern Xíng Mountain.

with an east-west passageway on the ridge,

The *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* states:
On the yǐyǒu day,
the Son of Heaven crossed the Xíngdèng westward,
and arrived southwest at Gǔ. This is the place.

flows northwest,
converges into one stream,
passes west by the south of Yáo City,

(The Fén River) then bends and flows west from the south of the county.
The Fén River passes north of the old city of Jiàng County.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* records:
In the 25th year of King Wǔ of Liáng (444 BCE),
the land in Jiàng split open,
cutting off the west at the Fén River.
The Fén River flows west past the north of the Sīqí Palace.
The Héng River has an old bridge,

Being in the water,
the materials could endure long without decay.
It then flows west past the south of Wèi's Zhèngpíng Commandery,
the former seat of the Eastern Yōng Province.
During the Tàihé era (477-499 CE),
when the imperial capital moved to Luòyáng,
the province was abolished and the commandery established.
It then flows west to where the Huì River enters at Wángzé.
(The Fén River) then passes south of Chángxiū County to the west.
The Fén River then joins the Gǔ River to the west.
The Gǔ River emerges from below Huángfù, west of the old city of Línfén County.
Its source is as large as a wheel,
flows southwest,

then west past the east of Xún City,
the ancient state of Xún.
The *Jíjūn Gǔwén* records:
Duke Wǔ of Jìn destroyed Xún and bestowed it upon Senior Official Yuán.
The Gǔ River then flows southwest into the Fén River.
The Fén River flows southwest past the south of the old city of Chángxiū County.
In the 11th year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn (196 BCE), it was made a marquisate,
enfeoffing Dù Tián.
The Xiū River emerges south of the county,
and flows southwest into the Fén River.
The Fén River flows west past the north of Qīngyuán City,
the former Qīngyáng Tíng.
North of the city is Qīngyuán,
where the Marquis of Jìn held a hunt at Qīngyuán,
and formed three armies.
The Fén River then passes south of Jì Tíng.
In the past, Jiù Jì, while on a mission, passed through the wilds of Jì,
and saw Xì Quē weeding,
with his wife bringing him food.
They treated each other with the respect of guests.
(Jiù Jì) spoke of this to Duke Wén,
who appointed him as a minister,
and restored Jì to him.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Present-day Píshì County in Hédōng has Jì Tíng,
the former capital of the ancient state of Jì.
Dù Yù's *Shì Dì* states:
Northeast of Píshì County in Píngyáng is Jì Tíng,
which is this亭.
The Fén River then joins the Huá River to the west.
The Huá River emerges from Huá Valley in the northern mountains,
flows southwest past the west of an old city,
commonly called Gěngyáng City,
but that is incorrect.
Gěngyáng is in Yúcì, not here.
According to the *Stele of the Former Hàn Prefectural Clerk and Chancellor of Hóu*:
The Hóu clan descended from Cāngjié.
Passing through the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
they divided according to clan names.
Some were prominent in Chǔ and Wèi,
others illustrious in Qí and Qín.
Wěi Sī, a minister of Jìn,
was their descendant.
He received Huáyáng as his fief,
which is present-day Běi Tíng of Púbǎn.
This is that city.
The water flows southwest and empties into the Fén River.
The Fén River passes north of Jì Mountain,
which lies about forty *lǐ* south of the river.
The mountain is twenty *lǐ* from east to west,
thirty *lǐ* from north to south,
and thirteen *lǐ* high.
It is fifteen *lǐ* west of Jiè Mountain.
On the mountain is a temple to Jì,
and at its foot is Jì Tíng.
In the 15th year of Duke Xuān of the *Chūnqiū* (594 BCE),

The Marquis of Jìn marshaled troops at Jì,
to seize territory from the Dí.
(The Fén River) then passes south of Píshì County to the west.
The Fén River flows west past the north of Kuíqiū,
which was the Fāngzé of the Hàn dynasty.
Jiǎ Kuí stated:
According to Hàn law,
sacrifices to the earth were performed every three years.
The Fényīn Fāngzé,
within the marsh there was a square mound,
hence it was called the Fāngzéqiū.
This is Kuíqiū.
Xǔ Shèn’s Shuōwén explains the character as having the radical yì,
with guǐ providing the phonetic.
It is a place name in Línfén, Hédōng,
located north of Jièshān,
which is the Fénshān.
This mountain stands alone,
with a circumference of seventy lǐ,
and a height of thirty lǐ.
Wén Yǐng said it was southeast of Píshì County,
which would be about thirty lǐ away,
but this is incorrect.
Based on current measurements, this mountain is probably over ten lǐ high.
On the mountain there is a spirit temple,
and beside the temple is a numinous spring.
On days of prayer and sacrifice,
the water circulates without diminishing,
and it is also commonly called the Zǐtuī Shrine.
Yáng Xióng’s "Hédōng Fù" says:
The divine carriage moves at a steady pace,
wandering leisurely all around,
to view Jièshān.
I sigh for Duke Wén and pity Tuī,
and admire Great Yǔ at Lóngmén.
The Jìn Tàikāng Jì, Dìdào Jì, and Yǒngchū Jì
all state that Zǐtuī fled and hid on this mountain,
but this is actually incorrect.
I note that the place where Jiè Tuī hid
was Miánshān.
Duke Wén encircled it and designated it
as Jiè Tuī’s fields,
naming the mountain Jièshān.
Dù Yù said:
It is located in Jièxiū County, Xīhé.
The Fén River then flows west past the north of Gěngxiāng City,
which was the capital of the Yīn.
Emperor Zǔyǐ moved here from Xiàng,

hence the preface to the Shū states:
Zǔyǐ’s capital at Gěng was ruined.
Dù Yù said:
It is Gěngxiāng, southeast of Píshì County, Píngyáng.
Pángēng, because Gěng was north of the river
and too close to mountains and rivers,
moved the capital from Gěng to Bó.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed Gěng
and granted it to Zhào Sù.
Later, Xiāngzǐ, along with Hán and Wèi, partitioned Jìn.
Hán Kāngzǐ resided in Píngyáng,
Wèi Huánzǐ made Ānyì his capital,
and they were called the Three Jìn,
this being one of them.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn traveled to Hédōng,
crossed the Fén River,
and composed the "Qiūfēng Cì" upon these waters.
The Fén River then flows west past the south of Píshì County.
The Zhúshū Jìnián records: In the twelfth year of King Xiāng of Wèi,
the Qín nobleman Gōngsūn Yuán led troops to attack us,
besieging Píshì.
Dí Zhāng led troops to relieve the siege of Píshì,
but was hindered by the west wind.
In the thirteenth year,
the walls of Píshì were built.
Pān Xì, Governor of Hédōng during the Hàn, channeled the Fén River to irrigate Píshì County.
The old canal still exists,
but now has no water.
Further west, it reaches Fényīn County,
and flows north then west into the Yellow River.
South of the water is a long ridge,
with its back to the Fén and facing the river.
The ridge is four or five lǐ long,
over two lǐ wide,
and ten zhàng high.
The Fén River passes along its northern side,
and enters the Yellow River to the west.
The Hànshū calls it the Fényīn Shuí.
Yìng Shào said:
Shuí
is a type of mound.
Gōngsūn Xiáng, a man from Fényīn, observed the vapors,
and saw the essence of a treasure ascending.
Xiáng reported this to Emperor Wǔ,
and Emperor Wǔ obtained a precious tripod from the water.
It was moved to the Gānquán Palace,
and the era name was changed to Yuándǐng,
all because of this place.
6.2 Huì River
6.2 Huì River
The Huì River originates from the Gāoshān east of Huìjiāo, east of Jiàng County in Hédōng.
The Huì River flows east from Jiànggāo Mountain,
also known as Hénán Mountain,
and also called Huì Mountain.
It passes west by the south of Yì City.
According to the "Shī Pǔ,"
Jìn Mùhóu moved the capital to Jiàng,
and by the time of his grandson Xiàohóu,
Jiàng was renamed Yì,
as Yì was the old capital of Jìn.
Later, Xiàngōng expanded the city to the north,
making it two lǐ square,
and again named it Jiàng.
Therefore, Simǎ Qiān's "Historical Records Chronological Tables" states,
in the ninth year of Xiàngōng,
the construction of the capital Jiàng began.
In the "Zuǒ Zhuàn," the twenty-sixth year of Duke Zhuāng,
it is recorded that the Jìn official Shì Wěi fortified Jiàng and deepened its palace.
The river then flows southwest and joins the Black Water,
which originates from the Black Water Valley to the northeast,
flows southwest past the north of Yì City,
and draws in the North River Water from the right,
which emerges from the flat plains,
flows south and joins it,
then mingles and flows southwest into the Huì River.
The Huì River then flows southwest and converges with several other waters,
called Huìjiāo.
The "Bamboo Annals" states:
In the twelfth year of Zhuāngbó;
the Marquis of Yì burned the crops of Qūwò and returned,
acting on behalf of Wéngōng.
There is also the Hè River,
which emerges from the eastern near plains,
flows southwest to Huìjiāo and enters the Huì River.
There is also the Gāoquán River,
which emerges from the southeastern near plains,
flows northwest toward Huìjiāo and joins the Huì River.
Further south,
the Zǐgǔ River emerges east from Báimǎ Mountain's Báimǎ River.
The "Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú" states:
Jiàng Mountain extends east to Báimǎ Mountain.
This refers to that mountain.
It passes west by Yíngtíng City,
then exits west through Zǐgǔ,
and joins the Gān River,
which is a tributary of the Jiào River.
The "Historical Records: Bái Qǐ Biography" states,
crossing the river to capture Hán's Ānyì,
and reaching east to the Gān River.
This water then joins the Tiánchuān River to the west,
which emerges from the eastern stream,
flows northwest to Huìjiāo and enters the Huì River.
There is also the Yújiā River, emerging from Yújiā Valley.
The "Bamboo Annals" states:
Zhuāngbó rebelled with Qūwò,
attacked Yì,
and Gōngzǐ Wàn came to rescue Yì,
while Xún Shū Zhěn pursued him to Yújiā Valley.
There is the Fànbì River emerging from below the cliffs,
flowing northwest together,
to Yìguǎng City.
In the past, when the Jìn army entered from the north,
Yìguǎng fortified it,
and thus named it after his surname.
The two rivers converge and flow northwest;
to Huìjiāo and enter the Huì River.
The Huì River then flows southwest and joins the Jiàng River,
commonly called the White River,
but this is incorrect.
The water emerges east of Jiàng Mountain,
with cold springs gushing forth,
sending waves northward,
cascading down into the ravines,
about ten zhang high.
The green cliffs appear like dots of ink,
the white rapids like unrolled silk,
making it an extremely wondrous sight.
This water flows northwest and joins the Huì River.
Yìng Shào said:
The Jiàng River is southwest of Jiàng County's mountain,
likely referring to the old Jiàng.
The "Historical Records" states,
Zhì Bó led Hán and Wèi to divert water to flood Jìnyáng,
leaving only three planks above water.
Zhì said:
I did not know before that water could destroy a state,
but now I know.
The Fén River could flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River could flood Píngyáng.
At that time,
Hán resided in Píngyáng,
and Wèi's capital was Ānyì,
Wèi Huánzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Hán Kāngzǐ stepped on Wèi Huánzǐ's foot,
their elbows and feet touching in the carriage,
and thus the Zhì clan perished.
Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked,
can a single word cause a state to perish,
is there such a thing?
Confucius thought it nearly so,
and I have seen Zhì's words,
the Fén River flooding Ānyì,
perhaps that happened;
but the Jiàng River flooding Píngyáng,
I do not know the reason.
It passes west by the south of the county,
In the "Spring and Autumn Annals," the sixth year of Duke Chéng,
Jìn Jǐnggōng planned to leave the old Jiàng,
wanting to reside in Xúnxiá.
Hán Xiànzǐ said:
The land is thin and the water shallow,
not as good as Xīntián,
where the Fén and Huì rivers carry away impurities.
So they settled in Xīntián.
It was also called Jiàng,
that is, Jiàngyáng.
Likely because it was north of the Jiàng and Huì rivers.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Huà Wúhài, the General of the Rapid Cavalry, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The county faces Jiàng Mountain to the south,
with two rivers before and behind.
The "Ancient Texts and Trivial Sayings" states:
Jìn Pínggōng and Qí Jǐnggōng rode to the banks of the Huì River,
and saw eight white-horsed chariots approaching,
with a large creature having a fox's tail and a wildcat's body,
following Pínggōng's carriage.
The duke asked Shī Kuàng,
who replied it was the god of Shǒuyáng,
with a wildcat's body and a fox's tail,
named Zhě,
who brings fortune when wine is offered,
and thus they made offerings,
likely by this river.
It then flows southwest past the south of Sīqí Palace,
which is forty lǐ west of the old city of Xīntián Jiàng County,
built by Jìn Pínggōng.
At that time, stones spoke in Wèiyú,
and the Marquis of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng about it,
Kuàng said:
Stones cannot speak,
but perhaps something possesses them.
I have heard that,
when actions are untimely,
and resentment stirs among the people,
then non-speaking things may speak.
Now the palaces are extravagant,
the people's strength exhausted,
is it not fitting that stones speak?
Shū Xiàng considered Zǐyě's words,
those of a gentleman.
As for the palace,
it faces the Fén River with its back to the Huì River,
and to the west is where the two rivers converge.
The "Bamboo Annals" states;
In the fifth year of Jìn Chūgōng,
the Huì River ceased at Liáng.
This is that river.

and empties into the Fén River.
When Jìn's Zhì Bó Yáo attacked Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Xiāngzǐ fled to defend Jìnyáng,
and Yuán Guò arrived later,
encountering three people at this marsh,
invisible from the waist down,
who gave Yuán Guò two sections of bamboo,
saying:
Deliver these to Wúxù for me.
Yuán Guò received them at this marsh,
which is called Wáng Marsh.
6.3 The Sù River
6.3 The Sù River
The Sù River emerges from the Shǔjiā Valley on the eastern mountains of Wénxǐ County in Hédōng.
The Sù River originates from here,
commonly known as Huá Valley.
It reaches Zhōuyáng and merges with the Táo River,
whose source flows east from Qīngyě Mountain.
People consider it to be Qīngxiāng Mountain.
Its waters flow east past the foot of the great ridge,
then flow westward out, called the Hán Pass.
Further west, it joins the Sù River.
Zhèng sent Zǐchǎn to inquire about Duke Píng of Jìn's illness.
Duke Píng said:
"The divination says Táitái is the cause of the haunting."
The historians do not know,
I dare to ask.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Gāoxīnshì had two sons,
the elder was Èbó,
the younger was Shíchén.
They could not tolerate each other.
The Emperor moved Èbó to Shāngqiū,
and moved Shíchén to Dàxià.
Táitái,
a descendant of Shíchén,
was able to continue his official duties.
The Emperor praised him for this,
and granted him a state in the Fén River region.
From this, it can be seen that
Táitái
is the deity of the Fén and Táo Rivers."
Jiǎ Kuí said the Fén and Táo
are the names of two rivers.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
"The Táo River originates from Wénxǐ County,
hence Wáng Mǎng designated the county as Táo Pavilion."
Then, could the Sù River also be a combined name for the Táo River?
Flowing west past the south of Zhōuyáng Town,
its southern side faces the Sù River,
and its northern side leans against the mountain plain.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xiàn of Jìn, in the first month,
the Dí people attacked Jìn,
and a white rabbit danced in the market of Zhōu.
This is the town.
Emperor Jǐng of Hàn enfeoffed Tián Shèng as a marquis here.
The Sù River flows west past the south of Dǒngzé Marsh,
which is the ancient pond,
four lǐ from east to west,
and three lǐ from north to south.
In the sixth year of Duke Wén of "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
"a hunt was conducted at Dǒng,"
referring to this marsh.
The Sù River also merges with the Jǐng River,
which originates from the northern valley of Jǐng Mountain.
"The Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"From Jǐng Mountain, one can look south to the Salt Merchant's Marsh,
and north to Shǎo Marsh.
Its grasses are mostly shǔyù and qínjiāo,
its northern side is rich in ochre,
and its southern side is rich in jade."
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"The Salt Merchant's Marsh is the salt pond of Xiè County."
According to the "Classic," it does not mention water,
but now there is water there.
It flows northwest
and empties into the Sù River.
Further southwest, it passes the south of Zuǒyì County.
The Sù River flows west past the north of Zhòngyóu Township,
and then west past the north of Tóngxiāng City.
The "Bamboo Annals" says:
"The Marquis of Yì attacked Qǔwò,
achieved a great victory.
Duke Wǔ sought peace with Yì,
and returned upon reaching Tóng."
"The Book of Hàn" says:
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ,
when he was about to visit Gōushì,
upon reaching Tóngxiāng in Zuǒyì,
he heard that Nányuè had been defeated,
and designated it as Wénxǐ County.
The Sù River further merges with the Shāqú River to the west,
which originates from the nearby streams to the southeast,
and flows northwest into the Sù River.
The Sù River flows southwest past the old city of Zuǒyì County,
which was formerly Qǔwò.
Duke Wǔ of Jìn moved here from Jìnyáng.
Qín renamed it Zuǒyì County.
This is what "The Book of Songs" sighs about, "following you to Hú."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
"A lower state has ancestral temples,
it is called a state."
In Jiàng, it is called the lower state,
which is Xīnchéng.
It was Wáng Mǎng's Táo Pavilion.
The Sù River flows past the west of the city,
its current swift and deep,
with no gentle fords.
Thus, the poet called it the "rushing waters,"
meaning it could not carry away bundled firewood.
By the water's side,
is where Hú Tū encountered Shēnshēng.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
In autumn,
Hú Tū went to the lower state,
and encountered the crown prince.
The crown prince made him ascend as his attendant and said:
"Yíwú has been disrespectful.
I have requested the Emperor to give him to Qín."
He replied:
"Spirits do not enjoy offerings from those not of their kind.
You should consider this."
The lord said, "Agreed.
Please meet me in seven days at the western side of Xīnchéng."
When the time came, he went
and met him at this place.
Thus, "The Annals" says that where ghosts and spirits rely,
there are times when they are trustworthy.
The Sù River flows west past the north of Wángguān City,
which is located on the southern plain.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals: Zuǒzhuàn," in the thirteenth year of Duke Chéng, fourth month,
records: The Marquis of Jìn sent Lǚ Xiàng to break with Qín, saying:
"Kāng still does not repent,
entered our Héqū,
attacked our Sù River region,
and captured our Wángguān."
Thus, the Battle of Héqū occurred.
Today, people still call this city Wángchéng.
Further southwest, it passes the west of Ānyì County.
Ānyì was the capital of Yǔ.
Yǔ married a woman of the Túshān clan,
who, longing for her homeland,
had a terrace built to gaze toward it.
Today, south of the city gate,
the terrace foundation still remains.
I note that according to the Rites,
for the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,
the gates, terraces, corners, and eaves merely descended in rank accordingly;
it need not have been exactly as recorded in the historical texts.
Thus, it was a city of Jìn.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Wèi Jiàng moved here from Wèi.
In the past, Lord Wén hung Shī Jīng’s qín at its gate,
using it as a warning against careless speech.
In the second year of Lord Wǔ’s reign,
Ānyì was again fortified,
likely expanded.
The First Emperor of Qín dispatched the Left Gēng and Bái Qǐ to capture Ānyì,
establishing the Hédōng Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Táoduì,
and the county was called Hédōng.
There was Xiàng Níngdū,
who studied the Way and ascended as an immortal,
but suddenly returned here;
in Hédōng, he was called the Rejected Immortal.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was also Mǐn Zhòngshū,
who lived in seclusion within the city,
known to few.
Later, he left after being recognized.
The Sù River flows southwest past the old city of Jiānyán County.
South of the city is the Salt Pond,
which receives water from the Salt River.
The river originates from the Bó Mountain in the southeast,
flowing northwest past the north of Wūxián Mountain.
The Geographical Records states:
The mountain lies south of Ānyì County.
The Classic of Regions Beyond the Seas: West says:
The country of Wūxián is north of Nǚchǒu,
with the right hand holding a green snake,
and the left hand holding a red snake,
at Dēngbǎo Mountain,
where the group of shamans ascend and descend.
The Classic of the Great Wilderness: West says,
within the great wilderness lies the Spiritual Mountain,
where the ten shamans—Wūxián, Wūjí, Wūfēn, Wūpéng, Wūgū, Wūzhēn, Wūlǐ, Wūdǐ, Wūxiè, and Wūluó—
ascend and descend from here,
and all medicinal herbs are found here.
Guō Jǐngchún says:
This means the group of shamans ascend and descend the Spiritual Mountain,
gathering herbs back and forth.
It is where divine shamans roam,
hence the mountain derives its name.
At the valley mouth on the ridge,
there is a shrine to Wūxián.
The river then flows past the old city of Ānyì,
and further west empties into the Salt Pond.
The Geographical Records states:
The Salt Pond lies southwest of Ānyì.
Xǔ Shèn calls it gǔ.
It is fifty-one lǐ long,
seven lǐ wide,
and one hundred sixteen lǐ in circumference.
The character derives from the radical for salt, with the ancient phonetic component.
Lǚ Chén says:
Sùshā first began boiling sea salt,
and the salt pond in Hédōng is called gǔ.
Today, the pond measures seventy lǐ east to west,
and seventeen lǐ north to south.
Its water is purple, clear, and still,
deep and stagnant.
The water produces rock salt,
naturally forming in imprints.
It is gathered in the morning and replenished by evening,
never diminishing.
Only when mountain floods suddenly arrive,
or heavy rains cause overflowing torrents,
does the salt pond diminish.
Therefore, both public and private efforts block the watercourses,
preventing excessive flooding.
This is called the Salt River,
also known as the Blocked River.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas calls it the Marsh of Salt Traders.
South of the marsh are layered mountains,
with towering cliffs and elegant clouds,
deep valleys and profound abysses.
The cliffs stand steep on both sides,
leaving no space for a carriage track.
This is called the Stone Gate.
A path runs through it,
named the Passage.
It leads south to Shàngyáng,
and north reaches the Salt Marsh.
West of the pond is another pond,
called the Female Salt Marsh.
It measures twenty-five lǐ east to west,
and twenty lǐ north to south,
located south of the old city of Yīshì.
In the sixth year of Duke Chéng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìn planned to abandon the old Jiàng.
The senior officials said:
Xún and Xiá
have fertile land near the gǔ.
Fú Qián says:
Level land with irrigation is called fertile;
gǔ refers to the salt pond.
The local custom involves channeling water to soak hemp,
distributing it across the fields.
When the water in the plots evaporates,
salt naturally forms on the soil.
This is the so-called xiáncuó,
but it tastes bitter.
It is called the Salt Fields.
The names salt and gǔ
originate from this.
Originally, it was the seat of the Salt Commandant,
who commanded over a thousand troops to guard it.
King Mù of Zhōu and Emperor Zhāng of Hàn both visited Ānyì to view the salt pond.
Thus, Dù Yù says:
Yīshì has a salt pond.
Later, the commandant’s office was abolished,
and Yīshì and Ānyì were divided,
establishing counties to guard them.
It then passes south of Xiè County to the east,
and flows southwest into Zhāngyáng Pond.
The Sùshuǐ River flows further west past the north of the old city of Yīshì County.
In the seventh year of Duke Wén of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìn defeated Qín at Línghú,
advancing as far as Kūshǒu.
Xiān Miě fled to Qín,
and Shì Huì followed him.
Kàn Yīn stated:
"Línghú is Yīshì."
Kūshǒu lies thirty lǐ to the west.
South of the county, it faces a marsh,
which is the former residence of Yī Dùn.
The Kǒng Cóng says:
Yī Dùn
was a poor scholar of Lǔ.
When he farmed, he was often hungry;
when he raised silkworms, he was often cold.
Hearing of Lord Zhū's wealth,
he went to ask him about his methods.
Lord Zhū told him:
"If you wish to become rich quickly,
you should raise five female animals."
Thereupon, he went to Xīhé,
and greatly raised cattle and sheep south of Yīshì.
Within ten years,
his profits were beyond calculation,
his wealth rivaling that of kings and dukes.
His fame spread across the land,
and he prospered in wealth at Yīshì.
Hence he was called Yī Dùn.
The Sùshuǐ River flows further west past Xúnchéng.
The Book of Songs says, "The Earl of Xún comforted them,"
likely referring to this old state.
Dù Yuánkǎi's Explanation of Places in the Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"Northwest of present-day Xiè County is Xúnchéng."
Fú Qián said:
"The state of Xún was east of Xiè County,
the ruins of the Xúnxiá clan."
I, based on the Bamboo Annals, note that
in the fourteenth year of Duke Huì of Jìn,
Duke Mù of Qín led troops to escort Prince Chóng'ěr,
besieged Línghú,
and Sāngquán and Jiùcuī both surrendered to the Qín army.
Hú Máo and Xiān Zhěn resisted Qín,
advancing as far as Lúliǔ.
Then they addressed Duke Mù of Qín,
sending Prince Zhí to come
and speak with the army about withdrawal.
They encamped at Xún,
and made a covenant in the army.
Jīng Xiàngfán's Names of Lands in the Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"Sāngquán and Jiùcuī are both southeast of Xiè."
It does not mention Xiè,
indicating they did not reach Xiè.
It can be seen that the text of the Spring and Autumn Annals
does not differ from the Bamboo Annals.
Now, twenty-four lǐ northeast of the old city of Xiè is an ancient city,
northwest of the old city of Yīshì.
Local custom names it Xúnchéng.
Examining Fú Qián's explanation,
it also matches local custom,
which is better than Dù's single text and isolated evidence.
The Sùshuǐ River flows further southwest past the south of the old city of Xiè County.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals,
when Duke Huì of Jìn returned to his state with Qín's help,
he promised Qín five cities beyond the river,
including Xièliáng within,
which is this city.
The Sùshuǐ River flows further southwest past Xiáchéng,
the old town of the Jìn minister Zhān Jiā.
In the thirtieth year of Duke Xī of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Qín
and Jìn besieged Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng sent Zhú Zhīwǔ to say to Duke Mù of Qín:
"Jìn promised you Jiāo and Xiá,
yet they set up defenses by evening after crossing in the morning."
Jīng Xiàngfán said: "Five lǐ southwest of present-day Xiè County in Hédōng is the old Xiáchéng."
The Sùshuǐ River flows further southwest past the east of Zhāngyángchéng.
The Bamboo Annals record:
"The Qí army pursued the Zhèng crown prince Chǐ,
who fled to the southern Zhèng of Zhāngchéng."
This is what the Book of Han calls Dōngzhāng.
In the second year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Cáo Shēn, acting as Left Chancellor,
separately joined Hán Xìn in attacking eastward.
The Wèi general Sūn Sù's army was at Dōngzhāng,
where they were utterly defeated.
Sū Lín said:
"It belongs to Hédōng,
and is this city."
The Sùshuǐ River flows further southwest and joins a marsh.
The marsh divides into two parts.
South of the city are two marshes,
with wetlands on the left and right.
The eastern marsh is commonly called Jìnxīng Marsh,
twenty-five lǐ from east to west,
eight lǐ from north to south,
facing Yándàoshān to the south.
To its west are stone cliffs a thousand xún high;
to the east, the Pánxī gorge is ten thousand rèn deep.
Square ridges coil among the clouds;
strange peaks rise like rosy clouds.
Solitary summits stand out beautifully,
overarching the tops of the mountain ranges.
Verdant pines shade the peaks;
clear springs bathe the summits.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"What the world calls 'mandarin duck broth'"
emerges above and flows hidden below.
Its summit is level and square,
and fine medicinal herbs grow there.
The Shénnóng's Materia Medica says:
"The land has species such as gùhuó, nǚshū, tóngyún, and zǐwǎn."
Therefore, black-robed thinkers of the profound
and deer-skin-clad seekers of unity
have journeyed there in successive generations.
The path emerges from the northern peaks,
often extremely precipitous.
Those coming and going all grasp vines and climb the heights,
seeking kudzu to descend into the depths.
To the east are linked trees;
one must ascend a hundred steps before descending beside the cliffs.
Traces of rope and chain
still remain today,
hence it is also called Bǎitī Shān (Hundred-Step Mountain).
The water flows north from the mountain for five lǐ and then disappears underground,
said to connect hiddenly with the marsh wetlands,
though this is not clearly understood.
The western marsh is Zhāngzé.
It lies fifteen lǐ northwest of Púbǎn,
twenty lǐ from east to west,
and four or five lǐ from north to south.
It accumulates water in both winter and summer,
though its level sometimes rises and falls.
6.4 Wénshuǐ
6.4 Wénshuǐ
The Wénshuǐ River originates from Wéngǔ in the western mountains of Dàlíng County,
flows east to that county,
turns south to the northeast of Píngtáo County,
and then flows east into the Fén River.
The Wénshuǐ flows past the west of the old city of Dàlíng County and then southward,
where the Mìshuǐ flows into it.
Southwest of the county at the foot of the mountain,
the Wǔ family dug a well for water supply.
The well was extremely deep,
but one day, the water overflowed onto level ground
and flowed southeast into the Wénshuǐ.
The Wénshuǐ then flows south past the east of the old city of Píngtáo County,
passes west through the city,
and flows south out of the outer walls.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Duōráng.
The Wénshuǐ continues south past the county,
where it meets the Yǐnquán mouth on the right.
The water originates from the summit of Yèquán Mountain.
It is commonly said that
when rain is delayed in season,
people come here to pray and supplicate,
hence the mountain got its name,
though the details are unclear.
The mountain's cliffs are perilously steep,
standing firm as if reaching the heavens.
Halfway up the cliff, there is a stone,
about fifty zhang above the ground.
Layered pines adorn the rocks,
and rows of cypresses offer a picturesque view.
Only on the western side is there a place where one can ascend by steps.
On the summit, there is a level area of about ten qǐng,
where the monk Shì Sēngguāng built two temples.
A spring emerges between the two temples,
flows east over the rocks,
and descends along the mountain.
Further east,
the waterway becomes hidden and does not flow consistently,
hence the name Yǐnquán (Hidden Spring).
When rainfall is abundant,
it flows into the Wénshuǐ.
The Wénshuǐ then flows south past the east of the old city of Zīshì County, forming Wén Lake,
which is fifteen lǐ from east to west
and thirty lǐ from north to south.
It is commonly called West Lake,
located ten lǐ directly east of the county.
On the western side of the lake,
there is another city by the lake,
called Zhūchéng.
Where water gathers is called dū,
also called zhū,
so the city is named after the water.
Wén Lake then flows east past the east of the old city of Zhōngyáng County.
According to the "Jìnshū Dìdào Jì" and "Tàikāng Dì Jì,"
there is a Zhōngyáng City in Xīhé,
which was an old county.
The Wénshuǐ then flows southeast,
merging with the Shèngshuǐ.
The Shèngshuǐ originates from Húqí Mountain in the west,
flows east past the south of Liùbì City,
where the Wèi dynasty once established six fortifications below it
to defend against various Hú tribes from Líshí,
making it a major garrison.
During the Tàihé period, the garrison was abolished,
and the Xīhé Commandery was established instead.
The Shèngshuǐ then flows east and merges with Yángquán Shuǐ,
which originates from Yáng Creek in the western mountains,
flows east past the north of Liùbì City,
and then flows southeast into the Shèngshuǐ.
The Shèngshuǐ then flows east past the south of the old Zhōngyáng City,
and further east merges with the Wénshuǐ.
The Wénshuǐ then flows southeast
and enters the Fénshuǐ.
6.5 Yuángōng Shuǐ
6.5 Yuángōng Shuǐ
Yuángōng Shuǐ originates from Yángtóu Mountain west of Zīshì County,
flows east past the north of the county.
The county
was originally established during the Qín dynasty.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn later enfeoffed Yíyáng Hóu Yīng as a marquis here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zītóng.
In the second year of the Huángchū era of Wèi,
Tàiyuán was divided,
and the Xīhé Commandery was reestablished.
During the Jìn dynasty, Chén Wáng Bīn was moved and enfeoffed in Xīhé,
so the county has a temple for Xīhé Mù Wáng Sīmǎ Zǐzhèng.
The inscription reads:
"Xīhé was originally located in mountainous forests.
During the late Hàn turmoil,
the people lost their homes.
When Wèi rose,
the territory was expanded,
and four counties were carved out of Tàiyuán
to form this commandery,
which lies by the mountains and borders the frontier."
The king, in the third year of Xiánníng,
had his fiefdom changed,
and in the twelfth month of the following year, the state was lost.
Officials such as Tàinóng Yán Chóng and Líshí Lìng Zōng Qún, along with 234 others,
carved a stone and erected a stele
to commemorate his merits and virtue.
North of the stele, the temple foundation still remains.
Further east, it enters the Fénshuǐ.
The water flows into Wén Lake
and does not reach the Fénshuǐ.
6.6 Dòngguò Shuǐ
6.6 Dòngguò Shuǐ
Dòngguò Shuǐ originates from the northern mountains of Zhān County.
The water flows westward,
merging with Nánxī Shuǐ,
which originates from the southern mountains,
flows northwest, and enters Dòngguò Shuǐ.
Dòngguò Shuǐ then flows northwest,
where Hēishuǐ emerges from the western mountains.
Three sources converge
into a single stream,
which flows east and then turns south,
passing east of the old city of Shòuyáng County.
According to the "Jìn Tàikāng Dì Jì,"
Lèpíng Commandery had a Shòuyáng County,
which is the place mentioned in Lú Chén's "Zhēngjiān Fù": "Passing Shòuyáng and gathering the reins."
The water then flows southwest into Dòngguò Shuǐ.
Dòngguò Shuǐ continues west,
where Púshuǐ emerges from Pú Valley in the south,
flows north, and enters it.
Dòngguò Shuǐ then flows west and merges with Yuánguò Shuǐ,
which is near the source of Biànshuǐ.
On a western hill, there is a Yuánguò Shrine.
It is said that he embraced the Way and harmonized with the spirits,
receiving a book from a heavenly envoy.
His deep feelings endured through the ages,
and his legacy was passed down to later generations.
Although the building has collapsed,
the clustered trees remain lush,
hence the water is named after him.
The water flows south
and enters Dòngguò Shuǐ.
It flows west past the south of Yúcì County,
and further west reaches the south of Jìnyáng County.
Yúcì County
was originally Túshuǐ Township,
the fief of the Jìn minister Zhì Xúwú.
In the eighth year of Duke Zhāo of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the Marquis of Jìn built the Sīqí Palace,
and stones were said to speak in Wèiyú of Jìn.
Fú Qián said that Wèi
was a Jìn town;
Yú
was the name of a district.
The "Hànshū" says:
"Yúcì."
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" considers it Túyáng County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Tàiyuán Tíng.
South of the county by the water, there is a Záo Terrace,
where Hán and Wèi killed Zhì Bó Yáo below it,
gutting him, severing his intestines,
and breaking his neck and jaw.
The water then flows southwest,
passing northwest of Wǔguàn City.
Lú Chén's "Zhēngjiān Fù" says:
"Passing the old outer walls of Wǔguǎn,
inquiring about the distance of the road."
Dòngguò Shuǐ then flows southwest, forming Chún Lake,
also called Dòngguò Marsh.
South of the marsh,
Túshuǐ flows into it.
The water originates from Tú Valley in Dàqiǎn Mountain northeast of Yángyì,
flows southwest past the south of Luómó Pavilion,
and merges with Jiǎnggǔ Shuǐ,
which originates from Jiǎng Creek southeast of the county.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
"From Jìnyáng City, 110 lǐ southeast to the mountains, there is the Jiǎng Valley main road,
crossing Xuānchē Ridge,
leading to Wǔxiāng."
The water flows northwest from Jiǎng Creek,
passing west of Jīchéng.
In the thirty-third year of Duke Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the people of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jī.
Dù Yù's "Shì Dì" says:
"The city is south of Yángyì."
North of the water is the old city of Yángyì County.
The "Zhúshū Jìnián" says:
"In the ninth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
it was associated with Hándān, Yúcì, and Yángyì."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Fánráng.
Jiǎng Creek then flows west and merges with Túshuǐ,
forming a chaotic flow northwest into Dòngguò Marsh.
It flows west into the Fénshuǐ,
which is the lower outlet of Jìnshuǐ.
When Liú Kūn was in Bìngzhōu,
Liú Yào led troops to intercept him,
and they battled at Dòngguò,
which is this water.
6.7 Jìnshuǐ
6.7 Jìnshuǐ
Jìnshuǐ originates from Xuánwèng Mountain west of Jìnyáng County.
The county,
was originally the state of Táng.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒ Zhuàn* state that before Shū Yú of Táng was born,
his mother, Yì Jiāng, dreamed that the Emperor said to her:
"I name your son Yú,
and will give him Táng,
entrusting him to the constellation Shēn."
When he was born,
he was named Yú.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
Shū Yú was living with King Chéng,
who plucked a paulownia leaf to make a ceremonial jade tablet,
and handing it to him said:
"I use this to enfeoff you."
Yú reported this to the Duke of Zhōu,
who requested:
"Is the Son of Heaven enfeoffing Yú?"
The King said:
"I was only joking."
The Duke said:
"The Son of Heaven has no joking words."
At that time, Táng had been extinguished,
so he was enfeoffed in Táng.
The county had the Jìn River,
and it was later renamed Jìn.
Therefore, Zǐ Xià, in his preface to the *Shī*, refers to this Jìn,
and calls it Táng,
frugal and practicing the rites,
retaining the legacy customs of Yáo.
The *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* and the *Shísān Zhōu Zhì* both say the Jìn River emerges from Lóng Shān,
also named Jiéchú Shān,
located northwest of the county,
but this is incorrect.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
from Xuánwèng Zhī Shān,
the Jìn River emerges,
which is now southwest of the county.
In the past, Zhì Bó dammed the Jìn River to flood Jìnyáng.
The river course flowed upstream from there,
and later people followed his traces,
storing the water to form a pond.
West of the pond, bordering the mountains and resting against the water,
stands the temple of Shū Yú of Táng.
Beside the water is a cool hall,
with a flying bridge constructed over the water.
