Further east, it reaches west of Chéngshì County,
where it divides into two branches:
In the thirty-first year of Duke Xī in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the land of Cáo was divided, extending east to the Jǐ River.
From here, the Jǐ River flows northeast,
emerging from the Great Marsh.
One branch flows southeast,
while the other flows northeast from the county,
entering the Jùyě Marsh.
To the south is the Hé Shuǐ,
to the north is the Jì Dú,
which passes by Chéngshì County and joins the Jì Qú and Pú Qú.
The Northern Jì flows north from Jìyáng County,
then northeast past the south of Zhǔzǎo City.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* states:
Yuānqú County has Zhǔzǎo City,
which is this place.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Gé Zhū was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Northern Jì then flows northeast past the north of the old city of Yuānqú County,
then northeast past the south of the old city of Lǚdū County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Qídū.
It then flows northeast past the north of the old city of Dìngtáo County.
In the sixth year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
because the Jì Shuǐ emerged north of it
and flowed east, branching at Liáng in Dìngtáo,
the state of Jìyīn was established,
named with reference to the Northern Jì.
It then flows northeast and joins the Pú Shuǐ.
This waterway receives the Jì Shuǐ at Fēngqiū County,
which is what the *Dìlǐ Zhì* calls the Pú Qú Shuǐ, whose head receives the Jì.
Kǎn Yīn said:
It first receives a separate branch of the Jì,
namely the Northern Jì.
Its old channel flows northeast from the Jì,
diverging left to form the Gāoliáng Bēi,
three *lǐ* square.
The Pú Shuǐ then flows east past the north of Kuāng City,
where Confucius, leaving Wèi for Chén,
encountered danger at Kuāng.
It then flows northeast,
where on the left it meets a separate branch of the Pú,
which receives water from the Hé at Suānzǎo County.
Thus Dù Yù stated:
The Pú Shuǐ emerges at Suānzǎo County,
first receiving the Hé.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* states:
In the tenth year, tenth month of King Xiāng of Wèi,
there was heavy continuous rain and fierce winds,
and the Hé River overflowed the outer wall of Suānzǎo.
It was blocked in the Hàn era,
hence Bān Gù's phrase "the writing blocked the Zǎo wilderness."
Now it has no water.
Its old channel flows northeast between the southern and northern Díchéng cities.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn*, fifth year of Duke Xiāng,
states: When Chǔ's Zǐ Náng attacked Chén,
the duke met at Chéngdí to rescue it.
The Pú Qú then flows northeast past the south of the old city of Suānzǎo County,
which belonged to the state of Hán.
Juàn Chēng said:
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven established states and named capitals,
sometimes using commendable names,
sometimes using mountains and forests.
Thus Yùzhāng took its name from a tree for the commandery,
and Suānzǎo took its name from the jujube tree for the region,
hence called Suānzǎo.
The *Hàn Guān Yí* states:
The former Riverbank Attendant resided west of the city.
West of it is the Hán King's Qì-observing Terrace.
Sūn Zǐjīng's "Preface to the Ode on the Old Terrace" says:
Outside the temple gate of Suānzǎo,
flanking the road on both sides are two old terraces.
Inquiring of the elders, they said:
They are the Hán King's Tribunal Terrace,
fifteen *ren* high.
Although the towers and pavilions have vanished,
their broad foundations resemble mountains.
Even the greatly worthy Shào Gōng
still abandoned the sweet pear tree [as a memorial].
For a petty state,
to have such lofty and elevated terraces and viewing towers,
displaying arrogance and excess to the world—
to serve as a mirror for the present and future,
I therefore composed an ode, saying:
"They dwarf the winding hills and mounds,
rivaling the towering peaks of the Five Sacred Mountains,"
speaking of their grandeur.
North of the city was the market ground of Hán.
Niè Zhèng, for Yán Zhòngzǐ of Púyáng, assassinated Hán's minister Xiá Lěi,
then flayed his face and died.
His elder sister wept for him here.
Within the city is a stele for Liú Mèngyáng, Magistrate of Suānzǎo in the Later Hàn.
The Pú Shuǐ accumulated northward, forming a lake,
five *lǐ* square,
called Tóngchí Bēi.
It then flows east past the east of Zuò Tíng and empties into it.
This was the ancient state of Zuò.
Fù Chén spoke of "Xíng, Máo, Zuò, and Zhài, the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu."
The Pú Qú then flows northeast past the south of Yān City,
the ancient state of Nán Yān of the Jí surname.
Because there was a Běi Yān,
this one was called Nán to distinguish it.
To the east is Yángqīng Lake,
five *lǐ* north-south,
thirty *lǐ* east-west,
also called Yānchéng Lake.
It passes south of Táo City,
which is the Suānzǎo and Xūtáo mentioned in the *Zhànguó Cè*.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Liú Xiāng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It then flows east and empties into the Pú,
commonly called Cháopíng Ditch.
The Pú Qú then flows northeast,
and again meets the old channel of the Suān Shuǐ.
The Suān channel first receives water from the Hé at Suānzǎo,
flows east past the north of Suānzǎo City and south of Yánjīn,
and is called the Suān Shuǐ.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* states:
Qín's Sū Hú led troops to attack Zhèng,
and Hán Xiāng defeated Qín's Sū Hú at the Suān Shuǐ.
The Suān channel water then flows northeast past the north of Yān City,
then east past the south of Huátái City,
then southeast past the south of Wǎ Tíng.
The *Chūnqiū*, eighth year of Duke Dìng,
records: The duke met the Jìn army at Wǎ.
Lǔ still held lambs [as gifts],
and from this meeting it began.
It then flows southeast and joins the Pú,
commonly called the Bǎichǐ Ditch.
Beside the Pú Qú is Qī City.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián*: In the sixteenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Hándān attacked Wèi,
took Qī and Fù and fortified the city.
It is also sometimes called Wǎnpú Tíng.
The *Chūnqiū*
records: Níng Wǔzǐ made a covenant with the people of Wèi at Wǎnpú.
Dù Yù said:
Southwest of Chángyuán,
near the Pú Shuǐ.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
It is Wèi territory.
As it is not a crucial point,
he did not know its exact location.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián*
states: In the fifth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
the nobleman Jǐng Jiǎ led troops to attack Zhèng.
Hán Míng fought at Yáng,
and our army was defeated and fled to the marsh.
To the north is Tánlíng Tíng,
also sometimes called Dàlíng City,
but its exact nature is not investigated.
There is also Guì City.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián*
states: In the seventeenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qí's Tián Qī attacked our eastern borders.
They fought at Guìyáng,
and our army was defeated and fled.
It is also called Guìlíng.
According to the *Shǐjì*,
King Wēi of Qí sent Tián Jì to attack Wèi,
defeating them at Guìlíng.
Qí then became strong,
proclaimed itself king,
and issued commands to the world.
The Pú Qú then flows east past the north of Pú City,
the ancient Pú town of Wèi.
When Confucius was going to Wèi,
Zǐ Lù came out from Pú.
The *Hánzǐ* says:
Lǔ, in mid-summer, began digging a long ditch.
Zǐ Lù was the magistrate of Pú
and used his private grain to feed the laborers.
Confucius sent Zǐ Gòng to destroy their vessels.
I note that the *Jiāyǔ* says
Zhòng Yóu, as magistrate of Hòu, repaired ditches and channels.
He gave them single-basket meals and gourd drinks.
The Master ordered Cì to stop him.
It does not mention the character for Lǔ.
Also, when entering his territory,
he praised his goodness three times.
He became a senior official
and ultimately died in the Wèi calamity.
The Pú Qú then flows east past the south of Wéi City,
which is the Wéi township of Báimǎ County.
Sīmā Qiān's *Records* states:
It is the ancient state of the Xià lord Shǐ Wéi.
The city wall protrudes westward and is not square.
Within the city are six large wells,
all with underground tunnels leading down,
commonly called Jiāng wells.
There is a raised imperial road
connecting the city to Chángyuán.
The Pú Qú crosses the imperial road eastward,
then flows east past the north of the old city of Chángyuán County.
This is Wèi territory,
formerly called Shǒuyuán.
Qín changed it to its present name.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Chánggù County.
The *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* says:
The county had defensive walls,
hence the county was named after them.
In the first year of the Jiànguāng era, Emperor Ān of the Xiào line
enfeoffed his maternal uncle Sòng Jùn as a marquis here.
The county has Jì City.
The Pú Qú passes north of it.
It was the town of Zhèng's senior official Jì Zhòng.
Dù Yù said:
Northeast of Chángyuán County in Chénliú is Jì City.
Quān Chēng also said that in Chángyuán County there was a Luó Pavilion.
This was the former Chángluó County.
During the Han dynasty, it was made the marquisate of the Rear General Cháng Huì.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
Wáng Mǎng changed Chángluó to Huìzé.
It was abolished and merged during the Later Han.
Chángyuán has the Chángluó Marsh,
which is where Wú Jìyīng herded pigs.
There are also the Chángluó Ridge and the Qú Bóyù Ridge.
The "Chénliú Customs and Traditions" states:
Chángyuán County has a Qú Bó Township,
also called Xīnxiāng,
where there are the Qú Pavilion, the Bóyù Shrine, and the Bóyù Tomb.
Cáo Dàgū's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition" says:
Arriving at the borders of Chángyuán,
I observe the residents of the farming countryside;
I see the mounds and ruins of Púchéng,
overgrown with dense brambles and thorns;
The Qú clan is to the southeast of the city,
and the people also face their burial mounds;
Only virtuous deeds are imperishable,
the body may perish but the name endures.
In the past, Wú Jìzhá visited the superior states,
arriving in Wèi,
he observed the archives, guesthouses, and the fields of the elders,
because Wèi had many gentlemen.
The Pú Canal further east divides into two waterways,
from which the Northern Pú emerges.
The Pú Canal then passes east of Xūchéng to the north.
The "Odes of Wèi" says:
I think of Xū and Cáo.
Máo states:
Xū
is a town of Wèi.
Zhèng states:
From Wèi eastward, passing through the towns,
hence the longing.
The Pú Canal then passes north of Xiāngqiū Pavilion to the south.
The "Bamboo Annals" states:
In the seventh year of King Xiāng,
Hán Míng led troops to attack Xiāngqiū;
in the ninth year,
Chǔ Shùzhāng led troops to join us,
and encamped at Xiāngqiū.
The Pú River then passes east of the old city of Púyáng County to the south.
In the past, Master Yán composed decadent music for Zhòu;
when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Master Yán fled east,
and threw himself into the Pú River to die.
Later, Duke Líng of Wèi was about to go to Jìn,
and set up lodging on the Pú River.
At night he heard new music,
and summoned Master Juān to receive it from this river.
The Pú River then passes east of the old city of Líhú County in Jìyīn to the south.
This is what Wáng Mǎng called Ruìhú.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" states:
It formerly belonged to Dōngjùn.
The Pú River then passes east of the old city of Jiāmì County to the north.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the third year of Duke Yuán,
Lǔ Jìsūn met Duke Yōu of Jìn at Chǔqiū,
captured Jiāmì,
and then fortified it.
The Pú River then passes northeast of Lùchéng to the south.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" states:
Chéngshì County in Jìyīn has a Lùchéng Township.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
an alliance was made at Lùshàng.
Jīng and Dù both say it is this pavilion.
The Pú River then joins with the Gōu Ditch to the east.
The ditch begins by receiving a branch of the Pú River southeast of Gōuyáng County,
passes south of the old city of Gōuyáng County,
which is the Gǔqiū of the "Spring and Autumn Annals".
The "Zuǒzhuàn" considers it Gōudòuqiū.
The county is situated on its southern side,
hence the county is named accordingly.
Further east, it enters Chéngshì County,
joins the Pú River on the left, and together with the Jǐ River enters Jùyě.
Therefore, the "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Pú River enters Jùyě from the south of Púyáng.
This is also what the "Classic" refers to as the Jǐ River dividing into two at Chéngshì County,
and entering Jùyě to the northeast.
The old course of the Jǐ River continues north,
joining the Hóng River on the right.
The river originates from Xuēxùnzhǔ in Jùyě,
passes northwest through the marsh,
and then passes west of Kànxiāng City to the north.
In the eleventh year of Duke Huán of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
the "Classic" records that the Duke met with the Duke of Sòng at Kàn.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" states:
Dōngpínglù has a Kàn Pavilion.
The "Imperial Overview" states:
The tomb of Chīyóu is in Kànxiāng City, Shòuzhāng County, Dōngjùn.
The tomb is seven chi high,
and sacrifices are often made to it in the tenth month.
Red vapor emerges like crimson silk,
and the people call it the Chīyóu Banner.
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
Shòuzhāng has a Chīyóu Shrine.
Further north, it joins with the Jǐ Ditch.
From the islet to the northern mouth is one hundred and twenty lǐ,
named the Hóng River.
Huán Wēn, in the fourth year of Tàihé, led troops northward,
and dug a canal to connect with the Jǐ River;
by the thirteenth year of Yìxī,
when Emperor Wǔ of Liú entered Cháng'ān from the west,
he further expanded the project.
Above the Hóng mouth,
it is also called the Huángōng Ditch.
From here, the Jǐ River flows northward.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Zhuāng of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
the "Classic" records that in summer, the Duke pursued the Róng west of the Jǐ River.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
This refers to the Jǐ River from Jùyě to Jǐběi.
Further northeast, it passes the western border of Shòuzhāng County,
south of Ānmín Pavilion,
where the Wèn River comes from the northeast and flows into it.
The Jǐ River continues north,
and the Wèn River flows into it.
This is what Dài Yánzhī called the Qīngkǒu.
Guō Yuánshēng's "Record of the Northern Expedition" states:
The Qīng River begins by receiving the Hóng River,
and flows north into the Jǐ River.
Some say the Qīng is the Jǐ River.
The "Tribute of Yu" states:
The Jǐ River meets the Wèn River to the northeast.
Now, a dry channel flows into the Great Marsh,
north of the Great Marsh is the Qīngkǒu,
where the Qīng River meets the Wèn River.
Lǐ Qīn said:
The Wèn River originates from Làiwú County in Tàishān,
and flows southwest into the Jǐ River.
The Jǐ River then passes east of Liángshān to the north.
Yuán Hóng's "Rhapsody on the Northern Expedition" says:
With Liángshān at our backs,
we cut across the waves of the Wèn River,
which is exactly this place.
Liú Chéngzhī cited this mountain to prove it was Liángfù,
which is unreasonable.
Southwest of the mountain is the tomb of Lǚ Zhòngtì.
On the eastern bank of the river is a stone bridge.
The bridge originally spanned the river,
but the river shifted,
so it now stands by the bank.
The elders say
this bridge was built when Lǚ Mǔ of Dōnghǎi raised troops.
Three lǐ north of the mountain is Lǚ Mǔ's residence,
and three lǐ east of the residence is the Jǐ River.
The Jǐ River then passes west of Xūqú City to the north.
The city lies adjacent to the Jǐ River,
hence it was the state of Xūqú.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
Zǐyú said:
Rén, Sù, Xūqú, and Zhuānyú
are of the Fēng surname.
They indeed preside over Tàihào,
and share in the sacrifices to the Jǐ River.
Dù Yù said:
Xūqú is northwest of Xūchāng County,
but this is incorrect.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
Northwest of Shòuzhāng is the city of Qú, which is correct.
West of the Jǐ River is Ānmín Pavilion,
north of the pavilion faces Ānmín Mountain,
and to the east, it borders the Jǐ River.
East of the river is the boundary of Wúyán County.
West of the mountain is the stele of Wáng Fēn, Inspector of Jìzhōu,
erected in the fourth year of Zhōnghé of the Hàn dynasty.
The Jǐ River then passes east of Wēixiāng to the north.
In the twenty-eight year of Duke Zhuāng of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
the "Classic" records the construction of Méi in winter.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
The "Gōngyáng Commentary" calls it Wēi.
Thirty lǐ northwest of Shòuzhāng County in Dōngpíng,
there is the old Wēixiāng,
a town of Lǔ.
Dù Yù said:
There is the tomb of Wēizǐ.
The Jǐ River then divides into two waterways to the north.
Its branch flows out to the northwest,
called the Mǎjiá River.
Further north, it passes west of Xūchāng County.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Xūqú,
is one state with two cities and two names.
It seems the capital was moved to Xūchāng,
while Qú was its original location.
The Qin established it as a county.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Zhào Yǎn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Jì River flows through the county,
and the Zhàogōu River flows into it.
The Jì River then flows north past the east of Yúshān,
where it joins the Mǎjiá River on the left.
The Mǎjiá River originates from the Jì River,
flows northwest,
passes north of Ānmínshān,
then flows west,
where the Zhàogōu River branches off,
flowing northeast into the Jì River.
The Mǎjiá River then passes east of Táochéng.
In the tenth year of Duke Huán of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the *Classic* records:
"The Duke met with the Marquis of Wèi at Táoqiū,"
which is in Wèi territory.
Dù Yù said:
"East of Dōng'ē County in Jǐběi is Táochéng,
which is Táoqiū."
The Mǎjiá River then flows northeast past the south of Yúshān.
The mountain
is also called Wúshān.
This is the "Wúshān píng" mentioned in Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Hùzǐ Gē."
On the mountain is Liǔshūchéng.
Cáo Zǐjiàn, Prince of Dōng'ē of Wèi, often climbed it,
and wished to end his days there.
When he died,
he was buried west of the mountain,
forty *lǐ* west of Dōng'ēchéng.
The river then flows east into the Jì River,
at a place called Mǎjiákǒu.
The Jì River flows north from Yúshān past the east of Qīngtíng.
In the fourth year of Duke Yǐn of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
"The Duke and the Duke of Sòng met at Qīng."
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Forty *lǐ* northeast of present-day Dōng'ē in Jǐběi,
there is an old Qīngtíng,
which is the Qīng mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Thus, the lower reaches of the Jì River are also called Qīngshuǐ.
The water is clear and deep,
justifying the name."
Therefore, the King of Yān said:
"I have heard that Qí relies on the clear Jì and the turbid Hé for defense,"
referring to this river.
Further north, it passes west of Gǔchéng County.
On the bank of the Jì River is Yǐnmǎolěi,
over forty *lǐ* south of Yúshān,
within the boundaries of Gǔchéng County.
This is the old Xiǎogǔchéng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Duke Huán of Qí fortified it in the twenty-third year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ,
and enfeoffed Guǎn Zhòng there.
Within the city is the Yíwú Well.
*The Wèi Tǔdì Jì* says:
"The county has Gǔchéngshān,
which produces patterned stone,
in the area of Yánggǔ.
In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Marquis of Qí and the Duke of Sòng met at Yánggǔ."
The county also has Huángshāntái.
This is where Huángshígōng made an appointment with Zhāng Zǐfáng.
There is also the Láng River,
which originates from Lángxī on Dàjiǎnshān to the southeast,
and flows northwest past west of Gǔchéng.
Further north is the Xīliú Spring,
which emerges from the mountains east of the city,
flows northwest past north of Gǔchéng,
and then flows west into the Láng River.
Because it flows west,
it is so named.
It then flows northwest into the Jì River.
Three *lǐ* northwest of the city
is the tomb of King Xiàng Yǔ,
partially ruined,
with a stone stele still standing,
inscribed:
"Tomb of King Xiàng."
*The Huánglǎn* says:
"The tomb is fifteen *lǐ* from the county,"
which is incorrect.
Now, southwest of Gǔyángchéng in Péngchéng,
there is another tomb of Xiàng Yǔ,
which is also incorrect.
I note that according to Simǎ Qiān's *Records*,
Lǔ held out for Chǔ,
and only surrendered after Hàn King showed them Xiàng Yǔ's head.
Lǔ then surrendered,
and Xiàng Yǔ was buried in Gǔchéng with the rites due to a Duke of Lǔ.
How could it be elsewhere?
The Jì River then flows north past west of Zhōushǒutíng.
In the eleventh year of Duke Wén of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, Zuǒ Qiūmíng says:
"In the second year of Duke Xiāng,
Wángzǐ Chéngfù captured Jiǎorú's younger brother Róngrú of the Chángdí,
and buried his head north of the gate of Zhōushǒu."
This is that city.
Nowadays it is called Lúzichéng,
the seat of Jǐběi Commandery.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"The present Lúzichéng, seat of Jǐběi,
is the old Zhōushǒu city of Qí."
Further north, it passes east of Línyì County.
*The Treatise on Geography* says:
"The county has a Jì River temple,
which was Gǔchéngtíng in Wáng Mǎng's time."
There is a stone gate on the river,
made of stone,
hence the name 'Gate of the Jì River.'
In the fifth year of Duke Yǐn of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
"Qí and Zhèng met at Shímén,
where Zhèng's chariots overturned while crossing the river."
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Shímén
is in Qí territory.
Sixty *lǐ* southwest of the old city of Lú County in present-day Jǐběi,
there is an old stone gate,
three hundred paces from the water.
It seems the river course shifted,
so it is now on the bank."
The Jì River then flows north past west of Píngyīnchéng.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
"The Marquis of Jìn sank jade in the Hé River,
met at the Lǔ Jì,
renewed the alliance at Júliáng,
and jointly attacked Qí.
The Marquis of Qí defended at Píngyīn."
Dù Yù said:
"The city is northeast of the old city of Lú County,"
which is incorrect.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Píngyīn
is in Qí territory,
ten *lǐ* southwest of the old city of Lú County in Jǐběi."
South of Píngyīnchéng is the Great Wall,
extending east to the sea,
and west to the Jì River.
Where the river passes through,
it is called Fángmén,
three *lǐ* from Píngyīn.
The Marquis of Qí dug a trench at Fángmén,
which is this place.
The water was drawn from the Jì River,
and the old channel still exists.
North of Fángmén today is Guānglǐ.
The people of Qí pronounce 'guǎng'
with the same sound as 'guāng,'
so this is the Guǎnglǐ mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* as being defended.
It is also said
that Wūshān is northeast of Píngyīn.
Once, the Marquis of Qí climbed it to observe the Jìn army,
but retreated in fear of their numbers.
Shī Kuàng and Xíng Bó heard the cries of crows,
and knew the Qí army was secretly retreating.
People and events have vanished,
but the geography remains clear,
which is more reliable than Dù's claim about the northeast.
Now, on Wūshān, there is a stone chamber,
commonly called the Filial Son Hall.
The Jì River bends to the right,
forming Měihú Lake,
over forty *lǐ* across.
The Jì River then flows northeast past west of Yuánmiáochéng,
formerly known as Luòdāngchéng.
Fú Tāo's *Běizhēng Jì* says:
"The Jì River merges with the Qīnghé River,
reaching Luòdāng."
When Emperor Wǔ of Sòng campaigned west to Cháng'ān,
he ordered Yuán Miáo to garrison here,
hence it is also called Yuánmiáochéng.
The Hé River flows northeast from the Sìdúkǒu and becomes the Jì River.
*The Wèi Tǔdì Jì* says:
"Ten *lǐ* from the branch of the Hé River at Méngjīn, it merges with the Qīngshuǐ River,
flows eastward in a disorderly course,
passes north of Luòdāngchéng,
where black and white waters flow separately,
distinct as the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
and then flows southeast."
Further northeast, it passes north of Lú County.
The Jì River flows northeast and joins with the Méi Gutter,
whose waters originate from Méi Lake,
flowing north to empty into the Jì.
The Ěryǎ states:
"Where water and plants meet is called méi,"
and "a valley that connects through is called wēi."
Jiànwéi Shèrén said:
"It is where water and plants within the water intermingle."
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"Wēi"
means a valley by the water's edge that connects through.
The Shìmíng states:
"Méi"
means "eyebrow,"
as it borders the water like an eyebrow borders the eye.
The Jì River then passes north of the old city of Lú County,
which is the seat of Jìběi Commandery.
In the second year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé of Hàn,
it was established by dividing off from Tàishān,
likely because the Jì River lies to its north.
The Jì River then passes north of Shí City,
a city bordering the water's edge,
originally a postal station.
Sūn Shí, a man from Zhù'ē,
moved his household to live there
to escape the troubles of the time,
hence it was called Shí City.
The Jì River then flows northeast and joins with the Zhōngchuān River,
which originates southeast from the watershed ridge of Shānchí County,
where a single stream splits into two branches,
the spring flow dividing equally,
also called the "Dividing Flow Junction."
Half the water flows south from Tàishān into the Wèn River,
and half flows from Shānchí County,
running northwest past the south of the Eastern Tàiyuán Commandery,
whose seat is Shānlú Fortress,
and north to join with the Bīn Creek.
The Bīn Creek originates from the Bīn Creek Valley on the southern Gé Mǎ Mountain,
flows north past the old city of Lú County and south of Chéndūn Garrison,
then northwest to join the Zhōngchuān River,
a place called Gé Mǎ Kou.
These waters then flow north past the east of the old city of Lú County,
and north into the Jì River,
commonly called the Shā Gutter River.
The Jì River then flows northeast,
and on the right joins with the Yù River.
The Yù River originates from Lǎnggōng Valley on Tàishān,
formerly called Kūnruì Creek.
There was a Buddhist monk, Zhú Sēnglǎng,
who in his youth served Fótúchéng,
profoundly learned and erudite,
especially skilled in astrology and prognostication,
who secluded himself in this valley,
hence it was called Lǎnggōng Valley.
Thus Chē Pín's Qín Shū states:
During Fú Jiān's time,
the monk Zhú Sēnglǎng
once traveled with the recluse Zhāng Jùhé.
Jùhé often lived in caves,
while Lǎng resided on Kūnruì Mountain,
building grand halls and residences,
with connected towers and layered pavilions.
Though their simple adornments differed,
both were renowned for attaining tranquility in seclusion.
This is that valley,
and the water is also called Kūnruì Water.
This water flows northwest past Yùfú Mountain,
and is also called Yù River.
It then flows northwest past the east of Liè Mountain,
then northwest, skirting the east of the old city of Zhù'ē County,
west of Yějǐng Pavilion.
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhāo of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Classic records that the Marquis of Qí condoled with the Duke at Yějǐng—this is the place.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the feudal lords made a covenant at Zhùkē,
which the Zuǒzhuàn calls Dūyáng.
When the Hàn arose,
it was renamed Ā.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Gāo Yì was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
which Wáng Mǎng called Ānchéng.
Thus, this water is commonly called the Zhù'ē Gully River,
flowing north to empty into the Jì.
In the fifth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Gěng Yǎn attacked Zhāng Bù from the east,
crossing troops over the river from the Cháoyáng Bridge,
which was at this location.
The Jì River then flows northeast,
where the Luò River enters it.
The Luò River originates southwest of the old city of Lìchéng County,
where the spring source surges upward,
and the water gushes forth like a wheel.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Huán of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jì at Luò—this is the place.
It is commonly called Éjiāng Water,
because at the spring source there is a temple to Shùn's consorts É and Yīng.
South of the city faces a mountain,
on which stands a shrine to Shùn.
At the mountain's base is a large cave,
called Shùn's Well,
perhaps comparable to Máo Mountain's Yǔ's Well.
The Shū
says Shùn plowed at Lì Mountain,
which is also said to be here,
though this is not certain.
North of this water is Dàmíng Lake,
to the west is Dàmíng Temple,
whose east and north sides border the lake,
making this water a pure pond.
Above the pond is a guest pavilion,
flanked by catalpa and paulownia trees.
Basking in the sun, looking up and down,
facing fish and birds,
with water and trees bright and clear,
one could speak of the nature of Háoliáng,
where things and self do not conflict.
From the lake, a channel is drawn
east into the western outer wall,
east to the west of Lìchéng, then skirting the city wall northward,
where the embankment water receives from the eastern city,
passing below the sacrificial site,
where spring sources vie to emerge.
This water flows north past the east of Lìchéng,
then north,
where water is drawn to form the Liúbēi Pond,
where state officials and guests feast,
and public and private gatherings often convene upon it.
It divides into two streams:
the right stream flows north out,
the left stream flows west past the north of Lìchéng,
northwest forming an embankment,
called Lì Water,
which joins with the Luò River.
Further north,
a branch of Lì Water first receives Lì Water east of Lìchéng,
flows northeast past the west of the eastern city and north out of the outer wall,
then north to empty into the Luò River.
Further north,
the Tīng River emerges.
The Luò River then flows north to empty into the Jì,
a place called Luòkǒu.
The Jì River then flows northeast,
where Huábùzhù Mountain stands as a solitary peak, lush and graceful,
not connected to hills or mounds to make itself tall;
like a tiger's tooth, towering and steep,
a lone summit, exceptionally lofty, piercing the sky.
Its green cliffs and verdant hues
appear from afar like dots of dark ink.
Below the mountain is Huá Spring,
thus Jīng Xiàngfán's Chūnqiū Tǔdì Míng states:
"Huá Spring
is the spring water below Huábùzhù Mountain."
In the second year of Duke Chéng of the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn,
Duke Qǐng of Qí battled Xì Kè of Jìn at Ān,
the Qí army was defeated,
and pursued,
circling Huábùzhù three times.
Féng Chǒufǔ exchanged places with the Duke,
and as they were about to reach Huá Spring,
the trace horse became entangled in a tree and stopped.
Chǒufǔ made the Duke dismount,
to go to Huá Spring to fetch drink,
and thus the Marquis of Qí escaped.
Hán Jué presented Chǒufǔ,
and Xì Zǐ was about to execute him.
He cried out:
"From now on, there will be none who take on their lord's troubles in his stead.
Here is one such man,
and he is about to be executed!"
Xì Zǐ said:
"A man who does not shrink from death to save his lord—
it would be inauspicious for me to execute him.
I shall pardon him to encourage those who serve their lords."
Thus he was spared.
This is Huá Water.
It crosses the Tīng Channel twenty li to the north,
and empties into the Jì.
Further northeast, it passes north of Tái County.
The Jùhé River flows north from the west of Jīshān,
passing west of the old Jùhé city.
When Gěng Yǎn campaigned against Zhāng Bù,
he defended Jùlǐ,
which is this city.
It has walls on three sides,
with a deep ravine to the west.
West of the ravine is where Gěng Yǎn encamped.
He battled Fèi Yì here,
and beheaded Yì at this place.
The Jùhé River further north joins the Guānlú River.
The Guānlú River originates from Mǎ'ěr Shān,
flows north past the west of Bótíng City,
and then northwest to Pínglíng City.
It converges with the Wǔyuán River.
The Wǔyuán River emerges from the flat marshes south of Tánchéng,
commonly called the Wǔyuán Deep.
It flows north past the east of Tánchéng,
colloquially known as Bùchéng.
Further north, it passes west of the old city of Dōngpínglíng County,
originally called Língchéng.
Later, the character "píng" was added.
This was the state of Tán.
When Duke Huán of Qí passed through Tán,
Tán did not show him courtesy.
In the ninth year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ's reign,
they again did not pay court visit.
In the tenth year, it was destroyed.
Outside the east gate of the city is the stele of Rén Zhàoxiān from Lè'ān.
This was the seat of Jǐnán Commandery.
In the sixteenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
it was established as a kingdom.
In the second year of Emperor Jǐng, it became a commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lè'ān.
The river further north passes east of Jùhé City.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Liú Fā, son of the Prince of Chéngyáng, as a marquis here.
This river joins the Guānlú River,
flows west, and empties into the Jùhé River.
The Jùhé River flows northwest past the old city of Tái County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Dài Yě, Commandant of Dōng Commandery, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It was called Táizhì under Wáng Mǎng.
The river flows northwest,
joined by the Báiyě Spring.
The Báiyě Spring emerges north of Báiyě Spring, southwest of Táichéng,
passes Liúshān and flows northwest,
then turns right into the Jùhé River.
The Jùhé River continues north,
joined by the Tīng River.
The Tīng River originates from the Luò River,
flows east, turns north,
then northeast,
and empties into the Jùhé River.
The mingled flow continues north into the Jì River.
The Jì River flows northeast,
converging with the Qíngōu River.
The Qíngōu River emerges southeast of the old city of Tái County,
flows northwest,
passes east of Táichéng,
then northwest into the Jì River.
Further northeast, it passes south of Jiān County.
The Jì River flows east past the old county city's south.
In the fourth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Bàijūn, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
To the right, it receives the Bǎimài River.
The Bǎimài River emerges west of the old city of Tǔgǔ County.
Its source spans a hundred paces square,
with a hundred springs gushing forth,
hence called the Bǎimài (Hundred Veins) River.
It flows northwest,
passing through the old city of Yángqiū County.
In the fourth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Liú Ān, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángqiū here.
It is commonly called Zhāngqiū City,
but that is incorrect.
South of the city is Nǚláng Shān,
on which stands a shrine,
commonly called the Nǚláng Shrine,
worshipped by the local people.
The river exits the city northwest,
flows north past Huángjīn Gù,
a stronghold where bandits gathered,
hence the name.
The Bǎimài River flows northeast into the Jì River.
The Jì River flows east,
joined by the Yángzhǔgōu River.
The Yángzhǔgōu River emerges twenty lǐ southwest of the old Fénglíng City,
flows northwest past east of Tǔgǔ City,
then northwest past east of Zhāngqiū City,
then north past west of Nìng Qī City,
and north into the Jì River.
Further east, it passes north of Liángzōu County.
The Lǒng River emerges south from within the Great Wall,
flows north to the west of the old city of Pānyáng County,
where it meets the Pān River from the south.
The Pān River originates from Lóngshān southeast of the county,
also commonly called Zuǒfù River.
It flows northwest past the county city's south,
called Jǐnán Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
Yìng Shào said:
The county lies north of the Pān River,
hence named accordingly.
The river bends south,
then west into the Lǒng River.
The Lǒng River flows north past the county,
northwest to the mouth of the Méng River.
The Méng River emerges from Jiǎshān to the southwest,
flows northeast past west of Méngshān,
then northeast into the Lǒng River.
The Lǒng River flows northwest to southeast of Liángzōu, converging with the Yúzǐgōu River.
The Yúzǐgōu River emerges from Liǔquánkǒu east of Chángbái Shān.
This mountain
is where Chén Zhòngzǐ and his wife lived in seclusion.
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
Zhòngzǐ
belonged to a noble family of Qí.
His elder brother Dài enjoyed a salary of ten thousand zhōng,
but Zhòngzǐ disapproved and refused to partake,
leaving his brother and mother,
and dwelling in Yúlíng.
This is that place.
The river flows past west of the old city of Yúlíng County.
It was called Yúlù under Wáng Mǎng.
In the fifteenth year of Emperor Shìzǔ's Jiànwǔ reign,
Hóu Bà's son Yù, Marquis of Zéxiāng, was re-enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The river flows north into the Lǒng River.
The Lǒng River
is the ancient Yuán River.
Thus Jīng Xiàngfán said:
In Liángzōu County of Jǐnán, there is the Yuán River.
The Lǒng River flows northwest past the old city of Liángzōu County,
then bends north past the city's west.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Wǔ Hǔ was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The river flows north into the Jì River.
Northeast of the city,
the Shí River also flows northwest into it.
Further east, it passes south of Línjì County.
The county,
was originally the territory of Dí.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Lìjū.
The *Hàn Jì* records:
In the second year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān,
it was changed to its present name,
because it bordered on Línjì.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
It was the seat of the Lè'ān Grand Administrator.
Yàn Mó's *Qí Jì* says:
There are southern and northern cities separated by the Jì River,
the southern city being the old city of Bèiyáng County,
bordering the Jì River to the north.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* says:
It was a marquisate.
Rú Chún states:
Also written as 'pí',
pronounced 'bà',
meaning 'exhausted army'.
The *Shǐjì Jiànyuán Yǐlái Wángzǐ Hóu Zhě Niánbiǎo* says:
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the state of Jìng Hóu Liú Yàn, son of Prince Xiào of Qí.
Now it is the seat of the Bohai Qiao Commandery.
The Jì River flows further northeast,
spreading out to form deep pools and islets,
called Píngzhōu.
To the side of Tàwò County lies the old city of Píng'ān,
commonly called Huìchéng,
which is incorrect.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* records:
Qiānchéng Commandery had a Píng'ān County,
a marquisate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Hóngmù.
Yìng Shào says:
Thirty *lǐ* southwest of Bóchāng County is the Píng'ān Pavilion,
the site of the old county.
The name Píngzhōu has been preserved to this day.
The Jì River flows further northeast past the west of the old city of Gāochāng County.
According to the *Dìlǐ Zhì*,
Qiānchéng Commandery had a Gāochāng County.
In the fourth year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Dǒng Zhōng was enfeoffed there as a marquisate.
It is commonly called Mǎchāng City,
which is incorrect.
The Jì River flows further northeast past the south of the old city of Lè'ān County.
Fú Chēn's *Qí Jì* says:
Fifty *lǐ* northwest of Bóchāng City are southern and northern cities,
thirty *lǐ* apart,
separated by the Shí and Jì rivers.
Referring to this as the northern city of Bóchāng,
is incorrect.
Lè'ān shares waterways with Bóchāng and Bógū,
all lying to the northwest.
Bógū is sixty *lǐ* from Qí City.
Lè'ān is farther across the water,
making the verification particularly clear.
Bān Gù says:
Qiānchéng Commandery had a Lè'ān County.
Yìng Shào says:
The name was chosen for its auspicious meaning.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Lǐ Cài was enfeoffed there as a marquisate.
Three *lǐ* west of the city are the tombs of Rén Guāng and others.
Guāng was a man of Wǎn County,
clearly not from Bóchāng.
The Jì River passes further north of Bógū City.
The *Hòu Hàn Jùn Guó Zhì* says:
Bóchāng County has Bógū City.
The *Dìlǐ Shū* says:
Lǚ Shàng was enfeoffed at Bógū in Qí Commandery.
The old city of Bógū is fifty *lǐ* northwest of Línzī County,
near the Jì River.
Sīmā Qiān says:
Duke Xiàn moved to Bógū.
Within the city is a high terrace.
In the twentieth year of Duke Zhāo of the *Chūnqiū*,
Duke Jǐng of Qí drank on the terrace,
saying:
If the ancients did not die,
what joy could compare to this?
Yǎn Píngzhòng replied:
Long ago, Shuǎngjiūshì first dwelt here,
Jìcè succeeded him,
Féng Bólíng succeeded him in turn,
Bógūshì succeeded him,
and then Tàigōng succeeded him.
Your servant believes that if the ancients did not die,
the joy would be that of Shuǎngjiūshì,
not Your Lordship's joy.
This was on that very terrace.
The Jì River flows further northeast past the west of Lángyágù and then flows northeast.
It flows further northeast past the west of Lì County.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* records:
Qí Commandery had a Lì County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Lìzhì.
Yàn Mó says:
The county is located
fifty *lǐ* north of Qí City.
It flows further northeast past Jiǎxiàyì,
and enters the [Yellow] River.
The Jì River reaches south of Jiǎxiàyì in the northeast,
then flows east past the north of the old city of Lánghuái County.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* says:
Eighty *lǐ* northeast of Bóchāng is Lángkuài Township,
the site of the old county.
The *Shānhǎijīng* says:
The Jì River, cutting across Jùyě, flows into the Bohai Sea,
entering northeast of Lángkuài in Qí.
Further northeast,
a branch of the [Yellow] River flows into it.
The *Shuǐ Jīng* considers this the Jì entering the [Yellow] River,
which is incorrect.
This is actually the [Yellow] River flowing into the Jì,
not the Jì entering the [Yellow] River.
It then flows further northeast into the sea.
Guō Jǐngchún says:
The Jì River, from Xíngyáng to Bóchāng in Lè'ān, enters the sea.
Now the [Yellow] River has dried up,
yet the Jì River still flows unceasingly.
The *Jīng* says it enters the [Yellow] River;
both explanations are mistaken.
However, the [Yellow] River, north of the Jì and Tà rivers,
flows separately into the sea.
What has ceased flowing now
is only the Tà River.
Guō perhaps thought the Jì flowed into it,
which is factually incorrect.
Examining the waterways according to the classics,
they are not as precise as the *Shānhǎijīng*.
One branch of the water flows southeast,
past the south of Chéngshì County.
The Héshuǐ River branches off from the Jì in the northeast of Dìngtáo,
merging from the southeast with Huáng Gōu branch stream on the right,
commonly known as Jiè Gōu.
It flows north past the western part of Yǐshì County's ancient city,
then further north past the east of Jǐngshān,
mentioned in Wèi Shī as the "Jǐngshān and Jīng."
Lord Máo said:
"Jǐngshān,
a great mountain indeed."
Continuing north past the west of Chǔqiū city,
the "Records of the Commanderies and States" states:
There is a Chǔqiū Pavilion in Chéngwǔ County.
Dù Yù states,
that Chǔqiū lies southwest of Chéngwǔ County,
where Wèi Yì Gōng was destroyed by the Dí,
and Wèi Wén Gōng moved eastward across the river,
settling in Cáo city.
Qí Huán Gōng established Chǔqiū to relocate him.
Hence, the "Spring and Autumn Annals" speak of Xíng moving back as returning home,
Wèi forgetting its loss.
This is what the "Shī" refers to as "ascending the void,"
overlooking Chǔ,
gazing at Chǔ with Táng,
and Jǐngshān with Jīng.
Therefore, Zhèng Xuán says,
to observe its neighboring towns and natural features.
Further northeast, it flows past the west of Chéngwǔ city,
then northeast past the east of Hòu city,
possibly moved to Hòu,
detailed information is not available.
Continuing northeast past the west of Liángqiū city,
the "Geographical Records" states:
Chāngyì County has Liángqiū village.
In the 32nd year of Duke Zhuāng in the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
the people of Sòng and Qí met at Liángqiū.
Dù Yù notes:
in the southwest of Gāopíng Chāngyì County, there is Liángqiū village.
Further northeast, it flows west of Chéngshì County and north into Héshuǐ.
Héshuǐ flows southeast past the south of Chéngshì County's ancient city,
which,
in the "Spring and Autumn Annals" is Chéngqiū.
As the "Local Customs Records" states:
Chéngshì County in Jìyīn,
was originally Sòng Chéngqiū village.
In the fifth year of Emperor Xiàojǐng of Hàn,
Liáng Xiào Wáng’s son Mǎi was made a marquis there.
The "Geographical Records" states:
Chéngshì County,
in the southeast of Sìshuǐ, reaching Suīlíng into Huái.
The "Records of the Commanderies and States" state:
Chéngshì has Sìshuǐ.
This is Hézé.
The "Shàngshū" mentions leading Hézé,
from Táoqiū northward,
eastward to Hé,
without mention of Sìshuǐ.
It also states:
leading Hézé,
covering Mèngzhū.
Mèngzhū lies northeast of Suīyáng County.
Kàn Yìn's "Record of the Thirteen Provinces" notes:
the lack of inlet mention but use of covering suggests,
it doesn’t always enter.
When water is abundant,
it eventually covers completely.
Marsh waters overflow,
joining Huái and Sì,
hence the record of Suīlíng entering Huái,
referring to it as Gǒusì.
Yet, numerous tributaries to Sì are not just this,
leading ultimately to Sìshuǐ,
making it conveniently called.
There could be more Sìshuǐ as multifaceted water,
specific details are unclear.
Further east past the north of Chāngyì County,
Héshuǐ flows east past the north of Chāngyì County's ancient city.
The "Geographical Records" states:
The county,
was originally Liáng.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng’s reign,
Liáng was divided as Shānyáng State,
in the fourth year of Emperor Wǔ Tiān Hàn,
it became Chāngyì State,
to enfeoff Chāngyì King Bixiě,
who was deposed,
the state abolished to Shānyáng Commandery,
under the rule of Jùyě Commandery by Wáng Mǎng.
Later it became Gāopíng Commandery,
later under the administration of Yǎn Province in Eastern Hàn.
County Magistrate Wáng Mì,
brought gold to present to Yáng Zhèn, Grand Administrator of Eastern Láii,
Zhèn refused,
exemplifying caution in matters of four unknowns.
To the northeast of the main city is Jīnchéng,
within the city is the stele of Yǎn Province Inspector Xuē Jì from Hédōng,
appointed Lángzhōng as governor of Yàn,
sweet dew descended on the orchard.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng, transferred the province,
the following year sweet dew again descended on trees before the hall,
official Féng Xún, Chief Clerk Huá Cāo, and others praised the trees,
commemorating the governance of Tang.
Westward is the stele of Màolíng Inspector Yāng Shūgōng of Yǎn Province,
established by officials like Sūn Guāng in the 4th year of Jiànníng,
northwest is the stele of Dōng Tàishān's native Bān Mèngjiān,
in the 10th year of Jiànhé,
appointed Right Minister of the Shàngshū as Yǎn Province Inspector by Qín Rùn officials and others,
they inscribed on stone praising good governance,
all steles are there.
Further east past the south of Jīnxīang County,
"Records of the Commanderies and States" states:
Shānyáng has Jīnxīang County.
Héshuǐ flows south past its ancient city,
commonly called the ancient county city north of Jīnxīang Mountain.
Further east past the north of Dōngmín County,
Héshuǐ flows east past the tomb of Hàn's General Píngdí Marquis Zhuā Fūgōu of Huáiyáng.
North of the tomb is a stone temple.
Héshuǐ flows east past the north of Dōngmín County's ancient city,
an ancient Sòng territory.
In the 23rd year of Duke Xī in the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
Qí Marquis attacked Sòng besieging Mín.
"Records of the Thirteen Provinces" state:
Shānyáng has Dōngmín County.
Zōu Yǎn stated:
I climbed Mín city overlooking Sòng capital.
In the 11th year of Jiànwǔ of Later Hàn's Shìzǔ,
Féng Yì's eldest son Zhāng was enfeoffed.
Further east past the north of Fāngyǔ County,
forms Héshuǐ.
The Hé River flows east past the south of Chóngxiāng City,
which is the place mentioned in the Zuǒzhuàn where Zāng Wénzhòng lodged at the Chóngguǎn.
The Hé River then flows east past the north of Wǔtáng Pavilion,
which the Gōngyáng considers a town on the Jì River.
The city has a terrace,
about two zhàng high,
with water below it.
In the past, the Marquis of Lǔ viewed fish at Táng,
referring to this place.
It is ten lǐ north of the old city of Fāngyú County,
and is the Hé River mentioned in the Jīng.
The Hé River then flows east past the north of Nímǔ Pavilion,
as recorded in the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn under the seventh year of Duke Xī:
in autumn,
an alliance was formed at Níngmǔ,
planning to attack Zhèng.
The Hé River then flows east and joins the Huáng River of Jùyě,
which is another name for Hézé.
The Huáng River originates from the various ponds of Jùzé,
which include Méngdiàn and Mángbēi.
The water from Huánghú flows east,
and is called the Huáng River.
There is also the Xuēxùnzhǔ River,
which flows from the islet past the front of Xuē Village,
dividing into two streams:
one flows east into the Huáng River,
and the other flows northwest into the marsh,
which is the Hóng River.
The Huáng River flows southeast,
and south of the river is the tomb of Lǐ Gāng, the Hàn Dynasty Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Lǐ Gāng, styled Shūyì,
was a native of Gāopíng in Shānyáng.
He died in the first year of the Xīpíng era.
His stele can be seen.
There are stone towers, a memorial hall, and three stone chambers,
with beams over a zhàng high,
carved stone rafters and tiled roofs,
constructed with a flat ceiling,
square wells with lotus-shaped beams and pillars on the sides,
and relief carvings on the four walls,
depicting rulers and ministers, officials and subordinates,
patterns of turtles, dragons, qílín, and phoenixes,
and images of flying birds and running beasts.
The craftsmanship is exquisite,
and it is not severely damaged.
The Huáng River then flows east past the north of Jùyě County.
Hé Chéngtiān said:
"The Jùyě Lake is vast,
connecting to the Zhū and Sì Rivers in the south,
and to the Qīng and Jì Rivers in the north.
The old county city was right in the middle of the lake,
so they intended to station troops in this city.
Where the city is located
is the Jùyě Lake."
To the northeast, it expands into Dàyě,
where in the past, a qílín was captured during a western hunt.
The Huánglǎn states:
"In Jùyě County of Shānyáng, there is a tomb of shoulders and thighs,
piled up in large and small sizes,
equal to the Guān Tomb."
It is said that Chīyóu fought with the Yellow Emperor,
and was defeated in the fields of Zhuōlù.
His body was dismembered,
so he was buried separately.
The Huáng River then flows east past the north of Xián Pavilion,
as recorded in the Chūnqiū under the seventh year of Duke Huán:
"The Jīng records the burning of Xiánqiū."
South of the river is Jīnxiāng Mountain,
which marks the eastern boundary of the county.
The several mountains of Jīnxiāng
all have hollow openings,
called tunnels.
Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēngjì states:
"A few lǐ north of Jiāoshì Mountain,
Lǔ Jùn, the Hàn Dynasty Colonel-Director of Retainers, excavated the mountain and found a white snake and a white rabbit.
He did not bury them there,
but reburied them south of the mountain,
where he excavated and found gold,
hence the name Jīnxiāng Mountain."
The mountain is steep and precipitous,
with stone memorial halls and temples in front of the tombs.
The four walls are all made of blue stone with relief carvings,
depicting images of loyal ministers, filial sons, chaste women, Confucius, and his seventy-two disciples since the beginning of writing.
Beside each image, inscriptions are carved in stone,
with clear and distinct characters.
There is also a stone bed,
eight chǐ long,
polished and gleaming brightly.
When struck, its sound can be heard from far and near.
At the time, Fù Zhēnzhī, a Gentleman of the Household of the Grand Commandant, and Zhōu Ānmù, a Consultant General, dismantled the stone bed,
each taking parts away.
They were sued by the descendants of the Lǔ family,
and both were dismissed from office.
East of Jiāoshì Mountain is Jīnxiāng Mountain,
where there is a tomb
called the Tomb of the King of Qín.
Two hundred steps up the mountain, one reaches the tomb entrance,
with a trench ten zhàng deep,
steep cliffs on both sides,
and a width of two zhàng.
Walking seventy steps inside,
one reaches the burial gate.
Outside the gate, there are empty spaces on the left and right,
capable of accommodating fifty to sixty people,
called the White Horse Hollow.
One zhàng inside the burial gate,
one reaches the outer hall.
Beyond the outer hall,
there is an inner hall.
Visitors all carry torches to walk through,
and although there are no other carvings,
the stonework is very refined.
Some say this is the tomb of the Mourning King of Chāngyì of the Hàn Dynasty,
but this is not certain.
To the southeast is the tomb of Fàn Jùqīng,
with its name and components still preserved.
Jùqīng's given name was Shì,
a native of Jīnxiāng in Shānyáng,
and a Governor of Jīngzhōu during the Hàn Dynasty.
He formed a stone-like friendship with Zhāng Shào of Rǔnán and Chén Píngzǐ of Chángshā,
and they were known as friends unto death.
The Huáng River then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Kàngfù County in Rènchéng Commandery,
which was the Rèn State of the Xiàhòu clan.
In the first year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
it was separately established as Rènchéng in the north,
which was the Yánjiù Pavilion of Wáng Mǎng.
The county has a Shī Pavilion,
which was the Shī State of the Chūnqiū period.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shùnfù.
According to the Dìlǐzhì,
it was a subordinate county of Dōngpíng.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Liú Lóng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The water here is called Duke Huán's Ditch,
which flows south to Fāngyú County
and enters the Hé River.
The Hé River then flows east past Qínliáng,
where stones are piled up along the banks for one lǐ,
two zhàng high.
It is said that this was built when Qín Shǐhuáng toured the east,
hence the name.
The Hé River then flows east past the south of Húlù County
and enters the Sì River to the east.
This is where the marsh waters converge.
The Shàngshū states:
"Floating on the Huái and Sì Rivers,
one reaches the Hé River."
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"Sū Mào killed the Governor of Huáiyáng,
seized his commandery,
and camped at Guǎnglè.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn besieged Mào,
but Mào led his elite troops and broke through to Húlíng,
where he joined forces with Liú Yǒng.
Troops from Jìyīn and Shānyáng crossed here."
Further southeast, it passes northeast of Pèi County,
where the Jì and Sì Rivers intermingle,
so the names Jì and Nà are used interchangeably.
The Dōngguān Hànjì, in the biography of Gài Yán, Marquis of Ānpíng, states:
"Yán served as General of the Tiger Teeth,
and fought against Yǒng and others.
Yǒng's army retreated in defeat,
with half drowning in the river.
He fought them again,
defeating them repeatedly,
and thus pacified Pèi and Chǔ.
Línhuái surrendered entirely.
Yán ordered Pèi to repair the temple of Emperor Gāozǔ,
appointing village heads, sacrificial officers, and musicians,
and held fasting ceremonies to worship at the temple of Emperor Gāozǔ."
Further southeast, it passes north of Liú County.
The old city of Liú County
is flanked by the Sì and Jì Rivers,
and was a city of Sòng.
This is the Lǚliú mentioned in the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn as invading Sòng.
Thus, Fán Xiūbó wrote in his Bìdìfù:
"In the morning, I set out from Sìzhōu;
in the evening, I lodge in Liúxiāng."
Zhāng Liáng devoted himself to the Hàn ancestor,
starting from here,
and eventually received a fief.
Within the city, there is a temple of Zhāng Liáng.
Further east, it passes north of Péngchéng County,
where the Huò River flows from the west and joins it.
The Jì River then flows south past the northeast corner of the old city of Péngchéng County,
not passing east.
The Huò River flows into it from the west,
and the city rests on the northern bank of the water.
The Jì River then flows south past the east of the old city of Péngchéng County,
not passing its north.
This is likely an error in the Jīng.
Further southeast, it passes north of Xú County.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The commandery of Línhuái,
was established in the fifth year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
with its seat at Xú County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Huáipíng,
and the county to Xúdiào.
This was the former state of Xú.
In the thirtieth year of Duke Zhāo in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Viscount of Wú captured the Viscount of Zhōngwú,
then attacked Xú,
damming the mountains to flood it,
and subsequently destroyed Xú.
The Viscount of Xú fled to Chǔ.
Chǔ attempted to rescue Xú but failed to arrive in time,
and so fortified Yí to settle him.
Zhāng Huá's *Records of the Investigation of Things* records the dispatch written by the Clerk of the Bureau of Compositions, Máo Wēn.
Liú Chéngguó's *Treatise on the Geography of Xúzhōu* says:
Regarding the strange tale of King Yǎn of Xú,
a palace woman of the Lord of Xú became pregnant and gave birth to an egg.
Considering it inauspicious,
she abandoned it by the waterside.
An old widow had a dog,
named Húcāng,
which was hunting by the water's edge,
found the discarded egg,
carried it back in its mouth,
and the old widow, considering it strange,
covered and warmed it,
and it turned into a child.
As he was born lying prone,
he was thus named.
When the Lord of Xú's palace heard of this,
they took him in again.
He grew up benevolent and wise,
and succeeded to the lordship of the state of Xú.
Later, when Húcāng was dying,
it grew horns and nine tails—
it was truly a yellow dragon.
King Yǎn buried it within Xú territory,
and today a dog mound can still be seen there.
When King Yǎn governed the state,
his benevolence and righteousness were widely known.
Wishing to travel by boat to the Central States,
he dug a canal between Chén and Cài.
He obtained vermilion bows and arrows,
which were considered auspicious signs from heaven.
He therefore took this as his name and title,
calling himself King Yǎn of Xú.
Thirty-six states among the lords of the Jiāng and Huái rivers submitted to him.
When the King of Zhōu heard of this,
he sent an envoy to Chǔ,
ordering them to attack him.
King Yǎn, loving his people and unwilling to fight,
was consequently defeated by Chǔ.
He fled north to the eastern hills of Wǔyuán County in Péngchéng.
Tens of thousands of the common people followed him.
Therefore, the place where he emerged was named Xú Mountain.
A stone-chambered temple was erected on the mountain,
possessing spiritual efficacy,
and the people pray there.
According to the texts and the events,
there seems to be some evidence,
but the ages are remote,
making it difficult to ascertain the details.
Today, outside Xú City, there is the tomb of the Lord of Xú,
where in the past Jìzǐ of Yánlíng untied his sword—
this is the so-called "not going back on a promise made in the heart."
Further east, it reaches south of Suīlíng County in Xiàpī,
and enters the Huái River.
The Jì River and the Sì River,
their waters mingled, flow southeast
to Jiǎochéng,
and together enter the Huái.
The *Classic* writes Suīlíng,
which is an error.
9 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Nine
9.1 Qīng River
9.1 Qīng River
The Qīng River originates from the Black Mountain north of Xiūwǔ County in Hénèi.
The Hēishān is located east of Báilùshān in the north of the county.
It is the source of the Qīngshuǐ,
which gathers from various ponds and scattered springs upstream,
accumulating to form a river.
Flowing southward, it then bends southwest.
A waterfall cascades over the cliffs,
suspended like a river pouring into a ravine over twenty zhang deep,
with a thunderous roar
that shakes the mountains and valleys.
On both sides, the stone cliffs are layered and deep,
with animal tracks and scorch marks intermingled.
Mist from scattered water in the ravine coalesces,
making it impossible to see the bottom.
On the southern peaks and northern ridges,
many reclusive monks have settled.
The eastern cliffs and western valleys
are also sites of temples and spiritual retreats.
The sentiments of bamboo and cypress
harmonize with the profound and mysterious spirit of the mind,
while the nature of benevolence and wisdom
resonates deeply with the mountains and waters,
making it an even more exceptional place.
The water flows through ravines in a flying stream,
clear and cool, offering a view into the cave,
and is called the Qīngshuǐ.
The stream is named Yáoxī,
also called Yáojiàn.
The Qīngshuǐ flows further south
and converges with the Xiǎoyáo Shuǐ,
which originates nearby from a remote stream in the northwest
and flows southeast into the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qīngshuǐ then flows southeast,
where the water from the Wúzé Pond flows into it.
This water originates from the Wú Pond northwest of the old city of Xiūwǔ County.
Xiūwǔ
was formerly called Níng,
and also known as Nányáng.
Mǎ Jìcháng said:
"The land of Jìn, from Zhāogē north to Zhōngshān, is called Dōngyáng;
from Zhāogē south to Zhǐ, it is called Nányáng."
Thus, Yìng Shào's *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
"Hénèi was the state of Yīn,
and the Zhōu named it Nányáng."
It also says:
"Jìn first opened up Nányáng."
This is the present city of Nányáng.
Qín Shǐhuáng changed its name to Xiūwǔ.
Xú Guǎng and Wáng Yǐn both state that it was changed by Qín Shǐhuáng.
Zàn, in his commentary on the *Book of Hàn*, says:
"According to the *Book of Hán Fēi*,
when Qín Zhāowáng crossed Zhào's Chángpíng,
he campaigned west against Xiūwǔ.
At that time, Qín had not yet unified the world,
so the name Xiūwǔ had long existed."
I note that the *Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* states:
"When King Wǔ campaigned against Zhòu,
he marshaled his troops at Níng,
and renamed Níng as Xiūwǔ."
When Wèi Xiànzǐ returned from hunting at Dàlù,
he died at Níng, which is this place.
In the eighth year of Hàn Gāodì,
he enfeoffed Commandant Wèi Chì as a marquis here,
also called Dà Xiūwǔ.
Since there was a smaller one,
this was called the larger.
Xiǎo Xiūwǔ is to the east,
where Hàn Gāozǔ and Lord Téng crossed from the Yùmén Ford
and lodged at Xiǎo Xiūwǔ.
Dàlù is the Wúzé.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
"Twenty lǐ northwest of Xiūwǔ City is the Wúzé Shuǐ."
The pond is about twenty lǐ from north to south,
and thirty lǐ from east to west.
To the west, the Chángmíng Gōu flows into it.
The water has two sources.
The northern water originates from the Jiè Gōu in the northeast border of Yěwáng County in Hénèi,
where a branch stream forms the Chángmíng Gōu.
It flows east past the south of Yōngchéng,
where the Hánquán Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates northwest of Yōngchéng,
with the spring flowing southward,
passing west of Yōngchéng.
In the twenty-fourth year of Duke Xī of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the king intended to use the Dí to attack Zhèng.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"Yōng
is the descendant of King Wén."
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"West of Shānyáng in present-day Hénèi is the old city of Yōng."
It then flows southeast into the Chángmíng Gōu.
The Chángmíng Gōu flows east past the north of Shèquǎnchéng.
Here, the Hàn Grand Marshal Zhāng Yáng was killed by Yáng Chǒu.
Suī Gù killed Chǒu and stationed his troops here,
intending to join Yuán Shào in the north.
The *Diǎnlüè* states:
"Suī Gù, styled Zìtù.
Someone warned Gù, saying:
'General, your style is Tù (rabbit),
and this city is named Quǎn (dog).
When a rabbit encounters a dog,
it is bound to be frightened.
You should leave quickly.'
Gù did not heed this advice."
In the fourth year of the Hàn Jiàn'ān era,
Wèi Tàizǔ executed him here.
He appointed Wèi Zhǒng as the Grand Administrator of Hénèi
to guard it.
When Yǎnzhōu rebelled,
Tàizǔ said:
"Only Zhǒng has not abandoned me."
But when Zhǒng fled,
Tàizǔ angrily said:
"If Zhǒng does not flee south to Yuè
or north to the Hú,
I will not let you go."
After Shèquǎn was pacified,
he captured him.
The Duke said:
"It is only because of his talent."
He released him and employed him.
The Chángmíng Gōu flows east into a stone ravine,
where the Cài Gōu flows into it.
This water originates north of Zhōu County,
branching east from the Báimǎ Gōu,
and is called the Cài Gōu.
It converges east with the Chángmíng Gōu water,
then flows east past the north of the Wútíng in Xiūwǔ County,
and enters the Wú Pond to the east.
Further north, the Gǒuquán Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates southwest of the old Xiūwǔ city in Shānyáng County,
sharing the same source but splitting into two streams.
It divides into two waters:
the southern one is the Gǒuquán,
and the northern one is the Wú Dú.
These two channels flow side by side,
both entering the pond to the east.
Twenty-five lǐ northeast of Shānyáng County is the Lùzhēn Fù.
To its south are the Huángmǔ and Mǎmíng springs,
which converge southeast and flow into the Wú Pond.
Northeast of the Lùzhēn Fù,
one finds the Fùfǔ Duī.
South of this mound are three springs,
spaced four or five lǐ apart,
flowing irregularly but converging,
and entering the pond to the south.
The springs are west of Zhuólùchéng.
In the twenty-fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
Wèi enfeoffed Hàn Xiàndì as the Duke of Shānyáng.
Zhuólùchéng
was where the Duke resided.
North of the pond water, at the edge of the marsh,
lies the Tuíchéng.
In the eleventh year of Duke Yǐn of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the king gave the fields of Minister of Justice Sū Fènshēng,
including Cuánmáo, Tuí, and ten other towns, to Zhèng.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"North of Xiūwǔ County in Hénèi is the old Tuíchéng,
solidly built.
Nowadays, it is commonly called Píyuán,
measuring four hundred paces square,
solidly built,
and eight zhàng high.
At the edge of the pond,
fifteen lǐ north across the water,
is what is commonly called Lánqiū,
measuring two hundred paces square.
Ten lǐ west is another mound at the foot of the mountain,
commonly called Chìqiū,
measuring five hundred paces square.
Their shapes are similar,
and it is suspected that this is the ancient Cuánmáo.
Dù Yù said:
"These two towns are north of Xiūwǔ County,"
but the details are unclear.
Further east,
the Chángquán Shuǐ flows into it.
Its source is southeast of Báilùshān,
flowing underground for thirteen lǐ,
then re-emerging as a strong source northwest of Dèngchéng.
It is also commonly called the Chóngquán Shuǐ.
It then flows east past the Qīxián Shrine,
where bamboo and reeds are planted in rows on both sides,
remaining verdant and steadfast through winter and summer.
Here, the Bùqiū Commandant of Wèi, Ruǎn Jí of Chénliú,
the Palace Attendant Jī Kāng of Qiáoguó,
the Jìn Minister over the Masses Shān Tāo of Hénèi,
the Minister over the Masses Wáng Róng of Lángyá,
the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Xiàng Xiù of Hénèi,
the Military Adviser Liú Líng of Pèiguó,
and the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng Ruǎn Xián,
all lived together in Shānyáng,
forming a carefree and self-contented group.
People of the time called them the "Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove."
This is what Xiàng Zǐqī referred to as the old residence in Shānyáng.
Later generations built a shrine at this site.
South of the shrine is another spring,
which flows southeast into the Chángquán Shuǐ.
As Guō Yuánshēng's *Shùzhēng Jì* records:
"Twenty-five lǐ southeast of Báilùshān is the former residence of Jī Gōng."
Because there were leftover bamboos when residing there,
it is likely referring to this.
The water then flows south past the east of Dèngchéng,
named the Dèng Ditch,
also called the Báiwū Water.
In the past, Sīmǎ Yì campaigned against Gōngsūn Yuān,
and upon returning reached Báiwū,
which is precisely here.
The water then flows southeast past the north of Tuíchéng,
and further southeast passes through marshes to empty into a pond.
The pond water flows east,
called the Bāguāng Ditch,
and eastward flows into the Qīngshuǐ,
named the Chángqīng River.
Eastward, it passes by the Yǒngfēng Wù of Zhōu,
where Dīnggōng Spring emerges to the right of Jiāo Spring.
Further east is Jiāo Spring,
which emerges to the left of Tiānmén and to the right of Tiānjǐng Ridge.
The rock of Tiānmén Mountain is hollow,
shaped like a gate,
three zhàng wide,
two pǐ high,
and over a zhàng deep.
Nothing else emerges from it,
and it is called Tiānmén by the world.
Over five hundred paces to the east,
there is a stone cave facing west,
barely large enough to admit a person.
Entering southeast,
the path leads directly to Tiānjǐng,
ascending straight up over three pǐ.
Climbing by pulling and stepping,
one reaches the upper level,
two hundred paces east-west,
seven hundred paces north-south,
with steep cliffs on all sides,
making it impossible to ascend.
Above is the Vihāra of the Bhikṣu Shì Sēngxùn,
the monastery having over ten monks.
Providing for them is difficult,
so many descend to the lower level,
with those of determination residing there.
Around the monastery are scattered trees,
with a stone spring,
over a square zhàng in size,
its clear water deep and still,
never increasing or decreasing.
Mountain dwellers rely on it for drinking.
To the north are two stone chambers,
formerly the dwelling of the recluse Niànyī,
now uninhabited.
The spring emerges from the northern hill,
flows south to form a stream,
called Jiāo Spring by the world.
Further east is Yúbào Spring,
further east is Zhāngbō Spring,
further east is Sānyuān Spring.
The Gěng River connects in succession,
the Nǚ constellation linked together.
These four springs are west of Chóngménchéng and together flow south into a single river.
Chóngménchéng:
In the past, Qí Wáng Fāng was deposed by Sīmǎ Shī,
and resided here in a palace,
which is what the "Wèi Zhì" refers to as sending Qí Wáng to Chóngmén in Hénèi.
The city is twenty lǐ northwest of the old city of Gòngxiàn.
South of the city is Ānyáng Pond,
further east is Zhuóshuǐ Pond,
further east is Bǎimén Pond,
the pond measuring five hundred paces square,
west of the old city of Gòngxiàn.
In the eighth year of Hàn Gāodì,
Lú Bàshī was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gòng,
which was the old state of Gònghé.
In the past, after Bó returned the imperial governance,
