Sixty lǐ northwest of Shānyáng in Hénèi is Kuí City.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the first year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Zhào's Marquis Chéng Yǎn and Hán's Marquis Yì Ruò attacked our Kuí,
which refers to this city.
The Dān River then bends south and turns west,
where the Guānggōu River originates.
The Dān River flows west past the north of Yuànxiāng City,
bends south and turns east,
passes south of the city,
flows southeast into the Qìn River,
where it is called Dānkǒu.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the fifth year of Duke Shān of Jìn,
the Dān River ceased to flow for three days;
in the ninth year of Duke Yōu,
the Dān River surged and reversed its course,
referring to this river.
The Qìn River flows further east,
where the Guānggōu River joins it.
The Guānggōu River originates from the Dān River,
flows southeast,
and gives rise to the Jiègōu River.
It then flows south into the Qìn River.
The Qìn River flows southeast past the north of Chéngxiāng City,
then east past the south of Zhōngdū Pavilion,
where it joins the Jiègōu River on the left.
The Jiègōu River originates from the Guānggōu River,
flows southeast,
and gives rise to the Chángmínggōu River.
It then flows south past the west of Zhōngdū Pavilion,
and south into the Qìn River.
Further east, it passes north of Zhōu County,
which
was formerly the state of Zhōu.
In the eleventh year of Duke Yǐn in the "Spring and Autumn Annals" and "Zuǒzhuàn,"
the Zhou court granted it to Gōngsūn Duàn of Zhèng.
Hán Xuānzǐ later moved to reside there.
The Báimǎgōu River joins it here,
originating from Báimǎ Lake.
The lake is also called Zhūguǎn Polder.
The polder receives water from the Chángmínggōu River.
The lake water flows southeast,
passing west of Jīn Pavilion,
where it divides into two streams.
One stream flows east as the Cài Ditch,
while the other flows south into the Qìn River.
Further east, it passes north of Huái County.
The "Hánshī Wàizhuàn" states:
When King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu and reached Xíngqiū,
he renamed Xíngqiū as Huái.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Red Dí attacked Jìn and besieged Huái, referring to this place.
Wáng Mǎng designated it as Hénèi,
which was the seat of the former Hénèi Commandery.
It was part of the old territory of the Three Hé.
Wéi Zhāo said:
Hénán, Hédōng, and Hénèi are the Three Hé.
North of the county is Qìnyáng City,
and the Qìn River passes south of it, flowing eastward.
Further east, it passes south of Wǔdé County,
then southeast to north of Xíngyáng County,
where it flows east into the Yellow River.
At the south of the county, the Qìn River
accumulates to form a polder,
connecting several lakes.
The Zhūgōu River joins it here,
originating from the Qìn River northwest of Qìnshuǐ County.
It flows southeast from Fāngkǒu,
where the Fènggōu River branches off to the right.
Further southeast,
it diverges to the right as the Shāgōu River.
The water then flows further southeast,
west of Yěwáng City,
where a branch canal diverges to the left
to irrigate the surrounding city.
It passes east of Yěwáng City,
then bends around the east of the city and flows north into the Qìn River.
The Zhūgōu River flows southeast from the branch canal,
passing south of Zhōu City,
then east past south of Huái City,
and further east past north of Yīn City.
Guō Yuánshēng's "Shùzhēng Jì" states:
On the north bank of the Yellow River,
in Huái County of Hénèi, there is Yīn City.
Some say it was governed by King Āng of Yīn
during the conflict between Chǔ and Hàn,
but this is incorrect.
I consulted the "Bamboo Annals," which records:
When the Qín army attacked Zhèng,
it encamped at Huái
and fortified Yīn City,
which refers to this city.
Thus, the name Yīn has existed for a long time,
indicating it did not originate with Āng.
In the past, Liú Yào appointed Guō Mò as Governor of Yīn Province,
overseeing military affairs along the Yellow River,
with his seat here.
The Zhūgōu River then flows southeast into the lake.
The lake receives the Shāgōu River on the right,
which branches off from the southern distributary of the Zhūgōu River.
It flows southeast past west of Ānchāng City.
In the fourth year of the Hépíng era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Chancellor Zhāng Yǔ was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Southeast of the city today, there is an ancient tomb,
which people call the Tomb of Zhāng Yǔ.
I consulted the "Book of Hàn,"
which states that Yǔ
was from Zhǐ in Hénèi,
but moved his family to Liánsháo.
In the first year of the Hóngjiā era,
Yǔ, due to old age, requested to retire,
and personally arranged his tomb and burial grounds.
He built a ancestral hall at the Féiniú Pavilion in Pínglíng,
near Yánlíng.
He petitioned for this,
and an edict ordered the relocation of the pavilion.
He died in the second year of the Jiànpíng era of Emperor Āi,
and was buried there.
Thus, this tomb is not his.
The Shāgōu River flows east past north of Xí City.
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xí in the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Dàshū was captured at Wēn
and killed at Xí City, referring to this place.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
It is southwest of Huái County.
It then passes west of Yīn City,
and flows southeast into the polder.
The polder water reaches Wǔdé County,
flows south to north of Xíngyáng County,
and then southeast into the Yellow River.
Earlier scholars also regarded this ditch as the Jì Canal.
Thus, Bān Gù and Kàn Yīn both stated that the Jì River reaches Wǔdé and enters the Yellow River.
It seems the branches of the Jì River divide and spread,
each bearing its own name,
and it also shares the designation of the Dān River.
9.3 The Qí River
9.3 The Qí River
The Qí River originates from Dàhào Mountain west of Lónglǜ County in Hénèi.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
The Qí River originates from the Jūrù Mountain.
The water emerges from the side of the mountain,
with cascading waves pouring down,
striking and surging against the transverse mountain.
The mountain is joined at the top and opens at the bottom,
spanning a width of about sixty to seventy paces,
where massive rocks lie piled,
accumulating across the moats and ravines.
The torrential waves surge turbulently,
with a force akin to rolling thunder,
churning the water and scattering mist,
creating a hazy appearance as if fog has gathered.
Further to the northeast,
the Zhān River flows into it.
This water originates from east of the Zhān Terrace in Húguān County,
where lofty stone cliffs rise,
towering and majestic, obscuring the sky.
A spring flows from the northwestern corner,
merging with the Jīngǔ Stream,
which is the western brook of the Zhān Terrace.
It converges with the Zhān River to the northeast,
then flows eastward into the Qí River.
The Qí River then passes through Nánluó Plain,
and further north of Sānluó City,
where it converges with the Nǚtái Stream to the northeast.
This stream originates from below the Three Nǚtái to the northwest,
flowing northeast into the Qí River.
The Qí River continues northeast through Qíyáng Plain,
passing northwest of Shíchéng,
a city situated on a plateau,
bordered by ravines and facing the Qí River.
The Qí River flows further northeast,
where the Xīliú Stream joins it.
This stream originates from below the eastern great ridge,
flowing westward past the south of Shílóu,
located on the northern ridge's stone cliffs,
where waterfalls hang like white silk, standing tall and majestic,
reaching extreme heights with its waters,
known as the Xīliú Stream.
It then flows east past the south of Féngdū Fortress,
commonly called Qíyáng City,
located thirty lǐ to the northwest.
The Qí River then emerges east from the mountains,
splitting into two streams.
The waters converge at a stone weir,
which holds back the water to irrigate the Báigōu Canal.
The left branch is the Yuàn River,
while the right remains the Qí River,
passing southeast of Yuánfǔ City and north of Zhāogē County.
The Bamboo Annals records:
In the eighteenth year of Duke Dìng of Jìn,
the Qí River ceased to flow through old Wèi,
referring to this location.
The Qí River flows further east,
converging on the right with the Quányuán Stream.
This stream has two sources:
one emerges northwest of Zhāogē City,
flowing southeast.
An old man, preparing to cross the water in the morning, hesitated, finding it difficult to ford.
King Zhòu inquired the reason,
and his attendants replied:
"The marrow of the elderly is not solid,
hence they feel the morning cold."
King Zhòu then had the man's shins broken here to examine the marrow.
The water flows south, then bends east,
passing south of Zhāogē City.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì states:
This was originally the Mò settlement.
The Book of Songs says:
"Where shall we gather the tang plant?
In the lands of Mò."
King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn first moved and settled here,
making it the capital of Yīn.
King Zhòu's capital was in the wilderness of Dàlù, as recorded in the "Tribute of Yǔ" section of the Yǔgòng.
This is the place.
Here occurred the events of the "Grain Hill" and "Wine Pond,"
with new decadent music,
giving the settlement the name Zhāogē.
Jìn Zhuó states:
The Shǐjì Yuèshū records
that King Zhòu composed the music of Zhāogē.
Zhāogē means
singing at improper times.
Therefore, when Mòzǐ heard of it,
he detested it and turned his carriage around,
refusing to pass through the settlement.
The Lúnyǔ Bǐkǎo Chèn states:
The settlement was named Zhāogē.
Yán Yuān would not stay,
the seventy disciples covered their eyes,
while Zǎi Yǔ alone looked back,
causing Zǐ Lù to stumble and fall from the carriage.
Sòng Jūn explains:
Zǐ Lù feared Zǎi Yǔ would gaze upon the inauspicious place,
so he kicked him with his foot, causing him to fall from the carriage.
Within lies the Yīn Lùtái,
where King Zhòu once threw himself into the fire.
The Bamboo Annals states:
King Wǔ personally captured Emperor Shòu Xīn at the Nándān Terrace,
thereby dividing the brilliance of Heaven.
The Nándān Terrace
is likely another name for the Lùtái.
King Wǔ enfeoffed King Zhòu's son Wǔ Gēng here with the remaining people of Yīn,
dividing the land into three parts,
called Bèi, Yōng, and Wèi,
appointing Guǎn Shū, Cài Shū, and Huò Shū to oversee them,
forming the Three Supervisors.
They rebelled,
and after Zhōu pacified them, Kāng Shū was enfeoffed as the ruler of Wèi.
Jīzǐ feigned madness in sorrow,
hence the Qíncāo includes the "Jīzǐ Cāo."
Passing through its ruins,
the land of his parents,
overwhelmed with grief,
he composed the "Song of the Wheat in Ear."
Later, it came under the control of Jìn.
Situated between the Hé and Qí Rivers,
during the Warring States period, it belonged to Zhào.
Men and women were licentious and unrestrained,
retaining remnants of King Zhòu's customs.
The terrain was perilous, with many bandits.
During the Hàn, Yú Xǔ was appointed magistrate.
Friends condoled with him, considering it difficult to govern.
Yú Xǔ said:
"Without encountering gnarled roots and tangled knots,
how can one distinguish a sharp tool?"
Further east, it converges with the left stream,
called the Mǎgōu Stream.
This water emerges north of Zhāogē City,
flowing east, then bending south,
passing east of the city.
It then flows east and merges with the Měigōu Stream,
which originates below the great ridge northwest of Zhāogē,
flowing east through Luòtuó Valley.
Within, it meanders through ninety bends,
hence it is commonly called Měigōu.
Passing twelve cliffs,
where streams cascade successively,
the sound of springs never ceasing,
the water swirls and rushes,
coiling back into deep ravines.
Between the ravines, a thousand passages are piled with stones,
and myriad water holes exist.
Observers, if their thoughts are not thorough,
lack the sentiment to appreciate and depict its form.
The water flows east past north of Zhāogē City,
then southeast into the Mǎgōu Stream,
and further southeast into the Qí River,
forming the Féi Spring.
Hence the "Odes of Wèi" states:
"I think of the Féi Spring,
and here I sigh long."
Máo's commentary says:
"Springs that share the same mountain but flow to different destinations are called féi."
The Ěryǎ states:
"Flowing from the same source but reaching different destinations is called féi."
The Shìmíng explains:
"When they first emerge together,
the water that soaks and moistens is little,
but the branches that disperse and return are many,
resembling fertility."
Jiànwéi Shèrén states:
"Water emerging separately and flowing,
yet converging together, is called féi."
Now, this water emerges separately but converges together.
The Bówùzhì calls it the Ào Stream.
The Book of Songs says:
"Look at that bend of the Qí,
where the green bamboos grow luxuriantly."
Máo explains:
"Lǜ"
refers to wángchú grass;
"zhú"
refers to biānzhú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn blocked the breached Yellow River,
cutting down bamboos and trees from the Qí Garden for use.
When Kòu Xún governed Hénèi,
he cut bamboos along the Qí River,
producing over a million arrows,
to supply military provisions.
Now, looking across the Qí River,
these things are no longer found.
Only the wángchú grass and biānzhú remain unchanged.
Máo Xìng further states,
"Ào"
means a bend.
Zhèng also does not consider it the source,
while Minister Zhāng exclusively regards it as water flowing into the Qí,
which is not thoroughly examined.
Yet this water is precisely the "spring-source water" mentioned in the Book of Songs.
Hence the "Odes of Wèi" states:
"The spring source is on the left,
the Qí River is on the right."
A maiden of Wèi, longing to return,
uses this as a metaphor for the left and right of the Qí River,
likely referring to the water's entry points as left and right.
The Qí River flows further south past the Fāng Weir,
the old mouth of the Qí River, flowing east through Líyáng County's boundary,
and south into the Yellow River.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Qí River originates from Gòng,
flowing east to Líyáng and entering the Yellow River.
The "Treatise on Ditches and Canals" states:
Eighteen lǐ west of Zhēhài Pavilion to the mouth of the Qí River is the location.
In the ninth year of the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
King Wǔ of Wèi placed large square timbers at the river mouth to form a weir,
diverting the Qí River eastward into the Báigōu to facilitate water transport,
so people of that time named the place Fāngtóu.
Therefore, Lú Chén's "Rhapsody on Hardships of Campaigns" says:
"Behind are the great square timbers and massive weir,
with deep channels and high embankments."
Afterward, it fell into disuse.
During the Xīpíng era of Wèi, it was reopened,
so the old channel passed north of Fāngchéng,
exiting eastward at the present watercourse,
breaking through the old dam.
The weir
used iron pillars, timber, and stone together,
and the old watercourse passed west of Fāngchéng to the south,
then further south divided into two streams:
one stream flowed south into the Qīng River,
the waters above and below connecting and flowing into each other;
when the Yellow River and Qīng River were in flood,
they entered the old channel northward, beginning from here.
The other stream flowed east,
passing south of Fāngchéng,
and eastward joined with Yuànkǒu.
The Yuàn River received water from the Qí River northwest of Yuánfǔchéng,
from east of the stone weir and west of Yuànchéng,
bending and passing south of the city,
then flowing southeast past northeast of Tǔjūn,
reaching the old stone diversion.
Originally, five waterways divided the flow,
known in the world as the Five Outlets,
but now only two waterways remain connected:
one stream flows west into the Qí River,
called Tiānjǐng Gōu,
and the other passes east of Tǔjūn and divides into Liǎo Gōu,
entering east into Báisì Bēi.
Further south, it divides and flows east into Tóngshān Bēi,
irrigating over seventy qǐng of fields;
the two marshes formed
are the Yě of Táiyīn.
The Yuàn River flows southeast into the Qí River.
The Qí River then joins the old Sùxū watercourse on the right,
which receives water from the Yellow River east of Zhēhài Pavilion and west of Lí Mountain in Dùnqiū County,
where a stone weir was built at its confluence with the Qí River to the north,
diverting the water to flow northeast.
When Wèi Wǔ excavated the Báigōu,
he utilized the old Sùxū watercourse and enhanced its function.
Therefore, Sū Dài said:
"If the mouth of Sùxū is breached,
Wèi will lose Dùnqiū."
This refers to this watercourse.
The Qí River then flows northeast,
called Báigōu,
passing south of Yōngyúchéng.
In the twenty-third year of Duke Xiāng of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Shūsūn Bào came to rescue Jìn,
and encamped at Yōngyú.
The Qí River then flows north past east of the city,
northeast past east of Tóng Mountain,
then northeast past west of Emperor Kù's tomb,
which the world calls Dùnqiū Tái,
but this is incorrect.
The "Imperial Overview" states:
Emperor Kù's tomb is south of Dùnqiūchéng in Púyáng, Dōngjùn,
within the Yě of Táiyīn.
Further north, it passes east of Báisì Mountain,
traverses Guǎngyáng Lǐ,
passes west of Zhuānxū's tomb,
commonly called the Tomb of the Yīn King,
but this is incorrect.
The "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
Zhuānxū was buried south of Dùnqiūchéng in Dōngjùn,
at the large tomb in Guǎngyáng Lǐ.
The Qí River then bends north and turns west,
passing north of Dùnqiū,
so as Yǎn Yīn stated:
Dùnqiū is south of the Qí River.
The "Ěryǎ" says:
A single-tiered mountain is called Dùnqiū.
The "Shìmíng" explains it as a mound formed in one rise,
without distinction of height, size, or slope.
The "Shī" says, "Seeing you off across the Qí,
reaching Dùnqiū."
Wèi relocated various Hú tribes from Jiǔyuán, Xīhé, and Tǔjūn,
settling Tǔjūn beside the mound,
hence it was also called Tǔjūn.
It then bends and passes west of the old city of Dùnqiū County,
which the "Old Text Shàngshū" identifies as Guān territory.
This likely refers to the fifth ruler among Tàikāng's brothers, called Wǔ Guān.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the thirty-first year of Duke Dìng of Jìn, Dùnqiū was walled.
The "Imperial Overview" states:
Dùnqiū
is a city gate name,
Dùnqiū Dào,
which the world calls Yīn,
but these are all incorrect.
It was named after the mound,
hence called Dùnqiū.
The Qí River flows northeast past east of Wǎngrén Mountain and west of Qiānchéng.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Dìng of the "Zuǒzhuàn" to the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi at Qiān.
Dù Yù said:
Northeast of Líyáng is Qiānchéng.
This is that city.
The Qí River then flows northeast past Shízhù Gǎng.
It flows northeast and empties.
Passing south of Nèihuáng County to the east,
it becomes Báigōu.
The Qí River then flows northeast past west of Bìngyángchéng,
which the world calls Pìyángchéng,
but this is incorrect.
It is what the "Treatise on Commanderies and States" calls Bìngyáng Jù in Nèihuáng County.
Báigōu continues north,
joining Dàng River on the left.
It then flows northeast past south of the old city of Nèihuáng County,
the county facing Huángzé on the right.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" states:
The county has Huángzé.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
Chénliú has Wàihuáng,
hence this is called Nèi,
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
Lián Pō of Zhào attacked Wèi and captured Huáng,
referring to this county.
Bending northeast from the county,
it joins the Huán River,
Báigōu passes east of Xìyángchéng north of the county,
which the world calls Yìyáng Jù.
In the tenth year of Duke Zhāo of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Xún Yíng of Jìn went to Qí to fetch a bride,
and on his return,
died at Xìyáng.
Báigōu then flows north past east of Gāochéng Tíng,
where the Huán River comes from the southwest and joins it.
It then flows north past east of Wèn Tíng,
which marks the boundary of Wèi.
The old city of Wèi County,
Yīng Shào said:
It was the secondary capital of Lord Wǔ of Wèi.
Within the city is Lord Wǔ's platform,
called Wèichéng Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
On the left, it joins Xīnhé,
a branch of the Huán River.
Báigōu then flows northeast past west of Tóngmǎchéng,
likely built when Emperor Guāngwǔ campaigned against the Tóngmǎ.
Hence the city got its name.
Báigōu then flows northeast past east of Luólèchéng,
further northeast,
the Zhāng River joins it,
called Lìcáo Kǒu.
From here, the Qīngzhāng, Báigōu, and Qí River
all share the same name.
Further northeast past north of Guǎntáo County,
and further northeast past west of Qīngyuān County,
Báigōu water flows northeast past west of Zhàochéng,
then north,
where the Ānán River emerges.
Likely channeled by General Ānán of Wèi,
to benefit the Héng watercourse,
hence it was named Ānán.
Báigōu then flows northeast past west of Kōnglíngchéng,
then north past west of Qiáotíngchéng,
fifteen lǐ east of the old city of Guǎntáo County,
the county
is what the "Spring and Autumn Annals" calls Guànshì,
and the seat of Yángpíng Commandery of Wèi.
The water then bends past north of the county,
then flows northeast past east of the old city of Píng'ēn County,
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
The county
was originally a separate township of Guǎntáo.
Established in the third year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
Enfeoffed as a marquisate for Xǔ Bó, the empress's father.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
Under Wáng Mǎng, it was Yánpíng County.
The water then flows east past west of the old city of Qīngyuān County,
and passing northwest of the county forms Qīngyuān,
hence the county has the name Qīngyuān.
The world calls it Yúchíchéng,
but this is incorrect.
The water then flows northeast past north of Yúyángchéng,
where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Tàicháng Jiāng Dé as a marquis.
Wén Yǐng said:
The fief was in Qīngyuān, Wèi Commandery,
which the world calls Qīngyuānchéng,
but this is incorrect.
Further northeast past east of Guǎngzōng County,
it becomes the Qīng River.
The Qīnghé River flows northeast past the old city of Guǎngzōng County.
In the fifth year of the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Hé,
the imperial crown prince Wànnián was enfeoffed here, establishing a kingdom.
Tián Róng stated that
the Zhào state established the Jiànxīng Commandery within the city,
and placed Línqīng County east of the river,
beginning from the time of Zhào Shí.
To the right of the Qīnghé River is the tomb of Lǐ Yún.
Yún, styled Xíngzǔ,
was a native of Gānlíng.
He was fond of learning,
excelled in yīn-yáng arts,
was recommended as a Xiàolián,
and promoted to Magistrate of Báimǎ.
The Palace Attendants Shàn Chāo and others,
established a commoner of the Yètíng, the Mǐn family, as Empress.
Four members of the Empress's family were enfeoffed,
and rewards amounting to hundreds of millions were bestowed.
Yún submitted a memorial, sending copies to the Three Excellencies, saying:
Confucius said,
"The term 'Emperor' (Dì)
means 'to examine carefully' (dì).
Now, appointments made by imperial decree (chǐ yī),
are not reviewed by the Emperor himself.
Does this mean the Emperor does not wish to examine carefully?"
The Emperor was enraged,
imprisoned him, and had him executed.
Later, when Jià Cóng, Inspector of Jìzhōu, was on an inspection tour, he passed by and paid respects at Yún's tomb,
erected a stone stele to honor him.
The stone pillar still exists today,
commonly called the Lǐ Family Stone Pillar.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the east of the Jièchéng Pavilion.
There is a large bridge over the water,
called the Jièchéng Bridge.
The *Records of Heroes* states:
Gōngsūn Zàn attacked the Huángjīn bandits of Qīngzhōu,
routed them greatly,
and returned to garrison Guǎngzōng.
Yuán Běnchù personally led an expedition against Zàn.
They joined battle twenty *lǐ* south of the Jiè Bridge.
Yuán Shào's general Qū Yì defeated Zàn at the Jièchéng Bridge,
and beheaded Zàn.
Yán Gāng, Inspector of Jìzhōu, also defeated Zàn's rear guard troops on the bridge.
This is that very bridge.
The world calls it the Gèchéng Bridge,
which is likely a corruption in transmission.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the west of Xìnxiāng.
The *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
Seventeen *lǐ* northwest of Gānlíng is Xìnxiāng,
an old county seat.
The Qīnghé River again flows north past the west of the old city of Xìnchéng County.
Yìng Shào said:
Fifty *lǐ* northwest of Gānlíng is the Xìnchéng Pavilion,
an old county seat.
The Zhào state established Shuǐdōng County at this city,
hence it is also called Shuǐdōng City.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the west of the old city of Qīngyáng County.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn established Qīnghé Commandery,
with its seat here.
In the third year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng,
the imperial son Chéng was enfeoffed here, establishing a kingdom.
It was called Pínghé under Wáng Mǎng.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Xiānyú Jì from Xīhé was appointed Grand Administrator of Qīnghé.
He began constructing an official residence but died before its completion.
Later, the Administrator Zhào Gāo estimated the project cost at two million,
while the Official Huáng Bǐng
and the Registrar Liú Shì stated:
four million cash.
Thereupon, Jì's ghost appeared in broad daylight,
entered the prefecture accompanied by attendants,
and confronted Gāo and Bǐng,
jointly checking and verifying the accounts.
It was determined that Shì and Bǐng had embezzled and concealed funds.
Jì then wrote a memorial stating his case, the gist being:
Gāo is of noble status but lacks integrity;
a man of the fields and mounds,
yet he sits arrogantly, leaving behind his kind;
scrutinizing details, he misses the crucial point;
his nature is that of a servant girl or concubine;
flattering the age to seek prominence;
stealthy, thieving, cruel, and base;
he brings disgrace to the office bestowed by Heaven;
the *Yì* admonishes against the unworthy occupying high position;
this truly describes Gāo.
I, your subject, cannot bear the ghost's words.
Respectfully, I report this via the thousand-*lǐ* postal relay.
I submit it to Gāo to forward upwards.
Then he went northwest for thirty *lǐ*,
where his carriage and horses vanished and were seen no more.
Bǐng and the others all fell to the ground and died.
Gāo reported the circumstances.
An imperial edict was issued,
returning Jì's fields, residences, wife, and children in Xīhé to him.
Furthermore, officials were appointed in succession,
to quell the grievances from the underworld.
In the third year of the Jiànhé era of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
Qīnghé was changed to the Gānlíng Kingdom.
Because the king engaged in sorcery and seditious talk,
he was transferred.
That year, Gānlíng Commandery was established,
with its seat here.
It again flows northeast past the west of Dōngwǔchéng County.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the west of Língxiāng.
Yìng Shào said:
Seventy *lǐ* southwest of Dōngwǔchéng is Língxiāng,
an old county seat.
In the Later Hàn, Grand Coachman Liáng Sōng was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Hence the world calls it Liánghóu City,
and subsequently Hóuchéng County was established with its seat here.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the west of the old city of Dōngwǔchéng County.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
Shèng, a prince of Zhào,
titled the Lord of Píngyuán,
for his merit in relieving Hándān,
was enfeoffed here.
As there was a Wǔchéng in Dìngxiāng,
this one was prefixed with "East" (Dōng).
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the west of the old city of Fùyáng County.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Right Marshal Chén Xū was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lèsuì.
The *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
Thirty *lǐ* northwest of Dōngwǔchéng is the Fùyáng Pavilion,
an old county seat.
The world calls it Jiànchéng,
which is incorrect.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast.
It passes the west of the old city of Zǎojiàng County.
The *Table of Enfeoffed Imperial Princes Since the Jiànyuán Era* in the *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
In the second year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Yàn, son of Huì, Prince of Guǎngchuān, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Yìng Shào's *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
Fifty *lǐ* northwest of Dōngwǔchéng County,
there is Zǎojiàng City,
an old county seat.
It again flows north past the east of Guǎngchuān County.
The Qīnghé River flows north past the south of the old city of Guǎngchuān County.
Kàn Yǐn said:
Within the county, a long river flows through,
hence it is called Guǎngchuān (Broad River).
Beside the water are Qiāng fortifications,
the former residence of the Yáo clan.
This is now the seat of Guǎngchuān County.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the south of the old city of Lì County.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
it was a subordinate county of Xìndū.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lìníng.
Yìng Shào said:
Thirty *lǐ* northwest of Guǎngchuān County is the Lìchéng Pavilion,
an old county seat.
Now the pavilion is located east and somewhat north of the county,
and the water crossing is still called the Lìkǒu Ferry.
It again flows east past the south of Xiū County.
It again flows northeast past the west of Dōngguāng County.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast,
where on the left it joins with the old course of the Zhāngjiǎtún Jiàng River,
now blocked by deep embankments and high barriers,
and no longer contains water.
It again passes the south of the old city of Xiū County,
bends and passes east of its city.
Xiū is pronounced "tiáo".
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiūzhì.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
It formerly belonged to Xìndū.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast,
where on the left it joins with the old branch course of the Qízhāng River.
It again flows northeast past the east of the old city of the Xiū Kingdom.
Emperor Wén of Hàn enfeoffed Zhōu Yàfū here as a marquisate.
Hence the world calls it Běixiū City.
The Qīnghé River again flows northeast past the east of Dǐgé City.
The city lies adjacent to the Qīnghé River.
It was the seat of Xiū County in the Jìn dynasty.
Within the city is a stele for Magistrate Kǒng Míng of the State of Lǔ.
The Qīnghé River again flows east to the west of Dōngguāng County,
then flows south past the Húsū Pavilion.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
Dōngguāng has the Húsū Pavilion.
The world calls it Qiāngchéng,
which is incorrect.
It again flows northeast,
where on the right it meets the old course of the Great River (Yellow River),
and again passes the west of the old city of Dōngguāng County.
In the Later Hàn, Gěng Chún was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
In the second year of the Chūpíng era,
three hundred thousand Huángjīn bandits entered Bóhǎi.
Gōngsūn Zàn defeated them within the boundaries of Dōngguāng,
pursued them fleeing to this river,
decapitated thirty thousand,
their blood dyeing the water red.
This is that very river.
It again flows northeast past the west of Nánpí County.
The Qing River flows further northeast,
where the Wúdì Ditch emerges.
It passes east by the old city of Nánpí County,
then east by the north of Lètíng,
which is the old city of Línlè County from the "Geographical Treatise,"
renamed Lètíng by Wáng Mǎng.
According to the "Jìnshū Dìdào Zhì"
and the "Tàikāng Dìjì,"
the state of Lèlíng had a Xīnlè County.
This is that city.
It then passes east by the north of Xīnxiāng City.
This is the old city of Gāolè from the "Geographical Treatise,"
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Wéixiāng.
The Wúdì Ditch further east divides into two channels.
The Wúdì Ditch flows east past the north of Lèlíng Commandery,
then bends northward,
turns east and passes by the old city of Yuànxiāng County,
then southeast by the old city of Gāochéng County,
where it merges with a branch channel.
This branch channel originates from the Wúdì Ditch,
flows south past the west of Lèlíng Commandery,
then southeast past the east of the old city of Qiāntóng County.
The "Shǐjì Jiànyuán Yǐlái Wángzǐ Hóu Zhě Niánbiǎo" states:
It was originally called Zhòng,
also written as Qiānzhōng.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Xiǎnyīn, son of the Prince of Héjiān Xiàn, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
Yìng Shào said:
Emperor Líng of Hàn renamed it Ráo'ān,
the seat of Cāngzhōu.
The branch channel bends southeast,
then flows northeast to join the Wú
dì Ditch.
The Wúdì Ditch flows northeast past the north of an old city,
commonly called Gōngchéng.
It then flows northeast past the northeast of Yán Mountain and enters the sea.
In the fourth year of Duke Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
when Qí and Chǔ made a covenant at Shàolíng,
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Long ago, Duke Shào Kāng granted our former lord, Tàigōng, domain boundaries,
reaching north to Wúdì."
This is likely the extent of those boundaries.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
According to an old account, Wúdì was in Gūzhú County of Liáoxī.
The two accounts differ,
and it is uncertain which is correct.
However, since Guǎn Zhòng cited this Wúdì to reprimand Chǔ,
this location seems more plausible.
As it has been traditionally accepted for a long time,
I record it based on what I have heard and seen.
The Qing River flows northeast past the west of the old city of Nánpí County.
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" says:
"Zhāngwǔ has a Běipí Tíng,
hence this is called Nánpí."
Wáng Mǎng named it Yínghé Tíng.
The "Shǐjì Huì Jǐng Hóu Zhě Niánbiǎo" states:
In the seventh year of the later period of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Péng Zǔ, nephew of Empress Xiàowén, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Cáo Cāo captured Yuán Tán at this city.
The Qing River flows north past the east of Běipí City,
where it joins the old course of a branch of the Hūtuó River on the left,
called Hékǒu,
and the city is called Héchéng.
The "Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì" says:
"Fifty lǐ north of Nánpí City is Běipí City,"
which is this city.
It then passes northeast by the west of Fúyáng County.
The Qing River flows northeast,
where the old course of the Fú River emerges.
According to the "Shǐjì,"
the southern boundary of Zhào had a Fú River.
The Fú River was to the south,
yet this place bears the name Fúyáng.
This is likely because the Fú River's flow,
with its converging and reversing currents,
mingled with the two channels of the Qīng and Zhāng Rivers,
following the old course of the Hé River.
The old trace of the Fú River
diverged again from here,
hence the county has the name Fúyáng.
It begins by receiving the Qing River within the county boundaries,
flows northeast past the north of Yuànxiāng City in Gāochéng County,
then east past the north of the old city of Zhāngwǔ County.
In the seventh year of the later period of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Dòu Guǎngguó, brother of Empress Xiàowén, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huánzhāng.
In the Tàishǐ era of Jìn, Zhāngwǔ Commandery was established,
with its seat here.
The old course of the Fú River flows east past the north of Qiè Mountain.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
"Fifty lǐ northeast of Gāochéng is Qiè Mountain,
seven lǐ long."
The Fú channel flows northeast past the south of the old city of Liǔ County.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Yáng, son of Prince Xiào of Qí, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
The "Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì" says:
"Fifty lǐ northeast of Gāochéng County is Liǔ Tíng,
which was formerly a county."
It is commonly called Pì Tíng,
but this is incorrect.
The Fú channel flows northeast past Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Wànghǎi Tái,
then east into the sea.
Yìng Shào said:
"Fúyáng County
is where the Fú River flows into the sea,
with tides coming and going
twice daily."
Now, the ditch no longer has water.
The Qing River further north divides into two channels,
with a branch flowing east,
also called the Fú channel.
The Qing River flows north past the west of the old city of Fúyáng County, which Wáng Mǎng called Fúchéng.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Liú Xīn, General Xiāoqí and Marquis of Píngxiāng, was re-enfeoffed here as a marquis.
It was the seat of Fúyáng Commandery.
Further northeast,
a branch of the Hūtuó River joins it,
called Hékǒu.
It then passes northeast by the north of Huìyì,
where the Huì River emerges.
It then passes northeast by the south of Xiāngyì.
The Qing River flows east,
dividing into two streams,
with a branch channel emerging on the right.
It flows east past the old terrace of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
"One hundred lǐ east of Zhāngwǔ County is Emperor Wǔ's Terrace,
with two terraces, north and south,
sixty lǐ apart,
with foundations sixty zhàng high.
It is commonly said
that Emperor Wǔ of Hàn built it while touring the eastern seas."
It then flows east into the sea.
The Qing River flows northeast past the south of Zhùgūyì,
commonly called Xīnchéng,
but this is incorrect.
It then passes northeast by the south of Qiónghéyì.
The Qing River flows northeast past the south of Qiónghéyì,
commonly called Sānnǚchéng,
but this is incorrect.
Northeast, it reaches Quánzhōu County,
and enters the Hūtuó River from the north.
The "Shuǐ Jīng" says:
"The Sìgōu flows southeast to Quánzhōu County and joins the Qing River,
from which point it becomes the Pài River's tail."
Further east,
the Quánzhōu Canal emerges.
It then passes northeast by Piāoyúyì,
and enters the sea.
The Qing River flows east past the old city of Piāoyúyì,
commonly called Jiǎofēichéng.
The "Zhào Jì" says:
"Shí Lè sent Wáng Shù to boil salt at Jiǎofēi,"
which is another name for this city.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
"One hundred lǐ northeast of Gāochéng County,
north to the end of Piāoyú,
east facing the vast sea,
the people all boil seawater,
relying on salt-making for their livelihood,"
referring to this city.
From here, the Qing River enters the sea.
9.4 Dàng River
9.4 Dàng River
The Dàng River emerges from the eastern mountains west of Dàngyīn County in Hénèi.
The Dàng River originates from Shíshàng Mountain west of the county,
its spring-fed stream passing by the old city south of the county,
and the county is named after the river.
When Jìn attacked Prince Chéngdū Yǐng,
the emperor was defeated south of this river.
Lú Chēn's "Sì Wáng Qǐshì" says:
When Emperor Huì campaigned against Prince Chéngdū Yǐng,
and was defeated in battle,
the eight bearers of the imperial carriage,
with the carriage still on their shoulders,
were all killed by competing soldiers.
The carriage fell to the ground,
and the emperor was wounded by three arrows.
All officials fled in disarray,
only the Palace Attendant Jī Shào supported the emperor.
Soldiers were about to attack him,
but the emperor said:
"He is my official,
do not harm him."
The crowd said:
"We have received the Tàidì's orders
to spare only Your Majesty alone."
They then beheaded him,
and his blood stained the emperor's sleeve.
When about to wash it,
the emperor said:
"This is Palace Attendant Jī's blood,
do not wash it away."
This is where Jī Yánzǔ met his end.
Further northeast to Nèihuáng County,
it enters Huángzé.
The Yǒu River originates from Hán Dàniú Spring northwest of Dàngyīn.
The "Geographical Treatise" states:
from the western mountains of the county,
the Yǒu River emerges.
The Yǒu River then flows east past the north of Hán Fùbì,
and further east flows past the north of Yǒu City,
which was the ancient Yǒulǐ.
The "Shǐjì Yīnyì" says:
Yǒulǐ is in Dàngyīn County.
The "Guǎngyǎ" states,
yǒu
means prison.
In the Xià dynasty it was called Xiàtái,
in the Yīn dynasty Yǒulǐ,
in the Zhōu dynasty Língyǔ,
all being circular earthen enclosures.
In the past, King Zhòu of Yīn, accepting the words of Chóng Hóuhǔ,
imprisoned the Western Earl here.
Sǎn Yíshēng and Nángōng Kuò visited King Wén,
who then expounded the "Yì" to clarify the principles of adversity and prosperity, beginning and end.
North of Yǒu City,
water accumulated to form an abyss,
over ten paces square,
more than one zhang deep,
flowing east to Nèihuáng where it meets the Fáng River.
The Fáng River emerges from Mǎtóu Ravine in the western mountains,
flows east past the north of Fáng City,
which is the Yuèfáng mentioned in Lú Chén's "Zhēng Jiān Fù".
This water flows southeast and pours into the Yǒu River,
then flows east through Huángzé and enters the Dàng River.
The "Geographical Treatise" says:
the Yǒu River reaches Nèihuáng and enters the Dàng.
The Dàng River then flows east and joins with the Chángshāgōu River.
Its source is the northern valley of Hēi Shān,
flowing east past the north of the old ramparts of Jìn Bǐ,
called Jìn Bǐ City,
also named Wèi Jiàng City.
In the past, Lord Wújì of Wèi forged an order and seized Jìn Bǐ's army here.
Thus Bān Shūpí's "Yóu Jū Fù" says:
passing Dàngyīn to mourn Jìn Bǐ,
condemning the lord for his disloyalty.
This water flows further east,
called Yíshī Ditch,
then flows east past the south of Dàngyīn County,
further east past Wǎngrén Shān,
northeast to Nèihuáng County,
entering the Dàng River from the right,
also called Huángquè Ditch.
This water
floods in autumn and summer,
and diminishes in spring and winter.
The Dàng River then flows past the south of Nèihuáng City.
Chénliú has a Wàihuáng,
hence this is called Nèi (Inner).
It flows east and empties into Báigōu.
9.5 Huán River
9.5 Huán River
The Huán River originates from Xuànshì County in Shàngdǎng.
The water emerges from Huán Shān,
which is in Zhǎngzǐ County.
It flows east past the north of Lónglǜ County.
North of the county is Lónglǜ Shān,
where Bó Zhònglǐ once roamed in spirit.
The county is named after the mountain.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Zhōu Zào was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Yìng Shào said:
the Shāng Emperor was named Lóng,
so it was changed to Lín.
The county has the Huánghuá River,
which emerges from the northern cliff of Huánghuá Valley on Shénqūn Shān.
The mountain is seventeen lǐ high.
The water emerges from the Mùmén Belt,
the belt being the third level of the mountain,
seven lǐ above the ground.
The suspended water pours southeast into the ravine,
plunging straight down the cliff,
its shape resembling a rooster's tail,
hence called Jīqiào Torrent,
comparable to
Tiāntāi and Chìchéng waterfalls.
The water flows east to the valley mouth,
submerges underground,
and re-emerges ten lǐ northeast,
named Liǔzhǔ,
the islet being four or five lǐ around,
this is the Huánghuá River's resurgence from a second source.
Flowing east,
it is joined by Wěiquán River,
which emerges from the marshes north of Línlǜ Shān,
flowing southeast,
and merging with Shuāngquán,
which emerges from Lǔbān Gate,
flowing east down into Wěiquán River.
Wěiquán River flows further southeast,
and pours into the Huánghuá River,
called Língyáng River.
Further east,
it enters the Huán River.
Further northeast, it exits the mountains,
passing south of Yè County.
The Huán River leaves the mountains,
flowing east past the north of Yīnxū.
The "Zhúshū Jìnián" says:
when Pángēng ascended the throne,
he moved from Yǎn to Běiméng,
called Yīn.
In the past,
Xiàng Yǔ and Zhāng Hán made a covenant here.
The Huán River flows further east,
where a distributary branches off,
flowing northeast past the south of Yè City,
called the Xīn River.
Further east,
it divides into two streams.
One stream flows north past beneath Dōngmíng Observatory.
In the past, Mùróng Jùn dreamed Shí Hǔ bit his arm,
awoke disturbed by it,
offered a reward for the corpse,
but none knew its location.
Later, a favored concubine of the rear palace said
Hǔ was buried beneath Dōngmíng Observatory.
Thereupon they dug there,
descended past three springs,
found his coffin,
opened it and removed the corpse.
The corpse was rigid and not decayed.
Jùn cursed it, saying:
"Dead barbarian,
how dare you dream of a living Son of Heaven!"
He ordered the Imperial Censor Zhòngwèi Yáng Yuē to enumerate his crimes and whip the corpse.
This was likely Hǔ's original burial place.
Further north, it passes the stone bridge of Jiànchūn Gate.
Not very tall,
the stonework is finely crafted and dense.
The old bridge had two stone pillars flanking its head,
with excellent chī-dragon bases and carved inscriptions.
When the imperial carriage journeyed south,
finding its construction splendid and exquisite,
they moved it to the west tower east of Píngchéng,
facing north towards the archery hall.
Green waters form a level pool,
emerald woods line the banks,
a place for leisurely strolls and rest.
This water flows west past the old Xuánwǔ Park of Wèi Wǔ,
the park originally had Xuánwǔ Pond,
for practicing with boats,
with fish weirs, fishing terraces, bamboo, trees, and thickets.
Now the pond and woods are utterly gone,
with hardly any trace remaining.
This water flows west and empties into the Zhāng.
The southern stream flows northeast past the north of Nǚtíng City,
further northeast past the south of Gāolíng City,
east joining Jiōng Ditch,
then east past Lúcí Slope,
north merging with Tái Slope water.
The slope is thirty lǐ east-west,
north-south emptying into the Báigōu River.
The ditch receives water from the Huán River upstream,
crosses the Xīn River northwards,
flows north past the east of Gāolíng City,
further north past the west of the old city of Chìqiū County.
The southern corner of the county has Chìqiū,
the county likely named after the hill,
hence Gānhóu.
The "Chūnqiū Jīng" records,
in the twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhāo,
the duke went to Jìn,
and halted at Gānhóu.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Táng Lì was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
Wáng Mǎng's Lìqiū.
It then bends past the north of the city,
flowing northeast and emptying into Báigōu.
The Huán River from Yè flows east past the north of the old city of Ānyáng County.
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" says:
Shí Zūn entered from north of Lǐ City,
and beheaded Zhāng Chái at Ānyáng, which is this place.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
forty lǐ south of Yè City is Ānyáng City,
north of the city the Huán River flows east.
The Huán River flows further east to Chánglè County,
where a branch ditch emerges on the left.
The Huán River then flows east past the south of the old city of Chánglè County.
According to the "Jìnshū Dìlǐ Zhì":
Wèi Commandery had Chánglè County.
Further east, it passes north of Nèihuáng County,
and enters Báigōu to the east.
The Huán River flows past the north of Nèihuáng County and runs eastward,
emptying into the Báigōu,
which is commonly known as Huánkǒu.
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén and Lǚ Chēn's Zìlín
both state that the Huán River originates between Jìn and Lǔ.
In the past, Shēng Bó dreamed of wading across the Huán River,
where someone gave him qióngguī beads to eat.
He wept, and then more qióngguī beads appeared,
filling his bosom.
He then sang:
"Crossing the waters of the Huán,
I am gifted with qióngguī.
To return,
to return,
qióngguī fills my bosom."
Later, when he spoke of this,
he died by evening.
This is the same river.
10 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 10
10.1 The Zhuózhāng River
10.1 The Zhuózhāng River
The Zhuózhāng River originates from Fājiū Mountain west of Zhǎngzǐ County in Shàngdǎng,
and the Zhāng River originates from Lùgǔ Mountain,
which is connected to Fājiū Mountain by the same ridge but lies to the south.
The Huáinánzǐ refers to it as Fābāo Mountain,
hence different names appear interchangeably.
On the left, the Yángquán River flows into it,
and on the right, the Sǎngài River joins it.
These three sources all emerge from the same mountain,
but are distinguished by their north and south locations.
It flows east past the south of the county,
then further east,
the Yáo River flows northeast from the western mountains,
passes north of the Yáo Temple,
and then east past the old city wall of Zhǎngzǐ County,
which was the fief of Xīn Jiǎ, an official of the Zhōu dynasty.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the people of Jìn captured the Wèi envoy Shí Mǎi in Zhǎngzǐ;
this is the same county.
The Qín dynasty established Shàngdǎng Commandery,
with its seat here.
The river flows northeast into the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River joins the Liáng River to the east,
which originates from Nánliáng Mountain,
flowing north past the old city wall of Zhǎngzǐ County.
The Zhúshū Jìnián states:
In the twelfth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Zhèng captured Túnliú, Shàngzǐ, and Niè.
Shàngzǐ
is another name for Zhǎngzǐ.
The Liáng River then flows north into the Zhāng River.
It bends and flows northeast from the county,
the Táo River emerges south from Táoxiāng,
flows north past the east of Zhǎngzǐ City,
turns west past the north of the city,
and empties east into the Zhāng River.
It then flows east past the north of Húguān County,
and further northeast past the south of Túnliú County,
the Zhāng River flows east past the south of Túnliú County,
then bends past the east of the city,
flowing northeast,
where the Jiàng River flows into it.
This river originates west from the valley of Fājiū in Gǔyuǎn County,
and is called the Làn River.
It flows east past the old city wall of Túnliú County,
which was the ancient state of Liúxū.
It belonged to the Lù clan.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the people of Jìn captured Sūn Kuǎi in Chúnliú, which is this place.
The river flows northeast into the Zhāng River.
Thus, Sāng Qīn states:
The Jiàng River originates southwest of Túnliú,
and flows east into the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River flows further east,
where the Dòng River joins it,
which originates west from Fājiū Mountain,
flows east past the old city wall of Yúwú County,
in the sixth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Jǐng Dān's son Shàng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Dòng River then flows east past the north of the old city wall of Túnliú County,
according to the Zhúshū Jìnián,
in the first year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Marquis Gòng of Hán and Marquis Chéng of Zhào moved Duke Huán of Jìn to Túnliú.
The Shǐjì records
that Marquis Sù of Zhào seized Duānshì from the ruler of Jìn and relocated him here.
The river then flows east and empties into the Zhāng River.
Thus, Xǔ Shèn states:
The river originates from Fājiū Mountain and enters the Zhāng River,
with the water radical,
and the phonetic component "dōng."
The Zhāng River then flows northeast past the west of the old city wall of Húguān County,
bends past the north of the city,
which was the ancient state of Lí.
There is a Lí Pavilion,
and the county has the Húkǒu Pass,
hence it is called Húguān.
In the first year of Empress Lǚ,
Wǔ, a son of Emperor Huì's harem, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
In the Hàn dynasty, an elder of Húguān named Gōngchéng Xìng submitted a petition defending Crown Prince Wèi,
and he was a native of this town.
The county lies east of Túnliú,
so it cannot be placed before Túnliū in sequence.
The Zhāng River passes Lùtái Mountain and merges with the Tóngtī River,
which originates from Shídèng Mountain northwest of Tóngtī County,
flows east and joins the Zhuānchí River,
which originates from Bātè Mountain,
and flows northeast into the Tóngtī River.
The Tóngtī River then merges with the Nǚjiàn River to the southeast,
which originates northwest from Hǎosōng Mountain,
flowing southeast,
with the Wěichí River and Gōngzhǔ River merging on the north and joining it from the right;
on the south, the Yújiāo River and Huánghòu River merge and enter from the left,
flowing together southeast,
and emptying into the Tóngtī River.
The Tóngtī River then flows east past the tomb of Lǐ Xǐ,
with a stele in front of the tomb,
though the stone is broken and fragmented.
The Lǐ family erected it in the first year of the Tàihé era.
The river then flows east past the north of the old city,
which sits atop a mountain ridge,
overlooking valleys below,
with three sides—east, west, and north—
protected by a two-lǐ-long wall,
commonly known as Duànliáng City,
which was the Shàngsī Pavilion of the old county.
The Tóngtī River then flows east past the north of the old city wall of Tóngtī County,
the city lies in the mountains south of the river,
and was the fief of Yángshé Chì, the Earl of Tóngtī, a senior official of Jìn.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn defeated Hán Wáng Xìn in this county.
The Tóngtī River then flows southeast past the west of Qǐng City,
which was the Xiàsī settlement of the county.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
The county has the Shàngsī Pavilion and the Xiàsī settlement.
The Tóngtī River then flows south past the west of Húyì,
bends east past the south of the city,
then flows east past Xiāngyuán County,
and enters the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River then flows northeast past the old city wall of Xiāngyuán County,
which was Wáng Mǎng's Shàngdǎng Pavilion.
North of Lù County,
The county
was originally the state of the Red Dí Lùzǐ.
Its minister Fēng Shū had outstanding talent,
but lacked abundant virtue.
Jìn’s Bó Zōng enumerated his five crimes,
and sent Xún Línfǔ to destroy it.
Kàn Yīn said:
There is the Lù River,
which is a marshland of Jìzhōu,
namely the Zhāng River.
I consulted the Yān Shū,
where Wáng Měng and Mùróng Píng met at Lùchuān.
Píng blocked the mountain springs,
selling water to the army,
at the price of one bolt of silk
for two dàn of water.
There being no other large river
that could serve as a marshland,
the only great waves and long rapids
were those of the Zhāng River.
Thus, people also call the Zhuózhāng the Lù River.
North of the county lies the old Táibì,
with the Zhāng River passing south of it.
It was originally established by the Lùzǐ,
and is commonly known as Táibì.
When Mùróng Chuí attacked Mùróng Yǒng at Zhǎngzǐ,
his army camped at Lùchuān.
Yǒng led elite troops to resist,
relying on the river for defense.
Chuí arrayed his forces at Táibì,
and defeated them in a single battle,
which took place here.
Here, the Zhāng River joins the Huángxū River mouth on the left.
The water emerges from beneath Zhāng Huì Cliff west of Táibì.
It is said that when the cliff turns red, the land suffers military disaster.
Thus, to avoid its unpredictable changes,
people constantly smear it with stone powder to whiten it,
hence it is commonly called Zhāng Huì Cliff.
The water flows south,
passes west of Táibì,
and then enters the Zhāng River to the south.
The Zhāng River then flows northeast past Wàngfū Mountain.
South of the mountain, a stone figure stands atop it.
Its posture suggests longing amid the clouds,
hence the name.
The Niè River flows east from Fùzèng Mountain in the west,
and joins the Xītāng Stream.
The water emerges from Tāng Valley in the western mountains of Niè County,
where five springs converge,
called the Five Converging Springs.
They flow southeast together,
known as the Xītāng River,
then flow southeast and join the Niè River.
The Niè River then flows east past the old city of Niè County,
which is named after the Niè River.
To the east, it joins the Báijī River.
The water emerges from the western mountains of the county,
flows east past the north of the county,
then southeast into the Niè River.
The Niè River flows further southeast,
where the Wǔxiāng River joins it.
The source is southwest of Wǔ Mountain,
passing west of the old city of Wǔxiāng County,
and south to the Qīnggǔ mouth.
The water emerges from Qīng Valley in the northeast’s Cháng Mountain,
flows southwest and joins the Bìběng and Báibì rivers,
then south into the Wǔxiāng River.
Further south is the Huángshuǐ mouth.
The Huáng River has three sources,
which converge in one gorge,
flow southeast and join the Yǐnshì River.
The water emerges northwest from Yǐnshì Mountain,
flows southeast into the Huáng River.
Then east into the Wǔxiāng River.
The Wǔxiāng River flows southeast into the Niè River.
The Niè River flows further southeast,
and joins the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River then flows east past north of Pányáng City,
where the Cānggǔ River joins it.
The water emerges from Cānggǔ Stream in Línlǜ County,
flows northeast past west of Lǔbān Gate,
where twin towers rise majestically,
and stone cliffs soar like rosy clouds.
On both sides, stone embankments are constructed,
with lofty foundations still remaining.
It flows north past east of Piānqiáo,
which is the Qiáolǐng Bàodú Fortress of Línlǜ.
Stone steps ascend westward,
climbing for over five lǐ.
The cliff path is interrupted for four or five zhàng,
with a wooden plank bridge in the middle,
barely passable,
hence the name Piānqiáo.
From above, one must still cling to vines and grasp creepers,
to cross safely.
At the mountain peak,
is where Yǔ Gǔn grew dizzy and fell.
Cānggǔ Stream further north joins the Báimù Stream.
The water emerges from Báimùchuān east of Húguān County,
flows east past north of Bǎimǔ City,
akin to the Qiúchí Hundred Qǐng.
It then flows east through Shímén Valley in Línlǜ County,
and joins Cānggǔ Stream.
Cānggǔ Stream flows north past east of Pányáng City and northward,
joining the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River then flows east past north of Gégōng Pavilion and eastward.
Further east, it passes Wǔ'ān County.
At the east of the county, the Zhāng River
is joined by the Qīngzhāng River from southeast of Shè County,
commonly known as the Jiāozhāng Mouth.
It then exits the mountains eastward,
passing west of Yè County.
The Zhāng River then flows eastward through the Sānhù Gorge to become the Sānhù Ford.
Zhāng Yàn said:
Sānhù
is a place name
located southwest of Liángqī.
Mèng Kāng stated:
Ford
is the name of the gorge
located forty lǐ west of Yè.
Further east,
the Wū River flows into it;
the river originates in the mountains of Wǔ'ān County,
flowing southeast past Wūchéng to the north.
In the past, Xiàng Yǔ and General Pú Yīngbù crossed from Sānhù,
defeating Zhāng Hán at this river.
The Wū River flows east into the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River continues eastward passing to the south of Wǔchéng,
which was commonly referred to as Liángqī City;
Liángqī was north of Yè,
and people also called it Liǎngqī City,
which was incorrect.
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Records of Counties and States" states:
In Yè County there is Wǔchéng,
which is indeed the city of Qī.
The Zhāng River further flows to the northeast, passing in front of the Xīmén Bào Shrine,
on the east side of the shrine is a stele,
with raised characters carved,
on the east headstone of the shrine's main hall is inscribed:
It was repaired during the time of Zhào Jiànwǔ.
Cào Pī in "Rhapsody on Search and Expedition" said:
Admiring Xīmén's fine traces,
suddenly gazing distantly at its sacred structure.
The Zhāng River joins with the Zhī River on the right.
This river originates from the Zhāng River at the west meeting point of Hán,
then separates eastward to join with the Hán River,
the river arises from the northeast of Hán Mountain,
passing west of the ancient city of Hánhuì County,
flowing north into the Zhī River,
thus called Hánhuì.
Zhāng Yàn explained:
A branch of the Zhāng River,
from the southwest of the city joins with the waters of Hán Mountain,
now there are still ditches beside the city.
In the second year of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's reign,
Zhào Jìngsù Wáng's son Liú Rén was enfeoffed as a ruler of a state.
The river continues northeast into the Zhāng.
In the past, the Marquis of Wèi appointed Xīmén Bào as magistrate of Yè,
channelling the Zhāng to irrigate Yè,
and the people benefited from its use.
Later, during Wèi Xiāng Wáng's time,
Shǐ Qǐ was appointed magistrate of Yè,
and again the Zhāng River was dammed to irrigate the fields of Yè,
making them fertile,
and the people sang of it.
Wèi Wǔ Wáng once more dammed the Zhāng River,
diverting its flow eastward,
calling it Tiānjǐng Dam.
Over twenty lǐ,
twelve weirs were constructed,
each three hundred paces apart,
allowing mutual irrigation,
a single source dividing into twelve streams,
each with a sluice gate.
Lù's "Record of Yè" states:
The places irrigated by the waters,
are called Yànlíng Marshes.
Thus Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Cápital of Wèi,"
described twelve weir flows,
sharing the same source with different mouths.
When Wèi Wǔ attacked Yè,
he diverted the Zhāng River to besiege it.
"Annals of the Last Emperor" recorded:
Sīkōng encircled the city of Yè, which was forty lǐ around,
initially shallow and narrow,
appearing crossable,
yet Shěn Pèi refused to yield and laughed at it,
Sīkōng fortified it overnight,
expanding and deepening it to two zhàng,
leading the Zhāng River to flood it,
finally capturing Yè.
It was initially established by Duke Huán of Qí,
as recorded in the "Guǎnzi":
Five Deer's, Zhōngmóu's, and Yè's constructions,
were to protect All-Under-Heaven.
Later it belonged to Jìn,
in the seventh year of Marquis Wén of Wèi's rule,
he began to establish this locality,
hence it was named Wèi.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
the Wèi Commandery was established,
governed by Yè County,
when Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wèi City.
Afterward, the Wèi Commandery was divided,
with east and west commandery captains established,
thus called "Three Wèi."
Wèi Wǔ, following the old division of counties and states,
rerouted the Zhāng flow from the west of the city to east within,
passing beneath the Tóngquè Terrace,
submerging and flowing east into the city,
known as the Chángmíng Canal.
The canal water flowed south beneath Zhīchē Mén,
as Wèi Wǔ erected the Northern Palace in Yè,
which contained the Wénchāng Hall.
Canal waters lined the avenue north and south,
and the branch streams drew irrigation,
allowing irrigation everywhere,
emerging east at the foot of the Shídòu Dam,
into the Huáng Water.
Hence Wèi Wǔ's "Rhapsody on Ascending the Terrace" said:
Draw from Chángmíng,
to water the streets and neighborhoods.
This referred to the canal.
The Shí family, upon the site of the old Wénchāng Hall,
constructed the East and West Tàiwǔ Halls on the Jìběi Gǔchéng Mountain,
using fine stone as the base,
with a base beneath housing five hundred guards.
Curved pillars and tile roofs
were all cast in bronze,
decorated with gold lacquer.
Also bronze figures from Cháng'ān and Luòyáng,
were placed before the hall,
to glorify the nation.
To the northwest of the city were three terraces,
each based on the city walls,
towering majestically,
as high as a mountain,
erected by Wèi Wǔ in the fifteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
with all paths smoothed out.
"The Ancient Lands of the Spring and Autumn" writes:
Kuí Hill,
a place name,
now are these three terraces west of Yè.
It states that the terrace is leveled,
while some view it differently,
the intention remains unexplored.
The central one is called Tóngquè Terrace,
ten zhàng tall,
with one hundred and one rooms,
upon completion,
he summoned all his sons up,
commanding them each to compose a rhapsody.
Chén Sī Wáng wrote it with ease,
praised instantaneously.
It was also where Wèi Wǔ favored Wáng Shūzhì at Fèngcháng.
In the past, Yán Cái and his associates assaulted the Yè Gate,
upon learning of the attack,
before vehicles and horses could arrive,
he led his officers on foot to the palace gate,
observed by the Supreme Ancestor from Tóngquè Terrace, saying,
"The one approaching must be Wáng Shūzhì."
Chancellor Zhōng Yáo remarked:
"With upheaval in the old capital,
how come every Court Minister remains in their office,
yet you arrived?"
Zhōng replied:
"Being nourished by its benefits,
how can I shun its difficulties?
While the palace may be old,
it is not the duty to avoid distress.”
It became a celebrated story of the time.
Shí Hǔ added two more zhàng,
establishing a structure,
connecting beams and eaves,
covering it entirely,
named Mìngzǐ Cave.
Also, atop the building was a five-story pavilion,
fifteen zhàng high,
rising to twenty-seven zhàng above ground,
with a bronze sparrow on the pinnacle,
spreading wings as if flying.
To the south was the Jīnhǔ Terrace,
eight zhàng high,
with one hundred and nine rooms.
To the north was the Bīngjǐng Terrace,
also eight zhàng tall,
with one hundred and forty-five rooms,
containing an ice chamber on top,
with several wells inside,
fifteen zhàng deep,
storing ice and graphite.
Graphite could be inscribed upon,
and when burned it doesn't easily exhaust,
also called coal.
Additionally, there were granaries for millet and salt,
for unforeseen needs.
Even now inscriptions remain on the granaries.
Zuǒ Sī’s "Rhapsody on Wèi Cápital" states:
The three terraces are arranged in a striking line.
The city has seven gates,
the southern is named Fèngyáng Gate,
the central is Zhōngyáng Gate,
next is Guǎngyáng Gate,
the eastern is Jiànchūn Gate,
the northern is Guǎngdé Gate,
next is Jiù Gate,
the western is Jīnmíng Gate,
and also known as Bái Gate.
The Fèngyáng Gate had three terraces with open passageways,
standing 35 zhang high.
The Shí family built a multi-story viewing tower atop them,
placing a bronze phoenix there,
its head one zhang and six chi tall.
On the eastern city wall,
the Shí family established the Dōngmíng Observatory.
On top of the observatory, they added a gilded Boshan censer,
calling it "Clanging Against the Heavens."
On the northern city wall stood the Qídǒu Tower,
surpassing all other pavilions,
solitary, lofty, and uniquely standing.
The city walls measured seven li from east to west,
and five li from north to south.
Their exterior was decorated with bricks,
with a tower every hundred paces.
All the various palaces and halls,
their gate towers and corner bastions,
were additionally fitted with viewing pavilions.
Layered roof ridges and upturned eaves,
soaring rafters brushing against the clouds,
were painted with vermilion and azure,
their colors light and plain.
At the height of its prosperity,
from sixty or seventy li away from Yè,
looking from afar, it appeared lofty and graceful,
majestic like an immortal's abode.
The Wei, inheriting the Han mandate,
again made Luòyáng their capital.
Considering Qiáo as the original state of their ancestors,
Xǔchāng as the place where the Han had resided,
Cháng'ān as the legacy of the Western Capital,
and Yè as the foundation of royal enterprise,
they thus designated them the Five Capitals.
Today, it is the seat of the Cìshǐ of Xiàng Prefecture and of Wèijùn Commandery.
The Zhāng River flows north from the Xīmén Bào Temple past the west of the Zhào dynasty's Yuèmǎ Terrace.
Its foundation was five zhang high,
with a row of viewing towers atop it.
Shí Hǔ would often conduct military reviews below it,
ascending the towers to observe.
Hǔ himself would shoot whistling arrows from the terrace,
using them as signals for the army's cavalry to advance or withdraw.
The Zhāng River then flows north past the west of the Jìmò (Sacrifice Path).
During the Warring States period,
it was the custom for sorcerers to procure brides for the River Earl (Hé Bó),
performing sacrifices on this path.
In the time of Marquis Wén of Wèi,
Xīmén Bào was the magistrate of Yè.
He made an agreement with the village elders, saying:
"When you are getting a bride for the River Earl,
I would be pleased if you informed me,
as I wish to send off the maiden."
They all replied:
"Yes."
When the time came,
the elders and the district officers levied taxes on the people,
collecting millions in cash.
The sorcerers and shamans traveled through the villages.
When there was a beautiful girl,
they would pray, declaring she should be the River Earl's bride.
They would then spend thirty thousand cash to betroth the girl,
bathing her, applying cosmetics, dressing her as if for marriage.
Bào went to attend the event.
The elders, sorcerers, officers, and people all gathered to watch.
The chief sorceress was seventy years old,
followed by ten female disciples.
Bào called for the bride to see her,
and deemed her not beautiful enough.
He ordered the old sorceress to go and inform the River Earl,
and threw her into the river.
After a while, he said:
"Why is she taking so long?"
He then ordered three disciples and an elder to go and report,
and threw them all into the river as well.
Bào bowed deeply and said:
"The elders are not returning.
What is to be done?"
He then intended to send the district officers and local magnates to hasten them,
but they all kowtowed until their heads bled,
begging not to procure brides for the River Earl anymore.
Although the illicit sacrifice was thus stopped,
the place retained the name "Sacrifice Path."
It is also the place where Mùróng Jùn threw Shí Hǔ's corpse.
Tián Róng believed it was the Zǐmò (Purple Path).
In the 11th year of Jiànwǔ of the Zhào dynasty,
a pontoon bridge was built over the water at Zǐmò.
For Fótú Chéng, a tomb was prepared during his lifetime at Zǐmò.
He died in the 15th year of Jiànwǔ,
and was buried there in the twelfth month,
which is this very place.
The Zhāng River also faces the Zhào family's Línzhāng Palace.
The palace was located in the Sāngzǐ Garden,
which had many mulberry trees,
hence the garden's name.
On the third day of the third month and during the month when sericulture began,
Hǔ would lead the empress and consorts to pick mulberry leaves here.
Today, the place has remnant mulberry trees,
but not a foot of the wall's battlements remains.
The Zhāng River flows further north,
where the Fǔ River joins it.
The Zhāng River then flows east past the south of Liángqī City.
The *Record of Geography and Customs* states:
"Fifty li north of Yè is Liángqī City,
which was an old county."
In the fifth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Rén Pòhú.
In the first year of the Yǒngxīng era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Piāoqí General Wáng Jùn sent the Wūhuán leader Kěmò straight to Liángqī.
When his scout cavalry reached Yè,
Chéngdū Prince Sīmǎ Yǐng sent General Shí Chāo to attack Mò,
but was defeated by Mò here.
[The river] also passes north of Píngyáng City.
The *Bamboo Annals* records:
"In the first year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
the army of Yè defeated the army of Hándān at Píngyáng."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
"Yè has a Píngyáng City,"
which is this very place.
[The river] then flows east past the south of Lièrén County.
The Zhāng River flows eastward,
passing to the right of Chìqiū County in the north,
and immediately south of the ancient city of Péi County.
During the reign of Wáng Mǎng, it was renamed Jìshì.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
"Sixty lǐ southwest of Lièrén County, there is the city of Jìpéi,
which is an ancient county."
The Zhāng River then flows northeast, passing the ancient city of Lièrén County in the south,
renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Lièzhì.
The "Zhúshū Jìnián" states:
"In the eighth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
King Huìchéng attacked Hándān and captured Lièrén."
In the county, the Bǎiqú ancient channel merges on the right.
The Bǎiqú River originates from Qīnkǒu Mountain in Wǔ'ān County, Wèi Prefecture,
flowing southeast, passing south of Hándān County,
then eastward, merging with the Jūjiàn River.
The water is sourced from Wǔshǐ East Mountain and Bǎiqú,
but locals still refer to this river as the Jū River.
The Jūjiàn River continues eastward,
and there the Niúshǒu River joins,
originating from Dǔ Mountain in the west of Hándān County.
It flows east and splits into two rivers,
with turbulent rapids rushing side by side,
reflecting in the two valleys.
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng in the Hàn dynasty,
the seven kingdoms rebelled,
and Qūzhōu Marquis Lì Jì was ordered to attack Zhào,
laying siege to Hándān,
fighting for seven months.
The city was flooded by diverting the Niúshǒu and Jū Rivers,
causing the city walls to collapse,
and the king committed suicide.
The water flows east into Hándān City,
passing south of the Wēnmíng Palace,
where Emperor Shìzǔ of the Hàn captured Wáng Láng and rested during the day.

then passes the old southern wall of Ānxiāng County,
as stated in the "Treatise on Geography":
it was a marquisate.
Further east, it passes Shì County,
and enters the Sīxiáo River.
The Sīxiáo River then flows east past the southern wall of Xīliáng City,
then northeast past the old southern wall of Lèxìn County,
as recorded in the "Treatise on Geography",
a subordinate county of Jùlù,
which was a marquisate.
Further east, it enters the Héngshuǐ.
The Héngshuǐ then flows north to Yuán Tán Crossing,
likely named because Yuán Tán traveled back and forth from Yè via this crossing,
hence the ferry acquired this name.
Further northeast, it passes west of Xiàbó County,
and the Héngshuǐ flows north past the east of the old Wū County city wall,
as recorded in the "Bamboo Annals",
in the thirtieth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qín enfeoffed Wèi Yāng at Wū,
and changed its name to Shāng,
which is precisely this place.
Hence Wáng Mǎng changed it to Qínjù,
as stated in the "Records of Geography and Customs":
north of the county is Wū Hill,
likely from which the county derived its name.
Further right, it passes the west of the old Xiàbó County city wall,
which Wáng Mǎng changed to Rùnbó.
Yìng Shào said:
Tàishān has a Bó,
hence this one is called Xià (lower).
When Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn traveled south from the Hūtuó River,
he lost his way upon reaching here,
not knowing where to go.
He encountered an old man in white clothes who said:
Xìndū is held for Cháng'ān,
eighty lǐ from here.
Shìzǔ proceeded there,
and Rèn Guāng opened the gates to admit him,
marking the beginning of the restoration of the Hàn dynasty.
Searching for the old man yielded no trace,
leading commentators to believe he was a deity.
The Héngzhāng further flows northeast past the west of Xiàbó City,
winding northeastward,
where it is called Jiǔlíng.
Westward, it passes the old southern wall of Lèxiāng County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Lèqiū.
Further east,
it draws in the Jiāshuǐ, which flows into it.
Further northeast, it passes north of Fùchéng County,
then northeast to Chāngtíng,
where it converges with the Hūtuó River.
The "Classic" places Fùchéng below Xiàbó
and above Chāngtíng.
Examining the geography, this does not match,
though the accounts are similar.
Bóhǎi's Fùchéng is further east of Dōngchāng,
thus it is known to be incorrect.
The Zhāngshuǐ further flows northeast past the south of Wǔyì Commandery,
which was established by Wèi.
Further east, it passes north of Wǔqiáng County,
then northeast past the old southern wall of Wǔsuì County,
according to the "Records of the Grand Historian",
Qín defeated Zhào general Hù Zhé at Wǔsuì,
beheading a hundred thousand,
which occurred at this very place.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huánsuì.
The Báimǎ River flows into it,
its upper course receiving water from the Hūtuó,
flowing east past north of Lèxiāng County,
south of Ráoyáng County,
then southeast past north of Wǔyì Commandery,
and east into the Héngshuǐ,
where it is called Jiāojīnkǒu.
The Héngzhāng further flows east past the old north wall of Wǔyì County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Shùnhuán.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn enfeoffed his son in this county as a kingdom,
later dividing Wǔyì, Wǔsuì, and Guānjīn to form Wǔyì Commandery,
with its seat here.
The Héngzhāng further flows northeast,
rightward converging at Zhāngpíngkǒu,
an old channel receiving water from the Wǔqiáng Deep,
southwest of the deep,
beside the water lies the old seat of Wǔqiáng County,
hence the deep derived its name.
As recorded in the "Dōngguān Hànjì":
Emperor Guāngwǔ appointed Wáng Liáng as Grand Minister of Works,
and enfeoffed him here as a marquisate.
Elders recount:
a villager traveling on the road
saw a small snake,
suspecting it possessed spiritual power,
took it and raised it,
naming it Dānshēng.
As it grew, it devoured people,
causing distress in the village,
so they captured and imprisoned it.
Dānshēng carried the prison and fled,
submerging the town into a lake,
and the county magistrate and clerks all became fish.
Now, about half a lǐ northeast of the county seat lies Luòshuǐ.
The deep water further flows southeast and converges into a lake,
also called Lángjūn Deep.
Elders also say:
on the day the county submerged,
the snake's offspring fled east,
and also sank here,
hence the deep acquired the name Lángjūn.
The deep water connects northward,
called Shíhǔkǒu,
and further northeast becomes Zhāngpíng Marsh.
Where the marsh water overflows,
it breaches the northern embankment,
called Zhāngdāo Channel,
flowing north into the Héngzhāng,
called Zhāngpíngkǒu,
also known as Zhāngpíng Channel.
When water overflows, it flows south;
when water diminishes, it ceases to flow.
The Héngzhāng further flows past the old north wall of Dōngchāng County,
which the "Classic" calls Chāngtíng,
renamed Tiánchāng by Wáng Mǎng,
commonly called Dōngxiāng,
likely because the sounds of Xiāng and Chāng are similar,
leading to this error.
West lies Chāngchéng,
hence this city is called Dōngchāng.
The Héngzhāng further flows northeast,
leftward converging with the old course of the Hūtuó River,
called Hékǒu.
The Héngzhāng further flows northeast,
dividing into two streams,
at the point where the water overflows,
it is named Lǐ Cōng Huàn.
Further northeast, it diverges north of Lèchénglíng County.
The Héngzhāng River has no separate watercourse branching off within the county.
What emerges north of the county
is actually a branch of the Hūtuó River,
formed by the winding and splitting of the old Hūtuó watercourse.
The Héngzhāng River then flows east,
where it divides into two streams.
The left branch emerges at Xiàngshìkǒu,
and it is here that the Dú River breaks in and joins it.
The Héngzhāng River continues east,
passing north of the old city of Gōnggāo County.
Emperor Wén of the Hàn enfeoffed Hán Tuídāng, son of King Hán Xìn, as a marquis here,
which was called Lèchéng Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
The Héngzhāng River then flows northeast,
where it joins the Bǎiliáng Zhà on the right.
This water originates from the Lǐ Cōng Huàn,
flows northeast as the Bǎiliáng Zhà,
passes east of the old city of Púlíng County,
where in the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn,
Liú Jiā, son of Prince Huì of Guǎngchuān, was enfeoffed as a marquis.
The *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
"Eighty *lǐ* northwest of Xiū County lies Púlíng Township,
which was formerly a county."
Further northeast, it meets the branch of the Sāngshè River,
then continues northeast past the north of Gōnggāo City,
and finally flows east into the Héngzhāng River,
where it is called Bǎiliángkǒu.
The Héngzhāng River flows further northeast,
where it joins the Sāngshè Ditch on the right.
This ditch originates from the Cóng Marsh,
commonly known as Lú Dá Cóng Bó,
also called the Móhē River.
It connects to the Qīnghé River in the southeast
and reaches the Héngshuǐ in the northwest.
During the autumn rains when it floods,
the area twenty *lǐ* north of Guānjīn City
becomes entirely a marshland,
where the waters converge.
Its watercourse passes north of the old city of Guānjīn County.
Yuè Yì surrendered from Yān to Zhào
and was enfeoffed here,
with the title Marquis of Wàngzhū.
Under Wáng Mǎng, it was called Shuòdìng Tíng.
It then bends south and flows east past the south of Dòu Shì Qīngshān.
Along the eastern embankment lies Qīngshān,
which is the tomb of Dòu Shàowēng, father of Empress Dòu of Emperor Wén of the Hàn.
Shàowēng was a native of this county.
During the chaos of the Qín dynasty,
he lived in seclusion, fishing,
but fell into a deep pool and died.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
the empress sent envoys to fill the pool and bury her father,
erecting a large mound southeast of Guānjīn City.
Thus, the people called it Qīngshān.
Further east, it passes south of Dǒng Zhòngshū's temple.
Zhòngshū
was a native of Guǎngchuān.
People still call it the Temple of Lord Dǒng,
where prayers and sacrifices are offered without cease in spring and autumn.
The old ditch then flows east past the north of the old city of Xiūshì County.
In the fourth year of the Běnshǐ era of Emperor Xuān of the Hàn,
Liú Yín, son of Prince Gāng of Qīnghé, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jūníng,
but it is commonly called Wēnchéng,
which is incorrect.
The *Records of Geography and Customs* states:
"Twenty *lǐ* northwest of Xiū County lies Xiūshì City,
which was formerly a county."
Further east, it meets the Cóng Marsh.
The marsh measures ten *lǐ* from north to south
and sixty paces from east to west.
When the water rises in the Zǐwǔ Pool,
it becomes deep and still,
also called Sāngshè Abyss.
From the southern part of the Cóng Marsh,
a branch flows east between embankments,
passing north of the old city of Xiū County,
and joins the Qīngzhāng River to the east.
