When the Zhāng River floods, it flows north;
when the marsh swells, it spreads south.
The waterways shift,
interconnecting with one another.
From the northern part of the Cóng Marsh,
a stream flows northeast and divides into two branches.
One branch flows north past the west of Gōnggāo City and then north into the Bǎiliáng Zhà,
while the other flows east past the south of Gōnggāo City.
Further northeast,
the Yángjīn Ditch Water emerges.
The Héngshuǐ flows east past the north of the old city of Fùchéng County and the south of the old city of Lèchéng County,
which was the seat of Héjiān Commandery.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"This was formerly part of Zhào."
In the second year of Emperor Wén of the Hàn,
it was made a separate kingdom.
Yìng Shào said:
"It lies between two rivers."
In the ninth year of Emperor Jǐng,
his son Dé was enfeoffed as the King of Héjiān,
known as King Xiàn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it,
changing the commandery to Shuòdìng
and the county to Lùxìn.
Master Chǔ said:
"In the third year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of the Hàn,
Huò Shān, nephew of the Grand General Huò Guāng, was enfeoffed as a marquis here."
Emperor Zhāng enfeoffed his son Kāi here,
and Emperor Huán posthumously honored his grandfather, King Xiàomù Kāi, as King Xiàomù.
Since his fief was used to maintain the imperial tombs,
the name 'Líng' (tomb) was added, making it Lèchéng Líng.
Today, within the city, there is an old pond
measuring eighty paces square.
In the past, the Héngshuǐ was channeled north into the city to fill the pond.
North of the pond stands a layered terrace,
its foundations and moats now overgrown and desolate,
preserving an ancient air.
Further northeast, it passes south of Chéngpíng County.
The Héngzhāng River then flows east past the south of the old city of Jiànchéng County.
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
it formerly belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery.
Master Chǔ said:
"In the third year of the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo of the Hàn,
Chancellor Huáng Bà was enfeoffed as a marquis here."
The old city of Chéngpíng County lies to the north.
In the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn,
Liú Lǐ, son of King Xiàn of Héjiān, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
which was called Zé Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
The two cities align north and south.
The Héngzhāng River then flows east and joins the Yángjīn Ditch Water on the right.
This water flows east from the marsh past the south of Fùchéng.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"Bóhǎi has a Fùchéng County."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wúchéng,
but this is not the Fùchéng mentioned in the *Classic*.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ further enfeoffed the Grand Minister of War Wáng Liáng as a marquis here.
The Yángjīn Ditch Water then flows northeast past Jiànchéng County,
enters the Héngshuǐ on the left,
and is called Yángjīnkǒu.
The Héngzhāng River continues east,
where it joins the old course of the Hūtuó branch river on the left,
then flows northeast into the Qīnghé River,
where it is called Hékǒu.
It then passes Běi Pí Tíng of Nánpí County,
flows northeast past the west of Fúyáng County,
and finally flows northeast into the sea.
Further northeast, it passes west of Zhāngwǔ County,
then northeast past south of Píngshū County,
and finally east into the sea.
The Qīngzhāng River passes west of the old city of Zhāngwǔ County,
which was formerly the town of Huì.
A branch watercourse emerges here,
called the Huìshuǐ.
It flows northeast past Cānhù Tíng,
where it divides into two watercourses.
Yìng Shào said:
"Fifty *lǐ* southwest of Píngshū County lies Cānhù Tíng,
which was formerly a county."
It is commonly called Pínglǔ City.
The branch water then flows east,
where it is called Càifú Ditch.
Further east, it accumulates to form a marsh.
One stream passes north of the pavilion,
then passes south of the old city of Dōngpíngshū County.
Since there was a Píngshū City in Dài Commandery,
'East' was added to distinguish it.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"It is a subordinate county of Bóhǎi."
The *Wei Land Records* says it was the seat of Zhāngwǔ Commandery.
Thus, it is commonly mistaken for the old city of Xīnwǔ,
but this is incorrect.
Further northeast, it divides into two streams.
One emerges on the right as a marsh,
while the other flows north into the Hūtuó River,
where it is called Huìkǒu.
The Qīngzhāng River flows turbulently eastward into the sea.
10.2 The Qīngzhāng River
10.2 The Qīngzhāng River
The Qīngzhāng River originates from Shàoshān Dàyàogǔ northwest of Zhān County in Shàngdǎng,
flows south past the west of the county,
then bends from the south of the county,
The Huáinánzǐ states:
The Qīngzhāng River emerges from the Yèlì Mountain.
Gāo Yòu says:
The mountain is in Zhān County.
Today, the Qīngzhāng River emerges northeast of the old city of Zhān County,
commonly called Zhān Mountain.
Later, the Hàn dynasty divided Zhān County to form the Lèpíng Commandery,
with its seat at Zhān County.
The water emerges from the boundary of Zhān County in Lèpíng Commandery.
Therefore, the Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Records states:
Lèpíng was formerly named Zhān County.
It is an old county of the Hàn dynasty.
The mountain is also called Lùgǔ Mountain,
and the water emerges from the Dàyào Valley,
flowing south past the east of the old city of Zhān County,
not passing its west.
It then flows south past Xīyáng City.
In the Zuǒzhuàn, the twelfth year of Duke Zhāo,
Xún Wú of Jìn pretended to rendezvous with the Qí army.
He borrowed a route through Xiānyú,
and then entered Xīyáng.
Dù Yù says:
This refers to Xīyáng City, east of Zhān County in Lèpíng.
The water then meets the mouth of the Liángyú River to the south,
which emerges from the Dàqiǎn Mountain west of Liángyú City.
The river has two sources:
the northern water flows southeast,
passes southeast of the city,
and joins the southern water.
The southern water also emerges from the western mountains,
flows east past the north of Wéndāng City,
then northeast past the south of Liángyú City,
which is the old city of Èyǔ.
When Qín attacked Zhào at Èyǔ,
King Huìwén sent Zhào Shē to rescue it.
Shē heeded Xǔ Lì’s advice,
and defeated Qín at Èyǔ,
referring to this place.
Sīmǎ Biāo and Yuán Shānsōng’s Treatise on Commanderies and States both state that Niè County had the Èyǔ settlement.
Lú Chén’s “Rhapsody on Hardships of Campaigns” says:
I visited the empty walls of Liángyú,
and mourned at the old capital of Èyǔ.
Kǎn Yīn also says:
Èyǔ
is today’s Liángyú City.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Féng Jiěsàn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The water joins the northern water on the left,
and the northern water flows southeast into the Qīngzhāng.
The Qīngzhāng then meets the Láo River to the southeast.
The Láo River emerges from Láo Mountain northwest of Láoyáng County,
flows south past the southwest of the old city of Láoyáng County,
then east to Sù City,
where it joins the Qīngzhāng.
[The Qīngzhāng] passes east of Shè County to the west,
turns and follows the south of the county.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
it is a subordinate county of Wèi Commandery.
Here, the Zhāng River is called the Shè River,
likely because the name changes with the locality.
It flows east to Shǔjiào Settlement south of Wǔ’ān County,
and enters the Zhuózhāng River.
11 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 11
11.1 The Yì River
11.1 The Yì River
The Yì River emerges from the western mountains of Yán Township in Gù’ān County, Zhuō Commandery.
The Yì River emerges from the Kuānzhōng Valley in the western mountains,
flows east past the south of Wǔdàfū City.
In the past, Wáng Tán, Marquis of Běipíng,
refused to follow Wáng Mǎng’s administration.
His son, Xīng, had five sons,
who all avoided the turmoil of the times,
and lived in seclusion in these mountains.
Therefore, their old residence
is known to the world as Wǔdàfū City,
which is this place.
The “Eulogy on Mountains” says:
The five kings are within,
vast and continuous like vines.
The Yì River then flows east and joins the Zǐzhuāng Stream on the left.
The water emerges north from Zǐzhuāng Pass,
flows south past the west of Wǔgōng City,
and turns to pass its south.
The Five Lords,
are the five sons of Wáng Xīng.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed them as five marquises:
Yuáncái as Marquis of Běipíng,
Yìcái as Marquis of Ānxǐ, Xiǎncái as Marquis of Púyīn,
Zhòngcái as Marquis of Xīnshì,
Jìcái as Marquis of Táng.
These are the so-called Five Kings of Zhōngshān.
Common people also call their residence “Five Lords.”
Both cities are about one lǐ square,
situated on ridges and mounds,
sloping upward and square below.
The water flows southeast into the Yì River.
The Yì River then flows east and meets the Nǚsī Valley Stream on the right.
The water emerges from the Nǚsī Ravine to the southwest,
flows northeast and joins the Yì,
called the Sānhuì Estuary.
The Yì River then flows east to the southwest of Guānmén City,
which is the Great Wall Gate of Yān.
It joins the Fánshí Mountain Stream,
whose source emerges west from Fánshí Mountain in Guǎngchāng County,
flows east past Fùfǔ Mountain,
and joins the Yì River.
The Yì River then flows east past the Great Wall of Yān,
then east past Jiànlí City to the south,
likely where Crown Prince Dān hosted Gāo Jiànlí.
The Yì River then flows east past the south of Wǔyáng City.
Since the Yì flows from Kuānzhōng past Wǔfū Pass eastward,
it also bears the name Wǔ River.
Therefore, the lower capital of Yān
is known as Wǔyáng.
On the left, it meets an old channel of a branch of the Rú River.
The small city southeast of the great wall of Wǔyáng
is the old city of Gù’ān County.
Emperor Wén of Hàn enfeoffed his chancellor Shéntú Jiā as a marquis here.
The city is two lǐ east-west,
and one and a half lǐ north-south.
Gāo Yòu says:
The Yì River passes south of Gù’ān City and flows east outside the city walls.
This is the same water.
Yòu was from Zhuō,
and his account is clear and accurate.
Today, the water reaches the southeastern corner of the city,
and people also call the Yì River the Gù’ān River.
Wǔyáng
was likely built by King Zhāo of Yān.
It is twenty lǐ east-west,
and seventeen lǐ north-south.
Therefore, Fù Dài’s “Rhapsody on Travels” says:
Departing from northern Jì,
passing through Liángxiāng,
ascending the Golden Terrace,
viewing Wǔyáng,
the two cities vast and distant,
their old traces dim and obscure.
This likely refers to this place.
The Yì River flows east and emerges into Fànyáng.
[It] passes east of Fànyáng County to the south,
then east of Róngchéng County to the south,
The Yì River passes by the south of the old city of Fànyáng County.
At the end of the Qín dynasty,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú were seizing territory for Chén Shèng,
and Yān and Zhào ordered Kuǎi Tōng to persuade them;
Fànyáng was the first to surrender.
In the second year of the middle period of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Dài, a surrendered king of the Xiōngnú.
It was called Shùnyīn under Wáng Mǎng.
In the past, when Mùróng Chuí was in Fànyáng,
he garrisoned it here.
He intended to plan a return to the capital,
but was hindered by travel,
and in haste did not succeed,
ultimately perishing.
The Yì River then flows east and merges with the Rú River.
The Rú River originates from the southern valley of Qióngdú Mountain, northwest of the old Ān County,
flows east and joins the Yuánquán Spring,
which emerges from a northern stream,
and flows southeast into the Rú River.
The Rú River then flows southeast past the west of Fán Wūqī’s lodge,
which is where he presented his head to Jīng Kē.
The Rú River then flows southeast past the north of Jīng Kē’s lodge.
In the past, Yān Dān accepted Tián Shēng’s advice,
honored Kē as a high minister,
and lodged him here.
The areas of these two lodges,
with winding streams and clear springs,
high mountains and dense forests,
mists and breezes lightly veiling,
touch the heart and invite lingering sentiments.
Those beyond the mundane world
still rely on the old dwellings,
finding delight in the woods.
The Rú River then flows east past the northwest of Wǔyáng City.
Formerly, a dam blocked the Rú River,
and a branch stream flowed south into the city, passing west of the Bǎi Tomb.
The tomb’s wall is beside the city,
which is a water pond.
The surrounding burial grounds are deep and vast,
resembling a city.
Beside the water are several mounds,
tall and imposing,
looking like green hills from afar.
Inquiring of the elders
and consulting historical records,
there is no written evidence.
Judging by personal sentiment,
they should be old graves from before the Yān capital,
though some say they are Yān burial mounds,
but this is not so.
The old channel of this water flows south,
bends and turns east,
then divides into two channels.
One flows past the west of the old Ān City,
runs along the south of the city, and enters the Yì River.
The embankments on both sides are lofty and steep,
with deep, high banks.
Within a hundred paces on either side,
there are two fishing platforms,
unevenly standing opposite each other,
distantly facing one another,
forming an even more beautiful sight.
The other channel flows east into the Jīntái Pond.
The pond is six or seven lǐ east-west,
and five lǐ north-south.
Northwest of the pond is a fishing platform over ten feet high,
about forty paces square.
North of the pond, more than ten paces away, is the Jīntái,
about eighty paces east-west on the platform,
and slightly less north-south.
North of it is a small Jīntái,
and north of that is the Lánmǎ Platform.
All are several zhang high,
standing elegantly opposite each other,
flanking the platforms on both sides.
Water flows through,
with long corridors and broad halls,
encircling the shore.
Beams and walls have all collapsed,
but the pillar bases remain,
so the foundation structure can still be traced.
The elders all say
that King Zhāo entertained guests,
widely inviting masters of esoteric arts,
such as Guō Wěi,
Yuè Yì and their like,
Zōu Yǎn, Jù Xīn and their peers,
officials, travelers, and persuaders,
many came from afar.
Not wanting the guests of the feudal lords
to spy on Yān,
he built the Lower Capital’s lodges at the southern edge.
It is said that King Zhāo initiated it earlier,
and Zǐ Dān continued it later.
Thus, the carved walls and ruined lodges
still bear engraved stones.
Though there are no records to rely on,
examining the ancient traces,
they seem to match old legends.
The Rú River flows east from the dam past the west of Zǐchí Fort,
bends and flows north,
and then the Húntánggōu Stream joins it.
This stream originates from the southern stream of Báimǎ Mountain, west of Qiú County,
and flows southeast into the Rú River.
The Rú River then flows east to Sāikǒu,
an ancient place where stone dams blocked the water.
An old branch of the Rú River flowed south into a large pond east of the city,
the pond being four lǐ square,
now dry.
Within the pond is a spring,
deep and still,
on the north side of the pool,
commonly called the Shèngnǚ Spring.
The Rú River then flows east to the Báiyángshuǐ mouth.
The water originates from below Báiyáng Ridge in the western mountains of Qiú County,
flows southeast into the Rú River,
and people of the time called it the Hǔyǎn Spring.
The Rú River joins the Tán River to the east.
The Tán River originates southwest of Tán Mountain, northwest of Qiú County,
flows south and meets the Shíquán Spring.
The spring emerges from the southeastern corner of Shíquán Gù,
the water about twenty paces wide,
and three zhang deep.
The gù is within many mountains,
in a flat plain,
surrounded by steep ravines blocking water,
over eight zhang high.
The rock is five zhang high,
with red soil on top,
another layer above,
standing straight up like a wall,
forty-five paces wide.
Where the water does not surround it,
the path cannot accommodate a cart,
only allowing people and horses to pass,
hence called Shíquán Gù.
On the gù, there long stood the Báiyáng Temple,
dedicated to the mountain god of Báiyáng Mountain.
Beside the temple, trees cast intertwined shadows,
thick branches hide the light,
the monk Shì Fǎchéng built a temple atop it,
making it an even more sublime place for contemplation.
The water flows south into the Chán River,
hence commonly called the Bìnggōu.
The water then flows southeast,
passes north of the old Ān County and flows south into the Rú River.
The Rú River flows southeast,
and east of Dàlì Pavilion, northwest of Róngchéng County, joins the Yì River and flows into the Jùmǎ River.
Thus, the “Geographical Records” says:
In Yánxiāng of old Ān County,
the Yì River originates,
and reaches Fànyáng to enter the Rú River.
Kàn Yīn also said this,
and also said the Rú River joins the Qú River.
Xǔ Shèn said:
The Rú River enters the Lái River.
The names Lái and Qú,
are alternative names for the Jùmǎ River.
However, both Yì rivers originate from the same district,
and together enter the Rú River,
the southern Rú.
The northern Yì reaches Fànyáng County in Zhuō Commandery and meets the northern Rú,
then together flow turbulently into the Lái River.
Thus, the Yì River and other waters interchangeably share names.
It flows east past the north of the old city of Róngchéng County,
turbulently flowing east,
and at Píngshū County in Bóhǎi, merges with the Yì River.
Kàn Yīn said:
The western boundary of Zhuō Commandery is the Yì River of Dài.
This water originates east of Yānwángxiāntái, northeast of Láng Mountain, southeast of Guǎngchāng County in Dài Commandery.
The platform has three peaks,
very lofty and steep,
clouds crown the peaks,
high mists flank the ridges,
gorges and ravines are profoundly deep,
shrouded in mist and fog.
The elders say:
It is where King Zhāo of Yān sought immortality.
To its east is called Shíhǔ Ridge.
Fàn Yè’s “Book of Hàn” says:
It is the burial place of Jiǎnwáng Yān of Zhōngshān.
His burial was lavish,
using stones from the mountains of Zhuō Commandery
to build the tomb grounds.
The tomb passage, steles, and stone beasts
all came from this mountain.
Two stone tigers were left behind,
later people thus named the ridge after them.
The eastern foothills of the mountain
are where the spring source emerges.
The “Classic” refers to it as the western mountain of Yánxiāng.
The water flows east,
and the Bì River joins from the south,
turbid waves together flowing,
commonly called the Báo River.
Sīmǎ Biāo’s “Records of the Commanderies and States” says:
The Báo River originates from old Ān County.
Emperor Shìzǔ ordered Gěng Kuàng to attack over ten camps of bandits under Wú Nàilífú on Báo River in the western mountains of old Ān,
and he defeated them all.
This is that river.
The Yì River flows east past the north of Kǒng Mountain.
At the foot of the mountain, there is a stalactite cave.
The cave produces fine stalactites.
Gatherers carry torches and search through the sand,
entering the cave for about a li,
crossing a stream,
where a hidden current flows and joins it.
Its depth is shallow enough to wade across.
Within, numerous caves branch off strangely,
causing those entering and exiting to become confused and lost, not knowing which way to go.
At every confusing fork,
there are always markers left behind.
Those returning then follow the openings to find their way out.
Above, there is also a large opening,
broad and wide, opening into a cavern,
hence the mountain is named Kǒng (Opening) Mountain.
The river then flows east past the south of the old Xī Gù'ān city wall,
which is the Yánxiāng city.
It passes north of the Sòng Jīng Ridge.
The elders say:
Yān Dān bid farewell to Jīng Kē here,
and thus it was named.
The era is already distant,
and the details are not fully known.
The legacy of the name, passed down through tradition,
cannot be left unrecorded,
in hopes of broadening what later generations hear and transmit.
The Yì River then flows east, bends, and passes west of the Great Wall,
then flows east and south past the south of Wǔsuì County,
and north of Xīnchéng County.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Zhào general Lǐ Mù attacked Yān,
and took Wǔsuì and Fāngchéng." This is the place.
Common people also call this waterway the Wǔsuì Ford.
North of the ford, facing the Great Wall gate,
it is called the Fén Gate.
The "Zhào Hereditary House" in Records of the Grand Historian states:
In the nineteenth year of King Xiàochéng,
Zhào exchanged territory with Yān,
giving Lóngduì
and Fén Gate to Yān;
Yān gave Géchéng
and Wǔyáng to Zhào.
This is it.
It is also called the Fénshuǐ Gate,
and also called the Liáng Gate.
The Yì River divides east to form the Liáng Gate Marsh.
The Yì River flows further east,
and the water from the Liáng Gate Marsh flows into it.
This water receives the Yì River at the Liáng Gate,
enters the Great Wall to the east,
and flows northeast into the marsh.
The marsh water connects north to the Fànyáng Marsh.
The marsh is ten li west of Fànyáng city,
fifteen li square,
commonly also called the Yántái Marsh.
The marsh water connects south to the Liáng Gate Lake,
three li square.
The lake water flows southeast,
exits the Great Wall and flows into the Yì,
called the Fàn River.
From this point downstream on the Yì River,
it is commonly referred to by the name Fàn River.
It then flows east past the old city wall of Fànyáng County,
which is what Yìng Shào called "north of the Fàn River."
The Yì River then flows east past the north of the old city wall of Fányú County.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Tiáo, son of Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wòfú.
The Records of Geography and Customs says:
"Twenty li east of Běi Xīnchéng County is the Fányú Pavilion,
the site of the old county."
The Yì River then flows east past the south of the old city wall of Róngchéng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
the Zhào general Yè was enfeoffed at Shēnzé.
In the third year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng,
the surrendered Xiōngnú king Wéi Xúlú was enfeoffed at Róngchéng.
Both were marquisates.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shēnzé.
The Yì River flows further east,
and the Ní River flows into it.
This water originates from two marshes southeast of Róngchéng County,
called the Great Ní Marsh and the Small Ní Marsh.
Their water flows south into the Yì River,
at a place called the Ní Cave Mouth.
Beside the water is the Húnní city.
The Yì River passes south of it,
and eastward joins the Kòu River.
Therefore, Sāng Qīn said:
"The Yì River emerges northwest of Běi Xīnchéng,
and flows east into the Kòu."
From this point downstream, the Kòu and Yì interchangeably receive each other's names.
The Yì River then flows east past the south of Yìjīng.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Gōngsūn Zàn killed Liú Yú at Jì.
At that time, a children's rhyme said:
"South of Yān's border,
north of Zhào's frontier,
only here can one escape the world."
Zàn considered the Yì region to match this,
so he moved from Jì to the banks of the Yì River,
calling it Yìjīng City,
located four or five li west of Yì City.
In the fourth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Zhào,
Shí Hǔ came from southwest of Liáo to Yìjīng.
Because the city's defenses were extremely solid,
he ordered twenty thousand men to demolish it.
Now,
the city walls are leveled flat,
but the foundation of its tower still remains,
still as high as a bolt of cloth.
On the remaining foundation, there is a well.
Generations have named it the Yìjīng Tower,
which is what Zàn defended.
Therefore, Zàn's Letter to His Son says:
"Yuán's attack
was like ghosts and gods;
assault ladders danced upon the tower,
drums and horns sounded from underground."
This refers to this tower.
The Yì River then flows east past the south of the old city wall of Yì County.
In the past, Duke Wén of Yān moved to Yì,
which is this city.
Kuà Yīn stated that Crown Prince Dān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín,
and with the guests who knew of the plan,
held a farewell ceremony on the banks of the Yì River.
The Tale of Prince Dān of Yān says:
When Jīng Kē entered Qín,
the Crown Prince and those who knew of the plan
all dressed in plain white clothes and caps to see him off on the banks of the Yì River.
Jīng Kē rose to offer a toast,
and sang:
"The wind sighs, oh! the Yì River is cold;
the brave man once gone, oh! returns nevermore."
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù,
Sòng Rúyì harmonized with him.
When they played heroic tones,
the men's hair all stood on end;
when they played mournful tones,
the men all shed tears.
It is suspected this happened here.
I, based on examining the legacy and old traces,
find they are mostly in Wǔyáng,
so it seems the farewell was not held here.
In the third year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
the surrendered Xiōngnú king Pú Dá was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Further east, it passes south of Āncì County.
The Yì River passes south of the county and north of the old city wall of Mào County,
flowing east to Wén'ān County where it joins the Hūtuó River.
The Records of the Grand Historian records
Sū Qín saying:
"North of Yān's Great Wall,
south of the Yì River,"
precisely refers to this river.
Therefore, scholars like Bān Gù and Kuà Yīn
all called this water the Southern Yì.
Further east, it passes south of Quánzhōu County,
and enters the sea to the east.
The Classic records the course of the water,
following its sequence as it flows into the sea.
11.2 The Kòu River
11.2 The Kòu River
The Kòu River emerges from Gāoshì Mountain in Língqiū County, Dài Commandery.
This is the water of Ōuyí.
It originates from Gāoshì Mountain northwest of the county,
as the Shānhǎi Jīng states:
From Gāoshì Mountain,
the Kòu River emerges,
flowing eastward to join the river.
Its waters flow southeast,
and on the mountain there is a stone inscription,
bearing the words:
Northern Boundary of Jìzhōu.
Thus, it is commonly called the Stone Inscription Pass.
The water then flows south past Hòutáng,
which is the name of the river.
Further east, it merges with the hot spring water,
which emerges from Xuān Valley to the northwest.
This water is as warm as hot soup,
capable of curing all ailments,
hence it is commonly called the hot spring.
It flows southeast past the north of Xīngdòu Pavilion,
which stands on the southern plateau,
tilting and unsteady,
so people refer to it as the Leaning City.
From the plateau, the water flows southeast into the Kòu River.
The Kòu River flows further east,
joined by the Shuāquán water,
which originates from Shuāquán and flows south.
Beside the water stands the Shuāquán Pavilion,
and it flows southeast into the Kòu River.
The Kòu River then flows east past the old city of Língqiū County,
as Yìng Shào noted:
King Wǔlíng of Zhào was buried twenty lǐ southeast of here,
hence the county is named after him.
The county,
anciently part of Dài,
was in the first year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
when Zāng Kùi, Chancellor of Zhōngshān, petitioned for it to be separately administered.
Zàn, in his Commentary on the Geographical Records, stated:
The name Língqiū
predates King Wǔlíng.
Furthermore, according to Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shǐjì,
in the ninth year of Lord Jìng of Zhào,
he defeated Qí at Língqiū,
so the name does not derive from King Wǔlíng’s deeds,
as Zàn’s Commentary indicates.
The Kòu River flows south from the county into a gorge,
called the Narrow Gate,
where a checkpoint was established in the gorge
to inspect and restrict travelers.
Passing through the southern mountains,
where lofty peaks obscure the sky,
and deep streams match the valleys,
the water follows the ravine westward,
passing south of the Imperial Archery Terrace,
which stands on the northern hill.
South of the terrace is the Imperial Archery Stone Stele,
and to the south, elegant ridges divide the clouds,
layered cliffs pierce the heavens,
with towering accumulations of rock,
sheer cliffs rising straight up.
Whenever the imperial carriage traveled along the river,
this was often a place for leisurely excursions.
The Kòu River flows westward,
then turns south and east, curving past the south of the stone monument of Prince Xiáng of Běihǎi,
and flows south between the stone pillars of the Imperial Archery Stele.
Southeast, it passes south of Guǎngchāng County,
the Kòu River flows east through Jiāyá River,
where a stream from the south joins it,
originating from the northern foothills of Héng Mountain.
Three streams converge at Zhìchuān,
flowing east past Jiāyá Pavilion and northward,
joining the Kòu River.
North of the water lies the mountain,
and beyond it is the boundary of Guǎngchāng County.
The Kòu River then flows east past Dǎomǎ Pass,
where the pass and mountains are perilous and narrow,
extremely steep and deep,
akin to the poet’s description of a high ridge troubling fine horses,
or Fù Xiǎn’s hardship with traveling carriages,
hence the pass derives its name.
The pass water emerges from a long stream to the southwest,
flowing northeast through the pass to join the Kòu River.
South of the Kòu River,
on the mountain, an imperial seat was established in the Pine Garden,
and a monastery was built in the eastern garden.
To the northeast and on two sides,
peaks and cliffs are lofty and deep,
cloud-shrouded summits hide the sun,
and the water appears clear and bright.
The depths harbor no hidden dangers,
and travelers passing through
rarely fail to linger, forgetting to return.
Further southeast, it passes north of Shàngqūyáng County in Zhōngshān,
where the Héng River flows from the west to join it.
The Kòu River flows south from Dǎomǎ Pass and merges with the Dàlǐng water,
which originates from below the great ridge southwest of the mountain,
flowing northeast out of the gorge.
On the right side of the gorge, by the mountain,
stands a monastery,
soaring over the hills,
with crimson platforms and rainbow-like bridges,
while a long river flows turbulently,
winding below it,
and flows northeast into the Kòu River.
The Kòu River then curves east and joins the Liǎnglǐng stream water,
which originates from the northern hill of Héng Mountain,
flowing northeast between two ridges.
Although the northern ridge rises layer upon layer into the clouds,
it pales compared to the southern peak’s steep elegance.
Walking south from the water toward the distant peaks,
the stone steps wind and twist,
following a path of nine bends,
and gazing upon the surrounding mountains,
all seem inferior,
perhaps akin to Yángcháng or Qiónglái.
When Qí and Sòng established peaceful relations,
the road passed through here.
The water flows northeast,
joining the Kòu River.
Further east,
it joins the Xuánshuǐ on the left,
which emerges from the mountain plateau at Pán Valley,
its light rapids descending swiftly,
splitting over rocks and cascading down,
over a zhang in length,
plunging directly to the mountain’s edge,
white waves surging,
forming its own pool and islet.
The water flows southeast,
its turbulent flow joining the Kòu River.
The Kòu River then flows east past Hóng Mountain,
commonly called Hóngtóu here,
likely the Hóngshàng Pass mentioned in the Jìnshū Dìdào Jì.
The pass commandant was stationed in Běipíng, with the frontier drawn northeast of Wàngdū,
not far from Běipíng,
and marking the county’s territorial limit.
Here, the Kòu River
receives the Hóngshàng water on the left,
which emerges from a nearby stream to the northwest,
flowing southeast into the Kòu River.
Further east, it passes south of Táng County.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing south of the Zuǒrén City.
Yìng Shào said:
Zuǒrén City is located forty li northwest of Táng County.
The county has the Báo River,
which is also sometimes called the Táng River.
The river originates from the west-northwest of Zhōngshān City.
Within the city, there is a small hill,
situated on the western side of the city, rising sharply,
resembling a pile of millet.
It is suspected that this is the "Millet Pile Pass" in Wàngdū County mentioned in the Dìdào Jì.
Common people, because the hill is within the city,
also call it Zhōngshān City;
because there is the Táng River within the city, it is also called Guǎngtáng City.
The Zhōngshān Jì considers it to be Zhōngrén City,
and also considers it to be Gǔjù,
which is quite erroneous.
It is said that there is a hill within the city,
hence the name Zhōngshān,
which is the seat of Zhōngshān Commandery.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Now, twenty li east of Wàngdū in Zhōngshān, there is the old Zhōngrén City.
East of Wàngdū City, there is a city called Yáogū City.
Originally, there was no tradition of Zhōngrén,
but Fán considered it to be Zhōngrén,
the details of which are unclear.
Regarding the Zhōngrén mentioned in the Zhōngshān Jì,
the city is located over ten li east of the old Wàngdū City,
but less than twenty li,
only it is not to the east,
and upon examining these differing accounts, all are found to be inconsistent.
Now, this city is located sixty li northwest of Lúnú City,
to the northwest of the city,
is the source of the spring,
which flows west past the north of Láng Mountain.
Láng and Táng are similar in pronunciation,
and indeed it shares the tradition of the Táng River.
It flows west, passes through Zuǒrén Pavilion, and empties into the Kòu River.
The Kòu River flows east again,
and on the left converges with another river,
which originates from the foot of Láng Hill north of Zhōngshān City,
and is also called the Táng River.
However, it is not to the west of the city,
and common people also call it the Báo River,
thus it bears both names.
It flows southwest into the Kòu River,
but all of this is unclear,
and is likely based on doubtful traditions.
The Kòu River flows east again,
and the Héng River flows from the west to join it.
From here onward, the Kòu River also takes on the general name of Héngchuān.
This is what the Yǔgòng refers to as "Héng and Wèi have been followed."
The Kòu River flows east again,
and on the right encompasses the Mànì River,
which originates from Mànì Mountain northeast of Shàngqūyáng City,
flowing northeast past Fú Pavilion.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì says:
Wàngdū County has the Mànì Pass.
The Zhōngshān Jì says:
Bādù Mànì.
This is a strategically important location in the mountainous region,
where the two passes are connected in position.
It is suspected that this city is where the pass commandant was stationed,
but the origin of the different names
is not detailed.
The Mànì River flows east and empties into the Kòu River.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing south of Zhōngrén Pavilion.
In the thirteenth year of Duke Zhāo in the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn,
Xún Wú of Jìn led an army to invade Xiānyú and Zhōngrén,
and returned with great spoils.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing north of Jīngqiū.
It is commonly called Jīnglíng,
facing south toward the tomb of King Qǐng of Zhōngshān of the Hàn dynasty.
North of the Kòu River faces Jūnzǐ'àn,
on the bank is the tomb of King Xiàn, son of King Āi,
below the bank is a spring source,
and the accumulated water is also called Quánshàng'àn.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing north of Báitǔ.
To the south are the tombs of King Kāng, son of King Jìng,
where three tombs stand side by side.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing north of Yuèyáng City.
The Shǐjì states that Marquis Wén of Wèi sent Yuèyáng to destroy Zhōngshān,
and it was likely built by the old Zhōngshān,
hence the city got its name.
The Kòu River flows east again, passing south of the old city of Táng County.
These two cities are both on the north bank of the Kòu River,
hence it is said that the Kòu River passes south of them.
West of the city, there is another river,
originating from the flatlands northwest of the county,
gushing forth as a spring,
commonly also called the Táng River.
It flows east to the northwest corner of Táng City,
where it is dammed to form a lake,
commonly called Táng Pond.
Lotus covers the water,
and many gather there for leisure and play,
truly a scenic spot.
The water flows south into a small ditch,
and empties into the Kòu River below,
from top to bottom,
it shares the name of Tángchuān.
Yìng Shào's Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì says:
Forty li west of Táng County, one reaches Zhōngrén Pavilion.
Now, taking Zhōngrén Township from this city,
it is indeed forty li.
The Táng River enters the Kòu River from the northwest,
which matches Yìng's account.
It also mentions Yáo Mountain,
but to the south, there is no mountain to correspond, so this is incorrect.
Qí Yīn's Shísānzhōu Zhì says:
Zhōngshān governed Lúnú,
and the old city of Táng County was seventy-five li north of the state.
Yīn's statement about the north is incorrect.
The Shǐjì says:
After the Dìkù clan declined,
the Dìyáo clan arose,
and was first enfeoffed at Táng.
Wàngdū County is to the south,
and now this city faces the old Lúnú City to the south,
but aside from that, there is no city to correspond.
Examining antiquity to understand the present,
the meaning and facts are entirely contradictory.
The common name for the old Wàngdū City is about eighty li,
and it is seventy li from Zhōngshān City.
Verifying the route and inferring the city,
it should be Táng City.
The city is five li north of Yáo Mountain,
which matches the claim of seventy-five li.
However, common people call it Dū Mountain,
which is Yáo Mountain,
located in the Wàngdū region northeast of Táng.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
Yáo Mountain is also called Dòu Mountain.
Now, the mountain is northeast of the city,
standing steep and isolated,
like a tiger's tooth rising abruptly.
South of the mountain is the Temple of Yáo,
which is the mountain that Yáo ascended.
The Dìlǐzhì says:
Yáo Mountain is to the south.
Now, examining the south of this city,
there is no mountain to correspond,
hence earlier and later commentators
all consider the account in the Dìlǐ Jì to be mistaken.
Also, the common claim that Táng City is Wàngdū City,
to the north, there is no city to correspond,
and even if there were,
the route would be circuitous and distant,
the geographical features would be entirely inconsistent,
and ancient evidence would be sparse and unreliable.
At the western foot of Dòu Mountain northwest of this city,
there is a spring source,
which flows northeast past Dòu Mountain and joins the Sū River,
then flows turbulently east into the Kòu River.
Could this be the Táng River?
The details are unclear.
Also, about ten li southeast of this city,
there is a city,
commonly called Gāochāng County City,
which may be the old city of Wàngdū.
The county is south of Táng,
and Huángfǔ Mì said:
They are fifty li apart.
Examining the cities and lands,
it is still fifteen li,
likely a textual error.
East of this city,
there is a mountain standing alone,
and because it is not connected to other hills,
it is called Gū Mountain.
Gū and Dū are similar in sound,
and it is suspected to be the so-called Dū Mountain.
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
It was the residence of Qìngdū, mother of Yáo,
hence the county was named Wàngdū.
Zhāng Yàn said:
Yáo Mountain is to the north,
and Qìngdū Mountain, mother of Yáo, is to the south.
Ascending Yáo Mountain, one can see Dū Mountain,
hence Wàngdū County got its name.
Táng was also a city of Zhōngshān,
the state of Duke Wǔ,
of the same surname as Zhōu.
During the decline of Zhōu,
the state faced troubles from the Chìdí.
Duke Huán of Qí dominated the feudal lords,
demarcated territories,
and sent Guǎn Zhòng to repel the Róngdí,
building cities to secure them.
Afterward,
Duke Huán neglected state affairs,
and the King of Zhōu asked Grand Historian Yú:
Among the feudal lords today,
who will perish first?
He replied:
Heaven created people and made distinctions among them,
to differentiate them from birds and beasts.
Now, Zhōngshān indulges in debauchery, revelry, and pleasure,
satisfying desires without restraint,
so it will perish first.
Two years later, it indeed perished.
Marquis Wén of Wèi enfeoffed his crown prince Jī here,
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn established Zhōngshān Commandery,
in the third year of Emperor Jǐng’s reign it became a princely kingdom,
and under Wáng Mǎng it was Chángshān.
In the second year of Huángshǐ of Wèi,
Zhōngshān was captured,
and Ān Prefecture was established.
In the third year of Tiānxīng,
it was renamed Dìng Prefecture,
with its seat at the old city of Lúnú County south of the river.
In former times, Gěng Bózhāo returned to Emperor Shìzǔ at this place.
To the right of the Kòu River,
the Lú River flows into it.
The river’s source is the Black Water Pond within the city.
The Geographical Treatise says:
“The Lú River emerges from Běipíng.”
This is likely an error or oversimplification.
Scholars such as Qí Yīn and Yìng Shào
all also stated this.
I have observed that in the northwest corner of Lúnú City there is water,
deep and stagnant,
measuring a hundred paces from north to south,
and over a hundred paces from east to west.
The water’s color is pitch black,
and it is commonly called the Black Water Pond.
Some say that black water is called lú,
and stagnant water is called nú,
hence this city derived its name from the water.
Northeast of the pond, by the water’s edge,
lies the site of the former palace of the Prince of Zhōngshān of Hàn.
Its towers, halls, viewing pavilions, and terraces
all followed the standards of the capital,
and Prince Jiǎn, being noble and honored,
made them even more magnificent.
He began by constructing two lǚ,
opened four gates,
pierced the northern city wall,
and piled stones to form a conduit,
channeling the pond’s water to flow into the city.
He built fish ponds, fishing terraces, and viewing platforms for horse performances.
Over the years, these fell into ruin,
but their foundations remain.
Now they have all been covered with earth
to serve as a temple and pagoda.
Around the pond,
residents live crowded together.
The area is cramped, filthy, and squalid,
yet the spring’s source never ceases.
In the seventh year of Jiànwǔ of Zhào Shí,
the Northern Central General was dispatched to begin constructing a small city,
raising a northern terrace,
and establishing palaces and halls.
Later, Yān utilized the old palace
and built its capital south of the small city of Zhōngshān,
further constructing a partitioned city,
restoring palaces and viewing towers.
Today, the prefectural terraces still preserve the old layout,
from Hàn through Yān.
The pond water passed through the stone conduit.
After the stone conduit was destroyed,
the watercourse was also cut off.
The water secretly flowed out of the city,
pooling and slowly swelling,
then trickling northeast to join the Kòu.
The Kòu River flows east past the north of the tomb of Prince Āi of Hàn.
The tomb mound has two graves,
so people call it the Tomb of Two Women,
but this is incorrect.
Prince Āi was the grandson of Prince Jìng
and the son of Prince Kāng.
The Kòu River flows further east,
and on the right joins the Chángxīng Channel.
The channel emerges from Chángxīng Islet northwest of Shàngqūyáng County.
The islet water flows east and merges with Luòguāng Water,
which emerges from Luòguāng Channel
and flows east into Chángxīng Water.
The mingled streams flow east past the north of the lower temple at Héng Mountain.
During the turmoil at the end of Hàn,
the mountain paths were impassable.
Here originally stood a lower-tier divine hall.
Since the middle ages,
annual rituals have been recorded by the Fǎ clan.
In Jìn and Wèi times, it was changed to have eastern and western temples.
In front of the temples are stelae and gate towers,
with altars and rows of cypress trees.
The water flows further east past the north of the old city of Shàngqūyáng County,
originally a town where feudal lords and officials stayed when attending court.
In ancient times,
when the Son of Heaven made inspection tours,
he would always arrive at the Northern Peak in the eleventh month.
Marquises and earls all had bath towns
for purification and cleanliness.
After King Zhāo of Zhōu went on a southern campaign and never returned,
the ritual of inspection tours was abandoned,
but the town walls remained.
When Qín abolished the well-field system,
a county was established here.
The city lies on the sunny side of a mountain bend,
hence called Qūyáng;
there is a lower one,
so this is the upper one.
Under Wáng Mǎng, it was Chángshān Pavilion.
Flowing further southeast,
Húquán Water joins it.
The water originates from Hú Spring,
passes south of Shàngqūyáng County,
then flows east past the north of Pínglè Pavilion,
and on the left meets Chángxīng Stream.
It flows southeast past the south of Lúnú City,
then northeast.
To the left of the stream channel is the tomb of the Zhāng family,
with a stele for Zhāng Píngzhòng, Hàn-era Governor of Shànggǔ and Court Gentleman for Consultation,
erected during the Guānghé period.
The stream channel flows further northeast to join the Kòu River.
The water sometimes dries up,
and does not always flow continuously.
Further east, it passes south of Ānxǐ County.
The county
was formerly Ānxiǎn.
The terrain is perilous,
with difficult paths and wells.
In the fifth year of Yuánshuò of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Yìng, son of Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Níngxiǎn,
and Emperor Zhāng of Hàn changed it to Ānxǐ.
The Records of Zhōngshān says:
“The county lies at a bend of the Táng River,
with high mountains and steep banks,
hence called Ānxiǎn (Secure Peril).
When the town prospered and the people were at peace,
it was changed to Ānxǐ (Secure Joy).”
During the Jiànyuán era of Qín,
the Táng River flooded,
causing high banks to collapse.
Beneath the city corner were large accumulations of timber,
crisscrossed like beams and pillars.
In the early years of Later Yān,
this timber was still present,
its origin unknown.
I have examined records and investigated doubts,
surmising that when the city site was first formed,
mountain waters surged and swept,
carrying down giant rafts,
which piled up here.
As sand settled and soil accumulated,
land gradually formed.
Once walls were built upon it,
the material naturally endured.
The Kòu River flows further east past the north of Xiāng City,
formerly a township of Lúnú.
The Records of Zhōngshān says:
“Lúnú had three townships,
this being one of them.”
Later it was attached to Ānxǐ.
South of the city walls is a stele for the filial son Wáng Lì from the time of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
Further east, it passes north of Ānguó County.
The Kòu River passes east of the county and divides into two streams.
One branch
flows southeast past the south of Xiědú Pavilion.
In the first year of Yángjiā of Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Shū, son of Prince Xiào of Héjiān, at Xiědú Pavilion.
His grandson Hóng
was Emperor Líng.
It flows further southeast past the south of Rénqiū City,
then southeast past the south of Ānguō Pavilion.
In the fifth year of Yuánshuò of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Chuánfù, son of Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān.
This water flows further southeast
and enters the Hūtuó River.
The Kòu River flows northeast past the north of Xiědú Pavilion and then flows northeast.
Further east, it passes south of Bólíng County.
The Kòu River flows northeast past the old city of Lǐwú County.
The Geographical and Customs Record says:
This county
was originally the Xiàxiāng district of Ráoyáng,
and was later separated from Héjiān and placed under Bólíng.
In the seventh year of the Yuánchū era (120 CE) of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
Yì, son of Héjiān King Kāi, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
In the fifth year of the Yǒngjiàn era (130 CE) of Emperor Shùn,
it was changed to a marquisate.
Further northeast, it passes the old city of Bólíng County,
which was the ancient Lùchéng.
In the second year of the Yuánshuò era (127 BCE) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Zhēn, son of Zhōngshān King Jìng, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
The Geographical and Customs Record says:
Bólíng County
was the old Lǐwú County mentioned in the Records of the Grand Historian.
In the first year of the Běnchū era (146 CE) of Emperor Zhì of Hàn,
he succeeded Emperor Chōng as emperor,
posthumously honored his father Yì's tomb as Bólíng,
and thus made it a county,
also establishing a commandery there.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
it was abolished and returned to Ānpíng.
During the Tàishǐ era (265–274 CE) of Jìn, it was restored as a commandery.
Today, this city is called Yěchéng.
The Kòu River further flows northeast past the old city of Hóushì County,
then northeast past the east of Língyáng Pavilion,
then north,
where it joins the Bó River on the left.
The Bó River originates in Wàngdū County,
flowing southeast past the old city of that county,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shùntiáo.
Further southeast,
it disappears underground.
The Bó River then flows southeast along a channel,
where its source re-emerges,
flowing southeast past the south of Sānliáng Pavilion,
which is suspected to be the ancient Sháoliáng.
The Bamboo Annals record:
The people of Yān attacked Zhào,
besieging Zhuólù.
King Wǔlíng of Zhào and men from Dài came to rescue Zhuólù,
defeating the Yān army at Sháoliáng.
Now, east of the eastern ridge of Guǎngchāng, there is a mountain
commonly called Zhuólùluó.
The city's location is not far,
and the terrain is adjacent,
so by this reasoning,
it might be close to the truth,
though the details are unclear.
The Bó River further flows southeast past the south of Gǔliáng Pavilion,
then east past Yángchéng County,
where it spreads into a marsh.
The marsh water accumulates and swells,
covering an area several li square.
Not only is it rich in reeds and bamboo shoots,
but it is also particularly abundant in water chestnuts and lotus roots.
As for the lovely young boys
and the tender-aged children,
some take a single boat to gather water chestnuts,
others in overlapping boats break off lotus stems,
singing long songs of spring,
loving the deep green water.
Those gathering them do not speak of weariness,
those singing ballads let their voices flow freely.
At such times, travelers passing by and gazing upon it
also find solace for their weary eyes.
The world calls it the Yángchéng Marsh.
The old city of Yángchéng County is nearby to the northwest,
hence the marsh gets its name.
The Treatise on Commanderies and States says:
Púyīn County has Yángchéng.
Now, the city is thirty li southeast of the county.
The water then flows underground along a channel,
reaching the northwest of Qīngliáng Pavilion,
where its source re-emerges.
The Bó River further flows east past the south of Báidī Pavilion,
then east past the north of the old city of Guǎngwàng County,
where in the second year of the Yuánshuò era (127 BCE) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Zhōng, son of Zhōngshān King Jìng, was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Further east, it joins the Kūgōu,
which receives water from the Qīngliáng Marsh.
Further north, it passes east of Qīngliáng City,
which is Jiāngliáng.
In the second year of the Yuánshuò era (127 BCE) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Cháopíng, son of Zhōngshān King Jìng, was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Its water flows northeast into the Bó River.
The Bó River further flows northeast,
where on the left the Rú River flows into it.
The Rú River originates south of Chāng'ān Fort, west of Púyīn County.
The Records of Zhōngshān says:
East of the fort is the Àishì Sweet Spring,
with a shrine to Shùn and his two consorts.
Checking various historical records,
there is no mention of this place,
so the era is distant,
and the origin of such differing accounts
lies here.
The water from its source flows east past the old city of that county,
with winding islets and swirling rapids,
mostly twisting and turning,
so it is also called the Qū'nì River.
Zhāng Yàn said:
The Rú River curves north of the city and flows west,
hence it receives this name,
so the county is also named Qū'nì after the river.
In the fourth year of Duke Āi of the Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒzhuàn (491 BCE),
Guó Xià of Qí attacked Jìn,
capturing Qū'nì.
When Emperor Gāo of Hàn attacked Hán King Xìn,
he passed through Qū'nì from Dài,
ascended the city walls,
saw many houses and buildings,
and said:
How magnificent!
In my travels across the world,
only Luòyáng and this place are like this.
He decreed to enfeoff Chén Píng as Marquis of Qū'nì.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shùnpíng.
The Rú River further flows east and joins the Sū River,
which originates from a mountain southwest of the county,
flows northeast past the south of Yáogū Pavilion,
then east past the county into the Rú River.
The Rú River further east reaches the mouth of the Pú River,
which originates from Bóyáng Mountain in the northwest,
flows southwest,
accumulates water to form a deep pool,
a hundred paces east-west,
over a hundred paces north-south,
deep and unfathomable.
The Pú River further flows southeast,
with an ancient shrine beside the water,
commonly called the Bǎi Shrine,
also known as the Púshàng Shrine,
though the details are unclear.
Further south, it passes east of Yáng'ān Pavilion.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì says:
Púyīn County has Yáng'ān Pass,
likely the seat of the Yáng'ān Pass Commandant,
and the common name for this area is Yáng'ān Kuàng.
The Pú River further flows southeast through the kuàng,
passes under Yáng'ān Pass,
and the pass's high ground is called Tángtóu Bǎn.
Exiting the pass, it flows north,
then east past the old city of Xiàwū,
which is truly steep and perilous.
The Bamboo Annals record:
Yīn Chén of Wèi and Gōngsūn Póu of Zhào attacked Yān,
then captured Xiàwū,
and fortified Qū'nì.
East of this city,
a wall was built following the slope,
commonly called the Widow's City,
constructed by Jiǎ Fù when following Emperor Guāngwǔ in pursuit of the Copper Horse and Five Banner armies in Běipíng.
Due to phonetic shifts in common speech,
it acquired this name.
The water further flows southeast past the north of the old city of Púyīn County.
The Treatise on Geography says:
The city is north of the Pú River.
In the second year of the Zhānghé era (88 CE) of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
while touring the Northern Peak,
he found the name Qū'nì inauspicious,
so based on the mountain and river names,
changed it to Púyīn.
On the right, the water joins the Yú River,
which originates from Yú Mountain southwest of Běipíng County.
The mountain rocks resemble a giant fish,
and the water emerges below it,
hence the common name for the river based on its appearance.
It flows east and empties into the Pú River,
then east into the Rú River.
Therefore, the Treatise on Geography says:
The Pú River and Sū River
both enter the Rú River east of the county.
Further northeast, it passes south of Lèchéng,
then east into the Bó River.
From here, the Bó River is also commonly called the Rú River.
In the seventh year of Duke Zhāo (535 BCE) of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Qí and Yān made a covenant on the Rú River.
Dù Yù said:
The Rú River originates northeast of Gāoyáng County,
and flows to Mò County in Héjiān, entering the Yì River.
Thus, the Rú River, Hūtuó, Kòu, and Yì are used interchangeably.
The Bó River further flows northeast,
where the Xú River flows into it.
The Xú River originates from the foot of the great ridge southeast of Guǎngchāng County,
commonly called Guǎngchāng Ridge.
The ridge is over forty li high,
and within twenty li, it twists and turns five times
before reaching the top,
hence the ridge is named Five Turns.
Looking down from above, the layered mountains
look like ant hills,
truly deserving the name Lone Mountain,
and it is also steep and lofty.
The Xú River has three extraordinary sources,
converging into one stream,
flowing east then turning north past the east of the mountain,
with an imperial archery stele west of the water.
The Xú River further flows north, then bends west past the foot of the southern cliff,
There is another stele at the water's shady side.
The Xú River again follows the mountain and turns south, passing below the eastern cliff,
and at the water's edge there is yet another stele.
All three of these inscriptions
face the layered peaks, with cliffs and barriers deep and high,
standing like walls and rising like rosy clouds.
The stone inscription reads:
In the twelfth month of the first year of the Tàiyán era,
the emperor's carriage made an eastern tour,
passing through the perilous depths of the Wǔhuí,
and viewing the lofty banks soaring high.
Then he halted his carriage by the roadside,
took up his bow and shot an arrow,
the flying arrow passed over the cliff mountain.
A stone was carved to praise his great achievement.
On either side of the stele are two layered platforms,
which are the very places where the imperial shooting took place.
On the back of the stele are listed the names of the officials who erected it.
The Xú River bends northeast, passing by Láng Mountain,
and then bends again, passing south of the mountain.
Numerous peaks vie to rise high,
like the upright wings of birds,
standing steep and precipitous,
also like the tips of swords,
reaching the utmost in lofty and sheer terrain.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Crown Prince Lì fled due to the witchcraft affair,
and his son fled far and hid in this mountain,
hence the world knows it as Láng Mountain.
South of the mountain is the "Stele of Lord Lángshān,"
the details are recorded in its text.
The Xú River also passes south of the temple of the Middle Son of Lord Lángshān, General Chùfēng,
in front of the temple there is a stele.
On the fourteenth day of the eighth month, the rén-yín day, in the first year of the Yǒngkāng era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
an edict was issued bestowing honors upon the lord and his son,
and a temple was established according to the law, with this stele.
In the seventh year of the Guāngchū era of Liú Yào,
the former Dùnqiū Prefect Láng Xuān, Běipíng Prefect Yáng Píngyì Zhèn, and others
jointly restored the old stele,
carving the stone and erecting a eulogy.
The Xú River also passes through Běipíng County,
within the county boundaries, in the fourth year of the Xīpíng era of Hàn, the two provinces of Yōu and Jì, by an edict issued on the wù-zǐ day,
dispatched Jì Province Attendant Wáng Qiú,
and Yōu Province Attendant Zhāng Zhāo to divide the borders of the commanderies and counties,
erecting stones to mark the boundaries,
the full text is inscribed on the stone.
The Xú River flows southeast again, passing through a stone gate,
commonly known as Lóngmén (Dragon Gate).
Its upper part is closed, the lower part open,
the open part is six zhàng high,
flying water passes through it,
emerging southward, riding the cliffs,
pouring down the ravine and cascading,
over seven zhàng in height,
the sound of rushing and surging,
strangely powerful and fierce,
striking the rocks to form wells,
the water depth is unfathomable,
white waves churn on their own,
billows surge on all sides,
those who gaze upon it are startled in spirit,
those who approach it are struck with awe.
It emerges southeast from the mountain and passes through the city,
where there is an old stele,
which is the stele of Lord Tàibái,
the eldest son of Lord Lángshān.
The water flows east again,
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn pursued the Tóngmǎ and Wǔfān rebels at Běipíng and defeated them north of the Shùn River,
chasing the defeated northward,
but was defeated by them,
in close combat,
Emperor Guāngwǔ threw himself down a cliff,
encountered the charging cavalryman Wáng Fēng,
who then gave him a horse, and he retreated to defend Fànyáng.
The Shùn River
is likely another name for the Xú River.
The Xú River flows east again, passing north of Púchéng,
then east, passing Qīngyuàn City,
then southeast, merging with the Lú River,
which emerges west of Púchéng,
commonly called Quántóu Water.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
Běipíng County has the Lú River,
which is this water.
It flows east past the city,
then southeast,
entering the Xú River from the left.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
East to Gāoyáng it enters the Bó River,
but now it does not.
The Xú River flows east again, joining the Cáo River on the left,
which emerges from Cáo Hé Marsh in Shuòníng County to the northwest,
flowing southeast,
joining the water from Qí Mountain on the left,
which emerges from Qí Mountain,
flows east past north of Xíng'ān City,
then southeast into the Cáo River.
The Cáo River flows southeast past the old city south of Běixīnchéng County,
which was Shuòpíng County under Wáng Mǎng.
The Cáo River then flows east into the Xú River.
The Xú River flows southeast again, passing north of an old city,
commonly called Jìyú City,
the details of which are unknown.
The Xú River then flows east into the Bó River.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
The Xú River emerges from Běipíng, east to Gāoyáng it enters the Bó River,
then east into the Kòu River.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
The Bó River from Wàngdū,
east to Gāoyáng enters the Kòu River, which is correct.
Then northeast into the Yì River.
The Kòu River flows northeast again, passing north of Yīchéng,
commonly called the Yīchéng River.
The "Discourse on Earth" does not mention the name Yīchéng,
it is the ancient Gěchéng.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" says:
Gāoyáng has Gěchéng,
which Yàn gave to Zhào.
The Kòu River flows northeast again, passing east of the old city of Ālíng County,
which was Ālù under Wáng Mǎng.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate to Left General Rén Guāng.
The Kòu River flows northeast to the Great Wall and enters the Yì River.
12 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 12
12.1 Shèng River
12.1 Shèng River
The Shèng River emerges from Shànggǔ,
the old land of Yān.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Shànggǔ Commandery was established.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìnshū‧Discourse on the Earth" says:
The commandery is at the head of the valley,
hence it was named Shànggǔ (Upper Valley).
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shuòdiào.
The water emerges from Shèngshuǐ Valley in the southwest of the commandery,
flowing southeast past the eastern end of Dàfáng Ridge, below Shǒu Mountain.
There is a stone cave,
open to the northeast,
four or five zhàng high and wide,
entering the cave, it becomes even deeper and more lofty,
there is water inside the cave.
According to old tales,
there was once a Buddhist monk named Shì Huìmí,
fond of exploring hidden wonders,
he once carried a torch to search it,
following the water into the cave for three lǐ,
the cave divides into two:
one cave is especially small,
exiting northwest,
its destination unknown;
one cave exits southwest,
entering the cave, it took five or six days to return,
and its depth remains unfathomable.
The water is cold in summer and warm in winter,
in spring and autumn, white fish emerge from the cave,
returning after several days.
Those who catch and eat them
find them delicious, a rare delicacy,
likely similar to the fine fish of Bǐng Cave.
This water flows northeast into the Shèng River.
The Shèng River flows east again, passing Yùshí Mountain,
called Yùshí Pass,
the mountain has much mǐn jade and yān stone,
hence named Yùshí (Jade Stone).
The water flows underground for over a lǐ,
its hidden source emerges eastward,
then east,
cascading waves pour into the ravine,
over one zhàng in height,
then bends and flows south.
It passes east of Liángxiāng County, south.
The Sacred River flows southward,
passes west of the county and turns,
then continues south, passing west of the old city of Liángxiāng County,
which was called Guǎngyáng during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
The Fáng River flows into it,
originating from the south of Dàfáng Mountain, northwest of the county,
and flowing southeast past the foot of Yángtóu Hill,
commonly known as Yángtóu Stream.
The water then flows southeast,
and enters the Sacred River east of the county.
The Sacred River then joins with the Lè River to the south,
which originates from the south of Dàfáng Mountain, northwest of the county,
flowing southeast,
passing west of the county and then southeast into the Sacred River.
The Sacred River then flows east, passing south of the old county city,
and continues east, passing south of Shèngjù,
likely named in association with the river.
It then flows east and merges with the Xiá River,
which originates from the eastern valley of Gānquán Plain, west of Liángxiāng County,
flowing east past the north of the old city of Xīxiāng County,
called Yífēng during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
It is commonly known as Dūxiāng City.
According to the *Geographical Records*,
Zhuō Commandery had Xīxiāng County but not Dūxiāng City,
indicating that the common name is incorrect.
It then flows east past the south of Liángxiāng County city,
and continues northeast into the Sacred River,
commonly known as Xiáhuó River,
also called the Unreasonable Ditch.
It then flows east past the north of Yángxiāng County.
The Shèng Shuǐ (Sacred River) flows east from Zhuō County and joins the Táo Shuǐ (Peach River).
The Táo Shuǐ originates by receiving the Lái Shuǐ at Liángxiāng, southeast of Xúchéng,
and branches westward from the Yuán Shuǐ (Wall River).
It is commonly called the Nán Shāgōu (Southern Sand Ditch),
which is the Táo Shuǐ.
It flows east past the north of Qiú County,
then east past the site of the old Zhuō County town, where it joins the Zhuō Shuǐ.
Some consider this to be the Zhuō Shuǐ,
while others also call it the Táo Shuǐ.
It emerges from a large depression eight lǐ east of the Qígōu (Strange Ditch), southwest of the old Zhuō County town.
Several springs issue forth together,
flowing east past the north of Táorénxū (Peach Kernel Ruins).
Some say the ruins were named after the river,
in which case it would be the Táo Shuǐ.
Others say it was the former residence of Zhōng Rén,
not Táo Rén.
I have examined the "Treatise on Geography" [Dìlǐ Zhì],
which states the Táo Shuǐ receives its flow from the Lái Shuǐ.
Since the source of this water [here]
does not match the "Treatise,"
I consider Zhōng to be correct.
Further northeast, it joins the Lèduī Spring,
which emerges east of the mound,
flowing southeast to pour into the Zhuō Shuǐ.
The Zhuō Shuǐ then flows northeast past the west of the old Zhuō County town and pours into the Táo.
Yìng Shào said:
"The commandery of Zhuō,
formerly part of Yān,
was established in the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
To its south is the commandery of Zhuō Shuǐ,
from which it likely took its name."
Kàn Yǐn also stated this.
Now, there is no water south of the Zhuō city wall corresponding to this,
the only such water lies to the southwest.
Yìng Shào also said:
"The Zhuō Shuǐ emerges from Zhuōlù County in Shànggǔ."
I note that the Zhuō Shuǐ flows east from Zhuōlù into the Lěi Shuǐ.
The Lěi Shuǐ flows southeast past Guǎngyáng Commandery, forming the boundary with Zhuō Commandery.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Zhuō Commandery was established by dividing Yān.
The name 'Zhuō'
must have been adopted from the general designation of the Zhuō Shuǐ,
hence the commandery and county were named after it.
However, the principles of waterways are subtly interconnected,
with sources emerging in various places.
Thus, among the Xiōngnú it is called the Zhuōyē Shuǐ.
Mountains and rivers create barriers and vast distances,
making it unreasonable for there to be a continuous flow connecting them.
Places that receive the name
are all related through hidden and visible connections,
with the name adopted from afar based on sentiment.
Reasoning from this,
the matter might be close [to the truth],
but it is not entirely satisfactory.
The Táo Shuǐ flows east past the north of the old Zhuō County town.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yuánhàn.
In the first year of the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
it was changed to Fànyáng Commandery.
The current commandery seat is at the site of the old Zhuō County town.
In the northeastern corner of the town wall is a stele for the Jìn Prince Kāng,
and east of the town is a temple stele for Simā Xiāo, Prince of Fànyáng.
The Táo Shuǐ flows northeast and meets the Yuán Shuǐ.
The Yuán Shuǐ receives its flow from the Lái Shuǐ,
branching from the Táo Shuǐ at Liángxiāng County.
It is commonly called the Běi Shāgōu (Northern Sand Ditch).
Thus, Yìng Shào said:
"The Yuán Shuǐ emerges from Liángxiāng,
flowing east past the north of the old Yuán County town."
The "Shǐjì Yīnyì" says:
"In Héjiān there is Wǔyuán County,
and in Zhuō there is Yuán County."
In the third year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Cì, a surrendered Xiōngnú king.
It was the Yuánhàn Tíng under Wáng Mǎng,
commonly called Qǐngchéng,
which is incorrect.
It flows east past Qǐng,
also a place name.
Hence there is the saying 'above Qǐng,'
and it is commonly called the Qián Hé (Front River) of Qǐng.
Further east,
the Luò Shuǐ flows into it.
The Luò Shuǐ receives its flow from the Míngzé Zhǔ (Singing Marsh Islet),
an islet fifteen lǐ square.
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he made an imperial visit to Míngzé,
which was here.
Fú Qián said:
"The name of a marsh,
located in the northern boundary of Qiú County" —
this is that marsh.
From the west, the Dúshù Shuǐ flows into it,
emerging from the northern mountains of Qiú County,
flowing east into the islet.
From the north, the Gānquán Shuǐ flows into it,
emerging from the western mountains of Liángxiāng,
flowing southeast past the west of Xīxiāng Town,
then south into the Míngzé Zhǔ.
The water from the islet flows east to become the Luò Shuǐ,
then east past the south of Xīxiāng Town,
then east past Yuán County and south into the Yuán Shuǐ.
The Yuán Shuǐ flows east past the north of Zhuō County,
then east to pour into the Táo.
Thus Yìng Shào said:
"The Yuán Shuǐ flows east into the Táo."
Kàn Yǐn said:
"It flows to Yángxiāng and joins it."
Now, examining the watercourses, it does not reach that far.
The Táo Shuǐ flows east past Yángxiāng,
then east to pour into the Shèng Shuǐ.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows east,
joined by the Guǎngyáng Shuǐ,
which emerges from the western mountains of Xiǎoguǎngyáng,
flowing east past the north of the old Guǎngyáng County town;
further east,
the Fúlù Shuǐ flows into it.
The Fúlù Shuǐ emerges from the western mountains,
flowing southeast past the south of the old Guǎngyáng County town,
then east into the Guǎngyáng Shuǐ.
The combined flow goes southeast to Yángxiāng County,
joining the Shèng Shuǐ from the right.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows southeast past the west of Yángxiāng Town,
not passing its north.
The county
was formerly the Yáng Tíng of Zhuō.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" [Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì] says:
"Fifty lǐ east of Zhuō County is Yángxiāng Tíng,
later divided off to form a county."
Under Wáng Mǎng,
it was renamed Zhāngwǔ,
which is Chángxiāng County.
According to the "Tàikāng Geographical Records" [Tàikāng Dìjì],
Zhuō had Chángxiāng but not Yángxiāng.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows east past Chángxīng Town's south wall,
then east past the north of the old Fāngchéng County town wall.
This is the Fāngchéng that Lǐ Mù captured when attacking Yān.
It was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Fàng under Wèi.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows east,
joining from the left with the Báisì Gōu (White Sacrifice Ditch).
The Báisì Gōu emerges east of Lóuchéng in Guǎngyáng County,
flowing southeast.
From the left it joins the Lóuchéng Shuǐ,
which emerges from level ground,
its source flowing southeast,
joining the Báisì Shuǐ from the right.
The combined flow goes southeast past the west of Chángdào Town,
formerly a township tíng.
It lies forty lǐ west of Chángxiāng Town,
enfeoffed in the third year of the Gānlù era of the Wèi young emperor Cáo Huàn.
It then flows southeast into the Shèng Shuǐ.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows southeast past the east of Hánchéng.
The "Hán Yì" chapter of the "Shī" says:
"Vast is that Hánchéng,
completed by the army of Yān.
The king bestowed on the Marquis of Hán
the Zhuī and the Mò tribes,
to hold all the northern states."
Zhèng Xuán said:
"Zhōu enfeoffed the Marquis of Hán,
who resided in Hánchéng as a feudal lord.
It is said that pressured by the Xiǎnyí,
he gradually moved eastward."
Wáng Sù said:
"In Fāngchéng County of Zhuō Commandery there is Hánhóu Chéng,
commonly called Hánhào Chéng,
which is incorrect."
The Shèng Shuǐ flows southeast,
joining from the right with the Qīngdiàn Shuǐ,
which issues from the Western Marsh,
flowing east to pour into the Shèng Shuǐ,
at a place called Liúgōng Kǒu.
Further east, it passes south of Āncì County,
and east into the sea.
The Shèng Shuǐ flows east past the south of the old Āncì County town of Bóhǎi,
which was enfeoffed as a marquisate in the third year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn
for Wáng Mǐn, Governor of Jīng Province.
It then flows southeast to pour into the Jùmǎ Hé, and does not reach the sea.
12.2 The Jùmǎ Hé (Giant Horse River)
12.2 The Jùmǎ Hé (Giant Horse River)
The Jùmǎ Hé emerges from Lái Mountain in Guǎngchāng County of Dài Commandery.
This is the Láishuǐ River.
It has two sources,
both originating from Láishān Mountain.
It flows east past the old city of Guǎngchāng County,
which was called Guǎngpíng during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The state of Wèi enfeoffed Yuè Jìn as a marquis here.
The Láishuǐ River then flows northeast past the southeast of Xīshèyú City and continues northeast;
it then passes by Dōngshèyú City to the south,
and bends around the east of that city.
The *Bamboo Annals* states:
"Xún Yáo attacked Zhōngshān and captured Qióngyú Hill."
The characters for "qióng" (窮) and "shè" (射) are similar,
so it is suspected this city is the one,
though the details are unclear.
The Láishuǐ River then passes west of Sānnǚ Pavilion,
and north of Lóu Pavilion.
To the left it connects to Báijiàn Creek,
which has two sources,
that join to form one stream.
The rocks in the stream are brilliantly white,
looking from afar like accumulated snow,
hence it received its name from this appearance.
This water then flows northeast,
and is called Shícáo Water.
It flows underground,
and when overflowing, it forms a thoroughfare and pours forth,
called Báijiànkǒu.
The Láishuǐ River continues northeast,
where Sānggǔ Water flows into it.
This water originates from Sāng Creek in the south,
and flows north into the Láishuǐ River.
The Láishuǐ River then flows north past the east of Xiǎohóng,
and east past the south of Dàhóng.
This was likely the place where Huò Yuán lived in seclusion and taught.
Xú Guǎng stated:
"Yuán lived in seclusion on Guǎngyáng Mountain,
teaching several thousand students.
He was killed by Wáng Jùn.
Though ages have passed and times are distant,
the names of the two 'hóng' still mark the place."
There are no stele inscriptions,
so it is ultimately unknown for certain who resided there.
The Láishuǐ River then flows northeast past Zǐshí Creek Mouth and joins with Zǐshuǐ River.
This water originates north from beneath Dàgèn Mountain north of Shèngrén City,
flowing southeast.
To the left it meets Lěiluǒ Creek,
likely because the mountain collapsed into the ravine,
piling rocks and submerging the moat,
so the creek and ravine received this name.
The water emerges from the northeast,
and flows southwest into Zǐshí Creek.
Zǐshí Creek then passes east of Shèngrén City,
and continues southeast,
where to the right it meets Dānchē Water.
This water emerges from Dānchē Gorge,
flows southeast past the south of Shèngrén City,
then flows south into Zǐshí Water,
and further south into the Láishuǐ River.
The Láishuǐ River then flows southeast past the south of Yúchéng,
and bends around the east of that city,
where it is called Yúchéng River.
The Láishuǐ River then flows south past Cángdāo Mountain.
Layered cliffs stand like walls,
soaring straight up to the sky.
Looking from afar at the side of the cliff,
it appears as if knives are piled up,
ring upon ring, side by side,
all uniformly facing west.
The Láishuǐ River flows east past the north of Xúchéng,
where an old channel diverges,
commonly called Shāgōu Water.
Further east,
the Dūgàng Channel diverges.
One stream flows southeast,
which is the Dūgàng Channel;
another flows southwest,
which is the old channel of the Láishuǐ River.
When water is abundant, it forms a long, broad flow;
when water diminishes, the waves recede and lie hidden.
The dual source reappears at Qiú County,
which is the old river course.
It passes east of Qiú County to the north.
The Láishuǐ River receives the old channel north of the county,
where the dual source re-emerges,
forming a long pool.
The pool is about a hundred paces wide,
and several hundred paces long.
On its left and right, small streams flank it,
controlling and drawing in numerous waters,
forming its own deep islets.
The long river flows gently down for about ten *li*,
then flows southeast past the old city of Qiú County to the east.
In the third year of the Zhōng era of Hàn Jǐngdì,
it was used to enfeoff the surrendered Xiōngnú king Lóng Jiāng as a marquisate.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Qiúpíng.
It is called the Jùmǎ River,
also known as Qúshuǐ.
It then flows southeast.
Yuán Běnchū sent his subordinate general Cuī Jùyè to attack Gù'ān but failed to capture it.
As he retreated,
Gōngsūn Zàn pursued and attacked him at the Jùmǎ River,
where six or seven thousand men died.
This is that river.
It then flows southeast past the old city of Fànyáng County to the north,
where the Yìshuǐ River flows into it.
It then passes east of Róngchéng County to the north.
The Jùmǎ River flows further east,
where the Lìtíng Ditch empties into it.
This waterway originates from the Dūkàng Ditch east of Qiú County,
flowing southeast,
passing east of the Zǐyuān.
My sixth-generation ancestor, the Prefect of Lèlàng,
moved from Zhuō County's Xiānxián Township to settle on its northern bank,
with the great river to the west,
and this water flanking to the east.
Its branching streams and connecting channels,
winding through villages and gardens,
not only provided abundant resources for farming and fishing to cherish,
but indeed were a superb place for spiritual wandering.
This water flows southeast,
and is also named the Lìtíng Ditch.
The water then turns southwest,
passes south of the Dàlì Pavilion, and enters the Jùmǎ River.
Further east, it passes north of the old city of Róngchéng County.
Continuing east,
the Dūkàng Ditch empties into it.
This waterway originates from the Lái River at Láigǔ,
where diverting it creates a long, winding flow,
and blocking it causes the small stream to cease.
The virtue of water lies in its harmony,
and its adaptability lies in our control.
It flows southeast past north of Nǎi County,
then east past south of Lóusāng Village in Lìtíng, Zhuō County,
which is the former hometown of Liú Bèi.
Further east, it passes the Dūkàng Marsh,
which encompasses Fāngchéng County.
This county originally belonged to Guǎngyáng,
but later was attached to Zhuō.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* states:
The county has a Dūkàng Pavilion.
Sūn Chàngzhī's *Shùhuà* includes a *Dūkàng Dìtú*,
stating that Yān Crown Prince Dān sent Jīng Kē to present it to Qín,
the King of Qín killed Kē,
and the map was also destroyed.
The *Dìlǐ Shū Shànggǔ Shèngxián Zhǒngdì Jì* states:
Dūkàng is located in Zhuō Commandery.
Today, south of Gù'ān County there is a Dūkàng path,
which is the southern boundary of Yōuzhōu.
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Hàng"
means "mǎng."
It describes something vast and boundless,
without limits or shores.
A "hàng" marsh without water
refers to saline-alkali land.
The water branches from the marsh,
flows east past the old city of Zhuō County,
then east past south of the tomb of Hàn Palace Attendant Lú Zhí,
further east,
disperses into marsh islets,
which is the Dūkàng Marsh.
It bends north and empties into the Táo River.
The Dūkàng Water flows further south,
called the Báigōu Water,
passes west of the Guǎngyáng Pavilion to the south,
and then south joins a branch ditch.
This ditch receives water from the Jùmǎ River to the west,
emerges eastward as a branch ditch,
then flows east into the Báigōu,
the Báigōu continues south,
and enters the Jùmǎ River.
The Jùmǎ River flows further southeast past Yìchāng County,
where the Hùdiàn Water joins from the right.
This water originates from the Hù Embankment west of the old city of Línxiāng County,
flows southeast past south of Línxiāng City,
