where Hàn enfeoffed Yún, son of the Prince of Guǎngyáng Qǐng, as a marquisate.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
Ten lǐ south of Fāngchéng is Línxiāng City,
an old county.
The Diàn Water flows further southeast past west of the old city of Yìchāng County,
and enters the Jùmǎ River to the south.
The Jùmǎ River flows east past south of the old city of Yìchāng County,
where Hàn enfeoffed Yīng, son of the Prince of Guǎngyáng Qǐng, as a marquisate,
which was Yǒuzhì under Wáng Mǎng.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
Eighty lǐ east of Fāngchéng County is Yìchāng City,
an old county.
Further east,
the Bāzhàng Ditch empties into it.
This water emerges from flat land northeast of Āncì County,
flows southeast past east of Āncì City,
southeast past west of the old city of Quánzhōu County,
then south,
where it joins the dry ditch of the Hūtuó River from the right.
This ditch runs from northwest of Āncì,
east past east of Chángdào City and west of the old city of Āncì County,
where Jìn Minister of Works Liú Kūn defended against Shí Lè.
Further southeast to southwest of Quánzhōu County,
it enters the Bāzhàng Ditch from the east,
then south into the Jùmǎ River,
merging chaotically and flowing east.
Further east, it passes north of Bóhǎi's Dōngpíngshū County,
and enters the sea to the east.
The *Dìlǐzhì* states:
The Lái River flows southeast to Róngchéng and enters the river.
The river,
is the Rú River,
likely clarifying their confluence interchangeably.
The Jùmǎ River, north of Píngshū City,
enters the Hūtuó to the south,
and together they return to the sea.
13 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Thirteen
13.1 The Lěi River
13.1 The Lěi River
The Lěi River emerges from Yīnguǎn County in Yànmén,
flows northeast past south of Sānggān County in Dài Commandery,
The Lěi River originates from the Léitóu Mountain,
also known as the Zhì River.
Its spring emerges from the side of the mountain,
flowing along the waves and passing through ravines,
then heading northeast out of the mountain.
It passes west of the old city of Yīnguǎn County,
which
was formerly the Lóufán Township.
It was established in the third year of the later reign of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Fùzāng.
In the third year of Huángxīng of Wèi,
when Qí was pacified,
its people were relocated to the county,
and the Píngqí Commandery was established.
The Lěi River then flows northeast,
where it joins the Sānggàn River on the left.
To the northwest of the county, the terrain is elevated and flat,
with seven springs gushing forth,
called the Sānggàn Spring,
which is the Suòguàn River.
Elders say:
This water flows underground,
connecting to the great pool north of Yānjīng Mountain in Fényáng County, Tàiyuán.
The pool lies atop the mountain plateau,
and is known to the world as the Tiānchí.
It is over a square lǐ in size,
clear and mirror-like,
deep and still without flowing,
resembling the Qiūyuān of Zhāonà in Āndìng.
Clear water flows into the pool,
shining brightly and reflecting the sky.
The pool has never had any weeds,
and whenever wind-blown leaves fall into it,
small emerald-green birds
dive into the depths to retrieve them,
like the yún birds of Kuàijī.
The water does not diminish in the sun’s heat,
nor does it overflow in heavy rains,
and none can fathom its depth.
According to ancient lore,
it is said that once someone was riding a cart by the pool’s edge,
when suddenly a great wind arose,
blowing them into the water.
Later, someone found their cart wheel in the Sānggàn Spring,
thus proving that the two waters are connected underground.
East of the pool, separated by a hill, is another stone pool,
about fifty or sixty paces square,
clear, deep, and mirror-like,
no different from the larger pool.
The Sānggàn River flows southeast from its source,
where it meets the Mǎyì Chuān River on the right.
This river originates from the western plains of Mǎyì,
commonly called the Mó Chuān.
This is likely a phonetic corruption in the Dí language,
as “Mǎ” and “Mó” sound similar.
The river flows east past the old city of Mǎyì County,
as Gān Bǎo’s Sōushénjì records:
In the past, the Qín people built a city within the Wǔzhōu Pass to defend against the Hú.
The city collapsed several times just before completion.
Then a horse ran around a certain spot,
circling back and forth.
The elders found this strange,
so they built the city following its path,
and the city did not collapse.
Thus, it was named Mǎyì.
Some say it was the Mǎchéng of Dài,
but records vary,
and the truth is unclear.
The Hàn enfeoffed Hán Wáng Xìn with this city,
but he was later besieged by the Xiōngnú,
and surrendered.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhāngzhāo.
This river flows east into the Sānggàn River,
which then flows southeast.
South of the river is an old city,
facing the river to the northeast.
Further southeast,
it joins the Lěi River on the right,
where the waters branch and flow south.
The Sānggàn River continues east,
joining the Wǔzhōu Pass River on the left.
This river originates from an old city,
flowing southeast out of the mountains,
passing south of the Rìmò City,
so named because the sun sets here,
and it was a city where war chariots gathered.
To the east is the Rìzhōng City,
and east of that is the Zǎoqǐ City,
also called the Shíshí City,
located in the northern bend of the Huángguā Hill.
The river flows east,
then joins the Sānggàn River on the right.
The Sānggàn River flows southeast past the western bend of the Huángguā Hill,
then curves around the southern side of the mound.
Xú Guǎng said:
This is where Yīlú exiled his eldest son, Lìsūn, to the Huángguā Mound.
Further east,
it joins a branch stream on the right,
which originates from the Sānggàn River,
flowing southeast past the north of the Sānggàn Commandery,
established by the Great Wèi because of the river,
and the commandery takes its name from it.
Further northeast,
it joins the Xiàwū Mountain River on the left.
This river emerges from the eastern stream of Xiàwū Mountain to the south,
flowing northwest past the north of an old city,
the details of which are unknown.
It then flows northwest into the Sānggàn branch stream,
which continues east,
its long currents forming waves,
connecting two lakes.
The eastern lake and western marsh
are linked by deep pools,
the water clear and deep.
Morning ducks and evening geese
float upon its surface,
while dark-shelled and white-scaled fish
leap and swim below,
filling the pools.
The scene delights fish and birds alike,
lacking only pure water.
It is commonly called the Nánchí,
and north of the pool lies the old city of Wāngtáo County,
hence the name Nánchí.
The Nánchí water flows northeast into the Sānggàn River,
becoming the Lěi River,
and from here onward, both names are used interchangeably.
The Lěi River flows northeast past the west of Shítíng,
which was built in the third year of Tiāncì of the Huáng Wèi.
The Lěi River then flows northeast past the south of the Báiláng Mound,
where Emperor Dàowǔ of Wèi Lièzǔ encountered the auspicious sign of a white wolf,
hence the name of this mound.
On the mound is an old palace,
with foundations of towers and terraces still lofty.
Every autumn, when hawks and falcons soar,
and on hunting days,
the clear fields are surveyed,
making it an ideal place for elevated viewing.
The Lěi River flows east for forty-nine lǐ,
passing north of the Jùwèi Pavilion,
then east,
where the Guō Chuān River flows into it.
This river emerges south of the old city of Guō County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Guōzhāng.
The county faces the Xuán Mountain to the south,
with the Guō Mountain to its back on the right,
situated between two mountains,
hence the name Guōzhāng.
The river flows west out of the mountains,
called the Guōkǒu,
then north past the east of the old city of Fánzhì County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Dāngyào.
Further north, it passes east of the Jùwèi Pavilion,
then north past the west of the old city of Jùyáng County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shànyáng.
According to the Shísānzhōu Zhì:
It is located one hundred and three lǐ northeast of Yīnguǎn County.
The river then flows east into the Lěi River,
which continues east past the south of Bānshì County,
where the Rúhún River flows into it.
This river originates over fifty lǐ southwest of Xuánhóng County in Liángchéng,
flowing east past the south of an old city,
which northerners call the Dúgǔ Gūchéng,
and the river is also named after it.
It joins the Xuánhóng Pool water to the east,
which emerges from below the eastern mountain of Xuánhóng County,
accumulating into a pool.
It draws water from the north via the Yú River,
which originates from the Yú Stream,
flowing south into the pool.
The pool water receives and discharges river flows,
forming a great marsh,
two lǐ from east to west,
and four lǐ from north to south.
To the north, it faces the southern pool of Liángchuān City,
a pool fifty lǐ square,
commonly called the Qǐfú Yuánchí.
Though separated by hills,
the bird’s flight path is not far,
and among the clouds and mist,
there are often
flows southwest past the south of Xuánhóng County,
joining the Rúhún River on the right,
thus combining the names of the two waters.

The stream flows north past the east of an old pavilion,
north of which there is a stone figure,
so it is commonly called Shírénchéng (Stone Figure City).
It then flows northwest into the Lián River.
The Lián River flows north past the west of the old city of Dāngchéng County.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Zhōu Bó pacified Dài and executed Chén Xī at Dāngchéng,
which is this very place.
Yìng Shào said:
A city was built facing Huándū Mountain,
hence the name Dāngchéng (Facing City).
It then passes the old eastern part of Dài and flows northwest into the Qíyí River.
West of the Qíyí River is Suí Mountain,
on which there is a temple,
called the Nǚláng Shrine,
worshipped by local customs.
The Qíyí River flows north past the east of the old city of Sānggān,
and then north into the Lěi River.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states:
The Qíyí River originates from Píngshū County,
flows north to Sānggān, and enters the Lěi River. This is correct.
The Lěi River flows northeast past the mouth of the Shíshān Stream,
which originates from the southern mountains,
flows north past the east of Kōnghóu City.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Ninety lǐ northeast of Dàichéng is Kōnghóu City.
The stream then flows northeast into the Lěi River.
The Lěi River flows east past the north of the old city of Pān County,
and east joins the Xiéyáng Pass Stream,
which originates from Xié Creek.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Ninety lǐ southwest of Xiàluò City is Xiéyáng Pass,
whose road leads west to Dài Commandery.
The stream flows northeast,
passes Jītóu Mountain.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Jītóu Mountain is south of Pān City,
which is this mountain.
It then flows north past the old city of Pān County,
and on the left joins the old channel of Pān Spring.
The channel originally received water from Pān Spring within Pān City.
Some say
this was the capital of Shùn.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Forty lǐ southwest of Xiàluò City is Pān City,
and three lǐ northwest of the city
is Lì Mountain,
on which stands the temple of Yú Shùn.
The *Shísān Zhōu Jì* states:
One hundred and ten lǐ northeast of Guǎngpíng City is Pān County.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states:
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shùwǔ.
The spring spreads over several tens of paces,
flows east out of the city,
and enters the Xiéyáng Pass Stream.
In heavy rain, it flows freely,
but in drought, it ceases,
leaving only a stagnant pool.
The Pass Stream then flows northeast,
into the Lěi River.
The Lěi River flows east past Yōngluò City.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Twenty lǐ southwest of Xiàluò City is Yōngluò City,
and the Sānggān River flows east south of the city.
The Lěi River flows east past the south of the old city of Xiàluò County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Xiàzhōng.
During the Wèi dynasty, it was the seat of Guǎngníng County and Guǎngníng Commandery of Yān Prefecture.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
It is fifty lǐ from Píngchéng,
and two hundred paces south of the city is the temple of Yáo.
The Lěi River flows east past the north of Gāoyì Pavilion,
then east past the north of Sāntái,
and further east past the north of Wúxiāng City.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
In the Yān dialect, "máo" is pronounced as "wú,"
and it is now renamed Yíxiāng.
The Lěi River flows further east,
and the Wēnquán Stream joins it.
This stream originates from a hot spring at the foot of Qiáo Mountain.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Forty lǐ southeast of Xiàluò City is Qiáo Mountain,
at the foot of which is a hot spring,
above which stands a sacrificial hall,
with carved eaves and splendid architecture.
Overlooking the bank,
a stone pool gushes with spring water,
flowing abundantly below.
Through the alternation of heat and cold,
the water remains scalding,
unchanged, and can cure all ailments,
attracting a constant stream of visitors.
The pool water flows north,
into the Lěi River.
The Lěi River flows further east,
and on the left meets the mouth of the Yúyán River.
This river originates from a small hill west of Chángchuān City, outside the frontier, in Róuxuán Garrison.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
Liángqú Mountain,
devoid of vegetation,
rich in gold and jade,
is the source of the Xiū River.
It flows southeast past the south of the old city of Qiěrú County.
Yìng Shào said:
Forty lǐ northwest of Dāngchéng is Qiěrú City,
an old county seat.
The name of Dài is not fixed and has changed over time.
Comparing the city walls,
they are far apart.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states:
It was the seat of the Central Commandant.
The Yúyán River originates north of the county, beyond the frontier,
which is the Xiū River.
The Xiū River flows southeast past the north of the old city of Mǎchéng County.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states:
It was the seat of the Eastern Commandant.
The *Shísān Zhōu Zhì* states:
Mǎchéng is two hundred and forty lǐ east of Gāoliǔ.
Locals call this river Hétóu,
as Hétou originates from the Róng region,
a local variation in name.
It then flows east past Língdīng City,
and on the right joins Yánxiāng Stream.
This stream originates from the western mountains of the county,
flows east past the north of the old city of Yánlíng County.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
Northwest of Dāngchéng is Yánlíng Township,
an old county seat.
Locals refer to it as Qíchéng.
It then flows east past Luó Pavilion,
further east past Mǎchéng,
and then east into the Xiū River.
Further southeast, north of Dàníng Commandery,
it joins the Yànmén River on the right.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
The water of Yànmén
originates from Yànmén Mountain.
Wild geese emerge from its gate,
located north of Gāoliǔ.
Gāoliǔ is within Dài,
and the mountain is layered with peaks,
soaring among clouds and mist,
its ranges faintly visible,
extending east beyond the Liáo frontier.
The river flows southeast past the north of the old city of Gāoliǔ County,
the former seat of Dài Commandery.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐ Huáng, the King of Zhào was captured,
and the state was converted into a commandery.
Wáng Mǎng called it Yàndí.
In the nineteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed the Chancellor of Dài, Kǎn, as a marquis here.
Long ago, Qiān Zhāo executed Hán Zhōng at this place.
The city is sixty or seventy lǐ southeast of Píngchéng,
which is northwest within Dài.
The Yànmén River flows further southeast,
bends past an old city,
backed by mountains and facing a marsh,
northern locals call it Chìxiǎn City.
The Yànmén River flows further southeast,
bends northeast,
and accumulates into a deep pool.
The pond is obliquely long rather than square,
extending over twenty lǐ northeast,
and fifteen lǐ wide,
where reeds grow densely.
The Dūn River joins it,
originating from the southern foothills of Shǎoxián Mountain in the northwest,
flowing east past the south of the old city of Cānhé County.
The *Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì* states:
Fifty lǐ north of Dàorén City is Cānhé Township,
It is an old county town.
Dūn Shuǐ flows eastward again,
where Yù Shuǐ flows into it.
The water emerges from below the eastern hill,
flows northwest past the north of the old city,
commonly called Hédūi Chéng,
then northward joins Dūn Shuǐ,
and the combined flow runs northeast into Yànmén Shuǐ.
Therefore, the Shānhǎijīng states:
From Shàoxián Mountain,
Dūn Shuǐ emerges,
flowing eastward into the waters of Yànmén.
Guō Jǐngchún says:
The water emerges from Yànmén Mountain,
referring to this water.
Yànmén Shuǐ flows northeast again into Yángmén Mountain,
where it is called Yángmén Shuǐ,
and joins Shénquán Shuǐ.
The water emerges north of Wěibì,
and there is a spirit in the water.
When dense clouds gather but no rain falls,
and the drought persists beyond its season,
many come here to pray and make requests.
The water has two streams,
which people call Bǐlián Quán.
One stream flows northeast past the east of an old city,
which people call Shíhǔ Chéng,
and then flows northeast into Yángmén Shuǐ.
It flows east again past the north of Sānhuì Tíng,
then east past the north of Xīsìdào Chéng,
and further east,
where Tuōtái Gǔ Shuǐ flows into it.
This water receives Shénquán north of Wěibì,
flows east past the south of Yángmén Mountain through Tuōtái Gǔ,
and is called Tuōtái Shuǐ.
Drawing from springs and streams,
it flows turbulently eastward,
and travelers must cross it more than ten times.
It flows east past Sānhuì Chéng,
then east past the north of Tuōtái Tíng,
then northeast past the north of Mǎtóu Tíng,
and finally flows northeast into Yànmén Shuǐ.
Yànmén Shuǐ flows east again past Dàníng Jùn,
established during the Tàihé era of the Northern Wèi.
Xiū Shuǐ flows into it,
which is the Xiū Shuǐ mentioned in the Shānhǎijīng as flowing east into Yànmén Shuǐ.
The Dìlǐzhì mentions Yúyán Shuǐ but not the names Yànmén and Xiū Shuǐ.
The Shānhǎijīng mentions Yànmén,
but does not discuss Yúyán Hé.
From here downward, it is also commonly called Yúyán Shuǐ.
There are mulberry groves along the water,
so people of the time also called this water Cóngsāng Hé.
This is because the northern lands lack mulberries,
and upon reaching this place and seeing them,
they named it accordingly.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows east again past the south of Gāng Chéng.
According to the Shǐjì, Cài Zé,
a man of Yān,
retired from the chancellorship due to illness,
and was enfeoffed by Qín as Lord Gāngchéng.
It is suspected that this was his fiefdom.
It is commonly called Wǔgāng Chéng.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows east again,
where it joins Níngchuān Shuǐ on the left.
The water emerges from the northwest,
flows southeast past the west of the old city of Xiǎoníng Xiàn,
and then flows southeast into Yúyán Shuǐ.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows east again,
passing the south of the old city of Xiǎoníng Xiàn.
The Dìlǐzhì calls it Níng Xiàn.
It was the seat of the Western Commandant.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Bókāng.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Twenty lǐ west of Dàníng Chéng is Xiǎoníng Chéng.
In the past, a local named Bān Qiū Zhòng lived by the water,
selling medicine in Níng for over a hundred years.
People thought he was long-lived,
but later, an earthquake destroyed his house,
and Zhòng, along with dozens of households in the village, died.
The people took Zhòng's corpse and threw it into Yúyán Shuǐ,
then took his medicine and sold it.
Zhòng, wearing his fur coat, followed and questioned them.
The person was terrified,
kowtowed and begged for mercy.
Zhòng said:
"I do not resent you,
I only wanted people to know of me."
"Go now."
Later, when a courier from the King of Fúyú came to Níng,
the locals called him a banished immortal.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows east again,
where Hēichéng Chuān Shuǐ flows into it.
The water has three sources,
emerging northwest of Hēitǔ Chéng.
The extraordinary sources merge and flow together,
forming a single stream.
It flows southeast past the west of Hēitǔ Chéng,
then southeast past the west of Dàníng Xiàn and south into Yán Hé.
Yán Hé flows east past the south of the old city of Dàníng Xiàn.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
It is Guǎngníng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Guǎngkāng.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
One hundred and thirty lǐ northwest of Xiàluò Chéng is Dàníng Chéng.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows southeast again past the north of the old city of Rú Xiàn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Gǔwǔ,
but it is commonly called Rúkǒu Chéng.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
The city is ten lǐ west of Míngjī Mountain,
with a main road to the south,
and reaching Níngchuān to the west.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows southeast again past the west of Míngjī Mountain.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Thirty lǐ northeast of Xiàluò Chéng, Yán Hé flows eastward,
with Míngjī Mountain to the north.
The Shǐjì states:
Zhào Xiāngzǐ killed the King of Dài at Xiàwū and annexed his territory.
Xiāngzǐ went to Dài to fetch his elder sister.
His elder sister
was the wife of the King of Dài.
Upon reaching this place, she said:
"Dài has perished.
Where shall I return to?"
She then sharpened her hairpin on the mountain and committed suicide.
The people of Dài pitied her,
and built a shrine for her,
naming the mountain Mójī Mountain.
Every night, wild chickens
crowed in flocks on the roof of the shrine,
so it is also called Míngjī Mountain.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Twenty-five lǐ southeast of Dài Chéng is Mǎtóu Mountain,
with stalactite caves on its side.
After Zhào Xiāngzǐ murdered the King of Dài,
he fetched his elder sister.
His elder sister, the wife of the King of Dài,
said:
"To favor my brother over my husband is not benevolent;
to resent my brother for my husband is not righteous."
She sharpened her hairpin and stabbed herself to death.
The envoy also committed suicide.
The people pitied them,
and built a divine shrine on the mountainside,
naming it Mójī Mountain.
It is unclear which account is correct.
Yúyán Shuǐ flows south again past the south of the old city of Qiějū Xiàn.
Wáng Mǎng called it Jiǔjū.
The water flows southeast,
and empties into Lěi Shuǐ.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
Yúyán Shuǐ flows east to Guǎngníng and enters Gū.
This is incorrect.
It flows east again past the north of Zhuōlù Xiàn.
The Zhuō River originates from Zhuōlù Mountain,
commonly known as Zhānggōng Spring.
It flows northeast past the old city of Zhuōlù County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Bùlù.
Huángdì fought Chīyóu on the plains of Zhuōlù,
and settled his people in the foothills of Zhuōlù,
which is precisely this place.
The river then flows northeast and joins with Bǎnquán,
whose water originates from the eastern spring of the county.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Sixty lǐ southeast of Xiàluò City lies Zhuōlù City,
and one lǐ east of the city is Bǎnquán,
above which stands a temple to Huángdì.
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìlǐ Jì states:
Bǎnquán is also a place name.
The spring water flows northeast and converges with Chīyóu Spring,
which emerges from Chīyóu City,
a city lacking an eastern wall.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì records,
six lǐ southeast of Zhuōlù City lies Chīyóu City,
where the spring water is deep and stagnant,
flowing only during heavy rains,
merging chaotically with Bǎnquán,
and entering the Zhuō River to the northeast.
The Zhuō River then flows east past the southern part of Píngyuán Commandery,
where Wèi relocated people from Píngyuán and established this area,
thus creating an immigrant commandery
to govern the displaced population.
The Zhuō River continues northeast past the north of Zuò Pavilion,
and then flows northeast into the Lěi River.
It is also said that a branch of the Zhuō River flows into Xiōngnú territory,
where it is called Zhuōxié River.
The geography is obscure and unclear,
difficult to fully ascertain,
and not within our knowledge.
The Lěi River flows further southeast,
where it converges on the left with Qīngyí River,
also known as Cāng River.
This river originates south of Cháng Pavilion,
flows west past the old city of Běichéng Village to the north,
then turns northwest,
where Píngxiāngchuān River joins it,
emerging west of Píngxiāng Pavilion,
and flowing northwest into Qīngyí River.
Qīngyí River then flows northwest past Yīnmò Pavilion,
located ten lǐ south of Jūyōng County.
Qīngyí River then flows west and converges with Mùniúshān River.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Eighty lǐ east of Jǔyáng City lies Mùniú Mountain,
below which are ninety-nine springs,
which are the upper source of Cāng River.
The mountain is thirty lǐ northeast of the county,
and atop it is a temple to Dàowǔ Huángdì.
Elders say
that at the foot of the mountain, a hundred springs also compete to emerge,
and a divine ox with a dappled body
descended from the mountain,
drank from the springs until they dried up,
hence the mountain's name.
Today, ninety-nine springs are channeled from the foot of the mountain,
accumulating to form a river,
which flows southwest,
where Gǔ River and Fútúgōu River join it.
These rivers emerge southwest of the old city of Yíyú County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Shuòdiào Pavilion.
Their waters flow southwest together,
and enter Cāng River.
Cāng River then flows southwest,
converging on the right with Dìliègōu,
which elders say
formed during a land fissure in the Jìn dynasty,
creating a gully in this boundary area.
A small stream,
commonly called Boundary Water,
flows south into Cāng River.
Cāng River then flows west past the old city of Jūyōng County,
the seat of Wèi's Shànggǔ Commandery.
Long ago, Liú Yú attacked Gōngsūn Zàn but failed,
retreated north to defend this city,
and was captured by Zàn.
Sù River joins here,
emerging west of the lower city of the county,
winding past the south of the county,
and flowing south into Cāng River.
Cāng River then flows west,
converging on the right with Yánggōu River,
which emerges northeast of the county,
flows southwest past the old city of Jūyōng County to the north,
then west past the south of Dàhé and Xiǎohé Mountains,
where towering peaks pierce the clouds,
layered ridges cut through the mist,
twin summits stand in shared elegance,
competing to rise above the surrounding peaks.
A local man named Wáng Cìzhòng,
showed extraordinary ambition from a young age,
and upon reaching adulthood,
transformed the ancient script of Cāngjié into the modern clerical script.
During Qín Shǐhuáng's reign, official affairs were burdensome,
and many found the script simplified by Cìzhòng convenient,
so the emperor, intrigued by its utility, summoned him,
but despite three summons, he never appeared.
Cìzhòng upheld truth and embraced the Way,
mastering the beauty of numerology.
The emperor, angered by his disrespect,
ordered him transported in a cage cart.
As Cìzhòng set out on the journey,
he transformed into a great bird,
emerged from the cart,
and flew away,
shedding two feathers on these mountains,
hence the peaks are named Dàhé and Xiǎohé.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Sixty lǐ northeast of Jǔyáng City lie Dàhé and Xiǎohé Mountains,
where the mountain deity is named Dàhé Shén,
and east of the mountain lodge is the mouth of Wēntāng Spring.
The mountain is twenty lǐ northwest of the county,
its peaks spanning forty lǐ,
and the temple atop it is Cìzhòng's temple.
To the right emerges Wēntāng Spring,
which cures myriad ailments.
The foothills from which the spring emerges
are commonly called Tǔtíng Mountain.
This water is far hotter than other hot springs,
capable of scalding human skin upon contact.
Those seeking treatment must carefully regulate its use,
and cannot speak of it lightly.
East of Dàhé Mountain,
the water flows southeast,
converging on the left with Yánggōu River,
and chaotically flows south into Cāng River.
Cāng River then receives the mouth of Qīngyí River on the left.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
Mùniú Spring flows west
and converges with Qīngyí River.
From here, the two rivers interchangeably share the name.
Qīngyí River then flows west,
where Língtíng River joins it,
emerging from the marsh west of Mǎlán,
where numerous springs flow into the marsh,
and the marsh water accumulates,
forming streams and channels.
The channel water then converges on the left with Mǎlánxī River,
which originates from Mǎlán City,
a city backed by mountains to the north,
following the contours and streams,
where the inhabitants rely solely
on this water for their needs.
It flows south out of the city,
and enters the marsh water to the southeast.
The marsh water then flows south past the north of Líng Pavilion,
bends past the east of Líng Pavilion,
where Cìzhòng's bird feathers fell.
Hence, this pavilion bears the name Líng Pavilion.
The water then flows south,
and enters Qīngyí River.
Qīngyí River then flows west and converges with Quángōu River,
which originates from the flatlands south of the river plain,
and flows north into Qīngyí River.
Qīngyí River then flows southwest and reaches Huángōng Spring,
named so because Duke Huán of Qí, during his hegemony,
campaigned north against the Shānróng,
passed west of Gūzhú on his western expedition,
bound his horses and suspended his chariots,
ascending the western extreme of Bēi'ěr Mountain,
hence the water bears this name.
The spring emerges east of Jǔyáng County,
and flows northwest into Qīngyí River.
Qīngyí River then flows west past the old city of Jǔyáng County to the north,
the seat of Qín's Shànggǔ Commandery,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shuòdiào Commandery,
and the county Jǔyīn.
Kuò Yīn said:
It is sixty lǐ from Zhuōlù northeast to Shànggǔ City.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states:
North of the city, Qīngyí River flows west.
The river then bends past the west of the city,
flows south, and enters the Lěi River.
The Lěi River reaches Mǎxíng Mountain to the south,
where it is called Luòmǎ Rapids.
It then flows southeast out of the mountains,
and the Lěi River flows south out of the mountains,
where waterfalls form flying bridges,
and suspended rivers pour into ravines,
with torrents cascading over ten zhàng,
called Luòmǎ Rapids,
comparable to Ménɡmén's currents.
The Lěi River emerges from the mountains to the south,
where it is called Qīngquán River,
commonly also known as Qiān River,
though this is incorrect.
The Lěi River then flows southeast past the northern boundary of Liángxiāng County,
passes south of Liáng Mountain,
where Gāoliáng River originates.
It passes north of Guǎngyáng Jì County.
The Lěi River flows east again, passing north of the old city of Guǎngyáng County.
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Han states:
Emperor Shìzǔ went out from Jì with Yáo Qī and arrived at Guǎngyáng,
intending to travel south.
This is that city,
called Lesser Guǎngyáng.
The Lěi River flows northeast again, passing south of the old city of Jì County.
The Record of the Land of Wèi states:
Seven lǐ south of Jì City is the Qīngquán River, but it does not pass north of it.
This is likely an erroneous annotation in the Classic.
In the past, King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of Yáo at Jì.
Today, in the northwestern corner within the city walls, there is Jì Hill,
and the settlement was named after the hill.
This is similar to Qūfù in Lǔ and Yíngqiū in Qí.
King Wǔ enfeoffed Shào Gōng in this former state.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐhuáng, Yān was destroyed,
and it was made into Guǎngyáng Commandery.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Lú Wǎn as the King of Yān here,
and its name was changed to the State of Yān.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Guǎngyǒu,
and the county was called Dàiróng.
Within the city were the Wànzǎi Palace and the Guāngmíng Hall.
Below the Eastern Side Gate,
was the former site where Mùróng Jùn erected a bronze horse statue.
In the past, Mùróng Huī had a fine steed,
reddish-white with extraordinary features,
whose exceptional strength lasted until Jùn's time.
In the first year of the Guāngshòu era,
it was forty-nine years old,
yet its vigor and fleetness were undiminished.
Jùn considered it remarkable,
comparing it to Bào's piebald horse.
He ordered bronze to be cast to depict its likeness,
personally composing an inscription in praise,
which was engraved beside it.
Once the statue was completed, the horse died.
Inside the eastern gate of the great city, on the left side of the road,
stands the stele of Liú Jìng, General Who Pacifies the North of Wèi, Marquis of Jiànchéngxiāng with the posthumous title Jǐng.
Wáng Mì, Colonel Director of Retainers of Jìn, petitioned regarding Jìng,
stating that his merits benefited the people,
and he deserved to be included in the sacrificial rites.
Therefore, on the twentieth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of Yuánkāng, a stone was engraved and a stele erected,
to extol his name for later generations.
The Lěi River flows east again and joins the Xiǎnmǎgōu Stream.
This stream receives water from the Jì River above,
flowing west into the Great Lake.
The lake has two sources;
the water flows from level ground northwest of the county.
The sources converge and form the West Lake.
The lake is two lǐ east-west,
and three lǐ north-south.
It was likely the former pond of Yān.
Its green waters are clear and placid;
viewing from the riverbank pavilion, one can see far,
making it also a fine spot for sightseeing and excursions.
The lake water flows east to become the Xiǎnmǎgōu Stream,
which flows east past the south side of the city's southern gate.
This is the place where Yáo Qī once brandished his halberd.
This water then flows east into the Lěi River.
The Lěi River flows east again, passing south of the tomb of the King of Yān.
The tomb has a hidden passageway,
leading northwest out to Jì City.
During the Jǐngmíng era, when building a pagoda and erecting a finial,
they dug deep into a spring and discovered this passage.
It was forbidden by the princely residence,
so no one has explored it.
It leads to a large tomb northwest of the city,
and here are two burial mounds.
Their foundations are solid as磐石,
still tall and imposing,
but ultimately it is unknown which king's tomb it is.
The Lěi River flows southeast again,
where the waters of the Gāoliáng River flow into it.
This water issues from level ground northwest of Jì City.
The spring stream flows east,
passing north of the tomb of the King of Yān,
then east past north of Jì City,
then southeast.
The Record of the Land of Wèi states:
Ten lǐ east of Jì are the waters of the Gāoliáng River.
This water then flows southeast into the Lěi River.
It then flows east to the west of Yōngnú County, Yúyáng Commandery,
and enters the Sì Ditch.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Kòu Xún, Governor of Yǐngchuān, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yōngnú.
Wèi sent Zhāng Hé and Yuè Jìn to besiege Yōngnú,
which is this city.
The Sì Ditch
is another name for the Lù River.
The Record of the Land of Wèi states:
The Qīngquán River receives water from the Sānggān River above,
flows east, and joins the Lù River.
The Lěi River enters Yúyáng from the east,
where it branches out in various places.
Hence the common saying:
"The Gāoliáng has no upper source,
the Qīngquán has no lower end."
This is because the Gāoliáng is a mere trickle, shallow and scant,
barely enough to form a crossing,
relying on tiny streams
to become a river channel.
The Qīngquán, upon reaching Lù,
branches out in various places,
becoming even more minute waterways,
scattered and difficult to trace.
14 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Fourteen
14.1 The Shīyú River
14.1 The Shīyú River
The Shīyú River issues east of the Jūyōng Pass in Shànggǔ Commandery.
The pass is located sixty lǐ southeast of Jǔyáng City, within the boundaries of Jūyōng,
hence the name of the old pass.
When the envoy of Gēngshǐ entered Shànggǔ,
Gěng Kuàng welcomed him at the Jūyōng Pass,
which is this pass.
The river originates from Guān Mountain,
flows south past the old pass below.
On the eastern bank of the stream is a three-story stone chamber;
its doors, windows, leaves, and panels
are all made of stone,
likely the watchtower of the old pass.
To the south is a deep ravine.
Stones were piled to form the pass walls,
with high ramparts and steep cliffs,
not a feat easily accomplished.
The mountain peaks are layered and deep;
the side paths are narrow and confined.
The forest barriers are profound and perilous;
the road is barely wide enough for a cart.
Birds at dawn and beasts at dusk
cry coldly in harmony.
Traveling officials and wandering sons,
those who hear it are all moved to sorrowful longing.
The water passes through the mountains southward, traversing the boundaries of Jūndū County,
and is also called the Jūndū Pass.
The Continued Book of Hàn states:
The Imperial Secretary Lú Zhí secluded himself at Mount Jūndū in Shànggǔ, which is this place.
The water flows south out of the pass,
called the Lower Mouth.
The water flow submerges and runs hidden for over ten lǐ.
It flows east past south of Jūndū County,
then flows east past north of Jì County.
The old course of the Shīyú River flows east past the old city of Jūndū County,
then east again,
where a second source emerges hidden,
accumulating to form a deep pool,
called the Shīyú Pool.
It flows east again,
where the Yìjīng River flows into it.
This water originates from the Qiānliǎo Spring in the northwest,
also called the Dīngliǎo River.
It flows southeast past west of Mount Yù,
and is called the Yìjīng River.
When Gōngsūn Zàn was defeated at Bàoqiū,
he fled to defend Yìjīng,
likely using this river as a defensive barrier.
The Yìjīng River flows east again,
joining the Hǔyǎn Spring water on the left.
It issues from the level plain,
flowing southeast into the Yìjīng River.
It then flows southeast and joins the water of Gū Mountain.
This water issues from the left side of the plain,
originating from Gū Mountain,
flowing southeast into the Yìjīng River,
and is called the Tǎjiè River.
It then flows east past Jì City,
then east past the old city of Chāngpíng County,
and is also called the Chāngpíng River.
The Record of the Land of Wèi states:
One hundred and forty lǐ northeast of Jì City is Chāngpíng City.
West of the city is the Chāngpíng River.
It then flows east into the Shīyú River.
The Shīyú River flows southeast again,
joining the Qínchéng River on the left.
This water issues from the northern mountains,
flows south past Qín City,
then southeast into the Shīyú River.
The Shīyú River flows southeast again, passing west of the old city of Ānlè.
Gēngshǐ sent the Court Gentleman Hán Hóng north to proclaim imperial authority,
who appointed Wú Hàn as Magistrate of Ānlè,
which is this city.
It then turns north, then southeast, reaching west of Húnú County,
and enters the Gū River.
In the past, Péng Chǒng sent Wáng Liáng, Magistrate of Húnú, south to aid Emperor Guāngwǔ,
who raised troops from this county.
The Shīyú River enters the Gū River from the southwest of the county, flowing east.
Therefore, the Treatise on Geography states:
The Shīyú River flows from Jūndū County east to south of Lù and enters the Gū River. This is correct.
14.2 The Gū River
14.2 The Gū River
The Gū River comes from beyond the frontier.
The Gū River originates from beneath the Dānhuā Ridge, ninety li northwest of the Yùyí Garrison.
It flows southeast,
where the Dàgǔ Water joins it.
This water issues from the Dàgǔ Stream north of the garrison,
flows southwest,
passes north of the Dú Shí,
a solitary rock,
standing alone, not relying on any slope.
Further south,
the Jiǔyuán Water joins it.
This water is guided from the northern plain,
with tributaries joining from left and right,
eight streams merging into one watercourse,
hence the name Jiǔyuán (Nine Sources).
This water flows south,
reaching Dú Shí and joining the Dàgǔ Water.
The Dàgǔ Water then flows south past the west of Dú Shí,
and further south past the west of the Yùyí Garrison wall.
During the Tàihé era of the Wèi,
it was established to defend against the northern Dí.
Further southeast,
the Jiāngǔ Water joins it.
This water originates from the Jiān Stream northeast of the garrison wall,
flows southwest past the east of the garrison wall,
then southwest to join the Dàgǔ Water,
their mingled flow then pours south into the Gū Water.
Further south, it exits a gorge,
with two fortifications flanking the banks.
These are commonly called the Dúgù Mén (Solely Secure Gate),
because, relying on the perilous and secure terrain,
they are easily defensible.
The cliffs rise steeply,
forming a passage like a gate,
hence the name.
The Gū Water flows further south,
joining on the left with the Gānxī Water.
This draws from the northern plain, flows southwest past the east of an old pavilion,
then southwest into the Gū Water.
The Gū Water then flows southwest past the east of Chìchéng.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Zhào,
the provincial governor Wáng Bà was defeated by Yān,
and retreated to defend this city.
The city is on a hill,
overlooking a deep moat below.
The name of the stream,
by association, changed its designation,
so the river gained the name Chìchéng.
The Gū Water flows southeast and joins with the Quègǔ Water.
This water has two sources.
The southern one is the Yánglè Water,
originating from Qiějū County.
The *Geographical Treatise* says:
The water issues from the county.
It flows southeast past the north of Dàhé Mountain and Xiǎohé Mountain,
passes by the old city wall of Nǚqí County.
The *Geographical Treatise* says:
This was the seat of the Eastern Commandant.
It was called Qí County under Wáng Mǎng,
commonly known as Héngshuǐ,
also called Yángtián River.
Further southeast it passes an old pavilion,
then east,
joining on the left with the Hòulǔ Water.
This water issues from the northwestern mountains,
flows southeast past the north of Hòulǔ Fortress,
which is two hundred li northwest of Jūyōng County,
hence the name Hòulǔ.
During the Tàihé era,
it was renamed Yùyí Garrison.
It then flows southeast into the Yánglè Water.
The Yánglè Water flows southeast along the south of Láng Mountain.
The mountain's rocks are strikingly white,
standing tall and isolated,
surpassing all surrounding peaks.
Further southeast it passes east of a hot spring,
the spring lies within a mountain bend.
It then passes west of Chìchéng,
bends around the south of the city,
and flows southeast into the Chìchéng River.
The river water flows further southeast,
joining on the right with the Gāofēng Water.
This water issues southeast of the Gāofēng Outpost,
the outpost is on the mountain.
The water flows southwest,
then bends southeast,
entering the Gū Water.
The Gū Water flows southwest out of the mountains,
passes west of the old city wall of Yúyáng County,
and south joins the Qīdù Water.
This water issues from the Huángbān Valley in the northern mountains,
hence also called Huángbān Water.
It flows southeast into the Gū Water.
The Gū Water flows further south,
where the Yú Water joins it.
This water issues from a平地泉流 (flatland spring stream) southeast of the county,
flows west past the south of the old Yúyáng County wall.
Yìng Shào said:
It is north of the Yú Water.
Examining various geographical accounts,
none mention this,
but tracing the watercourse and seeking the river,
there is basis for it.
Now the city lies north of this water,
matching the explanation,
so the name Yúyáng likely belongs here.
The Qín conscripted the left-behind commoners to garrison Yúyáng.
This was the city.
The Yú Water flows southwest into the Gū Water.
The Gū Water flows south and joins with the water from Luó Mountain.
This water issues from a small hill south of the Yúyáng city wall.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* says:
Five li south of the city is Luó Mountain.
Its water flows southwest into the Gū Water.
The Gū Water flows south past the east of the old city wall of Ānlè County.
The *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* says:
The Jìn enfeoffed Liú Shàn as a duke here.
It is commonly called the Western Lù Water.
It passes north of Húnú County, Yúyáng,
joins southwest with the Shīyú Water,
forming the Lù River.
The Gū Water flows southwest past the west of Húnú Mountain,
then south past the west of the old Húnú County wall.
The Yúyáng Grand Administrator Zhāng Kān,
opened paddy fields in the county,
taught the people planting and cultivation,
and the common people became prosperous.
A children's ditty sang:
Mulberry trees without side branches,
Wheat sprouts with double heads,
Lord Zhāng governs,
Joy knows no bounds.
He served for eight years,
and the Xiōngnú dared not invade the frontier.
The Gū Water flows further south,
where the Yángchónggōu Water joins it.
This water issues from Húnú Mountain,
turns south, passes west of Húnú City,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jǔfú.
It flows along the south side of the city,
joining the Gū Water on the right.
The Gū Water flows further south,
where the Shīyú Water joins it.
The Gū Water flows further south,
joining on the left with the Bàoqiū Water,
commonly called the Eastern Lù.
The Gū Water flows south past Lù County, becoming the Lù River.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* says:
Thirty li west of the city is the Lù River.
Further southeast it reaches west of Yōngnú County,
becoming the Sìgōu.
The Lěi Water enters here,
commonly called the Hé Kǒu (Confluence).
Further east,
the Bàoqiū Water emerges east from the northwest of the county.
Further southeast it reaches Quánzhōu County,
joins with the Qīng River,
and flows east into the sea.
The Qīng River
is the tail of the distributary river.
The Gū River flows southeast past the east of the old Quánzhōu County wall,
which Wáng Mǎng called Quándiào.
The Gū Water flows southeast and joins the Qīng River,
now dry.
The Qīng, Qí, Zhāng, Huán, Kòu, Yì, Lái, Rú, Gū, and Hūtuó
all return to the sea.
Therefore, the *Classic* says it is the tail of the distributary river.
14.3 Bàoqiū Water
14.3 Bàoqiū Water
The Bàoqiū Water comes from beyond the frontier,
passes east of Yúyáng County to the south,
The Bàoqiū River originates from within the northern frontier of Yùyí,
flowing south past the east of Jiǔzhuāng Ridge,
commonly known as the Dàyú River.
Further south, it passes ninety lǐ southeast of Zhèn and west of Xī Mìyún Garrison,
then continues south,
where it joins on the left with Dàorén Creek,
which originates from Běichuān,
flows south past the west of Kǒng Mountain,
then passes east of Mìyún Garrison,
joining on the left with Mèngguǎng Ridge Water,
which emerges from beneath the ridge.
The ridge is extremely steep and layered,
towering majestically above all other mountains.
This water flows west past the south of Kǒng Mountain,
atop which is a bright, open cavern,
hence the local custom of calling it the Kǒng Mountain flow.
The ridge water then flows southwest to the east of Mìyún Garrison,
turning west to join Dàorén Creek,
and the mingled streams flow southwest past the south of Mìyún Garrison’s city wall,
where they meet on the right with the Dàyú River.
There is an old Dōng Mìyún city, hence this one is called Xī.
The Dàyú River then flows southeast,
joined by Báiyáng Spring Water,
which emerges from Báiyáng Creek in Wànglí to the north,
and enters on the right into the Dàyú River.
Further southeast,
Lóngchú Creek Water enters from the north into the Dàyú River, which then flows southeast out of the gorge,
passing south of the old Huáyán County of Ānzhōu’s former Yùyáng Commandery,
joining on the left with the county’s Northern Creek Water,
which originates from the south of the broad, long moat north of the county.
During the Tàihé era,
this moat was dug to defend against the northern Dí tribes.
This water flows south past the east of the old city of Huáyán County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Kuāngdé,
and Hàn Míngdì changed to Yántián.
The Right Assistant Administrator governed here,
and it was commonly called Húyán City.
Two hundred lǐ northwest of Yùyí Garrison,
it flows south into the Bàoqiū River,
which then flows south past the east of the old city of Sīxī County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Dūndé.
The Bàoqiū River then flows southwest past the east of the old city of Guǎngpíng County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Píngguǎng.
Further south, it joins with Sānchéng Water,
which originates from Jiùlǐ Mountain,
flows west past Sānchéng,
hence called Sānchéng Water.
It then passes by Xiāngxíng Mountain,
where fragrant gǎoběn plants grow all over the mountain,
hence the name.
Further west, it passes south of a stone cavern,
which is spacious inside,
providing shelter for travelers;
inside the cavern is water,
deep and still,
which those dwelling nearby draw from.
Further northwest, it passes south of Fúlíng Mountain and joins with Shímén Water,
which originates from Fúlíng Mountain.
The mountain is lofty and steep,
with cold, deep cliffs and barriers,
where snow accumulates on the shaded slopes,
and ice congeals even in summer,
reminiscent of the “é’é” (towering) ode in the “Lísāo,”
hence people named the mountain accordingly.
One stream flows southwest into it,
this water bearing the name Sāng Valley,
likely because it flows along Sāng Creek.
Further southwest, it passes southeast of Guǎngpíng City,
then enters on the right into the Bàoqiū River.
The Bàoqiū River then flows southeast past the south of the old city of Yúyáng County,
the seat of Yùyáng Commandery.
Established in the 22nd year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Tōnglù,
and the county Déyú.
The Bàoqiū River then flows southwest,
where after Gōngsūn Zàn had killed Liú Yú,
the Wūwán, remembering the virtue of the Liú clan,
welcomed his son Hé,
gathered a host of one hundred thousand,
and defeated Zàn upon this river.
Ten thousand heads were taken.
The Bàoqiū River then flows southwest past the east of Húnú City,
then flows southwest into the Gū River,
mingling and flowing south.
Further south, it passes west of Lù County.
The Bàoqiū River flows into the Lù River,
thus gaining the name Lù River.
The Gāoliáng River flows into it,
its headwaters receiving water from the Lěi River at the Lìlíng Weir.
North of the river is Liáng Mountain,
where the tomb of Yānlà King Liú Dàn is located,
hence the weir is named Lìlíng.
The water branches off from the weir,
flows east past the southern side of Liáng Mountain,
then northeast past the northern side of Liú Jìng’s stele.
The inscription reads:

“Liú Jìng, Marquis of Jiànchéngxiāng of the Pèi State, General of the Northern Expedition, Commissioner with Imperial Authority, and Commander of Military Affairs in the Héběi Circuit of the Wèi Dynasty,
styled Wéngōng, ascended Liáng Mountain to observe the source and flow,
surveyed the Lěi River to assess the terrain,
admired the canal-building achievements of Wǔ’ān,
and envied the prosperity of the Qín people.
He then ordered his subordinate Dīng Hóng,
to oversee a thousand soldiers,
and in the second year of the Jiāpíng era,
built a dam on the river,
channeled the Gāoliáng River,
constructed the Lìlíng Dam,
and opened the Chēxiāng Canal.
The dam’s inscription states:
‘The Gāoliáng River
originates from Bīngzhōu,
a tributary of the Lù River.
A long, sturdy embankment
was built straight across the midstream,
using stone-filled baskets as the main dam,
standing ten feet high,
thirty zhang long from east to west,
and over seventy paces wide from north to south.
A sluice gate was built on the northern bank,
four zhang wide,
with a water depth of ten zhang.
When mountain floods erupt,
the water flows eastward over the dam;
under normal flow conditions,
it enters from the northern gate,
irrigating two thousand qǐng of farmland annually.
In total, the enclosed land
amounts to over a million mǔ.’
In the third year of the Jǐngyuán era, the xīnyǒu year,
an imperial edict noted the increasing demand for food
and the insufficiency of dryland farming,
so the court sent the courtier Fán Chén to renovate the sluice gate,
limiting the farmland to a thousand qǐng,
demarcating four thousand three hundred and sixteen qǐng,
distributing it to commanderies and counties,
and readjusting the total farmland to five thousand nine hundred and thirty qǐng.
The water flows along the Chēxiāng Canal,
from the northwest of Jì County past Chāngpíng,
extending eastward to Lù County in Yúyáng,
irrigating an area
spanning four to five hundred lǐ,
with over ten thousand qǐng of farmland watered.
High and low lands were leveled,
plains and marshes were smoothed,
irrigation channels were opened for watering,
and drainage ditches were dug for dispersion.
The canal mouth was directed to serve as a floodgate,
and the overflowing water was channeled into ponds as a beneficial resource,
bringing benefits at the time,
and extending its legacy to later generations.
In the fourth year of the Yuánkāng era of the Jìn Dynasty,
Liú Hóng, the youngest son of the lord, General of the Xiāoqí Cavalry and Marquis of Píngxiāng,
was appointed Commissioner with Imperial Authority to oversee military affairs in Yōuzhōu,
concurrently serving as Colonel Protecting the Wūhuán and General Níngshuò.
The dam had stood for thirty-six years
when, in the summer of the fifth year, in the sixth month,
a great flood erupted,
destroying three-quarters of it,
leaving only over seventy zhang of the northern bank.
The upper canal, Chēxiāng,
overflowed everywhere.
Reflecting on the merits of the earlier dam construction,
he personally surveyed the mountains and rivers,
gave instructions on the plan,
and ordered Sima Guānnèihóu Péng Yùn,
along with over two thousand soldiers both inside and outside,
to rebuild the long embankment,
construct a stone canal,
repair the main dam,
and restore the sluice gate,
which was four zhang wide,
with a water depth of five feet.
The restoration revived the benefits of regulating water flow,
following the old system,
with over forty thousand laborers employed in total.
Various tribal kings and nobles
came without being summoned,
carrying their children on their backs to participate,
numbering in the thousands.
As the Book of Songs says, ‘Begin the work without haste,’
and the Book of Changes states, ‘The people forget their toil,’
which aptly describes this.
Then, the civil and military officials of the two offices,
moved by the achievements of the Qín state’s Zhèng Guó Canal,
and the Wèi people’s reverence for Bào Sì,
admired benevolent governance from afar,
and recorded these accomplishments.
On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the fifth year of Yuánkāng,
a stone was erected with an inscription,
to commemorate these great deeds,
and record the dam’s construction,
serving as a model for future generations.
These events are recorded in the stele’s inscription.
The river then flows southeast,
passes north of Jì County,
continues east to Lù County,
and empties into the Bàoqiū River.
It then flows south past the west of the old city of Lù County,
which was called Tōnglùtíng during Wáng Mǎng’s reign.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn sent Wú Hàn and Gěng Yǎn to defeat the Tóngmǎ and Wǔfān rebels east of Lù,
referring to this county.
The river then bends and flows southeast,
passing south of Lù City.
Emperor Shìzǔ appointed Péng Chǒng as the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng,
governing here.
Péng Chǒng rebelled,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ sent Guerrilla General Dèng Lóng to attack him,
stationing troops south of this river.
Emperor Guāngwǔ predicted his defeat,
and indeed, Péng Chǒng defeated him,
with remnants of walls and old fortifications still remaining.
The Bàoqiū River then flows southeast into Xiàzé,
a marsh extending over ten lǐ southward in winding islets,
bordered by Qiānzé to the north,
with a vast, boundless view.
It then flows south to the north of Yōngnú County,
bends eastward, and empties into the sea.
The Bàoqiū River flows northwest from the old city of Yōngnú County.
In the past, it branched off from the Sìgōu River, which flowed eastward.
Now the Sìgōu River's course is cut off.
Numerous streams flow eastward,
merging into a single watercourse.
It passes east of the county's north side,
then further east joins the Jū River.
The Jū River originates from Báiyáng Valley on the western mountains of Wúzhōng County in Yòuběipíng.
It flows northwest past Pínggǔ County,
bends and flows southwest,
where the Dúlè River joins it.
The Dúlè River emerges from the south of Bàodúgù to the north,
passes east of the old city of Pínggǔ County,
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era of the Later Hàn (25 AD),
Emperor Guāngwǔ dispatched twelve generals to pursue the Dàqiāng and Wǔfǎn rebels, reaching Pínggǔ,
where they decisively defeated them in this county.
This river flows south into the Jū River.
The Jū River then joins the Pánshān River on its left,
which originates from the mountain.
The mountain is steep and perilous,
rarely trodden by human feet.
From about thirty *lǐ* away,
looking at the water on the mountain,
it appears over twenty *lǐ* high,
with white rapids gleaming brightly.
The cascading waves pass through ravines,
flowing downstream,
turning from the northwest to pour into the Jū River.
The Jū River then flows southeast past the old city of Pínggǔ County,
and southeast meets the Rù River.
The Rù River emerges from the northern mountains,
which lie southeast of the old city of Sīxī County.
It flows southeast past the north of the old Bólù city,
then bends around the east of the city.
It is commonly called Pínglù City,
but this is incorrect.
By imperial edict of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed the Grand Marshal Huò Guāng as a marquis here.
Wén Yǐng said:
"Bólù means 'vast and level land,'
taking its auspicious name without it being a county,
with estates in Běihǎi and Hédōng."
Xuē Zàn said:
"According to records, there is a Bólù City in Yúyáng,
referring to this one."
The city now lies on the southern side of Qiějū Mountain,
situated on level ground,
encircled by flowing streams,
facing and commanding four waterways.
What Wén meant by "without a county designation"
refers to its auspicious and beautiful name.
The Rù River then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Pínggǔ County,
and flows southeast into the Jū River.
The Jū River then flows south past the east of Yǎngchéng,
and south joins the Wǔbǎi Gōu River.
This river emerges north of Qīshān,
flows east past the south of Yǎngchéng in Pínggǔ County,
and enters the Jū River from the east.
The Jū River then flows southeast past the north of Línjū City,
bends and passes east of the city,
then exits along the south side of the city.
The *Bamboo Annals* record:
In the sixteenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng (354 BC),
the Qí army battled the Yān army at the Jū River,
and the Qí army fled.
This is the same river.
The Jū River then flows south into the Bàoqiū River.
The Bàoqiū River then flows east and meets the mouth of the Quánzhōu Canal,
an old channel that once drew water from the Hūtuó River at Quánzhōu County.
Hence it was named after Quánzhōu.
It flows north past the east of Quánzhōu County,
then north past the east of Yōngnú County,
about one hundred twenty *lǐ* west of the old city of Yōngnú.
From the Hūtuó River northward, it enters the lower reaches,
passing through marshes and lakes for one hundred eighty *lǐ*,
then enters the Bàoqiū River,
called the Quánzhōu Estuary.
Chén Shòu's *Records of the Wèi* states:
"When Tàdūn harassed the borders,
Tàizǔ of Cáo (Cáo Cāo) planned to campaign against him,
and had a canal dug from the Jū Estuary passing through Yōngnú and Quánzhōu to connect with the rivers and sea."
It is now dry.
The Bàoqiū River then flows east,
where the Gēng River joins it.
The Gēng River emerges from the northern frontier of Xúwú County in Yòuběipíng,
flows south past Xúwú Mountain, receiving the Hēiniúgǔ River,
then the Shāgǔ River,
both issuing from the western mountains,
flowing east into the Gēng River.
In the past, Tián Zǐtài took refuge here,
and the population grew to five thousand households.
The *Kāishān Tú* says:
"The mountain produces wood that does not turn to ash,
and stones that produce fire."
According to the commentary:
"The wood is black like charcoal but leafless;
there are stones red like cinnabar.
Rubbing two such stones together,
produces fire,
which can ignite the ashless wood,
and last a lifetime."
They are no longer found today.
The river then passes east of the old city of Xúwú County,
which was called Běishùn Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
"One hundred ten *lǐ* northeast of Yòuběipíng City lies Xúwú City."
The river then flows southwest and joins the Zhōulú Xī River,
which emerges from Xúwú Mountain,
flowing southeast into the Gēng River.
The Gēng River then flows southwest,
where the Lěi River joins it.
The Lěi River originates from Jùnmí County in Yòuběipíng,
called Jùnmá under Wáng Mǎng.
It flows southeast,
commonly called the Chēfàn River.
It then flows southeast and joins the hot spring waters,
which emerge from the Wēn Xī (Warm Stream) on the northern mountain,
i.e., the warm source.
Those convalescing cannot bathe in its scalding flow,
because it is excessively hot.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
"East of Xúwú City there are hot springs,"
referring to this.
The water flows south for one hundred paces,
then disappears underground,
flowing openly only when water is abundant.
The Lěi River then flows southeast past Shímén Gorge,
where the mountains are towering and sheer,
with cliffs standing like an open cavern,
commonly called Shíménkǒu (Stone Gate Pass).
In the fourth year of the Zhōngpíng era (187 AD),
Zhāng Chún of Yúyáng rebelled,
killing Liú Zhèng, Governor of Yòuběipíng, and Yáng Hóng, Governor of Liáodōng.
In the fifth year of Zhōngpíng (188 AD),
an imperial edict ordered General Mèng Yì to lead Gōngsūn Zàn against Zhāng Chún.
They battled at Shímén,
where he was decisively defeated.
The Lěi River then flows southeast,
called the Northern Huáng River,
bends and becomes the Southern Huáng River,
then flows southwest past Wúzhōng Mountain,
where Bó Zhònglǐ compounded his divine elixir.
He also produced five thousand catties of gold on this mountain to aid the common people.
The mountain has Yáng Wēngbó's Jade Field.
Northwest of the county is Yáng Gōng's Altar and Shrine,
the former residence of Yáng Gōng.
The *Sōushén Jì* records:
"Yōng Bó,
a man of Luòyáng,
was of utmost sincerity and filial piety.
When his parents passed away,
he buried them at Wúzhōng Mountain.
The mountain is eighty *lǐ* high,
yet had no water on its summit.
Yōng Bó provided drink there.
Someone came to drink,
gave him a peck of stones,
and told him to plant them.
Jade grew in his field.
A Xú family of Běipíng had a daughter,
whom Yōng Bó sought to marry.
They demanded a pair of white jade discs as betrothal gift.
When the matchmaker conveyed the demand,
Bó went to the Jade Field and obtained five pairs.
The Xú family gave him their daughter in marriage,
and he settled his household there."
The *Yángshì Pǔ Xù* states:
"Wēngbó was a grandson of King Jǐng of Zhōu, enfeoffed at Yángfán.
At the end of the Spring and Autumn period,
he moved to Wúzhōng,
and changed his surname from Yángfán to Yáng.
He loved people and bestowed widely.
Heaven blessed him with the Jade Field.
His stele inscription says:
'He resided at Wēngtóng Mountain, sixty *lǐ* north of the county.
Later, he moved to below the western mountain,
and Yáng Gōng relocated there again,
receiving the gift of the Jade Field.
Having no fondness for treasure,
the Jade Field departed on its own.'
It is still called Yùtiányáng (Jade Field Yáng) today.
Gān Bǎo said:
"At the stone-planting site,
four large stone pillars were erected at the corners,
each one *zhàng* high,
marking a central area of one *qǐng*,
named the Jade Field.
This has been passed down to this day.
The name 'Jade Field'
originated from this,
but its location is now unknown,
consistent with the *Pǔ Xù*'s statement that it 'departed on its own.'"
The Lán River joins it,
emerging from the northern mountains,
flowing east, bending south,
passing east of the old city of Wúzhōng County.
The old city
was the state of the Earl of Wúzhōng.
In the fourth year of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ (569 BC),
Jiāfù, Earl of Wúzhōng, sent Mèng Lè to Jìn,
Because Wei Jiàng presented tiger and leopard skins,
and requested peace with the various Rong tribes,
thus it became the land of Yān.
In the twenty-second year of Qín Shǐ Huáng, Yān was destroyed,
and the Right Běipíng Commandery was established,
governing this place,
which is what Wáng Mǎng called Běishùn.
During the Hàn dynasty, Lǐ Guǎng served as the commandery governor,
and once went out and encountered a crouching stone,
thinking it was a tiger,
he shot it, and the arrow sank in up to its feathers,
which was at this very spot.
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
One hundred and thirty lǐ northwest of Right Běipíng City is Wúzhōng City.
This water then flows south into the Lěi Shuǐ,
and the Lěi Shuǐ flows southwest into the Gēng Shuǐ.
The "Geographical Treatise" says:
The Lěi Shuǐ originates south of Jùnmí County,
and flows east to Wúzhōng, where it enters the Gēng Shuǐ.
The Gēng Shuǐ,
is also commonly called the Zhè Shuǐ.
It flows south past the foot of Yānshān,
and on the side of the cliff there is a stone drum,
over a hundred zhàng above the ground,
looking like a granary holding several hundred shí,
with a stone beam piercing through it,
southeast of the drum,
there is a stone drumstick,
shaped as if in the act of striking.
The elders say,
when the stone drum of Yānshān
sounds, then there will be war in the land.
The Gēng Shuǐ then flows south past the west of Běipíng City,
and south into the Bàoqiū Shuǐ,
called the Zhèkǒu.
The Bàoqiū Shuǐ then flows east past the old city of Right Běipíng Commandery,
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" says:
Three hundred lǐ northeast of Jìchéng is Right Běipíng City.
The Bàoqiū Shuǐ then flows east,
and the Jùliáng Shuǐ flows into it,
this water originates from Chéngōng Shān north of Tǔyín County,
flows southwest past Guānjī Shān,
and is called Guānjī Shuǐ.
East of the water is Guānjī Temple,
within the temple a great hall was built,
very tall and spacious,
capable of accommodating a thousand monks,
the lower part is entirely constructed of stone,
with plaster added on top,
the foundation is hollowed out and connected,
with branches and channels spreading out,
outside the rooms beside the foundation,
cooking fires are lit on all sides,
the heat flows inward,
warming the entire hall.
Because this land is bitterly cold,
and the frosty air is severe and fierce,
the monks who have left home,
are mostly poor and thinly clad,
the donors, concerned that their religious practice might be hindered,
therefore built this structure,
so that many who are devoted to the Way take refuge here.
This water then flows southwest,
and on the right joins the Qūluò Shuǐ,
which originates from the mountains north of the county,
flows southeast into the Jùliáng Shuǐ.
The Jùliáng Shuǐ then flows south past the west of the old city of Tǔyín County,
and on the left meets the Hándù Shuǐ,
which originates northeast of the county,
flows southwest to the county,
and on the right empties into the Liáng Hé.
The Liáng Hé then flows south,
and the Jiànyú Shuǐ flows into it,
which originates from the northeast mountains,
flows southwest past the east of the old city of Tǔyín County,
then southwest into the Jùliáng Shuǐ.
The Jùliáng Shuǐ then flows southeast,
and on the right joins the Wǔlǐ Shuǐ,
which originates from Wǔlǐ Shān northeast of Běipíng City,
hence it is commonly called the Wǔlǐ Ditch,
also named Tiánjìquán,
it flows west then bends south,
passes east of Běipíng City,
flows southeast into the Jùliáng Hé,
and chaotically flows into the Bàoqiū Shuǐ.
From here, south of this water,
extending south to the Hūtuó,
west to Quánzhōu and Yōngnú,
and east to the sea,
is called the Yōngnú Marsh.
Within this marshland there are ninety-nine lakes,
with branches and streams dividing,
often interconnected,
not only do the Liáng Hé and Bàoqiū flow into the sea.
14.4 Rú Shuǐ
14.4 Rú Shuǐ
The Rú Shuǐ comes from beyond the frontier,
flows southeast past the north of Liáoxī Língzhī County,
The Rú River originates southeast of Yùyí Fortress,

It then flows northwest past the east of the old Yùyí City,

this water originates east of the old city,

the pond water is deep and does not flow,
this water then bends west and flows north,
then east past the north of the old city,
connecting two marshes,

It then flows northeast and joins the Nán River,
on the right of the Nán River the Wū River enters,
this water originates south of the Eastern Wù,

230 lǐ northeast of the fortress,
it flows northwest into the Nán River,
Rú and Nán are similar in sound,
a distortion in the Dí people's dialect.

flows northeast,

it flows southeast into the Lǚquán River.

then northeast,
the Nìliú River joins it,
this water originates southeast,
guided from a spring it flows west,
bends right and flows northeast to join,
the Mùlínshān River converges with it,
this water originates south of the mountain,
flows east into the Nìliú River,
the mingled streams flow northeast into the Rú River.
The Rú River then flows east,
the Pánquán River enters,
this water flows from northwest to southeast,
joining the Rú River.
The Rú River then flows southeast,
its course winding and bending,
called the Qū River.
300 lǐ northeast of the fortress,
it then flows east out of the gorge into the Ān Prefecture boundary,

The "Geographical Treatise" says:
the Rú River originates in the northern Mán region of the county,

It then flows southeast,

The Yāo River then flows southeast,
passes Báitán County and flows southeast,

The Rú River then flows southeast,

It then flows south,

The Rú River then flows southeast,
the Wǔliè River enters,
its waters from three streams branch and merge,

merging with the Pánquán River.
The spring issues 15 lǐ east of the prefecture,

The Xīzàng River then flows southwest,
the Dōngzàng River joins it,
this water originates from the eastern ravine,

merging with the Zhōngzàng River,
this water is guided from the central ravine,

Therefore the plain is called Sānzàng Plain,
the water Sānzàng River.
The Dōngzàng River then flows south,

the mingled streams on the right converge with the Lóngquán River,
this water originates below the eastern mountain,

its water flows southwest,

The Sānzàng River then flows southeast,
merging with the Lóngchú River,
which originates west from the Lóngchú ravine,
flows east into the Sānzàng River.
It then flows southeast past Wǔliè Ravine,
called the Wǔliè River.
Flowing southeast past below Shítǐng,

a solitary rock rising like a cloud,
perched on a perilous cliff,
perhaps over a hundred rèn high,
when governors passed through,
they ordered selected skilled men,
to draw bows and arrows,
yet none could reach its lofty summit.
Its waters flow east and merge into the Rú.
The Rú River then flows southeast,

originally Sānhuì City.
This water flows south into the Wǔdù Pond,

The Rú River then merges with the Gāoshí River,

east to Qīng Pass.
The peril of Lúlóng,
steep slopes winding and twisting,
thus it has the name Nine Bends.
In the second year of Yuánxǐ of Yān Jǐngzhāo,

burning mountains and cutting stone,
making it passable for square-axled carts,
carved a stone inscription on the ridge,
to record the achievement,
its inscription still exists.
Yet Yǔ Gǎozhī's annotation to the "Yángdū Fù" states,
Lúlóng Mountain is north of Pínggāng City,
which is quite reckless,
far from the facts.
I note that Lúlóng extends east past Qīng Pass,
to Fán City about two hundred lǐ,
from Fán City going northeast,
heading to old Pínggāng City is about 180 lǐ,
toward Huánglóng then five hundred lǐ,
thus Chén Shòu's "Wèi Zhì" records,
Tián Chóu led troops out of Lúlóng Pass,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys,
over five hundred lǐ passing Báitán,
traversing Pínggāng,
ascending Báiláng,
viewing Liǔchéng.
Pínggāng is far northeast of Lúlóng.
Yet Zhòngchū says it is to the south,

The Rú River then flows southeast past the east of old Lúlóng City,

the Rú River then flows southeast,

flowing south into the sea.
The Xīn River continues east,
with a left branch forming the Běiyáng Gū Diàn.
The waters of the diàn cross the Xīn River to the right,
and flow south into the sea.
The Xīn River then flows east to join the Rú.
The Rú River flows southeast to Léi County's Jiéshí Mountain.
Wén Yǐng said:
Jiéshí is in Léi County, Liáoxī,
called Xuǎnwǔ under Wáng Mǎng.
Léi County was incorporated into Línyú,
and Wáng Mǎng changed Línyú to Féngdé.
*The Treatise on Geography* says:
The great Jiéshí Mountain is southwest of Líchéng County in Yòuběipíng,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Jiēshí.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn also once climbed it to gaze upon the great sea,
and had an inscription carved on the stone here.
Now, along the coast, there is a stone like a paved path for several tens of lǐ.
At the mountain's summit is a large stone shaped like a pillar,
often visible,
standing in the midst of the great sea.
When the tide rises high, it is submerged,
and when the tide recedes,
it remains motionless and unsubmerged.
Its depth is unknown,
and it is commonly called the Tiānqiáo Pillar.
It appears man-made,
yet surely was not created by human strength.
Wéi Zhāo also identified this as Jiéshí.
*The Sān Qí Lüè Jì* says:
The First Emperor built a stone bridge in the sea,
and the sea god erected pillars for it.
The First Emperor requested to meet him.
The god said:
"My form is ugly,
do not depict my likeness.
I shall meet with the Emperor."
He then went forty lǐ into the sea,
and saw the sea god.
His attendants were forbidden to move,
but a craftsman secretly sketched the god's form with his foot.
The god angrily said:
"The Emperor has broken the agreement,
leave quickly!"
The First Emperor turned his horse to return.
As his front foot was still planted,
the ground behind him collapsed.
He barely managed to reach the shore.
The one who sketched drowned in the sea,
and the stones from all the mountains poured in.
They still lean perilously eastward today,
likely referring to this.
The Rú River here enters the sea to the south,
and does not pass west of Hǎiyáng County.
This is likely an error in the *Jīng*.
Also, according to the *Guǎnzǐ*,
in the twentieth year of Duke Huán of Qí,
he campaigned against Gūzhú.
When he was ten lǐ from Bēi'ěr Stream,
he suddenly halted,
stared wide-eyed,
took up his bow to shoot,
drew but did not release,
and asked his attendants:
"Do you see something ahead?"
The attendants replied:
"We do not see."
The Duke said:
"I see a figure a foot tall, fully formed,
wearing a hat,
with the right sleeve of its garment pulled back,
running before my horse.
Can there be a person like this?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that the god of Qǐ Mountain has a thief-like spirit,
a foot tall and fully formed.
When a ruler destined for hegemony arises,
then the god of Qǐ Mountain appears.
Moreover, it runs before the horse—
'running'
means guiding;
'pulling back the sleeve'
indicates water ahead;
'pulling back the right sleeve'
indicates crossing from the right side."
When they reached Bēi'ěr Stream,
there was a guide for the water.
Crossing from the left,
the depth reached their hats;
crossing from the right,
the depth reached their knees.
After crossing, they were greatly relieved.
Duke Huán bowed and said:
"Zhòngfù's sagacity reaches such heights!
I have long been deserving of punishment."
Now, proceeding south from Gūzhú,
one reaches the great sea.
And within the vast sea,
many mountains are visible.
However, a stream like the Zàn Stream at Bēi'ěr
is also unknown in location.
In former times, during the Hàn dynasty,
the sea waves swelled,
swallowing vast expanses of land.
It was likely together with Jiéshí
that they were engulfed by the great waves.
14.5 The Great Liáo River
14.5 The Great Liáo River
The Great Liáo River originates from Wèibáipíng Mountain beyond the frontier,
flows southeast into the frontier,
and passes west of Xiāngpíng County in Liáodōng.
The Liáo River is also said to originate from the Dǐshí Mountain.
Flowing eastward from beyond the frontier,
it passes directly west of Wàngpíng County in Liáodōng,
which was called Chángshuō during Wáng Mǎng's time.
It bends and flows southwest, passing west of the old city of Xiāngpíng County.
In the twenty-second year of Qín Shǐhuáng's reign, Yān was conquered and Liáodōng Commandery was established,
with its seat here.
In the eighth year of Hàn Gāodì's reign,
Jì Tōng was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and it was called Chāngpíng during Wáng Mǎng's time.
It was also the seat of the former Píng Province.
Further south, it passes west of the old city of Liáoduì County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shùnmù.
Gōngsūn Yuān sent General Bì Yǎn to resist Sīmǎ Yì at Liáoduì,
which was this very place.
Further southeast, it passes west of Fáng County.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*,
Fáng
was formerly a subordinate county of Liáodōng.
The Liáo River joins the Báiláng River on the right.
The Báiláng River originates southeast of Báiláng County in Yòuběipíng,
flowing north and then bending northwest,
passing south of the old city of Guǎngchéng County,
which was called Pínglǔ during Wáng Mǎng's time,
and is commonly known as Guǎngdū City.
Further northwest,
the Shíchéng Chuān River flows into it.
This river originates from Shíchéng Mountain to the southwest,
flowing east and passing south of the old city of Shíchéng County.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*,
Shíchéng County was in Yòuběipíng.
It bends north, passing west of Báilù Mountain,
which is Báiláng Mountain.
The *Wèishū Guózhì* states:
The Xiōngnú Chányú Tàdùn of Liáoxī was particularly powerful,
and was favored by the Yuán clan,
so Yuán Shàng sought refuge with him.
He repeatedly invaded and caused harm.
The Duke (Cáo Cāo) marched out of Lúlóng,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys for over five hundred *lǐ*,
and when he was still two hundred *lǐ* from Liǔchéng,
Yuán Shàng and Tàdùn led tens of thousands of cavalry to engage him in battle.
The Duke ascended Báiláng Mountain and looked toward Liǔchéng.
Suddenly encountering the enemy,
he took advantage of their disarray,
and unleashed his troops to attack them.
The enemy forces collapsed in great disorder,
Tàdùn was beheaded,
and over two hundred thousand Hú and Hàn people surrendered.
The *Yīngxióng Jì* states:
Cáo Cāo then struck his saddle on horseback, splitting it into ten pieces—
this happened here.
The *Bówùzhì* states:
Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) encountered a lion while on horseback,
and ordered his men to fight it.
Many were injured or killed.
The King then personally led several hundred of his regular strong attendants to attack it.
The lion roared and leaped fiercely,
startling everyone around.
Suddenly, the King saw a creature emerge from the forest, resembling a wildcat.
It leaped onto the yoke of the King's carriage.
As the lion approached,
this creature jumped onto the lion's head,
and the lion immediately crouched down, not daring to rise.
They then killed it,
and returned with the lion.
When they were still forty *lǐ* from Luòyáng,
all the chickens and dogs in Luòyáng fell silent, not crowing or barking.
The river then flows northeast into Guǎngchéng County,
and east into the Báiláng River.
The Báiláng River flows north, passing east of the old city of Báiláng County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Fúdí.
The Báiláng River flows further east,
and the Fāngchéng Chuān River flows into it.
This river originates from a mountain to the southwest,
flowing east and then bending north,
passing west of an old city,
commonly known as Quèmù City.
It bends east, passing north of Fāngchéng,
and flows east into the Báiláng River.
The Báiláng River flows further northeast, passing west of the old city of Chānglí County.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*,
this was Jiāolí,
the seat of the Eastern Commandant,
and was called Qínlǔ during Wáng Mǎng's time.
Yìng Shào said:
This is present-day Chānglí.
The Gāopíng Chuān River flows into it.
This river originates from the Píngchuān to the northwest,
flowing east and passing north of Wōchéng,
likely settled by people from Wō (Japan).
Further southeast, it passes north of Rǔlóu City,
likely passing through a Róng settlement,
a place with mixed barbarian names.
Further southeast, it flows into the Báiláng River.
The Báiláng River flows further northeast,
and the Zìlǔ River flows into it.
This river originates from distant mountains to the northwest,
flowing southeast into the Báiláng River.
The Báiláng River flows further northeast, passing west of Lóng Mountain.
Mùróng Huàng of Yān considered the area north of Liǔchéng and south of Lóng Mountain
a blessed land,
