so he ordered Yáng Yù to build Lóngchéng.
In the twelfth year, he renamed Liǔchéng as Lóngchéng County.
A black dragon and a white dragon appeared on Lóng Mountain.
Huàng personally observed them.
The dragons were two hundred paces away.
He offered two grand sacrificial animals,
and the dragons playfully intertwined their heads and soared,
then shed their horns and departed.
Huàng was delighted,
granted a great amnesty,
named the new palace Hélóng Palace,
and established a Lóngxiáng Shrine on the mountain.
The Báiláng River flows further north, passing east of Huánglóng City.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* states:
The Commandant of the Dependent State of Liáodōng governed Chāngliáo Circuit, where there was a Huánglóng Pavilion.
It was the seat of the Wèi Provincial Governor of Yíng Province.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
Southwest of Huánglóng City is the Báiláng River,
which flows northeast, passing along the northeast side of the city—
this is it.
Further northeast,
the Lànzhēn River originates beyond the northwestern frontier,
flowing southeast through layered mountains,
and southeast into the Báiláng River.
The Báiláng River flows further northeast out,
and its eastern flow divides into two branches.
The right branch
is likely the Yú River.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*,
the Yú River first receives water from the Báiláng River,
flowing southwest along the mountains,
passing west of an old city,
commonly known as Hélián City.
It is likely the old city of Línyú County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Féngdé.
The Yú River flows south, then bends east,
and joins another river,
commonly known as the Bànlún River,
likely a variant barbarian name.
It is likely the Hóu River mentioned in the *Geographical Treatise* as flowing north into the Yú River.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* states:
The Hóu River flows south into the Yú River.
The *Geographical Treatise* likely describes it as flowing from north to south.
Further southwest, it flows into the Yú River.
The Yú River flows further southeast, passing east of an old city,
commonly known as Nǚluó City.
Further south, it passes west of Yíngqiū City.
Although Yíngqiū was in Qí, it was given this name in the Liáo-Yān region,
likely because Yān and Qí were distant,
and this was a place of transplanted divisions.
The river flows southeast into the sea.
According to the *Geographical Treatise*,
the Yú River flows south from beyond the frontier into the sea.
One branch flows northeast out of the frontier as the Báiláng River,
then flows southeast to Fáng County and into the Liáo River.
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states:
The Báiláng River flows down into the Liáo River.
Further east, it passes west of Ānshì County,
and flows south into the sea.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* states:
The Great Liáo River flows southwest from beyond the frontier to Ānshì and into the sea.
14.6 The Small Liáo River
14.6 The Small Liáo River
Further, in Gāogōulì County of Xuāntú Commandery, there is Liáo Mountain,
from which the Small Liáo River originates.
The county
was formerly Gāogōulì,
the state of the Hú people.
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Hàn Wǔdì,
Yòuqú was pacified,
and Xuāntú Commandery was established here,
called Xiàgōulì during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The river originates from Liáo Mountain,
flowing southwest past Liáoyáng County, where it joins the Dàliáng River.
The Dàliáng River originates beyond the northern frontier,
flowing southwest to Liáoyáng and into the Small Liáo River.
Thus, the *Geographical Treatise* states:
The Dàliáng River flows southwest to Liáoyáng and into the Liáo River.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* states:
The county
was formerly part of Liáodōng,
but later came under Xuāntú.
The river flows southwest,
hence it is called the Liáng River.
The Small Liáo River flows further southwest past Xiāngpíng County, forming Dànyuān,
which dried up in the third year of the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn.
The Small Liáo River then passes Liáoduì County and enters the Great Liáo River.
When Sīmǎ Xuānwáng pacified Liáodōng,
he beheaded Gōngsūn Yuān on this river.
Further southwest to Liáoduì County,
it enters the Great Liáo River.
14.7 The Pèi River
14.7 The Pèi River
The Pèi River originates from Lòufāng County in Lèlàng,
flowing southeast past Línpèi County,
and enters the sea to the east.
Xǔ Shèn states:
The Pèi River originates from Lòufāng,
and enters the sea to the east.
Another account says it originates from Pèishuǐ County.
The *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
Pèishuǐ County is located northeast of Lèlàng,
and Lòufāng County is east of the commandery.
It likely flows south from that county, passing through Lòufāng.
In the past, Wèi Mǎn, a man from Yān, traveled west from the Pèi River to Cháoxiǎn.
Cháoxiǎn
was originally the state of Jīzǐ.
Jīzǐ taught the people righteousness,
promoting agriculture, weaving, trustworthiness, and honesty,
establishing eight laws,
so that those below knew the prohibitions,
and thus formed customs of propriety.
During the Warring States period,
Wèi Mǎn then became its king,
establishing his capital at Wángxiǎn City,
with a territory spanning several thousand *li*,
until his grandson Yòu Qú.
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he dispatched General of Tower Ships Yáng Pú and General of the Left Xún Zhì to attack Yòu Qú,
defeating him at the Pèi River,
and thus destroying the state.
If the Pèi River flows east,
there would be no reason to cross it,
and its location is now the capital of the state of Gāogōulí.
I inquired with foreign envoys,
who said the city lies on the north bank of the Pèi River.
The river flows west past the former Lèlàng Cháoxiǎn County,
which was the seat of Lèlàng Commandery,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
and then flows northwest.
Therefore, the *Treatise on Geography* states:
The Pèi River flows west to Zēngdì County and enters the sea.
Moreover, when the Hàn dynasty arose,
considering Cháoxiǎn distant,
they followed the old frontier of Liáodōng to the Pèi River as the boundary.
Examining past and present,
there are discrepancies in the accounts,
likely due to errors in the *Classic*.
15 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll Fifteen
15.1 The Luò River
15.1 The Luò River
The Luò River originates from Huānjǔ Mountain in Shàngluò County, Jīngzhào.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
The Luò River originates from Zhǒnglǐng Mountain.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
It originates from the western mountains of Shàngluò.
It also states:
Huānjǔ Mountain,
is where the Luò River originates,
flowing east to join the Dān River,
which originates east of Zhú Mountain in the northwest,
flowing south into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Shī River joins it,
which originates from Shī Mountain in the north,
flowing south into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east and meets the Rǔ River,
which originates from Liángyú Mountain in the north,
flowing south into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east and converges with the Lóngyú River,
which originates from Gǔwěi Mountain,
flowing east into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east to Yángxū Mountain,
where it joins the Xuánhù River.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
The Luò River flows northeast,
and joins the Xuánhù River.
It also states that from Lùtí Mountain to Xuánhù Mountain,
there are nine mountains in total,
and Xuánhù is also a mountain name,
together with Huānjǔ,
forming the sequence of the nine mountains.
Therefore, the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
These two mountains lie between the Luò River.
From this, it is known that the Xuánhù River
originates from Xuánhù Mountain,
so both the mountain and the river share the same name.
The river flows past the foot of Yángxū Mountain.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* also states:
Yángxū Mountain
overlooks the Xuánhù River,
and this is the confluence of the Luò River.
The *Jade Tablet of the River Chart* states:
When Cāngjié was emperor,
he toured the south,
ascended Yángxū Mountain,
and overlooked the waters of Xuánhù and the confluence of the Luò River.
A divine turtle bore writings,
with red shells and green patterns, and presented them to him,
which occurred at this river.
The Luò River flows further east past Qīngchí Mountain,
and joins the Wǔlǐ River to the east,
which originates from Wǔlǐ Mountain in the south,
flowing northeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Mén River branches off.
This is what the *Erya* refers to as the Luò River branching into waves.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Yāo River joins it,
which originates from Sānyào Mountain in the south,
flowing northeast past the west of Jùyáng City,
and then northeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east and joins the Huò River,
which originates from Huòyú Mountain in the south,
commonly called the Bèi River.
It flows northeast through Huòyú Plain,
locally known as Què Plain,
flowing northeast,
into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east past the north of Xióng'ěr Mountain,
as mentioned in the *Tribute of Yu*: "The Luò River is guided from Xióng'ěr."
The *Records of the Broad Expanse* states:
The Luò River originates from Xióng'ěr,
which refers to the opening of its source.
It flows northeast past the south of Lúshì County.
The Luò River passes north of the Dǎoqú Pass.
The Dǎoqú River emerges south from Dǎoqú Mountain,
which is also known as Xúnqú Mountain.
Its waters have a single source that divides into two streams;
the river flow splits in half.
One stream flows northwest,
then bends northeast,
and enters the Luò River.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
From the Xióng'ěr Mountains,
the Fúháo River emerges,
flows northwest, and pours into the Luò River.
It is suspected that this is the same water.
Xúnqú
is likely an alternative name for Xióng'ěr,
much like Tàiháng is also called Guīshān.
Therefore, the *Dì Shuō* states:
The Xióng'ěr Mountains
are the Earth's Gate,
and the Luò River emerges from between them.
This is also a general name.
The other stream flows northeast past the west of Dǎoqú City,
which was formerly a fortified city.
This water flows northeast
and pours into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the old city of Lúshì County.
According to the *Zhúshū Jìnián*,
in the nineteenth year of Duke Chū of Jìn,
Hán Lóng of Jìn captured the city of Lúshì.
It was called Chāngfù during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The Lúshì Chuān River flows into it;
this water emerges north from Lúshì Mountain,
flows southeast past the east of Lúshì City,
and then flows southeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where it converges with three streams
that all emerge from the southern mountains of the county,
flowing northeast into the Luò.
The *Kāishān Tú* states:
Lúshì Mountain is suitable for the five grains
and can protect against flood disasters.
It is also commonly called Shíchéng Mountain.
The mountain lies southwest of Yíyáng Mountain.
Mountains of a thousand names
are all contained within it.
With its hills, mounds, plains, and lowlands,
it is easy to find a place to settle.
There is also the Gémàn Valley Stream,
which flows from the southern mountains into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of Gāomén City,
which is the place mentioned in the *Sòng Shū* where the Rear Army's external forces commander, Páng Jìmíng, entered Lúshì and advanced to the wooden city of Gāomén.
The Luò River eastward joins with the Gāomén River;
this water emerges from the northern mountains,
flows southeast and merges with a distributary of the Luò River.
This distributary branches off from the Luò River,
flows northeast past the north of Shílè City,
then east past the north of Gāomén City,
and east into the Gāomén River,
where the mingled streams flow south into the Luò.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Sōngyáng Stream flows into it.
This water emerges from Sōngyáng Mountain,
flows north, and enters the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of Huáng Pavilion,
and further east joins with the Huáng Pavilion Stream.
This water emerges from Tíhú Mountain.
The mountain has two peaks,
extremely lofty, reaching the sky;
high cliffs rise into the clouds,
with steep rocks offering no steps.
Even monkeys lose their agility here,
and flying squirrels concede their lightness and skill.
Only when long mists envelop the ridges
and layered clouds crown the peaks
can one begin to distinguish their relative heights.
Hence, they are named the Greater and Lesser Tíhú.
The stream flows southeast past the pavilion below,
and is called the Huáng Pavilion Stream.
It then flows southeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River further east reaches the mouth of the Xúngōng Stream.
This water emerges from the Xúngōng Ravine in the southern mountains,
which is the Xúngōng Valley that Páng Jìmíng entered.
The water flows northeast through the valley
and pours into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of Tán Mountain.
This mountain stands isolated, sheer on all four sides.
On the mountain is a fortified settlement,
commonly called Tán Mountain Fortress.
During the Yìxī era,
when Liú Gōng advanced west to Cháng'ān,
his fleet reached
and stopped at Luòyáng.
He ordered his staff officer, Dài Yánzhī, and the government attendant, Yú Dàoyuán, to take boats upstream
to thoroughly explore the Luò River region,
wishing to know how far the naval forces could reach.
Dài Yánzhī reached this point and turned back,
ultimately failing to reach the river's source.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Kù Valley Stream flows into it.
This water emerges south of Yíyáng Mountain,
where three streams converge
into a single brook,
flowing northeast into the Luò.
The Luò River further east reaches the mouth of the Tíhú Stream.
This water emerges north from the Tíhú Ravine,
flows southeast, and enters the Luò River.
The Luò River then passes north of the Púgǔ Pavilion,
where it joins on the left with the Northern Stream.
This water emerges from the northern mountains,
flows southeast, and enters the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Hóu Valley Stream emerges from the southern mountains,
flows north, and enters the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the north of Lóngxiāng City.
General Lóngxiāng, Wáng Zhèn'è,
followed Liú Gōng west to Cháng'ān,
and this was the route taken by land,
hence the city acquired its name.
The Luò River flows further east,
where on the left it joins with the stream from the northern mountains of Yíyáng.
This water flows south from the northern ravine into the Luò.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Guǎngyóu Ravine Stream flows into it.
This water emerges from the Yóu Stream in the southern mountains,
flows north past the east of Lóngxiāng City,
and then north into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where on the right it receives the Zhígǔ Stream.
This water emerges from the southern mountains,
flows north past Tún City,
and then northwest into the Luò River.
It then flows northeast past the south of Lǐchéng Town.
West of the town is a fortress stream,
emerging from a mountain four *lǐ* to the north.
The plateau is twenty-five *zhàng* high.
This was formerly the seat of Miǎnchí County.
To the south, it faces Jīnmén Fortress.
Five *lǐ* south of the water
was the old seat of Yíyáng County.
The Luò River on the right meets the Jīnmén Stream.
This water emerges south from Jīnmén Mountain,
flows north past Jīnmén Fortress,
and then northwest into the Luò River.
The Luò River further east joins with the Kuǎn River.
This water has two sources that emerge together;
the two streams flow and converge,
and it is called the Great Kuǎn River.
They join and flow southeast into the Luò.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Shǔliáng Valley Stream enters it.
This water emerges south from Jīnmén Mountain.
The *Kāishān Tú* states:
The mountain has many strongholds and is located in Hán.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
General of Strong Crossbows, Chén Jùn, attacked and captured Jīnmén and Báimǎ in succession,
defeating them all.
This is the place.
The stream flows northeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River flows further east,
where on the left it joins with the Northern Stream,
which flows south into the Luò.
It then flows east past the south of Yángshì Town,
and further northeast past the south of Yúfù Town.
The Water of Taiyīn Valley flows south from the Taiyīn Stream,
and runs northward to empty into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east and joins with the Water of White Horse Stream.
This water originates from Yíyáng Mountain.
In the ravine there is a large rock,
whose shape resembles a horse,
hence the stream and ravine received their name from its appearance.
The stream water flows northeast and empties into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east, and the Water of Chāng Ravine flows into it.
This water originates from Yíyáng Mountain in the northwest,
and flows southeast,
passing south of the old commandery of Yíyáng,
which was formerly the market town of Yángshì.
It was originally the seat of the Luòyáng Capital Agricultural Supervisor,
but was later changed to a commandery.
This water then flows south and empties into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of Yīhé Fort.
The fortress is on the plain north of the river,
twenty *zhàng* high.
Its southern, northern, and eastern sides
are sheer natural barriers,
so only the western side needed to be fortified to make it secure.
The name "Yīhé" (One Fortification)
originated from this.
When Liú Yào's general attacked Hénán,
the Jìn general Wèi Gāi fled here,
so it was also called Gāi's father's town.
The Luò River then flows east and joins with the Water of Dùyáng Ravine.
This water originates from Dùyáng Stream in the northwest,
flows southeast past Yīhé Fort,
joins with the Water of Pán Valley to the east,
and then the combined flow runs southeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east.
The Water of Qú Valley originates from Nǚjī Mountain south of Yíyáng County,
flows northeast past the left side of Yúnzhōng Fort.
Above, the terrain rises steeply in layers,
with flowing mists hanging halfway down,
like ribbons girdling the hills,
hence the fort received its name.
The Water of Qú Valley then flows northeast into the Luò River.
Zāng Róngxù's *Jìn Shū* records
that Sūn Dēng once passed through Yíyáng Mountain.
Charcoal makers saw him and spoke to him,
but Dēng did not respond.
The charcoal makers sensed his spirit and demeanor were extraordinary,
and all spread the story.
Tàizǔ heard of it,
and sent Ruǎn Jí to observe him.
He spoke to him,
but again Dēng did not respond.
Jí then let out a great whistle.
Dēng laughed and said:
"Do it again with the same sound."
Jí whistled again,
and asked Dēng to come out with him.
Dēng refused,
so Jí took his leave and departed.
Dēng ascended the peak, walking and whistling,
producing sounds like those of flutes, panpipes, reed pipes, and mouth organs,
the sound shaking the mountain valleys.
Jí, puzzled, asked the charcoal makers,
and they said:
"That is indeed the sound of that man."
Jí searched for him again,
but did not know where he had gone.
After inquiring for a long time,
he finally learned his name.
I note that Sūn Chuò, in his preface to *Gāoshì Zhuàn*,
says it was at Sūmén Mountain,
and also separately wrote *Dēng Zhuàn*.
Sūn Shèng's *Wèi Chūnqiū* also says it was at Sūmén Mountain,
and does not list his name.
Ruǎn Sìzōng was moved by him,
and wrote *Dàrén Xiānshēng Lùn*,
saying, "I do not know this man.
He roams in spirit, self-content,
and does not interact with things."
Even the Ruǎn clan could not stir his noble integrity;
how then could anyone else know his name?
[The Luò River] then flows northeast past the south of Yíyáng County.
North of the Luò River is Xióng'ěr Mountain,
with twin peaks vying in height,
shaped like a bear's ears.
This is a separate mountain,
not the same as the Xióng'ěr from which the Luò River is guided in the *Yǔ Gòng*.
In the past, when Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn defeated Fán Chóng of the Chìméi,
the piled armor and weapons reached level with Xióng'ěr;
this is that mountain.
At the mountain's edge there is a pool,
whose water flows southeast.
Beside the water is another pool,
which the world calls Miǎnchí.
[The water] then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Yíyáng County,
where it is called the Xīdù Water.
It then flows southeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east past the south of the old city of Yíyáng County.
King Wǔ of Qín appointed Gān Mào as Left Chancellor,
and said:
"I wish to open the way to Sānchuān and spy upon the Zhōu court;
then I would die without regret."
Mào requested a pact with Wèi to attack Hán,
beheading sixty thousand,
and then captured Yíyáng City.
This was originally Hán territory,
later made a county.
Emperor Āi of Hàn enfeoffed Xīfū Gōng as a marquis here.
At the city's west gate,
Fán Chóng of the Chìméi, along with Péngzǐ and the senior generals,
presented the imperial seal, ribbons, sword, and jade disc.
Shìzǔ did not see them immediately.
The next day,
he arrayed troops by the Luò River and met Péngzǐ and the others.
He said to Péngzǐ's chancellor Xú Xuān:
"Do you have no regrets?" Xuān replied:
"No regrets."
The Emperor sighed and said:
"You are the brightest among the mediocre,
the most clanging among iron."
The Luò River then flows east and joins with the Water of Yànrǎn.
This water originates from the great marsh of Fù Mountain north of the county.
The mountain has no grass or trees.
The water flows north from the marsh,
bends and flows southeast,
and is called the Wǔyán Water by the world.
It then flows southeast past the east of the old city of Yíyáng County,
and flows southeast into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows southeast.
The Water of Huángzhōng Ravine originates from a northern hill,
with two extraordinary sources,
which combine into one stream
flowing east into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east,
and the Water of Lù Spring flows into it.
This water emerges from a nearby stream in the north.
The Luò River then flows east,
and the Gòng Water enters it.
This water originates from Chángshí Mountain in the north.
The mountain has no grass or trees.
To its west there is a valley,
named Gòng Valley,
from which the Gòng Water emerges.
Flowing south, it reaches the mouth of Yǐn Stream.
This water originates from Yǐn Valley in the northwest,
and flows southeast into it.
The Gòng Water then flows southwest and meets the Water of Left Ravine.
This water emerges from a nearby stream in the east,
and flows west into the Gòng Water.
The Gòng Water then flows south and joins with the Water of Lǐ Valley.
This water originates from Lǐ Stream in the northwest,
and flows southeast into the Zhēn Water.
The Zhēn Water originates from Zhēn Valley,
flows southwest and joins with the Water of Lǐ Valley,
then flows southwest into the Gòng Water.
The Gòng Water,
called Shítóu Spring by the world,
flows south into the Luò River.
The Luò River then flows east.
The Water of Black Ravine originates from the western mountains of Lùhún in the south,
passes through Black Ravine,
and enters the Luò River from the northwest.
The Luò River then flows east,
and the Water of Líntíng Stream flows into it.
This water originates from a nearby stream in the northwest,
flows southeast and meets the Water of Long Ravine.
This water emerges from the northern mountains and flows south into the Líntíng Water.
[The Líntíng Water] then flows southeast past the west of Jiǔqū,
and flows south into the Luò River.
[The Luò River] then flows northeast out from the south of Sànguān.
The Luò River flows east past the south of Jiǔqū,
an area ten lǐ in extent,
with a slope called Jiǔqū.
This is what the *Account of King Mù* refers to when it says,
"The Son of Heaven journeyed westward,
ascending Jiǔ'ē."
The Luò River then flows east and converges with the Háo River,
which originates from Mì Mountain in Xīn'ān County,
flows south past the east of Jiǔqū,
and then south into the Luò River.
Beside the Luò River is Shímò Mountain,
whose rocks are entirely black,
suitable for writing letters,
hence the mountain is named Shímò (Inkstone).
The Luò River flows further east,
where a branch channel diverges to the left.
It exits east through a pass,
crosses the Huì River,
and passes south of Qīngnǚ's tomb,
which is on Běi Mountain.
The *Records of the Elders* states:
"This woman was pure, chaste, elegant, and ancient in virtue,
her legacy manifest to this day."
The branch channel then flows east past Zhōu Mountain,
atop which is the tomb of King Líng of Zhōu.
The *Imperial Overview* says:
"King Líng of Zhōu was buried on Zhōu Mountain, southwest of Hénán City."
It is said that because the king was born divine,
he was posthumously titled 'Líng' (Spiritual).
His tomb
is continuously worshipped by people.
Further northeast, it passes south of Bǎi Pavilion.
The *Imperial Overview* says:
"Zhōu Mountain lies northwest of Bǎi Pavilion,"
referring to this pavilion.
It then flows northeast past the northeast of the Three Kings' Tombs and exits.
The Three Kings
are said to be King Jǐng, King Dào, and King Dìng of Zhōu.
Cuī Hào, Minister over the Masses of Wèi, annotated the *Rhapsody on a Westward Journey*, stating:
"Dìng should be Jìng.
When Zǐ Cháo stirred trouble,
Western Zhōu's governance weakened and its people scattered.
Kings Dào and Jìng,
along with King Jǐng, were all buried here,
hence later generations named the tombs the Three Kings' Tombs."
The *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* states:
"King Jǐng was buried at Díquán,
which is the large tomb within the Tàicāng in present-day Luòyáng."
Yet it is also said to be here,
which is unclear.
Moreover, regarding Kings Dào and Jìng,
consulting historical records,
there is again no burial site recorded.
East of the tombs now stands a stone stele,
listing the names and titles of kings from King Nǎn upward.
Examining the stele's record,
it clearly identifies them as Zhōu tombs.
The branch channel flows northeast past Zhì Township,
passes west of the royal city in Hénán County,
and traverses Jiárǔ Path.
Dù Yù's *Explanation of Places* states:
"West of the county lies Jiárǔ Path,"
referring to this.
The branch channel then flows north into a valley,
likely first opened during the Zhōu period,
but the channel has long been abandoned and unrepaired.
The Luò River, from the branch channel, flows east out of the pass,
with the Huì River joining from the right.
It is commonly called the Bāguān River.
Dài Yánzhī's *Record of a Westward Journey* calls it Bāguān Marsh,
which is the Sǎn Pass mentioned in the *Classic*,
a barrier extending from the southern mountains,
crossing the Luò River,
and connecting north to the Yellow River,
all being passes and fortifications,
built by the household servants of Yáng Pú.
The Huì River originates from the southern side of Báishí Mountain,
flows southeast and merges with the Zhān River,
which originates east from Lóuzhuó Mountain
and flows south into the Huì River.
The Huì River flows further southeast,
while the Xiè River originates north from Zhānzhū Mountain;
flowing southeast,
there is also the Jiāochù River,
originating north from Guī Mountain,
flowing south,
both merging with the Huì River.
The Huì River then flows south past the north of Guānchéng,
a distance of twenty lǐ.
The city is blocked by walls to the west,
and rests upon the Huì River to the east.
In the first year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn (184 CE),
Hé Jìn, Governor of Hénán, was appointed Grand General,
leading troops from five barracks to station at Dū Pavilion,
establishing eight passes: Hángǔ,
Guǎngchéng, Yīquē, Dàgǔ, Huányuán, Xuánmén, Xiǎopíngjīn, and Mèngjīn.
The commandant's office was established here,
with Hángǔ Pass as the foremost,
included among the eight passes.
Thus, people collectively referred to them
as the Eight Passes.
The river then flows south into the Luò River.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"From the southern side of Báishí Mountain originates the Huì River,
which flows south and empties into the Luò."
This refers to this river.
The Luò River then converges with the Guó River,
which originates from Fúzhū Mountain,
flowing north into the Luò River.
To its south
lies Lùtí Mountain,
commonly called Fēi Mountain.
This mountain
has steep, sheer cliffs a hundred rèn high on its northern side,
while the southern side consists of elevated plains and level land.
The Gān River originates from its eastern foothills,
flowing north into the Luò River.
Further northeast, it passes south of Hénán County.
The *Book of Zhōu* states that when the Duke of Zhōu was about to return governance,
he built the great city of Chéngzhōu in the central region,
connecting it to the Luò River in the south,
and relying on Jiá Mountain in the north,
making it the great convergence of the realm.
The *Apocryphal Treatise on the Classic of Filial Piety* states:
"Across the breadth of the eight directions,
Zhōu and Luò are the center,
called Luòyì."
The *Bamboo Annals* records:
In the twentieth year of Duke Dìng of Jìn (492 BCE),
the Luò River cut off from Zhōu.
In the ninth year of King Xiāng of Wèi (310 BCE),
the Luò River entered Chéngzhōu,
with mountains and waters greatly emerging.
To the south is Gānluò City,
called Gānchéng in the *Treatise on Commanderies and States*.
The *Geographical Records* states:
"The Luò River flows northeast past Wǔlíng Péiwěi,
north where it merges with the Jiàn and Chán Rivers."
These two rivers
flow east into the Qiānjīn Canal,
whose old channel remains.
Further east, it passes south of Luòyáng County,
where the Yī River flows from the west and joins it.
Luòyáng,
was the city of Luòyì built by the Duke of Zhōu.
Therefore, the "Luò Gào" says:
"We divined east of the Chán River,
and only Luò was favorable."
Its city wall measured seven hundred and twenty zhàng square,
connected to the Luò River in the south,
and bordered by the Jiá Mountain in the north,
making it the convergence point of the world.
It spanned six hundred lǐ in area,
and with the addition of eight hundred lǐ to the west,
it became a thousand lǐ.
In the thirty-second year of Duke Zhāo of the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn gathered the feudal lords and ministers to garrison the city of Chéngzhōu,
hence it was also called Chéngzhōu.
Sīmǎ Qiān's "Preface" states:
"The Grand Historian lingered in Zhōunán."
Zhì Zhòngzhì said:
"The ancient Zhōunán
is today's Luòyáng.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn initially intended to establish his capital here,
but moved by Lóu Jìng's words,
he departed within a day.
During the restoration under Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the imperial residence was in Luòyì,
and through the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
both made it their dual capital.
Therefore, the "Wèi Lüè" says:
"The Hàn dynasty, following the fire element, avoided water,
so they removed the water radical and added the 'zhùi' radical.
Wèi followed the earth virtue,
and earth is the mate of water.
Water flows when it meets earth,
and earth becomes soft when it meets water,
so they removed the 'zhùi' radical and added the water radical."
The "Chángshā Qíjiù Zhuàn" records:
Zhù Liáng,
styled Zhàoqīng,
served as the magistrate of Luòyáng.
During a year of severe drought,
when the Son of Heaven's prayers for rain failed,
Zhù Liáng exposed himself in the courtyard,
confessed his faults with sincerity,
and from morning until noon,
purple clouds rose and water gathered,
bringing sweet rain in abundance.
People sang:
"The heavens long withheld rain,
the people lost their way.
The Son of Heaven went forth himself,
Magistrate Zhù suffered especially,
his sincerity moved the spirits,
and pouring rain fell."
The county office and the Governor of Hénán administered it.
The Sīlì,
an official of the Zhōu dynasty,
was appointed by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn to oversee convict laborers
and supervise the capital region. Later,
it was named the Sīzhōu.
The "Dì Jì" says:
"The Luò River flows east into the Zhōngtí Mountains,
and eastward merges with the Yī River."
In ancient times, during the era of the Yellow Emperor,
a great fog covered the sky for three days.
The Emperor traveled to the banks of the Luò River,
saw a great fish,
and sacrificed five kinds of livestock to offer libations.
Then, heavy rain fell from the sky,
and after seven days and nights, the fish drifted away,
finally yielding the diagrams and writings,
which are now the "Hétú Shì Méng Piān."
In the past, Prince Jìn loved playing the phoenix pipes,
inviting Daoist priests,
and roaming the banks of the Yī and Luò rivers with Fú Qiū.
Hán Shǐ also received the auspicious sign of the jade chicken in these waters,
and this is also where the Luò River goddess, Fúfēi, resides.
The Luò River flows further east,
and the Hé River emerges from the Bànshí Mountain in the south,
flowing north past the Hé River Fort,
then northeast into the Gōnglù Gully.
However, due to popular mispronunciation,
it is called the Guānglù Gully,
which is incorrect.
Above it lies Yuán Shù's stronghold,
surrounded by steep ravines on all sides,
towering hundreds of rèn high,
and spanning four or five lǐ in width.
There is a body of water,
deep and stagnant,
so the stream and gully are named after it.
The Hé River merges north with the Liú River,
which originates from the eastern Bànshí Mountain,
flowing northwest past the Liú settlement,
surrounded by ravines on three sides,
located southwest of Gōushì.
It was the state of Liúzi within the Zhōu royal domain,
hence it is called the Liú Gully.
Its waters flow northwest into the Hé River,
and the Hé River flows north into the Luò River.
Further east, it passes south of Yǎnshī County.
The Luo River flows east past Jìsùzhǔ,
during the middle period of the Jin dynasty,
it was where tribute and accounts from a hundred states were halted,
hence the islet got its name.
It also runs straight south of the old Yǎnshī county seat,
sharing the watershed with Gōushì,
further east,
the Xiū River flows into it from the south,
this river originates from Shàoshì Mountain,
flows west past the south of Xué Mountain,
then north where it merges with the waters of Shàoshì Mountain,
which emerge from the northern stream of Shàoshì,
flowing southwest into the Xiū River.
The Xiū River then joins the Nánxī River on the left,
which rises from the southern mountain of Dàxué,
flowing north into the Xiū River.
The Xiū River then turns southwest and bends north,
flowing underground in a hidden course,
its old channel bends north and emerges from a gorge,
called Dàxué Kǒu,
passing north east of Fùfǔ Duī,
likely named for its resemblance to an object.
Further east, it reaches Língxīng Wù,
where the water flows hidden underground,
and a second source emerges,
beside the Gōushì Plain,
which the "Kāishān Tú" calls Gōushì Mountain.
It is also said that immortals ascended here,
referring to Prince Jìn controlling his crane on this mound,
while King Líng watched but could not approach,
raised his hand in farewell and departed.
His family found his left-behind shoes,
commonly also called Fǔfù Duī,
on the mound is a shrine to Zǐ Jìn.
Some say it is at Jiǔshān, not here,
but generations have passed,
and it cannot be verified. Liú Xiàng's "Lièxiān Zhuàn" states:
the sounds of flutes and pipes are heard in the world.
The Xiū River then passes south of Yánshòuchéng,
the seat of Gōushì County,
formerly Huá Fèi,
the capital of the state of Huá in the "Spring and Autumn Annals."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhōngtíng,
which is Gōushì City.
The city has a shrine to immortals,
called the Immortal's Temple,
the Xiū River then turns west and bends north,
passing west of the city,
southwest of the water is the stele of the temple of Sīkōng Mìlíng Yuánhóu Zhèng Mào.
The text is damaged and can no longer be read.
There is also the stele of Jìn Chéngmén Xiàowèi Chāngyuán Gōnghóu Zhèng Zhònglín,
erected in the sixth year of the Tàishǐ era of Jin.
The Xiū River then flows north into the Luo River.
The Luo River then flows east past the north of Bǎigǔ Wù,
Dài Yánzhī's "Xīzhēng Jì" says:
the fort is south of the river,
built high as a fort,
over ten zhàng tall,
when Liú Wǔwáng entered Cháng'ān from the west,
it was defended by his naval forces.
The Luo River then flows north,
where the Yángqú River flows into it.
The "Zhúshū Jìnián" records:
in the sixth year of Duke Xiāng of Jin,
the Luo River was cut off at Jiǒng.
This is the place.
The Luo River then flows north past east of Yǎnshī City,
northeast through Rǔzhōng,
south of the water is called Nán Xún,
also known as Shàng Xún.
It passes west of Zīchéng,
what Sīmǎ Biāo called Zī Jù,
and the Xún River flows into it,
originating from the Xún Stream of the northern mountains,
this river flows south,
commonly called the Hot Spring River.
Beside the water is the Jiāngrén Cave,
inside the cave is a stiff corpse,
Dài Yánzhī's "Cóng Liú Wǔwáng Xīzhēng Jì" says:
there is this corpse,
the corpse is still there today,
there is no principle that things do not transform,
no way that the soul does not move on,
yet this corpse has no consciousness,
like a wooden puppet,
to illustrate its slow change,
it is not as swift as the proper form's transformation.
The Xún River then flows southeast,
entering the Luo River east at the northwest of Zīchéng.
Thus Jīng Xiàngfán said:
now north of the Gǒngluò crossing,
there is the Xúngǔ River flowing east into the Luo,
called Xià Xún.
Hence the names Shàng Xún and Xià Xún,
also called Běi Xún,
thus there are the terms Nán Xún and Běi Xún.
There is also Xúnchéng,
likely the old town of Zhōu Grand Master Xún Xī.
The Luo River then flows east past north of Zīchéng,
further east,
the Luó River flows into it,
originating from Luóchuān of Fāngshān,
flowing northwest,
the Púchí River flows into it,
originating from Púbēi in the south,
flowing northwest to join the Luó River,
called Chángluó Chuān.
Also called Luózhōng.
Likely because Xīzǐ Xúnluó once resided here,
hence the river got its name.
The Luó River then flows northwest,
where the Báimǎxī River flows into it,
originating from the northern foothills of Sōngshān,
passing east of Báimǎ Wù,
and north into the Luó River.
Flowing northwest,
the Báitóngjiàn River flows into it,
originating from Tóngxī at the foothills of Sōngshān,
flowing north past east of Jiǔshān,
further north,
the Jiǔshānxī River joins it.
Originating from the eastern valley of Bǎichēng Mountain,
this mountain has a solitary peak standing out elegantly,
towering and distinct.
Zhòng Chángtǒng said:
in the past, there was a diviner named Bǔ Chéng from Mì,
who roamed atop Jiǔshān,
in a realm of carefree liberation,
referring to this mountain.
At the mountain's edge is the Jiǔshān Temple,
in front of the temple is a stele stating:
the Lord of the Nine Manifestations Divine Mansion,
first son of Tàihuá,
listed among the nine yang,
titled Lord of the Nine Mountains.
To the south it borders Sōngyuè,
to the north it girdles the Luo marshes,
in the ninth month of the second year of Yuánkāng of Jin,
the year being wù,
the emperor dispatched Diànzhōng Zhōnglángjiàng, Guānnèihóu Fán Guǎng,
Gōushì Magistrate Wáng Yǔ,
Chief Clerk Fù Yǎn,
to carry out the imperial decree,
and establish the temple hall.
There is also the "Stele of the Hundred Insects General's Manifestation,"
the stele states:
the general's surname is Yī,
personal name Yì,
courtesy name Tuí'ái,
the second son of Emperor Gāoyáng, Bó Yì.
On the seventh day of the seventh month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Jin,
the local people Wú Yì and others built the hall and temple,
on the twentieth day of the second month of the first year of Yǒngpíng, they carved the stone and erected the eulogy,
to praise and show later worthies.
This water flows northeast into the Báitóngjiàn,
then north past east of Yuángōng Wù,
likely Yuán Lù originally had this,
hence the name Yuángōng.
Flowing north into the Luó River,
the Luó River then flows northwest past north of Yuángōng Wù,
then northwest past the tombs of Pān Yuè and his father,
in front is a stele,
Pān Yuè's father Pān Zǐ,
was Governor of Lángyá,
the stele is broken and the text is damaged.
The "Pān Yuè Stele" inscription reads:
Stele of Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Gate Pān.
The stele states:
he met disaster from Sūn Xiù,
his entire family suffered calamity,
thus his disciples, moved by the overturned meat sauce to increase their grief,
erected a stele to record the event.
These are the words of Tàicháng Pān Ní.
The Luó River then enters the Luo River northeast of Zīchéng.
Further northeast, it passes east of Gǒng County,
then north into the Yellow River.
The Luò River flows eastward,
where the Mínglè Spring joins it.
The spring emerges from the southern plain,
with three springs flowing together,
hence it is commonly called the Wǔdào Spring,
which is the ancient Míngxī Spring.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, the twenty-second year of Duke Zhāo,
the army encamped at Míngxī.
The Luò River then flows east past the old city of Gǒng County,
the residence of the Eastern Zhōu,
originally the state of Gǒng Bó within the royal domain of the Zhōu.
As mentioned in the Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals, Yǐn Wénfù crossed at Gǒng,
which was here.
The Luò River flows further east,
where the Zhuó River joins it,
which is the ancient Huáng River.
It emerges from the southern plain.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Three lǐ north of Zīchéng is the Huáng Pavilion,
which is this pavilion.
This is the Huáng mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals where the army encamped.
The Luò River flows northeast,
where the Jiǒng River originates from the Shíquán Spring in the southern stream,
also commonly called the Shíquán Spring.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
East of Gǒng is a place called Kǎnkǎn,
east of the Jiǒng River,
likely referring to this river.
It then flows east of Pángǔ Wù,
also commonly called the Pángǔ River.
In Sīmǎ Biāo's "Records of Commanderies and States,"
Gǒng has the settlement of Kǎnkǎn.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, the twenty-fourth year of Duke Xī,
the king departed and reached Kǎnkǎn.
Fú Qián also considered it a town east of Gǒng.
Examining the texts now, it seems plausible,
though not precisely verifiable.
The "Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Records" and "Jìnshū Dìdào Records"
both state it is west of Gǒng,
which is incorrect.
The river then flows north into the Luò,
and the Luò River flows northeast,
entering the Huáng River.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
The Luò River
enters the Huáng River west of Chénggāo.
This is called Luòruì,
also known as Shígǔ.
Thus, Zhāng Yí advised Qín:
Send troops to Sānchuān,
block the mouth of Shígǔ.
This refers to this river.
The "Shǐjì Yīnyì" says:
Gǒng County has the Xúngǔ River.
The Yellow Emperor traveled east to the Huáng River,
passed the Luò,
built an altar and sank jade discs,
receiving the "Dragon Chart" from the Huáng River,
and the "Turtle Script" from the Luò River,
with red characters on a green background.
Emperor Yáo also built an altar at the Huáng and Luò Rivers,
selected auspicious times to sink discs,
glorious light emerged from the Huáng River,
auspicious air filled the surroundings,
white clouds rose,
whirlwinds passed,
red characters on a green background,
measuring nine chǐ in length and width,
with patterns evenly arranged,
containing divisions of constellations,
measures of the seven luminaries,
and the "Records of Emperors and Kings" detailing the numbers of rise and fall,
which were bestowed upon Yáo.
He then sank writings east at Rìjì,
red light arose,
a black turtle bore the writings,
with red characters forming on its back shell,
and he abdicated to Shùn.
Shùn also followed Yáo's rites,
sinking writings at Rìjì,
red light arose,
a black turtle bore the writings to below Jì,
glorious light and auspicious signs arrived,
a yellow dragon curled its armor,
unfurled a chart beside the altar,
with red characters and green patterns, bestowing it upon Shùn.
Shùn then abdicated to Yǔ.
King Tāng of Shāng observed east at the Luò,
practiced rites at Yáo's altar,
lowered jade discs and sank them three times,
but glorious light did not arise.
Instead, two yellow fish leaped,
emerging and crossing at the altar,
a black crow bathed,
following the fish upward,
transforming into black jade with red-bordered writings,
and a black turtle with red-character inscriptions.
Tāng used this to attack Jié.
Thus, the "Chūnqiū Shuōtící" says:
The Huáng River, following Kūn, emits heaven's essence;
the Luò River, flowing through plains, reveals earth's talismans.
Kings sink offerings here.
The "Bamboo Annals" says:
Luò Bó Yòng fought with Hé Bó Féngyí,
likely the spirits of the Luò River.
In ancient times, when Tàikāng of Xià lost governance,
he was pursued by Yì,
and his five brothers
waited at Luòruì,
composing the "Songs of the Five Sons,"
which took place here.
15.2 The Yī River
15.2 The Yī River
The Yī River originates from Mànqú Mountain west of Lǔyáng County in Nányáng.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
Mànqú Mountain,
from which the Yī River emerges.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
The Yī River emerges from Shàngwèi Mountain.
The "Geographical Records" say:
It emerges from Xióng'ěr Mountain, with similar foothills,
though ridges and peaks differ.
The Yī River flows northeast from Xióng'ěr past north of Luánchuān Pavilion.
The Jiān River emerges from Jiān Mountain,
flowing north along the east of the city and then north into the Yī River.
People call the Yī River the Luán River,
and the Jiān River the Jiāo River,
hence naming this area Luánchuān.
Further east, it forms deep pools,
turbid as if boiling,
with unfathomable depth.
The Yī River then flows northeast past south of Dōngtíng City,
bends around east of the pavilion,
and flows northeast.
Northeast, it passes Guōluò Mountain.
The Yáng River emerges from Yángxī Stream on Yáng Mountain,
commonly called Tàiyáng Valley,
from which the river takes its name.
It flows east into the Yī River.
The Yī River flows further east,
where the Běixiān River joins it.
It emerges from Xiān Mountain,
flowing north into the Yī.
The Yī River then merges with the Mán River,
which emerges from Mángǔ Valley in Lúshì County,
flowing east into the Yī.
Further northeast, it passes south of Lùhún County.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
The Yōngyōng River
originates from Lí Mountain,
flows southward, and empties into the Yī River.
Today, the river emerges from the Wángmǔ Jiàn in the southwest of Lùhún County.
North of the jiàn, on the mountain, there is a shrine to Wángmǔ,
hence later generations named the stream accordingly.
It flows eastward and empties into the Yī River,
which is precisely the Yōngyōng River.
The Yī River passes through Yá Kǒu,
a mountain gorge.
The cliffs on either side are deep and lofty,
standing sheer like gate towers.
On the cliff there is a wù (a small fortified settlement),
and the Yī River flows beneath it,
passing through the gorge and flowing northward.
This is the ancient Sāntú Mountain.
Dù Yù, in his Explanation of Geography, states:
The mountain lies south of the county.
Kàn Yīn, in the Records of the Thirteen Provinces, says:
The mountain lies to the southeast.
Today, this mountain is located about eighty lǐ southeast of the old city of Lùhún.
The Book of Zhou records
King Wǔ of Zhōu asking Grand Duke Wàng:
"I intend to base myself at the dwelling place of the Xià,
looking southward beyond the Sāntú,
and gazing northward toward the Hé (Yellow River)."
In the fourth year of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Simǎ Hóu said:
"The Sì Yuè, Sāntú, Yángchéng, Tàishì, Jīngshān, and Zhōngnán
are the strategic strongholds of the Nine Provinces."
Fú Qián stated:
"Sāntú, Dàháng, Huányuán, Xiáo, and Miǎn
are not what is meant by 'looking southward'."
Jīng Xiàngfán, in his work Geographical Names of the Spring and Autumn Period,
also says:
It is a mountain name.
According to Master Fú's explanation,
"tú"
means "road" or "path".
Considering the phrase "looking southward" from the Book of Zhou,
some say it should refer to Huányuán, Dàgǔ, and Yīquè,
but these are all incorrect.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records
that Jìn attacked Lùhún,
and requested to perform rituals at the Sāntú.
From this, it is clear that it refers to a mountain.
The Qīgǔ River flows into it.
The river originates from the Qīxī Mountain south of the Nǚjī Mountain in the west.
On the mountain, there is a shrine to the Queen Mother of the West.
It flows southeast and empties into the Yī River.
Further north,
the Zǎogǔ River flows into it.
This river originates from the eastern valley of Nǚjī Mountain,
flows east past the south of an old pavilion,
and then east into the Yī River.
The Yī River then flows northeast past the east of Fúliú Ridge.
On the ridge, there is a shrine to Lúnkūn,
where people still pray.
Liú Chéngzhī, in his Records of the Yǒngchū Era, states
that west of Lùhún County there is a place called Fúliú Bǎn.
Today, the mountain is located about thirty lǐ north of Yá Kǒu in the county's south.
His statement that it is west is incorrect.
To the north, it merges with the Wēnquán River.
This river originates from the southwestern foothills of Lánggāo Mountain in Xīnchéng County.
It flows southwest and joins the Yī River.
The Yī River then flows northeast past Fúdǔ Ridge.
On the left, it receives the Jiāo Jiàn River.
This river originates from Lùbó Mountain in the west,
flows east past the south of Gū Mountain.
This mountain stands solitary and prominent on the plain,
uniquely lofty and isolated.
Therefore, later generations call it Fāng Mountain,
which is precisely the "solitary mountain in the county" mentioned by Secretariat Director Liú Chéngzhī.
It flows east past the south of Fúdǔ Ridge,
then east into the Yī River.
The Yī River flows further northeast,
where the Juān River flows into it.
This river originates from the western mountains of Lùhún,
which was the capital of Lùhún.
Seeking the former residence of Guō Wén,
visiting the traces of Hú Zhāo,
but time has passed without cease,
and none can identify their locations.
This river has two sources,
both flowing eastward.
Guó Lüè is located ninety lǐ west of Lùhún County.
Sīmǎ Biāo, in the Treatise on Commanderies and States, states:
"West of the county lies the land of Guó Lüè."
This is what the Spring and Autumn Annals refers to as "eastward reaching Guó Lüè."
The northern stream flows east and merges with the Hóu Jiàn River.
This river originates from Hóu Stream in the northwest,
flows southeast, and empties into the Juān River.
The Juān River then flows east past the north of the old city of Lùhún County.
When King Píng moved the capital eastward,
Xīn Yǒu traveled to the Yī River region.
He saw someone with disheveled hair performing sacrifices in the wild and said:
"In less than a hundred years,
will this land become Róng territory?"
In the 22nd year of Duke Xī of Lǔ,
Qín and Jìn relocated the Lùhún Róng to the Yī River region.
Hence, the county is named after them.
The Juān River flows southeast,
and on the left merges with the Southern River.
This river originates from the Qīgǔ in the western mountains,
and is also called the Qīgǔ River.
It flows eastward along the jiàn,
passes south of the county,
then turns east,
and further south, on the left, meets the Northern River.
Their flows intermingle,
and on the left, they join the Chánzhǔ River.
This river receives water from the Chánzhǔ east of Lùhún County.
The zhǔ (marsh) is situated on the plain,
a marshland ten lǐ square,
abundant with fish and reeds.
This is what the Classic of Mountains and Seas refers to as "looking southward to the Chánzhǔ,
where Gǔn, the father of Yǔ, transformed."
Guō Jǐngchún (Guō Pú) annotates:
"Chán"
is also pronounced "nuǎn".
"Gǔn transformed in the Yǔyuān, yet also here. However, having already become a strange creature,
there is no place he does not transform."
Later generations call this marsh the Shènwàng Pō.
The water from the pō flows south into the Juān River.
The Juān River then flows southeast and empties into the Yī River.
In ancient times, a woman of the Yǒushēn clan was picking mulberry leaves by the Yī River.
She found an infant in a hollow mulberry tree.
It is said his mother became pregnant by the banks of the Yī River.
She dreamed a deity told her:
"When water comes from the mortar, flee eastward."
The next morning, the mother looked and saw water indeed coming from the mortar.
She warned her neighbors and fled.
Looking back at her town,
it had all become water.
His mother transformed into a hollow mulberry tree,
and the child was inside it.
The woman of Yǒushēn took him and presented him.
He was ordered to be raised in the kitchen,
and when he grew up, he possessed virtuous talent.
The Yīn dynasty appointed him as minister,
and he was called Yī Yǐn.
(The Yī River) then flows further northeast past the south of Xīnchéng County.
The Mǎhuáiqiáo Chángshuǐ originates from the Western Mountains of Xīnchéng County,
flowing east past the south of the stele of Zōng Jūn, the Jin dynasty's Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers and General Who Conquers the South.
Jūn, whose courtesy name was Wénpíng,
was a native of the county.
His stele
was erected in the twelfth month of the third year of the Tàishǐ era.
The water then flows east and enters the Yī River.
There is also the Míngshuǐ, which originates from Lánggāo Mountain west of Liáng County,
commonly called the Shíjiànshuǐ.
It flows northwest past the south of Yáng Liàng's fortification,
then northwest joins the Kāngshuǐ,
which also originates from Lánggāo Mountain,
flows northeast past the north of Fàn Wù and joins the Míngshuǐ,
then flows southwest and enters the Yī River.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"From Fànggāo Mountain,
the Míngshuǐ emerges,
flowing south and pouring into the Yīshuǐ." This is it.
The Yīshuǐ also meets the Dàjǐshuǐ,
which originates west of Liáng County,
having two sources.
The northern water emerges from Guǎngchéng Marsh,
flows southwest past the north of Yáng Zhì Wù and joins the southern water.
The source of the southern water emerges from Guǎngchéng Marsh in the south,
flows west past the south of Lùhún County.
The *Hénán Twelve Counties Regional Register* states:
"Guǎngchéng Marsh is at Huángfù within the boundaries of Xīnchéng County."
It flows northwest,
bends eastward,
passes south of Yáng Zhì Wù,
then bends north past the east of that fortification,
and again passes north of the fortification,
together pouring into the Lǎodǎo Jiàn,
commonly called the Lǎodǎo Jiànshuǐ,
then flows west into the Yī River.
The Yīshuǐ then flows north past the east of Xīnchéng and meets the Wújiànshuǐ,
which originates from the western mountains of the county,
flows east then bends south,
passes west of the county's old city,
then turns east and passes south of the county,
which was formerly the state of the Mánzǐ.
The county had the settlement of Màn,
now called Mánzhōng.
The county was established in the fourth year of Emperor Huì of Han.
The water then flows northeast
and pours into the Yīshuǐ.
The Yīshuǐ then flows north past the west of Dāngjiē City,
where the Dàkuángshuǐ enters it.
This water originates east from Dàbēn Mountain in Yángchéng County.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"Dàbēn Mountain has much Túfú jade.
On its southern side,
the Kuángshuǐ emerges,
flowing southwest.
In it are many three-legged turtles.
Those who eat them suffer no major illnesses
and can cure swellings."
The Kuángshuǐ then flows west past the south of the old city of Lúnshì County.
The *Bamboo Annals* state:
"Chǔ's Wúdé led troops and, together with Qín, attacked Zhèng and besieged Lúnshì."
It joins the Yǐbóshānshuǐ on the left,
which originates north from Yǐbó Mountain,
flows south past the west of Huáng City,
then south past the east of the old city of Lúnshì County,
and flows south into the Kuángshuǐ.
The Kuángshuǐ flows further west,
where the Bāfēngxīshuǐ pours into it.
This water originates north from Bāfēng Mountain,
flows south past the west of the old city of Lúnshì County,
then southwest into the Kuángshuǐ.
The Kuángshuǐ, flowing further west, reaches the mouth of the Sānjiāoshuǐ.
This water has three sources,
each leading a stream,
all emerging from the mountain, flowing south and converging,
hence the world calls it Sānjiāo (Three Crossings).
On the rocks are sweetflag,
with nine nodes per cùn,
most excellent for medicine.
Taking it long transforms one into an immortal.
The water flows southwest into the Kuángshuǐ.
The Kuángshuǐ then flows west past the north of Fǒugāo Mountain,
southwest joining the Yīnshuǐ.
This water emerges from the Yīn Valley in the northeast,
flows southwest past the northeast of Wǔlín Pavilion,
bends past the south of that pavilion,
then flows southwest past the east of Yīnyáng Pavilion,
likely naming the pavilion after the water,
then flows southeast into the Kuángshuǐ.
The Kuángshuǐ then flows west past the south of Yīnyáng City.
Then west past the south of Dāngjiē City,
and flows west into the Yī River.
The Yīshuǐ flows further north,
where the Tǔgōushuǐ emerges west of Xuánwàng Mountain,
flows east past the south of Xuánwàng Mountain,
then east past the north of the old city of Xīnchéng County,
and flows east into the Yīshuǐ.
The Yīshuǐ flows further north,
where the Bǎnqiáoshuǐ enters it.
This water originates from the western mountains,
flowing east into the Yīshuǐ.
The Yīshuǐ then flows north and meets the Yànjiànshuǐ,
which originates from the western mountains,
flows east past the south of Shěnchuí Pavilion.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒ Tradition*, seventeenth year of Duke Wén,
autumn,
record: "Zhōu's Gān Shuò defeated the Róng at Shěnchuí."
Fú Qián said:
"Shěnchuí is south of Gāodū."
Dù Yù's *Explanations of Places* states:
"North of Xīnchéng County in Hénán is Shěnchuí Pavilion."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
"Xīnchéng has Gāodū City."
Now the pavilion is seven lǐ south of the city,
its foundation remains.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Old accounts say Shěnchuí is south of Gāodū,
now Shàngdǎng has Gāodū County."
I say Jīng's discussion is distant,
insufficient for proof,
not as precise as Fú's explanation.
The water then flows east into the Yīshuǐ.
The Yīshuǐ then flows north past the east of Gāodū City.
Xú Guǎng's *Shǐjì Pronunciation and Meaning* states:
"Now Xīnchéng County in Hénán has Gāodū City."
The *Bamboo Annals* record,
in the seventeenth year of King Huichéng of Liáng,
"Eastern Zhōu and Zhèng benefited from Gāodū."
Also, the Láirúzhīshuǐ emerges from Bànkǒu Mountain,
flows southwest past the north of Bīnlún City,
passes west through Ài Jiàn,
because its water flows west,
it is also called the Xiǎokuángshuǐ.
The water then flows southwest past the south of Dàshí Ridge,
the so-called Dàshí Mountain in the *Chart of Opening Mountains*.
Below the mountain is the *Dàshí Ridge Stele*,
erected by Tōngmíng, a recluse of Hénán,
on the Wùchén day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
at the mountain hall.
The writing is shallow and crude,
nearly illegible.
Emperor Wén of Wèi hunted on this mountain,
a tiger leaped at the imperial carriage,
Sūn Lǐ drew his sword and threw it at the tiger on this mountain.
The mountain is south of Luòyáng,
but Liú Chéng says it is northeast of Luò,
which is incorrect.
In the mountain's recess is the Gāopíng Tomb of Emperor Míng of Wèi.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn History* states:
"Emperor Huì sent Commandant Chén Zǒng, styled Zhòngyuán, to Luòyáng Mountain to pray for rain.
Zǒng abolished all minor sacrifices,
preserving only the great stone and prayed to it.
After seven days, heavy rain fell."
This is the mountain.
The Láirúzhīshuǐ then flows southwest past the south of Chìméi City,
then west to the east of Gāodū City and enters the Yīshuǐ,
called the Qūshuǐ.
It then flows northeast through Yīquè.
The Yī River flows past the west of Qián Pavilion.
In the twenty-second year of Duke Zhāo (520 BCE), as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn,
Jī Yí, Yuè Zhēng, and Yòuháng Guǐ of Jìn led their troops across
and captured Qiánchéng.
Jīng Xiàngfán stated:
"Qián Pavilion is now located fifty lǐ southwest of Luòyáng, outside the Yīquè."
Fú Qián said:
"Qián is pronounced as Quán,
and it is a place in Zhōu."
The Yī River then flows north into the Yīquè.
In ancient times, the Great Yǔ dredged it to allow water passage.
Two mountains stand opposite each other,
appearing like a gate when viewed from afar.
The Yī River flows northward between them,
hence it is called Yīquè,
which is the Què Sài mentioned in the Chūnqiū.
In the twenty-sixth year of Duke Zhāo (516 BCE),
Zhào Yǎng sent Nǚ Kuān to guard Què Sài, referring to this place.
Lù Jī said:
"Luò has four gates,
and this is one of them."
On the eastern cliff and western ridge,
stone caves were carved and pavilions opened.
Tall ridgepoles span the peaks.
Below the western side's Líng Cliff,
a spring flows eastward
and enters the Yī River.
Fù Yì's "Fǎndū Fù" states:
"Through the Dragon Gate, transformation is spread;
by opening the Yīquè, wisdom is reached."
On the left wall of the gate, a stone inscription reads:
"On the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, the xīnsì day, in the fourth year of the Huángchū era (223 CE),
a great flood occurred,
reaching a height of four zhàng and five chǐ,
level with this point and below."
This likely records the rise and fall of the water.
On the right wall, another stone inscription states:
"In the fifth year of the Yuánkāng era (295 CE),
the Governor of Hénán Prefecture, following the path of the Great Yǔ,
dispatched the Inspector Xīn Yào and the Magistrate of Xīnchéng, Wáng Kūn,
along with the Supervising Clerics Dǒng Yī and Lǐ Bāo,
to cut through the banks and open the rock,
clearing and opening the Yīquè.
The stone inscription remains to this day."
Further northeast, it reaches the south of Luòyáng County,
and flows north into the Luò River.
The Yī River flows northeast from the gate,
with a branch channel diverging to the right.
It is channeled northeast for irrigation,
then meets the Héshuǐ to the east,
together flowing into the Gōnglù Jiàn
and entering the Luò River,
though it is now dry.
The Zhànguócè records:
"When Dōngzhōu wanted to farm,
Xīzhōu would not release water.
Sūzǐ went to see the Lord of Xīzhōu and said:
'By not releasing water now,
you are enriching Dōngzhōu,
as the people will plant other crops.
If you wish to impoverish them,
it would be better to release water to harm them.
Dōngzhōu will surely plant rice again,
and once they plant rice, you can seize it again.
Thus, Dōngzhōu will be at your command.'"
Xīzhōu then released the water,
which refers to the old channel of this water.
The Yī River flows further northeast,
with a branch channel diverging to the left.
The water accumulated into a lake,
flowing north into the Luò River,
though it is now dry.
The Yī River flows further northeast to the south of Luòyáng County,
passing east of the Yuánqiū (Circular Mound),
which was built by the Great Wèi for suburban sacrifices to Heaven, following the precedents of the Hàn.
The "Treatise on Suburban Sacrifices" in the Hòuhànshū states:
"In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era (26 CE),
the suburban altar was first established seven lǐ south of Luòyáng.
It was a circular altar with eight steps,
with an inner altar in the center.
The positions of Heaven and Earth were placed atop it,
both facing south.
On the outer altar,
positions for the Five Emperors were arranged above,
and beyond that was the enclosing wall.
The double enclosures were all purple,
to resemble the Purple Palace."
According to the Lǐ,
the Son of Heaven wore a great fur robe and ceremonial cap
to sacrifice to the Vast Heaven and Supreme God here,
but now the dragon robe and crown are used.
The altar enclosures are no longer purple.
The Yī River flows further northeast
and empties into the Luò River.
The Guǎngzhì states:
"The ní fish makes a sound like a child crying,
has four legs,
and a shape like the línglǐ fish.
It can be used to treat cattle
and comes from the Yī River."
Sīmǎ Qiān called it the 'human fish,'
so in his Shǐjì he wrote:
"For the burial of the First Emperor,
human fish oil was used for candles."
Xú Guǎng said:
"The human fish resembles a catfish but has four legs,
which is the ní fish."
15.3 Chán River
15.3 Chán River
The Chán River originates from the northern mountains of Gǔchéng County in Hénán.
North of the county is Qián Pavilion.
The Chán River emerges from the north of Zǐzé,
Zǐzé
being a place name.
North of the marsh, facing the elevated plain,
is where the Péi family cemetery is located,
with steles and gate towers still present.
The water flows southeast through the marsh.
To the west of the water is an elevated plain,
level and open on top,
the site of the ancient Qián Pavilion.
This is what Pān Ānrén referred to in his "Xīzhēng Fù" as crossing the street relay station.
To the east, it joins the Qiānjīn Canal.
The Zhōushū states:
"We divined west of the Chán River,"
referring to this water.
It flows southeast,
and southwest of the water is the tomb of Bó Zhònglǐ.
In front of the tomb is a stele,
inscribed:
"Stele of the True Man, Lord Bó."
Zhònglǐ's given name was Hù,
a native of Bā Commandery in Yìzhōu.
Erected in the eleventh month of the second year of the Yǒngníng era (302 CE).
The Chán River flows further southeast
and empties into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River flows east from the Qiānjīn Dam,
which is called the Qiānjīn Canal.
Further east, it passes south of Luòyáng County,
then east past Yǎnshī County,
and finally east into the Luò River.
15.4 Jiàn River
15.4 Jiàn River
The Jiàn River originates from Báishí Mountain south of Xīn'ān County.
The Shānhǎijīng states:
"From Báishí Mountain,
the Huì River emerges from its southern side,
flowing southeast into the Luò River.
The Jiàn River emerges from its northern side,
flowing north into the Gǔ River."
This mountain is commonly called Guǎngyáng Mountain,
and the water is called Chì'àn Water,
also known as Shízǐ Jiàn.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
"The Jiàn River is in Xīn'ān County,
flowing southeast into the Luò River."
This is accurate.
It flows northeast past the eastern slope east of Hángǔ,
called Bātè Slope.
It then flows southeast into the Luò River.
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"The Jiàn River originates from Miǎnchí Mountain."
Now, northwest of Xīn'ān County, there is a river
that emerges from the Miǎnchí border to the north,
flows southeast past Xīn'ān County,
and then southeast into the Gǔ River.
What Ānguó referred to must be this water.
However, the Gǔ River originates from Miǎnchí,
and downstream it joins the Jiàn River,
sharing the same name.
Thus, it may also be referred to as the Jiàn River.
This is not entirely clear.
Now, ten lǐ east of Xiàoshuǐ, there is a river
commonly called Cíjiàn,
also known as the Jiàn River.
According to the Shānhǎijīng, this is actually Shǎoshuǐ,
not the Jiàn River,
likely a customary error.
Also, in Hénán, there is Líshān Water,
called the Jiàn River.
This water emerges northwest from Lí Mountain,
flows southeast past Jiá Mountain,
and south of Gǔchéng County, it flows east into the Gǔ River.
It originally flowed together with the Gǔ River
and entered the Luò River to the south.
Now, the Gǔ River flows east into the Qiānjīn Canal,
and the Jiàn River flows with it,
entering the Luò River to the east.
Some believe this water was also divined by the Duke of Zhōu.
Lǚ Chén said:
"Now, in Hénán, there is a dead water,
which may be this river."
However, the meaning is unclear,
so it is recorded here for reference.
16 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 16
16.1 Gǔ Shuǐ
16.1 Gǔ Shuǐ
The Gǔ Shuǐ originates from the Gǔyáng Valley in Fánzhǒng Forest, south of Miǎnchí County in Hóngnóng.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
West of Fù Mountain there is a forest,
called Fánzhǒng.
The Gǔ River originates there,
flows eastward and empties into the Luò River,
and within it are many jūn jades.
Today, the Gǔ River originates from the Gǔyáng Valley on Mǎtóu Mountain east of Qiānxiáo,
flows northeast past the Miǎnchí Plain,
which was originally the territory of Zhōngxiāng.
In the second year of the Zhōngyuán era of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
a city was first built here,
and ten thousand households were relocated to establish a county,
which was named after the Miǎnchí of Xiáo.
It is also sometimes called Péngchí.
Thus, Xú Guǎng's Shǐjì Yīnyì states:
"Miǎn"
is sometimes written as "Péng,"
and this is the source of the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the south of the two cities of Qín and Zhào.
Sīmǎ Biāo's Xù Hànshū states:
"The Red Eyebrows, coming from Miǎnchí and Zìlìyáng to the south,
intended to head toward Yíyáng."
People call this place the Jùlì City.
Elders say:
In the past, during the meeting between Qín and Zhào,
each occupied one city.
The King of Qín made the King of Zhào play the sè,
and Lìn Xiàngrú forced the King of Qín to strike the fǒu here.
Féng Yì also defeated the Red Eyebrows on this plain.
Thus, Emperor Guāngwǔ's Imperial Edict states:
"Though initially they drooped their wings at Huíxī,
in the end they soared at Miǎnchí."
This can be said to be "losing in the east,
but gaining in the west."
The Gǔ River then flows east past the north of Tǔxiáo,
which is what is called the Sānxiáo.
The Gǔ River continues east,
where it joins the North Stream on the left.
The stream originates from Miǎnchí Mountain to the north,
flows southeast, and empties into the Gǔ River.
It is suspected to be the Jiàn River mentioned by Kǒng Ānguó.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the old city south of Xīn'ān County,
with the north flanked by the flow and the west connecting to Xiáomiǎn.
In the past, when Xiàng Yǔ entered Qín from the west,
he buried alive two hundred thousand surrendered soldiers here.
It is fitting that
his state perished and he met his end.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the south of the Qiānqiū Pavilion.
The pavilion's walls are built of piled stones,
and people call it the Qiānqiū City.
Pān Yuè's "Xī Zhēng Fù" states:
"The pavilion bears the name of 'a thousand autumns,'
but my son did not live to seventy days."
He was referring to this pavilion.
It then flows east past the Yōnggǔ Stream,
where winding ridges twist and turn,
and the stone path is obstructed by a gorge,
hence it is also called the Xiáshí.
The Gǔ River passes alongside,
and on the left, it merges with the North Plain River.
The river has two sources,
both originating from the North Mountain,
flowing southeast to combine into one stream,
entering from the northwest to the southeast,
and emptying into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River then flows east past Quēmén Mountain.
The mountain ridge is disconnected for over a li,
hence it got this name.
Two cliffs vie for height,
towering steeply and chaotically,
looking west at the twin peaks,
the right appears as level as a whetstone.
The Gǔ River flows east from the gate,
and the Guǎngyáng Plain River empties into it.
The water originates from the north of Guǎngyáng Mountain,
flows southeast, and empties into the Gǔ River.
Looking south at Wēi Mountain,
clouds and peaks intermingle chaotically.
The Gǔ River then flows past the south of the Báichāo Fortress.
Dài Yánzhī's Xī Zhēng Jì states:
"Next, we arrived at the Báichāo Fortress,
fifteen li from Hángǔ.
The fortress was built facing the main road,
with mountains standing on both sides,
about a hundred paces apart.
Going north from between them,
is the old pass city,
not what is called the Báichāo Fortress."
This fortress is fifteen li east of Quēmén,
and beside the fortress, there was formerly an earthen fort,
which was the site of the old ironworks.
During the Wèi and Jìn periods,
the Gǔ River was diverted for water-powered ironworks,
to supply the state's needs,
and the ruins still remain.
The Gǔ River continues east,
and the Shímò Stream originates from the eastern foothills of Wēi Mountain at Shímò Stream,
flowing northeast into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River then flows east,
and the Sòng River flows north into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the south of the tomb of Mǔqiū Xīng, the Wèi General of Works,
where two steles remain.
He was the father of Guànqiū Jiǎn.
The Guǎn Lù Biézhuàn states:
Lù once followed the army on a western campaign,
passed by his tomb and sighed,
saying to his scholarly friends:
"The Black Tortoise hides its head,
the Azure Dragon has no feet,
the White Tiger holds a corpse,
the Vermilion Bird weeps mournfully.
With these four perils all present,
it is fated that the clan will be exterminated."
Indeed, it turned out as he said.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the south of Hángǔ Pass,
turns northeast,
and the Zàojiàn River empties into it.
The water originates from Xīn'ān County,
flows southeast past the east of Mǔqiū Xīng's tomb,
then south past the west of Hángǔ Pass.
The pass is high, perilous, and narrow,
with the road emerging from the outskirts of the city.
In the third year of the Yuándǐng era of Hàn,
General of Tower Ships Yáng Pǔ, having achieved many great merits,
was ashamed to live outside the pass,
requested to use seven hundred of his household servants
to build fortifications and move the pass to Xīn'ān.
This is the place.
In the past, Guō Dān entered the pass from the west,
and sighed with emotion below it, saying:
"Unless I ride in a high carriage drawn by four horses,
I will never leave this pass."
After leaving home for twelve years,
he indeed achieved his ambition.
The Zàojiàn River then flows east into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River then flows northeast past the east of Hángǔ Pass City,
and on the right, joins the Shuǎng River.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Fifty li west of Báishí Mountain is Gǔ Mountain,
with many paper mulberry trees on its summit,
and many mulberry trees below.
The Shuǎng River originates there."
People call it the Zhùmá Stream,
flowing north into the Gǔ River,
and within it are many green jades.
The Gǔ River continues east,
and the Jiàn River empties into it.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Forty li west of Lóuzhuō Mountain is Báishí Mountain,
and the Jiàn River originates there,
flowing north into the Gǔ River."
Zhì Zhòngzhì's Sānfǔ Juélù Zhù states:
"The five Mǎ brothers
lived together at the confluence of the Jiàn and Gǔ Rivers,
and built five guest gates,
hence naming their residence after it."
Now it is forty li west of Hénán.
Comparing with The Classic of Mountains and Seas,
the distance matches what Zhòngzhì recorded,
and at the confluence, the old residence still exists.
This is indeed the Jiàn River,
which is what the Zhōushū refers to as "we divined east of the Jiàn River."
It speaks of this river.
From here downward, the Jiàn River is commonly referred to as the Gǔ River as well.
Thus, the Shàngshū states:
"The Yī, Luò, Chán, and Jiàn
all flow into the Hé River."
But it does not mention the Gǔ River by name,
indicating that the names are interchangeable.
Liú Chéngzhī states:
"Xīn'ān has the Jiàn River,
originating north of the county,
and also has the Yuān River,
but its source is unknown."
I have examined various geographical records,
and none mention a Yuān River.
However, the characters for "yuān" and "jiàn" are similar,
and sometimes "jiàn" was mistakenly written as "yuān."
Thus, Kuài Yīn's Dìlǐ Zhì states:
"The Yuān River in the Yǔgòng
is thus known to be a transcription error,
with characters mistaken and truth distorted.
Chéngzhī failed to consider this."
Since there is no such river,
how can one seek its source?
The Gǔ River continues east,
and the Bō River empties into it.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Thirty li west of Zhānzhū Mountain is Lóuzhuō Mountain,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant metal and jade.
The Bō River originates from its northern side,
and people call it the Bǎidá River.
It flows north into the Gǔ River,
and within it are many zǐ stones and patterned stones."
The Gǔ River continues east,
and the Shǎo River empties into it.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Thirty li west of Guī Mountain is Zhānzhū Mountain,
On its southern side there is much gold,
on its northern side there is much patterned stone,
and a small stream emerges from its northern side.
It draws in and channels numerous brooks,
accumulating them to form a river,
which flows eastward and empties into the Gǔ River,
and it is commonly called the Cí Jiàn.
The Gǔ River flows further east,
and the Yúsuí River flows into it.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
Ten lǐ west of Píngpéng Mountain is Guī Mountain,
on its southern side there is much Tūfú jade,
and the Yúsuí River emerges from its northern side,
flowing northward and emptying into the Gǔ River.
It is commonly called the Xiào River.
Pān Yuè’s *Xīzhēng Fù* says:
"I bathed in the Xiào River to wash my hat strings,
praising the fine name that lies here."
This river is over ten lǐ west of Hénán City,
so Lǚ Chēn said:
"The Xiào River is in Hénán."
However, Dài Yánzhī claims it is west of Hángǔ Pass.
Liú Chéngzhī further says it emerges from Tán Mountain.
Tán Mountain is west of Yíyáng County,
south of the Gǔ River,
so there is no reason for it to flow southward.
Examining and tracing these claims,
they likely stem from erroneous records in Yuán Shēng’s *Shùzhēng*.
Yuán Shēng traveled as a soldier,
inquiring along the journey,
and since it was not his native land,
he had no way to investigate thoroughly.
Now the river flows northward,
clear and reflecting, with muddy banks—
how could one say it is dried up?
All these accounts are inaccurate and far-fetched.
It passes northeast of Gǔchéng County to the north,
with the county seat bordering the Gǔ River to the west,
hence the county derives its name from it.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the south of Gǔchéng,
not passing its north,
and further east,
a branch of the Luò River flows into it,
though now there is no water.
It then passes north of Hénán County to the east,
and flows southeast into the Luò River.
To the northwest of the King's City in Hénán,
on the right side of the Gǔshuǐ River, there is a rocky shoal.
To the south of the shoal emerges the Dead Valley,
and to the north emerges the Lake Channel.
In the fourth year of the Tàihé era of the Wèi dynasty,
a sudden flood raised the water level by three zhàng,
and this low-lying area retained the water, forming a lake and islets.
A channel was constructed to drain the water,
stretching ten lǐ from east to west,
and the lake was breached to channel water into the Chánshuǐ River.
The Gǔshuǐ River again passes to the northwest of the King's City in Hénán,
which is what is called Chéngzhōu.
The Gōngyáng Commentary says:
What is Chéngzhōu?
It is the Eastern Zhōu.
Hé Xiū states:
It is named Chéngzhōu because
the way of Zhōu was first completed here,
and it was the capital of the king.
The Treatise on Geography says:
Hénán County in Hénán
was originally the land of Jiá and Rǔ.
Jīng Xiàngfán says:
Jiá is the name of a mountain;
Rǔ is the name of a settlement.
Divination determined the years and the tripods were set,
establishing the eastern capital of the king,
called the New City,
which is the King's City.
The southeastern gate of this city is called the Tripod Gate,
likely because the Nine Tripods entered through here,
hence this area is called the Center of the Tripods.
When the Viscount of Chǔ attacked the Róng of Lùhún,
he inquired about the tripods here.
The Record of Military Campaigns says:
The Gǔ and Luò rivers
originally converged to the northeast of the King's City,
which is called the clash of the Gǔ and Luò.
Today, there is a gap of a thousand paces to the southeast of the city,
and people also call it the site of the clash of the Gǔ and Luò,
but both are incorrect.
I have examined historical records:
During the time of King Líng of Zhōu,
the Gǔ and Luò rivers clashed and destroyed the royal palace.
The king intended to block them,
but Crown Prince Jìn admonished the king,
who did not listen.
