The remnants of the three dikes still exist.
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xiāng in the Zuǒzhuàn,
the people of Qí fortified Jiá,
and Mù Shū went to Zhōu to offer congratulations.
Wéi Zhāo states:
The Luò River flows south of the King's City,
and the Gǔ River flows north of the King's City,
entering the Chán River to the east.
By the time of King Líng,
the Gǔ River surged out to the west of the King's City
and flowed south to merge with the Luò River.
The two rivers opposed each other,
resembling a clash,
and destroyed the southwestern part of the King's City.
Yǐng Róng, in his Regulations of the Spring and Autumn Annals, states:
The dry water area at the Liáng Gate of the western city
is what people call the Dead Valley.
Only then did I realize that Yuánshēng, in his hasty travels,
entered the passes and studied the old accounts,
but they contradicted reality.
King Kǎo enfeoffed Duke Huán of Zhōu here as Western Zhōu,
and by the time of his grandson, Duke Huì,
he enfeoffed his youngest son in Gǒng as Eastern Zhōu,
hence the names Eastern and Western Zhōu.
When Qín destroyed Zhōu,
it established the Sānchuān Commandery.
Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed Shēn Yáng as the King of Hénán.
The Hàn dynasty established it as Hénán Commandery,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Bǎozhōngxìn Qīng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ made Luòyáng his capital,
establishing it as the Yǐn.
Yǐn
means to rectify,
overseeing and rectifying the capital region,
and setting an example for all commanderies.
The Gǔshuǐ River flows east and passes north of the Gānjì Gate,
which was opened by Jìn
during the rebellion of Zǐ Cháo.
It extends east to the Qiānjīn Dam.
The Register of the Twelve Counties of Hénán says:
Fifteen lǐ east of Hénán County's city lies the Qiānjīn Dam.
The Records of Luòyáng says:
The Qiānjīn Dam originally dammed the Gǔshuǐ River.
During the Wèi period, this dam was repaired,
and it was called the Qiānjīn Dam.
Stones were piled to build the dam, and five channels were opened,
called the Five Dragon Channels.
A dam was erected above the channels,
and at the eastern end of the dam,
a stone figure was erected.
Inscribed on the belly of the stone figure are the words:
"On the eighth day of the second month in the fifth year of Tàihé, the gēngxū day, this dam was constructed.
Channels were opened here, and this water balanced the channels above.
The water helped solidify it,
and it must endure for years and generations.
Therefore, a stone figure was erected to record this."
This was likely Emperor Míng of Wèi continuing the legacy of Wáng and Zhāng.
The dam was built by Chén Xié, the Commissioner of Waterways.
The Forest of Sayings says:
Chén Xié often offered wine to Ruǎn Bùbīng.
Later, when King Wén of Jìn wanted to repair the Nine Dragon Dam,
Ruǎn recommended Xié,
and King Wén employed him.
Six ancient bronze water dragons were excavated from the ground,
and the dam was completed.
The water passed east of the dam,
called the Qiānjīn Channel.
By the time of the Jìn dynasty,
a great flood suddenly poured in,
damaging the channels and ditches,
and extensive repairs were undertaken.
The inscription below the eastern flank of the stone figure says:
"On the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the seventh year of Tàishǐ,
a great flood surged violently,
rising three zhàng above the normal flow,
destroying two dams.
The Five Dragons discharged water,
flowing south and pouring down.
Over the years, erosion worsened,
and every flood caused damage.
Over the years, great efforts were wasted.
Now, to prevent further blockage,
a new discharge channel was opened to the west,
named the Dàilóng Channel.
The terrain is level and even,
making it ideal for discharge.
The Qiānjīn Dam does not contend fiercely with the water's force,
so it is unlikely to be damaged.
However, due to its low elevation,
water can overflow and erode it.
Now, the Qiānjīn Dam has been raised by one zhàng and four chǐ from its original height,
ensuring the Five Dragons will endure for generations without trouble.
If the Five Dragons deteriorate over time,
two more dams and channels can be opened to the west.
This would require a total of 235,698 workdays.
Construction began on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of that year.
The work was heavy, and laborers were few,
so it was completed on the twentieth day of the fourth month in the eighth year.
The Dàilóng Channel is the Nine Dragon Channel.
Later, when Zhāng Fāng entered Luòyáng,
he destroyed the Qiānjīn Dam.
In the early years of Yǒngjiā,
Lǐ Jǔ, the Grand Administrator of Rǔyīn, and Yuán Fú, the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán, repaired it
to facilitate water transport,
benefiting both public and private interests.
Over the years, the channels and dams deteriorated,
and the stonework was nearly exhausted.
The remnants of the foundation still exist.
During the Tàihé era, the court restored the old dam.
According to the inscription below the western flank of the stone figure at the Qiānjīn Dam:
"If the channels remain blocked for long,
those who wish to draw water deeply should, north of Hénán City and west of the rocky shoal,
open a new channel flowing north,
directing it toward Húqiū.
The old channel flows eastward,
and following the old route is easier due to the firmness of the shoal.
When the work is completed in due time,
it will become evident.
However, as border affairs are numerous,
and labor is scarce,
and the channels and dams are newly built,
they are not yet threatened by water,
so we dare not preemptively repair and open them.
If future efforts are to be made,
they should focus on the western shoal.
Therefore, this is recorded in stone
to leave for later generations of wise individuals."
Although the rocky shoal has deteriorated,
the old traces can still be relied upon.
Based on the text,
a channel was led north and joined the old watercourse to the east.
The old watercourse continues east,
and Emperor Huì of Jìn built a stone bridge over the water.
According to the inscription on the southern cheek of the western gate of the bridge,
it states: "On the twentieth day of the eleventh month in the second year of Yuánkāng of Jìn,
the stone lane and water gate were repaired.
The vertical beams were removed,
replaced with box beams,
and covered beams were erected.
Steps were added in front and behind, and stone barriers were installed continuously,
allowing entry from the north and south banks.
The eroded areas were repaired,
and stones were broken to create slopes."
The work was completed on the fifteenth day of the third month in the third year.
The width, length, and depth of the gate and lanes were recorded on both sides.
The east-west length is seven chǐ,
the north-south width of the dragon tail is twelve zhàng,
and the height of the lane and ditch opening is three zhàng.
This is called the Gāomén Bridge.
Pān Yuè, in his "Rhapsody on a Western Journey," wrote:
"I halted my horse at Gāomén."
This is the very place.
The Gǔshuǐ River flows further east,
Another stone bridge was constructed,
spanning the water to control the city.
This is the Western Bridge.
The Gǔ Shuǐ (Valley River) flows eastward again,
and on the left, it meets the Jīngǔ Shuǐ (Golden Valley River).
The water originates from Tàibái Yuán (Great White Plain),
flowing southeast past Jīngǔ (Golden Valley),
and is thus called Jīngǔ Shuǐ (Golden Valley River).
It flows southeast past the former residence of Shí Chóng, the Jìn dynasty Wèiwèiqīng (Commandant of the Guards).
Shí Jìlún (Shí Chóng) wrote in the preface to his *Jīngǔ Shījí* (Golden Valley Poetry Collection):
"In the seventh year of Yuánkāng (297 CE),
I left the position of Tàipú (Grand Coachman) to become Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Subdues the Caitiffs).
I had a separate residence within the boundaries of Hénán, in the Jīngǔ Jiàn (Golden Valley Ravine).
There were clear springs and lush trees,
with an abundance of fruit trees, bamboo, cypress, and medicinal plants.
The Jīngǔ Shuǐ (Golden Valley River) then flows southeast into the Gǔ Shuǐ (Valley River).
The Gǔ Shuǐ (Valley River) flows east past the north of Jīnyōng Chéng (Golden Rampart City).
Emperor Míng of the Wèi dynasty built it at the northwestern corner of Luòyáng City,
and it was called Jīnyōng Chéng (Golden Rampart City).
A multi-story tower was erected at the northeastern corner.
The *Jìn Gōnggé Míng* (Record of Jìn Palaces and Pavilions) states:
"Jīnyōng has a Chóngtiān Táng (Hall of Venerating Heaven),"
which is this very one.
A wooden pavilion was built atop the structure,
hence it was also called the White Tower.
When the imperial residence was first relocated,
and the palace complex was not yet completed,
the emperor halted his carriage here.
A night pavilion was constructed upon the old terrace,
which is what is meant by 'the terrace for pausing the carriage.'
To the south was the Qiánguāng Mén (Gate of Drying Light),
flanked by two watchtowers.
Below the watchtowers, a vermilion bridge spanned the moat,
serving as the imperial road.
To the east was the Hánchūn Mén (Gate Embracing Spring).
To the north was a retreat gate.
On the western side of the city wall were watchtowers,
with battlements every fifty paces.
On the roof platform, a bell was placed to harmonize with the water clock and drums.
To the northwest, connected corridors provided shade,
with walls lining broad pavilions.
During the sweltering summer days,
the emperor would often ascend here to escape the heat.
There was also a green water pool,
located within Jīnyōng.
The Gǔ Shuǐ (Valley River) flows past the north of Luòyáng's small city,
which relied on the old city's terrain,
and was connected to Jīnyōng,
hence it was called the Xiàng Chéng (Facing City).
During the turmoil of Yǒngjiā,
it was fortified into a stronghold,
called the Luòyáng Stronghold.
Therefore, the *Luòyáng Jì* (Record of Luòyáng) states:
"West of Língyún Tái (Soaring Cloud Terrace) is the Jīn Shì (Golden Market),
and north of the Jīn Shì (Golden Market) faces the Luòyáng Stronghold."
Further east, it passes beneath Dàxià Mén (Great Summer Gate),
which was the former Xià Mén (Summer Gate).
Lù Jī wrote in his *Letter to His Younger Brother*:
"The gate has three layers,
reaching a height of one hundred chǐ.
It was built by Emperor Míng of Wèi.
Inside the gate, on the eastern side,
along the city wall, is Jǐngyáng Shān (Sunny Mountain) built by Emperor Míng of Wèi,
and its remaining foundations are still present."
Sūn Shèng's *Wèi Chūnqiū* (Annals of Wèi) states:
"In the first year of Jǐngchū (237 CE),
Emperor Míng further enhanced the palaces with carved decorations and viewing towers.
He obtained white quartz, purple quartz, and large stones of five colors from the Tàiháng Gǔchéng mountains,
and erected Jǐngyáng Shān (Sunny Mountain) in the Fānglín Yuán (Fragrant Forest Garden).
Pine, bamboo, trees, and grasses were planted,
and birds and beasts were captured to fill it.
At that time, numerous labor projects flourished,
and the emperor personally dug the earth,
leading all officials down to the Sāngōng (Three Excellencies),
none of whom failed to exert their strength.
East of the mountain,
there was formerly the Jiǔjiāng (Nine Rivers).
Lù Jī's *Luòyáng Jì* (Record of Luòyáng) states:
"The Jiǔjiāng (Nine Rivers) were made into circular waterways.
In the water, three circular altars were built, breaking the flow,
allowing passage between them along the water."
The *Dōngjīng Fù* (Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital) says:
"At Zhuólóng (Washed Dragon) and Fānglín (Fragrant Forest),
with nine valleys and eight streams,
lotus covers the water,
and autumn orchids clothe the banks."
But now,
the mountain stands alone as a mere mound.
Of the rivers, not even a trace remains.
The Gǔ Shuǐ (Valley River) flows east again,
and a branch splits off south into Huálín Yuán (Flowery Forest Garden).
It passes south of Shū Pǔ (Sparse Garden),
within which is an ancient jade well.
The well is entirely made of mǐn jade,
with a black stone rim.
The craftsmanship is exquisite,
and though ancient,
it remains dazzlingly new.
It then flows south of Yáohuá Gōng (Jade Flower Palace),
and north of Jǐngyáng Shān (Sunny Mountain).
On the mountain is a capital pavilion hall, atop which a square lake was formed,
and in the lake, a royal seat stone was erected.
Before the royal seat, Pénglái Shān (Penglai Mountain) was constructed.
Winding pools reached the banquet mats,
and flying streams brushed the seats.
Facing south were archery targets,
flanking the mats, standing martial and imposing.
Behind the mountain hall,
the stone paths were rugged,
the cliffs steep and perilous.
Cloud terraces and wind-viewing towers,
encircled ridges and girded hills.
Visitors ascended and descended through multi-storied pavilions,
entering and exiting via rainbow stairways,
appearing from a distance like ducks diving or phoenixes soaring.
Within, water was channeled to flying banks,
creating cascading torrents and waterfalls.
Sometimes it wound through islets with murmuring rivulets,
gurgling incessantly.
Bamboo and cypress shaded layered rocks,
and embroidered thickets clustered by the springs.
When a gentle breeze briefly stirred,
fragrance filled the six directions of space,
truly a divine abode.
The water flows east into Tiānyuān Chí (Heavenly Abyss Pool).
In the pool is Emperor Wén of Wèi's Jiǔhuá Tái (Nine Splendors Terrace).
The hall's foundation was entirely built from old steles accumulated from Luòyáng,
and now a fishing terrace has been constructed atop it.
South of the pool stands straight Emperor Wén of Wèi's Máocí Táng (Thatched Hall),
before which is the *Máocí Bēi* (Thatched Hall Stele),
erected during the Huángchū era.
The water exits Huálín Yuán (Flowery Forest Garden) east from Tiāyuān Chí (Heavenly Abyss Pool),
flowing south of Tīngsòng Guān (Hall for Hearing Litigation),
which was formerly Píngwàng Guān (Terrace for Gazing Afar).
Emperor Míng of Wèi often said,
"Legal cases
are the lifeblood of the empire."
Whenever major cases were adjudicated,
he would often visit the hall to listen.
In the third year of Tàihé (229 CE),
it was renamed to its current name.
Northwest of the hall connects to Huálín (Flowery Forest),
where the convict registry office was located, formerly the place where Liú Zhēn ground stones.
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* (Biographies of Literary Men) states:
"When Emperor Wén was still Crown Prince,
he feasted various literary scholars.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he ordered Empress Zhēn to come out and greet them.
All those seated prostrated themselves,
except Liú Zhēn, who looked at her directly.
Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) considered this disrespectful
and sent him to the convict registry office.
Later, Tàizǔ rode a step-pulled carriage up the city wall
and descended to inspect the convict labor.
All the convicts showed respect,
but Zhēn remained seated defiantly,
grinding a stone without moving.
Tàizǔ said:
'Is this not Liú Zhēn?
How can a stone be so stubborn?'
Zhēn replied:
'The stone comes from beneath the dark cliffs of Jīng Shān (Jīng Mountain).
Externally, it displays the pattern of five colors;
internally, it holds a firm and steadfast will.
Carving it does not increase its markings;
grinding it does not add to its luster.
It receives a pure and upright essence,
its nature is entirely natural.'
Tàizǔ said:
'Is its fame then unfounded?'
And restored him to the literary academy."
The pool water then flows east into the southern pond of Luòyáng County.
This pond
is the former Dí Quán (Di Spring).
It measures one hundred and ten paces north-south,
and seventy paces east-west.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
"King Dào buried King Jǐng at Dí Quán (Di Spring),
which is the large mound within Luòyáng's Tàicāng (Great Granary)."
In the first year of Duke Dìng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (509 BCE),
Jìn's Wèi Xiànzǐ assembled the ministers of the various feudal lords at Dí Quán (Di Spring),
to begin the covenant to fortify Zhōu's capital.
Bān Gù, Fú Qián, and Huángfǔ Mì all stated that Dí Quán (Di Spring) was northeast of Luòyáng,
within the burial grounds of the Zhōu dynasty.
Now, it is verified that King Wēiliè of Zhōu was buried in the northeastern corner inside Luòyáng city,
King Jǐng's mound is within Luòyáng's Tàicāng (Great Granary),
and Dí Quán (Di Spring) lies between these two mounds,
beside the road east of Guǎngmò Mén (Gate of Vast Solitude),
north of the road to Jiànchūn Mén (Gate Establishing Spring).
This road
is the Dōnggōng Jiē (Eastern Palace Street),
which is to the northeast within Luòyáng.
Later, the Qín state enfeoffed Lǚ Bùwéi as Marquis of Luòyáng with a fief of one hundred thousand households.
He enlarged the city,
and it then encompassed King Jǐng's mound,
which is indeed within the burial grounds.
In the first year of Jìn's Yǒngjiā era (307 CE),
the ground at Bùguǎng Lǐ (Broad Step Lane) northeast of Luòyáng collapsed,
and two geese emerged.
The azure-colored one flew soaring into the sky.
The white one stopped there.
Dǒng Yǎng, a Filial and Incorrupt candidate from Chénliú, said:
Bùguǎng
was the Díquán of the Zhōu,
a place of alliances and meetings.
Now its color is greenish and chaotic in appearance;
can it be fully described?
Five years later,
Liú Yào and Wáng Mí entered Luòyáng,
and the emperor resided in Píngyáng.
Lù Jī’s “Record of Luòyáng” states:
Bùguǎng Lane was within the walls of Luòyáng city.
East of the palace was where Díquán was located;
it was not southwest of the Tàicāng Granary.
Jīng Xiàngfán, together with Minister of Works Péi Yànjì, compiled the “Map of Jìn Territories”
and wrote “Geographical Names of the Spring and Autumn Period,”
also stating that the pond southwest of the Tàicāng Granary was named Díquán.
He further said:
According to an old account, Díquán was originally north of Luòyáng in Chánghóng City,
and Chéngzhōu was built around it.
Dù Yù, relying on one piece of evidence,
asserted it must be Díquán, but in reality it was not.
Later it became the Eastern Palace pond.
The Jìn “Record of the Central Provinces” states:
When Emperor Huì was crown prince,
he went out and heard the sound of frogs.
He asked whether they were official frogs or private frogs.
Attendant Jiǎ Yìn replied:
Those on official land are official frogs;
those on private land are private frogs.
The prince ordered:
If they are official frogs,
they may be given provisions.
Previously there had been a prophecy:
Frogs shall become noble.
In the past, the Jìn court detained Crown Prince Mǐnhuái in the rear pond,
which was this pond.
One watercourse flows east from the Dàxià Gate past the Xuānwǔ Tower,
which was built against the city wall,
without adding additional walls.
On both sides were rows of covered walkways,
unevenly arranged like wings.
To the south one could see the Tiānyuān Pond,
to the north overlooked the Xuānwǔ Parade Ground.
“Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove” states:
Wáng Róng was elegant and handsome from childhood.
Emperor Míng of Wèi had cages for tigers set up on the Xuānwǔ Parade Ground,
and made strong men bare their torsos
to wrestle with them in turn,
allowing the common people to watch.
Wáng Róng, then seven years old,
also went to watch.
A tiger seized the moment to press against the cage and roar,
its sound shaking the ground.
All the spectators were startled and fell over,
but Wáng Róng stood calmly unmoved.
The emperor, seeing him from the gate tower,
sent someone to ask his name and was greatly impressed.
West of the parade ground was the former residence site of Jiǎ Chōng.
The Gǔ River flows east again past the north of the Guǎngmò Gate,
which was the Gǔ Gate of the Hàn.
To the north it faces the Máng Hills,
a continuous range stretching long,
encompassing all the mountains,
starting from the Luòkǒu,
extending west past Píngyīn—all are the Máng ridges.
“Records of the Wèi” states:
Emperor Míng wanted to level the Northern Máng Hills,
so that from the tower one could see Mèngjīn.
Attendant-in-Chief Xīn Pí remonstrated:
If the Nine Rivers overflow and surge,
and floods cause disaster,
with all the hills leveled,
how could we defend against it?
The emperor then stopped.
The Gǔ River turns east then south,
flowing under the stone bridge at the Jiànchūn Gate,
which was the Shàngdōng Gate.
Ruǎn Sìzōng’s “Poem of Cherishing Thoughts” says:
“I walk out of the Shàngdōng Gate.”
Also called the Shàngshēng Gate,
in Jìn times called the Jiànyáng Gate.
“Treatise on the Hundred Officials” states:
Luòyáng had twelve gates,
each gate had one guard officer,
with a salary of six hundred shi.
“Eastern Observatory Records of the Hàn” states:
Zhì Yùn was the guard officer of the Shàngdōng Gate.
Emperor Guāngwǔ once went out
and returned at night, ordering the gate opened to enter.
Zhì Yùn would not admit him.
The emperor ordered him to recognize his face through the gate crack.
Zhì Yùn said:
“The torchlight is distant and unclear.”
He thus refused to open,
and from this the emperor esteemed him even more.
This was also where Yuán Běnchū hung his official tally.
At the head of the bridge stand two stone pillars.
The “Inscription on the Right Pillar” of the bridge says:
In the fourth year of Yángjiā, on the yǐyǒu day of the rénshēn month,
an imperial edict ordered that the canal under the city wall,
connecting east to the Hé and Jì Rivers,
and drawing south from the Jiāng and Huái Rivers,
through which tribute and supplies
arrive,
be overseen by Palace Attendant Mǎ Xiàn of Qīngyuān, Wèi Commandery, to supervise the construction of the stone bridge’s beams and pillars.
He strictly commanded the craftsmen to employ the utmost skill and ingenuity,
erecting layered stones,
piling them high and spanning the distance.
The bridge work is extensive, the road broad,
facilitating flow for ten thousand li, and so on.
Governor of Hénán Pī Chóngwéi, Assistant Bóhǎi Hézhòng Shuāngfú, Water Official Rèn Fǎng of Zhōngmóu, Clerks Wáng Yìn and Zhào Xīng, Construction Official Shēn Xiáng of Suīyáng,
Road and Bridge Official Bēi Guó of Chénggāo,
Magistrate of Luòyáng Jiāng Shuāng,
Assistant Píngyáng Jiàng, Supervisor Official Wáng Téngzhī,
Chief Stoneworker Shān Zhòng of Yòuběipíng,
began work in the third month,
completed in the eighth month.
The water follows the pillar,
then from Lèlǐ Road turns east and emerges at the Yáng Canal.
In the past, Lù Jī, serving as Chéngdū King Yǐng, entered Luòyáng but was defeated and returned.
South of the water was the Horse Market;
old Luòyáng had three markets,
this was one of them.
It was also where Jī Shūyè was killed by Sīmǎ Zhāo.
To the north was the old neighborhood of Báishè.
In the past, Sūn Zǐjīng met Dǒng Wēiniǎn at Báishè,
referring to this place.
He considered sharing a carriage with him an honor,
hence there is a “Picture of Wēiniǎn.”
Further east it passes the stone bridge at the Horse Market.
South of the bridge are two stone pillars,
both without inscriptions.
When the Hàn Minister of Works, Wáng Liáng of Yúyáng, served as Governor of Hénán,
he planned to divert the Gǔ River to irrigate the capital.
The canal was completed but water did not flow,
so he was dismissed from his post.
Later, Zhāng Chún dammed the Luò River to facilitate water transport,
and both public and private sectors in Luòyáng prospered abundantly.
This canal now draws water from the Gǔ River,
likely Zhāng Chún’s creation.
According to Lù Jī’s “Record of Luòyáng” and Liú Chéngzhī’s “Record of Yǒngchū,”
on the west side of the city was the Yáng Canal,
constructed by the Duke of Zhōu.
In the past, the Zhōu relocated the people of Yīn to Luòyì.
The city walls were cramped and narrow,
a lowly and crude place.
The Jìn built the old city of Chéngzhōu for King Jìng to reside in.
The Qín further expanded it
to enfeoff Lǚ Bùwéi.
From this we can infer
it was not solely the Duke of Zhōu’s work.
It is also called the Jiǔqū Ditch.
“Register of the Twelve Counties of Hénán” states:
The Jiǔqū Ditch is west of Gǒng County, Hénán,
extending west to Luòyáng.
Also, according to Fú Chàng’s “History of Jìn”:
Director of Waterways Chén Láng excavated a transport canal,
entering from Luòkǒu and flowing into the Jiǔqū to the Dōngyáng Gate.
Hence, as Ruǎn Sìzōng’s “Poem of Cherishing Thoughts” says: “In the morning I go out the Shàngdōng Gate,
Gaze afar at the Shǒuyáng peaks”;
and also says: “In the distant Jiǔqū region,
Wandering, where shall I go?”
The Yáng Canal water reaches south to the Chānghé Gate,
which was the Shàngxī Gate of the Hàn.
“Records of the Hàn Palaces” states:
The reason the Shàngxī Gate was not purely white
was because the Hàn dynasty’s misfortune lay in the xū hour,
so it was decorated with red carvings.
During the Tàihé capital relocation,
the gate was moved to the south side.
The water north rides the high canal,
branching into upper and lower courses,
passes east of the old stone bridge and enters the city,
flows past the Wàngxiān Temple.
Inside is a stele.
The side of the stele imitates the “Stele of Zǐdān” in dragon and square design,
considered excellent by contemporary standards,
but inferior compared to antiquity.
The canal water flows east again past the south of the old Gold Market,
straight to the Qiānqiū Gate,
which is a right palace gate.
A branch flows into stone channels, goes underground,
and empties into the Língzhī Nine Dragons Pond.
During the Tàihé era of Wèi,
when the imperial capital moved to Luòyáng,
constructing palaces and halls,
repairing streets and canals,
they sought out hidden features.
They excavated and inspected the stones,
which were completely undamaged.
Moreover, the stonework was fine and dense,
not something modern knowledge can replicate.
It was also remarkably precise and exquisite,
so they used it accordingly.
One watercourse flows south from the Qiānqiū Gate past the Shénhǔ Gate,
facing east toward the Yúnlóng Gate.
On the lintels of both gates
are carved depictions of cloud dragons and wind tigers,
inlaid with fire-pearl foil.
When the morning light first rises,
and the evening sun slants its rays,
the frost-like patterns shimmer with emerald radiance,
dazzling the eyes with their variegated splendor.
It then flows south past the Tōngmén and Yèmén gates to the west,
turns eastward as it continues south,
and passes south of the Chānghé Gate.
According to the Rites,
the king had five gates:
namely, the Gāomén, Kùmén, Zhìmén, Yìngmén, and Lùmén.
The Lùmén was also called the Bìmén,
or the Hǔmén.
Emperor Míng of Wei, modeling himself on the Tàijí Palace in Luòyáng,
built the Tàijí Hall in the Southern Palace on the former site of the Hàn dynasty's Chóngdé Hall,
and renamed the Zhìmén as the Chānghé Gate.
In the Hàn dynasty,
the inscriptions on the gates of the Luòyáng palaces
were mostly in large seal script,
said to be the work of Cài Yōng and others.
After Dǒng Zhuó burned the palaces,
and Tàizǔ of Wei pacified Jīngzhōu,
Liáng Mènghuáng, the Hàn Minister of Personnel from Āndìng, who excelled in the clerical script style of Shī Yíguān,
sought to redeem his death sentence
by his calligraphy.
Tàizǔ admired his skill,
often hanging his works in his tent to admire,
considering him superior to Shī Yíguān.
The inscriptions in the Northern Palace
were all in the style of Hè script,
and after the Southern Palace was built,
Emperor Míng ordered Wéi Dàn, a palace attendant from Jīngzhào, to write them in ancient seal script.
When the capital moved to Luòyáng,
he ordered Shěn Hánxīn, a secretary in the Central Secretariat, to write them in clerical script.
During the Jǐngmíng and Zhèngshǐ eras,
he further ordered Jiāng Shì, the Director of Tallies, to replace them with large seal script.
The current inscriptions on the beams and plaques
are all in Jiāng Shì's hand.
The Zhōuguān states:
The Grand Steward hangs the laws on the Xiàngwèi in the first month.
The Guǎngyǎ says:
A què
is called the Xiàngwèi.
The Fēngsútōng says:
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ erected two observation towers at the gate,
which were called què,
derived from the character for "gate,"
with the sound jué.
The Ěryǎ says:
A guàn is called a què.
The Shuōwén says:
A què
is a gate tower.
The Hàn Guān Diǎnzhí says:
From Yǎnshī, forty-five lǐ from Luòyáng,
one could see the Zhūquè Què,
its towering height merging with the sky,
a testament to its majestic loftiness.
The Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng records the Zhūquè Què, Báihǔ Què, Cānglóng Què, and Běi Què,
which were the Southern Palace què.
The Dōngguān Hànjì says:
When Gēngshǐ departed from Luòyáng,
Lǐ Sōng, leading the carriage and horses, collided with the iron pillar gate of the Běi Què,
and three horses died,
referring to this què.
The Báihǔtōng says:
Why must a gate have què?
Què
serve to adorn the gate
and distinguish between noble and humble.
Now, outside the Chānghé Gate, large què are erected on both sides,
to correspond with celestial constellations.
Although not fully in accordance with ritual,
they still resemble the Xiàngwèi,
with fùsī added on top,
replacing the guàn.
The Guǎngyǎ says:
Fùsī is called a píng.
The Shìmíng says:
A píng
is for self-concealment;
fúsī is outside the gate,
with fú meaning "to repeat."
When ministers are about to enter to present matters,
they reconsider them here.
During the military uprisings at the end of the Hàn,
the fúsī of the imperial tombs were destroyed,
so that the people would not long for the Hàn again.
Thus, the Yántiělùn says:
"Walls, què, and fúsī,"
referring to the screens erected at corners.
Yǐng Róng also said:
A què
is where superiors' faults
can be written below by inferiors,
to seek public discussion and judgment,
hence it is called què.
Now, south of the water in front of the què, on the right side of the road,
a drum is placed to receive petitions.
In ancient times, Huángdì established the discussion hall of the míngtáng,
Yáo had the questioning room at crossroads,
Shùn had the banner for reporting goodness,
Yǔ had the drum for inquiries,
Tāng had the street for public criticism,
and King Wǔ of Zhōu had the Língtái for responses,
all to widely establish means for correcting errors.
The canal water then branches off,
flowing south along both sides of the road,
passing between the quarters of the Grand Commandant and the Minister of Education,
known as Copper Camel Street.
Previously, Emperor Míng of Wei placed bronze camels and other animals on the street south of the Chānghé Gate.
Lù Jī said:
"The camels are nine feet tall,
and their backs rise above the Grand Commandant's quarter."
To the west of the water is the Yǒngníng Temple,
first built during the Xīpíng era,
with a nine-story pagoda.
The pagoda's base is fourteen zhàng square,
and from the golden dew plate to the ground, it is forty-nine zhàng tall.
Modeled after the seven-story pagoda in Dàidū,
but taller and broader,
even the splendor of the two capitals,
the wealth of the five cities,
and the magnificent pagodas and temples
could not match this structure.
According to the Shì Fǎxiǎn Xíngzhuàn,
in the Western Regions, there is the Juélí Pagoda,
whose height resembles this one,
making both the Eastern Capital and the Western Regions equally magnificent.
This site was the former residence of Cáo Shuǎng.
During its construction,
in the southwest corner of the temple grounds, Cáo Shuǎng's underground chamber was discovered,
descending about a zhàng into the earth.
The walls were entirely built of stacked square stones,
finely and densely crafted,
with no damage at all.
All the stones were used for the temple's construction.
If not for Cáo Shuǎng,
even ordinary craftsmen would find it hard to replicate this.
As the Huán family said,
"Cáo Zǐdān gave birth to this piglet calf,"
truly so.
To the left of the canal is the former site of the Wèi and Jìn ancestral temples,
now all residential areas,
with no remaining walls.
The canal water then flows west between the temple and the altar,
emptying south into the Southern Canal.
The temple and altar are distinguished by their respective colors.
According to the Zhōulǐ,
the ancestral temple and the main hall
are both like the míngtáng,
with additional resting chambers.
Only the distant ancestral temple lacks these.
Later generations combined them into a single temple,
arranging the main chambers below,
with no further resting chambers.
The Rites state:
When the Son of Heaven establishes a state,
he places the temple on the left and the altar on the right,
with stone as the main material,
and wears the xīmiǎn for sacrifices.
Now, many princes and dukes oversee the affairs,
and the king does not personally perform the rituals.
In the first year of Xiánníng,
a great wind struck Luòyáng,
breaking the trees at the imperial altar.
A blue aura reached the heavens,
and as the Yuán King crossed east,
the Wèi altar replaced the flourishing one.
The canal water flows east from Copper Camel Street past the south of the Sīmǎ Gate.
Emperor Míng of Wei first built it,
but the què collapsed,
killing hundreds of people,
so it was never rebuilt,
leaving no què gate.
In the southern screen wall, there was once a place for bronze statues,
but as the golden figures were lost,
the site was also stripped,
with only broken stones remaining.
From here, it runs straight south to the Xuānyáng Gate,
with thoroughfares connecting in all directions,
all lined with imperial roads.
The restrictions on travel
were the same as in the two Hàn dynasties.
Cáo Zǐjiàn once traveled on the imperial street,
violated the gate restrictions,
and was thus slighted for it.
The canal water then flows east past what Dù Yuánkǎi called the north of Díquán,
which now has no water.
The pit is nine zhàng and six chǐ square,
over two zhàng deep,
seeming man-made rather than a natural spring or pond,
which is one piece of evidence against it.
Also, Huángfǔ Mì's Dìwáng Shìjì says:
"When the royal house was settled, they moved to reside there.
Chéngzhōu was small,
unfit for the royal capital,
so they destroyed Díquán to expand it.
Once the spring source was blocked,
it clearly left no trace,
which is the second piece of evidence against it."
Dù Yù stated:
Díquán is located southwest of the Tàicāng,
since it is said to be southwest,
it cannot be northeast of Luòyáng,
which is the third piece of evidence proving it is not.
Examining geographical accounts,
the matter is almost clear,
it cannot be Díquán.
The Qúshuǐ passes in front of the Sikōng’s office,
goes by the south of the Tàicāng,
exits beneath the stone bridge at the Dōngyáng Gate,
and flows into the Yángqú.
The Gǔshuǐ flows south from the Chānghé Gate and passes east of Tǔshān,
three lǐ west of the water is a slope,
on the slope is Tǔshān,
built by the Hàn Grand General Liáng Jì,
who piled earth to form a mountain,
planted trees to create a garden,
Zhāng Fán’s *Hàn Jì* says:
the mountain had many steep slopes,
resembling the two Xiáo Mountains,
amassing gold and jade,
capturing birds and beasts,
to fill it,
if someone killed a rabbit in the garden,
they would pursue each other in turn,
resulting in thirteen deaths.
It flows south past the Xīyáng Gate,
formerly the Xīmíng Gate of the Hàn dynasty,
also called the Yōng Gate.
The old gate was to the south,
during the Tàihé period, because the old gate was misaligned,
it was moved to this gate,
facing east toward the Dōngyáng Gate.
The Gǔshuǐ flows south past the east of Báimǎ Temple,
in the past, Emperor Míng of Hàn dreamed of a great being,
golden in color,
with a white light around its neck.
He asked his ministers,
and one replied:
In the west there is a deity called Buddha,
whose form resembles what Your Majesty dreamed,
could it be this?
Thereupon, he sent envoys to Tiānzhú,
to copy scriptures and images,
initially using yútǎng to hold the scriptures,
a white horse carrying the images,

This yútǎng was later moved to the pagoda of Mǐnhuái Crown Prince within the city,

and thus the golden light shone,
the Dharma wheel turned eastward,
beginning from this.
The Gǔshuǐ flows south past the east of Pínglè Observatory,

Then the illustrious Pínglè Observatory was established,

Emperor Líng built a great altar beneath the Pínglè Observatory,

After the ceremony,
the Son of Heaven personally donned armor,

Therefore, the *Eastern Capital Rhapsody* says:
To the west is the Pínglè capital grounds,
an observatory to show distant peoples,

Yìng Shào said:
Fēilián is a divine bird,
able to summon wind,

In the fifth year of Emperor Míng’s Yǒngpíng era,

Now, outside the Shàngxī Gate, there are no other foundations or observatories.

It is also said that a young imperial princess died,

Jìn Zhuó said:
Fēilián,
has a deer’s body, a head like a sparrow,

Dǒng Zhuó melted it down for gold,

Wáng Zūn was a minister,
the water cut off his feet,

The Gǔshuǐ flows east past the south of the Xuānyáng Gate,

When the imperial capital moved to Luò,

Therefore, the *Eastern Capital Rhapsody* says:
facing the Luò, turning away from the Hé,
with the Yī to the left and the Chán to the right.
Examining Luòyáng in the central plains,
divination favored Luò for settlement,
it is indeed divine.
To the left of the gate is where the Luòyáng Pond was located.

now blocked.
North faces the Nángōng of Luòyáng,
so Cài Yōng said:
the Píngchéng Gate,
the Zhèngyáng Gate,
connects to the palace,
the most honored gate for the imperial procession during suburban sacrifices,
*Luòyáng Zhū Gōng Míng* says:
the Nángōng has a Yí Platform overlooking the Zhào Platform.
The *Eastern Capital Rhapsody* says:
to the south is the Yí Gate,
with winding pavilions leaning against the city moat.
The *Commentary* says:
the Yí Gate,
is the ice chamber gate;
zǔ,
means to lean against;
xù,
is the moat beneath the city wall.
All winding and leaning, following the city moat as the path.
Therefore, *Shuōwén* says:
huáng,
is the city moat.
With water it is called chí,
without water it is called huáng.
The Yí Gate is the Xuānyáng Gate,
inside the gate is the Xuānyáng ice chamber,
*Zhōulǐ* mentions ice keepers,
who store ice when the sun is in the northern mansion and retrieve it in the western mansion,
bringing it out at dawn.
The ice chamber was originally inside the Xuānyáng Gate,
hence the name.
The gate is now blocked,
and the ice chamber is also abandoned.
The Gǔshuǐ passes the Líng Platform,
from which clouds and phenomena are observed.
Built by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
six zhàng high,
twenty paces square.
Emperor Shìzǔ once feasted at this platform,
catching a flying squirrel on the platform,

the youngest son of Dìwǔ Lún,

no fields or homes in his hometown,
he stayed at the Líng Platform,
sometimes going ten days without cooking,
the Sīlì Commandant Nányáng Zuǒ Xióng,

all former Xiàolián and Gōngcáo under Lún,
each offered gifts and provisions,
but he declined them all,

The Gǔshuǐ flows east past the south of the Píngchāng Gate,
formerly the Píng Gate.
It then passes north of the Míngtáng,
established in the first year of Emperor Guāngwǔ’s Zhōngyuán era.
Examining its foundation and structure,
round above and square below,
with nine chambers, double corners, and twelve halls.
Cài Yōng’s *Yuèlìng Zhāngjù* agrees,
thus water was channeled beneath it to form the Bìyōng.
The Gǔshuǐ flows east past the south of the Kāiyáng Gate,
*Jìn Gōng Gé Míng* says:
formerly the Jiànyáng Gate.
*Hàn Guān* says:
when the Kāiyáng Gate was completed,
it had no name overnight,
once a pillar came,
On the upper floor.
Lángyá Kāiyáng County reported:
A pillar from the southern city gate flew away.
Emperor Guāngwǔ sent someone to investigate,
and upon inspection, it was indeed true.
They then firmly bound it,
and inscribed the year, month, and day to mark it.
Hé Tāng, styled Zhònggōng,
once served as a gatekeeper.
When the emperor returned incognito at night,
Hé Tāng closed the gate and refused entry,
for which the court praised him.
Further east, it passes north of the Stone Classics at the Imperial Academy.
The "Rites of Zhōu" mentions the Imperial Academy,
which taught the methods of balanced education.
The "Record of Learning" states:
In ancient times,
there were village schools in households,
township schools in districts,
prefectural schools in regions,
and national academies in the state.
There were also the upper and lower schools of the Yúshì clan,
the eastern and western schools of the Xiàhòu clan,
the left and right schools of the Yīn people,
the eastern school of the Zhōu people,
and the Yú school.
The "Royal Regulations" state:
The elderly of the state were nurtured in the upper school,
and the common elderly in the lower school.
Thus, there were the Great Academy and the elementary school,
which educated the children of the state,
known as the "Guózǐ" (sons of the state).
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
the Imperial Academy was established in the Guózǐ Hall.
In the sixth year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of the Eastern Hàn,
stone tablets inscribed with the Five Classics were erected,
placed in front of the lecture hall of the Imperial Academy,
all on the eastern side.
In the fourth year of the Xīpíng era, Cài Yōng,
along with Tángxī Diǎn, General of the Household,
Yáng Cì, Grand Master of the Palace,
Mǎ Rìdī, Grand Master of Remonstrance,
Zhāng Xún and Hán Shuō, Court Gentlemen for Consultation,
and Shàn Yáng, Grand Astrologer, among others,
petitioned to correct and standardize the texts of the Six Classics.
Emperor Líng approved,
and Cài Yōng personally wrote the text on the tablets in vermilion ink,
had craftsmen carve them,
and erected them outside the gate of the Imperial Academy.
Thereafter, later scholars and students
all took them as the standard.
When the tablets were first erected,
those who came to view and copy them
filled the streets with over a thousand carriages daily,
clogging the roads.
Today, the tablets are inscribed with the names of Cài Yōng and others.
During the Zhèngshǐ era of the Wèi dynasty,
the "Three Script Stone Classics" in ancient, seal, and clerical scripts were erected.
The ancient script originated in the time of the Yellow Emperor,
when Cāngjié based characters on bird tracks,
taking their derived forms,
thus giving rise to the six principles of character formation.
After the Qín dynasty adopted seal script
and burned earlier classics,
the ancient script was lost.
When Lǔ Gōngwáng obtained the books from Confucius' residence,
he did not recognize the ancient script,
calling it "tadpole script"
because the name "tadpole"
resembled its shape.
It is said that the large seal script emerged during the reign of King Xuān of Zhōu,
created by the historian Zhòu.
When King Píng moved east,
the script became corrupted.
Lǐ Sī and Húmǔ Jìng of Qín
further modified the seal script, calling it small seal script,
thus distinguishing between large and small seal scripts.
However, Xǔ Shèn's "Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters" focused on seal script
and did not trace back to the ancient script.
It is said that clerical script originated in the Qín dynasty,
as seal script was too complex
for handling urgent affairs.
Thus, the simplified script used by clerks
was called clerical script.
Some say it was modified by Chéng Miǎo in Yúnyáng,
meaning that clerical script
is a simplified form of seal script.
Sūn Chàngzhī once heard Fù Hóngrén, Governor of Qīngzhōu, say that when people in Línzī excavated an ancient tomb,
they found a paulownia coffin with clerical script inscribed on the front and sides,
claiming it was the coffin of
the sixth-generation descendant of Duke Tài of Qí, Duke Hú.
Only three characters were ancient,
while the rest matched modern script,
proving that clerical script originated from ancient script
and did not begin in Qín.
In the early Wèi dynasty,
the ancient script was transmitted by Hándān Chún.
The ancient script on the Stone Classics
deviated from Chún's method.
They were erected west of the hall,
each stone eight feet long,
four feet wide,
with stones arranged below,
totaling forty-eight tablets,
spanning thirty zhàng in width.
Emperor Míng of Wèi also inscribed six tablets of the "Canonical Discourses,"
placing them alongside.
Lù Jī stated
that the "Eulogy of the Imperial Academy" was on a separate tablet,
west of the lecture hall,
with the "Stone Tortoise Tablet" below,
inscribed with the names of Cài Yōng, Hán Shuō, Tángxī Diǎn, and others.
The "Eulogy of Imperial Academy Disciples" was another tablet,
inside the outer gate.
Today, both tablets are missing.
East of the Stone Classics, there is a tablet
erected in the first year of the Yángjiā era of Emperor Shùn of Hàn.
The inscription reads:
"The Imperial Academy was built in the twenty-seventh year of the Jiànwǔ era.
Over the years, it fell into disrepair.
In the sixth year of the Yǒngjiàn era, in the ninth month,
an imperial edict ordered the restoration of the Imperial Academy.
The year was inscribed on stone,
using 112,000 laborers.
The work was completed in the eighth month of the first year of the Yángjiā era."
The south side of the tablet bears a eulogy,
with characters carved on both sides,
still intact and unbroken.
North of the Hàn Stone Classics is the Jìn dynasty "Tablet of Rituals at the Pìyōng,"
erected in the second year of the Tàishǐ era.
The tablet is broken in the middle.
But as times change,
things do not remain constant.
The Stone Classics have been damaged,
some half-destroyed, others nearly gone.
To speak of permanence
is indeed lamentable.
Examining antiquity, there are records of three types of schools,
but today, the Spiritual Terrace and Imperial Academy
no longer have a Pìyōng site.
During the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
when Wáng Mí and Liú Yào entered Luòyáng,
they burned both academies,
though traces of the former foundations remain.
The Gǔ River branches north at the southeastern corner of the city,
passing east of the Qīngyáng Gate,
formerly the Qīngmíng Gate,

or the Máng Gate.
Further north, it passes east of the Dōngyáng Gate,
formerly the Zhōngdōng Gate.
Further north, it passes west of the former Great Granary.
The "Records of Luòyáng" states:
"East of the great city is the Great Granary,
where thousands of transport ships often gather."
This is the place.
Further north, it enters the Luòyáng Ditch.
The Gǔ River then turns east and branches left into a pond,
and further east, branches right into Square Lake,
190 paces east-west,
70 paces north-south,
formerly the site of the Water Balance Office.
The Gǔ River then turns southeast and bends eastward,
called Ruǎn Bend,
said to be the former residence of Ruǎn Sìzōng.
The Gǔ River then flows east into the Hóngchí Pond.
The "Records of Officials" states:
"Hóngchí
is the name of a pond.
It is located twenty lǐ east of Luòyáng,
with one assistant official,
earning two hundred dàn of grain."
The pond is a thousand paces east-west,
1,100 paces north-south,
surrounded by embankments,
with an east-west transverse embankment in the middle.
Water flows through it,
so Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Hóngchí Pond" says:
"The pond of Hóngzé,
planned by the sage kings,
its source flows east,
emerging from the city moat."
The water then flows east,
joining the Qīlǐ Stream on the left.
The Jìn "Later Summary" states:
Chéngdū King Yǐng sent the Wú native Lù Jī as vanguard commander
to attack the capital.
Advancing recklessly,
he was ambushed by the Luò army,
suffering a major defeat at Deer Park.
People trampled each other,
dying in trenches and the Qīlǐ Stream,
filling the stream,
which is this very stream.
The stream has a stone bridge,
namely the Traveler's Bridge.
In the past, Sūn Dēng did not wish to stay long in Luòyáng,
knowing that the Yáng clan's prosperity would not last,
and desired to retreat to the forested countryside,
to live in seclusion and avoid a meaningless death.
Yáng Jùn buried it east of this bridge,
and Yáng Jùn later perished.
The Sōu Shén Jì states,
at the end of the Tàikāng era, the capital and Luòyáng began to have the "Zhé Yáng" song,
which contained lyrics about the hardships of war.
Yáng Jùn was later executed,
the Empress Dowager died in confinement,
which was the response to the "Zhé Yáng" song.
All these bridges,
were built by piling stones,
and were also tall and sturdy.
Their construction was excellent,
although over time they have suffered damage,
they have not ceased to serve travelers.
Zhū Chāoshí’s letter to his elder brother says,
the bridge is six or seven lǐ from the Luòyáng Palace,
all made of large stones,
with rounded bottoms to allow water to flow through,
capable of accommodating large boats passing underneath.
An inscription on it reads:
construction began in the eleventh month of the third year of Tàikāng,
employing seventy-five thousand people daily,
and ended in the fourth month.
This bridge fell into disrepair,
but was later repaired,
and now no inscription remains.
The Yángqú River flows east past the temple of Lì Yìjī, Marquis of Guǎngyě of the Hàn, to the south,
the temple is on the northern mountain,
which is what Chéng Gōngsuí called the Western Mountain of Yǎnshī.
The old foundation on the mountain still exists,
the temple faces east,
with two stone figures leaning against each other at the gate,
the inscription on the chest of the northern stone figure reads:
Gate Pavilion Chief Stone Figure.
To the west are two stone watchtowers,
although they have collapsed and been damaged,
they are still over ten feet high.
West of the watchtowers,
is the original site of the temple.
In front of the foundation is a stele,
the text on it is worn and incomplete,
no longer legible,
Zǐ'ān admired the enduring fragrance through the ages,
praised the pure virtue in the temple's images,
and the text is collected there.
The Yángqú River flows east past Bóyīn to the south,
where Pángēng once moved the capital,
changing the name from Shāng to Yīn, beginning here.
Bān Gù said:
Shīxiāng,
was the former capital of Shāng Tāng.
Therefore, it is also called Táng Pavilion.
Xuē Zàn’s "Annotations to the Book of Hàn" and Huángfǔ Mì’s "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings,"
both consider this incorrect,
believing it was the capital of Emperor Kù.
The "Jìn Tàikāng Jì" and "Dìdào Jì,"
both state that Tián Héng died at this pavilion,
so it was renamed Shīxiāng, but this is incorrect.
I refer to Sīmǎ Biāo’s "Jùnguó Zhì,"
which considers it the Shīshì of the Spring and Autumn period.
Its marshland,
lies between the wilderness and the plains,
with many tombs and mounds around the outer walls.
This is where Lù Shìhéng met Wáng Fǔsì.
Yuán’s "Preface to the Poems of Wáng and Lù" says,
when Jī first entered Luòyáng,
he stopped at Yǎnshī in Hénán,
when suddenly the sky darkened,
he saw what looked like a dwelling on the left side of the road,
so he went to stay there,
and met a young man,
whose demeanor was dignified and profound,
who discussed metaphysics with Jī,
Jī admired his ability but could not counter his arguments,
and when he posed a question,
Jī discussed ancient and modern matters,
and examined names and realities,
but the young man was not very impressed or understanding.
As dawn approached,
he left,
and stopped at an inn,
where an old woman said:
Where did you stay last night?
For dozens of lǐ east, there are no villages,
only the tomb of the Wáng family of Shānyáng.
Jī then felt strange and regretful,
looked back at the road from yesterday,
the empty wilderness was shrouded in clouds,
dense trees blocked the sun,
and he realized that the one he had met,
was indeed Wáng Bì.
This mountain is the former residence of Zhù Jīwēng.
The Sōu Shén Jì says:
Zhù Jīwēng,
was a man of Luòyáng,
who lived at the northern foot of Shīxiāng Mountain,
and raised chickens for over a hundred years,
with more than a thousand chickens,
each with a name,
and when he wanted to catch one,
he would call its name,
and it would come according to its breed.
Later, he went to Wú Mountain,
and no one knows where he went.
The Gǔ River flows east past the south of Yǎnshī City,
Huángfǔ Mì said:
Emperor Kù established his capital at Bó,
which is Yǎnshī.
This is what Wáng Mǎng called Shīshì.
The Gǔ River flows east and empties into the Luò River.
16.2 Gān River
16.2 Gān River
The Gān River originates from Lùtí Mountain in Yíyáng County, Hóngnóng,
the mountain is northwest of the old city of Lùhún County in Hénán,
commonly called Zòng Mountain.
The source of the water,
emerges from a bend in the mountain,
so people call it Gānzhǎng.
It flows northeast to the south of Hénán County,
and enters the Luò River from the north.
The Gān River originates and flows northeast,
then turns north past an old city to the east,
which is on Fēi Mountain,
commonly called Stone City.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
some say on the western mountain of the Gān River,
there is an old Gān City on level ground,
twenty-five lǐ west of Hénán City,
referring to this city.
I note that about ten lǐ east of the Gān River, south of Luò City,
there is an old Gān City,
facing the old Hénán City to the north,
commonly called Jiànluò City,
Jiàn and Gān sound similar,
so it is the old Gān City,
which was the former fief of Prince Dài.
Therefore, Zhāoshū was called the Duke of Gān.
The Gān River also meets the Fēi Mountain River,
which originates from the eastern valley of Fēi Mountain,
and flows east into the Gān River.
The Gān River enters the Luò River northwest of Hénán City.
The "Jīng" says south of the county,
which is incorrect.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
now southwest of Hénán County is the Gān River,
which enters the Luò River from the north.
This is correct.
16.3 Qī River
16.3 Qī River
The Qī River originates east of Yú Mountain in Dùyáng County, Fúfēng,
and flows north into the Wèi River.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
From the Yúcì Mountains,
the Qī River originates,
flowing northward into the Wèi River.
This suggests a direction from north to south.
The "Tribute of Yu" in the Book of Documents and the "Basic Annals of Yu" by the Grand Historian state:
The Wèi River is guided northeast to the Jīng River,
then eastward past the Qī and Jǔ Rivers, entering the Yellow River.
Kǒng Ānguó said:
The Qī and Jǔ Rivers
are names of a single river,
also called the Luò River,
originating north of Féngyì.
When King Tàiwáng of Zhōu left Bīn,
he crossed the Qī River and passed over the Liáng Mountains,
settling below Qí.
Thus, the Book of Songs says:
"When the people first arose,
they came from the lands of Jǔ and Qī."
It also says:
"Following the western bank of the river,
they reached below Qí."
This aligns with the accounts in the "Tribute of Yu" and the "Basic Annals of Yu."
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén Jiézì states:
The Qī River originates from the Qí Mountains in Dùyáng County of Yòufúfēng,
flowing east into the Wèi River,
with the water radical,
and the phonetic component "qī."
It further says:
Another name is the Qī River pond.
Pān Yuè's Guānzhōng Jì states:
Within Guānzhōng, there are the Jīng, Wèi, Bà, Chǎn, Fēng, Hào, Qī, and Jǔ Rivers.
Among them, the Fēng, Hào, Qī, and Jǔ Rivers
are located in Hù County, southwest of Cháng'ān.
The Qī and Jǔ Rivers both flow southward,
while the Fēng
and Hào Rivers flow northward.
The Kāishān Tú states:
Northwest of Lì Mountain lies the Wēn Pond.
Eighty lǐ southwest of the Wēn Pond is Qí Mountain,
located north of Dùyáng.
West of Cháng'ān, there is a canal
called the Qī Canal.
Bān Gù's "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Qī River lies west of Qī County.
Yán Yīn's Shísānzhōu Zhì further states:
The Qī River originates west of Qī County,
flowing north to Qí Mountain,
then east into the Wèi River.
Today, there is a river originating from the Qī Stream north of Qí Mountain in Dùyáng County,
called the Qī Canal,
flowing southwest into the Qí River.
However, the terrain and waterways are peculiar,
and current accounts vary,
making it difficult to verify through classical texts and histories.
Each account has its basis,
but with limited knowledge and superficial understanding,
it is impossible to determine the truth.
16.4 Chǎn River
16.4 Chǎn River
The Chǎn River originates from Lántián Valley in Jīngzhào,
flowing north into the Bà River.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Chǎn River originates from Lántián Valley in Nánlíng County,
flowing northwest and merging with another river,
which originates from Mǎng Valley to the southwest,
flowing northeast into the Chǎn River.
The Chǎn River then flows north through Lántián Plain,
entering the Bà River.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Chǎn River flows north to Bàlíng, entering the Bà River.
16.5 Jǔ River
16.5 Jǔ River
The Jǔ River originates from Zhílù County in Běidì,
flowing east past the north of Duìxǔ County in Féngyì,
and east into the Luò River.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Jǔ River emerges west of Zhílù County,
flowing east into the Luò River.
Now the water flows southeast from Zhílù County,
passes east of Qiáoshí Mountain and flows southeast,
traverses Tántái Plain,
commonly called Tántái Water.
It bends and flows west between mountains,
then flows southwest through Yíjūn Plain,
also called Yíjūn Water by later generations.
It then reaches the mouth of Huángqīn Water,
which emerges from Huángqīn Valley at Shímén Mountain in Yúnyáng County to the northwest,
flowing southeast to join Yíjūn Water.
It then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Duìxǔ County,
established in the second year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn.
Its southern waters merge with Tóngguān Water,
which emerges northeast of the county,
flows southwest through Tóngguān Plain,
and is called Tóngguān Water.
It then flows southwest past the east of Duìxǔ County,
flows southwest along the southern plain below the city,
and joins Yíjūn Water to the southwest.
Yíjūn Water then emerges south from the west of Tǔmén Mountain,
and is again called Jǔ Water.
It then flows southeast along the southern plain below Tǔmén,
east past Huáidé City,
with the southern city on the northern plain.
It then flows east past the north of the Mausoleum of the Grand Emperor of Hàn,
with the mausoleum on the southern plain.
Jǔ Water flows east into the Zhèng Canal.
In the past, Hán wanted to prevent Qín from campaigning east,
so it sent the hydraulic engineer Zhèng Guó to infiltrate Qín and dig a canal to divert water from the Jīng River,
called the Zhèng Canal.
The canal head draws water from the Jīng River at Zhāihùkǒu west of Zhōngshān,
which is called Hùzhōng.
The "Ěryǎ" identifies it as Zhōu's Jiāohuò.
The canal runs along the northern mountains,
flowing east into the Luò River for over 300 lǐ,
intended for irrigating fields.
During construction, the plot was discovered,
and Qín wanted to kill Zhèng Guó.
Zhèng Guó said:
"Initially, I came as a spy,
but the canal also benefits Qín."
They eventually let him complete the canal.
Upon completion, it was used to channel silt-laden water,
irrigating over 40,000 qǐng of saline-alkali land,
yielding one zhōng per mǔ.
Guānzhōng became fertile land,
with no more bad years.
Qín grew wealthy and strong,
eventually annexing the feudal lords,
and named it the Zhèng Canal.
The canal flows east past the north of Yíqiū City,
then east past the south of Zhōngshān.
The "Treatise on Rivers and Canals" says:
"The Jīng River was diverted from west of Zhōngshān."
The "Treatise on the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
records that Emperor Wǔ of Hàn obtained a precious tripod at Fényīn,
and intended to present it at Gānquán.
When the tripod reached Zhōngshān,
a yellow cloud canopy appeared, misty and dense.
Xú Guǎng's "Shǐjì Yīnyì" says:
"There is a Zhōngshān in Guānzhōng,
not the one in Jìzhōu."
This refers to this mountain,
commonly called Zhòngshān,
which is incorrect.
The Zhèng Canal then flows east past the south of Shěchē Palace, crossing Yěgǔ Water.
The old course of the Zhèng Canal then flows east past the south of Jiéxuē Mountain,
north of the old city of Chíyáng County,
then east across Qīngshuǐ.
It then flows east along the northern plain,
where Zhuóshuǐ joins it.
Above Zhuóshuǐ,
there is now no water.
Zhuóshuǐ draws from the large black spring east of Yúnyáng County,
flowing southeast as Zhúogǔ Water,
then emerging southeast from the plain,
and joining the Zhèng Canal.
It then flows east across the plain past the north of Qūliáng City,
then east past the southern plain below the Grand Emperor's Mausoleum,
bends north past the east of the plain and merges with Jǔ Water,
dividing into two streams.
One stream flows southeast out,
which is Zhuóshuǐ,
meeting Zéquán at the Bái Canal,
commonly called Qīshuǐ,
also called Qījǔshuǐ.
It crosses the Bái Canal,
flows east past the north of the old city of Wànnián County as Yuèyáng Canal,
the city
being Yuèyáng Palace.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn buried his father in this county,
raised a tomb mound,
designated the town's name,
and changed it to Wànnián.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
"Féngyì's Wànnián County,
established by Emperor Gāozǔ,
was renamed Yìchì by Wáng Mǎng."
Thus, Xú Guǎng's "Shǐjì Yīnyì" says:
"Yuèyáng
is now Wànnián."
Kǎn Yīn said:
"West of the county are the Jīng and Wèi Rivers,
north is a small river,
referring to this water."
This water then bends south,
renamed Shíchuān Water,
flows southwest past the west of Guōlǒu City and merges with a branch of the Bái Canal,
then flows south into the Wèi River.
The other stream flows east out,
which is Jǔ Water,
east merging with Zéquán,
which emerges from a marsh east of Jǔ,
separated from Jǔ Water by a plain,
fifteen lǐ apart,
commonly called this water Qīshuǐ.
It flows east past the south of Bó Zhāo's tomb,
with the tomb mound on the northern plain.
It then passes north of Huáidé City,
flows southeast into the Zhèng Canal,
merging with Jǔ Water.
It then directly crosses from Jǔ to join Zhuóshuǐ,
meeting at the Bái Canal,
hence Zhuóshuǐ gains the name Qījǔ.
Jǔ follows the Zhèng Canal,
flowing east past Dāngdào City south.
The city is south of the old city of Pínyáng County,
being Pínyáng Palace,
established by Duke Lì of Qín.
North of the city is Pín Mountain,
with a hall of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn on the mountain,
built with stone frames.
The county is south of the mountain,
hence called Pínyáng.
Yìng Shào said:
"The county is north of Pínshuǐ."
Now, to the left and right of the county,
there is no water corresponding to this,
what can match it
is only the Zhèng Canal and Jǔ Water.
It then flows east past the north of the old city of Liánsháo County.
The "Shísānzhōu Zhì" says:
"The county is named after a plant."
Jǔ Water then flows east past the north of the old city of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
then east past the north of the old city of Sùyì County,
renamed Sùchéng by Wáng Mǎng.
Later, Hàn enfeoffed Cavalry Commandant Gěng Kuí as a marquis here.
The water then flows northeast,
and joins the Luò River.
17 Commentary on the Water Classic, Volume 17
17.1 Wèi River
17.1 Wèi River
The Wèi River emerges from Niǎoshǔ Mountain south of Wèigǔtíng in Shǒuyáng County, Lǒngxī.
The Wèi River emerges from the southern valley of Wèishǒutíng on Shǒuyáng Mountain in Shǒuyáng County,
with the mountain northwest of Niǎoshǔ Mountain.
This county has Gāochéng Ridge,
with a city on the ridge,
called Wèiyuán City,
from which the Wèi River emerges.
Three sources converge and flow,
northeast past the west of Shǒuyáng County, merging with another source,
which emerges south from Wèishuǐgǔ at Niǎoshǔ Mountain.
This is what the "Shàngshū Yǔgòng" refers to as "the Wèi emerges from Niǎoshǔ."
The "Dì Shuō" states:
"Niǎoshǔ Mountain
is a branch of Tóngxué.
The Wèi River emerges from within it,
flowing northeast between the branches of Tóngxué.
Since it mentions passing through,
it is clearly not a single mountain."
It then flows northeast and converges with a different source.
The Wèi River flows southeast,
past the south of Shǒuyáng County,
receiving Fēngxī Water on the right,
then Guǎngxiàngxī Water further south,
then Gònggǔ Water further east,
with Tiānmǎxī Water on the left,
then Bóyánggǔ Water further south,
all irregularly flanking and joining,
chaotically flowing southeast out.
It flows northeast past the north of Xiāngwǔ County.
The Guǎngyáng River originates from the Western Mountains,
where two sources converge and flow together,
forming a single watercourse.
It runs northeast and empties into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River then flows southeast past the northeast of Xiāngwǔ County,
where the Jīngtóu River joins it.
This river originates from the Jīng Valley in the Niǎoshǔ Mountains southwest of Xiāngwǔ,
flowing northeast past the old city north of Xiāngwǔ County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiānghuán.
It was here that Wēn Xù, the Hàn Protector of the Qiāng, while on an inspection tour,
was captured by Gǒu Yǔ, a general under Wěi Xiāo,
and bit his own beard before committing suicide.
The river flows northeast and empties into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River generally flows southeast,
not northeast.
Further east,
the Xǐ River joins it,
originating from the Quèfù Valley to the southwest,
flowing northeast past the south of Xiāngwǔ County,
and then northeast into the Wèi River.
According to the *Wèi Zhì*,
in the second year of the Tàixī era,
a report from Xiāngwǔ stated
that a giant appeared,
over three zhàng tall,
with footprints three chǐ and two cùn long,
white hair,
wearing a yellow single-layered robe and headcloth,
leaning on a staff and calling out to the people’s king.
He began by saying:
“Peace shall now reign,
and in the twelfth month, the heavenly mandate of the Wèi will end forever,
as the succession of dynastic fortunes belongs to Jìn.”
Thus, they abandoned Wèi and submitted to Jìn.
Further east, passing south of Huándào County,
on the right is the Cénxī River,
next the Tóng River,
both joining from the left,
followed by the Guò River joining from the right.
The Wèi River then flows southeast past the old city west of Huándào County.
Long ago, Duke Xiào of Qín campaigned west and beheaded the Huán king of the Róng tribes.
Yìng Shào said:
“Huán
was a Róng settlement.”
In the fifth year of the Zhōngpíng era under Emperor Líng of Hàn,
it was separately established as Nán’ān Commandery.
The Chìtíng River originates from the Chì Valley in the eastern mountains of the commandery,
flows west past the north of the city,
and enters the Wèi River from the south.
The Wèi River then passes south of the city and meets the Sù River,
which originates from the Āndū Valley to the southwest,
flowing northeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River continues east,
where the Xīnxīng River originates from the Niǎoshǔ Mountains to the southwest,
its two sources merging,
flowing northeast to join the Zhāng River.
The Zhāng River originates from a stream below the southwestern mountains,
flowing northeast to the south of Zhāng County.
Originally, this was the seat of the Gùdào Frontier Captain,
but later, during the Hàn dynasty, it became a county.
In the first year of the Yǒngyuán era,
Emperor Hé enfeoffed Gěng Bǐng as a marquis here.
The Wànnián River originates from the southern mountains,
flowing northeast to join it,
then further northeast into the Xīnxīng River.
It then flows northeast past the north of Xīnxīng County,
which, according to the *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì*,
was a subordinate county of Nán’ān.
The river then flows northeast to merge with the Nánchuān River,
which originates from below the southwestern mountains,
joins the Běi River to the northeast,
and then flows northeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River then flows east past the west of Wǔchéng County,
where the Wǔchéng River joins it.
This river’s source
emerges from the Lùbù Western Mountains,
where two streams converge,
flowing northeast past the south of Lùbù,
and is also called the Lùbù River.
Further northeast,
the Chāngqiū River originates from below the southwestern hills,
flowing northeast into the Wǔchéng River,
then merging chaotically northeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River then flows east into the Wǔyáng River,
with the Guānchéng River joining from the south,
and the Ānchéng Valley River joining from the north,
both irregularly emptying into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River continues east,
where three valley streams from the Luòmén Western Mountains flow east and join it,
the three rivers uniting
and flowing northeast into the Wèi River.
There is the Luòmén settlement,
where long ago Féng Yì attacked Luòmén
but died before capturing it.
In the tenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Lái Xī attacked it again,
capturing Wěi Xiāo’s son, Wěi Chún,
thus pacifying Lǒngyòu.
The Wèi River flows east from Luòmén to the Hēishuǐ Gorge,
with six rivers flanking it on both sides:
on the left are the Wǔyáng Stream,
and further east, the Tǔmén Valley River,
both originating from the northern mountains,
flowing south into the Wèi River.
On the right are the Wēngǔ River,
further east the Gùchéng Stream,
further east the Lǘlǐ Stream,
also called the Xí Stream,
and further east the Hēishuǐ River,
all originating from the southern mountains,
flowing north into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River then flows east out of the Hēishuǐ Gorge,
passing through Jìchuān.
Further east, it passes north of Jì County.
The Wei River flows from the Heishui Gorge to the Cen Gorge,
with eleven tributaries from the north and south flowing into it.
To the north is the Wengu River,
which originates from the Wenxi stream on the southern mountain of Píngxiāng County,
flowing northeast past the old southern city of Píngxiāng County,
formerly the settlement of the Xiāng Róng people,
which Wáng Mǎng called Píngxiàng.
This river flows southeast,
passes south of the Sānduī,
then turns east and south,
traverses the Huánghuái River,
the Gěngjīn Canal,
which ceases to flow in winter,
but in spring and summer when the water is abundant,
it connects to the river and flows into the Wei.
Next is the Niúgǔ River,
which flows south into the Wei River.
To the south is the Chángqiàngǔ River,
further east is the Ānpúxī River,
further east is the Yīgǔ River,
all originating from the Zhūyǔ Mountain to the south,
which is located in the Wúzhōng settlement.
There is a stone drum on the mountain,
which sounds without being struck,
and when it sounds, warfare arises.
In the third year of the Hóngjiā era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
a large stone on the southern mountain of Jì in Tiānshuǐ sounded by itself,
its noise rumbling like thunder,
and after a while it stopped.
It was heard as far as Píngxiāng, two hundred and forty lǐ away,
and wild chickens all crowed.
The stone was thirteen zhǎng long,
with roughly equal width and thickness.
It was attached to the cliff face,
over a hundred zhàng above the ground,
and the common people called it the stone drum,
saying that when the stone drum sounds, warfare will occur.
That year, a prisoner in Guǎnghàn attacked and killed others,
stole weapons from the armory,
plundered officials and commoners,
wore embroidered clothes,
and called himself the Immortal Lord.
His followers gradually grew in number,
and the following winter he was executed.
Over three thousand people surrendered voluntarily,
proving the omen to be true and verified.
The river flows north past the northern side of Jì County's city,
which was established in the tenth year of Duke Wǔ of Qín after he attacked the Jì Róng people.
It was made a county,
and was the seat of the former Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhènróng,
and the county was called Jìzhì.
In the seventeenth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
it was renamed Hànyáng Commandery.
The city
was where Wěi Xiāo declared himself the Earl of the West.
Later, when Mǎ Chāo of the Eastern Hàn besieged Jì,
Yán Bójiǎn, the Assistant Inspector of Liángzhōu, secretly escaped through the water,
intending to report the emergency to Xiàhóu Yuān,
but was captured by Mǎ Chāo.
Mǎ Chāo ordered him to tell the city that no help was coming,
but Bójiǎn said:
"The great army is about to arrive,"
and all shouted "Long live!"
Mǎ Chāo angrily rebuked him,
and Bójiǎn said:
"Do you want an elder to utter unjust words?"
So he was killed.
The Wei River flows east and joins the Jì River,
which originates from the Jì Valley.
Further east is the Zhuógǔ River,
further east is the Dānglǐxī River,
further east is the Tuōlǐ River,
further east is the Qúgǔ River,
further east is the Huángtǔchuān River,
all originating from the southern mountains,
flowing north past the east of Jì City,
and then north into the Wei River.
The Wei River flows east out of the Cen Gorge,
enters the Xīnyáng River,
passes south of the lower city of Xīnyáng,
where the Xīgǔ and Chìhāo rivers both originate from the southern mountains,
flowing northeast into the Wei River.
The Wei River flows east and joins the Xīnyángyá River,
which is the Lǒng River,
originating northeast from Lǒng Mountain.
This river flows west and passes south of Wǎtíng,
where Wěi Xiāo, upon hearing of the fall of Lüèyáng,
sent Niú Hán to guard Wǎtíng,
which is this very pavilion.
Another river also originates from Lǒng Mountain,
flowing southeast past north of Wǎtíng,
then southwest, merging into one river,
called the Wǎtíng River.
It flows southwest past north of Qīngbīn Creek,
then southwest joins the Heishui River.
The Heishui River originates north of Hēichéng,
flows southwest past west of Hēichéng,
then southwest,
where the Mòwúnánchuān River flows into it,
which originates northeast from Lǒngchuí,
flows southwest past Hēichéng,
and south into the Heishui River.
The Heishui River flows southwest out of the Xuánjìng Gorge,
then southwest into the Wǎtíng River.
There is also the Huàn River,
which joins from the west,
commonly known as the Lùjiǎo Mouth.
It then flows south past the east of the old city of Āyáng County,
where in the first year of the Zhōngpíng era,
the Qiāng and Hú people from Běidì, along with Biān Zhāng, invaded Lǒngyòu,
and Gài Xūn, the Chief Clerk of Hànyáng, stationed troops at Āyáng to resist the rebels,
which is this city.
The river then flows south and joins the Yānwú River,
which originates from the eastern mountain of Yánfā,
flowing west into the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River flows further south,
where it meets the Fāngchéng River from the left,
which flows west into the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River flows south past the east of Chéngjì County,
traverses the Chánglí River,
which is called the Chánglí River.
It meets the Chéngjì River from the right,
which originates from the Dāngtíng River in the northwest,
flows east out of the Pòshí Gorge,
where the flow is cut off,
and the old channel flows east past Chéngjì County,
the birthplace of the ancient Emperor Tàihào, Fúxī.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was made part of Tiānshuǐ Commandery,
and the county
was the seat of Wáng Mǎng's Āyáng Commandery.
Further east,
a hidden source emerges,
connecting to the Chéngjì River,
which flows southeast into the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River flows further southeast,
meeting the Shòuqú River,
which originates east from Dàlǒng Mountain,
flows west past north of Shòuqú Pavilion,
then southwest into the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River flows further southwest,
traverses the Jiāngrén Gorge,
where on the cliff beside the road, there is a cave with a dead, withered corpse,
hence the gorge is named after it.
If one dismounts and climbs straight up to the cave,
it is about a hundred rèn high,
with a winding stone path,
barely wide enough for a single person to pass.
The withered corpse leans against the cave,
its bones still intact,
only lacking skin and hair.
When inquiring with the local residents,
they said that when their elders were children,
they had already heard from their ancestors' tales
that this must be a skeleton several hundred years old.
The river then flows southwest and joins the Lüèyángchuān River,
which originates west of the Xiānggǔ valley on Lǒng Mountain,
flowing west,
with the Dānxī River flowing into it from the right,
and the Gěchuān River entering from the left.
The river then flows west past the outskirts of Púchí,
where the Shílǔ River originates from the Shílǔ Creek to the southeast,
flowing northwest into it.
The river then flows west through the Lüèyáng River,
where it meets the Pòshègǔ River from the west,
further west meets the Píngxiànggǔ River,
further west meets the Jīnlǐgǔ River,
further west meets the Nánshì River,
further west meets the Tígǔ River,
all originating from the southern mountains,
flowing north past the east of Lüèyáng City,
with waves surging north into the river.
It then flows west past the north of the old city of Lüèyáng Circuit,
where the Níqú River originates from the southern mountains,
flows north through the Ní Gorge and enters the city from the north.
In the eighth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the Court Gentleman Lái Xì, along with Jì Zūn's subordinate Protector of the Army Wáng Zhōng and Right Assistant General Zhū Chǒng, led two thousand men,
all carrying halberds, knives, and axes,
from Yángchéng in Ānmín County.
In the second year of the Yuánshǐ era,
Emperor Píng abolished the Hūtuó Park of Āndìng and established Ānmín County,
building government offices and market districts,
from Fānxū and Huízhōng,
cutting down trees,
opening mountain roads to Lüèyáng,
and launching a night attack on Wěi Xiāo's defending general Jīn Liáng and others,
killing them all,
thus securing the city.
When Wěi Xiāo heard that Lüèyáng had fallen,
he mobilized all his forces to attack Lái Xì,
damming the river to flood the city.
Emperor Guāngwǔ personally led troops to rescue them,
and Wěi Xiāo fled to Xīchéng,
where Emperor Shìzǔ met with Lái Xì.
The river flows north from the city into the river,
one river with two branches,
which was likely the dam Wěi Xiāo built to flood Lüèyáng.
The river meets the Báiyáng Spring from the west,
further west meets the Púgǔ River,
further west meets the western branch of the Púgǔ River.
Further west, we come to the Longwěi Stream,
which joins the Púgǔ Stream,
both originating from the Southern Mountains,
their clear waters flying northward into the river.
The river then flows southwest to the Shuǐluò Estuary,
whose source lies eastward from Lǒng Mountain,
passing west by the Shuǐluò Pavilion,
and flowing southwest,
it meets the Dúnú Stream Estuary,
which emerges from Lǒng Mountain,
passes west through Dúnú Plain,
then west by the south of Shuǐluò Pavilion,
and flows northwest to join it,
mingling together southwest through Shímén Gorge,
called the Shímén River,
and flowing southwest into Lüèyáng Plain.
The Lüèyáng Plain River then flows northwest into Wǎtíng River,
which flows southwest out of Xiǎnqīn Gorge,
where the Shídàng River joins it,
emerging from the Northern Mountains,
on whose summit stands the temple of Nǚwā,
for after Fúxī there was the sovereign Nǚwā,
who, together with Shénnóng, formed the Three Sovereigns.
This river flows south to join the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River then flows southwest past the southeast of the old city of Xiǎnqīn County,
which in Han times was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Dòu Gù, the Grand Herald.
After Shídàng, we next encounter the Hámá Stream,
then the Jīnhēi Stream,
and then the Yídū Stream,
all emerging from left and right,
joining the Wǎtíng River in succession.
Further southeast, it meets the Ānyí Plain Estuary,
whose source lies east in Hú Valley,
flowing northwest through Yíshuǐ Plain to join the Dōngyáng Plain River,
called the Qǔyáng Junction.
Further west, it receives the Hédàng Plain River,
and further west, the Luóhàn River,
both flowing from northeast and southwest into the Yí River,
which then flows west past the south of Xiǎnqīn County,
and west into the Wǎtíng River.
The Wǎtíng River then flows southeast to the Dàhuá Valley Stream.
Further southeast, it meets the Zhélǐ Stream,
and further east, the Liùgǔ Stream,
all emerging from nearby gorges with rushing streams,
joining the Wǎtíng River.
Then southeast, it flows out of Xīnyáng Gorge,
where cliffs and peaks stand like walls,
and the water emerges between them,
called the Xīnyáng Cliff River,
which flows southeast into the Wèi River.
Further east, it passes Shàngguī County,
The Wèi River flows east past the northern side of Guī Mountain in the county,
passes east of Gù Ridge to the northeast,
then flows southeast.
Lánqú River originates from the northern mountains,
gathers numerous streams along its course,
and flows south to join the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows southeast and converges with Shénjiàn River,
