which is the Língquán Pond mentioned in the *Kāishān Tú*.
It is commonly known as Wàndàn Bay,
unfathomably deep,
truly a place of spiritual mystery.
Many who have ventured there recklessly
have met their demise.
The Wèi River further southeast receives Lìquán River,
which originates from Lìquán Stream to the north,
flows southeast, and joins the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows southeast past the west of Qiáo Pavilion,
then south to the mouth of Jiè River.
Jiè River originates from the western mountains,
where hundreds of streams converge,
forming a single river.
It flows east through Dāngtíng River,
which is the seat of Dāngtíng County.
To the left is Dāngtíng River,
and to the right, Zēngxí River joins it.
Further east, it converges with Dàbiàn River,
which originates from the western mountains,
where two sources merge and flow east,
passing through Dàbiàn River,
then southeast to join Jiè River.
Jiè River flows southeast and converges with Zhúlǐng River,
which originates from Zhú Ridge in the southern mountains,
where two sources flow together,
northeast into Jiè River.
Jiè River flows northeast past Shàngguī County,
with four tributaries on its left:
to the east, it meets Zhànxī River;
further east is Dàlǔgǔ River;
further east is Xiǎolǔgǔ River;
further east is Yángfǎngǔ River.
All originate from the northern mountains
and flow into Jiè River.
Jiè River is flanked by four tributaries on its right:
east of Zhú Ridge is Luànshíxī River;
further east is Mùméngǔ River;
further east is Luóchéngxī River;
further east is Shāngǔ River.
All originate from the southern mountains
and flow north into Jiè River.
Jiè River flows east,
and Huángguā River joins it.
Huángguā River originates from Xī Valley of Huángguā,
flows east past the north of Huángguā County,
then east,
flanked by Qīngxī and Báishuǐ on both sides,
then northeast,
where Dàhàngǔ River emerges from Hàn Stream in the south,
flows north through ravines,
with springs and streams meandering,
all joining Huángguā River.
Huángguā River flows northeast through Chì Valley,
and all flow into Jiè River.
Jiè River flows east and receives Máoquángǔ River,
then east past the south of Shàngguī City,
receiving Héquán River,
both originating from the southern mountains and flowing north into Jiè River.
Jiè River is also known as Yáng River.
To the north, Méng River joins it,
originating from Guī Mountain northwest of the county,
gathering numerous streams,
forming a river,
flowing east then bending south,
passing west of the old city of Shàngguī County,
skirting the south of the city and emerging from Shàngguī.
The old Guī
was a state of the Róng people.
In the tenth year of Duke Wǔ of Qín, he attacked Guī,
established it as a county,
which was the former seat of Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
Five cities were connected,
and within the northern city was a lake,
from which a white dragon emerged,
followed by wind and rain.
Therefore, in the third year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was renamed Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
The dwellings in its villages were all roofed with wooden planks,
as described in the *Book of Songs* as the "plank houses of the Western Róng."
Méng River flows south into Jiè River.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
Guī Mountain,
from which Méng River originates,
flows south into Yáng River,
referring to this river.
Jiè River flows east and receives Yánggǔ River,
then Dànggǔ River,
both originating from the southern mountains,
flowing north into Jiè River.
Jiè River flows east and converges with Duànxī River,
which originates from Mǎmén Stream in the southwest,
flowing northeast to join Jiè River.
Jiè River flows east into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows south past Qiáo Pavilion,
then east past Miánzhū County,
converging with Dōngtíng River,
also known as Qiáo River.
Qīngshuǐ is sometimes used as a general name.
Its source is east at Xiǎolǒng Mountain,
where numerous streams converge,
forming a single river,
flowing west into Dōngtíng River,
becoming Dōngtíng River,
converging with Xiǎozhī and Dàzhī Rivers.
Further northwest, it receives Nánshéngǔ River,
where three rivers originate from the southeast,
flowing in succession.
There is also Máipú River,
flanked by two streams,
converging with Yán River and flowing southwest into Dōngtíng River.
Dōngtíng River flows west,
with Tàngōu River on the right,
and further west, Qūgǔ River,
which originates from two streams in the southeast, flowing northwest,
into Dōngtíng River.
To the right of Dōngtíng River,
Wēngǔ River originates from Xiǎolǒng Mountain,
and further west,
Suōgǔ River originates from Suō Stream in the southern mountains,
flowing southwest into Dōngtíng River.
Dōngtíng River flows west to the mouth of Qīngshuǐ,
which originates from Lǒng Mountain in the northeast,
with two sources emerging together,
flowing southwest out of Lǒng Pass to form a single river,
then southwest through Xìyě Gorge,
passing Qīngchí Valley,
then east of the old city of Qīngshuǐ County,
which was Shímù County under Wáng Mǎng.
This river flows southwest to join Dōngtíng River,
and from here onward, it is also commonly called Qīngshuǐ.
It flows south past Qīngshuǐ City,
then west to converge with Qín River,
which originates from Qín Valley at Dàlǒng Mountain in the northeast,
with two sources flowing together,
passing three springs,
merging into one river,
then through Qín River Valley,
where the old Qín Pavilion stands,
the fief of Qín Zhòng.
The name "Qín"
began from here.
Qín River flows west past the old city of Jiànglǒng County,
then southwest,
where Zìhài and Sōngduō Rivers originate from Lǒng Mountain,
converge and flow southwest,
passing north of Jiànglǒng City,
then southwest into Qín River.
Qín River flows southwest through Lǒng River Valley,
passing Liùpán Pass,
by Qīngshuǐ City,
then southwest into Qīngshuǐ.
Both upstream and downstream of Qīngshuǐ,
it is called Qín River Valley.
Further west,
Qiāng River joins it,
originating from Qiāng Valley in the north,
gathering numerous streams,
forming a river,
where waters converge like stars,
called Xiǎoqiāng River.
It flows southwest,
with Chánggǔ River joining from the left,
and Dōngbù River entering from the right.
Qiāng River flows south into Qīngshuǐ.
Qīngshuǐ flows southwest to the mouth of Miánzhū River,
which originates from Miánzhū Stream in the northwest.
To the southeast is Chángsī River,
originating from Chángsī Stream in the north,
flowing south into Miánzhū River,
then southeast past the old city of Miánzhū Circuit,
southeast into Qīngshuǐ.
Qīngshuǐ flows southeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows southeast and converges with Jīnggǔ River,
which originates from Jīnggǔ Mountain in the southwest,
flowing northeast to converge with Héng River,
which originates from Héng Valley in the southeast,
flowing northwest past Héngshuǐ Kuàng,
then northwest into Jīnggǔ River.
The combined flow exits northwest through Jīnggǔ Gorge,
then northwest,
where Xuānyuángǔ River joins it,
originating from Xuānyuán Stream in the southern mountains.
Yáo Zhān of Nán'ān believed that the Yellow Emperor was born in Tiānshuǐ,
at Xuānyuán Valley, seventy lǐ east of Shàngguī City.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
He was born at Shòuqiū,
which is north of the eastern gate of Lǔ.
It is unknown which is correct.
This river flows north into Jīnggǔ River.
Jīnggǔ River flows northwest,
with Báichéng Stream flowing northeast,
and Bái'é Spring originating from its west.
The White City River flows eastward.
The White City River then flows northeast and enters the Jīng Valley River.
The Jīng Valley River flows northeast past Dǒng Tíng below,
where Yáng Nándāng sent his nephew Bǎo Zōng to garrison Dǒng Tíng,
which is this very pavilion.
The river flows northeast and empties into the Wèi River.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"From the Jīng Valley Mountain,
the Jīng River emerges,
flows southeast,
and empties into the Wèi River." This is correct.
The Wèi River flows eastward,
where the Bóyáng Valley River joins it.
The river originates from the Bóyáng Valley of the Xíngmǎ Mountain,
flows northward,
while the White River emerges from the White River Stream to the southeast,
and flows northwest to join the Bóyáng River.
The Bóyáng River flows northwest through the valley,
gathering and controlling the various streams,
and empties northward into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows eastward past Dàlì,
then southeast,
where the Miáo Valley River joins it.
The river emerges from the Xíngmǎ Mountain to the south,
flows north past Píngzuò to the northwest,
passes through Miáo Valley,
bends eastward past the south of Bóyáng City,
and is called the Bóyáng Plain.
It is said that when Lǐ Ěr traveled westward,
this was the route he took.
Thus, the mountains, plains, fields, and valleys
often bear his name.
The Wèi River flows southeast,
with numerous streams cascading like waves,
flowing in succession like geese in flight:
On the left, the Bóyáng Eastern Stream River joins it,
further east is the Wàngsōng River,
further east is the Máoliù Stream River,
further east is the Pízhōu Valley River,
further east is the Huángdù Eastern Stream River,
which emerges from the northern mountains,
and flows south into the Wèi River;
On the right is the Míng Valley River,
further east is the Qiū Valley River,
further east is the Qiū Valley Eastern Stream River,
further east is the Qiányán Valley River,
all emerging from the southern mountains,
and flowing northeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows southeast out of Shímén,
crosses the Xiǎolǒng Mountain,
passes south of Nányóu County,
and joins the Chǔ River to the east,
commonly known as the Chángshé River.
The river originates from the Shùlì Mountain in Qiān County.
It flows south past the east of the Chángshé Garrison,
which was built in the third year of the Hépíng era of the Wei dynasty,
to relocate displaced people and guard against invaders from Lǒng.
The Chǔ River flows south and empties into the Wèi River.
Kàn Yīn identified this river as the Qiān River.
The Wèi River flows eastward,
where the Qiān and Wū Rivers join it.
I have examined various geographical records,
which state that the Qiān River emerges from the northwest of Qiān County.
Kàn Yīn's Records of the Thirteen Provinces agrees with this,
and further identifies the Qiān River as the Lóngyú River,
likely because its waterways connect and share common names.
The Wèi River flows east into Sànguān.
The Biographies of Divine Immortals by Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Lǎozi traveled westward out of the pass,
and the pass official Yǐn Xǐ observed the qi,
knowing that a true man would travel westward.
He encountered Lǎozi
and insisted that he write a book.
Lǎozi had no choice
and wrote the Two Classics of the Way and Virtue,
which is called the Book of Lǎozi."
There is a temple of Lǎozi.
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural says:
"When Lǎozi was about to enter the pass westward,
the pass official Yǐn Xǐ, a lover of the Way,
saw that a true man was heading west
and invited him on the road."
Huángfǔ Shì'ān's Biographies of High-Minded Men says:
"Lǎozi served as the Archivist of the Zhou court,
and when the Zhou dynasty declined,
he retired from office,
serving as the Keeper of the Zhou Archives for over eighty years.
He preferred anonymity and detachment,
so the world did not know he was a true man.
In the tenth year of King Jǐng of Zhou,
when Confucius was seventeen,
he went to Zhou to meet Lǎo Dān."
However, when King Yōu lost the Way,
and King Píng moved the capital east,
the passes shifted for defense,
and people relocated for their duties.
Yǐn Xǐ observing the qi
could not have happened here.
As for the route taken,
this might be plausible.
The Wèi River flows east past the north of Xīwǔgōng,
commonly mistaken for Sànguān City,
but this is incorrect.
Mr. Chǔ said:
"Wǔgōng
is a small town on the western border of Fúfēng.
It is the entrance to the Shu plank roads,
close to the mountains, with no other prominent figures easily rising to power."
The Wèi River then joins the Hàn River,
which emerges from Zhōudào Valley,
flows north past the west of the old city of Gùdào County in Wǔdū,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shànzhì.
Gùdào County has the Nùtè Shrine.
The Tales of Marvels says:
"In Gùdào County of Wǔdū, there is the Nùtè Shrine,
which says the deity was originally a large catalpa tree in the southern mountains.
In the twenty-seventh year of Duke Wén of Qin,
they cut it down,
but the tree's wounds healed immediately.
Duke Wén of Qin then sent forty men with axes to chop it,
but it still would not break.
One exhausted soldier,
injured in the foot and unable to leave,
lay under the tree
and heard ghosts talking to each other:
'Is this battle tiring?'
One said:
'The foot is indeed tired.'
Another said:
'Duke Qin will surely persist without stopping.'
The reply was:
'What can he do to me?'
Another said:
'What about scattering red ashes on you?'
There was silence.
The lying man reported this,
and they ordered the soldiers to wear red clothes
and scatter ashes where they chopped.
The tree broke and transformed into an ox, entering the water.
Thus, the Qin people built a shrine for it."
The river flows northeast past Dàsànguān and enters the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows southeast,
joining the Five Streams River from the southern mountains on the right,
which flows between the ravines and empties into it.
It then flows east past the west of Chéncāng County.
The county has Chéncāng Mountain,
on which stands the Chénbǎo Jīmíng Shrine.
In the past, Duke Wén of Qín, moved by Bóyáng's words,
went hunting at Chéncāng,
encountered it on this slope,
and obtained a stone-like object,
its color resembling liver.
He returned and enshrined it as a treasure,
hence the name "Chénbǎo."
Its arrival came from the southeast,
with a brilliant glow and a sound like thunder,
causing all wild chickens to crow,
hence it is also called the "Jīmíng Shén."
The "Geographical Records" states:
There are shrines for Shànggōng Míngxīng, Huángdì's grandson Shùn's wife, and the Blind Tomb;
there is the Yǔyáng Palace,
built by King Wǔ of Qín.
Yìng Shào said:
The county is named after Chén Mountain.
Yáo Mù said:
Huángdì's capital was at Chén,
meaning it was here.
Róng's "Kāishān Tú Zhù" states:
Fúxī was born in Chéngjì and moved his capital to Chéncāng,
not the state of Chén.
Emperor Míng of Wèi sent General Hǎo Zhāo of Tàiyuán to build Chéncāng Fortress.
After its completion,
Zhūgě Liàng besieged it.
Liàng sent Jìn Xiáng, a fellow townsman of Zhāo, to persuade him,
but he did not surrender.
Liàng attacked Zhāo with tens of thousands against his thousand-plus men,
using cloud ladders, battering rams, and tunnels to press and shoot at Zhāo;
Zhāo used fire arrows and continuous stones to repel them,
and Liàng, finding the situation unfavorable, withdrew.
Today, the Qiān River faces Liàng's fortress,
which is where he confronted Zhāo.
The Chéncāng River originates from Chéncāng Mountain,
flows southeast, and empties into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows east and merges with the Suíyáng Stream,
whose upper reaches receive the Xié River.
The water from the Xié Valley divides and flows into the Suíyáng Stream,
reaching north to Chéncāng and entering the Wèi.
Therefore, Zhūgě Liàng wrote in his "Letter to Elder Brother Jǐn":
There is the Suíyáng Small Valley,
though its cliffs are extremely steep,
and its streams crisscross,
making it difficult for military movement,
in the past, patrols came and went,
and the main road provided access.
Now, I have ordered the vanguard to clear and repair this road,
heading toward Chéncāng,
which is sufficient to pin down the enemy's forces,
preventing them from dividing their troops and moving east.
The Wèi River flows east past the old city of Yùyí County,
The "Geographical Records" states:
There is a Qiān River Shrine,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yùpíng.
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
Wěi Xiāo besieged Lái Xì at Lüèyáng,
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict:
The Táohuā River emerges at Chuánpán,
all reaching Yùyí and Chéncāng,
dividing and advancing.
The Qiān River enters here,
originating from the Xiánzhōng Valley in Pǔgǔ Township of Qiān County,
breaking out to form the Xiánpú Marsh.
The "Ěryǎ" states:
Water breaking out forms a marsh, called qiān.
The name Qiān
indeed encompasses this meaning.
The river has two sources:
one originates from the western mountains of the county,
commonly known as Xiǎo Lǒng Mountain,
with steep cliffs and high dangers,
impassable for carts.
Therefore, Zhāng Héng's "Four Sorrows Poem" says:
The one I long for is in Hànyáng,
I wish to go to him, but the Lǒng slopes are long.
This water flows northeast,
dripping through ravines,
forming deep pools,
with unfathomable depths,
producing multicolored fish.
Common folk consider them spiritual,
and none dare to catch them,
hence calling this water the Lóngyú River,
and downstream it is also commonly called Lóngyú Chuān.
The river water flows east past the old city of Qiān County to the north.
The "Shǐjì" records:
Duke Wén of Qín hunted east in the Qiān fields,
and subsequently established his capital there.
Further east, it passes through marshes,
merging into one stream.
To the right is the Báilóng Spring,
with a diameter of five feet,
its source gushing forth,
creating ripples that spread in all directions,
flowing northeast into the Qiān.
The Qiān River flows east and meets another stream,
originating from the western side of the southern mountain,
commonly known as Wú Mountain.
Its three peaks rise like rosy clouds,
layered in beauty against the sky,
with collapsing ridges and steep slopes,
the mountain peaks supporting each other,
appearing perpetually on the verge of collapse.
The "Geographical Records" states:
Wú Mountain lies west of the county,
the "Ancient Texts" call it Qiān Mountain,
which is the Yú mentioned in the "Guóyǔ."
At the foot of the mountain is a stone cave, four feet wide,
seven feet high,
water overflowing the stone cavity,
cascading down sideways,
roaring and shaking,
forming a river at its source,
flowing north into the Qiān.
From the confluence upstream and downstream,
all call it Lóngyú Chuān.
The Qiān River flows southeast past the old city of Yúmí County,
renamed Fútíng by Wáng Mǎng.
In the past, Guō Xī, ashamed of Wáng Mǎng's summons,
retreated and lived here in seclusion.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Gěng Kuàng as a marquis here.
The Qiān River flows southeast past Cí Mountain,
then southeast past the old city of Píngyáng in Yùyí County.
The "Shǐjì" records:
In the second year of Duke Níng of Qín, he moved to Píngyáng.
Xú Guǎng said:
This was the Píngyáng Pavilion of old Méi.
North of the city stands the stele of Zhào Róng, Governor of Bīn Prefecture during the Hàn,
erected in the first year of Emperor Líng's Jiàn'ān era.
The Qiān River flows east and empties into the Wèi.
To the right of the Wèi River,
the Pánxī Stream joins it,
originating from the Zī Valley of the southern mountains,
descending from heights with rushing currents,
pouring into the stream.
Within the stream is a spring,
called Zī Spring.
The spring water accumulates into deep pools,
naturally forming ponds and islets,
which is the Zī Spring where Tàigōng fished, as mentioned in "Lǚshì Chūnqiū."
Nowadays, people call it Wán Valley.
The stone cliffs are deep and high,
secluded and dense,
with forests forming beautiful barriers,
rarely trodden by humans.
In the southeastern corner is a stone chamber,
likely where Tàigōng resided.
On the flat rocks by the water where he fished,
is where Tàigōng cast his line.
The marks of his kneeling and baiting,
the imprints of his two knees, still remain,
hence the name Pánxī.
The water is clear, cool, and mysteriously potent,
flowing north for twelve lǐ before entering the Wèi,
seventy lǐ north of Wéiduī City.
The Wèi River flows east past Jīshí Plain,
also known as the Northern Plain.
In the second year of Qīnglóng,
Zhūgě Liàng marched out of Xié Valley,
while Sīmǎ Yì stationed his troops south of the Wèi.
Guō Huái, Governor of Yōng Prefecture, strategized that Liàng would certainly contend for the Northern Plain and station there,
so he occupied it first.
When Liàng arrived,
he indeed could not advance.
The Wèi River flows east past the north of Wǔzhàng Plain.
The "Wèishì Chūnqiū" states:
Zhūgě Liàng occupied the southern plain of the Wèi River,
and Sīmǎ Yì said to his generals:
If Liàng advances toward Wǔgōng,
turning east along the mountains,
that would show his courage.
If he heads west to Wǔzhàng Plain,
then you gentlemen have nothing to worry about.
Liàng indeed stationed on this plain,
confronting Yì.
The Wèi River flows east past the old city of Méi County.
The "Geographical Records" states:
The seat of the Right Assistant Commandant.
The "Wèi Chūnqiū" records:
Zhūgě Liàng invaded Méi,
and Sīmǎ Yì occupied Méi to resist Liàng,
which is this county.
The Wèi River flows east past the south of Méi Fortress.
The "Hàn Xiàndì Zhuàn" states:
Dǒng Zhuó conscripted soldiers to build Méi Fortress,
as high as the walls of Cháng'ān,
storing grain for thirty years.
He himself said:
If successful,
he would dominate the world;
if not,
guarding this would suffice to live out his days.
Such was his folly.
18 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 18
18.1 The Wèi River
18.1 The Wèi River
flows east again, passing north of Wǔgōng County.
The Wei River passes through the county,
and the Xie River flows from the south to join it.
The river originates from the Yá Lǐng Mountain southwest of the county,
flows north through the Xie Valley,
passes east of the Wǔzhàngyuán,
as Zhūgě Liàng wrote in his "Letter to Bù Zhì":
"My forward army is stationed at Wǔzhàngyuán,
which lies ten lǐ west of Wǔgōng."
The remaining water flows from Wǔlì County,
hence it is also called the Wǔgōng River.
Therefore, Zhūgě Liàng stated in his "Memorial":
"I dispatched the Tiger Step Supervisor Mèng Yǎn to occupy the east bank of the Wǔgōng River.
Sīmǎ Yì took advantage of the rising water to attack Yǎn's camp.
I constructed a bamboo bridge,
crossed the river to shoot at them,
and once the bridge was completed, they fled."
This river flows north and empties into the Wei.
The "Geographical Records" states:
"The Xie River originates from Yá Lǐng,
flowing north to Méi, where it joins the Wei."
The Wei River then flows east past the north of Mǎ Zhǒng.
Zhūgě Liàng wrote in his "Letter to Bù Zhì":
"Mǎ Zhǒng lies over ten lǐ east of Wǔgōng.
It occupies a high position,
making it inconvenient to attack,
which is why I left it untouched."
The Wei River then passes north of the old city of Wǔgōng County,
which was called Xīnguāng during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The "Geographical Records" states:
"The county has the Tàiyī Mountain,
which the 'Ancient Texts' identify as Zhōngnán,
and Dù Yù identifies as Zhōngnán as well.
It is also called Tàibái Mountain,
located south of Wǔgōng County,
two hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān.
How high it is remains unknown.
A common saying goes:
'Wǔgōng's Tàibái,
three hundred lǐ from heaven.'
When troops march at its foot,
they must not beat drums or blow horns,
for doing so will bring fierce wind and rain."
Dù Yàndá said:
"Tàibái Mountain connects southward to Wǔgōng Mountain,
and among all the mountains, it is the most splendid and majestic.
Snow accumulates in both winter and summer,
making it appear brilliantly white from afar."
On the mountain is the Gǔ Chūn Shrine.
Chūn,
a native of Yuèyáng,
died of illness during Emperor Chéng's reign,
yet his body remained warm.
Later, he suddenly appeared at the south gate of Yuè and the Guāng Gate,
and then entered Tàibái Mountain.
The people erected a shrine for him on the mountain ridge,
where he would come to stay during spring and autumn."
At the foot of the mountain is the Tàibái Shrine,
where the people offer sacrifices.
During Liú Yào's time,
this mountain collapsed,
and a man from Cháng'ān named Liú Zhōng obtained a piece of white jade from the collapse,
one chǐ square,
with inscriptions reading:
"The emperor perishes, the emperor perishes, Zhào Chāng is defeated.
The well water dries up,
five beams are constructed.
È Yǒu declines slightly, Xiāo perishes.
Alas, alas,
the red ox struggles with the traces—is it all over?"
At the time, all the officials came to offer congratulations,
but the Secretariat Director Liú Jūn stepped forward and said:
"This is an omen of the state's destruction.
How can it be celebrated?"
It turned out just as he said.
The Wei River flows further east,
and the hot spring water joins it.
The water originates from Tàiyī Mountain,
boiling and surging like hot water.
Dù Yàndá said:
"It can cure all diseases.
When the world is peaceful, illnesses are healed;
when the world is chaotic, it has no effect."
This water merges with the stream below,
flows north for thirteen lǐ, and enters the Wei.
The Wei River then flows east past the old city of Tái County,
which was the ancient Tái City,
the fiefdom of Hòu Jì.
This is what the "Book of Songs" refers to as "establishing a household in Tái."
Northeast of the city is the Jiāng Yuán Shrine,
and one hundred paces southwest of the city is the Jì Shrine,
which is the Tái Pavilion of Méi.
When Wáng Shàolín served as the magistrate of Méi County,
he passed by this pavilion.
The pavilion chief said:
"This pavilion is haunted and kills people."
Shàolín replied:
"Benevolence overcomes evil.
What ghost would dare oppose me?"
He then stayed overnight.
In the middle of the night, he heard a woman's voice crying out for justice.
Shàolín said:
"Come forward and state your case."
The woman said:
"I have no clothes and dare not approach."
Shàolín threw his clothes to her.
The woman came forward and pleaded:
"My husband was the magistrate of Fú.
On his way to assume office,
he stayed overnight at this pavilion
and was killed by the pavilion chief."
Shàolín said:
"I will redress your grievance.
Do not harm innocent people again."
He then laid his clothes on the ground,
and she suddenly vanished.
The next day, he confronted the pavilion chief,
who confessed to the crime.
The pavilion was thus cleansed and peaceful.
The Wei River then flows east past the south of Yōng County,
where the Yōng River joins it.
The water originates from Yōng Mountain,
flows southeast through Zhōngláo Stream,
commonly known as Zhōngláo Water,
also called Bīngjǐng Water.
It flows south past the east of Hú City,
a local name.
This was likely the former residence of Duke Huì of Qín,
known as the Qínián Palace.
Duke Xiào also called it the Tuóquán Palace.
According to the "Geographical Records":
"It is located in Yōng."
Cuī Yīn said:
"The tomb of Duke Mù is beneath the Qínián Observatory of the Tuóquán Palace."
The "Imperial Overview" also states this.
Liú Xiàng said:
"Duke Mù was buried without a mound."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"When Duke Mù died,
177 people followed him in death.
The good ministers of the Zǐchē clan—Yǎnxī, Zhòngháng, and Zhēnhǔ—
were among those who followed him in death.
The people of Qín mourned them
and composed the poem 'Yellow Bird' for them."
I believe Cuī Yīn and the "Imperial Overview"
are mistaken.
Dukes Huì and Xiào
were both descendants of Duke Mù,
successive rulers.
How could descendants build a palace on the tomb of their ancestor?
From this, it can be inferred
that these two accounts are not accurate.
The Yōng River flows further east,
where it joins the Zuǒyáng Water on the left,
commonly known as the West Water.
This water originates from the Zuǒyáng Stream in the north,
flows south past the west of Qízhōu City,
where the Wèi dynasty established the seat of the Qízhōu Governor.
The Zuǒyáng Water then flows south and empties into the Yōng River.
The Yōng River also merges with the East Water,
a local name.
It originates from the Hétáo Valley in the north,
flows south, and joins the southern source on the right,
commonly known as the Fǎnyǎn Spring.
The combined flow passes east of Qízhōu City,
and then south to join the Yōng River.
The prefecture lies between these two rivers,
with the south being the confluence of the two streams,
also locally known as the Cuìkōng Water.
It flows east,
and the Dènggōng Spring joins it.
The water originates north of the Dèng Ài Shrine,
hence the name Dènggōng Spring.
Several sources all arise south of the old city of Yōng County.
The county
was the former residence of Duke Dé of Qín.
The "Jìnshū Dìdào Jì" identifies it as the land of the Western Guó.
The "Hànshū Dìlǐzhì" identifies it as Western Guó County.
The "Tàikāng Dìjì" states:
"It was the state of Guó Shū.
There was a Guó Palace.
When King Píng moved east,
Shū moved from here to Shàngyáng,
becoming the Southern Guó."
Yōng has the Five Altars Shrine,
where sacrifices are offered to the Five Emperors.
In the past, Duke Wén of Qín hunted between the Qiān and Wei rivers
and dreamed of a yellow snake descending from heaven to the earth,
its mouth resting at Fūyǎn.
Believing it to be the spirit of the Supreme God,
he built the Fū Altar to sacrifice to the White Emperor.
Duke Xuān of Qín built the Mì Altar south of the Wei River
to sacrifice to the Green Emperor.
Duke Líng then built the Upper Altar at Wúyáng
to sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor,
and the Lower Altar to sacrifice to the Red Emperor.
Duke Xiàn built the Qí Altar at Yuèyáng to sacrifice to the White Emperor.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn asked:
"Heaven has Five Emperors,
so why are there only four now?"
The scholars did not know the reason.
The Emperor said:
"I know it.
It awaits me to make five,"
and thus established the Northern Altar to sacrifice to the Black Emperor.
Yìng Shào said:
"A place elevated on all four sides is called Yōng."
Kàn Yīn said:
"It is suitable as a secluded place for deities,
hence numerous shrines were established there."
There were also the Phoenix Tower and the Phoenix Maiden Shrine.
During the time of Duke Mù of Qín,
there was a man named Xiāo Shǐ,
skilled at playing the xiāo flute,
able to attract white swans and peacocks.
Duke Mù's daughter, Nòng Yù, admired him,
so the Duke built a Phoenix Tower for them to reside in.
After several decades,
one day they followed a phoenix and departed.
It is said that in the Yōng palace, the sound of xiāo and guǎn flutes could be heard through the ages.
Now the tower has collapsed and the shrine is ruined,
and it is no longer so.
The Dèng Spring flows east and joins the Yōng River.
From this point onward, although it meets other waterways,
it is still commonly referred to as such,
hence the Yǔ Gòng mentions the confluence of the Yōng and Jǔ rivers.
The Yōng River flows east past the south of the Shào Pavilion,
commonly called the Shù Pavilion River.
This is likely because the sounds of "Shào" and "Shù" are similar,
leading to the error.
The pavilion
was the former fief of Duke Shào.
Jīng Xiàng Fán said:
"The pavilion is fifty lǐ south of Zhōu City's southern wall."
The Hòu Hàn Jùn Guó Zhì states:
"Méi County has the Shào Pavilion," referring to this.
The Yōng River flows southeast and joins the Héng River.
The Héng River originates from Dùyáng Mountain.
This river flows south,
called the Dùyáng River.
It flows southeast,
and on the left joins the Qī River.
The Qī River originates from the Qī Stream in Dùyáng County,
called the Qī Channel.
Thus, Xú Guǎng said:
"The Qī River originates from Qí Mountain in Dùyáng," which is correct.
The Qī Channel flows south,
and the Dàluán River joins it.
The Dàluán River originates from the Dàdào River in the northwest,
flowing southeast into the Qī River.
This is the ancient Qí River.
The Huái Nán Zǐ states:
"The Qí River originates from Shíqiáo Mountain,
flowing southeast."
Xiàng Rú's Fēng Shàn Shū says:
"Turtles were collected at Qí."
The Hàn Shū Yīn Yì states:
"Qí
is the name of a river."
It refers to this river.
The two rivers flow together,
merging into one stream.
To the south, it joins the Héng River.
From this point onward, it is also called the Qí River.
Commonly known as the Xiǎo Héng River,
or sometimes called the Mǐliú River.
It passes west of Qí Mountain,
then bends and passes south of Zhōu City.
The city lies on the southern side of Qí Mountain, closer to the west,
which is what is meant by "dwelling on the southern side of Qí."
It is not only named after the mountain
but also takes its name from the river.
It further passes below the Zhōu Plain.
To the north is the Zhōngshuǐ Township and Chéngzhōu Settlement,
hence it is called "having Zhōu."
North of the river
lies Qí Mountain.
This is where thieves once stole and ate Duke Mù of Qín's horses.
The Qí River flows east past the south of Jiāngshì City, becoming the Jiāng River.
According to the Shì Běn:
"The Flame Emperor,
surnamed Jiāng."
The Dì Wáng Shì Jì states:
"The Flame Emperor,
Shénnóngshì,
surnamed Jiāng.
His mother, Nǚ Dēng, traveled to Huáyáng,
was moved by a deity and gave birth to the Flame Emperor,
who grew up by the Jiāng River."
This is that place.
It flows east into the Yōng River.
The Yōng River flows south,
passing through the Zhōngtíng River in Měiyáng County,
where it joins the Wǔ River.
The Wǔ River originates from the side of the Dà Ridge in Dùyáng County.
It measures three hundred paces east-west,
and two hundred paces north-south.
Commonly known as Chìní Xiàn,
it flows along valleys and ravines,
and is popularly called the Dà Héng River.
It is likely the Dù River.
This river flows southeast,
passing east of the old city of Dùyáng County.
Commonly known as the Gùxiàn River,
also, the old Guó County had Dùyáng Mountain.
North of the mountain is Dùyáng Valley,
with a cave entrance leading northward,
its end unknown.
It lies south of Tiānzhù Mountain,
hence the county derived its name from it.
It also refers to this river for its name,
which is Wáng Mǎng's Tōng Dù.
Thus, the Dì Lǐ Zhì states:
"The county has the Dù River."
The Dù River flows east,
and the Èrkēng River joins it.
This river has two sources.
One originates from the northwest,
joining the Dú Tuí River,
then flows east past Wǔjiāng Mountain,
and further joins the Xiānggǔ River.
The Xiānggǔ River originates from the Xiāng Stream,
flowing southeast into the Dù River,
called the Xiānggǔ River.
Further south,
the Mò River joins it.
The Mò River originates east of the Liáng Mountain Great Ridge in Hǎozhì County,
flowing south past the west of Liáng Mountain Palace.
Thus, the Dì Lǐ Zhì states:
"Hǎozhì has Liáng Mountain Palace,
built by Qín Shǐ Huáng."
East of the river is the old city of Hǎozhì County,
Wáng Mǎng's Hǎo Estate.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of General Gěng Yǎn, Marquis of Jiànwēi.
It further flows south through the Zhōngtíng River in Měiyáng County,
joining the Yōng River,
called the Zhōngtíng River.
The Yōng River flows south past the west of Měiyáng County.
In the second year of Zhānghé,
it was re-enfeoffed as the marquisate of Zhāng Hóu Gěng Bǐng.
The river further flows south and joins the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows east,
and the Luògǔ River originates from the Luò Valley in the southern mountains.
It flows north past the west of the Great Wall.
In the third year of Gānlù of Wèi,
Shǔ dispatched Jiāng Wéi through Luò Valley,
besieging the Great Wall,
which is this place.
Further east,
the Máng River flows from the south and joins it.
The Máng River originates from the Máng Valley in the southern mountains.
It flows north past the Jade Maiden Chamber.
By the riverbank at the mountain's edge is a stone chamber,
commonly called the Jade Maiden Chamber.
The Máng River further flows north through the bamboo garden of Zhōuzhì County,
where it divides into two streams.
Emperor Chōng of Hàn decreed:
"Dí Yì rebelled in the east,
Huò Hóng relied on the Máng bamboo of Zhōuzhì."
This refers to here.
The river divides into two branches.
One branch flows northeast as a distributary,
while the other flows north into the Wèi River.
19 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 19
19．1 The Wèi River
19．1 The Wèi River
Further east, it passes south of Huáilǐ County,
then east,
where the Láo River flows from the south and joins it.
The Wei River passes by the old southern city of the county,
as noted in the "Collected Commentaries on the Book of Han,"
Lǐ Qí called it Xiǎo Huáilǐ,
which is the western city of the county.
Further east,
it merges with a branch of the Máng River,
which draws water from the Máng River at the Bamboo Garden,
flows northeast,
then bends northward and enters the Wei River.
The Wei River then flows northeast past the southern side of Huángshān Palace,
which is the Huángshān Palace mentioned in the "Treatise on Geography"
as having been built in the second year of Emperor Hui's reign.
The "Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò" states:
Emperor Wǔ traveled incognito
and journeyed west to Huángshān Palace.
Thus, later generations called it the Wandering City.
The Jiù River flows into it,
originating from the Jiù Valley in the southern mountains,
flowing north past the western side of the Great Mound,
which people call the Mound of Lǎozi.
In ancient times, Lǐ Ěr served as the Archivist of Zhōu,
and as the world declined, he entered the Róng region,
leaving a tomb here.
This matter lacks classical evidence,
but Zhuāng Zhōu, in his writings, said:
When Lǎo Dān died,
Qín Shī mourned him,
and after three cries, he departed.
This is not a statement about immortality.
Humans are endowed with the essence of the Five Elements,
and as yīn and yáng undergo transformations,
there is no principle of not changing.
Based on this reasoning,
perhaps it is as the tradition says.
The ancients allowed doubtful matters to be passed down,
so both accounts are preserved.
The Jiù River passes north of the Bamboo Garden,
merging with the Hēi River,
which originates from three springs to the right of the Jiù River.
These three springs emerge wondrously,
said to converge into a single stream,
flowing north,
and joining the Jiù River from the left.
The Jiù River then flows north and empties into the Wei River.
The Wei River further east merges with the Tiánxī River,
which originates from the Tián Valley in the southern mountains,
flows north past the western side of Chángyáng Palace,
then north past the old western city of Zhōuzhì County,
and further northeast merges with another stream.
This stream originates from the southern source of Zhōuzhì County,
flows north past the eastern side of the county,
then north past the western side of Sīxiāng City,
and finally north into the Tiánxī River.
The Tiánxī River then flows north
and empties into the Wei River.
North of the county is the Ménglóng Canal,
which draws water from the Wei River at Méi County,
flows east through Wǔgōng County as the Chénglín Canal,
passes north of the county,
and is also called the Língzhǐ Canal.
The "Treatise on Rivers and Canals" states that it draws water from the Dǔ River.
Xú Guǎng said:
"It is also called the various rivers."
The Wei River then flows east past the old southern city of Huáilǐ County,
which was the ancient settlement of Dàqiū.
King Yì of Zhōu made it his capital.
During the Qín dynasty, it was called Fèiqiū,
also known as Shūqiū.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
Emperor Líng enfeoffed the Left General of the Palace Guard Huángfǔ Sōng as a marquis here.
The county faces the Wei River to the south
and is backed by a canal to the north.
The "Annals of Qín" in the Records of the Grand Historian states:
In the third year of King Wǔ of Qín,
the Wei River ran red for three days.
In the thirty-fourth year of King Zhāo of Qín,
the Wei River again ran red for three days.
The "Treatise on the Five Phases" in the Hóngfàn states:
Red
is the color of fire.
When water turns completely red,
it is fire overwhelming water.
The Wei River
is a major river of Qín.
When yīn and yáng are disordered,
and Qín employed harsh punishments,
it was an omen of ruin and chaos.
Later, Xiàng Yǔ entered Qín,
enfeoffing Sīmǎ Xīn as the King of Sài,
with his capital at Yuèyáng;
Dǒng Yì as the King of Dí,
with his capital at Gāonú;
and Zhāng Hán as the King of Yōng,
with his capital at Fèiqiū.
These were the Three Qín.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn pacified the Three Qín from the north,
diverted water to flood the city,
and thus destroyed Zhāng Hán.
In the third year,
it was renamed Huáilǐ,
and Wáng Mǎng changed it to Huáizhì.
People called it Dà Huáilǐ,
and during the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
it became the seat of Shǐpíng Commandery.
The city is surrounded by embankments,
and the old canals still remain,
which is what the Book of Hàn refers to as the encircling dikes of Huáilǐ.
To the east is the Lòu River,
originating from the Chì Valley in the southern mountains,
flowing northeast past the eastern side of Chángyáng Palace.
The palace had tall poplar trees,
hence its name.
The Lòu River then flows north past the western side of the Reed Garden,
also called Xiānzé.
It then flows north past Wàngxiān Palace,
and further northeast,
the Gěnggǔ River flows into it.
The Gěnggǔ River originates from the Gěng Valley in the southern mountains,
flows north and merges with the Liǔquán,
then northeast past the western side of Wǔzuò Palace.
Chángyáng and Wǔzuò Palaces
are eight lǐ apart,
both named after trees,
much like Táo's establishment being named after five willows.
Thus, Zhāng Yàn said:
"The palace has five oak trees,
located west of Zhōuzhì County."
The river flows north past the eastern side of Xiānzé,
then north past the eastern side of Wàngxiān Palace,
then north merges with the Chì River,
then north past the eastern side of Sīxiāng City,
and finally north empties into the Wei River.
The Wei River then flows east and merges with the Gān River,
which originates from the Gān Valley in the southern mountains,
flows north past the western side of Fùyáng Palace of King Wén of Qín,
then north past the eastern side of Wǔzuò Palace,
then north past the western side of Gān Pavilion.
East of the river is Hù County,
where in ancient times, Xià Qǐ launched a campaign against the Yǒuhù and made a pledge at this pavilion.
Thus, Mǎ Róng said:
"Gān
is the name of a place in the southern suburbs of Yǒuhù."
The Gān River further east meets the mouth of the Láo River,
which originates from the Láo Valley in the southern mountains,
flows north past the eastern side of the Hàn-era Yíchūn Observatory,
then north past the old western city of Hù County.
The Láo River passes north of the city and merges with the Měibēi River,
which originates north of the Yíchūn Observatory,
flows northeast, and empties into the Láo River.
The Láo River flows north into the Gān River,
and then chaotically enters the Wei River.
This was the former site of the Shànglín Park.
Dōngfāng Shuò recounted that during the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ, he traveled incognito,
north to Chíyáng,
west to Huángshān,
hunted south at Chángyáng,
and toured east at Yíchūn.
At the tenth mark of the night clepsydra,
he went out with palace attendants, regular attendants, imperial guards, scholars awaiting appointment, and skilled horsemen and archers from Lǒngxī and Běidì,
gathering at the palace gates,
hence the term "Qímén" (Gate of Assembly).
At dawn,
they descended the mountains,
galloping and shooting deer, boars, foxes, and rabbits,
hand-to-hand combat with bears and brown bears,
and the emperor greatly enjoyed it.
The emperor then ordered the Grand Master of the Palace Yúqiū Shòuwáng and scholars skilled in calculation awaiting appointment
to survey the lands south of Āchéng,
east of Zhōuzhì,
west of Yíchūn,
calculating the acreage and its value,
and annexing the southern mountains to establish the Shànglín Park.
Dōngfāng Shuò admonished that the construction of the Ēpáng Palace by Qín led to chaos in the empire,
and thus presented the matter of the Six Auspicious Signs of the Tàijiē constellation.
The emperor then appointed him Grand Master of the Palace and Palace Attendant,
bestowing upon him a hundred catties of gold,
and ultimately established the Shànglín Park.
Thus, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú requested to compose a rhapsody on the emperor's hunting excursions,
featuring Master Wūyǒu and Lord Wúshì, and presented the "Shànglín Rhapsody."
Further east,
the Fēng River flows from the south and empties into it.
The Fēng River originates from Fēng Creek,
flowing northwest and dividing into two streams:
one stream flows northeast as a branch channel,
the other flows northwest,
then north,
where the Jiāo River enters from the east,
then north again,
where the water from Kūnmíng Pond flows into it,
then north past the west of Língtái,
and further north until it reaches Shídùn and empties into the Wèi River.
The Dì Shuō states:
The Wèi River flows east and meets the Fēng River within Duǎnyīn Mountain,
where the confluence lacks any high mountains or unusual peaks,
having only plateaus, hills, and rocky rapids.
There was formerly a Biànmén Bridge over the water,
directly opposite the Biànmén Gate,
built in the third year of Emperor Wǔ's Jiànyuán era.
Zhāng Chāng said:
The bridge is northwest of Cháng'ān, east of Màolíng.
Rú Chún said:
It is forty lǐ from Cháng'ān.
The Wèi River then flows past the north of Tàigōng Temple,
in front of which stands the "Tàigōng Stele,"
its text worn and incomplete,
now untraceable.
The Wèi River then flows northeast and merges with the Hào River,
which receives water from Hào Pond north of Kūnmíng Pond,
the former capital of King Wǔ of Zhōu.
Thus, the Shī Jīng says:
The king divined,
dwelling in this Hàojīng,
the turtle confirmed it,
and King Wǔ accomplished it.
Since Emperor Wǔ of Hàn dredged Kūnmíng Pond in this area,
its foundations have collapsed and been lost,
now impossible to investigate.
The Chūnqiū Hòuzhuàn says:
The envoy Zhèng Róng entered Bǎigǔ Pass,
reached Píngshū Station,
and saw a plain carriage and white horse on Huà Mountain,
which asked Zhèng Róng where he was going.
He replied:
To Xiányáng.
The person in the carriage said:
I am an envoy of the Lord of Huà Mountain,
and wish to entrust a letter to the Lord of Hào Pond.
When you pass Hào Pond on your way to Xiányáng,
you will see an inscribed stone beneath a large catalpa tree.
Take it and knock on the catalpa,
and someone will respond.
Give them the letter,
do not open it recklessly,
and delivering it will fulfill your desires.
Zhèng Róng traveled to Hào Pond.
He saw that beneath a catalpa tree there was indeed an inscribed stone,
took it and knocked on the catalpa,
and a response came:
Yes.
Zhèng Róng felt as if waking from sleep and saw palace gates,
resembling a king's residence.
A receptionist came out,
received the letter, and went inside.
After a while,
he heard a voice saying the Ancestral Dragon had died.
The ways of spirits are obscure,
difficult to discern and fathom,
so it is impossible to grasp their profound mysteries.
The Hào River flows north,
then northwest, merging with Biāo Pond,
which originates west of Hào Pond,
and flows north into the Hào River.
The Máo Shī states:
Biāo,
means flowing waves.
Yet tradition has taken it as a water name.
Zhèng Xuán said:
Between Fēng and Hào,
the water flows north.
The Hào River flows north past the west of Qīnglíng Terrace,
then past the west of the Císhí Gate,
which stood before the Ēpáng Palace,
entirely made of magnetite,
hence its name.
It was meant so that when foreign envoys came to court,
anyone concealing armor or weapons would be restrained upon entering, demonstrating its divine power,
thus also called the Quèhú Gate.
The Hào River then flows north into the Wèi River.
North of the Wèi River is the Dùyóu Pavilion,
seventeen lǐ from Xiányáng,
now called Xiàolǐ Pavilion,
containing a shrine to Bái Qǐ.
Alas,
though he had the merit of decisive victory,
he lacked the benevolence of Yǐn and Shāng,
and this is the place where he fell on his sword.
The Wèi River then flows northeast past the south of Wèichéng,
which Wén Yǐng believed was the old Xiányáng.
It was the detached palace where Duke Xiào of Qín resided.
Duke Xiàn made Lìyáng his capital,
where gold rained from the sky.
The Zhōu court historian Dān met Duke Xiàn and said:
Zhōu and Qín were once united, then separated,
after five hundred years apart they will reunite,
and seventy years after reuniting a hegemon king will arise.
By Duke Xiào's time, Xiányáng was built, the Jìquè towers erected, and the capital moved there.
Thus, the "Xījīng Fù" says:
Qín's territory to the north,
indeed is Xiányáng.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
Cháng'ān
was formerly Xiányáng.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn renamed it Xīnchéng,
and in the third year of Emperor Wǔ's Yuándǐng era,
it was separately made Wèichéng,
located north of Cháng'ān on the northern bank of the Wèi River,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jīngchéng.
Initially under Fúfēng Commandery,
later merged into Cháng'ān.
To the south, the Jué River flows into it,
which receives water from Huángzǐ Pond in Fánchuān,
an area that was the Fán Township of Dù.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn reached Lìyáng,
he awarded General Fán Kuài for flooding Fèiqiū most effectively,
granting him an estate in this township.
The water flows northwest past the west of Dùjīng in Dù County,
then northwest past the south of Dù Bó's tomb.
Dù Bó and his friend Zuǒ Rú served King Xuān,
Zuǒ Rú was unjustly killed though innocent,
Dù Bó died for him,
and ultimately was able to take revenge on King Xuān.
Thus, Chéng Gōngzǐ'ān's "Five-Character Poem" says:
Who says ghosts lack awareness?
Dù Bó shot King Xuān.
The Jué River flows northwest past Xiàdù City,
which was the state of Dù Bó.
The Jué River then flows northwest and joins an old canal,
which has two branches,
receiving water from the Jiāo River,
converging at Gāoyáng Plain,
then flowing north past the east of Héchí Pond,
and north into the Jué River.
The Jué River then flows north and meets the old Kūnmíng Pond,
then north past the east of Qín's Tōngliù Foundation,
then north past the east of Èshuǐ Pond,
then north receiving pond water,
which comes from that pond,
flowing northeast into the Jué River.
The Jué River then flows north past Cháng'ān City,
west merging with the water of Kūnmíng Pond,
which receives water from the pond at Kūnmíng Terrace,
where Wáng Zhòngdū once lived.
Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn records that Emperor Yuán fell ill,
and widely sought alchemists,
whereupon Hànzhōng sent the Daoist Wáng Zhòngdū.
The emperor asked what he could do,
and he replied:
I can endure cold and heat.
So on an extremely cold midwinter day,
he was ordered to ride bare-chested in a four-horse carriage on the ice of Kūnmíng Pond in the Shànglín Park,
circling the ice at a gallop.
The driver, bundled in thick fox furs, shivered with cold,
yet Zhòngdū alone showed no change in expression,
lying on the pond's terrace,
calm and composed.
On a sweltering summer day,
he was made to sit exposed,
surrounded by ten braziers of fire,
without speaking of heat,
nor sweating.
The pond water flows north past the east of Hàojīng and west of Qín's Ēpáng Palace,
the Shǐ Jì says:
In the thirty-fifth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
because Xiányáng was overcrowded
and the former kings' palaces were small,
he built a court palace south of the Wèi River,
also called Ēchéng.
Shǐhuáng first built the front hall, Ēpáng,
which could seat ten thousand people,
and beneath which a fifty-zhàng banner could be raised.
Covered passageways circled it,
stretching from the hall straight to the Southern Mountains.
The mountain peaks were marked as watchtowers,
and a raised walkway crossed the Wèi River from Ēpáng,
connecting to Xiányáng,
mirroring the celestial pole,
with the passageway spanning the Milky Way to reach the constellation Yíngshì.
The Guānzhōng Jì says:
Ēpáng Hall was twenty lǐ southwest of Cháng'ān,
a thousand paces east-west,
three hundred paces north-south,
its courtyard able to hold a hundred thousand people.
The water then bends and flows past its north,
northeast into Èshuǐ Pond.
The pond water exits north,
flowing past the east of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Jiànzhāng Palace,
south of the Fèngquè Tower,
east into the Jué River.
The Jué River then flows north past the east of the Fèngquè Tower,
the Sānfǔ Huángtú says:
Jiànzhāng Palace,
Built by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it spanned over twenty lǐ in circumference,
with thousands of gates and doors.
To its east stood the Phoenix Tower,
seventy-five chǐ in height,
commonly called the Chaste Maiden Tower,
which is incorrect.
The "Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn" states:
the tower was two hundred chǐ tall.
The "Records of Guānzhōng" says:
the round tower of the Jiànzhāng Palace,
facing the northern road,
had a golden phoenix atop it,
over ten chǐ tall,
hence it was named the Phoenix Tower.
Thus Fán Qīn’s "Rhapsody on the Phoenix Tower of Jiànzhāng" says:
The scale of Qín and Hàn,
vastly destroyed and vanished,
only the Jiànzhāng Palace and Phoenix Tower,
stand towering alone,
though not in the style of the Xiàngwèi Gate,
they remain a grand spectacle of an era.
The Jué River then flows north,
dividing into two streams:
one flows northeast,
the other passes north by the east of the Shénmíng Terrace,
attached to the palace halls.
It is said that the emperor built the Shénmíng Terrace and Jǐnghán Tower within the Jiànzhāng Palace,
both over five hundred chǐ tall,
all constructed with suspended pavilions,
connected by carriage paths.
The "Illustrated Guide to the Three Capital Regions" states:
the Shénmíng Terrace was within the Jiànzhāng Palace,
with nine chambers atop,
now called the Nine Sons Terrace,
though this is actually incorrect.
The Jué River then passes east of the Jiàn Terrace,
the "Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn" says:
north of the Jiànzhāng Palace was the Tàiyè Pond,
within which stood the Jiàn Terrace, three hundred chǐ tall.
Jiàn,
means to immerse,
as it was gradually submerged by the pond water,
another interpretation is that it is a star’s name.
To the south were three layers of the Bì Gate,
over three hundred chǐ tall,
with twelve halls in the middle,
stairs and platforms all made of jade,
a copper phoenix cast fifty chǐ tall,
adorned with gold,
the rafters atop the tower’s roof,
were thinly inlaid with jade discs.
Thus it was called the Jade Gate.
The Jué River then flows north into the Wèi River,
and this water is also called the Jué River.
Thus Lǚ Chēn said:
the Jué River originates from Dùlíng County.
The "Annotations to the Hànshū" says:
Jué,
is the sound of water,
not the name of a river.
It is also called the Gāodū River,
at the end of the Western Hàn,
the five marquises of the Wáng family extensively built ponds and residences,
diverting the Jué River into Cháng'ān City.
Thus the common people sang of it:
When the five marquises first rose,
Qūyáng was the most arrogant,
breaching the Gāodū River,
ultimately connecting the five Dù estates,
with earthen hills and the Jiàn Terrace,
resembling the western White Tiger.
This refers to this river.
Further east, it passes north of Cháng'ān County,
The Wèi River splits eastward into two streams,
the Guǎngyǎ states:
a stream emerging from the Wèi is called Xué,
much like the Yōng emerging from the Hé.
This watercourse flows northeast past the south of the stele of Guō Huái, Governor of Yōng Province under Wèi,
then southeast it joins another stream,
passing north of two stone figures.
When Qín Shǐhuáng built a bridge,
the iron anchor was too heavy to move,
so stone statues of strongmen like Mèng Bēn were carved to make offerings to them,
and the anchor could then be moved.
Further east, it passes north of the Yánghóu Shrine.
When floods rose, offerings were made here,
for this deity could create great waves,
and thus was worshipped alongside Hé Bó.
Later generations mistook it for a shrine to Dèng Ài.
How lamentable,
that slander prevailed and virtue declined,
and loyal dedication met with harm.
This stream then flows east and empties into the Wèi River.
Over the water is a bridge,
called the Wèi Bridge,
a structure from the Qín dynasty,
also known as the Biànmén Bridge.
Qín Shǐhuáng built detached palaces north and south of the Wèi River,
to mirror the celestial palaces,
thus the Sānfǔ Huángtú states:
The Wèi River traverses the capital,
to mirror the Milky Way;
a bridge spans across southward,
to emulate the Herd Boy.
To the south was the Chánglè Palace,
to the north the Xiányáng Palace.
To connect these two palaces,
this bridge was built.
It was six zhàng wide,
three hundred eighty bù from north to south,
with sixty-eight spans,
seven hundred fifty pillars,
and one hundred twenty-two beams.
North and south of the bridge were embankments,
with stone pillars erected firmly.
South of the pillars,
the jurisdiction fell to Jīngzhào,
north of the pillars,
to Féngyì.
There were directors and assistants,
each commanding fifteen hundred laborers.
At the northern end of the bridge,
stones were piled in the water,
hence it was called the Stone Pillar Bridge.
Formerly, there was a statue of the deity Cǔnliú.
This deity once spoke to Lǔ Bān.
Bān asked him to come out,
but Cǔnliú said:
"My appearance is very ugly,
and you are skilled at depicting forms,
I cannot come out."
Bān then clasped his hands and said:
"Just show me your head."
Cǔnliú then revealed his head,
whereupon Bān traced the ground with his foot.
Cǔnliú sensed this,
and immediately submerged back into the water.
Therefore, his statue was placed in the water,
with only his back and above standing above the surface.
Later, when Dǒng Zhuó entered the pass,
he burned this bridge.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi restored it,
and the bridge was then three zhàng six chǐ wide.
As for the statue of Cǔnliú,
when Cáo Cāo rode by and saw it, he was startled,
and ordered it removed.
The Yāndānzǐ states:
Yān Crown Prince Dān was held hostage in Qín,
and the Qín king treated him disrespectfully,
so he sought to return home.
The Qín king built a bridge with a triggering mechanism,
intending to trap Dān.
When Dān crossed the bridge,
the mechanism did not activate.
Another account says,
intertwined dragons supported his carriage and the mechanism did not trigger.
It is merely said,
but now its exact location is unknown.
The Wèi River further east joins a distributary of the Jué River.
This stream originates from the Jué River,
flowing northeast past the south of the Dèng Ài Shrine,
then splits eastward into two streams.
One stream flows east into the Xiāoyáo Garden and empties into the Lotus Pond.
Within the pond are pavilions and towers,
lotus covering the banks,
with beautiful blooms delightful to behold.
The other stream flows north and empties into the Wèi.
The Wèi River then flows east past the north of Cháng'ān City.
Construction began in the first year of Emperor Huì of Hàn,
and was completed in the sixth year,
on the site of Xiányáng.
The Qín detached palaces had no walls,
so walls were built for this city.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Cháng'ān.
There were twelve gates facing east:
The first gate on the northern end,
originally named Xuānpíng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Chūnwáng Gate Zhēngyuè Pavilion.
Also called the Eastern Capital Gate,
its outer gate was also called Eastern Capital Gate,
which is where Páng Méng hung his official cap.
The second gate,
originally named Qīngmíng Gate,
also called Kǎi Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Xuāndé Gate Bù'ēn Pavilion.
Inside was the Jítían Granary,
so it was also called Jítían Gate.
The third gate,
originally named Bàchéng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Rénshòu Gate Wújiāng Pavilion.
The people, seeing the gate's color was blue,
also called it Blue City Gate,
or Blue Brocade Gate,
also simply Blue Gate.
Outside this gate, fine melons were once produced.
Formerly, Shào Píng of Guǎnglíng was Marquis of Dōnglíng under Qín.
After Qín's fall,
he became a commoner
and grew melons outside this gate.
His melons were excellent,
so the world called them Dōnglíng Melons.
Thus Ruǎn Jí wrote in his "Yǒnghuái Poem":
"Long heard of Dōnglíng melons,
near just outside the Blue Gate,
fields stretch across paths and lanes,
mother and child linked like hooks."
This refers to this gate.
The first gate on the eastern end of the southern wall,
originally named Fù'àng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Yǒngqīng Gate Chángmào Pavilion.
To its south was Xiàdù City.
Yìng Shào said:
"It was the lower settlement of old Dùlíng,
hence called Xiàdù Gate,
also called Duān Gate,
facing north toward the Chánglè Palace."
The second gate,
originally named Ān Gate,
also called Dǐnglù Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Guānglǐ Gate Xiǎnlè Pavilion.
It faced north toward the Armory.
The third gate,
originally named Píng Gate,
also called Biàn Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Xìnpíng Gate Chéngzhèng Pavilion.
Also called Western Peace Gate,
it faced north toward the Wèiyāng Palace.
The first gate on the southern end of the western wall,
originally named Zhāng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Wànqiū Gate Yìnián Pavilion,
also called Guānghuá Gate.
The second gate,
originally named Zhí Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Zhídào Gate Duānlù Pavilion,
formerly the Lónglóu Gate.
Zhāng Yàn said:
"On the gate tower was a bronze dragon."
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states:
"The second gate on the western side of Cháng'ān,
is this gate."
The third gate,
originally named Xīchéng Gate,
also called Yōng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Zhāngyì Gate Zhùyì Pavilion.
North of its water entrance was Hánlǐ,
the people called it Hánlǐ Gate,
also called Tū Gate.
The first gate on the western end of the northern wall,
originally named Héng Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Bàdū Gate Zuǒyōu Pavilion.
Rú Chún said:
"Pronounced guāng,
hence called Guāng Gate."
Its outer wall had a Capital Gate and a Jí Gate.
Xú Guǎng said,
"The Jí Gate is north of the Wèi."
Mèng Kāng said:
"North of Cháng'ān,
it was a palace gate in Qín times."
Rú Chún said:
"The Sānfǔ Huángtú states the Jí Gate is outside the Héng Gate."
According to the Hànshū,
Xú Lì stationed troops here to guard against the Xiōngnú.
There were also Tōng Gate and Hài Gate.
The second gate,
originally named Chú Gate,
also called Cháo Gate,
was renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Jiànzǐ Gate Guǎngshì Pavilion.
Also called Gāo Gate.
Sū Lín said:
"Gāo Gate,
is the northern gate of Cháng'ān City,
inside which, to the east, were the Cháng'ān kitchen offices."
Hence it was named the Kitchen Gate.
Rú Chún says:
Now it is called the Broad Gate.
The third gate,
originally named the Dù Gate,
was also called the Lìchéng Gate.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it the Jìnhé Gate Línshuǐ Pavilion.
Outside it there were guest lodgings,
so the people called it the Guest Lodgings Gate,
and also the Luò Gate.
All these gates
all led to broad thoroughfares reaching in nine directions,
with three passageways opened wide,
reinforced with metal piles,
and surrounded by trees and woods.
Exiting on the left and entering on the right,
they formed paths for coming and going.
Travelers ascended and descended,
with distinctions between upper and lower levels.
When Hàn Emperor Chéngdì was Crown Prince,
Emperor Yuándì once urgently summoned him.
The Crown Prince exited the Lónglóu Gate but dared not cross the Imperial Thoroughfare.
He went west to the Zhíchéng Gate before he could cross.
The Emperor wondered at his delay,
asked the reason,
and the Crown Prince reported the circumstances.
The Emperor was pleased,
and thus issued an edict allowing the Crown Prince to cross the Imperial Thoroughfare.
The Wèi River flows east and joins the old Kūnmíng Canal.
The canal receives water from the eastern outlet of Kūnmíng Lake,
flows east past the north of Héchí Marsh,
also called the Nǚguān Marsh.
Further east it joins the Jué River,
also called the Cáo Canal.
Further east it passes south of Cháng'ān County,
and east past the south of the Míngtáng.
This was formerly the place where water was channeled for the Bìyōng,
located seven lǐ southeast of the Dǐnglù Gate.
Its structure was round above and square below,
with nine halls and twelve chambers,
and five rooms facing the four directions.
Three hundred paces north of the hall was the Língtái,
established in the fourth year of the Yuánshǐ era of Hàn Emperor Píngdì.
South of the canal was the old circular mound of the Hàn,
where in the second year of the Jiànshǐ era of Emperor Chéngdì,
the five suburban altars at Yōng were abolished,
and sacrifices to the Supreme Emperor of Heaven began at the southern suburbs of Cháng'ān.
Yìng Shào says:
"The suburban altar to Heaven was south of Cháng'ān,"
which is this place.
North of the old canal were the Báitíng and Bówàng Gardens,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn for the Crown Prince,
to enable him to receive guests,
pursuing his preferences.
When the Crown Prince's affair involving witchcraft and curses came to light,
he hacked his way out east through the Dù Gate.
Shǐ Liángdì died,
and was buried north of the garden.
Emperor Xuāndì made it the Lì Garden,
and with a thousand musicians and performers, he had music played in the rear garden temple in remembrance,
hence it was also called Qiānxiāng.
The old canal then flows east and turns north past outside the Qīng Gate,
where it meets a branch canal of the Jué River.
The canal receives water from the Jué River west of the Zhāng Gate,
with a flying aqueduct channeling water into the city,
east to the Cāngchí,
which is west of the Wèiyāng Palace.
Within the pool is the Jiàntái.
When the Hàn troops rose up,
Wáng Mǎng died on this terrace.
Further east it passes north of the Wèiyāng Palace.
When Gāozǔ was east of the passes,
he ordered Xiāo Hé to complete the Wèiyāng Palace.
Hé cut into Lóngshǒu Mountain to build it.
The mountain extends over sixty lǐ,
its head facing the Wèi River,
its tail reaching Fánchuān.
The head is twenty zhàng high,
the tail gradually descends,
to five or six zhàng high.
The soil is red and firm.
It is said that in the past a black dragon emerged from the southern mountains to drink from the Wèi River,
and its path formed traces along the mountain.
The mountain served as the foundation,
and the towers required no artificial construction,
towering above the Cháng'ān city wall.
To the north is the Xuánwǔ Tower,
which is the northern tower.
To the east is the Cānglóng Tower,
within which are the Chānghé, Zhǐchē, and other gates.
East of the Wèiyāng Hall are the Xuānshì, Yùtáng, Qílín, Hánzhāng, Báihǔ, Fènghuáng, Zhūquè, Yuānluán, Zhāoyáng, and other halls,
and the Tiānlù, Shíqú, and Qílín three pavilions.
North of the Wèiyāng Palace
is the Guì Palace.
It is over ten lǐ in circumference,
and within are the Míngguāng Hall, the Zǒugǒu Terrace, and the Bǎiliáng Terrace.
Formerly, elevated passageways were used
for communication between them.
Thus Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
"Beyond the Gōuchén,
the elevated passageways soar aloft,
connecting Chánglè and Míngguāng.
Passing north, they reach the Guì Palace."
The old canal flows between these two palaces,
and is called the Míng Canal.
Further east it passes north of the Armory.
Formerly, Chūlǐzǐ was buried here.
Chūlǐzǐ's personal name was Jí.
He was the younger half-brother of King Huì of Qín,
witty and clever,
and the people of Qín called him the "Sack of Wisdom."
He was buried west of King Zhāo's temple,
at Chūlǐ in Yīnxiāng south of the Wèi River,
hence he was commonly called Chūlǐzǐ.
He said, "A hundred years after my death,
there will be palaces of the Son of Heaven flanking my tomb."
Jí
died in the seventh year of King Zhāo's reign,
and was buried east of Zhāngtái, south of the Wèi River.
By the Hàn dynasty,
the Chánglè Palace was to its east,
the Wèiyāng Palace to its west,
and the Armory directly faced his tomb.
A Qín folksong said:
"For strength, Rén Bǐ;
for wisdom, Chūlǐ indeed."
The Míng Canal further flows east past north of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn's Chánglè Palace,
originally the Chánglè Palace of Qín.
It is twenty lǐ in circumference,
with bronze statues arrayed before the hall.
West of the hall are the Chángxìn, Chángqiū, Yǒngshòu, Yǒngchāng, and other halls.
Northeast of the hall is a pool,
north of which is a tiered terrace.
Commonly this pool is called the Wine Pool,
but this is incorrect.
North of the old canal is a tower,
where stands the stele of Sīmǎ Wényù, Governor of the Capital of Hàn.
The old canal then exits the city east and divides into two canals,
which are the so-called Wáng Canal mentioned in the *History of the Hàn*.
Sū Lín says:
"The Wáng Canal
is an official canal,
like the present-day Imperial Moat."
Jìn Zhuó says:
"It is the name of a canal,
located outside the Fù'àng Gate east of the city."
One watercourse passes under the Yáng Bridge,
which is the Qīngmén Bridge.
It runs along the north side of the city, passes west of Dèng Ài's shrine,
and flows north into the Wèi River,
but now has no water.
The other watercourse enters right into the old Kūnmíng Canal,
flows east past south of the Liánmíng Garden in Guǎngchéng Township of Fèngmíng County.
The Imperial Grandson Shǐ and Lady Wáng were buried north of the outer city walls.
Emperor Xuāndì moved the garden south,
divined it to be the Dào Garden,
added sixteen hundred households to tend the garden,
and established Fèngmíng County
to serve the two gardens.
The garden was at the Eastern Capital Gate.
King Hè of Chāngyì, from Bà, rode in the imperial chariot,
with the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace Gōng Suì as his carriage attendant,
and arrived at the Guǎngmíng Eastern Capital Gate.
The old canal flows northeast past west of the tomb of Xiàhóu Yīng, Grand Commandant of Hàn.
On the day of burial,
the hearse horses neighed mournfully,
and the light carriage would not advance.
Below was found a "Stone Coffin Inscription" saying:
"Alas, Lord Téng dwells in this chamber."
Thus he was buried there.
The tomb is eight lǐ east of the city and four lǐ south of the Yìnmǎ Bridge,
so people of the time called it the Horse Tomb.
The old canal further north divides into two canals:
one flows east past the Tiger Enclosure and east into the Bà River;
one watercourse joins the Wèi River to the north,
but now has no water.
Further east it passes north of Bàlíng County,
where the Bà River flows from the northwest of the county and joins it.
Bà is a place name on the water,
anciently called Zīshuǐ.
Duke Mù of Qín achieved hegemony,
and renamed Zīshuǐ as Bàshuǐ,
to manifest his hegemonic achievements.
The water originates from Lántián Valley in Lántián County,
which is said to be rich in jade.
To the northwest is Tónggǔshuǐ,
and further east is Wǎnggǔshuǐ.
These two waters converge and flow westward,
then further west into Níshuǐ.
Níshuǐ then flows west past Yáoguān,
north through Yáoliǔchéng,
where there are two cities, east and west.
Wèi established the Qīngní Army within the city,
which is also called Qīngníchéng.
In the third year of Qín Èrshì,
Hàn Gāozǔ entered,
attacking Qín from Wǔguān,
and Zhào Gāo sent a general to resist at Yáoguān.
The *Tǔdì Jì* says:
South of Lántián County is Yáoguān,
the place name is Yáoliǔdào,
leading to Jīngzhōu.
The *Jìn Dìdào Jì* says:
The pass is northwest of Shàngluò County.
Níshuǐ then flows northwest into Bà,
and Bàshuǐ flows north through Lántiánchuān,
passing east of Lántián County.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* records:
In the third year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qín's Zǐ Xiàng was appointed Lord of Lán.
This was likely Zǐ Xiàng's former fief.
The river plain contains the tomb of Hàn's Línjiāng King Liú Róng.
Emperor Jǐng summoned him for a crime,
and as he was about to depart,
he performed the ancestral farewell ceremony at the north gate of Jiānglíng.
The axle of his carriage broke,
and the elders wept, saying:
Our king will not return.
When Róng arrived,
the Commandant of the Capital, Zhì Dū, harshly interrogated the king.
The king was young,
and in fear, he committed suicide.
He was buried in this river plain.
Tens of thousands of swallows
carried earth and placed it upon his tomb mound,
and the common people pitied him.
Bàshuǐ then joins with Chǎnshuǐ on the left,
passes east of Báilùyuán,
which is west of Bàchuān,
formerly Zhǐyáng.
The *Shǐjì* records:
King Xiāng of Qín was buried at Zhǐyáng,
which is here.
It is called Bàshàng.
Emperor Wén of Hàn was buried upon it,
and it is called Bàlíng.
On it are four drainage channels to discharge water,
located thirty *lǐ* southeast of Cháng'ān.
Thus, Wáng Zhòngxuān composed a poem saying:
Ascending the banks of Bàlíng to the south,
I turn my head to gaze upon Cháng'ān.
Emperor Wén of Hàn once wished to gallop west down the steep slope from Bàlíng,
but Yuán Àng seized the reins at this spot.
The emperor said:
The general is timid.
Àng said:
Your servant has heard that the child of a household worth a thousand in gold
does not sit under the eaves,
and the child of a household worth a hundred in gold
does not stand leaning against the carriage rail.
A sage does not court danger.
Now galloping down an unpredictable slope,
if the horse were startled and the carriage wrecked,
what would become of the High Ancestral Temple?
The emperor then desisted.
Bàshuǐ flows further north,
and Chángshuǐ flows into it.
The water originates from Báilùyuán in Dù County,
flows northwest,
and is called Jīngxī.
Further northwest,
it joins on the left with Gǒujiāchuānshuǐ.
This water has two sources.
The western stream originates from Zhuópángǔ in Kuǐshān;
further east is Kǔgǔ, and the two waters converge
and flow northeast past the west of Fēngliángyuán.
The *Guānzhōng Tú* says:
West of Lìshān,
within the river plain is a mound
named Fēngchúnyuán,
located on the northern side of Kuǐshān,
a blessed land of Yōngzhōu,
which is this plain.
The water flows north alongside the stream and enters,
and on the plain is the temple of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
This water joins on the right with the eastern stream,
which originates from Shíméngǔ in the southern mountains.
Further east is Mènggǔ,
further east is Dàgǔ,
further east is Quègǔ,
further east is Tǔméngǔ.
These five waters emerge north from the valleys,
flow northwest past the east of Fēngliángyuán,
and then north to meet the western stream.
The plain is the confluence of the two waters.
The mingled flow passes north past the east of the tomb of Empress Xǔ of Emperor Xuān,
ten *lǐ* north of Dùlíng.
Hence, this river plain has the name Gǒujiā.
East of the plain is also called Báilùyuán,
upon which is Gǒujiābǎo.
The *Sān Qín Jì* says:
West of Lìshān is Báilùyuán,
upon which is Gǒujiābǎo.
During the time of Duke Xiāng of Qín,
a large dog came.
If there were bandits below, the dog would bark at them,
and the fortress would be without trouble.
Thus, the river plain obtained this name.
The river water flows further north past the east of Dùlíng.
In the first year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Yuán,
Emperor Xuān was buried at Dùlíng,
fifty *lǐ* north of Cháng'ān.
Northwest of the tomb is the old city of Dù County.
In the eleventh year of Duke Wǔ of Qín, it was made a county.
In the first year of the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
the eastern plain of Dù was made the initial tomb site,
and Dù County was renamed Dùlíng,
which was Wáng Mǎng's Ráo'ān.
The water then flows north into Jīngxī.
Jīngxīshuǐ flows further north past Bà County,
and there is a hot spring that flows into it.
The water issues from beneath the plain,
enters Jīngxīshuǐ,
and the mingled flow enters Bà.
It is commonly called Chǎnshuǐ,
but this is incorrect.
The *Shǐjì Yīnyì* states:
Emperor Wén exited the Ānmén,
and notes:
In Bàlíng County,
there is an old pavilion,
which is the Chángméntíng mentioned in the *Jùn Guó Zhì*.
The *Shǐjì* says:
Bà, Chǎn, and Chángshuǐ,
although not included in the sacrificial canon,
due to their proximity to Xiányáng, the capital of Qín and Hàn,
Jīng, Wèi, and Chángshuǐ
all received rites comparable to major rivers.
Formerly, Emperor Wén resided north of Bàlíng,
and facing the riverbank, he pointed toward the road to Xīnfēng, showing it to Lady Shèn, saying:
This is the road to Hándān.
Thereupon, he had Lady Shèn play the *sè*,
and the emperor himself leaned against the *sè* and sang,
sorrowful and mournful in his thoughts.
Turning to his ministers, he said:
If one uses stone from the northern mountains for the outer coffin,
and fills the gaps with hemp fiber and lacquer,
how could it be moved?
Zhāng Shìzhī said:
If there is something desirable inside,
even if sealed with Nánshān, there would still be gaps.
If there is nothing desirable,
even without a stone outer coffin,
what sorrow would there be?
Emperor Wén said:
Well said.
He appointed him Commandant of Justice.
Wéi Zhāo said:
A riverbank flanked by high cliffs is called *cè*,
and now this plain is flanked by two waters.
Bàshuǐ flows further north and meets two streams,
and further north,
an old canal branches off to the right.
Bàshuǐ flows further north past the south of Wáng Mǎng's Nine Temples.
In the first year of the Dìhuáng era of Wáng Mǎng,
he extensively recruited craftsmen from across the land,
dismantled over ten palaces and halls including Xīyuàn and Jiànzhāng,
and used their materials and tiles to build the Nine Temples.
He levied assessments on officials and commoners,
compelling them to contribute money and grain
to aid in completing the Nine Temples.
The temple halls all had double roofs.
The temple of the Great Primordial Ancestor
was forty *zhàng* in each direction, east, west, south, and north,
and seventeen *zhàng* high.
The remaining temples were half that size.
They had bronze column capitals,
adorned with gold and silver carvings,
exhausting the skill of all craftsmen.
They leveled heights and filled depressions,
the labor and cost amounting to hundreds of millions,
and ultimately tens of thousands died.
Bàshuǐ flows further north past Zhǐdào,
which is thirteen *lǐ* east of Cháng'ān County,
with Wáng Mǎng's Nine Temples to its south.
In the Hàn era, there were white swans flying in flocks
from the eastern capital gate past Zhǐdào.
Empress Lü performed the purification rite at Bàshàng.
Returning, he saw a blue dog,
which stood with bristling fur on this path.
There was a bridge over the water,
called the Bà Bridge.
In the third year of the Dìhuáng era,
a fire broke out on the Bà Bridge, starting from the east.
Several thousand soldiers used water to douse it, but it could not be extinguished,
and by evening it had burned completely.
Wáng Mǎng detested this,
and issued an edict saying:
"The fire on the bridge occurred on Jiǎwǔ day,
which is also the day of Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring).
I, by the divine mandate of the sacred ancestors,
inherited the legacy of Huángdì and Yú, and received the mandate.
Up to the fourth year of Dìhuáng,
it has been fifteen years.
Precisely at the end of winter in the third year,
the Bà Bridge was destroyed by fire.
I wish to use this to prosper and establish the new dynasty,
and unify the way of eternal existence.
Therefore, I rename the Bà Bridge as the Chángcún (Eternal) Bridge."
The Bà River flows further north,
where on the left it receives the Cáo Canal,
which cuts across the Bà River and emerges on the right.
It passes east by the north of Bàchéng,
and further east by the north of Zǐchǔ's tomb.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
"King Zhuāng of Qín was buried at Lìshān in Zhǐyáng,
which is the Bàlíng Mountain southeast of Jīngzhào."
Liú Xiàng said:
"King Zhuāng enlarged the name and erected a tomb mound."
The *Strategies of the Warring States* states:
"King Zhuāng's courtesy name was Yìrén,
later changed to Zǐchǔ,
so people still refer to the tomb by the name Zǐchǔ."
Further east, it passes by Xīnfēng County,
where on the right it joins an old canal.
This canal receives water from the Bà River upstream,
flowing northeast past the old city south of Bàchéng,
which was the Bàlíng County of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
renamed by Wáng Mǎng as Shuǐzhāng.
In the first year of the Jǐngchū era of Emperor Míng of Wèi, when the capital was moved to Cháng'ān,
the bronze statues were too heavy to transport,
so they were left south of Bàchéng.
Someone saw Jì Zǐxùn with elders rubbing the bronze statues, saying:
"I witnessed the casting of these,
and counting the days since then,
it has been nearly five hundred years."
The old canal flows further northeast past the west of Liú Gēngshǐ's tomb.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ,
