he was killed by the Chìméi rebels.
The former Palace Attendant Liú Gōng went at night to retrieve and bury him.
Emperor Guāngwǔ sent Minister over the Masses Dèng Yǔ to collect and bury him in Bàlíng County.
Bào Yǒng, who served as Imperial Secretary and acted as Grand General under Gēngshǐ,
was sent as an envoy to pacify Hédōng.
Hearing of Gēngshǐ's death,
he submitted to Emperor Shìzǔ,
and was promoted to Colonel Director of the Retainers.
While touring the county, he passed by Gēngshǐ's tomb,
dismounted, bowed, and wept,
expressing his grief before leaving.
The Emperor asked his ministers,
and Grand Master of the Palace Zhāng Zhàn said:
"Benevolence does not abandon the old,
loyalty does not forget the ruler—
these are acts of high virtue."
The Emperor then released him.
Further east, it passes by Xīnfēng County,
where on the right it joins the Cáo Canal,
which was dug by Zhèng Dāngshí, the Grand Minister of Agriculture of Hàn.
Because the Wèi River was difficult for grain transport,
he ordered the water engineer Xú Bó from Qí to mobilize laborers to dig a canal diverting water from the Wèi.
This canal started from Kūnmíng Pond,
ran south along the mountains,
and extended east to the Yellow River,
serving both for irrigation and transport,
greatly facilitating matters.
Now it has no water.
The Bà River flows further north past the east of the Qín tiger enclosure.
The *Biographies of Eminent Men* states:
"King Zhāo of Qín summoned the King of Wèi,
but the King of Wèi did not go,
sending Zhū Hài instead with a pair of jades.
The King of Qín was furious,
and placed Zhū Hài in the tiger enclosure.
Hài glared at the tigers,
his eyes splitting and blood spurting onto them,
and the tigers dared not move.
This is the place."
The Bà River flows further north into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows east and joins the old Chéngguó Canal.
This canal,
was dug by Wèi Zhēn, Left Imperial Secretary of Wèi, during the campaign against Shǔ,
and was called the Chéngguó Canal,
used for irrigation.
Its channel receives water from the Qiān River east of Chéncāng,
flowing east past Méi and north of Wǔgōng and Huáilǐ counties.
To the left of the canal is the tomb of Liáng Yán of Āndìng,
with steles still extant.
Further east, it passes south of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Màolíng,
formerly the Mào Township of Huáilǐ.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Emperor built his own tomb,
over eighty *lǐ* northwest of Cháng'ān."
The *Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn* states:
"After the Emperor's death, he appeared in form,
and said to the tomb warden Xuē Píng:
'Though I have lost power,
I am still your ruler.
How can you allow officials and soldiers to come to my tomb to sharpen their swords?'
From now on,
you must forbid this."
Píng kowtowed in apology,
and the apparition vanished.
Upon investigation around the tomb,
they indeed found a square stone
suitable for whetting,
which officials and soldiers had often stolen to sharpen their swords.
Huò Guāng wanted to execute them,
but Zhāng Ānshì said:
"The ways of spirits are obscure;
it is not appropriate to use this as a basis for punishment."
So they desisted.
Thus Ruǎn Jī's *Poems of My Heart* says:
"Power can be lost in an instant,
yet they come with swords to my mound."
One *lǐ* west and north of the tomb,
is the tomb of Lady Lǐ,
with a three-tiered mound,
commonly called Yīnglíng.
Her elder brother Lǐ Yánnián was musically gifted,
especially skilled in singing and dancing.
The Emperor loved him,
and whenever he composed new melodies,
listeners were invariably moved.
He often danced before the Emperor,
singing:
"In the north there is a beauty,
peerless and alone.
One glance overturns a city,
a second glance overturns a state.
Yet one would not mind the city overturned, nor the state overturned—
for such a beauty is hard to find again."
The Emperor said:
"Is there really such a person in the world?"
Princess Píngyáng said:
"Yánnián's younger sister."
The Emperor summoned her,
and she was enchanting and skilled in singing and dancing.
She gained favor,
but died young.
The Emperor grieved for her,
burying her with the rites of an empress,
and his sorrow was unceasing,
composing poems to mourn her.
The old canal flows further east past the old city south of Màolíng County,
established in the second year of the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"It was made a county under Emperor Xuān,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xuānchéng."
The old canal flows further east past north of Lóngquán,
which people now call Wēnquán (Hot Spring),
but that is incorrect.
North of the old slope north of the canal,
is the Lóngyuān Temple.
Rú Chún said:
"The *Plans of the Three Capital Regions* mentions a Lóngyuān Palace,
and now west of Cháng'ān city there is a temple site,
likely the remains of the palace."
The old canal flows further east past north of Jiāngyuán,
and north of the canal is the tomb of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn,
seventy *lǐ* southeast of Cháng'ān.
Further east, it passes the old city south of Pínglíng County.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"Established under Emperor Zhāo,
renamed Guǎnglì by Wáng Mǎng."
South of the old canal is the Dòu Family Spring,
and north is the Páihuái Temple.
Further east, it passes south of the tomb of Dòu Yīng, Marquis of Wèijī and Grand General of Hàn.
Further east, it passes south of Emperor Chéng's Yánlíng.
Five *lǐ* northeast of the tomb,
is the slope of Emperor Píng's Kānglíng.
The old canal flows further east past south of Wèilíng.
In the fourth year of the Yǒngguāng era of Emperor Yuán,
the Shòulíng Pavilion plain in Wèichéng was chosen as the initial tomb site,
with an edict not to establish a county town.
Further east, it passes south of Emperor Āi's Yìlíng.
Further east, it passes south of Emperor Huì's Ānlíng.
North of the tomb is the old city of Ānlíng County.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"Established under Emperor Huì,
renamed Jiāpíng by Wáng Mǎng."
Beside the canal is the Dùyóu Pavilion.
Further east, it passes north of Wèichéng.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"The county had the Lánchí Palace."
Qín Shǐhuáng traveled incognito,
and encountered bandits at Lánchí,
but its location is now unknown.
Further east, it passes south of Chánglíng.
It is also called Chángshān.
In the Qin dynasty, the tombs of the Son of Heaven were called "mountains,"
in the Han dynasty they were called "mounds,"
hence the general term "mountain-mounds."
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Mound"
is something naturally formed by heaven;
now the tombs of kings and dukes are called mounds.
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Nánlíng
is the tomb of Xiàhòu Gāo."
The *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* states:
"Hill"
means tomb;
"grave"
means to plant;
it is a planted tomb,
arrayed against the mountain,
distinguishing the names of low and high.
Thus the canal further east passes south of the tomb of the Han Chancellor Zhōu Bó,
north of which is the tomb of Yàfū.
To the southeast of the canal is what is called Zhōushìqū,
and further southeast it passes south of the Yánglíng Mound of Emperor Jǐng of Han,
then southeast it flows into the Wèi River,
but now it is dry.
The Wèi River further east passes north of Bàchéng County,
where it divides waters with Gāolíng.
South of the water is the temple of Dìngtáo Gōngwáng,
and the mound of Empress Dowager Fù.
When Emperor Yuán died,
Consort Fù followed the king back to his fief,
and was called Empress Dowager of Dìngtáo.
Ten years later,
Gōngwáng died,
and his son succeeded as king,
was summoned to be Crown Prince,
and when the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
he established a temple for Gōngwáng in the capital,
following the precedent of Emperor Xuān's father, the Mourning Emperor.
In the first year of Yuánshòu,
Empress Fù died,
and was buried together at Wèilíng.
Pān Yuè's *Guānzhōng Jì* states:
Han emperors and empresses shared the same burial ground,
but were buried together in separate mounds;
the feudal lords were all like this.
The temple of Gōngwáng is northwest of Bàchéng,
northwest of the temple
is the mound of Empress Dowager Fù,
not sharing the same burial ground as Emperor Yuán.
Wèilíng
does not refer to Emperor Yuán's mound.
It is probably south of the Wèi River,
hence called Wèilíng.
That the mound is level with Emperor Yuán's
means they are both twelve *zhàng* high.
Wáng Mǎng petitioned to destroy Empress Dowager Fù's tomb;
the tomb collapsed,
crushing hundreds to death.
When the coffin was opened,
the stench could be smelled for several *lǐ*.
All the high officials in position
flattered Wáng Mǎng's wishes,
contributing money and silk, sending disciples and students, and people from the four barbarian tribes,
totaling over a hundred thousand people,
who took up tools
to assist the Director of Construction in digging up Empress Dowager Fù's tomb.
In twenty days it was leveled,
and thorns were planted around the site
as a warning to the world.
Now the accumulated earth at that place is still high,
and the world calls it "Zēngchí,"
also called "Zēngfù."
Commonly it is also said to be the site of Emperor Chéng's initial mound,
but this is not clear.
The Wèi River further passes north of the tomb of Marquis Píng'ē Wáng Tán,
beside the tomb is a stele,
and to the left the Jīng River flows into it.
The Wèi River further east passes west of Zhāng County,
which is probably the relocated Zhāng of Lǒngxī Commandery.
The Wèi River further east meets a branch of the Báiqú,
and further east joins with the Wǔzhàngqú.
The water originates from Shímén Mountain in Yúnyáng County,
and is called Qīngshuǐ.
It flows southeast past the west of Huángqīn Mountain,
then south into Duìxǔ County,
passes south of the plain and emerges,
where it is called Qīngshuǐkǒu.
It flows southeast across the Zhèngqú,
then southeast into Gāolíng County,
passing west of Huángbáichéng,
originally the Qūliáng Palace.
South it crosses the Báiqú,
turns and flows east,
and is called Qūliángshuǐ.
Further southeast it passes north of the old city of Gāolíng County,
southeast it crosses the Báiqú channel,
then southeast into Wànnián County,
where it is called Wǔzhàngqú.
Further it passes east of Ǒuyuán,
and flows southeast into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River on the right passes north of the old city of Xīnfēng County,
east it meets with Yúchíshuǐ.
The water originates northeast of Lìshān,
originally flowing north from its source,
but later when Qín Shǐhuáng was buried north of the mountain,
the water curved around it,
flowing east then turning north.
When Shǐhuáng built his tomb,
he took earth from this place,
and the deep pit accumulated water to form a pool,
called Yúchí.
It is five *lǐ* northeast of Qín Shǐhuáng's tomb,
with a circumference of four *lǐ*.
The pool water flows northwest,
passing north of Shǐhuáng's tomb.
Qín Shǐhuáng greatly promoted lavish burials,
constructing his tomb at Lìróng Mountain,
also called Lántián.
Its northern side is rich in gold,
its southern side rich in jade.
Shǐhuáng, coveting its fine reputation,
thus was buried there.
They cut through mountains and chiseled stone,
sealing it down to the triple springs,
using bronze for the outer coffin.
The side passages circled over thirty *lǐ*,
above painted with images of the heavenly constellations,
below using mercury to represent the Four Waterways, the hundred rivers, the Five Peaks, and the Nine Provinces,
depicting the configuration of the earth.
Palaces, towers, and the hundred officials,
rare vessels and precious treasures,
filled it completely.
He ordered craftsmen to make crossbow mechanisms,
so that if anyone bored near,
they would shoot automatically.
They used lamp oil from human-fish,
choosing it for its long-lasting, inextinguishable nature.
Palace women who had no children
were all made to accompany him in death, a great many.
The tomb mound was fifty *zhàng* high,
with a circumference of over five *lǐ*.
Seven hundred thousand laborers worked on it,
and it took years to complete.
But by then Zhōu Zhāng's army of a million
had already reached its foot,
so he made Zhāng Hán lead the laborers to resist the disaster,
but could not stop it.
When Xiàng Yǔ entered the pass,
he opened it,
and even with three hundred thousand men working for thirty days, they could not exhaust the goods.
Bandits from east of the pass
melted the outer coffin to take the bronze.
A shepherd looking for his sheep set fire to it,
and the flames lasted ninety days without being extinguished.
Ten *lǐ* north facing Hóngmén,
the pool water further flows northwest.
Southwest of the water is a hot spring,
used by the world to cure illnesses.
The *Sānqín Jì* says:
"Northwest of Lìshān is hot water.
If you sacrifice you may enter,
if you do not sacrifice it will rot human flesh."
Common saying:
Shǐhuáng traveled with a goddess and offended her will,
the goddess spat on him and he developed sores.
Shǐhuáng apologized to her,
and the goddess brought forth hot water for him.
Later people thus used it to wash sores.
Zhāng Héng's *Wēnquán Fù Xù* says:
"I left Lìshān,
viewed the hot spring,
bathed in the divine well,
admired the widespread bestowal of its great bounty,
and thus composed this rhapsody."
This hot spring
does not burn human bodies.
The pool water further passes west of Hóngmén,
and further passes east of the old city of Xīnfēng County,
formerly the land of Lìróng.
When Gāozǔ became king in Guānzhōng,
the Grand Supreme Emperor longed to return east,
so imitating the old hometown,
he established this new settlement,
built city walls and altars,
planted white elms,
made the streets and courtyards uniform,
and relocated people from Fēng to populate this settlement,
hence naming it Xīnfēng.
In the third year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng of Han,
it was changed to Dūxiāng,
and enfeoffed to Duàn Jiǒng as a marquisate.
Later Yīnpánchéng was established.
The water passes north of the city and emerges,
and the world calls this water Yīnpánshuǐ.
Further north it crosses the Cáoqú,
and flows north into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River further east passes north of Hóngmén,
the old name for the slope mouth descending north from the main road.
To the right is the Hóng Pavilion.
The Book of Hàn records:
Gāozǔ was about to meet Xiàng Yǔ.
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Chǔ and Hàn states:
King Xiàng was at Hóngmén,
Yàfù said:
I sent someone to observe the Duke of Pèi,
his aura soared to the heavens,
intertwined with five colors,
sometimes resembling a dragon,
sometimes resembling clouds,
it is not the aura of a subject,
he should be executed.
When Gāozǔ met Xiàng Yǔ,
Fàn Zēng signaled to Yǔ with his eyes,
but Yǔ did not respond.
Fán Kuài, leaning on his shield, barged in,
ate a pig shoulder here,
and Yǔ admired his courage.
The Records of Commanderies and States states:
East of Xīnfēng County is the Hóngmén Pavilion.
Guō Yuánshēng’s Record of Travels states:
Some say the south gate of Bàchéng is called Hóngmén.
Xiàng Yǔ intended to take advantage of the meeting to endanger Gāozǔ,
but Yǔ, being benevolent, hesitated to act,
Fàn Zēng’s advice was not heeded,
and Xiàng Bó ultimately protected Gāozǔ, allowing him to escape harm.
After reaching Bàshàng,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Hàn.
According to the Annotations to the Book of Hàn,
Hóngmén is seventeen lǐ east of Xīnfēng,
so Bàshàng should be a hundred lǐ away.
According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Xiàng Bó rode overnight to inform Zhāng Liáng,
Liáng went with him to see Gāozǔ,
and then sent him back overnight.
Examining the distance,
this could not have been possible.
Now, the elders say it is several tens of lǐ from the south gate of Bàchéng,
which makes more sense.
According to Yuánshēng’s record,
although he consulted the Records of the Historian and the Book of Hàn,
he recounted what he saw during his travels,
which can be said to be learning without thinking.
Now, three lǐ east of the old city of Xīnfēng County, there is a slope,
over two lǐ long,
cut through the plain to form a passage,
open from north to south,
resembling a gate,
called Hóngmén.
Mèng Kāng said,
it is seventeen lǐ east of Xīnfēng,
but this is not the case.
He likely referred to the county seat,
not the city itself.
From the old city of Xīnfēng west to Bàchéng is fifty lǐ,
ten lǐ west of Bàchéng is the Bà River,
and twenty lǐ west is Cháng’ān City.
Yìng Shào said:
Bà,
is a place name on the river,
twenty lǐ east of Cháng’ān,
which is Bàchéng.
This was where Gāozǔ once stationed his army.
Since it is far east of Xīnfēng,
how could Xiàng Bó have met Gāozǔ overnight with Zhāng Liáng?
From this,
it is clear that Yuánshēng’s record is erroneous.
The Wèi River flows east again,
and the Shíchuān River flows into it from the south.
The Wèi River flows east again,
and the Xì River flows into it.
The Xì River originates from Fénggōng Valley on Lìshān,
flowing northeast,
then north, passing east of Lìróng City.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records:
In the fifth year of Duke Xiàn of Jìn, he attacked it,
and captured Lì Jī in this city.
Lìróng,
was a state of the Róng people,
of the Jī surname,
and later became the Lìyì of Qín.
Continuing north,
it converges with three rivers on the right,
passes east of Hóngmén,
and then north, passing east of the Xì Pavilion.
Yìng Shào said:
Xì,
is the western boundary of Hú County in Hóngnóng.
But it is separated by several counties,
so it cannot be the west of Hú County.
Sū Lín said:
Xì,
is the name of a settlement,
forty lǐ southeast of Xīnfēng.
Mèng Kāng said:
It is the name of a river,
and the Xì Pavilion is located there.
In the past, King Yōu of Zhōu was fond of Bāo Sì,
but Sì never laughed.
The king then beat drums and lit beacon fires to summon the feudal lords.
When the lords arrived,
there was no enemy,
and Bāo Sì laughed,
which greatly pleased the king.
When the Quǎnróng arrived,
the king again lit beacon fires to summon the feudal lords,
but they did not come.
Thus, King Yōu was defeated on the Xì River,
and died north of Lìshān.
Therefore, the Discourses of the States says:
King Yōu perished.
In the second year of the Jiànshǐ era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Yánlíng was built as the initial mausoleum,
but it was deemed inauspicious,
so another was constructed south of the Bàqǔ Pavilion.
In the first year of the Hóngjiā era,
Chānglíng County was established in Xì Township of Xīnfēng,
to serve the initial mausoleum.
In the first year of the Yǒngshǐ era,
an edict stated that Chānglíng was low-lying,
with poor imported soil,
unsuitable for an eternal resting place.
The construction of the mausoleum was halted,
and officials and people were ordered to return,
while the Minister of Works, Xiè Wànnián, was exiled to Dūnhuáng.
The Records of Guānzhōng states:
Chānglíng is twenty lǐ east of Bàchéng,
soil was taken from the eastern mountains,
costing as much as grain,
expending vast sums,
yet after years, it remained unfinished.
This is the place.
The Xì River further divides into two branches to the north,
both flowing into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows east again,
and the Líng River joins it.
The Líng River originates from Fèifú Mountain in the south,

20 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Twenty
20.1 The Yǎng River
20.1 The Yǎng River
The Yǎng River emerges from Mount Bōzhǒng in Dìdào County, Lǒngxī Commandery,
and flows east to Jù County in Wǔdū Commandery, where it becomes the Hàn River.
Cháng Qú's Huáyáng Guózhì states:
The Hàn River has two sources:
the eastern source emerges from the Yàng Mountain in Dīdào County of Wǔdū, forming the Yàng River,
as mentioned in the Yǔ Gòng: "The Yàng is guided eastward to become the Hàn";
the western source emerges from the Bōzhǒng Mountain in Xī County of Lǒngxī, joins the Bái River, passes through Jiāméng, and enters the Hàn.
The initial source is called the Miǎn.
According to records, the Miǎn River emerges from the Eastern Láng Valley,
passes through Jù County, and enters the Hàn.
The Hànzhōng Jì states:
east of Bōzhǒng,
all waters flow eastward;
west of Bōzhǒng,
all waters flow westward.
This is due to the terrain and the direction of the water flow,
hence it is commonly said that Bōzhǒng is the watershed.
Thus, it is impossible for the Miǎn River to flow westward.
Liú Chéngzhī says:
there is a river that flows from the south of Āyáng County to Zǐtóng and Hànshòu, entering a large cave,
which secretly connects to Gāng Mountain.
Guō Jǐngchún also mentions this.
The cave at Gāng Mountain is small.
Originally, it could not contain water,
but the water formed a great marsh and flowed to join the Hàn.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng further states:
the Hàn River flows south from Wǔsuì Chuān into the Màngě Valley,
crosses Yěniú, passes through to Guānchéng, and joins the Western Hàn River.
Therefore, most who speak of the Hàn River
say that the Western Hàn River reaches Jiāméng and enters the Hàn.
It is also said:
the initial source is called the Miǎn.
Thus, the Jīng states:
the Yàng River emerges from Dīdào County,
flows east to Jù County to become the Hàn River,
and flows southeast to the Bái River in Guǎngwèi.
Examining its course,
it seems to align with these three theories,
but does not fully trace the source of the Western Hàn.
However, both the eastern and western rivers
bear the names Miǎn and Hàn,
perhaps for this reason.
Bān Gù's Dìlǐ Zhì,
Sīmǎ Biāo and Yuán Shānsōng's Jùnguó Zhì,
all state that the Hàn has two sources:
the eastern one emerges from Dīdào,
the western one from Bōzhǒng Mountain in Xī County.
Kàn Yīn says:
the Hàn is sometimes called Yàng,
and the Yàng River emerges from the northwestern corner of Kūnlún,
reappearing at Dīdào as the Yàng River.
He also says:
in Xī County of Lǒngxī,
Bōzhǒng Mountain lies to the west,
from which the Western Hàn River emerges,
flowing south into the Bái River of Guǎngwèi.
He further states:
the Yàng River emerges from Huándào,
flowing east to Wǔdū to join the Hàn.
Xǔ Shèn and Lǚ Chén both state:
the Yàng River emerges from Huándào in Lǒngxī,
flowing east to Wǔdū to become the Hàn River.
They do not mention Dīdào,
but Huándao is northwest of Jì,
separated by several rivers,
with no water flowing south into it,
so it is suspected that mentioning Huándào is an error.
It is also said:
the Hàn
is the Yàng,
and to the east, it becomes the Cānglàng River.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
from Bōzhǒng Mountain,
the Hàn River emerges,
flowing southeast into the Jiāng.
Thus, both the eastern and western rivers
emerge from Bōzhǒng and are collectively called the Hàn River.
Kǒng Ānguó says:
when a spring first emerges, it is called Yàng,
still turbid.
But Cháng Qú specifically mentions Yàng Mountain and Yàng River,
likely because the author attached these as distinct names for the mountain and river.
I refer to the Shānhǎi Jīng:
the Yàng River emerges from the northwestern corner of Kūnlún,
flowing south into the Chǒutú River.
The Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn states:
the Son of Heaven traveled west from Chūn Mountain,
reaching the Chìwū clan.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
he traveled north,
on Gēngchén,
he crossed the Yáng River,
on Xīnsì,
he entered Cáonú.
The people of Cáonú, named Xì,
toasted the Son of Heaven on the Yáng River,
and presented nine hundred fine horses,
seven thousand cattle and sheep.
The Son of Heaven sent Péng Gù to receive them,
and bestowed upon Xì a golden deer,
which Xì received with a bow.
During the Tàihé era, I accompanied the High Ancestor on a northern inspection,
and the Dí people still made such offerings.
Though times differ between ancient and modern,
the tributes remain unchanged.
However, rivers flow hidden and concealed,
making it difficult to examine them in detail.
Geography is obscure and hidden,
subject to change without fixed rules,
so one cannot entirely say Kàn's view is wrong.
Though tributaries branch off,
and side channels differ in course,
tracing back to the origin and following to the end,
the hidden flow may be one.
Thus, both bear the names Hàn and Yàng,
and adopt local designations.
Hence, there are names such as Hànchuān, Hànyáng, Guǎnghàn, and Hànshòu,
some based on the beginning,
some on the end.
Even if different names appear interchangeably,
they still refer to Hàn and Yàng.
Rivers share the same designation though names differ,
perhaps for this reason.
Now, Bōzhǒng Mountain in Xī County
is the source of the Western Hàn River.
However, it is a mere trickle,
like a thin veil,
barely a stream.
It flows west and joins the Mǎchí River,
which emerges over sixty lǐ southwest of Shàngguī,
called the Lóngyuān River,
said to be where a divine horse emerged from the water,
similar to the wonders of Yúwú and Láiyuān,
hence the name.
The Kāishān Tú states:
on the Shénmǎ Mountain in Lǒngxī, there is a deep pool,
where dragon-horses are born.
This is that river.
The water flows west, called the Mǎchí Chuān,
and further west enters the Western Hàn River.
The Western Hàn River flows southwest,
receiving the Lánqú Stream on the left,
then the Shānlí Valley Stream to the west,
then the Tiě Valley Stream to the west,
then the Shídān Valley Stream to the west,
then the Nán Valley Stream to the west,
all emerging from the southern mountains,
rushing northward.
On the right, it receives the Gāowàng Valley Stream,
then the Xī Stream to the west,
then the Huánghuā Valley Stream to the west,
all emerging from the northern mountains, cascading southward.
The Western Hàn River flows further southwest,
joined by the Zī River,
which emerges from Zīchuān to the north,
originating from four valleys,
flowing south to Zī Gorge,
where it converges into one river,
emerges from the gorge flowing southwest,
and enters the Western Hàn River.
The Western Hàn River flows southwest to the mouth of the Xiáshí River,
which emerges from three streams: Yuàntíng, Xīcǎo, and Hēigǔ,
flowing southwest to the Xiáshí mouth,
converging into one channel,
flowing southeast,
turning south to enter the Western Hàn River.
The Western Hàn River flows southwest and joins the Yánglián Chuān River,
which emerges from the Western Valley,
where multiple streams pour down,
forming one river,
flowing southeast past the old city of Xī County to the north.
Qín Zhuānggōng attacked the Western Róng,

Wáng Yuán sought rescue from Shǔ,

When Yú Xǔ governed the commandery,

Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
"The Qīngshuǐ River comes from Qíshān to join the Báishuǐ River."
This is reckless talk.
The water originates from below Zhǔlěigèn northeast of Píngwǔ Commandery,

Zhāng Zǎi's Inscription says:
"With one man guarding the perilous pass,
ten thousand men hesitate."
Truly so.
Thus, when Lǐ Tè reached Jiàngé, he sighed:
"The Liú clan possessed such a place yet surrendered to others bound,
are they not mere slaves?"
The Xiǎojiàn Shuǐ emerges southwest from Jiàngǔ,

Xī Jìnshòu
was the fief of Jiāméng, younger brother of the King of Shǔ, enfeoffed as Marquis of Jǔ,

There is a ferry pass on the water.

Further southeast, it passes Làngzhōng County of Bà Commandery,

This water emerges from the Liáo region,

20.2 Dān Shuǐ
20.2 The Dān River
The Dān River originates from the Zhǒnglǐng Mountain northwest of Shàngluò County in Jīngzhào,
also known as Gāozhū Ridge.
The Dān River flows southeast and converges with the Qīngchí River,
whose source emerges from the Qīngchí Mountain to the northeast,
flowing southwest into the Dān River.
It passes southeast by the south of the county,
the county
formerly belonged to Jīngzhào,
and was divided into a commandery during the Jìn dynasty.
The Dìdào Jì states:
The commandery is located above the Luò River,
hence the name.
The Zhúshū Jìnián records:
In the third year of Duke Liè of Jìn,
the people of Chǔ attacked our southern borders,
reaching as far as Shàngluò.
The Chǔ River flows into it,
its source emerging from the Chǔ Mountain southwest of Shàngluò County.
In the past, the Four Hoary Ones reclused in the Chǔ Mountain,
which is this very mountain.
The waters of its two sources converge east of the Temple of the Four Hoary Ones,
then flow east past the south of Gāochē Ridge,
gathering numerous streams,
turning north to enter the Dān River.
On the ridge stands the Temple of the Four Hoary Ones.
The Dān River, from Cāngyě, flows east past the Tùhé Mountain,

Qì was first enfeoffed at Shāng.

It is on the southern side of Tàihuà.
Huángfǔ Mì and Kàn Yīn both considered it to be Shāng County in Shàngluò.

originated from this.
The Dān River flows southeast from Shāng County,

Yìng Shào said:
It is the southern pass of Qín,

The Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn, the fourth year of Duke Āi,

Jìn and Chǔ have a covenant,

Otherwise, we will pass through Shàoxí to await orders.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Chǔ's passage to Shàngluò
is a narrow route.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn descended upon Xī and Lì,

Wǔguān is 170 lǐ west of Xī County,

The Xī River originates from Dàhāo Mountain in Lúshì County, Hóngnóng, northwest of Xī County,

was the northern township of Xī.
It then flows east into Xī County,

The matter being extraordinary,

The water further flows east past the old city of the county to the north,

The Zuǒzhuàn, the eighteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
records Chǔ sending Prince Shèng to move Xǔ to Xī, referring to this.
Guō Zhòngchǎn said:
It is traditionally said that this city was built by Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
but this is incorrect.
I have examined the Shǐjì,
which states that in the first year of King Xiāng of Chǔ,

slaughtered fifty thousand troops,

When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered the pass,

This does not imply there was no city;

The Xī River further passes east of the county,

In the past, when Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered the pass,

This city is suspected to have been built by Wáng Líng.
The Dān River further flows southwest of the old city of Dānshuǐ County.
The county has the Mìyáng Township,

Ten days before the summer solstice,

Net them and catch them,

The Dān River flows southeast to the south of the county.

flows south past the south of Dānshuǐ County, and enters the Dān River.

Now in Xīn'ān County of Hénán, there is a Shímò Mountain,

The Dān River further flows south past the northeast of the old city of Nánxiāng County.
During the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty, the western region of Nányáng was divided to form Nánxiāng Commandery.

but he paid no heed.

The Dān River further flows east past the north of Nánxiāng County.
At the end of the Xīngníng era,

The northern half of the city is situated in the water,

The Dān River flows between the two counties,

which is the so-called Shāngwū.

21.1 The Rǔ River
21.1 The Rǔ River
The Rǔ River originates from Tiānxī Mountain west of Miǎn Township in Liáng County, Hénán.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
It emerges from Gāolíng Mountain,
which is Měng Mountain.
It is also said to emerge from Dàyú Mountain in Lǔyáng County of Nányáng,
and further said to emerge from Huánguī Mountain in Lúshì County of Hóngnóng.
The "Records of the Investigation of Things" states:
The Rǔ River emerges from Yànquán Mountain.
These are all different names.
During the Yǒngpíng era, I was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Lǔyáng,
and it happened that the imperial court issued a "Map of Mountains and Rivers" for the lower officials,
but as the local records were inconsistent,
I was ordered to trace the river's source and course.
These officials were not scholars,
making it difficult to obtain complete information,
but since I personally witnessed the terrain,
I could not refrain from recording it.
Now, the Rǔ River emerges west of Dàyú Mountain in Lǔyáng County, from Méngbǎi Valley,
where cliffs and barriers are deep and high,
mountain peaks dense and secluded,
rocky paths rugged,
and human footprints barely intersect.
To the west lies the boundary of Lúshì County.
The water flows northeast past the west of Tàihé City,
then eastward past the north of the city,
where deep pines are planted in rows on both banks,
with bamboo and cypress intertwining to cast shade,
the place where Yǐn Gōngdù found spiritual repose.
Further east, it reaches the western ridge of Yáo Mountain,
where the flow splits into two,
one branch flowing east past the south of Yáo Mountain,
forming the Zhì River.
This is what the "Classic" refers to as the Zhì River emerging from Yáo Mountain.
The other branch flows northeast to become the Rǔ River,
passing through Méngbǎi Valley,
where ravines and valleys on both sides vie in depth,
and mountains and hills compete in height,
with layered pines and lush cypresses lining the water,
shading the hills and islets,
hence the name by which people know it.
The flow continues unceasingly,
northward passing Chángbáishākǒu,
where Húbái Stream joins it,
the sandbanks on both shores rising like snow,
hence the name.
This water emerges south from Húbái Plain,
flowing north to join the Rǔ River,
and the Rǔ River then flows northeast toward Lánggāo Mountain.
Southeast, it passes north of the county.
The Rǔ River flows eastward from the gorge of Lánggāo Mountain,

scattered among them,
attracting many who follow the Way.

Liáng and Huò

After Qín destroyed the Western Zhōu, its ruler was relocated here,

Southwest of Hénán County, there is Liáng City,

In Liáng County of Hénán, there is Zhùchéng.

In the thirty-second year of Marquis Wén of Wèi,

The county,

Yǎng

This channel sometimes flows and sometimes dries up,
hence it is also called the Dry Canal.
The river flows northeast to the north of Fùchéng County,
where it joins the Áo River on the right,
and their mingled streams flow northeast into the Rǔ River at Jiá.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast,
converging on the left with the Lán River.
The Lán River originates from the Chónglǐng Mountain in Yángdí County,
flowing southeast past Jìshìchéng.
To the west is a layered terrace,
called the Jìshì Terrace.
The *Continued Book of Hàn* records:
When Emperor Shìzǔ's imperial carriage campaigned west,
bandits rose in groups.
The magistrate of Jiá, Féng Fáng, was attacked by the bandit leader Yán Póu,
and, exhausted,
went up to Jìshì.
The bandits surrendered there,
which is this place,
located over ten *lǐ* northeast of Jiáchéng.
The river then flows southeast past the east of Huángfù,
and south into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast,
converging with the Báigōu River.
The Báigōu River originates west of Xiàtíngchéng,
flows south past the west of Lóngchéng,
northwest of the city,
which is Móbēi,
measuring about fifteen *lǐ* in length and width.
In the first year of the Qīnglóng era of Wèi,
a dragon appeared at Móbēi in Jiá.
Emperor Míng went to the pond to observe the dragon there,
renaming Móbēi as Lóngbēi (Dragon Pond),
and the city as Lóngchéng (Dragon City).
The river then flows south into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast and converges with the Lóngshān River.
The Lóngshān River originates from Lóngxī in Lóngshān,
flowing north past the east of the old city of Fùchéng County.
In the past, King Píng of Chǔ greatly fortified Chéngfù
to house Crown Prince Jiàn.
Thus, Dù Yù said:
This is Fùchéng County of Xiāngchéng.
Féng Yì occupied it to surrender to Emperor Shìzǔ,
repaying the kindness shown at Jīnchē.
The river then flows northeast and converges with two other streams,
both originating from Lóngshān,
which flow north into it,
and then northeast into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the old city of Xiāngchéng County.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* states:
It was built by King Líng of Chǔ.
Liú Xiàng's *Shuōyuàn* records:
On the day Lord Xiāngchéng was first enfeoffed,
he wore emerald-green robes,
adorned with jade pendants,
and lingered by the flowing water.
This is that river.
It is the place where the Chǔ minister Zhuāng Xīn spoke.
Later, it became a county.
In the first year of Empress Lü,
Yì, a son of Emperor Huì's harem, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiāngchéng.
The Yellow Emperor once encountered a shepherd boy in its fields,
hence the *Eulogy by Jí Shūyè* says:
How wondrous and unfathomable,
the young boy of Xiāngchéng,
weary of roaming the six directions,
came to rest in this land.
To the south of the city lies Fànchéng.
When King Xiāng of Zhōu left Zhèng and resided in Fàn,
it was this city.
In the twenty-sixth year of Duke Xiāng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
crossed the Fàn River, and returned.
Dù Yù said:
They crossed the Rǔ River at Fànchéng.
It was the seat of the Jìn-era Xiāngchéng Commandery.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
King Xiāng of Zhōu resided here,
hence it was called Xiāngchéng.
Now a pass is established below it.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the south of Xībùgēngchéng.
In the twelfth year of Duke Zhāo of the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
King Líng of Chǔ said:
In the past, the feudal lords distanced themselves from me and feared Jìn.
Now I have greatly fortified Chén, Cài, and Bùgēng,
each with a thousand war chariots in levies.
Will the feudal lords not fear me?
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* records:
Chariot and Cavalry General Mǎ Fáng, for his previous service in administering medicine,
and diligent service at the palace,
was granted an additional fief of 1,250 households at the Gēngtíng of Xiāngchéng.
This is that very tíng.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past Fánqiūchéng,
and exits to the southeast.
It then flows southeast past the north of Dìnglíng County.
The Zhàn River originates from the Yúchǐ Mountain north of Chōu County,
flowing southeast,
passing by the foot of Yúchǐ Mountain to form Zhàn Pǔ,
which is over fifty paces square.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìn attacked Chǔ,
in retaliation for the battle of Yángliáng.
Prince Gé of Chǔ engaged the Jìn army
at Zhàn Bǎn,
where the Chǔ army was defeated,
and subsequently invaded beyond Fāngchéng.
Nowadays, the area north of the river is entirely bordered by mountainous ridges,
east-south of Fùchéng and north of the Zhàn River,
where there is a long slope on the mountain,
likely named Zhàn Bǎn after the Zhàn River,
hence the name Zhàn Bǎn.
The Zhàn River then flows southeast past the north of Púchéng,
as Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"North of Kūnyáng County lies Púchéng,
and north of Púchéng is the Zhàn River."
The Zhàn River continues east,
entering the Rǔ River north of its nine bends.
Dù Yù also identified this water as the Zhàn River.
According to the Rites of Zhōu,
the rivers of Jīngzhōu include the Yǐng and Zhàn.
Zhèng Xuán remarked:
"I have not heard of this,"
likely an occasional oversight.
Examining the geography now shows no discrepancy with the land,
and the description of the waters aligns with the Classic.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the old city of Dìnglíng County,
where in the third year of the Yuányǎn era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Chúnyú Cháng, the Palace Guard Commandant.
Wáng Mǎng later renamed it Dìngchéng.
The Records of the Eastern Pavilion states:
When Emperor Guāngwǔ attacked Wáng Mǎng,
the two dukes returned,
reaching the Rǔ River,
where they drank water from the bank with their hands,
washing the dust from their faces,
and said to Fù Jùn:
"Today we are exhausted,
but are the others also weary?"
This refers to this river.
To the right of the river, the Zhì River enters from the left,
while to the left, the Bǎichǐ Ditch emerges.
The ditch water flows between high banks,
also called the Bǎichǐ Dike.
From north of Dìnglíng City, it connects to the Yǐng River at Xiāngchéng County.
When the Yǐng River swells, it spreads south,
and when the Rǔ River overflows, it flows north.
East of the ditch lies a clear pool,
named Lóngyuān,
about four lǐ north of the Rǔ River,
one hundred paces from north to south,
two hundred paces from east to west,
with exceptionally clear and deep water,
never drying up,
abundant in fish and bamboo shoots.
When the lake overflows, it flows east into the Kuò River.
The Rǔ River continues southeast,
where the Kūn River joins it,
originating from Tángshān in Lǔyáng County,
flowing southeast past the west of the old city of Kūnyáng County.
In the first year of the Gēngshǐ era,
Wáng Mǎng conscripted those skilled in military strategy from across the land,
selected and trained guards,
recruited fierce warriors,
with banners and supplies
stretching for a thousand lǐ without end,
and even drove fierce beasts such as tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants to bolster his might.
Since the campaigns of Qín and Hàn,
such grandeur had never been seen.
Emperor Shìzǔ intercepted them with a few thousand troops at Yángguān,
but his generals, seeing the strength of Xún and Yì's forces,
retreated into Kūnyáng.
Emperor Shìzǔ then left Duke Wáng Fèng of Chéngguó
and General Wáng Cháng, the Commandant of Justice, to hold the city,
while he rode out at night with thirteen cavalry through the south gate,
to gather troops at Yǎn.
Xún and Yì besieged the city with dozens of layers,
using cloud towers over ten zhàng high,
overlooking the city,
with crossbows firing indiscriminately,
arrows falling like rain.
People inside the city carried doors to fetch water,
and Wáng Fèng requested to surrender,
but was refused.
Emperor Shìzǔ led his camp forces in a coordinated advance,
repeatedly breaking through,
and with three thousand daring warriors,
charged directly at Xún and Yì's troops,
defeating their main force by this river,
and killing Wáng Xún.
The city defenders also charged out with loud shouts,
combining forces inside and out,
their roars shaking heaven and earth.
A great storm arose,
with roof tiles flying,
and Wáng Mǎng's troops were utterly routed.
The Kūn River then bends past the south of the city,
and during the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Fù Jùn, the Palace Attendant.
Thus, the Later Hàn Records of Commanderies and States mentions Kūnyáng County,
likely named after the river.
The Kūn River then flows east past the south of Dìnglíng City,
and further east joins the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River continues southeast past the northwest of Qí'é City,
now the seat of the Nányǐngchuān Commandery.
The Fén River originates here,
also commonly called the Dàyīn River.
The Ěryǎ states:
"The Hé River has its Yōng,
the Rǔ River has its Fén."
Thus, the Fén
is a tributary of the Rǔ.
Therefore, the settlements along its banks
still bear the name Rǔyáng,
perhaps because the sounds of "fén" and "yīn" are similar,
or because it merges with the Yīn and Yǐng rivers downstream,
sharing their names.
Further southeast, it passes north of Yǎn County.
The Rǔ River flows past Qí'é City to the west and then southeast,
with the city surrounded by two rivers,
and flanked by twin streams.
The Rǔ River continues southeast, passing by the north of the old city of Yǎn County,
which was a subordinate city of Wèi.
According to the "Shǐjì," Zhāo Yáng of Chǔ attacked Wèi and captured Yǎn.
The Rǔ River flows further east to meet Lǐ Shuǐ,
which originates in Zhì County of Nányáng.
It is also said to stem from Zhìhéng Mountain,
the same Héng Mountain mentioned in "Shānhǎijīng."
Guō Jǐngchún considers it the Southern Peak,
but this is incorrect.
Mǎ Róng's "Guǎngchéng Song" states:
"Facing Héngyīn,"
referring to this mountain.
It is within the boundaries of Zhì County,
hence it has been called Zhìhéng Mountain over the ages.
According to "Shānhǎijīng,"
there is no mention of water.
However, Lǐ Shuǐ flows east past the foot of Táng Mountain,
which is the mountain where Gāo Fèng lived in seclusion.
Lǐ Shuǐ continues southeast to join with Gāo Shuǐ,
which rises from Gāo Mountain.
Guō Jǐngchún says it might be noted as Zhāng Mountain,
flowing eastward into Lǐ Shuǐ.
Lǐ Shuǐ flows southeast past the north of Táng City,
entering the city from the south, flowing west, then out of the city,
thus deriving its name from the mountain.
Lǐ Shuǐ meanders southeast,
passing by the north of the old city of Yè County,
mentioned in "Chūnqiū" when Duke Zhāo moved to Yè in the fifteenth year.
The state of Chǔ thrived while Zhōu declined,
controlling the southern lands,
seeking to dominate central China,
and built numerous cities in the north,
to pressure Huáxià,
thus naming this city Wànchéng,
sometimes written as 'fāng.'
Táng Lè's "Zòu Tǔ Lùn" says:
"We are Chǔ."
Dominating the southern lands,
from Yuè to Yè,
extending the border for ten thousand miles,
thus named Wànchéng.
According to "Chūnqiū,"
Qū Wán was at Zhàolíng
and said to the Marquis of Qí:
"Chǔ uses Fāngchéng as its defense."
Dù Yù says:
Fāngchéng is
a mountain name,
south of Yè.
It is unclear which is correct.
King Huì of Chǔ bestowed upon Zhū Liáng Zǐgāo the title of Yè Gōng City.
It was originally the fief of Zǐgāo.
Yè Gōng loved dragons,
and mythical dragons descended to the east of the river.
When Wáng Qiáo was the governor of Yè,
each full moon,
he would visit the tower to greet the emperor,
curious about his frequent arrivals without sight of his entourage.
Xiǎn Zōng secretly ordered the astrologers to observe him,
witnessing a pair of mandarin ducks flying in from the southeast,
they set nets when the ducks approached,
capturing only a single shoe.
Upon inspection by the artisans of the court,
it was identified as the shoe given to the minister within four years.
Whenever it was time for court,
the drum at the gate of Yè would sound on its own,
reaching the capital.
Later, a jade coffin appeared before the hall,
officials and citizens tried to move it,
but it remained immobile.
Qiáo said:
"Is the heaven's emperor summoning only me?"
He bathed and dressed, lying inside it,
instantly covered and buried to the east of the city,
with soil forming a tomb.
That night,
all oxen in the county sweat profusely and panted,
yet people were unaware.
The people built a temple,
naming it the Shrine of Lord Yè,
every regional leader recorded it,
all first visiting to pay respect,
officials and citizens prayed for its blessings,
and any violation would invite a curse.
The emperor then retrieved the drum,
placing it below the county pavilion,
where it remained silent henceforth.
Some say:
This is the ancient immortal Wáng Qiáo,
thus recorded by the Gān family in Shénhuà.
Lǐ Shuǐ then flows east past the east of the city to merge with Shāochē Shuǐ,
which flows west from Kǔcài Mountain,
running east past the south of Yè City,
to join with Lǐ Shuǐ.
Lǐ Shuǐ further flows east past the north of Yè Gōng Temple,
where there is the "Shěn Zǐgāo Zhū Liáng Stele."
In the times of Qin and Han,
there were twin towers with ceremonial platforms at the temple,
but during the Yellow Turban Rebellion,
were destroyed.
In the times of Wèi's Tàihé and Jǐngchū,
they were restored by the local officials,
and later Chén Xī of Rǔnán erected a stele in the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
though the words on the stele are damaged,
some content remains visible,
as seen on the stele.
Lǐ Shuǐ continues east and meets Yè's West Bank River,
with Fāngchéng Mountain to the south of the county,
mentioned by Qū Wán about Fāngchéng as Chǔ's fortification.
The mountain has a spring that flows north,
stored to form a reservoir,
covering two square miles,
its water spreads,
flowing east past the south of Yè City, and northeast into Lǐ Shuǐ.
Lǐ Shuǐ further flows east to Yè's reservoir,
the reservoir is ten miles from east to west,
seven miles from north to south,
the reservoirs were dammed by Zhū Liáng.
The reservoir's water flows east past the north of Wǔyáng County's old city,
then east passing south of Dìnglíng City,
merging with Qín Gōu Shuǐ,
whose source is from Yè County,
flowing east past the north of Wǔyáng City,
then east past south of Dìnglíng County,
then southeast into Lǐ Shuǐ.
The water flows between Kūn and Lǐ,
winding through four counties,
possibly the Xiàn Shuǐ mentioned by Lǚ Chén.
Now at Dìnglíng, there is no other water,
this is certainly it.
Lǐ Shuǐ flows east past the south of the old city of Yǎn County,
joining with the Rǔ on the left.
"Shānhǎijīng" states:
Lǐ Shuǐ flows east into Xiàn Shuǐ.
The Rǔ River continues southeast past the west of Dèng City,
as mentioned in the "Chūnqiū Zǔozhuàn," Duke Huán's second year,
where the Marquis of Cài and the Earl of Zhèng met at Dèng.
The Rǔ River flows further southeast,
joined by Wǔ Shuǐ.
Again southeast past the west of Shàngcài County in Rǔnán,
Rǔnán Commandery,
formerly divided by Chǔ,
established in the fourth year of Hàn Gāozǔ,
renamed Rǔfén by Wáng Mǎng.
The county,
formerly the state of Cài,
was granted to Shū Dù, the younger brother of King Wǔ of Zhōu after conquering the In (Yīn) Dynasty,
"Shì Běn" says:
"It was the Upper Cài,"
with Xiàcài in Jiǔjiāng,
thus named Upper.
"The Zhúsū Jìnián" states:
"Wèi Zhāng led troops with Zhèng's forces against Chǔ to capture Shàngcài."
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Emperor Ān enfeoffed Dèng Zhì as its prince.
The Rǔ River further flows east past the north of Xuánwù City,
Wáng Zhìshēn says:
"Rǔnán prefect Zhōu Jīn raised an uprising at Xuánwù."
Now the prefecture of Yùzhōu's Rǔnán Commandery is governed to the northwest of the city,
where a tributary of the Rǔ branches off to the left,
flowing northwest,
then turning west to east,
southwest to rejoin the Rǔ,
shaped like a hanging calabash.
The elders say:
"The northern part of the city was called Mǎwān,
with several acres of ground,
and a chestnut orchard on top,
small chestnuts,
incomparable in quality to those from Gù'ān,
yet it produced three hundred bushels annually,
presented to the imperial treasury.
The water islet is now Liǔ Zhōu,
densely wooded,
appearing like a cloud of fog from afar.
In the forest there stands a chestnut temple,
with spacious archery grounds,
frequented by officials and scholars.
On the northwest corner of the wall,
during Tàihé, Emperor Gāozǔ once visited Xuánwù,
King of the South Píng built a high platform at the small city,
constructing a multi-story building at the corner,
its base near the water's edge,
with a view over Lǐu Zhōu, surrounded by pavilions on both sides,
all rising unevenly,
creating a magnificent scene.
Continuing southeast, it passes south of Píngyú County.
The Zhēn River originates from the Qīngyī Mountain north of the Fúshí Ridge,
and is also called the Qīngyī River.
It flows southeast past the west of the old Lǎnglíng County city,
Yīng Shào said:
To the southwest is Lǎnglíng Mountain,
and the county was named after it.
During the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Zāng Gōng, the Commandant of the City Gates, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
The Zhēn River then bends south and flows past the south of the county,
then flows northeast past the north of the old Běiyīchūn County city,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Xuānchán.
Since there was a Yíchūn in Yùzhāng,
this one was prefixed with "north."
In the third year of the Yuánchū era,
Emperor Ān enfeoffed Yán Chàng, the father of the empress and a Palace Attendant, as a marquisate here.
The Zhēn River then flows northeast past the north of Mǎxiāng City,
and then flows northeast into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the south of Píngyú County,
and the north of the old Ānchéng County city,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Zhìchéng.
In the sixth year of the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Cāng, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast,
where the Bēi River flows into it.
The water originates from the Shènyáng County old city south bēi, receiving water from the Shèn River.
The bēi water divides into two branches,
one branch flows north from the bēi, encircling Shènyáng City with a moat on all sides.
Xún Shū of Yǐngchuān met Huáng Shūdù, a native of the county, at an inn,
and after conversing with him for a long time,
said:
You, sir,
are a model teacher for me.
Fàn Yì commented:
Huáng Xiàn's words and refined intent,
were not transmitted by hearsay.
Yet whenever gentlemen and scholars met him,
none failed to be impressed by his depth and far-sightedness,
and to rid themselves of flaws and pettiness.
Was it because his Way was complete and his nature whole,
that he was beyond praise?
The moat water then flows northeast from the channel and empties into the northern bēi.
The other branch flows northeast from the bēi and accumulates to form the Tóng Bēi.
The bēi water then flows northeast and further collects to form another bēi,
which people call the Jiào Bēi.
The bēi water receives water from the northern bēi of Shènyáng County,
flows northeast and accumulates to form the Tǔ Bēi,
the bēi water then flows east to become the Jiào Bēi,
the bēi water then flows southeast and empties into the Bì Bēi,
the bēi water then flows northeast to become the Tài Bēi,
the bēi water then flows east into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the north of Pínglíng Pavilion,
and then flows southeast past the north of Yángsuì Township.
The Rǔ River then flows east past the north of Lì Pavilion,
which is the Jílì mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Dù Yù said:
Northeast of Xīncài County in Rǔyīn is Lì Pavilion.
The present city is northwest of the old Xīncài city,
with half of the northern city wall submerged in water.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the south of the old Xīncài County city.
In the past, Guǎn and Cài slandered the royal house,
so Cài Shū was exiled and relocated here.
His son, Hú,
was able to follow virtue and reform his conduct.
The Duke of Zhōu recommended him to be a high minister,
and presented him to the king.
The king commanded him to rule over Cài,
which was land of Shēn and Lǚ,
to continue the sacrifices for Shūdù,
and he became Cài Zhòng.
Sòng Zhōng said:
Therefore, the place was named Xīncài (New Cài).
This is what Wáng Mǎng called Xīnqiān.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Wú Guó was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
The *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* says:
Zhèng Jìng of Xīncài,
courtesy name Cìdūwéi,
served as Commandant of Merit for the commandery.
Before the office hall of Gāo Yì there was a pagoda tree,
on which white dew resembling sweet dew appeared.
Yì asked his subordinates,
and they all said it was sweet dew.
Only Jìng said:
Your administration's governance has not yet brought about sweet dew;
this is merely tree sap.
Yì was displeased,
and Jìng feigned illness and left.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast,
where on the left it meets the Yì River.
The water originates from a separate branch of the Rǔ River east of Qí'é City,
flows southeast to become Liàn Ditch,
passes west of Zhàolíng County,
flows southeast and empties into the upper reaches west of Cài, where north of Gāng Ridge it forms the Huánglíng Bēi.
The bēi water flows east,
and east of the upper Cài Gāng it becomes the Cài Pond.
It then flows east past the south of the old Píngyú County city,
and becomes the Yì River.
The county
was formerly the state of Shěn,
and had a Shěn Pavilion.
In the fourth year of Duke Dìng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Cài destroyed Shěn,
and took Shěn Zǐ Jiā back,
later Chǔ made it a county.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
The Qín general Lǐ Xìn attacked Píngyú,
and was defeated here.
In the thirtieth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Yáo Tǒng here as a marquisate.
It was originally the seat of Rǔnán Commandery.
In the past, Fèi Chángfáng was a market officer,
and saw Master Hú Gōng hanging a gourd in the commandery market.
Chángfáng followed him,
and thus from afar entered this gourd together with him,
disappearing into the path of immortals.
His bones dissolved and his spirit was embraced,
he returned without meeting anyone,
and though he could command ghosts and spirits,
in the end he transformed along with all things.
Over a lǐ south of the city is a spirit temple,
which people call the Temple of Prefect Zhāng Míngfǔ.
When floods or droughts were irregular, people prayed there.
In front of the temple is a tablet,
but the writing is fragmented and disordered,
and can no longer be deciphered.
Beside the tablet is a small stone casket.
According to the *Illustrated Eulogies of Former Worthies of Guìyáng*,
Zhāng Xī of Línwǔ,
courtesy name Jìzhì,
served as magistrate of Píngyú.
At that time there was a great drought,
and Xī personally prayed for rain.
Not receiving a favorable response,
he piled up firewood and set himself on fire.
The Registrar Hóu Chóng and the minor official Zhāng Huà followed him,
and Xī burned there.
After the fire had blazed up,
heaven's numinous power responded,
and rain immediately poured down.
This is the place where Xī burned himself.
The Yì River then flows southeast,
and on the left branches off to become the Gé Bēi.
The bēi is several tens of lǐ square,
and its aquatic creatures contain numinousness,
nurturing many things.
In the past, Fèi Chángfáng threw his staff into the bēi,
and that is where the dragon transformation occurred.
He also summoned the Lord of the Eastern Sea to this bēi.
The bēi water flows east out to become the Tóng River,
commonly called the Sānzhàng Bēi,
also called the Sānyán River.
The river flows past the south of the old Tóngyáng County city,
Yìng Shào said:
The county is on the north bank of the Tóng River.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Yīn Qìng, son of the Commandant of the Guards Yīn Xìng, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
The county has a Gélíng City.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Yáo Dān, Marquis of Ānchéng, was re-enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Northeast of the city is the tomb of King Wǔ of Chǔ,
which the people call the Chǔ King's Lute.
Below the Zhùshè Lǐ north of the city,
a bronze tripod was found in the earth,
with an inscription saying:
King Wǔ of Chǔ,
thus it is known to be the tomb passage of King Wǔ.
The Tóng Bēi flows east and becomes the Fù River.
Where the water accumulates,
it is called a bēi pond.
Fords and channels interweave,
branching out across the rivers and lowlands.
The Yì River flows southeast from the Gé Bēi past the east of the old Xīncài County city,
and then flows southeast into the Rǔ River.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past Xiàsāng Lǐ,
and on the left branches off to become the Héngtáng Bēi,
and then further northeast becomes the Qīng Bēi.
The Rǔ River then flows southeast past the north of Húqiū City,
which was formerly territory of Chén.
In the ninth year of Duke Wén of the *Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Chǔ invaded Chén and captured Húqiū,
because it had submitted to Jìn.
The Rǔ River then flows east and joins with the Qīng Bēi.
The water receives water from the Shèn River at the right ditch of the Upper Shèn Bēi in Shènyáng County,
flows north and empties into the Mǎchéng Bēi.
West of the bēi is Huángqiū Pavilion.
The bēi water then flows east past the north of Xīnxī Pavilion,
and then east becomes the Chóu Bēi.
The bēi water then flows past Xīnxī County,
and collects to form the Qiáng Bēi.
The bēi water then flows east past the southeast of Suì Township and becomes the Bì Bēi,
and then further east becomes the Qīng Bēi.
East of the bēi faces Dàlǚ Pavilion.
The *Outer Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
During the time of Chéngzhōu,
to the south were the Jīngmán, and Shēn and Lǚ of the Jiāng surname.
This was where Cài Pínghóu was first enfeoffed.
To the southwest is Xiǎolǚ Pavilion,
hence this one is called "great."
South of the side bēi is the Qīng Bēi Temple,
in front of the temple is a bēi.
In the third year of the Jiànníng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
Lǐ Yán, the magistrate of Xīncài County from Gōushì in Hénán,
submitted a request to restore the Qīngbēi reservoir.
Minister Sītú Xùn and Minister Shàngshū Xí memorialized for approval at the Luòyáng Palace,
and a stele was erected south of the eastern embankment of Qīngbēi.
The stele states that Qīngbēi is located in the southwest of the county,
its source arising from a separate stream of the Tóngbǎi and Huái rivers,
entering the Chányuán,
passing through the Qiángbēi of Xīnxī County and extending into the Bāoxìn County boundary,
irrigating over five hundred qǐng of land.
The reservoir water then divides eastward into two streams:
one flows south into the Huái River,
and the other flows southeast past the north of Báitíng,
then east past the south of Wúchéng.
According to the *Shǐjì*,
in the second year of King Huì of Chǔ,
Zǐxī summoned Shèng, the son of Crown Prince Jiàn, from Wú,
and Shèng came to reside there,
hence it is called Wúchéng.
It then turns northeast, passing east of Húqiū and flowing north,
emptying into the Rǔ River,
commonly known as Bóxī water.
The Rǔ River then flows east past the old city north of Bāoxìn County and continues eastward.
Further east, it reaches Yuánlù County.
The Rǔ River flows southeast past the west of the old county city,
as Dù Yù explains in *Shìdì*:
"Yǔyīn has Yuánlù County."
It then flows south into the Huái River.
This is the so-called Rǔkǒu,
beside which lies the Rǔkǒu garrison,
the confluence of the Huái and Rǔ rivers.
22 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 22
22.1 Yǐng River
22.1 Yǐng River
The Yǐng River originates from Shàoshì Mountain northwest of Yángchéng County in Yǐngchuān.
In the seventeenth year of Qín Shǐhuáng, Hán was conquered,
and its territory was established as Yǐngchuān Commandery,
likely named after the river.
In the second year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
it was made the Kingdom of Hán,
and under Wáng Mǎng, it was part of Zuǒduì.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"The Yǐng River originates from Shàoshì Mountain."
The *Dìlǐzhì* states:
"It originates from Yángqián Mountain in Yángchéng County."
Today, the Yǐng River has three extraordinary sources:
the right stream emerges from the Yǐng Valley of Yángqián Mountain,
where Yǐng Kǎoshū of the *Chūnqiū* period served as the fēngrén.
This water flows northeast.
The middle stream originates from the connecting ridge of Shàoshì,
flowing southeast past the east of Fùshǔtíng.
In the sixth year of Duke Dìng of the *Chūnqiū*,
Zhèng attacked Féng Huá at Fùshǔ.
Féng Jìngtōng's *Xiǎnzhìfù* says:
"Seeking the whereabouts of Shànjuàn,
I met Xǔ Yóu at Fùshǔ."
Jīng Xiàngfán states:
"Fùshǔ is located twenty-seven lǐ southwest of Yángchéng County in Yǐngchuān,
commonly known as Huángchéng."
Some also call this water the Yǐn River,
which joins the right stream to the east.
The left stream emerges from the southern stream of Shàoshì,
merging eastward with the Yǐng River.
Thus, authors variously mention both mountains
when referring to the river's source.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
Biànsuí, ashamed to accept Tāng's abdication offer,
threw himself into this river and died.
Zhāng Xiǎn's *Yìmínzhuàn* and Jī Shūyè's *Gāoshìzhuàn*
both say he threw himself into the Jiǒng River and died.
It is uncertain which is correct.
The river flows southeast past the south of the county.
The Yǐng River continues east,
where the Wǔdù River joins it.
This water originates from the eastern stream of Tàishì Mountain northeast of Chónggāo County.
The county
was established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
to serve Tàishì Mountain,
commonly called Sōngyángchéng.
During spring and summer rains,
water cascades from the mountaintop,
with streams overlapping,
forming twenty-eight pools.
In drought, the streams dry up,
but the stone pools do not diminish.
Travelers resting along the road
may only drink from them;
none dare bathe in them.
If one violates this custom,
they will surely fall ill for several days,
so travelers fear it.
At the mountain's base lies a large pool,
several lǐ in circumference,
clear, deep, and pure.
Within the water stands a rock,
over ten zhàng high,
and about twenty paces wide,
with a very flat top.
Scholars, both lay and monastic,
often boat there and ascend it,
seeking to indulge in serene feelings.
The water flows southeast past the west of Yángchéng,
where stone streams wind and twist,
requiring five crossings upstream,
hence it is also called the Wǔdù River.
It flows southeast into the Yǐng River.
The Yǐng River passes the old city south of the county.
Long ago, when Shun abdicated to Yǔ,
Yǔ avoided Shāngjūn,
and Bóyì avoided Qǐ,
all occurred here.
It is also where the Duke of Zhōu used a tǔguī to measure the sun's shadow.
In the first year of the Yǒngshǐ era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Zhào Lín was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
South of the county faces Jīshān,
on which lies the tomb of Xǔ Yóu,
enfeoffed by Yáo.
Thus, the Grand Historian said:
"I ascended Jīshān,
and upon it lies the tomb of Xǔ Yóu."
At the mountain's base is the Qiānniúxū,
beside the Yǐng River lies the Dú Spring,
where Cháofù returned the ox,
and ox hoofprints remain on the stone.
There is also a temple to Xǔ Yóu,
with stele and gate towers still standing,
erected by Zhū Chǒng, Governor of Yǐngchuān during the Hàn.
The Yǐng River passes north of it,
merging east with the Lóngyuān River.
This water originates from Lóngyuān,
flowing southeast past the north of Yángchéng,
then southeast into the Yǐng.
The Yǐng River continues east,
where the Píngluòxī River joins it.
This water emerges from the Píngluò Stream below the Yùnǚ Terrace,
commonly called Píngluò water.
Lǚ Chén's mention that Shuò water originates from Yángchéng Mountain
likely refers to this water.
It flows southeast
and empties into the Yǐng.
The Yǐng River then flows east out of Yángguān,
passing south of Kāngchéng.
Emperor Míng of Wèi enfeoffed Wèi Zhēn, Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, as Marquis of Kāngxiāng,
and this was his fief.
It then flows southeast past the north of Yángdí County.
The Yǐng River flows southeast past the Yángguān Market,
where two settlements face each other across the water.
This is commonly called the Eastern and Western Tǔchéng.
The Yǐng River then flows past the west of Shàngjíchéng,
and bends to flow past the south of this city.
According to the "Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn," in the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng,
the state of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and used Shàngjíchéng as a crossing point over the Yǐng River.
To the west of the county, there is an old weir.
The stones of the weir have collapsed,
but the remains of the foundation still exist.
In the past, it was used to direct the branches of the Yǐng River.
The ancient channel flows southeast past the north of Sānfēng Mountain,
but now there is no water.
A spring flows into the channel,
which people call the Yúshuǐ,
then it flows east past the east of Sānfēng Mountain,
and continues southeast past the west of Dàlíng Mountain connecting to the hills.
This is also called Qǐshì Pavilion.
Qǐ offered sacrifices to the deities on Dàlíng Mountain,
which is Jūntái.
The "Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"In the summer, Qǐ had a feast at Jūntái."
Dù Yù said:
"There is a Jūntái south of Yángdíng County in Hénán."
The water then flows southeast,
accumulating to form a lake,
which is ten lǐ square.
It is commonly called Jūntái Lake,
named after the platform.
It flows southwest past the west of Xiàtíng City,
then bends southeast to form the Mi Polder of Jiǎ.
The Yǐng River flows from the dam east past the north of the old city of Yángdíng County.
Hòu Yǔ first established the Xià state here,
so when King Wǔ of Zhōu arrived, he said:
"Could this be the residence of Xià?"
Thus, he planned Lùoyì.
Xú Guǎng said:
"Yángchéng in Hénán,
is indeed the territory of Xià."
In the "Chūnqiū Jīng," it records,
"In the autumn,
Earl Tū of Zhèng invaded Lì."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" of the 15th year of Duke Huán mentions that
Tū killed Tán Bó and resided there.
Fú Qián said:
"Tán Bó is the governor of Lì for Zhèng;
Lì
is a major city of Zhèng."
Sòng Zhōng said:
"This is now Yángdíng."
At the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
Hán Jǐnghóu relocated the capital from Xīnzhèng to here.
Wáng Yǐn said:
"Yángdíng was originally Lì."
It was the administrative seat of Yǐngchuān Commandery.
To the west of the city, there is a stele of Guō Fèngxiào,
and beside the water, there is a stele of the Jiǔshān Shrine,
where cypress trees still flourish,
and it leans against the river flow to the north.
The river flows southeast past the west of Yǐngyáng County,
then southeast again past the southwest of Yǐngyīn County.
Yīng Shào said:
"The county lies on the sunny side of the Yǐng River,
hence its name."
Referring to the "Eastern Han Records,"
General Mǎ Fáng was ennobled with a marquisate.
Fáng was a gate commander,
holding a position as a peerless officer.
The Yǐng River then flows south past the west of Yǐngxiāng City,
with the old Yǐngyīn County city to the northeast.
It was formerly a prefecture governed by Xiànchāng.
Later, it became a county,
and Emperor Wéi Mingdi conferred it upon Shìzhōng Xīn Bǐ as a marquisate.
The Yǐng River continues southeast past the east of the Bǎicī Bend,
and passes south of Gāngqiū City,
the former city of Fénqiū.
In the "Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn," during the 18th year of Duke Xiāng,
Marshal Gēng of Chǔ organized troops in Fén.
Sīmǎ Biāo said
that in Xiāngchéng County, there is Fénqiū.
Dù Yù said:
"It is to the northeast of Xiāngchéng County."
It passes north of the former county of Fánchāng,
with Fányáng Pavilion in Qūléi.
The "Wèi Shū Guó Zhì" states:
In the first year of Yánkāng under Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
he reached Qūléi,
ascended the altar to accept the abdication,
and renamed the era to Huángchū.
In that year,
the Fányáng Pavilion in Yǐngyīn was renamed Fánchāng County.
Inside the city, there are three terraces,
referred to by people as the Fánchāng Terrace.
In front of the altar, there are two steles,
where Emperor Wèi Wéndì accepted the abdication.
After descending from the altar, he said:
"Like the matters of Shùn and Yǔ,
I understand them well."
Therefore, the stone inscription reads:
"Henceforth a spiritual altar was built in Fánchāng."
Later, six characters on the stele began to produce gold,
which critics believed signified the Sīmǎ family's golden course,
leading to the transition of the Cáo family from Wèi to Jìn.
The Yǐng River flows southeast past the north of Qīnglíng Pavilion,
opposite the north of Qīnglíng Lake,
which is twenty lǐ in length and breadth.
The Yǐng River flows north of it,
branching and flowing into the lake.
To the west of the lake, the Kuòshuǐ flows into it,
originating under the town of Xiāngchéng County,
flowing east into the lake,
and the lake waters continue east into Lín Yǐng County's Láng Lake.
The Yǐng River further flows southeast through Lín Yǐng County.
It flows southeast past the south of Lín Yǐng County,
and further southeast past the north of Rǔnán's Qiāng County,
where the Wěi River flows from Mì County in Hénán eastward and converges.
Lín Yǐng is an old county.
The Yǐng River enters from the west of the county,
with the small Qiāng River originating there.
The "Erya" records:
"The Yǐng Wang Bī" is sandy.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"All the large rivers overflow,
and the different water branches have names as well,
just like the Jiāng separates into the Tuó."
The Yǐng River flows southeast past the north of Gāo City,
which is the ancient Gāochéng Pavilion.
The "Chūnqiū Jīng" records:
"The Duke and feudal lords met at Gāo Yù,"
with Gāo and Zé being similar in script,
but their names different."
The Yǐng River flows east past the south of Yángchéng,
and the "Zhúshū Jìnián" states:
"Sūn Hé captured Yáng."
Qiāng City lies to the northeast,
so the Yǐng River cannot flow north of it.
The Yǐng River continues southeast,
where the Yúshuǐ converges,
not to be mistaken with the Wěi River.
It flows east past the north of Xīhuá County,
which Wáng Máng renamed Huáwàng.
There is a statement that follows with a phrase indicating east, thus the reference to west.
During the Jiànwǔ period of the Guāngwǔ Emperor Shǐ Zǔ,
Dèng Chén was enfeoffed with a marquisate.
The Hàn Jìbèi Dài's fief,
with the courtesy name Píngzhòng,
was located in Xīhuá.
When there were droughts,
he lamented the inability of his achievements to move heaven.
Thus, he heaped wood and sat on it, intending to self-immolate.
The fire ignited, and a torrent of rain suddenly poured.
Leaders from afar praised and admired him.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was summoned as Grand Minister.
To the north of the county, there is Xíyáng City,
where the Yǐng River flows to the south,
as the "Jīng" refers to the Wěi Water flowing into it.
The river then flows south past the north of Nǚyáng County.
To the south of the former city of the county, there is a branch of the Rǔshuǐ,
from which the county derives its name.
Kàn Yǐn said:
"Originally, it was a separate flow of the Rǔshuǐ,
but later dried up and was called the Dead Rǔshuǐ,
thus the character has no water radical."
I propose that Rǔ and Nǚ are simply regional pronunciations,
hence the character was changed according to pronunciation,
and it might not confirm fully to Kàn's theory,
as pronunciation changes can sometimes alter characters.
The Yǐng River flows east again,
where the large Qiāngshui joins it.
It then flows southeast past the east of the old city of Bóyáng County,
which is forty lǐ north of Nándùn County.
During the reign of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Bǐng Jí was granted a marquisate as a national lord,
but Wáng Máng later renamed it Lèjiā.
It flows southeast past the north of Nándùn County,
where the Qiāngshui flows from the west to join it.
The Qiāngshui enters the Yǐng River at Lèjiā County,
but does not reach Dùn.
Dùn is an old state of the Dùn people,
of the same family as Zhōu.
In the 25th year of Duke Xī of the "Chūnqiū",
when Chǔ attacked Chén,
the Dùnzi returned to Dùn,
traditionally called Yǐngyīn City.
But this is not correct.
The Yǐng River flows southeast past the south of Chén County,
and then southeast,
where it meets at the confluence of several streams.
Further southeast, it reaches north of Xīnyáng County,
where the Làngdàng Canal flows in from the northwest and joins it.
The Classic states that Làngdàng Qú is
another name for the Hundred-Foot Ditch.
The Yǐngshuǐ converges southward with the Jiāokǒu Xīngōu,
and from here flows eastward.
On the Yǐngshuǐ there is a weir,
called the Xīnyáng Yàn,
commonly known as the Shānyáng È,
which is incorrect.
The Xīngōu flows east from the north of the Yǐngshuǐ,
emerging from the county, which lies north of the water.
Therefore, Yìng Shào said:
"The county lies on the sunny (south) side of the Xīnshuǐ."
Now, the old county town is to the east,
clearly indicating that the Yǐngshuǐ does not flow north of it.
This is likely an error in the Classic.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows southeast from the weir,
passing north of the old town of Xiàng County.
In the seventeenth year of Duke Xī of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Lǔ destroyed Xiàng, referring to this place.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further east,
converging on the right with the Gǔshuǐ.
This water originates from various ponds in Píngxiāng,
flowing northeast past the old town of Nándùn County to the south,
then turning east along the city wall.
As mentioned in the Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals, Dùn was pressured by Chén and fled to Chǔ.
Since Dùn moved south,
it was called Nándùn (Southern Dùn).
Now, its town lies over thirty lǐ south of Dùn.
Further east, it passes through the town of Xiàng.
King Xiāng of Chǔ fortified this outer wall,
making it a secondary capital.
Within the capital, the small town in the southwest
is the old town of Xiàng County,
formerly the seat of Yǐng Prefecture.
The Gǔshuǐ passes north of the small town,
then east past the north of the temple of Jiǎ Kuí, Governor of Yù Province of Wèi.
Wáng Yǐn stated
that the temple was north of the town,
which is incorrect.
The temple is east of the small town.
In the past, when Wáng Líng was captured by Marshal Simǎ Yì of Xuān,
he arrived at the temple and sighed, saying:
"Jiǎ Liángdào,
Wáng Líng,
a loyal minister of Wèi,
may your spirit know this."
He then drank poison and died.
In front of the temple is a stele,
and on the stele stone, gold grew.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The gold could be mined,
an auspicious sign for the revival of Jìn."
The Gǔshuǐ flows further east out of the town,
and empties east into the Yǐng.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further east,
and beside it lies the Gōnglù Chéng,
built by Yuán Shù.
Therefore, later generations named the town after his courtesy name.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further east past the north of Línyǐng Chéng.
The town faces the water, lacking a southern wall.
Further east, it passes between the two towns of Yúnyáng,
flanked by water to the north and south,
though not fully equipped.
Further east, it passes Qiūtóu.
Qiūtóu rests on the water to the south.
The Wèishū Jùnguó Zhì states:
"The army of Xuānwáng camped at Qiūtóu,
and Wáng Líng surrendered with hands bound by the water."
Hence, it was named Wǔqiū.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further southeast,
passing north of an old town,
where the Xìshuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from the Yángdū Pō.
The pond water branches off,
flowing southeast to become the Xìshuǐ.
It flows east past the north of the old town of Xīnyáng County,
then southeast past the north of the old town of Sòng County.
This county is the so-called Qīqiū.
When Qín attacked Wèi and captured Qīqiū,
it referred to this city.
In the first year of the Suīhé era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
an edict granted a fief in Pèi to the descendants of the Yīn dynasty,
to preserve the three orthodoxies.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshǐ era of Emperor Píng,
it was renamed Duke of Sòng.
In the fourth year of the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng,
the fief was moved here,
hence named Xīnqī,
as the Duchy of Sòng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xīnyán.
The Xìshuǐ flows further south past Xìyáng County,
where the Xīngōu Shuǐ flows into it.
This ditch begins at Jiāokǒu,
flowing northeast past the south of the old town of Xīnyáng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Lǚ Qīng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xīnmíng.
Therefore, Yìng Shào said:
"The county lies on the sunny (south) side of the Xīnshuǐ."
Now, there is no water,
only the old course of the ditch remains.
It flows east into marshlands and disperses into the Xìshuǐ.
The Xìshuǐ flows further southeast past the south of the old town of Xìyáng County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lèqìng.
During the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Cén Péng's son, Cén Zūn, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Xìshuǐ flows further southeast,
accumulating to form a pond,
called Cìtáng.
Both public and private parties draw from it,
to irrigate fields.
It flows further southeast,
bends southwest, and enters the Yǐng.
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
"The Xìshuǐ originates from Xìyáng County,
and flows southeast into the Yǐng."
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further southeast past the east of Hú Chéng.
This is the old state of Hú.
In the fifteenth year of Duke Dìng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Chǔ destroyed Hú,
capturing Húzǐ Bào and taking him back.
Dù Yù's Shìdì states:
"Northwest of Rǔyīn County lies Hú Chéng."
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further southeast,
where a branch of the Rǔshuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from a separate channel of the Rǔshuǐ, thirty lǐ east of Qíluò Chéng.
It is commonly known as the Dà Yīnshuǐ.
It flows southeast past the south of the old town of Zhàolíng County.
In the fourth year of Duke Xī of the Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Duke Huán of Qí stationed his army at Zhàolíng,
reproaching Chǔ for not paying tribute.
This is the place.
Within the town is a large well,
several zhàng in diameter,
with clear and deep water.
Kàn Yīn said:
"Zhào means
high."
The land is hilly and elevated,
and the well is several zhàng deep,
hence the name.
Further southeast, it passes Zhēngqiāng County,
formerly the Ānlíng Village and Ānlíng Pavilion of Zhàolíng County.
In the eleventh year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was granted to the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary Lái Xī.
Xī was rewarded for his campaign to pacify the Western Qiāng,
hence renamed Zhēngqiāng.
Kàn Yīn quoted the Zhànguó Cè, suggesting that King Zhāo of Qín wanted to exchange land here,
which is incorrect.
The separate channel of the Rǔshuǐ flows further east past the north of the Gōnglù Tái.
The platform overlooks the water,
a hundred paces square,
built by Yuán Shù.
Another branch of the Rǔshuǐ flows east past Xīmén Chéng,
also known as Nánlì.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn enfeoffed Liú Chāng, son of the Prince of Guangling, as a marquis here.
Thirty lǐ north of the county lies Shú Chéng,
called Běilì.
Thus, the old channel flows between these two Lì,
passing through Nǚyáng County,
commonly known as the Dead Rǔ County.
It takes its name from the water,
hence called Nǚyáng.
