Further east, it passes north of the old town of Nándùn County,
then southeast past north of Tóngyáng Chéng,
then east past north of Dǐxiāng Chéng,
then east past north of the old town of Gùshǐ County.
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
"This county
was formerly Jìn."
Jìnqiū lies to the south,
hence the county was named after the hill.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Rùnzhì.
Sūn Shū'áo, because the land was thin and poor,
took it as his fief,
thus ensuring lasting succession.
North of the town, there is still a stele for Shū'áo.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Minister of Works Lǐ Tōng, admiring Shū'áo's acceptance of the fief,
was praised by Emperor Guāngwǔ,
and it was renamed Gùshǐ.
Another branch of the Rǔshuǐ flows east past north of Cài Gāng.
On the hill lies the tomb of Cài Zhāo, Chancellor of Píngyáng.
Zhāo, styled Shūmíng,
was a descendant of Hòu Jì of Zhōu.
The tomb has a stone gate tower,
with two steles in front.
The inscriptions on the steles are worn and fragmented,
no longer legible.
The stone sheep and tigers are tilted and low,
barely remaining.
The branch of the Rǔshuǐ flows northeast past the south of Hú Chéng,
then east past the northwest of the old town of Nǚyīn County,
and enters the Yǐngshuǐ to the east.
The Yǐngshuǐ flows further east past the north of the old town of Nǚyīn County.
The Shǐjì Gāozǔ Gōngchén Hóu Zhě Niánbiǎo states:
"In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Xiàhóu Yīng was enfeoffed as a marquis here."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Rǔ Fén.
The county lies on the shady (north) side of the Rǔshuǐ.
Therefore, it is named after the Rǔ River.
West of the city, there is another city,
which was the old Táoqiū Township.
It is the seat of the Rǔyīn Commandery.
Outside the city, in the northeastern corner, there is an old terrace that rises like a wing of the city, resembling a hill.
Commonly called the Nǚláng Terrace,
although it has collapsed and been destroyed,
it remains broad and lofty.
On top, there is a well,
which is suspected to be from the old Táoqiū Township,
though the details are unclear.
Further east to the east of Shèn County,
it flows south into the Huái River.
The Yǐng River flows southeast,
joining on the left with the Shàngwú and Bǎichǐ Rivers,
both of which originate from the Cìtáng and Xìbēi ponds,
flowing south and emptying into the Yǐng River.
The Yǐng River continues southeast,
where the Jiāngbēi River flows into it.
This water comes from the Dàchōng Pond,
which flows south,
accumulating to form the Jiāngbēi Pond.
It passes south of Shèn City to the west,
and flows along the south side of the city into the Yǐng River.
The Yǐng River then passes by the old city of Shèn County.
The county,
originally a town of the State of Chǔ, was where Lord Bái resided to resist the State of Wú.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Āi of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*,
the people of Wú attacked Shèn,
and Lord Bái defeated them.
It was called Shènzhì during the reign of Wáng Mǎng.
During the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Liú Cì was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Yǐng River flows southeast past the east of the Tiáoliáo Outer Wall,
commonly called the Zhèng City.
It then flows southeast into the Huái River.
In the twelfth year of Duke Zhāo of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the King of Chǔ hunted in Zhōulái,
and camped at the end of the Yǐng River,
likely where the Yǐng River meets the Huái River.
22.2 Wěi River
22.2 Wěi River
The Wěi River originates from the Mǎlǐng Mountain southwest of Mì County in Hénán.
The water flows from the foot of the mountain,
and it is also said to originate from the Yángchéng Mountain in Yǐngchuān.
The mountain is northeast of Yángchéng County,
and it is considered part of the Mǎlǐng range.
The Wěi River flows southeast,
passing south of an old terrace,
commonly called the Yángzǐ Terrace.
It then flows east past the north of the Mǎlǐng Fortress,
which is located on the mountain.
Below the fortress, a spring flows north,
also considered a separate source of the Wěi River,
and empties into the Wěi River.
The Wěi River flows east,
where it meets the Suí River.
The Suí River originates from the Suí Stream on Fāng Mountain,
which is the Fúxì Mountain mentioned in the *Shānhǎi Jīng*.
It flows southeast,
passing by the tomb of Zhāng Bóyǎ, the former Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng during the Hàn Dynasty.
The tomb precinct is surrounded on all sides,
with stones piled to form walls.
The corners and curves descend gradually,
arranged along the northern bank of the Suí River.
At the Gēng gate, two stone towers stand as markers,
with stone animals flanking the towers below.
In front of the tomb, there is a stone temple,
with three steles planted in a row.
The steles say:
"His virtue name is Bóyǎ,
a native of Mì in Hénán."
Beside the steles, two stone figures stand,
along with several stone pillars and various stone animals.
In the past, the Suí River was diverted south into the tomb precinct,
forming a pond.
The pond is located in the Chǒu direction,
with toads spouting water,
and stone gutters channeling the flow. South of the pond,
stone towers and a stone temple were built,
with various animals arranged in front like wings.
However, as things decay and time passes,
they have nearly all been destroyed and ruined.
Wealth without righteousness
is like floating clouds,
so how much more so is this?
Wángsūn and Shì'ān
understood this well.
The Suí River flows southeast past the south of Shàngguō Pavilion,
and empties southeast into the Wěi River.
The Wěi River continues east,
where the Xiānghé River flows into it.
This water originates from the Zǐjié Stream to the north,
also called the Zǐjié River,
flowing southeast and emptying into the Wěi River.
The Wěi River then flows east and meets the Lìdī Spring,
which emerges from the side of a deep stream.
The spring flows for over a zhang,
with water cascading and scattering,
hence it is commonly called the Lìdī Spring.
It flows south into the Wěi River.
It flows southeast past the south of the county.
The Wěi River flows southeast again,
merging with the two streams of Chéngyún,
both originating from Chéngyún Mountain.
The two sources flow in parallel,
running southeast to pour into the Wěi,
and are commonly known as the Eastern and Western Chéngyún Waters.
The Wěi River flows east again,
where the Wēi River joins it.
This water emerges from Wēi Mountain,
flowing northeast into the Wěi.
The Wěi River then passes east by the old city wall of Mì County,
which is called Xīnchéng in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
In the sixth year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
the feudal lords gathered to attack Zhèng and besieged Xīnmì,
which is why Zhèng did not fortify the city at the proper time.
Now, on the southern side of the eastern gate of the county town,
there is a shrine to Zhuō Mào, the Hàn-dynasty magistrate of Mì.
Mào, styled Zǐkāng,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
He was gentle, benevolent, broad-minded, and refined,
respectful and courteous.
Once, someone claimed his horse was theirs,
and Mào said to them:
"If this is not your horse,
I hope you will return it to me at the chancellor's office."
Then he pulled his carriage and left.
Later, the horse's owner recovered the horse,
apologized, and returned it.
He served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate under the Hàn,
was promoted to magistrate of Mì,
promoted the virtuous and taught the people,
never uttering harsh words.
His moral influence spread widely,
so that no one picked up lost items on the road,
locusts did not enter the region,
and the common people erected a shrine for him,
where sacrifices have continued without cease.
The Wěi River then joins the Suǒquán Water on the left,
which emerges west of the Yù Pavilion,
flowing north into the Wěi River.
The Wěi River flows southeast again and merges with the Mǎguān Water,
which emerges below the Yù Pavilion,
flowing northeast past Mǎguān,
hence called the Mǎguān Water.
It then flows northeast into the Wěi.
The Wěi River flows east again and joins the Wǔdìng Water,
which emerges north from Wǔdìng Ridge,
flowing southwest,
then bends southeast,
passing west of the Língniǎo Fortress.
It flows southeast alongside the fortress,
where water beside the fortress
cascades into the ravine,
over a zhang in height,
plunging straight into the stream below,
accumulating into a deep pool.
Those who come for leisure gaze upon it,
marveling at its splendid view.
Commoners, seeing this water hanging beside the fortress,
named it the Língniǎo Water.
It flows southeast into the Wěi.
The Wěi River flows east again and merges with the Hǔdú Mountain Water,
which originates from the Hǔdú Stream on the southern mountain,
flowing northeast into the Wěi.
The Wěi River flows southeast again,
where the Chìjiàn Water joins it.
This water emerges from Wǔdìng Ridge,
flowing southeast past the foot of Huángtái Ridge,
then east of the ridge,
and southeast into the Wěi.
The Wěi River flows southeast again,
where the Zhēn River joins it.
The Wěi River then passes southeast by the south of Kuài City.
The Shìběn states:
Lù Zhōng married the younger sister of the Guǐfāng clan,
called Nǚ Tuí.
She gave birth to six sons,
after a pregnancy of three years.
Opening her left flank,
three came out;
breaking her right flank,
three came out.
The fourth was called Lái,
said to be the ancestor of the Kuài people.
The Kuài people
are the Zhèng.
Duke Huán of Zhèng asked Shǐ Bó,
saying:
"The royal house faces many troubles;
where can I escape death?"
Shǐ Bó replied:
"Guó and Kuài
are your people;
you may move there."
The Zhèng clan moved east,
and Guó and Kuài offered ten cities.
Liú Zhēn said:
"Kuài lies north of Wàifāng in Yùzhōu,
bordering Guó to the north,
south of the capital at Xíng,
with Jǐ to the left and Luò to the right,
situated between two rivers,
nourished by the Zhēn and Wěi."
Xú Guǎng said:
"Kuài is in Mì County,
of the Yún surname,
and cannot be north of Wàifāng."
The Wěi River then passes east by the north of Yīnbǎn,
where there is a bridge over the water,
commonly called this crossing the Shēnchén Crossing.
In the ninth year of Duke Xiāng in the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Jìn attacked Zhèng,
crossed at Yīnbǎn,
and encamped at Yīnkǒu before returning.
Dù Yù said:
"Yīnbǎn
is a ford on the Wěi."
Fú Qián said:
"South of the water is called yīn;
kǒu means
the mouth of the water."
Shēn and yīn sound similar,
likely a mispronunciation in transmission.
Moreover, Jìn occupied the division of Shēn,
the land of Shí Chén,
while Zhèng was in the wilderness of Dàchén, the land of È Bó.
When armies encamped there,
the crossing thus gained its name.
Further east, it passes south of Zhèng County,
where the Zhēn River flows from the northwest to join it.
The Wěi River flows eastward through the old city of Xīnzhèng County.
According to the *Zuǒzhuàn*, in the first year of Duke Xiāng,
Hán Jué and Xún Yǎn of Jìn led the feudal lords to attack Zhèng,
entered its outer wall,
and defeated its infantry on the Wěi River.
The *Zhúshū Jìnián* records that in the second year of Marquis Wén of Jìn,
Duōfǔ, son of King Huì of Zhōu, attacked Kuài and conquered it,
then settled at Zhèngfù Hill,
naming it Zhèng,
and was called Duke Huán.
Huángfǔ Shì'ān’s *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
Some say the county was originally the ruins of the Yǒuxióng clan,
the capital of the Yellow Emperor.
The Zhèng clan moved and settled there,
hence it was called Xīnzhèng (New Zhèng).
Inside the city, there is an old shrine,
named Zhāngchéng.
The Wěi River flows eastward and becomes the Wěiyuān Water.
The *Chūnqiūzhuàn* says:
“Dragons fought outside the Shímén Gate at Wěiyuān,”
referring to this pool.
Now the Wěi River enters from the northwest of Zhèng City and flows southeast,
passing through the south gate inside the southern wall of Zhèng City.
In the past, an outer snake fought with an inner snake,
and the inner snake died.
Six years later,
the senior official Fù Xiá killed the ruler of Zhèng
and installed Duke Lì,
which was an omen of this event.
South of the water is Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng’s Terrace for Gazing at His Mother.
Lady Zhuāng Jiāng disliked the duke because he was born feet-first,
and she lived with Duàn in Jīng.
Duàn did not behave as a younger brother should,
and Lady Jiāng showed no restraint.
Duke Zhuāng placed his mother in Chéngyǐng,
vowing:
“Not until the Yellow Springs [death]
shall we meet again.”
Thus, he built a terrace to gaze at his mother,
to express the longing in his heart.
Moved by Kǎoshū’s words,
he rejoiced in the ode of the great tunnel,
and the gentle kindness was praised,
while the harmonious filial piety was restored.
The Wěi River flows eastward and joins the Huáng River.
What the *Jīng* calls the Zhēn River
is incorrect.
The Huáng River originates from the Huáng Spring south of Tài Mountain,
flowing southeast past the west of Huá City.
Shǐ Bó said to Duke Huán of Zhèng:
“This is the land of the lord of Huá.”
Wéi Zhāo said:
“Huá
is the name of a state.”
The *Shǐjì* records that
in the thirty-third year of King Zhāo of Qín,
Bái Qǐ attacked Wèi,
captured Huáyáng,
drove away Máng Mǎo,
and beheaded 150,000 men.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
“Huáyáng
is the name of a station,
located in Mì County.”
Jī Shūyè often gathered herbs in the mountains and marshes
and learned the qin from the ancients
at this station.
The Huáng River flows southeast
and joins another stream,
which originates from the southern ridge of Huá City.
One source divides into two,
with springs and streams branching off.
The eastern branch is the Qīhǔ Jiàn Water,
while the western flow is this stream.
This stream flows southwest and empties into the Huáng River.
Huáng
is what the *Chūnqiū* calls Huángyá.
Thus, Dù Yù said:
“West of Yuànlíng County is the Huáng River.”
It flows further southeast,
and beside the water are two terraces,
called the Jīsǔ Terrace.
East of the terrace
is where the two streams converge.
The Bǔzhāng Mountain Stream flows into it,
originating east of Bǔzhāng Mountain
and flowing west into the Huáng River.
The Huáng River flows south to the north of Zhèng City,
turns east at the northeast corner of the city,
and joins the Huáng Gōu,
which originates from Bǔzhāng Mountain,
flows southeast to Zhèng City,
and enters the Huáng River from the northeast.
The Huáng River flows southeast past the east of Lóngyuān,
where the Qīlǐ Gōu Water flows into it.
This water originates from level ground southeast of Xìhóu Pavilion,
flows east,
then bends and flows south,
passing east of Shēng City,
then flows south past the west of Zhú City,
which was the fief of Zhèng senior official Zhú Zhīwǔ.
It then flows south and empties into the Wěi River.
Further southeast, it passes north of Chángshè County.
The Wěi River flows southeast,
and the Southern Pú and Northern Pú streams flow into it.
Pú is pronounced “pú.”
The Wěi River flows southeast and joins the Lóngyuān Water,
which originates northwest of Chángshè County.
There is an old channel that receives water from the Wěi River.
When the water is abundant, it flows into the Lóngyuān Water;
when it decreases, the channel stops flowing.
In the channel, springs flow south,
turning east to form an abyss.
Green waters form a level pool,
clear, pure, and deep.
Looking down at the swimming fish,
they seem to float in midair,
as the saying goes, “No fish hides in the abyss.”
It flows east past the old city north of Chángshè County,
which was the Chánggé settlement of Zhèng.
In the fifth year of Duke Yǐn of the *Chūnqiū*,
the people of Sòng attacked Zhèng
and besieged Chánggé.
Later, a community altar tree grew violently,
hence the name Chángshè (Long Altar).
It was the seat of the Wèi commandery of Yǐngchuān.
I, during the Jǐngmíng era, served as magistrate of this commandery.
On the west side of the southern city, I built a guesthouse.
When the construction began,
a tree root was found underground,
very large and robust,
suspected to be the old altar tree that grew wildly.
Consulting old records,
the county had no name “Lóngyuān Water,”
so it likely emerged in recent times.
Jīng Xiàngfán’s *Chūnqiū Tǔdì Míng* says:
“North of Chángshè is the Bǐng River.”
However, this water is channeled from the moat,
not what is referred to as the northern boundary.
Also, according to the *Jīng Dù Dìmíng*,
both state that north of Chángshè County is the Chánggé district,
indicating the county was moved south.
Thus, this water is the Bǐng River.
It flows southeast past the north of Jí City,
where, according to the *Zuǒzhuàn*, the ruler of Chǔ attacked Zhèng to rescue Qí
and camped at Jízé.
The Bǐng River flows east,
and from the left, empties into the Wěi River.
The Wěi River divides into two streams southeast,
with a branch flowing northeast into the sand.
One stream flows east past Xǔchāng County,
the old state of the Earl of Xǔ,
of the Jiāng surname,
descendants of the Four Peaks.
The *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn* says the Son of Heaven met the Earl of Xǔ on the Wěi River.
In the fourth year of the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Mǎ Guāng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhùqī* says:
“The Hàn lost the empire because of Xǔ.”
When Wèi succeeded the Hàn mandate,
it was renamed Xǔchāng.
Inside the city are the foundations of the Jǐngfú Hall,
built during the Tàihé era of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
costing over eight million.
The Wěi River flows east into the Wèncāng City,
commonly mistaken as the Wèn River,
hence the name Wèncāng.
This is incorrect;
it is actually a warehouse of the Wěi River.
The Wěi River flows east past the old city south of Yānlíng County.
Lǐ Qí said:
“During the Warring States, it was called Ānlíng.”
In the past, Qín demanded an exchange of territory,
and Táng Jū was sent as an envoy here.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Commandant Zhū Pì was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zuǒtíng.
The Wěi River flows east,
and the Yānlíng Bēi Water flows into it,
originating from the southern slope of Yānlíng,
flowing east, west, and south into the Wěi River.
Further southeast, it passes northeast of Xīnjí County.
The Wěi River flows east from Yānlíng past the south of Tóngqiū,
which is commonly called Tiānjǐng Ridge,
also known as a hill,
but this is incorrect.
The Wěi River then bends and flows south,
with a bridge over the water,
called Tóngmén Bridge,
named after Tóngqiū,
and also said to be named after the Tóngmén Pavilion,
though the location of the pavilion is unknown,
and the details are unclear.
The Wěi River then flows southeast past Tóngqiū City,
as recorded in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*, in the 28th year of Duke Zhuāng,
when the State of Chǔ attacked the State of Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng fled to Tóngqiū.
This is the city referred to.
Dù Yù’s *Explanations of Place Names in the Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
northeast of Xǔchāng City in Yǐngchuān.
Jīng Xiàngfán says:
It is in the territory of Zhèng.
Though it does not appear on current maps, the city still exists,
about thirty-five lǐ southwest of the old city of Xǔchāng,
commonly called a dike.
South of the city is a long dike,
which serves as the northern embankment of the Wěi River.
To the west lies Tóngqiū,
and the city is elongated rather than square,
likely taking its name from the hill,
hence the city’s name.
The Wěi River then flows east past the old city of Xīnjí County,
which was established in the second year of the Shénquè era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn in the Jíxiāng area of Xǔ, in the Qūwěi City,
and because there was already a Jí County in Hénèi,
it was named “New.”
The city lies on the southern dike of the Wěi River,
and further east,
the Wěi River branches off to the right to form the Huò Marsh.
The Wěi River then flows past the south of Kuāng City,
which is the Kuāng Pavilion in Fúgōu.
Further east,
the Wěi River branches off to the left to form the Yāzi Marsh,
also called the Great Opening.
It then flows southeast past the northeast of Máochéngyì,
from the Great Opening, the Wěi River flows southeast past the west of Wěiyáng City,
south past the northeast of Máochéng,
then further south,
where it joins the Jiǎgēng Ditch on the left,
which originates from the Wěi River,
branching off northeast of the Great Opening,
flowing east past the old city of Wěiyáng,
commonly called Fùyáng City,
but this is incorrect.
This is likely due to the similarity in characters and pronunciation between “Wěi” and “Fù.”
During the Jiàn’ān era of the Hàn Dynasty,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate to Guō Fèngxiào, the Minister of Ceremonies.
The water then flows southeast to form the Yāzi Marsh,
which is fifteen lǐ wide,
with its remaining flow entering the Jiǎgēng Ditch to the south,
flowing west into the Wěi River,
and northeast into the sand.
The Wěi River then flows south past the west of an old city,
commonly called Sīxiāng City,
which lies fifteen lǐ west of the Wěi River.
The Wěi River then joins the Huò Marsh water on the right,
which originates from the Wěi River at Xīnjí County,
flowing south past the east of the old city of Xīnjí County,
then accumulating to form a marsh,
with Chángshè City to the northwest of the marsh.
The marsh water extends east along the Wěi River dike,
with Máo Yì to the west,
and from the north gate of the city, a dike road extends,
reaching this hill.
It is still commonly called Máo Ridge,
which is the Máochéngyì mentioned in the *Classic*.
The marsh water flows north, then east into the Wěi River crossing,
and west receives northern tributaries.
Further east, it passes the west of Xíyáng City,
then turns into the Yǐng River.
The Wěi River then flows southeast past the east of Chén Pavilion,
commonly called Tián City,
but this is incorrect.
This is likely because “Tián” and “Chén” sound similar,
and “city” and “pavilion” are phonetically related.
As recorded in the *Classic*,
in the 11th year of Duke Xuān of Lǔ,
the rulers of Chǔ, Chén, and Zhèng formed an alliance at Chénlíng.
Jīng Xiàngfán says:
There is an old Chén Pavilion in Chángpíng, Yǐngchuān.
Dù Yù says:
There is a Chén Pavilion southeast of Chángpíng County.
Now, this city lies northwest of Chángpíng City,
with Chángpíng City to the southeast,
which may be an error by Dù,
or a mistake in the transmitted texts.
Southeast of Chángpíng, on the northern bank of the Lín Marsh, there is a mound,
about one lǐ from east to west,
and about fifty paces from north to south,
commonly called the New Pavilion Terrace,
and it is suspected to be the Chén Pavilion mentioned by Dù, though the details are unclear.
The Wěi River then flows south past the west of the old city of Chángpíng County,
which was called Chángzhèng under Wáng Mǎng.
The Wěi River then splits into two branches to the south,
with the eastern branch,
called the Wǔliáng Ditch,
flowing past the north of Xíyáng City,
then east past the south of Zhěqiū,
where there is an old city on the hill.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
Chángpíng originally belonged to Rǔnán,
and the county has Zhěqiū City,
which is this city.
It then flows east past the south of Chángpíng City,
and empties east into the Láo Marsh.
The southern branch of the Wěi River,
called the Jīlóng Water,
gives the confluence the name “Cage Opening.”
The Wěi River then flows east past the west of Xíyáng City,
turns southwest, and enters the Yǐng River.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
The Wěi River flows southeast to Chángpíng County and enters the Yǐng River.
22.3 The Yì River
22.3 The Yì River
The Yì River originates from the Dàguī Mountain in Mì County, Hénán.
Dàguī,
is Jùcí Mountain.
The Yellow Emperor ascended Jùcí Mountain,
climbed onto the great embankment,
and received the "Divine Fungus Diagram" from the Huágài youth,
which is this mountain.
Yìshuǐ emerges from its slope,
flows and forms a reservoir,
commonly called the Jade Maiden Pond.
It passes east by the north of Xíng Mountain,
as recorded in the "Records of the Grand Historian": in the sixth year of King Xiāng of Wèi,
he defeated Chǔ at Xíng Mountain.
On the mountain is the tomb of Jì Zhòng of Zhèng,
west of which is the tomb of Zǐchǎn,
built with piled stones into a square mound.
East of the mound is a temple,
both facing northeast toward the city of Zhèng.
Dù Yuánkǎi said this shows they did not forget their roots.
Beside the temple, there was an old withered cypress tree,
from its decaying roots and old stump,
many young cypresses grew into a grove,
lush and verdant,
a sight both wondrous and admirable.
Yìshuǐ then flows southeast past the northwest of Chángshè City,
where the two rivers, Nán Pú and Běi Pú, emerge.
Liú Chéngzhī, in his "Records of the Yǒngchū Era," states:
the "Water Classic" mentions Púshuǐ,
originating from Dàguī Mountain,
flowing northeast into the Sì River,
where Duke Líng of Wèi heard music on the water.
This is quite mistaken.
I note that the "Water Classic" refers to Yìshuǐ, not Púshuǐ.
This river first receives Yìshuǐ,
with dual channels,
both flowing east into Wěishuǐ.
Wěishuǐ and it pass through sandy areas,
where branches and streams become disordered,
and they interchangeably share names.
Thus, in the ninth year of Duke Zhāo of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the people of Chéngfù were moved to Chén,
and the western fields of Yí Pú were added to them.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
it means adding the western fields of Yí Pú.
Dù Yù also stated,
that the fields of Yí west of Púshuǐ were given to the people of Chéngfù.
Fú Qián said:
Pú,
is the name of a river.
Moreover, the characters are similar and the pronunciation is the same,
but the waterways are distant and distinct,
so it cannot be the upper source of Běi Pú,
where Master Shī transmitted music upon it.
Yìshuǐ then flows south past the west of Zhōng Pavilion,
then southeast past the west of Huáng Terrace,
then southeast past the west of Guān Pavilion.
Then southeast past the west of Wǎn Pavilion,
the old town of Wǎn Shèquǎn, a senior official of Zhèng.
Yìshuǐ then divides into two streams.
One stream flows south past the east of Hú City,
formerly the Húrén Pavilion of Yǐngyīn County.
This water gathers south to form a reservoir,
called the Húchéng Reservoir.
Yìshuǐ from a branch channel flows east past the east of Qūqiáng City,
where Huángbēi Water flows into it,
originating from the north of Qī Nǚ Ridge at Huáng Terrace in the northwest,
Huángbēi is the ancient Zhuózé of Chángshè County.
As recorded in the "Records of the Grand Historian,"
in the first year of King Huì of Wèi,
Marquis Yì of Hán and Marquis Chéng of Zhào joined forces to attack Wèi,
and battled at Zhuózé.
North of this reservoir faces Jīmíng City,
which is Zhuó City of Chángshè County.
The reservoir water flows southeast past the north of Húquán City,
formerly the Húzōng Township of Yǐngyīn County.
It then joins east with the water of Húchéng Reservoir,
which receives water from Huángbēi,
and flows southeast into Huángshuǐ,
called the Hézuò Mouth,
then flows east past the north of Qūqiáng City,
and east into Yìshuǐ.
People of the time called it Chìshuǐ,
but this is incorrect,
as Chì and Yì sound similar,
hence the character changed according to sound.
Yìshuǐ then flows between the Eastern and Western Wǔ Pavilions,
two cities facing each other,
likely the ancient Ànmén,
as Sīmǎ Qiān mentioned: "Xīshǒu fled to Ànmén."
Xú Guǎng said:
Yǐngyīn has an Àn Pavilion, but it is uncertain if this is it.
Yìshuǐ then flows south past the east of Shèquǎn City,
which is the city of Gōngsūn Shèquǎn of Zhèng.
This is likely a common error.
Yìshuǐ then flows south past the west of the old city of Yǐngyīn County,
where Emperor Míng of Wèi enfeoffed Minister of Works Chén Qún as a marquis.
The water then flows southeast past the south of Xǔchāng City,
then southeast joins with Xuānliángbēi Water,
which receives water from Lángbēi southwest of Yǐngyīn City,
the reservoir is twenty lǐ north-south,
ten lǐ east-west,
as recorded in the "Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuo Commentary":
the Chǔ army attacked the Zhèng army at Lángyuān.
This water flows southeast into Xǔchāng County,
passes north of Jùlíng City,
which is Zhèng territory.
As recorded in the "Zuo Commentary" to the "Spring and Autumn Annals," in the fourteenth year of Duke Zhuāng,
Duke Lì of Zhèng captured Fù Xiá at Dàlíng.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
twenty-five lǐ northeast of Línyǐng County in Yǐngchuān is the old Jùlíng Pavilion,
the ancient Dàlíng.
This water then gathers east to form a reservoir,
called Xuānliángbēi.
The reservoir water then flows southeast into Yìshuǐ.
Yìshuǐ then flows southwest past the west of Táo City,
then southeast past the east of Táobēi.
It flows southeast into Yǐngshuǐ.
22．4 Zhēnshuǐ
22．4 Zhēnshuǐ
Zhēnshuǐ emerges from level ground northwest of Zhèng County,
Zhēnshuǐ emerges from below Jīluò Wù northwest of Kuài City,
flows southeast past the west of Jiǎ Fù City,
flows southeast,
joins left with Fànshuǐ,
which emerges from Jiǎ Fù City,
flows southeast into Zhēnshuǐ.
Zhēnshuǐ then flows south,
joins left with Chéngyúnshān Water,
which emerges from Chéngyún Mountain in the northwest,
flows southeast past the east of Húnzǐ Ridge,
the ridge gorge is called Wǔmíngkǒu,
flows southeast into Zhēnshuǐ.
Zhēnshuǐ then flows southeast,
passes through Xiàtián Plain,
flows west of Kuài City,
called Liǔquánshuǐ.
Thus, Shǐ Bó replied to Duke Huán:
with the people of Chéngzhōu,
you uphold justice to punish the guilty,
if you conquer Guó and Kuài, their lands are yours,
with Huà Mountain in front and the Yellow River behind,
the Luò River on the right and the Jǐ River on the left,
rely on Fúguī and live by Zhēn and Wěi,
uphold laws and guard them,
and you can achieve some stability.
This refers to here.
Zhēnshuǐ then flows south,
cascading down into a ravine,
plunging over ten zhàng,
forming a deep pool below,
about forty paces wide,
deep and unfathomable.
It then flows south into Wěishuǐ.
This is what the "Book of Songs" calls Zhēn and Wěi.
It is also commonly called Kuàishuǐ.
It passes east north of the county,
then southeast east of the county,
then south into Wěishuǐ.
From Kuài and Zhēn eastward,
there are no other waterways,
so it cannot pass Xīnzhèng and join Wěishuǐ.
What enters Wěishuǐ east of Zhèng City,
is Huángyáshuǐ,
likely an error in the "Classic."
Qú emerges from the northern river of Xíngyáng,
flows southeast past the north of Zhōngmóu County.
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
A canal is
where water resides.
The Qú River water flows in a mixed course from the Huáng Hé and Jì River,
passes east by the north of Xíngzé,
splits southeast from the Jì,
passes through the Pǔtiánzé in Zhōngmóu County,
and divides the waters north with Yángwǔ.
The marsh has much ephedra grass,
thus the *Shùzhēngjì* says:
Step into the county's borders and you will see this plant;
when it ends you know you have crossed the boundary.
Although this is not the case now,
it is likely not mistaken.
This is what the *Shī* refers to as "east there is the marsh grass."
Huáng Wǔzǐ said:
Zhèng having Yuánpǔ
is like Qín having Jùyòu.
The marsh lies west of Zhōngmóu County,
bounded west by the Great Wall,
reaching east to Guāndù,
girded north by the Qú River,
about forty *lǐ* east-west,
about twenty *lǐ* north-south.
Within are sand ridges,
with twenty-four ponds above and below,
their waters connecting directly,
deep pools linking one to another,
each having its name:

Dàjiàn, Xiǎojiàn, Dàhuī, Xiǎohuī, Yìlǔ, Liànqiū, Dàbáiyáng, Xiǎobáiyáng, Sànhè, Yúzhōng, Yángjuàn, Dàgǔ, Xiǎogǔ, Lóngzé, Mìluó, Dà'āi, Xiǎo'āi, Dàcháng, Xiǎocháng, Dàsuō, Xiǎosuō, Bóqiū, Dàgài, Niúyǎn, etc.
When the pond waters are full, they flow north;
when the canal overflows, it spreads south.
Thus the *Zhúshū Jìnián* records:
In the tenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
he channeled the river water into Fǔtián,
and also dug a large ditch to draw the Fǔ water.
There is also another channel,
which receives the river at Suānzǎo, guided from the Pú Channel, passes through Suānzǎo, goes by south of Yángwǔ County and exits;
the world calls it Shízìgōu and it connects to the canal.
Some say this channel was dug in the year of Liáng Huì,
but it cannot be verified in detail.
These ponds are where waters gather,
forming the deep marshes of Zhèng's lowlands.
The Qú River water then joins the Wǔchí Ditch on the right,
the ditch receives water from the marsh above,
flows down and empties into the canal,
called Wǔchí Kǒu.
In the third year of Jiāpíng of Wèi,
Sīmǎ Yì led the central army to suppress Grand Commandant Wáng Líng at Shòuchūn,
and returning from there,
the Emperor sent Palace Attendant Wéi Dàn to reward the army at Wǔchí.
Now that place is Wǔchí Township.
The Qú River water flows east again,
and the Bùjiā Ditch water flows into it,
the water originates from the north stream of Méi Shān southeast of Jīng County.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng of *Chūnqiū*,
Chǔ's Wěi Zǐ and Féng Gōngzǐ Gé led a crack force to invade Fèi,
turning right around Méi Shān.
Dù Yù said:
It is northeast of Mì,
and this is that mountain.
Its water flows northeast from the stream past west of Guǎnchéng,
which is the ancient state of Guǎn,
where King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Guǎn Shū.
King Chéng being young and weak,
the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
Guǎn Shū spread rumors saying:
The Duke will do harm to the child,
the Duke recited "*Chīxiāo*" to attack him,
which refers to the army of Dōngshān.
In the twelfth year of Duke Xuān of *Zuǒzhuàn*,
the Jìn army came to rescue Zhèng,
Chǔ encamped at Guǎn to await them.
Dù Yù said:
Northeast of Jīng County there is Guǎnchéng, and this is it.
Commonly called Guǎn Shuǐ,
it flows northeast further,
divides into two streams,
one flows northeast into Huángquè Ditch,
called Huángyuān,
the pool's circumference is a hundred paces.
The other stream crosses the Great Wall eastward,
flows northeast,
the water accumulates into a pool,
two *lǐ* north-south,
a hundred paces east-west,
called Bǎichǐ Shuǐ,
enters Pǔtiánzé northward,
splits into two streams,
one flows northeast past north of Dōngwǔqiángchéng.
The *Hànshū Cáo Cān Zhuàn* records:
He attacked Yǔ Yīng at Kūnyáng,
pursued to Yè,
returned to attack Wǔqiáng,
and thus reached Xíngyáng.
Xuē Zàn said:
According to this, Wǔqiángchéng is in Yángwǔ County,
which is this city.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed Cavalry General Zhuāng Bùshí as a marquisate here.
It flows northeast further,
joins the canal on the left,
which is the Bùjiā Shuǐkǒu.
The other stream flows east,
then bends southward,
turns southeast and empties into Báigōu.
The Qú River water flows east again,
and Qīngchí Shuǐ flows into it,
the water originates from level ground southwest of Qīngyángtíng,
flows northeast past south of Qīngyángtíng,
flows east,
which is the old Qīngrénchéng.
This is what the *Shī* refers to as "the Qīng people are at Péng."
Péng was Gāo Kè's city.
Thus Dù Yù's *Chūnqiū Shìdì* states:
West of Zhōngmóu County there is Qīngyángtíng, and this is it.
Qīng Shuǐ bends and flows north to Qīngkǒuzé,
where Qīhǔjiàn Shuǐ flows into it,
the water originates from the southern ridge of Huáchéng,
one source with two branches,
the streams diverge in course,
the west enters Huángquè Ditch,
the east becomes Qīhǔ Xī,
also called Huá Shuǐ.
It flows northeast further,
and Zǐguānggōu Shuǐ flows into it,
the water originates northeast of Huáyángchéng and flows east,
commonly called Zǐguāngjiàn,
then flows northeast and empties into Huá Shuǐ.
Huá Shuǐ flows east further past north of Fěichéng,
which is Běilíntíng.
In the *Chūnqiū*,
Duke Wén feasted with the Earl of Zhèng at Fěilín,
where Zǐjiā recited "*Hóngyàn*."
In the first year of Duke Xuān of *Chūnqiū*,
the feudal lords met at Fěilín to attack Zhèng,
Chǔ came to aid Zhèng,
and they met at Běilín.
Fú Qián said:
Běilín
is southern territory of Zhèng.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Now in Yuànlíng County of Xíngyáng there is the old Línxiāng,
north of Xīnzhèng,
thus called Běilín.
I note that the old Línxiāng city is east of Xīnzhèng,
about seventy *lǐ* as the crow flies,
the old Yuànlíng city is about fifty *lǐ* southeast,
it cannot be north of Xīnzhèng.
Examining the statements of Jīng and Fú,
both are inaccurate.
Dù Yù said:
Southwest of Zhōngmóu County in Xíngyáng there is Líntíng,
north of Zhèng,
now this pavilion is about forty *lǐ* south of the old city of Xīnzhèng County,
probably because there is Línxiāngtíng to the south,
thus Dù Yù based on this considered it Běilín,
which is most accurate.
Also considering Línxiāng as Fěi,
there may be doubts.
The feudal lords met at Fěi,
Chǔ encountered them here,
how could one know it was not here but point elsewhere?
Ancient traditions passed down,
the matter may not be mistaken.
It flows northeast further past north of Lùtái Nángāng,
emerges as Qīhǔjiàn,
flows east,
Qī Shuǐ flows into it,
the water originates from level ground northwest of Qīchéng,
commonly called Lóngyuān Shuǐ.
It flows northeast,
then north past west of Qīchéng,
then north to join Qīhǔjiàn,
called Hǔxī Shuǐ,
flows east in a mixed course past north of Qīchéng,
and meets Qīngkǒu Shuǐ eastward.
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Jùnguózhì* states:
Zhōngmóu has Qīngkǒu Shuǐ,
and this is that water.
Qīng Shuǐ flows northeast further,
and Báigōu Shuǐ flows into it,
the water has two sources,
the northern water originates from Méi Shān in Mì,
flows southeast then east,
passes Jìngchéng south and joins the southern water,
the southern water originates from Tài Shān, flows northwest to south of Jìngchéng,
joins the northern water on the left,
which is Chéng Shuǐ.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
Chéng Shuǐ originates from the north of Tài Shān,
flows northeast and empties into Yì Shuǐ,
commonly also called Jìngjiàn Shuǐ.
It flows northeast further,
and Tài Shuǐ flows into it,
the water originates from level ground east of Tài Shān,
the *Shānhǎijīng* states:
Tài Shuǐ originates from the south of Tài Shān,
and flows southeast to empty into Yì Shuǐ,
commonly called Lǐ Shuǐ.
It flows northeast past the west of Wǔlíng City,
and northeastward pours into Chéng Shuǐ.
Chéng Shuǐ again flows northeast into Huángwèng Jiàn,
northward passing west of Zhōngyáng City.
Within the city there is an old terrace, very elegant;
beside the terrace is a pond,
its waters clear and deep.
The stream water then bends east, passing north of the city.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the seventeenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Marquis Lí of Zhèng came to court at Zhōngyáng.
The water flows northeast, becoming Bái Gōu,
then flows northeast past the north of Bóqín City.
It is likely that when Bóqín went to Lǔ,
this was the route he took.
It bends and flows southward,
then eastward pours into Qīng Shuǐ,
which is what Pān Yuè in his "Dūxiāng Stele" referred to as from the old county of Zhōngmóu westward,
west to Qīng Gōu.
He was pointing to this water.
The waters flow disorderly east past the south of the temple of Magistrate Lǔ Gōng of Zhōngmóu.
During the Hàn Emperor Hé's time,
Lǔ Gōng of Yòufúfēng,
styled Zhòngkāng,
was promoted from a Tàiwèi clerk to magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
His governance focused on moral transformation,
not relying on punishments,
officials and people respected and trusted him,
and locusts did not enter the territory.
Yǐn Yuán'ān of Hénán doubted this was untrue,
and sent his subordinate clerk Féi Qīn to inspect.
Gōng accompanied Qīn through the fields,
sat under a mulberry tree,
a pheasant stopped beside him.
There was a small child.
Qīn said:
"Child, why don't you strike the pheasant?"
He replied:
"It is with its chicks."
Qīn rose and said:
"Locusts not entering the territory—first marvel;
transformation extending to birds and beasts—second marvel;
a young child cherishing benevolence—third marvel."
"To stay long is not to honor the worthy,
I request to return."
That year, auspicious grain grew in the county courtyard,
Ān praised his governance,
and reported the circumstances upward.
He was summoned to serve as Erudite and Palace Attendant.
Whenever the imperial carriage went out,
Gōng often accompanied riding alongside,
the emperor consulted him on civil affairs,
he concealed nothing,
thus he could leave behind affection,
from ancient times his temple has been offered sacrifices to this day.
Qīng Gōu Shuǐ again flows northeast past Shěnqīng Tíng,
suspected to be Bólàng Tíng.
Fú Qián said:
"Bólàng is a place name south of Yángwǔ,
now there is a pavilion,
the details are unclear."
It passes through Bólàng Zé,
where formerly Zhāng Liáng, avenging Hán against Qín,
struck Qín Shǐhuáng with a metal hammer but missed,
hitting his secondary carriage here.
Further north it divides into two waterways,
a branch flows east into Qīng Shuǐ.
Qīng Shuǐ from the branch flows north into the canal,
called Qīng Gōu Kǒu.
The canal water then passes left of the old city of Yángwǔ County,
east becoming Guāndù Shuǐ,
then passes north of Cáo Tàizǔ's fortifications.
There is a high terrace,
called Guāndù Tái.
The crossing is at Zhōngmóu,
so later generations also call it Zhōngmóu Tái.
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ camped at Guāndù,
Yuán Shào held Yángwǔ,
Shào connected camps gradually advancing,
basing encampments on sand mounds,
stretching several tens of lǐ east-west.
The Duke also divided camps to defend,
engaging in battle unfavorably.
Shào advanced to Guāndù,
erecting earth mounds and tunnels to press the fortifications.
The Duke also raised a high terrace to resist,
which is Zhōngmóu Tái.
Now north of the terrace the earth mound still exists,
east of the mound all are Shào's old camps,
remnants of foundations remain together.
The canal water again flows east past the north of Tián Fēng's temple.
Yuán Běnchū, ashamed not to accept his advice,
harmed him.
People of the time admired his sincere counsel,
innocently slain,
thus erected a temple here,
to show the appropriateness of the Yuán clan's downfall.
Further east,
Yì Shuǐ flows into it.
The water emerges east of Xìhóu Tíng west of Yuànlíng County,
people call this pavilion Quèchéng,
which is incorrect,
likely because "xì" and "què" sound similar.
Zhōngpíng Bēi,
commonly called Níquán,
is the ancient Yì Shuǐ.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"From Yì Mountain,
Yì Shuǐ emerges,
flowing north into the river."
Suspected to be this water.
It flows northeast past the old city of Yuànlíng County,
northeast past east of Jiāochéng and west of Yángqiū Tíng,
commonly called Jiāo Gōu Shuǐ.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the sixteenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qín's Gōngsūn Zhuàng led troops to attack Zhèng,
besieging Jiāochéng but not capturing it.
This is that city.
Commonly called Yìchéng,
which is incorrect.
Yì Shuǐ from Yángqiū Tíng flows east,
passing north of Shānmín City,
becoming Gāoyú Yuān.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
In the sixteenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qín's Gōngsūn Zhuàng led troops to fortify Shàngzhǐ and Ānlíng,
and Shānmín.
Further northeast it becomes Cù Gōu,
then further northeast,
Lǔ Gōu Shuǐ emerges from it.
Yì Shuǐ again flows northeast,
Ní Gōu Shuǐ emerges from it,
then further northeast becomes Bāzhàng Gōu.
Further east,
a branch of Qīng Shuǐ flows into it,
the water branching east from Shěnchéng,
pouring into Yì Shuǐ.
Yì Shuǐ again flows east past south of Cáo Gōng's fortifications,
east merging with Mò Shuǐ.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"From Mò Mountain,
Mò Shuǐ emerges,
flowing north into Yì."
Now this water emerges southwest of Zhōngmóu City,
suspected to be Mò Shuǐ.
It flows northeast past west of the old city of Zhōngmóu County.
Formerly, Xiàn Hóu of Zhào moved his capital here from Gěng.
Bān Gù says:
"Zhào moved here from Hándān."
During the time of Xiāngzǐ of Zhào,
Fóxī rebelled with Zhōngmóu,
placed a cauldron in the courtyard,
boiling those not with him,
where Tián Yīng lifted his robe to go to the cauldron.
Xuē Zàn annotates the "Book of Hàn":
"Zhōngmóu in the Spring and Autumn period was a borderland of Zhèng,
and when the three ministers divided Jìn,
it was within Wèi's territory,
Zhào from north of Zhāng did not reach here."
The "Spring and Autumn Commentary" says:
"The Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn passing Zhōngmóu,"
not the route from Wèi to Jìn.
The "Ancient Texts of Jí Commandery" says:
"The Qí army attacked Zhào's eastern border,
besieging Zhōngmóu."
This Zhōngmóu is not east of Zhào.
According to this, Zhōngmóu should be above Tà Shuǐ.
According to the "Spring and Autumn Annals":
"Qí attacked Jìn's Yíyí,
Jìn had a thousand chariots at Zhōngmóu."
"The Marquis of Wèi passed Zhōngmóu,
the people of Zhōngmóu wanted to attack him.
Wèi's Chǔshī Gù was in exile at Zhōngmóu,
said:
'Wèi though small,
its ruler is present,
cannot be defeated.
The Qí army, having taken the city, is arrogant;
encountering them would surely defeat them.'
Then they defeated the Qí army."
Fú Qián did not specify where Zhōngmóu was.
Dù Yù said:
"Now Xíngyáng has a Zhōngmóu,
but it is far,
suspected to be incorrect."
However, geography is irregular,
land has no constant domain,
following strength and weakness,
they swallow each other,
boundaries shift,
how can it be uniform?
Where war chariots point,
routes wind and are hard to know.
Since Wèi moved to Dàliáng,
Zhào exchanged Zhōngmóu with Wèi,
thus the southern boundary of Zhào
extended as far as the Fú Shuǐ,
not exclusively along the Zhāng.
After Zhào took Zhōngmóu from the west,
the Qí army attacked its eastern border,
which should have been of no concern.
Yet Zǎn directly pointed to the Luò Shuǐ,
merely stating the location of Zhōngmóu,
without providing evidence.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Shànfǔ Shèng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Mò Shuǐ then flows northeast and joins the Yì Shuǐ.
In the past, when Tàizǔ of Wèi turned against Dǒng Zhuō,
he traveled discreetly and passed through Zhōngmóu,
where he was detained by a local constable.
Guō Chánggōng’s *Shìyǔ* states:
he was held by the county authorities,
but a merit official requested his release.
The Yì Shuǐ continues northeast past the Zhōngmóu Marsh,
where Zhèng Tàishū attacked the bandits of Huánpú in this marsh.
The water flows east, then turns north and joins the Qú.
This is what the *Xù Shùzhēng Jì* refers to as the ten lǐ from Jiàngkuí Chéng to Cùgōu.
The Qú Shuǐ then flows east and joins the Yuān Shuǐ on the left,
which originates from the Shèngnǚ Bēi,
a pond with a circumference of over two hundred paces.
The water never diminishes,
remaining clear and full,
and flows south into the Qú.
The Qú Shuǐ then flows southeast and enters Dàliáng.
Further east, it reaches Jùnyí County.
The canal water flows southeast past the north of Chìchéng,
which Dài Yánzhī referred to as the northwest having a Dàliáng Pavilion,
but this is incorrect.
The Bamboo Annals
record that in the twenty-eighth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Ráng Cī led troops and engaged Zhèng Kǒng
in a night battle at Liánghè,
where the Zhèng army was defeated and fled.
This refers to this city.
To the left, an old channel emerges here.
In the twentieth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Wáng Bēn cut off the old canal,
diverting the water to flow southeast to flood Dàliáng,
which was called the Liáng Ditch.
It then flows east past the south of Dàliáng City,
originally the Yángwǔ Gāoyáng Township of the Spring and Autumn period,
and during the Warring States period, it was Dàliáng.
This was the former residence of Liáng Bó of the Zhōu dynasty.
Liáng Bó was fond of construction projects,
expanding his city,
and named it Xīnlǐ.
The people grew weary and rebelled,
and Qín subsequently seized it.
Later, King Huì of Wèi moved his capital here from Ānyì,
hence it was called Liáng.
The Bamboo Annals
record that in the sixth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng, on the jiǎyín day of the fourth month,
he moved the capital to Dàliáng, which is this.
After Qín destroyed Wèi, it was made a county.
Emperor Wén of Hàn enfeoffed King Xiào in Liáng.
King Xiào, finding the land low and damp,
moved east to Suīyáng,
and it was again renamed Liáng.
From then on, it was established as a county.
Because Dàliáng City was vast,
he resided east of the Yímén Gate in its eastern city.
Yímén
was where Hóu Yíng guarded the gate.
The Continued Account of Military Expeditions identifies this city as Shī Kuàng City,
stating that Guō Yuánshēng once visited this town,
stepped upon Yímén,
ascended the Chuītái,
and that ancient traces
were all vaguely present there.
I say this was actually the terrace gate of the Liáng family,
the capital residence of King Huì of Wèi,
not the Chuītái.
This must be an erroneous identification.
The Record of a Western Journey claims that the border official of Yí was from this county,
which is also incorrect.
The Bamboo Annals
record that in the thirty-first year of King Huìchéng of Liáng, in the third month,
a large ditch was dug north of the outer wall,
to channel the water of the Pǔtián marshes.
The Traditions of Chénliú states:
North of the county is the Jùnshuǐ River,
which was modeled and imitated,
hence it was called Jùnyí.
I say the old Biànshā became the Yīngōu.
It was dredged,
so it was called Jùn.
Is this not like the dredging of the Zhū River in the Spring and Autumn period?
The Jùnyí River of the Hàn dynasty
was nothing else;
it was all a change of name.
The region had many ponds and marshes.
At times, a divine sword emerged from a pond,
and to this day, the people imitate it and make it,
calling it the sword of the Dàliáng clan.
The canal water then bends north,
dividing into two streams.
The Continued Account of Military Expeditions says:
Biànshā reaches Jùnyí and divides.
Biàn flows east, while Shā flows south.
This water flows further south,
passing east of King Liáng’s Chuītái.
The Traditions of Chénliú states:
The county has the city of Cāngjié and Shī Kuàng,
above which is the Chuītái of the assembled immortals.
To the north is the Mùzé Marsh,
from which orchids and cattails emerge.
Above, there are many outstanding talents,
girdling the Mùzé Marsh,
which is fifteen lǐ square.
Commonly called the Púguānzé Marsh,
this is what is referred to.
King Liáng expanded and built it up,
making it the Chuītái.
The city walls have been destroyed,
leaving only traces of the old site.
Now, the layered terrace stands alone to the right of the Mùzé Marsh.
This terrace is about one hundred paces square.
It is the one mentioned in Ruǎn Sìzōng’s “Poems from the Heart”: “Setting forth from the Wèi capital by carriage,
I gaze south toward the Chuītái.
The sound of flute and pipe still lingers,
but where is King Liáng now?”
During the turmoil of the Jìn dynasty,
refugees took up residence here,
cutting and leveling the old foundation,
so it became two layers.
The upper foundation is still about forty or fifty paces square,
over one zhàng high.
It is commonly called the Qǐhuótái,
also known as Fántái City.
Here, the canal water
is also called Yīngōu or Hónggōu.
When Xiàng Yǔ and Liú Bāng divided the realm as kings,
they pointed to this water as the boundary between east and west.
Sū Qín, persuading King Xiāng of Wèi, said:
“Your Majesty’s territory
has the Hónggōu to the south,” referring to this.
Thus, Wèishì County has Bō Township, Bō Pavilion, Hónggōu Township, and Hónggōu Pavilion,
all named after this water.
Now, west of Xiāo County there is also a Hónggōu Pavilion,
and east of Suīyáng County in the state of Liáng there is a Hóngkǒu Pavilion.
Later discussants
also point to this as the boundary between Chǔ and Hàn when they divided the realm,
but this is incorrect.
It is likely what the Spring and Autumn period called the Hóngzé Marsh.
The canal water then joins with the Fànshuǐ River on the right.
This water receives the Yìshuǐ River upstream at Yuànlíng County.
The county was the old capital of Zhèng.
It was the Zuǒtíng County of Wáng Mǎng.
A branch of the Yìshuǐ River flows east, forming the Fànshuǐ River,
but common people call it Nígōushuǐ.
The Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals, year thirty of Duke Xí,
records that the Marquis of Jìn and the Earl of Qín besieged Zhèng,
with the Jìn army at Hánlíng
and the Qín army south of Fàn,
referring to the eastern Fàn.
This water then flows northeast past the south of Zhōngmóu County,
and further northeast past Zhōngmóu Marsh, where it joins the Yuānshuǐ River.
The Yuānshuǐ emerges north of the old city of Zhōngmóu County.
The city has a layered terrace.
According to Guō Chánggōng’s Shìyǔ and Gān Bǎo’s Jìn Jì,
both state that in the lower pond of the Yùtái of the former Wèi Rènchéng in Zhōngmóu County,
there was an iron awl from the Hàn dynasty,
six chǐ long,
buried three chǐ in the ground,
its head pointing southwest, immovable,
but aligning itself correctly on the first day of the first month.
This was considered an auspicious sign for the revival of the Jìn dynasty.
But now, its whereabouts are unknown.
Some say it is at the Chítái in Zhōngyáng City,
but it is unclear which is correct.
The Yuānshuǐ flows out from the west of the pond,
bends past the west of the city,
and flows southeast into the Fànshuǐ.
The Fànshuǐ then flows east past the south of Dàliáng Pavilion,
and further east past the south of Liáng Terrace, then east into the canal.
The canal water flows southeast past Kāifēng County,
where the Suī and Huàn rivers emerge.
To the right, the Xīngōu flows into it.
This water originates from Féngchí Pond.
The pond receives the Yìshuǐ River upstream at Yuànlíng County,
branching off as the Lǔgōushuǐ River.
It flows southeast past the north of the old city of Kāifēng County.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Táo Shě was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Records of Chénliú mentions Ruǎn Jiǎn,
courtesy name Màohóng,
who served as magistrate of Kāifēng.
When bandits were near the county,
and reports outside came urgently and repeatedly,
Ruǎn Jiǎn was in the middle of a wéiqí game, whistling leisurely.
The clerk said:
“The bandits are urgent.”
Ruǎn Jiǎn replied:
“On the board, there is also a ‘capture’ that is very urgent.”
Such was his indulgence in pleasure.
Thus, the Forest of Sayings states:
“Wáng Zhōngláng considered wéiqí as ‘sitting in seclusion,’”
or it was also called “hand conversation,”
and also “the sage of chess.”
The Lǔgōushuǐ reaches Fùchéng to the south,
flows southeast into the Bǎichǐbēi,
which is the ancient Féngzé Marsh.
Xú Guǎng’s Shǐjì Yīnyì says:
“Qín sent the young official Gōngzǐ to lead troops to meet the feudal lords at Féngzé.”
The Bamboo Annals from the tombs of Jíjùn record that Duke Xiào of Qín met the feudal lords at Féngzé.
This is the place.
Thus, Yìng Déliǎn’s “Rhapsody on a Western Journey” says:
“The carriage turns eastward,
halting at Féngzé.”
This water flows northeast as the Xīngōu.
The Xīngōu flows further northeast past the north of Niúshǒu Township,
called Niújiànchéng.
It then flows northeast into the canal,
which is the Shāshuǐ River.
Pronounced cài,
Xǔ Shèn correctly gives it as shā,
meaning water disperses over stones.
The character is composed of water (shuǐ) and few (shǎo),
where little water reveals the sand.
East of Chǔ, there is the Shāshuǐ River,
referring to this water.
It then bends south, reaching the north of Fúgōu County.
The Shā River flows southeast past the east of Niúshǒu Township,
where the Lǔgōu River originates,
also known as the Sònggōu.
It then passes by the old city of Chénliú County to the south,
Mèng Kāng said:
"Liú,
was a town of Zhèng,
later annexed by Chén,
hence called Chénliú."
The Lǔgōu River flows southeast past the old city of Yǔ County to the north,
the county suffered from the troubles of Chǔ,
they repaired their weapons to defend against the calamity,
hence called Yǔ,
or said to be a name for the borderlands.
It passes through Wànrén Sàn.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the Grand Administrator of Dōng Commandery, Zhái Yì, raised troops to attack Mǎng,
Mǎng sent General Fènwēi Sūn Jiàn to strike him north of Yǔ,
Yì's army was greatly defeated,
corpses piled up in the tens of thousands,
blood flowed and overflowed the road,
the place was named Wànrén Sàn,
the common people mourned and made sacrifices there.
It also passes through Lǔgōu Pavilion,
then southeast to the west of the old city of Yángxià County,
in the sixth year of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he enfeoffed Chén Xī as a marquisate.
The Lǔgōu River flows south into the Guō River,
now it is without water.
The Shā River flows southeast past the west of Dǒuchéng.
In the Zuǒzhuàn, the thirtieth year of Duke Xiāng,
Zǐchǎn buried Bó Yǒu's corpse,
his ministers interred him here.
The Shā River flows southeast past the east of Niúshǒu Pavilion,
in the Zuǒzhuàn, the fourteenth year of Duke Huán,
the people of Sòng with the feudal lords attacked the eastern suburbs of Zhèng,
and took Niúshǒu,
commonly called Chēniúchéng.
The Shā River flows southeast,
where the Bālǐgōu River originates.
It then flows southeast past the west of Qiúshì Pavilion in Qiúshì Township of Chénliú County,
and past the east of Dàntái Zǐyǔ's tomb,
joining with the Bālǐgōu River.
According to the Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn:
In Qiúshì Township of Chénliú County is the tomb of Dàntái Zǐyǔ,
and also a shrine to Zǐyǔ,
where the people pray.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Now in Wǔchéng County south of Tàishān is the tomb of Dàntái Zǐyǔ,
he was a man of that county.
It is unknown which is correct,
based on the local records' account,
it is recorded here accordingly.
The Bālǐgōu River receives water from the Shā River and flows southwest,
passing south of Niúshǒu Pavilion,
joining with the Bǎichǐ Bēi water,
which flows from the south of the bēi past Sānlǐ Gǎng east of Kāifēng City,
turning left to flow west then south,
entering the Bālǐgōu River.
Further south it reaches the mouth of the Yětù River,
which originates from the Yětù Bēi north of Tùshì Pavilion in the southwest,
land of Zhèng.
The Chūnqiūzhuàn says:
The Earl of Zhèng entertained Qūshēng at Tùshì.
The bēi water flows northeast into the Bālǐgōu River.
The Bālǐgōu River flows south past the west of Shícāng City,
then south past the east of Tùshì Pavilion,
then south past the west of Zhàolíng Pavilion,
and east into the Shā River.
The Shā River flows south past the east of the old city of Fúgōu County,
the county was originally Gǔpíng Township of Yǐngchuān,
there was a Fú Pavilion,
and also a Wěishuǐ ditch,
hence the county has the name Fúgōu.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Hàn Guāngwǔ enfeoffed General Píngdí Zhū Wěi as a marquisate.
The Shā River flows east and joins with the Kānggōu River,
which receives water from the Wěi River east of Chángshè County,
flowing northeast past the west of Xiàng Gǎng,
which was Xiàng Township of Zhèng.
Later people blocked its upper mouth,
now when water is abundant it flows north,
when water is low it ceases to flow.
Also, the Chángmínggōu River flows into it,
originating northwest of the old city of Yuànlíng County,
the county has two cities,
this is the western city,
east of the two cities,
there are many marshes and lakes,
which are the ancient Zhì Marsh.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Land of Zhèng.
Dù Yù said:
The marsh is east of Yuànlíng County in Xíngyáng,
which is the Zhì Field of the Chūnqiū.
Northwest of the old city, flat ground produces a spring,

the spring water flows past the west of Língqiū Pavilion,
further west,
the Chóngquán water flows into it,
originating from flat ground northwest of the city,
the spring surges and flows south,
passing west of Língqiū Pavilion,
flowing southwest into Lóngyuān water.
Lóngyuān water flows southeast past the west of Fányáng Pavilion,
then south into Báiyàn Bēi,
the bēi is northeast of Chángshè County,
seven lǐ east-west,
ten lǐ north-south,
southwest of Lín Township,
Sīmǎ Biāo's Jùnguózhì says:
Yuànlíng has Lín Township Pavilion.
Báiyàn Bēi also channels a stream flowing south,
called Chángmínggōu,
turning east then bending north,
then east past the north of Xiàng City,
the city is beside Xiàng Gǎng,
in the Zuǒzhuàn, the eleventh year of Duke Xiāng,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng,
their army was at Xiàng.
Further east,
it branches right to become Rǎnzé Bēi,
and flows east into Càizé Bēi.
The Chángmínggōu River flows east past the south of the old city of Wèishì County,
Juàn Chēng said:
"Wèishì,

From here the stream divides into three,
the northern branch becomes the Kānggōu,

in the first year of Empress Gāo,
she enfeoffed Lǐ, son of King Yuán of Chǔ, as a marquisate,
in the first year of Jiànwǔ, because the households were fewer than three thousand,
it was abolished and became Língshù Township of Wèishì County.
There is also a Língshù Pavilion,
in the Jiàn'ān period of Hàn,
Shàngshū Xún Yōu was enfeoffed as Marquis of Língshù Township.
Hence the Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn says:
"Língshù Township,
was formerly Pínglù County."
North is a large marsh,
named Chánglè Jiù.
The Kānggōu flows east past the north of Bái Pavilion in Fúgōu County,
the Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn says:
Fúgōu County has Bó Township and Bó Pavilion,
named among the seven townships and twelve pavilions.
The Kānggōu flows east past Shǎoqū Pavilion,
the Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn says:
Wèishì County has Shǎoqū Pavilion,
commonly called Xiǎochéng.
It then flows southeast past the east of the old city of Fúgōu County,
and southeast into the Shā River.
The Shā River flows south and meets the Nánshuǐ,
which flows south,
then divides into two streams,
one flows south past the east of Guān Pavilion,
then southeast,
joining with the left stream,
which flows south from a branch stream past the west of Zhàolíng Pavilion,
suspected to be the pavilion of Fúgōu,
and southeast joins the right stream.
People consider this water and the Yānlíng Bēi water as twin channels,
also called Shuānggōu.
It then flows southeast into the Shā River.
The Shā River flows south and joins with the Càizé Bēi water,
which originates northwest of Yānlíng City,
in the Chūnqiū, the sixteenth year of Duke Chéng,
Jìn and Chǔ met at Yānlíng,
Lǚ Qí shot and hit the king's eye,
the king summoned Yǎng Yóujī to shoot and kill him,
also where Zǐfǎn got drunk and brought about his own death.
The bēi is five lǐ east-west,
ten lǐ north-south,
the bēi water flows east past the north of Kuāng City,
the city is east of Xīnjí County,
north is Kuāng Pavilion of Fúgōu.
The pavilion is in Kuāngchéng Township,
in the Chūnqiū, the first year of Duke Wén,
the feudal lords paid court to Jìn,
Duke Chéng of Wèi did not attend court,
he sent Kǒng Dá to invade Zhèng,
attacking Miánzī and Kuāng,
which is this town.
Now south of Chángyuán County in Chénliú is Kuāng City,
which is Kuāng Pavilion of Píngqiū.
Xiāngyì also has Chéngkuāng City,
but Kuāng lies between Chén and Wèi,
and there are often different towns.
The bēi water flows southeast to the north of Fúgōu City,
then southeast into the Shā River.
The Shā River flows south past the west of Xiǎofú City,
and flows southeast,
the city is Píngzhōu Pavilion of Fúgōu County,
in the Yǒngyuán period of Emperor Hé of Eastern Hàn,
Cān, son of Prince Jìng of Chén, was enfeoffed as a marquisate.
The Shā River flows southeast past the west of Dàfú City,
the city is the old city of Fúlè.
Two li north of the city is the stele of Yuán Liáng,
which states that Liáng
was a native of Fúlè in the state of Chén.
In the seventeenth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ of the Later Hàn,
Liú Lóng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fúlè,
and this city was the location.
Here the Guō River divides,
so it cannot be that it splits into two streams north of Fúgōu.
One of these
flows southeast past the north of Chén County.
The Shā River further flows southeast past the west of Dōnghuá City,
then southeast,
where a branch of the Shā River flows southwest to reach the Wěi River,
called the Jiǎgēng Ditch,
which is now dry.
The Shā River then flows south and joins the Guǎngcáo Canal,
which receives water from the Pángguān Marsh,
said to have been excavated by Dèng Ài.
Although the water flow has ceased and revived,
the ditches and channels remain numerous.
In the past, Jiǎ Kuí, as the Inspector of Yùzhōu for the state of Wèi,
opened a transport canal over two hundred li long,
which is also called the Jiǎhóu Canal.
However, the rivers and channels meander and intertwine,
crisscrossing fields and paths,
making it impossible to distinguish them.
The Shā River further flows east past the old city of Chángpíng County to the north,
then southeast past the city of Chén to the north,
which was the old state of Chén.
Both Fúxī and Shénnóng made it their capital.
About thirty li northeast of the city,
there is still the solid-walled Xī City.
Guī Mǎn, a descendant of Shùn,
served as the Pottery Master for the Zhōu,
and King Wǔ, relying on his utensils,
married him to his eldest daughter, Tàijī, and enfeoffed him in Chén,
to complete the Three Honored Families.
Tàijī was fond of sacrifices,
hence the line in the *Shījīng*: "They beat their drums,"
"Below Wǎnqiū."
Wǎnqiū is east of the road south of Chén City.
Wáng Yǐn said it was gradually leveling out,
and now its location is unknown.
The state of Chǔ attacked Chén,
killing Xià Zhēngshū at the Lì Gate,
and made it the Xià Prefecture.
Later, inside the east gate of the city, there was a pond,
seventy paces from east to west,
about eighty paces from north to south,
with extremely clear and clean water,
which never diminished or dried up,
and where no fish or plants grew.
In the water was the site of an old terrace,
the "pond by the east gate" mentioned in the *Shījīng*.
Inside the city was a stele erected by the Hàn Chancellor Wáng Jūn for the official residences of four counties,
but the text is worn and damaged,
and cannot be fully read.
It roughly says:
"This state of Chén,
formerly called the Huáiyáng Commandery," and so on.
"His purity and benevolence were widely known,
and he was both feared and loved by the people.
He sought out worthy men and supported scholars,
over a thousand in number,
granting them fields, houses, and official residences,
reducing his own salary,
to help them complete the residences."
"The Assistant to the Five Officials, Xīhuá Chén Qí, and two hundred and five others,
in the second year of the Yánxī era," and so on.
Thus the eulogy says:
"Cultivating virtue and achieving merit,
the four counties returned to allegiance."
Now, to the left and right of the stele,
remnants of the walls still exist,
and the foundations remain.
People today no longer seek evidence from the stele,
saying it is a Confucian temple school,
which is incorrect.
Later, King Xiāng of Chǔ, when his state was destroyed by Qín,
moved his capital here.
Wén Yǐng said:
"This is Western Chǔ."
Of the Three Chǔ,
this is one.
Inside the southern outer city,
there is another city,
called Huáiyáng City,
established by Zǐchǎn.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn, it was made the state of Huáiyáng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it,
the commandery as Xīnpíng,
and the county as Chénlíng,
formerly the seat of Yùzhōu.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* states:
"North of the city is an old sandbar,
called Dead Sand,
but now the water flows freely,
and it is used for canal transport."
The Shā River flows east and then bends south,
passing east of Chén City,
where it is called the Bǎichǐ Ditch.
It then divides into two streams to the south,
from which the Xīn Ditch water emerges.
The ditch water flows southeast,
and the Gǔ River joins it,
its source receiving water from the Láo Marsh,
which lies northwest of Chén City,
extending south to Luò City,
all of which is marshland.
The marsh water flows east and is called the Gǔ River,
passing north of Láo City to the east.
Wáng Yǐn said:
"North of Luò is the Gǔ River, that is correct."
Luò is Chēng.
The *Chūnqiū* records the Duke meeting with Qí and Sòng at Chēng.
Dù Yù said:
"Chēng is Luò,
but it is incorrect to say it is northwest of Chén County.
Chēng
is a small city,
southwest of Chén Commandery."
The Gǔ River further flows east past the south of Chén City,
then east into the Xīn Ditch water,
then southeast into the Yǐng River,
at a place called Jiāokǒu,
where there is a large dam by the water,
the ancient Bǎichǐ Dam.
The *Wèishū Guózhì* says:
"Sīmǎ Xuānwáng attacked Grand Commandant Wáng Líng,
and his army suddenly arrived at the Bǎichǐ Dam,"
which is this dam.
Nowadays, it is commonly called the Shānyáng Dam,
which is incorrect.
Since the Xīn River first receives water from the Yǐng at the Bǎichǐ Ditch,
the dam also bears the name Xīnyáng.
From this, it can be inferred
that the common name is mistaken.
Further southeast to the north of Xīnyáng County in Rǔnán,
the Shā River flows east from the Bǎichǐ Ditch past the old city of Níngpíng County to the south.
The *Jìnyángqiū* records that when the Grand Tutor of Jìn, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Sīmǎ Yuè, fled east,
Shí Lè pursued him,
and burned the corpses here.
Hundreds of thousands of people
were slaughtered without resistance.
Lè had his cavalry surround and shoot them,
and the corpses piled up like a mountain.
Wáng Yífǔ died here.
I say that the wise use intelligence to surpass the masses,
and the eloquent use rhetoric to dispel confusion.
Although Yífǔ possessed outstanding talent,
and was skilled in persuasive speech,
he dishonored his sovereign and parents,
and incurred the wrath of Jié Lè.
Historians compare him to Huà and Wáng,
which is indeed praise.
The Shā River further flows east and accumulates into a marsh,
called the Yángdū Marsh.
The Míng River flows into it,
its source receiving a branch of the Shā River,
flowing east past the old city of Yílù County in Rǔnán Commandery to the north,
which was the Shǎngdū Post Station under Wáng Mǎng.
The Míng River further flows northeast into the marsh,
and the marsh water flows southeast, called the Xì River.
It further flows east past the north of Xīnyáng County,
then east,
where the Gāobēi water emerges to the east.
The Shā River further divides into two streams to the east,
which are the so-called Yí and Pú waters in the *Chūnqiū*.
A branch flows north past the old city of Qiáo County to the west,
and enters the Guō River along the city wall.
The Shā River flows southeast past the southwest of Chéngfù County,
where a branch emerges,
commonly called the Zhāng River.
One stream flows east,
which is the Pú River,
commonly called the Ài River.
It flows east past the old city of Chéngfù County to the south,
and then flows eastward.
Further southeast past the north of Shānsāng County,
the old city of Shānsāng is north of the Guō River,
so it is clear that the Shā River cannot pass north of it.
The *Classic* says it passes north,
which is an error.
Further southeast past the south of Lóngkàng County,
the Shā River passes north of the old city,
then southeast past the north of Báilù City and flows east.
Further southeast past the west of Yìchéng County,
and south into the Huái River.
Yìchéng County originally belonged to Pèi,
and later was attached to Jiǔjiāng.
The Shā River flows eastward and empties into the Huái,
which is called Shāruì.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
This is the eastern territory of Chǔ.
In the "Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuo Tradition," the twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhāo,
the Chǔ prime minister Zǐcháng led a naval force to Shāruì and then returned.
Dù Yù said:
Shā is the name of a river.
23 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll Twenty-Three
23.1 Yīngōu River
23.1 Yīngōu River
The Yīngōu River originates from the Làngdàng Canal in Yángwǔ County, Hénán.
The Yīngōu first receives the Great River at Juàn County.
Its old course flows southeast past the old city of Juàn County,
then east past the north of Méng City.
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states,
in the first year of King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín,
Méng Áo attacked and captured Chénggāo and Xíngyáng,
and initially established the Sānchuān Commandery.
It is suspected that this was built by Áo,
but the details are unclear.
The old course divides into two eastward,
and people call it the Yīngōu River.
Jīng Xiàngfán believed it originated from the Jì of the Yellow River,
but this is not thoroughly investigated.
Both flow east and cross the Jìsuì.
The right branch flows southeast past the north of Yángwǔ City,
crosses the Great Wall to the southeast,
passes north of Ān Pavilion,
and then northeast joins the left branch.
The left branch also flows east and crosses the Great Wall,
passing south of Yuányōng City.
In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn defeated Chǔ in battle,
and King Xiāng of Zhōu rewarded him here.
Therefore, the "Spring and Autumn Annals" records that on the jiǎwǔ day, he arrived at Héngyōng,
and built a royal palace at Jiàntǔ.
The "Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
This is where the Son of Heaven was honored at Héngyōng.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and States" says:
Juàn County has the Yuányōng City,
which is the Yuányōng that Hán presented to Qín as recorded in the "Records of the Grand Historian."
It then flows east past the south of Kāiguāng Pavilion,
then east past the south of Qīngyáng Pavilion,
and then east joins the right branch.
It then flows southeast past Fēngqiū County,
and crosses the Jì River.
Southeast, it reaches Dàliáng,
and joins the Làngdàng Canal.
After the Liáng Ditch was opened,
the old course of the Làngdàng Canal was also called Yīngōu and Jùnyí,
hence it is said to originate from Yángwǔ.
It flows southeast past the north of Dàliáng City,
and bends left to join the Liáng Ditch.
Both flow southeast together,
and are collectively called the Hónggōu and Shā River.
The branch that flows east from the left at the confluence of these rivers
is the Biàn River,
which is a variation in the name of the source.
Therefore, the "Classic" says the Yīngōu originates from the Làngdàng Canal.
Southeast, it reaches Pèi,
and becomes the Guō River.
The Yīngōu Canal initially flows turbulently through Làngdàng,
eventually diverging at Shā,
from which the Guō River emerges.
The Guō River receives the Shā River at Fúgōu County.
Xǔ Shèn also stated:
The Guō River originates from the Làngdàng Canal in Fúgōu County, Huáiyáng,
and cannot be called the Guō River until reaching Pèi.
The *Erya* says:
Guō is Xún.
Guō Jǐngchún noted:
A large river overflowing forms a small stream.
Lǚ Chēn said:
Xún
is the Guō River.
The Guō River passes west of Dàfú City.
Northeast of the city,
lie the old tombs of the various Yuán clan,
with steles and structures tilted and low,
stone sheep and tigers broken and shattered.
Only the steles of Minister of Education Pàng, Governor of Shǔ Commandery Téng, and Magistrate of Bópíng Guāng still preserve legible characters.
Aside from these,
nearly nothing else can be found.
The Guō River then flows southeast past Yángxià County to the west,
then east past Miǎochéng to the north,
a solid-walled city facing west.
There is a gap in the outer wall.
The Guō River then flows east past Dàjí City to the south,
formerly the Dàjí Township of Yān.
In the second year of Duke Xuān of *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Huà Yuán of Sòng fought Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng at Dàjí,
and Huà Yuán was captured.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* records:
Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed his soldiers,
but did not include his charioteer.
As they were about to engage in battle,
the charioteer Yáng Zhēn said:
"Yesterday, you decided about the sheep;
today,
I decide the course of events."
He then drove the chariot into Zhèng territory,
leading to Huà Yuán's capture.
Later, this land was annexed by King Zhuāng of Chǔ.
Thus, Juàn Chēng stated:
Dàjí,
a territory of Chǔ,
contains the tomb of Crown Prince Jiàn of Chǔ and the fishing terrace of Wǔ Yuán,
with ponds and marshes still present.
The Guō River then flows east past the old city of Ānpíng County to the north.
The *Chénliú Customs Biography* says:
Dàjí Township
was formerly Ānpíng County.
The local people are honest and simple,
easy to govern.
The Guō River then flows east past Lùyì City to the north,
commonly called Hǔxiāng City,
which is incorrect;
it is the Mínglù of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Dù Yù noted:
Southwest of Wǔpíng in Chén State is the Lùyì Pavilion.
Ten *lǐ* south of the city stands the stele of Jìn’s Court Gentleman for Consultation Hú Jūn,
erected in the eighth year of Yuánkāng.
North of the Guō River is the stele of Hàn’s Magistrate of Wēn Xù Xù,
whose courtesy name was Sìgōng,
a native of Chén State.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng,
appointed Gentleman of Consultation,
promoted to Magistrate of Wēn,
with the stele erected during the Yánxī era.
The Guō River then flows east past the old city of Wǔpíng County to the north.
About seven *lǐ* southwest of the city is the stele of Hàn’s Imperial Secretary Yú Xǔ,
inscribed:
"Stele of Lord Yú."
His given name was Xǔ,
courtesy name Dìng'ān,
descendant of Yú Zhòng,
served as Magistrate of Zhāogē and Governor of Wǔdū.
The text is largely damaged,
and can no longer be deciphered.
According to Fàn Yè’s *History of the Later Han*,
Yú Xǔ’s courtesy name was Shēngqīng,
a native of Wǔpíng, Chén State.
His grandfather was a county jailer,
known for leniency and forgiveness.
He once said:
"Yú Gōng built the village gate,
and his son became Chancellor.
Though I may not match Yú Gōng,
my descendants may still rise to the Nine Ministers."
Thus, he named his grandson Xǔ with the courtesy name Shēngqīng.
Dìng'ān
was likely his childhood name.
King Wǔ of Wèi was initially enfeoffed here,
ultimately ruling Wǔpíng and Huáxià.
The Guō River then flows east past Guǎngxiāng City to the north.
Juàn Chēng stated:
Xiāngyì has the Shéqiū Pavilion,
formerly Guǎngxiāng.
It was renamed Guǎngshì.
In the fourth year of Yángjiā under Emperor Shùn of Later Hàn,
Palace Attendant Zhì Tián was enfeoffed here as a marquis,
which is Guǎngxiāng.
The Guō River then flows east southwest of Kǔ County,
dividing into two streams.
A branch flows northeast,
entering a valley at Lài City,
known as the Dead Guō.
The Guō River then bends southeast,
passing the old city of Kǔ County to the south.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
It is the Xiāng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
renamed Làilíng by Wáng Mǎng.
The city’s four gates have imperial roads:
the eastern one starts at Lài Township,
the southern from the South Gate,
crossing the river directly to the old terrace on the west side;
the South Gate road
leads straight to the Guǎngxiāng road;
the West Gate imperial road
reaches Wǔpíng to the west;
the North Gate imperial road
extends to the North Terrace.
The Guō River then bends northeast,
reaching west of Lài Township,
where the Gǔ River flows into it.
The Gǔ River originates from the Huàn River east of Xiāngyì County,
flowing east past Chéngkuāng City to the east.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records: In summer, Shū Zhòng Péngshēng met Xì Quē of Jìn at Chéngkuāng.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
They plotted against the states following Chǔ.
Jīng Xiàngfán noted:
Thirty *lǐ* west of present-day Xiāngyì, Chénliú, lies old Chéngkuāng City.
The Gǔ River then flows southeast past the old city of Jǐwú County to the west.
The *Chénliú Customs Biography* says:
The county was formerly part of Sòng,
mixed with territories of Chén and Chǔ,
originally the Zhǒnglóng Township relocated from Nínglíng County of Liáng State.
During the Chéng and Āi eras,
households reached eight to nine thousand,
prompting the gentry to request establishing a county.
In the eleventh year of Yǒngyuán,
the King of Chén ceded territory,
and in the twelfth year, Dàjí Township and Zhíyáng Township were transferred from Yān,
given the auspicious name Jǐwú,
still retaining Chén and Chǔ customs.
The Gǔ River then flows east past the old city of Zhè County to the east.
The *Treatise on Geography*
lists it as a county under Huáiyáng.
Inside the city is Magistrate Xǔ’s *Ode to Pure Virtue*,
though the stone is broken and the text disordered,
only this inscription remains on the stele.
About one *lǐ* southwest of the city,
stands the stele of Hàn’s Magistrate of Yángtái Xǔ Shūzhǒng,
erected during the Guānghé era.
There is also the stele of the late Hàn Magistrate of Lèchénglíng and Assistant to the Grand Commandant Xǔ Yīng,
courtesy name Yúqīng,
son of the Colonel-Director of Retainers,
erected in the first year of Jiànníng.
Other steles have fragmented texts,
no longer legible,
likely similar to those of the Colonel-Director.
The Gǔ River then flows east through the old city of Kǔ County.
When the water rises, it surrounds the city moat;
