when it recedes, it flows alone in a single channel.
The Gǔ River then flows east past Làixiāng City to the south.
The city is solid-walled,
with a terrace slightly higher at the northeast corner.
Locals believe this terrace is north of the Gǔ River.
The city is also called Gǔyáng Terrace,
which is incorrect.
From here, the Gǔ River flows east into the Guō River.
The Guō River then flows north past the east side of Lǎozǐ’s Temple.
In front of the temple are two steles,
outside the south gate.
Emperor Huán of Hàn dispatched Palace Attendant Guǎn Bà to sacrifice to Lǎozǐ,
ordering Chancellor Biān Sháo of Chén to compose the text.
North of the steles is a pair of stone gate towers, very orderly.
On the south side of the stone towers,
an inscription by Emperor Wén of Wèi during the third year of Huángchū, carved while passing through Qiáo;
on the northeast side of the towers,
stands the Temple of Confucius.
In front of the temple is a stele,
on the west side erected by Chancellor Kǒng Chóu of Lǔ State, Chén, in the third year of Jiànhé.
To the north is the Temple of the Old Lord,
with nine wells in the eastern courtyard.
Further north,
beside the Guō River is also the Temple of Lǐ’s Mother,
north of Lǎozǐ’s Temple.
In front of the temple is the tomb of Lǐ’s Mother,
with a stele east of the tomb,
erected by Magistrate Wáng Fù of Chángshā, Qiáo, in the first year of Yǒngxīng.
The stele states:
Lǎozǐ was born between Qū and Guō.
The Guō River then bends east past the old city of Xiàng County to the south.
The city is low, small, and solid-walled.
Biān Sháo’s *Stele Inscription for Lǎozǐ* says:
Lǎozǐ
was a native of Xiàng County, Chǔ.
Xiàng County is now desolate and abandoned,
currently belonging to Kǔ,
though the old city still remains.
East of Làixiāng,
the Guō River flows along its southern side,
suggesting this is likely the city in question,
though it has no outer wall to correspond to it.
The Guō River then flows east past the north of the old Qiáo County city walls.
According to the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*, in the 22nd year of Duke Xī,
Chǔ general Chéng Déchén led troops to attack Chén,
capturing the cities of Qiáo and Dùn before returning.
This was the Yánchéng Tíng of Wáng Mǎng's time.
The Wèi state established Qiáo Commandery here,
which became the seat of Yǎn Province.
The Shā River branches north from its southern course,
flows north past the west of Qiáo city,
and then turns north to join the Guō.
The Guō River encircles the city on all sides.
South of the city is the tomb of Cáo Sōng,
north of the tomb is a stele,
north of the stele is a temple hall,
whose foundations remain,
and whose pillar bases are still in place.
North of the temple stand two stone gate towers,
sixteen feet high.
The brackets and pillars are all carved with cloud patterns,
though the upper latticework is already broken.
North of the towers is a pointed-top stele,
inscribed:
"Stele of the Late Hàn Dynasty's Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Coachman of Chánglè Palace, Specially Advanced, Marquis of Fèi Tíng, Lord Cáo."
Erected in the 3rd year of Yánxī.
The back of the stele also bears an imperial edict,
the text matching the other stele.
Flanking the stele to the east and west,
stand two stone horses facing each other,
eight feet five inches tall.
The stonework is crude and clumsy,
not matching the stone horses lining the spirit path of Emperor Guāngwǔ's tomb.
There is the tomb of Cáo Sōng's elder brother,
east of the tomb is a stele,
inscribed:
"Tomb of the Late Hàn Dynasty's Governor of Yǐngchuān, Lord Cáo."
He died in the 9th year of Yánxī,
but the year of the stele's erection is not recorded.
North of the tomb mound is the tomb of his eldest son, Cáo Chì,
east of the tomb is a stele,
inscribed:
"Stele of the Late Hàn Dynasty's Colonel of Chángshuǐ, Lord Cáo."
He served as Grand Master of the Palace, Chief Clerk of the Minister of War, and Palace Attendant,
before being promoted to Colonel of Chángshuǐ.
He died at age thirty-nine.
The stele was made in the 6th year of Xīpíng.
The tomb of Cáo Chì's younger brother, Cáo Yìn,
east of the tomb is a stele,
inscribed:
"Stele of the Late Hàn Dynasty's Receptionist, Lord Cáo."
Erected in the 6th year of Xīpíng.
East of the city is the old residence of Cáo Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo).
Its location backed against the outer wall and faced the market,
beside the moat and near the water.
The *Wèi Shū* states:
When Tàizǔ served as a Gentleman Consultant,
he requested leave due to illness and returned to his hometown,
building a house outside the city walls.
In spring and summer, he studied books and commentaries,
in autumn and winter, he practiced archery and hunting for his own amusement.
Emperor Wén (Cáo Pī) was born here in the 4th year of Zhōngpíng of the Hàn,
with a green cloud like a carriage canopy above,
which lasted all day before dispersing.
This is that very place.
Later, Emperor Wén visited Qiáo in the 1st year of Yánkāng,
feasting the elders grandly.
He erected an altar at the old residence site,
with a stele in front of the altar,
the stele inscribed "Stele of the Grand Feast."
Northeast of the stele,
south of the Guō River,
is the tomb of Sīmǎ Shìhuì, Prince Dìng of Qiáo.
In front of the tomb is a stele,
erected in the 3rd year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn.
About two hundred paces south of the stele are two stone pillars,
over ten feet tall.
The lower half is carved with interwoven bamboo patterns,
the craftsmanship extremely fine.
A stone plaque reads:
"Spirit Path of the Tomb of the Late Jìn Dynasty's Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yáng Province and Jiāng Province,
General Who Pacifies the East, Prince Dìng of Qiáo, Lord Sīmǎ of Wēn in Hénèi."
The Guō River then flows east past the north of Zhū Guī's tomb,
turning southeast.
The tomb mound rests against the road to the south,
with a stele,
inscribed:
"Stele of the Late Hàn Dynasty's Governor of Yōu Province, Lord Zhū."
Guī, styled Bólíng,
died in office in the 6th year of Guānghé.
His former subordinate, Assistant Clerk,
Nián Huà of Wúzhōng, Yòuběipíng,
had this made in the 2nd year of Zhōngpíng.
The back of the stele lists the names of former subordinates,
all from places like Jì, Zhuō, Shànggǔ, and Běipíng.
The Guō River flows southeast past the north of Céngqiū,
a hill standing alone in its elegance,
towering and isolated.
This was the site of an ancient fortress.
The Guō River then flows southeast past the north of the old Chéngfù County city walls.
A branch of the Shā River flows into it here,
this waterway connecting with the Shā River at Sīshàn County,
commonly called Zhāng Water,
hence the name Zhāngtóu.
It flows northeast past the west of the old Chéngfù County city,
then along the city's side northeast into the Guō.
The Guō River then flows east past the north of Xiàchéngfù.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
Shānshāng County has the settlement of Xiàchéngfù.
The Guō River then bends, flowing past the east of this settlement and west of Láng Mountain,
then turns southeast past the south of Láng Mountain.
East of the mountain is the settlement of Chuíhuì,
commonly called Lǐchéng.
Yuán Sōngsōng's *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
Shānshāng County has the settlement of Chuíhuì.
This is that city.
The Guō River then flows southeast past the north of Guōyáng city,
bordering the Guō River.
During the Tàihé era of Wèi, it was the seat of Guō Province,
with Gài Biǎo appointed as Governor.
Later, the province was abolished and a commandery established,
a strategic garrison point.
The Guō River then flows southeast past the south of the old Lóngkuàng County city walls.
In the 13th year of Jiànwǔ of Hàn,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Fù Chāng as a marquis here.
Hence the saying:
"From Lóngkuàng in Pèi state to Shānshāng."
The Guō River then bends south, flowing out through a stone bridge,
the bridge stones collapsed and scattered.
Accumulated stones on both banks are twenty feet high,
the water passes between them,
then flows southeast,
passes north of Jīng Mountain and flows eastward.
Further southeast, it reaches Huáilíng County of Xiàpī,
and enters the Huái River.
The Guo River flows further east,
where it joins with the Beifei River on the left.
The Beifei River originates from the marshlands northwest of Shānsāng County,
flowing southeast.
On both its left and right sides, it is flanked by several tributaries,
which, though emerging from different sources, converge into the same course,
resembling delicate veins trickling and merging.
It flows southeast past the southern side of Shānsāng Town,
commonly referred to as Běipíng City.
In the past, Wén Qīn was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shānsāng,
and it is suspected that his fief was located in this city.
To the southeast, there is a stele,
but the inscription on the stele is entirely damaged and unverifiable.
Only the names of former officials on the back of the stele remain legible,
erected in the first year of the Xīpíng era by Yìshì Méngshēng of the Pei State, Xiāo Liú Dìngxīng.
The Beifei River flows further east past the old city of Shānsāng County,
commonly called Dūtíng,
but this is incorrect.
Today, on the eastern side within the city walls, a mountain pavilion still stands tall,
situated on a lofty and steep hill,
unmatched by any grand terrace.
As recorded in the *Shísān Zhōu Zhì*,
"a mountain grew within the town,
and mulberry trees flourished by its pavilion,"
hence the county was named accordingly.
East of the outer city walls lies the tomb stele of Wén Mù,
who served as a two-thousand-bushel official for three generations.
Wén Mù held the position of Hù Cáo Shǐ in the commandery,
was summoned to serve as a Tàicháng Chéng after passing the examination for Erudites,
and, due to his expertise in observing celestial phenomena,
was promoted to Shìzhōng and Right Zhōngláng Jiàng.
He was later transferred to the three commanderies of Jiǔjiāng, Péngchéng, and Chénliú,
and passed away during the Guānghé era.
The stele was erected by his former subordinates, including Péngchéng's Lǚ Qián, the Grand Administrator of Zhuōjùn.
The Beifei River flows further east and accumulates into a pond,
known as the Xiá Pond.
The pond water flows southeast past the southern side of Xiá City.
According to the *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*, in the sixteenth year of Duke Chéng,
the Chu army returned and reached Xiá,
which refers to this city.
Thus, Jīng Xiàngfán stated:
"Xiá
is a territory of Chu."
The Beifei River flows further southeast past the old city of Xiàng County.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* records:
"This was the former state of Xiàng."
The *Shìběn* states:
"Xǔ, Zhōu, Xiàng, and Shēn
are all of the Jiāng surname,
descendants of the Yán Emperor."
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Xiàng
was a county of the Pei State,
now incorporated into Lóngkàng of the Qiáo State."
Dù Yù noted:
"East of Lóngkàng County lies Xiàng City."
In the thirteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ of the Han dynasty,
Fùbō Hóu Wáng Bà was further enfeoffed as a marquis here,
referring to this city.
It is commonly called Yuán City,
but this is incorrect.
The river flows further southeast past the southern side of Yìchéng,
commonly referred to as Chǔ City,
but this is also incorrect.
It then flows east into the Guo River.
The Guo River flows east and empties into the Huái River.
The *Jīng* states that it enters the Huái at Xiàpī Huáilíng,
but this is erroneous.
23.2 The Biàn River
The Biàn River emerges from Yīngōu north of Jùnyí County.
The Yīngōu (Dark Ditch),
is the Làngtàng Canal,
also said to be the Biàn River receiving the Zhānrán River's water,
and also said that the Dān and Qìn rivers flow together,
cutting off the Yellow River at Wǔdé,
entering south into Xíngyáng and joining the Biàn,
hence the Biàn also bears the name of the Dān River.
When the Yellow River and Jì River waters were cut off,
the Biàn received the Zhānrán and flowed east.
Since Wáng Bēn flooded Dàliáng,
the water emerged south of the county and did not pass north of it.
During summer floods,
this channel then became navigable,
so this canal is the Yīngōu,
and north of Dàliáng it is also called the Jùn River.
Therefore, Quān Chēng, in his *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* (Traditions and Customs of Chénliú), wrote:
"The Jùn River passes north of it."
Further east,
the Biàn River emerges from it.
Therefore, the *Jīng* (Classic) says: "The Biàn emerges from the Yīngōu north of Jùnyí County."
The Biàn River flows east past the south of Cāngyuán City,
which is the Cāngyuán Pavilion of Jùnyí County.
The city borders the Biàn River; Chénliú Chancellor Bì Miǎo governed here.
When General Zhēngdōng Xún Xī headed west,
Miǎo fled back to the capital.
Xī sent Sima Dōnglái Wáng Zàn to take over and hold Cāngyuán,
cutting off the supply transport by water.
The Biàn River flows east again past the north of Píngxiāng Pavilion in Chénliú County.
The *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* says the county has Píngxiāng Pavilion,
which is this pavilion.
The Biàn River flows past the south of the old city of Xiǎohuáng County.
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals) mentions Líng Shòuguāng,
a man of Fúfēng,
who died at the home of Hú Wǎng in Jiānglíng.
Wǎng buried him.
Over a hundred days later,
someone saw Shòuguāng in this county,
who sent a letter to Wǎng.
Wǎng opened and looked at it,
only a pair of shoes remained.
The Biàn River flows east past the south of Míngyàn Pavilion.
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*, year 16 of Duke Chéng,
records: "The Marquis of Wèi attacked Zhèng,
reaching Míngyàn."
Dù Yù's *Shìdì* (Explanation of Places) says:
"It is northwest of Yōngqiū County,
and common people still call it Báiyàn Pavilion."
The Biàn River flows east past the north of the old city of Yōngqiū County,
and passes Yánglè City's south.
The *Xīzhēng Jì* (Record of a Western Campaign) says:
"The city is one *lǐ* north of the Biàn,
five *lǐ* in circumference,
within Yōngqiū County's boundaries."
The Biàn River flows east again,
and an old canal emerges from it,
connecting south to the Suī River,
called the Dǒngshēng Cut.
Some say Dǒng started a rebellion,
diverting water south to connect to the Suī River,
hence this water got its name.
Now it has no water.
The Biàn River flows east again,
and a distributary emerges,
commonly called Luòjiàkǒu.
The *Xīzhēng Jì* says:
"Luòjià,
is a water name."
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* (Continued Record of Campaigns) says:
"It is two *lǐ* downstream from the Dǒngshēng Cut."
The Biàn River flows past the south of Wàihuáng County,
and east past the north of Yǒucāng City.
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"Yǒucāng City is twenty *lǐ* from Dàyóu's Tomb."
It flows east past Dàqí City's south.
The *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* says:
"Wàihuáng County has a Dàqí Pavilion."
It flows east past the north of Kē City.
The *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* says:
"The county has a Kēlǐn Pavilion,
which is this Kēlǐn Pavilion."
The Biàn River flows east past the south of Xiǎoqí City,
and south past the south of Lìwàng Pavilion.
The *Fēngsú Zhuàn* says:
"It was formerly Chéng'ān."
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* (Treatise on Geography),
a Chénliú county name,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Hán Yánnián as a marquis here.
The Biàn River flows east again,
and the old channel of Lóngmén emerges.
The channel formerly connected to the Suī River,
so the *Xīzhēng Jì* says:
"Lóngmén,
is a water name."
North of the gate is an earthen platform,
over three *zhàng* high,
with a top several tens of paces across.
The Biàn River flows east past the south of the old city of Jìyáng Kǎochéng County,
forming the Zīhuò Canal.
Kǎochéng County,
was a fief in the Zhōu,
and in the Spring and Autumn period was the state of Dài.
The *Zuǒzhuàn*, year 10 of Duke Yǐn,
autumn,
records: "Sòng, Wèi, and Cài attacked Dài."
In autumn of the 11th year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed Péng Zǔ as a marquis here.
The *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* says:
"It was the Qín county of Gǔ."
Later, due to the Hàn uprising,
the city had many calamitous years,
so it was renamed Zī County.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Jiāgǔ.
When Emperor Zhāng toured east and passed the county,
he issued an edict:
"Chénliú Zī County,
its name is not good.
Emperor Gāozǔ despised the city of Bóren,
Emperor Shìzōng rested at Wénxǐ and received the auspicious response of Huòjiā,
enjoying good fortune and great portents,
grateful for the imperial spirit's regard,
bestowing brilliance upon Yuè,
considering Emperor Wǔ's achievements,
change Zī County to Kǎochéng."
This channel likely got its name from the county.
The Biàn River flows east past the north of Shāyáng Pavilion in Nínglíng County,
formerly the state of Shāsuí.
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*, year 16 of Duke Chéng, autumn,
records: "Met at Shāsuí,
to plan an attack on Zhèng."
Dù Yù's *Shìdì* says:
"It is Shāyáng Pavilion north of Nínglíng County in Liáng State."
Later generations think it is Táng City,
but that is wrong.
The Biàn River flows east past the north of Huánghāo Wù,
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"From Táng City to Huánghāo is twenty *lǐ*."
The Biàn River flows east past below Xié City.
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"From Huánghāo to Xié City is five *lǐ*."
The *Chénliú Súfēng Zhuàn* says:
"Kǎochéng County has a Xié Pavilion."
The Biàn River flows east past the side of Zhōu Wù.
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"Three *lǐ* east of Xié City,
during the Yìxī era of Jìn,
Duke Liú sent Zhōu Chāozhī from Péngchéng along the old Biàn ditch,
cutting trees and opening a path over seven hundred *lǐ*,
to open a water route,
and moored here.
Hence this wù (enclosure) got its name."
The Biàn River flows east past the north of Gě City,
formerly the state of Earl Gě.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Earl Gě did not sacrifice.
Tāng asked:
'Why do you not sacrifice?'
He said he had nothing to supply for the sacrifices.
Tāng sent [supplies] to Earl Gě,
but Earl Gě still did not sacrifice.
Tāng asked him again,
and he said:
'I have no animals for sacrifice.'
Tāng sent them again,
but he still did not sacrifice.
Tāng asked him again,
and he said:
'I have no grain for the offerings.'
Tāng sent people from Bó to go
and plow for the elders,
with the old and weak bringing food.
Earl Gě again led his people to seize it,
killing those who would not give it.
Tāng then attacked Gě."
Gě, during the Warring States, belonged to Wèi.
King Ānxī of Wèi enfeoffed it to Prince Wújì,
titled Lord Xìnlíng.
The place, Gěxiāng,
is this city,
ten *lǐ* west of Nínglíng County.
The Biàn River flows east past Shénkēng Wù,
and east past Xiàhóu Cháng Wù.
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"From Xiàhóu Wù to Zhōu Wù,
each is five *lǐ* apart."
The Biàn River flows east past the north of the old city of Suīyáng County in Liáng State,
and east passes south of Xiāngxiāng Wù.
The *Xùshù Zhēngjì* says:
"Twenty *lǐ* west from Xiàhóu Wù,
and one *lǐ* east,
is the Xiāngxiāng Pagoda."
The Biàn River passes its south.
It was established by a certain gentleman during the Xīpíng era of Hàn.
He died and was buried there.
His younger brother carved a stone and erected a stele,
to display his virtue.
In front of the tomb path were lions and heavenly deer,
with piled bricks forming eight sets of hundred-step pillars,
now overgrown and ruined,
mostly decayed and fallen.
Further east, it reaches Méng County in Liáng Commandery,
where it becomes the Huò River.
Its remaining waves flow south into Suīyáng City.
The Biàn River then passes east along the south of Shì City,
commonly called Bó City,
but this is incorrect.
Kàn Yǐn's *Record of the Thirteen Provinces* considers it Guàn City,
located northwest of Méng County.
In the second year of Duke Xī of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Marquis of Qí, the Duke of Sòng, and the states of Jiāng and Huáng formed an alliance at Guàn.
Dù Yù identifies this as Shì.
He states that the characters for Shì and Guàn are similar.
Guàn was in Qí,
referred to as Guànzé,
which is correct.
This is not the place.
Now, there are no other cities in this area,
only this town northwest of Méng.
Examining the texts and verifying the location,
it is clearly the town of Shì,
and not Bó, as can be known.
The Biàn River then passes east along the north of the old city of Méng County,
commonly called Little Méng City.
The *Record of a Western Campaign* states
the city is fifteen or sixteen lǐ south of the Biàn River,
which was the original hometown of Zhuāng Zhōu,
who served as the official of the lacquer garden in Méng.
This is the "proud official in the lacquer garden" mentioned by Guō Jǐngchún.
Mourning the death of Huì Shī,
he closed his doors in this town.
The Biàn River flowed out south of the county,
but now there is no longer any water.
Only south of Suīyáng City is there a small stream flowing south into Suī City.
Two lǐ south is the tomb of Qiáo Zǎi, a Clerk under the Grand Tutor of the Hàn,
with a stele recording his courtesy name as Yuánbīn,
a native of Suīyáng in Liáng State.
The stele was erected by Gōngzǐ Xī of Suīyáng in the fifth year of the Xīpíng era.
One hundred paces east of the city is a stone chamber,
inscribed:
"Shrine of Qiáo Rén, Hàn Court Usher."
Five lǐ north of the city are stone tigers and stone pillars,
but no stele or record,
so it is unknown when they were built.
The Biàn River then passes east along the north of Great Méng City.
Since ancient times, there has been no record of two Méngs,
so it is suspected to be Méng Bó,
which is called Jǐngbó, the Northern Bó.
Jiāo Jǔ said:
"King Tāng of Shāng received the mandate at Jǐngbó."
Kàn Yǐn stated:
"It was the capital of Tāng."
Bó was originally the ruins of Emperor Kù,
located between the Yellow River and the Luò River in Yùzhōu according to the *Tribute of Yǔ*,
which is now Shīxiāng Pavilion, twenty lǐ west of Yǎnshī City in Hénán.
Huángfǔ Mì believed that examining the facts,
scholars are mistaken.
As Mèngzǐ said, Tāng resided in Bó,
neighboring Gé,
meaning Bó was adjacent to Gé.
Tāng's territory was seventy lǐ,
and Gé was only a small state.
Their domains were limited,
yet Nínglíng is eight hundred lǐ from Yǎnshī,
so it would be impossible for children to deliver provisions and plow for them.
Now, Liáng State itself has two Bós.
The Southern Bó is in Gǔshú,
and the Northern Bó is in Méng,
not Yǎnshī.
The *Ancient Text of Zhòng Huǐ's Announcement* states:
"The Earl of Gé was hostile to the provisions,"
"the campaign began from Gé."
This aligns with Mèngzǐ's words.
Cuī Yīn said:
"Tāng's tomb is north of Bó County in Jìyīn."
The *Imperial Overview* states:
"Three lǐ east of the northern outer wall of Bó City, on level ground, is Tāng's tomb."
The tomb is square,
each side measuring ten paces,
seven chǐ high,
with a flat top."
In the first year of the Jiànpíng era of Emperor Āi of Hàn,
the Grand Minister of Works' Clerk Xì Chángqīng inspected flood damage,
and thus visited Tāng's tomb.
It belonged to Fúfēng in Hàn times,
and now, in Zhēng, Huíqú Pavilion has Tāng's Pond and Zhēng Mò.
However, this is not commonly seen,
making it difficult to verify in detail.
According to the *Basic Annals of Qín Nínggōng*:
"In the second year, he attacked Tāng."
"In the third year, he battled Bó."
"The King of Bó fled to the Róng,"
"and thus Tāng was destroyed."
Thus, during the time of King Huán of Zhōu, there was a King of Bó named Tāng,
who was destroyed by Qín,
belonging to the Western Róng state,
and was buried in Zhēng,
not the Shāng Tāng.
Liú Xiàng stated,
expressing doubt that there is no burial site for Shāng Tāng.
Dù Yù said:
"North of Méng County in Liáng State is Bófá City."
"Within the city is the tomb of Chéng Tāng,"
"and west of it is the tomb of Jīzǐ."
Now, within the city is an old tomb with a square mound,
suspected to be the tomb of Tāng referred to by Dù Yuánkǎi,
but commonly called the tomb of Wángzǐ Qiáo.
Beside the tomb is a stele inscribed:
"The Immortal Wángzǐ Qiáo."
The stele states:
"Wángzǐ Qiáo
was a true man of ancient times."
It is heard he became an immortal,
but it is unknown in which era he flourished.
Extensively inquiring among Daoist masters,
some say he was from Yǐngchuān,
others say he was born in Méng.
When this city was first built,
this mound already existed.
Transmitted by the ancients, it is said:
"In the first year of the Yǒnghé era, in the twelfth month of winter,
during the time of the Là sacrifice,
at night,
there were sounds of crying,
very sorrowful in tone."
A nearby resident, Wáng Bó, found it strange,
and at dawn, he made an offering and observed.
At that time, swan geese descended in the snow,
with no human footprints,
but there were large bird tracks at the sacrificial site.
All around believed it to be divine.
Later, someone wearing a large hat,
a crimson unlined garment,
and leaning on a bamboo staff stood before the mound,
calling to the firewood-gathering youth, Yī Yǒngchāng:
"I am Wángzǐ Qiáo.
Do not take the trees from my grave mound."
Suddenly, he disappeared.
The magistrate at the time, Wàn Xī of Tàishān,
investigated the words of the elders,
moved by the response of the auspicious omen,
then built a numinous temple
to house his spirit.
Thereupon, followers of the Dao gathered from afar,
some playing the qín and singing of Tàiyī,
others deeply contemplating to reach Dānqiū.
They knew that the abode of supreme virtue
was truly the ancestral resting place of a true man.
In the eighth month of autumn in the eighth year of the Yánxī era,
the emperor dispatched an envoy with sacrificial animals,
to perform rites and offerings,
purifying it,
with reverence and solemnity.
The Chancellor of the state, Wáng Zhāng of Dōnglái,
courtesy name Bóyí,
believing that where the divine and sage arise,
there must be inscriptions and markers,
together with the Chief Clerk Biān Qián, erected a dark stone,
recording and eulogizing the遗留的功业.
Reading the stele text,
its meaning seems not distant,
and since it is seen along the route,
it cannot but be recorded here.
23.3 The Huò River
23.3 The Huò River
The Huò River originates from the Biàn River north of Méng County in Liáng Commandery.
South of Xiāo County is a mountain,
which the world calls the Southern Mountain of Xiāo City.
Dài Yánzhī called it Tóngxiào Mountain,
saying it took its name from the village where Liú Dé, Marquis of Yángchéng of the Hàn, resided.
Liú Chéngzhī said:
South of the county is Mào Mountain.
It is unclear which is correct.
The mountain has a Jī Valley,
whose waters flow north into the Huò River,
and the world calls it the West-Flowing Stream,
saying the water originates from the Wútóng Pond,
and because the pond water flows west, it was named accordingly.
I once passed through the town of Xiāo,
and to the right of the city, only this water flows north into the Huò River,
with no other watercourses,
so I suspect this is the Suī River mentioned in the "Classic."
The city faces the Huò River on its east, west, and south sides,
which is why the administrative seat of Pèi Commandery was also located here.
South of the city was formerly a place where a stone bridge had collapsed,
and stones were piled to form a beam,
twenty zhàng high,
but now it is nearly completely ruined and desolate,
and it is also unknown who built it.
The county was originally the state of Shū of Xiāo,
a vassal of Sòng,
which Chǔ later destroyed.
In the twelfth year of Duke Xuān of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Chǔ attacked Xiāo,
and Xiāo collapsed.
Shēn Gōng Wūchén said:
"The soldiers are suffering from the cold."
The king inspected the three armies and comforted them,
and the soldiers all felt as if wrapped in silk wadding,
which was surely due to the king's kindness.
A daughter of Xiāo was married to Qí and became the mother of Duke Qǐng,
whom Xì Kè referred to as Xiāo Tóngshū's daughter.
The Huò River flows east past Lóng City,
though it is unknown who first built it.
The Huò River then flows east past the north of Tóngxiào Mountain,
on whose northern slope is the tomb of King Yuán of Chǔ,
round on top and square at the bottom,
built with piled stones,
over ten zhàng high,
about a hundred paces wide,
with more than ten burial mounds,
all constructed of stone.
The Huò River flows further east,
where the Jìngjìng Ditch flows into it,
its waters originating from the Wútóng Pond,
flowing northwest,
which is what Liú Zhōngshū Chéngzhī called the Báigōu Stream.
It then flows north into the Huò River,
commonly known as the Jìngjìng Ditch.
Further east, it reaches the north of Péngchéng County,
and flows east into the Sì River.
The Huò River flows east from the Jìngjìng Ditch past the north of the Āyùwáng Temple,
which some say was built by King Yīng of Chǔ,
though this is not certain.
It likely follows the legacy of King Aśoka,
hence the name.
It joins with the Ānpō Waters,
which originate from the remaining flow of the Ān Pond,
flowing north past the Āyùwáng Temple.
Beside the water is a bridge,
called the Xuánzhù Bridge.
Next to the water is a stone tomb,
long since excavated,
with exquisitely crafted stonework,
remarkably grand in structure,
though it is unknown whose tomb it is.
I suspect it is the tomb Líng referred to by Chéngzhī.
The water flows north into the Huò River.
The Huò River flows east past the north of Mílí City,
which Liú Chéngzhī's "Records of the Yǒngchū Era" mentions as a city southwest of the main city.
The Huò River turns southwest of Péngchéng and flows north,
passing Péngchéng.
Northwest of the city was formerly the residence of Gōng Shèng, a senior official of Chǔ,
where an elder of Chǔ wept for Shèng.
The Huò River then turns east, passes north of the city, and flows east into the Sì River.
Three lǐ to the north is a stone tomb that has been opened,
said to be the tomb of Liú Xiàng, grandson of King Yuán of Chǔ,
though this is uncertain.
The city was originally the state of Lǎo Péng, a senior official of Yīn.
During the Spring and Autumn period, it was part of Sòng territory,
but Chǔ attacked Sòng and annexed it,
granting it to Yú Shí.
Cuī Zǐ Jìguī's "Ode to the Beginning" says:
"Thinking of Huáng Gōng at Pī Yí,
and toiling for Yú Shí at Péngchéng,"
referring to this county.
Mèng Kāng said:
"Jiānglíng was formerly called Southern Chǔ,
Chén was Eastern Chǔ,
and Péngchéng was Western Chǔ."
Wén Yǐng said:
"Péngchéng
was originally Eastern Chǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ made it his capital,
calling it Western Chǔ."
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn pacified the realm,
he made it the Chǔ Commandery,
enfeoffing his younger brother Jiāo as King of Chǔ,
who made it his capital.
In the first year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān,
it was renamed Péngchéng Commandery,
and Wáng Mǎng changed it to Hélè Commandery,
with Xúzhōu administered from here.
Within the city are several steles, including those of Yuán Ān, the Hàn Minister over the Masses, and Xú Shù, the Wèi General of the Household,
all erected along the right side of the street,
as they all once served as Chancellors of Chǔ.
Within the great city is a Jīn City,
and a small city to the northeast,
which Duke Liú further expanded,
with stone walls four zhàng high,
surrounded by moats.
West of the small city is another city,
built by the Grand Marshal, the King of Lángyá,
who began construction on the foundation of Xiàng Yǔ's former terrace,
erecting palaces, halls, gates, and towers,
all newly constructed.
In the twelfth year of the Yìxī era,
heavy rains fell incessantly,
and the Biàn River swelled violently,
causing the city walls to collapse.
The son of General of the Champion, Duke Liú of Péngchéng, ascended and rebuilt them,
entirely with bricks,
making them grand, sturdy, and imposing,
with towering watchtowers and dazzling splendor,
unmatched anywhere north or south.
Sòng's General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Xúzhōu, Xuē Āndū of Hédōng, surrendered the city to Wèi,
and Wèi sent Gōng Wèi Gǒurén of Bólíng and Gōng Kǒng Bógōng of Chéngyáng to assist him,
restoring the city gates and towers to their original state,
with the appearance unchanged from the past.
Later, they were demolished,
all at once,
though some exquisitely carved remnants remain,
still displaying dragons and clouds in dynamic forms,
remarkably refined and exquisite.
At the northeastern corner of the city, a multi-story tower was built,
called the Péngzǔ Tower.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
"Péngchéng County
was the ancient state of Péngzǔ."
The "Shìběn" says:
"Among the sons of Lù Zhōng,
the third was Jiǎn,
who was Péngzǔ.
This is Péngzǔ City,
and below is Péngzǔ's tomb."
Péngzǔ lived eight hundred years,
enjoying eternal longevity,
and here lies his tomb,
a testament to the boundless transformations of the universe.
Beside this tower,
it is bordered by the Biàn River and girded by the Sì River,
with the northeast being the confluence of these two waters.
Gazing out over the plains and rivers,
taking in the clear, open fields,
this is indeed a splendid place.
24 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 24
24.1 The Suī River
24.1 The Suī River
The Suī River originates from Yān County in Liáng Commandery,
The Suī River originates from the Làngdàng Canal west of Chénliú County,
flowing northeast.
The "Geographical Records" states:
The Suī River first receives the Làngdàng water from Jùnyí in Chénliú.
The "Classic" says it originates from Yān,
which is incorrect.
It then passes east by the old Gāoyáng Pavilion to the north,
commonly called the Northern City of Chénliú,
which is also incorrect.
Sū Lín said:
Gāoyáng
is a northern county of Chénliú.
According to records, it is in Liú,
an old village name.
There is a stele for the temple of the Hàn dynasty's Guǎngyě Jūn.
In the sixth year of Yánxī, twelfth month,
the magistrate of Yōngqiū, Dǒng Shēng, admiring the lingering glory of a thousand years past,
and following the splendid beauty of a bygone era,
ordered the county resident Zhǎng Zhào to compose a text,
to make manifest an immortal virtue.
It roughly states:
Ceasing to wash and sharing meals,
consulting on imperial strategies,
with achievements at Zhuōlù for Chén and Zhèng,
and no war at Mùyě between the sea and Tài,
greatly pacifying Huáxià,
calming and settling the people,
since the birth of humanity,
no achievement has been more lofty.
Now the old dwelling is unheard of,
and a solitary stele stands alone.
The "Chénliú Customs Biography" says:
The Lì clan resided in Gāoyáng.
When the Lord of Pei attacked Chénliú County,
Lì Yìjī rendered meritorious service,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāoyáng.
There was Lì Jùn,
styled Wénshān,
who rose to the post of Clerk in the Ducal Office and Great General.
For his meritorious service,
he received a fief in Zhuō,
thus moving from Chénliú to Zhuō.
The county has the Bǐng Pavilion and Bǐng Township.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Wáng Cháng as a marquisate here.
The Suī River then passes east by the old city of Yōngqiū County to the north.
This county
was formerly the state of Qǐ.
King Tāng of Shāng and King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of the Xià ruler here,
to continue Yǔ's lineage.
Chǔ destroyed Qǐ,
and Qín made it a county.
Juàn Chēng said:
The county has the name "Five Mounds,"
hence it was named for the clan.
Within the city is a temple to the Xià ruler.
In the past, during the two dynasties,
sacrifices were offered without cease.
The First Emperor of Qín thus built its outer walls into a large city,
and made it a county.
The Suī River flows further east,
where water accumulates to form a lake,
commonly called the White Sheep Marsh.
The marsh is forty lǐ square.
To the right, the water of the Jiānliáng Marsh flows into it.
This water originates from the marsh,
passing northeast by Yōngqiū City to the north,
then dividing east into two channels,
called Shuāng Gōu (Double Ditches),
both entering the White Sheep Marsh.
The marsh water joins east with the Luòjià Outlet.
This water originates from the Biàn River,
called Luòjià Water,
flowing southeast into the Suī River.
The Suī River then passes east by the old city of Xiāngyì County to the north,
and further east by Yōngqiū City to the north.
The Suī River then passes east by the old city of Nínglíng County to the south,
formerly the state of Gé Bó.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Kāngshàn.
It passes by Yān County to the north.
The two cities are fifty lǐ apart north to south,
hence the "Classic" has the text about originating from Yān.
Seven lǐ east of the city,
by the water's edge, are two steles for the brothers: Magistrate of Shànfǔ, Yáng Yàn,
and Imperial Secretary Lang, Yáng Shàn, styled Wénjié,
erected during the Hàn dynasty's Guānghé period.
It passes east by Suīyáng County to the south.
The Suī River flows east past the north of Héngchéng.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuo's Commentary, the twenty-first year of Duke Zhāo,
Yuè Dàxīn defended against Huá and Xiàng at Héng.
Dù Yù said:
South of Suīyáng County in Liáng State there is a Héng Pavilion.
Now it is southwest of Suīyáng County,
the world calls it Guāngchéng,
probably because the sounds of "guāng" and "héng" are similar,
but this is an erroneous popular transmission.
The Suī River then flows past the north of Xīnchéng,
which is the Xīnchéng Pavilion of Sòng.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuo's Commentary, the fourteenth year of Duke Wén,
the Duke met with the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Chén, the Marquis of Wèi, the Earl of Zhèng, the Baron of Xǔ, the Earl of Cáo, and Zhào Dùn of Jìn,
and they swore a covenant at Xīnchéng.
The Suī River then flows east past the north of Gāoxiāng Pavilion,
and further east past the north of Bóchéng,
which is Southern Bó,
the capital of Tāng.
The Suī River then flows east past the old city south of Suīyáng County.
King Chéng of Zhōu enfeoffed Wēizǐ Qǐ with Sòng to continue the line of Yīn,
and it became the capital of Sòng.
Formerly, Duke Yuán of Sòng dreamed of a river envoy riding in a covered carriage,
dressed in embroidered robes,
who came to pay respects to Duke Yuán.
Duke Yuán, moved by Wèi Píng's words, sought him from the man Yú Qiě of Quányáng,
who presented the divine turtle here.
In the twenty-second year of Qín Shǐhuáng, it was made Dàng Commandery.
Hàn Gāozǔ once appointed the Lord of Pèi as Administrator of Dàng Commandery.
After the empire was settled,
in the fifth year it became the State of Liáng.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Wén,
he enfeoffed his youngest son Wǔ as King of Liáng,
the beloved son of the Empress Dowager and the favored younger brother of Emperor Jǐng.
Therefore, his guards and attendants,
his adornments, were like the Son of Heaven's.
He stored up treasures and accumulated valuables,
much imitating the capital.
He recruited and extended hospitality to heroes and outstanding men,
and scholars all returned to him.
Men like Chángqīng,
having left office, came to wander here.
He expanded the Suīyáng city wall to seventy lǐ,
greatly built palaces, observatories, terraces, gardens, screens, and pavilions,
their scale matching the imperial residence.
Regarding the construction,
the laborers, while flowing with sweat, would sing,
and always sang the "Suīyáng Melody."
The creation and transmission of this tune began from this.
The west gate of the city is the place where Kòu Xiān played the qin.
Xiān was fond of fishing,
and lived by the Suī River.
Duke Jǐng of Sòng asked him about the Way, but he did not answer,
so the Duke killed him.
Ten years later,
he stopped at this gate, played the qin, and then left.
The people of Sòng, household after household, made offerings to him.
The south gate is called the Lú Gate.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Huá clan, dwelling in Lú Gate Lane, rebelled.
Dù Yù said:
The Lú Gate
is the south gate of the Sòng city.
Sīmǎ Biāo's Treatise on Commanderies and States says:
Suīyáng County has a Lú Gate Pavilion.
Inside the city there is a high terrace,
very elegant and broad,
standing majestically alone,
rising loftily and solitary.
It is called the Lí Terrace,
also known as the Shēng Terrace.
In its former days of full flourishing,
it truly vied with the clouds and mist in distance.
The Continued Record of Campaigns says:
The winding path resembles a snail shell (lí),
therefore it is called the Lí Terrace.
This is incorrect.
I consult the Quēzi,
which states that Duke Jǐng of Sòng had a craftsman make a bow,
and it took nine years to complete.
The Duke said:
Why so slow?
He replied:
I will not see you again, my lord.
My essence is exhausted in this bow.
He presented the bow and returned home,
and died after three days.
Duke Jǐng ascended the Tiger Enclosure Terrace,
took the bow, faced east, and shot an arrow.
The arrow passed over Mèng Shuāng Mountain,
and landed east of Péngchéng.
Its remaining force, swift and strong,
still sank its feathers into the stone bridge.
Thus, the Lí Terrace is the Tiger Enclosure Terrace,
probably where Sòng kept tigers in captivity.
In the Tàihé era of Jìn,
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn advanced to the river,
and ordered Yùzhōu Governor Yuán Zhēn to open the Stone Gate.
The Xiānbēi firmly garrisoned this terrace.
Zhēn halted his armored troops below the fortified city,
and, failing to achieve his goal, returned.
West of the Lí Terrace,
there is another terrace,
commonly called the Nǚláng Terrace.
Northwest of this terrace,
within the city, there is a Liángmǎ Terrace.
East of the terrace is a winding pool,
north of the pool are two fishing terraces in a row,
the water's circumference being six to seven hundred paces.
Directly east of the Lí Terrace,
there is another terrace,
the world calls it the Què Terrace.
North of the east-west road within the city,
there is the memorial stele for the tomb of Princess Consort Wáng of Jìn Liáng,
with two stelae standing side by side.
The stele says:
The consort's taboo name was Càn,
courtesy name Nǚyí,
a person of Qǔchéng in Dōnglái.
Granddaughter of the Lord of Běihǎi of Qí,
youngest daughter of the Sikōng, Jǐng Hóu of Dōngwǔ.
In the first year of Xiánxī, she was betrothed to the Sīmǎ clan.
In the second year of Tàishǐ, she became consort of the state.
In the fifth year of Tàikāng, she passed away.
Her tomb was constructed at Xīnméng.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng, the stele was erected.
East of this is the Chuī Terrace of the King of Liáng.
Its foundation, steps, and plinths still remain.
Now the Zhuīmíng Temple is built there.
East of the old palace is the former site of Ānliáng,
level and about five to six hundred paces around,
with water and a row of fishing terraces.
East of the pool is another terrace,
the world calls it the Qīnglíng Terrace.
The north city wall, leaning against the corner,
also forms a pool terrace.
Jìn Zhuó said:
Some say the Píng Terrace is in the northeast corner of the city,
or that the Rabbit Garden is beside the Píng Terrace.
Rú Chún said:
The Píng Terrace
is where the detached palace was located.
Now, twenty lǐ east of the city there is a terrace,
broad and wide but not extremely high,
commonly called the Píng Terrace.
I consult the Hànshū, Biography of King Xiào of Liáng, which states:
The King, by merit and kinship, held a great state.
He built the Eastern Park, three hundred lǐ square,
expanded the Suīyáng city wall to seventy lǐ,
greatly built palaces and chambers,
constructed elevated walkways,
from the palace connecting to the Píng Terrace for over thirty lǐ.
The elevated walkway exited east from the palace at the Yáng Gate.
The left Yáng Gate
is the east gate of Suīyáng.
Connecting to the Píng Terrace would be close,
but connecting to the city corner would be impossible.
Thus, it is known that the Píng Terrace was not within the city.
The King of Liáng, along with men like Zōu, Méi, and Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
roamed to the utmost upon it.
Therefore, the Preface to the Mountain Dwelling of the Suí Commandery King of Qí says: "The Western Garden had many scholars,
the Píng Terrace was full of guests.
The guests of Zōu and Mā were all present,
the song of cutting wood was repeatedly presented."
Thus, they pursued the fragrance of past pleasures,
their spirits wandered through ancient times.
This was indeed a grand event of the age.
Xiè's "Rhapsody on Snow" also says:
"The King of Liáng was displeased,
and wandered in the Rabbit Garden."
Now, the singing hall has sunk into ruins,
the pitch pipes have buried their sounds.
The solitary foundation stands in a lump,
no longer possessing the vista of former days.
Five or six lǐ north of the city,
one finds the tomb of the Hàn Grand Commandant Qiáo Xuán.
East of the tomb mound is a temple,
the place where Cáo Mèngdé personally poured a libation.
Cáo Cāo was originally of humble background,
and once paid a visit to Xuán.
Xuán said:
"The world is about to fall into chaos.
The one who can bring it peace,
is it not you, sir?"
Cáo Cāo felt he had met a true friend who understood him.
Later, passing by Xuán's tomb,
he made an offering, saying:
"Cáo, with my stubborn nature,
was received by you, a gentleman.
A scholar dies for one who knows him.
I hold this in my heart, never forgetting.
I also received your pledged words:
After my passing,
if your path leads you by,
should you not offer a cup of wine and a single chicken,
to pour a libation as you pass,
and your carriage passes three paces beyond,
do not complain of a stomach ache.
Though these were playful words spoken at the time,
if not for the closest kinship and deepest affection,
how could one be willing to utter such words?"
With sorrowful reverence, we offer sacrifices,
to express our long-held sentiments.
At the tomb stand several steles.
One was erected by the Confucian scholars, talented individuals, and wise men of the Han dynasty, who were moved by the virtuous conduct of the Qiáo family.
Together, they carved the stone and set up the stele
to show it to later generations.
Another stele was commissioned by former officials such as Cuī Liè, the Minister of Education from Bólíng, and Wú Zhěng, the Minister of Justice from Hénán,
who believed that supreme virtue resides within oneself,
yet its promotion depends on others.
If it is not clearly recorded,
how can it be examined?
Thus, they jointly engraved the fine stone
to illuminate the noble legacy.
Another stele was erected by Zhì, the Chief of Běicìmòdàng Garrison in Fúhǎn, Lǒngxī, who served as the Left Commandant, and Zhào Féng Xiàogāo of Yuándào, Hànyáng.
As Lord Qiáo once governed Liángzhōu,
they were moved by the principles of the Three Bonds,
admired the virtue of compliance and support,
and believed that Lord Qiáo’s meritorious deeds
should be proclaimed in his homeland.
Thus, they erected a stele with inscriptions
to illuminate his fine virtues.
In the seventh year of the Guānghé era,
Lǐ Yǒu, the Chief Clerk,
styled Zhòngliáo, composed the stele text.
On the back of the stele, there is a text about the Right Tripod, which records his appointment as Minister of Works in the third year of the Jiànníng era.
There is also a text about the Middle Tripod, recording his appointment as Minister of Education in the fourth year of the Jiànníng era.
And there is a text about the Left Tripod, recording his appointment as Grand Commandant in the first year of the Guānghé era.
The inscription on the tripods reads:
Former officials and disciples
jointly recounted Lord Qiáo’s conduct and deliberated on its essence.
Thus, his civil virtues were inscribed on the three tripods,
and his military achievements were engraved on the battle-axes.
These were written on the back of the stele
to illuminate his glorious virtues.
There is also an inscription on the battle-axes,
stating that they carved stones and created images,
making these battle-axes and military drums,
which were displayed on the eastern steps,
also to illuminate Lord Qiáo’s civil and military achievements.
To the south of the temple stand two pillars.
East of the pillars are two stone sheep.
North of the sheep are two stone tigers.
Northeast of the temple front is a stone camel.
Northwest of the camel are two stone horses.
All are tall and large,
and not severely damaged.
Only the temple structure has collapsed,
leaving behind rough remnants of the walls.
The stone drums still remain,
but the battle-axes are now nowhere to be found.
The Suī River flows south of the city,
accumulating to form the Fénghóng Pond.
Southwest of this pond is another pond.
Further east, it merges with the Míng River,
which originates from a large pond south of the city.
This pond spans a thousand paces in circumference.
Flowing south, it meets the Suī River and is called the Míng River.
It then cuts through the Suī River and flows into the Huàn River.
The Suī River continues southeast,
passing through a bamboo garden.
Along the banks, green bamboo shades the islets,
lush and verdant, a truly splendid sight.
People say this is the bamboo garden of the King of Liáng.
The Suī River then flows east past the old city of Gǔshú County to the north.
The Suī River continues east,
where the Qí River branches off.
The Suī River then flows east past the old city of Sù County to the north.
The *Geographical Records* state:
It was a marquisate.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Chéngfù.
The Suī River then flows east past the old city of Tàiqiū County to the north.
The *Geographical Records* state:
It was formerly called Jìngqiū.
In the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn dynasty,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate to Liú Zhèng, the Jié Marquis and son of Lǔ Gōngwáng.
Emperor Míng of the Hàn later changed it to its current name.
The *Biographies of Immortals* states:
The immortal Wén Bīn,
a native of this town,
made a living selling boots and shoes.
On the first day of the first lunar month, he met an old woman at the western shrine of the village pavilion,
who taught him the methods of immortality through diet and practices.
This is the very place.
The Suī River then flows east past the old city of Máng County to the north.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn dynasty,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate to Ér Zhí.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhuànzhì.
Emperor Shìzǔ later changed it to Línsuī.
Two lǐ west of the city,
south of the river, stands the stele of Huáng Yù, an Attendant Officer of Yùzhōu.
He died while serving under the Provincial Governor,
a victim of the crimes of Yīn Jūn.
He was twenty-five years old at the time.
Lǐ Jūn, the Magistrate of Línsuī from Píngyú,
along with the two-thousand-dan Assistant Xià Wénzé of Lúnshì, admired his conduct and mourned his death.
The province and state lamented,
honoring his gate and marking his tomb,
to illuminate his fine virtues
and serve as an example for later generations.
Inside the city stands the stele of Wáng Jūn, the Magistrate of Línsuī from Zuǒfěngyì.
He excelled in governance and achieved merit,
eventually rising to the position of Commandant of Guànghàn Dependent State.
Officials and people cherished his virtue.
Chén Shèngsūn, a Clerk in the Prefectural Office and a native of the county,
along with Ér Dìngxīng and Liú Bólí, both Gentlemen of the Palace,
jointly erected a stone to record his governance,
to preserve his distant achievements.
North of the county, it shares a watershed with Dàng County,
where Mount Dàng is located.
Between Máng and Dàng counties,
the mountains and marshes are deep and secure,
harboring much divine wisdom.
Immortals such as Juānzǐ and Zhǔzhù
both secluded themselves in Mount Dàng and attained the Way.
Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn dynasty once hid here,
and Empress Lǚ detected his presence by observing the aura.
This is the very place.
Jīng Fáng’s *Divinations of the Changes* states:
How can one know when a worthy person is in seclusion?
The master said:
Look to the four directions. If there are often great clouds,
displaying five colors but not bringing rain,
then beneath them, a worthy person is in seclusion.
Further east, it passes south of Xiàng County,
turns and flows north of the city eastward,
reaches south of Xiāo County,
and enters a pond.
Xiàng County,
was originally territory of Sòng.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
it was made part of Sìshuǐ Commandery.
In the fourth year of Hàn Gāodì,
it was renamed Pèi Commandery,
which administered from here.
In the sixth year of the Yuánshòu era of Hàn Wǔdì,
Jū Wēng, the Guìlín Supervisor of Nányuè, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate,
called Xiāngchéng.
Wáng Mǎng changed the names,
the commandery to Wúfú,
and the county to Wúfú Tíng.
The Suī River flows east past Shímǎ Tíng,
west of which is the tomb of the former Hàn General Fúbō, Mǎ Yuán.
The Suī River again flows east past the old southern wall of Xiàng County,
which was the capital of Duke Gòng of Sòng.
Within the state's palace gardens,
there still remains the foundation of Bó Jī's Yellow Hall.
The hall caught fire one night,
and those around her said:
"My lady, please withdraw a little."
Bó Jī said:
"According to a woman's duty,
if her guardians and tutors are not present,
she does not descend from the hall at night."
Thus she perished in the fire.
This hall is the place where Bó Jī was burned to death.
West of the city is the tomb of Bó Jī.
In the past, Zhèng Hún served as Grand Administrator of Pèi Commandery,
and in Xiāo and Xiàng counties he constructed dams and weirs.
The people benefited from them,
and carved a stone to praise him,
calling them the Zhèng Dams.
The Suī River then joins on the left with the Báigōu River,
whose waters originate from the Wútóng Dam.
Beside the dam is Wútóng Mountain.
The dam's waters flow southwest,
pass east of Xiàng City and then flow south to empty into the Suī.
When the Suī is in flood, it flows north into the dam;
when the dam overflows, it flows northwest into the Suī.
Flowing in and out in a circuit,
they alternately connect and feed each other.
Therefore, the Classic has text about entering the dam.
The Suī River again flows east past the east of Língbì in Péngchéng Commandery,
flowing southeast.
The Hànshū states:
"Xiàng Yǔ defeated the King of Hàn east of Língbì,"
which is this place.
It also says,
"It connects east to the Gǔ and Sì rivers."
Fú Qián said:
"It is a river name."
Located within the boundaries of Pèi State and Xiàng, its details are unknown.
The Suī River passes Gǔshú,
where it splits into two, forming the Qí River.
Thus, where these two rivers are, branches divide,
and they are commonly referred to together.
The name Gǔ River
likely changed due to the locality.
Thus, the Gǔ River is the Suī River.
It is also said:
"When the Hàn army was defeated,
the Suī River ceased to flow because of it."
The Suī River again flows southeast past the old southern wall of Zhú County.
The Dìlǐzhì says:
"It was called Dǔ Tíng by Wáng Mǎng."
Lǐ Qí said:
"It is now Zhúyì County."
The Suī River again flows east and joins with the Bóhú River,
whose waters originate from the Pì Dam in Zīqiū County.
It is over a hundred lǐ from north to south,
and forty lǐ from east to west.
To the east it reaches Cháojiě Tíng,
to the west it borders the old eastern wall of Zīqiū County in Péngchéng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shànqiū.
Its waters from the dam connect south to the Suī River.
Further east,
south of the Suī River,
the old Bāzhàng Gōu River empties into it.
Its waters originate from the Qí River and join the Suī River from the north.
It then flows east past the old northern wall of Fúlí County.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshòu era of Hàn Wǔdì,
Lù Bódé was enfeoffed here as a marquisate,
called Fúhé by Wáng Mǎng.
The Suī River again flows east past the old northern wall of Qǔlǜ County in Línhuái Commandery.
In the past, Bù Yóuzhāng from Rǔnán lost his mother when young.
When he became County Magistrate,
he encountered his mother here.
He then made his fine horse hesitate,
and his light carriage halt,
to inquire after the sick old woman—
and it was his mother.
Truly, sincere longing lodged in the heart,
and darkly moved spirits gave clear proof.
The Suī River again flows east and joins with the Wūcí River,
which emerges from Wūcí Zhǔ southwest of the county.
Its pool swells and flows northeast,
joining with the old Chángzhí Channel.
The channel originally received water from the Qí River,
flowed north for eighty-five lǐ,
and emptied into the Wūcí River.
The Wūcí River again flows east past the south of Qǔlǜ County,
then bends east past the east of its city,
and flows north to empty into the Suī.
The Suī River again flows east past the old northern wall of Suīlíng County.
In the first year of the Yuánshuò era of Hàn Wǔdì,
Liǔ Chǔ, son of Yì, King of Jiāngdū, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate,
called Suīlù by Wáng Mǎng.
The Suī River again flows east and meets with the old channel of the Tóng River.
It originally received water from the Tóng Dam southwest of Tóng County,
flowed northeast past the old northern wall of Tóng County,
then northeast past Suīlíng County,
and below joined the Suī River.
The Suī River again flows southeast,
past the old southern wall of Xiàxiàng County.
In the twelfth year of Gāozǔ,
Marquis Zhuāng Líng Ěr was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Xiàng River emerges from Xiàng County in Pèi State,
therefore 'lower' is added here."
Thus, Xiàng is another name for the Suī River.
It flows southeast into the Sì River,
called the Suī Estuary.
The Classic stops at Xiāo County,
which is incorrect.
This is what is called grasping one but losing the other.
24.2 Hùzǐ River
24.2 Hùzǐ River
The Hùzǐ River emerges from the north of the river at Púyáng County in Dōng Commandery.
The Hù River then flows left past the north of Léizé,
which is a marsh located over ten lǐ northwest of the old city of Chéngyáng County.
This is where Huáxū once trod upon the giant footprint.
The embankment measures over twenty lǐ from east to west,
and fifteen lǐ from north to south.
It is where Shùn fished.
Southeast of the marsh lies Chéngyáng County,
hence the Records of the Grand Historian states:
King Wǔ enfeoffed his younger brother Shūwǔ at Chéng.
Yìng Shào said:
Later, it was moved to the north of Chéng,
hence it was called Chéngyáng.
The Treatise on Geography says:
Chéngyáng has Yáo’s tomb and the Língtái.
Now, two lǐ west of Chéngyáng City is Yáo’s mausoleum.
One lǐ south of the mausoleum is the tomb of Yáo’s mother, Qìngdū.
Relative to the city, it lies to the southwest.
It is called Língtái.
The township is called Chóngrén,
and the settlement is named Xiūyì.
Temples have been erected at both sites.
Water surrounds them on all sides,
forming deep pools that do not flow.
The marsh connects to springs,
and the springs never dry up.
Fish and bamboo shoots are abundant,
but people dare not catch or gather them.
In front, several stone steles stand in a row.
There are several cypress and juniper trees,
and sandalwood and horse-chestnut trees form a grove.
The two mausoleums lie north and south of each other.
A straight imperial road runs between them,
paved with bricks,
and is still well-maintained.
Over fifty paces east of Yáo’s mausoleum and west of the city is the temple of the Lady of Zhōngshān,
who was Yáo’s consort.
The stone walls and steps remain as before.
To the south, west, and north,
tall oaks form a continuous shade,
spreading densely for over a lǐ.
South of the Lady of Zhōngshān’s temple is the tomb of Zhòngshānfǔ.
West of the tomb is a stone shrine,
with stone sheep and tigers tilting and low,
mostly broken and nearly destroyed.
Relative to the city, it lies to the southwest,
northeast of the Língtái.
According to Guō Yuánshēng’s Account of a Journey,
from the Hàn to the Jìn dynasties,
many officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank, as well as assistants and commanders,
inscribed stones with narratives.
From Yáo’s accession to the third year of Yǒngjiā,
a total of 2,721 years,
is recorded at Yáo’s consort’s temple,
as seen on a stele erected in the fifth month of the fifth year of Jiànníng of the Hàn,
by Guǎn Zūn, the magistrate of Chéngyáng.
North of Yáo’s mausoleum and south of Zhòngshānfǔ’s tomb,
between the two tombs, there was a temple for Wǔ Yuán,
established during the Tài’ān era of the Jìn.
One stele was erected during the Yǒngxīng era,
but now both the stele and the temple are gone.
It is also said that Yáo’s mausoleum is nine lǐ south of the city,
the Lady of Zhōngshān’s temple is two lǐ south of the city,
and six lǐ southeast,
is the tomb of Yáo’s mother, Qìngdū.
Two lǐ north of Yáo’s mausoleum is the tomb of Zhòngshānfǔ.
Examining the geography and verifying the descriptions,
these accounts are all inaccurate,
likely based on hearsay and dubious records.
About ten lǐ southwest of Léizé is a small hill,
standing alone and steep,
tall and majestic,
called Lìshān.
North of the hill is a small mound,
extending south to the northeast of the marsh.
There is Táoxū,
as Yuánshēng said:
This is where Shùn farmed and made pottery.
The mound and the ruins are connected,
bordering the Hù River.
Zhèng Xuán said:
Lìshān is in Hédōng,
and now there is Shùn’s well.
Huángfǔ Mì said that the present Lìshān in Jìyīn is the same.
It is adjacent to Léizé.
I believe Zhèng Xuán’s statement is correct.
Thus, Yáng Xióng’s Ode to the Hé River says:
Ascending Lìguān and gazing afar,
I wander along the banks of the river.
Now, Léishǒu Mountain lies to the west, resting against the great river.
Comparing it with maps and texts, this seems accurate.
Shì’ān also said:
Táoqiū southwest of Dìngtáo
is where Shùn made pottery.
He did not say it was here,
so Yuánshēng was mistaken.
North of the Hù River is Lǐnqiū County.
Wáng Yǐn’s Records of the Jìn Dynasty Geography says:
Lǐnqiū
is the Qí settlement mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
marking the eastern border.
The Bamboo Annals records:
In the eleventh year of Duke Liè of Jìn,
Tián Dàozǐ died.
Tián Bù killed his senior official Gōngsūn Sūn,
and Gōngsūn Huì rebelled against Zhào with Lǐnqiū.
Tián Bù besieged Lǐnqiū.
Zhái Jiǎo, Zhào Kǒngxiè, and Hán’s army came to rescue Lǐnqiū,
and fought Tián Bù at Lóngzé,
where Tián’s army was defeated and fled.
The Hù River and the Pú River flow east together.
This is what the Classic means by “passing Lǐnqiū to become the Pú River.”
South of the county and north of the Hù River is Yángjiǎo City.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
Wū Yú took Wèi’s Yángjiǎo and then attacked our Gāoyú.
Heavy rain entered through a hole,
flooding the armory.
They climbed the city wall,
captured it, and took the city.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
It is a Wèi settlement.
Now, south of Lǐnqiū County in Dōngjùn is Yángjiǎo City.
Gāoyú
is a Lǔ settlement.
Now, northeast of Lǐnqiū is the old Gāoyú City,
commonly called Jiāoyú City,
and Yángjiǎo is called Jiāozhú City,
but these names are incorrect.
The Hù River then passes south of Yángjìn City.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Sū Qín advised Qí, saying:
Passing through Wèi’s Yángjìn road,
one traverses the perilous Kàngfù.
Now, Yángjìn City is over ten lǐ southeast of Lǐnqiū City,
flanking Dūguān on both sides.
Zhāng Yí said:
If Qín sends troops to attack Wèi’s Yángjìn,
it will block the world’s vital passage.
Xú Guǎng’s Pronunciation and Meaning of the Records of the Grand Historian says:
“Block” could also be read as “open.”
To the east lies Kàngfù,
which is the route.
North of the Hù River is also Chéngdū City.
In the fifth year of Duke Yǐn of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Chéng invaded Wèi.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Thirty lǐ south of Lǐnqiū County in Dōngjùn is the old city of Chéngdū.
Master Chǔ said:
During the Hàn, Jīn Ānshàng was enfeoffed here as a marquis,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Chénggǔ.
The Hù River then flows east past the old city of Lí County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Lízhì.
Mèng Kāng said:
It is now Líyáng.
Xué Zàn said:
According to records, Líyáng is in Wèijùn,
not Lí County.
It is commonly called the city of the Marquis of Lí.
In the past, Lí took refuge in Wèi.
As the Book of Songs says, “Why are you in the mud?”
Máo’s commentary says:
“In the mud”
is the name of a settlement,
likely referring to this city.
The land is low and muddy,
but the city sits on a small mound.
It was the seat of the Wèi Púyáng Commandery.
The Hù River then flows east past the old city of Chú County.
The Treatise on Geography says:
It is a county under Jìyīn.
Master Chǔ said:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Jīn Mìdī here as a marquis.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wànsuì,
and it is still called Wànsuì Pavilion.
The Hù River then flows east past the south of Yùn City.
The Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals, sixteenth year of Duke Chéng, says:
The duke returned from Shāsuí
and waited at Yùn.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
The Gongyang Commentary writes it as “Yùn.”
Now, eighty lǐ east of Lǐnqiū County in Dōngjùn is the old Yùn City,
which is this city.
Further north, it passes northeast of Fàn County in Dōngjùn,
becoming the Jì Canal,
and joins with the Jiāng Canal.
The Hù River flows northeast from Yùnchéng,
passing by Fàn County and merging with a branch channel of the Jǐ and Pú Rivers.
This old channel originates from the Jǐ River at Chéngshì County,
flows north past Fàn County,
and receives the Hù River from the left.
Therefore, the Classic refers to it as the Jǐ Channel.
Further north, it joins the Jiāng Channel.
The Jiāng Channel receives water from the Yellow River northwest of Fàn County,
flows southeast past the south of Qín Pavilion.
Dù Yù's Explanation of Geography states:
"Northwest of Fàn County in Dōngpíng is Qín Pavilion."
It then flows southeast past the old city of Fàn County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jiànmù.
During the Xīngpíng era of the Hàn,
Jìn Yǔn served as Magistrate of Fàn.
When Cáo Tàizǔ campaigned east against Táo Qiān in Xúzhōu,
Zhāng Miǎo welcomed Lǚ Bù,
and commanderies and counties responded in support.
Chéng Yù persuaded Jìn Yǔn, saying:
"You must firmly hold Fàn,
while I guard Dōng'ē.
Then the achievements of Tián Dān can be established."
This refers to this very city.
The Jiāng Channel then flows east to meet the Jǐ Channel.
From this point onward, it is commonly called the Jiāng Channel.
It flows north past the east of Fàn City.
Vulgarly, it is also called Zhào Ditch,
but this is incorrect.
Further northeast, it passes east of Dōng'ē County.
The old course of the Hù River flows northeast and joins a branch of the Jiāng Channel from the left.
This branch originates from the Jiāng Channel at Fàn County,
flows northeast past the north of Fàn County,
then northeast past the south of Dōng'ē City,
and enters the old course of the Hù River from the east.
Further north, it passes east of the old city of Dōng'ē County.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records: "In winter, [the Duke of Lǔ] made a covenant with the Marquis of Qí at Kē."
The Zuǒ Tradition states:
"In winter, they made a covenant at Kē,
beginning peace with Qí."
Dù Yù said:
"Dōng'ē is the city of Kē."
According to the Discourses of the States,
Cáo Mò held a dagger against Duke Huán of Qí to force his compliance,
and subsequently was enfeoffed with this city.
Further northeast, it passes west of Línyì County.
Further northeast, it passes east of Chípíng County,
becoming the Dènglǐ Channel.
From below Xuānfáng
to above the Jiāng Channel,
there is no longer any water.
The water of the Jiāng Channel
first receives from the Yellow River,
and from the north becomes the Dènglǐ Channel.
Further northeast, it passes Zhù'ē County,
becoming the Jǐ Channel.
The river water emerges from the Sìdú mouth as the Jǐ River.
The two channels of the Jǐ River converge and flow east into Zhù'ē.
Further northeast, it reaches west of Liángzōu County,
where it divides into two:
Tracing the watercourse to Liángzōu,
the Jǐ River has no two streams;
this is likely an error in the Classic.
The northeastern branch is the Jǐ River,
and the eastern branch is the Shí River.
Further northeast, it reaches west of Jǐ.
The Jǐ River flows northeast into the sea.
The Shí River flows east to west of Línzī County,
bends south past east of Huà County in Tàishān,
then south to Fèi County,
and enters the Yí River from the east.
Shí
is the Ér River,
pronounced "ér".
In the third year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Qí and Jìn made a covenant at Ér.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Now in Línzī, there is only the Huà River,
which flows northwest into the Jǐ."
This is the Rú River mentioned in the Treatise on Geography.
Ér and Rú sound similar;
thus, the Huà River is the Ér River.
Since Huà and Shí merge,
they share the name.
The Shí River divides into two streams southwest of Xī'ān City.
A branch diverges,
flows west,
and receives the Déhuì River.
The Déhuì River originates from Huáng Mountain in Chāngguó County,
flows northwest past the old city of Chāngguó County.
In the past, Yuè Yì attacked Qí
and rendered meritorious service to King Zhāo of Yān,
who enfeoffed him with this county,
making him Lord of Chāngguó.
The Déhuì River flows further northwest,
and the Wǔlǐ Spring joins it.
The spring originates from Huáng Hill south of the county,
flows north past the west of the city,
enters the Déhuì River from the north,
then continues northwest.
It is commonly called the Cāngláng Ditch.
Further north, it flows into the Shí River.
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The Déhuì River originates northwest of Chāngguó,
and flows to Xī'ān, entering the Rú River."
The Shí River then flows west through Dōng Gāoyuàn City and continues west.
Common people diverted it to flow south of the city,
then it bends past the south of the city.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
In the fifteenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Qí was divided to form the Jiāoxī Kingdom,
with its capital at Gāoyuàn.
Xú Guǎng's Pronunciation and Meaning states:
"Lè'ān has the city of Gāoyuàn,
hence it is commonly called Dōng Gāoyuàn."
The water then flows north into the old channel,
continues west,
and receives the Gàiyě Ditch.
Its source arises northeast of Yánxiāng City,
emerging as a spring from level ground,
and flows northwest past the north of Yánxiāng City.
The Treatise on Geography states:
Qiānchéng had Yánxiāng County.
People call the old city Cóng City.
Yán and Cóng characters are similar;
the reading changed with the character,
but the details are unclear.
It flows northwest,
commonly called Gàiyě Ditch,
continues northwest,
passes north of Gāoyuàn County, and enters the Shí River.
The Shí River then flows west past the old city of Xī Gāoyuàn County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Bǐng Qiàn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It was called Chángxiāng under Wáng Mǎng.
The water flows west of the city.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Now in the southern boundary of Bóchāng County in Lè'ān, there is the Shí River,
which connects west to the Jǐ.
Its source originates from Pányáng,
flows north to Gāoyuàn,
and below there is the dead Shí,
where the middle section has no water."
Dù Yù also said:
"The Shí River in Lè'ān
has branches that dry up in drought,
which is the 'dry Shí' of the Spring and Autumn Annals."
The Zuǒ Tradition, ninth year of Duke Zhuāng: the battlefield of Qí and Lǔ,
where the Lǔ army was defeated.
The Shí River flows northwest to Liángzōu City and enters the Jǐ River.
It is not the Jǐ entering the Shí;
rather, the Shí comes to join the Jǐ.
If the Jǐ divided and flowed east,
clearly it could not be named Shí.
Investigating the Shí and Jǐ, there are no other streams extending south to Huà and Fèi.
This is an error.
24.3 Wèn River
24.3 Wèn River
The Wèn River originates from Yuán Mountain in Láiwú County of Tàishān,
and flows southwest past the south of the county.
Láiwú County lies southwest of the Qí capital city,
and Yuán Mountain is further southwest of the county, about sixty lǐ away.
According to the *Geographical Records*,
both the Wèn River and the Zī River originate from Yuán Mountain,
flowing southwest into the Jì River.
Therefore, it cannot pass south of this county.
The *Record of Campaigns* states:
The Wèn River emerges from the county and flows southwest;
it also says that upon entering the Láiwú Valley,
the road is flanked by continuous mountains for over a hundred lǐ,
with the riverbed often running through rocky gorges.
Medicinal herbs grow here,
pines and cypresses abound,
forests and thickets stretch densely,
cliffs and precipices face each other,
sometimes steep peaks block the path,
sometimes winding cliffs cut off the valley.
Clear winds rustle through the branches,
echoing through the mountain ravines.
Ascending heights and descending depths,
one feels both awe and trepidation;
perilous trails and broken paths
present the hardship of crossing suspended routes.
Before exiting the valley for over ten lǐ,
there is a separate valley on a solitary mountain.
The valley has a clear spring,
and several zhàng above the spring are two stone openings,
large enough for a person to pass through.
Entering the openings for over a zhàng,
the height is about nine chǐ,
and the width is four or five zhàng.
It is said this was where people lived in the mountains in ancient times,
and traces of firewood ashes and soot still remain.
The valley’s forests are dense,
and few travelers can reach it.
There are also some small mountain fields,
with traces of irrigation channels still visible.
Exiting the valley, there is a flat hill,
facing the mountains and beside the water.
The local people all grow wheat here,
saying this hill is unsuitable for millet or broomcorn millet but ideal for wheat.
The people of Qí have passed down this practice for generations.
It is believed this is the Màiqīu where the Foolish Old Man’s Valley is located.
How deep, secluded, and shaded it is,
a place where one can settle and live contentedly!
When I passed through here,
I lingered in contemplation,
turning back to gaze repeatedly.
I note that Màiqīu and the Foolish Old Man are still remembered in the valleys of Qí,
not in Lǔ.
This is likely an error by the recorders.
The Wèn River then flows southwest past the old city of Yíng County.
According to the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*, in the third year of Duke Huán,
the duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Yíng,
and the marriage alliance with Qí was concluded.
Further southwest, it passes north of Fènggāo County.
Fènggāo County
was established in the first year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
to oversee sacrifices to Mount Tài,
and it served as the seat of Tàishān Commandery.
North of the county is the tomb of Wú Jìzhá’s son,
located in a southern bend of the Wèn River.
When Jìzhá was on a diplomatic mission to the central states,
his son died between Yíng and Bó,
which is this very place.
The *Record of Campaigns* states:
Sixty lǐ west of Yíng County,
there is the tomb of Jìzhá’s son.
The tomb is round,
and its height is such that one can hide behind it.
In front, there is a stone inscription,
erected by the Magistrate of Fènggāo during the late Hàn dynasty.
It contains no narrative,
serving only as a marker.
In the past, local households were regularly assigned to clean it,
but this is no longer done.
The stone tablet has crumbled,
leaving nothing behind,
only the old pedestal remains.
The river bends and flows southwest from the county.
The Wèn River emerges from beneath the southwestern mound of the old city of Mù County,
commonly called Húlú Duī.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The Wèn emerges from Fúqí."
Gāo Yòu notes:
"It is a mountain name."
Perhaps this is the mound.
The old city of Mù County lies to the northeast,
the ancient state of Mù.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the people of Mù paid court to Lǔ,
thus Yìng Shào said:
"It was a dependency of Lǔ."
Commonly, this water is called the Mùwèn.
It then flows southwest past the west of the old city of Fènggāo County,
and flows southwest to join the Wèn River.
The Wèn River flows further south,
and on the right joins the Běiwèn River.
This water emerges from the Fēnshuǐ Stream,
its source dividing the waters from Zhōngchuān.
It flows southeast past the east of Mount Tài,
and on the right joins the water from the stream below Tiānmén.
This water emerges from the valley below Tiānmén on Mount Tài,
flowing east.
In ancient times,
when emperors ascended to perform the fēng sacrifice,
they all rested by this water.
On the water, stone holes often remain,
likely places where lodgings were built and crossed in ancient times.
The Shū of Mǎ Dìbó states:
"When Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
Dìbó followed him up the mountain.
Twenty lǐ from level ground,
looking south to the extreme distance,
nothing was unseen:
Its height
was like gazing at floating clouds;
its steepness,
with stone cliffs deep and cavernous,
as if there were no path.
Gazing from afar at the people,
some appeared as white stones,
or as snow.
After a long while,
the white things moved past,
and then one knew they were people.
Looking up at the cliffs, rocks, and pine trees,
lush and verdant,
as if amidst clouds;
looking down at the streams and valleys,
they appeared indistinct, unable to be measured in zhǎng or chǐ.
Ascending directly seven lǐ to Tiānmén,
and looking up at Tiānmén,
it was like viewing the sky from within a cave."
Yìng Shào's Hàn Guān Yí states:
"The mountaintop southeast of Mount Tài,
is named Rìguān.
The Rìguān
is where at the first crow of the cock, one sees the sun,
just beginning to emerge,
about three zhàng long,
hence it is so named."
This water flows east from the stream,
with surging waves pouring into the ravine,
flowing southeast,
passing through the fields of Guīyīn.
Mount Guī is fifteen lǐ north of Bó County.
In the past, the Master grieved over the decline of governance,
and gazing upon the mountain, cherished his integrity;
thus the Qín Cǎo contains the "Guī Shān Cǎo."
North of the mountain are the fields of Guīyīn.
In the tenth year of Duke Dìng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the men of Qí came to return the fields of Guīyīn—this is it.
It further joins the Huán River.
This water emerges from the southern stream of Mount Tài,
flowing south past between the Middle and Lower Temples.
The Cóngzhēng Jì states:
"Mount Tài has three temples: Lower, Middle, and Upper.
Their walls and gate towers are stern and orderly.
Within the temples, cypress trees flank both sides of the steps,
over twenty arm-spans in girth,
likely planted by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The Chìméi once chopped one tree,
and upon seeing blood, stopped;
the axe marks remain to this day.
The gates and towers are triple-layered,
with four pavilions and terraces,
and one three-tiered altar,
over one zhàng high,
eight chǐ wide.
Before the trees is a large well,
extremely fragrant and cold,
different from ordinary water.
It is unknown in which era it was dug,
yet though not regularly dredged, it neither decreases in drought nor increases in flood.
In the storehouse are ancient musical instruments from the Hàn period, as well as divine chariots and wooden figures,
all exquisitely crafted and beautiful.
There is also a golden horse, one pǐ, presented by Zhāng Yú, Marquis of Yǒngguì, in the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ of the Shí Hǔ period,
over two chǐ high,
its form and craftsmanship very fine.
The Middle Temple is five lǐ from the Lower Temple,
its buildings even more lofty and splendid
than the Lower Temple.
The temple is flanked east and west by ravines.
The Upper Temple is at the mountaintop,
the very place of the fēng and shàn sacrifices."
This water then bends and flows east,
and further southeast passes below the Míngtáng.
In the first year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
after performing the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài and descending,
he sat in the Míngtáng at the northeastern base of the mountain.
Emperor Wǔ considered the ancient site perilous, narrow, and inconspicuous,
and wished to build a Míngtáng beside Fènggāo but did not understand its design.
Gōngyù Dài of Jǐnán presented the Míngtáng Tú from the time of the Yellow Emperor.
In the drawing was a hall,
with no walls on four sides,
thatched roof,
with water channeled through,
a circular palace wall with a covered walkway,
above which was a tower entered from the southwest,
named Kūnlún.
The Son of Heaven entered from there,
to worship and sacrifice to the Supreme Deity.
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered Fènggāo to build a Míngtáng on the Wèn River,
according to Dài's drawing.
The ancient place where water was channeled for the Bìyōng,
its watercourse remains,
and the world calls this water the Shíwèn.
