The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"The Huán River emerges from Mount Tài,
flowing east to join the Wèn."
This is that water.
The Huán River then enters from the left into the Wèn River.
The Wèn River, receiving the confluence of several streams,
flows further southwest past the west of Mount Cúlái.
The mountain has many pines and cypresses,
the "pines of Cúlái" mentioned in the Shī.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
"Dàozǐ is a pine."
The Bàopǔzǐ, citing the Yùcè Jì, states:
"In pines a thousand years old,
there are creatures,
some like green oxen,
some like green dogs,
some like humans,
all living ten thousand years."
It also states that on Tiānlíng there are pines with reclining canopies,
the so-called 'tower pines.'
The Lǔliánzǐ states:
"Pines and firs are ten rèn high without branches,
not because they worry the main hall lacks pillars."
The Ěryǎ states:
"With pine needles and cypress trunk, it is called cōng."
The Zōushān Jì states:
"Mount Cúlái lies within the boundaries of Liángfǔ, Fènggāo, and Bó counties.
It still has fine pines,
and is also called Mount Yóulái.
It was the stronghold of Fán Chóng, leader of the Chìméi,
hence Chóng styled himself the Elder of Yóulái."
East of the mountain is the temple of Cháofù.
The mountain is ten lǐ high.
Below the mountain is a pond,
about a hundred paces square,
with three channels flowing into it.
One water flows northeast along the stream downward,
bends past the south of the county,
and flows northwest into the Wèn;
one water flows north through the ravine,
and flows west into the Wèn;
one water flows south past the south of Yángguān Pavilion.
In the seventeenth year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
it was where Zāng Hé was met from Yángguān.
It then flows west into the Wèn River.
It passes northwest of Bó County.
The Wèn River flows south past the east of the old city of Bó County.
In the eleventh year of Duke Āi in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
it records the meeting with Wú to attack Qí and capture Bó.
Guàn Yīng defeated Tián Héng beneath the city walls.
The river bends, following the south of the city and flowing westward,
not to the northwest.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the old city of Lóngxiāng to the south.
In the second year of Duke Chéng in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Marquis of Qí besieged Lóng.
The people of Lóng imprisoned Lú Pú Jiùkuí, a favorite of Duke Qǐng,
killed him, and exposed his body on the city walls.
The Marquis of Qí personally beat the drums to capture Lóng.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
the herald Chén Shǔ was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the east of Tíngtíng Mountain,
where the Yellow Emperor performed the shàn sacrifice.
The mountain has a temple to the gods,
and on the water there is a stone gate,
formerly the point where the water was divided for irrigation.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the west of the old city of Yángguān,
originally the Yángguān post station of Jùpíng County.
Yáng Hǔ occupied it to rebel,
and when attacked,
he burned the Lái Gate and fled to Qí.
The Wèn River again flows south,
where on the left it meets the Zī River.
The Zī River originates east of Liángfù County of Tàishān,
flowing southwest past the north of Tùqiú City.
In the eleventh year of Duke Yǐn in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, it was built,
and the duke said to Yǔfǔ:
"I shall retire there in my old age."
Therefore, the *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
"Liángfù has the settlement of Tùqiú."
The Zī River again flows past the south of the old city of Liángfù County,
north of which is Liángfù Mountain.
The *Kāishān Tú* says:
"Tàishān is on the left,
Kàngfù is on the right.
Kàngfù governs life,
Liángfù governs death."
When the king fēngsacrificed at Tàishān,
he performed the shàn sacrifice at Liángfù,
hence the county takes its name from this.
The Zī River again flows southwest past the north of the old city of Chái County.
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
it is a subordinate county of Tàishān,
commonly called Cháiwèn.
The Zī River again flows past the north of Chéng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Dǒng Xiè was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the army of Qí besieged Chéng,
and the people of Chéng attacked Qí,
watering their horses at this river.
Once, Confucius was traveling in the wilderness of Chéng,
and there he met Róng Qǐqí.
Wearing a deerskin robe,
with disheveled hair,
playing the qín and singing,
he expressed the joy of three happinesses.
The Master praised his ability to be content.
The Zī River again flows west past the south of Yángguān City,
then flows westward into the Wèn River.
The Wèn River again flows south past the east of the old city of Jùpíng County,
then flows southwest.
East of the city is the Lǔ Road,
mentioned in the *Book of Songs* as "the Lǔ Road is broad and smooth,
by which the lady of Qí returns."
Now, on both banks of the Wèn River, there is the Wén Jiāng Terrace.
The Wèn River again flows southwest.
The *Book of Songs* says, "The Wèn River flows on and on."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"When a raccoon dog crosses the Wèn River, it dies."
The nature of heaven and earth,
with its hidden complexities, is difficult to fathom,
and indeed cannot be exhausted by reason or principle.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the north of Wènyáng County of the State of Lǔ.
It was called Wèntíng under Wáng Mǎng.
North of the county is the Qūshuǐ Pavilion.
In the twelfth year of Duke Huán in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the *Classic* records the duke meeting with the Marquis of Qǐ and the Viscount of Jǔ,
forming an alliance at Qūchí.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"To make peace between Qǐ and Jǔ."
Therefore, Dù Yù said:
"North of Wènyáng in the State of Lǔ is the Qūshuǐ Pavilion."
In the second year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāngdì of Hàn,
during his eastern tour of Tàishān,
he established a traveling palace at Wènyáng.
Gěng Gōng, the Commandant of the Capital, stationed troops at Wènshàng.
The foundations and moats of the city gates remain,
commonly called Quèlíng City.
The Wèn River again flows west past the north of the old city of Wènyáng County and flows westward.
Further southwest, it passes south of Shéqiū County.
The Wèn River again flows west,
where the Guāng River flows into it.
It again flows west past the south of Shéqiū County.
The county has the city of Zhùxiāng.
In the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*,
it is recorded that Xuānshū married a woman from Zhù.
Dù Yù said:
"It is the Zhùxiāng City, the seat of Shéqiū County in Jìběi."
Further southwest, it passes north of Gāng County.
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
Gāng
was formerly Chǎn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Róu.
Yīng Shào said:
"The *Spring and Autumn Classic* records the people of Qí capturing Huān and Chǎn,
and now the Chǎn Pavilion is here."
Dù Yù's *Explanations of Places in the Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
"Chǎn is north of Gāng County.
East of Gāng City is a small pavilion,
which is now the seat of Gāng County.
Common people also call it the Chǎn Pavilion."
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Forty lǐ west of Gāng County is the Chǎn Pavilion."
It is unknown which is correct.
The Wèn River again flows west,
where the Shé River flows into it.
The Shé River originates from Tàishān northeast of the county,
flowing southwest through the fields of Wènyáng,
which were encroached upon by Qí.
North of the Wèn River,
the land is flat and open as far as the eye can see.
Duke Xī granted it to Jì Yǒu.
The Shé River again flows southwest past the west of Zhù City.
This is the so-called Shéyuān Park in the *Zuǒzhuàn*.
Therefore, Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Now in Jìběi, there is Shéqiū City.
Below the city is water,
which is the park of Lǔ."
Commonly called Zhuóxū Water,
but this is incorrect.
The Shé River again flows southwest past the south of Xiàhuān City.
The *Classic* records the duke meeting with the Marquis of Qí at Xiàhuān.
Now commonly called Xiàhuān City.
Probably in the third year of Duke Huán in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒzhuàn*,
Prince Huī went to Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí escorted Lady Jiāng to Xiàhuān.
This was against ritual.
Hence, the name Xiàhuān has been passed down.
The Shé River again flows southwest into the Wèn River.
The Wèn River again flows west,
where the Gōu River flows into it.
The Gōu River originates from Mǎ Mountain in the northeast,
flowing southwest past the south of Jí Pavilion.
In the third year of Duke Chéng in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the *Classic* records that in autumn, Shūsūn Qiáorú led troops to besiege Jí.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"When taking the fields of Wènyáng,
Jí did not submit,
so it was besieged."
It is eighty lǐ south of the Wèn River.
It again flows southwest past the east of Suì City.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
"The Suì Township of Shéqiū
was formerly the State of Suì."
In the thirteenth year of Duke Zhuāng in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Qí destroyed Suì and garrisoned it.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"Suì is ten lǐ northeast of Shéqiū."
Dù Yù also believed this.
However, there is no city northeast of the county to match this.
Now, the city is northwest of Shéqiū.
Probably Dù Yù's transmission of doubt is incorrect.
It again flows west past the west of Xiàhuān City and enters the Wèn River.
The Wèn River again flows west past the north of Chūn Pavilion.
Examining antiquity, there is no name "Chūn."
Only Pínglù County has a Chóngyáng Pavilion.
However, this pavilion is forty lǐ east of Gāng City.
Comparing with Fán's annotations, it matches,
but the details are unclear.
Further southwest, it passes south of Zhāng County of Dōngpíng.
The Treatise on Geography states:
Dōngpíng State,
was formerly Liáng.
In the sixth year of the middle period of Emperor Jǐng's reign,
it was separately established as Jìdōng State.
In the first year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ,
it became Dàhé Commandery.
In the second year of the Gānlù era of Emperor Xuān,
it became Dōngpíng State,
which Wáng Mǎng called Yǒuyán.
Zhāng County,
according to the Shìběn, was a state of the Rén surname.
It was where the people of Qí surrendered Zhāng.
Its old city was fifty lǐ northeast of Wúyán County.
The Wèn River again flows southwest,
where the Mì River flows into it.
The water emerges from the White Plain east of Féichéng County,
and flows southwest past the old city of Féichéng County.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said to his disciples:
"When you go to Qí and pass Féi,
there are gentlemen in Féi."
To the left, it passes north of the Gōuyǔ Pavilion.
In the second year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng,
phoenixes gathered at the Gōuyǔ Pavilion in Féichéng.
[The emperor] exempted their taxes and toured Tàishān.
This is that pavilion.
The Mì River again flows southwest past the old city of Fùchéng County to the west,
which Wáng Mǎng called Chéngfù.
Its waters again flow southwest and empty into the Wèn.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the old city of Táoxiāng County to the west,
which Wáng Mǎng called Zhàngtíng.
People of the time considered this to be Zhàng City,
but it is not.
It was probably due to the old name of Jùxīn.
It again flows southwest past the south of Wúyán County,
again flows southwest past the north of Shòuzhāng County,
again flows southwest to the Ānmín Pavilion,
and enters the Jì.
The Wèn River divides into four branches at Táoxiāng.
At the place where the streams separate,
it is called the Sìwènkǒu.
On its left,
two waters flow side by side,
southwest to the south of the Hòuxiāng city wall in Wúyán County,
the old fief of Hòu Zhāobó.
Disaster arose from cockfighting.
The Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals, the twelfth year of Duke Dìng,
states: "The Shūsūn clan razed Hòu."
Today, that city has no southern wall.
The Wèn River again flows southwest past the north of the old city of Dōngpínglù County.
Yìng Shào said:
"It was the ancient state of Jué."
Today, there is a Jué Pavilion.
The Wèn River again flows west past the south of Wēishān,
which people call Lóngshān.
The "Biographies of the Six Kings of Emperors Xuān and Yuán" in the Hànshū states:
During the time of Emperor Āi,
the earth of Wēishān in Wúyán spontaneously rose up,
covering the grass in the manner of an imperial highway.
Also, the stones of Húshān turned and stood upright.
Jìn Zhuó said:
"The Hànzhù writes it as Bàoshān.
A single stone from the mountain's flank,
turned and stood upright,
nine chǐ and six cùn high,
with a side length of one zhàng and a width of four chǐ."
King Dōngpíng Yún and his consort Yè said:
"The Han dynasty stone standing upright
is an omen of Emperor Xuān's rise."
They went themselves to the stone's location to sacrifice,
fashioned a stone image,
erected a stone at Bàoshān,
doubled the grass offerings to the east,
and performed joint sacrifices there.
In the third year of the Jiànpíng era,
Xīfū Gōng reported them.
The king committed suicide,
Consort Yè was executed in the marketplace,
and the state was abolished.
The Wèn River again flows west,
converges into a single watercourse,
and flows southwest into the Màodū Diàn.
Diàn
is another name for a marsh.
The water of the diàn flows out to the southwest,
called the Jùyě Ditch.
It again flows southwest past the south of Zhìmì City.
The Treatise on Commanderies and States states:
"Xūchāng County has Zhìmì City,
the ancient Zhōngdū."
This was the district where the Master served as magistrate.
He established regulations for nurturing the living and sending off the dead,
and rituals for elders and youth, men and women.
Lost articles were not picked up on the road,
and utensils were not elaborately decorated or fake.
The Jùyě Ditch again flows southwest and enters north of the Huángōng River.
The water emerges from the diàn to the west,
called the Jùliáng Water.
It flows southwest past the north of Zhìmì City,
then flows southwest and empties into the Hóngdú.
The next Wèn branch flows west past the north of the Hòu Pavilion,
and again west to the east of the old city of Shòuzhāng,
where it forms a marsh and islet.
In the third year of the Chūpíng era,
Lord Cáo attacked the Yellow Turbans east of Shòuzhāng.
Bào Xìn died in battle here.
The rightmost Wèn branch
flows west past the south of the old city of Wúyán County,
the old state of Sù.
It was the old fief of Queen Xuān of Qí,
the so-called ugly woman of Wúyán.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Qìng, son of the Gong King of Chéngyáng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngpíng,
which was this district.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yǒuyán Pavilion.
The Wèn River again flows west past the south of the Hòuxiāng city wall.
This is what the Treatise on Geography calls "Wúyán having Hòuxiāng."
The Wèn River flows southwest,
past the north of the old city of Shòuzhāng County.
This was the Liáng district of the Spring and Autumn period.
The district had a Shòu settlement,
called Shòuliáng in Hàn times.
Yìng Shào said:
"The world-honoring emperor's [Emperor Guāngwǔ's] paternal uncle was named Liáng,
therefore Emperor Guāngwǔ changed it to Shòuzhāng."
In the twelfth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the world-honoring emperor enfeoffed Fán Hóng as a marquis in this state.
The Wèn River again flows southwest,
where the Chángzhí Ditch water flows into it.
The water emerges from south of Gǔyáng Mountain northeast of Xūchāng City.
It passes east of Xūchāng City,
and again south,
where the Qī Ditch water flows into it.
The water emerges from five lǐ northeast of Wúyán City at the foot of Fù Mountain,
flows west past the north of the old city of Wúyán County.
Beside the water is the tomb mound of King Xiàn of Dōngpíng, Cāng,
with stele and towers still extant.
In the second year of the Yuánhé era,
Emperor Zhāng visited Dōngpíng,
sacrificed with the Great Tàiláo offering,
personally bowed at the sacrificial seat and bestowed an imperial sword before the tomb mound.
This water again flows west and empties into the Chángzhí Ditch.
The ditch water strangely divides into two,
one branch flowing west past the south of Xūchāng City and entering the Jì,
one branch flowing south and emptying into the Wèn.
The Wèn River again flows west and enters the Jì.
Therefore, the Huáinánzǐ states:
"The Wèn emerges from Fúqí,
flows west and joins the Jì."
Gāo Yòu said:
"Fúqí,
is a mountain name,
located east of Zhūxū County."
I note that Yòu's explanation is correct,
but it refers to the Dōngwèn,
not the one mentioned in the Classic as entering the Jì.
This is probably an erroneous citation.
25 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll Twenty-Five
25.1 The Sì River
25.1 The Sì River
The Sì River emerges from the northern mountains of Biàn County in Lǔ.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
It emerges from Chéngshì County in Jìyīn.
It also says:
It emerges north of Biàn County.
The *Classic* mentions the northern mountains,
but these are all incorrect.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
The Sì River emerges from the northeast of Lǔ.
In the past, due to official duties,
I traveled along Xú and Yǎn,
passing by the Zhū and Sì rivers,
and thus ordered an investigation into their sources and courses.
The water emerges northwest of Táoxū, southeast of the old city of Biàn County.
In the seventh year of Duke Zhāo of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Xiè Xī, heeding Jì Sūn's words,
ceded the Mèng clan's fortified city of Chéng to Jìn and moved to Táo.
Dù Yù states:
Southeast of Biàn County in the state of Lǔ is Táoxū, commonly called Táoxū,
where Shùn made pottery.
The well is called Shùn's Well,
but these are also incorrect.
The ruins contain Lòuzé,
a marsh fifteen *li* square,
with clear, still water,
three *zhang* deep, as if diminished.
To the west of the marsh lies a hill,
commonly called Guītíng Mountain.
Since there are tales of Táoxū and Shùn's Well,
the name Guītíng also came to be.
Beside the hill are three stone caves,
three to four *chi* wide and round,
some caves are connected, others not,
the water within them sometimes fills, sometimes leaks.
When it leaks, within a few nights,
the slopes empty and the marsh dries up.
The local residents,
knowing when it is about to leak,
prepare wooden curved channels in advance,
blocking the cave entrances,
causing fish and turtles to leap and scales to scatter,
too numerous to carry away.
From here, ridges connect to hills,
extending northwest for about forty *li*.
At the western edge of the ridge,
lies the source of the Sì River.
The *Records of the Investigation of Things* states:
The Sì emerges from Péiwěi,
which likely refers to this hill.
Stone caves discharge water,
with five springs all flowing forth.
Each spring cave is about a *chi* in diameter.
South of the water source stands a temple,
with cypress and pine forming a grove,
called by contemporaries the Yuánquán Shrine,
though its origins are unclear.
The Sì River flows west past the old city south of the county.
In the twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiāng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Jì Wǔzǐ captured Biàn,
saying:
"I heard the defender of Biàn was about to rebel,
so I led my troops to subdue him." This is the event.
To the south lies the old city of Gūmiè.
In the first year of Duke Yǐn of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the Duke and Zhū Yífǔ made a covenant at Miè.
The water emerges between these two towns,
flowing west past the north of Wú City.
In the seventh year of Duke Wén of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the *Classic* records the Duke attacking Zhū.
On the jiǎxū day of the third month, he took Xūjù,
and then fortified Wú.
Dù Yù states:
It is a town of Lǔ.
South of Biàn County lies Wú City,
prepared against Zhū's threats.
The Sì River flows from Biàn and converges with the Zhū River.
It flows southwest past the north of Lǔ County.
The Sìshuǐ River flows southwest,
passing through Lǔ County where it divides into two streams.
Beside the water stands a city,
which is the point where the two waters converge,
the northern one being the Zhū Canal.
In the ninth year of Duke Zhuāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Classic records: "In winter, the Zhū was dredged."
Jīng Xiàngfán, Fú Qián, and Dù Yù
all state that the Zhūshuǐ is north of the Lǔ city,
and it was dredged deeper as a precaution against Qí.
To the south is the Sìshuǐ River.
The Master taught between the Zhū and Sì rivers,
and now, between the two waters north of the city,
is the place where the Master led his disciples.
The Record of Campaigns says:
The Zhū and Sì rivers meet seventeen lǐ northeast of the Lǔ city.
Quèlǐ backs against the Zhū and faces the Sì,
measuring one hundred and twenty paces from north to south,
and sixty paces from east to west.
Each of the four gates has a stone threshold,
and the north gate is over a hundred paces from the Zhūshuǐ.
In the early years of the Later Hàn,
the thorns and brambles at Quèlǐ cleared themselves,
from the lecture hall to a distance of nine lǐ.
Bào Yǒng served as chancellor,
and he restored the sacrificial temple,
using it to execute the Lǔ rebels Péng Fēng and others.
Guō Yuánshēng says:
The Sìshuǐ is south of the city,
but this is incorrect.
I refer to the Discourses of the States,
which states: "Duke Xuān fished in the deep pool of the Sì in summer,
and Lǐ Gé cut the net and discarded it."
Wéi Zhāo notes:
The Sì is north of the Lǔ city.
The Records of the Grand Historian, the Tomb Records, and Wáng Yǐn's Records of Geography
all state that Confucius was buried north of the Lǔ city on the banks of the Sìshuǐ.
Today, south of the Sìshuǐ is the Master's tomb.
The Spring and Autumn Annals: Confucius's Prophetic Charts says:
A bird transformed into a book,
which Confucius held up to report to heaven.
A red sparrow carried the book in its beak,
and it transformed into yellow jade above,
inscribed with the words:
"Kǒng received the mandate,
established the responding laws,
and created the red system."
The Explanatory Texts says:
When Confucius died,
he was buried north of the Lǔ city with the yellow jade he had received,
which is also the place where Zǐgòng built a hut to mourn by the tomb.
Qiáo Zhōu says:
After Confucius's death,
over a hundred families from Lǔ settled around the tomb,
forming a community,
named Kǒnglǐ.
The Kǒng Collection says:
The Master's tomb mound covers an area of one square lǐ,
located six lǐ north of the Lǔ city on the banks of the Sìshuǐ.
Over fifty tombs of the Kǒng clan are located there,
with names arranged according to lineage order,
though they can no longer be identified.
There are three inscribed steles,
and stone animals and tablets still remain.
The Imperial Overview says:
The disciples each brought rare trees from all directions to plant,
so there were many unusual trees,
but no thorny trees or prickly grass. Today, not a single branch remains.
The Sìshuǐ flows south from north of the city, passes southwest of the Lǔ city, and merges with the Yíshuǐ.
The Yíshuǐ originates northwest of Níqiū Mountain southeast of the Lǔ city.
This mountain is where Yán Mǔ prayed and gave birth to Confucius.
Ten lǐ east of the mountain,
there is a temple to Yán Mǔ.
Several lǐ south of the mountain,
is the burial place of Confucius's father.
This is the "collapse of the Fáng tomb" mentioned in the Rites.
A spring emerges from level ground,
flows past the old city of Lǔ County to the south,
and outside the east gate north of the water,
is where the yuánjū bird once rested.
The Discourses of the States says:
A sea bird called yuánjū
rested outside the east gate of the Lǔ city for three days.
Zāng Wénzhòng made offerings to it,
and Zhǎn Qín criticized him.
Thus, Zhuāngzǐ said:
"A sea bird rested in the suburbs,
and the Marquis of Lǔ entertained it with wine,
played grand music for it,
and served it the grand sacrifice of beef, pork, and lamb.
After three days, it died.
This was nurturing it in a way it was not meant to be nurtured."
Outside the city gate and walls,
is also the place where Róng Yí died.
The Annals of Lü Buwei says:
Once, Róng Yí left Qí for Lǔ.
The weather was extremely cold, and he arrived at the city gate late with his disciple,
staying outside the outer gate.
As it grew even colder,
he said to his disciple:
"If you give me your clothes,
I will live;
if I give you my clothes,
you will live.
I am a man of great talent,
valued by the world.
You are an unworthy man,
not worth sparing."
The disciple said:
"How can an unworthy man share clothes with a man of great talent?"
Róng sighed and said:
"Alas, it cannot be done."
He took off his clothes and gave them to his disciple,
and died at midnight.
North of the Yíshuǐ faces the Jì Gate.
In the past, the stableman Luò was exceptionally strong,
and could throw a cover over this gate.
Fú Qián says:
"He could throw a weight of a thousand jūn,
over the top of the gate."
Dù Yù says he could run and catch the rafters of the roof,
and flip over the top of the gate.
In the twentieth year of Duke Xī of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Classic records: "In spring,
the south gate was newly built."
The Commentary of Zuǒ says:
"It was recorded as untimely."
Dù Yù says:
"Originally named the Jì Gate,
Duke Xī enlarged it,
and now it is still unlike the other gates,
renamed the High Gate."
Its remaining foundation is still over eight zhàng high,
and it is also called the Yú Gate.
In the tenth year of Duke Zhuāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals and Commentary of Zuǒ,
Prince Yǎn attacked the Sòng army,
secretly exiting through the Yú Gate covered with a tiger skin.
South of the gate, across the water,
is the Yú Altar,
three zhàng high,
where Zēng Diǎn desired to dance in the wind.
About one lǐ from the High Gate,
west of the road, is the stele of Dào'érjūn,
erected by Chancellor Chén of Lǔ.
Once, Zēng Shēn lived here,
and owls did not enter the outer city.
The county
is the location of Qūfù,
the ruins of Shàohào,
with the storehouse of Dàtíngshì,
which was attacked by Shù Niú in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Thus, Liú Gōnggàn's "Ode to the Capital of Lǔ" says:
"Store weapons in the storehouse of Yǒuyán,
and release warhorses in the wilderness of Jùyě."
King Chéng of Zhōu enfeoffed Jī Dàn at Qūfù,
naming it Lǔ.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
it was made the Xuē Commandery.
In the first year of Empress Gāo of Hàn,
it became the Kingdom of Lǔ.
On the mound is the residence of the Jì family,
with Wǔzǐ's Terrace.
Though now collapsed and leveled,
it is still several zhàng high.
A hundred paces west of the terrace is a large well,
three zhàng wide,
over ten zhàng deep,
lined with stones,
shaped like chime stones.
In the twelfth year of Duke Dìng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Gōngshān Bùniǔ led the people of Fèi to attack Lǔ,
and the duke entered the palace of the Jì family,
ascending Wǔzǐ's Terrace.
Two lǐ northwest of the terrace is the Terrace of Duke Zhōu,
five zhàng high,
with a circumference of fifty paces.
About four lǐ south of the terrace is the Temple of Confucius,
which is the former residence of the Master.
The residence covers one qǐng,
and the hall where he lived
was later turned into a temple.
In the thirteenth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn, he passed through Lǔ
and sacrificed to Confucius with the grand sacrifice.
Since the Qín burning of the Book of Songs and Documents,
the classics were lost and incomplete.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, Prince Gōng of Lǔ demolished Confucius's old residence
and discovered the Book of Documents, Spring and Autumn Annals, Analects, and Classic of Filial Piety.
At that time, people no longer knew about ancient script,
calling it tadpole script.
The Hàn dynasty kept it secret,
and few ever saw it.
At that time, the sound of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments was heard in the hall,
so it was not demolished.
The temple has three rooms:
The Master is in the western room,
facing east;
Yán Mǔ is in the central room,
facing south;
the Lady is separated in the eastern room,
facing east.
Xiàqiū,
a town in Lǔ,
was the Fùxiá of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
In the seventh year of Duke Āi,
Jì Kāngzǐ attacked Zhū,
and imprisoned them at Fùxiá, which is this place.
Yìng Shào said:
Xiàqiū is southwest of the county.
In the past, the Wèi minister Gōngshū Wénzǐ ascended Xiàqiū,
and Qú Bóyù followed.
Wénzǐ said:
How delightful is this hill!
When I die, I wish to be buried here.
Bóyù said:
If you, sir, delight in it,
then Yuàn requests to go first.
This satirizes his desire to harm the people's good fields.
The name Xiàqiū
likely originated from this to mark its designation.
Zēngzǐ offered condolences at Fùxià,
and both Zhèng Xuán and Huángfǔ Mì said it was in Wèi territory.
Though Lǔ and Wèi are different,
the land is the same.
The Huǒ River originates from Héxiāng County in Dōnghǎi.
In the seventh year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
Mǎ Guāng's son Lǎng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
This river flows southwest into Zhū.
In the second year of Duke Āi in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jì Sūn Sī attacked Zhū and seized the fields east of Huǒ and west of Yí, which is this.
The Huǒ River then passes southeast of Zōu Mountain in the state of Lǔ and flows southwest.
This is the Yì Mountain mentioned in the Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
It was where Duke Wén of Zhū relocated.
The present city lies on the southern side of Zōu Mountain,
relying on cliffs and barriers for fortified walls,
hence the state of Zhūlóu,
of the Cáo surname,
was the town of Shūliáng Hé.
Confucius was born here,
and it was later made a county,
taking the name of Zōu Mountain as the county's surname,
which was Zōu Tíng under Wáng Mǎng.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Yì Mountain is north of Zōu County,
and the town of Yì relied on it for its name.
The mountain stretches twenty lǐ east to west,
tall and outstanding, standing alone,
with piled rocks facing each other,
almost devoid of soil.
Among the rocks are many holes and caves,
interconnected and open,
often with spaces as large as several rooms.
Locals call them Yì holes.
In times of turmoil, people would take their families into the Yì holes.
Though external bandits were numerous,
they could do no harm.
During the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
the Grand Commandant Xī Jiàn led the local community to defend this mountain,
and the Hú bandits could not capture it despite attacking and besieging.
Now, south of the mountain is a large cave,
named Lord Xī's Cave.
North of the mountain is a sheer cliff.
When Qín Shǐhuáng observed rituals in Lǔ,
he ascended Yì Mountain
and ordered Chancellor Lǐ Sī to inscribe an inscription on the mountain ridge in large seal script,
naming it the Gate of Day.
This is what the Book of Songs refers to as "holding Fú and Yì."
The Huǒ River then flows southwest past the old city of Fān County
and then west past the north of the old city of Xuē County.
The Treatise on Geography says:
This was the state of Xī Zhòng, the chariot master of Xià.
According to the Bamboo Annals,
in the thirty-first year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Pī moved to Xuē,
and renamed it Xúzhōu.
South of the city, on the mountain, is the tomb of Xī Zhòng.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records of Jìn says:
The tomb of Xī Zhòng is on the mountain twenty-five lǐ south of the city,
and the common people consider it divine.
Qí enfeoffed Tián Wén here,
bestowing the title Lord Mèngcháng.
He was known for his kindness and wisdom.
Now, beside the outer wall, there is still Wén's tomb,
constructed with stones forming an outer wall,
built solidly and strictly,
gleaming and beautiful, still traceable.
Travelers coming and going
all make a point to visit,
considering it a remarkable sight.
The Huǒ River then flows west past the north of Zhònghuǐ City.
The Tàikāng Geographical Records of Jìn says:
Xī Zhòng moved to Pī,
and Zhònghuǐ resided here, serving as Tāng's left minister.
Later, during the Zhōu dynasty, it was enfeoffed as a marquisate,
but was later invaded and diminished,
demoted by the hegemon to a earldom,
of the Rén surname.
Yìng Shào said:
Pī is in Xuē.
Xú Guǎng's Shǐjì Pronunciation and Meaning says:
Yǐng Kè, son of King Yuán of Chǔ,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Shàngpī in the second year of Empress Lǚ's reign.
There is a Xiàpī,
hence this is called Shàngpī.
The Jìnshū Treatise on Geography says:
Zhònghuǐ City is thirty lǐ west of Xuē City.
The Huǒ River then flows west to Húlù County and enters the Sì River.
Thus, Jīng Xiàngfán said:
The Huǒ River at Xuē County originates from Fān County,
and flows west into Húlù in Shānyáng, which is this.
The Classic says east of Xiàqiū,
which is an error.
It then flows south past the west of Píngyáng County.
The county
is the Nánpíngyáng County of Shānyáng Commandery.
The Bamboo Annals says:
In the twenty-ninth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qí Tián Xī and men of Sòng attacked our eastern borders,
besieging Píngyáng.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Miǎnpíng.
The Sì River then flows south past the west of the old city,
which is commonly called Qīxiāng.
Yìng Shào's Records of the Thirteen Provinces says:
Qīxiāng
is a town of Zhū.
Dù Yù said:
Northeast of Píngyáng is Qīxiāng.
Now, southwest of the old city is seen
a square area of two lǐ,
but the details are unclear.
It then flows south past the west of Gāopíng County,
and the Guāng River flows from the northwest into it.
The Sì River flows south past Gāopíng Mountain.
The mountain is ten lǐ east to west,
five lǐ north to south,
and four lǐ high.
It connects with other mountains,
but this mountain is the highest,
with a flat top,
hence it is called Gāopíng Mountain,
and the county is also named after it.
The Sì River then flows south past the west of the old city of Gāopíng County.
In the third year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Chancellor Wèi Xiàng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāo,
General Chén Zhě was enfeoffed as Marquis of Tuó.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
it is a county under Shānyáng.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Gāopíng.
Yìng Shào said:
Emperor Zhāng changed it.
According to the original records:
Wáng Mǎng renamed it,
and Emperor Zhāng followed it.
What is called the Guāng River
is actually the Zhū River.
It is likely that Guāng and Zhū converge,
and they are interchangeably referred to.
It then flows south past the east of Fāngyǔ County.
In the fourth year of the Jiànpíng era of Emperor Āi of Hàn,
a woman named Tián Wúsè from the county gave birth to a child.
Two months before birth,
the child cried in the womb.
When born,
it was not raised,
but buried on the roadside.
After three days,
people passing by heard crying,
and the mother dug it up and raised it.
The Hé River flows from the west and joins it.
The Hé River is where the Jǐ River collects and forms lakes and marshes,
and eastward it joins the Sì River sixty lǐ west of Húlíng County, below Gǔtíng City,
commonly called the Huángshuǐ Estuary.
The Huáng River connects northwest to the Jùyě Marsh,
likely because the Huáng River flows into the Hé,
hence it is named accordingly.
It then turns southeast,
passing south of Húlù County,
and the Juānjuān River flows from the northeast into it.
The Treatise on Geography states,
this was the former Húlíng County.
The Hé River is to the south,
and Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Húlù.
Yìng Shào said:
It was also called Húlíng.
Emperor Zhāng enfeoffed the son of Dōngpíng King Cāng as the Marquis of Húlù,
and it was renamed Húlù.
The Sì River then flows east past the north of the city built by Xī Jiàn,
and further east past the southeast of Húlíng City.
In the past, when Huán Wēn advanced north,
Fàn Huān captured Mùróng Zhōng here.
To the east of the city is the stele of Dù Shàng.
The Sì River then joins the Nánliáng River on the left.
The Treatise on Geography states:
The river originates from Fān County.
Now, to the northeast of the county,
a spring emerges from the flat marshland like a wheel.
It forms a stream at its source,
flows southwest, and divides into two branches.
The northern branch emerges,
flows west past the north of Fān County,
and further west past the north of Téng City.
The Spring and Autumn Annals and the Zuǒ Commentary records:
In the eleventh year of Duke Yǐn,
the Marquis of Téng and the Marquis of Xuē came to court,
and they disputed over precedence.
The Marquis of Xuē said:
I was enfeoffed first.
The Marquis of Téng said:
I am the divination officer of Zhōu,
while Xuē is of a lesser surname.
I cannot be placed after him.
The Duke sent Yǔfǔ to request of the Marquis of Xuē:
Since you have condescended to visit me,
there is a Zhōu proverb that says:
When a mountain has trees, the craftsman measures them;
when a guest has propriety, the host selects it.
In the ancestral alliances of Zhōu,
those of different surnames are placed later.
If I were to visit Xuē,
I would not dare to rank with the Rén clan.
If you would condescend to favor me,
I would ask that the Lord of Téng be given precedence.
The Marquis of Xuē agreed,
and thus the Marquis of Téng took precedence.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Xiàhóu Yīng as a marquis here,
and he was called Lord Téng.
Dèng Chén said:
This is now Gōngqiū in Pèi Commandery.
The water also irrigates the hills here.
The old county city lies northwest of Téng.
The city wall is twenty lǐ in circumference,
and within it is an inner city.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
this is Téng,
which was enfeoffed to Cuò Shūxiù, the son of King Yì of Zhōu, as Duke Wén.
It was destroyed by Qí,
and Qín made it a county.
In the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Shùn, the son of Prince Gōng of Lǔ, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Generations have used this water to irrigate our fertile fields,
reaching up to a hundred zǐ,
hence it has the name of Two Canals.
The Nánliáng River flows southwest from its branch canal past the east of the old city of Fān County in the State of Lǔ.
Commonly, because it is south and adjacent to the Huǒ,
it is also called the Western Huǒ River.
The Nánliáng River then bends and flows past the south of the city.
Yìng Shào said:
The county
was the ancient town of Xiǎozhū.
The Treatise on Geography states:
The water flows west and empties into the Jì Canal.
The Jì is west of Húlù and joins the Sì on the left.
The Sì and Jì flow together,
so some geographical records say the Jì enters the Sì,
while others say the Sì enters the Jì.
They interchangeably receive each other's names,
hence there is the text stating it enters the Jì.
Kǎn Yīn's Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
It flows west to Húlù and enters the Sì, which is correct.
The Classic does not mention the name Nánliáng,
but refers to it as Juānjuān,
which is likely this river.
Dài Yánzhī's Record of the Western Campaign also says southeast of Húlù County,
there is the Juānjuān River,
but makes no mention of Nánliáng,
claiming it is the canal dug by the King of Wú.
I note that southwest of Húlù, there is only this river.
Yánzhī probably based it on the Discourses of the States, which says:
King Fūchāi of Wú raised an army,
intending to meet north at Huángchí,
and dug a canal between Shāng and Lǔ,
connecting north to the Yí
and west to the Jì.
Based on this,
he called this water the canal dug by the King of Wú,
but this is incorrect.
I have examined it via waterways,
and there is only the Sì River.
It likely reached north to the Yí,
flowed northwest through Shāng and Lǔ,
and connected to the Jì.
Wú merely widened it,
not that it started from the northeast,
receiving the Yí and flowing southwest to the Jì.
Even if there was a connection,
it was not the route taken by Wú.
The years are indeed distant,
but human reasoning remains close.
Using the present to infer the past,
I am even more convinced that Yánzhī's account lacks reason.
The Sì River then flows south,
and the Huǒ River joins it.
It further flows past the west of the Shàngpī City of Xuē,
and empties southward.
It then flows east past the east of Pèi County.
In ancient times, Xǔ Yóu lived in seclusion at Peize,
which is this county.
The county likely took its name from the marsh.
After Sòng was destroyed, it belonged to Chǔ.
It lies on the banks of the Sìshuǐ River,
and under Qín, it was the seat of Sìshuǐ Commandery.
Huángshuǐ flows into it.
Huángshuǐ originates from Huánggōu in Huángxiāng, Xiǎohuáng County.
The Guóyǔ states:
"The ruler of Wú met with the feudal lords at Huángchí."
Huángshuǐ flows east past the old city wall of Wàihuáng County.
Zhāng Yàn said:
"Wèi Commandery has a Nèihuáng County,
hence this one is called 'Outer'."
Xuē Zàn said:
"The county has Huánggōu,
hence the county is named after it."
Quān Chēng's Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn says:
"South of the county is Qúshuǐ.
In the Spring and Autumn period, it was Qūjí Village of Sòng,
an alternate capital of Sòng.
In the 25th year of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ,
Duke Yuán of Sòng died at Qūjí, which is this place.
Huà Yuán of Sòng resided at Jì Village.
In the 15th year of Duke Xuān,
Chǔ and Zhèng besieged Sòng.
Xiè Yáng of Jìn defied Chǔ
and delivered his mandate here.
The people of Sòng were afraid
and sent Huà Yuán to climb the wall at night and enter the Chǔ army camp.
He ascended Zǐ Fǎn's bed and said:
'My humble ruler sends Yuán to report our distress.
In our poor city, we exchange children to eat
and split bones for fuel.
A covenant made under the city walls
is something we cannot accept.'
Zǐ Fǎn withdrew thirty lǐ,
and Sòng and Chǔ made peace.
Today, east of the city on the wall, there is still a shrine to Huà Yuán,
where offerings are made without cease.
North of the city is Huà Yuán's tomb."
Huánggōu flows east from south of the city past Kuíqiū below.
In the 9th year of Duke Xī of Lǔ,
Duke Huán of Qí met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū.
Zǎi Kǒng said:
"The Marquis of Qí does not cultivate virtue but diligently pursues distant campaigns.
He campaigns north against the Shānróng,
south against Chǔ,
and holds this meeting in the west.
Whether he campaigns in the east is unknown,
but in the west he does not.
Is he not inviting disorder?
My lord should focus on quelling disorder,
not be diligent in such journeys."
The Marquis of Jìn then returned,
and this is the very place."
Huánggōu then flows east into a great marsh,
where reeds and rushes grow.
This is what the world calls Dàqí Bēi.
The water of the bēi flows northeast past Dìngtáo County south,
then east past the Chǔqiū Pavilion of Chéngwǔ County, Shānyáng Commandery, north.
Huánggōu then flows east past the old city wall of Chéngwǔ County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Chéng'ān.
Huánggōu then flows northeast past Gào City north.
In the 2nd year of Duke Huán of Lǔ,
the Jīng records taking the Gào great tripod from Sòng.
On the wùshēn day,
it was placed in the ancestral temple.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"Sòng's Dū attacked Kǒng Fǔ and took his wife,
killed Duke Shāng and set up Gōngzǐ Féng,
and bribed the duke with the Gào great tripod.
Zāng Āibó admonished that this was contrary to ritual."
The Shísānzhōu Zhì says:
"Today, southeast of Chéngwǔ County is Gào City,
commonly called Northern Gào."
Huánggōu then flows east past the old city wall of Pínglè County south,
then east,
and on the right joins Pàoshuǐ,
which is the upper source of Fēngshuǐ.
The water above receives Dàqí Bēi,
flows east past Shì City north,
then east past the old city wall of Sìshì County north,
which Wáng Mǎng called Sìshàn.
The county has the tomb of Yī Yǐn.
Cuī Yīn said:
"During the time of Wò Dīng, emperor of Yīn,
Yī Yǐn died
and was buried at Bó."
The Huánglǎn says:
"Yī Yǐn's tomb is in Pínglì Village, Sìshì, Jìyīn."
Huángfǔ Mì said:
"Yī Yǐn died at over a hundred years old.
A great fog lasted three days.
Wò Dīng buried him with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
personally attending the funeral,
to repay his great virtue."
It then flows east past Mèngzhū Marsh.
Dù Yù said:
"The marsh is northeast of Suīyáng County, Liáng State."
It then flows east past the old city wall of Gàochéng County south.
According to the Dìlǐzhì,
it is Shānyáng County.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Gàochéng,
hence the world speaks of Southern Gào and Northern Gào.
It then flows east past the old city wall of Shànfù County south,
where in ancient times Mìzǐ Jiàn governed.
Confucius sent Wūmǎ Qī to observe his administration.
Entering his territory,
he saw people fishing at night
and asked:
"Why do you release the fish you catch?"
They replied:
"The small ones,
our grand master wishes them to grow, hence we do so."
Upon hearing this, the Master said:
"Sincerity there, manifestation here.
Zǐ Jiàn has grasped it well.
Alas, Bù Qí,
what he governs is small."
Wáng Mǎng changed this county's name to Lìfù.
In the 13th year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Mào.
It then flows east past Pínglè County,
and on the right joins Pàoshuǐ.
The water above receives Suīshuǐ at the boundary of Xiàyì County,
flows northeast and joins another stream.
Above, it receives Suīshuǐ at the boundary of Zhùqiū County and flows north.
The world also calls it Húlúgōu.
The water accumulates to form an islet,
and the water of the islet flows northeast.
Two channels draw it in pairs,
joining Fēngshuǐ on the left.
Commonly called Èrpào,
from here downward,
Fēng and Pào are both used interchangeably.
Thus the Dìlǐzhì says:
"Pínglè is a marquisate.
Pàoshuǐ emerges from here."
It then passes Fēngxī Marsh,
called Fēngshuǐ.
The Hànshū states that Gāozǔ escorted convicts to Lìshān,
many convicts fled,
and arriving at Fēngxī Marsh,
a great snake blocked the path.
He drew his sword and cut it down.
This is the place where Hàn Gāozǔ cut the snake.
It then flows east past a great dam,
where the water divides into two.
It then flows east past the old city wall of Fēng County south,
which Wáng Mǎng called Wúfēng.
The water flows northeast along the city's east side,
and on the right joins a branch stream.
Above, it receives the great dam west of Fēng,
branches and flows northeast past Fēng City north,
and flows east into Fēngshuǐ.
Fēngshuǐ then flows east and joins Huángshuǐ,
which people of the time called Kuángshuǐ.
Likely because 'kuáng' and 'huáng' sound similar,
a vulgar tradition that lost the truth.
From here downward, Huángshuǐ is also commonly used.
Above the water was formerly a bridge,
called Pào Bridge.
Wáng Zhìshēn's Sòngshǐ says:
"Sòng's Grand Commandant Liú Yìgōng, from Péngchéng, sent Army Commander Jī Xuánjìng north to the city
to reconnoiter the Wèi army.
The Wèi army, west of Qīng, saw Xuánjìng's troops.
Wèi's Marquis Nánkāng, Dù Dàojùn, hastened toward Pào Bridge.
The people of Pèi County preemptively burned Pào Bridge
and beat drums in the woods.
Jùn thought the Sòng army had arrived in force
and vied to cross Pàoshuǐ.
The water was deep and bitterly cold,
and nearly half froze or drowned."
Qīngshuǐ is another name for Pàoshuǐ.
Shěn Yuē's Sòngshū says the Wèi army wanted to cross west of Qīng,
which is incorrect.
Pàoshuǐ then flows east past the old city wall of Pèi County south.
At the end of Qín, when uprisings began,
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn welcomed Hàn's founder at this city.
In the 11th year of Gāozǔ,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Héyáng Marquis Liú Zhòng's son.
Within the city is a temple to Hàn Gāozǔ,
with three steles in front,
erected in the Later Hàn.
The temple foundation is made of blue stone,
and the steps still remain.
When Liú Bèi was over Xúzhōu,
he administered from here.
Yuán Shù sent Jì Líng to attack Bèi.
Bèi sought help from Lǚ Bù.
Bù rescued him
and encamped at Xiǎopèi.
He summoned Líng and invited Bèi to drink together.
Bù said to Líng:
"Xuándé
is Bù's brother.
Bù's nature dislikes joining fights,
but enjoys resolving them."
He then planted a halberd at the gate.
Lǚ Bù drew his bow and said:
"Watch me shoot the small branch of the halberd.
If I hit it,
you should each withdraw your troops;
if I miss,
you may stay and decide the battle."
With one shot he hit it,
and thus the conflict was resolved.
This is the place where Lǚ Bù shot the halberd branch.
The Shùzhēng Jì states:
"The city is extremely large,
with moats on all sides connecting to the Fēng River.
The Fēng River flows east into the Sì River south of the city,
which is the Pào River."
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
"The Pào River flows from northeast of Pínglè County to Pèi, where it enters the Sì River."
The Sì River flows south past the east of Xiǎopèi County.
The county seat is located on an old mound south of the ancient city.
On the eastern bank is the Sìshuǐ Pavilion.
Hàn Gāozǔ served as the Sìshuǐ Pavilion Chief,
and this is that very pavilion.
The old pavilion now has a temple to Gāozǔ,
with a stele in front of the temple,
erected in the tenth year of Yánxī.
The temple gate towers have collapsed and deteriorated,
with almost nothing remaining intact.
In the water is the site of an old stone bridge,
and remnants of the stones still exist.
When Gāozǔ defeated Qíng Bù,
he passed through here,
held a banquet at Pèi Palace,
and while drinking and singing,
he sighed with emotion, saying:
"A wanderer longs for his hometown."
The Sì River then flows southeast past the old city of Guǎngqī County.
In the first year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Zé was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lìjù.
The Sì River then flows past Liú County and south past the east of Chá City.
Southwest of the city is a temple to Chóng Hóu Hǔ.
Though his virtue has faded and his legacy is forgotten,
it is unclear why such a distant memorial exists for him.
The Sì River then flows south past the west of the tomb of Huán Tuí, a senior official of Sòng.
The mountain rests against the Sì River,
with stone covering its western slope,
carved to form the tomb,
which people now call the Stone Outer Coffin.
The outer coffin has two layers,
and the stonework is exquisite.
The Master believed it would be better to decay quickly in death.
Further southeast, it passes northeast of Péngchéng County.
West of the Sì River is Lónghuá Temple,
established by the monk Shì Fǎxiǎn after traveling far to the Western Regions,
sailing back east across the sea,
and bringing the "Lónghuá Diagram."
He first established this tradition,
and the spread of the Dharma in China
began with Fǎxiǎn.
The two stones from India that he brought
are still in the niche on the eastern foundation of the southern veranda,
and the stones remain smooth and lovely.
The Sì River flows further south,
where the Huò River joins it,
and then passes east of the old city of Péngchéng County.
In the forty-second year of King Xiǎn of Zhōu,
the Nine Tripods sank into the depths of the Sì River.
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng, the tripods appeared in these waters.
The emperor, believing his virtue matched that of the Three Dynasties,
was overjoyed
and sent thousands of men to dive and retrieve them,
but they failed,
which is called "the tripods lying hidden."
It is also said that they were tied and pulled,
but before they emerged,
a dragon's teeth bit through the ropes.
Thus, the saying goes:
"Rejoicing too early severs the tripod's ropes."
This is likely an unfounded tale.
The Sì River then flows past the south of Gōng Shèng's tomb,
where the tombstone still stands.
It also passes east of Yàfù's tomb.
The Huánglǎn states:
"Yàfù's tomb is in the Jūcháo Pavilion east of the city wall of Lújiāng County,
with Yàfù's Well nearby.
Officials and commoners, when handling affairs,
all made offerings to Yàfù in the Jūcháo Hall.
Later, a shrine was built east of the city wall,
and it is still worshipped there today."
According to the Hànshū·Xiàng Yǔ Zhuàn,
Fàn Zēng of Lìyáng
died of a carbuncle before reaching Péngchéng,
with no mention of Jūcháo.
Now, south of Péngchéng is Xiàng Yǔ's Liángmǎ Terrace,
and on the southwestern foothills of the terrace,
is his tomb.
Zēng did not emulate Fàn Lǐ's actions
but ended his life here,
which can be called narrow-minded.
Examining historical records,
his tomb should be near this location.
Further southeast, it passes south of Lǚ County.
Lǚ was a city of Sòng.
In the first year of Duke Xiāng of the Spring and Autumn period,
the Jìn army attacked Zhèng and reached Chén.
Chǔ's Zǐ Xīn came to Zhèng's aid,
invading Sòng's Lǚ and Liú.
The county faces the Sì River.
In the third year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
white-necked crows and black crows
fought in flocks in the county.
The white-necked crows were defeated,
fell into the Sì River,
and thousands died.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn states:
"Turning against one's kin
brings the omen of white and black crows fighting."
At that time, the rebellions of Wú and Chǔ occurred.
On the Sì River, there is a stone bridge,
hence it is called Lǚliáng.
In the past, Duke Jǐng of Sòng, using a bow made by a master bowyer,
drew the bow and shot eastward.
The arrow landed east of Péngchéng,
embedding its feathers in the stone bridge,
which is this very bridge.
The hanging torrents rush violently,
truly a perilous stretch of the Sì River.
As Confucius said, "Even fish and turtles cannot swim here."
It is also said
that the waterfall is thirty ren high,
with froth flowing for ninety li.
Nowadays, this is no longer the case.
Perhaps the mountain's metaphor
does not fully capture the brilliance of heaven.
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìjì states:
"The water produces qìng stones,"
which is what the Shū refers to as "floating qìng stones from the banks of the Sì."
The Sì River flows further southeast,
where the Dīngxī River joins it.
The Dīngxī River originates from the Sì River at Lǚ County,
flowing southeast
and bordered to the north by wide lowlands,
with mountains towering above as it empties into the Sì River basin.
The Sì River is shallow and sluggish in winter and spring,
often requiring dredging to clear the channel,
so travelers frequently use this stream.
As Lù Jī's "Xíngsī Fù" says:
"Riding the swift banks of the Dīng River,
clearing the accumulated sand of the Sì River."
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán of Jìn,
General Xiè Xuán of the Left, at Lǚliáng, dispatched Supervisor Wénrén Shì with ninety thousand laborers
to dam the water and construct seven sluice gates,
to facilitate water transport.
Further southeast, it passes west of Xiàpī County.
The Sì Shuǐ passes through various counties, skirting the eastern side of Géyì Mountain,
which is the Péiyì to which Xī Zhòng relocated.
The Sì Shuǐ then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Xiàpī County,
continuing southeast,
where the Yí Shuǐ flows into it.
This was formerly a county under Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Yìng Shào said:
"Xī Zhòng moved here from Xuē,
hence it is called Xiàpī."
The Hàn transferred Hán Xìn, King of Qí, to be King of Chǔ,
and made this his capital.
Later it was made a county,
which Wáng Mǎng called Rùn Jiǎn.
It was the seat of Dōngyáng Commandery.
Wén Yǐng said:
"Qín Jiā
was a man of Dōngyáng Commandery,
which is present-day Xiàpī."
Jìn Zhuó said:
"Dōngyáng County
was originally under Línhuái Commandery.
Emperor Míng transferred it to Xiàpī,
and later it was transferred to Guǎnglíng."
Therefore, Zhāng Yàn said:
"Dōngyáng Commandery
is present-day Guǎnglíng Commandery."
Emperor Míng of Hàn established Xiàpī Commandery.
The city had three layers of walls.
Within its great wall were four steles: for Grand Marshal Shí Bāo, General Zhèndōng Hú Zhì, Minister over the Masses Wáng Hún, and Army Supervisor Shí Chóng.
The southern gate was called the White Gate;
here Cáo Cāo captured Chén Gōng.
The middle walled city
was where Lǚ Bù defended.
The small walled city
was the administrative seat of Xún Xiàn and Xī Tán, Generals of the Northern Headquarters during the Jìn restoration.
Long ago, Wú Bówǔ of Tàishān was orphaned young,
and was separated from his younger brother Wénzhāng for over twenty years.
They met in the county market,
and Wénzhāng was about to beat Bówǔ,
but feeling deep sorrow in his heart,
they inquired of each other,
and realized they were brothers.
The county is at the confluence of the Yí and Sì rivers.
Also, the Wǔyuán Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates northwest of Wǔyuán County in Péngchéng,
converges and flows into the marsh to the south,
passes west of its city,
which Wáng Mǎng called Hélè Pavilion.
East of the county is Xúmiào Mountain,
named for the Xú people's migration,
hence it bears this name.
On the mountain is a stone chamber,
the Xú Temple.
The Wǔyuán Shuǐ flows south and joins the Wǔ Shuǐ,
called the Jiā Shuǐ.
It flows south past Gāngtíng City,
then further south to Xiàpī, where it enters the Sì,
called the Wǔyuán Shuǐ Mouth.
Also, the Tóng Shuǐ originates from Róngqiū County in Dōnghǎi to the northwest,
flowing southeast to Xiàpī and entering the Sì.
The Sì Shuǐ flows southeast past the east of the old city of Xiàxiàng County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Cóng Dé.
Northwest of the city is the tomb of Hàn Grand Commandant Chén Qiú.
Before the tomb are three steles,
erected by his disciples Guǎn Níng, Huá Xīn, and others.
In the fourth year of the Chūpíng era,
Cáo Cāo attacked Xúzhōu,
defeated it,
and captured counties such as Qǔlǜ, Suīlíng, and Xiàqiū.
Because his father had taken refuge here and was killed,
he slaughtered a hundred thousand men and women,
so that the Sì Shuǐ ceased to flow,
and from then on, these counties were left without a trace of people,
a truly brutal act.
The Sì Shuǐ flows southeast to the mouth of the Suī Shuǐ.
The Sì Shuǐ then passes west of Sùyù City,
and further passes south of the city.
This was formerly Sùliú County of Xiàpī,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Kāng Yì.
When Emperor Yuán of Jìn was Prince of Āndōng,
he supervised the transport of military supplies
and established a storehouse here.
During the Tàihé era of Wèi,
it was the seat of Nánxúzhōu,
later reduced to a garrison.
When Liáng general Zhāng Huìshào advanced north,
his naval forces made camp here,
relying on the strength of this city,
and further repaired its outer walls and moats,
channeling water to encircle it on all sides,
so that the city now stands within the Sì Shuǐ.
Further southeast, it enters the Huái.
The Sì Shuǐ flows east past Língzhà to the south.
The *Xīzhēng Jì* says:
"This was formerly the seat of Líng County."
The Sì Shuǐ flows southeast past the north of Huáiyáng City,
which faces the Sì Shuǐ.
Here long ago, Zīqiū Xīn watered his horse, slew a flood dragon, and lost an eye.
The Sì Shuǐ flows southeast past the north of Wèiyáng City,
which rests upon the Sì riverbank.
Líng Jī's *Xíngsī Fù* says:
"Traveling by the winding shores of Wèiyáng."
Since there never was a Wèiyáng,
it is suspected to be the old city of Sìyáng County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Huáipíng Pavilion.
It was likely along the route Emperor Wén of Wèi took on his visit to Guǎnglíng,
though the details of the change are unclear.
The Sì Shuǐ flows east past the north of Jiǎochéng,
then flows southeast to pour into the Huái.
Examining various geographical accounts,
some say the Sì Shuǐ enters the Huái at Suīlíng,
others say it enters at Xiàxiàng,
but these are not accurate records.
25.2 The Yí Shuǐ
25.2 The Yí Shuǐ
The Yí Shuǐ originates from Ài Mountain in Gài County of Tàishān.
Zhèng Xuán states:
It emerges from Yí Shān,
or it is also said to emerge from Línlè Shān.
The water has two sources:
the southern source originates from what is commonly called Zuò Quán;
the northern water emerges from what is popularly called Yúqióng Quán.
Both flow southeast and converge into a single stream,
then join Luòyù Shuǐ on the right,
which emerges from Luòyù Shān,
flowing northeast to pour into it.
Yí Shuǐ flows southeast,
joining Sāngyù Shuǐ on the left,
which emerges north from Sāngyù Shān,
flowing east to pour into Yí Shuǐ.
Yí Shuǐ continues southeast,
where Tángláng Shuǐ enters it,
emerging from Lǔ Shān,
flowing southeast,
and pouring into Yí Shuǐ on the right.
Yí Shuǐ then flows east past the old city of Gài Xiàn,
joining Liánmián Zhī Shuǐ to the east,
which originates from Liánmián Shān,
flowing south past the east of Gài Chéng and then south into Yí.
Yí Shuǐ then flows east past Fúlái Zhī Shān,
where the "Spring and Autumn Annals" records that the Duke and the people of Jǔ held a covenant at Fúlái.
This is Gōnglái Shān,
located west of Pí Xiāng,
hence it was called the pass of Pílái.
Fúlái Zhī Shuǐ pours into it,
this water controls three streams on the left,
joins Gān Shuǐ on the right, and then pours into Yí.
Yí Shuǐ then flows south past the west of Bào Shān,
which has two peaks,
separated by one lǐ,
both ridges equally elegant,
standing round and uniform as one.
Yí Shuǐ then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Dōngguǎn Xiàn,
merging with Xiǎo Yí Shuǐ.
Mèng Kāng says:
The county,
formerly the settlement of Yùn,
is now Yùn Tíng.
In the second year of Yuánshuò during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Jí, son of the Prince Gòng of Chéngyáng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngguǎn.
During the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén of Wèi, it was established as Dōngguǎn Commandery.
The "Dōngyàn Lù" calls it Tuán Chéng.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liú campaigned north against Guǎnggù,
he ascended it to observe Wáng Nán.
It was the seat of the Southern Qīngzhōu of Wèi.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
Jǔ and Lǔ contended over Yùn,
for a long time indeed.
Now north of the city is Yùn Tíng.
Jīng Xiàngfán says:
Forty lǐ south of Gūmù Xiàn in Lángyá is Yuán Tíng,
formerly the Yùn settlement of Lǔ,
but over time the characters changed,
which is incorrect.
The "Jùn Guó Zhì"
states that Dōngguǎn has Yùn Tíng.
Now located forty lǐ northeast of Tuán Chéng,
it is still called the old Dōngguǎn city.
Xiǎo Yí Shuǐ emerges from Huánggū Shān,
flows southwest past the north of the city,
and pours into Yí to the southwest.
Yí Shuǐ then flows south and merges with Lǘ Shān Shuǐ,
which emerges from Lǘ Shān,
flows southeast,
is flanked by two streams on the right,
and all converge into Yí.
Yí Shuǐ flows south past the east of the old city of Dōng'ān Xiàn,
then merges with Shímì Shuǐ to the south,
which emerges from Shímì Shān,
land of Jǔ during the Spring and Autumn period.
The "Zuǒzhuàn"
records that the people of Jǔ returned Gòng Zhòng to Lǔ,
and he died at Mì.
Shímì Shuǐ flows east,
passes south of Dōng'ān Chéng,
where Emperor Hàn enfeoffed Qiáng, son of Prince Xiào of Lǔ, as Marquis of Dōng'ān.
Shímì Shuǐ then flows southeast into Yí.
Yí Shuǐ continues south,
Sāngquán Shuǐ emerges north from Wǔnǚ Shān,
flows southeast,
where Jùwéi Shuǐ pours into it,
emerging from Jùwéi Zhī Shān,
flowing southeast into Sāngquán Shuǐ.
Sāngquán Shuǐ continues southeast,
where Tángfù Shuǐ enters it,
this water originates from Tángfù,
as recorded in the ninth year of Duke Zhuāng of "Spring and Autumn,"
when Guǎn Zhòng requested imprisonment,
Bào Shū accepted him,
and released him at Tángfù.
Dù Yù says:
this refers to Yíwú Tíng northwest of Méngyīn Xiàn in Dōngguǎn.
Tángfù Shuǐ then flows southeast into Sāngquán Shuǐ,
Sāngquán Shuǐ then flows southeast past the north of the old city of Méngyīn Xiàn,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Méng'ēn.
It then flows southeast and merges with Sǒugù Shuǐ,
which has two sources that converge,
then flows east as a single stream,
commonly called Wèn Shuǐ.
It flows east past Méngyīn Xiàn and pours into Sāngquán Shuǐ,
then Lúchuān Shuǐ pours into it from the southeast,
emerging from Lùlǐng Shān,
flowing southeast,
with two streams converging on the left,
and Zhūgě Quányuán on the right.
These waters rush turbulently,
pass through Lú Xiàn of Chéngyáng,
formerly Lúshàng Lǐ of Gài Xiàn.
In the second year of Yuánshuò during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Xī, son of the Prince Gòng of Chéngyáng, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhùshàn.
It then flows southeast into Sāngquán Shuǐ.
Sāngquán Shuǐ continues southeast,
merging with Méngyīn Shuǐ on the right,
which emerges from the northern side of Méng Shān,
flowing northeast.
In the past, Chéng Gōng of Lángyá
took refuge on this mountain to avoid turmoil,
being by nature benevolent,
and not contending with others.
When someone falsely claimed his millet,
he relinquished it and departed.
This water flows northeast into Yí.
Yí Shuǐ then flows south past the east of the old city of Yángdū Xiàn,
the county
formerly being the state of Yáng.
It was an ally of Qí,
but Qí coveted its land and relocated it.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
General Dīng Fù was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Yí Shuǐ then flows south and merges with Méngshān Shuǐ,
which emerges from the northern side of Méng Shān,
flows east past the south of Yángdū Xiàn,
and pours into Yí Shuǐ to the east.
Yí Shuǐ then merges with Wēn Shuǐ on the left,
which originates from Wēnquán Bēi upstream,
and flows southwest into Yí Shuǐ.
It passes east of Línyí Xiàn in Lángyá to the south,
then passes east of Kāiyáng Xiàn to the south,
The Yíshuǐ flows south past the west of Zhōngqiū City,
as recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the seventh year of Duke Yǐn,
during the summer,
Zhōngqiū was fortified.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
it was recorded because it was not done at the proper time.
The Yíshuǐ then flows south past the east of the old city of Línyí County.
According to the Records of the Commanderies and States:
Lángyá has Línyí County,
which originally belonged to the Dōnghǎi Commandery.
The Zhìshuǐ flows into it,
originating from Guànshí Mountain in Wǔyáng County, south of Tàishān.
The Treatise on Geography states:
Guànshí Mountain
is the source of the Zhìshuǐ.
Yìng Shào's Records of Geography and Customs says:
the Wǔshuǐ originates there.
This is likely an alternative name for the same river.
It flows east past the foot of Méng Mountain,
where there is a shrine.
The Zhìshuǐ then flows southeast past the north of Zhuānyú City.
According to the Records of the Commanderies and States:
the county has Zhuānyú City.
When the Jì family was about to attack it,
Confucius said:
In the past,
the former kings made it the lord of Dōngméng,
a minister of the state.
Why attack it?
Rǎn Yǒu said:
Now, Zhuānyú
is strongly fortified and conveniently close to Fèi.
The Zhìshuǐ then flows southeast,
passing the south of the old city of Fèi County.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
it is a county under Dōnghǎi.
It was the fief of Jì Sūn of Lǔ.
Zǐlù was about to dismantle it.
Gōngshān Fúrǎo led troops to attack Lǔ but did not succeed.
Later, the Jì family was captured by Yáng Hǔ,
and Fúrǎo rebelled from Fèi.
This was the fief.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Chén Hè was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shùncóng.
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
the Yíshuǐ originates east of Fèi County in Dōnghǎi,
flows west into the Sì River,
with the water radical,
and the phonetic component jīn.
Lǚ Chén's Zìlín also says the same.
The direction in which this river flows southeast,
with the Yíshuǐ to the west,
cannot be said to go southeast.
These are all errors,
so common people call this river the Xiǎo Yíshuǐ.
The Zhìshuǐ then flows southeast past the south of Bēng City.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the eighth year of Duke Yǐn,
the Earl of Zhèng requested to relinquish the sacrifices at Tàishān,
and instead sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu, sending Wǎn to return the Bēng of Tàishān and exchange it for the fields of Xǔ.
Dù Yù's Explanation of Places states:
Bēng
was the town where Zhèng sacrificed to Tàishān,
located southeast of Fèi County in Lángyá.
The Zhìshuǐ then flows southeast and empties into the Yíshuǐ.
The Yíshuǐ then flows south past the east of the old city of Kāiyáng County.
The county
was originally the state of Yǔ.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuǒzhuàn, in the eighteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
the people of Zhū attacked Yǔ,
capturing everyone and taking them back.
The lord of Yǔ said:
I have nowhere to return.
He followed his family to Zhū.
Later, it was renamed Kāiyáng.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the third year of Duke Āi,
the text records Jì Sūn Sī and Shūsūn Zhōuqiú
leading troops to fortify Qǐyáng.
The county
was originally the seat of Lángyá Commandery.
It then flows east past the east of Xiāngfēi County,
turns and flows west from the south of the county,
then turns south past the west of Tán County.
According to the Lǔ Liánzǐ,
Lùzǐ said to King Mǐn of Qí:
The forces of Lǔ Fèi,
my armored soldiers are stationed in Xiāngfēi.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhāngxìn.
Tán was an ancient state.
Descendants of Shàohào.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the seventeenth year of Duke Zhāo,
the lord of Tán paid a visit to the Duke of Lǔ and feasted with him.
Zhāozǐ, Shūsūn Ruò, asked:
Shàohào named his offices after birds.
Why?
The lord of Tán said:
He is my ancestor,
I know about this.
Huángdì and Yándì used clouds and fire to name offices,
Tàihào used dragons,
Shàohào had the auspicious phoenix,
and established a system of bird-named offices.
Deliberations on governance were held there,
and Confucius went to learn from him.
Later, he told others:
The Son of Heaven lost the official system,
but learning exists among the four barbarians.
According to the Bamboo Annals,
in the fourth year of Duke Liè of Jìn,
Yuèzǐ Mòjú destroyed Tán,
and took the lord of Tán, Gū, back.
The county
was originally part of Lǔ,
the seat of Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Qín Shǐhuáng made it Tán Commandery.
In the second year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was renamed to its current name.
This is what Wáng Mǎng called Yípíng.
It then flows south past the west of Liángchéng County,
then south past the west of Xiàpī County,
and enters the Sì River from the south.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuǒzhuàn states:
In the thirteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn met the lord of Wú at Liáng.
The lord of Wú declined, saying the waterways were impassable,
and the Jìn forces turned back.
The Treatise on Geography states:
Liángchéng
was renamed Chénghàn by Wáng Mǎng.
The Yíshuǐ flows west north of Xiàpī County,
dividing into two streams.
One stream enters the Sì River southwest of the city's north,
and one flows east of the city, turns from the south of the county,
and also empties into the Sì River,
called the Xiǎo Yíshuǐ.
There is a bridge over the river,
called Yí in the Xú and Sì regions.
In the past, Zhāng Zǐfáng met Huángshígōng on this bridge,
which is this very place.
In the second year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Cáo Cāo besieged Lǚ Bù here,
diverting the Yí and Sì Rivers to flood the city and capture him.
25.3 Zhūshuǐ
25.3 Zhūshuǐ
The Zhūshuǐ originates from Línlè Mountain in Gài County, Tàishān.
The Treatise on Geography states:
Línlè Mountain
is the source of the Zhūshuǐ,
which flows northwest to Gài and enters the Sìshuǐ.
Sometimes written as "Chí,"
but "Gài" is a mistake.
The Zhūshuǐ flows northwest from the mountain past Gài County.
In the fifth year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
the emperor's brother-in-law Wáng Xìn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It then flows west past Dōngpíngyáng County in Tàishān.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the eighth year of Duke Xuān,
winter,
Píngyáng was fortified.
Dù Yù said:
This is present-day Tàishān's Píngyáng County.
Since there is a Píngyáng in Hédōng,
this one is called Dōng (east).
In the ninth year of the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Xīntài County.
It flows southwest to Biàn County,
and enters the Sì River.
The Zhǔ River flows southwest,
and the Dàoquán Spring flows into it.
The spring emerges from the northern side of Biàn Mountain, northeast of Biàn City.
The Shīzǐ states:
When Confucius arrived at dusk,
he did not lodge by Dàoquán,
and though thirsty, he did not drink from it,
for he detested its name.
Thus, the Lúnyǔ Bǐkǎochèn says:
The water is named Dàoquán,
and Zhòngní would not rinse his mouth with it.
This is the very spring.
It flows northwest and joins the Zhǔ River.
The Zhǔ River continues southwest past the west of Biàn City,
then flows southwest into the Sì River.
The mingled streams flow southwest to the northeast of Lǔ County,
where they split into two waterways.
Beside the water stands an ancient city,
at the point where the two streams divide and converge.
The Zhǔ River flows northwest past the north of Kǒnglǐ,
which is known as the area between the Zhǔ and Sì rivers.
The deepening of the Zhǔ River mentioned in the Chūnqiū
does not refer to its initial channeling,
but rather to its deepening and widening.
The Zhǔ River continues southwest,
where a distributary branches off.
It then flows south past the east of Xiáqiū City,
and enters a stone gate to the south,
an ancient water gate constructed of stone,
spanning across the water.
Flowing southwest,
it is commonly called the Dùwǔ Ditch.
The Zhǔ River continues southwest past the west of Xiǎnlǘ Pavilion in Nánpíngyáng County,
which was a Zhū settlement.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Xiāng of the Chūnqiū,
the Jīng records
that Zhū Shùqí fled here with Qī and Lǚqiū.
Dù Yù states:
North of Píngyáng is Xiǎnlǘ Pavilion.
The Shísānzhōu Jì says:
In Nánpíngyáng County of Shānyáng, there is also a Lǚqiū Township.
The Cóngzhēng Jì states:
What Dù calls Xiǎnlǘ
is Lǚqiū.
Now, it is noted that Qī Township lies northeast of the county,
and ten lǐ northeast of Qī Township,
one can see Lǚqiū Township.
Thus, Xiǎnlǘ is incorrect,
and Xiǎnlǘ must be a separate pavilion.
It is unclear which is accurate.
Further south,
the Guāng River flows into it.
Lǚ Chén states:
The Guāng River originates from Dōngpíngyáng,
receiving water from the Wèn River east of Chǎn Pavilion, west of Gāng County.
The Ěryǎ says:
The Wèn River diverges into the Chǎn,
just as the Luò River has the Bō.
The Guāng River flows southwest past the west of Shèngxiāng City.
Jīng Xiàngfán states:
Southwest of Gāng County lies Shèngxiāng City.
It then flows south past the west of the old city of Níngyáng County in Tàishān.
In the third year of Yuánshuò during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Tián, son of Prince Gòng of Lǔ, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Níngshùn.
Further south,
a distributary of the Zhǔ River flows into it.
This waterway draws from the Zhǔ River,
flows southwest past the north of Xiáqiū City,
then west past the south of Níngyáng City,
and finally southwest into the Guāng River.
The Guāng River continues southwest past the east of the old city of Chéngqiū County in Tàishān Commandery.
In the twentieth year of Sùhóu of Zhào,
the Hán general Jǔ fought against Qí and Wèi at Chéngqiū,
which is this county.
In the fifth year of Yuánshuò during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Jiàngyè, son of Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Guāng River then flows southeast and joins the Zhǔ River.
The Zhǔ River continues south to Gāopíng County,
where it flows south into the Sì River.
To the west lies Máoxiāng City,
thirty lǐ east of Gāopíng.
Jīng Xiàngfán states:
Thirty lǐ west of present-day Gāopíng County is the old Máoxiāng City.
26 Commentary on the Water Classic, Volume 26
26.1 The Shù River
26.1 The Shù River
The Shù River originates from the northwestern mountains of Dōngguǎn County in Lángyá,
where Dàbiàn Mountain and Xiǎotàishān share a continuous ridge but have different names.
Drawing from numerous streams,
they converge to form a river,
flowing southeast past the south of Pī Township,
which lies about eighty lǐ south of the county.
The city has three sides but is not enclosed to the south,
hence it is commonly called Bànchéng (Half City).
The Shù River continues southeast,
where it joins the Xiàn River on the left.
The Xiàn River originates from the north of Dàxiàn Mountain,
flows southeast past the east of Pī Township,
and then southeast into the Shù River.
Passing east of the county to the southeast,
the Shù River on the left merges with the water from Jī Mountain.
This water emerges from the west of Jī Mountain in Zhū County,
and Liú Chéngzhī mistakenly believed it to be the place where Xǔ Yóu lived in seclusion,
which is a grave error.
This water flows southwest into the Shù River.
Further southeast, it passes east of Jǔ County.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
Jǔ was the state of the Jǔzi,
of the Yíng surname,
descendants of Shàohào.
The Liènǚzhuàn says:
When Qǐliáng Zhí of Qí attacked Jǔ and died in battle,
his wife went to join him.
On the way, she encountered Duke Zhuāng of Qí,
who intended to offer condolences.
Qǐliáng’s wife said:
If Zhí died guilty,
why would you, my lord, demean yourself with condolences?
If Zhí was innocent,
our ancestral humble cottage remains,
and I dare not accept condolences in the suburbs.
The duke then turned his carriage and offered condolences at her home.
The wife wept beneath the city wall,
and after seven days, the wall collapsed.
Thus, the Qíncāo states:
After Zhí’s death,
his wife took up the qín and sang:
No joy surpasses that of new acquaintances,
no sorrow exceeds that of parting in life.
Her grief moved Heaven,
and the city wall crumbled.
This is the very city.
The city has three layers of walls,
all lofty and steep,
with only one gate open to the south.
The inner city measures twelve lǐ square,
and the outer wall spans about forty lǐ in circumference.
The Shīzǐ states:
The lord of Jǔ was fond of ghosts and sorcery, leading to the state’s downfall.
During the turmoil of Wúzhī,
Xiǎobái fled here.
When Yuè Yì attacked Qí,
Jǔ held its defenses and preserved the state.
Qín Shǐhuáng made it a county.
At the rise of the Hàn, it became the Chéngyáng Kingdom,
enfeoffed to Marquis Zhāng of Zhūxū,
with its seat at Jǔ.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jǔlíng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ merged Chéngyáng Kingdom into Lángyá Kingdom,
enfeoffing it to Prince Jīng, his son.
Prince Jīng was fond of palaces,
employing the utmost craftsmanship,
with wall bands adorned in gold and silver.
During the reign of Emperor Míng,
Jīng grew uneasy in Jǔ
and moved the seat to Kāiyáng.
The Shù River continues south,
and Yuángōng Water emerges from Qīng Mountain to the east, flowing along the southwestern course and joining the Shù River.
The Shù River flows further south,
where the Xún River flows into it.
The Xún River originates from Jùgōng Mountain,
flows southwest,
and was historically dammed to irrigate fields,
spanning twenty lǐ east to west
and fifteen lǐ north to south.
The Xún River then flows southwest into the Shù River.
The Shù River continues south and meets the Gěbēi Water.
This water originates from Sānzhù Mountain,
flows southwest past the south of Pìtǔ City,
commonly called Pìyáng City.
The Shǐjì Jiànyuán Yǐlái Wángzǐ Hóuzhě Niánbiǎo states:
In the second year of Yuánshuò during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Zhuàng, son of Prince Gòng of Chéngyáng, was enfeoffed as Marquis Jié here.
The water accumulates near the settlement to form a lake,
called Pìyáng Lake.
It flows southwest
and joins the Shù River.
Further south, it passes east of Yángdū County
and flows into the Yí River.
The Shù River flows from Yángdū County,
then south to meet the Wǔyáng Gōu Stream.
This stream originates east from Cāng Mountain.
On the mountain is an old city,
commonly called the Jiānguān City,
but this is incorrect;
it is actually the ancient Yǒulì City.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (125 BCE),
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Dīng, son of the Prince Gòng of Chéngyáng.
The city's foundation is built upon the mountain.
The stream flows from below the mountain,
running northwest,
and is called Wǔyáng Gōu.
It then flows west to Jíqiū County,
where it empties into the Shù.
The Shù River continues south past Jíqiū County of Dōnghǎi Commandery,
which was Zhùqiū in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
In the fifth year of Duke Huán (707 BCE),
the *Annals* records that the Marquis of Qí and the Earl of Zhèng went to Jì to fortify Zhùqiū.
The *Zuǒ Tradition* states:
"Qí and Zhèng paid court to Jì,
intending to attack it."
The Hàn established it as a county.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jiùxìn.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
"It was transferred from Dōnghǎi to Lángyé."
Kuài Yǐn said:
"Jí and Zhù
are pronunciations from Lǔ.
The character's reading likely changed over time."
The Shù River continues south past Hòuqiū County of Dōnghǎi,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Zhùqí Tíng.
Here it divides into two channels.
One channel flows southwest,
now dry,
commonly called the Dry Shù.
The other channel flows south past the east of the old city of Jiànlíng County.
