In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn (151 BCE),
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Wèi Wǎn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Fù Tíng.
The Shù River continues south past the west of Jiànlíng Mountain.
During the Zhèngguāng era of Wèi (520-525 CE),
when the Prince of Qí was stationed in Xúzhōu,
a large dam was built to block the water and divert it westward.
At the confluence of the two channels,
a defensive fort was established called Qūshù Shù.
From the dam, the water flowed thirty *li* west to join the old channel of the Shù River,
called the New Canal.
The old channel flows southwest from Hòuqiū,
joins the New Canal on the left,
and enters Sùyù County of Huáiyáng, emptying into the Sì River.
This is what the *Treatise on Geography* refers to as "reaching Xiàpī and emptying into the Sì."
The *Classic* says it enters the Yí at Yángdū,
which is incorrect.
The left channel of the Shù River was cut off by the great dam.
The old channel flows southeast,
receiving the Sāngyàn Stream.
This stream originates from Xiāngfēi County,
its springs flowing east.
The Shù channel continues south,
joining the Hénggōu Stream on the left.
This stream issues from the right of the channel,
flowing east into the old channel of the Shù.
Further south it reaches the dam.
The water flows southwest past the east of Sīwú Mountain,
then past the west of the old city of Sīwú County.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals Zuǒ Tradition* records:
"Chǔ captured the Lord of Zhōngwú and made it Sīwú County."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xīwú.
It then flows southwest to Sùyù, emptying into the Sì River.
The old channel of the Shù River flows southeast from the lower dam past the east of Sīwú City,
then southeast through Zhākǒu City.
The Zhā River originates from the Zhā territory of Chǔ.
In the tenth year of Duke Xiāng (563 BCE),
the *Annals* records the duke meeting with Jìn and other lords with Wú at Zhā.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"It is Sòng territory.
Now northwest of Bīyáng County in Péngchéng is the Zhāshuǐ Gōu,
eighty *li* from Bīyáng."
It flows southeast past the northeast of the old city of Fùyáng County.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
"It was the ancient state of Bīyáng."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals Zuǒ Tradition*, tenth year of Duke Xiāng, records:
In summer,
on the fourth month, day Wùwǔ,
they met at Zhā.
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gài of Jìn requested to attack Bīyáng and enfeoff it to Sòng's Xiàng Xū.
Xún Yīng said:
"The city is small but strong.
Victory would bring no glory,
defeat would be a laughingstock."
They insisted,
and on Bǐngyín they besieged it,
but could not take it.
Qín Jǐnfù, a retainer of the Mèng clan,
transported supplies for the campaign.
The men of Bīyáng opened the gate,
and the lords' warriors rushed the gate.
The portcullis was released,
but Zhōu's Hé held it up to let those inside out.
Dí Sīmí raised a large chariot wheel,
covered it with armor,
and used it as a shield.
Holding it in his left hand,
and wielding a halberd in his right,
he formed a single troop.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"This is what the *Odes* call 'having strength like a tiger.'"
The defenders hung down cloth,
Jǐnfù climbed it,
but they cut it when he reached the parapet.
He fell,
they hung it again,
and after reviving, he climbed again three times.
The defenders then desisted,
and he withdrew,
wearing the severed cloth as a sash and parading before the army for three days.
The lords' armies lingered long at Bīyáng,
and requested to return.
Zhì Bó angrily said:
"If you do not capture it in seven days,
you shall take it to atone for your crime."
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gài attacked,
personally enduring arrows and stones,
and finally destroyed it.
They took the Lord of Bīyáng back,
presenting him at the Wǔ Palace as a 'barbarian captive.'
Bīyáng
had the surname Yún.
The Hàn made it a county.
In the third year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (126 BCE),
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Jiù, son of Prince Xiào of Qí.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Fǔyáng.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
"Bīyáng has the Zhā River."
The Zhā River flows southeast,
mingles with the Yí and empties into the Shù,
called Zhākǒu,
from which the city gets its name.
It flows southeast to Qú County, enters the Yóu River, and empties into the sea.
26.2 The Jùyáng River
26.2 The Jùyáng River
The Jùyáng River originates from Mount Tài in Zhūxū County,
flowing north past the west of the county.
Mount Tài
is the Lesser Eastern Mount Tài.
The Jùyáng River
is the Jù River mentioned in the *Discourses of the States*.
Yuán Hóng called it Jùmèi,
Wáng Sháozhī considered it Jùmiè,
and it is also sometimes called Qúmí,
all referring to the same river,
with variations in the name.
The river flows north past the west of the old city of Zhūxū County.
In the second year of Emperor Huì of Hàn (193 BCE),
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Liú Zhāng, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí.
The *Records of Geography and Customs* says:
"Dān Mountain lies to the southwest,
source of the Dān River,
which flows east into the sea.
The Dān River originates from the hills of Zhūxū."
Thus it is said west of Zhūxū City is a long, steep slope,
named Pòchē Xiàn.
Twenty *li* northeast of the city is Dān Mountain,
commonly called Fán Mountain.
The county lies to the southwest,
not the mountain.
The characters for Dān and Fán are similar,
and the pronunciation changed with the character.
The Dān River has two sources,
each from a separate mountain,
commonly called the Eastern Dān and Western Dān Rivers.
The Western Dān River flows north from Fán Mountain,
past the east of the old city of Jù County,
where the Eastern Dān River joins it.
The Eastern Dān River originates from Fāng Mountain.
The mountain has two streams,
one being the Eastern Dān River.
It flows north past the county, joins the Western Dān River, and their waters mingle.
It then flows northeast past the north of Yībó Jiàn.
The Yī River also originates from Fāng Mountain,
flows into Píngshòu County,
accumulates to form a marsh.
When the water is high, it flows north,
then southeast,
bends and flows northeast,
past the west of the old city of Píngshòu County,
and north into the Dān River,
called Yúhé Kǒu.
The Dān River continues northeast past the east of Wànghǎi Tái,
flows northeast into the sea,
likely the namesake of the county.
It then flows north past the east of Línqú County.
The Jùyáng River flows north from Zhūxū into Línqú County,
where the Xūnyě Spring empties into it.
The spring originates from the Western Stream,
with a flying cascade cascading down the side of a deep ravine.
Above the spring and stream,
beside the source at the mountain's foot,
there is a shrine,
named the Yěquán Shrine.
According to the "Guǎngyǎ,"
the metal spirit is called Qīngmíng.
This place was likely the site of an ancient metalworking office,
hence the water derives its name from it.
The water is clear and bright, exceptionally cool and pure,
with no hidden rocks in its depths,
only shallow patterns carved in the sand.
Within it lies an ancient altar,
standing unevenly opposite each other.
Later generations made slight embellishments,
turning it into a place for leisurely excursions.
The steep banks on the north and south soar into the sky,
with sparse trees intertwining.
My late father served as the regional governor of Hǎidài during the Tàihé era.
In my childhood years,
I accompanied him on his official duties in the eastern provinces.
During the scorching heat of summer,
weary from idle thoughts in seclusion,
I would take up my qin and summon friends,
enjoying leisurely pastimes throughout the day.
We would pole bamboo rafts along the waves,
and light forests would sway with the ripples.
As the qin melodies harmonized,
our contemplative spirits also flowed freely.
This was a place to dwell and linger,
truly a spot to lean upon and find solace.
To the east, there is a small lake,
abundant with fresh bamboo shoots.
Not only are they as fragrant as peonies,
but they are also as pure as flying fish scales.
The water from this lake flows northeast into the Jùyáng River,
and is called the Xūnyě Spring.
It then passes east of the old city of Línqú County.
The city
was the ancient fief of the Bó clan.
In the first year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Nú, son of Prince Yì of Zīchuān.
Yìng Shào said:
"Línqú
is the name of a mountain,
hence the county is named after it;
Qú,
is also the name of a river."
The city lies beside the Línqú River,
which is why Wáng Mǎng used it to denote its appellation.
Along the riverbanks above and below the city,
are all the sites of the camps and fortifications from Liú Wǔhuáng's northern expedition to Guǎnggù.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast past the east of Wěisǔ Mountain,
a solitary peak standing elegantly,
shaped like a pile of grain.
Further northeast,
the Yáng River empties into it.
The Yáng River originates from the Shígāo Mountain in the northwest at Shíjiàn Pass,
flowing southeast past the west of the Féng Mountain Shrine.
The Yáng River then flows further southeast,
passing beneath Féng Mountain,
which is also Shígāo Mountain.
The mountain's base has three tiers,
with cliffs rising straight up.
On the mountain, there is a stone drum,
which sounds in years of calamity.
Guō Yuánshēng's "Xù Shùzhēng Jì" states:
"Féng Mountain is thirty lǐ south of Guǎnggù,
with a shrine,
and a stone drum.
When the Qí region is about to fall into chaos,
stone figures strike the stone drum,
and the sound can be heard for tens of lǐ."
The Yáng River flows along its northern side and then northeast,
commonly called the Shígōu River.
It flows northeast out of the north of Wěisǔ Mountain,
and east into the Jùyáng River,
at a place called Shígōu Pass.
However, the lower reaches of this river
sometimes flow and sometimes are blocked.
In spring and summer when the water rises,
the river flows continuously without cease,
and it is also sometimes called the Lóngquán River.
According to the "Geographical Records,"
Shígāo Mountain
is the source of the Yáng River.
Nowadays, in this county,
only this watercourse corresponds to it,
which seems to align with various pieces of evidence.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast to the mouth of the Pī Spring,
whose source emerges from level ground to the west,
flowing east into the Jùyáng River.
The Jùyáng River then flows north to meet the Jiàndé River,
which originates from the foothills of Féng Mountain to the west,
and flows east into the Jùyáng River.
Further north, it passes west of Jù County.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast to join the Kānglàng River,
which originates from Jiǎo Mountain southwest of the county.
The mountain has no trees,
but stands round, steep, and solitary,
with jagged peaks standing apart.
Zuǒ Sī's "Ode to the Capital of Qí" says:
"Jiǎo Ridge anchors its left," referring to this.
The Kānglàng River flows north into the Jùyáng River.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast past the west of the old city of Jù County,
which was the ancient state of Jì.
In the fourth year of Duke Zhuāng of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the Marquis of Jì could not submit to Qí,
so he gave the state to his younger brother Jì,
and left his country for good,
to escape the troubles with Qí.
Later, it was renamed.
Jù. Hence, "The Discourses of Lǔ Lián" states:
"The people of Qú and Jù
are skilled debaters."
In the eighteenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
it was separately made the state of Zīchuān.
Later, it was merged into Běihǎi.
In the second year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Cuò, son of Prince Yì of Zīchuān.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Yú County.
North of the city, there is an old terrace,
and west of the terrace is a square pond.
Yàn Mó said:
"It is ninety-seven lǐ west of the city of Qí."
When Gěng Yǎn defeated Zhāng Bù at Línzī,
he pursued him to the banks of the Jùyáng River,
where corpses lay in heaps,
referring to this river.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast past the east of the tomb of Pìlǘ Hún, the Jìn Dynasty General of the Dragon-Soaring Army and Governor of Yōuzhōu,
and then flows northeast.
Beside the tomb, there is a burial mound,
very large and tall,
which people of the time all call Mǎlíng,
but no one knows whose grave it is.
The Jùyáng River then flows northeast past the east of the old city of Yì County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Dídàng.
Yàn Mó said:
"It is fifty lǐ south of the city of Qí."
When Sima Xuānwáng attacked Gōngsūn Yuān,
he relocated people from Fēng to live in this city,
and thus renamed it Nánfēng City.
Further northeast, the river accumulates to form a deep pool,
from which a branch watercourse emerges,
called the Bǎichǐ Ditch.
It flows northwest past Běiyìdū City,
which in the second year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Liú Hú, son of Prince Yì of Zīchuān.
It then flows further northwest,
and empties into the Jùdiàn.
Further northeast, it passes west of Shòuguāng County.
The Jùyáng River flows northeast from Jùdiàn Lake,
passes west of the old county town,
which was the Yìpíng Pavilion of Wáng Mǎng’s time.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed Lǐ, the son of Gēngshǐ, as a marquis here.
Southwest of the city,
east of the river, there is a stone chamber of Kǒngzǐ,
the former temple hall.
Inside is a statue of Kǒngzǐ,
with disciples asking about the classics.
Since there are no stele records,
the details of its establishment are unknown.
The Jùyáng River flows further northeast,
where the Yáo River joins it.
The Yáo River originates from Jiǎobēng Mountain south of Jù County,
which is the old Yì Mountain.
Common people called it Jiǎobēng Mountain because its peak looked like a collapse,
hence the name Jiǎobēng Mountain,
also known as Jiǎolín Mountain,
both being popular corruptions of the name.
This river is the Ruí River.
The *Geographical Records* states:
Jù County has Yì Mountain,
from which the Ruí River originates.
It flows north past the east of Xī Mountain,
commonly called Qīng Mountain.
The Yáo River flows northeast between the eastern and western Shòuguāng cities.
Yìng Shào said:
Shòuguāng County has Guàn Pavilion.
Dù Yù said:
It is southeast of the county,
the state of Zhēnguàn.
He also said Zhēn Pavilion is southeast of Píngshòu County.
The old Píngshòu city is west of the Báiláng River,
now the seat of Běihǎi Commandery.
The river receives the lower flow from Yínglíng County,
flows northeast past the east of the city,
enters west into Biéhuà Lake,
also called Zhènhuái Lake.
The lake is twenty *li* east-west,
thirty *li* north-south,
and flows northeast into the sea.
Zhēn Pavilion is east of the Gài River.
The Gài River originates from Fùzèng Mountain east of Sāngdú Pavilion.
The pavilion
was the old seat of Gāomì Commandery,
commonly called the old commandery city.
The mountain is called Tǎ Mountain,
the river Lùmèng River,
also Lìmèng River,
both incorrect.
The *Geographical Records*
states Sāngdú
is a subordinate county of Běihǎi,
with Fùzèng Mountain,
from which the Gài River originates,
flowing north past northwest of Zhēn Pavilion to join the Báiláng River.
According to the *Geographical Records*,
Běihǎi has Zhēn County.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
The old state of Zhēnxún,
descendants of Yǔ,
ninety *li* northwest of Tíngguàn.
The Gài River flows north past west of Hán Pavilion into Biéhuà Lake.
The *Commandery and State Records* states:
Píngshòu has Zhēn City and Hán Pavilion.
Xuē Zàn’s *Collected Annotations on the Book of Han* states:
According to the *Ancient Texts of Jí Commandery*,
Xiáng resided in Zhēnguàn,
which is Guàn in Dōng Commandery.
Emperor Míng enfeoffed it to descendants of Zhōu,
renaming it Wèi.
Zhēnxún is in Hénán,
not Píngshòu.
It also says:
Tàikāng resided in Zhēnxún,
Yì also resided there,
and Jié resided there as well.
The *Preface to the Book of Documents* states:
Tàikāng lost the state,
and five brothers waited at Héruì.
This was Tàikāng’s residence,
near Luò.
I examined what Zàn based his account on:
now Hénán has Xún territory,
and Wèi state has Guān territory.
The *Discourses of the States* states:
Qǐ had Wǔguān,
called treacherous sons.
Wǔguān
is likely their name,
and the place they resided
was called Guān.
Huángfǔ Mì said:
Territory of Wèi.
He also said,
Xià Xiáng moved to Dìqiū,
relying on the Zhēnxún clan, a feudal lord of the same surname.
This matches the *Jízhǒng Texts*,
which say Xiáng resided in Zhēnguàn.
Since he relied on Zhēnxún,
it is clear Zhēnxún was not a single residence.
After Qiónghòu used his archery to usurp Xiáng,
Hánzhuó also had Péngméng assassinate Yì.
He resided there and produced Ào,
and from his house came Yì.
Thus, in the fourth year of Duke Xiāng of *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Wèi Jiàng said:
Ào used troops to destroy Zhēnguàn and the Zhēnxún clan,
placed Ào in Guō,
and placed Yì in Gē.
Therefore, Wǔ Yuán said to the Lord of Wú:
“Guō Ào killed Zhēnguàn to attack Zhēnxún.”
A surviving minister of the Xià, named Mí,
served Yì.
After Yì’s death,
he fled to the Gé clan,
now Gé County.
He gathered the remnants of Zhēnguàn and Zhēnxún,
killed Hánzhuó, and established Shǎokāng,
who destroyed them,
and the Yǒuqióng thus perished.
This likely means the place gave rise to the name,
and the residence marked the territory.
Even if transmitted texts have discrepancies,
and pavilions and walls have legends,
one cannot say that because there is a Guàn name there,
this one is wrong,
or abandon this name
to affirm that one.
Using geography to infer tradition,
Yìng Shào’s basis can also be examined.
The Yáo River flows northeast into the Jùyáng.
Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó both said Yáo once halted here,
hence the name,
but this is incorrect.
The *Geographical Records* states:
The Ruí River flows from Jù northeast to Shòuguāng into the sea.
Following its course,
this is the river.
It flows further northeast into the sea.
The Jùyáng River flows northeast past west of Wànghǎi Terrace,
northeastward.
Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó both said Píngwàng Pavilion is eighty *li* northwest of the old Píngshòu city in the ancient county,
and some say Qín Shǐhuáng ascended it to view the sea,
hence called Wànghǎi Terrace,
but details are unknown.
According to the *Records of the Grand Historian*,
in the second year of Yuánshuò of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed Liú Shǎng, son of Yì, Prince of Zīchuān, as a marquis here.
It flows further northeast into the sea.
26.3 Zī River
26.3 Zī River
The Zī River originates from Yuán Mountain in Láiwú County, Tàishān.
The Zī River originates from the mountains southwest of the county,
and is commonly known as Yuánquán.
The *Geographical Records* states:
Yuán Mountain,
is the source of the Zī River.
Therefore, the *Classic* contains the discussion of Yuán Mountain.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
the water flows from Yí Mountain,
which is likely another name for the mountain.
It flows northeast through the Láiwú Valley,
turns and flows northwest,
passing by the old city wall of the county.
The *Records of Campaigns* states:
the city is located in the Láiwú Valley,
blocked by two mountains along the road,
with a path passing through the southern and northern gates.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was Fàn Shǐyún who served as the magistrate of Láiwú,
saying that Láiwú was in Qí,
not under Lǔ's jurisdiction.
Citing an old account, it says:
Duke Líng of Qí destroyed Lái,
and the people of Lái scattered and settled in this valley,
where the settlements became desolate and overgrown,
hence the name Láiwú.
This is what the *Tribute of Yǔ* refers to as the Lái Yí.
At the meeting of Jiāgǔ,
the Marquis of Qí sent the Lái people with troops to threaten the Marquis of Lǔ,
and Xuānní remarked that the Yí did not disturb the Huá—this is the event.
I note that Tài, Wú, Lái, and Zuò,
are all mountain names,
from which the commandery and county derive their names,
established by Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Granted the Wú Mountain and Lái and Zuò"—this is the reference.
Yìng Shào's *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* says:
Láiwú County in Tàishān,
was the Lái and Zuò settlement of Lǔ.
The Zī River then turns northwest and flows past the west of the city,
and further northeast merges with another stream,
which originates southeast of the county,
commonly called the Jiāsāng Valley Stream.
The *Records of Campaigns* names it Shèngshuǐ.
The *Biographies of Immortals* states:
Lùpígōng,
was a man of Zīchuān,
who in his youth served as a minor clerk in the prefecture.
He was skilled and ingenious,
able to fashion tools with his hands.
On the mountain peak, there was a divine spring,
inaccessible to people.
The minor clerk reported to the prefect,
requesting thirty carpenters with axes,
to construct a pulley system,
and build a suspended pavilion.
His ideas flowed freely,
and in several tens of days, a ladder path was completed.
He ascended to the summit and built a shrine,
staying beside it,
securing himself in two rooms,
consuming magical herbs,
and drinking from the divine spring,
for over seventy years.
When the Zī River surged to the foot of the mountain,
he summoned over sixty members of his clan,
ordering them to ascend halfway up the mountain.
The water rose and flooded the entire commandery,
drowning tens of thousands.
The minor clerk dismissed his family,
instructing them to descend the mountain,
donned a deer-skin robe,
ascended the pavilion, and departed.
Over a hundred years later,
he sold medicine in the markets of Qí.
This stream flows northwest and joins the Zī River,
which then emerges north from the mountains,
called the Láiwú Outlet,
and flows northeast.
It passes east of Línzī County to the northeast.
The Zī River flows northeast from the mountains,
passes west of Niú Mountain,
then east past the old southern wall of Línzī County,
and eastward reaches the mouth of the Tiānqí Stream.
The stream emerges from beneath the southern foothills,
and is called the Tiānqí Abyss.
Five springs gush forth together here,
stretching three hundred paces from north to south,
and ten paces in width.
The mountain
is Niú Mountain.
Zuǒ Sī's "Ode to the Capital of Qí" says:
"Niú Ridge guards its south."
This water is among the eight shrines of Qí.
The name 'Qí'
originates from this.
The "Records of Geography and Customs" states:
"The reason Qí is called Qí
is precisely because of the name Tiānqí Abyss."
This water flows north and empties into the Zī River.
The Zī River then flows east past the north of the tombs of the Four Lords.
South of the river, at the foot of the mountain, are four tombs,
with square bases and round mounds,
each seven chǐ high,
aligned east to west in a straight row.
These are the tombs of the four kings of the Tián clan.
The Zī River then flows northeast past the west of Dàngyīn Village.
East of the river is a tomb,
with one base and three mounds,
measuring eighty paces east to west.
These are the graves of the warriors Gōngsūn Jiē,
Tián Kāijiāng,
and Gǔ Yězǐ.
Yànzǐ despised their valor for lacking propriety,
and by offering a peach caused their deaths.
They were buried in Yáng Village upon death,
which is this place.
The Zī River then flows north past the east of the city.
The city faces the Zī River,
hence it is called Línzī (Facing Zī).
It was called Qílíng County under Wáng Mǎng.
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"When water emerges in front and to the left, it is Yíngqiū."
King Wǔ enfeoffed this land to Grand Duke Wàng,
bestowing upon him the four borders,
and made Yíngqiū the capital of Qí.
Some say the capital was Yínglíng.
The "Shǐjì" records
that King Chéng of Zhōu enfeoffed Master Shàngfǔ at Yíngqiū.
As he journeyed east to his state,
his travel was slow and he lodged along the way.
The Marquis of Lái contended with him for Yíngqiū.
An innkeeper said:
"I have heard that opportunity is hard to gain and easy to lose.
The guest sleeps peacefully;
he is surely not one going to take possession of his fief."
When the Grand Duke heard this,
he dressed at night and hastened to Yíngqiū.
'Líng'
also means 'qiū' (hill).
Duke Xiàn moved from Yíngqiū to Línzī.
I note that south of Yínglíng city there is no water,
only north of the city is there a stream,
commonly called the Báiláng Stream.
It emerges west from Dān Mountain,
popularly called Fán Mountain.
It flows northeast from there.
Given the "Ěryǎ" text about 'emerging in front and to the left,'
it cannot be considered Yíngqiū.
Yíngqiū
is the name of a hill.
As the "Shī" says: "You went to Yíng,
and met me in the passes of Náo."
Many authors treat the names 'qiū' and 'líng' as equivalent,
and Yuánlíng is also rather close to Lái.
All say it was where the Grand Duke was enfeoffed.
Examining the "Chūnqiū,"
the "Classic" records the feudal lords fortifying Yuánlíng.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"They moved Qǐ."
The "Máoshī" with Zhèng's "Annotations"
both lack the character 'Yíng.'
Zuǒ Sī considered this incorrect.
Now within Línzī city there is a hill,
inside the inner wall,
with a circumference of three hundred paces,
and a height of nine zhàng.
The northern slope descends one zhàng and five chǐ.
The Zī River emerges in front of it,
hence it bears the name Yíngqiū,
which matches the "Ěryǎ."
The city faces the Tiānqí Abyss,
therefore the old city has the name Qí City.
Thus Yànzǐ said:
"First, Shuǎngjiūshì dwelled here,
then Péng Bólíng dwelled here,
then the Grand Duke dwelled here."
He also said:
"Our former lord, the Grand Duke,
built his capital at Yíngqiū."
When Jì Zhá observed the customs,
upon hearing the music of Qí, he said:
"Vast and grand is the great air!
To represent the Eastern Sea,
is it not the Grand Duke?"
When Tián Bā entered Qí,
he crossed the Zī and saw his reflection.
Guō Jǐngchún stated:
"Yíngqiū of Qí
has the Zī River passing its south and east."
Clearly it is not Yínglíng.
Duke Xiàn's move
is like the Jìn clan deeply engraving the name Jiàng at Yì;
it does not mean he moved from Yínglíng to there.
Its outer wall
is the Línzī city to which Duke Xiàn moved.
It is commonly called Lǔchéng (Captives' City),
because when King Mǐn of Qí attacked Yān,
King Kuài of Yān died,
and his people were captured and settled within the outer wall,
hence the name.
In the thirty-fourth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Qí was destroyed and made a commandery,
administered from Línzī.
In the sixth year of Hàn Gāodì,
his son Féi was enfeoffed at Qí as a kingdom.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jǐnán.
The "Zhànguócè" says:
"When Tián Dān was Chancellor of Qí,
he crossed the Zī River.
An old man, fording the Zī, emerged
unable to walk,
and sat in the sand.
Dān then removed his fur robe upon this water."
[The Zī River] then flows east past the east of Lì County.
The Zī River flows northeast from the county, passing north of the Dōng'ānpíng City.
Further east, it passes south of the old city of Jùdiàn County.
In the fourth year of the Zhēnghé era,
Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty visited Dōnglái,
reaching the great sea.
In the third month,
he plowed at Jùdiàn,
which is precisely this place.
Southeast of the county lies Jùdiàn Lake,
likely named after the water.
The Zī River continues northeast, passing south of the old city of Guǎngráo County.
During the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty,
Liú Guó, son of the Prince Jìng of Zīchuān, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Zī River flows further northeast,
where the Mǎchēdú River joins it,
receiving water from Jùdiàn,
which is where the Zhuó River flows into.
Lǚ Chēn said:
The Zhuó River is also called the Hùn River.
It originates from Wéi Mountain in Guǎng County,
commonly known as Yělǐng Mountain.
Flowing northeast, it passes west of Guǎnggù City.
The city lies four lǐ northwest of Guǎng County,
surrounded by steep ravines,
with deep moats forming natural barriers.
During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn Dynasty,
it was built by Cáo Yí of Dōnglái.
Beside the water, at the mountain's edge, is the Wǔlóngkǒu (Five Dragon Mouth).
In the fifth year of the Yìxī era,
when Emperor Wǔ of the Liú-Sòng Dynasty attacked Mùróng Chāo at Guǎnggù,
due to the treacherous terrain,
the troops were exhausted.
Xuán Wén of Héjiān advised Yù, saying:
"In the past, when Zhào attacked Cáo Yí,
those who observed the qi believed that the Miǎn River encircled the city,
making it impregnable.
If the Wǔlóngkǒu were blocked,
the city would surely fall."
Shí Chù followed this advice,
and Yí surrendered.
Five days after the surrender,
heavy rain and thunder occurred,
causing the blockage to burst open.
Later, when Mùróng Kè attacked Duàn Kān,
he could not capture it for a hundred days.
After blocking the mouth, Kān surrendered.
Not long after the surrender,
it burst open again.
The old foundation still exists.
It would be advisable to try repairing it."
Yù blocked it,
and Chāo and all the men and women in the city grew weak in the legs,
with more than half falling ill.
Chāo then fled,
and was captured by the Jìn forces.
However, the city's location
truly relied on the natural terrain for its defense,
and its vulnerability lay precisely in this.
The Zhuó River flows northeast,
passing east of Yáo Mountain.
The *Cóngzhēng Jì* states:
"Three lǐ north of Guǎnggù City is the Yáo Mountain Shrine.
Emperor Yáo ascended this mountain during an inspection tour,
and later generations named the mountain after him.
The temple is on the left foothill of the mountain,
with the statue facing east.
The splendid hall is well-maintained,
and the imperial images are solemnly adorned.
The dignified appearance of the emperor and his officials is awe-inspiring.
On the mountain's summit,
there was once an upper shrine,
now destroyed and abandoned,
with no remaining traces of its form.
On the flat rocks, there are still imprints of men and horses,
but they are merely yellow stones.
Only the traces of swords and blades appear strikingly real.
As for the blades of Yān, the edges of Dài,
the swords of Wèi, and the points of Qí,
they are no different from today's swords.
By closely examining and copying them,
one can tell they were made by human skill."
Looking west, one sees Húgōnglíng.
Sūn Chàng said:
"Fù Hóngrén, Governor of Qīngzhōu, claimed to have found a bronze coffin with clerical script there."
The Zhuó River flows further northeast, passing north of Dōngyáng City.
Flowing northeast, it merges with the Chángshā River.
This river originates from the northern foothills of Féng Mountain,
commonly known as the Yáng River.
It flows northeast, passing west of the old city of Guǎng County,
formerly the seat of the Governor of Qīngzhōu,
also called Qīngzhōu City.
The Yáng River flows further northeast,
where the Shíjǐng River joins it.
This river originates from the southern mountains,
where the mountain peak opens like a cave,
resembling a gate when viewed from afar.
Locals call this mountain Pìtóu Mountain.
The water flows north into a well,
located east of Guǎng City.
The well is surrounded by rocks on three sides,
over a zhàng in height and depth.
The long stream surges with waves,
cascading down like a waterfall,
with a roaring sound
that startles the river and echoes through the valley.
The force of the rushing water
resembles that of a great river.
It flows north into the Yáng River.
I grew up in eastern Qí
and often roamed beneath it.
For a long time, I was cut off from it,
accumulating years of longing.
Later, due to official duties,
I returned to the region of Hǎidài.
Guō Jīn and Zǐ Huì
composed poems together at Shíjǐng,
discussing ideas all day long.
The joy and entertainment greatly comforted my wandering heart,
but I regret that this river sometimes flows and sometimes stops.
The Yáng River flows east, passing south of the meditation hall of the old Qījí Temple.
North of the river, long corridors stretch everywhere,
with pavilions rising among the forests.
Seats are arranged in orderly rows,
and alms bowls are placed intermittently.
These are the diligent monks,
dwelling in secluded meditation.
The Yáng River flows further east, passing southeast of Dōngyáng City.
During the Yìxī era,
Yáng Mùzhī, Governor of Qīngzhōu under the Jìn Dynasty, built this city.
Because it lies north of the Yáng River,
it is called Dōngyáng City.
This is because the Zhuó River is commonly known as the Xīyáng River.
The flow of water sometimes ceases and sometimes resumes,
truly a spiritual phenomenon.
In the past, during the Sòng Dynasty,
this river stopped flowing and then resumed.
Liú Huǎng composed the *Tōngjīn* ode about it.
During the Tàihé era of the Wèi Dynasty,
this river dried up again,
ceasing to flow for years.
When my late father took office in the province,
before his term was complete,
the river resumed flowing,
clear and full, reflecting the surroundings.
This is what is called: "The dry valley overflows again,
the exhausted spring resumes its flow."
Scholars of Hǎidài
again composed the *Tōngjīn* ode.
Sūn Dàoxiāng of Píngchāng, a commoner, praised:
"That Miǎn Spring,
dry for over three years,
offerings of jade exhausted,
sacrifices of livestock spent.
The Way follows rise and fall,
its flow depends on sage wisdom."
The elder Zhào Yí of Héjiān praised:
"Before the term of governance was complete,
profound grace secretly bestowed.
Dry sources surge with waves,
parched rivers cleanse the banks."
Guō Qīn of Běihǎi said:
"Previous administration stopped the flow,
our lord opened the waters."
However, the praises are extensive and verbose,
difficult to record in full.
The Yáng River turns north, passing east of the temple of Liú Zhāng, Prince Jǐng of Chéngyáng of the Hàn Dynasty,
and flows east into the Jùyáng River.
Later, people built a dam to divert it,
directing it north into the Zhuó River.
At the time, people commonly referred to the Zhuó River as the Yáng River,
hence the terms Nányáng and Běiyáng Rivers.
The two rivers merge,
commonly called the Chángshā River,
or sometimes collectively referred to as the Miǎn River.
Thus, Yàn Mó and Fú Chēn, in their *Qí Jì*,
both stated:
"Since Dōngyáng City lies north of the Miǎn River,
it should be called Miǎnyáng City."
This is incorrect.
People also call the Yáng River the Yáng River,
but I have consulted various texts,
which clearly state that the Yáng River originates from Línqú County,
while the Yáng River originates from Guǎng County.
Although the two counties are adjacent,
their rivers and soils differ,
raising doubts about this matter.
The Zhuó River flows north, passing west of Zāngshì Terrace,
then north, passing west of Yì City,
and finally flows north into Jùdiàn.
The *Geographical Records* state:
"Wéi Mountain in Guǎng County
is the source of the Zhuó River,
which flows northeast to Guǎngráo and enters Jùdiàn."
To the west of Jùdiàn,
the Nǚ River also flows into it.
This river originates from Shétóu Mountain in Dōng'ānpíng County.
The *Cóngzhēng Jì* states:
"West of the river is the tomb of Duke Huán,
very large and lofty,
with a mound measuring over seventy zhàng in circumference."
It is forty zhang high,
and the circular mound measures over twenty zhang in circumference.
It is seventy zhang high,
and there is another tomb that is seven zhang square.
These two mounds—
Yàn Mó said:
According to the "Líng Jì," this is not a proper burial ritual;
it is as if following an old custom,
where he and his mother share the same tomb but have separate mounds.
Fú Chēn did not provide further details.
East of the tomb, at the foot of the mountain, lies the source of the Nǚshuǐ, where the temple of Duke Huán was originally located.
Shìqí Héng memorialized that it was established by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi.
He said:
"Recently, while passing through the outskirts of Qí,
I gazed upon the tomb mound of Duke Huán,
nestled in the southern mountains.
I request that a shrine be established
to serve as the solitary master of this place."
Guō Yuánshēng’s "Shù Zhēng Jì" states:
"The tomb of Duke Huán of Qí is located twenty lǐ south of Qíchéng.
The tomb was built against the mountain.
East of the large tomb lies the Nǚshuǐ.
Some say the tomb of Duke Huán’s daughter is situated above it,
hence the water is named after her.
The Nǚshuǐ flows northeast from its source,
and it is said to possess great spiritual power.
When governance is prosperous, the water flows abundantly;
when governance is weak, the river dries up.
In the sixth year of the Jiànpíng era of Yān,
the water suddenly dried up violently.
Xuánmíng took this as an ill omen,
fell ill, and died.
In the fourth year of the Tàishàng era of Yān,
the Nǚshuǐ dried up again.
Mùróng Chāo took this as an ill omen,
and the fortunes of Yān subsequently declined.
The Nǚshuǐ flows northeast past the old city of Dōng'ānpíng County.
The "Xù Shù Zhēng Jì" states:
"The Nǚshuǐ reaches the south of Ānpíng City, flows underground for fifteen lǐ,
then reemerges
and flows north into the Yángshuǐ.
The city
was originally the Xī Tíng.
In the third year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ in the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
Jì Jì surrendered Xī to Qí.
The "Gōngyáng Zhuàn" states:
"Who is Jì?
He is the younger brother of the Marquis of Jì.
He was praised for submitting to punishment,
offering Xī to serve the five sacrifices."
This was the former fief of Tián Chéngzǐ Dān.
Later, it was made a county.
Since Bólíng already had an Ānpíng,
this one was prefixed with "Dōng" (East).
In the seventh year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate to Liú Mào, son of the Prince of Zīchuān.
It then passes east of Dōng'ānpíng City,
flows northeast past the east of Lǒngqiū,
and enters Jùdiàn from the northeast.
The "Geographical Treatise" states:
"From the Tùtóu Shān,
the Nǚshuǐ originates,
flowing northeast to Línzī, where it enters Jùdiàn."
Further north, it becomes the Mǎchē Dú,
joins the Zīshuǐ to the north,
and continues north,
where the Shímiǎnzhīshuǐ flows into it.
The Shíshuǐ originates twenty-five lǐ northwest of Qíchéng,
emerging as a spring from level ground.
It is also called the Rúshuǐ,
and also known as the Yuánshuǐ.
Because the water is dark in color,
it is commonly referred to as the Hēishuǐ.
It flows northwest past the east of Huángshān,
then north past the east of Yúgōng Shān,
where the tomb of Yúgōng is located.
The Shíshuǐ then bends and flows north of Dù Shān,
where the Yúgōng Valley lies.
During the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
a lord lived in seclusion in this valley.
A neighbor falsely accused him of stealing a colt,
and the lord gave it to him.
The mountain
is a prominent ridge of Dù Shān.
Because the man appeared foolish,
he was called Yúgōng.
There is a stone bridge over the water,
so it is also called the Shíliángshuǐ.
The Huàshuǐ also flows into it,
originating from the Shíshuǐ,
eighteen lǐ east of Línzī City.
This is the so-called Huàzhōng.
Locals call the Huàshuǐ the Sùliúshuǐ,
which flows northwest into the Shíshuǐ.
When Mencius left Qí,
he stayed for three nights before departing from Huà,
hence later generations changed the name of the water accordingly.
South of the water, west of the mountain, lies the tomb of Wáng Chù.
In the past, when Yuè Yì attacked Qí,
he admired Wáng Chù’s virtue and offered to enfeoff him,
but Chù refused,
and hanged himself to death.
Along the water, fields were irrigated by diverted water,
and traces of the irrigation channels still remain.
The Shíshuǐ then flows northwest past the old city of Xī'ān County,
originally called Qúqiū.
This was the fief of Yōng Lǐn, a senior official of Qí.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Dōngníng.
The Shíshuǐ then flows west to the Shíyáng Weir, where it divides into two streams,
known as the Shíyángkǒu.
A branch flows northwest to Liángzōu and enters the Jìshuǐ.
The Shíshuǐ then flows north past the west of Xī'ān City,
continues north,
where the Jīngshuǐ and Xìshuǐ flow into it.
The water originates southwest of Qíchéng,
and is commonly called the Hánquán.
It flows northeast directly west of the Shēn Gate.
Jīng Xiàngfán and Dù Yù both stated:
"The Shēn Gate is the first gate on the western side of the southern wall of Qíchéng."
This is the Shēn Pond.
In the past, Duke Yì of Qí was traveling at the Shēn Pond,
when Bǐng Chù and Yán Zhí,
assassinated him among the bamboo groves.
Today, the pond no longer resembles its former state,
but along the water’s edge, small bamboo groves still grow,
sprouting from time to time.
In the commentary to Zuǒ Sī’s "Ode to the Capital of Qí,"
it states: "The Shēn Pond is by the seashore,
a marshland of Qí."
I examined the "Spring and Autumn Annals," under the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng,
when Jìn attacked Qí.
On the wùxū day,
they cut down the catalpas at the Yōng Gate.
On the jǐhài day,
they burned the Yōng Gate.
On the rényín day,
they burned the northeastern and northwestern outer walls.
On the jiǎchén day,
they advanced eastward, reaching south of the Wéishuǐ and the Yíshuǐ.
But it does not mention plundering northward by the sea.
Moreover, Xiànzǐ of Jìn did not hesitate to risk death to achieve his ambitions—
how could he have refrained from punishing his enemies
and instead ravaged the vegetation by the sea?
Furthermore, during the scorching summer heat,
it was not the season for distant travels.
Duke Yì was assassinated,
likely because, like a white dragon disguising itself as a fish,
he was trapped in the outskirts.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng neglected the nearby and cited the distant,
so his historical inquiry is flawed.
Dù Yù’s statement
is based on inference.
The Xìshuǐ flows north along the city wall,
passing west of the Yáng Gate.
Along the water’s edge is an old enclosed site,
known as the Jìxià of Qí.
During the Warring States period,
because King Xuān of Qí was fond of literature,
itinerant persuaders such as Zōu Yǎn, Chúnyú Kūn, Tián Pián, Jiēzǐ, and Shèn Dào—seventy-six in total—
were all granted official residences,
appointed as senior ministers,
and engaged in discussions without administrative duties.
Thus, the scholars of Jìxià in Qí flourished once more,
numbering in the hundreds.
Liú Xiàng’s "Bié Lù" states that Jì was the name of a city gate in Qí.
Persuaders and debaters
would gather under the Jì Gate,
hence the name Jìxià.
In the "Zhèng Zhì,"
Zhāng Yì asked about the "Shū Zàn," saying:
"Our late teacher, the scholar under the jujube tree—
when did he live?"
Zhèng Xuán replied:
"During the Tián clan’s rule in Qí,
it was a gathering place for learned scholars.
The people of Qí called him the scholar under the jujube tree,
but he was not a specific individual."
I examined the "Zuǒ Zhuàn," under the twenty-second year of Duke Zhāo,
when the ruler of Jǔ went to Qí,
and they swore an alliance outside the Jì Gate.
During the Hàn dynasty, Shūsūn Tōng was appointed as a court academician,
and was titled the Jìsì Jūn.
The "Shǐjì Yīnyì" states:
"He wished to continue the legacy of the Jìxià tradition of Qí."
However, "under the jujube tree" is also a place name within the city of Lǔ.
In the "Zuǒ Zhuàn," under the eighth year of Duke Dìng,
Yáng Hǔ seized the duke and attacked the Mèng clan,
entering from the Upper East Gate,
fighting inside the South Gate,
and also fighting under the jujube tree.
This was likely also a gathering place for Confucian scholars.
Thus, Zhāng Yì raised his doubt and asked,
and Zhèng Xuán explained and clarified it.
Although the names differ and appear interchangeably,
their essence is largely the same.
Within the city, there is an old terrace,
the Yíngqiū,
and the old temple of King Jǐng,
which is the temple of Marquis Zhāng of Zhūxū.
The "Jìn Qǐjū Zhù" states:
In the state of Qí, there was a great serpent three hundred paces long,
carrying a small serpent over a hundred paces long,
passing through the marketplace,
where all the market people watched.
It entered from the north gate.
Two hundred paces northeast outside the north gate,
there was the tomb and residence of Yàn Yīng, the chancellor of Qí.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records
that Yànzi’s residence was near the marketplace.
Duke Jǐng wanted to move him,
but Yīng refused to change.
He made a vow, saying:
“In life, I lived near the marketplace;
in death, how could I change my resolve?”
Thus, he was buried at his former residence,
and later people named the place Qīngjié Lǐ.
The Xì River then flows north past the west gate of Línzī City and northward,
then turns west past the south of the Wú Palace.
In the past, when the state of Chǔ sent an envoy to Qí,
the King of Qí feasted him at the Wú Palace—
this is that palace.
The place is still called Wútái Lǐ.
The terrace is very layered and elegant,
over a hundred paces from east to west,
and slightly less from north to south.
This is the terrace of the ancient Wú Palace.
East of the terrace is where the so-called “Yān stone” was obtained by the foolish man of Sòng, as mentioned by Quèzi.
West of the terrace is the Stone Shrine Stele,
which still exists.
It was erected in the fifth year of the Xīpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn.
Its inscription reads:
“Wútái Lǐ.”
The Xì River then flows west past the north of Kuíqiū.
In the eighth year of Duke Zhuāng in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Duke Xiāng sent Lián Chēng and Guǎn Zhìfù to garrison Kuíqiū.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
“Fifty lǐ west of Qí is the place called Kuíqiū.
If so,
there was no need to garrison it.”
In the ninth year of Duke Xī,
Duke Huán of Qí met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū.
Zǎi Kǒng said:
“The Marquis of Qí does not devote himself to cultivating virtue but strives for distant campaigns.”
This shows that Kuíqiū was not in Qí.
He cited Kuíqiū in Fényīn east of the Yellow River,
and Kuíchéng northwest of Shānyáng, suggesting it should be there,
but this is incorrect.
I examine the Zuǒ Zhuàn:
When Lián Chēng and Guǎn Zhìfù were garrisoning Kuíqiū,
they set the melon season as the time for rotation.
They requested a replacement but were not allowed.
They planned to cause chaos in Qí,
so they ordered their unattractive sister to wait for the duke in the palace.
Taking advantage of Wúzhī’s demotion,
they harmed Duke Xiāng.
If they were stationed far away without replacement,
how could they have plotted with a woman
to cause chaos in the ducal house?
Therefore, Dù Yù, examining the essence of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
annotated the tradition accordingly, placing it west of Línzī. One cannot abandon the near for the distant
merely to establish one’s own differing view.
If the difference can be distinguished,
then the meaning is upheld.
Thus, the garrison at Kuíqiū
was indeed this place.
West of the Xì River,
it branches left to form a deep pool.
Further west,
it passes south of the relocated commandery of Gāoyáng,
established by the Wèi.
It then flows northwest
and empties into the Shí River.
The Shí River then flows northeast,
and the Miǎn River joins it.
The Miǎn River originates east of Yíng City,
and is commonly called the Hàn Zhēn River.
It flows northwest past the north of Yíng City.
In the fourth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Liú Xìndū, son of Prince Dàohuì of Qí, was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
The Miǎn River then flows west past the old city of Bóchāng County in Lè’ān.
Yìng Shào said:
“The Chāng River originates from Chāngyáng County in Dōnglái.
The distance is too far to reach,
so they took its auspicious name.”
Kàn Yīn said:
“The county is situated on level ground,
hence the name Bóchāng.”
The Miǎn River flows west past Bèiqiū.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
“South of Bóchāng County, near the Miǎn River,
there is a place called Bèiqiū,
forty lǐ northwest of the city of Qí.”
In the eighth year of Duke Zhuāng in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Marquis of Qí was hunting at Bèiqiū
when he saw the boar of Prince Péngshēng standing and weeping.
The Marquis of Qí fell from his chariot and injured his foot at this place.
The Miǎn River then flows northwest into the Shí River.
The Cóng Zhēng Jì also states:
“The river originates from Línzī County,
flows north past the southern border of Lè’ān Bóchāng,
and enters the Shí River from the west.”
From here downward, it is commonly called the Miǎn.
In the past, when the Marquis of Jìn feasted with the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Qí said:
“There is wine like the Miǎn.”
He was referring to this river.
The Shí River then bends northeast,
passing north of Bóchāng City.
The Shí River then flows northeast past the old city of Qílì County,
then northeast past the old city of Jùdiàn County,
then northeast past the old city of Guǎngráo County,
and enters the Zī River from the northeast.
The Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì states:
“The Zī flows into the Rú.”
The Huáinánzǐ records:
Duke Bái asked subtly:
“If water is poured into water,
what happens?”
Confucius said:
“When the waters of Zī and Miǎn merge,
Yì Yá can taste and distinguish them.”
He was referring to these waters.
Further northeast, it enters the sea.
The Zī River enters Mǎchē Dú,
flows chaotically northeast past the old city of Lánghuái,
then northeast past the north of Mǎjǐng City,
intermingling with the waters of the Shí and Miǎn Rivers, sharing names interchangeably.
Thus, the settlements inherit their designations.
Further northeast, it reaches Píqiū Kēng
and enters the sea.
Therefore, both Yàn Mó and Fú Chēn state:
“The waters of Zī and Miǎn merge west of Píqiū Kēng.”
The Dìlǐzhì states:
“Mǎchē Dú reaches Lánghuái and enters the sea,”
likely referring to the county.
26.4 Wèn River
26.4 Wèn River
The Wèn River originates from Mount Tài in Zhūxū County.
On the mountain is the Great Wall,
connecting to Mount Dài in the west
and extending to the vast sea of Lángyá in the east,
stretching over a thousand lǐ.
It was built by the Tián clan.
The Zhúshū Jìnián records:
In the twentieth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
Qí built fortifications to form the Great Wall.
The Zhúshū also states:
In the twelfth year of Duke Liè of Jìn,
the king ordered Hán Jǐngzǐ, Zhào Lièzǐ, and Zhái Yuán to attack Qí,
and they entered the Great Wall.
The Shǐjì mentions that King Wēi of Qí crossed Zhào to invade us,
attacking the Great Wall.
Both Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó state:
The river originates from Wū Mountain southeast of the county,
which is east of Lesser Mount Tài.
It passes north of the county to the east.
The Wèn River flows northeast from the county past the north of Wú City.
The Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì states:
“Forty lǐ east of Zhūxū County is Wúchéng Pavilion,
the site of an old county.”
Further northeast, it passes east of Guǎn Níng’s tomb.
Thus, Yàn Mó said:
“Southwest of Chái Fù is the tomb of Guǎn Níng, the solitary gentleman of Wèi.”
Before the tomb is a stele.
Further northeast, it passes north of Chái Fù Mountain.
East of the mountain is the tomb of the recluse Bǐng Yuán,
with stele inscriptions still extant.
The Wèn River then flows northeast past the tomb of Sūn Sōng, Governor of Qīngzhōu in Hàn,
with a stele to the west.
The Wèn River then flows east past the old city of Ānqiū County.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
General Zhāng Yuè was enfeoffed here as a marquis.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
“It is the Zhì of Wáng Mǎng.”
Mèng Kāng said:
“This is now Qúqiū Pavilion.”
Both Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó’s Qí Jì state:
“Jǔ Qúqiū Pavilion is ten lǐ northeast of Ānqiū City.”
This is incorrect.
The city faces Móu Mountain.
Southwest of the mountain are the tombs of Sūn Bīnshuò and his brothers,
with stele inscriptions still extant.
Further north, it passes west of Chúnyú County,
then northeast into the Wéi River.
This was the state of Zhēnguàn of the Xiàhòu clan.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed the Duke of Chúnyú here,
calling it the state of Chúnyú.
In the sixth year of Duke Huán in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
in winter,
the Duke of Zhōu went to Cáo.
The Zhuàn states:
“The Duke of Chúnyú went to Cáo,
judging his state to be in danger,
and never returned.”
Northeast of the city,
two rivers converge.
26.5 The Wéi River
26.5 The Wéi River
The Wéi River originates from Wéi Mountain in Jī County of Lángyé.
Lángyé
is the name of a mountain,
and it was the former state of King Gōujiàn of Yuè.
After Gōujiàn annexed Wú,
he desired to dominate the Central States,
and moved his capital to Lángyé.
In the twenty-sixth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he destroyed Qí and made it a commandery.
The city walls were built by the Qín emperor.
He then ascended the great Lèzhī Mountain of Lángyé,
and built a tiered terrace upon it,
which was called the Lángyé Terrace.
The terrace is located ten lǐ southeast of the city,
standing alone and prominently,
rising above the surrounding mountains.
Its circumference, from top to bottom, is over twenty lǐ,
and it borders the vast sea.
The Qín king delighted in it,
and thus stayed for three months.
He then relocated thirty thousand households of commoners to the foot of Lángyé Mountain,
exempting them from taxes for twelve years.
The terrace's foundation has three tiers,
each tier being three zhàng high.
The top level is flat and spacious,
measuring over two hundred paces square,
and five lǐ wide.
Stone inscriptions were carved and steles erected,
to record the merits and virtues of Qín.
On the terrace, there is a divine abyss,
which is extremely numinous.
If defiled by people, it dries up;
if purified through fasting, it flows freely.
The shrine is among the eight temples of Qí,
and Hàn Wǔdì also once ascended it.
In the seventh year of Empress Lü of Hàn Gāodì,
it was made a kingdom.
In the third year of Emperor Wén,
it was renamed a commandery.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Tiányí.
The Wéi River originates from Wéi Mountain.
Xǔ Shèn and Lǚ Chén stated:
The Wéi River originates from Jīwū Mountain.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The Wéi River originates from Fùzhōu Mountain.
These are likely different names for the same place.
It flows northeast past the west of the old city of Jī County,
then west,
where the Xīquán River flows into it.
The Xīquán River originates from Sōng Mountain north of Xīquán County,
flows southeast past the east of Xīquán County,
then southeast past the east of Zhònggù Mountain,
and enters the Wéi River from the north.
The Geographical Treatise says:
It enters the Wéi River north of Jī County.
The Wéi River then flows northeast past the west of the old city of Zhū County.
In the twelfth year of Duke Wén of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ fortified Zhū and Yùn.
The Commentary says:
He fortified their subordinate cities.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhūbìng.
The Wéi River then flows northeast,
where the Juān River flows into it.
The Juān River originates from Mǎ'ěr Mountain,
which is one hundred zhàng high.
On its summit, two rocks stand side by side,
resembling the ears of a horse when viewed from Qí,
hence the name given by later generations.
It is thirty lǐ east of Cháng Mountain.
The Juān River emerges from its northern side,
flows north past the east of Lóuxiāng City.
In the fifth year of Duke Zhāo of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Classic records that in summer, Móuyí of Jǔ, Móulóu, Fáng, and Zī fled here.
The eastern part of Zhū County was also separated to form Hǎiqū County,
so commoners call this city Dōngzhū City.
The Juān River then flows north into the Wéi River.
It flows northeast past the west of Dōngwǔ County.
The county town was built on a ridge,
with a circumference of thirty lǐ.
In the sixth year of Hàn Gāodì,
Guō Méng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiángshàn.
Further north,
it joins the Fúqí River on the left.
The Fúqí River originates from Cháng Mountain to the southwest,
and flows northeast into the Wéi River.
Yàn Mó and Fú Chēn both considered the Wéi River to be the Fúqí River,
and the Fúqí River to be the Wéi River,
which is incorrect.
According to the Classic's description of the waterways,
the Wéi River flows north from Jī County past the northwest of Dōngwǔ County,
where it joins the Fúqí River.
Yàn Mó and Fú Chēn said:
The water two lǐ northwest of Dōngwǔ City is the Wéi River,
which is actually the Fúqí River.
The Wéi River then flows north and joins the Lú River on the right,
which is the Jiǔtái River.
The Geographical Treatise says:
The river originates from the old mountain in Héng County of Lángyé,
which Wáng Mǎng called Lìngqiū.
The mountain is southeast of the old city of Dōngwǔ County,
and is commonly called Lú Mountain.
It flows northwest past the west of the old city of Chāng County, then northeast.
The Qí Local Records say:
Southeast of Dōngwǔ City, there is the Lú River.
Beside the river, there is a fire-resistant tree.
Locally, it is called Chēngzi.
Even if burned by wildfire,
its charcoal does not extinguish,
hence Dōngfāng Shuò called it the "unburnable wood."
The river then flows northeast past the east of the old city of Dōngwǔ County,
and enters the Wéi River from the northwest.
The Geographical Treatise says:
The Jiǔtái River flows southeast to Dōngwǔ and enters the Wéi River.
This is what the Shàngshū refers to as "the Wéi and Zī rivers follow their courses."
Further north, it passes east of Píngchāng County.
The Wéi River then flows north past the west of the old city of Shíquán County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Yǎngxìn.
The Geographical and Customs Records say:
Forty lǐ southeast of Píngchāng County, there is the Shíquán Pavilion,
which was formerly a county.
The Wéi River then flows north past the east of the old city of Píngchāng County,
where the Jīng River flows into it.
The Jīng River originates from the Jīngshān Hill south of the county,
and flows northeast past the east of the old city of Píngchāng County.
Emperor Wén of Hàn enfeoffed Áng, son of Qí Dàohuì King Féi, as a marquis here.
At the southeastern corner of the city, there is a terrace,
and below the terrace, there is a well,
which connects with the Jīng River.
If something falls into the well,
it can be retrieved from the Jīng River.
In the past, dragons often appeared here,
so it is also called Lóngtái City.
The Jīng River then flows northeast into the Wéi River.
The Wéi River then flows north,
where the Wú River flows into it.
The Wú River originates from Wú Mountain,
commonly called Jùpíng Mountain.
The Geographical Treatise says:
Língmén County has Gāozhè Mountain and Hú Mountain, from which the Wú River originates,
flowing northeast into the Wéi River.
Now, this mountain connects with Wú Mountain to the west.
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
The river originates from Língmén Mountain,
commonly called the Wúwèn River.
The river flows northeast past the east of the old city of Gūmù County.
The county has five-colored soil.
When the king enfeoffed feudal lords,
he bestowed it according to their directions,
hence it was the state of the Bógū clan.
Kǎn Yīn said:
During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
Bógū and four other states rebelled.
Duke of Zhōu destroyed them,
and enfeoffed Tàigōng here.
Therefore, the Geographical Treatise says:
Some say it is Bógū.
Wáng Mǎng called it Jìmù.
Yìng Shào said:
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The state of the Bógū clan,
where Tàigōng was enfeoffed.
Xuē Zàn's commentary on the Hànshū states:
Bóchāng has the city of Bógū.
It is unclear which is correct.
The Wú River then flows northeast past the north of the old city of Píngchāng County.
In ancient times, a dam was built on this river to irrigate fields,
and it flows south into the Jīng River.
The Wú River then flows northeast
and enters the Wéi River.
Further north, it passes west of Gāomì County.
Yìng Shào said:
The county has the Mì River,
hence it has the name Gāomì.
However, what is nowadays called the Hundred-Foot Water
is actually the Mì River.
The river has two sources:
the western source emerges from Yì Mountain,
also called Zhàngrì Mountain.
The mountain is lofty and steep,
blocking the sunlight.
Yàn Mó said:
The mountain's shape blocks the sun,
hence it has this name.
Fú Chēn said:
The mountain blocks the sun,
therefore it is named Zhàngrì Mountain.
Its waters flow northeast,
the eastern source emerges from Wǔnǔ Mountain,
flows northwest and together they pour into one ravine,
commonly called the Hundred-Foot Water.
The ancients built a dam to irrigate several tens of qǐng of fields.
It flows north past the west of Gāomì County,
then flows down into the Wéi River.
From here downward it is also commonly referred to by that name.
The unruly flow passes west of Bēichǎn Mountain west of the county,
then further northeast,
where there is an old weir on the water.
In the past, stones were cut and pillars erected to block the Wéi River,
spanning about sixty paces wide.
The eastern bank was excavated,
channeling the water into a long canal.
It flows northeast past the old city south of Gāomì County.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Dèng Zhèn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Ten lǐ south of the county,
water was stored to form a pond.
It was over twenty lǐ square,
what was anciently called the Southern Capital of Gāomì.
It irrigated about one qǐng of fields.
The pond water dispersed and flowed,
descending into the Yí'ān Marsh.
The Wéi River flows north from the weir past the old city west of Gāomì County.
In the sixteenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
it was separately made the Jiāoxī Kingdom.
In the first year of the Běnshǐ era of Emperor Xuān,
it was changed to the Gāomì Kingdom,
which was Zhāngmóu under Wáng Mǎng.
The Wéi River flows further north.
In the past, Hán Xìn and the Chǔ general Lóng Jū faced each other across the Wéi River and arrayed their troops here.
Xìn ordered over ten thousand bags to be made at night,
filled with sand to block the Wéi River.
He led his troops to attack Jū and feigned retreat.
Jū pursued him northward.
Xìn breached the water,
and a great flood came.
Half of Jū's army could not cross,
and Lóng Jū was beheaded at this river.
West of the river is Lì Mound,
on which is the tomb of Hàn Minister of Agriculture Zhèng Kāngchéng,
and a stone stele still remains.
It flows further north past the old city east of Chāng'ān County.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Dèng Xí was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The *Records of the Commanderies and States* says:
It was restored in the first year of the Yánguāng era of Emperor Ān of Hàn.
It flows further north past east of Chúnyú County.
The Wéi River flows further north,
and on the left converges with the Wèn River.
It flows north past west of Píngchéng Pavilion,
then further northeast past west of Mìxiāng Pavilion.
The *Records of the Commanderies and States* says:
Chúnyú County has Mìxiāng.
The *Treatise on Geography*
states that both were subordinate counties of Běihǎi.
Yìng Shào said:
Sixty lǐ northeast of Chúnyú County is Píngchéng Pavilion,
and another forty lǐ further is Mìxiāng Pavilion,
which was an old county.
The Wéi River flows further northeast past the old city west of Xiàmì County.
East of the city is Mì Mound.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
There is a Sānhù Mountain shrine.
I note that
Yìng Shào said:
"Mì" is a river name,
hence there is the name Xiàmì.
It is commonly used to name the mound,
but this is incorrect.
It flows further northeast past east of Dūchāng County.
The Wéi River flows northeast past the tomb of Páng Méng.
Méng
was a man of this county.
In his youth, he had great integrity.
Ashamed to serve in the county offices,
he crossed the sea to Liáodōng.
Later he returned
and pursued secluded studies on Bùqí Mountain.
Emperor Míng sent a carriage with cushioned seats to summon him,
but Méng feigned madness and was excused.
It flows further north past the old city east of Dūchāng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Zhū Zhěn was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Chancellor of Běihǎi, Kǒng Róng, was besieged in Dūchāng by the Yellow Turban bandit Guǎn Hài.
Tàishǐ Cí sought Liú Bèi's aid for Róng,
breaking through the encirclement with his bow at that place.
It flows further northeast into the sea.
26.6 The Jiāo River
26.6 The Jiāo River
The Jiāo River emerges from Jiāo Mountain in Qiánzōu County,
flowing north past the west of the county.
The *Records of Qí* says:
The Jiāo River emerges from Wǔnǔ Mountain,
which is probably a different name for Jiāo Mountain.
It flows north past the old city east of Zhùzī County.
During the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Yán, son of the Prince of Jiāodōng Kāng, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It flows further past the old city west of Fú County.
The *Treatise on Geography*
states it was a subordinate county of Lángyé.
In the first year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Lǚ Píng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Jiāo River flows further north past the old city west of Qiánzōu.
Yuán Shānsōng's *Records of the Commanderies and States* says:
The county has a Jiè Pavilion.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
It was the old state of Jiè.
In the ninth year of Duke Xī of *The Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Jiè Gélú came to court.
Hearing an ox low, he said:
"This one bore three sacrificial oxen, all of which have been used."
Upon inquiry, it was indeed so.
Yàn Mó and Fú Chēn both said:
The county has eastern and western cities,
forty lǐ apart,
with the Jiāo River between them.
This is incorrect.
This is actually the Jù'ài River.
The river emerges from Jù'ài Mountain southwest of the county,
which is the Qián'ài Mountain mentioned in the *Records of Qí*.
It flows northeast past the old city west of Jù County.
This was Fútóng under Wáng Mǎng,
commonly called Wángchéng.
This water is also called the Yáng River.
It flows further northeast.
This is what Yàn and Fú called the Jiāo River forty lǐ west of Qiánzōu City.
It flows further east into the sea.
The *Treatise on Geography*
states that Lángyé had Jù County.
The Gēn'ài River emerges there,
flowing east into the sea.
This is that river.
Now the Jiāo River flows north,
passing east of Western Qiánzōu City.
Yàn and Fú said that Qiánzōu County was adjacent to Gāomì Commandery.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
The Jiāo River emerges from Fū County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Chúndé.
I suspect this is that county,
but it is not clearly known.
It flows further north past east of Yí'ān County.
The county
was originally named Yuántíng by Wáng Mǎng.
Yìng Shào said:
It was originally the town of Láiyí.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
Yàn Píngzhòng
was a man of Láiyí and the town.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Dèng Zhēn was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
forty lǐ west of the Wéi River.
The Jiāo River flows north past the east of Jiāoyáng County,
both Yàn and Fú called it Dōngtíng.
From the pavilion, a road connects,
leading south to Yí'ān.
The "Geographical and Customs Record" says:
Fifty lǐ southeast of Chúnyú County is Jiāoyáng Pavilion,
which was originally a county.
It flows northeast further,
and joins a stream on the left,
commonly known as Zhāngnú Stream,
which originates from the southeastern mound of Yí'ān County,
flows northwest past Jiāoyáng County, and empties into the Jiāo River.
To the left of the Jiāo River is a marsh,
about a hundred lǐ to the northeast,
called Yí'ān Pond,
the pond is forty lǐ in circumference,
and is also fed by a branch of the Wéi River.
The Jiāo River flows northeast further past the old city of Xiàmì County to the east,
then northeast past the old city of Jiāodōng County to the west,
in the first year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was made a separate state,
Emperor Jǐng enfeoffed his son Jì as king of this state,
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yùzhì,
now the seat of Chángguǎng Commandery.
Fú Chēn and Yàn Mó said,
the Jiāo River flows northeast, winding for a hundred lǐ north of Jiāodōng City,
and empties into the sea.
Further north, it passes west of Dānglì County,
and enters the sea to the north.
The county
was originally renamed Dōnglái Pavilion by Wáng Mǎng.
Further north, it passes Píngdù County,
in the second year of Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Yǎn, son of Prince Yì of Zīchuān, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Lìlú.
The county has an earthen hill,
the Jiāo River flows north past the earthen hill and empties into the sea.
South of the sea,
north of the earthen hill,
are all salt flats,
where salt boiling has been carried on continuously.
Looking north at the vast sea,
boundless and obscure,
the horizon divides into two,
white and black distinctly separated,
this is what is called the Míng Sea.
Thus the "Geographical Treatise" says:
The Jiāo River flows north to Píngdù and enters the sea.
27 Commentary on the Water Classic, Scroll 27
27.1 Miǎn River
27.1 Miǎn River
The Miǎn River originates from the Eastern Wolf Valley in Jù County of Wǔdū,
The Miǎn Shuǐ is also called the Jù Shuǐ.
Kǎn Yīn said:
Because it initially emerges from a swampy area,
it is called the Jù Shuǐ,
and the county also takes its name from it.
It originates and flows south,
and the Quánjiē Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from Hé Chí Xiàn,
flows southeast into Jù Xiàn,
and joins the Miǎn.
The Miǎn Shuǐ then flows southeast past the Jù Shuǐ Shù,
and flows southeast to join the Hàn,
at the so-called Jùkǒu, which is where the Miǎn and Hàn meet.
The *Shàngshū* says:
"From Bōzhǒng, the Yàng is guided,
flowing east to become the Hàn."
This is what the *Shānhǎi Jīng* refers to as the Hàn emerging from Fùyú Shān.
Flowing northeast, it reaches the mouth of the Xiàn Shuǐ.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
This water flows south to Guānchéng and joins the Xī Hàn Shuǐ.
The Hàn Shuǐ then flows northeast to join the Jùkǒu,
together forming the source of the Hàn Shuǐ.
Therefore, as Rú Chún said:
"People in this region call the Hàn Shuǐ the Miǎn Shuǐ."
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"The Yàng Shuǐ flows east to become the Miǎn,"
probably because it joins with the Miǎn.
When it reaches Hànzhōng, it becomes the Hàn Shuǐ,
so the names are used interchangeably.
The Miǎn Shuǐ then flows east past the south of Báimǎ Shù,
where the Jìn Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from the north in the Dí region of Wǔdū,
and flows south past the east of Zhāng Lǔ Chéng.
Lǔ
was the grandson of Zhāng Líng from Pèi Guó.
Líng studied the Way at Hèmíng Shān in Shǔ,
passed his teachings to Héng,
and Héng passed them to Lǔ.
Lǔ governed with leniency and benevolence,
and the people were devoted to him.
For the expenses of the Way,
rice was limited to a dǒu,
so his teachings were called the "Five Dǒu of Rice Way."
During the Chūpíng era,
Liú Yān appointed Lǔ as the Dūyì Sīmǎ,
stationed in Hànzhōng to block the valley roads.
He used Yuǎnchéng as his base,
relying on the steep ridges,
with a circumference of five lǐ.
To the east, it faced a deep valley,
profound and a hundred xún deep.
To the northwest and on two sides,
peaks and cliffs connected,
with no end in sight.
From the south, a winding path
ascended for over two lǐ.
The Jìn Shuǐ then flows south past the east of Zhāng Lǔ's base.
On the mountain west of the water, there is a hall of Zhāng Tiānshī,
which the people still revere today.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng called the mountain Báimǎ Sāi,
and the hall Zhāng Lǔ's base.
To the east, it faces Báimǎ Chéng,
also called Yángpíng Guān.
The Jìn Shuǐ flows south into the Miǎn,
called Jìnkǒu.
The city is bordered by the Jìn Shuǐ to the west,
and faces the Miǎn river to the south.
It lies at the confluence of the two waters,
so it is also called Jìnkǒu Chéng.
The Miǎn Shuǐ then flows east past the south of Wǔhóu Lěi,
where Zhūgě Wǔhóu resided.
It rests against the Miǎn Shuǐ to the south,
and south of the water is Liàng's fortress,
backed by mountains and facing the water,
with a small city inside,
isolated and difficult to access.
The Miǎn Shuǐ then flows east past the old city of Miǎnyáng Xiàn.
The city
is traditionally said to have been built by Xiāo Hé
when Hàn Gāozǔ was in Hànzhōng.
In the 24th year of the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn,
Liú Bèi annexed Liú Zhāng,
secured Hànzhōng in the north,
and erected an altar,
proclaiming himself King of Hànzhōng here.
The city faces the Hàn Shuǐ to the south,
and is connected to the north by a thoroughfare.
One-third of its southern side has collapsed into the water.
Observing its remnants,
its form is still occasionally recounted.
To the south, it faces Dìngjūn Shān.
When Cáo Gōng campaigned south to Hànzhōng,
Zhāng Lǔ surrendered,
and he ordered Xiàhóu Yuān and others to guard it.
Liú Bèi crossed the Miǎn Shuǐ south from Yángpíng Guān,
beheaded Yuān,
and secured Hànzhōng.
When Zhūgě Liàng died,
he ordered to be buried on this mountain.
Following the natural terrain,
no mound was raised,
only deep pines and lush cypresses,
clustering densely over the hills and streams,
so no one knows the exact location of the tomb.
East of the mountain is a place called Gāopíng,
where Liàng once camped,
and there is a temple to Liàng.
After Liàng's death,
the people made offerings in the wild.
The Infantry Commandant Xí Lóng
and the Secretariat Lang Xiàng Chòng jointly memorialized:
"We have heard that the people of Zhōu, remembering the virtue of Shào Bó,
refrained from cutting down the sweet pear tree.
The King of Yuè, cherishing the achievements of Fàn Lǐ,
cast a bronze statue to preserve his likeness.
Liàng's virtue reached far and wide,
his merits overshadowed later generations.
The preservation of the royal house
truly relied on this man.
Yet to have the people making offerings in the alleys,
and the barbarians sacrificing in the wild,
is not the way to honor virtue and remember merits,
or to follow the practices of the past.
If we fully comply with popular sentiment,
it would be excessive and without precedent to establish it in the capital,
and it would also encroach upon the ancestral temples.
This is why the sage ruler is hesitant.
We propose that it is appropriate to establish it near his tomb,
in Miǎnyáng,
to stop private sacrifices,
and to uphold proper rites."
Thus, permission was granted to establish this temple,
which was likely initiated by this proposal.
Zhōng Shìjì, campaigning against Shǔ, made a detour to set up a shrine.
East of the tomb mound,
is the Eight Formations Diagram.
Its remnants are roughly still there,
though collapsed and difficult to discern.
The Miǎn Shuǐ then flows east past the north of Xīlè Chéng.
The city is on a mountain,
with a circumference of thirty lǐ,
very steep and fortified.
Beside the city is a valley called Róngqiú Gǔ,
with a road leading to Yìzhōu,
and many groups of Lǎo people in the mountains.
Zhūgě Liàng built it for defense.
The Governor of Liángzhōu, Yáng Liàng,
relying on its steep and fortified position,
held and resided there,
but was defeated by Fú Jiān.
Later, Governors Jiāng Shǒu and Pān Měng
also successively guarded this city.
East of the city,
the Róngqiú Xī Shuǐ flows into it,
commonly called the Luò Shuǐ.
This water originates from Bā Lǐng Shān to the south,
flows northeast,
and on the left of the water is an old city,
relying on the mountain and its steepness.
It is cut off on all sides.
Long ago, the First Sovereign sent Huáng Zhōng to occupy it,
to resist Cáo Gōng.
The stream then flows north past the east of Xīlè Chéng,
and flows north into the Hàn.
The Hàn Shuǐ then receives the Dùkǒu Shuǐ on the left,
which originates from the northern mountains of Yángpíng.
The water has two sources:
one called Qīng Jiǎn,
produces fine eels;
the other called Zhuó Jiǎn,
produces good crucian carp.
They are often caught in the second and eighth months,
considered delicacies of regular taste.
The Dù Shuǐ flows south past the east of the old city of Yángpíng Xiàn,
then south past the east of the old city of Miǎnyáng Xiàn,
and flows southwest into the Hàn Shuǐ.
The Hàn Shuǐ then flows east,
and on the right meets the mouth of the Wēnquán Shuǐ.
This water emerges from level ground north of the mountain,
covering an area of several tens of paces.
The spring source boils and surges,
hot and steaming in winter and summer.
Looking at it, one sees a vast white vapor.
It is said to cure all kinds of illnesses.
Those who bathe in it all smell of sulfur,
and there are often hundreds of people gathering.
The pool water flows into the Hàn Shuǐ.
The Hàn Shuǐ then flows east,
and the Huángshā Shuǐ flows into it from the left.
This water originates from distant mountains to the north,
with deep and perilous valleys,
where human footprints are rare.
The stream is called Wǔzhàng Xī.
Beside the water is Huángshā Tún,
opened by Zhūgě Liàng.
The water flows south into the Hàn.
South of the water is Nǚláng Shān,
on which is the tomb of a maiden.
Looking from afar at the mountain tomb,
Towering and lofty in appearance,
upon reaching the location,
only a mound-like shape is discernible.
A straight path descends from the mountain,
where no grass or trees grow.
People call it the Nǚláng Path.
Below are the Nǚláng Temple and a stone for pounding clothes,
said to be associated with Zhāng Lǔ’s daughter.
A small stream flows north into the Hàn River,
called the Nǚláng Stream.
The Hàn River then flows east and converges with the Bāo River,
which originates from the Yálǐng Mountain in the northwest,
passes southeast through the Great Stone Gate,
traverses the old plank road in the valley below,
commonly referred to as “a thousand beams without pillars.”
Zhūgě Liàng wrote in his “Letter to Elder Brother Jǐn”:
“Previously, when Zhào Zǐlóng retreated his troops,
he burned the gallery roads north of Chìyá,
stretching over a hundred lǐ along the valley.
The beams of these galleries were embedded into the mountainside on one end,
while the other end was supported by pillars in the water.
Now the water is high and swift,
making it impossible to secure pillars.
This is the extreme difficulty,
which cannot be forced.”
He also wrote:
“Recently, a great flood surged forth,
destroying all bridges and galleries south of Chìyá.
At that time, Zhào Zǐlóng and Dèng Bómiáo,
one garrisoned Chìyá for farming,
the other garrisoned the mouth of Chìyá,
and they could only communicate along the cliff with Bómiáo.”
Later, when Zhūgě Liàng died at Wǔzhàngyuán,
Wèi Yán retreated first and burned the roads,
referring to this very route.
Since then, those who repaired the roads according to the old ways
no longer used pillars in the water.
Travelers crossing the floating bridges would feel them shaking,
causing hearts to tremble and eyes to dizzy.
The Bāo River then flows southeast past Sānjiāochéng,
so named because the city lies at the confluence of three rivers.
One river flows north from Cháng’ān,
one flows northwest from Qiúchí,
and one flows northeast from Tàibái Mountain.
This is how the city got its name.
The Bāo River then flows southeast to the mouth of the Bǐng Stream,
which originates from the Bǐng Cave.
The cave produces fine fish,
which usually emerge in the third month
and retreat in the tenth month.
The cave entrance is about five or six chǐ wide,
seven or eight chǐ above the flat ground.
A spring cascades down,
and fish pass from the cave into the water below.
The cave entrance faces the direction of Bǐng (south-southeast),
hence the name Bǐng Cave.
The water flows down into the Bāo River.
Thus, Zuǒ Sī praised, “Fine fish emerge from the Bǐng Cave,
and fine timber clusters in the Bāo Valley.”
The Bāo River then flows southeast past the Small Stone Gate,
a passage carved through the mountain,
over six zhàng in length.
An inscription reads:
“During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
this was opened by the Colonel-Director of Retainers, Jiānwéi’s Yáng Jué.”
In the second year of the Jiànhé era of Emperor Huán,
the Governor of Hànzhōng, Wáng Shēng of the same commandery, praised Jué’s achievement in opening the passage,
carved a stone to extol his virtue,
and named it the Stone Ox Road.
Lái Mǐn’s “Běn Shǔ Lùn” states:
“King Huì of Qín wanted to attack Shǔ but did not know the way,
so he made five stone oxen,
placing gold beneath their tails,
claiming they could excrete gold.
The King of Shǔ, relying on his strength,
ordered five strong men to pull them, thus creating a road.
The Qín envoys Zhāng Yí and Sīmǎ Cuò followed this road to conquer Shǔ,
hence it was called the Stone Ox Road.”
Yáng Jué likely expanded it based on this.
The “Shūdū Fù” says:
“Barricaded by the Stone Gate.”
This refers to it.
The gate lies west of Hànzhōng,
north of Bāozhōng.
The Bāo River then flows southeast past Bāokǒu,
the southern entrance of the Bāo Valley.
The northern entrance is called Xié,
hence the saying “north emerges at Bāoxié.”
The Bāo River then flows south past the east of the old city of Bāo County,
which is Bāozhōng County,
originally the State of Bāo.
