It was established in the sixth year of the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn.
The Bāo River then flows south into the Hàn River.
The Hàn River then flows east past Wànshíchéng below,
a city situated on a high plain,
over ten zhàng high,
surrounded by flat land on all sides,
shaped like an overturned jar.
To the south, water forms a barrier,
while to the northwest, it is bordered by the Hàn River.
The city has long been inhabited by mixed migrants,
so people also call it the Liúzáchéng (Migrant City).
The Hàn River then flows east past Hànmiàoduī below,
where a Hàn maiden once roamed.
A fishing platform was built beside the water,
and later a temple was erected on the platform.
People saw its vast, elevated foundation,
thus calling it Hànmiàoduī (Hàn Temple Mound).
The name was inaccurately transmitted,
and it was also called Hànwǔduī (Hàn Wǔ Mound).
This is incorrect.
[The river] passes east south of Nánzhèng County.
The county
was originally a vassal of Bāo.
During the reign of King Xiǎn of Zhōu,
the Shǔ region possessed the lands of Bāo and Hàn.
By the time of the Six States,
the Chǔ people annexed them.
When King Huái grew weak,
Qín seized them by force.
In the second year of King Nǎn of Zhōu,
King Huì of Qín established the Hànzhōng Commandery,
named after the river.
The *Records of Elders* states:
The name Nánzhèng
originated with Duke Huán of Zhèng.
After Duke Huán died fighting the Quǎnróng,
his people fled south,
hence the name Nánzhèng (Southern Zhèng).
This became the seat of Hànzhōng Commandery.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered Qín,
Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed him as King of Hàn.
Xiāo Hé said:
"Tiānhàn (Celestial River/Milky Way)
is an auspicious name."
Thus, he made Nánzhèng his capital.
The great walled city had a circumference of forty-two *lǐ*.
Within the city was a smaller walled city,
resting against the river ford to the south,
and connected to a ring of defensive walls to the north.
The golden battlements and lacquered wells
were all built during the Hàn dynasty.
The land was fertile and the rivers strategic.
Cáo Cāo compared it to "chicken ribs."
He said:
"To abandon a fine steed and not ride it,
and anxiously seek another instead."
He then left Dù Zǐxù to guard Nánzhèng and returned.
During the Xiánkāng era of Jìn,
the Governor of Liángzhōu, Sīmǎ Xūn, cut off one-third of the eastern side of the small city,
to serve as the seat of Nánzhèng County, Hànzhōng Commandery, Liángzhōu.
From Qí, Sòng, to Wèi,
this arrangement was maintained.
South of the river is the city of Hànyīn,
traditionally said to be where Empress Lǚ resided.
The Lián River flows from Mount Bálǐng,
running north past Liánchuān,
hence the river gets its name.
The Lián River then flows north into the Hàn River.
To the right of the Hàn River, it joins the Chí River,
which flows from Mount Hàn.
At the foot of the mountain is a shrine,
with twelve stone pillars erected,
their origin unclear,
likely objects of earth-god worship.
The common people pray there in all four seasons.
It is commonly called the Liáozi River.
It irrigates the fields on both sides,
and its scattered streams flow left into the Hàn River.
The Hàn River flows east further to the Chángliǔ Crossing,
Chángliǔ
being the name of a village.
Here lies the tomb of Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù of Hàn,
the stele inscription still exists,
but the writing is worn away,
and can no longer be read.
The Hàn River flows east past the south of Húchéng.
In the fifteenth year of the Yìxī era,
dense clouds and fine rain gathered over the city,
displaying five brilliant colors.
People together called it auspicious clouds and a favorable omen.
At dawn, when the clouds cleared,
they realized the city wall had collapsed,
with about half sinking into the water.
Twelve bronze bells emerged.
Inspector Suǒ Miǎo presented and sent them to Luòyáng,
delivering them to the residence of the Duke of Sòng.
To the south, facing Biǎnquè City,
this was likely an old place traversed by Biǎnquè,
hence the settlement retains his name.
The Hàn River flows out between these two cities,
and to the right meets the Pányú River.
This water flows from the southern mountains on the Bálǐng range.
The spring stream divides into two,
its clear waters cascading and branching,
the southern branch entering the Shǔ River,
the northern branch flowing into the Hàn River ford,
called the Pányú Estuary.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
"Pányú is twenty *lǐ* from Húchéng."
The Hàn River then joins the Wén River to the left,
this water being the Mén River,
which emerges from a stone cave in the northern mountains of Húchéng.
The elders say:
"In Dùyáng there is an immortal's palace,
the stone cave is the front gate of the palace."
Therefore, the river valley is called Ménchuān (Gate Valley),
and the water Ménshuǐ (Gate Water).
It flows southeast past the north of Húchéng.
The three cities stand in remarkable opposition,
spread across the valley,
with deep moats and solid ramparts,
and high towers facing each other.
The Mén River flows right into the Hàn River,
called the Gāoqiáo Creek Estuary.
The Hàn River flows further east,
where the Hēi River flows into it.
This water comes from the northern mountains,
flowing south into the Hàn.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
"Hēishuǐ is thirty *lǐ* from Gāoqiáo."
In *Zhūgě Liàng's Memorial* it is written:
"Depart Nánzhèng at dawn,
lodge at Hēishuǐ by dusk,
a distance of forty or fifty *lǐ*."
This refers to this river,
though the actual road is about a hundred *lǐ*.
It then flows east past the south of Chénggù County,
and further east past the south of Ānyáng County, Wèixīng Commandery,
where the Cén River, flowing from Mount Hàn, enters it from the north.
Cháng Qú's Huáyáng Guózhì states:
Shǔ made Chénggù into Lèchéng County.
Ānyáng County originally belonged to Hànzhōng,
Wèi divided Hànzhōng to establish Wèixīng Commandery,
and Ānyáng was placed under it.
Cén Shuǐ emerges from the southwest and flows northeast into the Hàn,
Zuǒgǔ Shuǐ emerges from the northwest,
which is Xù Shuǐ.
It originates from Tīng Shān in the north,
at the foot of the mountain there is a cave water,
the cave water flows southeast through the flat plain,
which is called Xùxiāng,
and the water is called Xù Shuǐ.
On the plain is the Táng Gōng Shrine,
Táng Jūn, styled Gōngfáng,
was a man of Chénggù,
studied the Way and attained immortality,
entered Yúntái Shān,
refined and ingested elixirs,
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight,
with roosters crowing in the heavens
and dogs barking amidst the clouds.
Only because he detested rats did he leave them behind,
whereupon the rats, feeling grateful,
on the last day of the month,
would vomit out their intestines and stomachs and regenerate them,
hence people of the time called them Tángshǔ (Táng rats).
On the day Gōngfáng ascended to immortality,
his son-in-law was traveling and had not yet returned,
so he could not ascend the cloud path together with him.
They agreed that this plain would be his dwelling place,
saying there would be no troubles of heavy frost, flood dragons, or tigers.
The local custom considered this to be true,
thus it was named Xùxiāng (Son-in-law's Village),
and consequently the water was also named accordingly.
The common people built a temple for him at that place.
They engraved stone and erected a stele,
to record and express these spiritual marvels.
Xù Shuǐ flows south past Xùxiāng, the stream emerges from the mountain and flows southeast,
passes south of Tōngguān Shì,
the mountain is over a hundred zhàng high,
on top is a Xiōngnú city,
five lǐ square,
with three layers of deep moats.
When Gāozǔ pacified Sān Qín in the north,
and Xiāo Hé guarded Hànzhōng;
wishing to repair the northern route to connect with Guānzhōng,
hence it was named Tōngguān Shì (Pass-Through Barrier).
Xù Shuǐ then flows east past the Qī Nǚ Zhǒng (Seven Maidens' Tombs),
the tombs flank the water,
arranged like the Seven Stars,
over ten zhàng high,
and several mǔ in circumference.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā,
a great flood broke the tombs,
the tombs collapsed,
revealing bronze beyond measure,
and a brick was obtained,
inscribed saying:
Xiàngshì Bó had no sons,
seven daughters built the tomb.
People suspect this is Xiàng Bó's tomb.
North of the water is the Qī Nǚ Chí (Seven Maidens' Pool),
east of the pool is the Míngyuè Chí (Bright Moon Pool),
shaped like a reclining moon,
they all connect and flow into each other,
called Zhāng Liáng Qú (Zhang Liang's Canal),
likely opened by Liáng.
Xù Shuǐ passes south of Fán Kuài Tái,
the platform is five or six zhàng high,
capable of holding about a hundred people on top.
It then flows southeast past north of Dà Chénggù,
the city rides the high terrain,
facing Xù Shuǐ to the north,
north of the water is Hán Xìn Tái,
over ten zhàng high,
capable of holding about a hundred people on top.
Tradition says Gāozǔ fasted for seven days,
set up an altar and arranged the ceremony of the nine guests,
to pay respects to Xìn.
Xù Shuǐ turns east and then south,
again passes east of the city and flows south into the Hàn Shuǐ,
this is called the Sānshuǐ Kǒu (Three Waters' Mouth).
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east and meets Yìkǒu Shuǐ,
which emerges from Yì Gǔ in the northern mountains,
flowing southeast into the Hàn Shuǐ.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east to south of Dǎnchéng,
where it joins Luògǔ Shuǐ.
This water emerges north from Luò Gǔ,
the valley connects north to Cháng'ān,
its water flows south,
on the right then Dǎn Shuǐ flows into it,
which originates from Xī Xī,
flowing southeast to merge into one stream,
the turbulent flow emerges south reaching the city's edge,
and flows southwest into the Hàn Shuǐ.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east past south of Xiǎo Chénggù,
the provincial seat is at Dà Chénggù,
the county was moved north,
hence called Xiǎo Chénggù city.
One hundred twenty lǐ to the north is Xīngshì Bǎn,
Zhūgě Liàng marched out from Luò Gǔ,
garrisoned Xīngshì,
and established a beacon tower there,
whose light illuminated the Hàn Shuǐ.
Eastward, it passes through Shàng Tāo,
and then passes by Lóng Xià,
likely due to submerged rocks and startling rapids,
with turbulent flows and raging torrents,
hence the names of the two rapids, Upper and Lower.
Lóng Xià,
is a place name.
There are burial mounds and tomb ruins,
formerly this lodge was called Lóng Xià Tíng.
From Báimǎ up to here,
then flat plains flank the terrain,
with abundant water and fertile soil,
its benefits rival those of Sān Shǔ.
Crossing this point and following the Hàn upstream,
marks the beginning of the mountain journey.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east past Shímén Tān,
a mountain gorge.
Eastward it meets Yǒu Shuǐ,
which emerges from Yǒu Gǔ in the Qín Lǐng,
flowing south through layered mountains and joining Hánquán.
This water emerges east from Hánquán Lǐng,
the spring gushes from the mountain top,
looking from afar it appears crisscrossed,
resembling a waterfall,
with cascading waves striking rocks,
scattering like rain sprinkling,
its force akin to the wind-and-rain pool of Yànyuán.
Its water flows west into Yǒu Shuǐ.
Yǒu Shuǐ then flows south into the Hàn,
called Yǒukǒu.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east past Guīxū Tān,
the Shìběn states:
Shùn dwelled at Guīruì,
in Xīchéng County of Hànzhōng.
Some say Guīxū is to the northwest,
where Shùn lived.
Some write it as Yáoxū.
Hence later some took the surname Yáo, some took Guī,
the difference between Guī and Yáo is baseless,
it is unknown what it follows.
I note Yìng Shào's words,
this place is northwest of Xīchéng.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east past Hóujìng Tān,
the mountains have many monkeys and apes,
fond of climbing perilous places and hanging to drink,
hence the rapid received this name.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east past south of Xiǎo and Dà Huángjīn,
the mountain has Huángjīn Qiào,
north of the water faces Huángjīn Gǔ,
there is Huángjīn Shù,
leaning against the mountain and cliff,
dangerously winding for seven lǐ.
The Dī plundered Hànzhōng,
and used this as a defensive garrison,
facing Tiěchéng opposite.
One city is on the mountain,
holding over a hundred people;
one city is at the mountain's foot,
capable of holding about a hundred people.
Speaking of their steepness and peril,
hence they were named with gold and iron.
Formerly, Yáng Nándāng ordered Wèixīng Tàishǒu Xuē Jiàn to hold Huángjīn,
and Jiāng Bǎo to hold Tiěchéng.
Sòng dispatched Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Sīhuà to campaign west,
Sīhuà ordered Yīnpíng Tàishǒu Xiāo Yuán to attack and capture them.
The bandits retreated to Yǒu Shuǐ.
Hàn Shuǐ then flows east and meets the mouth of Qúchú Xī,
the water emerges north from Jiù Gǔ,
southwest of Cháng'ān,
its water flows south past west of Bāxī Shù,
then flows south past east of Yángdū Bǎn,
the slope from top to bottom,
winds and twists in nineteen bends,
connecting west to Hánquán Lǐng.
The Hànzhōng Jì states:
From Xīchéng, crossing Huángjīn Qiào, Hánquán Lǐng, and Yángdū Bǎn,
with steep cliffs a hundred layers deep,
sheer precipices ten thousand xún high,
having reached its peak,
one thinks they have surpassed Sōng and Dài,
but looking ahead at the next ridge,
it is again twice as high.
Speaking of climbing Yángcháng,
surpassing the realm of mist and clouds,
looking back at the path traveled,
it is remote and unfathomably perilous.
The mountains abound with wild cattle and wild sheep,
leaping across cliffs and crossing ridges,
running as if flying,
colliding with trees,
even those ten arm-spans around all topple.
The mountains exhaust rugged barriers,
the land reaches the limit of perilous terrain.
Its water flows south through Qúchú Xī,
called Qúchú Shuǐ.
and flows southward into the Hàn River,
which is called the Chúkǒu.
The Hàn River then flows east,
where it meets the Yáng Shuǐ on the right,
a river that flows broadly and expansively,
spanning nearly a li in width.
The Yáng Shuǐ originates from Bā Shān,
flowing northeast past Píngyáng Chéng.
The *Hànzhōng Jì* states:
This was originally the seat of Xīxiāng Xiàn.
It lies 380 li south from Chénggù,
and 480 li from Nánzhèng.
Yángchuān
is the birthplace of Qī Fūrén of the Hàn dynasty.
Emperor Gāozǔ obtained her favor and doted on her.
The lady longed for her hometown,
craving the rice of Yángchuān.
The emperor had it delivered by post to Cháng'ān,
exempted her hometown from taxes,
and renamed it a county.
Therefore, the place was also called Xiángchuān,
to signify the auspiciousness of the lady's birthplace.
The city is now Dìngyuǎn.
In the seventh year of the Yǒngguāng era of Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
Bān Chāo was enfeoffed with Xīxiāng of Nánzhèng Xiàn in Hànzhōng Jùn,
as the Marquis of Dìngyuǎn,
which is precisely this place.
The Yáng Shuǐ then flows northeast into the Hàn River,
which is called the Chéngyáng Shuǐkǒu.
The Hàn River then flows east past Áotóu,
where granaries and storehouses were established in the past.
A road runs alongside the mountain,
making it a convergence point for water and land hazards.
It was the seat of Ānkāng Xiàn of Wèixīng,
with a garrison,
overseeing transient and mixed populations.
The Hàn River then flows east and joins the Zhí Shuǐ,
which emerges north from beneath the cliffs of Zǐwǔ Gǔ,
then branches southward,
flowing east into the Xún Shuǐ,
then south past the foot of the Suōgé,
where a garrison is situated on the mountain,
placed atop a lofty mound,
overlooking a deep abyss below.
Zhāng Zǐfáng burned and destroyed the plank roads,
to show there was no turning back.
It then flows southeast through Zhígǔ,
passes west of Zhíchéng,
and flows south into the Hàn River.
The Hàn River then flows east past the south of Zhíchéng,
then east past Qiāndù until reaching Xiāmá Fǔ,
passing Hànyáng and Wǔkǒu to arrive at Péngxī and Lóngzào.
These are all names of streams, ravines, shoals, and gravel banks.
The Hàn River then flows east past the south of Níngdū Xiàn of Jìnchāng Jùn,
whose seat is at Sōngxīkǒu.
It then flows east past Guǎngchéng Xiàn of Wèixīng Jùn,
whose seat is at Wánggǔ.
The valley road leads south to the Bāliáo region,
where there are salt wells,
but consuming the salt causes goiter disease.
The Hàn River then flows east past Yúfǔ Gǔkǒu,
where the former Xīchéng and Guǎngchéng counties
used this valley as their boundary.
It then flows east past the south of Xīchéng Xiàn.
The Hàn River flows east past the south of Biēchí and Jīng Tān.
Jīng,
means large.
The "Shǔdū Fù" says:
The flowing Hàn is vast and mighty,
Its startling waves thunderously surge,
Gazing from afar, the sky seems distant,
Approaching it, clouds appear dim.
The Hàn River flows east past the north entrance of Lángǔ,
Where peaks are remote and streams deep,
Ravines and gorges perilous and profound,
The air is desolate and rustling,
The wind whistles and howls,
Hence the river valley claims its name.
The Hàn River flows further east,
On the right it meets Dàshì,
Where the terrain is obstructed by a swift stream,
Therefore it is also called Jíshì.
A city was built against the mountain,
The city wall measures two lǐ in circumference,
Located on a steep mountain,
It was the seat of Jí Yì, the Protector of Liángzhōu.
Fú Jiān dispatched the partial army of Wéi Zhōng to attack Yì,
Yì held firm for two years and could not be taken,
But without reinforcements, it eventually fell.
The Hàn River faces Yuègǔkǒu on the right,
The mountain has Bānyuèchuān,
Within it lies fertile yellow soil,
Mulberries and hemp are planted in rows,
Excellent and abundant paddy fields.
Thus Mèng Dá wrote in his "Letter to Zhūgě Liàng",
Praising its fertile and beautiful river land.
The Hàn River flows east past the old city of Xīchéng County,
According to the "Geographical Records",
It was a county under Hànzhōng Commandery.
In the late Hàn dynasty, it became Xīchéng Commandery.
In the 24th year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Liú Bèi appointed Shēn Yí as the Grand Administrator of Xīchéng.
Yí occupied the commandery and surrendered to Wèi,
Emperor Wén of Wèi changed it to the seat of Wèixīng Commandery,
Which was the old city of Xīchéng County.
The Dí people raided Hànchuān,
And Liángzhōu moved its seat here.
Within the city are the Shùn Shrine and the temple of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Nine households were established,
To perform sacrifices seasonally.
The Hàn River flows east to become Zhān Tuān,
Where great waves surge and toss,
Crashing billows like collapsing clouds.
Ancient elders said,
A sturgeon fish would flap its fins against the current,
Gazing at the waves and swimming straight upstream,
But reaching here, its gills would burst and it could proceed no further,
Hence the rapid was named accordingly.
The Hàn River flows east and joins Xún Shuǐ.
The water emerges north from Xún Shān,
Flows southeast past Píngyáng Shù below,
And branches off from Zhí Shuǐ to flow eastward.
It passes through Píngyáng Shù and enters Xún Shuǐ.
Xún Shuǐ flows southeast past Xúnyáng County and merges with Zuò Shuǐ,
Which emerges west from Zuò Xī,
Flows south past Chóngyán Bǎo,
Turns west then east past the south of the fort,
And flows southeast into Xún Shuǐ.
Xún Shuǐ flows southeast past the south of Xúnyáng County,
On the northern mountain of the county is Xuánshūyá,
Fifty zhàng high,
With characters carved into the stone,
People cannot climb up,
And do not know what they say.
Below the mountain is a stone altar,
Above which are five horse hoof prints,
Named Mǎjì Shān.
Xún Shuǐ flows southeast into the Hàn,
Called Xúnkǒu.
The Hàn River flows east past the south of Mùlán Zhài,
On the right bank is a city,
Named Jìlíng Chéng,
Several lǐ in circumference,
On the left bank are dozens of rows of piled stones,
Layered for several tens of lǐ,
It is said this place is called Mùlán Zhài.
Here the Wú court dispatched troops to rescue Mèng Dá.
The Hàn River flows further east,
On the left it meets Yù Xī, where Xìngjìn and Xúnyáng counties
Divide their boundaries at this valley.
The Hàn River flows east and joins Jiǎ Shuǐkǒu,
The water emerges from Qínlǐng Shān,
Flows southeast past the south of Jīnjǐng Chéng,
Then east past the north of Shàngyōng Commandery,
And merges with Guānfù Shuǐ.
This water emerges from Qīngní Xīshān north of Yángtíng County in Shàngluò,
Flows south past the west of Yángtíng Jù.
Commonly called Píngyáng Shuǐ.
It merges south with Fēngxiāng Chuān Shuǐ,
Which emerges from Dōngshān in Fēngxiāng, Hóngnóng,
Flows southwest past the old city of Fēngxiāng.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
Nánxiāng Xī County has the old Fēngxiāng,
Which is the Fēngxī mentioned in the "Spring and Autumn Annals".
According to the "Geographical Records", it belonged to Hóngnóng.
Now it belongs to Nánxiāng.
It then flows southwest and merges with Guānfù Shuǐ.
Guānfù Shuǐ flows south into Shàngjīn and enters Jiǎ Shuǐ.
Jiǎ Shuǐ flows east and south past the south of Xìngjìn County in Wèixīng Commandery,
Established in the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Jiǎ Shuǐ flows further east,
And enters the Hàn River on the right.
The Hàn River flows east to become Lóngyuān,
Above the abyss is Húbí Shān,
So named because the rocks resemble the noses of foreigners.
Below it overlooks Lóngjǐng Zhǔ,
The abyss is several zhàng deep.
The Hàn River flows east past the old city of Xī County in Wèixīng Commandery,
Becoming Báishí Tān.
The county,
Was the land of Xīxué in the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
Originally part of Hànzhōng,
It was Xīzhì under Wáng Mǎng.
The county has Xīyì Shān,
A hundred lǐ in circumference,
Shaped like a city.
It has gates on all four sides,
Above is a stone altar,
Several tens of zhàng long,
Traditionally said to be where immortals dwelled,
Now there are Daoist priests with unbound hair consuming zhú,
Constantly several tens of them.
The mountains are high and valleys deep,
Growing much wēihéng grass,
Which does not bend in the wind,
But sways alone when there is no wind.
The Hàn River flows east past the south of Chánglì Gǔ,
Entering the valley is the old city of Chánglì,
An old county.
The Hàn River flows east past Yáofāng,
Likely because descendants of Shùn settled here,
Hence the place retains the name Yáo.
28 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 28
28.1 Miǎn Shuǐ
28.1 Miǎn Shuǐ
It flows further east past Dǔyáng County,
Dǔ Shuǐ emerges from Shàngfěn County,
Flows north and enters it.
The Dǔ River originates from the Gùtíng Valley at the boundary of Jiànpíng Commandery,
flowing east through Xīnchéng Commandery.
This commandery
was formerly Fánglíng County of Hànzhōng.
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Dèng Chén.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, it was made Fánglíng Commandery.
Emperor Wén of Wèi combined Fánglíng, Shàngyōng, and Xīchéng,
establishing them as Xīnchéng Commandery,
appointing Mèng Dá as its Grand Administrator,
with his seat at the old county town of Fánglíng.
There was a Fěnshuǐ County situated upstream,
hence it was called Shàngfěn County.
Beside the Dǔ River is a separate stream,
where the soil on its banks is a bright yellow color.
It is said to be edible,
and some claim that drinking this water
makes one free from illness and long-lived.
Can this be true?
There is also Báimǎ Mountain,
whose rocks resemble horses,
appearing lifelike when viewed from afar.
The water beside it is called Báimǎ Pass.
When Mèng Dá was the defending commander,
he climbed it and sighed, saying:
"Liú Fēng and Shēn Dān held a thousand-mile fortress,
yet they lost it."
He composed the "Shàngdǔ Yín",
its melody mournful and poignant,
deeply moving to the heart.
Even now, people still sing it by the waterside.
The Dǔ River then flows northeast past Shàngyōng Commandery,
which was the ancient state of Yōng.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Wén of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the men of Chǔ, Qín, and Bā destroyed Yōng.
Yōng was a small state,
attached to Chǔ.
When Chǔ suffered disaster, it did not come to its aid,
instead rallying the various Mán tribes to rebel.
Therefore, it was destroyed and made into a county,
belonging to Hànzhōng Commandery.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, it was further divided to form Shàngyōng Commandery.
The city walls face the water on three sides.
The Dǔ River then flows east past the south of Fāngchéng Pavilion,
northeast under the Cēn Mountain,
then north past the south of Dǔyáng County,
flowing north into the Hàn River,
where it is called the Dǔkǒu.
The Hàn River flows further east,
where it is called Láotān.
In winter, the water is shallow and there are many large rocks below.
Further east is Jìngtān,
where summer floods are swift and powerful,
the river full of rapids and whirlpools,
causing hardship for travelers.
Hence the proverb says:
"Winter Láo, summer Jìng,
halt official missions,"
meaning these two rapids are obstructive.
Further east, it passes south of Yúnxiāng.
The Hàn River flows east past the Western Mountain south of Yúnxiāng County,
on top of which is a stone toad.
At a casual glance,
it is indistinguishable from a real one.
The Hàn River then flows east past the old city of Yúnxiāng County,
where it is called Yúnxiāngtān.
This county
was formerly Lí,
that is, the Yúnxiāng of Chánglì.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"There is a Yún Pass."
Lǐ Qí considered it the state of Yúnzǐ.
In the fifth year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
it was established as a county.
The Hàn River then flows east past the mouth of Pípá Valley,
where the borders of Liáng and Yì provinces meet,
hence it is called the Pípá Boundary.
It then flows northeast,
bends southeast,
and passes northeast of Wǔdāng County.
Forty *lǐ* northwest of the county,
in the middle of the Hàn River, there is an islet,
named Cānglàng Islet.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng's *Records of the Hàn River* calls it Qiānlíng Islet,
which is incorrect.
This is a corruption in common speech,
where the sound and characters have changed.
The *Dì Shuō* states:
"The water emerges from Jīng Mountain,
flowing southeast to become the waters of Cānglàng,
which is near the capital of Chǔ.
Therefore, the 'Song of the Fisherman' says:
'When the Cānglàng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat-strings therein;
when the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet therein.'"
I note that the *Tribute of Yu* in the *Book of Documents* states:
"Channeling the Yǎng River,
it flows east to become the Hàn,
and further east becomes the waters of Cānglàng."
It says 'becomes' rather than 'passes',
clarifying that it is not another river breaking in.
It seems that the Hàn and Miǎn rivers are commonly referred to as Cānglàng downstream.
Winding through Yān and Yǐng,
connecting with the lands of Jì and Ruò,
all were capitals of Chǔ.
The fisherman sang of it,
which does not contradict the water's location.
Examining the classics and commentaries,
the *Book of Documents* should be considered correct.
The Hàn River flows further east to become Héngzǐ Tán,
in which there is a rocky shoal islet,
sixty *zhàng* long,
eighteen *zhàng* wide.
People also say that because Héngzǐ buried his father here,
the pool got its name,
though the details are unclear.
The Mǎn River flows southeast past the old city of Wǔdāng County,
which Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed as the marquisate of Táng, son of Dèng Chén.
Inside is a stele,
its inscription worn away,
no longer legible.
Common tradition holds
that it is the inscription of Lord Huá,
but it is also unclear from which era this Lord Huá was.
The Hàn River flows further east,
where the Píngyángchuān River flows into it.
This water emerges from Fúqīn Mountain north of the county,
flows south through Píngyángchuān,
passes below the old city of Píngyáng,
then flows south into the Miǎn.
The Miǎn River flows southeast past the old city of Wǔdāng County,
then east,
where the Zēng River flows into it.
This water originates from Wǔdāng Mountain south of the county,
also called Tàihé Mountain,
or Cēnshàng Mountain.
The mountain's form is exceptionally beautiful,
and it is also called Xiānshì (Immortal's Abode).
The *Supplementary Records of Jīngzhōu Maps* states:
"The mountain's form is exceptionally beautiful,
different from other peaks.
The summit resembles a Boshan incense burner,
towering loftily in the distance.
Those seeking longevity through medicinal herbs gather here."
During the Xiánhé era of Jìn,
Xiè Yǔn of Lìyáng, relinquishing his post as magistrate of Luó, retreated to this mountain.
Hence it is also called Xièluó Mountain.
The Zēng River originates at the mountain's foot,
passes along the mountain's northern side,
flows northeast into the Miǎn,
where it is called Zēngkǒu.
The Miǎn River flows east past Lóngcháo Mountain,
which is in the middle of the Miǎn River,
fifteen *zhàng* high,
one *lǐ* and two hundred thirty *bù* in circumference.
The mountain is steep and precipitous,
with lush forests and abundant trees on top,
remaining verdant even in deep winter.
Further southeast, it passes northeast of Shèdū City,
which is an old village name.
According to the *Treatise on Commanderies and States*,
Zhùyáng County had the Shèdū Township.
In the first year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Jiā, son of the Marquis of Jiàng, Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi, was enfeoffed here as a marquisate.
The Jūn River enters the Miǎn at this county,
where it is called Jūnkǒu.
Further southeast, it passes southwest of Cuó County.
The county seat is at the old city,
facing the Miǎn River to the south,
where it is called Cuótóu.
In the fifth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the marquisate of Xiāo Hé.
Xuě Zàn said:
"This is present-day Nánxiāng Cuótóu."
The *Màolíng Book* states:
"It is in Nányáng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Nángēng."
Further south, it passes east of Gǔchéng,
then south, passing west of Yīn County.
The Miǎn River flows east past the south of Gǔchéng, not passing its east.
The city is on Gǔchéng Mountain,
which was the fief of Gǔ Bó Suí in the Spring and Autumn period.
The city walls and gates are in ruins,
but the foundations and moats still remain.
The Miǎn River then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Yīn County,
which was formerly known as Xiàyīn.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Zhāo of the Spring and Autumn period,
Chǔ’s Minister of Works, Chì, moved Yīn to Xiàyīn, which is this place.
East of the county there is a burial mound,
where the county magistrate Liú Xī of Jǐnán,
courtesy name Déyí,
who governed the county during the Wèi period,
was fond of antiquity,
established teaching and erected a stele,
recording over a hundred students,
those who died before completing their studies,
were buried at this site,
called the "Living Tomb."
The Miǎn River then flows southeast to the mouth of Luò Creek,
which originates from Jíchí Marsh northwest of the county,
flows southeast past Luòyáng City,
which lies north of Luò Creek,
and the creek flows southeast into the Miǎn River.
Further south, it passes east of Zhùyáng County,
where the Zhù River originates from Fánglíng County,
flows east past the county and south into the Miǎn River.
The Miǎn River then flows south,
where the Fàn River joins it,
which originates from Làngyáng County in Liángzhōu.
Wèi sent Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé to conquer Bāxī,
advancing to Dàngqú,
while Liú Bèi’s army was stationed at Fànkǒu,
which is where this river originates.
Zhāng Fēi took a separate route to ambush Zhāng Hé at this river,
Hé was defeated,
abandoned his horse and climbed the mountain,
fleeing back to Hànzhōng.
The Fàn River then flows east past Bāxī,
through Bāqú, Běixīnchéng, and Shàngyōng,
east past the old city of Fànyáng County,
which was established during the Jìn period by dividing Zhùyáng.
Upstream from the county,
the mountains are deep and the waters swift,
with winding shores and turbulent rapids,
making travel by land and water difficult.
Further east, it passes south of Xuéchéng,
which lies along the main road of Liángzhōu.
According to old accounts, someone once established a school here,
but during times of turmoil,
the students had no support,
so they built a city together for defense,
hence the city’s name.
The Fàn River then flows east into the Miǎn River,
called Fànkǒu.
The Miǎn River then flows south past the east of Quèlín Mountain,
which lies along the main land route of the commandery.
East of the mountain are two steles,
one of which records Quèlín Mountain.
The inscription says:
"A ruler of a state should not raise heights or fill in lowlands."
Earlier,
some had cut through the mountain ridge to create a level road,
but many people suffered from illness,
so the governor, Zhāng Zhòngyú of Guànjūn, together with the locals, restored the old mountain road,
and composed this inscription.
The other stele is for Master Guō,
whose given name was Fǔ,
courtesy name Fǔchéng,
known for his filial piety, friendship, and love of learning.
His daughter erected this stele for him here,
but it lacks a reign year,
so it is unknown from which era he lived.
The Miǎn River then flows south past east of Zhùyáng County,
further south,
the Zhù River joins it,
which Dù Yù identified as the Péng River.
The river originates from the border of Wèichāng County in Xīnchéng Commandery of Liángzhōu,
which was established during the Huángchū era by dividing Fánglíng.
The Zhù River flows southeast past Zhùyáng County,
where a solitary rock rises from the water,
beneath which lies a clear pool.
Sometimes, the roots of this rock are seen to resemble yellow bamboo roots,
and those who see it often meet with misfortune,
so it is collectively called the "Rock of Misfortune,"
though the details are unclear.
The Zhù River then flows east past the old city of Zhùyáng County,
which
was originally a vassal of Chǔ.
After Qín pacified Yān and Yǐng,
it was established as a county,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yìhé.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Wú Xū as a marquis here.
The Zhù River then flows east into the Miǎn River,
called Zhùkǒu.
The Miǎn River then flows south past the east of Gāotíng Mountain,
where a spirit resides,
worshipped by the local people,
and their prayers are answered.
The Miǎn River then flows east to Qī Tān,
where Shāndū County of Xīnyě Commandery borders Shùnyáng and Zhùyáng,
with the boundary at this shoal.
Further east, it passes northeast of Shāndū County,
where south of the Miǎn River lies Gùchéng,
situated beside the Miǎn River,
which is the seat of Shāndū County in Xīnyě,
formerly known as Chìxiāng in Nányáng.
Qín established it as a county,
and in the fourth year of Empress Gāo of Hàn,
General of the Guards Wáng Tiánqǐ was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
North of the Miǎn River lies Héchéng,
which is the Héchéng Jù of Wǔdāng County mentioned in the "Treatise on Commanderies and States,"
and Shāndū County was once governed here,
so this place is also called the "Old County Shoal."
Several li north of the Miǎn River’s bank is a large rock rapid,
called the "Five Maidens Rapid."
It is said that the father of five maidens was harmed by others,
and they lived in Gùchéng.
The five maidens sought to avenge their father,
so they built the rapid to attack the city.
The northern part of the city is now submerged in water.
It is also said that someone was buried north of the Miǎn River,
and the tomb was about to be destroyed by water.
The deceased had five daughters but no sons,
and they were all very wealthy,
so they built this rapid to protect the tomb.
The construction of the rapid was very skillful.
Another account says that a woman married a stubborn son of Yīn County,
whose family possessed ten thousand in gold.
Since childhood, he never obeyed his father’s words.
On his deathbed,
the father wished to be buried on the mountain,
but fearing his son would not comply,
he deliberately said, "Bury me on the rocky shoal below the islet."
The stubborn son said:
"I have never followed your instructions,
but this time I will obey."
He then spent all his family wealth to build a stone tomb,
piling earth around it to form an islet,
several hundred paces long.
During the Yuánkāng era, it began to be damaged by water,
and now the stones are about half the size of a couch,
with hundreds gathered in the water.
This stubborn son lived in the Western Hàn period.
The governor of Xiāngyáng, Hú Liè, implemented benevolent governance,
repairing broken dikes,
and the people benefited from his efforts.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of the Jǐngyuán era,
the people carved a stone inscription in his honor,
erecting a stele here.
The Miǎn River then flows east, where it becomes shallow,
and in winter, it can be forded,
called Jiāo Lake.
During military conflicts,
many crossed here.
During the Tàikāng era of Jìn, a resonant stone was found here,
which, when struck by water, could be heard for several li.
The Miǎn River then flows east past the north of Lè Mountain,
where Zhūgě Liàng was fond of singing the "Liángfǔ Yín,"
and wherever he climbed or traveled,
the mountain was popularly named Lè Mountain.
The Miǎn River then flows east past Lóngzhōng,
passing north of Kǒngmíng’s former residence.
Liàng said to Liú Shàn:
"The late emperor visited me three times in my thatched cottage,
consulting me on the affairs of the world,"
which refers to this residence.
When the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Liú Jìhé of Pèiguó, was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
he visited this residence with Lǐ Ān of Qiánwéi,
and ordered Ān to compose an "Inscription for the Residence," which says:
"The Son of Heaven commanded me north of the Miǎn River,
listening to the drums and reflecting deeply,
aspiring to the lingering glory of the ancient sages."
More than sixty years later,
in the fifth year of the Yǒngpíng era,
Xí Zàochǐ also composed an inscription for this residence.
Further east, it passes north of Xiāngyáng County.
The Miǎn River flows east past the north of Wàn Mountain.
On the mountain is the stele of Zōu Huī,
erected by Lǔ Zōngzhi.
In the pool below the mountain is the stele of Dù Yuánkǎi.
Yuánkǎi was fond of leaving a name for posterity,
so he made two steles both recording his own achievements.
One stele was sunk in the waters of Xiàn Mountain,
and one stele was lowered into this pool,
saying:
"A hundred years from now,
who knows if deep valleys will not become hills?"
In the bend of the water below the mountain,
it is said the Hàn maiden once roamed.
Therefore, Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Southern Capital" says:
"The roaming maiden plays with pearls at the bend of Hàngāo."
Hàngāo
is another name for Wàn Mountain.
The Miǎn River then flows east and joins the Tán Stream.
The water emerges from Liǔzǐ Mountain west of the county,
flowing east to form Duck Lake.
The lake lies northeast of Mǎ'ān Mountain.
Prince Wǔlíng admired its peak's beauty,
and renamed it Wàngchǔ Mountain.
The stream water divides into two from the lake.
The northern channel is the course of the stream.
It flows north past the west of Hànyīn Terrace.
Facing the stream and gazing afar,
surveying the fields and gardens,
one's feelings wander to watering vegetables,
and thoughts settle on Hànyīn.
Thus, the terrace was named accordingly.
Further north, it passes Tán Stream,
called Tán Stream water.
Beside the water is the temple of the monk Shì Dào'ān.
The stream's name
is used to identify the temple.
South of the stream are the former residences of Xú Yuánzhí and Cuī Zhōupíng.
All are now inhabited by others.
Therefore, Xí Zàochǐ wrote in his "Letter to Xiè Ān":
"Whenever I visit my maternal uncle,
gazing freely at Tán Stream,
and think of the friendship between Cuī and Xú,
I cannot help but beat my chest in hesitation,
feeling melancholy all day long."
The stream water flows alongside the city walls and pours in.
Long ago, when Liú Bèi was plotted against by Jǐng Shēng,
he rode his horse Dí Lú westward,
and fell into this stream.
Westward, over a li from the city,
it flows north into the Miǎn.
One watercourse flows southeast out.
Yìng Shào said:
"The city lies north of the Xiāng River,
hence called Xiāngyáng."
This water should be the Xiāng River.
The city's north rests on the Miǎn River,
which is the old city of Xiāngyáng County,
called Xiāngyáng under Wáng Mǎng.
It was the northern ferry garrison of Chǔ,
now the western rampart of the great city.
The land was formerly of Yān, Ruò, Lú, and Luó.
When Qín destroyed Chǔ,
it established the Nán Commandery,
naming this area the northern part.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
when Wèi Wǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
he divided Nán Commandery to establish Xiāngyáng Commandery,
making it the seat of the Jīngzhōu Governor.
The dwellings were prosperous,
officials' carriages were seen everywhere,
a hub of the region.
East of the southern gate road are three steles:
one is the stele of Jìn Grand Tutor Yáng Hù,
one is the stele of General Zhènnán Dù Yù,
and one is the stele of General Ānnán Liú Yǎn,
all erected by students.
Two hundred paces outside the eastern gate is the tomb of Liú Biǎo.
During Tàikāng, it was excavated by someone,
and the bodies of Liú Biǎo and his wife were intact,
their complexions unchanged,
as if in life.
The fragrance from the tomb could be smelled from three or four li away,
lasting for months without fading.
Today, the tomb mound and ancestral hall remain tall, prominent, and well-kept.
The city's north rests on the Miǎn River,
where people often suffered from flood dragon harm.
Xiāngyáng Grand Administrator Dèng Xiá, relying on his courage and resolve,
drew his sword and entered the water.
The flood dragon coiled around his leg,
but Xiá swung his sword and beheaded it.
The blood dyed the water red.
From then on, the trouble was eliminated,
and there were no more flood dragon difficulties.
Long ago, when Zhāng Gōng met his end,
his sword was also lost in this water.
Later, when a man named Léi served as a Junior Clerk under Jiàn'ān,
passing by Lài Stream,
the sword left behind
suddenly leaped from his bosom into the water.
At first, it was still a sword,
but later transformed into a dragon.
Therefore, Wú Jūn's "Poem on Sword and Mount" says:
"The sword is two flood dragons."
Zhāng Huá's words are not without proof.
The Miǎn River then flows past Pínglǔ City's south.
The city
was built by Lǔ Zōngzhi,
hence the city obtained its name.
Eastward, it faces Fán City.
Fán
was the fief of Zhòng Shānfǔ.
The "Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū" records:
When Emperor Huán visited Fán City,
all the common people came to watch,
except one old man who kept plowing without stopping.
Court Gentleman Zhāng Wēn sent someone to ask him,
but the old man smiled without answering.
Wēn then spoke with him directly,
asking his name,
but he left without telling.
The city wall is four li in circumference,
with the southern half submerged in water.
During the Jiàn'ān period,
Guān Yǔ besieged Yú Jìn here in this city.
Just then, the Miǎn River flooded,
rising over three zhàng,
and the city fell, with Jìn surrendering.
Páng Dé brandished his sword,
boarded a boat, and fled for his life to the eastern ridge.
Wèi Wǔ said:
"I have known Yú Jìn for over thirty years,
yet when facing danger and entrusted with a mission,
he is even less reliable than Páng Dé."
Southwest of the city is Cáo Rén's flood record stele,
re-inscribed by Dù Yuánkǎi,
with later additions recording the campaign against Wú.
Then, from east of the county, it bends southwest,
where the Yù River flows from the north to join it.
East of Xiāngyáng City lies East White Sand,
north of White Sand are three islets,
northeast is Wǎnkǒu,
where the Yù River flows in.
In the Miǎn River is Fish Beam Islet,
where Páng Dégōng resided.
Shìyuán lived on the north bank of the Hàn River,
at South White Sand,
hence people have long called this place White Sand Bend.
Sīmǎ Décāo’s home was on the sunny side of the islet,
facing each other across the way,
their joyful friendship naturally connected,
boating and lifting robes,
freely relaxed and content—
how could it compare to returning a thousand miles by oar,
offering deep feelings in eternal longing?
South of the water is a layered terrace,
called Jǐngshēng Terrace,
built by Liú Biǎo when he governed Xiāngyáng.
It is said Biǎo often roamed here,
regularly stopping to rest.
Biǎo had a fondness for hawks;
once he climbed this terrace
and sang the song “Wild Hawk Comes,”
its melody resembling Mèng Dá’s “Shàngdǔ Chant.”
The Miǎn River then passes east of Táolín Pavilion,
and passes east of Xiàn Mountain.
On the mountain is a city built by Huán Xuān,
where Sūn Jiān died.
There is also a stele for Huán Xuān.
When Yáng Hù garrisoned Xiāngyáng,
he once climbed it with Zōu Rùnfǔ.
After Hù died,
later people erected a stele at the old site;
those who gaze upon it feel sorrow,
and Dù Yuánkǎi called it the “Falling Tears Stele.”
On the mountain is also the stele of General Zhēngnán Hú Pí,
and the stele of General Zhēngxī Zhōu Fǎng.
In the water below the mountain
is where Dù Yuánkǎi sank his stele.
The Miǎn River then flows southeast past Cài Islet, where Hàn’s Chángshuǐ Commandant Cài Mào lived,
hence named Cài Islet.
West of the islet’s east bank is Huí Lake,
holding water over several dozen acres,
several lǐ long,
nearly a hundred paces wide,
its water always green.
Yáng Yí lived at Upper Huí,
Yáng Yóng lived at Lower Huí,
opposite Cài Islet.
At Guǎngchāng Village south of Xiàn Mountain,
it also joins with Xiāngyáng Lake’s waters.
The water above receives from Duck Lake,
flows southeast past the west of Xiàn Mountain,
then southeast into White Horse Marsh waters,
then east into the fish pond of Palace Attendant and Marquis of Xiāngyáng Xí Yù.
Yù followed Fàn Lǐ’s fish farming method to build a large pond,
the pond sixty paces long,
forty paces wide,
with a fishing platform in the center.
North of the pond is a pavilion,
where Yù’s tomb lies.
Pines and bamboos are planted in rows along the pond’s side on the Miǎn River,
where Yù resided.
He also built a stone conduit,
channeling the large pond’s water north of his residence to make a small fish pond,
seventy paces long,
twenty paces wide,
bordered by a main road to the west,
with high embankments to the northeast and southeast,
catalpas and bamboos planted along both sides,
lotus and foxnuts covering the water—
a famous spot for outings and feasts.
When Shān Jìlún garrisoned Xiāngyáng,
whenever he visited this pond,
he never failed to return greatly intoxicated,
always saying, “This is my Gāoyáng Pond.”
So people of the time sang of him:
“Where does Lord Shān go?
Off to Gāoyáng Pond.
At dusk he returns slumped in his carriage,
dead drunk and unaware.”
Its waters flow down into the Miǎn.
West of the Miǎn River is also the Filial Son’s Tomb.
A man of the Qín family from Hénán was extremely filial,
serving his parents tirelessly.
After his parents passed,
he carried earth to form a grave mound,
often weeping tears of blood by the tomb.
When someone recited the poem “Lù’é,”
he wept bitterly,
overcome with grief.
Falling ill at the tomb,
unable to eat,
a tiger often nursed him,
until he died after over a hundred days.
Now the woods are dense and serene,
called the “Filial Son’s Tomb.”
South of it is Cài Mào’s burial mound,
with a stone carved in front into the shape of a large deer,
very large,
its head nine feet high,
exquisitely crafted.
The Miǎn River then flows southeast past the north of Yì City,
the fief of Marquis of Xiāngyáng Xí Yù,
hence called Yì City.
The Miǎn River then flows east to join Dòngkǒu,
whose water emerges from Dàfù Mountain northeast of the old city of Ānchāng County,
flowing southwest called White Water.
It then flows south past the east of old Ānchāng City,
bends past the south of the county.
The county
was originally the White Water Township of Càiyáng.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn, because Chángshā was low and damp,
divided White Water and Shàngtáng townships to form Chūnlíng County.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he changed it to Zhānglíng County,
establishing a garden and temple there.
In the second year of Wèi’s Huángchū era,
it was renamed as it is today,
formerly the seat of Yìyáng Commandery.
White Water then flows southwest and joins Kūn Water on the left,
which originates from a small hill southeast of the city,
flows west past north of Jīn Mountain,
then southwest past the south of the county,
and flows west into White Water.
North of the water is White Water Marsh,
on its sunny side is the former residence of Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ,
its foundations still remain.
This is the so-called White Water Township,
where Sū Bó’ā observed the auspicious aura.
When Guāngwǔ campaigned against Qín Fēng,
he visited his old fief,
held a feast with great joy.
Zhāng Píngzǐ considered him a true man,
who toured south to see his old home.
The “Dōngguān Hànjì” says:
Emperor Míng visited Nányáng,
sacrificed at the old residence,
summoned school officials’ children to perform elegant music,
played “Lù Míng,”
and the emperor himself played xūn and chí to accompany,
entertaining the guests—
again at this residence.
White Water then flows west to join Jìn Water,
which emerges from Yángzhōng Mountain northeast of Xiāngxiāng County,
flows west past the north of old Xiāngxiāng County city.
According to the “Jùn Guó Zhì,”
it was a subordinate county of Nányáng.
Jìn Water then flows west past the east of old Càiyáng County city,
flows southwest into White Water.
It then flows west past the south of the city.
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Chéngyáng King Zhǐ’s heir Běn as a marquis here.
Yìng Shào said:
Cài Water emerges from Càiyáng,
flowing east into the Huái.
Now south of this city there is no other water,
only this water can match it.
The river flows west,
regrettably not eastward,
and the Huái’s source is obstructed,
mountains and rivers make it impossible to enter—
likely Yìng Shào’s error.
Dòng Water then flows southwest into the Miǎn River.
It then passes east of Zhōnglú County,
with Wéi Water from Wéi Mountain in Fánglíng County flowing east into it.
The county,
was the state of the Lúróng in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
South of the old county town, there is a river flowing from the western mountains,
where a stone cave in the mountains produces horses,
hence called Mǎxué Shān (Horse Cave Mountain).
During the Hàn dynasty, several hundred horses emerged from it,
the horses were small in shape,
resembling the horses of Bā and Diān.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
Lù Xùn attacked Xiāngyáng,
and from this cave obtained several tens of horses, which were sent to Jiànyè.
When a Shǔ envoy arrived,
there was someone whose home was in Diānchí,
who recognized the color of the horses' coats,
saying they were the horses his father had ridden,
and wept upon seeing them.
The river flows east for one hundred and forty lǐ past the south of the city,
named Yùmǎ Gǎng (Bathing Horse Harbor),
meaning that when these horses were first obtained,
they were washed here,
hence the name.
It is also said that when riding out, they bathed at the Miǎn River's edge,
also called Xǐmǎ Jiù (Washing Horse Stable).
The place where they crossed the Miǎn River and stayed overnight,
was named Qítíng (Rider Pavilion).
However, the various Mán tribes to the south dammed this river,
blocking it to the south at Wéichuān,
to irrigate the surrounding fields,
and the lower flow enters the Miǎn River.
The Miǎn River flows southeast past the west of the old city of Líqiū,
below the city facing Zhōuzhōu,
where Qín Fēng resided,
hence renamed Qínzhōu.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
Qín Fēng held his troops at Líqiū.
Líqiū city is two lǐ west of Guànchéng,
in the third year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Guāngwǔ sent Zhēngnán Cén Péng to attack Fēng,
in the fourth year,
Zhū Yù from Guànchéng captured Fēng at Líqiū.
The Miǎn River further south joins with the Shū River,
which originates southwest of Zhōnglú County,
flows east to the northern border of Qǐ County,
and enters the Miǎn River to the east,
called Shūkǒu.
In the water, there is a creature like a three- or four-year-old child,
with scales like a pangolin,
arrows cannot penetrate it,
in the seventh and eighth months,
it likes to bask on the gravel banks,
its knee-head resembles a tiger,
its paws and claws often submerged in water,
when it emerges its knee-head,
children unaware,
wanting to catch and play with it,
it will kill people.
Some say,
if someone captures it alive,
and removes its gāoyàn,
it can be controlled to a small extent,
named Shuǐhǔ (Water Tiger).
Further south, passing northeast of Qǐ County,
to the left of the Miǎn River is Qíchéng (Rider City),
with a circumference of two lǐ,
and a remaining height of one zhàng six chǐ,
which is Qítíng.
The county,
originally a Chǔ town,
was made a county by Qín,
in the eleventh year of Hàn Emperor Gāozǔ,
Huáng Jízhōng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
South of the county are the Huáng family tombs,
in front of the tombs are twin stone towers,
exquisitely carved,
commonly called Huánggōng Què (Lord Huáng's Towers).
Lord Huáng's name was Shàng,
who served as Sītú of Hàn.
The Miǎn River flows east past Zhūlán Qiáo (Pig Orchid Bridge),
originally named Mùlán Qiáo (Magnolia Bridge),
to the left and right of the bridge grew abundant reeds.
East of the bridge,
Liú Jìhé raised many pigs,
the governor of Xiāngyáng said:
"Here it smells of pig dung,
it should be renamed Zhūlán Qiáo,"
and the common people thus named it.
North of the bridge is Xí Yù's residence,
beside the residence is a fish pond,
the pond requires no artificial work,
naturally connected by channels,
sixty to seventy bù long,
ten zhàng wide,
often producing famous fish.
The Miǎn River further south meets the Mùlǐ Shuǐ,
during the Chǔ period, a canal was dug east of Yíchéng,
its upper opening three lǐ from the city,
Hàn's Nánjùn governor Wáng Chǒng further excavated it,
channeling Mán Shuǐ to irrigate fields,
called Mùlǐ Gōu.
It passes east of Yíchéng and flows northeast into the Miǎn,
called Mùlǐ Shuǐkǒu.
Further south, passing east of Yíchéng County,
the Yí Shuǐ originates from Fánglíng,
flowing east to join it.
The Yí River,
is the Mán River.
Because Huán Wēn's father was named Yí,
it was renamed the Mán River.
The Yí River originates from Kāngláng Mountain in the territory of Zhōnglú County,
which is adjacent to Jīng Mountain.
The water flows southeast past the western mountains of Yíchéng,
where it is called Yí Creek.
Further southeast, it passes by Luóchuān City,
the former state of Luó.
It is also called the Yān River,
as mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*: "The men of Chǔ attacked Luó and crossed the Yān."
The Yí River flows further southeast and merges with the Líng River,
which is the Qí River.
It connects upstream to Mòchéng Mountain in Mòyáng County of Liángzhōu,
the route taken by Sīmǎ Yì when he departed from Jǔ.
The water flows east past Qíxiāng County in Xīnchéng Commandery,
which was established from a division of Fánglíng,
and is called the Qí River.
Further east, it passes Língxiāng,
where it is called the Líng River.
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn pacified Wú,
he divided the northern district of Línjū and the southern district of Zhōnglú to establish Shànghuáng County,
with its seat at Língxiāng.
The Qí River flows further east past the western mountains of Yíchéng,
where it is called Qí Creek.
It flows east and merges with the Yí River,
at a place called Qíkǒu.
Mingling with the Yí River, it flows eastward,
where it is called the Qí River.
It passes south of Mánchéng,
which lies thirty *lǐ* south of Yíchéng.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records: "Mò Áo, after being defeated at Luó, retreated to Yān,
and crossed the Qí River in disorder."
The Yí River then flows east and empties into the Miǎn.
In the past, Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
diverting the water from the long valley west of the mountains,
which was this very river.
The old dam was about a hundred *lǐ* from the city.
Water flowed from the west of the city to irrigate the east,
forming a deep pool,
which is now known as Yùndǒu Pō.
The water breached the northeastern corner of the city,
and the people were swept away by the current.
Hundreds of thousands died east of the city,
and the entire eastern part of the city reeked,
so the pond was named Chòu Chí (Stinking Pond).
Later, people used its channels
to create ponds and fields west of the city.
The pond,
called Xīn Pō (New Pond),
covered several dozen *qǐng*.
To the northwest was Tǔmén Pō,
extending from Pínglù Canal in the north to Mùlán Bridge in the south, bounded by Tǔmén Mountain in the west and crossing the main road in the east.
Water flowed freely throughout,
entering the city from Xīn Pō in the east.
The city,
formerly the old capital of Yānyǐng,
was made a county by Qín.
In the third year of Emperor Huì of Hàn,
it was renamed Yíchéng.
The water flows through the great city,
passing north of the tomb of Qín Jié, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng during the Hàn.
Before the tomb stand two steles.
Jié
was a native of Ruò.
He served as Commandant of Jiāngxià before becoming Grand Administrator of Nányáng.
While passing through Yíchéng,
he saw a house facing east.
Jié stopped his carriage to look at it
and said:
"This dwelling could serve as a tomb."
Later, he died in Nányáng,
and when his funeral procession returned,
reaching the place where he had once stopped his carriage,
the carriage refused to advance.
Thus, his former subordinates purchased this residence to bury him,
and the solitary grave remains intact.
South of the city lies the residence of Sòng Yù.
Yù,
a native of this city,
was a man of exceptional talent and eloquence,
skilled in writing and knowledgeable in music.
The water then passes before Jīnchéng,
where an ancient stele still stands at the southern gate of the county.
The water flows east out of the city
and empties into Chòu Chí.
Chòu Chí irrigated the fields,
and the pond water dispersed,
flowing further into Zhūhú Pō.
Zhūhú Pō also irrigated the fields below.
The remaining water flowed down into Mùlǐ Ditch,
an old canal dug by Wáng Chǒng, Grand Administrator of Nán Commandery during the Hàn,
which diverted water from the Yān River
to irrigate seven hundred *qǐng* of land.
Bái Qǐ's canal irrigated three thousand *qǐng*,
making the land rich and fertile,
turning it into even more productive soil.
The county has Tài Mountain,
at the foot of which stands a temple
where famous scholars of the late Hàn resided.
Dozens of Inspectors, Officials of Two Thousand *Dàn*, Ministers, and Elders,
in their vermilion carriages and ornate canopies,
gathered together at the temple.
When the Inspector of Jīngzhōu passed through and saw this,
he greatly admired the grandeur
and named it Guāngài Lǐ (District of Officials' Canopies), inscribing a stone to commemorate it.
This stele was destroyed during the Yǒngjiā era,
but some of the text has been preserved.
It reads:
"Lofty is the southern peak,
brilliant is the shining light.
Here indeed flourish the talented and wise,
from which gentlemen are born.
These gentlemen,
are the flowers of the Hàn.
Their virtue shines like a dragon's glory,
their fame spreads like a crane's cry."
This mountain collapsed in the third year of Jiàn'ān,
with a sound heard for fifty or sixty *lǐ*.
Pheasants crowed from the rooftops,
and the people of the county, troubled by this,
consulted the Palace Attendant, Páng Jì.
Jì said:
"When mountains collapse and rivers run dry,
it is an omen that the state will perish."
In the thirteenth year,
when Cáo Cāo (Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) pacified Jīngzhōu,
the region south of the Miǎn River fell into decline.
The Miǎn River flows past the old city of Ruò County,
the ancient state of Ruò.
Between Qín and Chǔ,
it moved here from Shāngmì,
becoming a vassal of Chǔ,
which later annexed it as a county.
The county borders the Miǎn River ferry to the south,
and south of the ferry is a stone mountain
with an ancient beacon tower on top.
North of the county is a great city,
where King Zhāo of Chǔ, fleeing from Wú,
relocated his capital from Jìyǐng.
This is the so-called land of Yān, Ruò, Lú, and Luó,
which Qín made into a county.
The Miǎn River flows further east,
where the Áo River joins it.
The Áo River originates northeast of Xīnshì County,
flows southwest past the western side of Tàiyáng Mountain,
and then south past the north of Xīnshì County.
Further southwest, it merges with the Zhī River on the right.
The Zhī River originates from Dàhóng Mountain,
flows southwest through the boundary of Xiāngyáng Ruò County,
passes southeast of Díchéng to the southwest,
and joins the Áo River from the left.
The Áo River then flows southwest and empties into the Miǎn,
at a place called Áokǒu.
The Miǎn River flows south past the west of Shíchéng,
a city fortified by the mountains,
established when Yáng Hù, Grand Tutor of Jìn, garrisoned Jīngzhōu.
In the ninth year of Yuánkāng during the reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the western part of Jiāngxià was divided to establish Jìnglíng Commandery, with its seat here.
The Miǎn River flows southeast and merges with the Jiù River,
which originates from Liáoqū Mountain northeast of Jìnglíng County,
also known as Lúqū Mountain,
and flows west into the Miǎn.
In the fourth year of Duke Dìng of Lǔ,
when the Wú army entered Yǐng,
King Zhāo fled to Suí,
crossing at Chéngjiù,
which refers to this river.
Further east, it passes east of Jīngchéng.
The Miǎn River flows southeast from Jīngchéng,
passing east of Zhāng Mountain in Dāngyáng County.
On the mountain stands an ancient city,
built by Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn when he attacked Dù Zēng.
This is the place referred to in the "Tribute of Yǔ" as "from Nèifāng to Dàbié."
Since it borders and is connected to the Miǎn River's flow,
it indeed corresponds to the text in the *Shàngshū*.
The Miǎn River flows east again,
and on the right joins Quánkǒu.
The water issues from Zhāng Mountain,
flowing southeast past the north of Quánchéng,
which was the ancient state of Quán.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
King Wǔ of Chǔ conquered Quán.
Quán rebelled,
so he besieged it and killed its ruler,
and moved Quán to Nàchù, which is this place.
To the southeast is Nàkǒu City.
The Quán River then flows east into the Miǎn.
The Miǎn River flows southeast again and joins with Yángkǒu.
The water above connects to Chì Lake in Jiānglíng County.
Northwest of Jiānglíng is Jìnán City,
to which King Wén of Chǔ moved from Dānyáng,
and which King Píng fortified.
Bān Gù states:
It was the capital Yǐng of Chǔ.
Southwest of the city is Chìbǎn Ridge,
below which is a watercourse
flowing northeast into the city,
called Zǐxū's Watercourse,
likely opened when the Wú army entered Yǐng.
It is called Xījīng Lake.
It then exits the city to the northeast,
flowing southwest into Lóng Slope.
The slope
is the ancient Tiānjǐng Water,
over two hundred paces in circumference,
located east of Líng Stream within the Jiāng dike.
The water is extremely deep,
and a dragon was seen within it,
hence the name Lóng Slope.
North of the slope is King Zhuāng of Chǔ's fishing terrace,
thirty-four chǐ high,
sixty chǐ from north to south,
and ninety chǐ from east to west.
The slope water then passes south of Yǐng City,
flowing northeast, where it is called Yáng Water.
Further northeast,
Lùbái Lake water flows into it.
The lake is north of Dàgǎng,
south of the gǎng is Zhōng Lake,
and below the southern dike is Hūnguān Lake.
The three lakes combine into one waterway,
connecting east to Huāng Valley.
On the eastern bank of Huāng Valley is Yěfù City.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary* says:
"Mò'áo hanged himself in Huāng Valley,
and the commanders were imprisoned in Yěfù,"
referring to this place.
When water is abundant in spring and summer,
it connects south to the Great River;
otherwise, it reaches the Jiāng dike to the south
and passes west of Fāngchéng to the north.
Fāngchéng
is the Southern Mán Prefecture.
Further north, it meets the three lakes,
so Shèng Hóngzhī said:
"East of the Southern Mán Prefecture are three lakes,
sharing a single source,"
likely referring to the relocation of the administrative seat to the Western Prefecture.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
a channel was opened to Lùbái Lake,
flowing down into Yáng Water,
to expand water transport.
Yáng Water then flows east past north of Tiānjǐng,
which is over a lǐ north of Fāngchéng,
two lǐ in circumference,
its depth unfathomable.
The well has a hidden chamber,
and weapons appear when seen.
On the western bank is Tiānjǐng Terrace,
built on the foundation of an old dike,
facing the water's edge,
an excellent place for leisure and rest.
Yáng Water flows northeast again,
and to the east receives the mouth of Chì Lake.
The lake is fifty lǐ in circumference,
and all the ponds below the city
converge here.
Northeast of the lake is Dàshǔ Terrace,
sixty chǐ high,
with a length and width of eight chǐ,
also called Qīngshǔ Terrace.
Its elegant structure and layered brightness
offer a broad and comprehensive view,
allowing visitors who ascend it
to express distant sentiments.
Yáng Water then flows east into Huáróng County,
where there is Líng Stream Water,
connecting west to the mouth of Chì Lake.
From here downward, there are many lakes,
fifty lǐ in circumference,
and all the ponds below the city
converge here.
There is also Zǐxū's Watercourse,
likely opened when entering Yǐng.
The water flows east into Lí Lake,
which is seventy-five lǐ east of the county.
This is the place mentioned in the *Guóyǔ* where King Líng of Chǔ excavated a stone outer wall and dammed the Hàn River to emulate Emperor Shùn.
Beside the lake is Zhānghuá Terrace,
one hundred chǐ high,
with a foundation one hundred fifty chǐ wide.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng said:
"Chǔ built a terrace atop Zhānghuá."
Wéi Zhāo believed Zhānghuá was also a place name.
When the king ascended it with Wǔ Jǔ,
Jǔ said:
"The terrace's height should not exceed what is needed to observe the auspicious or ominous signs of the state,
and its size should not exceed what is needed to accommodate the ritual vessels for banquets,"
criticizing its extravagance and admonishing against its excess.
It is said that this watercourse was used for transporting supplies
when King Líng built the terrace.
The water flows north into Yáng Water.
Yáng Water then flows northeast and joins with Zuò Stream Water.
The water issues from north of Jiānglíng County,
likely converging from various scattered pools,
accumulating to form a river.
It flows east past Lǔ Zōngzhī's fortifications,
facing the postal road to the south.
There is a large bridge over the water.
In the third year of Lóng'ān,
Huán Xuán attacked Yīn Zhòngkān in Jiānglíng.
Zhòngkān fled north
and hanged himself on this bridge.
Zuò Stream then flows east into Chuánguān Lake.
The lake water flows northeast into Nǚguān Lake.
The lake water flows east again,
entering Yáng Water.
Yáng Water then flows north past west of Jìnglíng County,
and further north,
it receives Jīn and discharges Zhè.
Zhè Water
is the lower Yáng Water.
Jīn Water issues from one hundred ninety lǐ from the county,
flowing west past Jīn City,
where the Jīn Water Garrison is stationed below the city.
In the second year of Yuánxī of the Jìn dynasty,
the Jīn Water Garrison in Jìnglíng Commandery obtained seven bronze bells,
which were reported to the higher authorities.
Jīn Water then flows west past north of Jìnglíng County,
flowing west into Yáng Water,
called Jīnkǒu.
West of the water is the ancient great city of Jìnglíng,
the ancient state of Yún.
It was governed by Lord Xīn of Yún,
referred to as Yúnxiāng.
In the past, Bái Qǐ captured Yǐng
and advanced east to Jìnglíng,
which is this place.
The Qín dynasty made it a county,
and Wáng Mǎng called it Shǒupíng.
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Liú Lóng was further enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Beside the city is Gānyú Slope.
In the thirteenth year of Duke Zhāo in the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
when Prince Hēigōng served as Lìngyǐn,
he encamped at Yú Slope.
Yáng Water then flows north into the Miǎn,
called Yángkǒu,
also known as Zhōng Xiàkǒu.
When Cáo Tàizǔ pursued Liú Bèi at Dāngyáng,
Zhāng Fēi held his spear at Chángbǎn,
allowing Bèi and a few riders to head obliquely toward Hànjīn,
and they crossed at Xiàkǒu.
The Miǎn River flows east and reaches Chǎnkǒu.
Its water receives the waters of Dà Chǎn, Mǎgǔ, and other lakes,
three to four hundred lǐ in circumference.
When summer floods converge,
it becomes vast like the sea,
with huge waves and deep pools,
connecting the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers.
Thus, Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"Beside it are Zhū, Chǎn, Dān, and Cháo."
Further southeast, it passes east of Yúndù County in Jiāngxià,
where Xià Water flows from the west and joins it.
This is the Dǔkǒu,
which is the central summer water.
The county
was formerly the Yún Pavilion.
The Zuǒzhuàn states,
"Ruò'áo married a woman from Yún."
The Yǔgòng mentions "Yún earth and Mèng becoming cultivated,"
hence the county derived its name from this.
The county has the Yúnmèng City,
located to the northeast.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east past Zuǒsāng.
In ancient times, when King Zhāo of Zhōu campaigned south,
the boatmen presented him with a boat sealed with glue.
As King Zhāo crossed the Miǎnshuǐ,
he sank midstream
and died in these waters.
During a meeting between Qí and Chǔ,
the Marquis of Qí said:
"King Zhāo campaigned south but did not return;
I inquire about this."
Qū Wán replied:
"You should ask the riverside."
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
Village elders say that the common people assisted with King Zhāo's funeral here,
completing the rites before departing,
hence it is called "assisting the funeral."
Zuǒsāng
is a corrupted form of the characters.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east and joins the Jùliàng Shuǐkǒu,
where water from the north connects to Jùliàng Lake,
and flows south to the Miǎnshuǐ.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east and reaches Héyìkǒu.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said,
elders from Xūdǎo Village mentioned that court couriers assembled for the king's funeral here,
hence the name.
Today, Xūdǎo Village has the Dàliànkǒu,
said to be where King Zhāo was encoffined.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east,
called Héngsāng,
said to be where King Zhāo's body was recovered.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east and is called Zhènggōng Tán,
said to be where Duke Wǔ of Zhèng drowned together with the king.
I say the generations are too far apart,
making it implausible.
This was the Zhèng Township of Chǔ,
where the local magistrate presumptuously called himself "duke,"
hence later generations called it Zhènggōng Tán.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east and reaches Sǐmiǎn,
said to be where King Zhāo crossed the Miǎnshuǐ and died,
hence the name "Dead Miǎn."
Could the king's corpse have floated upstream?
But over the ages, it has become obscure,
hard to clarify clearly,
though inferring from similar events,
it seems plausible yet not entirely accurate.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east and joins Lìkǒu,
where the Āishuǐ originates from the Chíhé Mountain southwest of Xīnyáng County in Jìnglíng Commandery,
flowing east past the south of Xīnyáng County,
whose seat is the old city of Yúndù,
established by dividing Yúndù.
The Āishuǐ flows southeast into the great lake south of Xiāochéng County,
then south into the Miǎnshuǐ,
which is called Lìkǒu.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows southeast,
where the Yúnshuǐ enters.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east past the Dùnshuǐkǒu,
where water connects south to the Tàibái Lake of the county,
and the lake water connects southeast to the river,
also called Dùnkǒu.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east past the north of Dùnyáng County,
located on the north bank of the Dùnshuǐ.
The Miǎnshuǐ flows east past the north of the old city of Línzhàng,
where in the second year of Jiànxīng of Jìn,
Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn governed Jīngzhōu,
stationed here.
It then flows south to the north of Shāyí County in Jiāngxià,
and enters the river from the south.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
Xiàkǒu is also called Miǎnkǒu.
The Shàngshū Yǔgòng states:
"The Hànshuǐ flows south to Dàbié and enters the river."
In the fourth year of Duke Dìng in the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn,
when the Wú army attacked Yǐng,
Chǔ's Zǐ Cháng crossed the Hàn and deployed troops,
from Xiǎobié to Dàbié.
Jīng Xiàngfán's Chūnqiū Tǔdìmíng states:
"Dàbié
is a mountain name east of the Hàn,
located south of Ānfēng County."
Dù Yù's Shìdì states:
"The two Bié are names near the Hàn,
so they cannot be in Ānfēng."
According to the Dìshuō,
"the Hànshuǐ flows east and strikes the slopes of Dàbié,
then joins the river to the south."
This matches the Shàngshū and Dù Yù,
but its exact location is now unknown.
29 Shuǐjīng Zhù Volume Twenty-Nine
29.1 Miǎnshuǐ
29.1 Miǎnshuǐ
The Miǎnshuǐ merges with the Jiāng,
then flows east past Pénglí Marsh,
which the Shàngshū Yǔgòng
calls the marsh where waters converge.
Zhèng Xuán said:
"Huì
means to circle."
The Hàn and Jiāng contend,
turning east to form this marsh.
It then flows northeast past the south of Jūcháo County,
the ancient state of Cháo.
When Tāng attacked Jié,
Jié fled to Náncháo,
which is Cháo Marsh.
The Shàngshū records
that during the Zhōu, the Earl of Cháo came to court.
In the twelfth year of Duke Wén in the Chūnqiū,
in summer,
the people of Chǔ besieged Cháo.
Cháo
was a Shū state.
Shū rebelled,
hence they besieged it.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
Emperor Míng of Hàn enfeoffed Liú Bān, Marquis of Zīqiū, as the marquis of this state.
The Jiāngshuǐ flows east from Rúxūkǒu,
then joins Zhàkǒu on the left,
where water originates from Cháo Lake,
flowing east past the north of Wūshàng City,
then east past the south of the relocated Nánqiáo Commandery city,
then east across the embankment,
past the north of Fùnóng Mountain,
then east,
joining Qīngxīshuǐ on the left,
which originates from the Qīngxī at Mǎzǐyàn to the northeast,
flowing east past Qīngxī City, then bending southwest,
passing the mountain and flowing southwest into Zhàshuǐ,
called Qīngxīkǒu.
Zhàshuǐ flows east,
joining Báishíshānshuǐ on the left,
which originates from Báishí Mountain,
flowing west past the south of Lǐquè City,
then southwest into Zhàshuǐ.
Zhàshuǐ flows southeast and accumulates into Dòu Lake,
with an islet in the middle. East of the lake is Hánzōng Mountain,
with a city on the mountain.
North of the mountain is the lake water,
which flows east to form the rear embankment north lake,
with the embankment to the south.
On the embankment is the old city of the relocated Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Dòu Lake water flows east,
called Dòuhúkǒu,
flowing east past the north of Cìshǐ Mountain,
then past the south of Hánzōng Mountain,
flowing between the two mountains,
emerging north of Wángwǔzǐ City,
which is on Cìshǐ Mountain.
The lake water flows east past the north of Yòutángxué, forming Zhōngtáng,
an embankment amid four waters.
Water originates north of Géhǔ Mountain,
with Hǔshān City on the mountain,
and Guōsēngkǎn City.
North of the water is Zhàozǔyuè City,
all part of the old Dōngguān City.
Formerly, Zhūgě Kè led troops to build the Dōngxīng Embankment to block Cháo Lake,
constructing a city against the mountain,
and assigning generals Quán Duān and Liú Lüè,
each with a thousand men to guard it.
Wèi sent Sīmǎ Zhāo to supervise Zhūgě Dàn, who led troops to attack the three cities of Dōngguān,
intending to destroy the embankment and block it.
The armies built a floating bridge,
deployed on the embankment,
and divided forces to attack the city.
Kè sent champion Dīng Fèng and others to ascend the embankment, shouting and attacking fiercely,
while Zhū Yì and others used the navy to attack the floating bridge.
Wèi's Zhēngdōng Hú Zūn's soldiers fought to cross,
the bridge collapsed,
and thousands drowned.
The embankment is Dōngxīng Embankment,
and the city is Guān City.
Zhàshuǐ flows southeast past the south of Gāojiāngchǎn City,
north of the old Jǐnglüè City,
then southeast past the south of Zhāngzǔxǐ City,
flowing southeast, then bending north,
past the west of Zhèngwèiwèi City.
These events of Wèi are long past,
hard to ascertain fully,
but by examining old records and seeking new information,
this is roughly the case.
It then bends northward,
where Púpǔ emerges,
and Zhàshuǐ flows southeast into the great river,
called Zhàkǒu.
It then flows east past the south of Niúzhǔ County,
and east to Shíchéng County.
The "Shíchéng County" mentioned in the Classic
refers to Shíchéng County of Xuānchéng Commandery.
Niúzhǔ is located within the boundaries of Gūshú and Wūjiāng counties,
approximately five hundred lǐ northeast of Shíchéng.
How could one pass through Niúzhǔ and then arrive at Shíchéng?
This is an error in the Classic.
It divides into two branches:
one flows northeast,
while the other passes north of Pílíng County,
forming the Northern River.
The "Treatise on Geography" states,
Pílíng County
was a subordinate county of Kuàijī.
Two hundred paces north of Dāntú County there is an old city,
which originally was the seat of Pílíng Commandery.
Formerly it was three lǐ from the river,
but the bank gradually eroded,
so it reached the city walls.
North of the city is the tomb of Liú Yáo, Governor of Yángzhōu,
which has sunk into the river.
This river is the Northern River.
The "Classic" recording it as the Northern River is acceptable.
But saying it flows east to Yúyáo is incorrect.
Examining its course,
one knows the error in the "Classic".
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
The River water, emerging east from Shíchéng and passing south of the State of Wú, becomes the Southern River.
The River water, entering east from Shíchéng, becomes the Guìkǒu,
flows east past the north of Shíchéng County,
established in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
and subordinate to Xuānchéng Commandery.
To the east it joins the Great Stream,
whose waters first receive the River,
flow north past the east of the old city of that county,
and then enter the Southern River from the north.
The Southern River then flows east and joins the waters of Guìcháng Pool,
which emerge from Láng Mountain south of the county,
flow north to become Guìcháng Pool,
and the pool waters then flow north and pour into the Southern River.
The Southern River then flows east past the south of Línchéng County of Xuānchéng,
and further east joins the Jīng River.
The Southern River then flows east and joins the Tóng River,
then flows east past Ānwú County,
where it is called "Ānwú Stream".
Further east,
the Xuán Stream waters pour into it.
These waters emerge from below Língyáng Mountain,
pass west of Língyáng County as the Xuán Stream waters.
This is the place where in former times, a man of the county named Yáng Zǐmíng caught a white dragon while fishing.
Three years later,
the dragon welcomed Zǐmíng up to Língyáng Mountain,
which rises over a thousand zhàng from the ground.
Over a hundred years later,
he called to the people below the mountain,
telling them to ascend halfway up the mountain to speak with him in the stream.
Zǐ'ān asked Zǐmíng where his fishing reel was.
Twenty years later,
Zǐ'ān died.
Below the mountain, a yellow crane perched in the trees on his grave mound,
and its cry often called "Zǐ'ān",
hence the county took its name from this.
In the fourth year of the Xiánkāng era of Jìn,
it was renamed Guǎngyáng County.
The stream waters then join the Eastern Stream waters from the north,
which emerge from Nánlǐ Mountain,
flow north past the east of that county.
Sāng Qīn said:
The Huái River emerges southeast of the county,
and enters the Great River from the north.
These waters then flow north past Shǔyóu Mountain,
and further north,
join the Xuán Stream on the left,
flow north past the east of Ānwú County,
which was established by division from Wǎnlíng
in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn.
South of the county is Luòxīng Mountain,
on which there is a hanging waterfall over fifty zhàng high,
falling into a deep pool below.
The pool waters flow northeast,
enter the Xuán Stream on the left,
and together pour into the Southern River.
North of the Southern River
is the boundary of Wǎnlíng County.
The Southern River then flows east past the south of Níngguó County,
established by division from Wǎnlíng in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn.
The Southern River then flows east past the south of old Zhāng County and the north of Ānjí County.
At the end of the Guānghé era,
when the empire was in great turmoil,
this district defended its strategic points and maintained its integrity,
for which the Hàn court commended it.
In the second year of the Zhōngpíng era,
