the southern district of old Zhāng was separated to form Ānjí County.
South of the county is Diàotóu Spring,
which gushes forth suspended from a height of one rèn,
then flows into the river,
and the river waters below join the Southern River.
The Southern River then flows northeast to become the Long Channel,
passes the lake mouth, and the Southern River flows east into Jùqū,
which is called the Mouth of the Five Lakes.
The Five Lakes
refer to Chángdàng Lake, Tài Lake, Shè Lake, Guì Lake, and Gé Lake.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"It pours into the Five Lakes, vast and boundless."
This speaks of the River water passing through the Five Lakes and then encompassing and pouring into Tài Lake.
Therefore, Zuǒ Qiūmíng, relating the "Discourses of the States", said:
"When Yuè attacked Wú,
they fought at the Five Lakes." This refers to this.
It also says:
"When Fàn Lǐ destroyed Wú,
he returned to the Five Lakes and took leave of Yuè."
This is then the comprehensive general name for Tài Lake.
Yú Fān said:
"This lake has five channels,
hence it is called the Five Lakes."
Wéi Zhāo said:
"The Five Lakes
are present-day Tài Lake."
The "Shàngshū" calls it Zhènzé.
The "Ěryǎ" considers it Jùqū,
with a circumference of five hundred lǐ.
In the lake is Bāo Mountain,
which the "Spring and Autumn Annals" calls Fūjiāo Mountain.
It has a cavern chamber that goes underground and travels hidden,
connecting north to Lángyé Dōngwǔ County.
Commonly it is called Dòngtíng.
Beside it is Qīng Mountain,
also called Xiàjià Mountain.
The mountain has a cave,
which secretly connects to Dòngtíng Mountain.
On it is a stone drum,
over a zhàng long.
When it sounds, there is warfare.
Therefore, the "Records of Wú" says:
"Tài Lake has Bāo Mountain,
over a hundred lǐ west of the state.
Several hundred families reside there,
producing timber for bows and crossbows.
Beside it is a small mountain,
which has a stone cave
connecting south to Dòngtíng,
so deep and far its end cannot be known."
The state of Sānmiáo,
had Dòngtíng on its left,
and Pénglí on its right,
which is present-day Gōngtíng Lake.
Taking Dòngtíng of Tài Lake opposite Pénglí,
then left and right can be understood.
I note that both lakes having Dòngtíng in their names also allows them to be divided into left and right.
It is merely a matter of orientation based on the direction one faces.
Since it concerns Sānmiáo,
it is appropriate to take the Xiāng River as the correct reference.
Therefore, Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Here are the caverns of Bāo Mountain and Dòngtíng,
the subterranean passages of Bālíng,
hiddenly reaching, connecting all around,
deep grottoes, secluded and remote."
The "Shānhǎijīng" says:
"Fúyù Mountain,
looking north one sees Jùqū.
Tiáo Water emerges from its northern side,
flows north and pours into Jùqū."
Xiè Kānglè said:
"The 'Shānhǎijīng' says Fúyù Mountain is five hundred lǐ east of Jūyú,
which would mean the eastern mountains of Jūyú County should enter the sea.
Jūyú is now northwest of Niǎodào Mountain in Yúyáo.
How could it look north to Jùqū?"
He considered Guō very ignorant of geography.
It is said that at the southern mouth of Dòngtíng is Luófú Mountain,
three thousand six hundred zhàng high.
Below the stone tower on east Luófú Mountain are two stone drums.
Striking them produces a clear, far-reaching sound—
these are the so-called divine bells.
The details are recorded in the "Record of Luófú Mountain".
Kuàijī Mountain should be directly south of the lake,
and there is also Shānyīn Stream water entering there.
Forty lǐ west of Shānyīn are two streams:
the Eastern Stream is one zhàng nine chǐ wide,
warm in winter and cool in summer;
the Western Stream is three zhàng five chǐ wide,
cool in winter and warm in summer.
The two streams flow north for over three lǐ,
reach Xú Village and merge into one stream,
over five zhàng wide, where warmth and coolness intermix.
This is probably the Tiáo Water mentioned in the "Shānhǎijīng".
It flows north past Luófú Mountain and then pours down into Tài Lake.
Therefore, it is said to emerge from its northern side
and enter Jùqū.
In the lake are the three mountains Dàléi and Xiǎoléi,
also called the Three Mountains Lake,
and also called Dòngtíng Lake.
Yáng Quán's "Rhapsody on the Five Lakes" says:
"Its head is at Wúxī,
its feet tread at Sōngjiāng,
bearing Wúchéng on its back,
embracing Tàiwú against its chest.
Zuòlǐng, lofty and towering,
arched and winding.
Dàléi and Xiǎoléi,
swift waves chasing one another."
This describes the lake's encompassing extent.
East of Tài Lake,
eighteen lǐ west of the State of Wú, is Zuòlǐng Mountain.
Common tradition says this mountain was originally in Tài Lake,
and Yǔ, in regulating the waters, moved it closer to Wú.
Further east and southwest are two small hills,
both having stones like rolled bamboo cables.
Common tradition says these are what Yǔ used to pull the mountains.
In Tài Lake there is a shallow area.
The elders say:
"This is the trace of Zuòlǐng Mountain's foot."
From here eastward, it gradually deepens,
and it is said to be the channel of Qiān Mountain.
This mountain is over thirty lǐ from Tài Lake.
To the east, Sōng River emerges.
It receives water from Tài Lake above,
then passes through Lìzé,
which lies to the south of Wú, on the left and right banks of Sōng River.
The Guóyǔ states:
Yuè attacked Wú,
and Wú defended itself at Lìzé,
with the Yuè army on the south bank of the river
and the Wú army on the north bank.
Yúshì said:
Sōng River flows north from Wú State for fifty lǐ,
and beside the river are the two mountains, Chéng and Xū,
each with a temple.
In the thirteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
Yuè sent two senior ministers, Chóu Wúyú and Ōuyáng, among others, to attack Wú.
The people of Wú defeated them,
capturing the two senior ministers.
After the ministers died,
temples were erected on the mountains,
named the two kings, Chéng and Xū.
On Xū Mountain, there is now an altar stone,
and the elders say:
It is the place governed by the spirit of Xū.
Below is a winding road with nine turns,
leading south to Tài Lake.
Héliǘ built it to travel to Gūxū Terrace,
from which to gaze upon Tài Lake.
Sōng River flows northeast from the lake for seventy lǐ,
where the river water divides,
called Sānjiāngkǒu (Three Rivers Mouth).
The Wúyuè Chūnqiū records that Fàn Lǐ left Yuè,
sailing out from the mouth of the three rivers,
and entered among the five lakes.
This also distinguishes the three rivers and five lakes,
although the names are confusing,
they do not match the Zhífāng.
Yǔ Zhòngchū’s annotation to the Yángdū Fù says:
Now Tài Lake flows east into Sōng River,
and seventy lǐ downstream there is a water mouth,
where the flow divides, entering the sea to the northeast as Lóu River,
and entering the sea to the southeast as Dōng River,
making three together with Sōng River.
The Wú Jì states:
One river flows southeast for seventy lǐ into a small lake, called Cìxī,
and emerging southeast from the lake is called Gǔ River.
Gǔ River emerges from the small lake in Wú,
passing by the old city of Yóujuàn County.
The Shényì Zhuàn states:
Yóujuàn County
was Chángshuǐ County in the Qín era.
During the time of the First Emperor,
there was a children’s rhyme in the county:
“When the city gate has blood,
the city will sink and become a lake.”
An old woman heard this and grew worried and fearful.
One morning, she went to spy on the city gate.
The gate guards wanted to bind her,
but the woman explained her reason.
After the woman left,
the gate guards killed a dog and smeared its blood on the gate.
When the woman went again,
she saw the blood, fled, and dared not look back.
Suddenly, a great flood rose, about to submerge the county.
The registrar ordered a subordinate to report to the magistrate.
The magistrate saw the subordinate and said:
“Why have you suddenly become a fish?”
The subordinate replied:
“Your Honor has also become a fish.”
Thus, it sank and became a valley.
Therefore, the water of Chángshuǐ City was named Gǔ River.
The Wú Jì states:
There is a city in the valley,
which was the seat of Yóujuàn County.
It was the Cháipì Pavilion of Wú,
originally the Zuìlǐ area of the Jiùlǐ Township.
The First Emperor of Qín, disliking its kingly aura,
ordered over a hundred thousand prisoners to defile its surface soil,
giving it a foul name,
and changed it to Qiújuàn,
also called Yóujuàn.
In the third year of Huánglóng of Wú,
auspicious grain grew in Juàn County,
so it was renamed Héxīng.
Later, because the crown prince’s name was Hé,
it was changed to Jiāxīng.
This is the Zuìlǐ City of the Chūnqiū.
Gǔ River flows southeast again, passing west of Jiāxīng County city.
Gǔ River flows southeast again, passing by the old city of Yánguān County.
It was formerly the seat of the Hǎichāng Commandant of Wú.
During the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
it was established by dividing from Jiāxīng.
The Tàikāng Dìdào Jì
states that Wú had Yánguān County.
Yuè Zī’s Jiǔzhōu Zhì says:
The county has Qínyán Mountain.
The First Emperor of Qín passed by here,
and a beauty died,
buried on the mountain.
Below the mountain is a beauty temple.
To the right of Gǔ River is Mǎgāo City,
the old city of the Salt Control Commandant.
King Bì of Wú boiled seawater for salt in this county.
Therefore, the Hànshū Dìlǐ Zhì states:
The county has a salt official.
Fifty lǐ east is Wǔyuán Township,
originally Yuè territory.
Qín established Hǎiyán County in this area.
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
The county
was originally Wǔyuán Township.
Later, the county sank and became Zhè Lake,
and the seat was moved to Wǔyuán Township,
renamed Wǔyuán County.
Wáng Mǎng named it Zhǎnwǔ.
During the reign of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
the land of Wǔyuán sank again and became a lake,
which is the present Dāng Lake.
Later, this county was moved.
To the south is Qínwàng Mountain,
which the First Emperor of Qín ascended to gaze upon the Eastern Sea,
hence the mountain got its name.
Gǔ River emerges from the county as Gǎnpǔ,
connecting to the vast sea.
In the first year of Guāngxī,
three hairy people gathered in the county,
likely blown by the wind.
Further east, it reaches Yúyáo County of Kuàijī,
and enters the sea to the east.
Xiè Língyùn stated:
Jùqū is in Yújì.
Thus, Yújì is another name for Yúyáo.
Now, south of Yújì,
northwest of Yúyáo,
the Zhèjiāng and Pǔyáng River converge and flow together into the sea.
However, the river names have already diverged,
and this is not the Southern River mentioned by Bān Gù.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
The Three Rivers are
the Mín River, the Sōng River, and the Zhè River.
However, the Zhè River originates in the southern barbarian regions,
and is not the same as the Mín River.
Authors describing geographical features
often say that the river reaches Shānyīn as the Zhè River.
Now, the river branches southward,
passes through Wūchéng County,
flows south to Yúháng County,
and then merges with the Zhè River.
Therefore, Kǎn Yīn's "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
The river reaches Kuàijī and merges with the Zhè River.
The Zhè River flows south from Línpíng Lake to the Pǔyáng River,
and east of Yújì, it joins the Pǔyáng River.
Branching from Qínwàng,
it flows east to Yúyáo County and becomes a river again.
Eastward, it merges with Chēxiāng Water,
which originates from Chēxiāng Mountain,
cascading from a high waterfall
over forty zhang in height.
Although there are floods and droughts, its flow neither increases nor decreases.
The river flows east past Huángqiáo,
by the river stands the former residence of Huáng Chāng, Governor of Shǔ Commandery during the Hàn.
The bridge was originally built by Huáng Chāng.
Huáng Chāng served as a clerk in the province,
and his wife was separated from him due to bandits.
Later, they reunited in Shǔ,
and restored their former affection.
The river flows east past the south of Zhě Mountain.
Yú Fān once climbed this mountain and looked out in all directions,
admonishing his descendants that they could live north of the river,
where they would enjoy official positions and emoluments for generations,
but living south of the river would bring no prosperity.
Indeed, those who lived north of the river
successively rose to prominence,
while those who lived south of the river
often declined.
Zhòngxiáng's words were thus proven true.
The river flows past the official granary,
which was the former residence of Yú Guó, Governor of Rìnán,
called Xīyú,
because his elder brother Yú Guāng lived east of the county.
This place is where the two wild geese escorted the former governor.
The river flows east past the old city of Yúyáo County,
whose walls were built by the Wú general Zhū Rán.
It faces the river to the south,
and backs against the vast sea to the north,
as the Master said: "The vast and boundless sea,
an abyss of ten thousand miles."
The county lies one hundred and forty lǐ west of Kuàijī,
and is named after the Gōuyú Mountain.
The mountain lies south of Yúyáo,
and north of Gōuzhāng.
The river flows east past Xuéhú Táng,
whose waters irrigate the entire county,
making it all fertile farmland.
The river flows east and empties into the sea.
This is what is called the Three Rivers.
Therefore, Zǐxū said:
The states of Wú and Yuè
are encircled by the Three Rivers,
and the people have nowhere to move.
However, the southeastern land is low-lying,
where myriad streams converge,
and tides and lakes overflow and breach,
forming rivers wherever they touch.
Branches and tributaries crisscross,
with numerous distributaries dividing,
so the old courses and channels
are difficult to fully ascertain.
Although roughly following the county boundaries,
and compiling what is recorded,
it may not necessarily capture the full reality.
29.2 Qián River
29.2 Qián River
The Qián River originates in Dàngqú County, Bā Commandery.
The Qián River
is likely a branch of the Hàn River that flows underground,
hence it bears this name.
Now there is a large cavern,
into which the Qián River flows,
passes beneath Gāng Mountain,
and emerges underground to the southwest, called the Fú River.
Some believe this is the ancient Qián River.
Zhèng Xuán said:
The Hàn River branches into the Qián,
its cavern originally small,
where water accumulates to form a marsh,
and its flow merges with the Hàn River.
When the Great Yǔ dredged and opened the Hàn River,
it became the Western Hàn River.
Therefore, the "Book" says:
Tuó and Qián were both regulated.
Liú Chéngzhī claimed the Bái River flows into the Qián,
but the Bái River merges with the Qiāng River and enters the Hàn,
which is still the Hàn River.
During the Yánxī era, the county
was separated from Bā to establish Dàngqú Commandery,
which was likely the ancient Cóng State.
Now there is Cóngchéng County,
and the Yú River,
along both banks of which,
all are inhabited by the Cóng people.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered the passes,
they followed to pacify the Three Qín,
these people being brave, robust, and fond of singing and dancing.
Gāozǔ loved and practiced their dances,
which are now called the Bāyú Dance.
Northwest of the county is the Xúcáo River,
which flows south past the county and empties into the Qián River.
In the county are the tombs of Chariot and Horse General Féng Gǔn and Governor of Guìyáng Lǐ Wēn.
The spirits of these two men
often return to their hometown in the third month,
and the Hàn River suddenly rises.
Officials and commoners of the commandery and county
all make offerings to them on the water,
now called Féng Lǐ.
Further south, it enters the Great River.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
Diéjiāng has a separate river originating in Jìnshòu County,
which is the Qián River.
Its southern source passes through Bāxī,
and this is the Western Hàn River.
29.3 Tuān River
29.3 Tuān River
The Tuān River originates from Fēn Mountain north of Lì County,
flows south past the east of the county,
and further south past the east of Guànjūn County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed Cháoyáng as Lìxìn County,
Yìng Shào said:
"The county is located on the north bank of the Cháo River."
Now the Cháo River flows past its north,
but does not emerge from its south.
It is likely that the city walls have shifted and submerged,
and the river channels have changed their course,
hence the old name is passed down,
while the remaining designation persists today.
Further east, it reaches the south of Xīnyě County,
and enters the Yù River from the east.
29.7 Bǐ Shuǐ
29.7 Bǐ Shuǐ
The Bǐ Shuǐ originates from Tàihú Mountain northeast of Bǐyáng,
flowing southeast past the south of the county,
where the Xiè Shuǐ joins it from the south.
Tàihú Mountain is located about thirty li northeast of Bǐyáng,
with a circumference of fifty to sixty li.
Zhāng Héng, in his fu "Nán Dū,"
refers to it as Tiānfēng Tàihú.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Bǐ Shuǐ originates from Bǐyáng County,
and enters Cài from the east."
The "Jīng" states:
"The Xiè Shuǐ joins it from the south."
However, there is no Xiè Shuǐ in Bǐyáng,
likely a mistaken reference to the Bǐxiè in Shòuchūn.
In the fourth year of Yánchāng,
I was appointed as the Governor of Dōngjīngzhōu,
with the administrative seat at the old city of Bǐyáng County.
South of the city lies the Cài Shuǐ,
which originates from Nánpánshí Mountain,
hence also called Pánshí Chuān.
It flows northwest and joins the Bǐ Shuǐ,
but it is not the Xiè Shuǐ.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"The state of Qí ordered Zhāngzǐ to attack Jīng with Hán and Wèi.
Jīng sent Táng Miè to respond,
and they stationed their armies on opposite banks of the Bǐ Shuǐ.
Wishing to observe the depth of the water,
the people of Jīng shot arrows but could not determine it.
A grass-gatherer said:
"If the troops are numerous, the water is shallow."
Zhāngzǐ launched a night attack,
and beheaded Miè on this river."
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows further west,
where the Ào Shuǐ joins it.
The Ào Shuǐ originates from Zǐqiū Mountain to the north,
flowing east, then bending and turning south,
and finally entering the Bǐ Shuǐ from the south.
According to the "Shānhǎi Jīng":
"The Ào Shuǐ enters the Shì River from the north,
and does not join the Bǐ Shuǐ."
I consulted Lǚ Chén's "Zìlín," "Nánzì," and "Ěryǎ," all of which state:
"The Yuē Shuǐ is in Bǐyáng."
Tracing the convergence of its river flow,
and examining the water and soil where it joins,
it should indeed be the Yuē Shuǐ,
pronounced as "yuē."
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows further southwest past the north of the old Yuèchéng on Chánggāng.
On the right, the Bǐ Shuǐ meets the Mǎrénbēi Shuǐ,
which originates from the northern mountains of Wǔyīn,
where springs converge competitively,
forming a lake,
covering about a hundred qǐng of land,
called Mǎrénbēi.
The water from the bēi flows past the county,
and is dammed to the southwest to irrigate fields.
Both public and private parties diverted its flow,
causing the watercourse to break,
though the old channel remains.
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows further south past Huìkǒu,
where it merges with a branch of the Dǔ Shuǐ.
The Bǐ Shuǐ then meets the Lǐ Shuǐ further south.
The Lǐ Shuǐ originates from Tóngbó Mountain,
sharing the same source as the Huái River but flowing separately westward,
hence also called the Pài Shuǐ.
The Lǐ Shuǐ flows northwest past the northeast of the old city of Píngshì County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Píngshàn.
Within the city lies a stele commemorating the Nányáng Dūxiāng Zhèngwèi Dànquàn.
The Fēng Shuǐ further northwest merges with the Sōu Shuǐ,
which originates from the northern mountains of Húyáng,
flowing west and bending north,
passing west of Píngshì City before entering the Fēng Shuǐ from the north.
The Lǐ Shuǐ then flows west and joins the Bǐ Shuǐ.
From here downstream, the Bǐ Shuǐ is also commonly referred to as the Pài Shuǐ.
In the past, Hàn Guāngwǔ defeated Zhēn Fù and Liángqiū Cì west of the Bǐ Shuǐ,
and beheaded them on this river.
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows further south,
where the Zhào and Lǐ canals diverge from it.
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows southwest,
where the Xiè Shuǐ joins it.
The Xiè Shuǐ originates north of Xièchéng,
its source being small,
but growing larger as it reaches the city.
The city is surrounded by water on all sides,
the capital of Shēnbó,
as mentioned in the "Shī": "Shēnbó, majestic and grand,
entered Xiè."
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ under Shìzǔ,
Fán Zhòng's youngest son, Dān, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xièyáng,
which was his fiefdom.
Thus, this water is indeed the Xiè Shuǐ.
With high banks and deep waters,
its flow is calm and gentle,
leading people to call it the Tíngyíng Shuǐ.
The city and garrison also adopted Tíngyíng as their name,
but this is incorrect.
To the west of the city,
was the old seat of Jíyáng County,
hence it is also called Jíyángchéng.
The Xiè Shuǐ flows southeast past Xīndū County,
and joins the Bǐ Shuǐ from the left.
The Bǐ Shuǐ flows southwest past the west of the old city of Xīndū County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Xīnlín.
The "Jùnguó Zhì" considers it the eastern district of Xīnyě,
formerly known as Xīndū.
Further west, it reaches Xīnyě County,
and enters the Yù River from the south.
The Bǐ River flows south of the ridge,
heading southwest,
with a garrison post situated atop the ridge.
The Bǐ River further flows southwest and converges with the two streams of Náncháng and Bǎnmén.
These waters originate northeast from the Lóng Mountain east of Húyáng.
On the western side of the mountain stands a stele for Hú Zhù, the Hàn Dynasty Governor of Rìnán.
His son, Zhēn,
served as a Cavalry Commandant and married the Eldest Princess, the Administrator of Húyáng,
who was the elder sister of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
The temple hall had steps and foundations made entirely of blue stone.
North of the temple was a stone hall.
Zhēn's great-great-grandson, Yáng, the Governor of Guìyáng,
in the fourth year of the Yánxī era, upon mourning his mother's passing,
erected a stone shrine beside the tomb,
with an inscription carved on the beam.
Though the stone structure has collapsed,
the characters on the beam remain undamaged.
Shèng Hóngzhī believed it to be the thunder-fearing chamber of Fán Zhòng's mother,
but this is likely a mistaken transmission of doubtful accounts.
South of Lóng Mountain lies a small hill,
on whose slope stand two stone tigers,
facing each other and flanking the passageway.
Though located in a remote, wild area,
they remain completely undamaged,
their craftsmanship is exquisite,
truly marvelous.
Consequently, people call it Shíhǔ Shān (Stone Tiger Mountain).
The waters flow southwest past the old city south of Húyáng County,
as stated in the "Geographical Records":
It was the ancient state of Liào.
The "Bamboo Annals" records:
King Gòng of Chǔ met with Duke Píng of Sòng at Húyáng.
Within the eastern city are two steles,
seemingly for Fán Zhòng,
fully inscribed with the names of former officials.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
Zhòngshānfǔ was enfeoffed at Fán,
hence taking it as his clan name.
He moved from Zhàiyáng to settle in Húyáng,
excelling at farming and cultivation,
amassing up to three hundred qǐng of land.
He extensively built houses and estates,
with tall towers and interconnected pavilions.
Channels irrigated the fields,
bamboo and trees formed forests,
the six domestic animals roamed pastures,
fish, snails, pears, and fruits,
sandalwood, jujube, mulberry, and hemp,
his closed gates formed a market,
weapons, crossbows, and equipment,
his wealth reached millions,
his construction projects
were works of enduring legacy,
their ingenuity beyond description,
his wealth rivaled that of a feudal lord.
In his youth, Emperor Shìzǔ
often visited his maternal relatives.
When he went to Cháng'ān for studies,
they provided generous provisions.
After Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored him as Marquis Jìng,
decreeing that Húyáng establish a temple for Zhòng,
with officials appointed to maintain sacrifices.
When touring Zhānglíng,
he often paid respects at Zhòng's tomb.
The waters encircle and irrigate the city.
Southeast of the city,
there are steles for the former Magistrate Fán Méng and the Palace Attendant Fán Ān.
South of the city are several steles,
without inscriptions.
There are also several stone shrines,
adjacent to the tombs.
Their beams and structures have collapsed,
leaving only stone walls,
and it is unknown to which descendants they belong.
The waters flow south into a great lake,
and the county's name, Húyáng,
derives from this lake.
The lake waters flow southwest,
converging with the dispersed waters from various ponds around Húyáng,
called Bǎnqiáo Water.
Further southwest, it joins the Lǐ Channel,
and the Zhào Channel also flows into it.
These two waterways originate from the Pài Water,
flowing south past the old city east of Xīndū County,
as twin channels drawing water,
converging south with the Bǎnqiáo Water.
The Bǎnqiáo Water further flows southwest to meet the Náncháng Water,
which originates from the dispersed flows of ponds around Tángzǐ and Xiāngxiāng.
The Tángzǐ Pond lies southwest of Tángzǐ Mountain,
where there is a Tángzǐ Pavilion.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, from Xīnyě, slaughtered the Tángzǐ district,
killing the Húyáng Commandant at this place.
The pond waters are clear and deep,
later regarded by Emperor Guāngwǔ as a divine abyss.
Flowing southwest to Xīnyě County,
it converges with the Bǎnqiáo Water,
then flows southwest into the Bǐ River.
The Bǐ River continues southwest,
emptying into the Yù River.
30 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Thirty
30.1 The Huái River
30.1 The Huái River
The Huái River originates from Tāizān Mountain in Píngshì County, Nányáng,
flowing northeast past Tóngbǎi Mountain.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
The Huái emerges from Yú Mountain.
It lies east of Cháoyáng,
west of Yìxiāng.
The "Book of Documents"
records guiding the Huái from Tóngbǎi.
The "Geographical Records" state:
Píngshì County in Nányáng,
called Píngshàn under Wáng Mǎng.
The "Comprehensive Meaning of Customs" states:
Tóngbǎi in Píngshì County, Nányáng,
with Dàfù Mountain to the southeast,
is where the Huái River originates.
Huái
means "equal."
The "Chunqiu Shuoti Ci" states:
Huái
means equalizing its force.
The "Explanation of Names" states:
Huái,
means to encircle,
encircling the northern boundary of Yángzhōu,
eastward to the sea.
The "Erya" states:
Huái is a bank,
yet the Huái River shares the same source as the Lǐ River, both issuing forth,
flowing west as the Lǐ,
flowing east as the Huái.
It flows underground for about thirty lǐ,
emerging east at the southern side of Dàfù Mountain in Tóngbǎi,
called Yángkǒu.
South of the water is Fùyáng County.
Kǎn Yīn stated:
Fùyáng County is the Lèxiāng district of Húyáng.
Established in the second year of the Yuányán era of Emperor Yuán,
located south of Dàfù Mountain in Tóngbǎi,
hence named Fùyáng.
The "Dongguan Hanji" records:
Zhū Yòu was orphaned young,
and returned to the Liú family of Fùyáng, his maternal relatives.
South of the mountain is the Huáiyuán Temple,
with a stele in front of the temple,
erected by Guō Bāo of Nányáng.
There are two more steles,
both made by the local governor during the Hàn Yánxī era.
Their inscriptions are crude and clumsy,
hardly worth viewing.
Therefore, the "Classic" states:
It flows northeast past Tóngbǎi.
The Huái River further flows east past Yìyáng County.
The county faces south toward Gùchéng Mountain,
where water cascades down the mountain for several zhàng,
with torrential waves drenching the slopes,
forming a giant well,
called Shíquán Water,
which flows north into the Huái.
The Huái River further flows past the old city south of Yìyáng County,
the seat of Yìyáng Commandery.
Commonly called Báimáo City,
the city is round rather than square.
Kǎn Yīn stated that
during the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty,
four counties—Ānchāng, Pínglín, Píngshì, and Yìyáng—from the eastern border of Nányáng were partitioned
to establish Yìyáng Commandery at Ānchāng City.
Also, both the "Tàikāng Records" and the "Jìnshu Didao Ji" mention Yìyáng Commandery,
named after a subordinate county of Nányáng.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Wèi Shān, Commandant of Běidì.
The Jiǔdù Water flows into it,
originating from Jīchì Mountain.
The streams and ravines wind and twist,
making nine crossings along the way.
It resembles the Jiǔdù Water of Língyáng,
hence also called Jiǔdù.
East of the stream, on the mountain, a watercourse issues from beneath the summit,
with a several-zhàng white torrent
plunging directly into cascading waves,
falling into a ravine hundreds of zhàng deep,
appearing like a flying silk ribbon.
It descends into the Jiǔdù Water,
which then flows north into the Huái.
It flows east past the north of Píngchūn County in Jiāngxià.
The Huái River flows east again,
and the Yóu River flows into it.
The river originates from Yóuxī in the southwest of the county,
flowing northeast past the old city of Píngchūn County.
In the fourth year of the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
he enfeoffed his son Quán as a king of a state.
The Yóu River then curves east,
and on the northern bank, there is an earthen cave,
one chǐ in diameter,
from which a spring flows down,
cascading for three zhàng along the waves,
and enters the Yóu River.
The river flows southward in a turbulent course,
then turns northeast and flows into the Huái.
The Huái River flows northeast again past the old city of Chéngyáng County.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
he enfeoffed the Marquis of Dìng, Xī Yì, as a marquisate,
which was called Xīnlì during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
It was the seat of the Wèi's Chéngyáng Commandery.
The Huái River flows northeast again and merges with the Dàmù River.
The river originates from Dàmù Mountain in the west,
which is where the Jìn General of Chariots and Cavalry, Zǔ Tì, moved his family from Chénliú to seek refuge.
The river flows east past the north of Chéngyáng County,
and then enters the Huái River to the east.
The Huái River flows northeast again,
and on the left, it meets the Hú River,
which originates from a remote stream in the southwest along the riverbank,
where its source is found.
The Huái River flows east again past the old city of Ānyáng County,
which was the state of Jiāng,
of the Yíng surname.
Today, there is a Jiāng Pavilion at this location.
In the fourth year of Duke Wén of the Spring and Autumn period,
the people of Chǔ destroyed Jiāng.
The Earl of Qín dressed in mourning attire and left his residence,
saying:
"An ally has been destroyed.
Though I cannot save it,
how dare I not show compassion?"
The Hàn later made it a county.
In the eighth year of Emperor Wén,
he enfeoffed Liú Bó, son of the Prince of Huáinán Lì, as a marquisate,
which was called Jūnxià during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
The Huái River flows east again and reaches the Sì Estuary.
The river originates from Dàkuì Mountain in the south,
flowing northeast,
flanked by three streams,
and flows northward in a turbulent course into the Sì River.
It then flows north past the west of Xiánshǒu Mountain.
It emerges again to the north and southeast,
curving past the south of Rénshùn City,
which was the former seat of Yìyáng Commandery,
established by dividing Nányáng.
In the early Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
it was enfeoffed to Ānpíng Xiànwáng Fú's eldest son, Wàng Běn.
The seat was originally on Shíchéng Mountain,
but due to the invasion and pressure of Liáng Xī,
it was moved to this city.
The Liáng Inspector of Sīzhōu, Mǎ Xiānpín, did not hold it,
and the Wèi established Yǐngzhōu here.
In the past, Cháng Zhēnqí sent three thousand cavalry from Xuánhù to aid Yìyáng,
and the official Páng Dìngguāng stationed troops at the Sì River.
The Sì River flows southeast past the north of Jīnshān,
a mountain without trees,
steep and towering in layers.
The Sì River flows east again past the north of the old city of Yìyáng,
which is situated on a mountain,
relying on the ridges and peaks,
with a circumference of three lǐ.
This was the former seat of the commandery.
Fifteen steps south of the city,
opposite the gate, there is a Tiānjǐng,
with a circumference of over a hundred steps,
and a depth of one zhàng.
It flows east past the old city of Zhōngwǔ County,
originally a subordinate county of Jiāngxià,
which was called Dānglì County during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
It flows east again past the north of Shíchéng Mountain,
a very high and steep mountain.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The Wèi attacked Míng'è."
The Yīnyì commentary says:
"Míng'è,
some say it is at Xiāngshān in Méng County."
According to the Annals of Lü Buwei,
it is one of the Nine Passes.
The Sì River flows past the old city of Méng County.
During the Jiànwǔ era, Emperor Shìzǔ enfeoffed Dèng Hán as the Marquis of Méng.
According to Sū Lín:
it is pronounced "máng."
The Sì River flows east again past the south of Qījǐnggǎng,
then flows northeast into the Huái River.
The Huái River flows east to Gǔkǒu,
where the Gǔ River originates from Xiānjīn Mountain in the south,
flowing north,
and the Sè River flows into it.
The river originates from Jùshān in the southwest,
flowing northeast past the east of Guāngyān City,
then north past the east of Qīngshān and the west of Luóshān,
commonly called Xiānjū River,
flowing northeast into the Gǔ River.
The Gǔ River flows northeast into the Huái River.
It flows east again past the south of Xīnxī County.
The Huai River flows east past the old city of Xī,
as recorded in the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, the eleventh year of Duke Yǐn,
when there was a conflict between Zhèng and Xī.
It is said that the Marquis of Xī attacked Zhèng,
but the Earl of Zhèng defeated him.
The Huai River then flows east past the north of Fúguāng Mountain,
also called Fúguāng Mountain,
which is Yìyáng Mountain.
It produces fine jade and black stones,
suitable for making game pieces.
The mountain overlooks the long Huai River,
often glowing with light.
The Huai River flows further east,
past the old city of Xīnxī County.
Yìng Shào said:
Xī later moved east,
hence the addition of "new."
It was called Xīndé under Wáng Mǎng.
In the nineteenth year of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Mǎ Yuán was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Inside the north gate of the outer city is the temple of Jiǎ Biāo, the magistrate of Xīnxī,
with a stele in front of the temple.
Facing south is also the stele of Chéng Xiǎo, the governor of Rǔnán under the Wèi.
During the Tàihé era of the Wèi,
the tribal leader Tián Yìzōng pledged allegiance,
and the Eastern Yù Province was established,
with Yìzōng appointed as its governor.
The Huai River then flows east and joins the Shèn River,
which originates west of Shènyáng County
and flows east past the old city of Shènyáng County,
from which the county takes its name.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Luán Yuè was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Liú Táo of Yǐngyīn served as the magistrate of the county,
and his governance flourished,
with lost items left untouched on the roads.
He resigned from office due to illness.
A children's song went:
"Melancholy and joyless,
we think of our Lord Liú.
When will he return,
to bring peace to us common folk?"
Such was the affection he inspired.
Yìng Shào said:
The Shèn River originates here,
flowing northeast into the Huai.
The Shèn River flows eastward,
accumulating to form Jiāo Pond.
The pond water flows southeast to become Upper Shèn Pond,
then east to become Middle Shèn Pond,
and southeast to become Lower Shèn Pond,
all dispersing and merging with the waters of Hóngquè Pond.
This pond system begins by receiving water from the Huai,
connecting to Hóng Pond on the left.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Zhái Fāngjìn petitioned to have it destroyed.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Dèng Chén, the governor of Rǔnán, sought to restore it.
Knowing that Xǔ Wěijūn understood watercourses well,
he summoned him for discussion.
Wěijūn said:
"Emperor Chéng followed Fāngjìn's advice and destroyed it,
but soon dreamed of ascending to heaven,
where the Heavenly Emperor angrily said:
'How dare you ruin my Zhuólóng Abyss!'
Since then, the people have lost its benefits."
At that time, a children's song went:
"He who ruined our pond,
is Zhái Zǐxián.
Things reverse and turn,
the pond shall be restored."
"My lord, revive the abandoned work.
The words of the children's song
will soon prove true."
Thus, he was appointed as the Director of Waterways,
and a dike over four hundred lǐ long was built,
benefiting the people.
The pond waters disperse and flow,
merging downstream with the Shèn River,
then flowing southeast past the north of Xī City,
and southeast into the Huai,
where it is called the Shèn Estuary.
The Huai River then flows east and joins the Shēn Pond waters,
which originate from Shēn Pond north of Xīnxī County,
flowing southeast
and dividing into two streams.
One stream passes west of Shēnqiū,
then curves past its south,
with the southern branch becoming Lián Lake waters,
flowing south into the Huai.
The Huai River then curves left,
forming two lakes,
called East and West Lián Lakes.
The Huai River flows further east,
joining the Hè River on the right,
which originates from Báishā Mountain.
It flows northeast past west of Chái Pavilion,
commonly called Chái River.
It then flows northeast and merges with Tánxī River,
which originates from Tán Valley,
flowing northeast
and joining the Chái River on the right.
The Chái River then flows east past west of Huáng City,
formerly Yìyáng County.
Inside the city are two walls,
the western one being Huáng City.
The Chái River then flows northeast into the Huai,
where it is called the Chái Estuary.
The Huai River flows northeast,
where a branch of Shēn Pond waters flows into it,
originating from the pond waters north of Shēnqiū.
It flows east past south of Diào Terrace,
which lies within a river bend,
with Qín Terrace north of it.
It then flows east past south of Yáng Pavilion,
and southeast merges with the Huai.
The Huai River then flows east past north of Huáiyīn Pavilion,
and east past south of Bái City,
the fief of Bái Gōng Shèng of Chǔ,
ten lǐ northeast of Bái Pavilion.
The Huai River then flows east past south of Chánglíng Garrison,
and further east,
where Qīng Pond waters flow into it,
branching from the eastern channel of Qīng Pond.
It flows southeast past west of Bái Pavilion,
then south to east of Chánglíng Garrison,
and southeast into the Huai.
The Huai River then flows northeast and joins the Huáng River,
which originates from Huángwǔ Mountain.
It flows northeast,
where Mùlíng Pass waters flow into it,
originating from Mùlíng Mountain.
It flows northwest into the Huáng River.
The Huáng River then flows east past south of the Western Yáng City of Jìn,
and east past south of Guāng City,
the seat of Guāng City Left Commandery.
It then flows northeast past south of Gāo City,
formerly the state of Xián.
It then flows northeast past east of Yìyáng Commandery,
where there is Yúqiū.
South of the outer wall is the temple of Zǐxū.
The Huáng River then flows northeast into the Huai,
where it is called the Huáng Estuary.
The Huai River then flows northeast past the old city of Bāoxìn County,
and flows eastward into it.
It then flows east past north of Qīsī County,
which was formerly the state of Jiǎng,
descended from the Duke of Zhōu.
As recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, the tenth year of Duke Wén,
the King of Chǔ hunted at Mèngzhū,
and the Duke of Qīsī, Fù Suì, served as Right Minister of War.
Chǔ later annexed it and made it a county.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Bēn Hè was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
In the northwest corner of the city is the temple of the Chǔ minister Sūnshū Áo,
with a stele in front of the temple.
The Huai River flows northeast,
where the Pì River flows into it.
The river originates from Chuí Mountain south of Yìyáng County,
flowing northwest past Yīnshān Pass,
between two cities,
historically a site of banditry,
where troops were stationed for defense.
It exits the mountains to the northwest,
then flows northeast past east of Xīnchéng Garrison,
and northeast reaches the mouth of Zhàoyú River,
twenty-five lǐ northwest of Yúqiū, outside Yìyáng.
The river originates from South Mountain,
flowing northeast past east of Zhàoyú Pavilion and north into the Pì River.
It then flows northeast into the Huai,
commonly called Báilù River.
It then flows east past south of Yuánlù County,
where the Rǔ River flows into it from the northwest.
The county
is the Lùshàng mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
As recorded in the Zuo Commentary, the twenty-first year of Duke Xī,
the people of Sòng held the covenant at Lùshàng,
seeking alliances with Chǔ.
In the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Shìzǔ re-enfeoffed Yīn Shí, the Marquis of Yīnxiāng and Palace Attendant Commander of the Capital Guard, as a marquis here.
It then flows east past northeast of Ānfēng County in Lùjiāng,
where the Jué River flows into it from the north.
The Huái River flows northwest of Shòuyáng County,
where the Féi River enters the Huái from the west and north of the city,
which is called the Féi Mouth.
The Huái River continues north,
where the Xiàféi River flows into it.
This river originates from the Shā River,
emerging on the right at Chéngfù County,
flowing southeast past the old southern city of Chéngfù County,
which was called Sīshàn during Wáng Mǎng’s time.
This county
was originally the territory of Jiāo Yí.
In the ninth year of Duke Zhāo in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒ Zhuàn*,
Chǔ’s Prince Qìjí moved Xǔ to Yí,
which is indeed Chéngfù.
He took the fields of Zhōulái and north of the Huái to augment it,
and Wǔ Jǔ granted the fields to the Lord of Xǔ.
Dù Yù said:
At this time, Chéngfù was renamed Yí,
hence the record indeed refers to it.
Rán Dān moved the people of Chéngfù to Chén,
augmenting it with the fields west of the Yí Pú River.
This refers to the Yí fields being west of the Pú River.
Thus, the Pú River is another name for the Shā River,
and it shares the general designation of Xiàféi.
In the first year of the Yǒngshòu era of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as a marquisate for Táo, the grandson of the Grand General Liáng Jì.
The Xiàféi River flows east from the county past the old southern city of Sīshàn County,
which was established in the third year of the Zhānghé era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
by dividing Chéngfù.
The Xiàféi River flows east further to become the Gāo Bēi,
then east again to become the Dà Chòng Bēi,
where the water divides into two streams:
the southern one is the Xiàféi River,
and the northern one is the Jī Bēi.
The Xiàféi River flows east,
joining the Jī River on the left,
which originates from the Jī Bēi,
flows east to become the Huáng Bēi,
then southeast to accumulate as the Máo Bēi,
and further east as the Jī River.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
A man of Sòng was traveling,
but his horse would not advance,
so he threw it into the Jī River—this is the place.
The Jī River meets the Xiàféi River on the right,
and they flow together eastward,
both entering the Huái.
The Huái River flows north through a mountain gorge,
called Xiáshí,
where two fortresses were built on the mountains on opposite banks to guard the strategic crossing.
On the mountain on the western bank, there are horse hoofprints,
traditionally said to be where Huáinán King rode his horse and ascended to immortality.
Now, southeast of the mountain,
there are over ten large and small hoofprints on the rocks,
which still exist today.
The Huái River flows north past the old eastern city of Xiàcài County,
originally the city of Zhōulái.
Wú’s Jì Zhá was first enfeoffed at Yánlíng and later at Zhōulái,
hence it was called Yánzhōulái.
In the second year of Duke Āi in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Cài’s Duke Zhāo moved from Xīncài to Zhōulái,
which was called Xiàcài.
On the eastern bank of the Huái, there is another city,
which is the new city of Xiàcài.
The two cities face each other,
guarding the banks of the Huái.
The Huái River flows east past the north of Bāgōng Mountain,
where there is a temple to Lǎozǐ on the mountain.
The Huái River passes south of Pánchéng,
where the Pánxī Garrison was established.
East of the garrison is Pánxī,
which discharges into the river and receives the Huái,
mutually drawing and flowing.
It flows east further past Liángchéng,
adjacent to the Huái River,
with Méichéng on the left bank of the river.
The Huái River bends left to form Méi Lake.
The Huái River also receives the Luò River on the right north of Xīqūyáng County,
where the water divides from Yánxī,
crosses Héngtáng to the north,
and flows north past the east of Xiāo Pavilion.
Further north,
the Quèfǔxī River flows into it,
originating from East Quèfǔ Valley and flowing northwest past the south of Quèfǔ Pavilion,
then northwest into the Luò River,
flowing north past the old eastern city of Xīqūyáng County,
which was called Yánpíng Pavilion during Wáng Mǎng’s time.
Yìng Shào said:
The county is on the northern side of the Huái bend,
and there is a Qūyáng in Xiàpī,
so this one is prefixed with “west.”
The Luò River flows north past Qíxū,
descends into the Huái,
which is called the Luò Mouth.
The *Classic* says the Huái River passes Shòuchūn County,
and the Běiféi River flows into it from the northeast of the county.
This is an error in the *Classic*.
Examining the rivers and confirming the land,
it is indeed incorrect;
this is the Luò River,
not the Féi River.
The Huái River flows north past the west of Mòxié Mountain,
with the old city of Yīnlíng County south of the mountain.
In the fifth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ fled from Gāixià with several hundred cavalry,
crossed the Huái at night to Yīnlíng but lost his way,
and fell into a large marsh on the left.
The Hàn general Guàn Yīng pursued him with five thousand cavalry and caught up with him in this county.
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
it was called Yīnlù during Wáng Mǎng’s time.
Later, it became the seat of Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
At that time, there were many tiger disasters,
and the people suffered greatly.
Zōng Jūn of Nányáng served as governor,
expelled the greedy and cruel,
promoted the loyal and good,
and the tigers all crossed the river to the east.
It flows east further past the north of Dāngtú County,
where the Guō River flows in from the northwest.
The Huái River flows northeast from Mòxié Mountain past the north of Mǎtóu City,
which was the seat of Wèi’s Mǎtóu Commandery,
originally the old city of Dāngtú County.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
Yǔ married a woman of the Túshān clan,
but did not let personal affairs harm public duties.
From Xīn to Jiǎ, four days later,
he returned to govern the floods.
Thus, the custom along the Jiāng and Huái rivers
is to use Xīn, Rén, Guǐ, and Jiǎ as auspicious days for marriage.
Yǔ’s ruins are southwest of the mountain,
and the county is located there.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
Dāngtú
was a marquisate.
Wèi Bùhài, as the Warden of Yǔ, captured the rebels Gōngsūn Yǒng and others from Huáiyáng,
and Hàn enfeoffed him there.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shānjù.
The Huái River flows northeast further,
where the Háo River flows into it.
This river originates from a northeast stream of Mòxié Mountain,
which flows northwest past the north of Yǔ’s ruins,
then west into the Huái.
The Huái River flows north further,
where the Shā River flows into it,
which the *Classic* calls the Làngdàng Canal.
West of the Huái is the old city of Píng’ē County,
called Píngníng during Wáng Mǎng’s time.
In the thirteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ further enfeoffed Gěng Fù as a marquis there.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* says:
Píng’ē County has Tú Mountain.
The Huái emerges between the left of Jīng Mountain
and the right of Dāngtú,
rushing between the two mountains
and surging northward.
In the tenth year of Duke Āi in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and *Zuǒ Zhuàn*,
a minister said to Mèngsūn:
Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Tú Mountain,
and ten thousand states brought jade and silk.
Dù Yù said:
Tú Mountain is northeast of Shòuchūn.
This is incorrect.
I refer to the *Guóyǔ*, which says:
When Wú attacked Chǔ,
they destroyed Kuàijī,
and obtained bones there
that filled a cart.
The Lord of Wú sent an envoy to inquire about them,
and the envoy held the bones and asked:
May I ask, why are these bones so large?
Zhòngní said:
I have heard that
in the past, Yǔ summoned the spirits to Kuàijī Mountain,
and Fángfēngshì arrived late,
so Yǔ killed him.
His bones filled a cart,
so these are the largest.
Qiūmíng personally received this sacred account,
and recorded it as factual evidence.
I also refer to Liú Xiàng’s *Shuōyuàn: Biànwù*
and Wáng Sù’s preface to the *Family Sayings of Confucius*, compiled by Kǒng Měng, the twenty-second generation descendant of Confucius, from ancestral writings,
both of which mention this event.
Thus, Tú Mountain shares the name Kuàijī.
Examining various texts and local records,
I suspect it is not this place.
It was likely where King Mù of Zhōu assembled.
The Huái River flows north of Jīng Mountain,
where the Guō River flows into it from the southeast.
It flows northeast further past the east of Yìchéng County in Pèi Commandery.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
Later, it was attached to Jiǔjiāng.
It flows east further past the north of Zhōnglí County.
The Shiben states:
Zhōnglí
is of the Yíng surname.
Yīng Shào says:
The county
was originally the state of Zhōnglízi,
which Chu destroyed and made into a county.
This is the Zhōnglí mentioned in the Chunqiu Zuozhuan
when Prince Guāng of Wú attacked Chǔ and captured Zhōnglí.
It was called Cánfù under Wáng Mǎng.
The Háo River originates north of Yángtíng in Yīnlíng County,
and at a small bend there is a stone cave,
its depth unfathomable.
It is said that stalactites emerge from the cave,
but the details are unknown.
The Háo River flows northeast past the west of the county,
then bends and turns south,
east past the south of its city,
then north past the east of its city,
and flows north past a small town before emptying into the Huái.
The Huái River then flows east past the south of Xiàqiū County.
Further east,
the Huàn River joins it,
its headwaters receiving the Làngdàng Canal at Kāifēng County.
In the twenty-first year of King Xī of Hán, as recorded in the Shiji,
he sent Bào Yuān to rescue Wèi,
but they were defeated by Qín,
and Yuān fled to Kāifēng.
It flows southeast past the north of Chénliú,
then further southeast,
entering from the west at Jiǔlǐ and joining it.
The Huàn River then flows southeast past the old city of Yōngqiū County,
then east past Chéngkuāng City,

This was originally the territory of Chéngkuāng and Xiāngniú of Sòng,

The Zhushu Jinian records:
In the seventeenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,

In the eighteenth year,
King Huìchéng, with the Hán army, defeated the allied forces at Xiānglíng,

which occurred here.
To the west is Chéngkuāng City,
mentioned in the Chunqiu
as the place of the meeting at Chéngkuāng.
Because Chéngkuāng was low and damp,
Qín Shǐhuáng moved the county to Xiānglíng and renamed it Xiāngyì,
which Wáng Mǎng called Xiāngpíng.
In the first year of the Jiànhé era of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
he enfeoffed Húgǒu, son of Liáng Jì, as a marquis here.
The Chenliu Fengsu Zhuan states:
South of the county is the Huàn River,
hence the tradition says:
Between Suī and Huàn, fine textiles are produced,
used for the emperor's ceremonial robes in suburban and ancestral temple rituals.
This is what the Shangshu refers to as "their baskets contain woven patterns."
The Huàn River then flows southeast past the old city of Jǐwú County,
then east past the north of Zēng City.
In the Chunqiu,
the first year of Duke Xiāng,
the Jing records that Hán Jué of Jìn led an army to attack Zhèng,
while Zhòngsūn Miè of Lǔ met with Qí, Cáo, Zhū, and Qǐ,

Dù Yù says:
Southeast of Xiāngyì County in Chénliú is Zēng City.
The Huàn River then flows southeast past the north of Yān City and south of Xīn City,

joining the Míng Ditch on the left,

It then passes north of Bó City,

Gǔshú is Southern Bó,
the capital of Tāng.
The Shisan Zhou Zhi states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn divided Gǔshú to establish it.
In the twelfth year of Duke Zhuāng of the Chunqiu,

The Huàn River flows east past the south of Gǔshú City,

It then flows east past the north of Yángtíng.

Jīng Xiàngfán says:
This is Sòng territory,
and thirty lǐ southeast of present-day Suīyáng is the old city of Yángliáng,
now called Yángtíng.
Commonly called Yuánchéng,
but this is incorrect.
It is eighty lǐ northwest of Liángguó.
The Huàn River then flows east past the old city of Jiànpíng County in Pèi Commandery,

It then flows east past the old city of Cuó County.

The Huàn River then flows southeast past the south of Fèitíng,

Téng, styled Jìxīng,

The Huàn River then flows east past the old city of Zhì County,

The Huàn River then flows east,

His ancestors moved from Kuàijī to Zhì County in Qiáo,

There is Jī Mountain in Qiáo,
and the family lived beside it,

During the Huángchū era of Wèi,

The Bāo River flows east into the Huàn.

The Dili Zhi states:
It was originally Zhuīxiāng.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn defeated Qíng Bù here,
and the county

There is an ancient stone bridge site on the water,

The Huàn River then flows east past Gǔyáng County,

The Huàn River then flows east past the south of Gǔyáng Garrison,

Yīng Shào says:
The city is on the north bank of the Gǔ River.
It then flows northeast into the Huàn.
The Huàn River then flows southeast past the south of Báishí Garrison,
then past the south of Hóng City,
where the Xiáo River joins it,

It flows southeast past Gǔyáng County,
where the old Bāzhàng Channel emerges,

The Xiáo River then flows southeast past the north of the old city of Xiáo County,

The Xiáo River originates here,

The Xiáo River enters the Huái from the south.

It flows south past Xiàqiū County in Pèiguó, crossing the Qí River.

then southeast to the west of Chánshí,
entering the Huái from the south.
The Huái River then flows east past Fú Mountain,

During the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty,
a dam was built between the two mountains,
contrary to the will of heaven and earth,
It goes against the expectations of the people and spirits,
and naturally, the water will break through and cause damage.
The Huái River then flows east past the south of Xú County,

The Huái River continues east,

flows past the old city south of Dōngchéng County,
where during the Hàn Dynasty, several thousand cavalry pursued Yǔ,
and Yǔ led twenty-eight cavalry to retreat to Dōngchéng,
relying on the Sìtuí Mountain,
he beheaded the enemy general and departed,
which is exactly this location.
According to the "Records of the Grand Historian," in the eighth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Liú Liáng, son of the Prince of Huáinán Lì, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The "Treatise on Geography" states,
that Wáng Mǎng renamed it Wǔchéng.
The Chí River then flows northeast between two mountains,
and enters the Huái River to the northeast,
which is called the Chí River Mouth.
The Huái River continues east,
and the Qí River flows into it.
The water first receives the Suī River northeast of Gǔshú City,

The Qí River then flows southeast past Qí County,

To the south, the Xiáo River emerges.
The Qí River continues southeast,

and the old channel of Chángzhí emerges,

crosses the Tóng River to the east,

then flows east into Xú County,
crosses Lìjiàn to the east,
then flows east past the old city south of Dàxú County,

The Huái River then flows east past Kè Mountain,
passing the old city south of Xūyí County,
the "Treatise on Geography" states:
it was the seat of the Commandant,
and in the first year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Méngzhī, son of the Prince of Jiāngdū Yì, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,

The Huái River then flows east past the city of Guǎnglíng Huáiyáng,

According to the "Record of Military Expeditions,"
it was the seat of the Governor of Huáiyáng,

It then flows northeast to the west of Huáiyīn County in Xiàpī,

The confluence of the Huái and Sì Rivers
is at Jiǎochéng.
The two rivers on the left and right
flank and converge with the two waters,
at the point where they break through and enter,

It then flows east past the north of Huáiyīn County,
where the Zhōngdú River emerges from Báimǎ Lake,

On the right bank of the Huái River is Huáiyīn,
and two lǐ west of the city is Gōnglù Pǔ,
where in the past Yuán Shù headed toward Jiǔjiāng,
intending to flee east to Yuán Tán,

It then flows east past the old city north of Huáiyīn County,

and in the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Hán Xìn was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jiāxìn.
In the past, Hán Xìn left Xiàxiāng and fished here.
East of the city are two tombs,
the western one being the tomb of the Laundry Woman.
It is several hundred paces in circumference,
and over ten zhàng high.
In the past, the Laundry Woman fed Hán Xìn in Huáiyīn,
and when Hán Xìn became king of Xiàpī,
he reportedly threw gold into the tomb mound to repay her.
The eastern mound is the tomb of Hán Xìn's mother.
The county has the Zhōngdú River,
which first receives the river at Jiāngdū County in Guǎnglíng Commandery,
and the county seat faces the river.
Yìng Shào's "Record of Geography and Customs" states:
the county is a gathering place for the capital,
hence it is called Jiāngdū.
The county has a river temple,
commonly known as the Temple of Minister Wǔ.
Zǐxū is only worshipped alongside,
with three sacrifices per year,
the same as for the Five Sacred Mountains.
This is the old course of the river.
In the past, when the Wú general planned to attack Qí,
and dominate the Central Plains to the north,
he built Hán City southeast of Guǎnglíng City,
and dug a deep moat beneath the city,
called Hán River,
also known as Hánmíng Channel,
which connected northeast from the river to Shèyáng Lake.
This is what the "Treatise on Geography" calls the Canal River.
It flows northwest to Mòkǒu and enters the Huái River.
Since the Yǒnghé era,
the water from Jiāngdū was cut off,
and its upper course received water from Ōuyáng Embankment,
diverting the river into the embankment,
and after sixty lǐ, it reached Guǎnglíng City.
Between the Chǔ and Hàn dynasties, it was Dōngyáng Commandery,
in the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ, it became the State of Jīng,
in the eleventh year, it became Wú City,
which was built by the King of Wú, Liú Bì.
In the fourth year of Emperor Jǐng, it was renamed Jiāngdū,
and in the third year of Yuánshòu under Emperor Wǔ,
it was renamed Guǎnglíng,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it again,
the commandery as Jiāngpíng,
and the county as Dìng'ān.
East of the city, there is a bridge over the water,
called Luò Bridge.
The Zhōngdú River flows north from Guǎnglíng, east of Wǔguǎng Lake,
and west of Lùyáng Lake.
The two lakes are aligned east to west for five lǐ,
and the water flows between them,
descending into Fánliáng Lake.
The old course went northeast,
reaching Bózhī and Shèyáng Lakes,
then northwest through Jiáxié,
and finally to Shānyáng.
During the Yǒnghé era,
due to concerns about the windy lake route,
Chén Mǐn dredged the northern mouth of Fánliáng Lake,
and the water descended into Jīn Lake, passing through a crossing,
where it took twelve lǐ to reach the northern mouth,
and then directly to Jiáxié.
During the Xīngníng era,
due to the windy conditions of Jīn Lake,
a channel was dug from the southern mouth of the lake,
along the eastern bank for twenty lǐ,
into the northern mouth,
and since then, travelers no longer passed through the lake.
Thus, Jiǎng Jì's "Discourse on the Three Provinces" states:
the Huái River and lakes are winding and distant,
with water and land routes differing,
and Shānyáng was inaccessible,
so Chén Mǐn dredged a channel,
and further excavated Mǎ Lài,
crossing the lake for a hundred lǐ.
From Guǎnglíng to Báimǎ Lake in Shānyáng,
passing west of Shānyáng City,
which is the old city of Shèyáng County.
Yìng Shào said:
it is located on the northern bank of the Shè River.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Xiàng Chán, the Left Lingyǐn of Chǔ, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.

and in the fifteenth year of Emperor Shìzǔ's Jiànwǔ era,

The city

The Zhōngdú River then flows east,

which is called Shānyáng Mouth.
It then flows east,
and two small streams flow into it.
The Huái River flows left past the south of Sìshuǐ State,
which was formerly the Dōng Hǎi Commandery.
Xú Guǎng’s Shǐjì Yīnyì states:
Sìshuǐ,
a state name.

the capital was first established at Líng,
and Sī Wáng Shāng, son of Xiàn Wáng of Chángshān, was enfeoffed as ruler of the state.

Wáng Mǎng changed Sìshuǐ Commandery to Shuǐshùn,
and Líng County to Shēnglíng.
The Líng River flows into it,
the water emerges from Líng County,
flows east past the east of the old city of that county,

Yìng Shào said:
The Líng River emerges southwest of the county and enters the Huái,

Further east it reaches Huáipǔ County of Guǎnglíng,
and enters the sea.
Yìng Shào said:
It is the Huái bank.
As it lies adjacent to the Huái watercourse,
it thus received this name.
The Huái River flows past the east of the old city of the county,
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Huáijìng.
The Huái River branches off at the county,
the northern branch being the Yóu River,
passing Qú County and merging with the Shù.
It further flows past the west of Qú Mountain,
beside the mountain is the old city of Qú County.
In the thirty-fifth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
a stone was erected at Qú County by the sea,
to serve as the eastern gate of Qín.
Cuī Yǎn’s Shù Chū Fù states:
Leaning on the high mast to gaze all around,
I behold the majestic gate of Qín.
Northeast in the sea there is a large island,
called Yùzhōu.
It is what the Shānhǎi Jīng calls Yù Mountain in the sea,
and it is said this mountain moved here from Cāngwú.
On the mountain there are still plants from the south,
now the seat of Yù Prefecture.
Thus Cuī Jìguī, in narrating the Shù Chū Fù,
said of Yùzhōu,
it is the former Cāngwú Mountain.
Delighted yet puzzled by this,
hearing that atop it were immortal scholars’ stone chambers,
he went to see them.
He saw a Daoist living alone,
serene, neither speaking nor responding,
realizing he was beyond his own reach.
This is what his fu describes,
“I crossed to Yùzhōu at dusk.”
The Yóu River further flows north past the east of the old city of Lìchéng County in Dōng Hǎi,
formerly Lìxiāng.
In the fourth year of the Yuán Shuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Yīng, son of Gòng Wáng of Chéngyáng, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Liúquán.
The Yóu River further flows north past the west of Yǔ Mountain,
the Dìlǐ Zhì states:
Yǔ Mountain lies southeast of Zhùqí County.
The Shàngshū states:
Yáo consulted the Four Peaks and obtained Shùn,
advanced sixteen clans,
and executed Gǔn at Yǔ Mountain,
who became Táowù,
sharing guilt with Huāndōu, Sānmiáo, and Gònggōng,

After Gǔn died,
his spirit transformed into a yellow bear,

and became the Xià suburban sacrifice,
