Thus the Liánshān Yì states:
There was Chóng Bó Gǔn,
who lay hidden in the wilds of Yǔ Mountain.
The Yóu River further flows north past the west of the old city of Zhùqí County,
the Chūnqiū Jīng records in summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Jiāgǔ.
The Zuǒzhuàn, tenth year of Duke Dìng,
the Duke made peace with Qí,
and met at Zhù,
which was actually Jiāgǔ.
Fú Qián said:
The place has two names.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Yóutíng,
east of the county is Jiākǒu Pǔ.
The Yóu River flows left past the west of the old city of Jìjīn County in Lángyá,
the Dìlǐ Zhì states:
The Lord of Jǔ first arose here,
later moved to Jǔ,
there was a salt office,
thus the age called it Southern Jǔ.
The Yóu River further flows northeast past the north of Gànyú County,
to the east lies the vast sea,
there is a stele of Qín Shǐhuáng,
on the mountain,
one hundred fifty paces from the sea.
When the tide comes,
it rises three zhàng above it,
when it recedes, three chǐ.
What is seen is a northeast-leaning stone,
one zhàng eight chǐ long,
five chǐ wide,
three chǐ eight cùn thick,
with one line of twelve characters.
The Yóu River further flows northeast past the old city south of Jìzhāng,
in the Chūnqiū, nineteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
Qí attacked Jǔ,
the Lord of Jǔ fled to Jìzhāng.
A woman of Jǔ, angered that the Lord of Jǔ had harmed her husband,
old yet entrusted with spinning,
took her hemp thread and at night let it down by rope,
the rope broke and there was clamor,
people on the wall also clamored,
Duke Gòng of Jǔ feared,
opened the west gate and fled,
and Qí then entered Jì.
Thus the state of Jì Zǐbó.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn states:
Our Bó Jī returned to Jì.
Dù Yù said:
Jìzhāng,
the place has two names.
Northeast of Gànyú County in Dōng Hǎi is the old city of Jì,
which is this city.
The Yóu River flows northeast into the sea.
In former times, Wú’s Yān-Dài route,
often crossing the vast sea,
fearing its perilous waves,
changed to follow this watercourse upstream,
and thus emerged.
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
The Yóu River enters the sea north from Huáipǔ.
The Ěryǎ states:
The Huái branches off to become Xǔ.
The Yóu River is also a branch designation.
31 Shuǐjīng Zhù Scroll Thirty-One
31.1 Zhǐ River
31.1 Zhǐ River
The Zhǐ River emerges from Yáo Mountain west of Lǔyáng County in Nányáng.
Liú Lěi, a distant descendant of Yáo,
fed dragons for Emperor Kǒng Jiǎ,
but when Kǒng Jiǎ sought more dragons,
he could not obtain them,
so Lěi, in fear, moved to Lǔ County,
where he established a shrine to Yáo on the Western Mountains,
which became known as Yáo Mountain.
Hence, Zhāng Héng’s “Rhapsody on the Southern Capital” states:
“To honor the former emperor and pursue filial piety,
they erected a Táng shrine at Yáo Mountain.”
Yáo Mountain lies northeast of Tàihé City in the Tàihé River valley,
from which the Zhī River flows.
Zhāng Héng’s “Rhapsody on the Southern Capital” says:
“Among its rivers and streams are the Zhī, Lǐ, Fán, and Jìn,
which spring from rocky caverns,
spreading broadly and expansively,
vast and overflowing,
gathering swiftly,
like arrows flying with the speed of the wind.”
The Zhī River then passes through the Tàihé River valley,
flows east past the Xiǎohé River valley,
and further east,
where the hot spring water joins it.
This water issues from a northern hill,
with seven sources wondrously emerging,
exceptionally hot.
Kàn Yīn said:
“The county has hot water
that can cure illnesses.”
Beside the hot spring there is also a cold spring;
though the terrain is no different,
the temperatures are contrasting,
so even on scorching summer days,
it feels as icy as a frosty valley.
The mingled streams converge in one channel
and flow south into the Zhī River.
The Zhī River then flows east past Húmù Mountain,
and eastward it meets the mouth of another hot spring,
whose water issues from a northern hill,
with a heat so intense and virulent
that those suffering from ailments
cannot bathe directly under its flow.
Those seeking relief from itching must step about ten paces away from the hot spring to a separate pool
before they can enter.
Beside the spring is a stone inscription that reads:
“The Imperial Princess Spring,
which can cure myriad diseases.”
Thus, Dù Yàndá said:
“It is boiling like hot water,
able to cook rice,
and drinking it cures a hundred illnesses.
Taoist practitioners cleanse their bodies and bathe here,
drinking from it three times a day,
in amounts as they please.
After forty days,
all ailments in the body are cured,
and the three worms die.
When studying the Way and encountering hardship or danger,
one will never harbor regret,
for it can fortify the spirit and preserve determination.”
This is what is referred to in “Rhapsody on the Southern Capital” as “the Hot Water Valley gushing behind it.”
However, Wǎn County has a Purple Mountain,
east of which lies a body of water,
fifteen li from east to west,
and two hundred paces from north to south,
deep and brimming,
with no outlet,
warm throughout winter and summer,
also called by the world the Hot Water Valley.
This is not the same as the counties of Lǔyáng or Nányáng.
Zhāng Píngzǐ broadly described the lands encompassed,
making clear it is not this one.
The Zhī River flows further east,
where the Fángyáng River water joins it.
This water originates from the Fángyáng River west of Zhì County in Nányáng,
flowing north into the Zhī River.
North of the Zhī River,
there are piled stones,
known to the world as Nǚlíng Mountain.
This mountain rises isolated from the plain,
not connected to ridges to achieve height;
its steep rocks stand alone,
not relying on terrain to appear distant.
Its four sides are sheer cliffs,
soaring with spiritual loftiness,
and from afar it appears slender and graceful,
like a single pillar piercing the clouds.
The northern face seems partially collapsed,
barely allowing passage,
so enthusiasts occasionally climb it.
The Zhī River then merges with the Bō River,
which issues from the eastern valley of the great ridge in the western reaches of Huòyáng,
commonly called Xiēmǎ Ridge,
and the river valley is called Guǎngyáng River valley.
This is incorrect.
It is what Yìng Shào referred to as Gū Mountain,
the source of the Bō River.
Mǎ Róng’s “Eulogy of Guǎngchéng” says:
“Flooded by the Bō and Zhà.”
This water then flows south past Mán City,
likely a separate settlement of the Mán people,
commonly called Má City.
This is incorrect.
The Bō River flows further south,
splitting into three streams east of Bái Pavilion,
all flowing south into the Zhī River.
From this point downstream,
the Zhī River also bears the general name of the Bō River.
Hence, Kàn Yīn wrote that it flows northeast to Dìnglíng and enters the Rǔ River.
The Zhī River then flows east past the old city of Lǔyáng County,
which was the former settlement of Liú Lěi.
There is Lǔ Mountain,
and since the county lies on its southern side,
it was thus named.
It was called Lǔ Mountain under Wáng Mǎng.
In ancient times, when it belonged to Chǔ,
Wénzǐ defended it,
and when battling Hán Jiù,
there was an omen of the returning sunlight.
Inside the city is a stele for the Nányáng Dūxiāng Zhèngwèi.
The Zhī River on the right joins with the Lǔyáng Pass water,
which issues from the valley between the split peaks of Fēntóu Mountain outside Lǔyáng Pass,
flowing northeast into the Zhī River.
The Zhī River then flows northeast and merges with the Niúlán River,
which rises from Niúlán Mountain north of the county,
flowing southeast past the east of Lǔyáng City,
beside which stands the stele of Hànyáng Hóu Jiāo Lì.
The Niúlán River then flows southeast and joins with the Báishù Stream,
which issues from the northern gorge of Lǔ Mountain,
flowing southeast past the west of Lǔ Mountain,
then south to merge with the Niúlán River,
and further southeast past the south of Lǔ Mountain.
Kàn Yīn said:
“Lǔyáng County—
now its territory is Lǔ Mountain.”
The water flows south into the Zhī River.
The Zhī River flows east past the south of Yìng City,
the old Yìng Township,
the state of the Marquis of Yìng.
This is the one referred to in the “Book of Songs” as “the Marquis of Yìng who followed virtue.”
The Péng River joins it here,
commonly called the Little Zhī River.
It rises from the eastern foothills of Péng Mountain, south of Lǔyáng County at Yǐwù,
flowing north past the west of Péng Mountain,
below which is the Péng Mountain Temple,
and in front of the temple stands the Péng Mountain Stele,
erected in the third year of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Huán of Hàn
by Dù Zhòngcháng.
The Péng River flows past its northwest,
east of the tomb of Yǐn Jiǎn, the former magistrate of Ānyì of Hàn.
West of the tomb mound is a stone temple,
in front of which are two stone watchtowers,
east of the towers is a stele tower,
south of which are two lions facing each other,
further south are two stone tablets,
and southwest of the stone pillars are two stone goats,
erected in the fourth year of the Zhōngpíng era.
The Péng River then flows northeast straight past the south of Yìng City and enters the Zhī River.
The Zhī River then on the left joins with the Qiáo River,
which issues from southeast of Shì Mountain north of Lǔyáng County,
flowing past the north of Yìng Mountain,
then south past the west of Yìng City.
The “Treatise on Geography” states:
“It was the Yìng Township of the old Fùchéng County,
where King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed his younger brother as a marquis.”
Yìng Shào said:
“The ‘Han’s Exoteric Commentary on the Songs’ recounts that King Chéng of Zhōu was playing with his younger brother,
and using a paulownia leaf as a jade tablet, said:
‘I enfeoff you with this.’
The Duke of Zhōu said:
‘The Son of Heaven does not speak in jest.’
The king then promptly enfeoffed him,
hence called the Marquis of Yìng,
and the township was also called Yìng Township.”
According to the “Lǚ’s Spring and Autumn Annals”:
“King Chéng used a paulownia leaf as a jade tablet to enfeoff Shū Yú,
not the Marquis of Yìng.”
The “Ancient Texts of Jí Commandery”
records that the state of Yìng already existed during the Shāng dynasty,
so it was not King Chéng.
It was also the fief of Fàn Jū during the Warring States period,
and the river is called the Yìng River.
The Zhī River then flows east past the old city of Chōu County.
In the first year of Duke Zhāo in the “Zuǒzhuàn,”
in winter,
Chǔ Prince Wéi sent Bózhōu Lí to fortify Chōu.
It emerges from below Yúchǐ Mountain.
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiāng in the “Spring and Autumn Annals,”
Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
encamping at Yúlíng,
and fording below Yúchǐ Mountain,
during heavy rain,
many in the Chǔ army froze,
and the laborers nearly perished.
When the Jìn people heard of the Chǔ army’s presence,
Shī Kuàng said:
“It is harmless;
I repeatedly sang the ‘North Wind,’
and then sang the ‘South Wind.’”
"The South Wind" is not strong,
filled with sounds of death,
Chǔ will surely achieve no success.
The water crossed here is the Zhǐ Shuǐ.
South of the water is the tomb of Zhōu Bāo, the Marquis of Jíchéng, who served as the Grand Servant of Chánglè and a Regular Palace Attendant of the Hàn dynasty.
In front of the tomb is a stele base,
resting against the western ridge of the hill,
with four gates opened,
each gate flanked by two stone beasts.
The burial mound has collapsed and the tomb is ruined,
the stele and beasts have shifted and sunk.
Someone unearthed one of the beasts,
which remained completely intact,
very tall and robust.
Its head was less than about one zhàng from the ground,
and its craftsmanship was exquisite.
On its left shoulder was carved the characters "bìxié."
Outside the gates, a stone bridge was built over the moat,
which remained undamaged over time.
The stele inscription reads:
"Six emperors and four empresses,
consulted and sought advice from him."
He began his service under Emperor Ān,
and died after Emperor Huán.
At that time, eunuchs monopolized power,
the Five Marquises tyrannized the age,
exploiting both public and private resources
to serve the dead and the living.
Enfeoffment is to honor the virtuous,
steles are to praise the meritorious.
Unless one belongs to such ranks,
what need is there for such extravagance?
Stone may last a thousand springs,
but it is better to decay swiftly.
Bāo's tomb may endure for ten thousand ages,
yet it only reveals ridicule and disgrace.
Alas,
how utterly foolish!
The Zhǐ Shuǐ flows eastward further,
where the Chōu Shuǐ joins it.
It is commonly called the Qiū Shuǐ,
but this is incorrect.
The water has two sources.
The eastern source emerges from beneath the eastern cliff of Jiàndú Mountain, southwest of the county,
with a surface about fifty paces across,
its depth immeasurable.
It flows northeast past the south of Chōu County,
then bends northeast around the east of the county,
and northward merges with the western source.
The western source emerges from the northern foothills of Pō Mountain, southwest of the county,
flowing northeast past the west of Chōu City,
then bends around the north of the county,
and eastward joins the right-hand water.
The mingled streams flow north into the Zhǐ Shuǐ.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered the passes,
he defeated Lǚ Yǐ, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng, east of Chōu,
precisely at this location,
on the northern bank of the Zhǐ Shuǐ.
The Zhǐ Shuǐ flows southeast further, passing north of the old city of Kūnyáng County.
Long ago, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn fought Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì at Kūnyáng and defeated them.
The fleeing troops trampled over one another,
and in their panic, they perished over a stretch of more than a hundred lǐ.
At that moment, torrential rain poured down,
and the Zhǐ Chuān swelled and overflowed.
Tigers and leopards trembled in fear,
while soldiers struggled to cross,
resulting in tens of thousands drowning.
The water became impassable due to the corpses,
and Wáng Yì, Yán Yóu, and Chén Mào, on light horses,
all crossed by stepping on the floating bodies.
(The Zhǐ Shuǐ) flows northeast past the northwest of Dìnglíng County in Yǐngchuān,
then east past the south of Yǎn County,
and eastward enters the Rǔ Shuǐ.
The Zhǐ Shuǐ flows east past the south of the Xībùgēng Pavilion.
North of the pavilion, it backs against the Rǔ Shuǐ north of Dìnglíng City.
It enters the Rǔ Shuǐ eastward,
with Yǎn County to the south,
so it cannot pass through it.
31.2 The Yù Shuǐ
31.2 The Yù Shuǐ
The Yù Shuǐ originates from the Zhīlí Mountain in Lúshì County, Hóngnóng,
flows southeast past the northwest of Xī'è County in Nányáng,
then east past the south of Wǎn County.
The Yù Shuǐ originates and flows eastward,
passing north of the old city of Lì Xiàn.
Guǒ Zhòngchǎn said:
The old city of Lì Xiàn is southeast of Zhīlí Mountain.
Lì,
is an old county.
The Sān Cāng states:
Fán, Dèng, Lì.
Lì has two cities,
this is the northern Lì.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered the passes,
he captured Xī and Lì,
which refers to this county.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows southeast past Héng Mountain of Zhì Xiàn,
passing east of the northern wall of Bǎizhāng Guō.
Further east,
the Lǔyáng Guān Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from the Fēnshuǐ Ridge south of Lǔyáng Xiàn.
The southern water flows south from the ridge,
while the northern water flows north from the ridge,
hence commoners call this ridge Fēntóu.
The water flows south past Lǔyáng Guān,
where mountains on both sides pierce the sky,
and splendid trees reach the clouds.
Therefore, Zhāng Jǐngyáng wrote in a poem:
"At dawn I climb Lǔyáng Guān,
the gorge path is steep and deep."
This is also where Sīmǎ Zhī and his mother encountered bandits.
The Guān Shuǐ flows southwest past Héng Mountain of Zhì,
passing west of Huánghòu Chéng.
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Shìzǔ dispatched Palace Attendant Fù Jùn with credentials to welcome Empress Guāngliè at Yùyáng.
Fù Jùn mobilized over three hundred soldiers,
to guard the empress on her journey back to the capital.
It seems this was where lodging was arranged,
hence the city gained its name.
On the mountain is a stone chamber, very ornate and clean,
traditionally called the "Empress's Bathing Chamber,"
which she also favored.
The Guān Shuǐ then flows southwest past the old city of Zhì Xiàn.
In the time of Duke Wén of Qín,
there was a man named Bó Yáng,
who encountered two boys,
named Yáo and Bèi.
These two boys,
were two pheasants.
He who obtained the female would become hegemon,
he who obtained the male would become king.
The two boys fluttered and transformed into a pair of pheasants.
Emperor Guāngwǔ captured a pheasant on this mountain,
considering it an auspicious sign for the restoration,
hence he established a county and named it accordingly.
The Guān Shuǐ then bends and flows southeast,
emptying into the Yù.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows southeast past the old city of Bówàng Xiàn to the east.
Guǒ Zhòngchǎn said:
It is 120 lǐ northeast of the commandery,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Colonel Zhāng Qiān accompanied General-in-Chief Wèi Qīng on the western campaign,
serving as the army's guide,
scouting for water and grass,
ensuring no shortages.
In the sixth year of Yuánguāng,
he was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Geographical Treatise states:
Nányáng has Bówàng Xiàn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yílè.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows southeast past the old city of Xī'è to the east.
Yīng Shào said:
Jiāngxià has an È,
hence this one is called Western È.
Long ago, when Liú Biǎo attacked Dù Zǐxù at Xī'è,
the Registrar Bó Xiàozhǎng heard the sound of war drums,
became frightened and closed his door,
covering himself with a quilt.
Gradually he climbed the city wall to watch,
saying courage can be learned.
The Yù Shuǐ flows further south,
and the Ěr Shuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from Xióng'ěr Mountain in Lúshì Xiàn of Hóngnóng Commandery,
flowing southeast past the north of Lì Xiàn,
then southeast past the north of Fángyáng Chéng.
In the fourth year of Emperor Āi of Hàn,
the Nányáng Grand Administrator Sūn Chǒng was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
commonly called Fángyáng Chuān.
It then passes south of Xī'è Xiàn.
North of the water is the tomb of Zhāng Píngzǐ.
East of the tomb,
beside the burial mound is Píngzǐ's stele.
The script is entirely in ancient characters.
The seal script heading contains Cuī Yuàn's inscription.
Shèng Hóngzhī and Guǒ Zhòngchǎn both said:
When Xiàhóu Xiàoruò governed the commandery,
he considered the text inferior,
and had another inscription carved on the reverse.
However, the two inscriptions on the reverse are actually by Cuī Zǐyù and Chén Xī,
not Xiàhóu Xiàoruò.
They are entirely in clerical script.
Both texts are preserved,
and have never been damaged.
It is also said there were two stelae at the tomb site,
but now only one is seen.
Perhaps it was because I traveled in summer heat,
weary and unable to investigate thoroughly.
South of the water by the road are two stone towers,
six or seven zhàng apart,
standing alone, equally tall,
about seventeen or eighteen chǐ high.
The pillars have a circumference of over two zhàng.
The stone surface is green,
and shines like a mirror.
Above, brackets and corbels support the arches,
with carved eaves on all four sides,
exquisitely crafted and elegantly carved,
a marvel of human artistry.
The inscription states:
The Shǔ Commandery Grand Administrator, surnamed Wáng,
styled Zǐyǎ,
was a man of Xī'è in Nányáng.
He had three daughters but no sons,
and the family wealth amounted to a thousand gold.
When the father died and was to be buried,
the daughters said to each other:
"Our late father bore us sisters,
with no male brothers.
Now we shall lay his spirit to rest in the dark abode,
conceal his soul beneath the earth.
To leave no posterity in the netherworld,
how can we manifest our lord's virtue?"
Each contributed five million cash,
one daughter built the tomb,
two daughters built the towers,
to express their filial devotion.
The inscription calls them "tomb towers."
East, under the woods,
near the burial mounds,
but their exact location cannot be determined.
The Ěr Shuǐ then flows southeast and empties into the Yù Shuǐ,
commonly called the Sì Shuǐ.
Sì and Ěr sound similar,
but this is incorrect.
The Geographical Treatise states:
Xióng'ěr Mountain produces three streams,
the Ěr Shuǐ is one of them,
flowing southeast to Lǔyáng and entering the Miǎn.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows south past the east of Yù Mountain.
On the mountain is a spirit temple,
commonly called Dú Mountain.
South of the mountain are the twin burial mounds of Wèi General of Chariots and Cavalry Huáng Quán and his wife,
with a subterranean passage connecting them.
Before the mounds are four stelae:
two erected by Emperor Míng of Wèi,
two by his son and his officials.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows southwest past the stele of Shǐ Dìngbó to the south,
then west to Guālǐ Ford.
Over the water are three bridges,
called Guālǐ Crossing.
From Wǎn, the road east leads to Dǔyáng,
west leads to Fāngchéng.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Shìzǔ entered from the west of Dǔyáng,
and General Pòlǔ Dèng Fèng, resentful of Hàn's plundering of Xīnyě,
blocked Guālǐ.
The Emperor personally engaged in combat,
and Dèng Fèng surrendered at Xīyáng Xià,
where he was subsequently executed.
The Treatise on Commanderies and States mentions
the existence of Guālǐ Ford and Xīyáng Settlement.
The obstructed bridge
is the site of Huán Wēn's old fortifications,
which he established in the fifth year of Shēngpíng when leading Fàn Wāng's troops north on campaign.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows southwest past the tomb of Jìn Shǔ Commandery Grand Administrator Dèng Yìshān to the south,
then south past the east of Wǎn City.
This city
was originally the capital of Shēnbó,
and King Wén of Chǔ destroyed Shēn and made it a county.
King Zhāoxiāng of Qín appointed Bái Qǐ as general,
attacked Chǔ and captured Yǐng,
and made this area Nányáng Commandery,
renaming the county Wǎn.
Wáng Mǎng changed the names again:
the commandery became Qiánduì,
the county became Nányáng.
Liú Shàn said:
It is south of the Central Plains and situated on sunny land,
hence the name.
The southwestern corner of the great city is the ancient Wǎn City,
the seat of the Jīng Province Governor,
hence also called Jīngzhōu City.
The present Nányáng Commandery
administers the great city.
Within its eastern city is an old palace foundation,
two hundred paces in circumference,
eight chǐ high,
with steps and stairs all paved with blue stone.
In the northwestern corner of the great city is another palace foundation,
one hundred paces in circumference,
five chǐ high,
likely built by Gēngshǐ.
Three lǐ west of the city,
There is an ancient terrace over thirty feet high,
built by Emperor Wén of Wèi during the Huángchū era when he
toured the southern regions.
The Yù Shuǐ then bends and flows past the south of the county,
which is what the "Rhapsody on the Southern Capital" refers to when it says

In the second year of the Dìhuáng era under Wáng Mǎng,
Zhū Wěi and others gathered the various generals south of the city,

and established Shèng Gōng as Son of Heaven upon this river.
The *Shìyǔ* states:
When Zhāng Xiù rebelled,
the Duke fought him,
was defeated,
and his son Áng, unable to ride,

The *Wèi Shū* states:
When the Duke campaigned south and reached Wǎn,

The Yù Shuǐ flows further south,
where the Méi Xī Shuǐ flows into it.
This stream originates from the south of Zǐ Shān north of the county,

Xī

The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
The ancestor of Lǚ Shàng was one of the Four Peaks,

he was enfeoffed at Lǚ,

Lǚ was in Wǎn County.

It is suspected that this is the place.

The Méi Xī flows further south past the east of Dùyǎn County.
The old city lies to the west.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,

Wáng Mǎng later renamed it Rùnyǎn.
The land is low-lying,

In the third year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,

The Méi Xī, further south, is called Shíqiáo Shuǐ,

South of the Yù Shuǐ,
there is also the Nánjiù Settlement,

Guō Zhòngchǎn states:
Thirty *lǐ* south of Wǎn City there is a town,
very low and small,
traditionally called Sāngōngchéng.

Shèng Hóngzhī, in his *Jīngzhōu Jì*,

I note that on the left and right banks of the Yù Shuǐ there were formerly two riverbanks,

the banks beside the water.
The settlement lies northeast of Yùyáng.
Examining antiquity and inferring from the terrain, this seems close.
Beside the town is a shrine to Fàn Lǐ.
Lǐ
was a man of Wǎn,
and the shrine is his former residence.
In the Later Hàn, there was a Fàn Zēng,

When campaigning against the Yellow Turban bandits,
he came to this shrine
and erected a stele for Lǐ.

When Xiàhóu Zhàn served in Nányáng,

East of the town is the former residence of the General-in-Chief Hé Jìn.

Sōng, courtesy name Zhòngshān,
was a man of Wǎn.
He and Fàn Shì of Shānyáng shared a bond of severed gold.
Being poor and unable to support his parents,
he hired himself out as a guard on Ā Street.
When sent to welcome Shì,
Shì descended from his carriage, took his arm, and said:
"You, a man of principle, are among the ranks of common soldiers—
is this not painful?"
Sōng replied:
"Hóu Yíng served in lowly tasks as a morning gatekeeper—
a humble and lowly position
that the ancients did not consider shameful.
What pain is there in this?"
Therefore, his eulogy says:
"Zhòngshān was perceptive and understanding,
rolling and unrolling without fixed pattern.
He bent his body to servile labor,
yet stood out elegant, containing fragrance."
The river bends further south past the east of Yùyáng County.
The Yù Shuǐ then flows south into the county,
passing by Xiǎocháng'ān.
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Treatise on Commanderies and States* states:
"The county has the Xiǎocháng'ān Settlement."
Xiè Shěn's *Hàn Shū* records that
Emperor Guāngwǔ attacked Yùyáng but could not take it,
so led his troops intending to attack Wǎn.
Reaching Xiǎocháng'ān,
he fought Zhēn Fù
and was defeated here.
The Yù Shuǐ flows further southwest past the old city south of the county.
In the seventh year of the Yánxī era of Emperor Huán,
he enfeoffed Dèng Bǐng as a marquis here.
The county
was formerly the seat of the Nányáng Director of Agriculture.
Later it became Yùyáng Commandery.
The commandery was abolished and the county restored.
To avoid the taboo name of Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jìn,
it was renamed Yúnyáng.
The Yù Shuǐ also flows north of the Ānlè Commandery.
In the first year of the Jiànhé era of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
he enfeoffed the Minister over the Masses, Hú Guǎng, as Marquis of the Ānlè Township in Yùyáng County.
Now, within his fief, the Lèzhái Garrison is established.
Guō Zhòngchǎn's *Xiāngyáng Jì* states:
Ninety *lǐ* south of Nányáng City is the former residence of Yuè Guǎng, President of the Imperial Secretariat of Jìn.
Guǎng, courtesy name Yànfǔ,
was skilled in pure conversation
and was highly regarded in his time.
The Prince of Chéngdū
was Guǎng's son-in-law,
and the Prince of Chángshā suspected him.
Guǎng said:
"Would I trade one daughter for five sons?"
Yet he was still suspected,
and ultimately died of worry in his old residence.
Now the garrison established there takes its name from this.
The river flows further south past the west of Xīnyě County.
The Yù Shuǐ (Yù River) flows further south into Xīnyě County.
A branch stream diverges and flows out southeastward,
spreading across low-lying wetlands and gathering into pools.
To the left (north), it accumulates to form a reservoir.
It measures nine lǐ from east to west,
and fifteen lǐ from north to south.
The fields irrigated by the reservoir's water
all become fertile and excellent land.
The Yù Shuǐ flows further south and converges with the Tuān Shuǐ (Tuān River).
It then flows south past the west of the old city of Xīnyě County.
When Shìzǔ (Emperor Guangwu of Han) was defeated at Xiǎo Cháng'ān,
his elder sister Yuán was killed.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he grieved deeply for his deceased sister.
He posthumously honored Yuán as the Xīnyě Cháng Princess of Integrity and Righteousness,
and this city is associated with that.
In the second year of the Xiánníng era of the Jin dynasty (AD 276),
the youngest son of the Grand Marshal, King Wǔ of Fúfēng, Xīn, was enfeoffed as Duke of Xīnyě Commandery.
Five districts from Nányáng—Jíyáng, Càiyáng, Rǎng, Dèng, and Shāndū—were carved out to form his fief.
Wáng Wénshū (Wang Chang) later established a new administrative division.
The west side became the commandery seat,
while the east side was residential.
The city's west side borders the Yù Shuǐ.
Further east, it joins with the Cháo Shuǐ (Cháo River).
The Cháo Shuǐ originates from the Chìshí Mountain to the northwest
and flows southeast through the territory of Guànjūn County,
a place named Shāqú.
It then flows southeast past the south of the old city of Rǎng County,
which was a separate town of the state of Chǔ.
After Qín captured Yān and Yǐng,
it was established as a county.
King Zhāo of Qīn enfeoffed his chancellor, Wèi Rǎn, with this as his marquisate.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Nóngrǎng.
It served as the seat of the Jīngzhōu Governor during the Wèi dynasty.
The Cháo Shuǐ further divides into two streams southeastward.
One branch flows northeast,
forming the Fánshì Reservoir.
This reservoir measures ten lǐ from east to west
and five lǐ from north to south.
It is commonly called the Fántíng Reservoir.
East of the reservoir lies the old estate of the Fán family.
After the Fán clan perished,
the Yǔ clan took possession of the reservoir.
Hence a proverb says:
"The reservoir is vast and deep,
the lower fields are fine;
When Master Fán lost his estate, Master Yǔ prospered."
In former times, during the Jin dynasty,
Dù Yù continued the work of Xìnchén (Shao Xinchen),
restoring the Liùmén Reservoir to hold back the waters of the six gates.
Below it, twenty-nine subsidiary reservoirs were connected.
The waters from these various reservoirs dispersed and flowed,
all entering the Cháo Shuǐ.
This is recorded in the "Liùmén Stele."
After the Liùmén Reservoir was established,
the other reservoirs were cut off.
The Cháo Shuǐ then flows east past the north of the old city of Cháoyáng County
and empties southeast into the Yù Shuǐ.
The Yù Shuǐ flows further southeast and joins with the Jí Shuǐ (Jí River).
The Jí Shuǐ receives its water from the Dǔ Shuǐ (Dǔ River).
The Dǔ Shuǐ originates from the northern mountains of Jíyáng County.
Several sources emerge together,
flowing south past Xiǎodǔ Township,
where it is called the Xiǎodǔ Shuǐ.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guangwu (AD 26),
Marquis Chéng'ān, Zāng Gōng, followed the Emperor in attacking Dǔ Township.
Its eastern source is about seven or eight paces wide.
The water surges and boils up,
hence it is commonly called the Téngfèi Shuǐ (Boiling Surge River).
It flows south through Dǔ Township,
where it is called the Dǔ Shuǐ.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ (AD 27),
Jì Zūn led troops south to attack Dǒng Xīn at Dǔ Township.
Because the river gave its name to the county,
it thus had the name Dǔyáng.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
"The county has the Dǔ Shuǐ."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yángchéng.
Emperor Āi of Hàn changed it to Shùnyáng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (AD 26),
Ānyáng Hóu Zhū Yòu was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Dǔyáng.
At the county, the Dǔ Shuǐ
was dammed to form a reservoir.
Ridges flank it east and west,
with the water spanning five or six lǐ between them.
In ancient and modern times, when the ridges were breached, the pooled waters would swell,
extending over ten lǐ from north to south.
When the water broke through, it would flood southward,
pouring down to form a bend.
The bend divides into two streams:
the western one is the Dǔ Shuǐ,
the eastern one is the Yíngyuán.
The Dǔ Shuǐ, with its irregular flow,
forms two lakes.
Hence they are named the Eastern Reservoir and the Western Reservoir.
The waters guided from these two reservoirs
branch out,
flowing southeast to the confluence where they enter the Bǐ Shuǐ (Bǐ River).
Therefore, the "Treatise on Geography"
states that both the Bǐ Shuǐ and the Dǔ Shuǐ flow into Cài,
due to their interconnected and interchangeable names.
The two lakes flow and pour forth,
merging to form the Huáng Shuǐ (Yellow River).
It receives all these waters.
It passes by the Huángchún Settlement of Jíyáng County,
and is also called the Huángchún Shuǐ.
Xiè Shěn's "History of the Later Han" records:
Zhēn Fù and others defeated Emperor Guangwu east of Xiǎo Cháng'ān,
then crossed the Huángchún Shuǐ southward in victory.
Their forward camp had its back to two rivers,
meaning it faced the Bǐ Shuǐ,
and they destroyed the bridge behind them,
showing no intention to retreat.
The Hàn troops attacked them,
their three armies were routed,
and twenty thousand men drowned in the Huángchún Shuǐ.
It then flows south past the west of the old city of Jíyáng County.
Yìng Shào said:
"The county lies south of the Jí Shuǐ."
Thus we know this river is the Jí Shuǐ.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gaozu of Hàn (200 BC),
Dù Déchén was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Later, when the Hàn uprising began,
they attacked Tángzǐ Township,
killed the commandant of Húyáng,
and advanced to capture Jíyáng.
Dèng Chén led his followers
to rendezvous with Emperor Guangwu at this county.
The Jí Shuǐ flows further south through Xīnyě County,
passing by the Huángyǒu Settlement.
In the third year of Emperor Guangwu's Jiànwǔ era (AD 27),
Fù Jùn and Cén Péng advanced to attack Qín Fēng,
first capturing Huángyǒu.
It is called the Huángyǒu Shuǐ here.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn defeated Qín Fēng on the banks of this river.
The settlement was entirely inhabited by Mán people,
and was still called the Huángyǒu Mán.
The Jí Shuǐ flows east from Xīnyě County and then southward,
entering the Yù Shuǐ,
at a place called Lìkǒu.
The sounds of "Jí" and "Lì" are similar,
so it should be Jíkǒu.
This is due to local dialect pronunciation,
hence the character changed according to the reading,
just as in the world, "Jízi wood" is called "Lìzi wood."
The Yù Shuǐ flows further southeast past the east of Shìlín,
which is the name of a garrison.
The garrison has a storehouse.
To the left (north) of the river is the great Yùzhāng Reservoir,
which irrigates over three thousand qǐng of fine farmland.
It flows south past the east of Dèng County.
This county
was originally the state of Marquis Wúlí of Dèng.
King Wén of Chǔ destroyed it,
and Qín made it a county.
The Yù Shuǐ joins with the Zhuó Shuǐ (Zhuó River) on the right (west),
commonly called the Ruògōu Shuǐ.
It receives water from the Bái Shuǐ at Cháoyáng County,
flowing southeast past the south of the old city of Dèng County.
Xí Zàochǐ's "Records of Xiāngyáng" states:
"When the King of Chǔ reached the Zhuó Shuǐ of Dèng,
which is twenty lǐ from Xiāngyáng,
it was this river."
The Zhuó Shuǐ flows further east past the north of Dèngsài.
This is a small hill southeast of Dèng City,
locally named Dèngsài.
Formerly, Sūn Wéntái (Sun Jian) defeated Huáng Zǔ below it.
The Zhuó Shuǐ flows east and empties into the Yù Shuǐ.
The Yù Shuǐ flows further south past the east of Dèngsài,
then past the east of Yōu City.
This was the ancient state of the Viscount of Yōu,
likely the southern border of Dèng.
Formerly, the Bā tribe requested friendship with Chǔ and Dèng,
but the people of Yōu seized their gifts.
This is that city.
Sīmǎ Biāo considered it the Yōu settlement of Dèng.
It flows south into the Miǎn Shuǐ (Miǎn River).
31.3 The Yǐn Shuǐ (Yǐn River)
31.3 The Yǐn Shuǐ (Yǐn River)
The Yǐn Shuǐ originates from the marshes south of Yǐnqiáng County,
and flows east into the Yǐng Shuǐ (Yǐng River).
The Yǐn River originates from Mount Shǎoshì in Yángchéng County of Yǐngchuān,
flowing eastward to join the Yǐng River.
It then meanders southeast,
passing northwest of Línyǐng County.
The Lesser Yǐn River branches off here,
flowing east past the old city of Línyǐng County to the north.
The Yǐn River continues east past the north of Yǐnyáng City,
then east past the old city of Yǐnqiáng County.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Jiān Chán, General Yánghuà, as a marquis here.
East of the Yǐn River lies the Táoshū Marsh.
I note that Yǐnyáng City is south of the Yǐn River,
yet this city is clearly named Yǐnyáng (Yang meaning “south of the river”).
This indicates that to the south,
there was still the Yǐn River,
hence this city was named Yáng (south).
South of the Yǐng River are two waterways.
The southern waterway flows southeast,
passes west of the Línyǐng Pavilion,
and enters the Rǔ River to the southeast.
It is now dry,
likely an old course of the Yǐn River.
West of Qíluò City, the Rǔ River
splits off eastward,
which people then called the Great Yǐn River.
It flows northeast,
with a branch channel diverging right,
known as the Dead Rǔ.
The separate Rǔ flows northeast past the north of Zhàolíng City,
where the Liàng Ditch originates.
Further east of the separate Rǔ,
the Fén Ditch originates.
The separate Rǔ flows east past the north of Zhēngqiāng City,
with the Fén Marsh south of the water,
colloquially pronounced as “fèn.”
The Fén River flows east from the separate Rǔ to form this marsh,
accumulating water four or five lǐ north of Zhēngqiāng City,
covering about thirty lǐ square.
The waterway joins the Lesser Yǐn River on the left.
The upper reaches of this water receive the Láng Marsh,
flowing south as the Gǒng River,
with water from the Qīnglíng Marsh joining from the east.
Turning east, it is again called the Lesser Yǐn River,
flowing south into the Great Yǐn River.
The name “Great Yǐn River”
likely derives from the confluence of Yǐn waters, collectively bearing the name.
It then flows east past the old city of Xīhuá County,
east past the old city of Rǔyáng County to the north,
and enters the Yǐng River to the east.
31.4 The Qú River
31.4 The Qú River
The Qú River originates from Mount Ào northwest of Wúfáng County in Rǔnán,
flows east past the north of the county,
and enters the Rǔ River.
Northwest of the county lies Tángxī City,
formerly the state of Fáng.
In the fifth year of Duke Dìng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Fūgài, brother of King Hélǘ of Wú, fled to Chǔ
and was enfeoffed at Tángxī,
hence the name Wúfáng.
In the eighth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Zhuāng Marquis Yáng Wǔ was enfeoffed here.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Chǎn, son of King Xī of Sìshuǐ, as Marquis of Tángxī.
In the mountain stream lies the White Goat Abyss,
where goats once emerged from the water.
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
a white goat emerged from this abyss,
and herders prayed and sacrificed to it.
There was a custom against clapping hands.
Once, a goat emerged from the water,
and a startled village woman clapped,
after which it ceased.
The abyss water joins the Qú River below,
which flows east past the old city of Qúyáng County to the west,
then east into the Qìn River,
meandering past the south of the county.
In the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Guāngwǔ’s Jiànwǔ era,
Dàn, grandson of Wú Hàn, was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The water then flows east into the Rǔ River.
31.5 The Qìn River
31.5 The Qìn River
The Qìn River originates from Mount Shàngjiè east of Wǔyīn County,
referred to as the Shì River in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.
Guō Pú’s commentary notes
that Shì should be Qìn,
originating from Mount Zhēn.
Xǔ Shèn states
it originates from Mount Zhōngyáng,
all being different names for the same mountain.
It flows east and joins the Bì River,
which originates from Mount Hàn in Wǔyīn County,
flowing northeast into the Qìn.
The Qìn River flows further northeast,
where the Shā River originates from Mount Dàshú to the southwest,
flowing northeast into the Qìn.
The Qìn River flows east,
joined by the Lún River,
which originates from Mount Xuān,
flowing southeast into the Qìn.
Further east, the Qìn River meets the mouth of the Ào River,
which originates from Mount Ào to the west,
flowing east into the Qìn.
It passes south of Wúfáng County,
then east past south of Qúyáng County.
Yīng Shào said:
The Qú River originates from Wúfáng County,
flowing east into the Qìn.
Northwest of the county
is where the two rivers converge.
It then passes south of Shàngcài County,
flowing east into the Rǔ River.
31.6 The Wǔ River
31.6 The Wǔ River
The Wǔ River originates from Mount Fúyǔ northwest of Wǔyīn County,
flowing east past the south of the county.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
From the Zhāogē Mountains,
the Wǔ River originates.
It flows southeast,
and pours into the Róng River.
The Classic records "Fúyǔ" —
is this an alternative name for that mountain?
The upper course of the Róng River receives the Dǔ River,
flows east,
and on the left joins the Western Liáo River.
Further east,
the Eastern Liáo River pours into it.
Both originate from the Northern Mountains,
flow south, and pour into the Róng River.
The Róng River then flows northeast,
and north of Wǔyīn County,
on the left, meets the Wǔ River.
Its course lies slightly to the west,
not passing south of the county.
The old city was on the southern side of the mountain.
During the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of the Han,
Cén Péng was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The Han established it as Yángshān County.
When Cáo Cāo fought Zhāng Xiù at Wǎn,
his horse, named Juéyǐng,
was hit by a stray arrow,
and the Duke was wounded in the right arm.
He withdrew to Wǔyīn,
which is this very place.
East of the city is the Mǎrén Embankment.
Guō Zhòngchǎn said:
The embankment is fifty lǐ west of Bǐyáng County.
It covers an area of about one hundred qǐng,
and the fields it irrigates extend over ten thousand qǐng.
Crops are rotated according to the year,
so the region never suffers a lean year.
The embankment water encircles the city moat three times.
An old channel runs southwest from the moat to join the Bǐ River.
Therefore, the Wǔ River could not have passed south of it again.
Moreover, the county is named Wǔyīn (Wǔ's Shade),
so it makes no sense for it to be south.
If it were south, it would be Yáng (Sunny).
This is not only incorrect,
but also illogical.
The Wǔ River then flows northeast,
and the Lǐ River pours into it.
This river originates from the Zhì Héng Mountains,
flows southeast past the east of Jiànchéng.
"Jiàn"
should be "Juǎn",
a misreading of the character.
The Records of the Commanderies and States states:
Yè County has the city of Juǎn.
The river then flows east into the Wǔ River.
The Wǔ River flows northeast past the west of the Eastern Mountains,
and flows west into the Wǔ River.
To the left of the Wǔ River is the Huángchéng Mountain.
A stream originates from Huángchéng Mountain,
flows northeast past Fāngchéng.
The Records of the Commanderies and States states:
Yè County has Fāngchéng.
Guō Zhòngchǎn said:
Between Kǔcài and Yúdōng is a small city,
named Fāngchéng,
facing the stream to the east.
Investigating the origin of this city's name,
it must have been named after the mountain.
Kǔcài is Huángchéng,
and together with Yúdōng,
they form Fāngchéng.
It is commonly called Fāngchéng Mountain.
The water flows east and pours into the Wǔ River.
Therefore, the Record of Tombs of Sages and Worthies states:
West of Fāngchéng in Yèyì, Nányáng,
is Huángchéng Mountain,
where Cháng Jū and Jié Nì plowed together.
There is an east-flowing stream,
which is where Zǐlù asked for the ford.
Shīzǐ states:
The madman of Chǔ, Jiēyú, plowed at Fāngchéng,
likely here.
Shèng Hóngzhī said:
Within the eastern boundary of Yè is an old walled city,
starting east of Chōu County,
reaching the Qìn River,
and extending to the boundary of Bǐyáng.
It stretches continuously for several hundred lǐ north and south,
and is called Fāngchéng,
also known as the Long Wall.
Lǐ County has one side of an old walled city,
its exact length unknown,
called the Long Wall.
This is the western corner of that city.
The distance between them is six hundred lǐ.
Although there is no constructed foundation on the northern side,
it connects continuously with the mountains.
The Hàn River flows to its south.
Therefore, Qū Wán replied to Duke Huán of Qí:
"For the state of Chǔ,
Fāngchéng serves as its wall,
and the Hàn River as its moat."
The Records of the Commanderies and States states:
Yè County has a long mountain called Fāngchéng,
referring to this walled city.
The Wǔ River then flows northeast past the old city of Wǔyáng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Han,
Fán Kuài was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
It then passes east north of Xīpíng County.
The county
was formerly the state of Bó.
The Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒzhuàn mention that Jiāng, Huáng, Dào, and Bó
were all friendly with Qí.
The Han named it Xīpíng.
West of it is the Lǚ ruins,
which is the Xīlíng Pavilion.
Xīlíng is level and open,
hence the name Xīpíng (Western Level).
In the third year of the Gānlù era of Emperor Xuān of the Han,
the Chancellor Yú Dìngguó was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xīntíng.
The Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Record states:
The county has Lóngquán water,
which can be used to whet swords,
making them exceptionally hard and sharp.
Hence, there is the debate on hardness and whiteness.
Thus, swords from Lóngquán
are treasures of Chǔ.
The county produces famous metal,
and in ancient times had an iron official.
It then passes east south of Yǎn County.
The old city of Yǎn County
is far from here,
so it cannot pass by it.
It then passes east north of Dìngyǐng County,
and flows east into the Rǔ River.
In the second year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān of the Han,
Dìngyǐng County was established from part of Shàngcài County in Rǔnán Commandery.
In the first year of the Yǒngjiàn era of Emperor Shùn,
Guō Zhèn from Yángdí was appointed Imperial Secretary,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dìngyǐng,
which is this city.
31.7 The Yǔn River
31.7 The Yǔn River
The Yǔn River originates from Càiyáng County,
The Yùnshuǐ originates from the Dàhóngshān to the southeast of the county.
The mountain lies to the southwest of Suízùn and
to the northeast of Jìnglíng.
The foundation upon which it sprawls
extends over a hundred *lǐ* in breadth and circumference.
Its peak is called Xuángōu.
Situated amidst the numerous hills of the plain,
it is the most outstanding among the various ridges.
At the foot of the mountain, there is a stone gate.
Cliffs press in on both sides, layer upon layer, steep and lofty.
The cliffs are several hundred *rèn* high.
Entering the stone gate,
one then reaches a stalactite cave.
Above the cave, a plain cliff stands sheer,
inaccessible to human footsteps.
Within the cave are many stalactites.
Congealed cream hangs down,
appearing as white as ice and snow.
Fine, subtle droplets
drip continuously.
The dark cave extends far and deep,
but travelers do not venture to its utmost depths,
because within the cave there is often a hot wind,
making it impossible to endure for long.
The Yùnshuǐ emerges from its northern side.
Initially, its flow is shallow and narrow,
but farther on it becomes broad and deep,
capable of floating boats and rafts—
a great river indeed.
People of the time, because the Yùnshuǐ originates here,
therefore also call it Yùnshān.
The Yùnshuǐ flows northeast and joins the Shíshuǐ.
The Shíshuǐ originates from Dàhóngshān,
flows northeast, and pours into the Yùnshuǐ.
It is called the Xiǎo Yùnshuǐ.
Then, the combined streams flow northeast
past the old city wall of Shàngtáng County.
This was originally the Shàngtáng Township of Càiyáng,
the old state of the Marquis of Táng.
In the third year of Duke Dìng of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Duke Chéng of Táng went to Chǔ.
He had two Sùshuāng horses.
Zǐcháng desired them,
but the duke did not give them.
He detained him for three years.
The people of Táng stole the horses and presented them to Zǐcháng,
and only then was the Marquis of Táng allowed to return.
The Yùnshuǐ flows east again,
and the Jūnshuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from Dàhóngshān,
flows northeast past the north of Tǔshān,
and then flows northeast into the Yùnshuǐ.
The Yùnshuǐ then bends and flows southeast.
It passes to the west of Suí County to the southeast.
The county
was the old state of Suí.
It is what the *Zuǒzhuàn* of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* refers to as the largest among the states east of the Hàn.
Chǔ destroyed it and made it a county.
During the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was established as a commandery.
The Zhàshuǐ originates from Huángshān to the northwest of the county.
It flows south past the west of Juéxī County,
then southeast,
where the Juéshuǐ joins it.
The Juéshuǐ originates from the southern side of Tóngbóshān.
Lǚ Chēn said:
"The water is in Yìyáng."
The Juéshuǐ flows southeast past the west of Juéxī County,
then southeast and pours into the Zhà.
The Zhàshuǐ then flows southeast past the west of the old city of Suí County.
In the fourth year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
King Wǔ of Chǔ attacked Suí.
The Lìngyǐn Dòu Qí and the Mò'áo Qū Chóng cleared the road and bridged the Zhà,
and the army approached Suí.
This refers to this water.
Beside the water is Duànshé Qiū.
The Marquis of Suí went out and saw a large snake cut in half.
He then lifted it up and applied medicine to it.
Therefore, it is called Duànshé Qiū.
Later, the snake brought a bright pearl to repay his kindness.
The world calls it the Marquis of Suí's Pearl,
also called the Divine Snake Pearl.
South of the hill is the pond of Suí's senior official Jì Liáng.
The water then flows south and joins the Yìjǐngshuǐ.
This water emerges southeast of Suí City.
The wellspring constantly surges and overflows, its moisture pouring forth,
unchanged in winter and summer.
Tradition calls it the Righteous Well.
Its lower stream joins the Zhà.
The Zhàshuǐ then flows south and pours into the Yùn.
The Yùnshuǐ also meets the Zhīshuǐ.
This water's source also originates from Dàhóngshān,
and it flows east and pours into the Yùn.
The Yùnshuǐ then passes south of Suí County and north of Suíchéngshān and flows southeast.
It then passes to the west of Ānlù County in Jiāngxià to the south.
The Suíshuǐ originates from Shílóngshān east of Yǒngyáng County in Suí Commandery.
It flows northwest,
then turns south, passing west of Yǒngyáng County,
and traverses Héngwěishān,
which is the Péiwěishān mentioned in the *Tribute of Yu*.
The Suíshuǐ then flows southwest to the old city of Ānlù County,
enters the Yùn to the west,
which is the old Yún City.
It uses the ridge as its wall,
steep without needing construction.
The Yùnshuǐ then flows south past the north of Shíyánshān.
In the past, Zhāng Chāng rebelled at its foot,
caging a colorful phoenix to delude the masses.
In the second year of Tài'ān of Jìn,
General Zhènnán Liú Hóng sent his subordinate officer Pí Chū
to battle Zhāng Chāng at Qīngshuǐ.
Zhāng Chāng was defeated,
pursued and beheaded at the riverbank.
This is the Qīngshuǐ mentioned in the *Zuǒzhuàn* of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, fourth year of Duke Dìng,
when Wú defeated Chǔ at Bǎijǔ,
pursued them,
and caught up at Qīngfā.
It seems the Yùnshuǐ also bears the name Qīngshuǐ.
It then flows southeast and joins the Fùshuǐ on the right.
The Fùshuǐ originates from Dàyángshān northeast of Xīnshì County in Jìnglíng Commandery.
The water has two sources.
The Dà Fùshuǐ emerges from the southern side of the mountain,
flows south, and joins the Xiǎo Fùshuǐ on the left.
The Xiǎo Fùshuǐ emerges from the eastern side of the mountain
and flows south past the east of Sānwángchéng.
At the end of the Former Hàn,
Wáng Kuāng, Wáng Fèng, and Wáng Cháng were stationed here.
Therefore, it is called Sānwángchéng.
Within the city is an old stele,
but the characters are missing and damaged,
and can no longer be read.
The water bends and flows southwest,
joining the Dà Fùshuǐ on the right.
It is commonly called Dà Bìshuǐ.
It then flows southwest past the west of Dùchéng,
which is the seat of Xīnshì County.
The *Treatise on Commanderies and States* considers it Nánxīnshì.
Since there is a Xīnshì in Zhōngshān,
this one is prefixed with "south."
It was established by dividing Ānlù County.
Also, Wáng Kuāng raised troops in the county at the beginning of the restoration,
and they were called the Xīnshì troops.
The Fùshuǐ then flows southeast into the territory of Ānlù,
joining the Tǔshānshuǐ on the left.
It is commonly called Zhāngshuǐ.
The water emerges from Tǔshān,
flows south past the west of the old city of Pínglín County in Suí Commandery,
commonly called Jiàngbēichéng.
It borders Xīnshì.
Therefore, at the beginning of the restoration,
the troops had the names Xīnshì and Pínglín.
It then flows south,
enters the Fùshuǐ on the right,
and the Fùshuǐ then flows east into the Yùn.
The Yùnshuǐ then passes south of Xīnchéng,
built by Huán Wēn, Grand Marshal of Jìn, in the fifth year of Yǒnghé.
The Yùnshuǐ then meets the Wēnshuǐ.
The Wēnshuǐ emerges from a marsh east of Xīnyáng County in Jìnglíng.
Its mouth is two *zhàng* and five *chǐ* in diameter.
The banks are layered with sand,
straight and clean, quite lovely.
If one observes it calmly,
the deep spring is like a mirror.
But upon hearing human voices, the water churns and surges,
and nothing can be seen again.
Its heat can scald a chicken.
After flowing over a hundred paces broadly,
it becomes cold like a frigid spring.
It flows southeast and pours into the Yùnshuǐ.
It then receives the Tóngshuǐ on the right.
The Tóngshuǐ originates from Tóngshān northwest of Qūlíng County in Jiāngxià Commandery.
It flows southeast past the south of the county.
The county seat is the old city of Shítóŋg.
The city is round, not square.
It flows east into Ānlù
and pours into the Yùnshuǐ.
It then flows southeast into the Xià.
The Yùnshuǐ then divides into two streams to the south.
The eastern one connects to the Shèshuǐ,
the western one enters the Miǎn.
This is called the Yùnkǒu.
32 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Thirty-Two
32.1 The Liáoshuǐ
32.1 The Liáoshuǐ
The Liáoshuǐ originates west of Píngchūn County in Jiāngxià.
Northeast of the Pì River,
on the right it meets the Tàgǔchuān Water,
which originates from the Tàgǔchuān in the southeast,
flows northwest,
and joins the Pì River from the left.
The Pì River then flows northwest past the west of Mǎhēng City,
and further northwest past the west of the old city of Lù'ān County.
This county
was originally the state of Gāoyáo.
Xià Yǔ enfeoffed his youngest son here,
to continue the sacrifices.
Now, within the county's Dūpō, there is a large mound,
which the people call Gōngqín,
and it is the tomb of Gāoyáo.
The Chǔ people call a mound "qín."
In the first year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
it was separately made the Héngshān Kingdom.
In the fifth year, it belonged to Huáinán.
In the sixteenth year of Emperor Wén,
it was again made the Héngshān Kingdom.
In the second year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Wǔ,
it was separately made the Lù'ān Kingdom.
Under Wáng Mǎng, it was called Ānfēng.
This is what the *Hànshū* refers to as "using Shū to slaughter Lù."
In the third year of Tàikāng of Jìn,
it was the seat of Lújiāng Commandery.
The Pì River further northwest divides into two streams,
from which the Quèbēi emerges.
It then flows north past the west of Wǔmén Pavilion,
and northwest past the west of the old city of Ānfēng County.
According to the *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì*,
it was a subordinate county of Ānfēng Commandery,
commonly called Ānchéng.
Further north, it meets the Rú Water,
and the mingled streams flow northwest and join.
It enters the Huái River from the north.
The point where the waters converge is called the Bǐkǒu.
32.5 Xiè Water
32.5 Xiè Water
The Xiè Water originates from Bó'ān County,
which
is the Bóxiāng County of the *Geographical Treatise*,
and which Wáng Mǎng called Yánglù.
The Xiè Water, from the county, receives the Bǐ Water upstream at Má Bùchuān,
emerges northwest and passes through Rúxī,
which is called the Rú Water.
It passes north of Quèbēi,
and westwards joins the Bǐ Water.
The Xiè Water from Rúxī passes by Ānfēng County,
flows north and joins the Pì,
also called the Rúxūkǒu.
It enters the Huái River from the northwest.
The mingled streams return together.
32.6 Féi Water
32.6 Féi Water
The Féi Water originates west of Guǎngyáng Township in Chéngdé County, Jiǔjiāng.
Lǚ Chén's *Zìlín* says:
The Féi Water originates from Liángyú Mountain,
commonly called Liánjiā Mountain,
and some also call it Dú Mountain.
Flowing north, it divides into two streams,
from which the Shī Water emerges.
The Féi Water then flows north past the east of Dí City,
and further north past the east of Díqiū,
where on the right it meets a branch of the Shī Water.
This branch receives the Shī Water east of Héféi County city,
flows west past Chéngdé County,
and joins the Féi Water.
It passes north of that county to the west,
and enters Quèbēi from the north.
The Féi Water from Díqiū flows north past the west of the old city of Chéngdé County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Píng'ē.
It then flows north past the east of Quèbēi,
and further north past the east of Sǐhǔtáng.
The Quèbēi channel receives water upstream from Jǐngmén,
and interconnects with Quèbēi,
hence the *Classic* says it enters Quèbēi.
The Féi Water further north,
on the right joins the Yánjiàn Water,
which receives the Shī Water upstream at Héféi County,
flows north past the west of Jùnqiú County,
and accumulates to form Yánghú.
The water of Yánghú from the pond flows northwest past the south of Sǐhǔ Pavilion,
and joins, flowing west between Héngtáng.
In the beginning of Tàishǐ of Sòng,
Sīmǎ Liú Shùn of Yùzhōu,
leading eight thousand troops, occupied the city and land,
to resist Liú Miǎn.
Zhào Shūbǎo with five thousand elite troops,
delivered provisions to Sǐhǔ,
but Liú Miǎn defeated them.
This pond water divides into two,
from which the Luòjiàn emerges,
and the Yánjiāng Water joins it.
This water receives from Quèbēi.
The pond water receives the Jiàn Water upstream south of Wǔmén Pavilion,
and separates as the Duànshén Water.
It then flows northeast past the east of Wǔmén Pavilion,
where the pavilion is at the confluence of the two waters.
The Duànshén Water further flows northeast past the east of Shénjì Pavilion,
and further north is called the Háo Water.
Though the names differ widely,
it is in fact the same watercourse.
It then flows northeast past the east of Báisháo Pavilion,
accumulates to form a lake,
called Quèbēi.
The pond is about 120 lǐ in circumference,
located 80 lǐ south of Shòuchūn County.
It is said to have been built by the Chǔ minister Sūnshū Áo.
Wèi Tàiwèi Wáng Líng
fought with Wú general Zhāng Xiū at Quèbēi,
which is this place.
The pond has five gates,
which intake and discharge river flow.
To the northwest is Xiāngménbēi.
The pond water flows north past the shrine of Sūnshū Áo,
called the Quèbēi channel.
Further north, it divides into two streams.
One stream flows east and joins the Líjiāng Water.
The Líjiāng Water flows east past the south of Líjiāng Pavilion.
When Wén Qīn rebelled,
the Wú army advanced north,
and Zhūgě Xù resisted them at Líjiāng,
which is this water.
It flows east and joins the Féi Water,
called the Líjiāng Shuǐkǒu.
Further north, it passes east of Shòuchūn County.
The Féi Water from Líjiāng flows north past the east of the old city of Shòuchūn County, forming Chánglàijīn.
Beside the ford is the Xiètáng North Pavilion,
a place of bustling arrivals and departures,
where boats, carts, and travelers on land and water gather.
Further northwest,
on the right it joins the Dōngxī stream, whose water is drawn from a channel emerging north,
flowing southwest past the west of Dǎogōng Temple.
Beside the temple, a five-story pagoda was built along the stream,
with spacious buildings,
lofty and serene, fostering enlightenment.
It then flows southwest and joins the Féi.
The Féi Water then flows west past below Dōngtái,
which is the pavilion on the northeastern corner of the outer wall of Shòuchūn.
To the east is a lake,
where in spring and summer,
red lotuses cover the water.
A channel draws water to the city moat,
accumulating into a deep pool,
called Dōngtái Lake,
also a distributary south of the Féi.
The Féi Water flows west past the north of the old city of Shòuchūn County,
and on the right joins the Běixī.
This water originates from the northern mountains,
with spring sources descending and washing over rocks,
tumbling down onto the water above the collapsed wall,
where tall forests reach the sky,
and lofty branches bear the sun,
emerging from the mountain forest.
To the right of the retreat,
and left of Shānyuān Temple,
monks and laypeople play and wander,
often gathering below,
drawing water inside and out,
the spring as pure as the seven purities.
The stream water flows along,
southwest past the retreat south of Lù Dàoshi's hermitage,
adjacent to the stream,
not overly large,
but sufficient for quiet dwelling,
also a scenic spot.
The stream water flows southwest and joins the Féi Water.
It enters the Huái River from the north.
The Fei River flows west and divides into two branches.
The right branch is the old channel of the Fei River,
dammed to form the Chuánguān Lake,
where boats and warships were stationed.
The left channel of the Fei River then flows west past the north of the Shíqiáo Gate,
also called the Cǎoshì Gate.
Outside, a stone bridge crosses to the northern islet,
upon which stands the Xīchāng Temple.
The temple is surrounded by water on three sides.
In the Buddha hall, three statues are enshrined,
their true appearances and marvelous forms,
with robes and adornments exquisitely brilliant,
were erected by Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng Dynasty.
West of the temple,
lies the Chuánguān Quarter,
where the Cāngsì and Dūshuǐ officials
managed and constructed [the facilities].
North of the lake faces the Bāgōng Mountain.
The mountain has no trees,
only bare hillocks.
On the mountain stands the temple of Huáinán King Liú Ān.
Liú Ān was the grandson of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
and the eldest son of King Lì.
He humbled himself to treat scholars with respect,
was deeply fond of Confucian learning,
and supported several dozen practitioners of esoteric arts,
all of whom were outstanding talents,
well-versed in secret methods of immortality and the teachings of the Hóngbǎo [text].
Suddenly, eight elders appeared,
all with white beards and eyebrows,
seeking an audience at his gate.
The gatekeeper said:
"Our king seeks longevity.
Since you gentlemen possess no arts to halt aging,
I dare not announce you."
The eight elders all transformed into youths,
and the king greatly revered them.
The eight scholars were all capable of refining gold and transforming elixirs,
moving freely without obstruction.
They then ascended the mountain with Ān, buried gold in the ground,
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
The remaining elixir in the vessel,
licked by chickens and dogs,
enabled them all to ascend as well.
At the place from which they ascended,
the trodden stones all sank,
and the footprints of men and horses remain there.
Thus, the mountain was named after the eight elders.
I climbed to its summit,
but heard no tales of the footprints of men and horses,
only the temple statues remain.
In the temple are depicted images of Ān and the eight scholars,
all seated on couches with canopies as in life,
wearing fine and elegant garments,
each holding feather fans and wearing skirts and capes,
with towels, pots, pillows, and other objects,
just as in their daily lives.
Before the temple stands a stele,
erected in the tenth year of the Yǒngmíng era of Qí.
On the mountain are a hermitage and a stone well,
which is what Cuī Yǎn referred to when he said:
"I descended to Shòuchūn,
climbed the northern ridge to the Huáinán Taoist chamber,
where the Bāgōng stone well is located."
It is also said:
Zuǒ Wú, along with Wáng Chūn, Fù Shēng, and others, sought Ān,
together visited Xuánzhōu and later wrote an account,
titled *The Record of the Eight Elders*.
It does not include the tale of the chickens and dogs ascending to the sky.
According to the *Hànshū*,
Ān rebelled and was executed.
Gé Hóng clarified that he attained the Dao,
with details recorded in the *Bàopǔzǐ* and *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
The Fei River then receives the Gǒubēi Channel from the left.
The channel water diverges from Líjiāng,
leading the channel north of Shòuchūn City,
passing right of the Sháobēi Gate,
and entering the city from the north.
Formerly, Shímíáo of Jùlù served as county magistrate,
and this is where he left his calf.
East of the channel lies the Dōngdū Street.
North of the left path along the street,
stands the temple of Sòng Dynasty Minister of Works Liú Miǎn.
Built in the second year of Yuánhuī of Sòng in the Xiàoyì Ward of the eastern township,
before the temple stands a stele.
The stele's construction began that year,
and it was erected in the first year of Yǒngmíng of Qí.
Shěn Yuē's *Sòngshū* states:
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
Yīn Yǎn, Governor of Yùzhōu, rebelled.
Emperor Míng appointed Miǎn as General Fǔguó to suppress him.
Yǎn surrendered,
and [Miǎn's troops] did not commit the slightest offense,
bringing relief to the people.
They erected a stele for him during his lifetime,
but the inscription exaggerated the facts.
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán,
his former subordinate Yán Yòumíng composed the temple inscription,
his former aide Páng Tǐng wrote the temple eulogy,
and Xiàhóu Jìngyǒu composed the temple ode,
all engraved on the sides of the stele.
The channel water then flows north past the east of the Xiàngguó City,
built by Emperor Wǔ of Liú-Sòng during his campaign against Cháng'ān.
The halls, chambers, and pavilions
still bear the name "Xiàngguó."
It then exits the city northward and flows into the Fei River.
It then flows west past the north of Jīnchéng,
and further west,
joins the Yángtóu Creek from the left.
The creek receives water from Sháobēi,
flows northwest through Yángtóu Creek,
and is called Yángtóu Jiàn water.
It flows north past Yùn Lake,
joins the Fēngshuǐ Channel from the left,
which receives water from the Huái River south of Fēng Village,
flows down into Yángtóu Creek,
passes alongside the west of Shòuchūn City,
then flows north past Xiàng Gate,
exits north from the Shāmén Gate under the Xiāoyáo Tower west of Jīnchéng's west gate,
and flows north into the Fei Channel.
The Fei River flows north into the old channel's Héngtáng,
which was the southern road of Xuánkāng's imperial highway,
connecting left to the Chuánguān Quarter.
The Fei River passes Xuánkāng City,
flows northwest,
and exits north at the water's edge,
where there is a Qūshuǐ Hall,
also a gathering place for leisurely excursions.
It then flows further northwest.
In former times, during the Jìn dynasty,
Xiè Xuán defended against Fú Jiān from the north,
prayed at Bāgōng Mountain,
and deployed his formation along the banks of the Fei River.
Jiān gazed upon the grass and trees on the mountain,
all appearing as human figures.
This was where Jiān was defeated in battle.
It was not that the spirits of the eight elders provided aid,
but rather the delusion of the impending downfall of the Fú clan.
The Fei River then flows northwest into the Huái River,
which is called the Féikǒu.
32.7 Shī River
32.7 Shī River
The Shī River also diverges from the Fei River at Guǎngyáng Township,
flowing southeast into the lake.
The Shī River receives water from the Fei River at Guǎngyáng Township,
flows southeast past Héféi County.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Xià River emerges southeast of Chéngfù,
and here joins with the Fei River,
hence called Héféi."
Kàn Yǐn also stated,
"It emerges east of Chéngfù in the Peì Kingdom,
and here merges to form the Fei."
I have examined the distinct courses and separate branches of the rivers,
and find no principle of one flowing into the other.
Thus, I know the theories of Yìng and Kàn
lack factual evidence.
It is likely that when the Xià River swells suddenly,
the Shī joins with the Fei,
hence called Héféi,
not referring to the Xià River.
The Shī River flows east from Chéngdé past the south of Héféi County's city wall,
the city situated within four waters.
Further east lies Xiāoyáo Ford,
where a bridge formerly spanned the water.
When Sūn Quán attacked Héféi,
Zhāng Liáo defeated him north of the ford.
The bridge was left with only two planks unremoved.
Quán, with Gān Níng, spurred his horse toward the ford,
Gǔ Lì whipped the horse from behind to add momentum,
and thus they managed to cross the bridge.
Líng Tǒng, clad in armor, fell into the water.
Later, pursuing the fleeing enemy,
he wept at the ford's shore.
The Shī River then divides into two branches eastward,
with a distributary flowing out northward,
descending into Yángyuān.
The Shī River then flows east past the Húkǒu Garrison,
enters Cháo Lake eastward,
which is called the Shīkǒu.
32.8 Jǔ River
32.8 Jǔ River
The Jǔ River originates from the Huái River in Fánglíng County of Hànzhōng,
flowing southeast past the boundaries of Línjū County.
The Ju River originates from Jǐng Mountain northwest of Jūyáng County in the Eastern Wènyáng Commandery,
which is the head of Jīng Mountain.
Its lofty peaks rise like rosy clouds,
soaring steeply through layered clouds.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Gold and jade are produced here."
It is also the source from which the Ju River flows.
Therefore, the Huainanzi says:
"The Ju River emerges from Jīng Mountain."
Gāo Yòu states:
"Jīng Mountain is located in Huáidé County of Zuǒ Féngyì,"
likely because the Luò River has the alternate name of Qījǔ.
This is erroneous evidence.
Dù Yù states:
"The water originates from Fā'ā Mountain in the southwest of Xīnchéng Commandery,"
which is likely a different name for the mountain.
The Ju River flows southeast past the southeast of Jūyáng County.
The county has the Tóng River,
which flows east past the south of the county
and then enters the Ju River.
The Ju River then flows southeast past the north of Wènyáng Commandery,
which is within the boundaries of Gāo'ān County.
The commandery seat is at Xīchéng,
and the county seat is located beneath the commandery city,
formerly a subordinate town of Xīnchéng.
In the early years of the Yìxī era,
it was separated from Xīnchéng to establish this county.
To the west, it is entirely bordered by layered mountains.
The Ju River flows south past the west of Línjū County.
The Qīngxī River flows into it,
originating from Qīng Mountain west of the county.
To the east of the mountain is the Làn Spring,
which is the source of the Qīngxī River.
Its mouth spans several zhàng in diameter,
and its depth is unfathomable.
The spring is exceptionally pure and numinous.
When the sun is scorching and oppressive,
or when there is untimely rain,
if foul objects are thrown into it,
it can immediately produce torrential rain.
The water flows eastward from its source,
and because it originates from Qīng Mountain,
it is named Qīngxī.
Following the source and floating along the stream,
the scenery is strikingly deep and steep.
Shèng Hóngzhī states:
"Dense trees grow alongside,
reaching into the sky and intertwining.
Precarious cliffs and leaning precipices
constantly seem on the verge of collapse.
The wind and springs echo beneath the green forests,
while rock-dwelling gibbons' calls drift above the white clouds.
Travelers often feel their eyes cannot fully take in the sights,
nor their emotions fully appreciate the beauty.
Thus, forest dwellers seek refuge here,
and cloud wanderers settle their hearts.
Beside the spring, many Taoist priests have built their retreats."
The Qīngxī River then flows east into the Ju River,
and the Ju River bends and flows past the south of the county.
During the Xiánhé era of the Jìn dynasty, it served as the seat of Jūyáng Commandery.
The Ju River then flows southeast past the north of the old city of Dāngyáng County.
The city relies on ridges for defense,
with its back resting against the Ju River to the north.
Its old city is located 140 lǐ to the east,
called the Eastern City,
south of the Chángbǎn slope in the Lǜlín region.
The Chángbǎn slope
is where Zhāng Yìdé brandished his spear.
The Ju River then flows southeast past the west of Lǘchéng and the east of Mòchéng,
and then south past the west of Màichéng.
This is where Guān Yúnchǎng pretended to surrender,
after which he rebelled.
The tradition states:
"Wǔ Zǐxū built Lǘchéng and Mòchéng to attack Mài City."
As the proverb says:
"With Lǘ to the east and Mò to the west,
Màichéng will fall on its own."
The Ju River then flows south past the tomb of King Zhāo of Chǔ,
which faces Màichéng to the east.
Thus, Wáng Zhòngxuān's fu "Ascending the Tower" states:
"To the west, it connects with Zhāoqiū."
The Ju River then flows south and merges with the Zhāng River.
It then passes east of Zhījiāng County to the southeast,
and enters the Yangtze River to the south.
The Ju River then flows southeast past the east of Chángchéng,
and further southeast flows into the Yangtze River,
where it is called the Jūkǒu.
32.9 The Zhāng River
32.9 The Zhāng River
The Zhāng River originates from Jīng Mountain east of Línjū County,
flows southeast past Liǎotíng,
and then east past the south of Zhāngxiāng.
Jīng Mountain is located over a hundred lǐ east of Jǐng Mountain, within the boundaries of Qíxiāng County in Xīnchéng.
Although many peaks compete in height,
Jīng Mountain stands out in solitary beauty.
The Zhāng River flows southeast,
then bends southwest,
passing south of Biān County.
The county's old city is located 140 lǐ to the northeast.
To the southwest is Gāoyáng City,
which moved its seat to the old city of Xǔ Mào.
The city faces the Zhāng River to the south,
and the river further flows south past the south of Zhāngxiāng in Línjū County.
In the past, Guān Yǔ defended Màichéng,
pretended to surrender and fled,
but Pān Zhāng beheaded him here.
The Zhāng River then flows south past Dāngyáng County,
and further south past the east of Màichéng.
Wáng Zhòngxuān ascended its southeastern corner,
faced the Zhāng River, and composed a fu, saying:
"Between the clear Zhāng's open tributaries,
leaning on the long isle of the winding Jū."
The Zhāng River then flows south,
where the Wěi River flows into it.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"The Wěi River originates from Yízhū Mountain in the northeast,
flows south, and enters the Zhāng River."
It then flows south to Wūfúyì north of Zhījiāng County,
and enters the Ju River.
The Treatise on Geography states:
According to the Tribute of Yu,
the southern range of Jīng Mountain,
located northeast of Línjū County,
is where the Zhāng River originates.
It flows east to Jiānglíng and enters the Yáng River,
which then flows into the Miǎn River.
This is incorrect. Now, the Zhāng River joins the Ju River from the right over a hundred lǐ southeast of Dāngyáng County.
32.10 The Xià River
32.10 The Xià River
The Xià River emerges from the Jiāngjīn River southeast of Jiānglíng County.
East of Yùzhāngkǒu at Jiāngjīn is Zhōngxiàkǒu,
which is the head of the Xià River,
a tributary of the Yangtze.
This is what Qū Yuán meant by "passing Xiàshǒu and floating west,
gazing toward Lóngmén but seeing it not."
Lóngmén
is the eastern gate of Yǐng City.
It then flows east past the south of Huáróng County.
The county
was formerly Róngchéng.
In the fourth year of Duke Dìng of Lǔ in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the state of Xǔ moved to Róngchéng.
It faces the Zhōngxià River to the north.
From the northeast of the county, it flows past the south of the old city of Chéngdū Commandery.
During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
when Western Shǔ was in turmoil,
Huáróng and other cities were ceded to form the fief of Prince Yǐng of Chéngdū.
The Xià River then flows past the north of the tomb of Hú Chǒng, Governor of Jiāozhǐ.
Hàn Grand Tutor Guǎng was buried in the imperial mausoleum,
yet beside this tomb stands a stele for Guǎng,
so people call it Guǎng's tomb,
but this is incorrect.
The inscription is said to be composed by Cài Bójiē.
It passes south of the tomb of Fàn Xīróng.
Wáng Yǐn's Records of the Lands from the Jìn History states:
"The tomb of Táo Zhū is in Huáróng County,
and the stele inscription says it is Fàn Lǐ of Yuè."
The Jìn Taikang Geographical Records, Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīngzhōu, and Liú Chéngzhī's Records
all state it is in the southwest of the county,
while Guō Zhòngchǎn says it is ten lǐ east of the county.
Examining the stele,
it is inscribed:
"Tomb of the late Magistrate of Xīróng, Lord Fàn."
The inscription is fragmented,
and the person is not clearly identified,
but it mentions that Lǐ was his ancestor.
The stele was erected in the second year of Yǒngjiā.
Considering its account,
it is the most thorough and detailed.
Having personally visited the site,
I diverge from the common theories
and correct them accordingly.
The Xià River then flows east past the south of Jiānlì County.
The county was established in the fifth year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
The land is low-lying, with many marshes and ponds.
From the eastern border of Zhōulíng to the southwest,
it flows through Yúndù and Dùnyáng,
forming the marshlands of Yúnmèng.
Wěi Zhāo states:
"Yúnmèng is in Huáróng County."
According to the third year of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
when the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ,
Zǐchǎn prepared hunting gear to hunt in the Mèng region south of the Yangtze.
Guō Jǐngchún states
that this refers to Bāqiū Lake southeast of Huáróng County.
Dù Yù states:
"Zhījiāng County and Ānlù County have Yúnmèng,"
which likely spans across rivers and marshes,
covering a vast area.
The Xià River then flows east,
where the Xiàyáng River flows into it.
The water originates from the Yáng River at Zhèkǒu in Jìnglíng County,
flows southeast, and merges with the Zhōngxià River,
forming the Xiàyáng River.
It then flows northeast past the north of Huáihuái County in Jiāngxià and continues northeast.
Further east, it reaches Yúndù County of Jiāngxià,
and enters Miǎn.
Yìng Shào's "Record of the Thirteen Provinces" states:
Where the Jiāng diverges and enters Miǎn is the source of the Xià River.
The name "Xià"
originates from the division of the Jiāng,
drying up in winter and flowing in summer,
hence it received this designation.
It is called Zhōngxià,
and also encompasses the name Dàxià.
Where it breaks through and enters,
it is called Dǔkǒu.
Zhèng Xuán, in his "Commentary on the Shàngshū",
states that the Cānglàng waters
are now called the Xià River,
as they converge, hence the name changed over time.
Liú Chéngzhī, in his "Record of Mountains and Rivers from the Yǒngchū Era", says:
The Xià River
is called Cānglàng in ancient texts,
as sung in "The Fisherman".
Based on this,
the water should flow from Miǎn.
Now, examining it, the Xià River is where the Jiāng flows into Miǎn,
not Miǎn entering Xià.
If Miǎn were to flow into Xià,
its course would be southwest,
contradicting the Shàngshū's description of "further east".
I also believe this is incorrect.
From Dǔkǒu downstream,
the Miǎn River is also called Xià,
and where it meets the Jiāng,
it is called Xiàruì.
Thus, the "Zuǒzhuàn" of the Chūnqiū records that when Wú attacked Chǔ,
Shěn Yīn Shè rushed to Xiàruì.
Dù Yù states:
Where the Hàn River curves and enters the Jiāng,
is Xiàkǒu.
32.11 Qiāng River
32.11 Qiāng River
The Qiāng River originates from Cānláng Valley in Qiāng territory,
locally called Tiānchí Báishuǐ.
"Geographical Records" states:
It originates from Qiāngdào in Lǒngxī,
flows southeast past the east of Dàngchāng City,
about five hundred lǐ northwest of Tiānchí.
The Qiāng River then flows southeast past the east of Dàngpóchuān City and turns southeast.
Long ago, when Jiāng Wéi invaded Lǒngyòu,
he heard that Zhōng Huì had entered Hànzhōng,
so he withdrew.
Learning that Zhūgě Xù, Governor of Yōngzhōu, was stationed at Qiáotóu,
and planning to take the northern route from Kǒnghán Valley,
Xù intercepted him on this road,
so Wéi changed to the northern route.
He crossed Qiáotóu and entered Jiàngé,
and Xù pursued but could not catch him.
The Qiāng River flows further southeast,
where Yángbù River joins it.
Yángbù River originates from Yángbù Stream in the northeast,
flows southwest past Ānmín Shù,
then southwest into the Qiāng River.
