Further southeast, it passes southwest of Wǔjiē City,
then southeast past the west of Jiālú City,
where Yángtāng River joins.
Yángtāng River originates from Tāng Stream north of Yīnpíng's northern border,
flows southeast past the north of Bùbù City,
then southeast past the south of Wǔbù City,
and southeast right where it joins Qiè River,
which emerges southwest from the source.
The Qiāng River then passes south of Jiālú City,
past south of Yú City,
and further southeast,
where it joins Wǔbù River on the left.
Wǔbù River has two sources,
from the southern and northern Wǔbù Streams,
which flow southwest and merge into one river,
then bend southeast into the Qiāng River.
The Qiāng River flows further southeast to Qiáotóu, where it joins Báishuǐ,
about ninety lǐ southeast of the old city of Báishuǐ County.
Further southeast, it reaches Báishuǐ County of Guǎngwèi,
and merges with the Hàn River.
Further southeast, it passes Làngzhōng County of Bājùn,
then south to the east of Diànjiāng County,
and south into the Jiāng.
32.12 Fú River
32.12 Fú River
The Fú River originates northwest of Fú County in Guǎngwèi,
from beyond the border of Gāngdīdào in Guǎnghàn Shǔguó,
flows southeast past the west of Fú County,
which was called Tǒngmù under Wáng Mǎng.
Zāng Gōng advanced and captured Fú City,
beheading Gōngsūn Huī at Fú.
Upstream from here,
the county has Chán River originating from Chán Mountain,
whose source has gold and silver mines.
Washing and smelting them
produces gold and silver.
Chán River passes Chán Pavilion and flows down into the Fú River.
The Fú River flows further southeast past the north of Miánzhú County,
where Zāng Gōng sailed upstream to Píngyáng,
and Gōngsūn Shù's general Wáng Yuán surrendered,
leading to the capture of Miánzhú.
The Fú River flows further southeast and joins Jiànshǐ River,
which originates from Xī Stream in Píngluòjùn,
flows southwest, bends, and turns southeast,
entering the Fú River.
The Fú River flows further southeast past the north of Jiāngyóu Shù,
where Dèng Ài, from Jǐnggǔ in Yīnpíng,
advanced on foot with troops and horses bound, entering Shǔ,
passing Jiāngyóu and Guǎnghàn.
The Fú River flows further southeast past the south of Nán'ānjùn,
then south where it meets Jīntáng River,
which originates from Xīndū County in Guǎnghàn,
flowing southeast into the Fú River.
The Fú River flows further south,
where a distributary branches off,
flowing west past Wǔchéng County in Guǎnghàn as Wǔchéng River,
then west to Chéngdū, entering the Jiāng.
South to Xiǎo Guǎngwèi,
it merges with Zǐtóng River.
Xiǎo Guǎngwèi
is the area of Guǎnghàn County,
renamed Guǎngxìn by Wáng Mǎng.
32.13 Zǐtóng River
32.13 Zǐtóng River
Zǐtóng River originates from the northern border of its county,
flowing southwest into the Fú River.
Formerly Guǎnghànjùn,
Gōngsūn Shù changed it to Zǐtóngjùn.
Liú Bèi, praising Huò Jùn for defending Jiāméng,
further divided the area north of Guǎnghàn,
establishing Zǐtóngjùn separately,
with Jùn as its governor.
The county had five women,
and the King of Shǔ sent five strong men to welcome them.
Upon arriving, they saw a large snake entering a mountain cave.
The five men pulled it,
causing the mountain to collapse,
crushing the five men and five women.
Thus, the mountain was named Wǔfù Mountain,
also called Wǔfùhòu.
Chí River originates here,
also called Wǔfù River,
or Tóng River.
Its water originates in the mountains,
flows south past Zǐtóng County,
renamed Zǐtóng by Wáng Mǎng.
From the county, it flows south past the east of Fú City,
then south into the Fú River,
called Wǔfù Shuǐkǒu.
Further southwest to the south of Xiǎo Guǎngwèi,
it enters Diànjiāng.
It is also said the Fú River here enters the Hàn River,
and is called Nèishuǐ.
It flows north past Diànjiāng.
Long ago, when Cén Péng and Zāng Gōng advanced from Jiāngzhōu up the Fú River,
Gōngsūn Shù ordered Yán Cén to station troops at Shěn River.
Gōng, with infantry on the left and cavalry on the right,
advanced with boats on both sides,
shaking the mountains and valleys.
They heavily defeated Cén's army,
beheading or drowning over ten thousand men,
turning the water turbid.
Shěn River originates from Guǎnghàn County,
flowing down into the Fú River.
32.14 Cén River
32.14 Cén River
Cén River originates from Hàn Mountain in the southeast of Nánzhèng County in Hànzhōng,
flows north to Ānyáng County,
and south into Miǎn.
The Cen River,
is also known as the Huang River.
It flows northeast past the north of the Southern City of Chénggù,
which is situated on a mountain.
Some say it was first established by Hán Xìn,
while others claim it was founded by Zhāng Liáng,
though the exact origin remains uncertain.
In the ninth year of the Yìxī era,
Suǒ Xiá served as the governor of Guǒzhōu,
and he administered from this location instead of Chénggù,
hence it was called the Southern City.
The city has a circumference of seven lǐ,
with ravines at its collar and valleys girding it,
featuring sheer cliffs a hundred xún high.
A city was built at the northern valley entrance,
and the eastern gate lies beside the mountain, following the ravine.
After more than five lǐ,
a winding path ascends,
finally reaching the city's administrative center.
North of the city, there was formerly a bridge over the water,
crossing the Cen River to the north.
North of the river is Zhào Jūn City,
and north of that city, there is another bridge,
crossing a tributary of the Miǎn River to the northern city,
which
is the seat of Dàchénggù County.
On the right bank of the Huang River is the Yuèguī Lodge,
with the Cen River flowing past its north,
continuing north to Ānyáng,
where it joins the Miǎn River from the left.
This is the mouth of the Cen River.
33 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Thirty-Three
33.1 The Jiāng River
33.1 The Jiāng River
Mín Mountain is in Dí Dào County of Shǔ Commandery,
where the Great River originates,
flowing southeast past the north of that county.
The Mínshān,
also known as Dúshān,
has a river called the Dúshuǐ,
and is also referred to as Wènfùshān.
It lies beyond the frontier,
and is the source from which the Jiāngshuǐ flows.
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
The spring source of the Dàjiāng
is what we now hear of,
beginning at the foot of Yángbó Lǐng.
Following the cliffs, it spreads out,
with hundreds of small streams,
hardly yet enough to float a wine cup.
Traveling southeast for over a hundred lǐ, one reaches Báimǎ Lǐng,
and passes Tiānpéng Què,
also called Tiānpéng Gǔ.
King Zhāo of Qín appointed Lǐ Bīng as governor of Shǔ.
Bīng saw Tiānpéngshān in Dīdào Xiàn,
where two mountains face each other,
shaped like a gate tower,
called Tiānpéng Mén,
also known as Tiānpéng Què.
The Jiāngshuǐ from here upward is extremely weak,
truly what is called "originating from a floating cup."
During the Yuányán era of the Hàn dynasty,
Mínshān collapsed,
blocking the Jiāngshuǐ,
so that it did not flow for three days.
Yáng Xióng's Fǎn Lísāo says:
"From Mínshān, I cast it into the river's flow,
to mourn Qū Yuán,
and named it Fǎn Sāo."
The Jiāngshuǐ flows east from Tiānpéng Què past Wènguān,
and then north of Dīdào Xiàn.
In the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the northern part of Shǔjùn was divided to establish Wènshānjùn to govern it.
The county
was originally established by Qín Shǐhuáng,
and later became Shēngqiān Xiàn.
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
From Báimǎ Lǐng, turning back for over twenty lǐ, one reaches Lónghù,
then eighty lǐ to Cánlíng Xiàn,
then sixty lǐ south to Shíjìng,
then over sixty lǐ to Běibù,
where it first becomes about a hundred paces wide;
then west over a hundred and twenty lǐ to the old Wènshānjùn,
where it widens to over two hundred paces;
then southwest a hundred and eighty lǐ to Shībǎn,
where the Jiāng grows somewhat larger.
Thus, its essence forms the well-constellation's brilliance,
and the Jiāng and Hàn rivers shine with spiritual power.
The Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng says:
"The essence of Mínshān
ascends to form the well-constellation,
where the Emperor gathers prosperity,
and the spirits establish blessings."
Therefore, the Shū states:
"Mínshān guides the Jiāng."
Its springs flow deep and far,
making it foremost among the Four Dú rivers.
The Guǎngyǎ states:
"Jiāng
means tribute."
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
"It produces precious things
that can be offered as tribute."
The Shìmíng states:
"Jiāng
means 'shared,'
as small streams flow into it,
making it public for all."
A hundred and forty lǐ to the northeast is Láishān,
from which the Zhōngjiāng flows,
eastward into the Dàjiāng.
Láishān
is Qióngláishān,
located in Yándào Xiàn of Hànjiā,
also called the southern mountain of Xīndào.
It has the Jiǔzhé Bǎn,
where ice forms in summer,
and extreme cold prevails in winter,
the place where Wáng Yáng reined in his horse.
Píng Héng said:
"This is the source of the Zhōngjiāng."
Guō Jǐngchún's Jiāng Fù states:
"Flowing two rivers from Jū and Lái."
Another hundred and fifty lǐ east is Jūshān,
from which the Běijiāng flows,
eastward into the Dàjiāng.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"Jūshān,
from which the Jiāngshuǐ flows,
eastward into the Dàjiāng,
with many strange snakes in it."
The Jiāngshuǐ then passes Wènjiāngdào.
The Wèn River emerges from beneath Yùlún Bǎn on Kūnshān west of the frontier and flows south,
then east past the county and eastward into the Dàjiāng.
Thus, Sū Dài warned Chǔ:
"The armor of Shǔ
can float boats on the Wèn,
ride the summer floods down the Jiāng,
and reach Yǐng in five days."
He referred to this river.
There is also the Jiānshuǐ that flows into it,
originating from Miánsīdào,
also called Yùlěishān in Miánsī Xiàn.
Lǚ Chēn said:
"Also called Bànhuànshuǐ,
it flows down into the Jiāng."
The Jiāngshuǐ then flows east and branches into Tuó,
dug by Kāimíng,
what Guō Jǐngchún called "Yùlěi marking the eastern branch."
The county
is the seat of Wènshānjùn,
established by Liú Bèi.
Crossing the river, there is a Zuóqiáo.
The Jiāngshuǐ then passes Dū'ān Xiàn,
where there are Táoguān and the temple of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Lǐ Bīng built a great dam here,
blocking the Jiāng to create a weir,
with left and right openings,
called Jiānpéng.
The Jiāng flows into Píjiāng,
and a check dam was built for navigation.
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"The Jiāng reaches Dū'ān,
where the right is dammed,
and the left is checked,
so the main flow goes east,
to the right of Píjiāng.
Using the mountain to channel water,
bamboo and wood are easily transported,
to irrigate the various commanderies."
He also dug Yángmójiāng and Guànjiāng,
west to Báishā Yóu below Yùnǚfáng,
erecting three stone figures in the water,
carved to admonish the river god:
water should not drop below their feet in drought,
nor rise above their shoulders in flood.
Thus, the people of Shǔ rely on it for irrigation in drought,
and in rain, do not block its flow.
Therefore, the Jì states:
"Water and drought follow human will,
with no knowledge of famine,
fertile fields stretching a thousand lǐ,
renowned as a 'land-sea,'
called the 'land of abundance.'"
The postal station is on the dam,
commonly called Dū'ān Dàyàn.
Also known as Jiānyàn,
and also called Jīndī.
Zuǒ Sī's Shǔdū Fù states:
"West beyond the Jīndī."
When Zhūgě Liàng marched north,
he considered this dam fundamental to agriculture,
vital to the state's resources,
so he assigned twelve hundred conscripts to guard it,
with a dam official.
When Huángfǔ Yàn, governor of Yìzhōu, reached Dū'ān,
he camped at Guānbǎn.
His assistant Hé Lǚ said:
"The place we are camping,
named Guānbǎn,
means 'looking up, looking down in rebellion,'
an ominous sign."
He did not listen,
and was indeed killed by the guard commander Zhāng Hé.
The Jiāngshuǐ then passes Línqióng Xiàn,
called Jiānqióng by Wáng Mǎng.
The county has fire wells and salt water,
which at night
glow with rising light.
The Jiāngshuǐ then passes Jiāngyuán Xiàn, renamed Qióngyuán by Wáng Mǎng.
The Yuánjiāngshuǐ flows from here.
The Jiāngshuǐ then flows northeast past Pí Xiàn.
A county resident named Yáo Jīng
was killed by rebel tribes,
who abducted his two daughters.
The two daughters appeared in a dream to their brother,
saying they would drown themselves in the river the next day,
and their bodies would arrive the day after,
so he could wait for them.
It happened as dreamed,
and he retrieved the two daughters' bodies from the water.
The commandery and county honored them as extraordinary.
The Jiāngshuǐ then flows east past Chéngdū Xiàn,
established in the second year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The county has two rivers,
flowing side by side beneath the commandery,
so Yáng Zǐyún's Shǔdū Fù says:
"Two rivers adorn its front."
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
"King Zhāo of Qín sent Lǐ Bīng as governor of Shǔ,
who dug the two rivers of Chéngdū,
irrigating ten thousand qǐng of fields.
The river god demanded two maidens yearly as brides.
Bīng offered his own daughter to marry the god,
went straight to the temple to urge wine on the god,
but the wine cup always remained full."
Bīng sternly reprimanded him,
and then suddenly disappeared.
After a long while,
two oxen were seen fighting on the riverbank.
After some time,
Bīng returned,
sweating profusely, and said to his subordinates:
"I fought fiercely,
and you should have helped me.
The one facing south with a white patch on its waist
is my ribbon.
The Registrar stabbed and killed the one facing north,
and the river god then died.
The people of Shǔ admired his courage and decisiveness,
and all robust and strong men
were thus named 'Bīng's sons.'
In the twenty-seventh year of King Huì of Qín,
Zhāng Yí and Sīmǎ Cuò, among others, were dispatched to conquer Shǔ,
and the Shǔ Commandery was subsequently established.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Dǎojiāng.
Yí built Chéngdū,
modeling it after Xiányáng.
During the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
the Shǔ Commandery became a kingdom,
and was later changed to the Chéngdū Neishi and the seat of the Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
The *Geographical and Customs Records* states:
"Huáyáng and the Black Water constitute Liángzhōu."
In the second year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liáng was renamed Yìzhōu,
as the newly opened territories of Qiánwéi, Zāngkē, and Yuèxī
expanded the borders of the province,
hence it was called Yì.
Initially, the seat was at Luò County in Guǎnghàn,
but was later moved here.
Thus, Lǐ Gù wrote in his *Letter to My Younger Brother Yuán*:
"I am now fifty-seven years old,
my hair and temples have already turned white.
As the saying goes, 'travel with a body to shelter,
leave with a full stomach.'
I have traveled throughout the world,
but have yet to see Yìzhōu."
In the past, Yán Fūzǐ often said:
"There are five classics,
I have studied four;
there are nine provinces,
I have traveled to eight."
I wish to emulate this man.
Initially,
the place where Zhāng Yí built the city and excavated earth
was ten lǐ from the city,
and was later used for fish farming—
this is now the Wànqǐng Pond.
North of the city, there is also the Lóngdī Pond,
east of the city is the Qiānqiū Pond,
west is the Liǔ Pond,
northwest is the Tiānjǐng Pond.
Their waters flow and connect,
never drying up in winter or summer.
On the two rivers to the southwest, there are seven bridges:
directly west of the city gate, over the Pí River, is the Chōngzhì Bridge;
southwest at the Shíniú Gate is the Shì Bridge.
When Wú Hàn entered Shǔ,
he first sent light cavalry from Guǎngdū to burn it.
Below the bridge is what is called the Shíxī Abyss.
Lǐ Bīng once made five stone rhinoceroses to suppress the water spirits.
He carved the stone rhinoceroses
and channeled the water through the southern river,
naming it Xīniú Village.
Later, two of the stone rhinoceroses were moved:
one was placed at the Shì Bridge Gate in the prefectural market,
and one was sunk into the abyss.
The south gate of the great city is called the Jiāng Bridge;
south of the bridge is the Wànlǐ Bridge;
to the west upstream is the Yíchéng Bridge,
and downstream is the Zuó Bridge.
East of the road on the southern bank is the School of Literature.
Initially,
when Wén Wēng was the governor of Shǔ,
he established a lecture hall
and built a stone chamber in the southern city.
After the Yǒngchū era,
the school building was damaged by fire,
and a later governor added two more stone chambers.
Later, the provincial authorities took over the commandery school,
moving it east of the road on the southern bank of the Yíchéng Bridge.
West of the road is the city,
formerly the Brocade Office.
It is said that when brocade workers wove brocade,
they would rinse it in the river's flow,
and the brocade would become exceptionally bright.
If rinsed in other rivers,
the color of the brocade would be dull.
Thus, it was named Jǐnlǐ.
In Shǔ, there is a river with treacherous currents,
where the river god once drowned people.
When Wén Wēng was governor,
he offered sacrifices to it,
but when the wine offering was not fully consumed,
he drew his sword and struck it,
and it ceased to cause harm.
The river flows east past Guǎngdū County,
established in the second year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jiùdū Tíng.
Lǐ Bīng discerned the water veins
and opened salt wells in the county.
West of the river is Wàngchuān Plain,
where mountains and cliffs were cut to channel water,
forming various ponds and reservoirs,
thus providing abundant resources for livelihood—
this is the Southern River.
Turning north from the Chōngzhì Bridge,
there is the Chángshēng Bridge.
Ten lǐ north of the city is the Shēngxiān Bridge,
where there is a farewell pavilion.
When Sīmǎ Xiàngrú was about to depart for Cháng'ān,
he inscribed on its gate:
"If I do not ride back in a high carriage drawn by four horses,
I will not pass beneath you."
Later, he went to Qióng and Shǔ,
and indeed fulfilled his ambition.
Lǐ Bīng built bridges along the water,
corresponding to the seven stars.
Thus, Emperor Shìzǔ said to Wú Hàn:
"The army should be stationed between the seven bridges and the stars."
Hàn advanced victoriously from Guǎngdū and pressed toward Chéngdū,
positioning his forces north and south with his deputy Liú Shàng,
encamping on both sides of the river,
with floating bridges facing each other.
Gōngsūn Shù sent Xiè Fēng to deploy troops at the Shì Bridge,
attacking Hàn from behind and defeating him.
Hàn fell from his horse into the water,
but managed to escape by holding onto the horse's tail.
He returned to camp, appointed generals,
and secretly crossed the river at night
to join Shàng in attacking Fēng,
killing him on the northern bank of this river.
North of the river, to the left, lies Fántián.
Wén Wēng also channeled the Jiānyú River to irrigate seventeen hundred qǐng of Fántián.
The Jiān River then flows east, crossing Miánluò,
passing through the Wǔchéng boundary to the northern bank of Guǎngdū,
and enters the river from the south—
this is called the Wǔchéng Water Mouth,
and it is the Northern River.
The river flows east to Nán'ān, where it forms the Bìyù Ford,
as Zuǒ Sī said:
"Eastward, crossing the Yù Ford."
It then flows southeast past Qiánwéi's Wǔyáng County,
where the Qīngyī River and Mò River come from the southwest,
converge, and flow into it.
The county
was originally the territory of the great Yèláng Kingdom.
In the sixth year of the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, it was opened up,
and commanderies and counties were established.
In the fourth year of the Tàichū era,
Rèn Ān, the Governor of Yìzhōu, built the city of Wǔyáng.
Wáng Mǎng changed the names,
the commandery was called Xīshùn,
and the county was called Jíchéng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ called it the Shìdàfū Commandery.
There is the Mín River flowing into it,
emerging from Jiāngyuán County,
its head receiving the Great River,
flowing southeast to Wǔyáng County where it empties into the River.
Below the county on the River,
there was formerly a great bridge,
one and a half lǐ wide,
called the Ānhàn Bridge.
In years of high water it was damaged,
and the people suffered from the repair work.
Later, the Grand Administrator Lǐ Yán cut through Tiānshè Mountain,
following the River to open a passage,
and this bridge was subsequently abandoned.
The county has the Chìshuǐ River,
which flows down into the River.
In the twenty-ninth year of the Jiàn'ān era,
a yellow dragon appeared in this river,
and after nine days it finally left.
This county uses the River to create a large weir,
opening six water gates,
to irrigate the area below the commandery.
Běi Mountain,
is the mountain which Wáng Qiáo of old ascended.
The River water further converges with the Wénjǐng River,
which was channeled by Lǐ Bīng.
From Zuódào it divides its waters with the Méng Stream,
reaching Línqióng County of Shǔ Commandery where it joins the Bùpú River.
This water emerges from beyond the frontier west of Chéngdū in Shěnlí Commandery.
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
using the western part of Shǔ's capital, the Qiáng and Zuó peoples,
he administered the Máoniú Road.
In the fourth year of the Tiānhàn era, a Commandant was established,
in charge of the outer Qiāng tribes,
located on the exterior of the Qiónglái Mountains.
Traveling west from Shǔ across the Qiáng and Zuó regions,
the road is extremely perilous,
with the difficulties of the Nòngdòng eight crossings,
and the obstacles of the Yángmǔgé Road.
The water comes from Bùpú west of the county,
dividing into two streams.
One stream passes along that road,
then east past Línqióng County,
entering the Wénjǐng River.
The Wénjǐng River then flows east past Jiāngyuán County,
the county borders the Wénjǐng River,
on the river is the Cháng family dike,
spanning forty lǐ.
There is the Zhū Pavilion,
south of the pavilion is Qīngchéng Mountain,
on the mountain grows fine grain,
below the mountain are squatting owls,
which are taro,
as the saying goes, "where there are squatting owls below,
one never goes hungry even to old age,"
this is why the Zhuó family gladly moved far away to here.
The Wénjǐng River then flows east to the foot of Tiānshè Mountain in Wǔyáng County and enters the River.
The other stream flows south past the west of Qióngdū County in Yuèxī Commandery,
southeast to Qīnglíng County of Yúnnán Commandery,
entering the Pú River.
The commandery was originally Yúnchuān territory,
established in the third year of the Jiànxīng era of Shǔ.
The Pú River then flows south past Xiélóng County of Yǒngchāng Commandery,
where it joins the Tān River,
which emerges from Qīnglíng County,
receiving water from the Qīnglíng River upstream,
passes Yèyú County,
then southeast to Xiélóng where it enters the Pú River.
The Pú River then passes through Jiànníng Commandery of Níngzhōu.
The province,
was originally the garrison of the Láijiàng Area Commander,
so southerners called it "Below the Garrison."
In the third year of the Jiànxīng era of Liú Shàn,
it was established by dividing off part of Yìzhōu Commandery.
Passing Shuāngbǎi County,
the Jí River enters there,
which emerges from Niúlán Mountain in Qínzāng County,
flows south to Shuāngbǎi County,
and empties east into the Pú River.
Further east to Láiwéi County it enters the Láo River,
which emerges from beyond the frontier,
flows east past that county and joins the Pú River.
The Pú River flows east to Mílíng County of Jiāozhǐ Commandery in Jiāozhōu,
then south into the sea.
The River from Wǔyáng east reaches Péngwáng Settlement.
In the past, Cén Péng and Wú Hàn sailed up the River into Shǔ,
their army camped at this place.
Learning of the name, they disliked it,
but as dusk fell they did not move camp,
and were subsequently assassinated.
It is called the Píngmó River,
also called the Outer River.
This place has the Péng tomb,
said to be the tomb of Péng Zǔ.
The River then flows southeast past the west of Ān'ān County,
there is the Xióng'ěr Gorge,
where mountains connect in steep competition,
ridges vie in height.
During the Hépíng era of Hàn,
mountains collapsed in an earthquake,
the River water flowed backwards,
forming a suspended irrigation rapid,
named Lěidǐ,
also called Yángài,
which was leveled by Lǐ Bīng.
The county seat is at the confluence of the Qīngyī River,
girded by the two rivers,
which was the former seat of Shǔ King Kāimíng.
Lái Mǐn's "Běn Shǔ Lùn" says:
A man from Jīng, the magistrate of Bì, died,
his corpse floated upstream,
the people of Jīng searched for it but could not find it.
The magistrate reached below Wèn Mountain and revived,
and met Wàngdì.
Wàngdì,
was Dù Yǔ.
A woman named Zhū Lì descended from heaven,
emerging from Jiāngyuán to become Yǔ's wife.
He then became king over Shǔ,
and was called Wàngdì.
Wàngdì appointed him as chancellor.
At that time, the Wū Mountain gorge was blocked and the Shǔ waters did not flow.
The emperor sent the magistrate to cut through the Wū Gorge to let the water through.
Shǔ then obtained dry land.
Wàngdì considered himself inferior in virtue,
and thus abdicated the state to him,
who was called Kāimíng.
South of the county is Éméi Mountain,
there is the Méng River,
which is the Dàdù River.
The water issues from Méng Stream,
flows southeast and joins the É River,
which emerges from beyond the frontier,
passes through Wènjiāng Circuit.
Lǚ Chén said,
the Zāi River emerges from Shǔ.
Xǔ Shèn considered it the É River,
emerging from beyond the frontier of Wènjiāng in Shǔ,
with the water radical,
and the phonetic element "wǒ".
South to Ān'ān it enters the Dàdù River,
and the Dàdù River then flows east into the River.
Therefore, the "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
The Méng River emerges from Hànyáng,
west into the River, west of Nièyáng.
Further southeast it passes north of Bódào County,
where the Ruò River and Yān River converge and come from the west to flow into it.
Further east,
the Zhǔ River flows north and empties into it.
The county
was originally inhabited by the Bó people.
The *Geographic and Customs Record* states:
Among the barbarians, they are the most benevolent,
possessing the way of benevolence,
hence their name is written with the character for “person.”
They are the wealthy Bó servants mentioned in the *Qin Annals*.
Their settlement
was walled in the sixth year of Empress Lü’s reign.
Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn, moved by Simǎ Xiàngrú’s words,
ordered the county magistrate to open a route south to Bódào,
but the effort expended achieved no success.
Táng Méng went south and cut a path through,
then chiseled through rock and opened a passage,
to connect with the southern regions,
reaching as far as Jiànníng,
a distance of over two thousand *lǐ*,
with mountain paths more than a *zhàng* wide,
and three or four *zhàng* deep.
The marks of their chiseling still remain.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Bózhì.
The mountains abound with *yóuhú* monkeys,
resembling monkeys but with short legs,
fond of playing among cliffs and trees,
leaping a hundred paces in one bound,
or three hundred *zhàng*,
going forward smoothly and returning inverted,
riding the air as if flying.
The county has the Shǔ king’s weapon rack,
where a deity created great difficulties.
The cliffs in the river were steep and perilously obstructed,
making it impossible to cut through.
Lǐ Bīng then piled up firewood and burned them,
hence the place has hanging cliffs,
which still display five colors.
Red and white shine upon the water,
and dark yellow fish come from Bó,
stopping here,
said to fear the cliffs and islets,
and go no further up.
The *Records of the Elderly in Yì Province* states:
Zhāng Zhēn’s wife
was a woman of the Huáng clan,
named Bó.
Zhēn’s boat capsized and sank,
and his body could not be found.
Bó went to the rapids at the place of his drowning,
looked up to heaven and sighed,
then threw herself into the deep pool.
After fourteen days,
Bó emerged from beneath the rapids holding Zhēn’s hand.
People of the time said in verse:
“Fú has Xiān Luò,
Bódào has Zhāng Bó.”
The river water further joins with the Fúhēi River,
which flows from Nánguǎng County in Nánguǎng Commandery of Níngzhōu.
The county was formerly a subordinate county of Qiánwéi.
It was established in the first year of the Tàichū era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
During the Yánxī era of Liú Shàn,
it was divided to form a commandery.
It originates from Fénguān Mountain,
flowing northward,
where the Dàshè River flows into it.
The Dàshè River emerges from Nánguǎng County,
flows north and empties into the Fúhēi River,
then continues north past Bódào and enters the main river,
where it is called the Nánguǎng Estuary.
As for the Zhǔ River, it has not been heard of.
Further east, it passes south of Jiāngyáng County.
The Luò River flows from the Sānwēi Mountains,
passes east south of Luò County in Guǎngwèi,
and flows southeast to join it.
The Luò River originates from the Zhāng Mountain in Luò County,
and it is also said to originate from the Bǎi Mountain in Zǐtóng County.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
Sānwēi is located south of Dūnhuáng,
connecting to the Mín Mountain,
with the Hēi River flowing along its southern side.
However, the "Shānhǎi Jīng" does not mention the source of the Luò River.
The "Jīng" says it originates from the Sānwēi Mountain,
but this is unclear.
Cháng Qú said:
Lǐ Bīng channeled the Luò River through the mountains,
and the water flowed from the Pùkǒu,
passing through Shífāng County.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Yōng Chǐ was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Měixìn.
The Luò River then flows south past the old city of Luò County,
which was the seat of Guǎnghàn Commandery.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was the King of Hàn,
he recruited men from Bā and Yú,
and marched north to pacify Sān Qín.
In the sixth year, he divided Bā and Shǔ,
establishing Guǎnghàn Commandery at Chéngxiāng.
Wáng Mǎng called it Jiùdū,
and the county was named Wúluò.
In the second year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
the seat was moved to Fúchéng,
and later returned to Luò County.
Previously, south of Luò County's city wall,
weeping could often be heard during overcast or rainy days,
audible even within the government offices,
and this persisted for several decades.
Chén Chǒng of Pèi State served as the governor,
and attributed this to the many deaths during the chaotic times,
with exposed bones left unburied.
He thus gathered and buried them all,
and the weeping ceased.
Liú Bèi personally led an attack on Luò,
and here Páng Shìyuán was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Yìzhōu traditionally considered Shǔ Commandery, Guǎnghàn, and Qiánwéi as the "Three Shǔ,"
with fertile and beautiful land,
and outstanding and talented people,
renowned throughout the province.
The county had Shěnxiāng,
located seven lǐ from the river,
where Jiāng Shìyóu resided.
Shī was extremely filial;
his mother enjoyed drinking river water
and eating sliced raw fish.
He often fetched water upstream from the river at cockcrow.
His son, sitting
to fetch water, drowned.
Fearing her mother-in-law would find out,
the wife claimed he had gone away to study,
and each winter and summer,
she secretly threw clothes into the river.
Then, such supreme filial piety reached the heavens,
and a spring gushed forth beside their home,
with water as sweet as the river's.
Shī had fields
bordering the saline marshes by the river,
but with the spring's irrigation,
they all became fertile land.
Moreover, from the spring,
a pair of carp emerged every morning,
providing food for them.
It can be said that filial piety and brotherly love arose from the heart,
and their beautiful virtue was made known for eternity.
The Luò River then flows south past Xīndū County.
Shǔ had three capitals:
namely Chéngdū and Guǎngdū,
and this was one of them.
It merges with the Mián River,
which originates west from Miánzhú County.
It also joins with the Jiān River,
also called the Pí River,
and some say it is the Fú River.
Lǚ Chěn said:
It is also called Jiān.
However, both these rivers converge with the Luò.
Flowing past Qiánwéi's Niúbǐ County, it becomes the Niúbǐ River.
In the past, Luó Shàng rode the Niúbǐ River east to attack Lǐ Xióng,
referring to this river.
The county was established in the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
It then flows east past Zīzhōng County,
and Hàn'ān County,
where it is called the Mián River.
In all the counties above,
it is used for irrigation.
Hence the saying:
"The Mián and Luò bring fertile abundance."
The Mián River reaches the Fāng Mountain at Jiāngyáng County and enters the river,
called the Mián River Mouth,
also known as the Zhōng River.
Jiāngyáng County lies between two streams.
It is situated at the confluence of the Jiāng and Luò rivers.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Sū Jiā, Chancellor of Zhào, was enfeoffed as a marquis here,
and it became the seat of Jiāngyáng Commandery.
It was formerly the Zhījiāng Commandant of Qiánwéi,
established in the eighteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era
by Liú Zhāng.
In the river, there are large and small rapids.
In the late spring months,
the Huánglóng sandbar submerges,
and the rapids become calm.
In the past, when Shìzǔ was still obscure,
he passed through Jiāngyáng County.
He had a son,
and a diviner who observed qi said
that Jiāngyáng had the signs of a noble child.
Wáng Mǎng sought him out, and the Liáo people killed him.
Later, Shìzǔ harbored resentment,
and established a shrine for his son in the county,
punishing the people
with cloth taxes for several generations.
Yáng Xióng's "Qín Qīng Yīng" says:
Yǐn Jìfǔ's son, Bó Qí, was extremely filial.
His stepmother slandered him,
and he threw himself into the river.
Covered in moss and algae,
he suddenly dreamed of a water spirit,
who bestowed upon him a wonderful medicine.
Thinking of caring for his parents,
he raised his voice in a mournful song.
Boatmen heard it and learned it.
When Yǐn Jìfǔ heard the boatmen's song,
it resembled Bó Qí's,
so he took up his qín and composed "The Melody of Zǐ'ān."
The river flows north of Hàn'ān County.
Though the county is pressed against mountains and rivers,
its land is exceptionally fertile,
with every household engaged in sericulture, fishing, and salt production.
The river flows east past Fánshí Rapids,
and then Dàfù Rapids,
passing through two dangerous stretches.
It then flows east past the north of Fú County, turning southeast,
where the Xíbù River flows from the Fú Pass northeast into it.
The county
was originally territory of the Bā barbarians.
In the sixth year of the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Táng Méng was appointed General of the Gentlemen of the Household,
leading ten thousand men out of the Bā Fú Pass.
It was established in the second year of the Yuándǐng era,
and Wáng Mǎng called it Fúxìn.
The county seat is at the confluence of the Ānlè River,
whose source connects south to Níngzhōu's Píngyí Commandery, Biē County,
flows north through the eastern boundary of Ānlè County,
and then passes below Fú County, entering the river from the north.
The county magistrate, Zhào Zhǐ, sent his subordinate, Xiān Níhé,
in the twelfth month of the first year of the Yǒngjiàn era,
to Bā Commandery.
He drowned in the Chéngtuān Rapids.
His son, Xián, searched for the body but could not find it.
His daughter, Luò, was twenty-five years old,
with two sons
under five years old.
By the fifteenth day of the second month of the second year,
the body was still not found.
Luò then took a small boat to where her father had drowned,
wept mournfully, and threw herself into the river.
She appeared in a dream to Xián, saying:
"On the twenty-first day, I will emerge together with Father."
On that day,
father and daughter indeed floated to the surface of the river.
The commandery and county reported this,
and a stele was erected for them,
to honor their filial sincerity.
As for the Xíbù River,
nothing more is heard of it.
Perhaps it is another name for this river,
but this is not certain.
It then flows northeast to the east of Jiāngzhōu County in Bā Commandery,
where five rivers—the Qiáng River, Fú River, Hàn River, Bái River, and Dàngqú River—converge,
flowing south into it.
The river flows eastward,
and on the right reaches the mouth of Jiàngguī Creek.
The Huáyáng Jì states:
Qúrěn County produces divine turtles.
In the first year of the Xiánxī era,
a turtle was presented to the Prime Minister's residence,
said to have come from this creek.
The river flows eastward and converges with the Southern and Northern Jíqú streams.
The southern stream originates from the boundary of Fúlíng County,
called Yáng Creek.
It flows northward past the west of Nánpǔ Qiáo County in Bādōng Commandery.
On the side of the creek gorge are three salt wells,
each several tens of paces apart.
Wooden barrels are used,
with a diameter of five feet,
and boiling continues without interruption.
The creek water flows northward into the river,
called the mouth of the Southern Jíqú,
also known as the mouth of Yúyáng Creek.
The northern stream originates from the divided creek at Gāoliáng Mountain north of Xīnpǔ County,
flows southward past the west of the county,
and continues south for a hundred lǐ to Qúrěn County,
where it enters the river from the south,
called the mouth of the Northern Jíqú,
also known as Bānkǒu,
or Fēnshuǐkǒu.
The Qúrěn County Commandant governs here.
The river flows eastward and on the right passes the mouth of Sì Creek,
likely where the river's overflow enters.
The river flows eastward past Shílóng and reaches between the two villages of Bóyáng.
There is a flat rock,
four hundred zhàng wide,
six lǐ long,
blocking the river.
It submerges in summer and emerges in winter,
its base connecting to the islets.
Further east, it passes Yángcháng Hǔbì Rapid.
When Yáng Liàng served as Governor of Yìzhōu,
his boat capsized here,
and he lamented the turbulent waves.
The people of Shǔ still call it Shǐjūn Rapid to this day.
The river flows eastward,
and Péng River joins it.
The water originates from the Liáo region in Bāqú Commandery,
flowing southeast past the east of Hànfēng County.
Qīng River joins it,
its source in the Liáo region south of Bā Ridge, northeast of Bāqú County in the northwest,
which is the Bāqú River.
It flows southwest to the county,
then west into a gorge,
where Tánjǐng Creek emerges.
It then flows west out of the gorge,
reaching east of Hànfēng County and flowing west into Péng Creek,
called Qīngshuǐkǒu.
Péng Creek flows further south,
passing sixty lǐ west of Qúrěn County,
and flows south into the river,
called Péngxīkǒu.
The river flows eastward,
and on the right passes the old city wall of Qúrěn County.
Cháng Qú said:
The county is 290 lǐ west of Bādōng Commandery.
The county seat is at the old city,
straddling the mountain slope,
facing the great river to the south.
On the southern bank of the river is Fāng Mountain,
square and steep in shape,
leaning against the riverbank.
The river flows eastward past Qúwū Rapid,
also known as Xiàqú Rapid,
or Bówàng Rapid.
On the left, Tāng Creek joins it.
Its source is over 600 lǐ north of the county in the Shàngyōng region,
flowing south through the county,
flanked by a hundred salt wells,
which supply Bā and Chuān.
The larger grains are one square cùn,
raised in the center,
shaped like an open umbrella.
Hence, it is called Sǎnzi Salt.
Those that are not fully formed
are also square in shape,
different from ordinary salt.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìnshū Dìdào Jì states:
Forty-three lǐ into Tāngkǒu,
there are stones that are boiled to make salt.
The larger stones are like a shēng,
the smaller ones like a fist.
When boiled, the water dries up and salt forms,
similar to Shǔ's fire wells.
The combination of fire and water yields excellent results.
Tāng Creek flows down and merges with Tán Creek.
The water above receives Bāqú River,
flows south through Tánjǐng Creek,
called Tánjǐng Water,
and enters Tāng Creek below.
Tāng Creek flows south into the river,
called Tāngkǒu.
The river passes Dōngyáng Rapid.
On the river are broken rocks,
so it is also commonly called Pòshí Rapid,
where Xún Yánguāng perished.
Cháng Qú said:
The waterway has several rapids like Dōngyáng and Xiàqú.
The mountains have the formations of large and small stone fortresses,
as well as língshòu trees and orange orchards.
Thus, the Dìlǐ Zhì states:
The county has an orange official,
and a civilian market.
The river passes the old tomb of Yúfù County.
The old commandery seat was two lǐ west of Gùlíng Creek in Gùlíng Village.
The creek is Yǒnggǔ.
The area has many papaya trees,
bearing fruit
as large as a wǔ,
with white-yellow flesh and a strong fragrance,
which is what the Ěryǎ calls mào.
The river flows east to Luòniú Rapid,
passing north of Gùlíng.
By the river are six large graves.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said:
These are burials from when Chǔ's capital was at Dānyáng,
similar to Zhǐ's Bālíng.
Hence, it is named Gùlíng.
A Yúfù County Commandant is stationed here.
On the left bank of the river,
is Bāxiāng Village.
The villagers excel at brewing,
so it is commonly said that Bāxiāngqīng Commandery produces famous wine.
Beside the village is a creek,
with many língshòu trees in it.
There are fish in it,
with heads like sheep,
plump flesh and few bones,
more delicious than other fish.
The creek water flows underground through Píngtóu Mountain, connecting to the lake of the old Nánpǔ County.
The land is flat and open, with lakes and marshes,
containing water chestnuts, foxnuts, crucian carp, and wild geese,
no different from the outer river.
All such things
are absent within the gorges.
The area is densely inhabited by fierce barbarians,
and one should not venture there lightly.
The river flows eastward,
and on the right passes Yèqīng and eastward through Cháoyáng Dàokǒu.
There is a county seat,
with a market below it,
held once every ten days.
The river flows eastward,
and on the left passes south of Xīnshì Field.
Cháng Qú said:
Bā historically established a market on the river,
which is now Xīnshì Village.
The river flows eastward,
and on the right converges with Yángyuán River.
The water originates east of Gāoyáng Mountain, southwest of Yángkǒu County,
flowing northeast past the south of the county,
then northeast,
where Bǐng River joins it.
The water originates from Bǎizhī Mountain southeast of the county.
Below the mountain is Bǐng Cave,
several zhàng square.
Inside are fine fish,
often swimming in the shallows in late spring,
and entering the cave in early winter,
similar to the Bǎohàn Bǐng Cave.
The water flows north into Gāoyáng Creek,
which then flows northeast into the river,
called Yángyuán Stone.
The river flows eastward through Nánxiāng Gorge,
eastward past the south of Yǒng'ān Palace,
where Liú Bèi died.
It is also where Zhūgě Liàng received his final edict.
The flat land here extends about twenty lǐ,
with vast river and mountains,
unmatched within the gorges.
The city wall spans over ten lǐ,
backed by mountains and facing the river.
The crumbling walls are in ruins on all sides,
overgrown with thorns and brambles.
The local residents
mostly cultivate within.
The river flows eastward past the south of Zhūgě Liàng's diagram fortifications.
The rocky terrain is flat and open,
overlooking both river and land.
There is the Eight Formations Diagram created by Liàng,
spanning eastward from the old fortifications,
all piled with fine stones.
West of the fortifications,
stones are arranged in eight rows,
with two zhàng between rows.
It is said:
Once the Eight Formations are completed,
from now on in military campaigns,
defeat shall be avoided.
All depict the strategies of troop deployment and movement,
which even later experts could not fully comprehend.
Now, with summer floods washing away,
and years of erosion,
the higher parts are only two or three chǐ tall.
The river flows eastward again,
and the Wūfēi River flows into it.
The river originates from the boundary of Lóuzhōng County in Tiānmén Commandery,
flows north past the south of Shāqú County in Jiànpíng Commandery,
then flows north past the south of Wū County,
and travels northwest along mountain paths for 370 lǐ before flowing into the river,
where it is called the Wūfēi Mouth.
The river flows eastward again past the old city of Wū County.
The county
was originally the Wū Commandery of Chǔ.
The Qín abolished the commandery and established a county,
placing it under Nán Commandery.
Sūn Xiū of Wú divided it to form Jiànpíng Commandery,
with its seat at Wū City.
The city walls follow the mountain ridges,
with a circumference of twelve lǐ and one hundred ten paces.
The east, north, and west sides all border deep valleys,
while the south faces the great river.
This was originally the state of Kuí.
The river flows eastward again,
and the Wūxī River flows into it.
The stream originates east of Xuānhàn County in Jìnxīng Commandery of Liángzhōu,
flows south past the south of Tàichāng County in Jiànpíng Commandery,
then past the west of Běijǐng County,
turns east and passes north of the county.
South of the water are salt wells,
and the wells are north of the county,
hence the county is named Běijǐng.
These are the resources for the entire Jiànpíng Commandery.
The salt water flows down to connect with the Wūxī,
so the stream is also called the Salt Water.
The stream then bends south and passes east of Wū County.
Three hundred paces northeast of the county is a sacred spring,
called the Kǒngzǐ Spring.
Its water gushes clear from a stone cave,
pure and as high as a spring,
flowing down into the stream.
The stream then flows south into the great river.
The river flows eastward again through the Wū Gorge,
which was dug by Dù Yǔ
to allow the river to flow through.
Guō Zhòngchǎn said:
According to the "Geographical Records,"
Mount Wū is southwest of the county,
but now Mount Wū is east of the county.
This is likely because the commandery and county seats were not fixed.
The river passes through the gorge eastward to Xīnbēng Rapids.
This mountain
collapsed in the twelfth year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé of Hàn,
and collapsed again in the second year of the Tàiyuán era of Jìn.
On the day of the collapse,
the water flowed backward for over a hundred lǐ,
and surged up several tens of zhàng.
Now on the rapids there are rocks,
some round like bamboo baskets,
some square like houses,
and there are many such rocks.
They all fell from the collapsing cliffs,
causing the turbulent flow to rage,
hence it is called Xīnbēng Rapids.
The remnants of the collapsed cliffs,
compared to the other ridges,
still stand tall and lofty.
Over ten lǐ downstream is the Great Mount Wū,
which is not only unmatched in the Three Gorges,
but can also rival the peaks of Mín and É,
and stand alongside the ridges of Héng and Yí.
Its wings embrace the surrounding mountains,
reaching up to the blue clouds,
and ascending to the heavens,
distinguishing its superiority.
This is where the deity Mèng Tú resided.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
Mèng Tú, a minister of Xiàhòu Qǐ,
was in charge of deities in Bā.
When the people of Bā brought lawsuits to Mèng Tú's place,
he would arrest those whose clothes were stained with blood upon request.
He lived on the mountain,
west of Dān Mountain.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
Dān Mountain is in Dānyáng,
which belongs to Bā.
West of Dān Mountain is Mount Wū.
Also, the daughter of an emperor lived here.
Sòng Yù spoke of the youngest daughter of the Heavenly Emperor,
named Yáo Jī,
who died before she could marry.
She was enfeoffed on the southern side of Mount Wū,
and her spirit became a plant,
which is the sacred fungus.
This is the so-called maiden of Mount Wū,
on the heights of Gāotáng.
In the morning, she becomes the drifting clouds,
and in the evening, the passing rain.
Morning after morning, evening after evening,
beneath the Yángtái,
when one looks at dawn,
it is indeed as described.
Thus, a temple was built for her,
named Zhāoyún.
The gorge stretches for 160 lǐ from end to end,
and is called the Wū Gorge,
likely named after the mountain.
Within the seven hundred lǐ of the Three Gorges,
the mountains on both banks are continuous,
with almost no gaps.
Layers of cliffs and overlapping peaks hide the sky and block the sun.
Unless it is midnight or noon,
one cannot see the sun or the moon.
When the summer floods rise to the hills,
travel upstream or downstream is blocked.
If there is an urgent imperial decree to be delivered,
sometimes one departs from Báidì at dawn
and reaches Jiānglíng by dusk,
covering twelve hundred lǐ in between.
Even riding a swift horse or harnessing the wind
would not match this speed.
In spring and winter,
there are white rapids and green pools,
with clear reflections swirling upside down.
On the steep cliffs grow many strange cypresses,
with hanging springs and waterfalls
cascading between them.
Clear, lush, lofty, and dense,
it is truly full of charm.
Whenever the sky clears after rain or on frosty mornings,
the woods are cold and the streams serene.
Often, high-up monkeys give long cries,
continuous and eerily mournful.
The empty valleys carry the echoes,
lingering mournfully for a long time before fading.
Thus, the fishermen sing:
"Of the Three Gorges in Bādōng, the Wū Gorge is the longest;
three cries of the monkeys, and tears soak one's clothes."
The river flows eastward again past Shímén Rapids.
On the north bank of the rapids is a mountain,
joined at the top and open at the bottom,
forming a passage from east to west,
which is the path along the river.
Liú Bèi was defeated by Lù Xùn
and fled through this gate.
The pursuers were pressing hard,
so Bèi burned his armor and blocked the road.
Sūn Huán served as Xùn's vanguard,
fighting desperately without regard for his life.
He cut off the road to Upper Kuí,
intercepting the crucial path.
Bèi crossed mountains and traversed dangers,
barely managing to escape.
Furious and resentful, he sighed:
"When I once went to the capital,
Huán was still a child,
yet now he presses me so hard
that it has come to this."
Thus, he died of rage.
Further east, it passes south of Zǐguī County.
The county,
formerly Guīxiāng.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
It was the state of Guīzǐ.
The "Musical Apocrypha" states:
In ancient times, Guī was in charge of harmonizing the musical pitches.
Sòng Zhōng states:
Guī is Kuí,
Guīxiāng,
is probably Kuíxiāng.
Among the legitimate heirs of ancient Chǔ, there was one named Xióng Zhì,
who, due to a disability, was not established [as ruler],
and resided in Kuí,
becoming a vassal of Chǔ,
later the king appointed him as the Viscount of Kuí.
In the 26th year of Duke Xī of the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
Chǔ, because he did not perform the sacrifices,
destroyed him.
Yuán Shānsōng states:
Qū Yuán had a virtuous elder sister,
who heard that Yuán had been exiled,
also came back,
admonished him to comfort himself,
the entire village hoped she would be heeded,
therefore the place was named Zǐguī,
which is what the "Lí Sāo" refers to as "Nǚ Xū, graceful and gentle, admonishing me."
The county town leans against the mountain on the northeast, following the slope,
its circumference is two lǐ,
its height is one zhàng five chǐ,
it faces the great river to the south,
according to ancient tradition,
it is called Liú Bèi City,
probably built when Bèi campaigned against Wú.
Several tens of lǐ northeast of the county are the old fields and residence of Qū Yuán,
although the ridges and banks are overgrown and dilapidated,
they still retain the name "Qū's fields."
One hundred sixty lǐ north of the county is Qū Yuán's former residence,
with piled stones forming the foundation of the house,
the place is named Lèpíng Lǐ,
sixty lǐ northeast of the residence is the Nǚ Xū Temple,
the clothes-beating stone still remains.
Therefore, the "Records of Yídu" states:
Zǐguī was probably the initial state of Chǔ's lord Xióng Yì,
and is the hometown of Qū Yuán.
Yuán's fields and residence still exist today.
This refers to that.
The river water again flows east past the north of a city,
this city relies on the ridge for its fortifications,
two hundred ten paces,
flanked by a stream and facing a valley,
occupying the mountain and resting against the river,
facing Dānyáng City to the north,
this city occupies the mountain and straddles the hill,
its circumference is eight lǐ two hundred eighty paces,
its eastern and northern sides,
all face sheer ravines,
to the west it borders Tíngxià Stream,
to the south it rests against the great river,
steep and cliff-like, standing erect,
truly a natural stronghold.
It is where Chǔ's lord Xióng Yì was first enfeoffed at Dānyáng and established his capital.
The "Treatise on Geography" considers it to be Wú's Dānyáng,
commentators say:
considering that Wú and Chǔ are far apart,
and the rugged Jīng Mountains,
it cannot possibly be far in Wú territory,
this is incorrect.
Moreover, the tombs of Chǔ's former kings are located there,
which is probably evidence.
The river water again flows southeast past the south of Kuí City,
which straddles and occupies the river and hill,
its circumference is one lǐ one hundred eighteen paces,
to the northwest it backs against a deep valley,
to the east it borders Xiāngkǒu Stream,
to the south it faces the great river,
within the city at the northwest corner is the Golden City,
at the northeast corner is the circular earth prison,
at the southwest corner is a stone well.
Its mouth diameter is five chǐ.
Xióng Zhì initially governed Wū City,
later moved here due to illness,
probably the relocation of Kuí.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" of the "Spring and Autumn Annals," 26th year of Duke Xī,
records Chǔ's Lingyǐn Zǐ Yù fortifying Kuí.
Fú Qián states:
It is south of Wū,
which is Zǐguī, Guīxiāng.
The river water again flows east past the north of the old city of Guīxiāng County,
Yuán Shānsōng states:
According to the elders' tradition,
after Yuán was exiled,
he suddenly briefly returned,
the villagers were overjoyed,
therefore it was named Guīxiāng (Returning Home).
Moreover, its mountains are beautiful and waters clear,
thus producing outstanding talents,
the terrain is perilous and the currents swift,
therefore their nature is also constrained.
The "Book of Songs" says:
The sacred mountain descends spirits,
giving birth to Fǔ and Shēn.
Truly so.
I say Shānsōng's words here can be said to use events to establish evidence,
but I fear this is not the original intent behind naming the county.
The county town faces layered ridges to the south,
backs against the great river to the north,
borders Xiāngkǒu Stream to the east,
the stream's source emerges several hundred lǐ southeast of the county,
flows northwest into the county,
passes west of Gǒu Gorge,
within a niche in the gorge cliff,
a stone protrudes resembling a dog's shape,
its form fully complete,
therefore the gorge is named after the dog.
Xiāngkǒu Stream again flows northwest past the county and enters the river,
this is called Xiāngkǒu.
The river water again flows east past the south of Xìnlíng County,
facing the great river,
bordering a deep stream to the east,
the stream's source arises north in the territory of Shàngyōng County, Liángzhōu,
flows south past the county and empties into the great river.
Again, it flows east past the south of Yílíng County.
The river flows from Jiànpíng to the Eastern Boundary Gorge,
which Shèng Hóngzhī called the Kōnglíng Gorge.
The gorge is extremely high and steep,
marking the boundary between the two commanderies of Yíjùn and Jiànpíng.
Looking into the distance from within it,
the ridges appear to intersect beyond the mountain ranges,
with five or six peaks rising unevenly.
Above, there are strange rocks resembling two figures with sleeves rolled up, facing each other.
Folklore says that the supervising couriers of the two commanderies disputed the boundary here.
The supervising courier of Yíjùn Commandery appears to lean slightly eastward,
and commentators consider this inferior.
The river passes through the gorge
and flows east past the Chāzào of Yíchāng County.
On the left bank of the river,
the sheer cliffs stand hundreds of *zhàng* high,
where even birds cannot perch.
There is a burnt-out torch,
inserted into the cliff face,
visible from a distance, measuring several *chǐ* in length.
The elders pass down the story
that during the great flood in ancient times,
people moored their boats by the cliff
and stuck the remaining torch into the rock face.
It has remained there to this day,
and thus, over generations,
it has been called Chāzào (Inserted Hearth).
The river then flows east past Liútóu Rapid,
where the water is swift, turbulent, and violent,
making it impossible for fish and turtles to swim,
and travelers often suffer from it.
A song says:
"At the rapid's head, white waves fiercely clash,
in an instant, swallowed forever, no return."
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"From Shǔ to here is over five thousand *lǐ*;
going downstream takes five days,
but upstream takes a hundred days."
The river then flows east past the north of Yíchāng County,
which was established from parts of Yídào and Héngshān.
The county seat is on the southern bank of the river,
resting against the great river to the north,
facing Yílíng across the boundary.
The *Yídū Jì* says:
"Crossing Liútóu Rapid for ten *lǐ*,
one reaches Yíchāng County."
The river then flows east past Lángwěi Rapid and then Rén Rapid.
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"The two rapids are two *lǐ* apart.
The water at Rén Rapid is extremely steep and swift.
On the southern bank, there is a bluish rock
that submerges in summer and emerges in winter.
The rock is lofty and rugged,
and within a few dozen paces, it is entirely shaped like human faces,
some large, some small.
The distinct ones
even have beards and hair fully formed.
Hence, it is named Rén Rapid."
The river then flows east past Huángniú Mountain,
below which lies a rapid
named Huángniú Rapid.
On the southern bank, ridges rise layer upon layer.
On the outermost high cliff, there is a rock
shaped like a man carrying a knife and leading an ox,
with the man black and the ox yellow,
clearly formed.
Since it is beyond human reach,
no one can investigate it further.
This cliff is already high,
and coupled with the river's winding torrents,
even after traveling for two nights,
one can still see this sight.
Thus, travelers chant:
"At dawn, we depart from Huángniú,
at dusk, we lodge at Huángniú,
after three dawns and three dusks,
Huángniú remains as before."
This means the waterway is winding and deep,
and looking back, it appears unchanged.
The river then flows east past Xīlíng Gorge.
The *Yídū Jì* says:
"Entering the Xīlíng boundary from Huángniú Rapid eastward,
to the gorge's mouth is about a hundred *lǐ*,
with winding mountains and rivers.
High mountains and layered barriers line both banks,
so unless it is noon or midnight,
the sun and moon are not visible.
The sheer cliffs sometimes reach about a thousand *zhàng*.
The rocks are colorful,
their forms often resembling various things.
The trees are tall and lush,
remaining so through winter and spring.
The gibbons' cries are exceptionally clear,
echoing through the valleys,
lingering endlessly.
This is one of the so-called Three Gorges."
Shānsōng said:
"I often heard that the water in the gorge is swift,
and both written records and oral accounts
all warn of the danger and fear,
never praising the beauty of the mountains and waters.
But when I came to tread this land myself,
upon arriving, I was delighted,
and finally believed that hearing is not as good as seeing with one's own eyes.
The layered cliffs and elegant peaks,
their strange structures and unusual shapes,
are truly difficult to describe in words.
The trees are dense and towering,
lush and flourishing,
reaching beyond the misty clouds.
Looking up or gazing down at the reflections,
the more familiar, the more beautiful it becomes.
Lingering for two nights,
I unconsciously forgot to return.
What my eyes have witnessed
is something I have never experienced before.
Since I delighted in discovering this wondrous sight,
if the mountains and waters have spirits,
they too should be astonished to find a kindred soul after millennia."
The river flows past Yǔ's Severed River to the south,
and north of the gorge lies Qīgǔ Village.
Between two mountains, there is clear, deep water,
forming a pool that does not flow.
Also, the *Qíjiù Zhuàn* says:
"In the past, this was part of the great river.
When Yǔ controlled the floods,
this river was too small to drain the water,
so Yǔ opened the present gorge mouth instead.
The water rushed through with combined force,
and this river was cut off.
To this day, it is called Duànjiāng (Severed River)."
The river exits the gorge and flows southeast,
passing Gùchéng Islet.
The islet is attached to the northern bank,
and its head is called Guō Islet,
two *lǐ* long
and one *lǐ* wide.
On it lies the old city of Bù Chǎn,
its shape matching the islet,
nearly filling its circumference.
The old city on Gùchéng Islet has a perimeter of five *lǐ*,
built by Bù Zhì, the Xīlíng commander of Wú.
In the first year of the Fènghuáng era of Sūn Hào,
Zhì's son Chǎn again became Xīlíng commander
and surrendered this city to Jìn.
Jìn sent Grand Tutor Yáng Hù to receive and aid him,
but before he arrived,
it was captured by Lù Kàng.
The river then flows east past the north of the old city,
which is called Lù Kàng's City.
The city uses the mountain as its walls,
with natural defenses on all sides.
On the southern bank of the river, there is a solitary, elegant mountain.
Looking up from the river,
it appears as a sheer, steep cliff.
When Yuán Shānsōng served as the commandery governor,
he once climbed it to gaze afar.
Thus, his *Jì* says:
"Now, ascending from the mountain's south to its ridge,
the ridge can accommodate about ten people.
Looking around at the various mountains from all sides,
one can roughly see their entire layout.
Looking down at the great river,
it resembles a coiled ribbon,
and boats appear like ducks and geese."
To the north lies the old city of Yílíng County,
whose southern side faces the great river.
This is where the Qín general Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
and after three battles, burned Yílíng.
Yìng Shào said:
"Yí Mountain lies to the northwest,
so the county was named after the mountain."
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Jūlì,
but in the first year of the Huángwǔ era of Wú,
it was renamed Xīlíng.
Later, it was again called Yílíng.
Thirty *lǐ* north of the county, there is a stone cave,
named Mǎ Chuān (Horse Passage).
Once, a white horse emerged from the cave,
and people chased it.
It entered the cave, traveled underground, and emerged in Hànzhōng.
People from Hànzhōng who lost horses also once emerged from this cave,
though the distance between them is several thousand *lǐ*.
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"North of the river, there are many connected mountains.
Climbing them to look at the mountains south of the river,
they appear in tens or hundreds of layers,
their names unknown.
The high ones reach a thousand *rèn*,
with many strange shapes and unusual forms.
Unless the mist disperses and the rain clears,
one cannot discern these distant mountains."
I have traveled back and forth about ten times,
and could only catch glimpses of the distant peaks.
The river then flows east past Báilù Cliff, where along the river, there are steep cliffs over a hundred *zhàng* high,
where even gibbons cannot roam.
There was once a white deer
that scaled the steep cliffs,
ascending along the rock face.
Hence, this cliff is popularly known as Báilù Cliff.
The river flows eastward through the area between Jīngmén and Hǔyá.
Jīngmén is to the south,
joined at the top and open at the bottom,
piercing through the southern part of the mountain.
There is a gate resembling tiger teeth,
located to the north,
with reddish stone cliffs,
interlaced with white veins,
resembling the shape of teeth,
both named after their physical resemblance.
These two mountains
are the western fortifications of Chǔ.
The water current is swift and steep,
hence Guō Jǐngchún's "Ode to the River" says:
"Hǔyá stands tall and precipitous,
Jīngmén soars aloft and spreads wide;
the deep whirlpools churn and surge,
the torrents roar like thunder and flash like lightning."
In the eleventh year of the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn dynasty,
Gōngsūn Shù dispatched his Grand Minister over the Masses Rén Mǎn and the River-Supporting King Tián Róng,
leading tens of thousands of troops,
to take advantage of the strategic terrain and build a pontoon bridge,
spanning the river to block the waterway,
with encampments stretching across the mountains,
to block the land routes.
Emperor Guāngwǔ dispatched Wú Hàn and Cén Péng with sixty thousand troops to attack Jīngmén.
Hàn and others led the naval forces to assault it,
charging directly at the pontoon bridge,
and taking advantage of the wind to set fires,
thus beheading Mǎn and others.
Further east, it passes north of Yídào County.
The Yí River flows from south of Hěnshān County,
and empties into it from the northeast.
Yídào County
was where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn campaigned against the southwestern barbarians,
and the route passed through here,
hence it was called Yídào.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Jiāngnán.
Because Huán Wēn's father's name was Yì,
it was changed to Xīdào.
Wèi Wǔ divided Nánjùn to establish Línjiāng Commandery.
Liú Bèi renamed it Yídū.
The commandery seat was located at the old city four hundred paces east of the county,
built by the Wú chancellor Lù Xùn,
at the confluence of two rivers.
To the north is Húlǐyuān,
above which orange trees cover the fields,
and mulberry and hemp obscure the sun.
Looking west at the various ridges of Hěnshān,
layered peaks rise in beauty,
with verdant greenery adjoining each other.
At times, rosy clouds and white mists
drift and linger above them.
Northeast of the city is Wàngtáng,
a particularly steep place,
overlooking the clear river below,
a famous spot for sightseeing.
North of the county is Nǚguànshān,
a high and prominent location,
offering distant views in all directions.
According to ancient tradition,
long ago, a pining woman whose husband served as an official in Shǔ,
and who repeatedly missed their autumn rendezvous,
climbed this mountain in despair,
and died of grief.
The mountain trees withered and became barren,
turning into a bald and desolate place.
The villagers pitied her,
and thus named this mountain Nǚguàn.
She was buried on the mountain top,
and her solitary grave remains to this day.
Further east, it passes south of Zhījiāng County.
The Jǔ River flows from the north and empties into it.
The river then flows east past north of Shàngmíng City.
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
when Fú Jiān invaded Jīngzhōu,
Governor Huán Chōng moved across the river to the south,
and had Liú Bō build it,
relocating the provincial seat to this city.
The land is level and open,
bordering the great river to the north.
The river branches into tributaries,
which flow east into the main river.
The county seat is on an island,
hence it is called Zhījiāng.
The "Treatise on Geography" says:
"The Jiāngtuó emerges from the west,
and flows east into the river." This is it.
This area
was the ancient state of Luó,
likely where Luó relocated.
Luó originally resided west of Yíchéng Mountain.
King Wén of Chǔ later moved them to Chángshā,
which is present-day Luó County.
Three lǐ west of the county is Jīnxiāng.
Jīnxiāng
is the name of a hamlet.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Zhuāng of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Bā people attacked Chǔ.
The ruler of Chǔ defended against them,
but suffered a major defeat at Jīn.
Yìng Shào said:
"Nánjùn's Jiānglíng has a Jīnxiāng."
But today it is no longer heard of.
Guō Zhòngchǎn said:
"Investigating Chǔ's defense against the Bā people,
Zhījiāng was their route.
This Jīnxiāng
is likely that place."
Shèng Hóngzhī said:
"The county was originally located in Jǔzhōng,
but later moved west of Bǎilǐzhōu,
one hundred and sixty lǐ from the commandery.
To the left and right of the county, several dozen islands are scattered in the river,
among which Bǎilǐzhōu is the largest.
Within it are mulberry fields and sweet fruits,
reflected in the river and leaning against the island.
From west of the county to Shàngmíng in the east and Jiāngjīn,
there are ninety-nine islands.
A Chǔ proverb says:
"If the islands do not number a hundred,
then a true king will not emerge."
Huán Xuán harbored ambitions for the throne,
so he added an island to make the count one hundred.
He usurped the title for several decades,
but his clan was exterminated and he was slaughtered.
When he fell,
the island also vanished.
Now that the emperor is in the west,
suddenly an island spontaneously emerged.
Sand and currents swirled around it,
forming in no time.
Not long after,
the dragon soared over the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Two lǐ east of the county is the former residence of the county native Liú Níngzhī.
Níngzhī, styled Zhì'ān,
had an elder brother, Shènggōng, who was noble and did not serve in office.
Níngzhī admired Lǎo Lái
and Yán Zǐlíng's way of life.
He built a house by the rivers and lakes,
and would not eat without working.
His wife was the daughter of Guō Quán, Governor of Liángzhōu,
and she too could endure poverty.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
the couple retreated to Héngshān,
and never returned.
Ten lǐ northeast of the county, on the northern bank of Tǔtái, is Yǐzhōu,
over ten lǐ long.
At the beginning of the Yìxī era,
this is where Lièwǔ Wáng executed Huán Qiān.
Twenty lǐ southeast of the county, on Fùchéngzhōu, is the hermitage of the Daoist Fàn Chái.
He claimed to be from Bādōng,
and traveled to Jīng in his youth,
often lingering within the county's borders.
He wore coarse clothes and ate simple food,
living freely and contentedly.
His predictions often came true,
but his words were cryptic.
If someone wished to see him,
he would suddenly appear to converse,
but if one sought him by appearance,
they would never find him.
Although he crossed various islands,
boatmen never saw him ferrying across.
Later, he traveled east to Guǎnglíng,
and died there.
Chái had no fixed dwelling,
only resting in a small hut.
His disciples admired him,
and at the places he once frequented,
they jointly built a hermitage,
to preserve his memory.
The county has a temple for Chénliú Wáng Zǐxiāng.
The inscription praises Zǐxiāng, who during the reign of Emperor Hé of Hàn,
served as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and implemented benevolent governance.
The emperor summoned him,
but he died on the way at the Zhījiāng post station.
Often, three white tigers would appear among the people,
escorting the funeral procession beyond the border.
The people, cherishing his memory like the sweet pear tree,
in the eighteenth year of the Yǒngyuán era, built a temple and established sacrifices,
engraving a stone to record his virtue,
and named him "Zhījiāng White Tiger Lord Wáng."
His descendants to this day still call him the White Tiger King.
The river then flows east to meet the Jǔ estuary,
which King Zhāo of Chǔ referred to as the Jiāng, Hàn, Jǔ, and Zhāng rivers,
the sacred rivers of Chǔ.
Further south, it passes south of Jiānglíng County.
North of the county lies an islet,
named Méihuí Zhōu.
From here, the river water splits into two,
forming the Southern and Northern Rivers.
On the Northern River is Gùxiāng Zhōu.
At the end of the Yuánxīng era,
when Huán Xuán fled westward,
Máo Yòuzhī and the army advisor Fèi Tián shot arrows at Huán Xuán on this islet.
Huán Xuán's son, Shēng, who was six years old at the time,
immediately pulled them out.
Wáng Shàozhī stated:
When Huán Xuán first fled,
he went a whole day without food.
When his attendants offered him coarse porridge, he could not swallow it.
Shēng embraced his father's chest and comforted him,
causing Huán Xuán to be overwhelmed with grief.
Later, at this place,
Féng Qiān, the Protector of Yìzhōu, beheaded Huán Xuán on this islet,
and Shēng was executed in Jiānglíng.
Downstream lies Lóng Zhōu,
and east of this islet is Chǒng Zhōu.
Between these two islets,
the waters have always been abundant with fish.
Fishermen cast their nets and spread their weirs,
but they often got tangled and torn.
A diver once swam down to investigate
and saw two stone oxen underwater,
which were the cause of damage to the nets.
Therefore, fishermen would all stir the waves to float their boats,
beat their oars, and depart.
Downstream is what is called Bǐnglǐ Zhōu.
On this islet is Gāoshā Lake.
Northeast of the lake, a small waterway connects to the river,
named Zēngkǒu.
The river then flows east past the north of Yānwěi Zhōu,
where it converges with Língxī Stream.
This stream has no spring source;
it gathers scattered surface water upstream,
combines to form a large stream,
and flows south into the river.
At the confluence of the river and the stream is the Língxī Garrison,
backed by hills and facing the river,
with Língxī Stream winding to its west,
hence the garrison derives its name.
Eastward, the river reaches Mǎmùkǒu,
where the river cuts through an islet to form a confluence.
The river then flows east past the old city of Jiānglíng County.
The "Tribute of Yu" states:
"From Jīng Mountain to Héngyáng is Jīngzhōu."
It seems the name was derived from Jīng Mountain,
and thus the province was named.
This was the territory of ancient Chǔ.
Zǐ Gé said:
"Our former lord resided in the remote Jīng Mountain,
serving the royal affairs,
and later moved to Jìyǐng."
The present city
was the site of the Chǔ shipyard,
the Zhǔgōng of the Spring and Autumn period.
In the twenty-ninth year of King Zhāoxiāng of Qín,
he sent Bái Qǐ to capture Yānyǐng,
and established Nánjùn with the lands south of the Hàn River.
The "Zhōushū" states:
"Nán
is a state name.
The Nán clan had two ministers,
equal in strength and power,
who competed for advancement and authority.
The ruler could not control them,
so the Nán clan split into two Nán states."
According to Hán Yīng's "Preface to the Odes":
"Its territory lay between Nánjùn and Nányáng."
This is what the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" refers to when it says, "Yǔ inspected the southern lands from Túshān."
The commandery took its name from this.
Later, Emperor Jǐng of Hàn enfeoffed it as the state of Línjiāng King Róng.
The king was accused of encroaching on temple grounds to build his palace
and was summoned to the capital.
As his carriage passed through the north gate, the axle broke.
The elders secretly wept,
saying:
"Our king will not return."
Thereafter, the north gate was never opened again,
likely because Róng met an unjust end.
In the second year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
it was renamed Jiānglíng County.
Wáng Mǎng changed the names again,
calling the commandery Nánshùn
and the county Jiānglù.
The old city
was built by Guān Yǔ.
When Guān Yǔ besieged Cáo Rén in the north,
Lǚ Méng launched a surprise attack and seized it.
Guān Yǔ said:
"This city was built by me;
it cannot be assaulted."
So he withdrew his forces.
When Dù Yuánkǎi attacked Jiānglíng,
the defenders on the wall tied a gourd around a dog's neck and showed it to him,
mocking Dù Yuánkǎi's goiter.
After the city fell,
he slaughtered the old and young within,
and blood flowed so profusely it soaked his feet.
Commentators of the time looked down on him for this.
The land of Jiānglíng City slopes to the southeast,
so it was reinforced with a golden dike,
starting from Língxī.
Huán Wēn ordered Chén Zūn to construct it.
Chén Zūn was skilled in surveying and engineering.
He had drums beaten
and listened from afar
to determine the high and low points of the terrain.
Based on this, he built the dike,
with almost no error.
West of the city is Qīxiá Tower,
overlooking the moat,
which channels the river flow.
South of the city is Mǎmù City,
with a horse path to its west.
This stretch of islets extends from Méihuí down to here,
over seventy lǐ in length.
On the islet is Fèngchéng,
formerly the seat of the Jiāngjīn Chief,
who was responsible for managing the crossing for the commanderies,
and transporting tribute to Luòyáng.
Hence it was called Fèngchéng [Tribute City],
also known as the Jiāngjīn Garrison.
South of the garrison faces Mǎtóu Bank.
In the past, Lù Kàng was stationed here facing Yáng Hù,
and they greatly upheld trust and righteousness.
Commentators considered them
a reappearance of Huá Yuán and Zǐ Fǎn in their time.
North of the garrison faces a large bank,
called Jiāngjīnkǒu,
from which the islet also derived its name.
Here the river begins to widen significantly.
The "Family Sayings of Confucius" states:
"When the river reaches Jiāngjīn,
unless one uses a double-hulled boat to avoid the wind,
it cannot be crossed."
Therefore, Guō Jǐngchún said:
"Crossing Jiāngjīn, the waters swell."
This describes its depth and breadth.
The river then flows east past the south of Yǐngchéng,
the city built according to Zǐ Náng's dying wish.
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
"A separate town of Chǔ."
It was the old Yǐng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yǐngtíng.
Within the city is the tomb of Zhào Táiqīng,
which Zhào Qí prepared for himself during his lifetime.
The tomb depicts images of host and guests,
to preserve their affection,
recounting his longstanding aspirations.
The river then flows east to Yùzhāngkǒu,
which connects to the Xià River.
To the northwest is Yùzhāng Ridge,
from which the place likely derived its name.
Some say it was named after the Yùzhāng Terrace of the King of Chǔ,
but this is not certain.
35 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 35
35.1 The River
35.1 The River
further flows east to the west of Huáróng County,
where the Xià River emerges.
The river branches left to form the Zhōngxià River,
while to the right, Zhōnglángpǔ emerges.
The river branch on the right curves southward and then turns west,
forming an extreme bend in the watercourse,
which people call the River Bend.
Further southeast, opposite the south of Huáróng County,
Yǒngshuǐ flows into it.
The river then flows east,
where Yǒngshuǐ joins it.
This waterway connects south from the Xià River to the main river,
and is called Yǒngkǒu.
Between these two waterways
is where, according to the "Spring and Autumn Annals," Yán Áo wandered at Yǒng and escaped.
The river then flows past the north of Lèxiāng City in Chánlíng County, Nánpíng Commandery,
which was built by Wú's Lù Kàng.
Later, Wáng Jùn attacked it
and captured Wú's naval commander Lù Jǐng on this islet.
Further southeast,
Yóushuǐ flows from the southeast to join it.
Further east,
it joins the Yóu River mouth on the right,
then flows east past the north of Gōng'ān County.
When Liú Bèi fled to Jiānglíng,
he had a fortress built and garrisoned here.
When Cáo Cāo heard that Sūn Quán had lent Jīngzhōu to Liú Bèi,
he dropped his brush in shock while writing.
After Dù Yù conquered the region south of the river,
he abolished Huáróng and established
what was called Jiāng'ān County,
the seat of Nánjùn Commandery.
The Wú state made the southern district of Huáróng into Nánjùn Commandery,
and in the first year of the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty (280 CE),
it was renamed Nánpíng.
The county has the Yóu River,
east of which is the Jǐng River mouth,
which marks the boundary of Wǔlíng Commandery.
East of the Jǐng River mouth is the Lún River mouth,
where the Lún River joins the Jǐng River from the south,
and further east connects to the Lǐ River and various lakes and ponds.
From here, deep pools and lakes are linked together,
all being military settlements of the Southern Man Commandery.
Thus, beside the river stands a large walled city,
traditionally known as the Granary Storage City,
which served as a depot.
The river joins the Gāo River mouth on the left,
a river inlet.
To the right, it faces Huángzhōu,
and the river then flows east to the old Shì River mouth,
where the waters connect with the Gāo River.
The river then passes north of Yángqí Mountain on the right,
which rests against the great river.
East of the mountain is a walled city,
the former seat of the Huáróng County Commandant.
The great river flows further east,
joining the Zǐxià River mouth on the left.
The river bends northward on the left,
connecting to the Xià River,
hence the name Zǐxià.
Further east, the great river meets the Hóutái River mouth on the left,
a river inlet.
On the right, it meets the Lóngxué River mouth,
an inlet bending to the right.
To the north, it faces Hǔzhōu Island,
