and north of the island is Lóngcháo,
a place name.
In ancient times, when Yǔ crossed the river southward,
two yellow dragons flanked his boat.
The boatmen were terrified and lost composure,
but Yǔ laughed and said,
"I have received my mandate from Heaven,
and I strive to nourish the people.
Life
is nature;
death
is fate.
Why fear dragons?"
Thereupon, the two dragons lowered their scales, turned their tails, and departed.
Hence, the water and land took their names from this.
From Lóngcháo, the river flows east to the Yú River mouth,
which exists when the Xià River floods in summer
but disappears in winter.
On the northern bank of the river is a small walled city,
the former seat of the Jiānlì County Commandant.
Further east are the Qīngyáng and Tǔwù River mouths,
both river inlets.
The great river passes north of Shíshǒu Mountain on the right,
then flows east past Zhěyāo.
Zhěyāo
is the name of an island,
located in the great river, downstream from Běihúzhōu Island.
On the left, the river meets the upper Fànkuāng River mouth,
which connects to the lower mouth in summer and autumn.
Between the upper and lower mouths,
the distance is over thirty lǐ.
Downstream from Zhěyāo is Yángzǐzhōu Island,
located in the great river.
Between these two islands,
people often suffered from flood dragon disasters,
until Jīng Cìfēi once crossed here,
encountered two flood dragons,
and slew them.
Since then, such calamities have rarely occurred.
On the right bank of the river
is the Qīngshuǐ River mouth,
above which is the Qiánguān office.
The water flows from Niúpí Mountain northeast to connect with the river,
facing Qīngshuǐzhōu Island to the north.
Downstream, it connects to Shēngjiāngzhōu Island,
and to the south is the Shēngjiāng River mouth,
which connects southward to the Lǐ River inlet.
On the left, the river joins the lower Fànkuāng River mouth,
an inlet where river waters enter.
Further on the right, the river meets the Shàngtán River inlet,
a river branch.
The river then flows east past the south of Zhútīng,
where in the river lies the Guānxiáng River branch.
East of the branch is a large island,
which splits eastward into Juézhōu Island.
South of the island faces the Xiāng River mouth.
Further east, it reaches the north of Xiàjuàn County in Chángshā,
where the Lǐ, Yuán, and Zī rivers converge
and flow east to join it.
All these waters
flow into the marsh of Dòngtíng Lake,
which is the Xiāng River,
not a branch of the great river.
The Xiāng River flows from the south to join it.
The river water converges with the Xiāng River on the right,
which is what is called the confluence of the river waters.
The river water then flows east,
and on the left, it receives the Èr Xià Pǔ,
commonly known as the Xījiāng Kǒu.
Further east, it passes by the south of Jìzhì Shān,
east of the mountain lies Yǐn Kǒu Pǔ.
On the right bank of the river is Chénglíng Shān,
on the mountain there is an ancient city,
which connects eastward to Wēiluò Shān,
also called Huīluò Jī.
The southern bank of the river is named Huángjīn Lài,
east of the lài are Huángjīn Pǔ and Liángfù Kǒu,
which are summer inlets.
Further east, it passes by Péngchéng Kǒu,
east of the water is Péngchéng Jī,
hence the water takes its name,
which is the Yù Jiàn Shuǐ,
originating from Yù Shān and Yù Xī east of Bāqiū Xiàn,
flowing northward into the river.
The river water from Péngchéng Jī flows east past the north of Rú Shān,
facing Yǐn Jī to the north,
between the two jī,
there is a solitary rock standing alone in the middle of the great river,
east of the mountain is a river inlet,
commonly known as Báimǎ Kǒu.
The river water then passes left by the south of Báiluó Shān,
and right past the north of Yālán Jī,
which is an island in the river.
To the east are Yā Lán and Zhì Pǔ, two inlets,
which are summer inlets.
The river water passes left by the south of Shàng Wūlín,
a village and place name.
Further east, it passes by Wūlí Kǒu,
a river inlet,
which is Zhōng Wūlín.
Further east, it passes by the south of Xià Wūlín,
where Wú’s Huáng Gài defeated Wèi Wǔ at Wūlín,
exactly at this place.
The river water flows further east,
and on the left, it receives Zǐliàn Kǒu.
It connects north to Liàn Pǔ,
and further east, it joins Liàn Kǒu,
a river inlet.
To the south lies Liàn Zhōu,
from which the name “Liàn” originates.
On the right bank of the river is Pú Jī Kǒu,
which is Lù Kǒu.
The water originates from Sānshān Xī west of Xiàjuàn Xiàn,
flowing east past the north of Lùchéng,
and further east past the south of Xiàjuàn Xiàn,
formerly an old county of Chángshā,
called Rùn Juàn under Wáng Mǎng.
In the sixteenth year of the Sòng Yuánjiā era,
it was transferred to Bālíng Jùn.
The Lù Shuǐ then bends and flows northwest,
passing north of the county,
facing Jīnchéng to the north,
where Wú general Lù Huàn was stationed.
The Lù Shuǐ then enters Púqí Xiàn,
flowing north past the west of Lǚ Méng Chéng,
where Sūn Quán once campaigned against Chángshā’s Líng and Guì and stationed troops.
The Lù Shuǐ then passes by Pú Jī Shān,
and enters the great river to the north,
called Dāohuán Kǒu.
Further east, it passes north of Pú Jī Shān,
facing Púqí Zhōu to the north,
also called Qíng Zhōu,
and also Nán Zhōu.
At the head of the zhōu,
lies the seat of Púqí Xiàn,
established in the first year of the Jìn Tàikāng era.
On the zhōu is Báimiàn Zhōu,
and south of the zhōu is also Hòng Kǒu,
where water originates from Ài Xiàn in Yùzhāng,
flowing east into Púqí Xiàn,
and entering the river at Yúyuè Shān northwest of Shāyáng.
The mountain lies in the middle of the great river, south of Yángzǐ Zhōu,
standing alone in the middle of the zhōu.
On the left of the river water is Zhōngyáng Shuǐ Kǒu,
and further east is Báishā Kǒu,
also called Shā Tún,
which is Má Tún Kǒu,
originally named Mièmò Kǒu,
a river inlet.
To the south lies Púqí Zhōu,
the water enters north for over a hundred lǐ,
where Wú troops were stationed.
Further passing north of Yúyuè Shān,
below is Jīnliáng Zhōu,
northeast of the zhōu facing Yuān Zhōu,
also called Yuānbù Zhōu,
a riverbank.
From the head of the zhōu upstream,
all are sheer cliffs with no banks,
passing from Púqí to Báishā before there are inlets,
making upstream travel very difficult.
In the river is Shāyáng Zhōu.
It is the seat of Shāyáng Xiàn,
the county was originally Shāyì of Jiāngxià,
renamed Shāyáng Xiàn during the Jìn Tàikāng era,
in the sixteenth year of the Sòng Yuánjiā era,
it was transferred to Bālíng Jùn.
On the right bank of the river is Yōng Kǒu,
also called Gǎng Kǒu.
Flowing northeast, it becomes Chángyáng Gǎng.
Further northeast, it passes by Shízǐ Gāng,
on the gāng is an ancient city,
which is the old city of Zhōulíng Xiàn.
As Zhuāng Xīn said,
it was the state of Zuǒ Zhōu Hóu.
Further east, it passes south of the new seat of Zhōulíng,
called Jiāngxià under Wáng Mǎng.
The gǎng water flows southeast into the river,
called Yáng Kǒu,
facing Lóngxué Zhōu to the south,
which is the lower end of Shāyáng Zhōu.
Within the zhōu is Jiàbù Kǒu,
in the second year of the Sòng Jǐngpíng era,
when welcoming Emperor Wén from Jiānglíng,
the imperial carriage stopped here,
hence the name.
When Emperor Wén’s carriage departed from Jiānglíng,
upon reaching here,
a black dragon leaped out,
carrying the emperor’s boat,
startling everyone on board,
the emperor said to Chief Secretary Wáng Tánshǒu,
“This is how Xià Yǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
what virtue do I have to bear this?”
Hence the name Lóngxué.
The river water flows further east and on the right receives Niè Kǒu,
a river inlet.
To the left facing Niè Zhōu,
the river water passes left by the south of Bǎirén Shān,
and right past the north of Chìbì Shān,
where Zhōu Yú and Huáng Gài once deceived Wèi Wǔ’s great army.
The river water flows east past the south of Dàjūn Shān,
east of the mountain is Shān Tún,
a summer inlet,
where the river water bends left.
In the river, a rock emerges,
called Jiédù Shí.
On the right, the Tú Shuǐ flows into it,
originating from Jīn Shān in Wǔchāng Xiàn, Wǔchāng Jùn of Jiāngzhōu,
flowing northwest past the old city south of the relocated Rǔnán Jùn,
during the Xiánhé era,
as northern invaders pressed south,
households crossed south,
and this jùn was established,
with its seat at Tú Kǒu.
The Tú Shuǐ passes west of the county and flows further northwest,
entering the river.
The river water flows further east past the south of Xiǎojūn Shān,
adjacent to the river crossing,
east of which is Xiǎojūn Pǔ.
The river water flows further east past the north of Jīchì Shān.
East of the mountain is Tǔchéng Pǔ.
Further northeast, it reaches northwest of Shāyì Xiàn, Jiāngxià,
where the Miǎn Shuǐ flows from the north into it.
The Dùn River receives water from the Tàibái Lake in Dùnyáng County,
flowing southeast as the Dùn River, passing south of Dùnyáng County,
and empties into the Yangtze River,
which is called Dùnkǒu,
where the Dùnyáng Commandant had his administrative seat.
In the sixth year of the Yǒngjiā era of the Jin Dynasty,
Wáng Dūn appointed Táo Kǎn as Governor of Jīngzhōu to garrison this place,
but he moved to Línzhàng the following year.
The Yangtze River then flows east past the Yànfù Mountain,
which faces south toward Yànzhōu,
also called Yànbù.
On the right bank of the Yangtze, opposite the southern end of Yīngwǔzhōu (Parrot Islet),
the river bends to the right,
forming what is called Yìzhǔ,
and by the end of the third month,
the water flows down to connect with the Fánkǒu River.
The Yangtze River then flows east past the south of Lǔ Mountain,
which was anciently called Yìjì Mountain.
The Dì Shuō states:
"The Hàn River joins the Yangtze north of Héng Mountain beside Yìjì Mountain."
On the mountain is the city where Lù Huàn, the Wú Administrator of Jiāngxià, had his seat,
likely named after the two rivers.
The Geographical Records state:
"The Xià River passes through the commandery and enters the Yangtze,
hence the name Jiāngxià."
The old administrative seat was in Ānlù,
established in the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
but Wú later moved it to this city.
Within it is a stele for Hú Fèn, the Jin General Who Conquers the South and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
as well as an inscribed stone by General Who Pacifies the South, Wáng Shìjiàng,
recording the campaign against Dù Zēng.
There are also the tomb and temple of Liú Qí.
To the left of the mountain is the mouth of the Miǎn River.
On the left bank of the Miǎn is Quèyuè City,
also called Yǎnyuè Fort,
built by Supervisor Dài,
which was formerly Qūlíng County.
Later, it became the administrative seat of Shāyí County.
In the past, it was defended by the Wèi general Huáng Zǔ,
until Dǒng Xí and Líng Tǒng attacked and captured him.
Mí Héng was also killed here.
Héng, relying on his talent and being unconventional,
acted recklessly and unrestrainedly in an unpredictable era,
failing to preserve himself,
and meeting a death not meant for him—
one could say his regrets ran deep.
On the right bank of the Yangtze is Chuánguān Pǔ,
extending west of Huánghú Jī and then south,
directly below the lower tail of Yīngwǔzhōu (Parrot Islet),
where the Yangtze River swirls, forming a bend called Fú Pǔ,
also known as Huángjūn Pǔ.
In the past, it was where the Wú general Huáng Gài and his army were stationed,
hence the name of the bend,
and it is also a gathering place for merchant boats.
East of Chuánguān Pǔ is Huánghú Mountain,
with beautiful forests and streams,
where Dài Zhòngruò of Qiáo Commandery lived in rustic attire.
Below the mountain is called Huánghú Àn,
and below the bank is a bay,
named Huánghú Wān.
Northeast of Huánghú Mountain, facing Xiàkǒu City,
which was built by Sūn Quán
in the second year of the Huángchū era of Wèi.
It leans against the mountain and borders the river,
with an open and clear layout,
its distant walls relying on the natural barriers,
and its high towers overlooking the flowing water.
Above, one can gaze over the flowing river,
while below, turbulent waves crash against rugged rocks—
truly a hardship for boatmen.
Across the river lies the entrance to the Miǎn River,
hence the city is named Xiàkǒu,
and it was also the administrative seat of Shāyí County.
On the left bank of the Yangtze River is Húkǒu,
where water connects to Tàibái Lake,
and further east, it joins Lièkǒu,
which receives water from the Yǔn River in Ānlù County,
flowing east past the north of Lièyáng County,
and then eastward into the Yangtze River.
The Yangtze River continues east,
and lake water flows from north to south into it,
called Jiāwújiāng.
On the right bank, two Xià Pǔ bends are frequently encountered,
facing north toward Dōngchéngzhōu,
and west of the bend is Yōngfú Garrison.
On the right bank of the Yangtze River,
to the east, is the mouth of Lóngxiāng River,
which originates from the northern mountains in the Mán region.
On the left bank of the Yangtze is Wǔkǒu,
where water connects upstream to Yántóu in Ānlù.
In the second year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng Dynasty,
General of the Guards and Governor of Jīngzhōu, Xiè Huì, held troops upstream,
but was defeated by General Who Conquers the North, Tán Dàojì,
and fled here,
where he was captured by the garrison commander Guāng Shùn.
Further south to Wǔchéng,
all flow into the great Yangtze River.
To the south lies Wǔzhōu,
which faces south toward the mouth of the Yángguì River,
where the Yangtze River flows southward.
It connects to the three smelting sites of Jīnnǚ, Dàwén, and Táobān,
which were old Wú garrison posts,
marking the end of the Jīngzhōu boundary here.
The Yangtze River flows east past the south of Ruòchéng,
and Yǔ Zhòngyōng's Jiāng Shuǐ Jì states:
"From Ruòchéng to Wǔchéngkǒu is thirty lǐ."
It faces south toward Guōkǒu,
a Xià Pǔ bend,
though it does not always flood.
To the east is Kǔcài Xià Pǔ,
and east of the bend is Kǔcài Mountain.
The Yangtze River passes north of it, hence the bend is named Kǔcài.
On the mountain grows a bitter vegetable that is edible.
On the left bank of the Yangtze River is Guǎngwǔkǒu,
a river bend.
On the right bank of the Yangtze is Lǐmǔ Pǔ,
a bend notably free from the nuisance of mosquitoes and gnats.
It faces north toward Zhēngróngzhōu,
where Champion General Liú Yì defeated Huán Xuán on this islet.
Xuán then fled west with the emperor to Jiānglíng.
Further east, it passes south of Zhū County.
The River flows east past the north of Báihǔ Jī,
the mountain overlooking the side of the riverbank.
Further east, it joins Chìxī,
at the mouth of Xiàpǔ,
where the River bends to the right.
It then flows east past the north of Bèi Jī,
which Yǔ Zhòngyōng called Pèi’àn.
On the right bank of the River is Qiūkǒu,
a river inlet.
Further east, it receives Wūshí Shuǐ,
which emerges from Wūshí Shān
and flows south into the River.
On the right bank of the River is Lí Jī,
and north of the jī is also called Lí’àn.
East of the mountain is Xiàfǔ,
and further east, it passes north of Shàngqì,
the name of a mountain.
Zhòngyōng called it Dà, Xiǎo Zhúqì.
On the north bank is Fēnghuǒ Zhōu,
also known as Jǔ Zhōu,
facing north toward Jǔkǒu.
Zhòngyōng wrote it as "Jǔ" (莒),
capturing the sound but forgetting the character,
which is incorrect.
Jǔ Shuǐ emerges from Guītóu Shān,
flows northwest past the south of Ménglóng Shù,
the seat of Liáng Dìngzhōu,
where the local chieftain Tián Xiùchāo served as governor.
Jǔ Shuǐ then flows west,
joining on the left with the waters of Chuíshān,
which emerge from the southern side of Chuíshān,
sharing the same source as Yìyáng Pì Shuǐ,
hence these waters converge.
East of the water is Nánkǒu Shù,
and further south, it passes west of Fāngshān Shù,
flowing west into Jǔ Shuǐ.
It then flows southwest past the east of Liáng Sīzhōu and Yùzhōu,
where the local chieftain Tián Lǔshēng served as governor,
administering from Húbēichéng,
also called Shuǐchéng.
Jǔ Shuǐ then flows southwest past the south of Yánchéng,
and further southwest past the west of Qí’ān Jùn,
where Dàoshuǐ flows into it.
Dàoshuǐ emerges from Huángwǔ Shān,
flows south past the west of Báishā Shù,
then southeast past the west of Liáng Dáchéng Shù,
and joins Jǔ Shuǐ to the southeast.
Jǔ Shuǐ then flows southeast past Chìtíng,
where it is called Chìtíng Shuǐ.
It then divides into two streams,
flowing south into the River,
called Jǔkǒu,
facing south toward Jǔ Zhōu.
According to the "Spring and Autumn Annals" and "Zuǒzhuàn," in the fourth year of Duke Dìng,
the states of Wú and Chǔ arrayed their forces at Bó Jǔ.
Jīng Xiàngfán said:
"This is east of the Hàn region."
In Jiāngxià, there is Jǔ Shuǐ,
sometimes written as "Jǔ" (举),
which is likely the same.
The left stream flows southeast into the River,
and the riverside is called Wénfāngkǒu.
On the right bank of the River is Fèngmíngkǒu,
a river inlet,
beside which is Fèngmíng Shù.
The River then flows east past the old city of Zhū Xiàn,
which King Xuān of Chǔ destroyed and relocated here,
hence the name Zhū.
In the first year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed Wú Ruì as King of Héngshān,
with his capital here.
During the Xiánhé era of Jìn,
Yǔ Yì served as governor of Xīyáng,
established by dividing Jiāngxià.
In the fourth year,
the governor of Yùzhōu, Máo Bǎo, and the governor of Xīyáng, Fán Jùn, jointly defended it,
but it fell to Zhāng Géduó, a general of Shí Hǔ,
and has since lain in ruins.
South of the city faces Lú Zhōu,
where during the old Wú period, guesthouses were built on the islet,
convenient for travelers to stay,
and it is also called Luó Zhōu.
North of È Xiàn,
The river further receives the Wěi Estuary,
which is a river inlet.
East of the inlet lies Wěi Mountain.
The river flows east past the north of the mountain,
where the northern cliff has the Dōnghú Estuary.
The river waves bend leftward,
their flow forming a lake,
hence it is called the Lake Estuary.
The river further flows east and reaches the Kōngshí Estuary.
A river inlet is on the right,
facing the river is Kōngshí Mountain.
To the south, it faces the Shíxué Islet,
upon which is located the seat of Qíyáng County.
Further east,
the Qí River flows into it.
The river further flows east past the old city wall of Qíchūn County.
In the thirtieth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Chén Jùn's son Fú was enfeoffed as a marquis here.
The river further flows east and reaches the Tónglíng Estuary,
which is a river inlet.
The Great River flows right past the north of Xiāmá Mountain,
and eastward meets the Hǎi Estuary.
The waters to the south connect to a great lake,
reaching north to the river,
with mountains flanking it on both sides.
The river flows past its north,
eastward joining the Zāng Estuary,
which is a river inlet.
The river further flows left past the south of Chángfēng Mountain,
reaching the Chángfēng Estuary,
which is a river inlet.
The river further flows east past the south of Jībù Mountain,
commonly called Jībù Jetty.
Also called Jībù Promontory,
it is what Yǔ Zhòngyōng referred to as Gāo Mountain.
This marks the boundary between the two commanderies of Xīyáng and Xúnyáng.
On the right bank is the Tǔfù Estuary,
a river inlet.
Flanking the inlet is Jiāng Mountain,
east of the mountain is the Hù Estuary,
a river inlet,
which Yǔ Zhòngyōng called the Cháo'èr Inlet.
Further east, it passes north of Xiàzhì County,
where the Lì River flows from the southwest of Dōnglíng and enters it.
The river flows east past the south of Pípá Mountain,
below which lies Pípá Bay.
Further east, it passes the south of Wàngfū Mountain,
and further east reaches the Kǔcài River Estuary,
a summer inlet.
On the right bank of the river,
the Fù River flows into it.
The water originates from the Qīngpén Mountain in Yángxīn County,
flowing northwest past Yángxīn County,
which was formerly a subordinate county of Yùzhāng.
The area has many nǚniǎo birds.
The Xuánzhōng Jì states:
A man from Yángxīn obtained one by the waterside,
and subsequently lived with it.
They bore two daughters,
who all donned feathers and flew away.
In the Yùzhāng region, when raising children, they do not expose their clothing,
saying that if this bird's dust falls on a child's clothing,
it will cause the child to fall ill.
Therefore, it is also called the yèfēi yóunǚ.
Further northwest, it passes Xiàzhì County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Rùnguāng,
later merged into Yángxīn.
On both sides of the water,
both public and private irrigation channels,
all turned into fertile land,
the former location of a Wú military garrison.
The river further flows east,
on the right reaching the Lánxī River Estuary,
also a river inlet.
Further east,
on the left reaching the Qīnglín Estuary.
The water originates from the Dōnglíng Township of Lújiāng Commandery.
Jiāngxià has a Xīlíng County,
hence this is referred to as Dōng (East).
The Shàngshū states:
"The river passes Jiǔjiāng and reaches Dōnglíng."
Flowing southwest,
the water accumulates into a lake.
West of the lake is Qīnglín Mountain.
In the first year of the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty,
Emperor Míng dispatched Shěn Yōuzhī to campaign west against Zǐxūn.
While cutting timber to build fortifications at Qīng Mountain,
they saw a youth of exceptional beauty,
who asked the woodcutters:
"Why are you taking this?"
They replied:
"We wish to campaign against the rebels."
The youth said:
"By the latter part of the month, it will be pacified.
Why trouble yourselves to cut this?"
Amidst the crowd,
he suddenly vanished,
hence it is called Qīnglín Lake.
The lake has crucian carp,
eating them is rich and delicious,
and they ward off cold and heat.
The lake water flowing west is called Qīnglín River.
Further southwest, it passes Xúnyáng,
dividing into two streams:
one stream flows east connecting to Dàléi,
one stream flows southwest entering the river,
which is the Lì River mentioned in the Jīng.
It faces right across to the Mǎtóu Bank.
From the Fù Estuary to here is over fifty lǐ,
with banks obstructed by the river and mountains.
36 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 36
36.1 Qīngyī River
36.1 Qīngyī River
The Qīngyī River originates west of Qīngyī County, east of Méng Mountain,
and joins with the Mò River.
The county
was originally the state of the Qīngyī Qiāng.
The Zhúshū Jìnián records:
In the tenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
a man from Xiáyáng, coming from Qín via the Mín Mountains and the Qīngyī River, returned.
In the fourth year of the Tiānhàn era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Shěnlí Commandery was abolished,
and two commandants were established.
One administered Qīngyī,
overseeing the Hàn people.
When Gōngsūn Shù held Shǔ,
Qīngyī did not submit.
Emperor Shìzǔ praised this,
and in the nineteenth year of Jiànwǔ, established it as a commandery.
In the first year of the Yánguāng era of Emperor Ān, a Shǔ Commandery Dependent State Commandant was established.
The prince of Qīngyī, admiring Hàn institutions,
petitioned to be incorporated.
In the second year of the Yángjiā era of Emperor Shùn,
it was renamed Hànjiā,
commending the acquisition of this fine vassal.
The county has Méng Mountain,
from which the Qīngyī River originates.
It flows east past the county,
and meets the Mò River at Língguān Circuit in Yuèxī Commandery.
The Qīngyī River further flows east,
where the Qióng River joins it.
The water originates from the Qiónglái Mountain in Yándào, Hànjiā,
flowing east to Línqióng County in Shǔ Commandery,
then east into the Qīngyī River.
Reaching Nán'ān County in Qiánwéi,
it enters the river.
The Qīngyī River passes Píngxiāng,
where it is called the Píngxiāng River.
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"The Píngxiāng River flows east past Éméi Mountain,
which lies within the boundaries of Nán'ān County,
a thousand lǐ south of Chéngdū.
On clear autumn days,
one can see two peaks,
standing opposite each other like eyebrows."
The Qīngyī River further flows east,
entering the Great River.
36.2 Huán River
36.2 Huán River
The Huán River originates from the Mín Mountains in Shǔ Commandery,
flows southwest through Qiāng territory,
and enters the Southern Sea.
The "Tribute of Yu" in the *Book of Documents* states,
"The Min and Bo mountains have been cultivated;
the Tuo and Qian rivers have been channeled;
the Cai and Meng mountains have been pacified;
and the Héyí region has achieved success."
Zhèng Xuán said:
"Hé
is the land where the upper barbarians dwell.
Hé is pronounced as Huán."
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"The Huán River originates from the Shǔ Mountains in Shǔ Commandery,
flowing southwest into the Qiāng territory."
The *Book of Documents* further states:
"From Xīqīng, they came by way of the Huán."
Mǎ Róng and Wáng Sù said:
"To govern the Xīqīng Mountains,
they came solely by way of the Huán River,
meaning there was no other route."
I, based on the *Classic* and referencing the *Book*,
note that both the Mín Mountains
and Xīqīng
have the Huán River.
The Huán River originates from the Xīqīng Mountains,
and there are no other tributaries;
the only watercourse guided is this river.
By floating on the Qián and Hàn rivers, one reaches the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers.
Therefore, the *Records of Geography* of the Jìn dynasty states:
"Liáng Province extends south to the Huán River,
west to the Black River,
and east to the Hánguān Pass."
The present-day regions of Hànzhōng, Bā Commandery, Wénshān, Shǔ Commandery, Hànjiā, Jiāngyáng, Zhūtí, Fúlíng, Yīnpíng, Guǎnghàn, Xīndū, Zǐtóng, Qiánwéi, Wǔdū, Shàngyōng, Wèixīng, and Xīnchéng
are all ancient territories of Liáng Province.
South of the Huán River is barbarian land,
as stated in the *Book*: "the Héyí region has achieved success."
However, what can be identified
is only this river and the Jiāng River.
The Huán River
is likely an alternative name for these two rivers,
serving as a general term for both waterways.
Zhèng Xuán, annotating the *Book of Documents*, said:
"Woven hides
refer to the states of the Western Róng.
Xīqīng
is a mountain in Yōng Province.
Between the territories of Yōng and Róng,
those who have business in the capital
must pass through this province.
Huán is the name of a slope in Lǒng,
and its path winds and twists,
spiraling upward,
hence it is called Huán.
Today, the people below refer to this winding slope as Pán.
This is Zhèng Xuán's unique interpretation,
but I fear it deviates from the meaning of 'by way of the Huán' in the *Book of Documents*,
and does not align with the text about floating on the Qián River into the Wèi."
I have examined various texts
to gather knowledge and insights.
Now, I will briefly compile the courses and tributaries of the rivers.
Although their appearances have changed over time,
based on common understanding,
I will roughly explain their origins.
From Xīqīng to Jiāméng, it flows into the Western Hàn River,
which is what Zhèng Xuán referred to as the Qián River.
From the Western Hàn River, going upstream to the boundary of Jìnshòu,
the Jǔ
and Yàng rivers branch southward through ridges and caves,
meandering to connect with the Hàn River.
Following this route into the Yàng River,
it aligns with the *Book*'s description: "floating on the Qián River and crossing the Miǎn."
Passing through Hànchuān to Nánzhèng County,
it joins the Bāo River.
Going upstream along the Bāo River to the south of Yálǐng,
the stream branches into the Xié River,
reaching Wǔgōng and flowing north into the Wèi River.
This is the connection between water and land routes,
the course the river repeatedly follows.
It does not contradict the *Tribute of Yu*'s account of entering the Wèi River,
and indeed matches the *Book of Documents*' description of crossing the Hé River.
36.3 Ruò River
36.3 Ruò River
The Ruò River originates beyond the frontier of Máoniú in Shǔ Commandery,
flowing southeast to the old pass,
where it is called the Ruò River.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"Within the South Sea,
between the Black Waters,
there is a tree named Ruòmù,
and the Ruò River flows from it."
It also says:
"On the Huīyě Mountain, there is a tree
with green leaves and red flowers,
named Ruòmù.
It grows west of the Kūnlún Mountains,
attached to the western extremity."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Ruòmù is west of Jiànmù.
The tree has ten flowers,
and their light shines upon the earth below."
Thus, Qū Yuán's "Heavenly Questions" in the *Lí Sāo* says:
"Before Xīhé basks in the sun,
how does the light of Ruòhuá shine?"
However, Ruòmù does not grow in only one place.
Between the Black Waters,
where such trees are planted,
water flows beneath them,
hence the river derives its name.
The Ruò River flows along its course,
traversing the land of Shǔ.
Huángdì's eldest son, Chāngyì,
whose virtue was insufficient to inherit the great throne,
descended to dwell by this river,
becoming a feudal lord.
He married a woman from the Shǔshān clan
and gave birth to Zhuānxū in the wilderness by the Ruò River.
Zhuānxū possessed sage virtue,
ascended the throne at twenty,
succeeded Shǎohào's rule of the metal office,
and upheld the mandate with the virtue of water.
The Ruò River flows southeast,
and the Xiān River joins it.
Also known as the Zhōu River,
the Dàdù River originates beyond the frontier,
flowing south into the Ruò River at the Máoniú route.
It then passes through Dàzuó County in Yuèxī and enters the Shéng River.
The Shéng River originates beyond the frontier.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"From the Bāsuì Mountain,
the Shéng River flows forth,
running southeast,
where it divides into two branches:
one branch flows east,
passing through Guǎngróu County,
and empties into the Jiāng River;
the other flows south along the Máoniú route,
reaching Dàzuó, where it merges with the Ruò River.
From there downward, it is also commonly called the Shéng River.
Zuó
refers to barbarians.
In Wénshān, they are called Yí;
in Nánzhōng, they are called Kūnmí;
in Shǔ, they are called Qióng;
in Hànjiā
and Yuèxī, they are called Zuó.
All are barbarian tribes."
It flows south past the west of Qióngdū County in Yuèxī,
directly south to Huìwú County,
where the Yān River flows southeast and joins it.
Qiōngdū County,
was established when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn opened up Qiōngzuó.
The county sank and became a pool,
and is now thus named Qiōngchí.
Southerners call it the Qiōng River.
In the river is Bàngguī Mountain.
Yìng Shào said:
There is Guī Water,
meaning crossing this water to display flourishing prosperity.
Later they rebelled again.
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng,
Hàn troops crossed Yuèguī Water to attack them,
and made it Yuèguī Commandery,
administering Qiōngdū County.
Wáng Mǎng sent Rèn Guì to serve as Lǐngróng Grand Governor to guard it,
and renamed it Jíguī.
The county
was originally the state of Qiōngdū.
Yuèguī Water is Ruò of Shéng,
seemingly renamed according to the water and land.
There is also Wēn Water,
hot in winter and summer,
its source can scald chickens and pigs.
Bathing and washing in its lower hot springs
can cure chronic illnesses.
This is where Lǐ Xiāng once defeated Lǐ Liú at Wēn Water.
Ruò Water also passes Huìwú County.
The county has Jùnmǎ River,
which flows from the high mountains east of the county.
The mountains have the Tiānmǎ Path,
where its traces remain.
The horse traveled a thousand lǐ in a day.
Commoners pastured their horses at the foot of the mountain,
and sometimes gave birth to fine foals,
said to be offspring of the heavenly horse.
In the river are bèizǐ tāi copper,
which can be obtained
by sacrificing a sheep.
There is also Sūn Water,
which flows from Táigāo County,
that is, Táidēng County.
Sūn Water is also called Báishā River.
It flows south past Qiōngdū County.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú pacified the southwestern barbarians,
bridging Sūn Water,
which is this water.
Further south, it enters Ruò Water at Huìwú.
Ruò Water then flows south past Suǐjiǔ County of Yúnnán Commandery.
Qīnglíng Water enters it,
flowing from west of Qīnglíng County,
east past the county below,
after which the county is named.
There is Shízhū Qí,
where in a long valley are stone pigs,
mothers and offspring numbering thousands.
Elders pass down the tale
that barbarians once herded here,
and one morning turned to stone.
To this day, the barbarians dare not go to herd there.
Tān Water flows from it.
Qīnglíng Water then flows east into Shéng Water.
Shéng Water then passes west of Sānjiàng County,
and passes Gūfù County,
north facing Sānjiàng County,
where Yān Water flows into it.
Sānjiàng is also called Xiǎo Huìwú,
hence the Classic says:
Yān reaches Huìwú and flows into Ruò Water.
Ruò Water also joins Mǔxuè Water,
which flows from Mǔxuè Valley on Nóng Mountain east of Nòngdòng County in Yìzhōu Commandery,
north past south of Sānjiàng County,
and north into Shéng.
Shéng Water then flows east,
where Tú Water flows into it,
which flows from Mùmí South Mountain in Jiànníng Commandery.
The county and mountain are both named after the grass.
The mountain is five hundred lǐ south of Wūjù Mountain northeast of the county.
The mountain grows mùmí grass,
which can detoxify poison.
When all plants are flourishing,
birds often eat by mistake,
and if their beaks are poisoned,
they must swiftly fly to Mùmí Mountain
and peck mùmí grass to detoxify.
Tú Water originates from Là Valley,
flowing northwest to enter Shéng at Yuèguī.
Shéng Water then passes Mǎhú County of Yuèguī Commandery,
called Mǎhú River.
It then joins Bēi Water on the left,
which flows from Bēishuǐ County,
and flows east into Mǎhú River.
Further northeast, it reaches west of Zhūtí County in Qiánwéi,
becoming Lújiāng River.
Zhūtí is the name of a mountain.
Yìng Shào said:
It is located southwest of the county,
and the county was named after it.
It was part of the Qiánwéi Dependent State,
situated about 1,800 lǐ south of the commandery.
In the 20th year of the Jiàn'ān era, Zhūtí Commandery was established,
with its seat at the old county town.
Two hundred lǐ southwest of the commandery lies the subordinate Tángláng County.
Traveling northwest,
one ascends a high mountain,
where a winding, sheep-gut path stretches over eighty lǐ.
Sometimes one climbs by grasping trees,
sometimes by pulling each other up with ropes.
Those climbing along it feel as if they are ascending to heaven.
Therefore, Yuán Xiūmíng's Bāshǔ Records states:
"High mountains tower steeply,
rocks lie piled and scattered,
the path twists and turns perilously,
overlooking sheer ravines below.
Travelers cling to the slopes,
pulling themselves up by ropes."
People from the Three Shǔ regions
and the various commanderies of Nánzhōng
consider it extremely dangerous.
There is the Lú Crossing,
located eighty lǐ east of the county.
The water is six to seven hundred paces wide,
over ten zhàng deep,
with much miasmic air,
and few travelers pass through.
In the second year of the Tàiníng era of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
Lǐ Xiāng and others invaded Yuèxī,
attacking Táidēng County.
Wáng Xùn, the Regional Inspector of Níngzhōu, sent General Yáo Yuè to attack them.
They battled at Tángláng,
and Lǐ Xiāng's army was heavily defeated.
Yáo Yuè pursued them to the Lú River,
where over a thousand men drowned in the water.
Wáng Xùn, angered that Yáo Yuè and others did not pursue them relentlessly,
flew into a rage,
his hair standing on end so fiercely that his cap split,
and he died.
According to records, Yǒngchāng Commandery has the Láncāng River,
which originates from Bónán County in the southwest,
established in the second year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
Bónán is the name of a mountain,
and the county was named after it.
The river flows northeast past Bónán Mountain.
During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's reign, the road through Bónán Mountain was opened,
crossing the Láncāng Crossing.
The land was extremely remote,
and travelers suffered greatly.
A song says:
"The virtue of Hàn is vast,
opening the unsubmissive lands.
Crossing Bónán,
traversing the Cāng Crossing,
crossing the Láncāng,
we become laborers."
The mountain is forty lǐ high.
The Láncāng River yields gold sand,
which the Yuè people collect to make gold.
There is also the Pearl-Light Cave,
which produces luminous pearls,
as well as amber,
coral,
and yellow, white, and green pearls.
The Láncāng River flows further northeast to Bùwéi County, where it joins the Lèi River.
The Lèi River originates from Suītáng County,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The Lèi River flows southwest,
twists and turns, then flows north,
and east to Bùwéi County, where it empties into the Láncāng River.
Further east, it merges with the Jìn River.
The Jìn River flows north from Yǒngchāng County, passing west of the commandery.
The area along the river is rich in rhinoceroses and elephants.
The mountains have hook snakes,
seven to eight zhàng long,
with forked tails.
The snakes dwell in mountain streams and rivers,
using their tails to hook people and cattle on the banks to eat them.
The miasmic air along this river is particularly vile.
Within the miasma, there is a creature,
invisible in form,
that makes a sound when active.
Striking trees, it breaks them;
striking people, it harms them.
It is called the "ghost projectile."
Only in the eleventh and twelfth months is it somewhat safe to cross.
From the first to the tenth month, passing through invariably harms people.
Therefore, when the commandery had criminals,
they were exiled to the banks of the Jìn River,
and none survived more than ten days.
The Jìn River flows north into the Lú Crossing River,
then east past the north of Bùwéi County and northeast.
Both banks are high mountains several hundred zhàng tall,
with Lú Peak being the most majestic,
towering孤高 over three thousand zhàng.
This mountain collapsed during the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
shaking the commandery and its towns.
Along the riverbanks,
only narrow paths for horses and pedestrians are barely passable,
and miasmic air is often present.
In the third and fourth months, passing through is certain death;
even outside these months, it causes nausea and vomiting.
After the fifth month,
travelers may pass without harm.
Therefore, Zhūgě Liàng wrote in his Memorial:
"In the fifth month, we crossed the Lú,
eating only every other day.
It is not that I do not cherish myself,
but because the royal enterprise cannot remain confined to Shǔ."
The Yìzhōu Records states:
"The Lú River's source is at Qūluóxī.
After flowing three hundred lǐ downstream, it is called the Lú River.
The two peaks harbor lethal air;
in the summer months, it was traditionally impassable.
Hence, Marquis Wǔ found crossing in summer arduous."
The Lú River further downstream converges with various waters,
collectively referred to by this name,
hence it is called the Lú River.
From Zhūtí to Bódào, there are water and land routes.
The water route includes the Hēishuǐ and Yángguān Shuǐ,
extremely perilous and difficult,
with three hazardous crossings that trouble travelers.
Thus, a common saying goes:
"Zhūxī and Chìshuǐ,
winding like a coiled snake in seven bends;
Pányáng and Wūlóng,
where the air reaches the heavens.
Gazing at Dūhuòcǐ,
halting at Zhùhūyī;
Láijiàng's merchants,
carry loads on left shoulders for seven lǐ."
There are also places like Niúkòutóu and Mǎbójiǎ Bǎn,
such are the hardships and dangers.
Further northeast, it reaches Bódào County
and enters the river.
The Ruò River, upon reaching Bódào,
is also called the Mǎhú River.
The Shéng River, Lú River, Sūn River, Yān River,
and Dàdù River
all converge and flow into it, sharing the common name.
Therefore, various texts recording these rivers
sometimes say they enter the Ruò,
sometimes say they flow into the Shéng,
yet all state they reach Bódào and enter the river.
Indeed, different waters flow along and merge,
becoming a single crossing,
with no other stream
that could match it.
There is the Filial Son Stone in the river.
In the past, a county man named Kuí Shūtōng
was extremely filial by nature.
He fetched water from the river for his mother,
and Heaven caused a flat stone to appear in the river channel.
It is still called the Filial Son Stone today.
This can be said to be utmost sincerity arising from within,
and a blessed response coming from Heaven.
36.4 Mò River
36.4 Mò River
The Mò River originates beyond the borders of Guǎngróu.
The county has Shíniǔ Township,
where Yǔ was born.
Today, the local tribes jointly protect it.
The area spans a hundred lǐ,
where no one dares to live or herd.
If a criminal flees into the wilderness,
pursuers do not press closely.
If he can hide for three years
without being captured,
he is collectively pardoned,
as it is said that the spirit of Great Yǔ protects him.
It flows southeast past Máoniú County to the north,
then east to Yuèxī Língdào County,
emerging south of Méng Mountain.
Língdào County,
also known as Língguān Circuit.
Under the Han system, circuits were established in regions inhabited by non-Han peoples.
The county has a copper mountain,
and also the Lìcí Islet.
In the ninth year of the Tàishǐ era of the Jin dynasty,
two yellow dragons appeared in Lìcí Pond.
The county magistrate Dǒng Xuánzhī led officials and commoners to observe them,
and reported it to the Inspector Wáng Jùn,
who submitted a memorial to the court.
The Jin court then changed the name to Hùlóng County.
The Mòshuǐ River originates west of Mínshān Mountain,
flows east past Hànjiā Commandery,
then flows south and strikes a high mountain.
The mountain is closed at the top and open at the bottom,
and the river passes through it.
This mountain
is Méngshān Mountain.
To the northeast, it joins the Qīngyīshuǐ River.
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
The two rivers, east of Qīngyī County in Hànjiā,
merge into one stream,
and from there down it is also called the Qīngyīshuǐ River.
The Mòshuǐ River flows further east,
passes by Kāikān County,
which was formerly Píngxiāng.
It was established in the early Jin dynasty.
The Mòshuǐ River flows east past the south of Línqióng,
and then emerges east at Jiāngyuán County.
It flows east into the Jiāng River.
In ancient times, the Mòshuǐ River, from Méngshān Mountain to the Hùnyá Cliff west of Nán'ān,
had a swift and turbulent current,
damaging boats and ships,
and was a perennial hazard.
The Governor of Shǔ Commandery, Lǐ Bīng, dispatched laborers to level the Hùnyá Cliff.
The river god became enraged,
so Lǐ Bīng took up a sword, entered the water, and fought the god.
Thus, it was pacified.
The Hùnyá Cliff was straightened,
and the waterway was opened.
This is the channel Lǐ Bīng excavated.
36.5 Yánjiāng River
36.5 Yánjiāng River
The Yánjiāng River originates from Nánguǎng County in Qiánwéi,
flows east to Bó County in Zāngkē,
then turns east and flows north.
Bó County
was the former seat of Qiánwéi Commandery.
The county has Qiánshān Mountain.
In the first year of the Jiànxīng era of the Jin dynasty, Píngyí Commandery was established.
The county has the Bóshuǐ River,
which originates from Bùlángshān Mountain west of Bó Town,
and flows east to join the Wēnshuǐ River.
The Wēnshuǐ River is also called Nuǎnshuǐ,
originating from Fú County in Qiánwéi and flowing south into the Qiánshuǐ River.
The Qiánshuǐ River also originates from Fú County,
and flows south to meet the Wēnshuǐ River.
Kàn Yīn called it the Kànshuǐ River.
Both flow south into the Bóshuǐ River.
The Bóshuǐ River, at that county, flows east into the Yánjiāng River.
The Yánjiāng River also joins the Hànshuǐ River,
which originates from the Shè Valley in Hànyáng Circuit, Qiánwéi.
This was called Xīntōng under Wáng Mǎng.
It flows east to Bó Town and enters the Yánjiāng River.
Reaching Fúlíng County in Bā Commandery,
it flows into the Gēngshǐshuǐ River.
The Gēngshǐshuǐ River
is the initial distributary of the Yánjiāng River.
The Yánjiāng River flows north into the Fúlíngshuǐ River.
The Fúlíngshuǐ River originates east of the county,
formerly the southern border of Bā Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Bātíng.
Wèi Wǔ partitioned the territory,
and established Fúlíng Commandery.
When Zhāng Kān was the county magistrate,
Gōngsūn Shù attacked him.
Loyal and righteous men,
selected skilled swimmers to ferry Zhāng Kān across on a raft at Xiǎobiéjiāng River,
which is this river.
This river flows north to Zhǐ County and enters the Jiāng River.
The Gēngshǐshuǐ River flows east into Nánpǔ County in Bādōng,
where the water flows into a channel mouth at Shímén.
The empty cavern is dark and deep,
the secluded ravine shadowy and dense.
The overhanging cliffs close above,
constantly threatening to collapse.
Travelers detour to avoid miasma,
and those who pass through
cannot help but feel anxious beneath them.
It is also called the Xīxiāngshuǐ River,
and also Xīxiāng Creek.
The creek winds for about two hundred *li*,
before emerging from the mountains.
It then flows on,
for another two hundred *li* or more,
and enters Qiānlíng County to the southeast.
Further southeast, it reaches Wǔyáng County in Wǔlíng,
and flows into the Yǒushuǐ River.
The *Wǔlíng Xiánxián Zhuàn* states:
Pān Jīng served long as the Registrar of the commandery.
The Grand Administrator Zhào Wěi held him in high esteem.
He asked Pān Jīng:
Why is your honorable commandery named Wǔlíng?
Pān Jīng replied:
Our humble commandery was originally named Yìlíng,
located within the boundaries of Chényáng County,
bordering the non-Han peoples,
and was frequently overrun by them.
During the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the seat was moved to the top of the eastern mountain,
and thus the name was changed.
The *Zhuàn* says:
'Stopping weapons constitutes *wǔ* (military prowess).'
The *Shī* says:
'A high plain is called *líng*.'
Hence, it was named thus.
On the north bank of the Yǒushuǐ River is Qiányáng County.
Xǔ Shèn said:
'The Wēnshuǐ River flows south into Qián.'
This is probably a general designation
for the waterways and tributaries downstream from the Bóshuǐ River.
Thus, the county received its name.
The mouth of Xīxiāng Creek is fifty *li* above the old city of Qiānlíng County,
where it joins the Yǒushuǐ River on the left.
The Yǒushuǐ River flows east past the north of its old city,
then east past the south of the old Wǔyáng County,
and emerges eastward.
The distance between the two counties
is about four hundred *li* by waterway,
and they meet at Wǔyáng.
The Yǒushuǐ River flows southeast to Yuánlíng County,
and enters the Yuán River.
36.6 Cúnshuǐ River
36.6 Cúnshuǐ River
The Cúnshuǐ River originates from Yèmǎ County in Qiánwéi,
which was called Chànmǎ under Wáng Mǎng.
The powerful clan leader Yōng Kǎi of Yìzhōu rebelled,
built fortifications on the mountain,
and tethered his horses to posts.
The posts grew into a forest,
which the non-Han people now call Yōng Wúliáng Forest.
Liáng
is the non-Han word for horse.
The Cúnshuǐ River flows southeast from the county,
passes north of Mùmí County,
then flows east past north of Qiělán County,
and emerges to the southeast.
Southeast, it reaches Dìngzhōu County in Yùlín,
where it becomes the Zhōushuǐ River.
The Cúnshuǐ River flows further east,
passes north of Wúliǎn County in Zāngkē Commandery,
and to the southeast joins the Wúliǎnshuǐ River.
The Wúliǎnshuǐ River first receives water from the Zāngkēshuǐ River,
flows east past Wúliǎn County as the Wúliǎnshuǐ River,
then flows east into the Cúnshuǐ River.
The Cúnshuǐ River flows east past Dìngzhōu County in Yùlín and becomes the Zhōushuǐ River,
indicating a change in the river's name.
Further northeast, it reaches Tánzhōng County,
and flows into Tán.
36.7 Wēnshuǐ River
36.7 Wēnshuǐ River
The Wēnshuǐ River originates from Yèláng County in Zāngkē,
The county
was originally the state of the Marquis of Yèláng.
Táng Méng opened it up and made it a county,
and Wáng Mǎng named it Tóngtíng.
The Wēn River flows from the northwest of the county,
passes by Tánggǎo and joins the Mí River.
The Mí River originates from Tánlǔ Mountain in Tónglài County of Yìzhōu Commandery to the west,
flows east past Tánggǎo County,
and enters the Wēn River from the right.
The Wēn River then flows west past the south of Kūnzé County,
and then past Wèi County.
This county
was originally the capital of the Diān state.
When Zhūgě Liàng pacified the southern region,
in the third year of the Jiànxīng era of Liú Shàn,
Jiànníng Commandery was established here by dividing Yìzhōu Commandery.
Both banks of the river are high mountains,
and in the mountains and along the river,
all are inhabited by the Mù'ěr Yí people.
Their language is different,
and their tastes and desires also differ.
Although they live in the mountains,
the land is relatively mild,
and there is no miasma or poison.
The Wēn River then flows southwest past Diānchí City.
The lake is northwest of the county,
with a circumference of about three hundred lǐ.
Its upper source is deep and broad,
while its lower flow is shallow and narrow,
seeming to flow backward,
hence it is called Diānchí.
Elders pass down the tale
that in the lake there are divine horses.
When domestic horses mate with them, they give birth to fine steeds
that can travel five hundred lǐ in a day.
In the fourteenth year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
Fèi Tǒng, the governor of Níngzhōu, reported:
"In Diānchí County of Jìnníng Commandery, there are two divine horses,
one white and one black,
frolicking upon the river's waters."
There is a Diān Prefecture.
In the third year of the Yuánfēng era, Yìzhōu Commandery was established,
with its seat at Diānchí City,
which under Liú Shàn became Jiànníng Commandery.
The Wēn River then flows west to join the Great Marsh,
and merges with the Pú River of Yèyú.
The Wēn River then flows southeast past Wúdān County of Zāngkē,
and during the Jiànxīng era,
Liú Shàn transferred it to Jiànníng Commandery.
The Qiáo River flows into it,
its waters originating from the Southern Pond of Yúyuán.
The county seat is on Lóngchí Isle,
with a circumference of forty-seven lǐ.
It is also called the Hé River,
and divides its waters with Xiélóng.
Later, Héyáng Commandery was established,
with its seat at Héyáng County,
which lies on Héyuán Isle.
Yúnpíng County is also located on this isle.
The Qiáo River flows east to Wúdān County,
and enters the Wēn River.
The Wēn River then flows southeast past the east of Wúzhuó County of Xīnggǔ Commandery,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Yǒuzhuó.
It joins the Southern Qiáo River,
which originates from Qiáo Mountain in the county,
flowing east,
where the Liáng River flows into it.
The Liáng River receives water from the Hé River at Yúyuán County,
and flows southeast past Shèngxiū County of Xīnggǔ,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Shèngbó.
The Liáng River then flows east past Wúzhuó County,
entering the Qiáo River from the left,
and the Qiáo River then flows east into the Wēn River.
The Wēn River then flows southeast past the south of Lǜgāo County.
In the third year of the Jiànxīng era of Liú Shàn,
Xīnggǔ Commandery was established by dividing Zāngkē,
with its seat at Wēn County.
According to the "Jìnshū Dìdào Jì,"
the seat was here.
The Wēn River then flows southeast past the south of Liángshuǐ Commandery.
The Wēn River joins with the Liáng River upstream,
so from here down it also bears the name Liáng River.
Therefore, Liú Shàn divided the southern part of Xīnggǔ,
establishing a commandery at Liángshuǐ County.
The Wēn River flows southeast past the north of Xúnfēng County,
and then past the east of Láiwéi County,
where the Pú River branches off to the right.
It then flows east to Guǎngyù County of Yùlín,
where it becomes the Yù River.
This was the Guìlín Commandery of the Qín dynasty,
renamed Yùlín Commandery by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn in the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era.
Wáng Mǎng called it Yùpíng Commandery.
Yìng Shào's "Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì" states:
"According to the 'Zhōulǐ,'
the Yù official was in charge of ritual vessels for libations.
For all libation ceremonies in sacrifices and for guests,
he blended yùchàng and filled the ritual vessels.
Yù
is a fragrant herb,
the flower of a hundred herbs,
boiled and blended with black millet for brewing,
used to invoke the spirits.
Some say it is what is now called yùjīnxiāng.
Another explanation is
that it was a tribute from the Yù people,
hence the commandery was named after it."
The Wēn River then flows east past Zēngshí County,
where the Wénxiàng River flows into it.
This river originates from Jūtǐng County of Zāngkē.
Yìng Shào said:
"This was the ancient state of Jūtǐng,
which Wáng Mǎng called Cónghuà."
The Wénxiàng River, Méng River, Lúwéi River, Láixì River, and Fá River
all flow from the east of the county through Guǎngyù to Zēngshí County,
and enter the Yù River.
It then flows east to the east of Lǐngfāng County,
where it joins the Jīnnán River.
The county has the Zhūyá River,
which originates from Línchén County,
flowing northeast,
where the Huān River flows into it.
The Huān River's source receives water from the Zāngkē River,
flowing east past Zēngshí County and then down into the Zhūyá River.
The Zhūyá River then flows northeast past Línchén County,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jiànchén.
The county has the Jīnnán River and Qīnlí River,
both of which pass by Línchén,
flow east into Lǐngfāng County,
and enter the Yù River.
They flow northeast into the Yù River.
The Yù River,
is the Tún River of Yèláng.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
there was a Bamboo King who rose by the Tún River.
A woman was washing clothes by the riverbank,
when a large bamboo of three sections floated to her feet.
She pushed it but it would not go away.
Hearing a sound from within,
she took it home and split it open,
obtaining a baby boy.
He later became powerful among the Yí and Pú tribes,
taking Bamboo as his surname.
The discarded, split bamboo
grew into a forest in the wild;
this is the bamboo grove at the present-day Bamboo King Shrine.
The king once stopped with his followers by a large rock.
He ordered them to make soup,
but his followers said:
"There is no water."
The king struck the rock with his sword, and water sprang forth;
this is the present-day Bamboo King Water.
Later, when Táng Méng opened up Zāngkē,
he beheaded the Bamboo King.
The Yí and Liáo tribes all resented this.
Because the Bamboo King was not born of flesh and blood,
they requested that a shrine be established for him.
The emperor enfeoffed his three sons as marquises,
and upon their deaths,
they were enshrined alongside their father.
The present-day Shrine of the Three Lords of Bamboo
venerates these deities.
The Tún River flows northeast past Tángǎo County,
then east past Qiělán County of Zāngkē Commandery,
where it is called the Zāngkē River.
The river is several *li* wide.
The county seat is situated on the riverbank,
being the former Marquisate of Qiělán,
also named Tóulán,
and the seat of Zāngkē Commandery.
The Chǔ general Zhuāng Jué,
sailed up the Yuán River to attack Yèláng.
He moored his boats by tying them to stakes (zāngkē),
hence naming Qiělán as Zāngkē.
It was opened in the sixth year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Tóngtíng.
There is the Zhùpǔ Pass.
Zāngkē
is also the name of two mountains facing each other in the middle of the stream.
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" says:
"Spitting waves at Zāngkē."
In the fifth year of Yuándǐng,
Emperor Wǔ attacked Nányuè,
dispatching elite troops from Yèláng down the Zāngkē River,
to converge at Pānyú.
The Zāngkē River flows southeast past the west of Wúliǎn County,
from which the Wúliǎn River emerges.
Further east,
the Huān River emerges.
It then passes through Guǎngyù County of Yùlín Commandery, becoming the Yù River.
It flows northeast past the north of Lǐngfāng County,
then east past the north of Bùshān County,
the seat of Yùlín Commandery.
Lù Jì of Wú said:
"From now on, in sixty years,
chariot tracks will be standardized,
and writing will be uniform."
By the first year of Tàikāng,
Jìn indeed conquered Wú.
It then passes south of Zhōngliú County and joins the Wēn River.
Further east, it enters Ālín County,
where the Tán River flows into it.
This river originates from Yù Mountain in Tánchéng County of Wǔlíng Commandery.
It flows east past Tánzhōng County of Yùlín Commandery,
where the Zhōu River comes from the southwest to join it.
The Tán River flows southeast and joins the Gāng River,
which originates west from Wúliǎn County of Zāngkē,
called Yǒuliǎn under Wáng Mǎng.
It flows east to Tánzhōng and enters the Tán River.
The Tán River passes east of Zhōngliú County and west of Ālín County,
then enters the Yù River from the right.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
"The Qiáo River flows east to Zhōngliú and enters the Tán River."
It also says:
"In Lǐngfāng County, there is also a Qiáo River."
I have examined its waterways,
and there are no other distinct tributaries.
It is precisely where the Qiáo and Wēn Rivers intermingle,
hence they share a common name.
Previous writers all say it reaches Zhōngliú and enters the Tán River.
The Tán River also acquires the combined name of Yù,
but the character should be Wēn,
not Qiáo River.
This is likely an error in writing the character.
To the right of the Yù River, the Liú River flows into it,
originating south from Bùshān County,
flowing down past Zhōngliú to enter the Yù River.
The Yù River flows east past Ālín County,
then east past Měnglíng County,
where the Yín River flows into it.
Further east, it passes Guǎngxìn County of Cāngwú,
where the Lí River flows into it.
The Yù River flows further east,
where the Fēng River flows into it.
This river originates west of Féngchéng County in Línhè Commandery,
from Niútún Mountain on the eastern border of Xièmù County.
It is also called the Lín River.
It flows southeast past the west of Méngzhǔ Ridge,
then further southeast,
joining the Qiáo River from the left.
Yǔ Zhòngchū said:
"The water emerges from Méngzhǔ Ridge,
flowing south into the Lín River."
The Lín River flows past the east of Línhè County,
then south to the commandery seat,
where it joins the Hè River from the left.
The Hè River originates from Luó Mountain northwest of Xīng'ān County in the northeast,
flowing southeast past the west of Xīng'ān County.
Shèng Hóngzhī's *Records of Jīngzhōu* says:
"By the water at Xīng'ān County, there is a flat stone,
on which are stone sandals,
said to be where the King of Yuè took off his sandals when crossing the stream."
The Hè River flows southwest to the east of Línhè Commandery,
then enters the Lín River from the right.
The commandery seat faces the confluence of these two rivers,
hence the commandery and county derive their names from this.
The Lín River flows southwest past the south of the commandery,
then southwest past the east of Fēngyáng County,
becoming the Fēngxī River.
Therefore, the *Treatise on Geography* says:
"The county has the Fēng River."
It flows southwest into Guǎngxìn County,
then south into the Yù River,
at a place called the Fēngxī River Mouth.
The Yù River flows east past Gāoyào County,
where the Láo River flows into it.
This river originates south in Hépǔ Commandery of Jiāozhōu,
with its seat at Hépǔ County,
established in the sixth year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
after pacifying Yuè.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huánhé,
and the county Huántíng.
In the seventh year of Huángwǔ of Sūn Quán,
it was changed to Zhūguān Commandery.
The commandery does not produce grain,
but gathers many pearls and treasures.
Previous administrations were oppressive and harsh,
causing the pearls to migrate to Jiāozhǐ.
Mèng Bózhōu of Kuàijī became the governor,
implementing benevolent governance,
and the pearls returned.
The commandery administered Línyǔn County,
called Dàyǔn under Wáng Mǎng.
The Láo River flows north from the county,
past Gāoyào County into the Yù River.
The Yù River flows south past the west of Nánhǎi Commandery of Guǎngzhōu,
where Yín Mountain rises.
Further south,
it receives the three waters of Xīsuí from the right,
then flows south past Sìhuì Inlet.
The waterway above connects to the ancient Lángjiū Inlet within the Cáo Estuary west of Lúróng County in Rìnán Commandery,
which Mǎ Yuán used for transport.
The water curves southeast,
bending to connect to Láng Lake.
The lake water receives the Jīnshān Lángjiū,
and the Jiū River flows north,
joining the Lúróng and Shòulíng Rivers from the left.
The Lúróng River originates from the high mountains south of Qūsù City in the southwest.
South of the mountains are long ridges,
connecting to a natural barrier reaching the sky.
West of the ridges, the Lúróng River converges,
winding hidden around the mountains, circling west and north of the guard post,
then flowing east past the north of Qūsù City.
Further east,
it joins the Shòulíng River from the right.
This river originates from the border of Shòulíng County.
In the ninth year of Zhèngshǐ of Wèi,
Línyì advanced and invaded,
reaching Shòulíng County, which became the boundary;
this is that county.
Shòulíng County is named for the convergence of waters,
hence the river derives its name.
It flows east past the old city of Qūsù,
but examining ancient records,
there is no mention of the name Qūsù.
Yīng Shào's *Records of Geography and Customs* says:
"Rìnán
was formerly the Xiàng Commandery of Qín."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn opened Rìnán Commandery in the sixth year of Yuándǐng,
with its seat at Xījuǎn County.
The *Records of Línyì* says:
"The city is over four hundred *li*
by footpath from Línyì."
The *Records of the Outer Regions of Jiāozhōu* says:
"From Rìnán Commandery south,
going to the state of Línyì,
it is over four hundred *li*."
The distances correspond,
so the city was formerly Xījuǎn County.
The *Treatise on Geography* says:
"The water enters the sea."
There are bamboos that can be made into walking sticks.
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Rìnán Tíng.
The Línyì Jì says:
Its city is situated between two rivers,
with mountains on three sides,
overlooking water to the north and south,
with streams and inlets to the east and west,
converging and flowing beneath the city walls.
The city’s western side bends at ten corners,
with a circumference of six lǐ and one hundred seventy bù.
Its east–west span measures six hundred fifty bù.
The brick wall is two zhàng high,
with a brick parapet one zhàng high built atop it,
pierced with square openings.
Planks are laid upon the bricks,
and on the planks stand five-tiered pavilions.
Houses are built upon the pavilions,
and towers are erected upon the houses.
The taller towers reach seven or eight zhàng,
while the shorter ones are five or six zhàng.
The city has thirteen gates.
All palaces face south.
There are over two thousand one hundred rooms in the buildings.
Markets and dwellings surround them.
The terrain is steep and perilous,
hence all the weapons and military equipment of Línyì
are stored in Qūsù.
There are many city fortifications.
Since the time of the Línyì king Fàn Húdá,
the remaining settlers from the Qín era
have assimilated to the local customs.
The old traditions of Rìnán
have completely changed.
People nest in trees and dwell on branches,
nestling against the city walls and clinging to the mountains.
Dense brambles and thick reeds
reach up to the clouds,
shrouded in deep mist and endless haze,
unfit for human habitation.
In Qūsù, eight gnomon markers were erected;
the shadow cast by the sun measured eight cùn to the south.
From here, shadows southward lie to the south of the sun,
hence the commandery was named accordingly.
Looking at the North Star,
it appears to fall at the edge of the sky.
The sun is in the north,
so they open north-facing doors to face the sun.
This is the general situation.
Fàn Tài’s Gǔjīn Shànyán says:
Zhāng Zhòng of Rìnán
went to Luòyáng to present accounts.
At the grand assembly on the winter solstice,
Emperor Míng asked:
“Does the Rìnán commandery look northward to see the sun?”
Zhòng replied:
“Nowadays, commanderies have names like Yúnzhōng and Jīnchéng,
but they do not necessarily correspond to reality.
The sun also rises in the east for all.
As for the warm and mild climate,
and the angle of the sun’s shadow,
officials and commoners dwell
according to their preferences, facing any direction,
east, west, north, or south,
with no fixed orientation.
The people are fierce and stubborn,
resolute in battle,
adept at navigating mountains and waters,
but unfamiliar with flat land.
The ancients said:
‘The Five Ridges
are the boundary between heaven and earth, separating the interior from the exterior.’
How much more so for the distant routes beyond the sea,
gazing at the nine ridges stretching far and wide?
It is no longer just a matter of obstructed roads,
but truly a remote and obscure frontier land.”
The Shòulíng River flows from south of the city,
eastward merging with the Lúróng River,
then eastward pouring into Lángjiū.
The waters accumulate there,
forming a deep lake below,
called Láng Lake.
At the mouth of the inlet lies the Qín-era Xiàng Commandery,
its ruins still remaining.
Looking south from the lake,
it connects outward to Shòulíng.
From Láng Lake, one enters Sìhuì Inlet.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā,
because Línyì was stubborn and hostile,
difficult to civilize over generations,
relying on its remoteness and numerous people,
disregarding authority and betraying virtue,
with northern tribute already arriving,
yet southern gold lacking in offerings,
the emperor ordered a deputy general and General Lóngxiāng, Governor of Jiāozhōu, Tán Hézhī, to deploy troops in Rìnán,
cultivating culture to subdue the distant.
In the twenty-third year,
they raised banners and entered Láng Lake from the mouth of Sìhuì Inlet,
stationing troops at Qūsù,
advancing to besiege the city.
Using scaling ladders and cloud bridges,
suspended towers to ascend the ramparts,
with drums and gongs resounding loudly,
fierce warriors raging like lightning,
winds fierce and flames soaring,
the city walls crumbled and the defenders fell.
They beheaded the king of Qūsù, Fàn Fúlóng.
Those above fifteen years of age
were slaughtered without mercy.
Blood rained from the towers and pavilions,
corpses piled into mounds.
Proceeding south from Sìhuì,
one reaches the mouth of Lúróng Inlet.
In the third year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty,
the post of Commandant of Dependent States in Rìnán Commandery was abolished,
and the former seat of Lúróng County was used to establish Rìnán Commandery and the old seat of Xiànglín County.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì says:
The commandery is two hundred lǐ from the mouth of Lúróng Inlet,
which was the former seat of Xiànglín County of the Qín-era Xiàng Commandery.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
the Western Expedition Commander Huán Wēn dispatched Supervisor Téng Jùn to lead troops from Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu to attack Fàn Wén at the old Lúróng County of Rìnán,
but was defeated by Wén,
precisely at this place.
He retreated to Jiǔzhēn,
and reorganized the troops.
Wén died of his wounds,
and his son Fó succeeded him.
In the seventh year,
Jùn and the Governor of Jiāozhōu, Yáng Píng, again advanced their troops to Shòulíng Inlet,
entering and stationing at Láng Lake,
to attack Fó at the old terrace of Rìnán. Fó gathered his forces like ants,
connecting fortifications over fifty lǐ.
Jùn and Píng defeated them,
and Fó fled into the marshes.
He sent a chieftain with hands bound behind his back
to plead for mercy at the army gate.
They dispatched warrior Chén Yán to console Fó,
made a covenant with him, and then withdrew.
Kāng Tài’s Fúnán Jì says:
From Línyì to the mouth of Lúróng Inlet in Rìnán is about two hundred lǐ.
Setting out southward from the mouth to the various states of Fúnán,
one often departs from this inlet.
Thus, the Línyì Jì says:
“Reaching the farthest bounds of the vast ocean,
extending to the utmost limits of flowing garments.”
The land borders the vast sea,
a thoroughfare for many states.
The Yù River flows south to Shòulíng,
which is one inlet.
The inlet receives water from the southern Dūguān Fort Inlet of Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
The Línyì Jì says:
The inlet connects to Tónggǔ, Wàiyuè, Āndìng, and Huánggǎng Xīnkǒu.
It is said that crossing at Tónggǔ
means entering Luòyuè territory.
There are bronze drums,
hence the name.
Mǎ Yuán took the drums to cast bronze horses.
Reaching the Záo Kǒu,
which was excavated by Mǎ Yuán,
it connects internally to Jiǔzhēn and Pǔyáng.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì
states that Jiǔdé Commandery has Pǔyáng County.
The Jiāozhōu Jì says:
The excavated southern pond
is the route through Jiǔzhēn,
five hundred lǐ from the province.
In the nineteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
it was opened by Mǎ Yuán.
The Línyì Jì says:
Wàiyuè borders Jìsù.
Looking from Dūwàng to Jìsù,
one exits at Pǔyáng.
Crossing Biànzhōu,
one reaches Diǎnyóu.
Crossing the old county,
one arrives at Xiánhuān.
Xiánhuān belongs to Jiǔzhēn.
South of Xiánhuān,
deer and muntjacs fill the hills,
calling to their companions,
their cries filling the wilderness.
Peacocks soar,
obscuring the sun and covering the mountains.
Crossing the Zhì Kǒu,
one reaches Jiǔdé.
According to the Jìnshū Dìdào Jì, there is Jiǔdé County.
The Jiāozhōu Wàiyù Jì says:
Jiǔdé County belongs to Jiǔzhēn Commandery,
located south of the commandery,
bordering Rìnán.
The Mán Lúyú dwelled in this land.
Upon his death,
his son Bǎogāng succeeded him.
His grandson Dǎng
submitted to Wú’s rule,
and it was established as Jiǔdé Commandery,
again becoming subordinate.
The Línyì Jì says:
Jiǔdé
is the farthest reach of the Nine Yí tribes,
hence the commandery is named accordingly.
The name of the commandery was established,
during the Zhou dynasty, it was the Yi state of the Yuèshang clan.
According to the "Zhōu Lǐ",
the nine Yi tribes extended as far as Yuèshang.
White pheasants and elephant tusks,
came through multiple translations.
From Jiǔdé, one reaches Lèikǒu,
the water source comes from the distant wilderness in the northwest,
passing through the boundaries of Níngzhōu.
Within the Jiǔdé estuary, it passes through the Yuèshang Jiū, Jiǔdé Jiū, and Nánlíng Jiū.
According to the "Jìn Shū Dìdào Jì",
Jiǔdé Commandery had Nánlíng County,
established during the Jin dynasty.
Zhú Zhī's "Fúnán Jì" states,
mountain streams and rapids are called jiū.
The "Dìlǐ Zhì" says:
The commandery has fifty-two small waterways,
all flowing alongside the great river,
these are what are referred to as jiū.
The "Línyì Jì" says:
In the ninth year of the Yìxī era,
the Governor of Jiāozhǐ, Dù Huìdù, built the Jiǔzhēn estuary,
and fought with the King of Línyì, Fàn Húdá,
capturing and beheading two of Húdá's sons,
taking over a hundred prisoners,
Húdá fled.
In the fifth month,
Huìdù went from the Jiǔzhēn estuary through Dūsù estuary,
again attacked Jiǔzhēn,
with a long encirclement crossing the mountains,
and heavy barricades cutting off the estuary,
driving elephants as the vanguard,
engaging in battle at the city walls,
fighting for several days,
causing casualties before retreating.
The "Dìlǐ Zhì" says:
Jiǔzhēn Commandery,
was established in the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
administered from Xūpǔ County,
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huānchéng.
The "Jìn Shū Dìdào Jì" says:
Jiǔzhēn Commandery had Sōngyuán County.
The "Línyì Jì" says:
West of Sōngyuán,
birds and beasts are tame,
unaware of the fear of bows,
widows live alone,
with disheveled hair until old age,
the southern shifting ridges,
steep but not exceeding a ren in height,
the orioles harbor spring in the north,
kingfishers bask in the light in the south.
Although the chirping sounds connect,
the city walls separate them distinctly,
it is difficult to travel alone,
due to the division of customs and surnames.
From Nánlíng Jiū, one exits the southern boundary,
the Mán people advance to Qíshān,
in the third year of the Tàihé era,
Fàn Wén invaded Jiāozhōu, dividing the boundary at Héngshān,
passing the Bǐjǐng Temple,
from Ménpǔ to Gǔzhàn Bay.
In the eleventh year of the Chìwū era of Wú,
the ninth year of the Zhèngshǐ era of Wèi,
Jiāozhōu and Línyì fought a great battle in the bay,
initially losing Qūsù.
Crossing Lúróng County, a subordinate county of Rìnán Commandery.
From Lúróng County to Wúbiàn,
passing the beacon fire to Bǐjǐng County,
at noon, the sun overhead,
the shadow falls directly beneath one's body,
the shadow aligns with the person.
Rú Chún said:
Therefore, the county was named Bǐjǐng.
Kàn Yīn said:
Bǐ,
is read as bì, meaning to shelter.
The shadow is below oneself,
meaning one is sheltered by one's own body.
The "Línyì Jì" says:
Crossing Bǐjǐng, one reaches Zhūwú.
The estuary of Zhūwú County,
marks the current boundary,
south of Zhūwú,
there are Wénláng people,
living in the wild without houses,
resting under trees,
eating raw fish and meat,
gathering incense as their livelihood,
trading with others,
like the people of the ancient sovereigns.
South of the county is Wénláng Jiū,
its lower flow passes through.
The "Jìn Shū Dìdào Jì" says:
Zhūwú County belonged to Rìnán Commandery,
two hundred lǐ from the commandery seat,
the people of this county,
during the Hàn dynasty, could not endure the two-thousand-dàn officials,
requested to lead Qūdū Gān to establish a state.
The "Línyì Jì" says:
Qūdū,
is an Yi people.
Within Zhūshí estuary, it connects to Wúláo Lake,
Wúláo Jiū water connects to Shòulíng estuary.
In the first year of the Yuánjiā era,
the Governor of Jiāozhōu, Ruǎn Mízhī, campaigned against Línyì,
Yángmài was away for a marriage and not present,
General Fènwēi Ruǎn Qiānzhī led seven thousand men,
first attacked Qūsù,
already passed Sìhuì,
but had not entered Shòulíng,
for three days and nights without a place to rest,
the sea congealed against the shore,
they encountered a great storm and were defeated.
Yángmài, bringing his marriage party,
led about three hundred ships of troops to provide aid,
Qiānzhī encountered the storm,
with only a few ships remaining,
at night, they met within Shòulíng estuary,
fighting a great battle in the darkness,
Qiānzhī personally shot Yángmài's helmsman,
the ships were thrown into disarray,
a single Kūnlún boat,
rescued Yángmài.
Qiānzhī, with the remnants after the storm and drowning,
found it difficult to achieve victory,
from here, he returned across Shòulíng,
to Wēngōng estuary.
In the third year of the Shēngpíng era,
Wēn Fàngzhī campaigned against Fàn Fó at the boundary of Yīnyáng Qí in the bay,
entered Xīnluó Bay,
reached Yānxià,
also called Ābēn estuary,
entered Pénglóng Bay to take shelter from wind and waves,
which is the sea islet of Línyì.
In the twenty-third year of the Yuánjiā era,
the Governor of Jiāozhōu, Tán Hézhī, defeated Qūsù,
already flying banners across the sea,
heading toward Diǎnchōng,
at the ghost pagoda on Pénglóng biàn,
fought a great battle with Línyì,
then crossed Diǎnchōng, Línyì entered the estuary,
ordered the army to advance greatly,
due to maintaining caution.
West of the estuary,
is the capital of Línyì,
administered from Diǎnchōng,
forty lǐ from the coast,
situated at the edge of the wild frontier,
the state is south of the borders of Yuèshang,
it was the Xiànglín County of the Xiàng Commandery during the Qín and Hàn dynasties.
To the east, it borders the vast sea,
to the west, it reaches Xúláng,
to the south, it connects with Fúnán,
to the north, it links with Jiǔdé.
Later, the names Xiànglín and Línyì were abandoned,
the state was founded at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
during the chaos of the Chūpíng era,
people harbored rebellious thoughts,
the Xiànglín official with the surname Ōu,
had a son named Kuí,
attacked the county and killed the magistrate,
proclaimed himself king,
taking advantage of the chaotic times,
Línyì was thus established,
later, succession passed to descendants,
during the tripartite division,
it did not align with any side.
Wú held Jiāozhōu territory,
bordering it,
advanced and invaded Shòulíng to establish the boundary.
After Ōu Kuí,
the state had no historical records,
losing the succession lineage,
the number of generations is difficult to ascertain,
the ancestral line was extinguished,
with no remaining descendants.
The grandson Fàn Xióng succeeded to the throne,
the people were willing to support him.
Later, Xióng died,
his son Yì succeeded,
there was Fàn Wén,
a slave of the Yi commander Fàn Zhuī from Xījuǎn County in Rìnán.
When Wén was a slave,
herding sheep in mountain streams,
in the stream water, he caught two carp,
hid them and brought them back,
planning to eat them privately,
the master found out and searched,
Wén was greatly ashamed and afraid,
quickly made an excuse, saying:
he brought back whetstones,
not fish.
The master went to where the fish were,
saw they were two stones,
believed it and left,
Wén then found it strange.
The stones had iron patterns,
he went into the mountains and smelted iron from the stones,
forging two knives,
He raised the blade toward the stone barrier,
and prayed, saying:
"If the carp transforms,
and smelted stone becomes a blade,
and if, upon striking the stone barrier, it breaks, then this blade has divine power,
and Wén shall obtain this,
to become the ruler of the state."
"If it does not cut in,
then this blade lacks divine power."
He advanced and struck the stone barrier,
and it cleaved like the swords Lóngyuān and Gānjiàng cutting through reeds,
and from then on, the people's hearts gradually attached to him.
The struck stone still exists today,
and the fish-blade is still preserved,
passed down to sons and grandsons,
like the sword that beheaded the serpent.
Chuí once sent Wén on a distant trading journey,
north to the Central States,
where he saw and heard much.
During the Jiànxīng era of Emperor Mǐn of Jìn,
he went south to Línyì,
where he taught King Fàn Yì to construct city walls and moats,
repair and prepare armor and weapons,
and begin planning the layout.
The king loved and trusted him,
making him a general,
and he was able to win the hearts of the masses.
Wén slandered the king's various sons,
causing some to be exiled and others to flee,
leaving the king isolated.
The king died in the sixth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng,
without an heir.
Wén brought a prince back from a foreign land,
and while sailing on the sea, he fetched water,
placed poison in a coconut,
and had the prince drink it, killing him.
He then coerced the people of the state,
and established himself as king.
He took the former king's wives and concubines and placed them in a tall tower;
those who submitted to him,
he took and kept;
those who did not submit to him,
he cut off their food and drink until they died.
The "Jiāngdōng Old Affairs" states:
Fàn Wén was originally a man of Yángzhōu.
In his youth, he was captured and made a slave,
sold and taken to Jiāozhōu.
At the age of fifteen or sixteen,
he committed an offense deserving of caning,
and in fear, he fled,
following Línyì merchants across the sea to a distant land.
He entered the service of the king,
and was greatly favored and loved.
After more than ten years,
the king died,
and Wén harmed the king's two sons,
deceitfully killed the marquises and generals,
established himself as king,
and imposed his authority over various states.
Some were barbarians with topknots and savage speech,
eating with their mouths and drinking through their noses;
some had tattooed faces and carved bodies,
naked and wild tribes.
Exiles from Hàn and Wèi,
all were employed by him.
In the second year of the Jiànyuán era,
he attacked Rìnán, Jiǔdé, and Jiǔzhēn,
causing the common people to flee in panic,
leaving a thousand li without smoke,
and then returned to Línyì.
Línyì lies 2,500 li west of Guǎngzhōu.
At the southwestern corner of the city,
there are high mountains and long ridges,
connecting to the sky barrier.
North of the ridges, they join with ravines.
The great source of the Huái River emerges from the distant borders of Nánuǎn,
passing through three layers of long islets,
winding around hidden mountains to the west,
guarding the north and turning east,
with the southern side of the ridges opening into ravines.
The small source of the Huái River emerges from mountain streams in the Sōnggēn border region,
winding around hidden mountains to the south,
curving through streets and turning east,
merging with the Huái flow to pour into Diǎnchōng.
The city borders mountains to the southwest,
and overlooks water to the northeast.
Double moats and flowing streams
encircle the city below.
Outside the southeastern moat,
close against the city walls,
it stretches long east to west,
narrow north to south.
At the western end of the northern side,
