it twists and turns inward.
The city's circumference is eight li and one hundred paces.
The brick wall is two zhàng high,
with a brick parapet one zhàng high on top,
opened with square gaps and holes.
On the bricks rest planks,
on the planks are layered pavilions,
on the pavilions are built houses,
on the houses are constructed towers,
the taller ones six or seven zhàng high,
the shorter ones four or five zhàng high.
Flying galleries and owl-tail ornaments,
greet the wind and brush the clouds,
following the mountains and overlooking the water,
lofty and precipitous,
but the construction is crude and clumsy.
According to ancient barbarian custom,
the city opens four gates.
The east is the front gate,
facing the banks of the two Huái streams.
On the winding road, there is an ancient stele,
with barbarian script praising the virtue of the former king Hú Dá.
The west gate faces the double moats,
turning north and ascending the mountain.
West of the mountain,
is the Huái River flow.
The south gate crosses two layers of moats,
facing Lord Wēn's fortifications.
In the second year of the Shēngpíng era,
Jiāozhōu Governor Wēn Fàngzhī killed Jiāozhǐ Prefect Dù Bǎo and Assistant Administrator Ruǎn Lǎng,
then campaigned against Línyì.
After repeated battles on water and land,
Fóbǎo City defended itself,
repeatedly seeking to submit,
and he granted it.
Today, five li south of Línyì's east city are Lord Wēn's two fortifications.
The north gate borders the Huái River,
the road cut off and impassable.
Inside the city is a small inner city,
with a circumference of three hundred twenty paces.
Halls with tiled roofs,
the southern wall unopened,
with long buildings at both ends,
ridges extending north and south,
the south designed to face away from the sun.
In the western district of the city,
a stone mountain faces the Huái River and the sun,
with an east-facing hall opened,
flying eaves and owl-tail ornaments,
green latticework and red steps,
rafters and purlins,
mostly following ancient methods.
The pillars of the pavilion hall
rise over a zhàng and five chǐ above the city wall.
Cow dung is used as plaster,
the walls gleaming,
winding through curved passages,
with elegant windows and purple shutters.
The pepper chamber for consorts and concubines,
no separate palaces or towers,
the main hall and long corridors,
all within the same hall.
Leaning over the eastern balcony,
he speaks directly to those below.
Sons, brothers, ministers, and attendants
are all not permitted to ascend.
There are over fifty buildings,
ridgepoles connecting and beams joining,
eaves and roofs layered upon each other.
Spirit shrines and ghost pagodas,
eight temples large and small,
layered terraces and double pavilions,
resembling Buddhist monasteries.
The outer walls lack markets or neighborhoods,
the city has few inhabitants.
The coast is desolate,
not a place for people to live.
Yet the first ruler established it for eternal peace,
and the state has been maintained for ten generations—
can it last long?
During the Yuánjiā era,
Tán Hézhī campaigned against Línyì.
Its king, Yángmài,
fled with the entire state by night into the mountains and marshes.
[Tán] occupied its cities,
seizing treasures worth hundreds of millions,
and after the army withdrew,
Yángmài returned to his state.
His home and state lay in ruins,
with few people remaining at the time.
He paced anxiously, collapsing in distress,
fainting in rage and reviving,
and died in the twenty-third year of Yuánjiā.
Earlier,
when Yángmài's mother was pregnant,
she dreamed someone spread a golden mat for Yángmài,
and her child fell onto the mat.
A golden light arose,
shining brilliantly and dazzlingly bright.
In Chinese custom, the finest gold is called purple-polished gold;
in barbarian custom, the finest gold is called Yángmài gold.
When his father Hú Dá died,
he succeeded to the kingship,
able to win people's hearts.
Taking the spiritual dream as
an auspicious sign for the state,
his crown prince was initially named Duō.
Later, after Yángmài died,
his son Duō, at the age of nineteen, succeeded him.
Admiring the virtue of his late father,
he changed his name back to Yángmài.
For two generations in the ancestral line,
father and son shared the same name,
which showed that Línyì was destined to fall.
Outside the city,
beyond the moats and trenches,
forests and thorns grew wild and tangled,
dense and gloomy with brambles,
vines twined and bamboo flourished,
intermingling and reaching to the sky.
Among them were groves of fragrant cassia,
where the air was clear and the mist pure.
Guìfù,
a native of the county,
dwelled in this forest,
consuming cassia and attaining the Way.
Birds of the season with rare plumage
soared and gathered, their calls filling the air,
including the bǐyì bird.
They would not fly unless paired,
and the bird was named guīfēi,
its call sounding like its own name.
This longing for home is profoundly sorrowful,
and reverence for one's homeland became a custom.
Yùzhāng's Yú Yìqī,
by nature upright and unyielding,
would not stoop to crooked customs,
and found no place to settle.
He traveled far to the south,
and in his "Letter to Hán Kāngbó" wrote:
"Only the betel nut tree
is worth seeing on travels to the far south,
but it cannot endure frost,
and cannot be planted in the north.
Not having been seen by elders,
it fills one with deep regret.
I once watched the flying birds longing for their homeland,
and it deepened my thoughts, so I convey my feelings,
saying that this bird has a green back,
a red belly,
its crimson heart exposed,
its mournful cry unexpressed.
All day long it flies homeward,
yet flies not ten thousand *li*,
with tens of thousands of *li* still ahead.
How can it ever return?"
Jiǔzhēn's governor Rèn Yán
first taught plowing with oxen,
transforming the customs of Jiāozhōu,
and his influence spread to Xiànglín.
Since the knowledge of plowing began,
over six hundred years have passed,
and the methods of fire-weeding and cultivation
are the same as in Huáxià.
They have fields called white fields,
where white grain is planted,
with fire applied in the seventh month,
and harvest in the tenth month;
fields called red fields,
where red grain is planted,
with work in the twelfth month,
and harvest in the fourth month.
This is the so-called double-harvest rice.
As for grasses and sprouts,
grains are planted in succession month by month,
with early and late varieties,
blooming every month without fail.
The labor of plowing and weeding is heavy,
but the profit from harvest is light,
because the ripening is swift.
The rice does not scatter outward,
so it is always a land of plenty.
Silkworms produce cocoons eight times a year.
This is what is called "eightfold silkworm silk" in the "Odes of the Three Capitals."
The small streams on the cliffs are veiled in mist,
often spouting flying cascades,
sometimes like drifting snow or rising sand,
clear, cold, and bottomless.
Dividing into streams and branching into gullies,
they connect and flow together.
The water flows from the northeast corner of the city,
where a high bridge is suspended over it.
Crossing to the north bank of the Huái,
one reaches the thoroughfare of Pénglóng and Qūsù.
It was here that Tán Hézhī fought the great battle at the eastern bridge,
where Yángmài was wounded and fell from his elephant.
This is the very place.
The water then flows southeast past Chuánguānkǒu,
beyond the sources of the Chuánguān River and Xúláng,
where the natives all go naked,
men covering themselves with bamboo tubes,
women with leaves to hide their forms.
They are called Lánghuǎng,
the so-called "Naked Country."
Although accustomed to nudity,
they still feel shame without cover,
so they rely on the dark of night
to trade with others.
In the darkness, they smell gold,
and can tell its quality,
and the next morning, upon inspection,
it is exactly as they said.
From here, traveling outward,
one can reach Fúnán.
According to Zhú Zhī's *Records of Fúnán*:
"Fúnán is four thousand *li* from Línyì,
accessible by water and land."
Tán Hézhī ordered his troops to enter the city's harbor,
occupying Chuánguānkǒu,
a city six *li* in size.
From Chuánguānkǒu, the water flows down into the eastern lake of the great inlet,
where the great waters flow continuously,
and the tide rises, flowing westward.
The tide rises seven or eight feet day and night,
and from here westward,
on the new and full moons, the tides combine,
rising once for seven days,
with the water rising sixteen or seventeen feet.
After seven days,
the tide divides into two cycles day and night,
rising one or two feet.
In spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
it follows a strict pattern,
with fixed highs and lows,
and the water neither increases nor decreases.
This is the sea's movement,
also called Xiàngshuǐ,
and it also bears the name Xiàngpǔ.
This is what the *Table of Jìn Dynasty Meritorious Officials* calls "the clear course of Jīnlín,
the pure source of Xiàngzhǔ."
In its streams, inlets, and islets,
there are tiny water insects
that gather on wood and eat through ships,
destroying them in several tens of days.
In the deep pools and clear rapids,
there are fresh fish,
black in color,
with bodies five *zhàng* long,
heads like those of horses.
They lie in wait for people entering the water,
and then come to harm them.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says:
"The countries of Lí'ěr and Diāotí
are both south of the Yùshuǐ."
The *Records of Línyì* says:
"The Hàn established nine commanderies,
and Dān'ěr was among them.
The people prefer to go barefoot,
and wear large, dangling ears as ornaments.
Although men and women expose themselves,
they do not consider it shameful.
The intense sun of summer
naturally darkens their skin,
and this habit becomes the norm,
with blackness considered beautiful.
This is the so-called 'Dark Country' of the *Lisāo*."
Thus, Dān'ěr is Lí'ěr.
Wáng's *Spring and Autumn Annals of Jiāo and Guǎng* says:
"The two commanderies of Zhūyá and Dān'ěr
were established together with Jiāozhōu,
all set up by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
In the great sea,
beyond the southern extreme,
opposite Héptǔ's Xúwén County,
on clear, windless days,
one can gaze directly at Zhūyá Island,
which appears as large as a granary.
Crossing from Xúwén,
with a north wind filling the sails,
one can reach it in a day and a night.
It measures over two thousand *li* in circumference,
with a diameter of eight hundred *li*.
The population numbers over a hundred thousand households,
all of different races and kinds.
They wear their hair loose and tattoo their bodies,
and the women are mostly beautiful,
fair-skinned, with long hair and lovely locks.
They gather like dogs and sheep,
and do not submit to virtuous teachings.
Dān'ěr was abolished first,
and Zhūyá rebelled repeatedly,
so Emperor Yuán abolished the commandery on Jiǎ Juānzhī's advice."
Yáng's *Record of Strange Things in the Southern Regions* says:
"Dān'ěr and Zhūyá
are both in the sea,
forming the eastern frontier.
Therefore, the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says:
'They are south of the Yùshuǐ.'"
The Yùshuǐ flows south from Shòulíng County into the sea.
In the past, Mǎ Wényuān piled stones to build a dike,
reaching Xiàngpǔ,
and erected a golden marker as the southern boundary.
Yú Yìqī wrote in a letter:
"Mǎ Wényuān set up two bronze pillars on the northern shore of Línyì.
Over ten households of soldiers were left behind and did not return.
They settled on the southern shore of Shòulíng, facing the bronze pillars,
and all took the surname Mǎ."
Since the intermarriages,
there are now two hundred households.
Jiāozhōu, because they lived as wanderers,
called them Mǎliú.
Their language, food, and drink
are still similar to those of the Huá people.
Mountains and rivers have shifted,
and the bronze pillar is now again in the sea.
It is precisely by relying on these people
that the old location can be recognized.
The *Línyì Jì* says:
In the nineteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Mǎ Yuán erected two bronze pillars at the southern border of Xiànglín,
dividing it from the Xītú Kingdom,
marking the southern frontier of Hàn.
The local people, because they lived as wanderers,
called them Mǎliú,
and they are known as descendants of the Hàn people.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
The Yù River originates from Xiàng Commandery and flows southwest into the South Sea,
entering east of Xūlíng.
Yìng Shào said:
The Yù River originates from Guǎngxìn,
and flows east into the sea.
This may be correct at the start,
but is wrong at the end.
37 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll 37
37.1 Yān River
37.1 Yān River
The Yān River originates beyond the borders of Suíjiǔ County in Yuèxī.
Lǚ Chēn said:
The Yān River is also called the Fù River.
It flows southeast to Qīnglíng County,
where there is Yútóng Mountain.
The mountain deity has a golden horse and a jade-green chicken,
whose light and shadows flicker fleetingly,
and the people often see them.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn sent the Grand Master of Remonstrance Wáng Bāo to offer sacrifices,
hoping to obtain the chicken and horse.
Wáng Bāo fell ill on the journey and died,
so this was not accomplished.
Wáng Bāo's "Ode to the Jade-Green Chicken" says:
"Respectfully moving the golden essence and spirit horse,
the ethereal jade-green chicken."
Thus, Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" says:
"The golden horse gallops with light, leaving no shadow;
the jade-green chicken flickers fleetingly, displaying its form."
Further east, it passes south of Gūfù County,
and flows east into the Ruò River.
The Yān River passes through Línchí Marsh of the county and flows northeast,
passing west of Yúnnán County,
and flows northeast into the Ruò River.
37.2 Yèyú River
37.2 Yèyú River
The Yèyú River of Yìzhōu
originates from the northern border of the county,
bends and flows northeast from the county.
The county
was originally the state of Diānchí Yèyú.
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Táng Méng was sent to open it up,
and it was made Yìzhōu Commandery.
The commandery had Yèyú County.
Eighty *lǐ* northwest of the county,
there is Diàoniǎo Mountain.
Hundreds and thousands of birds gather in flocks,
and when they assemble,
they chirp and chatter noisily.
Each year, they arrive from the seventh to eighth month,
and stop around the sixteenth or seventeenth day,
coming six times a year.
Pheasants and sparrows come to mourn.
At night, people light fires to wait and catch them.
Those without a crop and do not eat,
as if specially grieving,
are considered righteous and are not taken.
It is commonly said
that the phoenix died on this mountain,
so all birds come to mourn,
hence the name Diàoniǎo (Mourning Birds).
East of the county is Yèyú Marsh,
where the Yèyú River accumulates to form this marshland.
It passes Bùwéi County,
which
was originally the state of Jiǔlóng Āiláo.
There is Láo Mountain.
Long ago, there was a woman named Shā Yī
who lived on Láo Mountain.
While fishing in the water,
she touched a sunken log and seemed to feel something,
became pregnant,
and gave birth to ten sons.
Later, the sunken log transformed into a dragon,
emerged from the water,
and nine sons fled in fright.
The youngest son could not leave,
so he sat with his back to the dragon.
The dragon then licked him.
His mother spoke in bird language,
calling the back "jiǔ"
and calling sitting "lóng,"
so she named him Jiǔlóng.
When he grew up,
his elder brothers together pushed Jiǔlóng to become king.
Later, at the foot of Láo Mountain, there was a husband and wife
who gave birth to ten daughters.
Jiǔlóng took them all as wives,
and thus they multiplied.
They all painted their bodies with dragon patterns
and wore clothing with tails.
After Jiǔlóng died,
for generations they did not communicate with the Central Plains.
In the twenty-third year of the Jiànwǔ era of Hàn,
the king sent troops
riding on leather boats southward,
attacking the Lùduǒ people of Hàn.
The Lùduǒ people were weak and small,
and were about to be captured.
Then, heaven thundered mightily,
with heavy rain and a south wind,
causing the water to surge and flow backward,
waves surging for over two hundred *lǐ*.
The leather boats sank,
and thousands drowned.
Several years later,
they again sent six kings
with about ten thousand men to attack Lùduǒ.
The king of Lùduǒ fought them,
killed the six kings,
and the elders of Āiláo buried them together.
That night,
tigers dug them up and ate them.
The next morning, only bones were seen.
Terrified, they withdrew,
and in fear said to their elders and petty kings:
"Āiláo has violated the borders
since ancient times.
Now, attacking Lùduǒ,
we were immediately punished by heaven.
Does the Central Plains have a king who has received the mandate?
How clearly heaven aids them!"
They immediately sent envoys to Yuèxī to offer tribute,
seeking to submit and attach,
to long protect the border passes.
In the twelfth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
it was established as Yǒngchāng Commandery,
with the commandery seat at Bùwéi County.
It is likely that Qín Shǐhuáng relocated the descendants of Lǚ Bùwéi here,
hence naming the county Bùwéi.
It is over six hundred *lǐ* north of Yèyú.
The Yèyú River does not pass through this county.
What flows north from Bùwéi
is the Lúcāng forbidden water.
The Yèyú River passes east of Suíjiǔ County from the south of the county,
and further passes west of Gūfù County,
joining with the Yān River.
It then flows southeast past Yǒngchāng Xiélóng County,
which in the third year of the Jiànxīng era, Liú Shàn placed under Yúnnán,
lying northeast of Bùwéi County.
It flows southeast out of the Yìzhōu border.
The Yèyú River flows southeast from Xiélóng County past Qínzāng County,
and to the south, together with the Pú River, it empties into the Diānchí Marsh at Liánrán and Shuāngbǎi counties.
From the marsh, the Yèyú River continues northeast past the south of Diānchí County,
then east past the south of Tóngbìng County,
then east past Lòujiāng County,
where it goes underground at the foot of a mountain,
reemerging at Fùkǒu,
and is called the Lòujiāng (Leaking River).
Zuǒ Sī’s "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" says:
"The Leaking River swirls underground, eroding its banks,
churning like the surging waves of the Valley of the Sun,
swelling like the swelling waves of the Mèngsì."
When Zhūgě Liàng pacified the south,
he fought south of this river.
The Yèyú River then flows past the north of Bēngǔ County,
where it joins the Pán River to the east.
The Pán River originates from the Xūtǐng Mountain southeast of Lǜgāo County,
flowing east past the north of Liángshuǐ Commandery and the south of Bēngǔ County.
The river is over a hundred paces wide,
and in its deepest parts reaches ten fathoms.
It is heavily plagued by miasma.
When Zhū Bāo rebelled,
Lǐ Huī pursued him as far as the Pán River.
In the nineteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
General Fúbō Mǎ Yuán submitted a memorial stating:
"Proceeding from Mílíng to Bēngǔ,
to attack Yìzhōu,
the Luòyuè troops under my command, numbering over ten thousand,
include more than two thousand soldiers skilled in combat.
Their bows are poisoned and sharp,
and they can shoot repeatedly,
their arrows falling like rain,
and wherever they strike, death follows.
I believe that advancing troops along this route is most advantageous,
as it relies on the benefits of the waterways,
making it swift and effective."
The Pán River then flows east past Hànxīng County,
where in the mountain streams,
Qíong bamboo and guāngláng trees grow abundantly.
The trees yield flour,
which the indigenous people rely on for sustenance.
Thus, "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" says:
"Qíong bamboo covers the ridges,"
and also:
"Flour comes from the guāngláng."
The Pán River flows north into the Yèyú River.
When Zhūgě Liàng entered the south,
he fought east of the Pán River.
Entering Xīsuí County of Zāngkē Commandery from the north, it becomes the Xīsuí River,
then flows east out of Jìnsāng Pass,
at Jìnsāng County,
which was the seat of the southern commandant of Zāngkē.
There is a pass over the river,
hence it is called Jìnsāng Pass.
Thus, Mǎ Yuán said:
"From the Mílíng waterway to the Jìnsāng Kingdom, then to Bēngǔ County in Yìzhōu,
transportation is convenient and unimpeded,
making it the route for military supplies and transport."
From Xīsuí to Jiāozhǐ,
lofty mountains and perilous terrain connect,
with a water route of three thousand lǐ.
The Yèyú River then flows southeast, crosses the Wēn River, and empties southeast into Jiāozhǐ.
Passing north of Mílíng County in Jiāozhǐ,
it divides into five waterways,
which crisscross Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
and at the southern boundary, they converge again into three waterways,
which flow east into the sea.
The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states:
Yáo extended his influence southward to Jiāozhǐ, which in the "Yǔ Gòng" is located at the southern frontier of Jīngzhōu,
beyond the remote wilderness,
hence it was called Yuè.
According to the *Zhōulǐ*,
among the eight southern barbarian tribes,
Diāotí and Jiāozhǐ
included people who did not eat grains.
The *Chūnqiū* does not mention them in its commentaries,
as they had no contact with Huáxià,
living on islands,
their people speaking bird-like languages.
Qín Shǐhuáng opened up the Yuè territory south of the mountains,
establishing the commanderies of Cāngwú, Nánhǎi, Jiāozhǐ, and Xiàng.
In the second year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he began to annex the Bǎiyuè,
opening up seven commanderies.
Thus, a Jiāozhì Cìshǐ was appointed
to oversee and govern them.
Initially, the administration was based in Guǎngxìn,
which is why it alone was not called a province.
At that time, Shuòfāng was also established,
signifying the opening of the northern frontier.
Subsequently, Jiāozhǐ was expanded in the south,
serving as a foundation for future generations.
Mílíng County
was opened in the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
and a Dūwèi was stationed there.
The *Jiāozhōu Wàiyù Jì* states:
The King of Yuè ordered two envoys to administer the people of Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn commanderies.
Later, the Hàn dynasty sent General Fúbō Lù Bódé to campaign against the King of Yuè.
When General Lù arrived at Hépǔ,
the King of Yuè ordered the two envoys
to present one hundred head of cattle,
a thousand jars of wine,
and the household registers of the two commanderies
to General Lù.
General Lù then appointed the two envoys as Tàishǒu of Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn,
while the various Luòjiàng continued to govern the people as before.
The commandery of Jiāozhǐ and the province were originally administered from here.
The province was named Jiāozhōu.
Later, a son of the Zhūyuān Luòjiàng named Shī
sought the daughter of the Mílíng Luòjiàng named Zhēng Cè as his wife.
Cè was a person of courage and daring.
Together with Shī, she raised a rebellion,
attacked and captured the province and commanderies,
and subdued the various Luòjiàng, all of whom submitted to Zhēng Cè.
She ruled as king from Mílíng County,
and exempted the people of Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn commanderies from taxes and levies for two years.
Later, the Hàn dynasty sent General Fúbō Mǎ Yuán to lead troops against Cè and Shī.
They fled into the Jīnxī Jiū,
and it took three years to capture them.
At that time, troops were also dispatched from Xīshǔ to jointly campaign against Cè and others.
All commanderies and counties were pacified,
and officials were appointed.
The mountains abound with large snakes,
called rán snakes.
They are ten zhàng long,
seven or eight chǐ in girth.
They often wait in trees for deer and other beasts.
When a deer or beast passes by,
they lower their heads and coil around it.
After a while, the deer dies.
First, they moisten it with saliva until it is wet,
then swallow it whole.
The antlers and bones pierce through the skin.
When the mountain tribes first see the snake motionless,
they impale it from head to tail with large bamboo spikes,
kill it, and eat it,
considering it a rare delicacy.
Therefore, Yáng's *Nányì Yìwù Zhì* states:
The rán is a great snake,
both massive and long,
its colors variegated and striking,
its patterns like brocade.
It devours pigs and swallows deer,
its fat nourishing its wounds.
At feasts and grand banquets,
it is served in dishes and cups.
This refers to the time when it is healing its wounds,
its fat is exceedingly rich.
If one throws a woman's garment at it while wrestling with it,
it will coil up and not rise,
making it easy to capture.
To the north are two rivers.
The left river flows northeast past the south of Wànghǎi County,
established in the nineteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era
by Mǎ Yuán during his campaign against Zhēng Cè.
It then flows east past the north of Lóngyuān County,
and further east joins the southern river,
which flows east from Mílíng County past the north of Fēngxī County.
The *Jiāozhōu Wàiyù Jì* states:
In ancient times, before commanderies and counties were established in Jiāozhǐ,
the land had Luò fields.
These fields rose and fell with the tides.
The people cultivated and ate from these fields,
hence they were called Luò people.
They established Luò kings and Luò marquises
to govern the various commanderies and counties.
The counties were mostly administered by Luòjiàng,
who held bronze seals with blue ribbons.
Later, a prince of Shǔ led thirty thousand troops to campaign against the Luò king and Luò marquises,
subduing the various Luòjiàng.
The Shǔ prince then proclaimed himself King Ānyáng.
Later, the King of Nányuè, Wèi Tuó, raised an army to attack King Ānyáng.
King Ānyáng had a divine man named Gāo Tōng
who assisted him from below,
crafting a divine crossbow for King Ānyáng.
With a single shot, it could kill three hundred men.
The King of Nányuè realized he could not engage in battle,
so he withdrew his troops and stationed them at Wǔníng County.
According to the Jìn *Tàikāng Jì*, this county belonged to Jiāozhǐ.
Yuè sent a crown prince named Shǐ
to surrender to King Ānyáng,
pledging allegiance and serving him.
King Ānyáng did not recognize Gāo Tōng as a divine man
and treated him improperly.
Tōng then departed,
saying to the king:
He who can wield this crossbow will rule the world;
he who cannot wield this crossbow will lose the world.
After Tōng left,
King Ānyáng had a daughter named Mèizhū.
Seeing that Shǐ was handsome,
Zhū had relations with Shǐ.
Shǐ asked Zhū
to fetch her father's crossbow for him to see.
When Shǐ saw the crossbow,
he secretly sawed it apart,
then fled back to report to the King of Nányuè.
Nányuè then advanced troops to attack.
When King Ānyáng fired the crossbow,
it broke, and he was defeated.
King Ānyáng boarded a ship and fled out to sea.
Today, in Píngdào County, the ruins of his palace city can still be seen.
According to the Jìn *Tàikāng Dìjì*,
the county belonged to Jiāozhǐ.
Yuè then subdued the various Luòjiàng.
Mǎ Yuán, considering the southwest distant to govern
and the road extending a thousand lǐ,
established this county for administration.
City walls were built, canals dug,
and irrigation channels opened,
benefiting the people.
The county has xīngxīng beasts,
shaped like yellow dogs,
and also resembling huān tún.
They have human faces,
with dignified and proper features.
They are skilled at speaking with people,
their voices beautiful and enchanting,
like those of lovely women.
When conversing face to face,
listeners cannot help but feel sorrow.
Their meat is sweet and delicious,
capable of sustaining one without grains,
and one never tires of it even after a full year.
Further east, it passes Làngbó,
where Mǎ Yuán, considering the terrain high,
advanced from Xīlǐ and stationed troops here.
It then flows east past the old city of Lóngyuān County,
and further east,
joins the northern river on the left.
In the twenty-third year of the Jiàn'ān era, when the province was first established,
dragons coiled around the southern and northern ferries.
Therefore, Lóngyuān was renamed Lóngbiān.
When Lú Xún invaded Jiāozhōu,
the Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu, Dù Huìdù, led naval and infantry forces to advance from the southern ferry at dawn,
attacking with fire arrows,
burning their ships and vessels,
causing them to scatter and flee instantly.
Xún was also struck by an arrow, plunged into the water, and died.
Thereupon, he was beheaded,
and his head was sent to the capital.
For his merit in beheading Xún,
Huìdù was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lóngbiān.
Liú Xīnqī's *Jiāozhōu Jì* states:
Zuǒ Fēi, a Gōngcáo of Lóngbiān County,
once transformed into a tiger,
and after several months returned to serve as an official.
Since it speaks of transformation,
transformation can occur anywhere.
When Niú Āi changed into a tiger,
he did not recognize his own elder brother.
When one assumes a transformed state,
how can one know it is an illusion?
The river then flows east past Qūyì County,
and eastward empties into Yínyù.
The *Jīng* states:
At the eastern boundary of the commandery, it reunites into three rivers.
This is the second of them.
The next river
flows east past the south of Fēngxī County,
then southwest past the south of Xīyú County,
then east past the north of Léiluǒ County,
then east past the south of Běidài County,
then east past Jīxú County,
where the Jīng River flows into it.
The river originates from the high mountains of Lóngbiān County,
and flows southeast into Jīxú County.
It flows into the Zhōngshuǐ River.
The Zhōngshuǐ River then flows east past the south of Léibēi County.
The *Jiāozhōu Wàiyù Jì* states:
This county
was originally the seat of Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
The *Línyì Jì* states:
Traveling south from Jiāozhǐ,
one emerges at the Dūguān Sài Ford.
The river flows east from the county past Āndìng County,
bordered to the north by the Chángjiāng River.
In the river is a bronze boat cast by the King of Yuè.
When the tide recedes,
people sometimes see it.
The river then flows eastward,
and across the water lies Nílí City,
said to have been built by King Ashoka.
It then joins the Nánshuǐ River to the southeast,
and the Nánshuǐ River flows southeast past the north of Jiǔdé Commandery.
The *Jiāozhōu Wàiyù Jì* states:
Within the boundaries of Jiāozhǐ Commandery lies the Fúyán Jiū,
located north of the commandery,
separated by a river crossing.
This is the river in question.
The river faces Zhūyuān County of Jiāozhǐ,
then flows east past the north of Pǔyáng County,
and further east past the north of Wúqiè County.
In the ninth month of the nineteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Mǎ Yuán submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject has carefully assembled twelve thousand elite troops from Jiāozhǐ,
combining them with the main army to form a force of twenty thousand men,
with two thousand vessels and carts of various sizes.
Since entering Jiāozhǐ,
this is now at its peak."
In the tenth month,
Mǎ Yuán advanced south into Jiǔzhēn,
reaching Wúqiè County.
The rebel chieftain surrendered,
and he proceeded into Yúfā.
The rebel leader Zhū Bó abandoned the commandery and fled into deep forests and vast marshes,
a gathering place for rhinoceroses and elephants,
with thousands of sheep and cattle,
where elephants were often seen in herds of several tens to hundreds.
Mǎ Yuán also dispatched troops into Wúbiān County,
which was the Jiǔzhēn Tíng under Wáng Mǎng,
reaching Jūfēng County.
The chieftain did not surrender,
and several tens to hundreds were beheaded.
Jiǔzhēn was thus pacified.
The river then flows east past Gōulòu County,
which is bordered by the Jiāngshuǐ River.
The Jiāngshuǐ River faces Āndìng County.
This is what the *Línyì Jì* refers to as Wàiyuè, Āndìng, and Jìsù.
In the county's river, there are submerged oxen,
resembling water buffalo in form.
They come ashore to fight,
and when their horns soften, they return to the river.
Once their horns harden, they emerge again.
The river then joins the Běishuǐ River to the east,
and further east flows into the Yù River,
where its course becomes chaotic and dissipates.
This is the third branch.
These are general terms for the various branches,
all ultimately flowing into the Yù Sea.
Therefore, the *Jīng* contains passages about entering the sea.
37.3 Yíshuǐ River
37.3 Yíshuǐ River
The Yíshuǐ River originates from the Jiāng River in Yúfù County of Bā Commandery.
The Yíshuǐ River,
also known as the Hěnshān Qīngjiāng River.
The water is so clear that one can see ten zhàng deep,
distinguishing sand from stones.
The people of Shǔ, seeing its clarity,
thus named it Qīngjiāng (Clear River).
In ancient times, Lǐnjūn floated an earthen boat on the Yíshuǐ River,
occupied Hànguān, and ruled over Bā.
Therefore, Fǎ Xiàozhí once said:
"Yúfù's Hànguān overlooks the river and controls the waters,
truly the gateway to fortune and misfortune for Yìzhōu."
The Yíshuǐ River then flows east past Shāqú County in Jiànpíng,
where the Wūchéngshuǐ River is located.
The mountain path along the southern bank stretches for five hundred lǐ,
and the river passes east of the county and emerges there.
It flows southeast past the south of Hěnshān County.
The Yí River enters from Shāqú County,
its flow shallow and narrow,
barely allowing boats to pass.
It passes east by the south of Nánliú City,
which is actually a mountain.
Standing alone, steep and precipitous,
on its western face, about a li up, one reaches a stone cave.
Holding a torch and walking about a hundred paces,
one finds two large stone pillars,
standing side by side in the cave,
separated by a zhang.
Commonly called the Yīn and Yáng Stones,
the yīn stone is always damp,
while the yáng stone is always dry.
Whenever floods or droughts occur,
the residents, dressed in ceremonial attire,
enter the cave,
and in times of drought, they whip the yīn stone,
whereupon rain falls in abundance;
in times of excessive rain, they whip the yáng stone,
and soon the sky clears.
According to tradition,
this method is often effective,
but those who wield the whip do not live long,
so people greatly dread it,
and thus refrain from doing it.
On the northeastern face, there is also a stone chamber,
capable of accommodating several hundred people.
Whenever chaos arises,
the people enter the chamber to avoid bandits,
as it is impregnable,
hence the name Nánliú City.
In ancient times, the Bā tribes had five clans,
without a ruler,
all serving ghosts and spirits.
They agreed to throw their swords into a stone cave,
vowing that whoever hit the target
would be honored as their lord.
Wù Xiàng, son of the Bā clan, hit the target.
They then ordered each to ride an earthen boat,
vowing that whoever floated
would be made lord.
Only Wù Xiàng floated,
so they jointly established him,
and he became Lǐn Jūn.
He then rode an earthen boat down the Yí River to Yányáng.
The Yán River had a goddess,
who said to Lǐn Jūn:
"This land is vast,
abounding in fish and salt.
I wish for you to stay and live with me."
Lǐn Jūn refused.
The salt goddess came each evening to stay,
and at dawn transformed into insects,
swarming and blotting out the sun,
darkening heaven and earth,
for over ten days.
Lǐn Jūn, seizing an opportunity, shot and killed her,
and the sky cleared.
Lǐn Jūn rode the earthen boat down to Yíchéng.
Yíchéng had steep, winding stone banks,
and its waters were also winding.
Lǐn Jūn gazed upon it and sighed,
causing the mountain cliffs to collapse.
Lǐn Jūn ascended it,
and above was a flat stone, two zhang and five chi square.
He then built a city beside it and settled there.
The four clans submitted to him.
Upon his death,
his spirit transformed into a white tiger,
so the Bā clan, believing tigers drink human blood,
thus offered human sacrifices.
The Yán River
is the Yí River.
There is also a salt stone,
which is the yáng stone.
Shèng Hóngzhī deduced from this
that it is likely the place where Lǐn Jūn shot the salt goddess.
Thus, it is understood that the yīn stone
was named in opposition to the yáng stone.
These events are so ancient
that they are difficult to verify clearly.
The Yí River then passes east by a stone chamber,
located atop layered cliffs.
The stone chamber faces south,
with water flowing beneath it.
The cliff is a thousand ren high,
visible directly from the water.
Those who climb the mountain ridge
grasp trees and tread cautiously,
yet none know who they are.
A villager named Luò Dū,
when young, came to this chamber to gather honey
and saw an immortal sitting on a stone bed.
Seeing Dū, the immortal stared fixedly without turning away.
Dū returned
and called the villagers to go again,
but they saw nothing more.
The locals now call it the Immortal's Chamber.
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"Dū's descendants still survive."
The Yí River then flows east and merges with three streams of hot springs.
A large stream flows between north and south banks,
with hot springs facing each other.
Warm in summer and hot in winter,
they are often shrouded in mist.
Sores and various ailments
are often healed by bathing here.
Elders say this spring once produced salt,
and even now the water has a salty quality.
The Yí River is also called the Yán River,
and this is one reason.
The Yí River then passes east by the old city of Hěnshān County,
named after the mountain.
Mèng Kāng said:
"Pronounced 'héng,'
it produces medicinal herbs."
Héng Shān is now pronounced with the sound of 'yín.'
It was formerly a county under Wǔlíng.
One li to the south, the Qīng River flows east.
To the south, facing Chángyáng Stream,
the stream water flows southwest into a hidden cave.
The cave is six or seven li east of Shètáng Village.
In the valley is a stone cave,
from which clear spring water gushes for about thirty paces,
then re-enters the cave.
This is the source of Chángyáng.
In the water are divine fish,
the largest two chi long,
the smallest one chi.
When residents fish,
they first state how many they need,
bow, and make their request.
After bowing, they cast their hooks and bait.
If they catch more than the stated number,
the water immediately surges with waves,
a sudden storm arises,
and trees are broken.
By the water grow unusual flowers.
Passersby wishing to pick them
must first make a request;
they cannot take them arbitrarily.
Northeast of the water source is Fēngjǐng Mountain,
winding with unusual formations.
The cave mouth is as large as a basin.
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"In summer, wind blows out;
in winter, wind blows in;
in spring and autumn, it is calm."
I went to observe it
in mid-fourth month.
Several zhang from the cave,
a cold gust suddenly arrived in an instant.
In mid-sixth month, it is especially unbearable.
Someone who passed by in winter
placed a bamboo hat in the cave,
and the wind sucked it in.
A month later, returning,
he found his hat at Bùyáng Stream,
thus realizing it connects underground.
The water has a dual source, visibly emerging,
flowing north into the Yí River.
This water is clear and cool,
more so than the large stream.
Even in the hottest days of summer,
one cannot bathe in its flow.
Over ten li north of the county is a divine cave.
Normally without water,
when someone is thirsty,
if they sincerely pray and beg,
water is obtained.
If someone mockingly asks,
the water never emerges.
About ten li east of the county is Pínglè Village.
There is also a stone cave from which clear spring water emerges.
Inside is a hidden dragon.
Whenever a great drought occurs,
the villages near Pínglè
carry grass and filth into the cave.
The dragon becomes angry,
and in an instant, water gushes out,
washing away the grass and filth,
and the fields nearby
are all irrigated.
Five or six li downstream from Pínglè,
the northern mountain of Dōngtíng Village is very high and steep.
The top is solid, the bottom hollow,
with a hollow opening east to west,
about two zhang wide,
rising as high as a house.
Inside is a stone bed,
very neat and orderly.
Wild chives grow beside it.
Those who go to ask for them
must receive the spirit's permission, indicated by the wind blowing them apart.
They take according to how they fall,
and cannot exceed the limit.
Taking without the wind blowing them apart brings misfortune.
Those who go to observe find the path unusually level when leaving,
and upon arrival, naturally become reverent and solemn.
Further east, it passes north of Yídào County.
The Yí River flows east past Hǔ Tān,
where the rocks on the bank bear the image of a tiger,
hence the name Tiger Shoal.
The Yí River then flows east past Fǔ Lài,
where the larger rocks resemble cauldrons,
and the smaller ones resemble dipper-shaped vessels.
Their shapes and colors are so lifelike,
only their solid interiors reveal they are not real.
The Yí River continues northeast,
where a stream joins it.
Its source extends for a hundred lǐ,
and it shares its origin with the Dān River from Wàngzhōu Mountain in the southwest.
The mountain is steep and lofty,
with exceptionally high and elegant peaks.
To the northeast, white cliffs stand sheer,
while to the southwest, a small path allows passage.
Ascending to its summit, one finds a level area,
about three mǔ in size.
Upon it stands an ancient city,
with water within the city walls.
From the city, one can see the entire territory of a zhōu,
hence the name Wàngzhōu Mountain (Gazing-at-the-Zhōu Mountain).
Due to colloquial corruption,
it is now called Wǔzhōng Mountain.
At the eastern foot of the mountain, a spring gushes forth to form a stream,
which is the source of the Dān River.
It flows down to feed the Dān River.
When the sky darkens and rain approaches,
a red vapor often appears,
hence the name Dān River (Cinnabar River).
The Dān River then passes by a pavilion,
beneath which lies a very deep stone cavern,
whose extent has never been measured.
Within the cavern, bats as large as crows
hang upside down in great numbers.
The Xuánzhōng Jì records:
"Bats that have lived for a hundred years hang upside down.
If captured and consumed,
they can make one an immortal."
At the mouth of the cavern is a spring,
warm in winter and cool in summer.
In autumn, it withdraws and hides,
while in spring, it emerges and flows freely.
In autumn, the local people dam the water outlet with orchids,
catching fish as long as four or five chǐ.
Their bones are soft, and their flesh is delicious,
different from other fish.
The Dān River flows further beneath it,
accumulating to form a deep pool.
Within the pool dwells a divine dragon.
Whenever there is a drought,
villagers throw ruì grass into the upper stream of the pool,
causing many fish to die.
Enraged, the dragon
brings forth heavy rain at once.
The Dān River then flows northeast,
with numerous tiger tracks on the rocks along both banks.
Some are deep, others shallow,
all naturally formed,
with no trace of human artifice.
The Dān River then flows north into the Yí River.
Its waters are clear and pure,
identical to those of the Great Stream.
The Yí River flows northeast past the north of Yídào County and then eastward.
Further east, it enters the Great River.
The Yí River also passes north of Yídū,
flowing east into the Great River.
It is comparable to the Jīng and Wèi Rivers,
and is also called the Northern Stream of Hěn Mountain.
The area through which the water flows consists entirely of rocky mountains,
with scarcely any earthen banks.
The water is so transparent and reflective
that looking down at the swimming fish,
they appear to be floating in midair.
In the shallows, multicolored stones abound.
In winter and summer, the swift currents churn the clear waters.
Along the banks are dense woods and hollow caves.
On quiet nights, listening closely,
one often hears clear echoes,
as birds of all kinds soar,
their plaintive calls harmonizing with one another.
Travelers passing by the tumbling waves
forget their weariness and lose track of time for returning.
37.4 Yóu River
37.4 Yóu River
The Yóu River originates from the western border of Chánlíng County in Wǔlíng.
The county has Báishí Mountain,
from which the Yóu River flows.
It runs east past the west of the county,
where it merges with the Wéi River.
The Wéi River originates from Wéi Mountain in Gāochéng County,
flowing east past the county,
then east to Chánlíng County,
where it enters the Yóu River.
Further east, it passes north of the county.
The county seat is an old city,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Chánlù.
Lady Sūn, wife of Liú Bèi,
was the sister of Sūn Quán.
She further renovated it,
with the city backing against the Yóu River and facing the marshes.
Further northeast, it enters the Great River.
The Yóu River flows northeast from Chánlíng County past the west of Gōng'ān County,
then turns north and flows into the Great River.
37.5 Lǐ River
37.5 Lǐ River
The Lǐ River originates west of Chōng County in Wǔlíng,
passes through the mountains eastward south of the county.
From the county eastward, the Lǐ River flows through the former boundaries of Línlǐ and Língyáng counties.
On the southern bank of the river,
two white stones stand side by side,
their shapes resembling humans,
each thirty zhàng tall,
and forty zhàng in circumference.
According to ancient legend,
long ago, the magistrate of Chōng County and the magistrate of Língyáng were disputing their borders,
and in the conflict, they harmed each other,
turning into stone.
The eastern one marks Língyáng,
the western one marks Chōng County.
Chōng County was later abolished,
and Línlǐ occupies its former territory.
The county
is the old seat of Chōng County,
adjacent to the Lǐ River,
hence the county's name.
It was established in the fourth year of the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty.
The Lǐ River flows further east,
where the Rú River joins it.
The Rú River originates from Lóngrú Mountain.
Its waters are clear and pure,
filtering through stones and separating sand.
When Zhuāng Xīn advised King Xiāng of Chǔ,
he spoke of "drinking from the flow of the Rú Stream."
The Rú River flows east into the Lǐ River.
Further east, it passes north of Língyáng County.
The Lǐshuǐ River flows east and meets the Wēnquánshuǐ River.
The water originates from a stone cave in the northern mountains,
stretching thirty zhang in length,
boiling and surging in both winter and summer,
always as if it were hot water.
The warm water flows south,
and pours into the Lǐshuǐ River.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east and joins the Língxīshuǐ River,
whose source emerges from the Língyáng Mountain to the south,
passing through the valley and flowing north into the Lǐshuǐ River.
The Lǐshuǐ River continues east,
where the Jiǔdùshuǐ River flows into it,
its water emerging from the Jiǔdù Mountain to the south,
with a stream at the foot of the mountain,
which is also named Jiǔdù.
All the mountain animals drink from this water,
and when they pass by other fords,
they do not drink from them.
The Jiǔdùshuǐ River flows north past the Xiānrénlóu,
beside which there is a stone,
extremely square and steep in shape,
known to the world as the Xiānlóu.
The water descends through the valley,
winding and meandering as it pours down,
making travel difficult,
often requiring one to lift one's clothes to wade upstream,
hence the name of the mountain and water,
likely arose from these circumstances.
The Jiǔdùshuǐ River then flows north and pours into the Lǐshuǐ River.
The Lǐshuǐ River continues east,
where the Lóushuǐ River enters,
its source originating from the border of Bādōng,
flowing east past the north of Lóuzhōng County in Tiānmén Commandery,
then east past Língyáng County,
and pours into the Lǐshuǐ River.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east past the south of Língyáng County,
a county renowned for the Língxī River.
The Lǐshuǐ River then passes by Xièyáng County,
where it meets the Xièshuǐ River on the right,
which originates from Jiànpíng Commandery,
flowing east past the south of Xièyáng County,
established during the Tàikāng era of the Jìn Dynasty.
The Xièshuǐ River then joins the Huángshuǐ River on the left.
The Huángshuǐ River emerges from the west of Língyáng County,
connecting north to the Wūshān Stream,
where realgar is produced,
possessing considerable mystical properties.
Mining is usually done in the winter months,
with rituals performed before quarrying the stone,
digging several zhang deep,
before obtaining fine realgar,
hence the stream is named after it.
The Huángshuǐ River flows north and pours into the Xièshuǐ River,
which then flows east into the Lǐshuǐ River,
known as the Xièkǒu.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east past the south of Lǐyáng County,
which lies south of the Lǐshuǐ River,
established as the seat of Tiānmén Commandery in the fourth year of Tàikāng of the Jìn Dynasty.
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān of the Wú Dynasty,
the Sōngliáng Mountain in Wǔlíng Commandery stood tall and solitary.
Its sheer white cliffs rose a thousand xún,
appearing lofty and graceful from afar,
resembling an incense burner.
A cave opened in the mountain,
dark and bright like a gate,
three hundred zhang high,
two hundred zhang wide,
with a bamboo growing from each corner of the gate,
hanging down and sweeping the ground,
called the "Tiānzhǒu."
Sūn Xiū considered this an auspicious sign,
and established Tiānmén Commandery by dividing Wǔlíng Commandery.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east past the Céngbù Mountain,
tall, elegant, and prominent,
with a steep stream at its foot,
where springs emerge,
flowing south into the Lǐshuǐ River.
Further east, it passes north of Zuòtáng County,
which was established
by dividing Chánlíng County during the Later Hàn Dynasty.
The Lǐshuǐ River enters the county,
where it joins the Cénshuǐ River on the left,
which originates from the border of Tiānmén Commandery to the northwest,
flowing south past the Cénpíng military settlement,
where the settlement dams the Cénshuǐ River,
irrigating several thousand qǐng of fields,
then flows southeast,
and pours into the Lǐshuǐ River.
The Lǐshuǐ River continues east,
where the Dànshuǐ River branches off.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows south past the east of the old commandery city,
turning east and passing south of Zuòtáng County.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east past the south of Nán'ān County,
established
by dividing Chánlíng County in the first year of Tàikāng of the Jìn Dynasty.
The Dànshuǐ River flows into it,
branching from the Lǐshuǐ River at Zuòtáng County,
flowing east past the north of the county,
then east into the Lǐshuǐ River,
known as the Dànkǒu.
Wáng Zhòngxuān's "Poem Presented to Shìsūn Wénshǐ" says:
"Vast and distant are the Dàn and Lǐ rivers."
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows east and meets the Chìshāhú Lake,
whose waters connect to the Jiāng River to the north and flow south into the Lǐshuǐ River,
known as the Shākǒu.
The Lǐshuǐ River then flows southeast into the Yuánshuǐ River,
called the Lǐkǒu.
This is likely a branch watercourse.
The "Lísāo" says:
"The Yuán has zhǐ, the Lǐ has lán."
Further east, it reaches the northwest of Xiàjuàn County in Chángshā,
and flows east into the Jiāng River.
The Lǐshuǐ River flows into Dòngtíng Lake,
commonly known as the Lǐjiāngkǒu.
37.6 Yuánshuǐ River
37.6 Yuánshuǐ River
The Yuánshuǐ River originates from Zāngkē, Qiělán County,
known as the Pánggōushuǐ River,
then flows east to Chánchéng County,
where it becomes the Yuánshuǐ River,
passing east by Wúyáng County.
The Wú River emerges from the ancient region of Gùqiělán,
flowing south to the old county of Wúyáng.
The county faces the Wú River,
and thus took its name from the river.
The Wú River then flows southeast into the Yuán,
where it is called the Wúkǒu.
The Yuán River flows east past Wúyáng County,
bordering the Yùn River to the south.
The source of the Yùn River is on the southeastern bank of Xǔ Mountain,
flowing northwest past the south of the county and then southward,
emptying into Xióng Creek.
Xióng Creek is bordered to the south by Yí Mountain.
Originally, the mountain was north of the water,
but during a night of wind and rain,
by morning the mountain had shifted south of the water.
Thus, the mountain was named Yí (meaning "shifted"),
akin to the strange mountains of Cāngwú Yùzhōu
and Dōngwǔ.
Xióng Creek flows down into the Yuán River,
and the Yuán River continues east past Chényáng County.
The county has Lóng Creek,
which emerges from Lóngqiáo Mountain to the south
and flows north into the Yuán.
The Yuán River flows further east,
where the Lài River joins it.
This river emerges from Fúyáng Mountain to the south
and flows north to meet the Yuán.
The Yuán River then flows east and converges with the Xù Creek,
which originates from Líliáng Mountain in Yìlíng County of Wǔlíng Commandery,
flowing northwest past Yìlíng County,
which was called Jiànpíng County under Wáng Mǎng.
Its seat was at Xù Creek.
This city
was built by Mǎ Liáng when he left Zǐguī under Liú Bèi's command,
venturing into the Five Creeks region
to pacify and appease the barbarian tribes.
Mǎ Liáng led the various barbarian tribes in constructing it.
The area governed by Xù Creek
is the most fertile land,
with several hundred qǐng of fine fields,
especially suitable for rice cultivation.
Cultivation never ceased,
and it then flows northwest into the Yuán.
The Yuán River flows east and joins the Xù River,
which originates from Xù Creek.
It flows north and empties into the Yuán.
The Yuán River flows east past the south of Chényáng County,
where it converges with the Chén River to the east.
The Chén River emerges from the valleys of Sān Mountain in the county,
flowing southeast,
where the Dúmǔ River joins it.
The source of the Dúmǔ River is on Lóngmén Mountain to the south,
passing through Dúmǔ Creek
before flowing north into the Chén River.
The Chén River then flows past the north of the county.
The old seat of government was on the southern bank of the Chén River,
hence the name Chényáng.
This is the place mentioned in the Chǔcí: "At dusk, I lodge at Chényáng."
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Huìtíng.
The Chén River then joins the Yuán River on the right,
and the confluence is called Chénxīkǒu.
There are Five Creeks in Wǔlíng,
namely Xióng Creek, Mán Creek, Wú Creek, and Yǒu Creek,
with Chén Creek being one of them.
The areas along these creeks are all inhabited by barbarian tribes,
hence they are called the Five Creeks Barbarians.
The river then flows past the west of Yuánlíng County,
where there is the Wǔ Creek.
It originates from Wǔ Mountain,
which is shared with Yǒuyáng,
and on the rocks at its source, the footprints of Pánhù are still preserved.
Pánhù
was a dog kept by Gāoxīnshì.
Its fur was of five colors.
Gāoxīnshì was troubled by the violence of the Quǎnróng,
so he offered a reward to anyone who could bring him the head of the Quǎnróng general, General Wú.
He promised to give his youngest daughter in marriage.
After the decree was issued,
Pánhù brought General Wú's head to the palace gate.
The emperor was overjoyed,
but did not know how to fulfill the reward.
The daughter heard of this
and believed that a promise should not be broken,
so she requested to go.
Thus, she was given to Pánhù.
Pánhù carried the girl into the southern mountains,
to a stone chamber on the heights,
a perilous and isolated place
where no human could reach.
The emperor grieved and longed for her,
but the messengers he sent could not proceed.
After two years,
she gave birth to six boys and six girls.
When Pánhù died,
they married among themselves,
weaving bark into cloth,
dyeing it with berries,
and favoring five-colored garments,
all tailored with tails.
Their mother reported to the emperor,
who granted them famous mountains.
Their descendants multiplied,
and they were called the barbarian tribes.
The barbarians of present-day Wǔlíng Commandery
are the descendants of Pánhù.
The dog's fur
is treasured and recorded by his direct descendants.
The Wǔ River flows south and empties into the Yuán,
and the Yuán River flows further east,
where the Shī River joins it.
The Shī River emerges from Shī Mountain Creek to the south,
and at its source is Yángqī Cliff,
whose cliffs are pure white,
appearing like accumulated snow.
Below are two stone chambers,
where people once lived.
Fine springs flow gently,
and streams vie to pour into the river,
making it indescribable.
The Shī River flows north to meet the Yuán,
and the Yuán River flows east past the north of Yuánlíng County,
which was the fief of the former Hàn marquis Wú Yáng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Yuánlù.
The county lies north of the Yuán River,
and the Yuán River flows east past the old seat of the county.
The county seat was moved north,
and the old city of the county
was made the seat of the Commandant's office.
It lies against hills and slopes,
with terrain encompassing rivers and ridges,
facing the Yuán and opposite the Yǒu,
at the confluence of the two rivers.
The Yǒu River originates from Línjiāng County in Bā Commandery of Yìzhōu,
specifically from Yǒuyuán Mountain in Chōng County of Wǔlíng.
It flows southeast past the old county of Wúyáng to the south,
then east through the boundaries of the old county of Qiānlíng,
where it joins the Xīxiāng Creek,
a branch of the Yán River,
the lower reaches of the Gēngshǐ,
called the Xīxiāng Creek mouth.
The Yǒu River then flows east past the old city of Qiānlíng County to the north,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Qiānlù.
The Yǒu River flows east past the old county of Yǒuyáng to the south,
which
was formerly Yǒulíng.
The Yǒu River then flows east past the north of Yuánlíng County,
and further southeast past the west of Pān Chéngmíng's fort. Chéngmíng campaigned against the Five Creeks Barbarians,
and this was the camp his army built.
The fort straddles mountains and rests against valleys.
The Yǒu River then flows south into the Yuán River,
which Kuò Yīn called the Shòu River.
The point where this water joins
is named the Yǒukǒu.
The Yuán River then flows past the side of Dòu Yìngmíng's city,
which Yìngmíng built during his campaign against the barbarians in the early Yuánjiā era.
The Yuán River flows further east,
where a creek emerges from Míng Mountain to the south.
The mountain is deep, winding, and perilous,
blocking both humans and beasts.
The creek flows north into the Yuán River.
The Yuán River then flows east and joins the Zhūyú Creek,
which emerges from Zhūyú Mountain to the north.
This mountain forms the boundary with Lǐyáng County of Tiānmén Commandery,
and the creek flows south to meet the Yuán.
The Yuán River flows further east,
where the Yí River joins it.
The Yí River emerges from Yí Mountain to the south
and flows north into the Yuán.
Yí Mountain connects eastward to Hútóu Mountain,
which is one hundred lǐ high
and three hundred lǐ in circumference.
At the foot of the mountain by the water's edge,
is the place where the Xīnxī Marquis Mǎ Yuán halted his army during his campaign against the Wǔ Creek Barbarians.
The path through Hútóu is winding and perilous,
with a thousand bends and shoals within.
Yuán advanced to Hútóu,
hoping for a swift victory,
but encountered miasmic poison on the way,
and ultimately perished here.
That such loyalty was slandered
is truly lamentable.
Liú Chéngzhī said:
The Yuán River branches off from Hútóu,
crossing thirty-three fords,
passes through Lóngbiān County in Jiāozhǐ,
and flows northeast into the sea.
Tracing the water's course and seeking its bridges,
this is not a matter of thorough investigation,
but since the ancients allowed doubtful accounts to be passed down,
I merely record what I have heard.
It then flows northeast past the south of Línyuán County.
Línyuán County and Yuánnán County are divided by water.
To the west of Yuánnán County lies Yíwàng Mountain,
which rises solitary in the midst of the river,
floating perilously, isolated on all sides.
In the past, barbarian people took refuge there to escape bandits,
hence it is called Yíwàng.
To the south is Yíwàng Creek,
which flows south from the layered mountains,
and from afar pours into the Yuán.
The Yuán River then flows east and reaches Guānxià Mountain,
which is girded to the east by Guān Creek,
cascading into the Yuán channel.
The Yuán River then flows east past the west of Línyuán County,
forming Míngyuè Pool and Báibì Bay.
The bay is shaped like a half-moon,
with clear, mirror-like depths.
Above, the wind whispers emptily;
below, the sound of springs never ceases.
Travelers all grasp their oars to play and roam,
lingering, fondly enjoying the scene.
The Yuán River then flows east past Sānshí Jiàn,
where three rocks stand like tripod legs, evenly poised,
elegant as if carved,
with lush, graceful bamboo at their sides,
truly delightful to behold.
Further east, it is girded by Lǜluó Mountain,
where green vines densely cover,
and crumbling cliffs overlook the water.
It is indeed a fine spot for fishing and poetic chanting.
The echoing sounds resemble bell tones,
truly a dwelling place for immortals.
The Yuán River then flows east past the west of Píng Mountain,
which faces south toward the Yuán River.
Cold pines shade above,
clear springs pour down below,
so that those who seek refuge cannot tear themselves away from its side.
The Yuán River then flows east past the south of Línyuán County.
The county faces south toward the Yuán River,
hence it is named accordingly.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Jiànyuán.
South of the county is the tomb of Gōng Xuánzhī, a recluse of the Jìn dynasty from Hànshòu,
with an inscription
erected by Chē Wǔzǐ during the Tàiyuán era.
The county seat lies under Wǔlíng Commandery,
originally the Qiánzhōng Commandery of Chǔ.
In the twenty-seventh year of King Zhāoxiāng of Qín,
he sent Sīmǎ Cuò to attack Chǔ with armies from Lǒng and Shǔ.
Chǔ ceded the area north of the Hàn River to Qín.
By the thirtieth year,
Qín further seized Chǔ's Wū, Qián, and the lands south of the river,
establishing them as Qiánzhōng Commandery.
In the second year of Hàn Emperor Gāozǔ,
the former Qiánzhōng territory was divided to form Wǔlíng Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Jiànpíng.
To the south, it faces Yuánnán County,
established during the Jiànwǔ era of the Later Hàn.
The county lies on the south bank of the Yuán River,
hence named Yuánnán.
The county seat is an old city,
formerly built by Mǎ Yuán during his campaign against Línxiāng.
The Yuán River then flows east past a small bay,
called Wǎngzhǔ.
About a lǐ east of the islet,
one reaches Wǎngrén Mountain.
To the west of the mountain lies a long creek over a hundred lǐ,
with lush, graceful bamboo,
spreading along the creek and shading the islet.
The long stream winds and flows,
pouring from afar into the Yuán.
The Yuán River then flows east into Lóngyáng County.
There, Dàn Water emerges from Yáng Mountain west of Hànshòu County,
flowing south, then east,
turning,
passing south of the county.
The county seat is Suǒ City,
the old city of Suǒ County.
During the Yángjiā era of Hàn Emperor Shùndì,
it was changed to its present name.
Yān Yīn believed it was where Xīng Water emerges and flows east into the Yuán,
but this water further flows east past various lakes,
then south into the Yuán,
also called Jiàn Water.
The place where the water enters
is called Dǐngkǒu.
The Yuán River then flows east past Fànzhōu in Lóngyáng County,
an islet twenty lǐ long.
Lǐ Héng, governor of Dānyáng under Wú,
planted citrus trees upon it.
On his deathbed, he instructed his son:
"On my islet, there are a thousand 'wooden slaves,'
requiring no food or clothing,
yet yielding a thousand bolts of silk annually."
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"A thousand orange trees in Jiānglíng
can equal a fiefdom."
This is what he meant.
At the end of Wú,
Lǐ Héng's citrus ripened,
yielding a thousand bolts of silk annually.
Even now, old roots and stumps remain on the islet,
likely his legacy.
The Yuán River then flows east past the north of Lóngyáng County,
with the city bordering the Yuán River.
The Yuán River then flows east and joins Shòu Creek,
which connects inland to Dàxīkǒu.
There are trees with interlocking branches,
their roots on opposite banks yet joining in the air above,
receiving waters from various lakes and pouring into the Yuán River.
Further east, it reaches the west of Xiàjuàn County in Chángshā,
and enters the river from the north.
The Yuán River pours into Dòngtíng Lake,
then converges with the river.
37.7 Yín River
37.7 Yín River
The Yín River emerges from the Yuán River valley north of Tánchéng County in Wǔlíng.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"From Dàoguò Mountain,
the Yín River emerges,
flowing south into the sea." This is it.
Southward, it reaches Tánzhōng County in Yùlín,
where it joins Lín Water.
Lín Water emerges from Wúyáng County,
which
was formerly Tánchéng.
During the Yìxī era of Jìn,
it was changed to its present name.
Commonly called Yí Creek,
the creek flows south through Tánzhōng,
pouring into the Yín River.
Further east, it reaches Měnglíng County in Cāngwú,
becoming Yù Creek.
Further east, it reaches Gāoyào County,
becoming Dà Water.
Yù Water emerges from Ālín County in Yùlín,
flowing east past Měnglíng County.
Měnglíng County lies southwest of Guǎngxìn,
called Měnglù by Wáng Mǎng.
At the county, the Yín River joins Yù Creek on the left,
their mingled flow passing Guǎngxìn County.
The *Geographical Records* state:
"Cāngwú Commandery seat,
established in the sixth year of Yuándǐng under Emperor Wǔ,
called Xīnguǎng Commandery by Wáng Mǎng,
the county called Guǎngxìn Tíng."
Wáng's *Annals of Jiāo and Guǎng* states:
"In the fifth year of Yuánfēng,
Jiāo Province moved its seat here from Yínglǒu County.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Wú sent Bù Zhì of Línhuái as governor of Jiāo Province,
leading four hundred military officers to Jiāo Province,
but the road was blocked.
Wú Jù of Chángshā, governor of Cāngwú,
held a force of five thousand.
Bù Zhì was suspicious of Wú Jù,
first sending an envoy to instruct him.
Wú Jù welcomed him at Línglíng,
thus allowing entry into the province.
After accepting Bù Zhì, Wú Jù later regretted it.
Bù Zhì, with few troops,
feared he could not maintain his position.
Wú Jù had a commander, Ōu Jǐng,
brave and resourceful like Wú Jù,
whose men served him well.
Bù Zhì disliked this,
and secretly sent someone to invite Wú Jù.
Wú Jù went and told Ōu Jǐng not to visit Bù Zhì,
but Bù Zhì persisted in inviting him.
Ōu Jǐng went as well,
and in the courtyard before the hall,
both were beheaded, and their heads displayed to the troops.
This happened here.
Yù Water then flows past Gāoyào County.
The *Jìnshū Geographical Records* state:
"The county lies five hundred lǐ east of the commandery.
The inspector, avoiding summer poison,
moved the county to reside on water."
The county has Húbēn Tíng,
where Sū Shī's wife Shǐzhū from Guǎngxìn,
as a ghost, brought a lawsuit before Hé Chǎng, governor of Jiāo Province,
similar to the case of the female ghost at Lí Tíng.
Wáng's *Annals of Jiāo and Guǎng* states:
"After Bù Zhì killed Wú Jù and Ōu Jǐng,
he readied boats and ships,
gathered twenty thousand troops,
and went south to take Nánhǎi.
Héng Yì and Qián Bó of Cāngwú,
formerly under Wú Jù's command,
raised troops to intercept Bù Zhì at Gāoyào Gorge in Cāngwú.
The two armies met there,
engaged in battle,
and Héng Yì, along with over a thousand of his men, threw themselves into the water and died."
Further east, it reaches the west of Pānyú County in Nánhǎi,
where it splits into two,
one branch flowing south into the sea;
Yù Water divides, and the Yín flows southward.
One branch flows east past the county's east,
then south into the sea.
The Yǐn River flows east, passing separately by Pānyú,
which the Classic of Mountains and Seas calls Bēnyú.
Jiāozhōu Administrator of Records Hé Pǔ Yáo Wénshì asked:
Why is it named Pānyú?
The reply was:
The Nánhǎi Commandery was formerly administered from within the present prefectural city,
adjacent to Pānyú County.
Now, within the city's southeast corner, there is a water hollow,
with a hill city leaning upon it.
I hear the people of this county call it Pān Mountain.
The county is named Pānyú,
perhaps meaning the corner (yú) of Pān Mountain.
The Book of Han says, "Floating down the Zāngkē,
descending the Lí Ford,
they converged at Pānyú."
They likely rode this water to enter Yuè.
When Qín unified the realm,
it conquered and pacified Yáng and Yuè,
establishing one commandant in the southeast,
one lookout in the northwest,
and opening Nánhǎi to relocate exiled people.
By the time of the Second Emperor,
the Nánhǎi Commandant Rén Xiāo
summoned Lóngchuān Magistrate Zhào Tuó, saying:
"I hear Chén Shèng has rebelled,
and powerful leaders are defying Qín.
I wish to raise troops,
block the new roads,
and rely on Pānyú's defensible terrain
to establish a state."
But he fell gravely ill,
with no one to confide in,
so he summoned you to convey this grand plan."
Xiāo died,
and Tuó took charge as Nánhǎi Commandant.
He then guarded the passes and set up defenses,
executed officials appointed by Qín according to law,
replacing them with his own partisans,
and declared himself king.
When Emperor Gāo stabilized the realm,
he sent Lù Jiǎ to formally establish Tuó as King of Nányuè,
exchanging tallies and opening diplomatic relations.
In the fifth year of Yuándǐng under Emperor Wǔ,
he sent General Fúbō Lù Bódé and others to attack the King of Nányuè.
After five generations and ninety-two years, it perished.
Its territory was made into the commanderies of Nánhǎi, Cāngwú, Yùlín, Hépǔ, Jiāozhǐ, Jiǔzhēn, and Rìnán.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Wú sent Bù Zhì to govern Jiāozhōu.
When Zhì reached Nánhǎi,
he observed the lay of the land,
viewed the old administrative site of Commandant Tuó,
backed by mountains and girded by sea,
vast and stretching as far as the eye could see.
The highlands were mulberry fields,
the lowlands fertile plains.
Forests, foothills, birds, and beasts—
what was not there?
Sea monsters, fish, and turtles,
giant softshell turtles, alligators, and fresh crocodiles,
rare and exotic creatures,
in thousands of kinds and myriads of types,
too numerous to record.
Tuó built a terrace on a ridge,
facing north toward Hàn.
Its round foundation spanned a thousand paces,
its sheer cliff rose a hundred zhang,
its summit covered three mǔ,
with winding covered walkways
meandering in twists and turns.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, he ascended to pay homage,
naming it the Cháotái (Audience Terrace).
Subsequent regional inspectors and commandery governors,
upon newly arriving to their posts,
would always ride carriages up to tread upon it,
leisurely enjoying themselves there.
Zhì climbed high and gazed afar,
beholding the vastness of the great sea,
observing the richness of the plains and marshes,
and said:
"This is truly fertile land on a sea island,
fit to be a capital city."
In the twenty-second year of Jiàn'ān,
he moved the prefectural seat to Pānyú,
built its inner and outer walls,
pacified and harmonized the Bǎiyuè,
and thus achieved peace and stability.
Jiāozhōu Administrator of Records Yáo Wénshì asked and answered:
"The Cháotái is thirty lǐ northeast of the prefectural city."
Péi Yuān's Records of Guǎngzhōu states:
"North of the city is the tomb of Commandant Tuó.
Behind the tomb is a large ridge,
called the Mǎ'ān Ridge.
In Qín times, prognosticators of qi said:
'The south has the qi of a Son of Heaven.'
The First Emperor conscripted people
to break open this ridge.
Blood flowed from the earth,
and the excavated site remains today.
Taking its appearance for its name,
the ridge thus received this designation."
Wáng's Spring and Autumn Annals of Jiāo and Guǎng states:
"King of Yuè Zhào Tuó
in life had the integrity to accept imperial authority and pledge allegiance as a vassal,
and in death had a secret, mysterious tomb.
For Tuó's burial,
they made a mound using the mountain.
His burial mound can be called extravagant and large,
interred with accumulated treasures.
During Wú times, envoys were sent to excavate his tomb,
seeking the coffin.
They cut through mountains and broke rocks,
wasting days and expending effort,
but in the end found nothing.
Though Tuó was extravagant and presumptuous,
he was cautious about his end,
so that later people would not know its location,
somewhat like Sōng and Qiáo moving their traces;
thus, even cowherds could not despoil it."
Dèng Démíng's Records of Nánkāng states:
"Formerly there was Lú Dān,
who served in the prefecture as Administrator of Records.
From youth he practiced immortal arts,
excelling at soaring through clouds.
Each evening he would ascend through the void to return home,
and at dawn return to the prefecture.
Once, during the New Year's court assembly,
he was late for the court ranks.
He transformed into a white swan and arrived before the palace gate,
circling and about to alight,
when the guards threw stones at him.
They obtained one of his shoes.
Dān, startled, returned to his place in the ranks.
All inside and out, left and right,
were astounded.
At that time, Bù Zhì governed Guǎngzhōu.
He deeply disliked this,
and reported the matter in writing,
leading to Dān's execution."
Records of Guǎngzhōu states: After Wú was pacified,
Jìn's Téng Xiū served as Regional Inspector.
A fellow villager told Xiū
that shrimp whiskers could be one chǐ long.
Xiū reproached him, considering it false.
The man then went to the Eastern Sea,
obtained shrimp whiskers four chǐ long,
hurried back to show Xiū,
and only then did Xiū accept it and apologize,
sending him off with generous gifts."
One branch of water enters southward,
a distributary of the Yù River,
passing through Sìhuì into the sea.
Another branch is the river flowing east separately past the city of Pānyú,
as the Book of Han says, "Floating down the Zāngkē,
descending the Lí Ford,
they converged at Pānyú."
They likely rode this water to enter Yuè.
The Yǐn River also flows east past Huáihuà County into the sea.
In the water are cuò fish.
Péi Yuān's Records of Guǎngzhōu states:
"Cuò fish are two zhàng long,
several arm-spans in girth.
Their skin can be used like a file.
They bear young,
and the small young follow their mother to seek food.
If frightened, they return into the mother's belly."
Wú's Geographical Records states:
"Cuò fish young
go out to seek food in the morning,
and return to the mother's belly at dusk."
Records of Nányuè states:
"At dusk they enter from the navel,
at dawn they emerge from the mouth.
Inside the belly are two cavities,
intestines storing water to nourish the young.
Each intestine holds two young,
so two intestines hold four."
The remaining water flows east to Lóngchuān,
becoming the Niè River,
bending north to enter the Yuán River.
A branch of the Yǐn River spreads and flows,
passing east from Pānyú through Zēngchéng County.
Records of Nányuè states:
"The county has many jùnyì birds.
Jùnyì
are mountain pheasants,
brilliant in color,
dazzling with five hues,
with sharp spurs, skilled at fighting.
If domestic chickens fight them,
they can be captured."
It also passes west of Bóluó County's border at Lóngchuān.
This is what Zuǒ Sī meant by "gazing at Lóngchuān and girded by wilds."
Zhào Tuó relied on this county to straddle and hold Nányuè.
The Yuán River flows southeast for fifteen hundred lǐ,
entering the South Sea.
It flows east past Jiēyáng County,
which was the Nánhǎi Post Station under Wáng Mǎng,
and then empties into the sea.
38 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Scroll Thirty-Eight
38.1 The Zī River
38.1 The Zī River
The Zī River originates from Lù Mountain in Dūliáng County, Línglíng Commandery.
The Zī River originates from Tángjiǔ Mountain on the border of Wúyáng County, Wǔlíng Commandery,
which is another name for Lù Mountain.
It is called the Great Stream.
It flows northeast past the south of Wǔgāng County, Shàolíng Commandery.
This county was established from a division of Dūliáng.
To the left and right of the county are two ridges facing each other,
layered and steep, equally beautiful,
with a gap of about two *li*.
Old traditions say that when the Later Han dynasty campaigned against the Five Streams barbarians,
the barbarians held these ridges,
hence the name Wǔgāng (Martial Ridge),
and the county is named after this.
The Great Stream flows past the south of Jiànxīng County,
and also past the south of Dūliáng County.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn dynasty,
it was made the fief of Jìnghóu Suì, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng.
West of the county is a small hill,
on which there is a still pool,
clear and shallow,
entirely filled with growing orchid plants,
with green leaves and purple stems.
Their fragrant breeze adorns the river,
the orchid fragrance wafts far,
and it is customary to call the orchid "dūliáng".
The hill is thus named,
and the county takes its name from it.
[The Zī River] flows northeast past Fūyí County.
The Fū River originates from Shàoyán Mountain on the border of Línglíng County, southwest of the county,
and flows northeast past the south of Fú County,
which was originally Fūyí County of Línglíng.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn dynasty,
it was made the fief of Jìnghóu Yì, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng.
The Fū River then flows east and joins the Shàolíng River,
called the Shàolíng Bank,
which is the river mouth.
[The Zī River] flows northeast north of Shàolíng County.
The county seat is under the commandery,
facing the Great Stream to the south,
while the river flows north of it,
called the Shàolíng River.
In the second year of the Xiánxī era of Wèi,
the first year of the Bǎodǐng era of Wú,
Sūn Hào divided the northern part of Línglíng and established Shàolíng Commandery at Shàolíng County.
The county
was formerly Zhāolíng.
Eastward, the stream reaches the mouth of the Gāopíng River.
This river originates from Shǒuwàng Mountain in Yuánlíng County, Wǔlíng Commandery,
flows southwest past the south of Gāopíng County,
then east into the borders of Shàolíng County,
and south into the Shào River.
The Shào River then flows east and meets the Yúnquán River.
This river originates from Yúnquán Mountain in Yǒngchāng County, Línglíng Commandery,
flows northwest past the south of Shàoyáng,
a county
which was formerly Zhāoyáng.
The Yúnquán River then flows north and joins the Shàolíng River,
called the Shàoyáng River mouth.
From here, it flows northeast out to Yìyáng County,
passing through mountain gorges along the way,
named the Zhūyú River,
which is a changed name for the watercourse.
It flows further northeast past the north of Yìyáng County.
The county has Guānyǔ Rapid,
the so-called Marquis Guān Beach,
facing south to the old fortifications of Gān Níng.
In the past, Guānyǔ stationed his troops north of the river,
and Sūn Quán ordered Lǔ Sù and Gān Níng to oppose him at this river.
Gān Níng said to Lǔ Sù:
"If Guānyǔ hears the sound of my cough or spit,
he will not dare to cross.
If he crosses, he will be captured."
Guānyǔ heard Gān Níng's arrangements at night,
and said:
"That is Xìngbà's voice."
So he did not cross.
The Zhūyú River flows east past the north of Yìyáng County,
and is also called the Zī River.
Yìng Shào said:
"The county is on the north bank of the Yì River."
Now there is no Yì River,
or perhaps it is a different name for the Zī River.
However, around this county,
there are deep pools everywhere.
Fishermen all let their light boats ride the waves,
singing folk songs in harmony,
which is what Luó Jūnzhāng described as their sounds being lingering and distant.
Ten *li* south of the river are several hundred wells,
the shallow ones four or five feet deep,
or three to five *zhàng*,
the deep ones also unfathomable. The elders pass down
that in the past, people struck the ground with a staff,
and it immediately became a well.
Some say it is where the ancients collected gold sand,
but the truth is not known in detail.
Further east, it joins the Yuán River in a lake,
and flows northeast into the [Yangtze] River.
The lake
is Dòngtíng Lake.
The place where it enters
is called the Yìyáng River mouth.
38.2 The Lián River
38.2 The Lián River
The Lián River originates west of Liándào County,
a branch of the Zī River.
It originates from the borders of Shàolíng County,
flows south past Liándào County.
The county
seat, the old city, is 160 *li* west of Xiāngxiāng County.
It controls and draws together numerous streams,
merging into a single creek,
which flows east into Xiāngxiāng County, Héngyáng Commandery.
