It passes by Shíyú Mountain,
which has much dark stone.
The mountain is over eighty *zhàng* high,
and ten *li* wide.
The stone is black in color, and its grain resembles mica.
When a layer is split open,
there is often a fish shape,
with scales, fins, head, and tail,
as if carved and painted,
several inches long,
the fish form fully complete.
When burned, it gives off a fishy odor like fish oil,
hence it is named after this.
The Lián River then flows past Xiāngxiāng County,
which faces the Lián River to the south.
It originally belonged to Línglíng,
[and was] the fief of Chāng, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng.
The Lián River then bends and flows past the east of the county,
and enters Xiāngnán County.
[The Lián River] flows northeast past the south of Xiāngnán County,
then northeast to the southwest of Línxiāng County,
and east into the Xiāng River.
The Lián River flows east from Xiāngnán County,
to the borders of Xiāngxī County, Héngyáng Commandery,
and enters the Xiāng River.
It is to the southwest of Línxiāng County.
38.3 The Xiāng River
38.3 The Xiāng River
The Xiāng River originates from Yánghǎi Mountain in Shǐ'ān County, Línglíng Commandery,
which is Yángshuò Mountain.
Yìng Shào said:
"The Xiāng emerges from Líng Mountain,"
which is probably a different name for the mountain.
The mountain is north of Shǐ'ān County.
The county
was formerly the southern part of Línglíng.
In the second year of the Xiánxī era of Wèi, the first year of the Gānlù era of Sūn Hào,
Shǐ'ān Commandery was established.
The Xiāng and Lí share the same source,
dividing into two rivers.
The southern one is the Lí River,
the northern one is the Xiāng River,
which flows northeast.
Luó Jūnzhāng, in his *Record of the Xiāng Region*, said:
"When the Xiāng River emerges from Yángshuò,
a wine cup can serve as a boat;
when it reaches Dòngtíng,
the sun and moon seem to rise and set within it."
[The Xiāng River] flows northeast past the east of Línglíng County.
The Yuèchéng Ridge Stream emerges south from the ridge of Yuèchéng,
which is the Western Ridge of the Five Ridges.
The Qín established garrisons at the Five Ridges,
and this was one of them.
[The stream] flows north to Línglíng County,
and empties into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River then flows past the south of Línglíng County,
and further northeast past Guānyáng County,
where it joins the Guān River.
This river originates from the borders of Xièmù County, Línhè Commandery,
flows northwest past the west of Guānyáng County.
The county
is probably named after the river.
It then flows northwest,
and empties into the Xiāng River,
called the Guān mouth.
[The Xiāng River] flows further northeast past the east of Táoyáng County.
The Táo River originates from the great mountains southwest of the county,
flowing northeast past the southern part of the county,
and it is from this river that the county derives its name.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty,
Jiéhóu Jū, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng, was enfeoffed here as a marquis,
and Wáng Mǎng later renamed it Táozhì.
The river flows eastward,
and empties into the Xiāng River.
It then continues northeast past the western side of Quánlíng County.
The Yíng River originates from the southern mountains of Língdào County in Yíngyáng,
flowing westward past the foot of the Jiǔyí Mountain.
Its base sprawls across the wilderness of Cāngwú,
with peaks standing majestic among several commanderies.
The layered cliffs rise in nine distinct masses,
each guiding a separate stream.
The mountain valleys bear rugged barriers,
with different ridges sharing the same imposing posture,
causing travelers to doubt their perception,
hence the name Jiǔyí Mountain (Mountain of Nine Doubts).
The Great Shùn was buried on its southern side,
and Shāng Jūn was interred on its northern side.
South of the mountain stands a temple to Shùn,
in front of which there is a stone stele,
but the characters are worn and missing,
making them no longer legible.
Looking up from the temple, the mountain appears extremely high,
rising steeply for over a hundred lǐ.
According to ancient tradition,
no one has ever reached its summit.
Within the boundaries of Língdào County to the northeast of the mountain,
there is another temple to Shùn.
South of the county is a stele for Shùn,
erected by Xú Jiǎn, the Grand Administrator of Línglíng.
The Yíng River then flows west past Yíngdào County,
where the Féng River joins it.
The Féng River originates from Féng Ridge northeast of Féngchéng County in Línhè Commandery,
its source being the Féng Stream.
It flows northwest,
and the county is named after it.
The Féng River gathers numerous streams,
merging them into a single watercourse,
known as Běizhǔ.
It passes north of the county and flows west to Guānxià.
Guānxià
is a place name,
where merchant vessels begin to change their rigging.
The Féng River then joins with the Méngzhǔ River on the left,
which flows south from the Méngzhǔ Ridge,
the fourth of the Five Ridges.
The mountain is rich in tin,
hence it is also called the Tin Region.
The Zhǔ River flows north past the west of Féngchéng County,
and then north to join the Féng River.
The Féng River then flows past Yíngdào County and meets the Yíng River on the right.
The Yíng River then bends northwest and flows past the west of Yíngdào County,
which was Wáng Mǎng's Jiǔyí Post Station.
The Yíng River then flows northeast past the south of Yíngpǔ County,
the seat of Yíngyáng Commandery.
In the second year of the Wèi's Xiánxī era (265 CE),
Sūn Hào of Wú partitioned it from Línglíng.
It lies on the northern bank of the Yíng River,
hence the commandery's name.
The Yíng River then flows north,
where the Dūxī River joins it.
The Dūxī River originates from Yǎng Mountain, twenty lǐ north of Chōnglíng County,
flowing south past the west of the county.
The county
was originally the Chōnglíng Township of Língdào County,
likely named after the Chōng Stream.
It was established as a county by the Dìng King of Chángshā of Hàn,
and in the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ (124 BCE),
he enfeoffed his middle son, Mǎi, as the Marquis of Chōnglíng.
East of the county's old city is another walled town,
facing east and west opposite each other,
each side measuring a hundred paces.
According to ancient tradition,
this was the old city of the Hàn family,
and the Hàn name still survives,
indicating it was the former fief of the Jié Marquis.
At the eastern corner of the city stands a stele,
but the characters are worn and missing,
making them no longer legible.
Thirty lǐ to the southeast, there is still a temple to the Jié Marquis.
The Dūxī River then flows south past the east of Xīnníng County.
The county lies beside the Dūxī to the east,
and the stream flows west past the south of the county,
where it joins with five streams on the left.
The county has five mountains,
each with a stream,
and the five waters converge at the county gate,
hence the name Dūxī (Converging Streams).
The Dūxī River flows northwest from the county,
passes north of Língdào County and merges with the Líng River.
The Líng River flows south from Jiǔyí Mountain,
then north past the southwest of the county.
The county is named after the Líng Stream,
which was Wáng Mǎng's Línglíng County.
The Líng River then flows north to join the Dūxī River,
and then northwest into the Yíng River.
The Yíng River then flows north into the Yíngyáng Gorge.
Continuing north, it emerges from the gorge at Guānyáng County,
the stretch between the large and small gorges
being extremely difficult for navigation upstream or downstream.
The Yíng River then flows northwest past the west of Quánlíng County,
which in the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (124 BCE)
was enfeoffed to the Jié Marquis Xián, son of the Dìng King of Chángshā.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Pǔrùn.
It is the seat of Línglíng Commandery,
originally part of Chǔ.
In the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ (111 BCE),
it was partitioned from Guìyáng.
The Grand Historian stated:
"Shùn was buried at Jiǔyí,
which is indeed Línglíng."
The commandery takes its name from this,
and it was Wáng Mǎng's Jiǔyí Commandery.
Chén Qiú of Xiàpī served as Grand Administrator of Línglíng.
When the rebel Hú Lán from Guìyáng attacked Línglíng,
diverting the river to flood the city,
Chén Qiú, from within, used the terrain
to reverse the flow and drown the rebels instead,
who were thus unable to capture the city.
The county has a Báitǔ Township.
The *Records of Former Worthies of Línglíng* states:
"Zhèng Chǎn, styled Jǐngzǎi,
was a man of Quánlíng.
He served as the Báitǔ village head.
During the troubled final years of Hàn,
when state resources were insufficient,
a poll tax was levied on every child one year old.
Many people did not raise their children.
Zhèng Chǎn then ordered the people not to kill their children,
and promised to pay the poll tax on their behalf.
He petitioned his commandery and county,
submitting a memorial to the throne.
The tax was subsequently abolished,
and Báitǔ was renamed Gēngshēng Township (Township of Renewed Life)."
The *Jìnshū Dìdào Jì* states:
"The county produces fragrant茅 (cogon grass),
with a very aromatic scent,
said to have been offered for filtering wine."
The Yíng River then flows north into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River then flows northeast and joins with the Yìng River.
The Yìng River originates from Shàolíng County,
passing through mountain cliffs,
scaling steep and treacherous terrain,
with sheer precipices thousands of fathoms high.
Clear springs lie deep below,
while the Yìng River surges above.
It flows southeast past the south of Yìngyáng County,
which was established by partitioning Guānyáng County during Jìn,
likely named after the Yìng River.
The Yìng River then flows southeast past the south of Yǒubí Xū (Ruins of the Nose).
Wáng Yǐn said:
"Yìngyáng County
was originally the northern part of Quánlíng.
Five lǐ to the east is Yǒubí Xū,
said to be the fief of Xiàng."
At the foot of the mountain is a temple to Xiàng,
said to be very efficacious
in bringing forth clouds and rain.
This is what I have heard.
The spirit of a sage is called 'líng' (numinous),
while the vital essence of a worthy becomes a ghost.
Xiàng was not wise in life,
so what could house his numinous spirit after death?"
The Yìng River then flows southeast into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River then flows northeast to the mouth of the Wú River.
The Wú River originates from Luó Mountain north of Yǒngchāng County,
flowing southeast past the east of Shíyàn Mountain.
The mountain has dark red stones shaped like swallows,
hence the mountain's name.
The stones vary in size,
resembling mother and child.
When thunder and wind clash,
the stone swallows fly in flocks,
soaring and diving like real swallows.
Luó Jūnzhāng said:
"Nowadays, the swallows do not necessarily fly again."
The river then flows southeast past the south of Yǒngchāng County,
and then east into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River then flows northeast past the south of Qíyáng County,
where the Yúxī River joins it.
The Yúxī River originates from Shàolíng County in Shàolíng Commandery to the northwest,
flowing southeast into the Xiāng.
Its waters churn clear and turbid,
creating two distinct colors.
The Xiāng River then flows north and joins with the Yíxī River.
The Yíxī River originates from east of the old Xīnpíng County, southwest of Xīnníng County in Xiāngdōng Commandery.
Xīnníng
was formerly Xīnpíng.
Numerous streams pour their waves,
converging into a single crossing.
It flows northwest,
and below the mountain on the eastern bank is a dragon cave.
The Yí River flows past below it,
and during droughts, if water is dammed and poured into it,
rain will fall.
The Yí River then flows northwest into the Xiāng.
The Xiāng River then flows northwest to the mouth of the Chōng River.
The Chōng River receives water from Tán Mountain northwest of Chōnglíng County in Yíngyáng,
flows north past the east of Xīnníng County,
then northwest,
and into the Xiāng River.
It then flows northeast past the east of Chóng'ān County,
and northeast past the west of Líng County,
where the Chéng River flows from the southeast to join it.
The Chéng River originates from the Xiéjiāng Mountain on the border of Shàolíng County, west of Chóng'ān County in Héngyáng.
It flows northeast to Chóng'ān County,
passes below the Shùn Temple,
which is located on the north bank of the Chéng River.
Further east, it joins the Lüètáng Pond.
Tradition holds that within this pond dwells a bronze deity.
Even now, the sound of bronze is occasionally heard from the water,
whereupon the water turns green and takes on a coppery smell,
causing the fish to die.
The Chéng River then flows northeast past the south of Chóng'ān County,
which was the fief of Dù, son of the Prince of Chángshā of the Hàn dynasty.
It was formerly the Zhōngwǔ County of Línglíng Commandery.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhōnghuán.
Here, the Wǔ River flows into it.
The Wǔ River originates from Biǎo Mountain southwest of Zhōngwǔ County,
flows east to the old city south of Zhōngwǔ County,
then turns northeast,
and joins the Chéng River at Chóng'ān County.
Reaching north of Línchéng County in Xiāngdōng,
it flows east into the Xiāng River,
at a place called the Chéngkǒu.
Línchéng was the former Líng County.
This county,
served as the seat of Xiāngdōng Commandery.
The commandery's original seat was east of the Xiāng River,
hence the name Xiāngdōng (East of the Xiāng) Commandery.
In the second year of the Zhèngyuán era of Wèi [255 CE],
the Wú ruler Sūn Liàng established it by partitioning the eastern part of Chángshā.
The county has a stone drum,
six *chǐ* high.
Where the Xiāng River passes by,
if the drum sounds, it foretells military conflict in the region.
Luó Jūnzhāng said:
"When struck, its sound can be heard for tens of *lǐ*."
This drum no longer produces sound.
East of Guānyáng County is Péi Rock.
Below it is a stone drum,
shaped like an overturned boat.
When struck, its clear sound carries far,
being of the same kind.
The Xiāng River then flows north past Yìnshí (Seal Stone).
The stone is located on the right bank of the Xiāng River, south of Héngshān County.
There are flat rocks, some large, some small,
bordering the water.
All the rocks bear marks,
square like seals,
arranged in rows,
with no writing.
This continues for about two *lǐ*,
hence it is named Seal Stone.
The Xiāng River then flows north past the east of Héngshān County.
The mountain lies to the southwest,
with three peaks:
one named Zǐgài,
one named Shíqūn,
and one named Fúróng.
The Fúróng Peak is the most lofty and striking.
Viewed from afar,
it rises majestically, obscuring the sky.
Therefore, Luó Hán said:
"Looking like battle clouds,
unless the sky is clear and bright in the morning,
its peak cannot be seen."
The Dān River surges to its left,
and the Lǐ Spring flows to its right.
The *Classic of Mountains* calls it Gǒulǒu,
which is the Southern Peak (Nányuè).
At the foot of the mountain is the Shùn Temple.
To the south is the tomb of Zhùróng.
During the reign of King Líng of Chǔ,
a landslide destroyed the tomb mound,
and the *Diagram of Yíngqiū with Nine Heads* was discovered.
When Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he sacrificed a horse of pure color to the mountain,
and obtained the *Book of Golden Tablets and Jade Characters*.
East of Fúróng Peak is a stone chamber of immortals.
When scholars pass by,
they often hear the sound of chanting.
Héng Mountain faces the Xiāng River on its eastern and southern sides.
From Chángshā to here,
along the seven hundred *lǐ* of the river,
the mountain appears nine times facing the traveler and nine times with its back turned.
Therefore, fishermen sing:
"The sail follows the twists of the Xiāng,
Gazing at Héng's nine faces."
On the mountain, a flying spring cascades down,
reflecting against the green woods,
plunging straight to the mountain's base.
Viewed from afar, it resembles a bolt of white silk hanging on the mountain.
The Xiāng River then flows northeast past the east of Xiāngnán County,
and further passes south of Xiāngxī County,
which was established from a division of Xiāngnán.
It is the seat of Héngyáng Commandery.
In the second year of the Gānlù era of Wèi [257 CE],
Wú's Sūn Liàng established it by partitioning the western part of Chángshā as the seat.
Hé Chéngtiān, Governor of Xiāngnán during the Jìn, later moved the seat to Xiāngxī.
The *Record of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
"The Rìhuá River originates from Rìhuá Mountain in Chēn County, Guìyáng,
and flows west to Xiāngnán County, where it enters the Xiāng."
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"Chēn County has the Lěi River,
which originates from Lěi Mountain,
and flows west to the western part of Xiāngnán County, where it enters the Xiāng."
The Xiāng River then flows north past the east of Lù Mountain.
This mountain faces the Xiāng River to the east,
with plains and lowlands to the west.
Those seeking tranquility of mind
often gather here.
Further northeast, it passes west of Yīnshān County;
the Mǐ River flows from the southeast and joins it;
further north, it passes west of Lǐlíng County,
where the Lù River flows from the southeast and joins it.
The *Continued History of the Later Han*, *Treatise on the Five Elements* states:
"In the eighth year of the Jiàn'ān era [203 CE],
a great mountain in Lǐlíng County, Chángshā,
often roared like the lowing of an ox.
After several years,
bandits from Yùzhāng attacked and overran the county's stations,
killing and plundering officials and commoners.
Therefore, it was taken as an omen."
The Xiāng River then flows north past Jiànníng County,
where there is the Kōnglíng Gorge.
Its terrifying waves thunder forth,
its depth rivaling the Three Gorges.
The Xiāng River then flows north past the old city of Jiànníng County below,
established during the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty [265-274 CE].
Further north, it passes west of Línxiāng County,
where the Liú River flows from the northwest of the county and joins it.
South of the county lies Shítán Mountain.
The Xiāng River flows past its west.
The mountain contains a stone chamber and a stone bed,
overlooking a clear stream.
The Xiāng River then flows north past the west of Zhāo Mountain.
At the mountain's foot is a swirling spring,
unfathomably deep.
Hence it is said that Zhāo Tán has no bottom;
it is also called Xiāngzhōu Tán.
The Xiāng River then flows north past the west of Nánjīn City.
To the west, it faces Júzhōu (Orange Isle),
sometimes written with the character '吉' (jí).
This is the southern end of Nánjīnzhōu.
West of the water is the Júzhōuzi garrison,
whose old outer wall still remains.
The Xiāng River continues north,
where on the left it meets the mouth of the Wǎguān River,
a tributary of the Xiāng.
It then passes west of the shipyard,
a place where merchant vessels of Xiāngzhōu moor.
To the north, it faces Chángshā Commandery.
The commandery seat is south of the city on the island in the river's east.
Its old administrative center was within the city,
but was later moved here.
The Xiāng River flows left past the east of Lù Mountain,
atop which is an old city.
North of the mountain is the mouth of the Báilù River,
a tributary of the Xiāng.
It then flows right past the west of the old city of Línxiāng County, where the county seat was located.
The Xiāng River flows along the bank, close to the river's side,
hence the name (Línxiāng, meaning 'facing the Xiāng').
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Fǔlù.
This was originally territory in the southern reaches of Chǔ.
After Qín conquered Chǔ,
it established Chángshā Commandery,
which was the area of Qīngyáng.
In the 26th year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
an edict stated:
"The King of Jīng shall present the lands west of Qīngyáng."
The "Biography of Zōu Yáng" in the *Hàn Shū* says:
"Crossing the waters to Chángshā,
returning the boats to Qīngyáng."
The commentary
by Zhāng Yàn states:
"Qīngyáng
is a place name."
Sū Lín states:
"Qīngyáng
is a county in Chángshā."
In the 5th year of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he enfeoffed Wú Ruì as the King of Chángshā,
and this city was built by Ruì.
In the 2nd year of Hàn Jǐngdì,
he enfeoffed Fā, son of Consort Táng, as king,
who made this his capital.
It was the Zhèn Mán Commandery under Wáng Mǎng.
According to the *Yǔ Gòng*, it lies within the region of Jīngzhōu.
In the 1st year of Yǒngjiā under Jìn Huáidì,
the various commanderies of central Xiāng within Jīngzhōu were separated to establish Xiāngzhōu,
with its administrative seat here.
Within the city walls,
west of the commandery office is a temple to Táo Kǎn.
It is said this was originally the site of Jiǎ Yì's residence.
Within it is a well,
dug by Yì,
extremely small but deep,
narrow at the top and wide at the bottom,
shaped like a pot.
Beside it is a one-footed stone bed,
barely large enough for one person to sit on.
Popular tradition holds
it was the bed Yì used to sit on.
There is also a large mandarin orange tree,
also said to have been planted by Yì.
Northwest of the city is an old market,
facing north towards the new administrative seat of Línxiāng County.
Northwest of the county seat is Běijīn City.
North of the county is the tomb of Wú Ruì,
over sixty-eight *zhàng* in breadth.
Ascending it offers a panoramic view,
making it an excellent resting spot overlooking the city.
Guō Bān's *Shì Yǔ* states:
At the end of the Huángchū era of Wèi,
men of Wú opened Ruì's tomb to obtain timber
for building a temple to Sūn Jiān in the county.
They saw Ruì's corpse, its appearance and clothing just as they had been.
After Wú was pacified, the tomb opener met Wú Gāng,
the Colonel of the Southern Mán, in Shòuchūn.
He said:
"Why does your appearance so resemble that of the King of Chángshā, Wú Ruì?
Only you are slightly shorter."
Gāng, startled, said:
"He was my ancestor."
From Ruì's death to the opening of his tomb was four hundred years,
and to meeting Gāng was over forty more years.
The Xiāng River, on the left, joins the mouth of the Shì River,
then northward reaches the mouth of the Shíguǒ River,
both being tributaries of the Xiāng.
On the right, it joins the mouth of the Máxī River,
a tributary of the Xiāng.
The Xiāng River then flows north past the east of Sānshí Mountain.
The mountain rests beside the north bank of the Xiāng River,
which is the mouth of the Sānshí River,
a tributary of the Xiāng.
North of the water is the Sānshí garrison,
the garrison town situated at the confluence of two rivers.
The Xiāng River then passes the Liúkǒu garrison storehouse,
facing north towards the Liú River.
Continuing north,
the Wéi River flows from the southwest and joins it.
The Wéi River originates from Mǎtóu Mountain in Yìyáng County.
It flows east past the south of Xīnyáng County,
which in the 1st year of Tàikāng of Jìn,
was renamed Xīnkāng.
The Wéi River then flows east into Línxiāng County,
passes east of the Wéikǒu garrison,
and flows south into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River then flows north to join the Duànkǒu,
and further north,
reaches Xiàyíngkǒu,
a tributary of the Xiāng.
On the left bank of the Xiāng River is the Gāokǒu River,
which emerges west of Yìyáng County.
It flows north past the south of the Gāokǒu garrison,
then northwest,
where the Shàngbí River, receiving water from the upper mouth of Bízhōu in the west, joins it from the west;
this is called Shàngbí Pǔ.
The Gāo River flows northwest to join Xiàbí Pǔ,
which at the lower mouth of Bízhōu first receives water from the Xiāng River,
connects west to the Gāo River,
and is called Xiàbíkǒu.
The Gāo River then flows northwest, bends right to form Língzǐ Tán,
and flows northeast into the Xiāng River at Língzǐkǒu.
The Xiāng River, east of the Gāokǒu garrison,
continues north,
where on the right it meets Bízhōu,
and on the left joins Shàngbíkǒu;
further north,
it faces Xiàbíkǒu on the right,
and then reaches Língzǐkǒu.
On the right bank of the Xiāng River,
Tóngguān Pǔ emerges.
The Xiāng River then flows north past Tóngguān Mountain,
which faces west towards the Xiāng River.
The mountain's soil is purple,
containing mica within,
hence it is also called Yúnmǔ Mountain.
It then flows north past the west of Luó County,
where the Mì River flows from the east and joins it.
The Xiāng River flows north again, passing east of the Xīkǒu garrison,
then continues north,
where a left branch is called the Xī River.
It flows northwest past the north of the Xīkǒu garrison,
then flows northwest,
bends northeast,
and empties into the Yù River.
This water originates from the Yùchí Pond in the northwest,
flows southeast and empties into the Xī River's inlet,
called the Yùchí Mouth.
The Xī River flows northeast again,
and the Dōnghú Lake empties into it,
the water of which receives from the Dōng Lake of the Yùchí Pond.
It flows south into the Xī River,
called the Sānyáng Channel,
with three garrisons south of the water.
It then flows northeast and empties into the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River emerges north from the Xīkǒu,
and further receives the Wàngtún Inlet,
an inlet of the Xiāng.
The Xiāng River flows north again,
a branch flows out north,
called the Mén Channel.
The Xiāng River meanders northwest,
and northeast joins the Mén River,
called the Mén Channel Mouth.
Further north, it reaches the Sānxī River Mouth,
whose water receives from the Great Lake in the east,
connects to the Xiāng Inlet in the west,
the confluence of three waters,
hence the name Sānxī (Three Streams).
Further north, it meets the Dàduì River Mouth in the east,
connecting to the Sānjīn Channel in the west.
The Xiāng River flows north again, passing west of the Huánglíng Pavilion,
and joins the Huánglíng River Mouth on the right,
whose water receives from the Great Lake.
The lake water flows west,
passing south of the Èrfēi Temple,
commonly called the Huánglíng Temple.
It is said that when the great Shùn went on an inspection tour,
the two consorts followed the expedition,
drowned in the Xiāng River,
their spirits roam the depths of Dòngtíng,
emerging and entering the inlets of Xiāo and Xiāng.
Xiāo means
water clear and deep.
The "Record of Xiāngzhōng" says:
"The Xiāng River is clear, illuminating five or six zhàng,
one can see the bottom stones like dice,
brightly colored,
white sand like frost and snow,
red cliffs like morning clouds,
this is the origin of the name Xiāo-Xiāng."
Therefore, the people built a shrine beside the water,
the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Liú Biǎo, engraved a stone and erected a stele,
placed it in the temple,
to commemorate the immortal legend.
The Huáng River flows west again into the Xiāng,
called the Huánglíng Mouth.
In the past, Wáng Zǐchēn had exceptional talent,
at twenty he had a nightmare,
wrote the "Rhapsody on Dreams,"
at twenty-one drowned in the Xiāng Inlet,
which is this river.
The Xiāng River flows north again, passing west of the Báishā garrison,
then north again,
joins the Dōngtīng Mouth on the right,
which is the Mì River.
The Xiāng River joins the Juéhú Mouth on the left,
whose water emerges from the Western Slope,
connecting east to the Xiāng Islets.
The Xiāng River flows north again,
the Mì River empties into it,
its water emerges east from the Huán Mountain in Ài County, Yùzhāng,
flows southwest past north of Wúchāng County,
and joins the Chún River,
whose source is the Chún Mountain southeast of that county,
flows northwest,
then east past south of the county,
then north past below the old city of the county,
the county was established by the Wú ruler Sūn Quán.
The Chún River joins the Mì River on the right again.
The Mì River flows west again past north of Luó County,
originally the state of Luózi,
formerly west of Yíchéng County in Xiāngyáng,
King Wén of Chǔ moved it here,
the Qín established the Chángshā Commandery,
and thus made it a county,
the water is also called the Luó River.
The Mì River flows west again past the Yùsì Mountain,
Luó Hán's "Record of Xiāngzhōng" says:
"To the left of the Qū Pool is the Yùsì Mountain,
Daoist masters bequeathed words,
this is a blessed land.
Also called Dìjiǎo Mountain."
The Mì River flows west further to become the Qū Pool,
which is the Mìluó Deep.
Qū Yuán, embracing sand,
drowned himself here,
hence the deep pool is named after Qū.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì and Sīmǎ Qiān,
both once passed here,
halted their oars on the river waves,
and cast their mourning into the deep.
North of the deep is the Qū Yuán Temple,
in front of the temple is a stele,
also the stele of Chéng Jiān, Governor of Hànnán,
placed in the original temple.
The Mì River flows west again past south of the Mìluó garrison,
flows west and empties into the Xiāng.
This is the Luó Ruì of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
commonly called the Mìluó Mouth.
The Xiāng River flows north again,
a branch divides and flows out north,
passes west of the Mìluó garrison,
then north past east of the Lěidàng Mountain,
then north past west of the Lěishí garrison,
called the Gǒudǎo Channel,
and north joins the Xiāng River.
The Xiāng River from the Mìluó Mouth flows northwest past west of Lěishí Mountain,
and north faces the Qīngcǎo Lake,
sometimes also called Qīngcǎo Mountain.
West faces the Xuánchéng Mouth,
the Xiāng River further north receives nine mouths,
all inlets of the Xiāng.
The Xiāng River flows northeast further to become the Qīngcǎo Lake Mouth,
joins the north mouth of the Gǒudǎo Channel on the right,
and joins the Láo Mouth,
further north receives the Tóngbàn Mouth,
all are rightward extensions of the Xiāng inlets.
Further north, it passes west of Xiàjuàn County,
the Wēi River flows from the east and empties into it.
The Xiāng River joins the Qīngshuǐ Mouth on the left,
which is the Zī River,
commonly called the Yìyáng River.
To the left of the Xiāng River,
it passes east of the Lùjiǎo Mountain,
to the right passes west of the Jǐntíng garrison,
then north joins the Chá Inlet,
then north receives the Wànshí Inlet,
all inlets of the Xiāng.
Beside the Xiāng Inlet north is the Wànshí garrison.
To the left of the Xiāng River, the Yuán River empties into it,
called the Héngfáng Mouth,
facing the Wēi Lake in the east,
sometimes called the Mí Lake.
To the right belongs the Wēi River,
which is the Wēi River mentioned in the "Classic of Waterways" as passing through Xiàjuàn,
flows west and empties into the river,
called the Mí Lake Mouth.
The Xiāng River flows north again,
passes the Jīnpǔ garrison,
north carries the Jīnpǔ water,
a lake marsh.
To the left of the Xiāng River, the Lǐ River empties into it,
commonly called the Wǔlíng River.
All these four rivers,
together empty into Dòngtíng,
north meet the Great River,
called the Five Islets.
The "Strategies of the Warring States" says:
"Qín fought with Jīng,
greatly defeated them,
and captured the Dòngtíng Five Islets."
The lake water is vast and round, over five hundred lǐ,
the sun and moon seem to rise and set within it.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"On the Dòngtíng Mountain,
dwell the two daughters of the Emperor.
The winds of Yuán and Lǐ,
meet the inlets of Xiāo and Xiāng,
emerging and entering often bring fierce winds and torrential rain."
In the lake are Jūn Mountain and Biān Mountain,
Jūn Mountain has a stone cave,
secretly connecting to the Bāo Mountain of Wú,
which is what Guō Jǐngchún called the underground passage of Bālíng.
This mountain,
is where the Goddess of the Xiāng roamed,
hence called Jūn Mountain.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng encountered wind here,
and asked his erudite scholars the reason.
They said:
"When the Goddess of the Xiāng emerges or enters, there is often wind."
The Qín king then scorched the mountain red.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn also ascended it,
and shot a jiāo dragon on this mountain.
Northeast faces Biān Mountain,
the mountain has much chí bamboo,
the two mountains are adjacent,
separated by several tens of lǐ,
standing opposite each other,
their solitary shadows seeming to float.
On the right bank of the lake is a mountain,
commonly called Dí Wūtóu Stone,
north of the stone, on the right joins the Wēng Lake Mouth,
whose water receives from Wēng Lake,
on the left joins the Dòng Inlet,
which is the so-called state of Sānmiáo,
left of Dòngtíng.
Further north, it reaches Bāqiū Mountain,
and enters the Jiāng.
The mountain lies on the right bank of the Xiāng River.
On the mountain stands the old city of Bālíng,
originally the Bāqiū Dǐgé Fortress of Wú.
In the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn, Bālíng County was established here.
Later, Jiànchāng Commandery was set up.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
Bālíng Commandery was established.
The city straddles ridges and hills,
bordering and controlling the three rivers.
West of Bālíng faces Chángzhōu,
which divides the Xiāng's waters to the south,
and reaches the Great River to the north.
Hence it is called the Three Rivers.
Where the three waters converge,
it is also sometimes called the Sānjiāngkǒu.
Between the mountains are arranged passes,
called Shèliè.
Further north, it faces Yǎngkǒu,
which is also a Xiāng watercourse.
The water's color is distinctively clear,
flowing northeast into the Great River.
There is a distinction between clear and turbid,
called the Jiānghuì.
38.4 Lí River
38.4 Lí River
The Lí River also originates from Yánghǎi Mountain.
The Lí River and the Xiāng River share the same mountain but have separate sources.
Between the Xiāng and Lí,
there is land over a hundred paces wide,
called Shǐ'ān Qiáo.
Qiáo,
is the Yuèchéng Qiáo.
The Qiáo River flows south from the sunny side of the Qiáo and joins the Lí,
named Shǐ'ān River.
Thus, Yǔ Zhòngchū's fu "Yángdū" says:
"Dividing the Five Ridges, the waters flow separately."
The Lí River flows south and joins the Wéi River,
which originates from the border of Shàolíng County to the northwest,
and flows southeast to Línglíng County,
passing west of Yuèchéng to the southwest.
In the sixteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era,
the Governor of Jiāozhōu, Lài Gōng,
gathered troops from Guǎngxìn at Xiǎolínglíng Yuèchéng to welcome Bù Zhì,
which was this very place.
The Wéi River flows southeast and joins the Lí River,
as mentioned in the "Hànshū": "Issuing from Línglíng, it flows into the Lí River."
The Lí River flows south and joins the Dànwán Stream,
which originates from Dànwán Mountain.
The mountain has a gushing spring,
whose rushing flow scours and impacts,
so that rocks in the mountain cliffs and stream resemble pellets,
naturally round like pearls,
shaped like pellets,
hence the mountain and stream are named accordingly.
Examining the mountain, there is a stone cavern,
descending several zhàng deep,
with deep and distant caves,
whose limits cannot be fathomed.
The stream flows east and joins the Lí River.
The Lí River flows south past the east of Shǐxīng County.
In the second year of the Xiánxī era of Wèi Yuándì,
Sūn Hào of Wú divided the southern part of Línglíng to establish Shǐxīng County.
The Lí River flows further south,
and joins the Luò Stream on the right,
which originates from Luòxī Mountain northwest of Yǒngfēng County,
flowing east past the north of the county.
The county,
was originally the northern township of Cāngwú,
and Sūn Hào carved it out to form a county.
The Luò Stream flows southeast past Shǐ'ān County and joins the Lí River to the east.
The Lí River flows southeast into Xīpíng County.
It passes Yánglài Mountain,
which overlooks the Lí River,
with rocks resembling sheep in color.
Further southeast, it passes Jīlài Mountain,
which borders the Lí River,
with rocks resembling chickens in color.
Thus, the two mountains are named after the forms of objects.
The Lí River flows south and reaches the mouth of the Xīpíng River,
whose source is Lóng Mountain east of the county,
flowing southwest past the south of the county,
then west to join the Běixiāng Stream,
which originates from Běixiāng Mountain northeast of the county,
flowing west past the north of the county,
then turning south as it flows west,
passing the west of the county.
The county,
was originally Fú Township of Shǐ'ān,
and Sūn Hào carved it out to form a county.
The stream flows south and joins the Xīpíng River,
which then flows west into the Lí River.
South of the county is the Zhāoxī Pond,
whose water issues from the southwest of the eastern mountain.
Water flows down from the mountain into the pond,
which increases and decreases twice daily,
rising and falling with the time,
never missing its schedule,
similar to the tides.
Hence, this pond is named Zhāoxī Pond.
The Lí River flows west through the boundary of Pínglè County,
joining the mouth of the Pínglè Stream on the left.
The stream originates south of Xièmù County in Línhè Commandery,
passing through mountains and flowing northwest,
passing southwest of Xièmù County,
flowing southwest to the southeast of Pínglè County,
where it joins the various streams of Xièmù on the left.
Branching streams converge,
flowing west past the south of Pínglè.
Sūn Hào carved out territory from Cāngwú to establish this county,
subordinating it to Shǐ'ān in the north.
The stream flows southwest and joins the Lí River,
called the Pínglè River.
Passing south through Lípǔ County of Cāngwú,
the Lài River originates east of Lǔ Mountain northwest of the county,
passing west of the county and joining the Rú River,
which originates from Rú Mountain northwest of Yǒngfēng County,
flowing southeast past the west of the county,
then southeast into Lípǔ County,
joining the Lài Stream,
and then joining the Lí River.
On the Lí River, there is a pass.
The Lí River flows further south,
joining the mouth of the Líng Stream on the left.
The stream originates from Fúlíng Ridge north of Fùchuān County in Línhè,
flowing south past the east of the county,
and then south into the Lí River.
Further south, it reaches Guǎngxìn County,
and enters the Yù River.
38.5 Zhēn River
38.5 Zhēn River
The Zhēn River originates south of Línwǔ County in Guìyáng,
winding northwest around the city and turning east to flow.
The Zhēn River originates southwest of the county,
flowing north past the west of the county,
and north to join the Wǔ Stream.
The "Shānhǎijīng" says:
"The Yì River originates southwest of Línwǔ,
and flows southeast into the sea.
It enters west of Pānyú."
The Yì River,
is likely another name for the Zhēn River.
The Wǔ Stream originates from Tóngbǎi Mountain northwest of Línwǔ County,
flowing southeast,
and joining the Zhēn River on the right.
The mingled flow passes southeast west of Línwǔ County,
called the Wǔ Stream.
The county lies east of the stream,
hence named Línwǔ County.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Dàwǔ.
The stream flows further southeast,
joining the Huángcén Stream on the left.
The stream originates from Huángcén Mountain in Chēn County,
flowing southwest,
and joining the Wǔ Stream on the right.
The Wǔ Stream flows south into the Chóng Mountains,
named Lánháo,
spanning five hundred lǐ in circumference,
all within the boundaries of Qūjiāng County.
The cliffs are steep and perilous,
the rocky ridges reach the sky,
with intertwined branches thick as clouds,
obscuring the sky and darkening the view,
called the Shuāngzhōng.
Suspended rapids whirl and pour,
crashing waves shake the mountains,
named the Shuāng River.
East to Ānnièyì east of Qūjiāng County,
it turns and flows southwest,
The Lóng Shuǐ flows southward out of the gorge,
which is called Lóngkǒu.
On the western bank is the city of General Rèn,
built by Rèn Xiāo, the Commandant of Nánhǎi.
After Xiāo's death,
Commandant Tuó from Lóngchuān began to reside there.
On the eastern bank is the temple of General Rèn.
The Lóng Shuǐ further south joins with the Líng Shuǐ.
The Líng Shuǐ originates east from Língjūn Shān,
a mountain
that stands alone in splendor among the clustered peaks.
In the eighteenth year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
a collapse of over ten zhàng occurred,
creating a hanging ravine where waterfalls cascade,
pouring their flow into the valley,
and the tumbling waves
empty into the Lóng Shuǐ.
The Lóng Shuǐ then joins with the Lín Shuǐ on the right,
which originates from Huán Shān northeast of the county.
Wáng Xīnzhī's *Records of Shǐxīng* states:
Within the source of the Lín Shuǐ is a stone chamber,
in front of which, on a flat rock, are arranged ten jars,
all filled with silver ingots.
Those who come across them while gathering wood cannot take them;
if they take them, they will inevitably become confused and fall ill.
In the early years of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
a servant of Fēng Qūzhī
secretly stole three ingots and returned home.
Upon opening them to look,
a large snake bit him, and he died.
The *Records of Xiāngzhōu* states:
That night,
Qūzhī dreamed of a deity saying:
"Your servant was not careful.
He stole three silver ingots,
and today he has been openly executed,
repaying with the silver."
Upon waking and looking,
the servant was dead, and the silver was there.
The Lín Shuǐ flows westward from its source into the Lóng Shuǐ,
and then joins with the Yún Shuǐ.
This water originates from the hot springs north of the county,
where the spring source boils and surges,
with vast vapors floating like clouds.
If something foul is thrown into it,
it becomes hot in a moment.
At times, small red fish swim within it,
yet they are not scalded.
It joins the Lóng Shuǐ to the northwest.
There is also the Jí Shuǐ,
which receives water from the Cāngmíng Shuǐ,
and there are islands within it.
This water takes in and discharges many streams,
flowing northwest into the Lóng Shuǐ.
The Lóng Shuǐ then flows south past Língjiù Shān,
a mountain
originally named Hǔjùn Shān,
also called Hǔshì Shān,
due to the frequent violence of tigers.
During the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
the monk Shì Sēnglǜ
built a dwelling in the cliffside recesses,
and the fierce tigers kept their distance.
This was likely due to the benevolence of Sēnglǜ,
so it was renamed Língjiù Shān.
The Lóng Shuǐ then flows south past the east of Qūjiāng Xiàn,
said to have been formerly called Qūhóng,
which
is the name of a mountain.
It connects eastward with the ridge.
Within the Lóng Shuǐ is a stele,
with text stating:
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
this is the old Qūjiāng Xiàn.
Wáng Mǎng called it Chúlǔ.
It is the seat of Shǐxīng Jùn.
In the second year of the Xiánxī era of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
Sūn Hào separated the southern part of Guìyáng to establish it.
East of the county, bordering the Lóng Xī,
it is called the Běi Lóng Shuǐ.
To the left of the water is the Dōng Xīkǒu.
The water originates from Shíyán Shān on the border of Nánkāng Xiàn, Jiāngzhōu, in Shǐxīng to the east,
flowing west to join with the Lián Shuǐ.
This water originates from Liángrè Shān Lián Xī in Nánkāng Xiàn,
a mountain
that is the Dàyǔ Lǐng,
the easternmost of the Five Ridges,
hence called Dōngjiào Shān.
This is where travelers change attire,
and the boat route below is named Lián Xī.
The Lián Shuǐ flows south,
emptying into the Dōng Xī,
called Liánkǒu.
Yǔ Zhòngchū referred to it as Dàyǔjiào Shuǐ.
The Dōng Xī is also called Dōng Jiāng,
or Shǐxīng Shuǐ.
Further west,
the Xiéjiē Shuǐ flows into it,
originating from Xiéjiē Shān southeast of the county.
The water has a separate source,
called Cháotóu.
Overlapping ridges embrace the torrents,
with rushing streams connecting one after another,
the twin sources pour forth,
merging into a single river.
Beside the water is the city of Bítiānzǐ,
Bítiānzǐ,
of whom nothing is known.
The Xiéjiē Shuǐ then flows northwest into the Dōng Jiāng.
The Jiāng Shuǐ then flows west past the south of Shǐxīng Xiàn,
and further west enters Qūjiāng Xiàn.
The Dǐ Shuǐ flows into it,
originating from Fúyuè Shān,
a mountain where stepping on one spot causes movement over a hundred paces, as if on water,
hence named Fúyuè Shān.
It flows south into the Dōng Jiāng.
The Dōng Jiāng then flows west to join with the Lì Shuǐ,
which originates from Sháoshí Běi Shān in the county,
flowing south past Sháoshí below.
It is a hundred rèn high,
with a circumference of five lǐ,
two rocks standing opposite each other,
one lǐ apart,
roughly equal in size, resembling twin gate towers,
named Sháoshí.
Ancient lore says,
long ago two immortals
parted and rested there,
and from then on the years were abundant,
lasting a full cycle of twelve years.
The Lì Shuǐ then flows south past Língshí below,
Língshí,
also called Táoshí,
thirty zhàng high,
with a circumference of five hundred zhàng.
Elderly traditions say,
the stone was originally from Wǔchéng Xiàn, Guìlín.
Due to a sudden thunderstorm one night,
it abruptly moved here.
People from there came and exclaimed:
"The stone has fled here!"
Hence named Táoshí.
Because it moved with spiritual power,
it is also called Língshí.
At its prominent spot,
it stands cliff-like by the river,
with mottled colors like embroidered patterns.
Water and stones create startling rapids,
their echoes unceasing,
merchant boats linger,
listening and enjoying without end.
The Lì Shuǐ flows south into the Dōng Jiāng,
which then flows west into the Běi Jiāng,
called Dōngjiāngkǒu.
From here, the Zhēn Shuǐ
takes on the names Shǐxīng and Dàyǔ,
and flows south into Zhēnyáng Xiàn.
Passing through Zhēnyáng Xiàn,
exiting Kuāngpǔ Guān,
it joins with the Guì Shuǐ.
The Zhēn River flows south past the west of Zhēnyáng County,
which was an old Han dynasty county.
It was called Qíwǔ during Wáng Mǎng's time.
East of the county is Zhēnshí Mountain,
thirty *li* in circumference,
its lofty peaks rising north of the great river,
its base coiling at the edge of the long watercourse.
On its southern side is a stone chamber,
where old fishermen used to rest.
In the past, when they tried to open a road north of the mountain to reach the commandery,
a great snake would always block the path,
so they did not succeed.
Therefore, travelers nowadays
must always take a boat in front of the stone chamber to cross.
The Zhēn River then flows southwest between Gāokǒu and Tàiwèi mountains,
which is called the Zhēnyáng Gorge.
The cliffs on both banks are magnificent and lofty,
standing sheer, cutting off the sky.
In the past, they once cut into the rock and built a gallery,
connecting the two banks to resist Xú Dàofù.
As the Zhēn River emerges from the left side of the gorge,
the Zhēn River flows into it.
This water originates west of Lóngchuān County in Nánhǎi,
flows past the south of Zhēnyáng County,
and enters the Zhēn River from the right.
Thus Yìng Shào said:
"The Zhēn River enters the Zhēn from the west" is correct.
The Zhēn River flows further southwest,
where the Kuāng River joins it.
As stated in the *Shānhǎi Jīng*: "The Huáng River originates from the northwest mountains of Guìyáng,
flows southeast and empties into Yì,
entering west of Dūnpǔ."
The Zhēn River then flows southwest past Zhōngsù County, where it meets the Yīlǐ River.
The place is narrow,
and is called Guānqí.
The connected mountains lie intertwined,
with sheer cliffs standing steeply.
Below is a temple of the gods,
backed by a hill and facing the stream.
Its altar and buildings are empty and solemn.
Around the temple's islet, rocks pile up jaggedly,
chaotically rising in the middle of the river.
When the seasonal floods arrive,
the water roars and boils,
and any floating timber that sinks
certainly never reemerges.
People believe it is the River Earl collecting timber.
During the Jin dynasty's central court period,
a county native on an official mission reached Luòyáng.
After finishing his business and about to return,
suddenly a man entrusted him with a letter, saying:
"My home is in front of Guānqí,
where vines hang among the rocks.
That is the place.
Just knock on the vines,
and someone will come to fetch it."
The envoy carefully followed his words,
and indeed two men came out,
took the letter and invited him into the water palace,
yet his clothes did not get wet.
This tale may seem far-fetched,
but within the workings of creation,
nothing is impossible.
King Mù traveled west
and discussed treasures with the River Patriarch.
Reasoning from this,
it is a similar case.
The Zhēn River then flows southwest past the south of Zhōngsù County,
which was established by Sūn Hào of Wú by dividing off the northern part of Sìhuì.
It enters the sea to the south.
The Zhēn River then flows south and empties into the Yù River, which then enters the sea.
39 Shujingzhu 39
39.1 Kuāng River
39.1 Kuāng River
The Kuāng River originates from Lújù in Guìyáng County,
its source is Lúxī at Shàngyì Mountain northwest of Guìyáng County,
called the Lúxī River.
It flows southeast past the old city of Guìyáng County,
and is called the Kuāng River.
The *Dìlǐzhì* states:
"The Kuāng River originates from Guìyáng,
flowing south to Sìhuì" is correct.
The Kuāng River flows further southeast,
where the Qiáo River joins it.
This water originates from the stream of Dūqiáo,
the stream flows down through a gorge,
emerging south from this gorge,
which is called the Zhēnnǚ Gorge.
The high cliff on the west bank of the gorge is named Zhēnnǚ Mountain.
At the mountain's base is a rock shaped like a person,
seven *chǐ* tall,
resembling a woman,
hence the name Zhēnnǚ Gorge.
Since ancient times it has been passed down
that several girls were gathering snails here,
when they encountered wind, rain, and sudden darkness,
and suddenly turned to stone.
This is truly a great marvel,
hard to believe upon hearing.
However, Qǐ was born from a stone,
and Zhì wailed in the hollow mulberry tree;
perhaps this is of the same kind.
The transformations of things—
can they truly be sought through reason?
The stream then joins the Kuāng River.
The Kuāng River flows further southeast into Yángshān County,
where it meets the Liánkǒu River from the right.
Its source is Shítáng Village, 110 *li* northwest of the county,
flowing southeast.
Beside the water is a camphor tree,
its trunk originally about two *zhàng* in diameter.
Its stump and roots still remain.
Though it was felled long ago,
the axe marks look fresh.
Birds fly around it ceaselessly,
and its many branches
flew off and scattered far, gathering in the countryside.
No one knows where they went,
only one branch is seen
remaining alone in the Hánkuāng River.
The Lián River flows southeast and empties into the Kuāng.
The Kuāng River flows further southeast and meets the Zhēn River from the right.
This water's source emerges nearby from beneath the eastern cliff,
the opening like a well.
Within a single day,
it overflows ten times and dries up ten times,
truly like the tides,
and flows into the Kuāng River.
The Kuāng River then flows south past the west of the old city of Yángshān County.
According to elders' tales,
in the past, whenever a magistrate governed this county,
he would quickly be promoted exceptionally high.
A grand astrologer passed by and observed,
saying the terrain caused this.
They dug and severed the connected ridge,
blood flowed and became a stream,
the city consequently collapsed,
and soon fell into ruin.
A large drum from the tower
flew to Línwǔ,
then to Guìyáng,
and was later named the "Sacred Drum."
From Yángshān to the Wǔbù post station in Guìyáng,
the route followed is the "Sacred Drum" road.
The road is like a trench,
reaching all the way to Gǔchéng.
The Kuāng River then flows past the south of Yángshān County.
This county
was originally the Táo Township of Hánkuāng County,
established as a separate county by Sūn Hào.
The Kuāng River then flows further southeast.
It passes southeast through Hánkuāng County.
Yìng Shào said:
The Kuāng Shuǐ flows northeast into the Yuán.
Zàn annotated the Book of Hàn,
stating that the Yuán is in Wǔlíng,
far from the Kuāng,
and separated by the Xiāng Shuǐ,
so it cannot flow into the Yuán.
The Kuāng Shuǐ flows southeast,
where on the left it joins the Wēng Shuǐ.
The Wēng Shuǐ originates from the Lìshān Lake to the northeast.
The lake is five lǐ in circumference,
and its water is purer than ordinary water.
It flows southwest and empties into the Kuāng,
where it is called the Wēng Shuǐ Kǒu.
Below the mouth, on the eastern bank, there is a Shèng Gǔ Zhàng,
which is the drumstick of Yángshān.
It lies horizontally by the riverbank.
Though struck by rushing waves,
it has never moved.
Birds soar and sing,
but none gather upon it.
If boatmen strike it with their poles while passing,
they invariably contract malaria.
The Kuāng Shuǐ flows further southeast,
where on the left it joins the Táo Shuǐ.
The Táo Shuǐ originates east from Yáoshān.
The mountain winds for several hundred lǐ,
with reddish cliffs rising in layers,
crowned by verdant forests,
their colors mingling with the clouds and mist.
On the mountain, there is white quartz,
and at its foot lies a flat ridge,
where the foundation of a great hall remains.
The elders say:
This was the traveling palace of Yáo.
The Táo Shuǐ flows west past the north of the county,
and empties into the Kuāng Shuǐ from the right.
The Kuāng Shuǐ then flows past the west of Hánkuāng County.
Wáng Xīn’s Records of Shǐxīng states:
The county has a Báilù Chéng,
and south of the city is Báilù Gāng.
During the Xiánkāng era,
a commandery resident named Zhāng Fáng served as magistrate of the county.
He governed with benevolent policies,
and white deer came to roam here.
Hence, both the city and the ridge were named after them.
To the south, it exits the Kuāngpǔ Pass,
becoming the Guì Shuǐ.
The pass is located in Zhōngsù County.
The Kuāng Shuǐ emerges from the pass and joins the Zhēn Shuǐ on the right,
where it is called the Kuāng Kǒu.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas calls it the Huáng Shuǐ.
Xú Guǎng said:
The Huáng Shuǐ is also called the Kuāng Shuǐ.
It originates from Guìyáng,
connects to Sìhuì,
and is also called the Cuǐ Shuǐ.
In the first year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Lù Bódé was appointed General Fúbō
to campaign against Nányuè.
He set out from Guìyáng,
descended the Huáng Shuǐ,
which is this very river.
Guì Shuǐ
is its alternative name.
39.2 Shēn Shuǐ
39.2 Shēn Shuǐ
The Shēn Shuǐ originates from Lújù in Guìyáng.
Lǚ Chén said:
The Shēn Shuǐ is also called the Suì Shuǐ.
It originates from Lúxī,
flows west into the Yíng Shuǐ,
mingles with the Yíng’s currents,
and together empties into the Xiāng’s crossing.
Xǔ Shèn stated:
The Shēn Shuǐ originates from Nánpíng County in Guìyáng.
The Classic records it as Guìyáng
because the county was originally under Guìyáng Commandery,
but was later transferred to Shǐxīng.
The county has Lúxī.
The Lújù Mountain
lies south of Nánpíng County,
east of the Jiǔyí Mountains.
It flows northwest past the south of Yíngdào County in Línglíng,
then northwest past the south of Yíngpǔ County,
then northwest past Quánlíng County.
Seven lǐ northwest, it reaches Yānshì,
where it bends and enters the Xiāng.
Above the water is Yānshì Hill,
which also gives its name to the settlement.
The water below is unfathomably deep,
and is called Lóngyuān.
39.3 Zhōng Shuǐ
39.3 Zhōng Shuǐ
The Zhōng Shuǐ originates from Dūshān in Nánpíng County, Guìyáng.
It flows north past the east of the county,
then northeast past the Sòngzhǔ Pavilion,
then north past the Zhōng Pavilion,
where it joins the Cuǐ Shuǐ.
Dūshān
is the Dūpáng Ridge,
the third of the Five Ridges.
The Zhōng Shuǐ is the Qiáo Shuǐ.
Yǔ Zhòngchū said:
The Qiáo Shuǐ flows south into the Zhēn Shuǐ of Shǐxīng,
emptying into the sea;
flowing north into Guìyáng,
the Xiāng Shuǐ empties into the Jiāng—this is correct.
The Cuǐ Shuǐ
is the Guì Shuǐ.
Cuǐ and Guì have similar pronunciations,
so the characters changed with the reading,
and the Classic perpetuated the error.
The Guì Shuǐ originates from the mountains on the northern border of Guìyáng County.
The mountain cliffs are lofty and steep,
with three sides particularly precipitous.
Stone springs cascade down,
forming waterfalls.
It flows north past Nánpíng County, then northeast to the Zhōng Pavilion,
where on the right it meets the Zhōng Shuǐ,
and together they form the Guì Shuǐ.
Thus, Yìng Shào said:
The Guì Shuǐ originates from Guìyáng,
flowing northeast into the Xiāng.
It then flows north past the east of Wèiníng County.
Wèiníng
was formerly Yáng’ān.
In the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn, it was renamed Jìnníng.
The county is located 120 lǐ east of Guìyáng Commandery.
To the south and west of the county,
it is bounded by clear streams.
It is impossible for the Guì Shuǐ to exit east of the county.
This is likely due to shifts in county boundaries,
as circumstances differed between ancient and modern times.
It then flows north into the Xiāng.
39.4 Lěi Shuǐ
39.4 Lěi Shuǐ
The Lěi Shuǐ originates from Nánshān in Chēn County, Guìyáng.
The Lěi Shuǐ’s source is at Wūlóng Báiqí Shān east of Rǔchéng County.
It flows northwest past the north of the county,
then west for thirty lǐ.
Along this stretch are fourteen rapids,
each several hundred bù long,
with swift, turbulent currents.
They follow one another like bamboo joints,
making travel and crossing difficult.
It then flows northwest past the north of Jìnníng County,
then west,
where on the left it joins the Qīngxī Shuǐ Kǒu.
The Qīngxī Shuǐ originates from Huángpí Shān east of the county,
flows southwest past the south of the county,
then northwest into the Lěi Shuǐ.
Rǔchéng County is over 300 lǐ east of the commandery,
and the mountain is further east of the county,
so it is impossible for the Lěi Shuǐ to originate from Nánshān.
It then flows north past the west of the county.
The county has a Lǜshuǐ,
which originates from Xiágōng Mountain east of the county,
flows northwest,
then bends south and empties into the Lěishuǐ,
called Chéngxiāng Creek.
The commandery established an office for wine,
brewing at the foot of the mountain,
named Chéng wine,
which was presented as tribute alongside Líng wine.
The Lěishuǐ flows further west,
where the Huángshuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from Huángcén Mountain west of the county,
which is the ridge of Qítián,
the second of the Five Ridges.
The Huángshuǐ flows northeast.
According to Shèng Hóngzhī:
Many mountain streams flow out and pour into a large creek,
called Héngliú Creek.
The creek water is very small,
yet does not dry up in winter or summer.
It is commonly called the Greedy Spring,
as those who drink from it become covetous of wealth and bribes,
similar to the Greedy Stream at Shímén in Guǎngzhōu.
Those who are honest and upright as high-ranking officials
do not drink from it.
In the past, Wú Yǐnzhī scooped water from it but remained uncorrupted.
How could greed be said to tarnish his integrity?
It is likely that he also disliked its name.
Liú Chéngzhī called it Yīyá Creek, connecting to Sìhuì,
which is quite reckless and not accurate.
Yǔ Zhòngchū said:
The ridge water flows south into Shǐxīng,
the Zhēnshuǐ empties into the sea,
meaning the Huángcén water enters the Wǔ Creek.
The northern water enters the Xiāngshuǐ in Guìyáng,
and empties into the Great River,
which is this water.
To the right, the Qiānqiūshuǐ flows into it.
This water originates from Wànsuì Mountain to the southwest,
where there is a stone chamber on the mountain,
with stalactites inside the chamber.
The mountain is entirely covered with Língshòu trees.
Below the creek is the Qiānqiūshuǐ.
Residents living by the water
call it Wànsuì Village.
This water flows downstream and merges with the Huángshuǐ.
The Huángshuǐ then flows northeast past the east of the county,
where it merges with the Chúquánshuǐ on the right.
This water originates from Xiāngbēi Village south of the county.
The village has a round pond,
about two hundred paces in diameter,
with one side warm
and the other side cold.
The cold side is extremely clear and green,
shallow enough to see the stones,
deep enough to see the bottom.
The warm side has white and turbid water.
The colors are distinct,
and the temperatures also differ.
It is named Chú Spring,
similar to the Bàntāng Spring in Jiāngchéng.
When the water is abundant, it overflows into Huáng Creek.
When the water diminishes, the flow through the ford stops.
Chēn is an old county,
and the seat of Guìyáng Commandery.
In the second year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was established by dividing Chángshā.
The "Geographical Records" says:
The Guìshuǐ originates here,
hence the name.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Nánpíng,
and the county Xuānfēng.
It was built when Xiàng Yǔ moved the Righteous Emperor.
South of the county is the tomb of the Righteous Emperor,
containing a stone tiger inside,
so it was called the White Tiger Commandery.
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
Cí Chōng, styled Zǐhé,
served as the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
The people were lazy,
and few wore coarse shoes,
so their feet were often cracked.
Cí taught them to make shoes.
Today, people south of the Yangtze River know how to weave shoes,
all due to Cí's teaching.
East of Huáng Creek is Mǎlǐng Mountain,
over six hundred zhàng high,
about forty lǐ in circumference.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, a commandery resident named Sū Dān roamed and dwelled on this mountain.
The "Guìyáng Biographies of Immortals" says:
Dān
was a native of Chēn County.
He was orphaned young,
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His speech was mystical and unfathomable,
so people of the time called him foolish.
He often herded cattle with other children,
taking turns as the leader,
ensuring the cattle did not scatter.
Whenever it was Dān's turn to lead,
the cattle would linger around him,
not straying and returning on their own.
The other children said:
"When it's your turn,
why don't the cattle run away?"
Dān replied:
"This is not something you can understand."
He then bid farewell to his mother, saying:
"My nature is destined for immortality,
and I must leave your care."
With tears, he also said:
"A great epidemic is coming,
and about half the people will die.
Dig a well and drink from it,
and you will be safe."
After this, there were very sorrowful cries,
and later, people saw Dān riding a white horse back to this mountain.
The common people built an altar and shrine for him,
and the people were safe, with bountiful harvests.
Thus, the people named it Mǎlǐng Mountain.
The Huángshuǐ flows north and empties into the Lěishuǐ,
called Chēnkǒu.
The Lěishuǐ flows west past the northern side of Huà Mountain,
also called Huáshí Mountain.
A solitary peak rises prominently,
flanked by two streams.
To the east is the confluence of Huáng Creek and the Lěishuǐ.
The Lěishuǐ flows eastward along its course,
unable to pass north of the county's west side.
The banks are lined with continuous mountains,
with stone springs cascading down.
Travelers often linger, captivated,
unable to contain their emotions.
It then flows north past the west of Biàn County.
This county
was formerly a marquisate granted by Emperor Huì to Wú Qiǎn, son of the King of Chángshā.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Biànpíng.
Within the county boundaries, there are hot springs,
located northwest of Chēn County.
There are several thousand mǔ of fields on either side,
irrigated by these springs.
Seeds are often sown in the twelfth month,
and the grain ripens by the third month of the following year.
Considering that this water is cold,
it cannot nurture seedlings,
but with irrigation from the warm water,
three harvests a year are possible.
The remaining water disperses and flows
into the Lěishuǐ.
It then flows northwest past the east of Lěiyáng County.
Lěiyáng is an old county,
named after the water.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Nánpíngtíng.
To the east lies the Lěishuǐ,
and east of the water, to the south,
is the old commandery city.
The county has a creek,
originating from Hóujì Mountain to the east.
Its water is clear and pure,
warm in winter and cool in summer.
It flows west,
called Féichuān.
North of the river is Lútáng Pond,
covering eight qǐng,
with unfathomable depth.
Large fish often come here,
and in the fifth month, they leap vigorously,
causing the water to surge several zhàng high,
with waves flooding the surrounding land.
Small fish flee in panic,
carried by the water onto the shore,
too numerous to count.
It is also said:
When the large fish are about to stir,
all the fish gather and float.
The water flows northwest along the side,
passing Cài Islet.
West of the islet,
is the former residence of Cài Lún,
with Càizǐ Pond beside it.
Lún
was a eunuch of the Hàn dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Shùn,
he pounded old fishing nets to make paper,
replacing bamboo slips and silk,
beginning from his time.
It then flows north past the east of Líng County.
In the county there is the Líng Lake,
within the lake there is an islet,
on the islet dwell residents,
the people there rely on it for sustenance,
brewing wine that is exceptionally mellow and fine,
called Líng wine,
which is annually presented as tribute.
By the lakeside there still remains the old seat of Líng County,
fifteen lǐ northwest of Línchéng County,
now subordinate to the provincial administration.
The Record of the Thirteen Provinces states:
The Dàbié River flows south from Mount Tài in Lěiyáng County,
north to Líng County, where it enters the lake.
It then flows north into the Xiāng River.
The Lěi River flows northwest to Línchéng County, where it turns right and joins the Xiāng River,
this is called the Lěi Estuary.
39.5 The Mǐ River
39.5 The Mǐ River
The Mǐ River originates from Shàngxiāng in Chálíng County,
flowing northwest past the west of the county.
The water originates from Mount Tàipíng in Guǎngxīng County, Ānchéng Commandery, Jiāngzhōu,
flowing northwest past the south of Chálíng County.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was enfeoffed as the estate of Jié Hóu Xīn, son of Dìng Wáng of Chángshā.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Shēngxiāng.
The Mǐ River then bends and passes the county,
flowing northwest to join another river.
The Treatise on Geography calls it the Ní River.
It then flows northwest past the south of Yōu County.
The Yōu River originates from Mount Fēnghóu in Ānfù County, Ānchéng Commandery, southeast,
flowing northwest past the north of the county.
The county borders the Yōu Stream to the north,
likely named after the stream.
In the fourth year of the Yuánshuò era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Zé, son of Dìng Wáng of Chángshā, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yōuyú,
which is the Yōu County mentioned in the Treatise on Geography.
The Yōu River then flows southwest into Chálíng County,
joining the Mǐ River.
It then flows northwest past the south of Yīnshān County.
The county,
originally Yángshān County,
still has the old city of Yángshān northeast of the county,
which was the estate of Zōng, son of Xiào Wáng of Chángshā.
It was said that its terrain was kingly,
so they cut through mountains and filled valleys,
renaming it Yīnshān County.
From Mount Hóután above the county, the Róng River flows down into the Mǐ River,
called the Róng Estuary.
There is a large cave in the water,
capable of holding a hundred shí,
from which water emerges,
hence the name.
The Mǐ River then flows northwest past the east of the county,
then west past the Lì Estuary,
where the Lì River from the county flows down into the Mǐ,
called the Lì Estuary.
The Mǐ River then flows northwest to meet the Yánghú Lake water,
which originates from Yánghú Lake below Lèsǒu Ridge northwest of the county,
the lake is seven lǐ from the ridge,
the lake water flows down into the Mǐ,
called the Yánghú Estuary.
Northeast of the Mǐ River is Mount É,
and northeast of the county is also Mount Wǔyáng Lóngwěi,
both places where immortals attained ascension,
with traces of immortals and dragon-horses above,
where leftover verses were found.
Though the spirits dwell in white clouds,
thoughts linger on the fragrant stream,
and the mind rests on the spring homeland,
the leftover verses remain here.
Reading the remaining chants,
one still feels the distant tranquility,
not merely longing for the traces in the clouds,
but cherishing the literary chants worth remembering,
thus I take up brush and paper,
to interpret the chants.
The summary reads:
Ascend Wǔyáng,
gaze upon Lèsǒu,
the thousand peaks of É Ridge at Yánghú Estuary,
command the flying dragon,
drive the white colt,
approach the heavenly waters,
heart hesitating,
a thousand years later,
who will know?
Truly a sublime appreciation of the divine homeland,
with elegant sentiments transcending the ordinary.
It then flows northwest into the Xiāng River.
39.6 The Lù River
39.6 The Lù River
The Lù River originates from Mount Lù east of Lǐlíng County,
flowing west past the south of the county.
Lǐlíng County,
in the fourth year of Empress Gāo’s reign, was enfeoffed as the state of Yuè, Chancellor of Chángshā.
The county borders the Lù River to the south,
the water originates east from Mount Wēnglíng in Ānchéng Township.
I say Lù and Lù sound similar,
later people conveniently used Lù as the name.
Though Wēnglíng is a different name,
it refers to the same foothills.
Bending from the west of the county, it flows northwest,
reaching Lùpǔ,
where it empties into the Xiāng River.
39.7 The Liú River
39.7 The Liú River
The Liú River originates from Liúyáng County southeast of Línxiāng County,
flowing northwest past the county,
northeast merging with the Láo River.
The Liú River originates from Mount Shǒupí in Yùzhāng County, Jiāngzhōu, east of the county,
its source flowing northwest,
passing south of the county,
the county is named after the stream.
It then flows northwest into Línxiāng County.
West into the Xiāng River.
39.8 The Mì River
39.8 The Mì River
The Mì River originates from Ài County in Yùzhāng,
The Spring and Autumn Annals: Zuǒ Tradition states:
Prince Qìngjì of Wú advised Fūchāi but was not heeded,
and resided in Ài, which is this place.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Zhìhàn.
It flows west past the west of Luó County in Chángshā,
the descendants of Luó moved here from Zhījiāng,
and it is still called the City of Marquis Luó.
The Mì River flows west and accumulates into a pond,
called Tǐng Lake.
It then flows west to Mount Lěishí,
entering the Xiāng River.
Mount Lěishí is to the north,
also called Mount Wǔmù,
the mountain is square and pointed like the shape of five wooden blocks,
hence commoners use this to name it.
The mountain is north of the Luó Estuary,
the Mì River is south of the Luó River,
flowing into the Xiāng, called the Eastern Tǐng Estuary.
39.9 The Gàn River
39.9 The Gàn River
The Gàn River originates from Nányě County in Yùzhāng,
flowing northwest past the east of Gàn County.
The Xū River originates in Nánchéng County,
flowing northwest past the south of Nánchāng County,
and empties westward into the Gàn River.
There is also the Zhuó River that flows into it,
which originates in Kānglè County,
formerly known as Yánglè.
The Zhuó River then flows east past Wàngcài County,
a county established because people from Shàngcài in Rǔnán named Píng settled in this land.
In the first year of the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
it was renamed Wàngcài County.
The Zhuó River then flows east past Jiànchéng County,
where in the fourth year of the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Liú Shí, son of the Prince of Chángshā Dìng, was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Duōjù.
The county produces burning stones,
as recorded in the *Yìwù Zhì*:
The stones are yellow-white in color with coarse grain,
and become hot when water is poured on them.
If a cauldron is placed on top,
it can cook food thoroughly.
When removed, they become cold;
when water is poured on them, they become hot again,
and this cycle repeats endlessly.
During the Yuánkāng era,
Léi Kǒngzhāng went to Luòyáng,
bringing a stone to show to Lord Zhāng.
Lord Zhāng said:
This is called a burning stone.
Only then did they know its name.
The Zhuó River then flows east to the east of Nánchāng County,
and enters the Gàn River.
The Gàn River then passes west of Báishè,
where the tomb of Xú Rúzǐ is located.
During the Jiāhé era of Wú,
Grand Administrator Xú Xī of Chángshā planted pines along the tomb path,
and Grand Administrator Xiè Jǐng of Nányáng erected a stele beside the tomb.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
Grand Administrator Xiàhóu Sōng of Liángjùn built a Sīxián Pavilion beside the stele.
The pines grew so large that it took an armspan to encircle them,
and the pavilion was maintained through the generations,
so that it is now called the Pìngjūn Pavilion.
The Gàn River then flows north past Nántáng,
east of which is Rúzǐ's residence,
situated on a small islet by the southern lake.
Rúzǐ's given name was Zhì,
and he was a native of Nánchāng.
He was of noble character and did not serve in office,
declining even when Grand Commandant Huáng Qióng summoned him.
Emperor Huán asked the Imperial Secretary Chén Fān:
Between Xú Zhì and Yuán Hóng,
who is superior?
Chén Fān replied:
Yuán is from a noble family,
polished without carving,
but as for Xú Zhì,
he stands out like a mountain above the plains,
so he should be considered superior.
Emperor Huán prepared elaborate rituals to summon him, but he did not come.
When Guō Línzōng of Tàiyuán was mourning his mother,
Xú Zhì went to offer condolences,
placing fresh grass in front of the mourning hut before leaving.
No one understood the reason,
but Guō Línzōng said:
It must be Rúzǐ.
As the *Book of Songs* says:
A bundle of fresh grass,
the man is like jade.
I am not virtuous enough to deserve this.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
The Gàn River then passes Gǔlù Islet,
also known as Liǎozi Islet,
formerly a place where large ships were built.
The Gàn River then flows north past the west of the old city of Nánchāng County,
which belonged to Chǔ during the Spring and Autumn period,
and was where Prime Minister Zǐ Dàng stationed troops in Yùzhāng.
During the Qín dynasty, it was made the southern part of Lújiāng.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Chén Yīng was appointed to establish Yùzhāng Commandery,
with its seat here,
which was built by Chén Yīng.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it,
calling the county Yíshàn,
and the commandery Jiǔjiāng.
Liú Xīn said:
Nine rivers, including Húhàn, flow into Pénglí,
hence the name Jiǔjiāng.
When Chén Fān served as Grand Administrator,
he appointed Xú Zhì as Gōngcáo.
Chén Fān did not receive guests while in the commandery,
but when Xú Zhì came,
he would set up a special couch for him,
and hang it up when he left.
This is the place where the couch was hung.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
it was renamed Xī'ān,
and during the Jìn dynasty, it was again called Yùzhāng.
The southern gate of the city was called Sōngyáng Gate,
inside which stood a camphor tree,
seventy-five feet tall,
twenty-five armspans in girth,
with lush, spreading branches and leaves,
casting shade over several acres.
Yìng Shào's *Hàn Guān Yí* states:
In Yùzhāng,
a camphor tree grows in the courtyard,
hence the commandery is named after it.
This tree once withered,
but during the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
it suddenly flourished again,
as lush as before,
and all took it as an auspicious sign for Emperor Zhōngzōng.
The *Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí* says:
When the ruler's governance is just and lawsuits are settled,
the camphor tree of Yùzhāng flourishes.
During the Tàixīng era,
Emperor Yuánhuáng indeed revived the great enterprise in the south,
so Guō Jǐngchún's *Nán Jiāo Fù* says:
The withered camphor tree flourished again in the ancestral city.
This is because Emperor Xuānwáng's ancestors were from Yùzhāng.
The Gàn River flows northward,
passing Dùzhī Bù to the northwest,
which was the site of the Jìn dynasty Dùzhī Colonel's office.
Bù
means a water landing.
The Gàn River then passes north of the commandery as a ferry landing,
where there is an old temple dedicated to Grand Administrator Jiǎ Méng.
Jiǎ Méng contended over land with Marquis Ān, Zhāng Pǔ,
and was killed by Zhāng Pǔ.
On that very day, his spirit appeared at the ferry landing,
so the people built a temple for him.
On the western bank of the river is a large rock,
called Shítóu,
which marks the ferry landing.
Twenty lǐ to the west is Sànyuán Mountain,
surrounded by layered peaks,
deep and secluded with charm.
At the end of the Lóng'ān era of the Jìn dynasty,
the monk Zhú Tánxiǎn built a monastery on the southern side of the mountain,
and monks from afar came one after another.
Five or six lǐ to the northwest is Hóng Well,
where water cascades down,
so deep it has no bottom.
It is said to be the well of Master Hóngyá.
Five or six lǐ to the north is the Wind and Rain Pool,
said to be where the mountain is high and the rapids swift,
striking the trees,
scattering mist like rain.
To the west is Luán Ridge,
where Master Hóngyá rested after riding a simurgh.
West of the ridge is Hú Ridge,
said to be where Wángzǐ Qiáo passed while controlling a crane.
There are two cliffs,
called Dà Xiāo and Xiǎo Xiāo,
said to be where Xiāo Shǐ roamed and gathered.
Léi Cìzōng said:
These are tales of chasing wind and catching shadows,
with no basis in reality to discern,
but they are recorded here as curious hearsay,
to broaden the ears of the well fish.
Also, according to Xiè Zhuāng's poem,
Xiè Zhuāng once traveled to Yùzhāng,
viewed the well, and composed a poem,
saying that Luán Ridge is surrounded by water,
called Luán Slope,
which seems not to be an unfounded claim.
East of the great lake is ten lǐ, two hundred and twenty-six paces,
aligned with the city to the north,
winding southward to Nántáng.
Originally connected to the Zhāng River,
its water level rose and fell with the river.
During the Yǒngyuán era of the Hàn dynasty,
Grand Administrator Zhāng Gōng built an embankment to open a southern road,
while also damming this water,
so that it neither increased in summer nor decreased in winter.
The water was clear and deep,
and the fish were plump and delicious.
However, every summer,
when the river overflowed the embankment,
many homes were flooded.
In the first year of the Jǐngpíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Grand Administrator Cài Jūn built a dike to the west,
opening a sluice gate in the embankment.
When the water was high or during droughts, it was closed;
when there was excess water inside, it was released.
Since then, the residents have suffered less.
The Gàn River then flows northeast past Wáng Bù,
beside which is a city,
said to be where Sūn Fèn garrisoned as Prince of Qí,
now called Wáng Bù,
likely the landing of the Prince of Qí.
More than twenty lǐ southeast of the commandery is another city,
called Qíwáng City,
connected by a built road,
likely a detached palace.
The Gàn River then flows north past the office of the Left Captain of Nánchāng,
where during the reign of Emperor Chéng of the Western Hàn,
Méi Fú of Jiǔjiāng served as Captain of Nánchāng and lived here.
Later, Méi Fú suddenly left his wife and children and departed.
The *Jiǔjiāng Zhuàn* says he attained immortality.
The Gàn River then flows north past the west of Lóngshā.
The sand is very clean and white,
high and steep yet sloping,
with the shape of a dragon,
stretching continuously for five li.
According to old customs, on the ninth day of the ninth month,
people would ascend to the high places.
In the past, someone found an old tomb in this sand,
with an inscription carved on a brick that read:
"Seven and a half li west of the river,
divination by stalks says it is auspicious,
but divination by turtle shell says it is inauspicious."
Now this tomb is nearly submerged by water,
which is what is meant by "the stalks are short, the turtle is long."
The Gàn Shuǐ then passes by the foot of Jiāoqiū City,
which was built in the fourth year of the Jiàn'ān era
by Sūn Cè.
The Gàn Shuǐ also passes beneath the Diàogé Dǐgé,
where the Duōzhī Xiàowèi was stationed,
and which Táo Kǎn, the Grand Commandant, moved and established here.
In the past, during the summer months,
the islet in front of the Dǐgé would submerge,
and the shore would be far away.
In the first year of the Jǐngpíng era,
the Xiàowèi of Yùzhāng,
using the power of transport,
gathered stones to form an islet at the edge of the shallows,
over sixty zhàng in length,
capable of accommodating several dozen boats.
The Gàn Shuǐ then flows north past Póyáng County,
which was called Yùzhāng County during Wáng Mǎng's time.
The Yú Shuǐ flows into it,
originating east of Yúgān County,
which Wáng Mǎng named Zhìgān.
The Yú Shuǐ flows north to Póyáng County and empties into the Gàn Shuǐ.
