The Gàn Shuǐ also converges with the Pó Shuǐ,
which originates east of Póyáng County,
flows west past the south of the county,
which is Wǔyáng Township.
The area has gold mines,
and Wáng Mǎng renamed it Xiāngtíng.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era, Sūn Quán
divided it to form Póyáng Commandery.
The Pó Shuǐ then flows west and empties into the Gàn Shuǐ.
There is also the Liáo Shuǐ that flows into it,
originating from Jiànchāng County,
which was established in the second year of the Yǒngguāng era of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
by dividing Hǎihūn.
The Liáo Shuǐ flows east past Xīnwú County,
established during the Zhōngpíng era of Hàn.
The Liáo Shuǐ also passes by Hǎihūn County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Yíshēng,
and is called the Upper Liáo Shuǐ,
also known as the Hǎihūn Jiāng.
It divides into two streams,
with a pavilion at the eastern ferry of the county,
which is crucial for crossing.
One stream flows northeast past Chāngyì City and then east into the great river of Yùzhāng,
called the Kǎikǒu.
In the past, when the King of Chāngyì of Hàn was enfeoffed at Hǎihūn,
he would often gaze eastward along the flow,
and return filled with indignation.
Hence, the name was given by later generations.
The other branch flows separately,
emptying into the Xún Shuǐ.
It then flows north past the west of Péngzé County.
The Xún Shuǐ originates west of Ài County,
flows northeast past Yùníng County,
formerly known as Xī'ān,
and was renamed to its current name in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Jìn.
The Xún Shuǐ then flows northeast past Yǒngxún County,
established in the second year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn.
The Xún Shuǐ then flows northeast and empties into the Gàn Shuǐ,
which collectively receives ten rivers,
converging into one watercourse,
and all emptying into Pénglí.
It then flows north into the Jiāng.
South of the great river,
the Gàn Shuǐ gathers vast flows,
stretching forty li from east to west,
with clear, deep pools and distant swells,
green waves still and pure,
converging and flowing into the Jiāngchuān.
39.10 Lú Jiāng Shuǐ
39.10 Lú Jiāng Shuǐ
The Lú Jiāng Shuǐ originates from Sāntiānzǐ Dū,
flows north past the west of Péngzé County,
and enters the Jiāng to the north.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
Three Son of Heaven Capital,
also called Son of Heaven Barrier.
Wáng Biāozhī's "Rhapsody on Mount Lú" preface says:
Mount Lú,
is a mountain of Péngzé.
Although not counted among the Five Sacred Mountains,
lofty and towering,
it is truly a famous mountain of extreme height.
Sūn Fàng's "Rhapsody on Mount Lú" says:
South of Xúnyáng Commandery lies Mount Lú,
the guardian peak of the Jiǔjiāng region.
It overlooks the marsh of Pénglí,
and connects to the level, open plains.
The Chart of Opening Mountains says:
The mountain is square,
its circumference over four hundred lǐ,
with layered barrier cliffs ten thousand rèn high,
embracing spiritual wonders,
and containing traces of immortals.
The Old Records of Yùzhāng say:
Lú Sú,
styled Jūnxiào,
originally surnamed Kuāng,
his father, the Prince of Dōngyě,
together with Póyáng Magistrate Wú Ruì, assisted the Hàn in pacifying the realm and died.
The Hàn enfeoffed Sú at Qiāoyáng,
as the Lord of Yuèlú.
Sú had seven brothers,
all fond of Daoist arts,
so they lodged their essence in the mountains of Gōngtíng,
hence the world calls it Mount Lú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn toured south,
saw the mountain and considered it divine,
enfeoffing Sú as the Great Illumination Duke, the Distant Master.
The Record of Mount Lú says:
During the time between the Shāng and Zhōu,
Master Kuāng Sú received the Dao from an immortal,
and together they roamed this mountain.
People of the time called their dwelling the hut of divine immortals,
hence the mountain was named accordingly.
Also, according to Zhōu Jǐngshì:
Mount Lú:
Kuāng Sú,
styled Zǐxiào,
originally a descendant of Dōnglǐzǐ.
During the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
he was born with divine intelligence,
repeatedly evaded summons and appointments,
and dwelled in a hut on this mountain.
People of the time revered and served him.
Sú later became an immortal and transformed,
his empty hut still remained.
His disciples saw the chamber,
grieved and wept for him,
morning and evening their actions resembled the wūháo bird's cry.
The world called him Lord Lú,
hence the mountain took this name.
This is hearsay,
not verified fact.
Therefore, the Records of Yùzhāng takes Lú as a surname,
using the hut to form a clan name.
Master Zhōu (or: the distant master Zhōu),
perhaps used admiration for the hut as a pretext,
borrowing the hut to create a name.
These two proofs are contradictory,
the two accounts conflict with each other.
Considering The Classic of Mountains and Seas was created by the Great Yǔ,
its records are ancient indeed.
Therefore, the "Classic of Regions Within the Seas: Eastern Part" says:
The Lú River emerges from the Three Son of Heaven Capital,
and enters the river west of Péngzé.
This shows the name Lú River,
mountain and water interdependent,
each raising distinct names,
clearly did not originate with Kuāng Sú.
It is merely gentlemen fond of tales,
forcibly drawing such parallels,
to complete their writings.
Also, according to Zhāng Huá's Records of the Investigation of Things, Biography of Cáo Zhù:
The spirit himself said his surname was Xú,
was enfeoffed at Mount Lú.
Later, Wú Měng passed by,
the mountain spirit welcomed Měng.
Měng said:
"Your Majesty has been in this mountain for nearly six hundred years,
your mandate is already exhausted,
it is not fitting to dwell here long,
it is not rightfully held."
Měng also presented a poem, saying:
"Gazing up at the row of immortal lodges,
Looking down upon the divine king's abode.
Through vast ages, my secluded feelings flow freely,
Meeting by chance, I entrust myself to the three bonds of friendship."
These are matters of spirits and the Dao,
and there are also changes and transfers,
their principles are difficult to detail.
Wú Měng,
was a recluse in the mountains who attained the Dao.
The Record of Xúnyáng says:
On Mount Lú there are three stone bridges,
tens of zhàng long,
less than a chǐ wide,
profoundly bottomless.
Wú Měng led his disciples up the mountain,
crossed these bridges,
saw an old man sitting under a cassia tree,
who offered Měng sweet dew in a jade cup.
They reached another place,
saw several people prepare jade ointment for Měng.
Měng's disciple secretly took one treasure,
wishing to show it to the world.
The bridge immediately shrank to the size of a finger.
Měng made him return the treasure,
took his disciple by the hand,
told him to close his eyes and led him across.
Its mountains and rivers are bright and pure,
winds and marshes clear and vast,
the air refreshing, the seasons harmonious,
the soil fertile, the people at ease.
Noble recluses,
continued their echoes in cave cliffs;
virtuous men, hidden dragons and phoenix talents,
went there and forgot to return.
Qín Shǐhuáng, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, and the Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
all ascended its cliffs,
gazed upon the Jiǔjiāng and looked afar towards Zhōnglíng and Péngzé.
North of Mount Lú is the Shímén Water,
which emerges from the ridge's end.
There is a solitary rock standing tall,
its shape like a gate,
hence it has the name Shímén (Stone Gate).
The water flows between twin rocks,
a hanging stream, a flying waterfall,
for nearly three hundred paces or so,
below spreading out for over ten paces.
Looking up from below, it seems to reach the sky,
as if dragging a flying silk ribbon through the heavens.
Below is a flat rock,
where several dozen people can sit.
Champion General Liú Jìngxuān
often climbed and ascended here.
The water passes through the ravine,
flows south past the Lóngquán Monastery,
built during the Tàiyuán era
by the Buddhist monk Shì Huìyuǎn.
This water flows down into the southern ridge of the river,
which is the Son of Heaven Barrier west of Pénglí Marsh.
The peaks and ridges are perilous and steep,
rarely trodden by human feet.
South of the ridge is a great road,
following the mountain down,
as if painted.
Tradition says:
It is the road to the river opened by Master Kuāng.
On the cliffs are the old foundations of three palaces,
ascending in order,
the highest reaching the mountain peak.
Below the mountain is also a spirit temple,
called the Gōngtíng Temple,
hence Péng Lake also has the name Gōngtíng.
I note the Ěryǎ says:
A great mountain is called gōng (palace).
The name gōng (palace),
probably originated from this,
not necessarily from the three palaces.
The mountain temple is very potent,
able to divide winds and split currents,
halt boats and dispatch messengers.
Travelers
must respectfully offer sacrifices when passing,
before they can depart.
Therefore Cáo Pí chanted:
"Dividing the wind into two,
Splitting the current into pair."
Formerly, Zhāng Gōngzhí, Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery,
was returning from his post upon recall,
his route passed by Mount Lú.
His children went to view the temple.
A maidservant pointed at a statue, joking it resembled the daughter.
That night, his wife dreamed of receiving a marriage proposal,
terrified, they hastily departed.
At dawn, in midstream,
their boat would not move.
Everyone on board was frightened,
saying:
"Loving one daughter brings calamity upon the whole family."
Gōngzhí could not bear it,
so he ordered his wife to put their daughter into the river.
His wife spread a mat on the water,
and used her deceased brother's daughter as a substitute.
The boat then could proceed.
Only then did Gōngzhí realize it was his brother's daughter.
Angry with his wife, he said:
"What face do I have to face the world?"
He then put his own daughter into the water.
As they were about to cross,
they saw from afar two girls on the bank.
Beside them stood an official, who said:
"I am the Registrar of Lord Lú.
Out of respect for the sovereign's righteousness,
he returned both women in full.
Therefore, Gàn Bǎo recorded this in his work on divine responses.
In Shāndōng, there is a stone mirror,
which emerges from the waters it reflects.
There is a round stone,
hanging from a cliff, clear and bright,
reflecting human forms.
When the morning light first disperses,
its radiance extends into the stone,
capturing every detail,
hence it is named the stone mirror.
There are also two springs that perpetually cascade,
resembling white clouds girding the mountain.
The "Record of Lúshān" states:
Báishuǐ lies south of Huánglóng,
which is the waterfall.
The water emerges from the mountain's belly.
It cascades down three to four hundred zhàng,
rushing through the forest canopy,
appearing from afar like a suspended silk ribbon.
Where it plunges, it forms a massive well,
unfathomably deep.
Its waters flow down into the river's depths.
South of Lúshān, there is Shàngxiāo Stone,
a towering cliff stretching afar,
connecting with the heavens.
In the thirty-sixth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
marveling at this distant peak,
he thus recorded it as Shàngxiāo.
South of Shàngxiāo,
Dà Yǔ carved a stone to mark its dimensions and distances,
and to this day, the name "carved stone" remains.
In the lake, there is Luòxīng Stone,
with a circumference of over a hundred paces,
and a height of five zhàng.
Bamboos and trees grow atop it.
Tradition says:
a star fell here,
hence it was named accordingly.
There is also a solitary rock,
standing alone in the great lake,
with a circumference of one lǐ,
soaring a hundred zhàng high,
towering and steep,
exceptionally magnificent.
Trees and woods grow atop it,
yet few birds gather there.
It is said that jade ointment can be gathered from it,
though this remains unverified.
The elders say:
long ago, when Dà Yǔ controlled the floods and reached this place,
he carved a stone to record his achievements.
Some say it was inscribed by Qín Shǐhuáng,
but as the years have long passed,
it is impossible to ascertain the truth.
40 Commentary on the Waterways Classic, Volume 40
40.1 Jiànjiāng River
40.1 Jiànjiāng River
The Jiànjiāng River originates from Sāntiānzǐdū,
The Classic of Mountains and Seas refers to it as the Zhèjiāng River.
The Treatise on Geography states:
The water originates from the southern barbarian region of Yīxiàn County in Dānyáng,
flowing north past the county.
To the south is Mount Bó,
on which there is a rock
that rises abruptly to a height of ten zhang,
its peak resembling the tip of a sword.
At times, a mysterious drum sound emerges from within,
and when the local magistrate is in office,
he uses the mountain drum as an omen:
if it sounds once, the official’s term lasts one year;
if it roars like thunder,
then the official’s tenure will be inauspicious.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows north past Mount Yī,
where the county seat lies on the southern side of the mountain,
hence the county is named after it.
In the second year of the Hóngjiā era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
it was established as the State of Guǎngdé,
and Yúnkè, grandson of Prince Xiàn of Zhōngshān, was enfeoffed here as king.
During the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty, it was made Guǎngdé County,
and placed under the jurisdiction of Xuānchéng Commandery.
Chén Yè of Kuàijī,
who maintained a pure and upright conduct,
withdrew and lived in seclusion on this mountain.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows north past Shèxiàn County,
where it merges with a small stream to the east.
This stream originates from Mount Wēng northeast of the county,
flows west past the old city’s southern side,
and then turns southwest to join the Zhèjiāng River.
Further east, it passes south of Suì’ān County,
where the stream is two hundred paces wide.
A bridge was built above for passage,
and the water is exceptionally clear and deep.
The fish in the pools are not hidden from view,
hence it was named Xīndìng,
established by partitioning Shèxiàn County.
During the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
it was renamed to its present name.
The Zhèjiāng River then joins Jué Creek on the left,
which originates west of Shǐxīn County
and flows east past the old county seat’s southern side,
forming the East and West Long Streams.
The stream has forty-seven rapids,
with turbulent and swift currents
that roar and clamor toward the sky.
Sūn Quán sent Hè Qí to suppress the mountain bandits of Yī and Shè.
The bandits fortified themselves on Mount Línlì in Yī,
a place of extreme steepness and inaccessibility.
They were also skilled in using prohibitive charms against weapons.
Hè Qí used iron stakes to scale the mountain,
ascending unexpectedly,
and struck them with white clubs,
rendering their charms ineffective.
Thus, he achieved a remarkable victory in pacifying the bandits.
Thereafter, the administrative seat of Shǐxīn was established in Huáxiāng of Shè,
with Hè Qí appointed to guard it.
Later, it was moved to Xīntíng.
In the first year of the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
it was renamed Xīn’ān Commandery.
The creek flows east and empties into the Zhèjiāng River.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows northeast past the south of Jiàndé County.
North of the county is Mount Wū,
at the foot of which there is a temple.
The temple is located seven lǐ east of the county seat.
On the temple’s islet, there is a large rock,
ten zhang high
and five chǐ in circumference.
When the water rushes and churns against it,
it can induce clouds and rain.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows east past the south of Shòuchāng County.
From Jiàndé to here, a distance of eighty lǐ,
there are twelve rapids,
all steep and treacherous,
making travel difficult.
South of the county is the tomb of the filial son Xià Xiān.
Xià Xiān lost both parents at a young age,
carried earth to build their tomb,
and after years of unbearable grief,
he passed away.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows north past Xīnchéng County,
where the Tóng Creek flows into it.
This water originates from Mount Tiānmù north of Yúqián County in Wúxīng Commandery.
The mountain is extremely lofty and steep,
with towering cliffs and overlapping ridges.
To the west, it overlooks a deep ravine.
On the mountain grows frost-resistant timber,
all trees several hundred years old.
It is called Xiángfèng Forest.
On the eastern side, there is a waterfall
that cascades into a deep pool covering several mǔ,
named Huànlóng Pond.
The pond water flows south past the west of the county,
forming the county’s West Creek.
The creek then flows southeast and merges with Zǐ Creek,
which originates from Mount Bǎizhàng west of the county,
also known as Mount Qián.
The mountain water flows southeast,
and is named Zǐ Creek. Along its middle course, flanked by water,
there are purple rock formations,
over a hundred zhang in length,
appearing like morning clouds when viewed from afar.
This water is also called Chìlài,
likely due to the reflection of the purple rocks in the water.
Zǐ Creek then flows southeast past the perilous Mount Báishí.
The mountain is extremely steep,
bordering Zǐ Creek to the north.
Further southeast,
the mountains line the water on both sides,
with two peaks standing opposite each other,
their summits and rocks facing one another,
often appearing to contend.
For over ten lǐ,
heaps of stones lie piled,
rising layer upon layer.
Below the ravine, white sand and fine pebbles
resemble frost and snow.
Water and trees reflect each other,
springs and rocks vie in brilliance.
This place is named Lóulín.
Zǐ Creek flows southeast past the east of Tónglú County, becoming Tóng Creek.
Sūn Quán took the creek’s name to designate the county,
carving out territory from Fùchūn to establish Tónglú County.
From the county to Yúqián,
there are sixteen rapids in total.
The second is Yánlíng Lài,
which winds around the mountain.
At the foot of the mountain, there is a stone chamber,
where during the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Yán Zǐlíng resided.
Thus, both the mountain and the rapid are named after him.
At the foot of the mountain lies a flat rock,
several tens of zhang in circumference,
resting by the pool’s edge,
likely where Yán Zǐlíng once roamed.
Tóng Creek then flows northeast into Xīnchéng County and joins the Zhèjiāng River.
The county
was originally part of Fùchūn.
Sūn Quán established it,
but it was later abolished and merged into Tónglú.
In the ninth year of the Xiánhé era,
it was reinstated as a county.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows northeast into Fùyáng County,
formerly known as Fùchūn.
During the Jìn dynasty, to avoid the empress’s name “Chūn,”
it was renamed Fùyáng.
To the east, it divides into Húpǔ.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows northeast past the south of Fùchūn County.
The county
was formerly called Zhūsuì under Wáng Mǎng.
South of the river, there is a mountain
where the ancestors of Emperor Wǔ of Sūn were buried.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
a glow appeared above the tomb,
like clouds reaching the sky.
In the fifth year of the Huángwǔ era,
Sūn Quán made Fùchūn the Dōng’ān Commandery,
dividing it into several commanderies
to suppress Shì Zōng.
The Zhèjiāng River then flows northeast past the west of Mount Tíng,
on which lies the tomb of Sūn Quán’s father.
It then passes north of Yúháng,
and flows east into the sea.
Bǐng smiled but did not respond,
and the house remained undamaged.
On another occasion, when he sought to cross a river,
the boatman refused him passage.
Bǐng then opened a canopy and sat within it,
letting out a long whistle to summon the wind,
and crossed the turbulent current.
The common people, awestruck,
followed him as if returning home.
The magistrate of Zhāng'ān, despising him, had him killed.
The people erected a shrine for him in Yǒngníng,
and mosquitoes and gnats could not enter it.
Bǐng upheld the Way and possessed arts,
yet could not preserve his life and avoid harm.
His case resembles that of Chánghóng,
or the tortoise of Sòng Yuán—
when calamitous fate arrives,
it is indeed difficult to avert.
The Gǔ Shuǐ flows eastward into Qiántáng County,
and then turns left into the Zhè Jiāng.
Therefore, the *Geographical Treatise* states:
"The Gǔ Shuǐ flows from Tàimò northeast to Qiántáng and enters the Zhè Jiāng." This is correct.
The Zhè Jiāng flows east past Língyǐn Mountain.
The mountain lies amidst four surrounding peaks,
with high cliffs and caverns.
To its left and right are three stone chambers.
There is also a solitary rock standing like a wall,
thirty arm-spans in circumference,
its top splayed open,
shaped like a lotus flower.
In the past, a Daoist priest
went there and never returned.
Perhaps because of this, the mountain was named "Linger."
At the foot of the mountain lies the old county seat of Qiántáng.
The Zhè Jiāng flows past its south.
Wáng Mǎng renamed it Quántíng.
The *Geographical Treatise* states:
"It was the seat of the Western Commandant of Kuàijī."
The *Qiántáng Records* state:
"The great seawall is about one lǐ east of the county seat.
Huá Xìn, a Commandery Consultant, proposed building this seawall
to guard against the sea.
Initially, recruitment began: anyone who could deliver one hú of earth
would be given one thousand coins.
Within ten days to a month,
people came flocking like clouds.
Before the seawall was completed, they stopped paying.
Those transporting earth and stones
all abandoned their loads and left.
Thus, the seawall was completed.
Therefore, it was renamed Qiántáng (Money Pond)."
South of the county, by the river, lies Míngshèng Lake.
Elders pass down the tale
that a golden ox appears in the lake.
Seen in antiquity,
its divine transformations are unfathomable.
The lake derives its name from this.
The county has Wǔlín Mountain,
from which the Wǔlín River flows.
Kuàiyīn states:
"The mountain produces Qián Shuǐ,
which flows east into the sea."
The *Wúdì Jì* says
the county only has the Zhè Jiāng;
this water [Qián Shuǐ] no longer exists.
East of the county are mountains such as Dìng and Bāo,
all facing west towards the Zhè Jiāng.
The river flows between two mountains.
The river currents are swift and deep, combined with tidal bores.
The tide comes twice daily,
arriving precisely on time.
It is especially large during the new moon and full moon,
reaching its peak in the second and eighth months,
towering over two zhàng high.
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* attributes this to the spirits of Zǐxū and Wén Zhǒng.
In the past, Zǐxū was loyal to Wú,
yet his corpse floated on the river.
The people of Wú pitied him,
erecting a shrine by the river,
named Xū Mountain.
The *Wú Lù* states:
"Xū Mountain is by Tài Lake,
less than a hundred lǐ from the river,
hence 'by the river.'"
Wén Zhǒng was loyal to Yuè,
and fell on his sword at Shānyīn.
The people of Yuè mourned him,
burying him in Chóng Mountain.
One year after Wén Zhǒng's burial,
Zǐxū came from the sea, carried Zhǒng away,
and they roam the rivers and seas.
Therefore, the waves that surge ahead of the tide
are Wǔ Zǐxū;
the following heavy waters
are Grand Master Zhǒng.
Therefore, Méi Chéng said:
"The tides leave no record."
Yet when the seawater rises with the tide,
and the river water flows backward,
it seems divine but is not,
manifesting here.
In the thirty-seventh year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he intended to tour Kuàijī.
Arriving at Qiántáng,
he faced the Zhè Jiāng,
but could not cross.
Therefore, he took the western ford of Yúháng.
The Zhè Jiāng joins north with Zhàoxī Lake.
The lake was originally named Zuò Lake.
Because Qín Shǐhuáng rested here during his inspection tour,
it gained the name Zhàoxī (Imperial Rest).
The Zhè Shuǐ flows east and joins Línpíng Lake.
The *Yì Yuàn* states:
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the bank at Línpíng in Wú Commandery collapsed,
revealing a stone drum.
Striking it produced no sound.
They asked Zhāng Huá about it.
Huá said:
"Take tóng wood from Shǔ,
carve it into the shape of a fish and strike it; then it will sound."
They followed his advice,
and the sound could be heard for tens of lǐ.
Liú Dàomín's poem says:
"Things distant may yet combine;
Shǔ tóng makes Wú stone sing."
Tradition says when this lake is choked with weeds,
the realm falls into disorder;
when the lake clears,
the realm is at peace.
In the first year of the Tiānxǐ era of Sūn Hào,
Wú Commandery reported:
"Línpíng Lake has been silted since the end of Hàn,
but now it has cleared again."
Furthermore, a stone casket was found by the lake.
Inside the casket was a small stone,
bluish-white in color,
four cùn long,
two cùn wide,
with the characters for 'Emperor' carved upon it.
Therefore, the era name was changed from Tiāncè to Tiānxǐ.
Sūn Shèng considered this an omen of Yuánhuáng's restoration,
a sign of auspicious stone from the Five Lakes.
The *Qiántáng Records* state:
During the troubles of Huán Xuán,
the lake water turned red,
glowing like cinnabar.
The lake water connects upstream to Pǔyáng River,
and flows down into the Zhè Jiāng.
It is called the Dōng Jiāng,
a route for travelers
to exit into the Zhè Jiāng.
The Zhè Jiāng flows past the north of Gùlíng City.
In the past, Fàn Lǐ built a city on the banks of the Zhè Jiāng,
saying it could be firmly defended,
hence called Gùlíng (Firm Mound),
which is present-day Xīlíng.
The Zhè Jiāng flows east past Zhātáng,
called Zhā Dú.
In the past, Grand Administrator Wáng Lǎng resisted Sūn Cè.
After several battles proved unfavorable,
Sūn Jìng indeed advised Cè, saying:
"Lǎng relies on the defensive strength of the city;
it is difficult to capture quickly.
Zhā Dú is several tens of lǐ from here,
and is a vital route.
If we go out from there,
attacking where he is unprepared,
we will surely defeat him."
Cè followed this advice,
and defeated Lǎng at Gùlíng.
There is Xīlíng Lake,
also called Xīchéng Lake.
West of the lake is Húchéng Mountain,
east is Xiàjià Mountain.
The lake water receives Yāogāo Creek upstream,
and flows down into the Zhè Jiāng.
[The river] also flows past Shānyīn County of Kuàijī.
There is Kǔzhú Village,
within which lies an old city,
said to be the fief granted by Gōujiàn to Fàn Lǐ's son.
The Zhè Jiāng flows east and joins Lán Creek.
South of the lake is Tiānzhù Mountain.
At the mouth of the lake is a pavilion,
named Lán Pavilion,
also called Lánshàng Village.
Grand Administrators Wáng Xīzhī and Xiè Ān and his brothers
frequently visited there.
Wú Commandery Grand Administrator Xiè Xù was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lán Pavilion,
likely taking this pavilion as his title.
Grand Administrator Wáng Yìzhī moved the pavilion into the water.
When Jìn Minister of Works Hé Wújì arrived in the commandery,
he built a pavilion on the mountain peak,
extremely high, commanding a full view.
Though the pavilion structure is ruined,
its foundation and steps remain.
The Zhè Jiāng flows past the north of the tomb of Yuè King Yǔncháng.
The tomb is in Mùkè Village.
Elders and worthies say:
"Gōujiàn sent workmen to cut róng timber for shields..."
He intended to present it to Wú,
but after a long time could not return,
and the craftsmen, filled with sorrow and longing,
composed the "Song of the Woodcutter."
Later generations thus named the place after it.
Gōu Jiàn made Lángyé his capital,
and wished to move Yǔncháng's tomb.
A wind that splits arose from the tomb,
blowing sand that struck people,
so that none could approach.
Gōu Jiàn said it was unwilling,
and so he stopped.
The Zhè River further flows northeast to the mouth of Cháng Lake,
the lake being five lǐ wide,
and one hundred and thirty lǐ from east to west.
Sixty-nine water gates were opened along the lake,
irrigating ten thousand qǐng of fields below,
and discharging north into the Long River.
South of the lake is Fùdǒu Mountain,
with a circumference of five hundred lǐ,
connecting north to Gǔchuī Mountain.
West of the mountain lies against a long stream,
whose waters flow down into Cháng Lake.
On the western ridge of the mountain is Hè Terrace.
When the Yuè people went to Wú
and returned, they completed it,
hence it is called Hè Terrace.
There is also Qínwàng Mountain,
directly south of the prefectural city,
the most outstanding among the many peaks,
visible upon entering the region.
The Shǐjì states:
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended it
to gaze upon the Southern Sea.
From the flat ground to the mountain top is seven lǐ;
the hanging steps are isolated and perilous,
the path extremely dangerous.
A record says:
One must pull on vines and grasp creepers
before being able to ascend.
The mountain has no very tall trees,
likely due to the exposed terrain and frequent winds.
South of the mountain is Jiāoxiàn,
within which lies a great walled city,
the old capital of King Wúyú of Yuè.
Therefore, the Wú Yuè Chūnqiū states:
Gōu Jiàn said to Fàn Lǐ:
"Our former lord Wúyú
had his state on the southern side of the southern mountains,
with the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temple south of the lake."
There is also Kuàijī Mountain,
the ancient Fáng Mountain,
also called Máo Mountain,
and also Dòng Mountain.
The Yuè Jué states:
"Dòng means to guard or stabilize."
It is likely the "guardian mountain" of Yángzhōu mentioned in the Zhōulǐ.
The mountain is square in shape,
with much metal and jade on its top,
and much jué stone below.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
"The Xī River issues from it,
flowing south into the lake."
The Wú Yuè Chūnqiū says that within Fùfǔ Mountain there is a "Book of Golden Tablets and Jade Characters,"
a prophetic text left by the Yellow Emperor.
Below the mountain is a temple to Yǔ,
within which is an image of the Holy Maiden.
The Lǐ Yuè Wěi states:
After Yǔ completed controlling the floods,
Heaven bestowed upon him a divine maiden, the Holy Maiden;
this is her image.
On the mountain is Yǔ's tomb.
In the past, after Great Yǔ had been on the throne for ten years,
he made an eastern inspection tour,
died at Kuàijī,
and was buried there.
Birds came
to weed for him,
pulling up grass roots in spring
and pecking away the weeds in autumn.
Therefore, the local officials forbade the people from harming these birds without cause;
violators were punished without pardon.
East of the mountain is a sunken well,
seven lǐ from the temple,
so deep the bottom cannot be seen.
It is called Yǔ's Well,
and it is said that many who traveled east explored its cavern.
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended Kuàijī Mountain,
carved a stone to record his achievements,
which still remains beside the mountain.
Sūn Chàngzhī's Shù Shū states:
It was inscribed in seal script by Chancellor Lǐ Sī.
There is also Shíkuì Mountain,
whose rocks resemble a chest.
Upon it is the "Book of Golden Tablets and Jade Characters."
It is said that Xià Yǔ opened it
and obtained the principles for managing all the rivers.
There is also Shèdì Mountain.
From afar, the mountain's target
looks like an archery target,
hence it is called Shèdì (the Archery Target).
West of Shèdì is a stone chamber,
named the Archery Hall.
Whether the harvest would be good or bad
was often divined by observing Shèdì,
using it as a standard for predicting high or low prices.
If the target was bright, rice was cheap;
if the target was dark, rice was expensive.
Hence the proverb:
"When Shèdì is white,
a hú of rice costs a hundred;
when Shèdì is black,
a hú of rice costs a thousand."
To the north is Shífān Mountain.
Northeast of the mountain is a solitary rock,
over twenty zhàng high,
eight zhàng wide,
looking from afar like a sail,
hence the name.
It faces the great lake to the north,
of unfathomable depth,
said to connect with the sea.
When Hé Cìdào served as commandery administrator,
he often caught cuttlefish in these waters.
Facing south is a retreat,
shaded above by tall trees,
overlooking cold springs below,
connecting west to Kuàijī Mountain—
all part of the same mountain range.
To the east it is girded by Ruòyé Stream.
The Wú Yuè Chūnqiū says that Ōu Yě obtained copper when it dried up,
and used it to forge five swords.
The stream's upper waters receive the Má Stream from Jiāoxiàn.
Below the stream,
a solitary pool several mǔ in circumference,
is extremely clear and deep.
A solitary rock overlooks the pool;
standing on the cliff and looking down,
startles the heart like monkeys would,
with cold trees covering the pool,
creating a somber, awe-inspiring view.
Above is a chestnut tree.
Xiè Língyùn and his cousin Huìlián often roamed here,
composing linked verses,
which they inscribed beside the tree.
Má Pool flows down into Ruòyé Stream.
The water is so clear it mirrors,
with the reflections of the many mountains,
a view like a painting when peered into.
During the Hàn dynasty, Liú Chǒng served as commandery administrator;
he had administrative achievements.
When about to leave his post and depart the administration,
the elders of this stream,
each holding a hundred coins, came out to see him off.
Chǒng accepted one coin from each.
However, for recluses dwelling in the mountains
and untrammeled folk hidden in the valleys,
when the Way prevails they appear;
things are valued for their ability to stir feelings from afar.
Presenting coins to convey respect,
the recipient thus considers one coin an honor.
How could it depend on the amount spent?
It is because the principle is weighty.
The stream's waters flow down into the great lake.
East of Yé Stream
is also Hán Stream.
North of the stream is Zhènggōng Spring,
several zhàng square,
warm in winter and cool in summer.
Hàn Grand Commandant Zhèng Hóng once lodged by the pool's side,
hence the spring was named after him.
Hóng in his youth maintained a life of austerity,
constantly gathering firewood himself,
to trade for food and provisions.
Whenever he crossed the stream's ford,
he often felt a divine wind escorting him.
Though he relied on his boat to move himself,
he had no labor of poling or rowing.
Villagers, coveting the aid of the wind,
often followed him back and forth.
If someone tarried,
his companions would say to him,
"Do you not wish to catch Zhèng's wind?"
Such was the inspiration he evoked.
The lake waters from the east
also flow into the river connecting to the sea.
By the water's side is Báilù Mountain.
North of the mountain, on the lake's embankment, there formerly was a pavilion.
Wú Attendant Gentleman Yáng Āimíng lived in Hóngxùn Lane.
Grand Administrator Zhāng Jǐng often went to visit him,
and had a canal opened and a dam constructed.
West of the dam a pavilion was built;
both the pavilion and the dam were named Yáng.
Sūn Ēn rebelled,
coming from the sea.
The Yáng Pavilion was burned,
but later rebuilt,
and its name remains.
To the east is Tóngniú Mountain.
The mountain has a copper cave some thirty zhàng deep.
Within the cave there is a large tree shrine,
on the mountain there is a smelting official,
north of the mountain, below the lake, there is Liàntáng Village,
as recorded in the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū*:
it is the place where Gōujiàn smelted copper and tin.
Charcoal was gathered from the southern mountains,
hence there is a charcoal stream in that area.
Gōujiàn submitted to Wú,
and the King of Wú granted Gōujiàn a territory of one hundred lǐ in Yuè,
extending east to the charcoal stream.
Nine lǐ south of the county is Hóu Mountain,
a solitary mountain standing in the middle of the long lake.
Kǒng Jìngkāng, the Jin dynasty General of Chariots and Cavalry,
in his youth retreated from the world
and lived in seclusion on this mountain.
North of the lake there are three small hills,
called Lùyě Mountain,
located six lǐ south of the county.
According to the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū*,
it was the deer park of Yuè.
On the mountain there is a stone chamber,
said to be a place where the King of Yuè rested and roamed.
South of the county, north of the lake, is Chényīn Mountain.
There was a skilled archer from Chǔ named Chén Yīn,
and the King of Yuè inquired of him about the art of archery.
Pleased with his discourse,
he then had selected soldiers practice archery outside the northern suburbs.
According to the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū*,
when Yīn died,
he was buried on the mountain west of the capital.
Now Chényīn Mountain is located five lǐ south of the capital,
north of the lake there is an archery hall and various official residences,
connected and extending continuously,
and also a dike was built in the lake,
pointing directly toward the southern mountains.
To the north was the great state of Yuè,
which the Qín dynasty changed to Shānyīn County,
the seat of Kuàijī Commandery.
The Grand Historian said:
Yǔ assembled the feudal lords
and held council here,
naming it Kuàijī.
Kuàijī means
"accounting assembly."
Initially named after the mountain,
it later became the name of the place.
Shàokāng of the Xià dynasty enfeoffed his youngest son, Zhù, to uphold the sacrifices to Yǔ, establishing Yuè.
Through the generations of Yīn and Zhōu,
until Yǔncháng,
it was recorded in the *Chūnqiū*.
After Yǔncháng's death,
Gōujiàn proclaimed himself king,
establishing his capital at Kuàijī.
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* mentions that the capital of the King of Yuè was at Pízhōng,
located in the northern boundary of Zhūjì.
In Kānglè Village of Shānyīn, there is a place named Yìzhōng,
which was where Yuè served Wú.
Therefore, its gate faced north,
with the east as the right
and the west as the left.
Thus, the twin watchtowers were outside the north gate,
and one hundred paces north of the watchtowers was Léi Gate,
a two-story gate tower
built by Gōujiàn,
and at that time there were old timbers from Yuè.
The buildings of the commandery and county offices,
the large roof tiles,
were also mostly relics from the time of Yuè.
When Gōujiàn dominated the age,
he moved the capital to Lángyé,
but later, when attacked by Chǔ,
he returned east of the Zhè River.
Outside the eastern wall of the city is Língsì,
where the water is very deep.
Old traditions say there is an underground passage below,
connecting to Zhènzé.
There is also the ancestral temple established by Gōujiàn,
located south of Gānpāng in Míng Village east of the city.
There are also the Yùsì, Zhúlín, Yúnmén, and Tiānzhù monasteries,
all built on the mountains,
with structures raised among the forests,
channels cut to extend the streams,
fully capturing the beauty of springs and rocks,
with flowing water passing through.
The Zhè River also flows north past the west of Shānyīn County,
and over one hundred paces outside the west gate is Guài Mountain,
originally a mountain from Dōngwǔ County in Lángyé Commandery,
which flew here and settled,
crushing several hundred households.
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* calls it Guài Mountain,
a mountain from the sea off Dōngwǔ.
Also called Zìlái Mountain,
the people found it strange,
hence the name Guài Mountain.
It is also said that
when King Wújiāng of Yuè was attacked by Chǔ,
he left Lángyé
and stopped at Dōngwǔ,
with people settling at the foot of the mountain.
From afar, this mountain
resembles a turtle in shape,
hence it is also called Guī Mountain.
Yuè built a spiritual terrace on the mountain,
and also constructed a three-story tower to observe the clouds and scenery.
The land and rivers are bright and beautiful,
making it a scenic spot.
Thus, Wáng Yìshǎo said:
"Traveling on the Shānyīn road
is like walking in a mirror."
On the Zhè River,
there are also Dà Wúwáng and Xiǎo Wúwáng villages,
which were the encampments of Hélǘ and Fūchāi when they attacked Yuè.
Now they are all inhabited by common people,
but the old names still remain.
In the past, when the King of Yuè was defeated by Wú,
with over five thousand troops,
he took refuge on Kuàijī Mountain,
humbling himself and treating his men well,
ensuring benefits reached all below.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"When the King of Yuè took refuge at Kuàijī,
he had wine poured into the river,
and the people drank from the stream,
their fighting spirit doubling."
The place where it was poured
was the Zhè River.
Xǔ Shèn and Jìn Zhuó both stated:
"The river reaches Shānyīn and becomes the Zhè River."
On the west bank of the river is Zhūshì Wù,
the territory granted to Gōujiàn,
extending west to Zhūshì,
referring to this place.
The Zhè River also flows northeast past the west of Chóng Mountain,
where Minister Wén Zhǒng is buried.
On the mountain is Báilóu Pavilion,
originally located at the foot of the mountain,
but County Magistrate Yīn Lǎng moved it to its current location.
Huán Yǎn of Pèiguó
sought refuge in Kuàijī,
and hearing of Chén Yè's noble and pure conduct,
went to visit but did not see him.
Later, Huán Yǎn sailed across the sea
south to Jiāozhōu.
Before leaving,
he left a letter for Chén Yè,
tying it to a pillar of Báilóu Pavilion without sending a messenger, and departed.
Ascending and gazing afar,
the mountains and lakes fill the view.
During the Yǒngjiàn era,
Zhōu Jiā of Yángxiàn submitted a memorial,
stating that the county was too distant
and attending meetings was extremely difficult,
requesting a division and separate administration.
Thus, the area west of the Zhè River became Wú,
and the area east became Kuàijī.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
it was one Wú,
later divided into three,
known in the world as the Three Wú.
Wúxīng,
Wú Commandery,
and Kuàijī are among them.
The Zhè River also flows east past Yù'ér Township.
The *Wànshàn Lì* says:
"In the first month of the sixth year of the Huángwǔ era of Wú,
Péng Qǐ was captured.
That year,
in the western township of Yóuquán, a child was born who could speak immediately upon falling to the ground,
saying:
'The sky is about to brighten,
the river will become clear,
the tripod's legs will break,
and gold will be born.'
Because of this, it was decreed to be called Yù'ér Township."
This is incorrect; the name Yù'ér is ancient.
It is merely that ignorant people,
relying on the place name,
fabricated stories through forced interpretations.
The *Guóyǔ* says:
"The territory of Gōujiàn
extended north to Yù'ér."
How can one cite the Huángwǔ era to verify the place name?
Wéi Zhāo said:
"The northern border of Yuè was at Jiāxīng."
The Zhè River also flows east past the south of Cháipì,
an old battlefield between Wú and Chǔ.
Defenses were stationed here,
hence it was called Pìsāi.
Therefore, the *Yuè Jué* states:
"In the past, Wú crossed from Yóuquán and Pìsāi to Kuàijī,
converging at Shānyīn."
It also flows past the north of Yǒngxīng County,
which is located one hundred twenty lǐ northeast of Kuàijī,
formerly Yújì County.
Yìng Shào said:
"It was the fief of Fūgài, younger brother of Hélǘ,
and called Yúyǎn by Wáng Mǎng."
A late Hàn dynasty children's rhyme said:
"The Son of Heaven shall rise between the three Yú in the southeast."
Therefore, Sūn Quán changed its name to Yǒngxīng.
The county borders the Zhèjiāng River,
and further east it joins the Pǔyáng River.
The river's source flows from Wūshāng County,
passes east through Zhūjì County,
and merges with the Xiè Creek.
The creek is several zhàng wide,
with two high mountains flanking it along its middle course,
their cloud-reaching cliffs standing sheer,
forming altogether five cascades.
The lowest cascade hangs over thirty zhàng,
ten zhàng wide;
the middle three cascades are inaccessible,
but by climbing the mountain and gazing from afar,
one can see them,
hanging over a hundred zhàng,
the water's force high and swift,
its roar shaking the air beyond the stream;
the uppermost cascade hangs over two hundred zhàng,
appearing from a distance like a cloud descending.
These are waterfalls,
which the locals call "xiè."
The river flows further east past the south of Zhūjì County,
the county facing the river's flow,
with an archery hall south of the river.
The county is backed by Wū Mountain to the north,
hence it is ancient Yuè territory,
formerly called Upper Zhūjì,
also known as Gōuwú.
Thus the *Guóyǔ* states:
The territory of Gōujiàn
extended south to Gōuwú.
It was called Shūlǔ under Wáng Mǎng.
The riverbanks have many inlets,
within which lies a great lake,
full of water in spring and summer,
shallow and drying in autumn and winter.
The river flows southeast past Shàn County, where it meets the water emerging from Báishí Mountain.
On the mountain is a waterfall,
with a hanging drop of thirty zhàng,
which pours down into the Pǔyáng River.
The Pǔyáng River flows east, then bends south,
then turns east and curves north,
passing east of Shàn County,
called Jìnzhōng under Wáng Mǎng.
The county opens its east gate toward the river,
the river over two hundred paces wide.
According to elders' tales since ancient times,
the county must not open its south gate;
opening the south gate would bring bandits and thieves.
The river flows past the county, curving around it,
hence there are eastern and western ferries.
The southern and eastern ferries lead to Línhǎi,
using single boats as floating crossings.
The western ferry leads to Dōngyáng,
with twenty-five boats joined to form a pontoon bridge.
By the river is Zhā Pǔ,
east of the inlet, traveling over two hundred lǐ,
it borders Gōuzhāng.
Within the inlet is an area of six lǐ,
with five hundred households,
all living along the inlet's banks,
their doors facing the water,
with very fertile fields.
There are Qīng Creek, Yúhóng Creek, Dàfā Creek, and Xiǎofā Creek.
On the river are six creeks,
the creeks' waters spreading out for irrigation before entering the river.
Along the creeks upstream and down,
crumbling cliffs seem to lean over.
To the east is Diàn Mountain,
to the south is Huáng Mountain,
and with Báishí Mountain, these three mountains
are the county's splendid peaks.
Below the mountains, numerous springs flow,
rushing over rocks, stirring waves,
cascading perilously in all directions.
The Pǔyáng River flows further east past a stone bridge,
eight zhàng wide,
four zhàng high.
Below is a stone well,
its mouth seven chǐ in diameter.
On the bridge is a square stone,
seven chǐ long,
one zhàng two chǐ wide.
At the bridgehead is a large flat stone,
capable of seating twenty people.
Both sides of the creek are entirely high mountains,
with stone cliffs some twenty zhàng high.
The waters clash within the creek,
their roaring echoes issuing outward,
audible several lǐ before reaching the bridge.
The river flows north past Shèng Mountain,
at the mountain's foot is a pavilion,
the pavilion backed by the mountain and facing the river,
with pine-covered ridges lush and dense,
and sandy islets calm and still.
The Pǔyáng River flows northeast past Chénggōng Ridge of Tū Mountain in Shǐníng County.
The ridge stands sheer, facing the river,
its steep path narrow and precipitous,
not allowing two to walk abreast.
Travelers pull themselves along by trees, advancing slowly,
not daring to look down.
West of the ridge is a mountain,
a solitary peak rising uniquely,
where birds rarely reach.
Once, herb gatherers,
following the mountain, saw a creek leading through,
and climbing up to the mountaintop,
found under a tree twelve square stones,
the ground very smooth and clean.
But when they tried to find it again,
they lost the former path.
It is said to be where various immortals rest and feast,
hence the mountain is named Tányàn.
North of the ridge is Tū Inlet,
at the inlet's mouth is a temple,
very efficacious.
Travelers and woodcutters
all pay respects there first;
if anyone trespasses or steals,
they are sure to be harmed by snakes or tigers.
To the north is Tū Mountain,
connecting with Shèng Mountain.
Though the two mountains are in different counties,
their ridges and peaks are linked.
Between them, deep ravines hold mist,
springs and creeks draw in fog,
breezes over fields carry fragrance,
touching the mountain caves, prolonging delight.
Therefore, Wáng Yuánlín called it a divine and enlightened realm,
as recorded in Xiè Kānglè's *Shān Jū Jì*.
The Pǔyáng River flows northeast from Tū Mountain past Tàikāng Lake,
the location of the estate of Chējì General Xiè Xuán.
To the right it borders the Long River,
to the left it leans against connected mountains,
with level ridges extending smoothly,
and the clear lake mirroring the distance.
By a river bend a tower was built,
beside the tower are all paulownia and catalpa trees,
towering and lush, delightful.
The residents call it the Paulownia Pavilion Tower.
The tower faces the river on two sides,
offering all the pleasures of ascending to gaze afar.
Reed gatherers and fishermen
float and fill the area.
A road was built across the lake,
leading from the eastern hill to the mountain,
the road very straight and level.
In the mountains are three retreats,
their high ridgepoles reaching into the void,
their hanging eaves touching the sky,
looking down upon level woods,
with misty depths below.
Water and land are peaceful and tranquil,
truly a place to retreat from the world.
On the river is Pípá Qí,
at the bend an ancient tomb fell into the water.
On a brick were characters in relief, saying:
"Divined auspicious, turtle omened ill,
after eight hundred years falls into the river."
Xiè Língyùn took the brick to the capital,
where all passed it around to see.
It matched the turtle-shell prophecy,
thus they knew the tomb was already eight hundred years old.
The Pǔyáng River flows further northeast past the west of Shǐníng County,
originally the southern district of Shàngyú.
In the fourth year of the Yǒngjiàn era of Hàn Emperor Shùn,
Zhōu Jiā of Yángxiàn submitted a memorial,
and it was first separated from the old administrative seat.
West of the water, there were often troubles from tides and waves.
At the beginning of the Jìn restoration,
the seat was moved to the present location.
Below the county is a small river,
its source emerging from [unknown] Mountain,
called [unknown] Inlet.
It passes below the county, flowing west to pour
into this inlet at Máo Mountain below Pǔyáng.
The inlet connects west to Shānyīn Inlet and reaches the river.
The river is a hundred zhàng wide,
narrowest at two hundred paces.
High mountains flank the river,
with dense shade covering the water.
On the river, fishermen and merchants gather,
on the streams, woodcutters and recluses cross paths.
Hence, with cassia oars and orchid rudders,
they vie for passage, gazing at the scenery.
South of the river is an old walled city,
built by Grand Marshal Liú Láozhī when he campaigned against Sūn Ēn.
The river flows east past the south of Shàngyú County,
called Kuàijī under Wáng Mǎng.
Originally the seat of the Director of Salt,
the place was called Yúbīn.
The Jìn *Tàikāng Dìjì* states:
Shùn avoided Dānzhū here,
hence the county's name.
The hundred officials followed him,
therefore north of the county is the Hundred Officials Bridge.
It is also said that after Yǔ finished meeting with the feudal lords on business,
they enjoyed music together here,
hence the name Shàngyú.
The two accounts differ,
and it is unclear which is correct.
To the south of the county lies Lánfēng Mountain,
which has few trees and many rocks.
The post road winds along the mountain,
and by the riverside path,
railings have been constructed all along.
The mountain has three ridges,
resting against the Long River,
towering in solitary peril,
appearing as if they might topple over.
The path along the mountain
overlooks a great river below,
and flying pavilions with railings have been built,
allowing travelers to cross by means of them.
These three ridges are called the Three Stone Heads.
Gě Hóng of Dānyáng
withdrew from the world and lived here;
the foundations and well remain.
Wáng Fāngpíng of Lángyá,
who loved mountains and rivers by nature,
also made his home at Lánfēng,
angling here,
passing the entire day.
Travelers passing by did not recognize him
and asked:
"Master Fish-seller, have you caught any fish to sell?"
Fāngpíng replied:
"I have not caught any,
and even if I did, I would not sell them."
This water is also called the Shàngyú River.
Outside the eastern wall of the county lies Yúpǔ,
where in the lake there are two mountains, Dàdú and Xiǎodú,
and also Fùzhōu Mountain.
Below Fùzhōu Mountain is the Yúpǔ King Temple,
which has now been moved into Lǐshān.
These three mountains stand isolated in the water.
Beyond the lake are Qīngshān, Huángshān, and Zélán Mountain,
with layered peaks and overlapping ridges,
rising unevenly into the clouds.
At the summit of Zélán Mountain is a deep pool;
the mountain's shadow falls upon the water,
and the water's color is bluish-green.
Within the mountains are several valleys,
and there is a stone weir,
with Báimǎ Tán to the right,
a pool of unfathomable depth.
It is said:
When the lake was first created,
the embankments repeatedly collapsed.
The people offered a white horse in sacrifice,
and thus the water was named.
To the south of the lake is the river crossing.
South of the river are the two villages of Shàngtáng and Yángzhōng,
separated by the lake to the south,
and often suffering from floods.
The prefect Kǒng Língfú dammed the lake in front of Fēng Mountain to create a dike,
and below the dike opened a channel
leading directly to Nánjīn.
He also built two water weirs for diversion,
so that this river would no longer suffer from flooding.
To the east of the county is Lóngtóu Mountain,
and within its cliffs
is a stone well,
with clear, cold spring water in both winter and summer.
To the south it borders the Long River,
and to the east it connects to Shàngbēi.
South of the river road
stands the Cáo É Stele.
É's father, Xū,
drowned while greeting the tidal bore.
É was fourteen years old at the time.
Grieving that her father's body could not be found,
she wailed and leaped along the riverbank,
then removed her clothing and threw herself into the water,
praying:
"If I encounter my father's body,
the clothing will sink;
if I do not,
the clothing will float."
As soon as it fell, it sank,
and É then threw herself into the water at that spot and died.
The county magistrate Dù Shàng
had his nephew Hándān Zǐlǐ compose the stele text
to honor her filial devotion and martyrdom.
By the riverbank is Mǎmù Mountain.
When the great tide rises,
the waves conceal this mountain,
submerging Shèng Tíng,
and affecting several counties in between,
making travel difficult.
To the northeast of the county is also the tomb of the filial son Yáng Wēi's mother.
Wēi lost his father when young
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
Once, while gathering firewood in the mountains with his mother,
they were threatened by a tiger.
Knowing he could not defend against it,
he embraced his mother
and, crying out, walked on.
The tiger, seeing his devotion,
lowered its ears and left.
If not for sincerity penetrating the subtle,
who could move a fierce beast with principle?
There is also the Wú Channel,
which cuts through the mountains at its source
and flows into the Xū River.
The Shàngyú River flows east past Zhōushì and into Yǒngxīng.
The *Geographical Records* states:
"The county has Qiú Tíng,
and the Kē River flows east into the sea."
Qiú Tíng is located ten *lǐ* northeast of the county.
The Kē River north of the river
is likely the same as this river.
Further northeast, it passes east of Yǒngxīng County
and merges with the Zhè River,
where it is called the Pǔyáng River.
The *Geographical Records* also states:
"The county has Xiāo Mountain,
source of the Pān River,
which flows east into the sea."
This is also suspected to be another name for the Pǔyáng River,
as there is no other watercourse that corresponds to it.
The Zhè River further flows east into the sea,
hence the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says:
"The Zhè River enters the sea northwest of Mǐn."
Wěi Zhāo regarded the Sōng River, Zhè River, and Pǔyáng River as the Three Rivers.
40.2 Jīn River
40.2 Jīn River
The Jīn River originates in Lóngbiān County of Jiāozhǐ,
flows northeast to Lǐngfāng County of Yùlín,
and empties east into the Yù River.
The *Geographical Records* states:
"It passes Línchén County
and reaches Lǐngfāng County, where it empties into the Yù River."
40.3 Twenty Rivers South of the River to Rìnán Commandery
40.3 Twenty Rivers South of the River to Rìnán Commandery
Róngróng,
Yè,
Zhàn,
Chéng,
Niúzhǔ,
Xūwú,
Wúrú,
Yíngjìn,
Huángwú,
Dìlíng,
Qīnlí,
The Qīnlí River originates in Jìnxīng Commandery of Guǎngzhōu,
which was established during the Tàikāng era by partitioning Yùlín,
and flows east to Línchén, where it enters the Yù River.
Wúhuì,
Chónglài,
Fūshěng,
Wúbiàn,
Yóupú,
Wángdū,
Róng,
Yǒngwài,
All these originate west of Rìnán Commandery
and flow east into the sea.
The Róngróng River is at the southern border,
and the names follow in order northward.
These twenty rivers
are located south of the river to Rìnán Commandery.
40.4 Locations of Mountains, Rivers, and Marshes in the *Tribute of Yu*
40.4 Locations of Mountains, Rivers, and Marshes in the *Tribute of Yu*
Sōnggāo is the Central Peak,
located northwest of Yángchéng County in Yǐngchuān.
The *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* says:
"Yin contains yang,
hence stones congeal to form mountains."
The *Discourses of the States* says:
"Yu divided the nine mountains."
Mountains
are accumulations of earth.
The *Erya* says:
"A mountain that is large and high is called sōng."
Combined, it is called Sōnggāo;
divided and named, it has two chambers:
to the southwest is Shǎoshì,
and to the northeast is Tàishì.
The *Records of Sōnggāo Mountain* says:
"Within the cliffs at the foot of the mountain is a stone chamber,
said to contain natural scriptures
and natural provisions."
It also says:
"The mountain has a Jade Maiden Terrace,
named because Emperor Wǔ of Hàn saw it,
and thus named the terrace."
Mount Tài is the Eastern Peak,
located northwest of Bó County in Tàishān,
and is known as Dàizōng.
Kings performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices on this mountain,
to demonstrate its elevated status.
There were ceremonies involving golden tablets and jade cases.
Mount Huò is the Southern Peak,
southwest of Qián County in Lújiāng,
and is known as Tiānzhù Mountain.
The Ěryǎ states:
"A large mountain encloses,
a small mountain is called Huò."
The Kāishān Tú says:
"Its summit intrudes upon the divine ether,
its base secures the deep springs."
Mount Huá is the Western Peak,
southwest of Huáyīn County in Hóngnóng,
and is the Dūnwù Mountain of ancient texts.
Mount Léishǒu is southeast of Púbǎn County in Hédōng,
Mount Dǐzhù is in the middle of the river east of Dàyáng County in Hédōng,
and Mount Wángwū is northeast of Yuán County in Hédōng.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor received the elixir formula on this mountain.
Mount Tàiháng is northwest of Yěwáng County in Hénèi,
where Wáng Liè obtained the stone marrow.
Mount Héng is the Northern Peak,
northwest of Shàngqūyáng County in Zhōngshān,
and Mount Jiéshí is in the water south of Línyú County in Liáoxī.
Great Yǔ split its rocks,
channeling the river to the right.
Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì both ascended it.
The sea waters encroached westward,
increasingly over the years,
enveloping the mountain.
Hence it is said to be in the water.
Mount Xīchéng is southwest of Huòzé County in Hédōng,
Mount Tàiyuè is in Yǒng'ān County in Hédōng,
Mount Húkǒu is southeast of Běiqū County in Hédōng,
Mount Lóngmén is west of Píshì County in Hédōng,
Mount Liáng is on the river northwest of Xiàyáng County in Féngyì,
Mount Jīng is south of Huáidé County in Féngyì,
Mount Qí is northwest of Měiyáng County in Fúfēng,
and Mount Qiān is west of Qiān County in Fúfēng.
Mount Lǒng, Mount Zhōngnán, and Mount Dūnwù
are southwest of Wǔgōng County in Fúfēng.
Mount Xīqǐng is southwest of Líntáo County in Lǒngxī,
the Middle Range Mountain mentioned in the Yǔ Gòng.
Mount Bōzhǒng is south of Dīdào County in Lǒngxī,
the Southern Range Mountain.
Mount Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué is southwest of Shǒuyáng County in Lǒngxī.
Zhèng Xuán said:
"On Mount Niǎoshǔ,
there is a bird
that flies and dwells with a rat.
There is also a mountain where they stop and share a burrow,
these are two mountains.
The bird is called tú,
resembling a duō but yellow-black in color.
The rat is like a house rat but with a short tail.
They dig burrows and dwell together,
the rat inside and the bird outside."
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"They form a pair, male and female."
Dù Yàndá said:
"They share a burrow for lodging,
raising their young by feeding each other,
and stop when grown."
Zhāng Yàn said,
"They do not mate,
hence the mountain is named accordingly."
Mount Jīshí is southwest of Héquān County in Lǒngxī,
the Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"The mountain is east of Dènglín,
where the river enters."
Lake Dūyě is northeast of Wǔwēi County,
the county is three hundred lǐ north of Gūzāng City,
and northeast is Lake Xiūtú.
Ancient texts refer to it as Zhūyě.
Its waters originate from Lake Wǔshǐ in Gūzāng,
the lake has two sources,
flowing northeast as one stream,
passing west of the old city of Gūzāng County,
flowing northeast,
with the Língyuān Pool beside the water.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
"In the late Hàn,
the erudite Hóu Jǐn from Dūnhuáng, skilled in esoteric studies,
told his disciples:
'The spring west of Liángzhōu City will dry up,
and twin towers will rise above it.'
During the Jiāpíng era of Wèi,
Tiáo Mào, Governor of Wǔwēi, established a school,
building towers at this spring.
The governor filled the water,
constructed a gate tower,
facing the school towers.
The spring source shifted and emerged again,
redirected here,
hence the name Língyuān (Divine Abyss)."
The lake water flows northeast past east of Mǎchéng,
the city is the old site of Xiūtú County,
originally the capital of the Xiūtú King of the Xiōngnú,
called the Mǎchéng River.
It flows northeast and joins the Héngshuǐ,
which emerges below Gūzāng City,
in Wǔwēi Commandery,
the seat of Liángzhōu.
The Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì states:
"In the third year of Yuánshuò of Hàn Wǔdì,
Yōng was renamed Liángzhōu,
because its land corresponds to the metal phase,
hence cold and cool."
It moved to Jì,
and Jìn relocated the seat here.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
"Liángzhōu has a dragon shape,
hence called Wòlóngchéng (Reclining Dragon City),
seven lǐ north-south,
three lǐ east-west,
originally built by the Xiōngnú."
During the Zhāng family's residence,
four additional city walls were built, each a thousand paces.
The east city cultivated gardens and orchards,
named Jiǎngwǔchǎng (Military Training Ground),
the north city cultivated gardens and orchards,
named Xuánwǔpǔ (Black Tortoise Garden),
all with palaces.
The central city had seasonal palaces,
for touring according to the seasons.
Together with the old city, they made five,
with interconnected streets,
twenty-two gates,
extensively renovating palaces, towers, and pavilions,
decorated with colorful silks,
emulating the Central Plains."
The water flows north along the city,
entering the Mǎchéng River.
The river flows northeast,
joined by the Qīngjiànshuǐ,
commonly called Wǔjiànshuǐ (Five Ravines Water).
It emerges east of Gūzāng City,
flowing northwest into the Mǎchéng River.
The river also joins the Chángquánshuǐ,
which emerges from Xūcì County east of Gūzāng,
called Bōdé under Wáng Mǎng.
It flows northwest past Huángshāfù,
then northeast into the Mǎchéng River.
It flows northeast past the old city of Xuānwēi County,
then northeast past east of Píngzé and Yànrán stations,
then northeast past east of the old city of Wǔwēi County.
In the fourth year of Tàichū of Hàn Wǔdì,
the Xiōngnú Húnyé King killed the Xiūtú King,
settling his followers as Wǔwēi County,
the seat of Wǔwēi Commandery,
renamed Zhāngyè by Wáng Mǎng.
The Dìlǐzhì states:
"The Gǔshuǐ emerges from the southern mountains of Gūzāng,
flowing north to Wǔwēi and entering the sea."
Here the water divides into two branches:
one flows north into Lake Xiūtú,
commonly called the Western Sea;
the other flows east for one hundred fifty lǐ,
entering Zhūyě,
called the Eastern Sea.
Collectively, they are called Dūyě.
Mount Hélí is northeast of Huìshuǐ County in Jiǔquán,
also called Mount Hélí.
The Liúshā Desert is northeast of Jūyán County in Zhāngyè.
The Jūyán Marsh lies northeast of the old city of the county,
which is what the *Book of Documents* refers to as the Flowing Sands.
Its shape resembles a five-day-old moon.
The Ruò River flows into the Flowing Sands,
which are called Flowing Sands
because sand and water move together there.
It is also said to originate from Zhōngshān,
flowing westward to the extreme Yānzī Mountains,
located north of the Xīhǎi Commandery.
The mountains have red and white stones,
and if two stones are struck together,
they become moist.
If struck continuously,
once the moisture is exhausted, fire emerges,
and all the mountain stones are like this.
The flames rise several zhang high,
lasting all day without extinguishing.
A great black wind
from the Flowing Sands Mountains suddenly covers them, and only then do they extinguish,
with the stones returning to their original state.
Speaking of the matter of stirring fire,
it can trigger illnesses lasting years,
so people dare not approach it lightly.
The Flowing Sands also pass by Fúzhǔ,
traverse the Hèshì Kingdom,
pass east of the Niǎoshān Mountains,
west of the Zhāoyún Kingdom,
travel southwest of the Kūnshān Mountains,
and emerge at the Guòyíng Mountains.
The *Classic of the Great Wilderness: West* states:
Beyond the southwestern sea,
the Flowing Sands emerge there,
passing east of Xiàhòu Kāi.
Kāi presented three female attendants to Heaven,
and obtained the *Nine Arguments* and the *Nine Songs* there.
They also pass west of the Yuánqiū Immortality Mountain,
and enter the Southern Sea.
The Sānwēi Mountains are south of Dūnhúang County.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says:
On the Sānwēi Mountains,
three blue birds dwell.
These mountains
span a hundred lǐ in breadth and circumference,
located west of the Niǎoshǔ Mountains,
which is what the *Book of Documents* refers to as "banishing the Sānmiáo to Sānwēi."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
The treacherous Yǔnxìng clan
dwelled in Guāzhōu.
Guāzhōu
is a place name.
Dù Lín said:
Dūnhúang
is ancient Guāzhōu.
The tribute goods of the province
included fine melons produced locally,
and the people took their name from this.
The Róng of Guāzhōu
were later annexed by the Yuèzhī.
In the sixth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was separated from Jiǔquán and established.
Seven lǐ to the south is the Míngshā Mountain,
hence it is also called Shāzhōu.
The Zhūyǔ Mountain is north of Tiānshuǐ and south of Jìchéng,
which is the mountain of Jì County.
There is a stone drum there,
and the *Kāishān Tú* calls it the Tiāngǔ Mountain.
When calamities arise in the Nine Provinces, it sounds,
with constant responses.
It is also said:
The Shígǔ Mountain has a stone drum,
corresponding to the star Hé Gǔ.
When the star moves, the stone drum sounds,
and when the stone drum sounds, the land of Qín faces disaster.
If the sound is shallow, it brings calamity to all things;
if deep, it brings calamity to the ruler.
The Mín Mountain is west of Jiāndīdào in Shǔ Commandery,
which the *Book of Hàn* identifies as the Dú Mountain.
The Xióng'ěr Mountain is east of Lúshì County in Hóngnóng,
and from this mountain,
the Gǔ River emerges from its northern forest.
The Jīng Mountain is northeast of Línjū County in Nán Commandery,
part of the eastern range.
Biàn Hé obtained the uncut jade in this mountain,
but the King of Chǔ did not have it worked.
Clutching the jade, he wept beneath the mountain.
Later, the king had a jade worker polish it,
resulting in what is called Hé's Jade.
The Nèifāng Mountain is northeast of Jìnglíng County in Jiāngxià,
noted in the *Tribute of Yǔ*,
as Zhāng Mountain.
The Dàbié Mountain is southwest of Ānfēng County in Lújiāng,
while the Wàifāng Mountain
is Sōnggāo.
The Tóngbǎi Mountain is southeast of Píngshì County in Nányáng.
The Péiwěi Mountain is northeast of Ānlù County in Jiāngxià.
The Héng Mountain is south of Xiāngnán County in Chángshā.
When Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he sacrificed a horse by blood at Héng Mountain,
and there obtained the *Book of Golden Slips and Jade Characters*.
Upon examining the jade characters,
he grasped the principles of water management.
The Jiǔjiāng region is northwest of Xiàxī County in Chángshā,
the Yúnmèng Marsh is east of Huáróng County in Nán Commandery,
the Dōnglíng region is northwest of Jīnlán County in Lújiāng,
and the Fūqiǎnyuán region is west of Lìlíng County in Yùzhāng.
The Pénglí Marsh is northwest of Péngzé County in Yùzhāng,
which is what the *Book of Documents* refers to as "Pénglí already dammed,
where the yang birds dwell."
The Zhōng River is southwest of Wúhú County in Dānyáng,
flowing east to enter the sea at Yángxiàn County in Kuàijī.
The Zhèn Marsh is fifty lǐ south of Wú County,
the Běi River is at the northern border of Pílíng,
flowing east into the sea.
The Yìyáng Mountain is west of Xiàpī County,
and the Yǔ Mountain is south of Zhùqí County in Dōnghǎi.
The county
is what Wáng Mǎng called Yóutíng.
The *Book of Documents*
says, "executed Gǔn at Yǔ Mountain,"
referring to this mountain.
West of the mountain is the Yǔ Abyss,
where Yǔ's father transformed,
his spirit becoming a yellow bear,
and entered the abyss.
Thus, the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"The floodwaters reached the heavens,
Gǔn stole the Emperor's swelling earth to dam the waters,
without awaiting the Emperor's command.
The Emperor ordered Zhùróng to kill Gǔn in the Yǔ suburbs."
Táoqiū is southwest of Dìngtáo County in Jìyīn,
and Táoqiū
is a double-layered mound.
The Hē Marsh is east of Dìngtáo County,
and the Léi Marsh is northwest of Chéngyáng County in Jìyīn.
The Hē River is south of Húlù County in Shānyáng,
the Méng Mountain is southwest of Méngyīn County in Tàishān,
the Dàyě Marsh is northeast of Jùyě County in Shānyáng,
and the Dàpī region is north of Chénggāo County in Hénán.
The *Erya* says:
"A single-layered mountain is called pī,"
thus Dàpī is a mountain name,
not a place name.
The Míngdū Marsh is northeast of Suīyáng County in Liáng Commandery,
the Yìzhōu Tuó River is southwest of Wènjiāng County in Shǔ Commandery,
and another is southwest of Pí County,
both returning to enter the Jiāng River.
In Jīngzhōu,
the Tuó River is in Zhījiāng County in Nán Commandery,
and the Sānshì region is north of the Tuó in Qǐ County in Nán Commandery.
The *Shangshu* says:
Guide the Hàn River,
passing the Three Shì.
The *Dì Shuō* says:
The Miǎn River flows east,
passing the Three Shì where they converge,
and strikes the slopes of the Dàbié Mountains.
Thus, Mǎ Róng, Zhèng Xuán, Wáng Sù, Kǒng Ānguó, and others
all considered the Three Shì to be the name of a river.
Xǔ Shèn stated
that "shì"
refers to an embankment added along the water's edge,
where local people dwell.
According to the *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*, in the sixteenth year of Duke Wén,
the Chǔ army encamped at Gōushì
to attack the various Yōng.
In the fourth year of Duke Xuān,
the Chǔ Prime Minister Zǐ Yuè stationed his troops at Zhāngshì.
In the fourth year of Duke Dìng,
the Left Minister of War, Wù,
defeated the Wú army at Yōngshì.
In the twenty-third year of Duke Zhāo,
the Minister of War, Wěi Yuè, hanged himself at Wěishì.
Fú Qián sometimes referred to these as settlements,
and other times as territories.
Jīng Xiàngfán and Dù Yù also said they were names for places along the water's edge or borderlands.
Now, between the two counties of Nányáng and Yùyáng,
along the banks of the Yù River,
there exist Nánshì and Běishì.
However, the discussions among various scholars
are divided between water and land,
and there is no clear source in the mountains,
nor defined routes or passes.
Only Zhèng Xuán and Liú Chéng claimed they were within the boundaries of Jìnglíng County.
The *Classic* states:
north of Qǐ County lies Tuó,
yet there are many tributaries named Tuó,
so commentators are doubtful
and unable to determine their exact locations.
The above covers the locations of mountains, rivers, and marshes in the *Yǔ Gòng*,
totaling sixty.
